facts.soil: Broken rock plus dead life. It takes a century to build a centimetre.
facts.sand: Rock ground to between 0.06 and 2 mm, mostly stubborn quartz.
facts.mud: Soil with enough water to lose its grip on itself.
facts.clay: Mineral sheets so fine they slide — the reason clay can be shaped.
facts.adobe: Mud and straw. Half the world's oldest surviving buildings.
facts.brick: Sun-dried mud, standardised. The first mass-produced object.
facts.pot: Fired clay. Once you can boil things, your diet changes forever.
facts.glass: An amorphous solid — no crystal structure. It does not flow, whatever you have heard.
facts.cullet: Crushed scrap glass — a sand substitute for aggregate, not the same mineral as sand itself.
facts.sea: 3.5% salt, and the destination of every mineral rivers carry.
facts.salt: The only rock humans eat. Wars have been fought over it.
facts.brine: Salt water strong enough to dehydrate any microbe that enters it.
facts.ice: Less dense than the water it came from, which is why lakes have fish.
facts.steam: Water carrying five times the energy it needed just to reach boiling.
facts.spark: A fragment of stone, briefly glowing. The start of everything.
facts.flint: Breaks in conchoidal curves, so every fracture leaves an edge. Unlocks Cut.
facts.fire: Carbon meeting oxygen fast enough to glow. Unlocks Heat.
facts.wood: Cellulose in lignin — a natural fibreglass, and a fuel.
facts.charcoal: Wood with everything but the carbon baked out. Burns far hotter.
facts.ash: The minerals a tree pulled from the soil, handed back.
facts.lye: Ash water. Caustic enough to dissolve fat, hair and skin.
facts.soap: One end of the molecule grips grease, the other grips water.
facts.tree: A plant that spends a fortune on a trunk to outgrow its neighbours.
facts.acacia: A savanna thorn tree armed with paired spines — one long and straight, one short and curved.
facts.straw: The stalk left after the grain is taken. Tinder, thatch and bedding.
facts.hay: Grass cut and dried in the sun — winter feed for grazing animals when nothing else grows.
facts.sprout: A seed that has committed. There is no going back into the shell.
facts.seedling: Roots first, leaves second. Plumbing before solar panels.
facts.plant: A machine that turns light and air into sugar, and asks for nothing.
facts.grass: Grows from the base, so grazing cannot kill it. Covers around 40% of the land.
facts.flower: An advertisement paid for in sugar, aimed at insects.
facts.leaf: A solar panel that must open its pores to breathe, and lose water doing it.
facts.root: Trades sugar with underground fungi for minerals it cannot reach.
facts.bulb: A whole next-season plant, packed in fat leaves, buried for safety.
facts.vine: Skips the cost of a trunk by climbing someone else's.
facts.herb: Leaves whose chemical defences we happen to find delicious.
facts.tea: Green, oolong and black are one plant. Only the oxidation differs.
facts.brewed_tea: Second most consumed drink on Earth, after water itself.
facts.meadow: Not scenery — the density of bloom that makes a pollinator colony viable.
facts.nectar: Roughly 25% sugar, made deliberately and given away on purpose.
facts.bee: Forages 5 km out and reports good ground back to the hive by dancing.
facts.honey: Under 18% water. Nothing can grow in it, so it never spoils.
facts.beeswax: Costs the hive 8 g of honey for every 1 g secreted.
facts.candle: The wick does not burn. It pumps liquid wax up into the flame.
facts.fruit: A bribe wrapped around a seed, aimed at anything that travels.
facts.yeast: A single-celled fungus living on fruit skins. Unlocks Ferment.
facts.chilli: Capsaicin repels mammals and does nothing at all to birds.
facts.grape: Picked near 24% sugar — exactly what yeast needs to reach 13% alcohol.
facts.cucumber: About 95% water, held up entirely by cell wall pressure.
facts.tomato: A berry, and unusually full of glutamate — which is why it reads as savoury.
facts.apple: Seeds never breed true. Every named variety is a clone of one lucky tree.
facts.olive: Inedibly bitter raw. Every olive you have eaten was cured first.
facts.wheat: Bred for 10,000 years above all to stop dropping its own seed.
facts.rice: Tolerates flooding, so the water itself does the weeding.
facts.sugarcane: A giant grass that stores sugar in the stalk instead of the seed.
facts.potato: Not a root — a swollen underground stem. That is why it has eyes.
facts.onion: Cut it and two chemicals that were kept apart meet, and you cry.
facts.garlic: Whole, it barely smells. The smell is a wound response.
facts.cabbage: Same species as kale, broccoli, sprouts and cauliflower. All of them.
facts.field: One plant, no competitors — the most productive and most fragile system in farming.
facts.harvest: The narrow window the entire calendar of settled life is built around.
facts.grain: A seed we eat before it ever gets to be a plant.
facts.flour: Ground grain. Porridge came 30,000 years before anyone baked it.
facts.malt: Barley sprouted then killed, its starch already turned to sugar.
facts.dough: Wet, worked flour: an elastic protein net strong enough to hold gas.
facts.pasta_dough: Egg instead of yeast. The protein sets the shape on cooking.
facts.pastry: Layers of flour separated by cold butter, waiting for steam.
facts.cake_batter: Sugar steals water from the flour, which is what keeps cake tender.
facts.risen_dough: Full of carbon dioxide the yeast exhaled and the gluten refused to let go.
facts.sourdough_starter: Wild yeast and lactobacilli, kept alive by daily feeding. Livestock, really.
facts.flatbread: The oldest bread. Steam alone puffs it, in under two minutes.
facts.bread: A foam of carbon dioxide, set solid by heat.
facts.sourdough: Slower, sourer, and it keeps for days because the acid holds mould off.
facts.noodle: The oldest found are 4,000-year-old millet noodles from Lajia, China.
facts.pasta: Al dente is the few seconds between the starch swelling and the protein firming.
facts.cake: Set the scaffold before the air escapes, or it falls.
facts.wort: Sweet barley water. Boiling it sterilised beer centuries before germ theory.
facts.beer: Boiled, and therefore safe. Older than writing, possibly older than bread.
facts.grape_juice: Crushing brings the wild yeast on the skin to the sugar inside.
facts.wine: Stops near 15% — the point where yeast is killed by its own waste.
facts.vinegar: Literally 'sour wine'. A second fermentation, by a different organism.
facts.apple_juice: Browns within minutes — the same enzyme reaction as a bruise.
facts.cider: Apples carry their own yeast and sugar. Left alone, juice becomes cider.
facts.olive_oil: Squeezed from fruit flesh. Cold press means pressure and nothing else.
facts.cane_juice: Must be crushed within a day, before the cane eats its own sugar.
facts.sugar: One of the purest substances in any kitchen — near 100% sucrose.
facts.caramel: Hundreds of new compounds, none of which were in the sugar.
facts.mead_must: Honey watered down until life can live in it again.
facts.mead: Honey, water and time. No field and no harvest required.
facts.sauerkraut: The bacteria that sour it were already living on the cabbage.
facts.kimchi: The same lactic fermentation as sauerkraut, run cold and spiced.
facts.pickle: A brined pickle is alive and souring. A vinegar one arrives sour.
facts.passata: Cooked tomato gives up far more lycopene than raw. Some food is better cooked.
facts.herb_oil: Aroma compounds dissolve in fat, not water. Oil is the better solvent.
facts.pasture: Humans cannot digest grass. Grazers are the machine that converts it.
facts.aurochs: 1.8 m at the shoulder, foul-tempered, extinct since 1627.
facts.cow: Every cow alive descends from roughly 80 tamed aurochs.
facts.milk: Around 90 kg of grass a day becomes some 28 litres — and only after a calf.
facts.chicken: Domesticated jungle bird. Around three alive per living human.
facts.egg: A chalk shell with seven to seventeen thousand pores, because the embryo breathes.
facts.fish: The first vertebrates. Your skeleton is a variation on their design.
facts.lizard: Over 7,000 species, and every one an ectotherm — basking in the sun is a requirement, not a habit.
facts.snake: Legless, with 175 to 400-plus vertebrae — and, in most species, only one working lung.
facts.turtle: A shell of 50 to 60 of its own bones — ribs and vertebrae, fused outward and capped in keratin.
facts.rattlesnake: Its rattle is hollow keratin segments — modified tail scales, buzzed by a dedicated muscle.
facts.salt_fish: Fed medieval Europe through winter and crossed oceans without ice.
facts.meat: Tenderness depends almost entirely on how hard that muscle worked.
facts.mince: Cutting across the fibres is why a burger beats the same cut whole.
facts.roast: The Maillard reaction: hundreds of aromas that did not exist raw.
facts.cured_meat: Salt does not kill the microbes. It leaves them nothing to drink.
facts.bacon: Wood smoke is genuinely antimicrobial. The flavour was a side effect.
facts.sausage: A way to make offcuts keep, and travel.
facts.meatball: Egg binds it. Without a binder, mince squeezes out its own juice.
facts.broth: Tough collagen dissolved into gelatin. Cheap cuts make the best.
facts.aspic: Proof in a bowl that the collagen really did dissolve.
facts.soup: Almost every cuisine on Earth begins one the same way: onion, slowly.
facts.cream: Fat floats. Cream is milk that has been left alone.
facts.butter: Fat globules battered until they break and stick to each other.
facts.ghee: Water gone, solids strained. Keeps for months without a fridge.
facts.yoghurt: The bacteria eat the lactose, which is why the intolerant can eat it.
facts.curd: Acid makes casein clump. The fastest cheese there is.
facts.cheese: Salted curd. From here, the only ingredient left is time.
facts.aged_cheese: Those crunchy crystals in old parmesan are free amino acids.
facts.mould: Its spores are in every room you have ever stood in.
facts.blue_cheese: Skewered with holes, because the mould needs air to grow inward.
facts.penicillin: An accident on a windowsill in 1928, and a decade of work to make it a drug.
facts.ice_cream: Stirring while freezing keeps the crystals microscopic. That is the trick.
facts.mayonnaise: Lecithin holds oil inside water that would rather not hold it.
facts.boiled_egg: White sets at 63 °C, yolk at 70 °C. Everything happens in between.
facts.cooked_rice: Raw starch is nearly indigestible. Cooked, it feeds most of the world.
facts.sushi_rice: Sushi began as preservation — fish kept safe in souring rice.
facts.baked_potato: Dry heat makes it floury. The same potato boiled stays waxy.
facts.chips: Escaping steam is what keeps the oil out. Cool oil means greasy chips.
facts.salad: Salt early and osmosis empties every cell. Dress it at the table.
facts.greek_salad: No lettuce in a real one. Just what ripens together, in the same soil.
facts.cheese_toastie: Young cheese flows; very old cheese has no water left and splits.
facts.pizza_base: A Neapolitan oven runs at 450 °C and is done in 90 seconds.
facts.pizza: Tomato on flatbread is far older than the flag story, and belonged to the poor.
facts.apple_pie: Pectin glues apple cells together and survives the oven.
facts.grilled_fish: Sets at 50 °C. Fish never had to hold itself up against gravity.
facts.dinner: Stone, water, sun and a seed. All of agriculture, on one plate.
facts.feast: Nutritionally unnecessary. Every human society does it anyway.
facts.philosopher_stone: Never found. Chemistry was the consolation prize.
facts.stone_soup: A fable about how to get a village to feed itself.
facts.gingerbread_man: Elizabeth I had them baked in the likeness of visiting dignitaries.
facts.corn_dolly: The last sheaf, woven into a figure to hold the harvest spirit.
facts.scarecrow: Crows learn its face in two days. It works on everything else.
facts.cornucopia: The broken horn of the goat that nursed Zeus. It refilled forever.
facts.ambrosia: Food of the gods, said to confer immortality on anyone who ate it.
facts.manna: Appeared each dawn, rotted by dusk. Nobody agrees what it was.
facts.golden_egg: A story about not understanding the system you live off.
facts.sickle: A curved flint blade. The tool that turned a field into a harvest.
facts.granary: Surplus, stored. It bought the first bad year, and the first bureaucracy.
facts.smoked_fish: Preserved by phenols before it is ever properly cooked.
facts.greenhouse: Holds heat by stopping warm air rising away, not by trapping infrared.
facts.early_crop: Borrowed warmth, and a harvest weeks ahead of the weather.
facts.barrel: Oak bent by steam. Storage that flavours what it stores.
facts.aged_wine: Oxygen through the staves, vanillin out of the oak.
facts.clean_hands: The cheapest public health intervention ever discovered.
facts.garlic_butter: Fat as a delivery system for a plant’s wound chemistry.
facts.garlic_bread: Bread is porous enough to drink fat. That is the whole idea.
facts.wrap: Flatbread used as cutlery, which is how most of the world ate.
facts.spaghetti_meatballs: Invented in New York, where meat was suddenly cheap.
facts.malt_vinegar: Beer that met the wrong bacteria, to everyone’s benefit.
facts.caramel_sauce: Fat and water blocking sugar from crystallising again.
facts.sundae: Your tongue reads the contrast, not the average.
facts.choucroute: Two autumn preservations, eaten together in midwinter.
facts.breakfast: A 1920s public relations campaign that never wore off.
facts.cheeseboard: Acid and sugar, cutting fat. Mechanics dressed as tradition.
facts.tzatziki: Yoghurt with the whey drained out, and the protein left behind.
facts.potato_salad: Dress it warm. Cold starch will not drink anything.
facts.egg_sandwich: Named after a man who would not leave the card table.
facts.fish_and_chips: Britain’s national dish, assembled entirely from imports.
facts.pilaf: Fat around every grain, so the starch never glues them together.
facts.salted_dough: Salt does not just season bread — it tightens the gluten and slows the yeast.
facts.creamed_butter: Butter and sugar beaten pale. The air whipped in is the leavening.
facts.cake_mix: Fat, sugar and egg, emulsified — before any flour goes near it.
facts.sweet_cream: Sugar lowers the freezing point, which is what keeps ice cream scoopable.
facts.breadcrumb: Stale bread, crushed. It holds moisture that would otherwise be squeezed out.
facts.meatball_mix: Mince and crumb, waiting for a binder.
facts.meatball_sauce: Simmered in tomato, which cooks them through and seasons the sauce back.
facts.garlic_yoghurt: Raw garlic stirred through yoghurt, which tames it without cooking it.
facts.olive_salad: Tomato, cucumber and olive — everything that ripens in the same month.
facts.batter: Flour and beer. The bubbles make it light; the alcohol boils off fast and crisps it.
facts.battered_fish: A raw coat of batter, sealing the fish before it ever meets the oil.
facts.fried_fish: The batter sets into a shell and the fish inside steams in its own moisture.
facts.rubbed_flour: Butter worked into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs. Water comes last.
facts.cured_mince: Salt draws out protein that makes the mince sticky enough to hold together.
facts.egg_mayo: Chopped egg bound in its own emulsion — yolk meeting yolk.
facts.kimchi_paste: Chilli and garlic, the flavour engine of the ferment.
facts.salted_cabbage: Brined until limp, so the paste can reach every leaf.
facts.tempered_clay: Clay cut with sand so it can dry and fire without cracking.
facts.limestone: Compacted seabed — shells and skeletons, pressed for aeons.
facts.cement_meal: Ground limestone and clay, waiting for the kiln.
facts.cement: The glue. Roughly a tenth of humanity's carbon dioxide.
facts.mortar: Cement paste with sand in it to stop it shrinking.
facts.concrete: Rock, glued. The most used material on Earth after water.
facts.river: Fresh to taste, but never pure — every river carries dissolved rock to the sea.
facts.goat: Domesticated from wild bezoars; browses scrub and rock where cattle starve.
facts.carbon: Four bonds in every direction. Every molecule life is built from hangs off it.
facts.oxygen: Most of your mass by atom count. Almost never found alone either — it pairs up on contact.
facts.hydrogen: The first element, made in the first minutes of the universe. Almost never found alone.
facts.nitrogen: Two atoms locked by the strongest bond there is, N2 — four fifths of the air.
facts.sulfur: Yellow, volcanic, and the reason two amino acids can staple themselves together.
facts.phosphorus: Carries the energy and holds DNA together. The scarcest of the six.
facts.legume: A plant that hosts bacteria in its roots and pays them in sugar.
facts.bone: Collagen for spring, calcium phosphate for stiffness. Neither works alone.
facts.shell: Calcium carbonate, laid down by a fringe of tissue called the mantle.
facts.carbon_dioxide: What burning makes and what leaves eat.
facts.glucose: What photosynthesis actually produces. Everything else is built from it.
facts.starch: Thousands of glucose units chained for storage.
facts.amino_acid: Twenty of them, in every living thing, all the same handedness.
facts.cysteine: The amino acid carrying sulfur. It can bond to another of its own kind.
facts.dipeptide: Two amino acids joined, and one water molecule gone.
facts.polypeptide: A chain in a specific order, written in DNA and read by a ribosome.
facts.protein: A chain folded into one shape. The shape is the function.
facts.disulfide: Two cysteines, cross-linked. What makes hair hair.
facts.keratin: Hair, nail, horn and hoof — all the same protein, differently packed.
facts.denatured_protein: Unfolded, tangled, set. This is what cooking is.
facts.atp: The cell spends its own body weight in this every day.
facts.nucleotide: Sugar, phosphate and a base. Four of them spell everything alive.
facts.dna: The instructions, in four letters, for building the thing holding it.
facts.membrane: Two layers of fat, tails inward. Life needs an inside.
facts.cell: The smallest thing that is unambiguously alive.
facts.tissue: Cells of one kind, doing one job together.
facts.muscle: Protein filaments ratcheting past each other.
facts.collagen: A third of all the protein in you, wound in triple helices.
facts.gelatin: Collagen unwound by heat, and it sets as it cools.
facts.enzyme: A protein with a pocket shaped to hold one particular molecule.
facts.alpha_helix: A chain coiled into a spring, held by hydrogen bonds four residues apart.
facts.beta_sheet: Chains lying side by side, pleated like a folded fan. Silk is almost nothing else.
facts.ribosome: Two thirds RNA — and the RNA, not the protein, is the part that does the chemistry.
facts.messenger_rna: A working copy of one gene. Short-lived on purpose, so the cell can stop just by letting it decay.
facts.resistance: The survivors of a course of antibiotics are, by definition, the ones it did not kill.
facts.hydrogen_gas: Two hydrogen atoms, bonded — H2. This is the form that actually exists in a jar.
facts.oxygen_gas: Two oxygen atoms, double-bonded — O2. The gas in every breath you take.
facts.ore: Rock with enough of a useful mineral in it to be worth digging up — usually a metal.
facts.cinnabar: Bright red mercury sulfide, and mercury's one and only important ore.
facts.rutile: Titanium dioxide, and — along with ilmenite — the only titanium ore that's ever been worth mining.
facts.iron: Iron ore needs a furnace hot enough to reach 1,500°C to give up its metal.
facts.copper: One of the few metals nature hands you pure — the first one anyone learned to smelt, around 5000 BC.
facts.gold: Chemically inert enough that it is still found lying around as pure metal — no smelting required.
facts.silver: For most of history this did not come from silver ore at all — it came out of lead.
facts.tin: Melts at just 232°C — one of the easiest metals there is to work.
facts.lead: So easy to coax out of its ore that people in the Near East were using it before recorded history began.
facts.zinc: Boils at 907°C — cooler than it takes to smelt its own ore, so the metal evaporates unless you catch it.
facts.mercury: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature — freed from its ore just by roasting it.
facts.aluminum: The commonest metal in Earth's crust — once so hard to isolate it cost more than gold, until 1886.
facts.nickel: Named after a mischievous spirit — miners dug up a copper-look ore and got no copper out of it.
facts.chromium: Pulled from its ore by a reaction hot enough to run on its own once lit — burning aluminium for the oxygen.
facts.titanium: So reactive that heating its ore with carbon — the trick that works for iron — just makes a ceramic instead.
facts.platinum: Melts at 1,768°C — so hot the first people to work it never melted it, just sintered the grains with gold.
facts.uranium: Named for a planet, and it took fifty years between finding the ore and finally isolating the metal itself.
facts.helium: First spotted in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse, not found on Earth for another 27 years.
facts.neon: Trace enough in air — 18 parts per million — that it took liquefying the whole atmosphere to find it.
facts.magnesium: The third most abundant element dissolved in seawater — and it burns at about 3,100°C.
facts.calcium: The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust, and the third most abundant metal.
facts.sodium: A metal that catches fire on contact with water — which is why it is never found free in nature.
facts.potassium: Reacts with water hard enough to ignite its own hydrogen, burning with a lilac flame.
facts.yellowcake: Powdered uranium concentrate — not the metal yet, just the ore boiled down to something worth shipping.
facts.flax: Humans were using wild flax for textiles 30,000 years ago, long before farming it.
facts.fibre: What is left of a flax stalk after the soft inner parts have rotted away.
facts.thread: The oldest known twisted fibre is around 50,000 to 40,000 BC — older than farming, pottery or metal.
facts.cloth: Two sets of thread interlaced at right angles: warp one way, weft the other.
facts.clothing: Cloth cut and stitched to the shape of a body — the point of the whole fibre chain.
facts.pulp: Cellulose fibre beaten loose and suspended in water, waiting to be drained into a sheet.
facts.paper: A thin sheet of matted cellulose fibres. The pulp process is credited to Cai Lun, a Han court eunuch.
facts.oak_gall: A wasp lays an egg in an oak bud and the tree grows a hard apple-like ball around the larva.
facts.ink: Iron gall ink was Europe's standard ink for the 1,400 years between the 5th and 19th centuries.
facts.mirror: Silver deposited on the back of a sheet of glass — Justus von Liebig's process, 1835.
facts.enriched_uranium: Natural uranium is over 99% U-238. Weapons grade means 85% or more of the rarer U-235.
facts.warhead: Critical mass is the least fissile material that will sustain a chain reaction. Past it, the rate only climbs.
facts.book: A stack of pages bound at one edge — the biggest advance in bookmaking before the printing press.
facts.pig: Domesticated twice over, independently: near the Tigris, and separately in China.
facts.lard: A semi-solid white fat, rendered straight out of a pig by steam, boiling or dry heat.
facts.sheep: Grazes grass flat where a goat would rather climb and browse the scrub instead.
facts.wool: Not just hair — the crimp and the microscopic scale are what let it felt and spin.
facts.horse: Its teeth never stop erupting, worn down by a lifetime of grazing.
facts.duck: Almost every domestic duck breed on Earth comes down from one wild bird: the mallard.
facts.turkey: Spends all day foraging the ground, then flies up into a tree every night to roost.
facts.wolf: Dogs and wolves share a common wolf ancestor — today's wolves are cousins, not quite the parents.
facts.deer: Lives in the seam between forest and open ground — cover on one side, grazing on the other.
facts.bear: Along parts of the Alaskan coast, this bear eats almost nothing but salmon while the run lasts.
facts.kangaroo: Hop it fast enough and it costs less energy, not more — the opposite of most ways of moving.
facts.koala: Eats almost nothing but eucalyptus — and out of 600-plus species on offer, sticks to about 30.
facts.dingo: A domestic dog gone wild — feral for well over 3,000 years, and now Australia's apex predator.
facts.platypus: A mammal that lays eggs, carries a venomous spur, and hunts by sensing electricity.
facts.elephant: Pushes over trees for a living, and does it thoroughly enough to turn woodland into grassland.
facts.lion: The most social cat there is — it lives in family groups where other big cats hunt alone.
facts.zebra: Those stripes are there to stop flies landing, not to help it hide or keep cool.
facts.giraffe: A heart that runs at roughly twice human blood pressure, just to get blood up to the brain.
facts.camel: The hump is fat, not water — up to 36 kg of it, burned for energy when food runs short.
facts.chromatin: DNA spooled round protein beads. Two metres of it fits in a nucleus six microns across.
facts.chromosome: Chromatin wound down about ten thousand times tighter. Only then can you see one down a microscope.
facts.gene: One stretch that codes for one thing. Barely 2% of your genome is doing that.
facts.nucleus: A double membrane with a few thousand doors in it, keeping the genome apart from the machinery.
facts.microtubule: A hollow tube of two proteins, 25 nm across. It builds the spindle and it drives the sperm's tail.
facts.mitosis: One cell into two identical ones. Nearly every cell you have was made this way.
facts.meiosis: Two divisions, one copy of the DNA. That is how you get half a set instead of a whole one.
facts.sperm: Head five microns wide, tail ten times longer. The testes make 200 to 300 million a day.
facts.ovum: One of the largest cells in your body, and the only one you can see without a microscope.
facts.polar_body: Meiosis in the female divides unfairly on purpose: three cells get chromosomes and almost nothing else.
facts.zygote: One cell, one full set of chromosomes again, and about thirty hours before it divides.
facts.morula: Sixteen cells in a ball. Named after a mulberry, which is the least clinical word in embryology.
facts.blastocyst: A hundred cells around a puddle. The cells pumped in the salt and the water followed.
facts.stem_cell: Undecided. Given the right signal it becomes any of the 200-odd cell types you are built from.
facts.gastrula: Where a ball of cells becomes layers, and the layers decide what everything will be.
facts.embryo: Eight weeks, and every major organ is at least started. None of them work properly yet.
facts.fetus: Latin for offspring. From week nine the organs are all there, unfinished and not all in place.
facts.human: Full term runs 39 to 40 weeks. Then labour ends the pregnancy and a newborn leaves the body it grew inside.
facts.cotton: A fibre that grows in a boll wrapped around the seeds. The plant grew it to help them travel.
facts.maize: Cannot sow itself. The kernels stay stuck to the cob, so without someone to plant it, it ends.
facts.popcorn: Steam at 135 psi bursting the hull, and the starch inside foaming out. Only one kind of maize does it.
facts.barley: Handles salty ground that would finish wheat. Most of the world crop is eaten by animals, not people.
facts.oat: Started life as a weed in other people's wheat fields and got domesticated more or less by accident.
facts.soybean: 36% protein and 20% oil by weight, and it makes its own nitrogen. A crop that asks for very little.
facts.tofu: Cheese, made from a bean. Curdle soy milk with a salt, press the curds, cut into blocks.
facts.pea: A monk grew several thousand of these, counted what came out, and got modern genetics.
facts.carrot: Purple, for most of its history. The orange one is a Dutch invention, and fairly recent at that.
facts.lettuce: 94.9% water, so it cannot be frozen, canned or dried. Eat it now or do not eat it.
facts.pumpkin: A berry. The record one weighed 1,246.9 kg, which is a great deal of berry.
facts.beet: The red pigment goes straight through some people. Pink urine, harmless, and it has a name: beeturia.
facts.lemon: Not a wild species at all — a hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, two other fruits entirely.
facts.strawberry: Not a berry. Each seed on the outside is an achene — a whole separate fruit with a seed in it.
facts.banana: A berry, growing on the largest herb on Earth. What looks like a trunk is not a trunk.
facts.pear: A pome, like the apple, but picked green and hard on purpose — it finishes ripening off the tree.
facts.cherry: Crack the stone, chew the kernel inside, and it releases hydrogen cyanide. So do not do that.
facts.fig: A fruit with all the flowers folded away inside, and a wasp that crawls in to reach them.
facts.coffee: Not a bean. It is the seed of a fruit called a cherry, and it tastes of nothing until it is roasted.
facts.brewed_coffee: Roasted, ground, steeped in hot water, then filtered back out. That is the entire method.
facts.cocoa: The pods grow straight out of the trunk. Raw, the beans inside are bitter and taste of nothing much.
facts.cocoa_bean: Heaped up for days until the pulp liquefies and ferments. Skip that and it stays harshly bitter.
facts.chocolate: Ground until the particles are under 20 micrometres — finer than the tongue can detect.
facts.glycine: The smallest of the twenty, and the only one with no handedness — its side chain is one hydrogen.
facts.alanine: The next simplest after glycine. Muscle uses it to post spare nitrogen back to the liver.
facts.serine: Named after silk. The nucleophile at the heart of a serine protease is one of these.
facts.proline: Its side chain loops back onto the backbone. That kink is what breaks an alpha helix.
facts.tyrosine: Made from phenylalanine, and turned into dopamine, adrenaline, thyroid hormone and melanin.
facts.aspartic_acid: Half of aspartame. In plants it is the parent of four amino acids you cannot make yourself.
facts.glutamic_acid: Savoury on its own. This is what umami is, and MSG is the salt they sell it as.
facts.glutamine: The most abundant free amino acid in your blood, and how the body moves ammonia around safely.
facts.asparagine: The first amino acid anyone ever isolated, out of asparagus juice, in 1806.
facts.arginine: The only thing your body makes nitric oxide out of, and the last stop before urea.
facts.valine: Swap a glutamate for one of these at position six of beta-globin and you have sickle-cell disease.
facts.leucine: Eat enough of it and muscle starts building protein. It is the signal as well as the material.
facts.isoleucine: One of only two of the twenty with two chiral centres, and it is built out of the other one.
facts.threonine: The last of the twenty to be found, in 1935, and one of only two with two chiral centres.
facts.methionine: AUG codes for this and nothing else, and AUG is where the ribosome starts reading.
facts.lysine: Cereal grains are short of it and pulses are full of it. That is why beans and bread go together.
facts.histidine: Its ring has a pKa near 6, close enough to swap a proton in a living cell. Active sites are full of it.
facts.phenylalanine: The one on the aspartame warning label. People with PKU cannot break it down.
facts.tryptophan: The biggest of the twenty, and the raw material for serotonin, melatonin and vitamin B3.
facts.quicklime: Limestone with the carbon dioxide cooked out of it. Add water and it gets hot enough to boil.
facts.fluorite: Named from *fluere*, to flow — it was a smelting flux long before anyone knew it held an element.
facts.kelp: Not a plant at all. A brown alga that grips rock instead of rooting, and can grow half a metre a day.
facts.borax: Traded down the Silk Road from Tibetan lake beds in the 8th century, long before anyone had heard of boron.
facts.chlorine: Named for its colour — khlōrós, pale green — and the first gas ever used as a weapon, at Ypres in 1915.
facts.fluorine: Reacts with everything but the lightest noble gases. The chemists who chased it are called fluorine martyrs.
facts.bromine: The only nonmetal that is liquid at room temperature. Named brômos, Greek for stench.
facts.iodine: Found by accident in seaweed ash in 1811, and named for the violet vapour that came off it.
facts.silicon: 27.2% of the crust by weight, second only to oxygen — and almost never found loose.
facts.boron: Claimed in 1808 and arguably not made pure until 1909 — a hundred and one years of nearly-boron.
facts.arsenic: Skips the liquid state entirely: heat it and at 614°C it goes straight from solid to gas.
facts.selenium: Named for the moon, because tellurium had already taken the earth. Nearly all of it comes out of copper.
facts.antimony: Egyptians were painting their eyes with its sulfide by about 3100 BC, which is where kohl comes from.
facts.germanium: Mendeleev left a gap for it in 1869 and called it ekasilicon. Winkler found it in a silver ore in 1886.
facts.tellurium: About as rare in the crust as platinum, and a 15 mg dose gives you garlic breath for months.
facts.argon: Third most abundant gas in the air, and nearly every atom of it was once a potassium atom.
facts.krypton: From 1960 to 1983 the metre was defined as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of one krypton-86 line.
facts.pyrolusite: Manganese dioxide — the black that Neanderthals painted caves with, and glassmakers' soap.
facts.molybdenite: Soft, grey, greasy and metallic — for centuries nobody could tell it from graphite or from lead ore.
facts.osmiridium: Hard grains of osmium and iridium, already alloyed, sitting in the river sand with the platinum.
facts.manganese: The reason steel bends instead of cracking — it ties up the sulfur that would split it while hot.
facts.cobalt: Named for a goblin. Miners got no copper out of the blue ore and blamed the kobold — same joke as nickel.
facts.tungsten: Melts at 3,422°C — the highest melting point of any metal, which is why light bulbs used it.
facts.molybdenum: Its name is just the Greek word for lead, because for centuries nobody could tell the two ores apart.
facts.vanadium: Named for a Norse goddess because its compounds are so colourful. Nine tenths of it is scraped out of slag.
facts.cadmium: Boils at 767°C, cooler than zinc does — which is exactly how it gets separated from the zinc it hides in.
facts.palladium: Over half of it is sitting in catalytic converters, turning car exhaust into something less poisonous.
facts.rhodium: Named after a rose, for the colour of one of its salts. Under one part per billion of the crust.
facts.iridium: A thin iridium layer in the clay worldwide is the fingerprint of the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
facts.osmium: The densest element that occurs in nature — 22.59 g/cm³, about twice the density of lead.
facts.ruthenium: About 100 parts per trillion of the crust, and roughly 30 tonnes a year. Named, in Latin, for Russia.
facts.rhenium: One part per billion of the crust, and no ore of its own — it is always somebody else's by-product.
facts.hafnium: Chemically almost indistinguishable from zirconium, so it hid inside it until 1923 — then it got Copenhagen.
facts.zirconium: Neutrons pass straight through it, which is why nuclear fuel is wrapped in zirconium and not in steel.
facts.tantalum: Named for the man in the myth who stood in water he could never drink, tantalised for eternity.
facts.niobium: Named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because for decades nobody could tell it from tantalum.
facts.scandium: Mendeleev left a gap in the table and described what belonged there. Ten years later, someone found it.
facts.yttrium: One small Swedish quarry, Ytterby, ended up with four elements named after it. This is the first of them.
facts.pollucite: A zeolite up to a quarter caesium by weight — most of the world's supply sits under one Canadian lake.
facts.monazite: Reddish phosphate sand, heavy enough to survive weathering and pile up on beaches. Full of rare earths.
facts.rare_earth: The lanthanides as they actually come: a mixture, and famously hard to separate into its members.
facts.baryte: Barium sulfate, better known as heavy spar. Most of what's mined goes down oil wells as drilling mud.
facts.lithium: The least dense metal there is, and one of only three that float on water — while reacting with it.
facts.caesium: The second is defined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of one caesium transition. This metal is the clock.
facts.rubidium: Named for the deep red lines in its spectrum. Parting it from caesium takes about 30 recrystallisations.
facts.beryllium: Nearly transparent to X-rays, which is why the window on an X-ray tube is very often made of it.
facts.strontium: Named after a Scottish village, and it is what makes the red in fireworks.
facts.barium: You drink it so your gut shows up on an X-ray — safe only because that one barium salt won't dissolve.
facts.radium: Painted onto watch dials to make them glow, by women told to lick their brushes to a point. It killed them.
facts.thorium: Three times as common as uranium, and for a century most of what was mined went into gas lamp mantles.
facts.plutonium: Not mined — made. Uranium-238 in a reactor swallows a neutron and, two beta decays later, is plutonium.
facts.polonium: Marie Curie found it first and named it for Poland. By mass it is 250,000 times more toxic than cyanide.
facts.cerium: As common in the crust as copper, and the one rare earth that will oxidise its own way out of the mix.
facts.lanthanum: Its name means 'to lie hidden' — it was found hiding inside what everyone took for pure cerium.
facts.neodymium: Nd2Fe14B — the strongest permanent magnets known. The name just means 'new twin'.
facts.samarium: The first element ever named after a person — and you get it by boiling it off a bath of lanthanum.
facts.europium: The red on old colour TV screens, and the glow in euro banknotes under UV. Also the softest lanthanide.
facts.gadolinium: Sticks to a magnet only below 20°C, and swallows neutrons better than any other stable nuclide.
facts.promethium: No stable isotope at all. About 560 grams exist in the entire crust, made by uranium quietly fissioning.
facts.noble_mix: What an air plant actually gives you: the two rarest stable gases, still mixed together.
facts.xenon: In 1962 it formed a compound, and "the noble gases do not react" quietly stopped being true.
facts.bismuth: Decays with a half-life a billion times the age of the universe, so everyone just calls it stable.
facts.smoke: An aerosol of soot, condensed tar and ash — the part of the fuel that never finished burning.
facts.forge: A hearth with a pipe into the fire. More air means a faster burn, and a faster burn means more heat.
facts.stockfish: Unsalted cod dried on open racks by cold wind. Loses about 80% of its water and keeps for years.
facts.bottle: A bubble of glass inflated down a hollow pipe, then worked into a shape.
facts.bone_char: Charred bone, porous and black. The standard decolouriser in cane-sugar refining.
facts.blackware: Fired black, because the starved fire took its oxygen from the iron in the clay.
facts.air: 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon — and the whole of it weighs about 5.15 × 10^18 kg.
facts.sky: Not a thing — a colour. Sunlight scattered by air molecules, blue scattered hardest.
facts.wind: Air levelling out a pressure difference the sun made by heating one place more.
facts.dust: Silt held up by air. Dry ground puts thousands of millions of tonnes up a year.
facts.cloud: Droplets condensed onto specks a hundredth their size, about 0.2 micrometres across.
facts.mist: The same droplets as fog, thinner. The only line between them is whether you can still see a kilometre.
facts.fog: A stratus cloud that reached the ground. It loses its Latin name the moment it touches.
facts.dew: Water that condensed onto something cold, not water that fell. It starts at the dew point.
facts.frost: Not frozen dew. Water vapour deposits straight onto a cold surface as ice, skipping liquid altogether.
facts.rain: Drops from 0.1 to 9 mm across, flattened rather than tear-shaped, and breaking up above that.
facts.snow: Crystals grown by vapour freezing onto them, then stuck together. The aggregate is the snowflake that lands.
facts.storm: Moisture, an unstable air mass, and something to lift it. Take one away and there is none.
facts.lightning: Charge sorted by ice striking ice in the updraught, then let go all at once.
facts.thunder: Air exploding away from a channel at about 30,000 K. Three seconds a kilometre.
facts.hail: Ice laid down in layers at least a millimetre thick, held up by an updraught for half an hour or more.
facts.rainbow: Always 42° out from the point opposite the sun. The geometry belongs to the drop.
facts.ozone: O3, named for its smell — ozein, Greek for 'to smell'. It damages what it is named for.
facts.hurricane: A storm that runs on warm water. Take it over sea much below 26.5 °C and it begins to die.
facts.blizzard: Defined by wind, not by snowfall: 56 km/h or more, visibility down to 400 m, for three hours or more.
facts.flood: Water arriving faster than the ground can absorb it or the channel can carry it.
facts.dune: Sand that grew itself: sand hitting sand tends to stick, sand hitting hard ground bounces away.
facts.loess: Wind-blown dust that landed and stayed. It weathers into some of the most productive farmland there is.
facts.fulgurite: A glass tube left in the ground by a lightning strike, following the path the current took down.
facts.steel: Iron with 0.02–2.14% carbon. The carbon jams the lattice so it cannot slip.
facts.bronze: Copper with about an eighth part tin. Melts near 950 °C and casts far better than copper.
facts.brass: Copper and zinc, roughly two to one. Change the ratio and you change the colour.
facts.solder: A tin-lead mix that melts at 183 °C — lower than either metal on its own.
facts.hide: Skin off the animal and untanned. Dries hard as board, and rots the moment it is wet again.
facts.tannin: A plant polyphenol that grabs protein and drops it out of solution. Named for tanning.
facts.leather: Tanned hide. Dries flexible instead of hard, and will not rot when it is wetted again.
facts.latex: A milky colloid that runs from a cut in the bark. Rubber is suspended in it, not dissolved.
facts.rubber: cis-1,4-polyisoprene, 100,000 to 1,000,000 daltons. Untreated, it goes sticky in heat.
facts.vulcanised_rubber: Rubber with sulfur chains stitched between its polymer strands. Goodyear, 1839.
facts.canvas: Plain weave in heavy yarn. The word comes from cannabis — it used to be hemp.
facts.silkworm: Bombyx mori has been bred until it cannot fly and does not exist in the wild.
facts.cocoon: One unbroken filament, 300 to 900 metres of it, spun in about two or three days.
facts.silk: A triangular fibre with rounded corners. It shines because it works like a prism.
facts.coin: The first ones were electrum — a natural gold-silver alloy nobody could value by eye.
facts.nail: Until about 1800 every one was forged singly by hand, and they were worth stealing.
facts.knife: A blade and a tang running back into the handle, so the grip does not snap off it.
facts.needle: The hard part was never the point. It was drilling an eye without splitting the bone.
facts.rope: Every layer is twisted against the one below. That fight is the only thing holding it.
facts.wheel: The potter's wheel came first. Cart wheels were plain wooden disks with a hole in them.
facts.lamp: A pool of oil and a wick reaching down into it. Lascaux had one 15,000 years ago.
facts.shoe: The oldest known one is 5,500 years old, one piece of hide, and its laces survived.
facts.pipe: Plumbing is named after lead: plumbum. Soft enough to bend, and that was the problem.
facts.plough: A share to cut the sod and a mouldboard to turn it over. Scratching the surface is not enough.
facts.peat: Dead plants that could not rot, because mud or sour water kept the oxygen off them.
facts.coal: Buried peat, squeezed and cooked for millions of years until mostly what is left is carbon.
facts.coal_tar: The black liquid that comes off coal heated without air. Phenol and cresols are in it.
facts.phenol: An alcohol that behaves like an acid. Runge pulled the first of it out of coal tar in 1834.
facts.wood_tar: What drips out of wood heated without air, next to the charcoal that stays behind.
facts.methanol: Wood alcohol. Boils at 64.7 °C, and 4 mL of it can take your sight permanently.
facts.formaldehyde: It stitches proteins to each other. That is what fixing, embalming and smoke tanning all are.
facts.galalith: Plastic made out of milk. Buttons, pen barrels and piano keys, from 1897 onwards.
facts.bakelite: The first plastic made from synthetic parts. Baekeland, 1907. Once set it cannot be melted.
facts.ethanol: Boils at 78.2 °C. Distilling stops at 95.6% — past that it and water boil as one thing.
facts.ethylene: More of it is made than any other organic compound, and half of that becomes polythene.
facts.polyethylene: The world's most used plastic, and it can be made from sugarcane instead of oil.
facts.oxo_degradable_plastic: Plastic with a metal-salt pro-oxidant blended in to fragment faster — banned across the EU since 2021.
facts.nurdle: A pea-sized pre-production pellet — the raw form nearly all plastic ships in before it's molded.
facts.magma: Molten rock while it is still underground. Every igneous rock there is froze out of it.
facts.lava: The same melt once it reaches the surface. Nothing changes but the address, and the name.
facts.basalt: Fine, dark and everywhere: nearly the whole floor of every ocean is basalt.
facts.granite: Quartz, feldspar and mica, grown big enough to see because the melt cooled slowly and deep.
facts.obsidian: Volcanic glass. It froze too fast for one crystal to start, so it has no crystals at all.
facts.pumice: Frozen volcanic froth, 64–85% holes by volume. It floats until it waterlogs and sinks.
facts.quartz: Silicon dioxide. It outlasts every other mineral, which is why sand is mostly quartz.
facts.feldspar: The commonest mineral group there is: about 41% of the continental crust by weight.
facts.mica: A silicate built in sheets, bonded so weakly between them that it splits into elastic plates.
facts.sandstone: Sand buried, squeezed and cemented. The grains are mostly quartz, because quartz survives.
facts.mudstone: Mud turned to rock. Mudrocks are half of all the sedimentary rock in the record.
facts.shale: Mudstone that splits: compaction lined its clay flakes up parallel, and it parts along them.
facts.conglomerate: Rounded pebbles set in finer sediment. Only fast water shifts stones that size.
facts.slate: Metamorphism, step one. It splits along the direction of the squeeze, not the old bedding.
facts.phyllite: Between slate and schist. Its silky sheen is mica just large enough to catch the light.
facts.schist: Mica grown big enough to see and all lying one way, so the rock splits into flakes.
facts.gneiss: High grade, and striped: over 600 °C the pale and dark minerals sort into separate bands.
facts.marble: Limestone recrystallised. The calcite grains grow and interlock, and the fossils go.
facts.quartzite: Sandstone whose grains have fused. Break it and the crack runs through them, not around.
facts.lignite: Brown coal: compressed peat, sometimes still three-quarters water. The lowest rank there is.
facts.anthracite: The last rank of coal: 86–97% carbon, hard and glossy, with the tar cooked out of it.
facts.corundum: Aluminium oxide, 9 on the Mohs scale. Pure it is colourless — the colours are impurities.
facts.diamond: Carbon rearranged. It is stable only 150 km down, so every one you see was carried up.
facts.ruby: Corundum with chromium standing in for a little of the aluminium. That alone makes it red.
facts.sapphire: Corundum with iron and titanium. An electron hops between the pair and the stone reads blue.
facts.emerald: Beryl coloured by chromium — the same element that makes ruby red, in a different crystal.
facts.opal: Hydrated silica, 3–21% water, in spheres even enough to diffract light into colours.
facts.up_quark: The lightest quark. Two of them and a down quark make every proton in the universe.
facts.down_quark: Heavier than the up quark, and the reason a neutron is a neutron. Two downs and an up.
facts.proton: Two up quarks and one down. Strip the electron off a hydrogen atom and this is what is left.
facts.neutron: One up quark and two down. Outside a nucleus it lasts about fifteen minutes.
facts.electron: 1/1836th the mass of a proton, and no known substructure. All of chemistry is these.
facts.atomic_nucleus: Tens of thousands of times smaller than its atom, and almost all of the atom's mass.
facts.photon: The quantum of the electromagnetic field. Massless, and it only ever travels at one speed.
facts.gamma_ray: The same stuff as light, at a million times the energy. Lead and concrete, not paper.
facts.plasma: Gas with its electrons torn off. An estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter is in this state.
facts.deuterium: Hydrogen with a neutron. About 156 atoms in every million of the hydrogen in seawater.
facts.tritium: Hydrogen with two neutrons. Radioactive, half-life 12.32 years, so none of it is original.
facts.fission_product: The two halves a split nucleus leaves. Caesium-137 and strontium-90 both take 30 years to halve.
facts.cosmic_dust: Grains from a few molecules up to 0.1 mm, condensed in the winds of dying stars.
facts.nebula: A luminous patch of the interstellar medium — hydrogen and dust, and where stars come from.
facts.star: A luminous spheroid of plasma held together by its own gravity. Nothing else is required.
facts.red_giant: A star that has run out of core hydrogen and swollen. The Sun will do this in 5 billion years.
facts.white_dwarf: A dead core the size of Earth with the mass of the Sun. One tonne per cubic centimetre.
facts.supernova: Several solar masses thrown outward at three per cent of the speed of light.
facts.neutron_star: 1.4 solar masses in a 10 km ball. A matchbox of it would weigh about 3 billion tonnes.
facts.black_hole: Gravity so strong that nothing, light included, can cross back out of the event horizon.
facts.planetesimal: A solid body about a kilometre across — big enough that its own gravity holds it together.
facts.planet: Round under its own gravity, and it has swept its orbit clear. Both halves matter.
facts.moon: Made from the debris of a Mars-sized body hitting the Earth about 4.4 billion years ago.
facts.comet: Rock, dust and frozen water, carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia. A dirty snowball.
facts.asteroid: The whole belt weighs 3% of the Moon. Jupiter threw out over 99% of what was there.
facts.gas_giant: Mostly hydrogen and helium — over 90% by mass. Jupiter and Saturn are the two here.
facts.ice_giant: Only about 20% hydrogen and helium. The rest is water, ammonia and methane.
facts.bacteria: DNA loose in the cytoplasm, no nucleus, no organelles. The other, older way to be a cell.
facts.archaea: A third domain, separated from bacteria in 1977. Its membranes use a chemistry nothing else does.
facts.mitochondrion: It keeps its own circular DNA and its own bacterial ribosomes, because it used to be a bacterium.
facts.chloroplast: A cyanobacterium that moved into a cell two billion years ago and never came out again.
facts.cyanobacteria: The first organisms known to have produced oxygen, and they filled the whole sky with it.
facts.alga: Photosynthetic, and mostly single-celled, with no roots, leaves or stems. Not one family.
facts.fungus: Neither plant nor animal. It digests its food outside its own body, then absorbs the result.
facts.spore: One cell that can build a whole fungus. Most fungal spores are carried by the wind.
facts.mycelium: The actual fungus: branching threads through soil. One can span thousands of acres.
facts.lichen: A fungus and an alga living as one thing. Under some conditions that counts as parasitism.
facts.mycorrhiza: Fungus fused to root. Found in 92% of plant families, and at least 460 million years old.
facts.root_nodule: A lump on a legume root, red inside, housing bacteria the plant lets in and then feeds.
facts.rhizobium: A soil bacterium the legume lets inside. In the nodule it starts breaking nitrogen apart.
facts.ammonia: NH3. Nearly every nitrogen atom in a living thing entered biology through this molecule.
facts.pollen: Not a sperm cell but a whole small organism, in a wall tough enough to survive fossilisation.
facts.polyp: A sac two cell layers thick with one opening, and that opening is both mouth and exit.
facts.zooxanthellae: Single-celled algae living inside an animal's own cells, in vacuoles, paying rent in sugar.
facts.coral: An animal taking up to 90% of its food from the algae growing inside its own tissue.
facts.reef: Under 0.1% of the ocean's area, and home to at least a quarter of all marine species.
facts.atoll: A ring of reef around a lagoon. The island it grew on sank, and the coral grew upward to keep pace.
facts.bleached_coral: White because the algae have gone. The animal is not dead yet; it is starving.
facts.detritus: Dead plant matter in pieces. More material goes down this chain than through anything's mouth.
facts.earthworm: Breathes through its skin, so it needs damp soil — and so rain does not drown it.
facts.humus: The dark residue when decay runs out of easy food. Much of it has sat there over a century.
facts.compost: A heap gets hot without being lit: 54–71 °C, all of it waste heat from microbes eating.
facts.cellulose: Glucose chained with the bond flipped. The most abundant organic polymer on Earth.
facts.rumen: The largest stomach compartment in a ruminant, and it holds no cellulase of the cow's own.
facts.fatty_acid: Acetate, propionate, butyrate. A cow's actual food, made for it by something else.
facts.lodestone: Magnetite that a lightning strike magnetised. The Earth's own field is far too weak to do it.
facts.magnet: Stroke iron with a lodestone and its domains line up. Hard iron keeps the alignment; soft iron loses it.
facts.magnetic_field: The region where a magnet or a current pushes. Iron filings on paper lie along its lines.
facts.copper_wire: Copper pulled cold through a die. It gets longer as it gets thinner, and never loses volume.
facts.voltaic_pile: Volta, 1800: zinc and copper discs stacked with brine-soaked card. The first steady current.
facts.generator: Faraday's disk, 1831. Spin a conductor through a field and the field pays back in current.
facts.current: A flow of charge. In a copper wire the electrons drift about a millimetre a second.
facts.electromagnet: A coil around iron. Its field can be thousands of times the coil's alone, and it switches off.
facts.electric_motor: A field pushes sideways on a current. The commutator flips the current so it keeps pushing.
facts.transformer: Two coils on one iron ring. Voltage out over voltage in is just the ratio of the turns.
facts.nichrome: 80% nickel, 20% chromium: 66 times the resistivity of copper, and it will not burn away.
facts.heating_element: A resistor whose whole job is to waste power. Heat goes as current squared times resistance.
facts.filament: A coil of a coil, so the hot gas only ever flows past the outside of it.
facts.light_bulb: A wire held at 2,500 °C in gas that will not react with it. Most of what leaves is heat.
facts.sulfuric_acid: The most-made industrial chemical. It pulls water out of things, including skin.
facts.lead_acid_cell: Planté, 1859 — the first battery you could refill with current instead of throw away.
facts.electrolysis: Push current through a solution and you can drive a reaction backwards, uphill.
facts.electroplating: Metal taken off one electrode and put back on another, an atom at a time.
facts.p_type: Silicon with boron in it. Boron is one electron short, so the gaps do the carrying.
facts.n_type: Silicon with phosphorus in it. Phosphorus has one electron spare and lets it go.
facts.diode: Two doped silicons meeting. Charge crosses the seam one way and not the other.
facts.led: Electrons falling into holes. The size of the gap they fall across sets the colour.
facts.transistor: A small current at one terminal ruling a large one at another. Everything modern sits on it.
facts.solar_cell: A diode in the light. The junction's field pulls the pair apart before they recombine.
facts.refrigerator: It does not make cold. It carries heat out of the box and dumps it behind the box.
facts.thyroxine: Two tyrosine rings joined, carrying four iodine atoms. T3 is the same molecule one iodine lighter.
facts.ascorbate: Vitamin C. Plants reach it from glucose by way of L-galactose; animals take another road from the same sugar.
facts.hydroxyproline: Proline given a hydroxyl after the chain was already built. Collagen is full of it.
facts.triple_helix: Three left-handed strands twisted into one right-handed rope, 3.3 residues to a turn.
facts.hydroxyapatite: Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 — 65 to 70% of the mass of bone, and more of tooth enamel.
facts.fluorapatite: Hydroxyapatite with fluoride sitting where the hydroxide was. Harder, and slower to give way to acid.
facts.porphyrin: Four pyrrole rings closed into a circle, four nitrogens pointing inward at a hole sized for one metal ion.
facts.heme: A porphyrin with an iron ion held in the middle. It carries oxygen, moves electrons and senses gas.
facts.hemoglobin: Four chains, four hemes, four oxygens — and it lifts blood's oxygen capacity seventyfold.
facts.myoglobin: One chain, one heme, and a firmer grip on oxygen than haemoglobin has.
facts.chlorophyll: Heme's ring with magnesium instead of iron. It is a poor absorber of green, which is why leaves are.
facts.cobalamin: Vitamin B12: a corrin ring around a cobalt ion. Only archaea and bacteria can build one.
facts.photosystem_ii: Four manganese ions and one calcium in a single cluster, counting to four so water can be split.
facts.iron_sulfur_cluster: Iron and sulfide at the corners of a cube, tied to the protein by cysteines.
facts.cytochrome_c_oxidase: Two hemes and two coppers. The last enzyme in the respiratory electron transport chain.
facts.ferritin: A hollow protein sphere of 24 parts, holding about 4,500 iron ions where they can catalyse nothing.
facts.zinc_finger: A loop too small to hold its own shape until a zinc ion pins it. Then it reads DNA.
facts.carbonic_anhydrase: One zinc ion, and up to a million reactions a second — ten million times faster than no enzyme at all.
facts.selenocysteine: The 21st amino acid, spelled with a stop codon. Cysteine with selenium where the sulfur was.
facts.glutathione_peroxidase: A selenoprotein. Its selenium is the atom hydrogen peroxide reacts with first.
facts.sulfite_oxidase: Carries molybdenum on a pterin ring, in the gap between the two mitochondrial membranes.
facts.superoxide_dismutase: Works as fast as molecules can collide. Built around copper, manganese, iron or nickel.
facts.sodium_potassium_pump: Three sodium out, two potassium in, one ATP. A nerve cell can spend most of its energy on this.
facts.action_potential: Sodium in, potassium out. Almost no ions actually move, and the voltage swings anyway.
facts.retinal: Half a beta-carotene, cut down the middle. The molecule that absorbs the light you see by.
facts.rhodopsin: A protein wrapped round one retinal. A photon straightens the retinal, and seeing starts there.
facts.magnesium_oxide: What is left after the flash. Prized as a refractory — it holds where other furnace linings fail.
facts.zinc_oxide: The alchemists' philosopher's wool: white fume off burning zinc, caught and collected.
facts.copper_oxide: Black powder that fires blue, green or red in a glaze, depending on what the kiln does.
facts.rust: Iron's failure mode. Flaky, friable, and offering the metal underneath no protection at all.
facts.litharge: Lead's oxide. Red below 486 °C, yellow above it — one compound, two crystal packings.
facts.mercuric_oxide: The red powder that gave up oxygen to Priestley in 1774, before the gas had a name.
facts.alumina: A film of this about 5 nm thick is the only reason aluminium looks unreactive.
facts.copper_sulfide: Chalcocite in the ground. Most of the world's copper is roasted out of this.
facts.zinc_sulfide: Doped with a trace of metal it glows when struck. The first particle detector was a screen of it.
facts.lead_sulfide: Galena. The main lead-bearing mineral, and mostly found sitting with zinc ores.
facts.tarnish: The black on old silver is not oxide. Silver ignores air; it is sulfur it cannot ignore.
facts.potassium_chloride: The other salt. Most of it goes on fields as potash; the rest into low-sodium table salt.
facts.potassium_iodide: What the word 'iodised' on a salt packet means. A few parts per million, against deficiency.
facts.sodium_fluoride: Trace amounts in water and toothpaste turn tooth enamel into fluorapatite.
facts.hydrogen_chloride: A gas until it meets water, and then it is hydrochloric acid — one of the strong ones.
facts.tungsten_carbide: As hard as corundum and close to diamond. The tip of the tool that cuts the steel.
facts.calcium_carbide: A rock that makes a flammable gas when it gets wet. It lit mines for fifty years.
facts.acetylene: Burnt with oxygen it passes 3,300 °C — the hottest flame any common gas pair makes.
facts.titanium_nitride: Brown as a powder, gold as a coating. The colour on a drill bit is hardness, not paint.
facts.magnesium_nitride: Proof that a magnesium fire does not care about oxygen: it burns in pure nitrogen too.
facts.carbon_monoxide: Colourless, odourless, flammable. The commonest fatal air poisoning in many countries.
facts.sulfur_dioxide: The smell of a struck match. Volcanic eruptions are the largest source of it there is.
facts.hydrogen_sulfide: Rotten eggs, briefly. It paralyses the nerve that smells it, and then you cannot.
facts.nitric_oxide: What lightning makes out of air. Colourless, and not for long once it meets oxygen.
facts.nitrogen_dioxide: The brown in a bad city sky. Nitric oxide plus one more oxygen atom.
facts.nitrate: The form a root can actually take nitrogen up in. Almost all of them dissolve in water.
facts.phosphate: PO4 — one phosphorus, four oxygens. It bridges DNA's sugars and it is what ATP spends.
facts.ribose: The five-carbon sugar in RNA. Glucose becomes it by the pentose phosphate pathway.
facts.deoxyribose: Ribose minus one oxygen. That missing hydroxyl is the whole difference between RNA and DNA.
facts.adenine: The A. Also the business end of ATP — the cell spells with it and pays with it.
facts.guanine: Named from guano, isolated from bird droppings in 1844. The crystals also make fish scales shine.
facts.cytosine: The C. Unstable enough that it turns into uracil on its own, which is why DNA has a repair crew.
facts.thymine: 5-methyluracil: uracil with one methyl group. DNA uses it where RNA uses uracil.
facts.uracil: RNA's U. Found in the Murchison meteorite, and in 2023 in a sample from the asteroid Ryugu.
facts.base_pair: A with T by two hydrogen bonds, G with C by three. That is the whole copying mechanism.
facts.rna: One strand, ribose, uracil. Chemically the more fragile of the two, and probably the older.
facts.transfer_rna: 76 to 90 nucleotides. Reads a codon at one end and holds an amino acid at the other.
facts.ribosomal_rna: About 60% of the ribosome by mass, and the part that does the chemistry.
facts.ribozyme: RNA that catalyses. Cech and Altman took the 1989 Nobel for finding RNA could do that at all.
facts.phospholipid: A phosphate head and two greasy tails. In water it builds a bilayer with no help at all.
facts.cholesterol: An animal molecule that stiffens or loosens a membrane. Most of yours is made, not eaten.
facts.vesicle: A bubble of bilayer with water inside. The cheapest inside there is.
facts.primordial_soup: Oparin's 1924 guess at the early ocean. Haldane supplied the word soup in 1929.
facts.protocell: A bilayer sac with replicating chemistry inside. Nobody has yet made one that lives.
facts.cytoplasm: About 80% water, and so crowded with protein that nothing dissolved in it behaves normally.
facts.virus: A genome in a protein coat, with no metabolism. Called organisms at the edge of life.
facts.binary_fission: One cell into two, no partner. E. coli does it about every 20 minutes at 37 °C.
facts.budding: The daughter grows out of the mother's side and leaves. Yeast does it; so does a hydra.
facts.cutting: A severed stem that grows its own roots. The new plant is a clone of the one it came off.
facts.tuber: A potato is not a root. It is a swollen underground stem, and every eye on it is a bud.
facts.runner: A stolon: a stem that crawls sideways and roots where it touches. Strawberries spread this way.
facts.glycogen: Starch's animal counterpart, branched far more. About 100 g in the liver, 400 g in muscle.
facts.methane: CH4, the simplest alkane. Some archaea make it, and nothing else alive does.
facts.cactus: Spines are modified leaves; the fat stem does the photosynthesis. Water can be 90% of its mass.
facts.malic_acid: A four-carbon acid. CAM plants build it in the dark and take it apart again in the light.
facts.stoma: A pore between two guard cells. Opening it to eat costs the plant water, every single time.
facts.xylem: Dead pipework. Wood is xylem that kept being added, one year's worth at a time.
facts.phloem: Living tissue, unlike xylem. It carries sugar downward, and it sits just inside the bark.
facts.sap: Two saps, running opposite ways. Neither of them is latex, and neither of them is resin.
facts.bark: Everything outside the vascular cambium. Strip a ring of it off and the tree usually dies.
facts.cork: Dead cells full of gas, walled with suberin. Stripped off a living oak, and it grows back.
facts.lignin: 20 to 35% of dry wood. Stiffens the cell wall, keeps water in the pipes, and resists rot.
facts.oak: Around 500 species. The tannin that makes acorns bitter is the tannin that tanned leather.
facts.pine: Evergreen and resinous. Over 90% of a conifer's timber is one cell type: the tracheid.
facts.hardwood: Wood from a flowering tree, with vessels. Balsa is one, so the name is not about hardness.
facts.softwood: Wood from a conifer, with no pores at all. Yew is a softwood and harder than many hardwoods.
facts.bamboo: A grass. Some species add 91 cm in a day, and a culm never gets thicker than it started.
facts.coconut: A drupe, not a nut. The husk is built for buoyancy, but people did most of the carrying.
facts.coconut_water: Liquid endosperm — the same tissue that later settles out as the solid white flesh.
facts.mangrove: Filters salt out at the root and dumps the rest in old leaves. Its seeds sprout on the tree.
facts.bast_fibre: Fibre out of the inner bark. Soft and flexible, unlike the stiff leaf fibres of sisal.
facts.sugar_beet: A taproot that is 12 to 21% sucrose. Breeding took it from 8% to 18% in two centuries.
facts.rubber_tree: Amazonian, and barely grown there: a leaf blight keeps plantations out of its own homeland.
facts.mulberry: In the fig's family. What looks like one fruit is many fruits packed against each other.
facts.willow: Roots from a broken branch lying on wet ground. Its bark sap is rich in salicin.
facts.salicin: Bitter as quinine. The gut turns it into salicylic acid — the compound aspirin was built on.
facts.winter_wheat: Sown in autumn. It will not flower until weeks of 1–7 °C have switched off its FLC repressor.
facts.gibberellin: A growth hormone, found first in a fungus that made rice grow too tall to hold itself up.
facts.semi_dwarf_wheat: Norin 10's Rht1 and Rht2, crossed in by Borlaug. Short straw, heavy head, and it stays upright.
facts.graft: Cambium pressed to cambium. The top keeps its own genes, so the fruit is the scion's.
facts.phytochrome: A light sensor built from a cracked-open haem ring. Red switches it on, far-red switches it back.
facts.foxglove: Rosette one year, spire the next, then dead. Leaves, flowers and seeds all carry the poison.
facts.digoxin: Isolated in 1930 from the woolly foxglove, not the garden one. It blocks the sodium-potassium pump.
facts.capsicum: One species. Capsaicin sits in the white pith the seeds hang off, not in the seeds themselves.
facts.paprika: Dried mild Capsicum annuum, ground. Red from carotenoids; as extract E160c it colours food.
facts.pectin: The glue between plant cells. Ripening enzymes cut it, and that is why fruit goes soft.
facts.lanolin: The grease sheep secrete to keep rain out of their fleece. Washed from the wool, it goes into ointments.
facts.tallow: Rendered beef or mutton suet. Solid at room temperature, and it keeps for months without a fridge.
facts.horn: A keratin sheath over a living bone core. Grown for life and never shed, which an antler is not.
facts.antler: Solid bone, grown and dropped every year. No other mammal bone grows faster.
facts.feather: Beta-keratin grown from a follicle. Barbs hook to barbs with tiny barbicels to make an airtight vane.
facts.down: The under-layer with no hooks on its barbules, so it traps air instead of making a flight surface.
facts.oyster: A filter feeder that builds its own stone house. One can pull 190 litres of water through its gills a day.
facts.pearl: Nacre wrapped around an intruder by the mantle. Rarely the grain of sand of the story.
facts.nacre: Aragonite tablets half a micrometre thick, stacked in protein. That thickness is why it shimmers.
facts.lac_insect: A scale insect that settles on a twig, feeds on sap, and coats the whole branch in resin.
facts.shellac: Insect resin melted, filtered and flaked. Dissolved in alcohol it is a varnish; pressed, it was a record.
facts.cochineal: A scale insect farmed on prickly pear. Up to a quarter of its dried weight is red dye.
facts.carmine: Carminic acid locked to aluminium. The red in yoghurt, sweets and lipstick, and a real allergen.
facts.rennet: Chymosin from the fourth stomach of an unweaned calf — the enzyme that sets milk into curd.
facts.whey: What runs off the cut curd: water, lactose, and the milk proteins rennet leaves alone.
facts.ricotta: Recooked. Heat coagulates the whey proteins that rennet could not touch.
facts.swim_bladder: A gas bag that holds a fish at depth without swimming. It is the same organ as a lung.
facts.isinglass: Dried fish swim bladder, nearly pure collagen. It drags the yeast out of beer.
facts.roe: The ripe egg mass of a fish. A single salmon redd can hold five thousand of them.
facts.whale: A mammal that went back to the sea. It breathes air and feeds its calf milk the thickness of paste. Its closest living relatives are the hippopotamuses — the two branched from a shared semi-aquatic even-toed ungulate about 60 million years ago.
facts.ambergris: Sperm whale gut secretion, weathered at sea for years until it stops smelling foul.
facts.baleen: Keratin plates that strain krill out of a mouthful of sea. Called whalebone, and it is not bone.
facts.ox: A castrated bull trained to pull. Calm, heavy and steady all day — the engine before engines.
facts.manure: Most of the nitrogen a grazing animal eats leaves again in the dung, ready for the next crop.
facts.parchment: Limed skin dried under tension, never tanned. It buckles whenever the air turns damp.
facts.sinew: Tendon: collagen all lined up one way. Enormously strong along it, useless across it.
facts.ivory: Dentine from a tusk that never stopped growing. Polished, it shows a crosshatch nothing else has.
facts.royal_jelly: Fed to a larva for the whole of its growth, it makes a queen out of a would-be worker.
facts.s_thermophilus: Named heat-liking, and it means it: best growth 35–42 °C. Turns milk's lactose into lactic acid.
facts.l_bulgaricus: Isolated from Bulgarian yoghurt in 1905 and named for the country. Grows best at 40–44 °C.
facts.l_acidophilus: Acid-loving, literally: grows most readily below pH 5. A gut and mouth organism, not a milk one.
facts.bifidobacterium: Branched and Y-shaped — bifid — and anaerobic. The commonest bacterium in an infant's gut.
facts.l_paracasei: Not a starter. It arrives later, grows in ripening cheese, and takes the proteins apart as it goes.
facts.l_plantarum: The plant one. Grows anywhere from pH 3.4 to 8.8, and at 15 °C but not at 45.
facts.leuconostoc: Lives on the skins of fruit and vegetables. Heterofermentative: it gives off CO₂ as well as acid.
facts.lactococcus: The cheese and buttermilk bacterium. Dairy strains are plant strains that shed the genes milk made useless.
facts.acetobacter: Turns ethanol into acetic acid, and needs oxygen to do it. Pasteur found the first one in 1864.
facts.penicillium: A soil mould of cool climates, over 300 species. One of them is why there is antibiotic in this game.
facts.koji: Aspergillus oryzae grown on steamed grain. Its aflatoxin genes are still there and no longer work.
facts.kefir_grains: Not an organism: bacteria and yeasts living in a matrix of the polysaccharide kefiran.
facts.lactic_acid: What homofermentative bacteria make from glucose: two lactate, two ATP, and no gas at all.
facts.acetic_acid: The sour in vinegar. Freezes to ice-like crystals just below room temperature, at 16.6 °C.
facts.yoghurt_culture: Each feeds the other: amino acids from milk protein one way, folic and formic acid the other.
facts.starter_culture: The culture that actually performs the fermentation, kept alive off the food by freeze-drying.
facts.pasteurised_milk: Heated enough to kill the pathogens and not enough to sterilise. Most bacterial spores come through.
facts.souring_kraut: Phase two in the crock: Leuconostoc has taken dominance, and the gas coming off is its doing.
facts.kefir: Sour, fizzy and faintly alcoholic — because yeasts ferment it alongside the bacteria.
facts.buttermilk: What is left in the churn after souring the cream. Under 0.5 per cent fat.
facts.miso: Soybeans, salt and koji, left until the mould's enzymes have taken the beans apart.
facts.camembert: Ripened from the rind inwards by a mould sprayed on the outside, for at least three weeks.
facts.beef: Cattle's meat. Beef and cow run back to one Indo-European root by two different roads.
facts.pork: The pig's meat, and the second most eaten meat in the world after poultry.
facts.mutton: A sheep past two years old. Tougher than lamb, and darker — colour tracks age.
facts.lamb: A sheep in its first year, and its meat. One English word does both jobs.
facts.venison: From Latin venari, to hunt. It once meant the meat of anything hunted, not only deer.
facts.calf: A dairy cow has to calve to keep milking, so a dairy makes calves whether it wants them or not.
facts.veal: The meat of a calf. Mostly the dairy's male calves, which will never give milk.
facts.poultry: Domesticated birds kept for meat, eggs or feathers. A wild bird shot for the pot is game.
facts.game: Not a species but a status: wild animals hunted for meat, and leaner than farmed ones.
facts.steak: Cut from the loin, which barely works. Tenderness rises with distance from hoof and horn.
facts.aged_beef: Held near freezing for weeks while the meat's own enzymes take its connective tissue apart.
facts.ham: The pig's hind leg, cured. Ham is Old English for the bend of the knee, gammon the French for it.
facts.stew: Slow, moist heat for the least tender cuts. The juiciness is collagen, not added water.
facts.carob: A Mediterranean legume that grows as an evergreen tree. The carat is named after its seed.
facts.locust_bean_gum: E410. The milled endosperm of a carob seed — 42 to 46% of the seed, and mostly galactomannan.
facts.guar_gum: E412. Ground guar-bean endosperm, with about eight times the thickening power of cornstarch.
facts.xanthan_gum: E415. Secreted by Xanthomonas campestris, the bacterium that causes black rot in cabbages.
facts.red_alga: Rhodophyta. Red from phycobilin pigments, and the source of both agar and carrageenan.
facts.carrageenan: E407. Sulfated galactose chains from red seaweed. Kappa gels with potassium and grips milk protein.
facts.agar: E406. Sets at 32–42 °C and will not melt again below 85 — a gap gelatin does not have.
facts.alginate: E401. Out of brown seaweed. Drop a solution of it into calcium and it gels on contact.
facts.citric_acid: E330. Nearly all of it is grown, not squeezed — a mould fed on sugar, since 1919.
facts.sodium_acetate: E262. Vinegar's acid, neutralised — a stable solid that holds food at a mildly acidic pH.
facts.msg: E621. The sodium salt of glutamate. Ikeda pulled it out of kombu in 1908 and named the taste umami.
facts.inosinate: E631. A nucleotide that meat and fish already carry at 80 to 800 mg per 100 g.
facts.guanylate: E627. The salt of GMP. Expensive, and almost never used unless glutamate is already there.
facts.ribonucleotides: E635. Inosinate and guanylate mixed. Two per cent of it in MSG quadruples the effect.
facts.maltodextrin: Starch cut short — three to seventeen glucose units. Past DE 20 the same stuff is glucose syrup.
facts.hydrolysed_vegetable_protein: Plant protein taken apart into free amino acids. Where the loose glutamate in savoury food comes from.
facts.silicon_dioxide: E551. Amorphous silica, not quartz — a branched powder that is nearly all surface.
facts.beta_carotene: E160a. The orange in a carrot, and one molecule of it is cut in the gut into two of vitamin A.
facts.annatto: E160b. Achiote seed. The colour sits in a waxy coat on the outside of the seed, not inside it.
facts.turmeric: A rhizome in the ginger family. It cannot seed itself — every plant is a piece of another.
facts.curcumin: E100. Turmeric's yellow. It barely dissolves in water and goes readily into alcohol or oil.
facts.betanin: E162. Beetroot red — a betalain, which carries nitrogen. No plant makes betalains and anthocyanins both.
facts.caramel_colour: E150. Sugar cooked with acid, alkali or salt until brown. More fully oxidised than caramel candy.
facts.ponceau_4r: E124. A synthetic azo dye, built from aromatic rings. Azo dyes do not occur in nature at all.
facts.sorbate: E200–203. Named for the rowan it was distilled from in 1859. Now essentially all synthetic.
facts.benzoate: E210–213. Named after gum benzoin, made now from toluene, and it only works in acidic food.
facts.sulfite: E220–228. Sulfur dioxide taken onto a salt. In wine it stops fermentation and blocks oxidation.
facts.nitrite: E249–250. It turns cured meat pink and holds back the spores that make botulinum toxin.
facts.hydrogenated_oil: Liquid oil with hydrogen added across its double bonds, so it sets solid. Normann's patent, 1902.
facts.trans_fat: A side reaction nobody wanted. Partial hydrogenation flips cis double bonds to trans as it goes.
facts.monoglyceride: E471. A triglyceride with two of its three fatty acids gone, so one end will accept water.
facts.lecithin: E322. Named from lekithos, the Greek for egg yolk, where Gobley found it in 1845.
facts.sorbitol: E420. Glucose with its aldehyde end reduced to an alcohol. About half as sweet as sugar.
facts.xylitol: E967. Wood sugar, reduced. Xylan out of timber, acid-split to xylose, then hydrogenated.
facts.aspartame: E951. Two amino acids joined and capped with a methyl ester. About 200 times as sweet as sugar.
facts.peanut: A legume, not a nut. It flowers above ground and then drives a stalk down to ripen its pods underground.
facts.sesame: Its capsules burst when the seed is ripe and scatter it. Cereals were bred out of that habit; sesame was not.
facts.almond: Nearly half the honeybee hives in the US are trucked to California each February, for this one crop.
facts.drupe: Stone fruit. The stone is hardened ovary wall, not seed coat — and that test rules out most nuts.
facts.mango: A drupe in the cashew family. Its skin and sap carry the oil that makes poison ivy poison ivy.
facts.urushiol: The oil in poison ivy. Also in mango skin, leaves and sap, and in the shell of a raw cashew.
