facts.sumac: A whole dried fruit, ground. Sour from malic acid, and Rome used it where we now use lemon.
facts.walnut: Not a true nut, and not quite a drupe. The shell is the stone; the green husk is not part of the fruit.
facts.juglone: 2–4% of a fresh walnut husk. Stains hands brown and stops other plants growing under the tree.
facts.black_pepper: A vine's unripe drupe. It is cooked before drying, and that is why the corn goes black.
facts.piperine: Pepper's heat. It opens the same channel capsaicin does, from a plant that is no relation.
facts.jalapeno: A pod type, not a species. Same plant as the sweet bell pepper, picked green and hotter if left red.
facts.chipotle: A smoked red jalapeño. Ten pounds of fresh pepper go in and one pound comes out.
facts.cumin: The seed is a whole dried fruit. Same family as carrot, celery, parsley and dill.
facts.marjoram: Origanum majorana. Oregano is the other species in the genus, and its other name is wild marjoram.
facts.lime: The Navy swapped lemon for lime and scurvy came back. Lime juice is the far weaker cure.
facts.makrut_lime: The leaf is the crop, not the fruit. It looks like two leaves because the stalk is winged.
facts.rhizome: A stem that runs sideways underground. It has nodes and buds; a root has neither.
facts.ginger: A rhizome, not a root, and turmeric's close relative. No wild form is left — every plant is a cutting.
facts.gingerol: Fresh ginger's heat: a yellow oil in the rhizome. Drying wrecks it into something hotter.
facts.shogaol: 160,000 Scoville. Why dried ginger bites harder than fresh — it is not the same molecule.
facts.celery: The strings are collenchyma, bundled outside the veins. A marsh umbellifer, like carrot and cumin.
facts.raisin: A grape resists drying. Its skin is waxed against water loss, which is the whole difficulty.
facts.lentil: The optical lens is named after this seed, not the other way round. Latin lens meant lentil first.
facts.split_pea: It splits where it was always going to: down the seam between its two cotyledons.
facts.farro: Not one grain. Einkorn, emmer or spelt — hulled wheats that will not thresh clean.
facts.sunflower: Mature heads do not follow the sun. They stop, facing east, and the morning warmth brings pollinators.
facts.oil: Generic vegetable oil. Deodorised at 232 °C, which is why the bottle need not name a plant.
facts.vitamin_a: Retinol. One reduction step from retinal, and the liver stores it as an ester until asked.
facts.vitamin_d: Not a vitamin. UVB builds it in your skin from a cholesterol precursor, so it is a hormone you make.
facts.soy_sauce: Koji, brine and months. 17–20% salt, so only the halophiles get to work.
facts.candied_fruit: Sugar traded for water, a little stronger each week, until nothing can grow in it.
facts.coconut_sugar: Tapped from the cut flower stem, not the nut. Sap that is 80% water, boiled down.
facts.parsley: Parsley seed holds apiol in enough quantity to be toxic — the leaf everyone eats does not.
facts.sage: Its oil contains thujone, a neurotoxin that can cause convulsions in high enough doses.
facts.rosemary: Its name means 'dew of the sea' in Latin, and it grows wild on cliffs above the Mediterranean.
facts.basil: Its name means 'royal plant' — from the Greek basilikón phytón, kingly herb.
facts.thyme: Thymol, its antiseptic oil, is the same compound now used as an active ingredient in Listerine.
facts.mint: A sterile hybrid of watermint and spearmint. It cannot set seed — every plant grows from a runner.
facts.tarragon: Named for its coiled roots — Latin dracunculus, 'little dragon'. French tarragon can't be grown from seed.
facts.dill: Its scent comes from carvone — flip the molecule to its mirror image and you get spearmint instead.
facts.coriander: A gene variant, OR6A2, makes some people taste soap instead of citrus in the leaf.
facts.chives: Its sulfur compounds repel most insects, but the flowers still draw bees in to pollinate.
facts.bay_leaf: Comes from an evergreen tree that can reach 20 metres — most kitchen herbs aren't trees at all.
facts.oregano: Gets stronger when dried, not weaker — the opposite of almost every other kitchen herb.
facts.thiamin: The first vitamin ever isolated — pulled from rice bran in 1910, the layer polishing removes.
facts.riboflavin: The reason whey glows yellow-green — first isolated from it in 1879, called lactochrome.
facts.niacin: Your body makes it from tryptophan at a steep, fixed rate: 60 milligrams in for 1 milligram out.
facts.folate: Named for the Latin word for leaf — first isolated by extracting it from spinach in 1941.
facts.vitamin_b6: Plants build it partly as their own sunscreen, a defence against UV-B. Animals never gained that trick.
facts.vitamin_e: Named tocopherol, Greek for 'to bear a child' — discovered in 1922 as the fertility factor rats needed.
facts.red_40: Invented in 1971 to replace amaranth, the red dye the FDA later banned for causing cancer.
facts.yellow_5: A 2024 discovery: this yellow dye can turn live mouse skin briefly transparent under light.
facts.yellow_6: Mixed with red dye amaranth to fake the brown of chocolate and caramel. Made from petroleum.
facts.blue_1: The same blue candy dye is also poured into rivers and soil to trace how water moves.
facts.gum_arabic: E414. Tapped from Acacia bark, from which the gum exudes on its own.
facts.gellan_gum: E418. About half the concentration of agar reaches the same gel strength.
facts.arrowroot: Its fine grain once made it a standard ingredient in carbonless copy paper.
facts.shiitake: Traditionally grown on cut logs set beside trees already carrying its spores.
facts.maitake: Called 'dancing mushroom' in Japanese; grows in clumps at the base of old oak trees.
facts.spirulina: Not algae or a plant — it's dried cyanobacterium biomass, farmed in alkaline ponds.
facts.creatine: Named for kreas, Greek for meat — Chevreul isolated it from a muscle extract in 1832.
facts.citrulline: Named for citrullus, Latin for watermelon — first isolated from the fruit in 1914.
facts.theanine: About 1-2% of green tea leaf by dry weight, discovered there in 1949, isolated in 1950.
facts.caffeine: Runge isolated it from coffee beans Goethe gave him, weeks after they first met, in 1819.
facts.alpha_gpc: Chemically stripped from lecithin — remove its two fatty tails and this is what is left.
facts.synephrine: Citrus makes its own stimulant: tyrosine, then tyramine, then this, in the unripe peel.
facts.horsetail: Absorbs silicon from soil and once scoured pewter — the old name for it is 'pewterwort'.
facts.dandelion: Named for its jagged leaves — French 'dent de lion', lion's tooth.
facts.aloe_vera: Its leaf holds two layers: a water-storing gel, and a laxative called aloin the FDA banned in 2002.
facts.ginseng: Chinese for 'person root' — named for a forked shape said to resemble a human body.
facts.psyllium: About a quarter of the seed's weight is mucilage, milled from its husk into dietary fiber.
facts.fos: Resists human digestive enzymes; gut bacteria ferment it instead — a genuine dietary fiber.
facts.pineapple: A bromeliad, not a tree. Its flowers fuse into one fruit even without pollination.
facts.spinach: Dioecious and wind-pollinated — separate male and female plants, unusual for a vegetable.
facts.acai: A palm-tree drupe from Amazon floodplains, borne in branched clusters of up to 900 fruit.
facts.pomegranate: Botanically a berry — one flower's ovary, ripened into a fruit holding up to 1,400 seeds.
facts.goji: A woody nightshade shrub — same family as tomato and potato, but no vine in sight.
facts.papaya: Its huge lobed leaves crown a single soft stem up to ten metres tall. No trunk, no wood.
facts.broccoli: Same species as cabbage, bred for the flower head instead of the wrapped leaves.
facts.alfalfa: A legume whose taproot can run past 15 metres, chasing water no shallow root reaches.
facts.biotin: First crystallized from egg yolk in 1936 — but raw egg white's avidin binds it too tightly to absorb.
facts.hyaluronic_acid: A glycosaminoglycan first pulled from a cow's vitreous humor in 1934 — now farmed from rooster combs.
facts.sucralose: E955. Sucrose with three hydroxyls swapped for chlorine — discovered when 'test' was misheard as 'taste.'
facts.stevia: The Guaraní called it ka'a he'ê, sweet herb — its glycosides taste up to 300 times as sweet as sugar.
facts.fish_sauce: Salted and sealed for up to two years — the longer it ferments, the less fishy it tastes.
facts.lithium_graphite: LiC6 — lithium ions parked between graphite's carbon sheets. This is what a battery anode actually is.
facts.lithium_fluoride: The one alkali halide water won't dissolve. Its crystal passes UV light nothing else can.
facts.lithium_chloride: So hungry for water it is used to dry air itself, one damp crystal at a time.
facts.lithium_iodide: The standard electrolyte inside a pacemaker battery — chosen for how long it lasts, not how well it conducts.
facts.lithium_nitride: The only stable alkali metal nitride. Lithium takes nitrogen straight from the air; the others cannot.
facts.sodium_bromide: A sedative for eighty years before anyone knew why — bromide calms nerves whatever salt carries it.
facts.sodium_iodide: Doped with thallium it lights up under radiation — the crystal at the heart of the first particle counters.
facts.potassium_fluoride: After hydrogen fluoride itself, this is chemistry's main working source of a fluoride ion.
facts.caesium_chloride: Spun in a centrifuge it forms its own density gradient — the trick that first separated DNA by weight.
facts.stainless_steel: Steel needs only 10.5% chromium to stop rusting. The chromium grows its own invisible, self-healing skin.
facts.beryllium_copper: Strikes without a spark — the one alloy safe to swing a wrench with beside an open gas line.
facts.niobium_titanium: Wound into coil and chilled near absolute zero, this is the wire inside four in five MRI magnets.
facts.rose_gold: Gold does not blush on its own. Copper mixed through it is the entire difference.
facts.hard_lead: Pure lead sags. A little antimony stiffens it — and, oddly, stops it shrinking as it cools.
facts.titanium_alloy: Aluminium in the lattice makes titanium fly. This one alloy is most of the titanium ever flown.
facts.iron_chloride: Rust-red and thirsty for grime — it clumps dirt out of drinking water and eats copper off circuit boards.
facts.galvanized_iron: Zinc rusts first on purpose. It sacrifices itself to a scratch so the iron underneath does not have to.
facts.silver_chloride: It darkens the instant light touches it — the whole of photography starts from that one fact.
facts.gold_amalgam: Mercury drinks up gold flour too fine to pan. Miners have used the trick, and paid for it, for centuries.
facts.dental_amalgam: Soft enough to pack into a cavity, hard within minutes: mercury and silver, filling teeth for two centuries.
facts.xenon_tetrafluoride: 1962: proof the noble gases were never entirely noble. The first one ever forced into a bond.
facts.lithium_oxide: A pinch in a glaze turns copper blue and cobalt pink — a flux that changes the colours around it.
facts.sodium_peroxide: Not a simple oxide — sodium burned in excess oxygen overshoots. It once breathed for submarines.
facts.potassium_superoxide: Scrubs carbon dioxide out of sealed air and hands back oxygen — a rebreather's whole trick in one rock.
facts.titanium_dioxide: The white in almost everything white — paint, paper, toothpaste — chosen purely for its brightness.
facts.nickel_oxide: Green as a pure crystal, black the instant it is not — an electrode inside the earliest nickel batteries.
facts.tin_dioxide: Suspended in a glaze it scatters light instead of passing it — the opaque white of old tin-glazed pottery.
facts.palladium_hydride: A palm-sized block of this metal can hold nine hundred times its own volume of hydrogen gas.
facts.neon_light: Thousands of volts through the gas itself, no filament at all. Pure neon burns a steady orange-red.
facts.silver_bromide: More light-sensitive than silver chloride — the compound most black-and-white film was built from.
facts.germanium_dioxide: Mixed into silica glass it bends light more without clouding it — the core of a fiber-optic cable.
facts.bismuth_telluride: Push current through this crystal and one face chills while the other warms — no moving parts.
facts.ferrovanadium: A little of this in the melt is a universal steel hardener — tougher, and better against heat and twisting.
facts.nicad_battery: A cadmium plate and a nickel plate in alkaline electrolyte — rechargeable long before lithium was.
facts.platinum_rhodium_gauze: Platinum wire mesh with a tenth rhodium worked in — the screen ammonia burns across on its way to fertiliser.
facts.platinum_iridium: 90% platinum, 10% iridium — for over a century, this exact golf-ball-sized bar WAS the kilogram.
facts.hardened_platinum: Pure platinum is too soft for a ring. A trace of ruthenium worked in is what actually holds the stone.
facts.tungsten_rhenium: A thermocouple wire good past 2,200°C — hot enough that almost nothing else can even measure it.
facts.rocket_nozzle_alloy: Niobium and hafnium, a whisper of titanium — this exact alloy steered the Apollo Lunar Module down.
facts.scandium_aluminum_alloy: Traces of scandium in aluminium raise its strength 50 to 70 MPa — enough to matter in a MiG or a bike frame.
facts.yag: Yttrium, aluminium and oxygen in a crystal clear enough to host a laser. Dope it with neodymium and it lases.
facts.rubidium_superoxide: Like potassium one row up, rubidium in excess oxygen skips the plain oxide and goes straight to superoxide.
facts.strontium_chloride: The active ingredient behind 'for sensitive teeth' — it plugs the tubules a receding gum has exposed.
facts.luminous_paint: Radium mixed into zinc sulfide, painted onto a watch face, glowing green in the dark since 1908.
facts.gas_mantle: 99% thorium dioxide, 1% cerium dioxide — a fabric mesh that turns an ordinary gas flame white-hot bright.
facts.ferrocerium: Scrape it and the sparks hit 3,300°C. This, not flint, is what actually lights a modern lighter.
facts.neodymium_magnet: Neodymium, iron, and boron this recipe cannot carry — the strongest permanent magnet you can buy.
facts.samarium_cobalt_magnet: Weaker than neodymium but happy past 300°C — the rare-earth magnet that survives an engine bay.
facts.red_phosphor: Half a gram to a gram of this sits inside every colour tube TV — europium is the only red they had.
facts.gadolinium_steel: As little as 1% gadolinium makes iron easier to work and far harder to oxidise hot.
facts.signal_paint: Promethium's beta rays hit a phosphor instead of your eye directly — a gentler glow than radium's ever was.
facts.nuoc_cham: One part fish sauce, one part sugar, two parts water, lime for the acid — Vietnam's dipping sauce.
facts.carbon_tetrafluoride: Burn carbon in pure fluorine instead of oxygen and this is what comes out — even graphite will burn this way.
facts.carbon_disulfide: For a century this reeking liquid was made by heating carbon and sulfur, before natural gas took the job.
facts.nitrogen_trifluoride: Nitrogen barely reacts with anything — an electric spark through nitrogen and fluorine forces this bond.
facts.chlorine_trifluoride: Made by fluorinating chlorine gas — and so reactive once formed it will set sand itself on fire.
facts.disulfur_dichloride: Lead chlorine gas into a flask of sulfur and the contents turn a golden yellow liquid at room temperature.
facts.phosphorus_trichloride: White phosphorus burning in chlorine gas — the industrial route to one of chemistry's most common reagents.
facts.sulfur_hexafluoride: Discovered in 1901 by simply exposing sulfur to fluorine gas — nothing about making it has changed since.
facts.phosphorus_pentafluoride: Phosphorus and fluorine combine directly, four molecules of each swapped for four of this at a time.
facts.phosphorus_sesquisulfide: Red phosphorus and sulfur, melted together above 450 K — this is the head of a strike-anywhere match.
facts.aluminum_chloride: Aluminium foil burns in chlorine gas at 650°C in an exothermic reaction run at industrial scale.
facts.aluminum_sulfide: Ignite aluminium and sulfur together and the reaction runs so hot the molten product can melt through steel.
facts.copper_chloride: Copper at red heat combines directly with chlorine gas — a very exothermic reaction with a molten result.
facts.magnesium_chloride: Alkaline earth metals all react with the halogens to form salts like this one — magnesium's own chloride.
facts.magnesium_sulfide: Formed directly when sulfur, or even just hydrogen sulfide gas, meets magnesium metal.
facts.calcium_chloride: The textbook example of an alkaline earth metal meeting a halogen — calcium and chlorine, straight to salt.
facts.sodium_sulfide: Sodium and sulfur combine directly, but almost every tonne made goes straight into pulping wood for paper.
facts.potassium_sulfide: Potassium and sulfur react cleanly together, dissolved in liquid ammonia to keep the reaction under control.
facts.tin_chloride: Chlorine gas over tin metal at 115°C, nothing more — a clean, direct route to a common industrial catalyst.
facts.lead_chloride: The most straightforward way to make it is also the most literal: chlorine gas, straight onto lead metal.
facts.gold_chloride: Robert Boyle proved gold could react with something in 1666: metallic gold, straight into chlorine gas.
facts.copper_fluoride: Copper metal and fluorine gas at 500°C — only half of it converts, but the half that does is genuine.
facts.aluminum_copper_alloy: Aluminium and a little copper, precipitated into a strengthening phase — its main home is an aircraft frame.
facts.magnalium: Aluminium and magnesium alloyed — light enough for engines, or loaded with magnesium for a firework's flare.
facts.nak_alloy: Sodium and potassium melted together stay liquid at room temperature — reactor coolant since the 1960s.
facts.tin_silver_solder: Tin dissolves silver readily — their eutectic, melting at 221°C, is the real alloy behind lead-free solder.
facts.lithium_bromide: A strong aqueous solution of this salt is the desiccant that dries the air inside a building's cooling system.
facts.potassium_bromide: The first medicine that worked against epilepsy — so widely prescribed 'bromide' became slang for dull.
facts.rubidium_fluoride: A white crystal built on the same cubic lattice as ordinary table salt, one row down the periodic table.
facts.rubidium_chloride: Dissolves into cells so readily that biologists use it to make bacteria absorb foreign DNA on command.
facts.rubidium_bromide: Its crystal lattice is table salt's own structure, just stretched to fit two heavier atoms.
facts.rubidium_iodide: Bottled as eye drops in Romania under its own brand name — eight milligrams of this salt in every millilitre.
facts.caesium_fluoride: The most reactive stable metal meets the most reactive nonmetal — chemists use the salt as a fluoride source.
facts.caesium_bromide: Grown into crystal optics, it splits light in spectrophotometers chemists use to identify compounds.
facts.caesium_iodide: The phosphor screen inside an X-ray image intensifier — this crystal is what turns radiation into a picture.
facts.krypton_difluoride: Krypton will not bond with fluorine on its own — only an electric spark, UV light, or a hot wire forces it.
facts.titanium_chloride: Cold titanium ignores chlorine completely. At 550°C the two combine violently instead.
facts.cobalt_chloride: Blue when bone dry, pink the moment it absorbs water — a colour change reliable enough to indicate humidity.
facts.chromium_chloride: Chromium metal chlorinated directly — the same element that grows its own rust-proof skin, made to react.
facts.lanthanum_oxide: Lanthanum tarnishes almost as fast as you can watch, turning black in hours as it burns to this oxide.
facts.cerium_oxide: Ce + O2 → CeO2, straight from the metal — then it scrubs a car exhaust or polishes glass flat.
facts.neodymium_oxide: Burns off the metal at just 150°C, and the flaking oxide keeps exposing fresh metal underneath to burn again.
facts.europium_fluoride: Europium metal reacts with every halogen there is. Fluorine gives this one: white europium(III) fluoride.
facts.europium_chloride: The same europium-plus-halogen reaction, run on chlorine instead — yellow crystals instead of white.
facts.gadolinium_oxide: Unlike most rare earths, gadolinium shrugs off dry air — only damp air tarnishes it down to this oxide.
facts.hydrogen_fluoride: The only common acid that eats glass, not metal — stored in plastic because it dissolves the bottle.
facts.lithium_ion_battery: Graphite anode, lithium cobalt oxide cathode — the pair that actually powers a phone.
facts.lithium_hydride: 2 Li + H2 → 2 LiH — fast even at low heat, faster still above 600°C.
facts.neptunium: Named for the next planet past Uranus — a neutron fired into uranium made the first atom of it in 1940.
facts.americium: A speck of americium-241 sits inside most household smoke detectors, ionizing air to sense smoke.
facts.curium: Named for Marie and Pierre Curie — first made in 1944 by firing alpha particles at plutonium.
facts.berkelium: Named for Berkeley, California — the same cyclotron there later made californium too.
facts.californium: Half a milligram gives off enough neutrons to start up a nuclear reactor or find oil in a well.
facts.protactinium: Named for the element it decays into — actinium — the step directly before it in nature's decay chains.
facts.actinium: So radioactive it visibly glows pale blue in the dark, one of only a few elements that do.
facts.technetium: The first element ever made artificially before being found in nature — its name literally means 'artificial'.
facts.astatine: So rare that less than a gram of it exists naturally in the entire Earth's crust at any moment.
facts.rutherfordium: Named for Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who first split the atom and mapped out its nucleus.
facts.dubnium: Named for Dubna, Russia — the lab whose decade-long priority dispute with Berkeley became legend.
facts.seaborgium: One of only two elements named for someone still alive at the time — chemist Glenn Seaborg himself.
facts.bohrium: Named for Niels Bohr, who put electrons into orbits around the nucleus like tiny planets.
facts.hassium: Named for Hesse, the German state — Hassia in Latin — home to the lab that first made it in 1984.
facts.meitnerium: The only element named specifically for a real woman — physicist Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of fission.
facts.darmstadtium: Named for Darmstadt, the German city whose heavy-ion accelerator has now made half a dozen elements.
facts.roentgenium: Named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and won physics' very first Nobel Prize.
facts.copernicium: Named for Copernicus, who worked out that the planets circle the Sun rather than the Earth.
facts.beryllium_fluoride: The fluoride base of FLiBe, the molten salt that carries heat through a liquid-fluoride nuclear reactor.
facts.beryllium_chloride: A Friedel-Crafts catalyst, and the raw material electrolysis splits apart to make pure beryllium metal.
facts.beryllium_bromide: Covalent, not ionic — beryllium is too small and too polarizing to make a true salt with a halogen.
facts.beryllium_iodide: Decomposed on a white-hot tungsten filament, it deposits beryllium metal purer than any ore ever gives up.
facts.magnesium_fluoride: Clear from deep ultraviolet to the infrared — the anti-reflective coating on camera and telescope lenses.
facts.magnesium_bromide: Once a nerve tonic and anticonvulsant; today it mostly survives as a catalyst in the aldol reaction.
facts.magnesium_iodide: Made dry, in ether — chemists use it to strip methyl groups clean off an aromatic ether.
facts.calcium_bromide: A dense brine pumped down oil wells as drilling fluid, and stirred into coal to trap mercury before it vents.
facts.calcium_iodide: An iodine supplement stirred into cat food today; an early photographic emulsion a century ago.
facts.strontium_fluoride: Carries radioactive strontium-90 inside a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, decaying for decades.
facts.strontium_bromide: Burned in a flare, it throws off the same deep red any strontium salt gives a firework.
facts.strontium_iodide: Doped with europium it catches gamma rays and flashes — a scintillator crystal grown a whole cylinder at once.
facts.barium_fluoride: Clear to infrared light and flashes at a gamma photon's touch — a crystal PET scanners use as a detector.
facts.barium_chloride: The standard lab reagent for weighing out exactly how much sulfate a solution is hiding.
facts.barium_bromide: Marie Curie used this salt's own crystallization habit to fractionate radium out of its barium ore.
facts.barium_iodide: The least-documented of barium's four halides — even its own reference entry names it no use at all.
facts.radium_fluoride: Crystallizes in fluorite's own cubic shape — the same column of the table, just heavier and radioactive.
facts.radium_chloride: The first radium compound ever isolated pure, by Curie herself — now also a prostate-cancer drug's core.
facts.radium_bromide: Discovered by the Curies in 1898; it later glowed on watch dials until the danger was understood.
facts.radium_iodide: A yellow, water-soluble radium salt — one of the rarest compounds here, one of Wikipedia's shortest pages.
facts.bacteriophage: A virus built to infect nothing but bacteria. The name is Greek for devourer of bacteria — and it means it.
facts.prophage: A phage genome stitched into a bacterium's own chromosome, copied for free at every division. Waiting.
facts.lysis: A cell bursting open once its own internal pressure overcomes a wall that phage enzymes have already breached.
facts.protozoan: A single eukaryotic cell living entirely on its own. Common wherever there's water, even a damp patch of soil.
facts.eimeria: An apicomplexan parasite genus, almost always locked to one host for life. Several live only in chickens.
facts.coccidiosis: An intestinal disease caused by coccidian parasites invading the gut lining. Spread through droppings.
facts.salmonella: A genus of rod-shaped bacteria behind roughly 1.2 million food-poisoning cases a year in the US alone.
facts.viroid: Bare circular RNA, no protein coat, about 1/80th the size of a typical virus. Only known to infect plants.
facts.salicylic_acid: Raffaele Piria split salicin into a sugar and a second piece, then oxidised that piece into this.
facts.aspirin: Felix Hoffmann acetylated salicylic acid in 1897 using acetic anhydride. Bayer called the result aspirin.
facts.streptomyces: Filamentous, spore-forming soil bacteria — as a genus they make over two-thirds of nature's known antibiotics.
facts.streptomycin: Isolated from Streptomyces griseus, 19 October 1943, out of New Jersey soil. The first cure for tuberculosis.
facts.pancreas: Ninety-nine percent of it is exocrine, making digestive enzymes. The other one percent makes insulin.
facts.insulin: Two peptide chains, A and B, held by two disulfide bonds — a third closes a loop inside the A chain.
facts.sweet_potato: A different family from potato entirely. Grown from cuttings of its own vine, not from seed.
facts.cauliflower: Same species as cabbage and broccoli — a head of flower buds that never opened.
facts.zucchini: A squash, picked immature — the seeds and rind are still soft enough to eat.
facts.eggplant: A nightshade, like chilli and tomato — a berry, botanically, that follows the flower.
facts.asparagus: The part eaten is a young shoot — spears sent up each spring by a perennial root.
facts.radish: Ready to pull within a month. Grows best in light, sandy soil for a straight root.
facts.turnip: A biennial root — it spends its first year storing food, and only flowers in its second.
facts.leek: An allium, like onion — grown for up to six months in loose, well-drained soil.
facts.brussels_sprout: A cabbage cultivar bred for its buds, which mature up a thick stalk over several weeks.
facts.kale: A cabbage cultivar whose leaves never form a head — hardy enough to survive -15°C.
facts.artichoke: A cultivated thistle. Its bud must be cut before the flower opens or it turns woody.
facts.okra: A mallow-family seed pod — cotton's cousin — that turns mucilaginous once cut.
facts.mushroom: Agaricus bisporus, the common button mushroom — grown on composted manure, not wood.
facts.avocado: A single-seeded berry. Named varieties are grafted onto rootstock, not grown from seed.
facts.arugula: A mustard-family salad leaf, ready in 40 to 50 days of full sun and moist soil.
facts.watercress: An aquatic mustard relative with hollow floating stems — grows straight in flowing streams.
facts.orange: A citrus hybrid — pomelo crossed with mandarin. Named varieties are grafted, same as lemon's own kin.
facts.grapefruit: An accidental hybrid of sweet orange and pomelo, first crossed in the 17th-century Caribbean.
facts.peach: A stone fruit that starts bearing within 2-3 years — and is finished within about 20.
facts.plum: A stone fruit of Prunus, kept pruned to a modest 5-6 metres for picking.
facts.apricot: A stone fruit. The kernel inside the pit is not a snack — it carries a real cyanide compound.
facts.nectarine: Not a hybrid — the same species as peach, missing fuzz because of one recessive gene.
facts.watermelon: 91% water. Botanically a pepo — a modified berry with a thick rind.
facts.cantaloupe: Cucumis melo — a true melon, the same genus as cucumber, not related to watermelon.
facts.kiwi: A berry from a woody vine — and the vine itself is either male or female, never both.
facts.raspberry: An aggregate of tiny drupelets. Its cane grows one year and only fruits the next.
facts.blackberry: Same aggregate-drupelet fruit as raspberry, but the core stays in when you pick it.
facts.cranberry: Harvested by flooding the bed — the ripe berries float free of the vine.
facts.blueberry: A true berry that changes colour three times before it's ripe — green, then red, then blue.
facts.date: A palm's drupe. Wild-pollinated by wind — growers do it by hand for a reliable crop.
facts.persimmon: Ripens after its own tree has already dropped its leaves for the year.
facts.guava: A myrtle-family tree berry — fruiting within two years of its own seed, for up to forty.
facts.rye: A wheat-tribe cereal that survives snow cover heavy enough to kill winter wheat.
facts.quinoa: Not a grain at all — a seed, from a plant related to spinach, not to wheat.
facts.buckwheat: No relation to wheat — it's a cousin of rhubarb, eaten like a grain only because of its starch.
facts.millet: Small-seeded, drought-tolerant grasses grown as a grain across dry regions worldwide.
facts.sorghum: A grass grain bred for drought and heat — nitrogen-efficient where most cereals struggle.
facts.chickpea: A pulse — each small pod on the plant holds only two or three seeds.
facts.bean: Phaseolus vulgaris — black, kidney and pinto beans are all one species, bred different colours.
facts.black_bean: The common bean, dried — anthocyanin pigment in the seed coat is what turns it black.
facts.pinto_bean: Spanish for 'painted' — named for the mottled speckling on its seed coat.
facts.kidney_bean: A common bean cultivar. Raw, it carries the highest lectin toxin load of any bean.
facts.semolina: A coarser grind than flour — the granules couscous and pasta both start from.
facts.couscous: Semolina rolled wet by hand into tiny pellets, then steamed light and fluffy.
facts.cinnamon: Inner tree bark, pried off in strips that curl into quills as they dry.
facts.nutmeg: A seed, sun-dried for up to 30 weeks until it rattles loose in its own shell.
facts.clove: Not a seed or a berry — a flower bud, picked before it ever opens.
facts.cardamom: Ginger's own family — triangular papery pods holding small black seeds.
facts.vanilla: An orchid's seed pod. Every plant grown today is hand-pollinated — its own flower can't self-pollinate.
facts.saffron: The dried stigma of an autumn crocus. A kilogram takes 150,000 flowers, hand-picked.
facts.fennel: Carrot's own family — its dried seeds are the spice, its bulb the vegetable.
facts.mustard_seed: Cabbage's own family — the small round seed the whole mustard condiment starts from.
facts.allspice: Picked green and unripe, then sun-dried until it looks like a large peppercorn.
facts.star_anise: A star-shaped fruit of 6 to 8 pods in a whorl, picked from the tree just before it ripens.
facts.wasabi: A real Brassicaceae rhizome, ground fresh — most 'wasabi' served is horseradish and dye.
facts.cashew: A drupe hanging off the cashew apple. Its shell carries a poison-ivy relative — toxic until roasted.
facts.pistachio: A drupe whose shell pops open on its own as it ripens — a trait people bred for.
facts.pecan: Not really a nut — a hickory drupe, a single stone inside a husk.
facts.hazelnut: A true nut, unlike most 'nuts' here — it drops free of its husk 7 to 8 months after pollination.
facts.macadamia: A Proteaceae tree native to Australia. Perfectly edible for people — toxic to dogs.
facts.mozzarella: Pasta filata — curd heated and kneaded until it turns into one smooth, stretchy paste.
facts.cheddar: Named for the process, not the place — curd repeatedly kneaded, cut, stacked and turned to drain the whey.
facts.parmesan: Hard and granular from unpasteurised cow's milk, aged a minimum of a year and often two.
facts.feta: Greek and brined — sheep's milk, or a mix of sheep and goat, never cow alone.
facts.cottage_cheese: Acid-set curds, drained and mixed straight back with cream — never aged, never pressed.
facts.evaporated_milk: Milk with 60% of its water boiled off, canned and heat-sterilised — no sugar added.
facts.condensed_milk: Evaporated milk with sugar stirred in at a roughly 9:11 ratio — the sugar is what keeps it shelf-stable.
facts.custard: Cream thickened by egg protein alone — coagulating between 70 and 80°C, curdling past it.
facts.ketchup: Tomato, sugar and vinegar — the vinegar and sugar are what keep it shelf-stable.
facts.maple_syrup: Boiled down from tree sap — it takes 20 to 50 litres of sap for one litre of syrup.
facts.peanut_butter: Roasted peanuts, ground twice — medium, then fine — until it's a paste.
facts.jam: Crushed fruit and sugar, boiled to 104°C — the fruit's own pectin is what sets it.
facts.cornstarch: Pure starch, milled out of the corn kernel's endosperm — nothing else left in it.
facts.baking_soda: NaHCO3 — releases carbon dioxide the moment it meets acid or heat, which is the entire trick.
facts.baking_powder: Baking soda pre-mixed with a weak acid and cornstarch — self-contained, unlike soda alone.
facts.worcestershire_sauce: A fermented anchovy-and-malt-vinegar sauce, invented by two Worcester pharmacists.
facts.hot_sauce: Chilli and vinegar, at its simplest — nothing more is required.
facts.tahini: Ground sesame seeds, toasted first — an oily paste, not unlike peanut butter's own process.
facts.vanilla_extract: Vanilla pods steeped in ethanol and water — carries hundreds of flavour compounds beyond vanillin alone.
facts.mustard: Ground mustard seed mixed with vinegar or another liquid into a paste.
facts.shrimp: A decapod crustacean built for swimming — an elongated body, not a crab's sideways scuttle.
facts.crab: Its tail is folded flat under its own body — that's the trait that lets it run sideways.
facts.lobster: Ten legs by the strict count — the two big front pincers are legs too.
facts.salmon: Born in a river, grown at sea, and it fights back upstream to the exact place it hatched.
facts.tuna: A fish that runs warmer than the water around it — one of only three that can.
facts.guacamole: Mashed avocado and salt, traditionally worked with a mortar and pestle.
facts.hummus: Cooked mashed chickpeas blended with tahini — the two ingredients that make it hummus.
facts.salsa: Chopped tomato and onion at its simplest — the base every other salsa builds from.
facts.coleslaw: Shredded raw cabbage in a dressing — cabbage is the only ingredient every recipe agrees on.
facts.omelette: Beaten egg, fried in butter — the whole dish is just that one transformation.
facts.pancake: A starch batter, cooked flat on a hot griddle — no patterned plates involved.
facts.waffle: Leavened batter, cooked between two patterned plates — the grid is pressed in, not poured.
facts.burger: Ground meat, cooked into a patty, inside a sliced bun — the whole definition in one line.
facts.hot_dog: A cooked sausage in a partially sliced bun — nothing more is required to call it one.
facts.sandwich: Any filling between two slices of bread — the bread is the only fixed part of the definition.
facts.fried_rice: Cooked rice, stir-fried — the day-old rice recipe every household reaches for.
facts.taco: A tortilla folded by hand around a filling and eaten straight from the hand.
facts.cassava: Unlike a potato's swollen stem, cassava's edible part really is a root — swollen with starch, and, raw, laced with cyanogenic compounds that processing has to remove.
facts.tapioca: Cassava root, grated and pressed until its starch washes out as a milky liquid, then dried into flour or pearls — raw cassava is toxic, so this processing is not optional.
facts.avibirnavirus: A double-stranded RNA genus, bare and non-enveloped. Its only member's natural hosts are chickens and turkeys.
facts.infectious_bursal_disease: Also called infectious bursal disease. Destroys a young chicken's B-lymphocytes right where they form.
facts.gammacoronavirus: A coronavirus genus from the avian gene pool. Goose, duck and chicken each carry their own species in it.
facts.infectious_bronchitis: A chicken-only coronavirus disease. Fouls the airway first, then can reach the kidney and the oviduct.
facts.e_coli: Normal gut flora in almost every warm-blooded animal, harmless there — until one strain gets the wrong genes.
facts.colibacillosis: What a virulent E. coli strain causes once it reaches tissue the harmless kind never goes. Costly to poultry.
facts.ascaridia_galli: A roundworm living nowhere but a bird's small intestine. Free-range chickens catch it from an earthworm.
facts.ascaridiasis: Heavy Ascaridia galli infection in a chicken's gut, from eggs that persist for years in soil and water.
facts.satellite: Bare RNA even smaller than a viroid's. It cannot replicate at all without borrowing a helper virus's proteins.
facts.cowpox: A real Orthopoxvirus — its usual wild host is voles, not cattle, which only catch it occasionally.
facts.vaccine: A weakened, killed, or fragmentary pathogen, given on purpose so the immune system meets the real one first.
facts.immunity: The immune system's memory of a pathogen it has already met — faster and stronger, the second time around.
facts.nitrophenol: Phenol with a nitro group on its fourth carbon. Bright yellow, and paracetamol's classical first step.
facts.aminophenol: Nitrophenol's nitro group, reduced to an amine. One reaction away from paracetamol.
facts.paracetamol: Relieves pain and fever. Exactly how is still not settled science, after more than a century of use.
facts.histamine: One amino acid, one step. The actual cause of a runny nose in an allergic reaction — not the allergen protein.
facts.arachidonic_acid: A polyunsaturated fatty acid built into cell-membrane phospholipids until an enzyme cuts it free.
facts.prostaglandin: Made from arachidonic acid by the enzyme painkillers target. The real signal behind pain, fever and swelling.
facts.beryllium_oxide: 2 Be + O2 → 2 BeO — though igniting beryllium in open air also throws off the nitride Be3N2 alongside it.
facts.strontium_oxide: Strontia — what strontium becomes the moment it meets oxygen.
facts.barium_oxide: 2 Ba + O2 → 2 BaO — barium's own exothermic answer to open air.
facts.caesium_superoxide: When caesium burns in air, CsO2 — not the plain oxide — is what actually forms.
facts.calcium_hydride: Calcium and hydrogen, combined directly at 300 to 400°C.
facts.magnesium_hydride: Magnesium, hydrogenated directly — though the first prep needed 200 atmospheres and 500°C.
facts.strontium_hydride: Sr + H2 → SrH2 — a clean yield takes oxygen-free hydrogen and redistilled strontium.
facts.barium_hydride: Barium and hydrogen, combined directly at 150 to 200°C.
facts.sodium_hydride: 2 Na + H2 → 2 NaH — industrially, molten sodium beaten into mineral oil under a hydrogen atmosphere.
facts.potassium_hydride: Potassium and hydrogen, combined directly between 200 and 350°C.
facts.rubidium_hydride: Rubidium metal, treated with hydrogen gas.
facts.caesium_hydride: Made from caesium carbonate and magnesium, heated together in hydrogen.
facts.beryllium_nitride: Beryllium powder, heated in dry nitrogen with oxygen kept well out of the way.
facts.calcium_nitride: 3 Ca + N2 → Ca3N2, straight from the elements.
facts.strontium_nitride: What's left when strontium metal burns in nitrogen instead of air.
facts.barium_nitride: Barium, like the rest of its column, reacts with nitrogen on heating.
facts.radium_nitride: The reason a piece of radium goes black in air: not oxide, nitride. 3 Ra + N2 → Ra3N2.
facts.bromine_trifluoride: Br2 + 3 F2 → 2 BrF3, first made in 1906 by reacting the two straight at 20°C.
facts.iodine_pentafluoride: I2 + 5 F2 → 2 IF5 — first made in 1891 by burning solid iodine in fluorine gas, and still the method today.
facts.bromine_monochloride: One part bromine, one part chlorine, forced together — an interhalogen like any other in its family.
facts.iodine_monochloride: I2 + Cl2 → 2 ICl — chlorine gas passed straight through iodine crystals leaves a dark brown liquid behind.
facts.iodine_monobromide: I2 + Br2 → 2 IBr — the two heaviest common halogens, combined directly.
facts.hydrogen_iodide: H2 + I2 → 2 HI — the reaction still used to make the highest-purity samples today.
facts.bull: Fertile from about seven months old. Only a few are kept intact — most male calves are castrated.
facts.heifer: A female that has not yet calved. Dairy heifers are often kept on to replace their own mothers.
facts.steer: A castrated male raised for beef. The same animal, elsewhere, might just as easily be called an ox.
facts.chick: Uses an egg tooth to break out of the shell after about 21 days, feeding at first on its last yolk.
facts.cockerel: A young male chicken — not yet the rooster he will grow into.
facts.pullet: A young female chicken, sexually immature — under about 22 weeks old in the poultry trade.
facts.rooster: A fertile adult male chicken. The word is an 18th-century American euphemism for 'cock'.
facts.hen: An adult female chicken. One bred for laying can produce more than 300 eggs a year.
facts.capon: A male chicken castrated or neutered young, traditionally to make the meat milder and fattier.
facts.ram: An intact male sheep, occasionally called a tup. Kept mostly for breeding.
facts.ewe: An adult female sheep. Pronounced 'yoo' — nothing like it looks spelled.
facts.wether: A castrated male sheep. Most male lambs not kept for breeding become one.
facts.kid: A juvenile goat. The word comes from Old Norse kið, carried in by Scandinavian settlers.
facts.buck: An intact adult male goat. Acquires a strong, distinctive odour during the autumn rut.
facts.doe: An adult female goat. Many breeders wait until she reaches 70% of adult weight before breeding.
facts.piglet: Newborn into a litter that was once yearly — by the 19th century, twice a year in Europe.
facts.boar: A male pig of breeding age, kept intact rather than castrated.
facts.gilt: A young female pig, not yet mated or not yet farrowed — the exact line shifts by local usage.
facts.barrow: A male pig castrated before puberty — a stag is the same operation done after.
facts.sow: A breeding female pig, or one after her first or second litter.
facts.foal: An equine up to one year old. A mare 'in foal' is pregnant; to 'foal' is to give birth.
facts.colt: A male foal — the term holds until the horse turns three or four.
facts.filly: A female foal — the term holds until the horse turns three or four.
facts.stallion: An intact adult male horse — a colt becomes one at three, or four in racing.
facts.mare: An adult female horse — a filly becomes one at three, or four in racing.
facts.gelding: A castrated male horse, of any age — the one horse term untouched by puberty.
facts.buffalo: Swamp-type buffaloes wallow on purpose, digging mudholes with their own horns.
facts.carabeef: Buffalo meat — the word is a 1970s Philippine-English portmanteau of carabao and beef.
facts.chevon: Goat meat. A 1922 trade-association coinage — chevre crossed with mouton — that never caught on.
facts.donkey: Descended from the African wild ass, at home in true desert rather than open grassland.
facts.rabbit: Livestock since at least the first century BC in Rome, kept for meat, fur and wool.
facts.drake: An adult male duck — 'duck' itself technically names the female, or 'hen' in ornithology.
facts.duckling: A young duck in downy plumage. In the food trade the word can also mean a tender young adult.
facts.goose: Paired with 'gander' it means specifically the female; alone it can mean either sex.
facts.gander: An adult male goose. Set beside 'goose' it draws a sex line the word alone does not.
facts.gosling: A young goose before fledging — not yet able to fly.
facts.poult: An infant turkey — 'chick' works too, but poult is the word specific to it.
facts.tom: An adult male turkey, also called a gobbler — up to twice the weight of the hen.
facts.turkey_hen: An adult female turkey, typically 2.5 to 5.4 kg — much smaller than the tom.
facts.basking_shark: Second-largest fish alive, filter-feeding zooplankton by swimming with its huge mouth held open.
facts.megamouth_shark: Undiscovered until 1976 and still one of the rarest sharks alive, with fewer than 300 ever recorded.
facts.sand_tiger_shark: Swims with its mouth open baring three rows of ragged teeth, yet has never killed anyone.
facts.great_white_shark: Can sprint at 24 km/h and keeps parts of its body warmer than the sea around it.
facts.mako_shark: The fastest shark alive, clocked bursting through the water at 74 km/h.
facts.salmon_shark: Keeps its stomach 16-19°C warmer than the cold Pacific water it hunts salmon in.
facts.thresher_shark: A tail as long as its own body, used to whip and stun the small fish it hunts.
facts.goblin_shark: Its jaws catapult forward from its skull to snatch prey — the fastest bite of any shark.
facts.eagle_ray: White-spotted and built to leap clear of the water, with teeth shaped to crush shellfish.
facts.manta_ray: The largest ray alive, and it carries the largest brain of any fish — up to 200 grams.
facts.catshark: Lays its eggs in a tendrilled ‘mermaid’s purse’ anchored to the seabed.
facts.tope_shark: Tagged individuals have crossed entire oceans, one swimming from Britain to Iceland.
facts.leopard_shark: Harmless to people, despite dark saddle-and-spot markings down a silvery back.
facts.tiger_shark: Eats almost anything — sea turtles turn up in a fifth of the stomachs studied.
facts.lemon_shark: Yellow-brown skin camouflages it over the sandy seafloor it hunts across.
facts.bull_shark: Tolerates fresh water so well it has been tracked 4,000 km up the Amazon.
facts.orca: The largest dolphin alive, and an apex predator that even hunts other whales.
facts.nautilus: A living fossil, little changed in hundreds of millions of years, with up to 90 tentacles.
facts.blacktip_shark: Leaps clear of the water and spins three or four times while chasing schooling fish.
facts.oceanic_whitetip_shark: Once so common around shipwrecks it earned the nickname ‘shipwreck shark’.
facts.silky_shark: Named for its smooth skin, and almost always found trailing a school of tuna.
facts.blacktip_reef_shark: The most common shark on Indo-Pacific coral reefs, patrolling shallow lagoons.
facts.grey_reef_shark: The first shark ever recorded performing a threat display before it charges.
facts.whitetip_reef_shark: Can pump water over its own gills and lie still — most sharks must swim or drown.
facts.great_hammerhead: A solitary hunter that pins stingrays down with its huge hammer-shaped head.
facts.scalloped_hammerhead: Schools hundreds strong near seamounts by day — most hammerheads hunt alone.
facts.octopus: Three hearts and copper-based blue blood — two-thirds of its half-billion neurons sit out in its arms.
facts.giant_pacific_octopus: The largest octopus species. A mother starves guarding her eggs for six months and dies as they hatch.
facts.blue_ringed_octopus: A bite can kill in minutes with no antivenom, yet it has never once been recorded attacking unprovoked.
facts.giant_squid: Eyes up to 27 cm across, the largest of any animal, built to watch the dark for one predator: the sperm whale.
facts.vampire_squid: Neither vampire nor squid — closer kin to an octopus, and it doesn't hunt: it collects sinking marine snow.
facts.box_jellyfish: 24 eyes with real lenses and corneas across four clusters, and among the most venomous animals alive.
facts.lions_mane_jellyfish: The largest jellyfish species — a bell over 2 m wide, tentacles once measured past 36 m long.
facts.man_o_war: Not a jellyfish — a colony of thousands of genetically identical zooids, all budded from one fertilised egg.
facts.sea_anemone: A single polyp that can span a metre, with no stony skeleton — clownfish live in it, immune to its sting.
facts.crown_of_thorns: A coral-eating starfish with up to 21 venomous arms — one can strip 6 square metres of reef a year.
facts.whale_shark: The largest fish alive, yet a filter feeder — it even eats clouds of egg and sperm from mass coral spawning.
facts.zebra_shark: Born striped like its namesake, then grows into a pattern of leopard-like spots as an adult.
facts.nurse_shark: Hunts muddy, sandy seafloors by night, using suction strong enough to pull prey from reef crevices.
facts.anglerfish: In the deep sea's permanent dark, it dangles a glowing lure grown from its own fin, lit by colonies of bacteria.
facts.pink_frogmouth: A rosy, loose-skinned 'sea toad' that sits on the continental shelf, sometimes half a kilometre down, waiting for prey.
facts.psychedelic_frogfish: No two share the same swirling pink pattern, and instead of swimming, it walks the seafloor on its fins.
facts.giant_grouper: The largest bony fish on the reef, big enough to swallow juvenile sea turtles and small sharks whole.
facts.stonefish: Camouflaged as a lump of encrusted rock on the seabed, it carries the most potent venom of any fish alive.
facts.common_lionfish: Its banded spines carry a real venom, and since slipping through the Suez Canal in 1991 it has spread across the Mediterranean.
facts.proailurus: About the size of a house cat and at least partly a tree-climber — most studies place it as the basal member of the whole cat family, and a likely ancestor of every cat alive today.
facts.pseudaelurus: Grew from cat-sized to about 5 feet as the animals it hunted grew bigger — the last common ancestor before the cat family split into today's small cats, today's big cats, and the extinct sabertooths.
facts.homotherium: A sabertooth, not a big cat — its subfamily split off from the rest of the cat family before the ancestors of any living species did, and it left no descendants among them.
facts.panthera_zdanskyi: Its 2.5-million-year-old skull, dug up in Gansu, China, is the oldest complete pantherine skull ever found — and closely resembles a modern tiger's.
facts.tiger: Popularly billed as the biggest cat alive — true of the largest individuals, though average size trades places with the lion depending which subspecies you compare. No two tigers share the same stripe pattern.
facts.javan_tiger: A tiger population isolated on Java when rising seas cut its land bridge to the mainland. Declared extinct in 2008 — the last confirmed sighting was in 1976.
facts.pakicetus: Wolf-sized and four-legged, foraging along Eocene rivers 50 Mya — earliest known cetacean, by its whale-type inner ear.
facts.ambulocetus: Its name means 'walking whale'. Crocodile-like, it bore weight on land but swam by paddling its hind feet.
facts.rodhocetus: A protocetid that paddled with its hind feet rather than walked — sacrum unfused, so on land it could only shuffle.
facts.basilosaurus: Fully aquatic, up to 20 m, serpentine — hind legs shrunk to a useless 35 cm. The name means 'king lizard'; it's a whale.
facts.dorudon: A smaller basilosaurid, ~5 m, sharing Eocene seas with Basilosaurus — and sometimes its prey. First true tail fluke.
facts.llanocetus: An early mysticete that still had teeth, not baleen — gripped and sheared prey instead of filtering. One of the oldest known.
facts.dog: The first animal humans ever domesticated, tens of thousands of years before any other — and still, formally, the same species as the wolf: Canis lupus familiaris.
facts.german_shepherd: Bred from traditional German herding dogs in 1899 by one man, Max von Stephanitz, for working ability over looks — now a mainstay of police, military and service work.
facts.border_collie: Often ranked the most intelligent dog breed; herds sheep with a silent, fixed stare called 'the eye' instead of barking or nipping.
facts.rottweiler: Descended from Roman legion drover dogs — by the Middle Ages it was the 'Rottweil butcher's dog,' herding cattle and pulling meat carts to market.
facts.saint_bernard: Bred at the Great St Bernard Hospice in the Alps to search for lost travelers in deep snow — one dog, Barry, is credited with saving 40 to 100 lives.
facts.siberian_husky: Bred by the Chukchi people of northeastern Siberia to pull sleds; its coat can withstand temperatures down to -50 to -60°C.
facts.basenji: Doesn't bark — its unusually shaped larynx makes a yodel-like sound instead, earning it the nickname 'the barkless dog.'
facts.greyhound: One of the fastest dogs alive, reaching peak speeds of at least 69 km/h (43 mph) on a large heart and a flexible spine.
facts.afghan_hound: A 'basal' breed that predates the 19th-century founding of most modern breeds — genetic studies place it among the oldest dog lineages alive.
facts.bloodhound: Its olfactory bulb is roughly 40 times bigger than a human's relative to brain size — trail identifications from it have been accepted as evidence in some courts.
facts.beagle: Bred to hunt rabbits and hares by scent; the USDA's 'Beagle Brigade' now uses beagles to sniff out banned food in airport luggage.
facts.dachshund: Its name means 'badger dog' in German — short legs, an elongated body and oversized paddle-shaped paws are all built for digging into a badger's burrow.
facts.jack_russell_terrier: Bred from 1819 by an English parson, Jack Russell, starting with a single terrier named Trump, to run with foxhounds and bolt foxes from their dens.
facts.bull_terrier: Its head is famously egg-shaped in profile, curving smoothly from skull to nose — one of the few dog breeds with triangular eyes.
facts.labrador_retriever: The most-registered dog breed across the UK, US, Canada and New Zealand for decades running; a 'soft mouth' lets it carry downed game without leaving a mark.
facts.golden_retriever: Developed in the 1860s by a single Scottish breeder, Lord Tweedmouth, by crossing a Flat-coated Retriever with a now-extinct Tweed Water Spaniel.
facts.chihuahua: The smallest recognized dog breed in the world, weighing as little as 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) fully grown.
facts.pug: Bred for centuries in China purely as an imperial companion — pet pugs were reportedly kept in luxury and guarded by soldiers.
facts.atlantic_cod: One female releases up to 15 million eggs in a season, yet overfishing crashed the Grand Banks cod by over 95% by 1992.
facts.atlantic_herring: Schools can hold four billion fish across four cubic kilometres of ocean — tight enough their ripples show from a mile off.
facts.rainbow_trout: Some stay in freshwater for life; others, called steelhead, swim to sea and back, spawning several times instead of dying after one run.
facts.northern_pike: An ambush predator that strikes in a fraction of a second — and eats smaller pike as readily as any other fish.
facts.common_carp: A bottom-feeder tough enough for water too muddy and low in oxygen for most fish; Romans farmed it in ponds two thousand years ago.
facts.goldfish: Bred from colour-mutated carp in China for a thousand years — kept in ceramic pots instead of open ponds so mutants survived to be bred.
facts.koi: An ornamental Amur carp bred for colour in Niigata, Japan since the 1820s — released to the wild, it reverts to its ancestor's plain colouring in a few generations.
facts.european_eel: Lives the reverse of a salmon: it grows for years in European rivers, then swims to the Sargasso Sea to spawn once and die.
facts.wels_catfish: Europe's largest native freshwater fish — scaleless, with six barbels it uses to smell out prey along the muddy riverbed.
facts.swordfish: Loses every tooth and scale by adulthood; organs by its eyes and brain keep its vision 10 to 15°C warmer than the cold water it hunts in.
facts.marlin: Reaching 5 metres and 800 kilograms, it flares blue and lavender stripes down its flanks in a flash just before striking prey.
facts.european_plaice: Hatches symmetrical like any fish; within weeks one eye migrates across its skull, and it settles flat onto the seabed for life.
facts.seahorse: The male gets pregnant, not the female — she deposits eggs into his brood pouch, and he carries them up to 45 days before giving birth.
facts.clownfish: Lives in a sea anemone's stinging tentacles, protected by mucus that mimics the anemone's own chemistry; the breeding male changes sex if the female dies.
facts.piranha: Its reputation as a pack hunter is a myth — most species are omnivores that school mainly to protect themselves, not to hunt in a frenzy.
facts.largemouth_bass: The male alone builds the nest and guards the eggs and fry for weeks — a level of care that's helped it invade rivers from Japan to Guatemala.
facts.nile_perch: Introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, it ate through the native cichlids so completely it's blamed for several hundred extinctions.
facts.butterfly: Inside the chrysalis, most of the caterpillar's tissue is broken down and the adult body is rebuilt from clusters of cells called imaginal discs.
facts.ant: A colony functions almost as a single superorganism: one or more queens do all the reproducing, and thousands of sterile female workers do everything else.
facts.ladybird: A seven-spot ladybird overwinters in large clusters, packed together under tree bark or among boulders, before waking in spring to hunt aphids.
facts.dung_beetle: Scarabaeus satyrus rolls its dung ball in a straight line at night by steering off the Milky Way — the first animal shown to navigate by the stars.
facts.firefly: Its glow comes from the enzyme luciferase acting on the compound luciferin, produced in special organs usually on a female's lower abdomen.
facts.dragonfly: It can see almost the full 360 degrees around it — nearly 80% of its brain is given over to processing what its eyes see.
facts.locust: The same grasshopper species can switch between a solitary, harmless form and a swarming, gregarious one — the change can be triggered just by how often its hind legs bump into another locust's.
facts.mantis: About a quarter of mating encounters observed in the wild end with the female eating the male.
facts.cockroach: Mainly nocturnal, it hides by day in narrow crevices and can stay active for a month without food before it needs to eat again.
facts.termite: It can't digest the wood it eats on its own — a gut community of bacteria and protists breaks down the cellulose for it.
facts.flea: Powerful hind legs launch it up to 110 times its own body length, and historically, rodent fleas carrying Yersinia pestis were a major route by which the Black Death reached people.
facts.spider: A spiderling can disperse for hundreds of kilometres by 'ballooning' — releasing a silk thread that catches the wind and carries it off, sometimes riding jet streams for weeks.
facts.scorpion: Every scorpion species glows blue-green under ultraviolet light, and unlike almost every other arachnid, it gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
facts.tick: It climbs to the tip of a blade of grass and 'quests' — legs outstretched, waiting to grab onto whatever brushes past — then feeds exclusively on blood.
facts.centipede: Injects venom through forcipules, a modified pair of legs just behind the head — and despite the name, no centipede has exactly 100 legs; the true count is always an odd number, from 15 pairs up to 191.
facts.millipede: No millipede has 1,000 legs either, but it does carry two pairs per body segment — twice a centipede's count — and some species defend themselves with a compound related to hydrogen cyanide.
facts.woodlouse: A crustacean fully adapted to life on land, breathing through gill-like structures that still need damp air to work — which is why it shelters under stones and bark by day.
facts.eoraptor: One of the earliest known dinosaurs, from Argentina 231 Mya — barely a metre long, reclassified since 2012 as a basal sauropodomorph.
facts.coelophysis: A slender Late Triassic predator, up to 3 m long — over 1,000 skeletons piled at New Mexico's Ghost Ranch, likely swept in by a flash flood.
facts.compsognathus: A chicken-sized Jurassic theropod that once held the title of smallest known dinosaur; both fossils preserve a lizard in the gut.
facts.allosaurus: Apex predator of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, up to 9.7 m long, its bite marks preserved in sauropod bone and stegosaur plates.
facts.spinosaurus: A sail-backed Cretaceous predator, among the largest theropods known, with isotope evidence for a semiaquatic, fish-heavy diet.
facts.tyrannosaurus: The last tyrannosaur, over 12 m long — cladistically a coelurosaur, not a carnosaur, closer kin to a chicken than to Allosaurus.
facts.velociraptor: A turkey-sized Mongolian predator, only 2 m long — nothing like the human-sized Jurassic Park raptors. Quill knobs prove it had feathers.
facts.deinonychus: A sickle-clawed predator whose 1969 description sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance' — the real model for Jurassic Park's raptors.
facts.archaeopteryx: A raven-sized Jurassic animal with flight feathers, teeth and a bony tail — the classic fossil bridging non-avian dinosaurs and birds.
facts.plateosaurus: A Late Triassic herbivore of Europe, known from over 100 skeletons — once called a 'prosauropod', a term now seen as an outdated grade.
facts.brachiosaurus: A Late Jurassic sauropod with forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, giving it a giraffe-like build that browsed 9 m off the ground.
facts.apatosaurus: A 21-23 m Jurassic sauropod first named Brontosaurus in 1879, ruled a duplicate in 1903, reinstated as its own genus by a 2015 study.
facts.stegosaurus: A Late Jurassic herbivore with bony back plates and a spiked tail — one spike's puncture wound matches a healed Allosaurus injury.
facts.ankylosaurus: One of the last dinosaurs before the extinction, armoured with a bone-club tail — despite its fame, one of the least complete ankylosaurids known.
facts.protoceratops: A sheep-sized Mongolian ceratopsian, famous for the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil locked with a Velociraptor — not a Triceratops ancestor.
facts.triceratops: A massive end-Cretaceous ceratopsian with three horns and a bony frill, now read mainly as display, not a defensive weapon.
facts.pachycephalosaurus: The largest dome-headed dinosaur, its skull cap solid bone up to 25 cm thick — lesion evidence supports head-to-head combat.
facts.stegoceras: A small Cretaceous dome-head, far less famous than Pachycephalosaurus, known from one of the most complete pachycephalosaur skeletons.
facts.iguanodon: Named in 1825 for teeth shaped like an iguana's — only the second dinosaur ever described, its reconstruction revised radically since.
facts.parasaurolophus: A duck-billed hadrosaur with a long, hollow, backward-curving crest, modelled as a resonating chamber for calling to the herd.
facts.quetzalcoatlus: Not a dinosaur — a pterosaur with a wingspan around 10-11 m, a leading candidate for the largest flying animal ever known.
facts.elasmosaurus: Not a dinosaur — a plesiosaur whose neck, built from 72 vertebrae, made up over two-thirds of its 10.3 m length.
facts.leptocyon: A fox-sized early canid of Oligocene-Miocene North America, weighing as little as 2 kg — the smallest canid that ever lived belonged to this genus. It ate small animals and fruit, not the specialised meat-only diet later canids evolved.
facts.eucyon: A jackal-sized omnivore that arose in the western United States around 10 million years ago, then did what almost no other North American mammal of its time managed: it crossed into Eurasia, around 6 million years ago.
facts.canis_lepophagus: One of the earliest members of genus Canis, in Miocene North America around 5 million years ago — coyote-sized, and the likely direct ancestor of the modern coyote as well as the wolf lineage.
facts.canis_etruscus: An Early Pleistocene wolf-like canid of about 2 million years ago — genetic and fossil evidence traces the gray wolf's own lineage back through this species.
facts.canis_mosbachensis: A Middle Pleistocene Eurasian wolf, smaller than a modern gray wolf and comparable in size to today's Indian wolf — the direct predecessor of Canis lupus itself.
facts.venus_flytrap: Two trigger hairs must be touched within 20 seconds of each other before the trap snaps shut in a tenth of a second.
facts.nepenthes: A wax-slicked rim tips ants and other insects into the fluid below — how it gets nitrogen from poor tropical soil.
facts.sundew: Greek for 'dewy' — its glistening mucilage traps an insect and finishes digesting it in about 15 minutes.
facts.mistletoe: A hemiparasite: its haustorium taps a host tree's water and minerals while its own green leaves still photosynthesise.
facts.rafflesia: No leaves, stem or roots of its own — just a flower up to a metre across, bursting from a host vine and reeking of rot.
facts.welwitschia: Grows exactly two leaves in its entire life and never sheds them — some Namib Desert plants are 2,000 years old.
facts.water_lily: Air channels called aerenchyma keep its floating leaves buoyant and pipe oxygen down to roots anchored in the mud.
facts.duckweed: The world's smallest flowering plants — Wolffia's flower is just 0.3mm — reproducing mostly by budding, not seed.
facts.orchid: Seeds are dust-fine with no food reserve of their own — almost every species needs a fungus just to germinate.
facts.giant_sequoia: The most massive tree alive by volume — bark nearly a metre thick shields it from the fires that pop open its cones.
facts.coast_redwood: The tallest tree species alive, over 116m — its needles pull fog straight through their skin, bypassing the xylem.
facts.moss: No roots or water-carrying vessels — just rhizoids for grip, and a film of water its swimming sperm need to fertilise.
facts.liverwort: Among the first plants to leave the water, 470 million years ago — raindrops still launch its spore-filled gemmae.
facts.bracken_fern: One of the world's most widespread plants, spreading mainly by rhizome — its ptaquiloside is a documented carcinogen.
facts.edelweiss: Dense white wool on its star-shaped flower head scatters UV radiation near the snowline, 1,800 to 3,400m up.
facts.saguaro: Its pleated trunk expands like an accordion to store rainwater — and it may take 75 years to grow its first arm.
facts.fly_agaric: Amanita muscaria, the classic red toadstool. Psychoactive, but no documented death from it in over a century.
facts.death_cap: Amanita phalloides causes about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Half a cap can be a lethal dose.
facts.chanterelle: Ridges instead of true gills, and a faint smell of apricots — a long-prized wild edible.
facts.porcini: Boletus edulis has pores, not gills, under its cap, and can grow to 3 kg — a huge, prized wild mushroom.
facts.morel: Its honeycomb cap is prized by chefs, but morels contain toxins that only cooking destroys — never eaten raw.
facts.puffball: A single raindrop can trigger it to eject over a million spores at around a metre a second.
facts.bioluminescent_fungus: Panellus stipticus glows along its gill edges — the chemistry behind 'foxfire', wood that glows at night.
facts.stinkhorn: Smells of carrion to draw flies, which carry off its spores. Can grow 15 cm taller in an hour.
facts.turkey_tail: Fan-shaped bands of colour tiled across dead logs. Eaten in China as 'Yunzhi' for thousands of years.
facts.slime_mold: Not a fungus at all — a brainless, single-celled amoeba that can still solve a maze.
facts.truffle: Grows entirely underground, fused to oak roots. Périgord black truffles have sold for over €1,000 a kilo.
facts.shaggy_mane: Its gills turn from white to black within hours as the whole cap dissolves itself into ink.
facts.birds_nest_fungus: A raindrop hitting its tiny cup flings egg-like spore packets up to a metre away.
facts.zombie_ant_fungus: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis drives an infected ant to clamp its jaws onto a leaf vein and die there.
facts.humongous_fungus: One Armillaria ostoyae in Oregon spans about 2,200 acres and is roughly 8,000 years old.
facts.dead_mans_fingers: Black, upright clubs push through bark at the base of rotting stumps — Xylaria polymorpha.
facts.witchs_butter: A gelatinous orange-yellow jelly fungus that parasitizes other wood-rotting fungi, not the wood itself.
facts.pyrite: Iron disulfide, FeS2 — brassy enough to fool a prospector, which is exactly its nickname.
facts.hematite: Iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3 — the world's most important iron ore, red streak and all.
facts.magnetite: Fe3O4, iron caught halfway oxidised — and the only mineral that turns into a lodestone.
facts.graphite: Pure carbon, the same as diamond, laid out in slippery sheets instead of a rigid cage.
facts.calcite: Calcium carbonate, CaCO3 — the mineral that limestone, marble and eggshell are all built from.
facts.malachite: Copper carbonate hydroxide — banded green, and the reason a weathered copper vein turns that colour.
facts.azurite: Deep-blue copper carbonate, and chemically restless — left alone it slowly turns into malachite.
facts.gypsum: Calcium sulfate dihydrate, soft enough to scratch with a fingernail — plaster's raw material.
facts.olivine: Magnesium iron silicate, olive-green and named for it — the first mineral out of a cooling basalt melt.
facts.garnet: An iron-aluminium silicate that grows inside metamorphic rock as an index of how hot it got.
facts.beryl: Beryllium aluminium silicate — colourless on its own; every gem colour in it comes from an impurity.
facts.aquamarine: Beryl tinted pale sea-blue by iron in its Fe2+ state — the mildest of beryl's colour tricks.
facts.serpentine: Mottled green and named for snakeskin — what olivine becomes once water gets into it.
facts.mosquito: Only females drink blood — for the protein to make eggs. Males live entirely on nectar.
facts.cat: Its ancestor is the African wildcat. Grain stores drew in rodents, and rodents drew in the cat.
facts.snail: A shelled gastropod. Some freshwater species are, indirectly, among the deadliest animals to people.
facts.plasmodium: A single-celled parasite genus that replicates inside red blood cells. Five species infect humans.
facts.toxoplasma_gondii: Cats are its only sexual host. Roughly half of people alive may carry it, mostly without symptoms.
facts.giardia: A tough cyst form can stay infectious in cold water for up to three months, waiting to be swallowed.
facts.entamoeba_histolytica: An amoeba that mostly infects humans and other primates, and almost nothing else.
facts.trichomonas_vaginalis: A flagellated protozoan spread by direct sexual contact — no other route reliably passes it on.
facts.cryptosporidium: Its oocyst shrugs off ordinary chlorine, which is why it's a real hazard even in treated water.
facts.ascaris_lumbricoides: Up to a billion people carry it. A single female can lay 200,000 eggs a day.
facts.hookworm: Doesn't wait to be swallowed — its larvae simply burrow straight through bare skin.
facts.enterobius_vermicularis: Its entire life cycle happens inside one human gut — humans are its only known host.
facts.trichinella_spiralis: The smallest nematode known to parasitize humans, yet one female can produce 1,500 larvae.
facts.wuchereria_bancrofti: Its larvae peak in the blood between 10 pm and 4 am, timed to when the night-biting mosquito feeds.
facts.taenia_solium: The pork tapeworm can grow past 8 metres long from a single scolex barely a millimetre wide.
facts.taenia_saginata: The beef tapeworm can top 22 metres and live in a human gut for 25 years.
facts.schistosoma: A blood fluke that needs a freshwater snail as a stepping stone before it can reach a person at all.
facts.clonorchis_sinensis: The Chinese liver fluke can live 30 years in one host, passing through a snail and a fish to get there.
facts.head_louse: Cannot jump or fly at all — it only spreads by direct head-to-head contact.
facts.body_louse: Lives and lays its eggs in clothing seams, not on the body it feeds from.
facts.scabies_mite: A burrowing female lays two or three eggs a day in a skin tunnel until her four-week life ends there.
facts.bed_bug: Never lives on its host — it hides in dark seams nearby, like a mattress, between blood meals.
facts.malaria: Fever comes in waves timed to red blood cells bursting open, all at once, every one to three days.
facts.toxoplasmosis: Caught from cyst-laden undercooked meat as easily as from a cat's litter box.
facts.giardiasis: Swallowing only a handful of cysts is enough to start an infection.
facts.amoebiasis: Kills more than 55,000 people worldwide a year, mostly through amoebic dysentery.
facts.trichinosis: First symptoms can appear in as little as twelve hours after eating the wrong meat.
facts.lymphatic_filariasis: Adult worms block the body's own lymph vessels — the swelling of elephantiasis follows from there.
facts.schistosomiasis: The second-most economically devastating parasitic disease on Earth, after malaria alone.
facts.gourd: A Cucurbitaceae fruit that, dried out, leaves a hollow, hard shell — a container waiting to happen.
facts.mbira: Zimbabwe's thumb piano: metal tines on a hardwood board, each tine a different length for a different pitch.
facts.gong: A bronze disc quenched from red heat so it can be hammered soft, then hardened again by reheating.
facts.cymbal: Cast bronze, lathed thin — cutting can shave off two-thirds the blank's weight, carving in the tone grooves.
facts.bell: Cast from bell metal, a bronze around 23% tin — the ratio empirically settled on for the best tone.
facts.xylophone: Wooden bars cut to length and struck — as with the marimba, longer bars ring lower, shorter bars higher.
facts.angklung: West Javanese bamboo tubes tuned to a note, shaken so the tubes knock inside their own bamboo frame.
facts.maraca: A dried gourd shell with a handful of pebbles or seeds sealed inside, shaken for the rattle.
facts.djembe: A West African goblet drum carved from one log while the wood is still green, headed with goatskin.
facts.tabla: The North Indian hand drum pair's black tuning spot, the syahi, is iron filings bound in a starch paste.
facts.timpani: A copper kettle under a skin head — almost alone among drums, it can be tuned to a definite pitch.
facts.daf: A Middle Eastern and Central Asian frame drum ringed inside with dozens of small jingling metal rings.
facts.guitar: A hollow wood body resonates strings plucked or strummed by hand, no bow and no hammer involved.
facts.violin: Its strings are bowed, not plucked — and the bow hair needs pine-resin rosin to actually grip and sound them.
facts.morin_khuur: Mongolia's horsehead fiddle: strings and bow both traditionally horsehair, scroll carved as a horse's head.
facts.sitar: A hollowed calabash gourd resonates metal strings — plus a set that vibrate on their own, never plucked.
facts.kora: A West African 21-string harp-lute: a gourd sliced in half and sealed with cow skin as its resonator.
facts.piano: A cast-iron frame holds up to 20 tons of string tension; felt-covered hammers strike the strings, not fingers.
facts.flute: Holes cut along a tube shorten or lengthen the vibrating air column inside it, and that sets the pitch.
facts.pan_flute: Many tubes of different lengths bound side by side, each one closed at the bottom and sounding one note.
facts.trumpet: Brass tubing bent twice into a loop; the player's own buzzing lips against the mouthpiece make the sound.
facts.didgeridoo: An Aboriginal Australian drone pipe — traditionally a eucalyptus branch termites hollowed out first.
facts.bagpipes: An airtight animal-skin bag, squeezed by the arm, feeds reed pipes so the sound never stops for breath.
facts.shofar: A ram's horn with no mouthpiece at all — heat softens its keratin enough to flatten and straighten it.
facts.theremin: Played without ever being touched: a hand's distance from an antenna changes the circuit's own pitch.
facts.electric_guitar: A vibrating steel string disturbs a magnet's field and induces current in a coil — no hollow body needed.
facts.synthesizer: Generates its waveform electronically from scratch, rather than amplifying a vibration that already exists.
facts.cane: Arundo donax, a giant cane grass in dense stands along riverbanks — source of nearly all woodwind reeds.
facts.reed: A thin blade shaved from cane, clamped by a ligature — it beats against the mouthpiece itself to sound.
facts.double_reed: Two cane blades bound onto a metal staple, cork-wrapped and sealed into the instrument — no mouthpiece at all.
facts.clarinet: A single cane reed beats against the mouthpiece; a cylindrical wood bore gives it a dark, covered tone.
facts.saxophone: The same single reed as a clarinet, but on a conical brass body — Adolphe Sax patented the family in 1846.
facts.oboe: Two cane blades beat against each other, no mouthpiece; a narrow conical wood bore gives its bright tone.
facts.bassoon: The oboe's double reed on a 2.54 m maple bore, folded back so the finished instrument stands only 1.34 m tall.
facts.free_reed: A thin brass tongue fitted to a slot just wide enough to swing freely through it, never touching the frame.
facts.bellows: A pleated chamber of leather and cloth: squeezing it forces out a jet of air, expanding draws more back in.
facts.harmonica: A wood comb holds brass free reeds — one set sounds on the blow, another on the draw, no bellows at all.
facts.accordion: Hand-squeezed bellows drive air across free reeds — Cyrill Demian patented the name in Vienna, 1829.
facts.reed_organ: A keyboard instrument with no pipes at all — foot-pumped bellows drive air over banks of free reeds instead.
facts.producer: Makes its own food from sunlight instead of eating anything — the base of every food chain.
facts.primary_consumer: Eats producers directly and nothing else — the first animal step in a food chain, a herbivore.
facts.secondary_consumer: A carnivore eating the herbivores that ate the plants — one rung above a primary consumer.
facts.decomposer: Fungi and bacteria that feed on waste and the dead, turning it back into nutrients plants can use.
facts.trophic_level: An organism's rung on the food chain — producer, then herbivore, then the carnivores above it.
facts.food_chain: A straight line of who-eats-whom, from a producer up through consumers to whatever eats last.
facts.food_web: Every real ecosystem's food chains tangled together — the actual network, not one single line.
facts.apex_predator: Sits at the top of a food chain with few or no natural predators of its own left to eat it.
facts.trophic_cascade: Remove a top predator and the effects ripple down every level below it — rarely simply, or fully.
facts.sea_urchin: Grazes algae and kelp holdfasts with its teeth; enough of them can strip a seafloor bare.
