facts.sea_otter: Bites through a sea urchin's spines from underneath and licks out the soft contents inside.
facts.kelp_forest: Dense underwater kelp, kept alive by otters eating the urchins that would otherwise graze it bare.
facts.keystone_species: A species whose effect on its ecosystem is far bigger than its numbers alone would suggest.
facts.mutualism: Two species, each genuinely better off for the other's presence — not one exploiting the other.
facts.commensalism: One species benefits from the other, which is left neither better nor worse off by it.
facts.parasitism: One organism lives on or in another and feeds off it, causing the host real, one-sided harm.
facts.whale_barnacle: Embeds in whale skin and filters passing plankton with feathery limbs, usually at no cost to the whale.
facts.pioneer_species: The first life to colonise bare ground — often lichen or moss — before anything else can take hold.
facts.succession: How a community of species changes over time, one wave of colonisers replaced by the next.
facts.climax_community: The stable, self-sustaining end stage of succession — the community that stops replacing itself.
facts.tundra: Permafrost keeps the subsoil frozen year-round, so nothing taller than moss and lichen can root.
facts.desert: Under 250 mm of rain a year defines it; little there stores water like a cactus's swollen stem.
facts.taiga: The world's largest land biome — a belt of pine, spruce and larch across the subarctic.
facts.rainforest: At least 1.68 m of rain a year, and a canopy so dense the forest floor gets 2% of the sunlight.
facts.limiting_factor: Growth is capped by whichever resource is scarcest, not by the total of everything available.
facts.carrying_capacity: The largest population an environment's food, water and space can sustain before growth stops.
facts.mountain: Continental crust that collided and had nowhere to go but up — the Himalayas are still rising.
facts.trench: The seafloor sagging where one plate bends and dives beneath another. The Mariana reaches 10,994 m.
facts.volcano: A vent to a magma chamber. Alternating layers of lava and ash, erupted again and again, build the cone.
facts.rift_valley: A continent stretched thin enough to crack: the block between two faults drops as the land splits.
facts.floodplain: Flat land beside a river, built up flood by flood from the thin layer of silt each overflow leaves.
facts.meander: Fast water wears the outer bank away, slow water drops sand on the inner one, and the bend migrates sideways.
facts.oxbow_lake: A meander looped back on itself until its own neck was cut through, stranding the old bend as a lake.
facts.delta: A river hits still water, slows, and can no longer carry its load — the sediment drops and builds land.
facts.canyon: A river cutting down through rock lifted thousands of feet beneath it — the Grand Canyon's whole story.
facts.waterfall: Hard rock over soft: the soft layer erodes faster, and the drop between them grows a little every year.
facts.sea_cliff: Waves cut a notch at the rock's foot; the overhang above eventually has nothing left to stand on.
facts.sea_cave: Waves force their way into a crack in the cliff and hollow it out — always along an existing weakness.
facts.sea_arch: A sea cave that finally breaks all the way through a thin headland, leaving an opening beneath the rock.
facts.sea_stack: An arch's roof gives way at last, and what is left standing apart from the cliff is the stack.
facts.estuary: Where a river's fresh water meets the moon-pulled tide and the two measurably mix, rather than staying apart.
facts.lagoon: Shallow water fenced off from the open sea by a narrow bar of sand, with only a thin inlet through.
facts.glacier: Snow that piled up faster than it melted, for centuries, compressed to ice, and is now sliding downhill.
facts.iceberg: A slab of a glacier that calved — broke free — and now drifts on the salt water it did not come from.
facts.fjord: A glacier gouges a valley far below sea level; the ice retreats, and the sea moves in to fill it.
facts.cavern: Rainwater turned faintly acidic by carbon dioxide dissolves limestone along a crack for centuries.
facts.sinkhole: A cavern hollowed out below keeps growing until the ground above it can no longer hold its own weight.
facts.plateau: High ground, flat on top: a broad slab of crust swollen upward by magma rising underneath it.
facts.mesa: A plateau's edge eaten back by weather until an isolated, flat-topped island of hard caprock remains.
facts.butte: A mesa worn narrower still, until almost nothing is left of the caprock that was protecting it.
facts.caldera: A magma chamber empties in a great eruption, and the volcano above it has nothing left to hold it up.
facts.geyser: Groundwater heated past boiling but held down by its own weight, until it flashes to steam all at once.
facts.eagle: Hunts open country from cliffside nests, diving at up to 320 km/h to take prey.
facts.jaguar: The only big cat that regularly cracks turtle shells, killing with a bite to the skull.
facts.turquoise: A hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium -- one of the oldest gemstones ever mined.
facts.quetzalcoatl: Aztec feathered-serpent god of wind, Venus and learning. The name means Precious Serpent.
facts.tezcatlipoca: Aztec god of night and sorcery. His name means Smoking Mirror, for the obsidian he is shown in.
facts.huitzilopochtli: Aztec sun and war god, patron of Tenochtitlan, born fully armed from Coatlicue.
facts.tlaloc: Aztec rain god known by his goggle eyes and fangs; ruled the paradise of Tlalocan.
facts.coatlicue: Aztec earth goddess, 'Serpent Skirt' -- mother of Huitzilopochtli and of the stars.
facts.tonatiuh: Aztec sun god of the current, fifth cosmic age; demanded sacrifice to keep moving.
facts.mictlantecuhtli: Skeletal Aztec god of the dead, king of Mictlan's lowest level.
facts.xiuhtecuhtli: Aztec fire god, the Turquoise Lord -- turquoise was fire's own stone to him.
facts.centeotl: Aztec young maize god, his face marked by a black line from brow to jaw.
facts.xolotl: Dog-headed Aztec god who guides the dead through Mictlan; the axolotl bears his name.
facts.fifth_sun: The current Aztec cosmic age, born when two gods leapt into a divine bonfire.
facts.sun_stone: A 24-tonne Aztec basalt disc carved under Moctezuma II, recording the cosmic ages.
facts.mictlan: Aztec underworld of nine levels; the dead take four years to reach the deepest one.
facts.kukulkan: Yucatec Maya feathered serpent; his shadow descends Chichen Itza's pyramid each equinox.
facts.itzamna: Maya creator god credited with inventing writing; often shown as an aged sky lord.
facts.ixchel: Aged Maya jaguar goddess of medicine, childbirth and water; consort of Itzamna.
facts.chaac: Maya rain god, long-nosed, who strikes clouds with a lightning axe to bring rain.
facts.ek_chuah: Maya god of merchants, travellers and cacao, honoured each year in its harvest season.
facts.popol_vuh: K'iche' Maya sacred text: creation, the Hero Twins, and a people's own history.
facts.hero_twins: Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the Maya Hero Twins who out-tricked the lords of Xibalba.
facts.xibalba: The K'iche' Maya underworld, 'place of fright,' ruled by One Death and Seven Death.
facts.cacao_of_the_gods: Cacao's mythic origin as a gift from the gods -- hence its genus name, 'food of the gods.'
facts.open_pit_mining: Dug in stepped benches, with haul roads spiralling up the walls — a million tons a day from the biggest pits.
facts.strip_mining: Digs a shallow seam one long trench at a time, burying each strip's waste in the void left by the last.
facts.mountaintop_removal: Blasts up to 120 metres off a summit to reach thin coal, dumping the rock in the next valley over.
facts.placer_mining: Washes loose sand and gravel through water and lets density sort out anything worth keeping.
facts.room_and_pillar_mining: Digs rooms out of a seam while leaving pillars of untouched rock standing to hold the roof up.
facts.longwall_mining: A shearer cuts a long coal face while supports advance and the roof is let collapse behind them.
facts.block_caving: Undercuts a huge ore column and lets gravity fracture it, falling into tunnels dug below.
facts.bauxite: Aluminium's ore, and it sits so close to the surface there's barely any overburden to remove.
facts.spodumene: A lithium aluminium silicate that crystallises in granite pegmatite — most hard-rock lithium's source.
facts.bastnasite: A rare-earth fluorocarbonate — almost all of Mountain Pass, California's rare earths ride in this one mineral.
facts.leopard: Leopards drag kills heavier than themselves into trees — once a giraffe calf hauled 5.7 m up.
facts.snow_leopard: Its tail is thick with stored fat and fur, worn like a blanket over its face while it sleeps.
facts.cheetah: Goes 0 to 97 km/h in under 3 seconds — faster off the line than most sports cars.
facts.cougar: Ranges from the Yukon to the southern Andes — the widest span of any wild land mammal.
facts.red_fox: Earthworms can supply over 60% of its calories some months — hunted mostly by ear.
facts.coyote: Hunts in loose bands to bring down prey too big for one alone, a habit noted since 1805.
facts.african_wild_dog: Some Serengeti packs specialise in hunting adult zebra six times their own weight.
facts.polar_bear: Waits motionless for hours by a seal's breathing hole in the ice, then strikes the instant it surfaces.
facts.giant_panda: Evolved an extra 'thumb' from a wrist bone just to grip bamboo, despite being classed a carnivore.
facts.sun_bear: The smallest bear has the longest tongue of any bear, for licking honey from tight spaces.
facts.gorilla: Western lowland gorillas eat far more fruit than mountain gorillas, who barely touch it.
facts.chimpanzee: Chimps strip leaves off twigs to fish termites from mounds, the first wild tool use ever recorded.
facts.orangutan: The most arboreal great ape — it crosses the canopy climbing and swinging, rarely touching ground.
facts.baboon: Troops hunt cooperatively on the open savanna, taking prey as large as young gazelles.
facts.lemur: Sunbathes every cold morning, sitting upright and facing the sun like a devotee.
facts.bald_eagle: Builds the largest tree nest of any North American bird — one weighed over a metric ton.
facts.peregrine_falcon: The fastest animal on Earth — it can exceed 320 km/h in its hunting dive.
facts.snowy_owl: Unlike most owls, it hunts mainly by daylight across the open Arctic tundra.
facts.turkey_vulture: Locates carrion by smell, an ability most birds lack, sniffing out decay from the air.
facts.king_cobra: Its genus name means 'snake-eater' — king cobras prey chiefly on other snakes.
facts.komodo_dragon: The world's largest lizard, up to 3 m and 150 kg, with a genuinely venomous bite.
facts.gila_monster: The only venomous lizard native to the US — it chews its venom in through grooved teeth.
facts.nile_crocodile: Its bite force measures about 22 kN — among the strongest of any living animal.
facts.american_alligator: The female guards her mud nest for 65 days, then carries hatchlings to water in her mouth.
facts.golden_poison_frog: The most toxic vertebrate known by weight — one wild frog carries enough poison for 10-20 people. It makes none of it itself: the batrachotoxin is sequestered from small arthropods in its diet, and frogs raised in captivity on other food lose their toxicity entirely.
facts.american_bullfrog: A voracious ambush predator whose stomach contents have included snakes, birds and bats.
facts.cane_toad: Introduced to Australia in 1935 to fight cane beetles that lived too high on the stalks to reach.
facts.axolotl: Unlike other salamanders, it never leaves the water or metamorphoses — it keeps its gills for life.
facts.fire_salamander: Its black-and-yellow pattern is a warning label for the neurotoxin it secretes from its skin.
facts.stem: The plant's upright main axis — bears leaves and buds, and pipes water and food between root and leaf.
facts.node: The point on a stem where a leaf attaches; buds and branches start here too.
facts.internode: The stretch of stem between two nodes — it elongates to space the leaves out.
facts.terminal_bud: The bud at a stem's growing tip; its auxin keeps the buds below it suppressed.
facts.axillary_bud: A dormant side-bud sitting in a leaf's axil, ready to become a new branch.
facts.leaf_scar: The corky mark a fallen leaf leaves behind, right where it once attached.
facts.lenticel: A loosely packed pore in bark that lets a woody stem's living tissue breathe.
facts.root_cap: The tough cap of cells shielding a root's tip as it pushes through soil.
facts.root_meristem: A knot of ceaselessly dividing cells behind the root cap — source of every new root cell.
facts.elongation_zone: Where new root cells stop dividing and stretch lengthwise, pushing the tip forward.
facts.root_hair: A fine tubular outgrowth that multiplies a root's surface for soaking up water.
facts.cotyledon: An embryonic seed-leaf, often the first green tissue to unfurl as a seed sprouts.
facts.monocot: A flowering plant that sprouts with one cotyledon — grasses, lilies, palms, orchids.
facts.dicot: A flowering plant that sprouts with two cotyledons — historically over half of species.
facts.kapok: Ceiba pentandra, the 'cotton tree' — a rainforest giant with huge plank buttress roots.
facts.buttress_root: Wide, thin plank roots that stop a tall, shallow-rooted rainforest tree toppling over.
facts.brace_root: Adventitious roots from maize's above-ground stem nodes, arching down to prop it up.
facts.ivy: Hedera helix: an evergreen climber that grips trees and walls with clinging roots.
facts.clinging_root: A root that glues itself to a surface for grip, instead of drinking from the soil.
facts.aerial_root: A green, chlorophyll-bearing root some orchids hang in open air — no soil needed.
facts.pneumatophore: A mangrove's snorkel root, poking up out of waterlogged mud to pull in air.
facts.movable_type: Cast from lead, tin and antimony in a hand mould — one reusable piece per letter.
facts.printing_press: A screw-driven bar presses inked type onto paper. Gutenberg, working from about 1436.
facts.telescope: A convex lens focuses light, a concave eyepiece spreads it out magnified. Galileo, 1609.
facts.steam_engine: Watt split the condenser from the cylinder in 1769, so the cylinder never cools between strokes.
facts.barometer: Mercury in a sealed glass tube, held up by the weight of the air alone. Torricelli, 1643.
facts.pendulum_clock: A pendulum's swing takes the same time regardless of its width, so it can pace a clock. Huygens, 1656.
facts.cotton_gin: Iron teeth comb cotton through slots too narrow for the seeds. Whitney, 1793.
facts.sewing_machine: An eye-pointed needle carries thread through cloth to meet a shuttle's thread below. Howe, 1845.
facts.elevator: A spring drives pawls into the guide rails' teeth the instant the hoisting rope goes slack. Otis, 1852.
facts.telegraph: A key switches current down a wire; the current switches an electromagnet at the far end. Morse, 1844.
facts.telephone: An iron diaphragm near a magnet turns sound into a matching current, and back again. Bell, 1876.
facts.radio: A discharging capacitor oscillates across a spark gap and radiates from a wire antenna. Marconi, 1896.
facts.vacuum_tube: A heated filament boils electrons into a vacuum; they cross to the plate only one way. Fleming, 1904.
facts.phonograph: A vibrating needle indents hill-and-dale grooves into tinfoil on a turning cylinder. Edison, 1877.
facts.x_ray: Electrons striking the wall of an evacuated tube throw off radiation that photographs bone. Röntgen, 1895.
facts.camera_obscura: Light through a small hole lands inverted and reversed on the far wall of a dark box.
facts.photographic_plate: Silver fumed with iodine forms silver iodide, a compound so light-sensitive that exposure darkens it.
facts.photograph: A camera projects onto a light-sensitive plate; mercury vapor develops the invisible result. Daguerre, 1839.
facts.ether: Sulfuric acid dehydrates ethanol into ether — the anesthetic Morton demonstrated in 1846.
facts.integrated_circuit: Every part of a circuit, not just the transistors, built into one block of semiconductor. Kilby, 1958.
facts.microprocessor: An entire CPU's arithmetic, logic and control on a single chip. Intel's 4004, 1971.
facts.internal_combustion_engine: Otto compressed the fuel-air mixture in a cylinder before igniting it, for far higher efficiency. 1876.
facts.airplane: A cambered wing lifts, warped wingtips steer, a chain-driven propeller pulls. Kitty Hawk, 1903.
facts.typewriter: A struck key swings a metal bar that prints its letter, reversed on the bar, through an inked ribbon.
facts.herrerasaurus: A basal saurischian near the theropod/sauropodomorph split; a bitten skull shows it fought its own kind.
facts.dilophosaurus: Early Jurassic theropod with air-filled, bird-like bones and a pair of thin display crests, not weapons.
facts.ceratosaurus: A blade-toothed predator named for the display horn on its snout, likely too fragile for real combat.
facts.carnotaurus: Paired brow horns and arms so tiny its fingers fused — the first theropod found with real skin impressions.
facts.giganotosaurus: A carcharodontosaurid rivaling Tyrannosaurus in size, with jaws built to slice prey, not crush its bones.
facts.baryonyx: Its huge thumb claw and crocodile-like snout matched a stomach holding fish scales and a young iguanodontid.
facts.therizinosaurus: A herbivorous theropod with the longest claws of any known animal, hooked to pull branches within reach.
facts.oviraptor: Named 'egg thief' for a skull found near a nest; later finds proved it died brooding its own eggs.
facts.gallimimus: An ostrich-mimic that could run 42-56 km/h, with a toothless beak suited to plants and small prey alike.
facts.microraptor: A crow-sized, four-winged dromaeosaur that glided between trees, its gut once holding fish, bird, and mammal.
facts.diplodocus: A long, low-browsing sauropod whose whip-thin tail held about 80 vertebrae and roughly half its body length.
facts.massospondylus: A basal, bipedal sauropodomorph whose nesting ground is the oldest known evidence of nest-site fidelity.
facts.euoplocephalus: An armored ankylosaurid with bony plates even over its eyelids and a tail club that could fracture bone.
facts.psittacosaurus: A parrot-beaked early ceratopsian, some found with quill-like bristles down the tail and gastroliths inside.
facts.styracosaurus: A centrosaurine with a long nose horn and a frill ringed by spikes, likely for display more than defense.
facts.pentaceratops: Its name means 'five-horned face' — a nose horn, two long brow horns, and two frill-edge cheek points.
facts.camptosaurus: A basal iguanodontian whose heavily worn teeth show a lifetime of chewing tough, fibrous vegetation.
facts.maiasaura: Its name means 'good mother lizard' — hatchlings with unworn legs but worn teeth show adults fed the nest.
facts.drilling_rig: Bores rows of blast-holes up to 27cm across and 40+ metres deep before a bench is ever blasted.
facts.dragline_excavator: Strip mining's biggest machine, almost always run on grid power through a trailing cable, not diesel.
facts.diesel_electric_drive: Skips the gearbox: a generator makes electricity, and motors turn it back into torque at the wheel.
facts.haul_truck: The largest, BelAZ's 75710, carries 450 tonnes on eight tyres 4 metres across.
facts.continuous_miner: A rotating drum rips coal straight off the face, replacing separate cutting, drilling and blasting crews.
facts.longwall_shearer: The machine longwall mining is named for: twin drums shear coal off the face as supports advance behind it.
facts.locomotive: Diesel-electric transmission reached railways before mining trucks — most freight locomotives use it.
facts.crusher: A gyratory or jaw crusher, essentially a moving steel jaw, breaks boulder-sized ore to fist-sized chunks.
facts.ball_mill: A rotating steel drum tumbling with forged steel balls grinds crushed ore down to sand-sized grains.
facts.flotation_cell: Blows air through a ground-ore slurry so valuable, chemically-treated grains stick to bubbles and float off.
facts.tailings: The roughly 99% of ground rock flotation doesn't want, pumped as slurry to a storage dam.
facts.conveyor_belt: A closed loop of reinforced rubber slung between pulleys — cheaper per tonne-kilometre than trucking.
facts.stockpile: Buffers a mine's day-to-day grade swings by blending many truckloads of ore into one consistent pile.
facts.ore_railway: A dedicated unit train, one commodity and one route — the record run was 7.35km long, 99,734 tonnes.
facts.port: Where ore stops being a stockpile and becomes an export — Port Hedland alone ships 500+ million tonnes a year.
facts.bulk_carrier: Capesize ships too big for the Suez or Panama Canal carry about 75% of the world's seaborne iron ore.
facts.piston: Grey cast iron pistons and rings carry their own lubricant: graphite already inside the metal.
facts.axle: A wheelset: two wheels fixed rigidly to one steel shaft, so they always turn together.
facts.bogie: A pivoted frame under a rail car holding two or more axles, so a long car can still take a curve.
facts.steam_locomotive: Steam pushes a piston; a connecting rod turns that push into a crank pin on the driving wheel.
facts.diesel_electric_locomotive: The diesel engine never touches the wheels — it spins a generator that feeds traction motors.
facts.electric_locomotive: No engine on board — current from an overhead wire or third rail drives the motors directly.
facts.freight_wagon: An unpowered steel-framed car riding on bogies, built to be coupled into a train of many.
facts.hopper_car: A sloped floor and bottom gates dump bulk coal, ore or grain without anyone shovelling.
facts.tank_car: A cylindrical steel vessel for liquid or gas — some are lined in glass to protect the shell.
facts.flatcar: No sides, no roof — an open deck for loads too big or heavy for any other kind of wagon.
facts.boxcar: A fully enclosed wagon with sliding doors, built to keep general freight dry.
facts.caboose: The crew's car at the back — a cupola let them watch the whole train roll by for trouble.
facts.coupler: Push two cars together and the knuckle locks itself shut — no one stands between them.
facts.roller_bearing: Hardened chromium-steel rollers between two rings — the axle turns on them, not against them.
facts.plain_bearing: No rolling parts at all — the axle just slides in a graphite-lubricated sleeve.
facts.air_brake: Compressed air presses the shoe to the wheel — and clamps shut if the line ever breaks.
facts.block_signal: One train per block, always — a rail circuit senses the train itself, not a fixed timer.
facts.rail: Hot-rolled steel, I-beam in cross-section — standard gauge sets the rails 1,435 mm apart.
facts.sleeper: The crosstie that holds the gauge — wood needs creosote against rot; concrete needs none.
facts.ballast: Sharp, angular crushed rock — the interlocking edges keep the sleepers from creeping.
facts.points_switch: A pair of tapered rails that pivot to send a train onto one track or another.
facts.rail_yard: Not a station — a ladder of switches sorts wagons onto tracks to build new trains.
facts.capacitor: Two conductors and an insulating gap. Glass, ceramic, paper, even air can serve as that gap.
facts.accelerometer: A silicon mass on springs. Acceleration shifts it, and a capacitor reads the shift as motion.
facts.photodiode: Silicon answers light from 190 to 1100 nanometres — deep into the infrared a remote control uses.
facts.click_wheel: A ring of electrodes under plastic. A fingertip's own capacitance tells it where the finger sits.
facts.flash_memory: A gate buried in oxide traps electrons there for years — a bit that survives the power going off.
facts.ipod: Apple, 2001. A hard drive of songs, then flash memory, controlled by a touch-sensitive wheel.
facts.nike_plus_sensor: A pad under the insole radios a packet to the iPod once a second, running or not, for ten more.
facts.midsole_foam: Foam rubber or EVA, both blown into closed gas cells — the give under a running shoe's arch.
facts.athletic_shoe: A foam midsole over a rubber outsole, tuned to how much the wearer's foot naturally rolls inward.
facts.polarizer: Iodine chains stretched straight through plastic film absorb light vibrating one way, pass the rest.
facts.liquid_crystal: Reinitzer heated cholesteryl benzoate in 1888 and it melted twice, through a cloudy phase between.
facts.thin_film_transistor: A transistor grown on glass instead of cut from a wafer — one per pixel, switching it alone.
facts.liquid_crystal_cell: One transistor, one crystal, repeated millions of times — every pixel twisted open or shut alone.
facts.lcd_screen: White light through two crossed polarizers with a twistable crystal between decides each pixel.
facts.imax_3d_projection: Two lenses, two polarizing filters at right angles — one image per eye, sorted out by the glasses.
facts.laser_diode: A diode's own cleaved faces work as mirrors, turning ordinary light emission into a coherent beam.
facts.dvd_player: A laser reads a spiral of pits by interference; Blu-ray's bluer laser reads pits four times smaller.
facts.photosite: A capacitor built in silicon. Light frees electrons and the capacitor holds them, pixel by pixel.
facts.ccd_sensor: Boyle and Smith, 1969. Each photosite's charge shuffles down the row like a bucket brigade to be read.
facts.digital_camera: A converter assigns each photosite's charge a binary number — light becomes a file, not a negative.
facts.magnetic_tape: A magnetizable coating on a strip of plastic film — sound and picture stored as magnetism, not light.
facts.vhs: JVC's format beat Sony's sharper Betamax in the 1980s because its decks were cheaper and taped longer.
facts.magnetron: A magnet spirals boiling-off electrons past cavities cut into a copper block, which ring at 2.45 GHz.
facts.microwave_oven: Percy Spencer, 1946. A field flipping 2.45 billion times a second spins polar molecules, not just water.
facts.scanner: Mirrors bounce light from the original onto a CCD array, one thin strip at a time as the head crawls.
facts.barcode_scanner: A spinning mirror sweeps a laser across the bars up to 1,200 times a second; a detector reads the flicker.
facts.fingerprint_scanner: A grid of capacitor plates under the surface — ridges sit closer than valleys, and that reads as a print.
facts.wii_remote: A camera tracks two infrared LED clusters for pointing while an accelerometer senses the swing.
facts.superconducting_magnet: Chilled below its critical temperature, its coil carries current with zero resistance.
facts.mri_scan: Aligns hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat, then reads them relaxing back.
facts.fdg: Ordinary glucose with one hydroxyl swapped for radioactive fluorine-18.
facts.positron: The electron's antimatter twin: identical mass, opposite charge.
facts.pet_scan: A detector ring times paired gamma rays, nanoseconds apart, to find where they began.
facts.transducer: A piezoelectric crystal that turns an alternating voltage into a beam of sound.
facts.sound_wave: A pressure wave in tissue, pitched far above the roughly 20,000 Hz a human ear can hear.
facts.echo: Sound bounced back at a tissue boundary; its timing and strength reveal depth and density.
facts.ultrasound_scan: Thousands of 3-D slices a second, stitched into motion — time as the fourth dimension.
facts.icsi_needle: A glass micropipette fine enough to carry one sperm straight through an egg's membrane.
facts.nerve: A cable of axons carrying electrical impulses at up to 120 metres a second.
facts.myoelectric_signal: An electrical twitch in a rerouted muscle, standing in for a hand that is no longer there.
facts.bionic_arm: One rerouted nerve's old command still moves a prosthetic hand, via a skin sensor.
facts.robotic_surgery: A surgeon's hand movements, scaled down and freed of tremor, move tiny remote instruments.
facts.hydraulic_pump: A motor-driven pump that shuttles fluid between two chambers to push blood along.
facts.artificial_heart: A titanium pump wired through the skin only by a magnetic field, never by a wire.
facts.reinforced_concrete: Steel rebar gives concrete the tensile strength it lacks entirely on its own.
facts.curtain_wall: A building's non-structural glass skin, carrying only its own weight, not the floors above.
facts.skyscraper: A steel-and-concrete core takes the load; a hung glass skin merely keeps the weather out.
facts.laser: Chromium ions in a flashed ruby rod drop back to the ground state in exact lockstep.
facts.holographic_plate: Silver-halide emulsion on glass, fine-grained enough to record an interference pattern.
facts.hologram: Not a picture: a recording of a light wave's phase, reconstructed by the same beam again.
facts.fullerene: Sixty carbon atoms closed into a cage shaped exactly like a soccer ball.
facts.nanotube: A single sheet of graphite's lattice, rolled into a seamless tube a few atoms wide.
facts.stm_tip: A tungsten wire etched electrochemically down to a point that ends in one atom.
facts.scanning_tunneling_microscope: Electrons cross a vacuum gap they classically shouldn't, mapping a surface atom by atom.
facts.hadron_collider: Superconducting magnets steer two proton beams to near light speed, then crash them together.
facts.wool_card: A paddle set with fine wire teeth that combs locked wool fibres straight and parallel.
facts.carded_wool: Every fibre now runs the same direction, and the trapped bits of straw and dirt are gone.
facts.felt: No thread, no loom. Wet wool's own microscopic scales lock together under heat and rubbing.
facts.spindle: A weighted rod that twists loose fibre into thread as it spins in the hand or against the thigh.
facts.spinning_wheel: The wheel drives the spindle instead of a hand doing it — over ten times faster.
facts.loom: A frame that holds the warp threads taut so the weft can be woven back and forth through them.
facts.flying_shuttle: Kay's 1733 shuttle rode on wheels, so one weaver alone could work cloth twice as wide.
facts.knitting_needles: Two tapered rods: one holds the loops, the other draws a fresh loop through each one.
facts.knitted_fabric: One yarn meandering into interlocked loops — not two sets crossing at right angles like cloth.
facts.indigo: A shrub in the bean family, field-grown across the tropics for the blue dye locked in its leaves.
facts.leuco_indigo: Indigo won't dissolve in water until fermentation turns it into this — pale yellow, not blue.
facts.madder: A root grown over a metre long on purpose — the whole point is the red dye packed inside it.
facts.alizarin: The exact anthraquinone molecule inside madder root that's actually responsible for the red.
facts.alum: A double sulfate of aluminium — for centuries, the dye trade's single most common mordant.
facts.rose_madder: Alizarin alone washes straight out. Bonded to alum, it becomes a dye that survives the wash.
facts.dyed_cloth: Colour bonded into the fibre itself, not sitting on top of it — the difference a mordant makes.
facts.atomic_clock: Quartz tuned to vibrate at the exact frequency of a caesium atom's transition.
facts.communications_satellite: A radio transceiver with nothing to plug into, kept running by solar cells.
facts.gps_satellite: 24 of these orbit twice daily, each one carrying an atomic clock.
facts.gps: Times signals from four-plus satellites and trilaterates one point where they agree.
facts.cellular_telephone: A telephone's mouthpiece and earpiece wired to a radio that hands off tower to tower.
facts.smartphone: A cellular phone with a general-purpose microprocessor added — it computes now, not just calls.
facts.computer: A microprocessor paired with memory for its program and data — the stored-program design.
facts.router: Reads each packet's address and switches it out the right wire, one hop closer.
facts.internet: Not one network but many, glued by routers forwarding packets hop by hop.
facts.film_reel: A cellulose strip coated with the same silver-bromide emulsion still photography uses.
facts.movie_camera: A camera obscura whose lens exposes a moving film strip one frame at a time.
facts.film_projector: A bright bulb shines through the same sprocketed film a camera exposed, onto a screen.
facts.cinematography: A camera at 24 frames a second and a projector running them past a lamp at the same rate.
facts.television: A radio tuned to a video channel instead of an audio one, feeding a screen.
facts.mutation: A change in the DNA sequence, from a copying mistake or damage. You carry about 60 unique to you.
facts.natural_selection: Mutations that help you survive or reproduce spread through a population; harmful ones tend to vanish.
facts.evolution: Heritable change in a population's traits across generations — natural selection, given enough time.
facts.common_ancestor: Every living thing on Earth traces back to one ancestral population, about four billion years ago.
facts.allele: A different version of the same gene. You carry two of almost every one, one from each parent.
facts.genetic_diversity: How many different alleles exist across a population's genes. Bigger pools survive change better.
facts.cystic_fibrosis: A faulty chloride-channel gene clogs the lungs and gut with thick mucus. Inherited, not contagious.
facts.sickle_cell_anemia: One swapped amino acid bends red blood cells into a sickle shape that jams in blood vessels.
facts.cancer: Mutations disable the brakes on cell division, and a mass of runaway cells forms a tumor.
facts.gene_therapy: Delivering a working copy of a gene into a patient's cells to make up for a faulty one.
facts.crispr: A bacterial defence system repurposed as molecular scissors that cut DNA at a chosen sequence.
facts.cloning: Producing an individual with DNA identical to another's — plants and labs both know how.
facts.parthenogenesis: An egg develops into an embryo without fertilization. The offspring is a clone of the mother.
facts.de_extinction: Splicing an extinct species' genes into a living relative's genome to bring back lost traits.
facts.dna_sequencing: Reading out the exact order of bases in a stretch of DNA, one letter at a time.
facts.mitochondrial_dna: DNA inside mitochondria, inherited only from the mother, unchanged down the maternal line.
facts.dna_profile: A person's unique pattern of DNA markers, precise enough to match evidence to one person.
facts.wing_spar: The beam running the length of the wing that carries almost all of its bending load.
facts.wing: A cambered airfoil at the right angle of attack turns air downward and gets pushed up in return.
facts.fuselage: The main body. In a stressed-skin design the outer shell itself carries structural load.
facts.tail_stabilizer: A small fixed aerofoil at the tail that balances the main wing's lift and holds the nose steady.
facts.aileron: A hinged flap at the wingtip's trailing edge. One goes up as the other goes down, and the aircraft rolls.
facts.rudder: A hinged panel on the fin at the tail, swinging the nose left or right — a ship's steering, borrowed.
facts.tail_elevator: A hinged panel on the tailplane's trailing edge. Deflect it and the nose pitches up or down.
facts.landing_gear: A wheel on an oleo strut, a telescoping tube of gas and oil that soaks up the shock of touchdown.
facts.propeller: A spinning airfoil, twisted so every point along the blade meets the air at a useful angle.
facts.petroleum: Buried marine algae and plankton, cooked by millions of years of heat and pressure into crude oil.
facts.jet_fuel: Kerosene: the fraction of crude oil that boils off between petrol and diesel.
facts.compressor: Alternating spinning and fixed blades squeeze incoming air into a fraction of its intake volume.
facts.combustor: Fuel burns continuously in a steady stream of compressed air, not stroke by stroke like a piston engine.
facts.turbine: Blades in the hottest gas in the engine, spun by the exhaust and geared straight to the compressor.
facts.jet_engine: A turbine drives a compressor on the same shaft, with fuel burning continuously in between.
facts.turbofan: A ducted fan bolted to the front of a jet engine; most of its thrust comes from air the core never touches.
facts.glider: An aircraft with no engine at all, trading height for speed and finding air that rises faster than it sinks.
facts.hot_air_balloon: Air heated by an open flame is less dense than the air around it, so the whole envelope floats.
facts.airship: Unlike a balloon, it steers: engines and control surfaces added to a gas-filled envelope.
facts.rotor: Long, narrow airfoils exactly like a wing's, spun around a hub so they make their own airspeed.
facts.helicopter: A spinning rotor lifts it straight up with no runway, and a tail rotor stops the fuselage spinning too.
facts.parachute: A wide canopy multiplies the drag of a falling body until it settles to a survivable speed.
facts.jet_airliner: A fuselage carried by engines that burn fuel continuously instead of turning a propeller.
facts.runway: A paved strip long enough to reach flying speed on wheels, numbered for the compass heading it points.
facts.hangar: A roof wide enough to clear a whole wingspan with no column standing in the way.
facts.taxiway: Paved like a runway but marked yellow, not white — where aircraft move on their own engines, not full speed.
facts.control_tower: A glass-walled cab high enough to see the whole airfield, sequencing aircraft entirely by radio.
facts.airport: Runways, taxiways, hangars and a tower, all working as one system to move aircraft, not just park them.
facts.dna_helicase: A motor protein that burns ATP to unwind the double helix at a replication fork.
facts.primase: Lays a short RNA primer on bare DNA — polymerase can only extend an end, never start one.
facts.dna_polymerase: Adds nucleotides to a primer's 3' end, one at a time, reading the template strand.
facts.okazaki_fragment: A short burst of DNA made on the lagging strand, later stitched together with the rest.
facts.dna_ligase: Seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments into one unbroken strand.
facts.dna_replication: Semiconservative copying: every new double helix keeps one old strand and one new one.
facts.rna_polymerase: Binds a promoter, pries the helix open, and builds RNA against the exposed template.
facts.transcription: DNA's sequence copied into RNA — the first of the two steps that build a protein.
facts.codon: Three mRNA bases in a row. 64 combinations, 61 of them each naming one amino acid.
facts.anticodon: The three bases on a tRNA that pair with a codon, matching amino acid to instruction.
facts.translation: The ribosome reads codons three at a time and strings amino acids into a protein.
facts.intron: Non-coding filler transcribed into pre-mRNA, then cut out before the message ships.
facts.exon: The coding pieces of a transcript left over once splicing removes the introns.
facts.splicing: The spliceosome cuts introns out and stitches exons together into mature mRNA.
facts.point_mutation: One base pair swapped for another — silent, missense, or nonsense depending on where.
facts.frameshift_mutation: Insert or delete bases not in threes and every codon downstream reads wrong.
facts.geological_mapping: Rock types and structures — faults, folds, intrusions — plotted onto a map before a single hole gets drilled; the oldest surviving one, the Turin papyrus, mapped Egyptian gold deposits 3,000 years ago.
facts.target_generation: Small basaltic intrusions and dense ore bodies both distort a magnetic field enough to show up as an anomaly — where the anomaly lines up with the mapped geology is where the drill gets pointed.
facts.exploration_drilling: A diamond-set bit wears away as it cuts, exposing fresh diamonds underneath — the same wearing action Rodolphe Leschot's 1863 core bit ran on.
facts.resource_estimation: A deposit gets carved into thousands of identically sized blocks, each one assigned its own grade — that block model is where a mine's tonnage and grade actually come from.
facts.feasibility_study: Scoping, pre-feasibility and definitive feasibility studies get progressively more precise about the same question: will this deposit actually turn a profit.
facts.haul_road: Built to the haul truck fleet's own weight and turning circle, not to any public road standard — width, grade and subbase all sized around the machine, not the other way round.
facts.mine_infrastructure: A power plant, water-management ponds and a camp to house the workforce, all built before a single tonne of ore moves.
facts.overburden: Soil and rock with no value at all, sitting on top of the deposit — has to come off first, every time, before the ore underneath is reachable.
facts.bench: An open pit isn't one hole — it's a stack of stepped terraces, each one worked, drilled and hauled a level at a time.
facts.nitric_acid: Made by burning ammonia over hot platinum — the Ostwald process, still how nearly all of the world's supply gets made.
facts.ammonium_nitrate: Doesn't burn on its own, but as an oxidiser it will accelerate almost anything else that does — which is exactly why it ends up in explosives.
facts.anfo: 94% ammonium nitrate prills soaked in 6% fuel oil — cheap and easy enough to mix at the borehole that it's now the mining industry's default explosive.
facts.blasting: Rows of drilled holes, loaded and detonated in a timed sequence — the step that actually breaks rock too solid for any bucket to just dig into.
facts.excavator: Hydraulic pumps, not cables and gears, drive the bucket — the actual 'load' half of load-and-haul.
facts.run_of_mine: Raw material exactly as it exists in the mine — loaded and hauled out, but not yet crushed, sorted or processed in any way.
facts.waste_rock: Mined, but never processed — it's fragmented by the same blast as the ore next to it and simply has nowhere useful to go.
facts.waste_dump: Also called a spoil tip, boney pile, or mine dump depending where you are — an engineered pile, not just wherever a truck happens to tip its load.
facts.assay: Accurate to one part in ten thousand on a bead of gold — still the most reliable way there is to measure exactly how much precious metal a rock actually holds.
facts.grade_control: Every load gets checked against the cut-off grade — the minimum worth processing at all — before it's allowed anywhere near the mill.
facts.magnetic_separation: Magnetite needs just one kilogauss of field strength to respond — weak enough that a modest magnet is all it takes to pull it out of a ground-ore stream.
facts.gravity_separation: No chemicals, low cost — density alone does the sorting, the same trick placer mining uses, just built into a machine.
facts.concentrate: What's left once nearly all the worthless rock is gone — a flotation copper concentrate can run 25-30% metal against roughly 0.5% in the ore it came from.
facts.cyanide: One carbon atom triple-bonded to one nitrogen atom, CN⁻ — simple enough that it also turns up naturally in interstellar clouds and comets.
facts.dore: A semi-pure gold-silver alloy, at least 70% precious metal by weight — an unrefined bar poured on-site, not yet investment-grade metal.
facts.heap_leach: Recovers roughly 60-70% of the copper in a heap of crushed low-grade ore — lower than a mill manages, but cheap enough on ore that low-grade to be worth it anyway.
facts.copper_cathode: 99.99% pure — the actual traded commodity form, whether it got there by smelting and electrorefining or by heap leach and electrowinning.
facts.matte: 30 to 70% copper, still mixed with iron sulfide — most of the impurities smelting hasn't burned off yet.
facts.blister_copper: About 98% pure — named for the pitted surface sulfur dioxide gas leaves behind as it escapes while the metal cools.
facts.tailings_dam: Designed, unlike almost anything else a mine builds, to hold its contents forever — often raised in stages using the tailings themselves as fill.
facts.road_freight: Zimbabwe alone trucked roughly 1.13 million tons of spodumene concentrate to port in 2025, before a dedicated rail line existed to replace it.
facts.slurry_pipeline: Tasmania's Savage River pipeline has carried iron concentrate slurry 85km since 1967, on one span 167 metres above the river below it.
facts.car_dumper: A 1909 rotary car dumper could already empty five loaded mine cars a minute; modern ones rotate a car without even uncoupling it from the train.
facts.port_stockpile: Built far bigger than anything the mine itself needed — the whole point is blending trainload after trainload into one grade a ship can load from without stopping.
facts.stacker_reclaimer: One machine stacks incoming ore into the yard; the other, often the very same gantry, pulls it back off again — blending as it goes.
facts.ship_loader: Its boom moves front to back and up and down on separate drives, so it can reach every part of a hold as the ship's own draught deepens while it fills.
facts.shango: Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning and drumming; deified after his reign as the third Alaafin of Oyo.
facts.obatala: Yoruba orisha of creation and purity, called King of White Cloth; molded humankind from clay and water.
facts.orisha: The Yoruba pantheon of intermediary spirits sent by Olodumare; tradition numbers them at four hundred and one.
facts.eshu: Yoruba trickster-messenger orisha who carries sacrifices between humans and the other orisha.
facts.elegua: Guardian of roads and crossroads in Cuban Santeria, given the keys to past, present and future by Olodumare.
facts.olorun: Supreme Yoruba sky god, also called Olodumare; worshipped indirectly, through the orisha he sends to earth.
facts.yemoja: Yoruba river goddess, her name means 'mother of fish children'; became a sea goddess in the diaspora.
facts.anansi: Akan trickster spider who won ownership of the sky god Nyame's stories -- still told today as Anansi tales.
facts.oya: Yoruba orisha of storms and the Niger River who can shapeshift into a buffalo; guardian of the ancestral dead.
facts.babalu_aye: Yoruba orisha of epidemic disease, his body wrapped in palm straw; also known as Sopona or Omolu.
facts.abassi: Efik supreme creator god who forbade the first humans to farm or have children; both rules were broken.
facts.bumba: Kuba (Bushongo) creator god who vomited up the sun, moon, stars and every animal out of primordial darkness.
facts.lotus: Aquatic flower rooted in mud; a 1,300-year-old seed from a dry lakebed still germinated when planted in 1994.
facts.swan: One of the heaviest birds still capable of flight, favoring slow rivers and larger lakes.
facts.veena: A South Asian string instrument, traditionally built from hollowed wood and a gourd resonator.
facts.conch: A large sea snail's shell; with its spire tip cut off, it becomes a blown ceremonial trumpet.
facts.trident: A three-pronged spear, used to harpoon fish and, forged in iron, carried as a weapon.
facts.mouse: A small rodent that thrives in fields and farmland as readily as in houses, alongside people.
facts.monkey: Old and New World monkeys together number well over 200 species, most of them tree-dwelling.
facts.brahma: Four-headed Hindu creator deity, one head reciting each of the four Vedas; his mount is a swan.
facts.vishnu: Hindu preserver god; reclines on the serpent Shesha in the cosmic ocean, holding a conch and lotus.
facts.shiva: Hindu destroyer god; carries a trishula trident, body ash-covered, a cobra coiled at his neck.
facts.saraswati: Hindu goddess of knowledge and the arts; plays the veena, a hamsa (swan) resting at her feet.
facts.lakshmi: Hindu goddess of wealth; four-armed, seated on a lotus, gold coins pouring from one hand.
facts.parvati: Hindu goddess, daughter of the Himalayan king Himavan; mother of Ganesha, her mounts a lion and tiger.
facts.durga: Hindu warrior goddess with up to eighteen arms, each bearing a weapon; slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
facts.kali: Fierce Hindu goddess of time and death, garlanded with skulls; calmed by standing on Shiva's chest.
facts.ganesha: Elephant-headed Hindu god of beginnings, one tusk broken; rides a mouse and removes obstacles.
facts.hanuman: Monkey god and son of Vayu; carried an entire Himalayan herb-mountain to Lanka to save Lakshmana.
facts.indra: King of the Hindu devas; wields the thunderbolt vajra and rides the white elephant Airavata.
facts.agni: Hindu fire god and messenger between humans and gods; exists as fire on earth, lightning in the sky.
facts.surya: Hindu sun god, driven across the sky in a chariot pulled by seven horses, Aruna at the reins.
facts.vayu: Hindu wind god and father of Hanuman; revered in the Upanishads as prana, the world's life-breath.
facts.axon: A neuron's single output cable, sometimes over a metre long in a human leg, built to carry one electrical impulse away from the cell.
facts.dendrite: A branching antenna studded with receptor proteins, built to catch neurotransmitter signals arriving from other cells.
facts.neuron: A cell body flanked by branching dendrites and a single long axon — roughly half the brain's 86 billion cells are built this way.
facts.glia: Roughly half the brain's cells, and none of them fire a signal — they feed, insulate, and clean up after the neurons that do.
facts.astrocyte: Star-shaped glial cells that wrap around brain capillaries and decide what crosses from blood into brain tissue.
facts.oligodendrocyte: A glial cell built to manufacture myelin, the fatty membrane that insulates a nearby axon.
facts.myelin_sheath: Concentric wraps of fatty membrane coiled around an axon, letting an impulse jump gap to gap instead of crawling the whole length.
facts.synapse: The junction between two neurons — a gap of about 20 nanometres that only a chemical messenger, not electricity, can cross directly.
facts.neurotransmitter: A chemical messenger, packaged in vesicles and dumped into a synaptic cleft the instant an arriving impulse lets calcium in.
facts.choline: The amine head-group of phosphatidylcholine, the most abundant phospholipid in a cell membrane, and the raw material for one neurotransmitter.
facts.acetylcholine: Choline with an acetyl group stapled on. Released at the neuromuscular junction, it is the one neurotransmitter nerve agents and nicotine both target.
facts.dopamine: Built from tyrosine in two enzyme steps. Reuptake of it is exactly what cocaine blocks, flooding the receiving neuron's receptors.
facts.serotonin: Built from tryptophan in two enzyme steps — the reason tryptophan-rich food gets credited, correctly or not, with lifting mood.
facts.glutamate: The same molecule that builds proteins as glutamic acid does a second job once packaged into a synaptic vesicle: the brain's main excitatory signal.
facts.gaba: One enzyme away from glutamate, its own excitatory opposite — snip a carboxyl group off and the brain's chief excitatory signal becomes its chief inhibitory one.
facts.noradrenaline: Dopamine plus one oxygen atom, added by an enzyme that borrows it straight from the air. Drives arousal and the fight-or-flight response.
facts.white_matter: Long-range nerve fibers sheathed in fatty myelin — about 60 percent of the brain's tissue by volume, wiring its regions to each other.
facts.gray_matter: Densely packed neuron cell bodies and their synapses, forming the brain's thin, wrinkled outer layer and the cores of its deeper nuclei.
facts.cerebral_cortex: A folded sheet about 2.5 millimetres thick, six layers of gray matter over a bed of white matter, doing sensory processing, language, and conscious experience.
facts.spinal_cord: About 45 centimetres of nerve tracts wrapped around a butterfly-shaped core of gray matter, running from the brain stem down through the vertebral column.
facts.brainstem: The stalk linking thalamus, forebrain, and spinal cord — its midbrain, pons, and medulla run the reflexes and rhythms that keep a body alive without being asked.
facts.thalamus: A thumb-sized relay station between cortex and lower brain. Every sense but smell is routed through it before the cortex gets to process it.
facts.hypothalamus: A finger-tip-sized cluster of nuclei below the thalamus, running temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and the hormone system that keeps the body in balance.
facts.pituitary_gland: A pea-sized gland taking direct orders from the hypothalamus — one lobe is even made of the hypothalamus's own nerve tissue, extended down a stalk.
facts.hippocampus: A seahorse-shaped fold of gray matter where new memories first form, before they're gradually handed off to the cortex for permanent storage.
facts.amygdala: A pair of almond-shaped nuclei tucked in the medial temporal lobe, best known for attaching fear to a stimulus and holding onto it.
facts.corpus_callosum: A dense band of white-matter tracts that is the brain's biggest single connection: everything one hemisphere knows can cross it to reach the other.
facts.cerebrum: The two-hemisphere bulk of the forebrain, cortex on the outside and joined across the middle by the corpus callosum — about 90 percent of the brain's weight.
facts.cerebellum: The 'little brain' behind the brain stem, its own tightly folded gray-matter surface holding more neurons than the rest of the brain put together.
facts.hindbrain: The evolutionarily oldest part of the brain — cerebellum plus brain stem — running the reflexes and movement coordination a body cannot live without.
facts.brain: About 86 billion neurons and roughly as many glia, split into a forebrain that does the thinking and a smaller midbrain and hindbrain that keep the body running.
facts.frontal_lobe: The cortex's front quarter, home to the primary motor cortex that sends the corticospinal tract down to the spinal cord to move the body on command.
facts.parietal_lobe: The cortex region the thalamus routes touch and body-position signals into — where a scattered sense of skin and joints becomes one coherent map of the body.
facts.temporal_lobe: The lobe that houses the amygdala at its medial edge, and on its surface carries the language and emotion processing the amygdala's neighbourhood implies.
facts.occipital_lobe: The cortex's rearmost lobe, reached by the optic radiation — a thick, myelinated white-matter tract that is vision's last stop before it becomes seeing.
facts.meninges: Three membranes — dura, arachnoid, and pia mater — wrapped around the brain so it never has to touch bone directly.
facts.cerebrospinal_fluid: A liter of fluid, mostly water, made inside the brain's own ventricles and replaced three to four times a day, floating the brain so its own weight can't crush it.
facts.blood_brain_barrier: Tight junctions between capillary cells, policed by astrocyte end-feet, that keep most of what's in the blood from ever reaching brain tissue.
facts.cranial_nerve: One of 12 nerve pairs that connect straight to the brain rather than routing through the spinal cord — 10 of them plug directly into the brain stem.
facts.spinal_nerve: One of 31 nerve pairs, one above each vertebra, each splitting into a sensory branch heading up and a motor branch heading back out to the body.
facts.peripheral_nervous_system: Every nerve outside the brain and spinal cord — built from the spinal nerves and cranial nerves that branch out to reach the entire body.
facts.central_nervous_system: The brain and spinal cord together — the two organs the rest of the nervous system exists to serve and connect to.
facts.nervous_system: Central plus peripheral: an organ system so extensive that all of one body's nerves, laid end to end, could circle the Earth two and a half times.
facts.autonomic_nervous_system: The involuntary branch of the peripheral nervous system, run by the hypothalamus, that keeps heart rate, digestion, and breathing going without being asked.
facts.sympathetic_nervous_system: The autonomic branch that emerges from the spinal cord's chest and abdominal segments to run the fight-or-flight response.
facts.parasympathetic_nervous_system: The autonomic branch carried chiefly by the cranial nerves, running the rest-and-digest state that undoes what sympathetic activation just did.
facts.short_term_memory: A held pattern of ongoing synaptic activity in the frontal lobe's prefrontal cortex, gone within seconds unless something consolidates it.
facts.long_term_memory: What a short-term memory becomes once the hippocampus finishes gradually reorganizing it into the cortex's own long-lived networks.
facts.neuroplasticity: Cells that fire together wire together: a synapse used repeatedly recruits more receptors and strengthens, while an unused one fades.
facts.neurogenesis: Neural stem cells dividing into working neurons — in adult mammals this still happens in the hippocampus, though how much it happens in adult humans is genuinely contested.
facts.hippopotamus: Grazes grasslands by night and cools in the river by day; its skin oozes a reddish natural sunscreen.
facts.jackal: Egypt's 'jackal' turned out on closer genetic inspection to be a distinct wolf species.
facts.ibis: A wading marsh bird, mummified by the millions in antiquity, that had vanished from Egypt by the 1850s.
facts.boat: A hollowed or lashed hull, buoyant long before anyone added a sail or an engine.
facts.egyptian_cobra: North Africa's hooding cobra, delivering venom by direct bite rather than a spray.
facts.heart: Cardiac muscle so packed with mitochondria for oxygen that it almost never fatigues.
facts.ra: Egyptian sun god who crossed the sky by day in one barque and the underworld by night in another.
facts.osiris: Egyptian king of the dead, murdered by his brother Set and made whole again by Isis.
facts.isis: Egypt's most powerful goddess -- a healer and magician who revived Osiris and raised Horus in hiding.
facts.horus: Falcon-headed son of Isis and Osiris; lost his eye to Set in battle, and Thoth restored it.
facts.set: Egyptian god of chaos, storms and the desert who murdered his own brother Osiris.
facts.anubis: Jackal-headed god of embalming who weighed the hearts of the dead against Ma'at's feather.
facts.thoth: Ibis-headed god of writing, wisdom and the moon, also shown as a baboon.
facts.bastet: Cat goddess of Bubastis, daughter of Ra, whose annual festival drew crowds by the hundred thousand.
facts.sobek: Crocodile god of the Nile's waters and marshes, merged with Ra as Sobek-Ra.
facts.hathor: Cow goddess of music and love -- the gentle form the rampaging Sekhmet settled back into.
facts.sekhmet: Lioness goddess of war and plague, daughter of Ra, sent to punish a rebellious humanity.
facts.nephthys: Sister of Isis and wife of Set, who helped gather and mourn Osiris's dismembered body.
facts.nut: Sky goddess arched above her husband Geb, mother of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys.
facts.geb: Earth god whose laughter was said to cause earthquakes; husband of the sky goddess Nut.
facts.shu: God of air and light who forced Geb and Nut apart; fog and cloud were called his own bones.
facts.khnum: Ram-headed god who fashioned human bodies and their life force from clay on a potter's wheel.
facts.ptah: Creator god of Memphis, patron of craftsmen, said to have conceived the world in his heart.
facts.amun: 'The Hidden One' -- a minor Theban god who rose to King of the Gods, merged with Ra as Amun-Ra.
facts.maat: Goddess of truth and cosmic order; her ostrich feather was weighed against the hearts of the dead.
facts.khonsu: Moon god of Thebes, son of Amun -- 'the Traveller,' credited with instant miraculous healings.
facts.taweret: Hippopotamus goddess who protected women in childbirth and sided with Horus against Set.
facts.serket: Scorpion goddess who guards against venom, carved guarding Tutankhamun's canopic shrine.
facts.wadjet: Cobra goddess of Lower Egypt who became the uraeus, the rearing serpent on the pharaoh's crown.
facts.apep: The 'World-Encircler' -- a giant serpent that attacked Ra's sun barque every night in the underworld.
facts.raven: A kleptoparasite of wolves -- it trails packs to steal from their kills, and has led wolves to prey.
facts.spear: The oldest wooden spears are 300,000 years old; stone, bronze and iron tips came later, bound on.
facts.hammer: Perhaps the oldest tool with definite evidence: unhafted stone hammerstones date to 3.3 million years ago.
facts.rune: Germanic letters cut in straight strokes -- a horizontal line would split the wood grain.
facts.odin: Chief of the AEsir. His ravens report the world to him each day; he traded an eye for wisdom.
facts.thor: Odin's son, god of thunder. Wields the hammer Mjolnir, gripped only with his iron gloves.
facts.loki: Shapeshifting trickster. As a mare he bore Sleipnir; he also fathered the wolf Fenrir and a serpent.
facts.freyja: Vanir goddess of love and war. Rides a cat-drawn chariot and owns the necklace Brisingamen.
facts.frigg: Odin's wife. Orion's Belt was known in Scandinavia as 'Frigg's Distaff,' her spinning tool.
facts.baldr: Odin and Frigg's son. Every object swore never to harm him except the mistletoe that killed him.
facts.heimdall: Watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost. His horn Gjallarhorn will sound the start of Ragnarok.
facts.tyr: God of law and single combat. Lost his right hand in the wolf Fenrir's jaws binding it.
facts.njord: Vanir sea god, father of Freyr and Freyja. His mountain marriage to Skadi failed within nights.
facts.skadi: Giantess of winter and skiing. Chose her husband by his feet alone, expecting the god Baldr.
facts.sif: Thor's wife, her golden hair cut off by Loki and replaced with real gold by dwarven smiths.
facts.bragi: God of poetry, said to have runes carved on his own tongue. Greets the slain into Valhalla.
facts.idun: Keeper of the apples that keep the gods young. The giant Thjazi once stole her, eagle-shaped.
facts.hel: Loki's daughter, half flesh and half corpse. Rules the dead who die of sickness or old age.
facts.vidar: Odin's silent, near-mightiest son. His huge shoe is made to kill the wolf Fenrir.
facts.freyr: Vanir god of harvest, rides the golden boar Gullinbursti; traded his sword for a giantess.
facts.mane: Hair, and only males grow one — starting at adolescence as testosterone rises, full size by about age four.
facts.ossicone: A bone core under skin, not a horn or antler — forms before birth, fuses to the skull only at maturity.
facts.tooth: Enamel is the hardest tissue a body makes — 96% mineral, laid down over a bony root.
facts.trunk: Nose and upper lip, fused in early fetal development. No bone at all — just up to 150,000 muscles.
facts.shoulder_hump: Pure muscle, not fat — a power source for digging that no other living bear has.
facts.sagittal_crest: A ridge of bone down the skull's midline, grown to anchor the muscle that powers a bite.
facts.claw: Keratin sheath over the last bone in a toe — the same protein as hair, horn, and hoof.
facts.cecum: A fermentation chamber off the gut — in a koala, about 2 metres long, the largest of any animal its size.
facts.pouch: A fold of skin over the mammary glands, so young barely past embryo stage can still nurse.
facts.red_blood_cell: Round in almost every mammal — oval in exactly one, a shape that keeps blood moving when dehydrated.
facts.hoof: Keratin grown into a hard wall around a single toe bone that carries the animal's whole weight.
facts.knuckle: Where finger bones meet — some apes lock this joint rigid and walk on the back of it.
facts.nuclear_envelope: A double membrane around the genome, its outer layer wired straight into the ER, perforated by thousands of pores.
facts.endoplasmic_reticulum: A network of membrane tubules threading through the cytoplasm, physically continuous with the nucleus.
facts.rough_endoplasmic_reticulum: Ribosomes stud its outer face, giving it a rough look under the microscope and a job making proteins.
facts.smooth_endoplasmic_reticulum: The same tubular network minus the ribosomes — its business is building lipids, not protein.
facts.nucleolus: The largest thing inside the nucleus, and a ribosome factory with no membrane of its own.
facts.golgi_apparatus: Stacked membrane sacs that take in what the rough ER ships out, then modify, sort and repackage it.
facts.lysosome: A membrane bag of over sixty digestive enzymes, budded straight off the Golgi apparatus.
facts.vacuole: Smaller vesicles fuse into one big one; in a mature plant cell it can fill most of the space.
facts.cytoskeleton: Microtubules plus actin filaments plus intermediate filaments: the scaffolding every cell builds itself from.
facts.centriole: Nine microtubule triplets ringed into a cylinder, always kept in a pair near the nucleus.
facts.cilia: Hundreds of short hairs beating in unison, each built on a nine-plus-two ring of microtubules.
facts.flagella: The same nine-plus-two core as a cilium, just one or two per cell instead of hundreds, and far longer.
facts.cell_wall: A rigid cellulose layer laid down just outside the membrane — a plant cell building its own exoskeleton.
facts.plasmid: A loop of DNA a bacterium keeps on the side, copying itself independently of the main chromosome.
facts.diffusion: Molecules drift from where they're crowded to where they're not — no energy required, no pump needed.
facts.osmosis: Diffusion's special case: water alone, crossing a selective membrane toward wherever solutes are thicker.
facts.active_transport: Moving a substance the wrong way down its own gradient — and it always costs a burnt ATP.
facts.endocytosis: The membrane folds around something outside, pinches shut, and the outside becomes an inside.
facts.exocytosis: The Golgi apparatus's shipping side in action: a vesicle docks at the membrane and empties itself outward.
facts.phagocytosis: A cell doesn't just absorb a bacterium — it wraps its whole membrane around it and swallows it whole.
facts.muscle_cell: Actin ordered into thousands of repeating sarcomeres, burning ATP directly to slide past itself.
facts.white_blood_cell: Its lysosomes are loaded and waiting for whatever it engulfs by phagocytosis.
facts.guard_cell: One of the only epidermal cells that keeps its chloroplasts — the other reason it can pump salt and swell.
facts.palisade_cell: Long, tightly packed cylinders under a leaf's upper skin, carrying more chloroplasts than any other leaf cell.
facts.goblet_cell: A secretory cell built around an oversized Golgi apparatus, its whole shape swollen with mucin granules.
facts.mucus: Ninety to ninety-five percent water; the rest is mucin, and together they trap whatever the air brings in.
facts.ciliated_cell: Hundreds of beating hairs on one cell, sweeping the trachea's mucus blanket up and out.
facts.blood: Mostly plasma by volume, but the two kinds of cell suspended in it do entirely different jobs.
facts.nitrogen_gas: N2 — two nitrogen atoms locked by a triple bond so strong almost nothing can break it, which is why it makes up 78% of the air and does almost nothing while it is there.
facts.fox: Most widely distributed member of the dog family, found across the entire Northern Hemisphere.
facts.bow: A flexed stave that stores energy in its limbs, released through a string to launch an arrow.
facts.taiko: Japanese drum family with cowhide heads stretched over a wooden shell, beaten with sticks.
facts.izanagi: Primordial Shinto god who churned the sea into Japan's islands, then fled the underworld Yomi in horror.
facts.izanami: Primordial Shinto goddess who died bearing the fire god Kagutsuchi and became ruler of the underworld Yomi.
facts.amaterasu: Shinto sun goddess and mythical ancestor of Japan's imperial line; hid in a cave, darkening the world.
facts.susanoo: Shinto storm god exiled from Heaven for his rampage; slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi.
facts.tsukuyomi: Shinto moon god who killed the food goddess Uke Mochi in disgust, forever separating day from night.
facts.kagutsuchi: Shinto fire god; his birth killed his mother Izanami, so his father beheaded and dismembered him in revenge.
facts.inari: Shinto kami of rice, fertility and industry, whose messengers are white foxes -- kitsune.
facts.ryujin: Shinto dragon king of the sea, ruling a palace of red and white coral beneath the waves.
facts.fujin: Shinto wind god, one of the eldest kami, shown carrying a huge bag of winds on his shoulders.
facts.raijin: Shinto thunder god who beats drums ringed with the tomoe symbol from atop the clouds.
facts.hachiman: Shinto god of war and archery, syncretic spirit of Emperor Ojin; guardian kami of the samurai.
facts.tenjin: Shinto god of scholarship -- the deified spirit of the exiled courtier-poet Sugawara no Michizane.
facts.uke_mochi: Shinto food goddess killed by Tsukuyomi; crops and livestock grew from her corpse afterward.
facts.mikaboshi: Shinto star god, the only deity who refused to submit to the heavenly gods' conquest of the earth.
facts.ame_no_iwato: The heavenly rock cave where Amaterasu hid after Susanoo's rampage, plunging the world into darkness.
facts.ame_no_uzume: Shinto goddess of dawn and mirth; her bawdy dance lured Amaterasu out of hiding and founded kagura dance.
facts.sarutahiko: Shinto guardian kami with a seven-span nose and eyes like mirrors; blocked the descent of the heavenly gods.
facts.tectonic_plate: Earth's brittle outer shell broken into semirigid slabs — seven major ones, a dozen or so smaller.
facts.divergent_boundary: Where two plates pull apart and magma rises to freeze into new crust, mostly along mid-ocean ridges.
facts.convergent_boundary: Where two plates are driven together — one dives beneath the other, or both crumple upward instead.
facts.transform_boundary: Where two plates grind sideways past one another along a fault, neither building crust nor destroying it.
facts.earthquake: The ground's sudden release of strain built up along a locked fault, radiating out as seismic waves.
facts.mid_ocean_ridge: A continuous seam of brand-new seafloor, welling up along a divergent boundary for about 65,000 km.
facts.taxonomy: The nested system — kingdom down to species — that gives every living thing exactly one place and one name.
facts.tree_of_life: A branching diagram connecting every classified group of life back through common ancestry.
facts.cladistics: Grouping organisms by shared derived traits, not overall looks — the method behind the whale-hippo surprise.
facts.island: Land walled in by water on every side. Isolation is exactly what makes island wildlife so distinctive.
facts.fossil: Ancient remains preserved in rock after minerals slowly replace the original bone or shell.
facts.genetic_drift: Random, chance shifts in a population's allele frequencies — strongest of all in small populations.
facts.gene_flow: Alleles moving between populations as individuals, pollen, or seeds cross from one to another.
facts.adaptation: A trait shaped over generations by natural selection to fit its bearer to its environment.
facts.sexual_selection: Mate choice or rivalry favouring traits that win breeding success, not just plain survival.
facts.artificial_selection: Humans, not nature, choosing which individuals breed — the same mechanism, a different judge.
facts.reproductive_isolation: Populations diverged enough that they can no longer produce fertile offspring together.
facts.speciation: The point at which diverging populations can no longer interbreed and become separate species.
facts.adaptive_radiation: One ancestral population fanning rapidly into many species, each fit to a different niche.
facts.homology: Shared underlying structure — the same bone plan in a wing, a flipper, and a hand — from common descent.
facts.vestigial_structure: A once-useful body part reduced to a nonfunctional leftover once selection stopped favouring it.
facts.fossil_record: The total, ordered archive of fossils across rock strata — evolution's clearest paper trail.
facts.transitional_fossil: A fossil bridging two groups, carrying features of both the ancestral and the descendant form.
facts.living_fossil: A living species so little changed from its fossil relatives it looks like it stepped out of deep time.
facts.extinction: The permanent disappearance of a species when the last individual dies without descendants.
facts.mass_extinction: A sudden, global loss of a large share of species all at once, resetting evolution's course.
facts.camouflage: Colouring or pattern that blends its bearer into the background — adaptation you can see at a glance.
facts.peacock: A pheasant relative native to South Asia; males spread an iridescent, eye-marked tail in courtship.
facts.owl: Comb-like serrations on its flight feathers muffle the wingbeat, letting it hunt almost silently.
facts.helmet: Protective head covering; Bronze Age Aegean warriors wore bronze and boar's-tusk designs.
facts.lyre: Ancient stringed instrument; its classic form used a hollowed tortoise shell as a soundbox.
facts.poppy: The scarlet corn poppy grows wild among cereal crops; a different species yields opium.
facts.arrow: A projectile shaft tipped with a point -- among the oldest weapons humans have made.
facts.cicada: Nymphs feed on root sap underground for years before emerging to moult into winged adults.
facts.cerberus: Three-headed dog, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, that guards the gates of the underworld.
facts.zeus: King of the Olympian gods, ruler of sky and thunder. Roman Jupiter. Won his throne from the Titans.
facts.hera: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage. Roman Juno. Homeric epithet Boopis, 'cow-eyed.'
facts.poseidon: God of the sea and earthquakes, 'the Earth-Shaker.' Roman Neptune. Carries a trident.
facts.hades: God of the dead and ruler of the underworld. Roman Pluto. Also called Plouton, 'the rich one.'
facts.athena: Goddess of wisdom and war strategy. Roman Minerva. Sprang fully armed from Zeus's head.
facts.apollo: God of prophecy, music and archery. Chief epithet Phoebus, 'bright.' Twin brother of Artemis.
facts.artemis: Goddess of the hunt, wilderness and the moon. Roman Diana. Twin sister of Apollo.
facts.ares: God of war and battle-frenzy. Roman Mars. Called by Zeus 'the most hateful of all gods.'
facts.aphrodite: Goddess of love and beauty. Roman Venus. Name means 'foam-arisen,' born of the sea.
facts.hermes: Messenger of the gods and guide of souls to the underworld. Roman Mercury. Patron of travelers and thieves.
facts.dionysus: God of wine, ecstasy and theatre. Roman Bacchus. Called the 'twice-born' god.
facts.demeter: Goddess of grain and the harvest. Roman Ceres. Her grief for Persephone brings winter.
facts.persephone: Queen of the underworld and goddess of spring growth. Roman Proserpina. Daughter of Demeter.
facts.hephaestus: God of fire, the forge and craftsmen. Roman Vulcan. Epithet Amphigyeeis, 'the lame one.'
facts.cronus: Titan king who ruled the Golden Age. Roman Saturn. Overthrew his father Uranus, and was overthrown by Zeus.
facts.gaia: Primordial personification of the Earth. Roman Terra. Mother of Uranus and the Titans.
facts.uranus: Primordial personification of the sky, first ruler of the cosmos. Castrated by his son Cronus.
facts.rhea: Titaness of motherhood, wife of Cronus. Roman Ops. Saved infant Zeus with a trick of stone and cloth.
facts.eros: God of desire and love. Roman Cupid. Ovid gives him gold arrows that kindle love and lead ones that repel it.
facts.nike: Winged personification of victory. Roman Victoria. Daughter of the Titan Pallas and the river Styx.
facts.helios: God who personifies the sun. Roman Sol. Drives a four-horse chariot across the sky each day.
facts.selene: Goddess who personifies the moon. Roman Luna. Sister of Helios and Eos.
facts.eos: Goddess who personifies the dawn. Roman Aurora. Homer's constant epithet: 'rosy-fingered.'
facts.pan: God of the wild, shepherds and flocks. Roman Faunus. Has the legs and horns of a goat.
facts.hypnos: God who personifies sleep. Roman Somnus. Twin brother of Thanatos, death, and son of Nyx, night.
facts.heracles: Greatest of the Greek heroes. Roman Hercules. Son of Zeus, famed for his Twelve Labors.
facts.odysseus: King of Ithaca, hero of the Odyssey. Roman Ulysses. Known for his cunning, metis.
facts.rhinoceros: Wart-like bumps armor its deeply folded skin — adults face almost no natural predator.
facts.hyena: A bite 40% stronger than a leopard's lets it crush bone that would defeat most carnivores.
facts.sloth: Leaves can take more than a month to digest — no other mammal's gut works that slowly.
facts.armadillo: The only armadillo that can roll its whole body into a sealed, armored ball.
facts.hedgehog: Its spines are just hair, stiffened with keratin — and two back muscles roll it into a spiky, sealed ball.
facts.meerkat: Eye sockets covering over a fifth of its skull power the binocular vision behind its sentry watch.
facts.large_intestine: Cecum, colon, rectum, anal canal in series — built to reclaim water and salt, not absorb nutrients.
facts.colon: Ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid — one tube bent twice, by the liver then the spleen.
facts.haustra: Segmented pouches once blamed on short muscle bands — now thought to be the enteric nervous system's work.
facts.rectum: Where the colon's muscle bands blend into one sheath and the pouches vanish: a smooth reservoir for feces.
facts.appendix: Reassessed since the early 2000s: not vestigial. Its wall is packed with immune tissue standing watch.
facts.peristalsis: A wave of muscle: relax ahead, contract behind. The colon mostly skips it for a few big daily pushes.
facts.gut_flora: The body's largest bacterial ecosystem — a relationship that's mutualistic, not just commensal.
facts.vitamin_k: Gut bacteria — E. coli among them — convert it between forms and can synthesize their own share.
facts.beak: A bony core sheathed in keratin — the rhamphotheca — its shape set entirely by what the bird eats.
facts.talon: A bird of prey's claw — the foot that does the killing; the hooked beak only tears flesh afterward.
facts.air_sac: Thin sacs that push air through the lungs one-way on both breaths — no other vertebrate manages that.
facts.hollow_bone: Marrow swapped for air and internal struts — lighter, and plumbed straight into the lung's air sacs.
facts.keel: The sternum's midline ridge, giving flight muscle leverage — ratites are literally named for lacking one.
facts.flight_muscle: Pectoralis for the downstroke, supracoracoideus for the up — pulling through a shoulder pulley tendon.
facts.flight_feather: The stiff, asymmetric-vaned feathers of wing and tail carry the whole aerodynamic load.
facts.hummingbird: A shoulder joint that rotates the whole wing — the only bird family that can truly hover and fly backward.
facts.penguin: Wings became short, stiff flippers — the same bones as a flying bird's wing, just built for the sea.
facts.flamingo: Comb-like lamellae line the bill, worked upside-down in the mud to filter out its food.
facts.albatross: A sheet of tendon locks the wing open at the shoulder, so it glides on the wind without spending muscle.
facts.ostrich: Only two toes per foot, not four — no other living bird is reduced that far.
facts.kiwi_bird: The only bird with nostrils at its bill-tip, smelling worms in soil it can't see or feel.
facts.toucan: A hollow, oversized bill covering up to half its body surface — used to reach fruit and dump heat.
facts.woodpecker: A hyoid bone wraps around the skull as an internal seatbelt, cushioning the brain from every peck.
facts.pelican: The throat pouch is a fishing net, not a pantry — it drains the water out before the fish goes down.
facts.heron: Twenty-plus neck vertebrae fold into a tight S, cocking the dagger bill to strike.
facts.cormorant: Stands wing-spread after a river dive — a study on the great cormorant found the pose dries its plumage.
facts.parrot: The upper beak hinges free of the skull instead of fusing to it, adding bite force.
facts.swift: Legs too short for much but clinging — it eats, mates and sleeps on the wing.
