facts.cartilage: Collagen-rich connective tissue with no blood supply of its own — firm but flexible where bone is rigid.
facts.whisker: A hair whose root carries 100–200 nerve endings — enough to feel a gap's width in the dark.
facts.floating_clavicle: A collarbone with no joint to the rest of the skeleton — anchored only by connective tissue.
facts.retractable_claw: Sheathed in skin and fur at rest, so the point never dulls on the ground.
facts.tapetum_lucidum: A riboflavin-and-zinc mirror behind the retina — nearly 130 times as reflective as a human eye.
facts.righting_reflex: A falling cat rights itself by inner ear, then twists its front half and rear half in turn.
facts.purr: Made possible by a fully bony hyoid — a big cat's stays gristly, so it roars instead.
facts.barbed_tongue: A muscle studded with backward-hooked keratin spines — a built-in hairbrush.
facts.vomeronasal_organ: A mouth-roof organ wired to its own nerve, not the main smell nerve — it reads pheromones.
facts.slit_pupil: Snaps to a vertical slit in bright light — stays round in a cat the size of a tiger.
facts.manx: A dominant mutation shortens the spine to nothing — lethal if inherited from both parents.
facts.siamese: A heat-sensitive enzyme switches pigment on only where the skin runs cool.
facts.sphynx: A recessive keratin-gene mutation stops each hair from growing a proper root.
facts.devon_rex: Its curl looks like the Cornish Rex's but comes from a mutation at a different gene entirely.
facts.scottish_fold: A dominant cartilage-gene mutation folds the ear — and softens joints all over the body.
facts.tide: Raised mainly by the Moon's pull on the sea, with a smaller pull from the Sun added in.
facts.intertidal_zone: Flooded and drained twice a day; barnacles mark its top, kelp its lowest fringe.
facts.tide_pool: Seawater stranded in a rocky hollow at low tide, a miniature and harshly changeable sea.
facts.barnacle: A crustacean, not a mollusk. It cements its head to rock and kicks food in with feathery legs.
facts.mussel: Anchors itself to rock with byssus, tough protein threads spun by a gland in its foot.
facts.periwinkle: Grazes rock on a mucus-lubricated foot, then seals its shell to the stone with the same mucus.
facts.limpet: Clings to rock with one powerful suction foot and homes back to its own worn scar after grazing.
facts.chiton: Eight overlapping shell plates on a muscular girdle; its teeth are capped with iron-rich magnetite.
facts.hermit_crab: Has no shell of its own. It lives in an empty snail shell and moves to a bigger one as it grows.
facts.sea_star: Moves on hundreds of tube feet run by a water-filled hydraulic system, not muscle alone.
facts.sand_dollar: A sea urchin flattened for burrowing in sand, its spines reduced to short, mobile ones.
facts.whelk: A predatory sea snail that uses a spine on its own shell's lip to pry open a barnacle's plates.
facts.bladder_wrack: A brown seaweed kept afloat near the surface by paired air bladders along its fronds.
facts.sea_lettuce: A green alga only two cells thick, simple enough to grow from seawater into a brackish estuary.
facts.razor_clam: Buried in shore sand, it can dig itself down almost as fast as a person can dig after it.
facts.brittle_star: Whips its thin arms in snake-like curves to move; a lost arm snaps off easily and regrows.
facts.porcelain_crab: A filter feeder closer kin to hermit crabs than true crabs, gripping kelp holdfasts with spiny legs.
facts.frogspawn: A clump of eggs wrapped only in jelly, no shell — most amphibians must lay it in water or it dries out.
facts.tadpole: A fully aquatic larva with a tail and gills, hatched from spawn — nothing like the frog it will become.
facts.gill: A feathery, blood-vessel-rich fringe that pulls dissolved oxygen straight out of water.
facts.lung: An air sac that only finishes growing once a tadpole's gills are on their way out.
facts.metamorphosis: Thyroid hormone remakes a gilled swimmer into an air-breather, tail eaten by its own cells.
facts.amphibian_skin: Little keratin, no scales — a permeable membrane that must stay damp to work at all.
facts.cutaneous_respiration: Breathing through the skin itself — some salamanders rely on it completely and have no lungs at all.
facts.indicator_species: Permeable skin and a water-bound larva make an amphibian population an early warning for pollution.
facts.lateral_line: A row of pressure-sensing "plaques" down the head and flanks, for water, not air.
facts.caecilian: Limbless and burrowing, built so much like an earthworm most people miss that it's a vertebrate.
facts.japanese_giant_salamander: Among the largest living amphibians at 1.5 m — its wrinkled skin exists purely to breathe underwater.
facts.surinam_toad: Eggs sink into the mother's back skin, which closes into pockets until a toadlet climbs out.
facts.batrachotoxin: The frog doesn't make its own poison — it concentrates it from the ants and mites it eats.
facts.olm: Blind and pale from a lifetime in cave rivers, larval for life — its tissues ignore thyroxine.
facts.siren: Keeps functioning lungs and external gills side by side for life, unlike any other salamander.
facts.gallium: Melts at 29.8°C, liquid in your palm — Mendeleev predicted it in 1871, four years before it was found.
facts.dry_ice: Frozen carbon dioxide. Below 5 atmospheres it has no liquid phase — it sublimates straight to gas.
facts.housefly: Musca domestica tastes through chemoreceptors on its feet, and has only one pair of wings, not two.
facts.rat: Rattus norvegicus. Its incisors never stop growing — about 12 cm a year — so it gnaws constantly.
facts.feral_pigeon: Descended from the rock dove, and it still nests on window ledges the way its ancestors nested on sea cliffs.
facts.garden_snail: Cornu aspersum. Hermaphrodite — a mating pair each fire a calcite 'love dart' before mating.
facts.common_toad: Bufo bufo walks on four legs rather than hopping, and returns every spring to the exact pond it hatched in.
facts.green_alga: Chlorophyta — chlorophyll a and b, starch storage, mostly fresh water. Land plants share all three.
facts.potassium_nitrate: KNO3, saltpetre. Bacteria turn manure's ammonia into nitrate; wash it through ash and it crystallises.
facts.glycerol: Named from the Greek for sweet — the backbone left once a fat's three fatty acids are split off it.
facts.toluene: Named for tolu balsam, the resin it was isolated from in 1841 — now mostly made from petroleum instead.
facts.tnt: 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, first made in 1863 as a yellow dye — a military explosive only from 1902.
facts.gunpowder: 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur — a ratio traced to its 11th-century Chinese origin.
facts.dynamite: Nobel's 1867 patent: nitroglycerin soaked into kieselguhr, a diatom silica, stable enough to ship.
facts.nitroglycerin: Sobrero made it first, in 1846, and was so alarmed by how easily it detonates he opposed weaponising it.
facts.wind_shear: Wind changing speed or direction with height. Enough of it over a thunderstorm tilts the updraft into a spin.
facts.tornado: A supercell's rotating mesocyclone, stretched and tightened by wind shear until it touches the ground.
facts.tsunami: Not a wind-driven wave — the whole water column shoved sideways by a subduction-zone earthquake.
facts.liquid_hydrogen: Boils at -252.87°C, just 20 degrees above absolute zero — colder than every other cryogenic liquid but helium.
facts.liquid_nitrogen: Boils at -196°C. Splashed on something warm it floats on its own vapour — the Leidenfrost effect.
facts.antiproton: The proton's antimatter twin — same mass, opposite charge — confirmed to exist in 1955 at Berkeley.
facts.antihydrogen: A positron bound to an antiproton — a whole antimatter atom, first made at CERN in 1995.
facts.pyrope: Magnesium aluminium silicate garnet, carried up from the mantle in basalt and kimberlite pipes.
facts.spessartine: Manganese aluminium silicate garnet — the orange member, grown in granite pegmatite and rhyolite.
facts.grossular: Calcium aluminium silicate garnet, grown where metamorphism cooks impure limestone.
facts.andradite: Calcium iron silicate garnet — swap in chromium and its demantoid variety outshines emerald in fire.
facts.uvarovite: Calcium chromium silicate garnet, always green, grown in chromium-rich serpentinite.
facts.heliodor: Golden beryl, coloured by iron in its Fe3+ state — grown in the same granite pegmatites as beryl itself.
facts.morganite: Pink beryl, coloured by manganese in its Mn2+ state — the same element that turns red beryl scarlet in a hotter state.
facts.red_beryl: Manganese-coloured beryl grown in volcanic gas cavities, not pegmatite — rarer than diamond.
facts.amethyst: Quartz coloured violet by iron impurities plus natural background irradiation.
facts.citrine: Quartz whose iron centres have been driven from purple to gold — most of it is heat-turned amethyst.
facts.rose_quartz: Quartz pink not from a dissolved impurity but from microscopic fibres of a mineral related to dumortierite.
facts.smoky_quartz: Quartz with aluminium standing in for a little silicon, smoked brown by the same irradiation that colours amethyst.
facts.aventurine_quartz: Quartz glittering with included flakes of fuchsite mica — the sparkle is reflection, not the quartz's own colour.
facts.tigers_eye: Silicified crocidolite — asbestos fibres replaced by quartz, then stained gold-brown by iron oxide.
facts.rutilated_quartz: Quartz grown around needles of rutile, titanium dioxide, that crystallised first and got trapped.
facts.chalcedony: Cryptocrystalline quartz, its crystals too small to see — deposited from silica-laden groundwater in rock cavities.
facts.agate: Chalcedony banded in successive layers as silica-bearing water deposits it again and again in the same cavity.
facts.carnelian: Chalcedony coloured brownish-red by impurities of iron oxide — hematite, specifically.
facts.jasper: Opaque chalcedony, its common red-brown colour is iron inclusions running right through it.
facts.chrysoprase: Chalcedony coloured apple-green by trace nickel — unlike emerald's chromium, in a completely different host.
facts.bloodstone: Green jasper flecked red — the spots are hematite inclusions, not literally blood, whatever the legend says.
facts.moss_agate: Chalcedony with dendrites of manganese or iron oxide branching through it like moss — no plant was ever involved.
facts.petrified_wood: Wood buried and starved of oxygen, its cell walls replaced molecule by molecule with chalcedony carried in by water.
facts.tourmaline: A boron silicate that crystallises in granite pegmatite — boron is what makes it tourmaline at all.
facts.schorl: Iron-rich tourmaline, black and by far the commonest kind — about 95% of all tourmaline found is this.
facts.dravite: Magnesium-rich tourmaline, brown, named for the Drave district where it was first described.
facts.rubellite: Manganese-rich tourmaline, pink to red — the lithium-bearing elbaite branch of the tourmaline family.
facts.indicolite: Blue tourmaline — an iron and titanium pair trading an electron back and forth, the same trick that colours sapphire.
facts.watermelon_tourmaline: A single crystal zoned pink to green as it grew — manganese ran out and iron took over partway through.
facts.padparadscha: Corundum needing both ruby's chromium and sapphire's iron and titanium together to land on pink-orange.
facts.spinel: Magnesium aluminium oxide — grown alongside ruby in metamorphosed limestone, and mistaken for it for centuries.
facts.sodalite: Sodium aluminosilicate with chlorine locked in its cage structure — a feldspar relative too low in silica to be one.
facts.hauyne: A sulfate cousin of sodalite, in the same feldspathoid family, first found in Vesuvius's ejected limestone blocks.
facts.lapis_lazuli: Not one mineral but a rock: sodalite-group lazurite for the blue, pyrite for the gold flecks.
facts.scapolite: A calcium-sodium aluminosilicate that traps chlorine, carbonate or sulfate in its structure — metamorphosed feldspar.
facts.zircon: Zirconium silicate — chemically nothing like the metal zirconium is cut from, though it is zirconium's ore.
facts.vesuvianite: A complex calcium-magnesium-aluminium silicate grown where limestone gets baked by an intruding melt — a skarn mineral.
facts.taaffeite: Beryllium magnesium aluminium oxide, close kin to spinel — it was sold as spinel for years before anyone noticed.
facts.benitoite: Barium titanium silicate, blue and fluorescent — first mistaken for sapphire before its own mineral was recognised.
facts.topaz: An aluminium silicate that locks fluorine into every unit — fluorine is what makes it topaz and not something else.
facts.chrysoberyl: Beryllium aluminium oxide — shares beryllium and aluminium with beryl, but is a completely different mineral.
facts.alexandrite: Chromium-bearing chrysoberyl that reads green in daylight and red under incandescent light — same trick as ruby's chromium, doubled.
facts.cymophane: Cat's-eye chrysoberyl — parallel needle-like inclusions focus light into one moving band across the stone.
facts.andalusite: Aluminium silicate, Al2SiO5 — one of three minerals with that exact formula, sorted out by pressure and heat.
facts.chiastolite: Andalusite grown around carbon and clay swept to its corners, leaving a black cross in cross-section.
facts.sillimanite: Al2SiO5 again, but andalusite's higher-temperature twin — the same formula, rearranged by more heat.
facts.kyanite: Al2SiO5 a third time — andalusite's higher-pressure twin, grown deeper where the rock is squeezed harder.
facts.enstatite: Magnesium silicate pyroxene, MgSiO3 — the iron-free end of a solid-solution series that runs to ferrosilite.
facts.hypersthene: Enstatite with enough iron mixed in to sit halfway to ferrosilite — common in both igneous rock and meteorites.
facts.iolite: Cordierite to a mineralogist: a magnesium iron aluminium silicate grown by baking clay-rich rock.
facts.peridot: Gem-grade olivine, specifically its magnesium-rich forsterite end — one of only two gems that form in the mantle, not the crust.
facts.sinhalite: Magnesium aluminium borate, close enough to spinel's own recipe that it was mistaken for peridot for decades.
facts.kunzite: Spodumene coloured lilac-pink by manganese — the same lithium aluminium silicate, a different trace element.
facts.hiddenite: Spodumene coloured green by chromium — kunzite's twin, with ruby and emerald's own colouring element instead.
facts.zoisite: Calcium aluminium silicate grown in calcium-rich schist — colourless until a trace element gets into it.
facts.tanzanite: Zoisite coloured blue-violet by vanadium, then heat-treated to burn off a brownish veil and leave the blue.
facts.thulite: Zoisite coloured pink by manganese — tanzanite's sibling, with manganese standing in for vanadium.
facts.moonstone: Feldspar that cooled slowly enough to separate into alternating orthoclase and albite layers, scattering light between them.
facts.labradorite: Calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar — thin exsolved layers inside it split light the way a soap film does.
facts.albite: The sodium end of the plagioclase feldspar series — pure NaAlSi3O8, calcium's opposite number.
facts.sunstone: Albite-type feldspar glittering with flat copper platelets grown inside it — Oregon's stone specifically owes its sparkle to copper.
facts.amazonite: A green-blue microcline feldspar, its colour tied to trace lead locked in the same triclinic structure.
facts.jadeite: A sodium aluminium pyroxene — one of two unrelated minerals both called jade, made only where plates subduct.
facts.nephrite: A calcium magnesium iron amphibole — jade's other mineral, chemically nothing like jadeite despite the shared name.
facts.chrysocolla: A hydrous copper silicate that grows where malachite and azurite weather further in silica-bearing water.
facts.dioptase: Hydrous copper silicate, deep emerald-green — grown in the same oxidised copper-deposit zone as malachite, with silica instead of carbonate.
facts.dolomite: Calcium magnesium carbonate — limestone with roughly half its calcium swapped for magnesium by passing groundwater.
facts.aragonite: Calcite's higher-pressure polymorph — identical formula, CaCO3, packed into a different crystal shape.
facts.rhodochrosite: Manganese carbonate, rose-red from Mn2+ — baked further by metamorphism and it turns into the silicate rhodonite.
facts.rhodonite: Manganese silicate — what rhodochrosite becomes when metamorphism drives off its carbon dioxide and leaves silicate behind.
facts.smithsonite: Zinc carbonate, grown the same way malachite is — in the weathered, oxidised cap above a metal-sulfide deposit.
facts.cerussite: Lead carbonate, formed the same way malachite is — weathering in carbon-dioxide-charged water above a lead deposit.
facts.anglesite: Lead sulfate — what galena becomes when it oxidises in air, the lead equivalent of pyrite turning to hematite.
facts.celestine: Strontium sulfate, precipitated out of evaporating water exactly the way gypsum is, with strontium standing in for calcium.
facts.titanite: Calcium titanium silicate, also called sphene — one of the few common minerals built around titanium.
facts.epidote: A calcium aluminium iron silicate that grows where hot fluids alter calcium-rich feldspar — iron is what turns it pistachio-green.
facts.staurolite: An unusually aluminium-rich silicate that grows in schist alongside garnet, twinning into a natural cross.
facts.danburite: Calcium borosilicate, grown where boron-bearing fluids cook limestone during contact metamorphism.
facts.datolite: Calcium borosilicate with a hydroxyl group — a classic mineral of gas cavities in basalt, grown alongside zeolites.
facts.axinite: A calcium aluminium borosilicate that grows where a granite intrusion's boron-rich fluids meet its contact zone.
facts.dumortierite: An aluminium borosilicate that grows fibrous in aluminium-rich rock cooked by regional metamorphism.
facts.prehnite: Calcium aluminium silicate, another classic mineral of gas cavities in basalt — named for the officer who first brought it to Europe.
facts.petalite: Lithium aluminium silicate, grown in the same lithium-bearing granite pegmatites as spodumene.
facts.euclase: A hydroxyl-bearing beryllium aluminium silicate — beryl's chemistry with water folded into the structure.
facts.brazilianite: Sodium aluminium phosphate, grown in phosphate-rich granite pegmatite — named for the country its type locality is in.
facts.beryllonite: Sodium beryllium phosphate — pegmatite chemistry that swaps beryl's silicate framework for a phosphate one.
facts.amblygonite: A lithium aluminium fluorophosphate, grown alongside spodumene as one more lithium mineral in the same pegmatite.
facts.phosphophyllite: A rare zinc iron phosphate, grown in hydrothermal veins — named for its leaf-like, phyllite-style cleavage.
facts.hambergite: Beryllium borate with a hydroxyl group — one of the few gem minerals built directly from beryllium and boron.
facts.scheelite: Calcium tungstate, CaWO4 — named for the chemist who discovered tungsten, and still an ore of it today.
facts.cassiterite: Tin oxide, SnO2 — the ore the Bronze Age's tin was smelted from, and still the main tin ore now.
facts.jet: Driftwood buried in marine mud and compressed for millions of years — lignite dense enough to carve and polish.
facts.amber: Fossilised conifer resin, sometimes with an insect from millions of years ago trapped inside as it set.
facts.tortoiseshell: Keratin scutes from a hawksbill sea turtle's carapace — the trade nearly took the species with it, and is now banned worldwide.
facts.australopithecus_afarensis: Walked upright by 3.7 million years ago -- the Laetoli footprints prove it -- with a brain a third our size.
facts.homo_habilis: ‘Handy man’ -- the first Homo species, named for knapping the Oldowan stone tools that made it famous.
facts.homo_erectus: First hominin with a humanlike stride, and the first to walk out of Africa into Asia and Europe.
facts.homo_heidelbergensis: Big-brained, organized big-game hunter, likely ancestor of both Neanderthals and modern humans.
facts.homo_neanderthalensis: Stocky and cold-built for Ice Age Europe. Buried its dead, and left DNA in most people alive outside Africa.
facts.sahelanthropus_tchadensis: A 7-million-year-old skull from Chad -- maybe the earliest hominin, though its bipedalism is disputed.
facts.orrorin_tugenensis: A 6-million-year-old Kenyan hominin known mainly from a femur shaped for upright walking.
facts.ardipithecus_ramidus: 'Ardi' -- a 4.4-million-year-old Ethiopian hominin that walked upright yet still climbed trees.
facts.australopithecus_africanus: South Africa's 'southern ape', known from cave finds like the Taung Child and Mrs. Ples.
facts.paranthropus_boisei: 'Nutcracker Man' -- huge molars and jaw muscles for grinding tough plants, an extinct side branch.
facts.homo_rudolfensis: A bigger-brained contemporary of Homo habilis, found near Kenya's Lake Turkana.
facts.homo_antecessor: Found in Spain's Atapuerca caves, with cut-marked bones showing its people practiced cannibalism.
facts.homo_naledi: A small-brained Homo species whose bones were found deep in a South African cave chamber.
facts.homo_floresiensis: The 'Hobbit' -- a metre-tall hominin that shrank on the Indonesian island of Flores.
facts.denisovan: Known almost entirely from DNA out of a Siberian cave -- a sister lineage to the Neanderthals.
facts.australopithecus_sediba: Found by a 9-year-old boy at Malapa, South Africa -- a mix of ape-like and human-like traits.
facts.oldowan_tool: The oldest recognized stone-tool kit: sharp flakes struck off a stone core with a hammerstone, nothing more.
facts.acheulean_handaxe: A teardrop struck symmetrically from both faces of a stone core -- the same design used for 1.5 million years.
facts.fire_drill: Spin a wooden shaft against a wooden board by hand until the hot dust it grinds off glows into an ember.
facts.bow_drill: A cord wound around the spindle and driven by a bow turns hand-spinning into fast, steady strokes.
facts.ochre: An iron-rich earth pigment, red from hematite, ground fine enough to paint or stain skin.
facts.cave_painting: Animal figures in mineral pigment on cave walls, like those at Lascaux and Altamira.
facts.venus_figurine: Faceless, wide-hipped female carvings found from Spain to Russia, most made 26,000 to 21,000 years ago.
facts.atlatl: A hooked shaft that extends the throwing arm, hurling a dart far harder than any bare hand can.
facts.mammoth: A tundra grazer built for cold -- shaggy coat, curved tusks -- eating roughly 180 kg of grass and sedge a day.
facts.mammoth_bone_hut: A dome of mammoth bones and tusks, weighted and covered with hide, on treeless Ice Age steppe.
facts.coke: Coal heated past 1,000°C with no air doesn't burn — it comes apart, leaving this near-pure carbon behind.
facts.pig_iron: Cast in branching sand moulds off one channel — piglets nursed by a sow is where the name comes from.
facts.deadly_nightshade: Atropa belladonna. Renaissance women dropped its juice into their eyes to dilate the pupils -- bella donna, beautiful lady.
facts.atropine: A tropane alkaloid that blocks the nervous system's rest-and-digest signal, which is why it dilates pupils and speeds a stopped heart.
facts.poison_hemlock: Purple-blotched hollow stems along streams and ditches. Socrates was made to drink a decoction of it in 399 BC.
facts.water_hemlock: Its tuberous root is widely cited as North America's most acutely toxic native plant -- seizures can begin within an hour.
facts.castor_bean: The mottled seed yields castor oil, a mild laxative -- and, left behind in the pressed mash, one of the most toxic proteins known.
facts.ricin: A ribosome-inactivating protein: it shuts down protein synthesis inside a cell so completely that a few milligrams can kill an adult.
facts.oleander: Every part of this Mediterranean shrub carries cardiac glycosides -- the same class of chemistry China has used medicinally to treat heart failure.
facts.aconite: Monkshood. Its hooded purple flower conceals aconitine in every tissue, historically smeared on arrow tips and used as wolf bait.
facts.autumn_crocus: Colchicum autumnale flowers leafless in fall. Its colchicine is still prescribed for gout, and used in labs to double a plant's chromosomes.
facts.mayapple: One umbrella-shaped leaf shelters a rhizome so rich in podophyllotoxin it became the starting material for the chemotherapy drug etoposide.
facts.yew: Every part except the sweet red aril carries taxine alkaloids. The bark's taxol was developed into paclitaxel, a chemotherapy drug.
facts.pokeweed: Birds strip its magenta-stemmed berry clusters unharmed and scatter the seed; the same fruit sickens the mammals that eat it.
facts.larkspur: Delphinium, named for the dolphin-shaped spur on its unopened bud. Its methyllycaconitine is the leading cause of cattle deaths on western rangeland.
facts.lily_of_the_valley: Its convallatoxin is potent enough that even the water a cut stem stands in becomes toxic -- Soviet-era medicine once paired it with alcohol to treat dropsy.
facts.giant_hogweed: Its sap contains furanocoumarins that bind skin's DNA when hit by sunlight, causing burns and blistering that can recur for years.
facts.strychnine_tree: Strychnos nux-vomica. Its bitter seeds concentrate strychnine, an alkaloid so effective a rodent poison it is still sold as one.
facts.rhododendron: Some species load their nectar with grayanotoxin -- Xenophon's soldiers recorded being poisoned by wild honey made from it in 401 BC.
facts.horse_chestnut: The glossy brown seed -- a conker -- is packed with the saponin aescin, toxic raw but processed medicinally to treat vein disorders.
facts.datura: Jimsonweed. Its trumpet flower points upward and opens toward dusk; British troops in 1676 Jamestown ate it and spent a fortnight out of their minds.
facts.angels_trumpet: Brugmansia. Its pendulous trumpet flowers hang downward, the mirror image of its herbaceous relative datura, which points its blooms up.
facts.cannabis: Resin glands on the female flower buds manufacture cannabinoids, chief among them the psychoactive THC.
facts.thc: Tetrahydrocannabinol, the cannabinoid mainly responsible for cannabis's psychoactive effects -- one of over sixty the plant produces.
facts.coca: Andean peoples have chewed its leaf, buffered with lime to raise its pH, for a documented 5,000 years without the dependence refined cocaine produces.
facts.cocaine: The coca leaf's alkaloid, isolated and concentrated: it blocks the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine at the nerve synapse.
facts.tobacco: Nicotiana tabacum manufactures nicotine in its roots as an insect defence; nearly all of the genus's 75 species can do the same.
facts.nicotine: An alkaloid absorbed easily through skin and lung alike. The old 40-60 mg lethal-dose figure was debunked in 2014; the real lower limit is closer to 500-1000 mg.
facts.opium_poppy: Papaver somniferum, not the wild corn poppy. Lancing its unripe seed pod oozes a latex resin that dries into raw opium.
facts.morphine: Isolated from opium in 1803 and named for Morpheus, the god of dreams -- medicine's benchmark analgesic ever since.
facts.peyote: Lophophora williamsii, a spineless button cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert, is the sole source of ceremonial peyote for the Native American Church.
facts.san_pedro_cactus: Echinopsis pachanoi, a fast-growing columnar cactus of the high Andes, used ceremonially for a documented 3,000 years.
facts.mescaline: A phenethylamine alkaloid, structurally closer to amphetamines than to most other plant hallucinogens, made independently by peyote and San Pedro.
facts.psilocybin_mushroom: Psilocybe cubensis fruits readily on the dung of grazing cattle in warm pastures, bruising blue-green wherever it is bruised or cut.
facts.psilocybin: A prodrug: the body converts it to psilocin, the compound actually responsible for the hallucinogenic effect.
facts.morning_glory: Ipomoea seeds contain LSA, an ergoline alkaloid related to LSD; the Zapotec used one Mexican species ritually for centuries before its chemistry was known.
facts.betel_nut: Chewed with lime inside a betel leaf, the areca palm's seed is consumed habitually by an estimated 600 million people worldwide.
facts.ayahuasca_vine: Banisteriopsis caapi's bark supplies beta-carboline MAO inhibitors that let an otherwise orally inactive tryptamine survive digestion when brewed together.
facts.salvia_divinorum: Diviner's sage. Its salvinorin A is the only known naturally occurring hallucinogen with no nitrogen atom in its structure at all.
facts.sweet_flag: Calamus. Its aromatic rhizome was chewed by pioneers as a stimulant and thirst-quencher, though its beta-asarone is now banned from US food products.
facts.mescal_bean: Sophora secundiflora's bright red seeds -- red hots -- concentrate cytisine, used in a Native American vision-seeking rite that predates peyote's spread.
facts.meteorite: A meteoroid that survives the trip through the atmosphere and reaches the ground — most don't.
facts.impact_crater: Struck near 20 km/s, rock is compressed past a million bar — melted, vaporized, or turned to coesite.
facts.tektite: Impact-melted terrestrial rock, quenched airborne into glass — no crystals, under 0.02% water by weight.
facts.moldavite: Green tektite glass from one event: the Ries impact, 15 million years ago, its melt landing 450 km away.
facts.australite: Tektite reshaped by a second trip through the atmosphere — the flanged button NASA modeled Apollo capsules on.
facts.krishna: Eighth avatar of Vishnu, raised among Vrindavan's cowherds; plays the bansuri flute, a peacock feather in his crown.
facts.radha: Krishna's foremost consort among the Vrindavan gopis; her own symbol, tradition says, is the Golden Lotus.
facts.yashoda: Krishna's foster mother in Gokul, wife of the chieftain Nanda; credited with two of his best-known childhood miracles.
facts.kansa: Tyrant king of Mathura and Krishna’s uncle, undone by the very prophecy he tried to escape.
facts.rama: Seventh avatar of Vishnu and prince of Ayodhya; broke Shiva's own bow to win Sita's hand, then defeated Ravana.
facts.sita: Found by King Janaka while ploughing a field and raised as his daughter; her own name means ‘furrow.’
facts.ravana: Ten-headed rakshasa king of Lanka and grandson of the sage Pulastya; an ardent devotee of Shiva.
facts.lakshmana: Rama's loyal younger half-brother, who chose fourteen years of exile at his side over life in Ayodhya.
facts.arjuna: Third of the five Pandava brothers and wielder of the celestial bow Gandiva; Krishna served as his charioteer.
facts.chisel: A wedge-shaped steel blade, driven into wood, stone, or metal by a mallet or hammer.
facts.stethoscope: Laennec's 1816 original was a hollow wooden tube; the binaural rubber-tubed design followed in 1851.
facts.dental_drill: Its cutting bur is usually tipped with tungsten carbide or diamond.
facts.compass: A magnetised needle, free to pivot, that aligns itself with Earth's magnetic field.
facts.fire_hose: Amsterdam fire chief Jan van der Heyden sewed the first leather fire hose in 1673.
facts.chalk: Most classroom chalk today is gypsum, not true calcium-carbonate chalk.
facts.carpenter: Trains as an apprentice for three to four years before becoming a journeyman.
facts.electrician: US apprenticeships run three to five years and 4,000 to 6,000 hours of paid on-the-job training.
facts.plumber: Installs and maintains the pipes that carry a building's water in and its waste out.
facts.astronomer: Now more often exposes a CCD camera for minutes than peers through an eyepiece.
facts.meteorologist: Reads pressure, temperature, and wind to forecast weather from local to global scale.
facts.astronaut: A sealed helmet exchanges breathable oxygen and carbon dioxide with the spacecraft.
facts.veterinarian: Completes a dedicated veterinary-medicine degree covering anatomy, pharmacology, and surgery.
facts.farm_manager: Plans the sequence from ploughing and sowing through to harvest.
facts.medical_doctor: Four to five years of medical school, then a supervised residency, before independent practice.
facts.dentist: Earns a B.D.S., D.M.D., or D.D.S. degree before treating patients.
facts.railroad_engineer: US train drivers must be certified, and recertified every two to three years.
facts.ships_captain: Legally responsible for a ship's safe navigation, seaworthiness, cargo, and crew.
facts.airline_pilot: Captaining an airliner requires an Airline Transport Pilot License, the highest pilot certificate.
facts.firefighter: Trains at a local, regional, or state-approved fire academy before active duty.
facts.paramedic: US certification takes 1,500-plus classroom hours and 500-plus clinical hours.
facts.chef: Typically apprentices for three to four years, mixing classroom instruction with kitchen work.
facts.photographer: Still frames light through a box and a lens, exactly as the first cameras did.
facts.jewelry_designer: Ancient jewelry favored 24-karat gold, more accessible then than silver.
facts.textile_designer: Interlaces a vertical warp yarn with a horizontal weft on a loom to design woven cloth.
facts.teacher: Requires professional qualification, typically including pedagogy -- the science of teaching.
facts.khufu: Commissioned the Great Pyramid; his only surviving portrait is a 3-inch ivory statuette found in 1903.
facts.great_pyramid: Khufu's tomb at Giza, roughly 2.3 million limestone and granite blocks. The only Wonder still standing.
facts.pheidias: Athenian sculptor (c. 480-430 BC) whose chryselephantine cult statues defined Greek monumental art.
facts.chryselephantine: Greek for 'gold and ivory' -- ivory flesh and gold-leaf robes built over a hidden wooden statue core.
facts.statue_of_zeus: Pheidias's roughly 12-meter seated, chryselephantine Zeus at Olympia -- lost by the 5th century AD.
facts.nebuchadnezzar: King of Babylon for forty-three years, who built the Ishtar Gate and destroyed the First Temple.
facts.ziggurat: Stepped Mesopotamian temple tower; Babylon's own, Etemenanki, may underlie the Tower of Babel story.
facts.ishtar_gate: Babylon's processional gate to Marduk's temple, its mudbrick fired under a lapis-blue glaze.
facts.hanging_gardens: Legendary terraced gardens; no Babylonian text or excavation confirms they ever stood at Babylon at all.
facts.croesus: Lydian king whose vast wealth gave English the phrase 'rich as Croesus.'
facts.temple_of_artemis: Ephesus's great sanctuary to Artemis; its final, marble version had over 127 columns.
facts.herostratus: Burned the Temple of Artemis in 356 BC purely to be remembered -- and still is.
facts.sostratus: Architect credited, though disputedly, with the Lighthouse of Alexandria; Ptolemy let him sign it.
facts.lighthouse_of_alexandria: The Pharos, over 100 meters tall on Alexandria's harbor island; stood for more than a thousand years.
facts.mausolus: Carian ruler (377-353 BC) who began his own vast marble tomb while still alive.
facts.artemisia_ii: Mausolus's sister-wife; ruled Caria alone for two years after his death in 353 BC.
facts.mausoleum_halicarnassus: Mausolus's tomb at Halicarnassus -- so famous its name now means any grand tomb.
facts.chares: Sculptor of Lindos, on Rhodes, who cast the Colossus of Rhodes over twelve years.
facts.colossus_of_rhodes: 108-foot bronze Helios at Rhodes's harbor; stood 56 years before an earthquake felled it.
facts.protostar: A collapsing cloud fragment gathering mass, glowing from infall — no core fusion yet.
facts.brown_dwarf: 13 to 80 Jupiter masses — too little to fuse hydrogen, so it just cools for the rest of time.
facts.supergiant: 8+ solar masses and up to a million times as luminous. Almost every one ends in a supernova.
facts.pulsar: A spinning neutron star sweeping a radio beam past Earth — found by Jocelyn Bell in 1967.
facts.crab_nebula: Wreckage of the supernova Chinese astronomers logged in 1054 CE, still expanding, pulsar at its core.
facts.spectroscope: Splits starlight into a rainbow crossed by dark lines — each line naming an element.
facts.radio_telescope: Karl Jansky's antenna caught radio hiss from the galactic center in 1932, founding the field.
facts.galaxy: Stars, gas, dust and dark matter bound by gravity. Up to 2 trillion of them, by one estimate.
facts.milky_way: Our barred spiral, 100-400 billion stars. The Sun orbits its center once every 240 million years.
facts.andromeda_galaxy: Proved a separate galaxy by Hubble in 1925, using Cepheids. 2.5 million light-years off, and closing.
facts.spiral_galaxy: A rotating disc of stars, gas and dust with arms of active star birth. About 60% of galaxies today.
facts.elliptical_galaxy: Smooth and featureless, red with old stars. The giants of this shape sit at the hearts of clusters.
facts.barred_spiral_galaxy: A spiral with a straight stellar bar through its core. About two-thirds of spirals have one — ours does.
facts.lenticular_galaxy: A lens-shaped hybrid: a disc like a spiral's, but no arms, and gas long used up like an elliptical's.
facts.local_group: Our galaxy group: 100+ members, dominated by two spirals — the Milky Way and Andromeda.
facts.galaxy_cluster: Hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound by gravity — the biggest bound structures in the universe.
facts.supercluster: A group of galaxy clusters and groups. The Local Group sits inside the Laniakea Supercluster.
facts.supermassive_black_hole: Millions to billions of solar masses. Almost every large galaxy has one anchoring its center.
facts.accretion_disc: Gas pulled from a companion star spirals in and heats enough to blaze in X-rays before it falls in.
facts.active_galaxy: A galaxy outshone by its own nucleus — matter falling onto a central supermassive black hole.
facts.quasar: The most luminous class of active galaxy — 3C 273 alone outshines the Milky Way by 100 times.
facts.seyfert_galaxy: An ordinary-looking spiral with an extraordinarily bright core — Carl Seyfert named the class in 1943.
facts.radio_galaxy: A giant elliptical blasting jets of radio-emitting particles for millions of light-years past its disc.
facts.exoplanet: A planet around another star. Mayor and Queloz confirmed the first one, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995.
facts.cepheid_variable: A star that swells and shrinks on a clock — its period reveals its true brightness. Leavitt, 1908-12.
facts.spectrum: Starlight fanned out by wavelength — its dark lines give away a star's elements, heat, and motion.
facts.redshift: Light stretched to longer wavelengths by recession or expansion. Hubble read it as the universe's growth.
facts.dark_energy: About 68% of the universe, and it's speeding up the expansion. Found in 1998 supernova redshifts.
facts.dark_matter: Unseen mass, about 27% of the universe — Vera Rubin found galaxies spinning too fast without it.
facts.cosmic_microwave_background: The universe's first light, redshifted down to 2.7 kelvin. Penzias and Wilson found it by accident in 1965.
facts.globular_cluster: Hundreds of thousands of ancient stars packed in a sphere, up to 12.7 billion years old.
facts.orion_nebula: The nearest big stellar nursery, 1,300 light-years off — naked-eye visible in Orion's sword.
facts.pleiades: The Seven Sisters: an open cluster of 1,000+ young stars, 444 light-years away, naked-eye visible.
facts.als: Also called Lou Gehrig's disease: a person's motor neurons die while their mind stays intact.
facts.echolocation: Bouncing sound off the world to see it: orcas and other toothed whales click and read back the echoes.
facts.biomimicry: Engineering copies nature's homework: a humpback's bumpy flipper now shapes wind-turbine blades.
facts.frozen_zoo: A bank of frozen sperm, eggs, and cells from over 1,300 endangered species, ready to thaw.
facts.ultraviolet: Light one octave bluer than violet, invisible to us -- it's what sunburns skin and makes minerals glow.
facts.fluorescent_mineral: Drinks invisible UV light and throws visible color back -- fluorite even gave 'fluorescence' its name.
facts.aerogel: Nicknamed 'frozen smoke': a solid that's up to 99.8% air, one of the lightest solids ever made.
facts.lichtenberg_figure: The branching, fractal scar a strong charge burns through an insulator as it discharges -- lightning is one.
facts.fuel_cell: Combines hydrogen and oxygen without burning them, making electricity, heat, and water -- no soot.
facts.afar_triangle: The one place on Earth where seafloor-spreading-style rifting is happening on dry land, not underwater.
facts.aardvark: Its claws tear open termite mounds; a single night's foraging can down 50,000 insects on its sticky tongue.
facts.beaver: A keystone engineer: its dams reshape rivers into wetlands, and its four incisors never stop growing.
facts.naked_mole_rat: A eusocial mammal with one breeding queen per colony, near cold-blooded, and immune to acid-triggered pain.
facts.pronghorn: The fastest land mammal in the Americas -- built to outrun a cheetah species extinct for 12,000 years.
facts.fennec_fox: Its ears are the largest of any canid relative to body size -- radiators for heat, dishes for sound.
facts.vampire_bat: Hunts only in total darkness, reading a warm vein through heat sensors in its nose before its bite.
facts.aye_aye: Taps wood eight times a second, listens for the echo of a hollow tunnel, then fishes out the grub inside.
facts.star_nosed_mole: Its 22-tentacled nose carries 25,000+ touch sensors and can identify prey in 120 milliseconds flat.
facts.barn_owl: Its two ears sit at different heights on its skull, letting it strike prey in pitch darkness by sound alone.
facts.satin_bowerbird: The male builds no nest -- he builds a stick bower and decorates it almost entirely in blue to court females.
facts.leatherback_turtle: Holds its core 18°C above cold water via countercurrent heat exchange, and dives deeper than any reptile.
facts.archerfish: Spits a shaped water jet to knock insects off leaves, correcting its aim for light bending at the surface.
facts.electric_eel: Not a true eel: 6,000 stacked cells fire up to 860 volts, and it curls around prey to shock it twice.
facts.mantis_shrimp: Its claw strikes at 23 m/s, fast enough to flash-boil a bubble that hits prey with a second, separate blow.
facts.pistol_shrimp: Snaps a claw shut fast enough to flash-heat a bubble past the Sun's surface temperature, at 218 decibels.
facts.bombardier_beetle: Mixes two stored chemicals to fire a near-boiling, pulsed spray it can aim almost anywhere on its own body.
facts.tardigrade: Dries itself into a glass-like 'tun' to survive years without water, -272°C to 149°C, and the vacuum of space.
facts.coconut_crab: The largest land arthropod alive; adults give up the borrowed shell of their hermit-crab kin entirely.
facts.neith: Warrior-weaver goddess of Sais, worshipped as a creator; crossed bows were her own emblem.
facts.seshat: Goddess of writing and measurement who founded temples with the king in the 'stretching of the cord' rite.
facts.nefertem: Young god who rose from the primordial waters as a lotus at Ra's own nostrils; member of the Memphis triad.
facts.nekhbet: Vulture goddess of Upper Egypt, worshipped at Nekheb; paired with Wadjet as the crown's 'Two Ladies.'
facts.min: Ithyphallic fertility god of Coptos and Akhmim whose festival carried his image to the fields at harvest.
facts.renenutet: Cobra goddess of the grain harvest, name meaning 'to nurse'; guarded granaries and nursed royal infants.
facts.bes: Dwarf protector of households and childbirth, shown facing forward instead of in profile to scare off evil.
facts.mut: Mother goddess of Karnak, wife of Amun and mother of Khonsu in the Theban Triad; wears both of Egypt's crowns.
facts.tefnut: Moisture goddess sneezed or spat into being by Atum-Ra; twin sister and consort of Shu, mother of Geb and Nut.
facts.sokar: Falcon god of the Memphis necropolis, fused into Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, patron of craftsmen and the dead.
facts.wepwawet: Wolf-formed 'opener of the ways' of Asyut, a standard-bearer who led the pharaoh's army and later the dead.
facts.griffon_vulture: A carrion-eating scavenger whose bald head sheds heat, soaring on one of the largest wingspans of any raptor.
facts.sponge: No true tissues, nerves or organs — just specialised cells filtering food from water pumped through its own pores.
facts.comb_jelly: Not a jellyfish — its own animal phylum, swum by eight rows of beating cilia that split light into rainbow bands.
facts.hydra: A freshwater cnidarian that clones a new body off its own side by budding, and barely seems to age.
facts.planarian: Cut it into pieces and each piece can regrow a whole worm — brain included — within a couple of weeks.
facts.leech: A segmented worm related to the earthworm — its bite injects an anticoagulant still used in modern surgery.
facts.ribbon_worm: Fires an eversible, sometimes venom-barbed proboscis at prey — possibly Earth's longest animal.
facts.bryozoan: A colony of thousands of near-identical animals under a millimetre long, sharing one skeleton — long mistaken for moss.
facts.lampshell: Looks like a two-shelled clam, but a brachiopod's valves sit top and bottom, not left and right.
facts.velvet_worm: Ambushes prey by firing two crossing jets of sticky slime from glands beside its jaws.
facts.horseshoe_crab: Its blue, copper-based blood clots on contact with bacterial toxins and still tests every batch of injectable medicine.
facts.sea_spider: Not a true spider — its body is so reduced that its own gut and gonads run out into its legs.
facts.tusk_shell: A tusk-shaped shell open at both ends, buried head-down in sand, catching prey with thread-like tentacles.
facts.sea_cucumber: When threatened, some species eject sticky internal organs through the anus to entangle a predator, then regrow them.
facts.feather_star: A sea-star relative filtering plankton with feathery arms, gripping the reef with claws instead of tube feet.
facts.slug: A land snail that lost its shell, or reduced it to an internal remnant, in several separate lineages.
facts.cuttlefish: Its porous internal cuttlebone works like a submarine's ballast tank, and its pupils are shaped like a W.
facts.foraminifera: A single cell that builds an elaborate calcium-carbonate shell — fossil shells like these built the Great Pyramid.
facts.radiolarian: A single cell in an intricate glassy skeleton, its geometry the inspiration for Ernst Haeckel's illustrations.
facts.dinoflagellate: The single-celled organism behind a glowing night wave — some species flash blue light the instant it's disturbed.
facts.diatom_organism: Encased in two interlocking glass shells fitting like a pillbox — makes a fifth or more of Earth's oxygen.
facts.euglena: Carries a plant's chloroplasts to photosynthesise in light, then swims off to swallow food like an animal in the dark.
facts.paramecium: Covered in thousands of beating hairs that row it through the water and sweep food into a mouth-like groove.
facts.stonewort: A freshwater alga often crusted in limestone, among the closest living algal relatives that land plants have.
facts.cycad: A palm-like gymnosperm older than the dinosaurs — several genera still make sperm cells that swim.
facts.ginkgo: The last living species of its plant order, famous for outliving almost anything thrown at it — even an atomic bomb.
facts.hornwort: Most cells hold just one giant chloroplast — unique among land plants — often housing nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
facts.clubmoss: Not a moss at all — a vascular, spore-dispersing lineage older than ferns, whose oily spores once lit stage magic.
facts.manatee: The gentle "sea cow" grazes seagrass and mangrove leaves in warm shallow water, and can chill to death below 20°C.
facts.dugong: The only truly marine grazing mammal — its seagrass-feeding trails across the seabed likely inspired mermaid legends.
facts.hyrax: A rabbit-sized rock-dweller whose closest living relatives are the elephant and the manatee.
facts.sengi: Not a shrew — its closest relatives are elephants, and it can outrun almost anything its own size.
facts.tenrec: Madagascar's answer to hedgehogs, shrews, and otters all at once — one species "talks" by rubbing its own spines.
facts.golden_mole: Blind and earless, it "swims" through loose sand — some species find prey by sensing vibration through the skull.
facts.colugo: Wrongly called a "flying lemur" — not a lemur, and can't fly, but glides on the largest skin membrane of any mammal.
facts.echidna: A spiny, egg-laying mammal — lays one leathery egg straight into its own temporary pouch, then hatches it there.
facts.pangolin: The only mammal covered in true scales, built from keratin — the same protein as hair and nail.
facts.tapir: Uses a short, flexible snout to grab leaves, and submerges in rivers to feed and let small fish groom parasites off it.
facts.giant_anteater: Has no teeth at all — a sticky tongue up to 60cm long, flicking around 160 times a minute, does all the work.
facts.opossum: North America's only marsupial — its famous "playing dead" is an involuntary fainting spell, not a decision.
facts.wombat: Digs vast burrow systems and produces cube-shaped droppings — an intestinal trick that stops them rolling away.
facts.mesite: A weak-flying, ground-foraging bird found only in Madagascar's forests.
facts.kagu: A near-flightless bird found only on New Caledonia, hunting earthworms with nostril flaps found on no other bird.
facts.sunbittern: When threatened, it fans its wings to reveal huge fake eyespots, briefly looking like a much larger animal.
facts.turaco: One of the only birds with true green and red feather pigments — most bird "green" is a trick of light, not colour.
facts.hoatzin: Digests leaves by fermenting them in an oversized crop, like a cow — and its chicks are born with claws on their wings.
facts.seriema: The closest living relative of the extinct terror birds, killing prey by beating it against the ground.
facts.cuckoo_roller: The only member of its own bird order — despite the name, unrelated to true cuckoos or true rollers.
facts.tuatara: New Zealand's "living fossil" reptile, the last of its order, with a light-sensing third eye on a hatchling's skull.
facts.amphisbaenian: A limbless burrower whose blunt tail looks so much like its head that some cultures call it "two-headed."
facts.cumulus: A heap cloud built by convection over warm ground, its flat base usually below 550 m.
facts.cirrus: Ice crystals 6,000 to 20,000 m up, combed by strong winds aloft into curls called mare's tails.
facts.stratus: A flat grey sheet under 2,000 m, named for lying in layers. Lower it to the ground and it is fog.
facts.cumulonimbus: A cumulus that kept growing until it hit the tropopause and spread into an anvil, often past 12,000 m.
facts.nimbostratus: A thick dark layer riding in on a warm front, wringing out steady rain or snow for hours.
facts.supercell: A thunderstorm organised around a mesocyclone, a deep updraught that keeps rotating for hours.
facts.monsoon: A seasonal wind that reverses because land heats and cools faster than the ocean beside it.
facts.anticyclone: Sinking air spreads out at the surface as high pressure, clearing the sky it descends through.
facts.low_pressure: A mid-latitude cyclone: a warm front and a cold front, rotating together round a shared low.
facts.warm_front: Warm air riding up and over a retreating wedge of cold, denser air — a slow, wide advance.
facts.cold_front: Dense cold air undercutting the warmer air ahead of it, moving up to twice a warm front's speed.
facts.sleet: Snow that melted crossing a warm layer aloft, then refroze into a hard pellet near the ground.
facts.drizzle: Droplets under 0.5 mm across, misted out of a low stratus deck — too light to fall as rain.
facts.anemometer: Four hemispherical cups on a shaft, spun by wind pressure. Robinson's design, 1846.
facts.rain_gauge: A funnel over a graduated cylinder. Korea's cheugugi, standardised in 1441, was the first of its kind.
facts.weather_vane: An asymmetric pointer that swings to face into the wind. Athens' Tower of the Winds carried a bronze one.
facts.hygrometer: Human hair lengthens as humidity rises. De Saussure built the first hair hygrometer from one in 1783.
facts.tropical_climate: Köppen's line for it: every month averages 18°C or warmer. There is no real winter here.
facts.arid_climate: Defined by evaporation outrunning rainfall, not by temperature — deserts and dry steppe both qualify.
facts.temperate_climate: The mid-latitude belt, 23.5° to 66.5°, where most of humanity lives through four real seasons.
facts.mercury_planet: 70% metal by mass, giving it the largest iron core of any planet by volume — 57% of it.
facts.venus: 96.5% carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat so well it beats Mercury for hottest planet.
facts.earth: The only known world with stable liquid water on its surface, covering 71% of it.
facts.mars: Iron oxide dust rusted red over billions of years — hence the nickname, the Red Planet.
facts.jupiter: Radiates more heat than it gets from the Sun, still shrinking from its own formation.
facts.saturn: The only planet less dense than water — a big enough bathtub and it would float.
facts.uranus_planet: Coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system, -224°C, though not the farthest out.
facts.neptune: Found by math before anyone saw it — Le Verrier calculated it, Galle spotted it in 1846.
facts.pluto: Largest known body in the Kuiper belt by volume, found by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930.
facts.io: The most volcanically active body in the solar system, squeezed by Jupiter's tides.
facts.europa: An icy shell over an ocean holding two to three times the water of every ocean on Earth.
facts.ganymede: Bigger than Mercury and the only moon known to make its own magnetic field.
facts.callisto: The most heavily cratered surface known — unchanged and un-resurfaced for 4.5 billion years.
facts.saturn_rings: 99.9% pure water ice, in pieces from dust grains to houses, spread out paper-thin.
facts.cassini_division: A 4,800 km gap Cassini spotted in 1675, swept clear by the moon Mimas's gravity.
facts.titan: The only moon with a thick atmosphere, and lakes of liquid methane on its surface.
facts.enceladus: Geysers of ice erupt from its south pole, feeding Saturn's E ring, seen by Cassini in 2005.
facts.mimas: One crater a third of its own width away from looking exactly like the Death Star.
facts.titania: Uranus's largest moon, half ice half rock, scarred by a 1,500 km canyon.
facts.oberon: Its reddish, crater-pocked face hides an unexplained 11 km peak near the south pole.
facts.miranda: Jumbled chevron terrain and a 20 km cliff suggest it was shattered and re-assembled.
facts.triton: Orbits Neptune backward — the sign of a captured world, not one born in place.
facts.phobos: Spiraling inward toward Mars; in 30-50 million years it will crash or shred into a ring.
facts.deimos: Found six days before its sibling Phobos, and drifting away from Mars, not toward it.
facts.charon: Pluto and Charon orbit a point outside Pluto itself, each always showing the other one face.
facts.ceres: Holds 40% of the asteroid belt's mass, a quarter of it water ice, found in 1801.
facts.eris: 27% more massive than Pluto — the discovery in 2005 that got Pluto demoted.
facts.great_red_spot: A storm wider than Earth, tracked continuously since 1878 and still shrinking.
facts.longship: Clinker-built Viking warship with one square sail of rough wool -- shallow enough to row up rivers.
facts.viking: Norse seafarers and raiders; their word vikingr is rare before the 1100s, mostly seen on runestones.
facts.lanse_aux_meadows: Norse base camp in Newfoundland, tree-ring dated to 1021 CE -- Europe's earliest footprint in the Americas.
facts.castle: Malbork Castle in Poland, finished 1406, is the world's largest brick castle -- walls enclosing 21 hectares.
facts.moat: A defensive ditch around a fortification, dry or water-filled, keeping siege engines off the walls.
facts.drawbridge: A castle's moat-crossing bridge, pivoted at the gatehouse and winched up by chain to seal the entrance shut.
facts.colosseum: Rome's amphitheatre, finished 80 CE, seated up to 80,000 for gladiator bouts and staged animal hunts.
facts.gladiator: Rome's arena fighters; the earliest were prisoners of war, named and armed after the enemies Rome just beat.
facts.great_wall: Ming builders bonded its bricks with mortar of slaked lime and sticky-rice soup -- stronger than lime alone.
facts.caravel: Portuguese ship with a narrow hull and lateen sails, able to sail closer to the wind than a square-rigger.
facts.columbus: Crossed the Atlantic in 1492 on a fleet including two caravels, and insisted for years he had reached Asia.
facts.hardtack: Flour, water, and salt baked into a dense unleavened cracker, dry enough to survive months at sea unspoiled.
facts.hoba: The largest intact meteorite ever found -- a 60-tonne iron-nickel mass a plough struck in Namibia in 1920.
facts.tickle: The cerebellum predicts the feel of your own touch and dampens it, which is why you can't tickle yourself.
facts.sneeze: A nerve reflex fired by nasal irritants; high-speed video has caught its plume carrying 8 meters.
facts.bitumen: Petroleum's heaviest fraction — what's left once everything lighter than 500°C boils away.
facts.archimedes_screw: A helical blade in a tube lifts water as it turns. Traditionally credited to Archimedes, 3rd century BC.
facts.elephant_clock: A sinking float trips a see-saw every half hour, dropping a ball to strike a bell. al-Jazari, 1206.
facts.crankshaft: Turns circular motion into back-and-forth motion, or the reverse. al-Jazari's water-raising pump, 1206.
facts.submarine: A leather-covered wooden hull, rowed underwater by oars sealed through the sides. Drebbel, 1620.
facts.thermostat: Expanding mercury pushes a lever that closes a damper — an early feedback-controlled device. Drebbel, 1620s.
facts.lightning_rod: A grounded iron point gives a stroke somewhere safe to go instead of the building beneath it. Franklin, 1752.
facts.bifocals: Two lenses' halves set in one frame, near vision below and far above. Franklin is generally credited, by 1784.
facts.centrifugal_governor: Spinning flyweights swing outward as speed rises and choke the throttle. Watt, 1788.
facts.heliography: Bitumen hardens where light strikes it; washing off the rest leaves the world's first photo. Niépce, c.1827.
facts.antiseptic_dressing: Cotton soaked in undiluted carbolic acid, packed onto a wound. Lister's first case, 1865.
facts.blasting_cap: A small charge that detonates a bigger one it can't ignite by itself. Nobel adds mercury fulminate, 1867.
facts.automobile: A single-cylinder engine bolted to a three-wheeled carriage — the first car built for sale. Benz, 1885–86.
facts.metal_detector: Two induction coils balance against each other until metal nearby throws them off. Bell, 1881.
facts.tesla_coil: Two coils tuned to the same resonant frequency step a spark-gap pulse up to very high voltage. Tesla, 1891.
facts.ac_induction_motor: A rotating magnetic field drags an unpowered rotor around with it — no brushes needed. Tesla, 1887–88.
facts.autogyro: A propeller pulls it forward while an unpowered rotor autorotates and lifts it. de la Cierva, 1923.
facts.liquid_fuel_rocket: Ethanol and liquid oxygen burn through an alloy nozzle built to survive it. Von Braun's V-2, 1942.
facts.enigma_machine: A keyboard and wired rotors light one of 26 lamps per keystroke, a different letter. Scherbius, 1918.
facts.bombe: Electromechanical drums replicate dozens of Enigma rotor settings at once, ruling most out. Turing, 1939.
facts.mercaptopurine: A purine ring with sulfur where guanine has oxygen — it jams DNA synthesis in dividing cells. Elion, 1953.
facts.hypertext: Text wired with links a reader can jump through, instead of reading straight down the page. Nelson, 1965.
facts.world_wide_web: Berners-Lee married hypertext to the Internet: one naming scheme, one protocol, one markup language. 1989–91.
facts.ichthyosaur: Joseph Anning found the skull in 1811; his sister Mary spent months excavating the rest of the skeleton.
facts.leprosy: Mycobacterium leprae divides so slowly that symptoms can take five years or more to appear.
facts.chaulmoogra_ester: Alice Ball turned chaulmoogra oil's fatty acids into ethyl esters in 1916 — finally soluble enough to inject.
facts.artemisinin: Sweet wormwood's antimalarial compound — heat destroys it, so the extraction has to stay cold.
facts.lamarckism: Lamarck's giraffe: a neck stretched in one lifetime, passed on already lengthened to the next.
facts.abo_blood_group: Mix the wrong two and red cells clump together — why blood gets typed before a transfusion.
facts.waggle_dance: A bee's waggle run points at an angle from vertical equal to the food's angle from the Sun.
facts.book_of_optics: Argued vision happens because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays.
facts.event_horizon_telescope: Linked telescopes worldwide into one Earth-sized dish and imaged a black hole's shadow, 2019.
facts.sapling: A young tree past the seedling stage: its stem has turned from soft and green to properly woody.
facts.cambium: A ring of dividing cells under the bark — it builds new xylem inward and new phloem outward each year.
facts.sapwood: The living outer wood of a trunk, still carrying water up from the roots before it hardens into heartwood.
facts.heartwood: The dead, dark core of an old trunk — chemically toughened sapwood that still braces the tree once it's gone.
facts.cone: A conifer's seed case — it ripens over months, and some species keep it sealed shut on the tree for years.
facts.conifer: Cone-bearing, needle- or scale-leaved, and mostly evergreen — pines, firs, cedars and cypresses among them.
facts.gymnosperm: A seed plant with naked seeds — no fruit wrapped around them, unlike an angiosperm's.
facts.abscission: The layer of cork cells a plant grows across a leaf stalk, which is what actually makes the leaf fall.
facts.deciduous: Sheds its leaves on a seasonal cue rather than keeping them through winter like an evergreen does.
facts.samara: A winged seed shaped like a tiny airfoil — maple and ash both spin theirs down like a helicopter blade.
facts.catkin: A dangling, petal-less flower spike built for wind pollination, not for attracting insects.
facts.larch: A conifer that breaks its own family's rule: it drops its needles every autumn like a broadleaf tree.
facts.cedar: A resinous evergreen conifer with barrel-shaped cones that disintegrate scale by scale on the tree.
facts.juniper: A conifer whose cone scales fuse into a fleshy, berry-like ball — the 'berries' that flavour gin.
facts.holly: Spiny, glossy evergreen leaves and red winter berries — festive to look at, mildly toxic if eaten.
facts.magnolia: An ancient flowering tree — its lineage predates bees, so beetles still do the pollinating.
facts.maple: Winged samara seeds, and in some species sap sweet enough to boil down into syrup.
facts.birch: Thin, papery bark that peels off in horizontal strips, and catkins instead of showy flowers.
facts.beech: Smooth grey bark and 'mast' — oil-rich beechnuts once used to fatten pigs before winter.
facts.elm: Its bark carries the beetle that spreads the fungus behind Dutch elm disease.
facts.eucalyptus: Oil-rich leaves toxic to most browsers — koalas are among the few animals that can stomach them.
facts.baobab: A trunk swollen enough to store up to 120,000 litres of water against the next drought.
facts.banyan: Sends roots straight down from its branches; each one thickens into another trunk until it's a forest.
facts.aspen: Its leaf stalks are flattened sideways, so even a light breeze sets the whole canopy quaking.
facts.rootstock: The rooted half of a graft — swap it and you can dwarf a full-size apple tree without touching the fruit.
facts.scion: The cutting grafted onto a rootstock — every graft of it is a genetic clone of one original tree.
facts.crabapple: Grow an apple from its own seed and you get this: small, sour, and nothing like its parent.
facts.chill_hours: The quota of winter cold a fruit tree must clock up before it will flower properly in spring.
facts.breadfruit: Starchy enough to be a staple food across the Pacific — baked, boiled or fried, never eaten raw.
facts.jackfruit: The largest fruit grown on any tree, up to 55 kg, in the same genus as breadfruit.
facts.lychee: A rind hiding a translucent, sweet aril wrapped around one seed — botanically, a drupe.
facts.rambutan: Lychee's spiky cousin in the soapberry family — its name is just Malay for 'hair.'
facts.longan: Lychee's other cousin, named for the way its black seed shows through the flesh like an eye.
facts.tamarind: A legume tree — its pod fruit is sour enough to season food across three continents.
facts.dragon_fruit: The fruit of a climbing cactus, one that scales trees for support without ever rooting in them.
facts.starfruit: Slice it crosswise and its five ridges turn every piece into a perfect star.
facts.soursop: A relative of the custard apple and cherimoya, with spiny green skin and soft, custardy pulp.
facts.akee: Jamaica's national fruit — and toxic until its own capsule splits open on the tree.
facts.curry_leaf: Fried in hot oil at the start of a dish, which is how its aroma actually gets released.
facts.control_rod: Slides into the reactor core to soak up neutrons and choke off the chain reaction on demand.
facts.nuclear_reactor: The same fission as a bomb, just held on the edge of runaway instead of let loose.
facts.corium: Chernobyl's 'elephant's foot' — fuel, control rods and structure melted into one radioactive lava.
facts.nuclear_power_plant: The reactor never spins anything itself — it just boils water for a turbine to do that.
facts.heat_shield_tile: Silica fiber fired so light it's 90% empty space, yet it shrugged off 1,260°C on re-entry.
facts.tunnel_boring_machine: A rotating steel cutterhead chews the tunnel face while hydraulic rams shove the machine forward.
facts.ct_scanner: An X-ray tube and detectors spin around the patient; a computer stacks the angles into 3D.
facts.hydroelectric_dam: Water drops through a penstock into a turbine — a whole river's fall, spent turning one shaft.
facts.stand_mixer: Named for its beater's own motion — it spins on its own axis while orbiting the bowl, like a planet.
facts.swashplate: A tilting plate that changes each rotor blade's pitch differently through the turn — how a helicopter steers.
facts.electric_car: No engine, no gearbox, no idle — a battery and a motor with full torque from a dead stop.
facts.icebreaker: Doesn't climb the ice and crush it — a reinforced bow bends and breaks it under the hull at speed.
facts.snow_groomer: A tracked tiller combs the piste into corduroy, winched up the steepest slopes on a cable.
facts.turboprop: A gas turbine that barely bothers with jet thrust — a gearbox sends nearly all its power to a propeller.
facts.abrams_tank: A tank engine borrowed from an idea more common in helicopters — a 1,500hp gas turbine, not a diesel.
facts.tiger_tank: Flat, vertical armor plates and an 88mm gun — no sloping, unlike its own stablemate the Panther.
facts.radar: Times a radio echo's round trip — half the delay, times the speed of light, is the range.
facts.stealth_aircraft: Faceted panels fling radar's echo away from the receiver instead of straight back at it.
facts.rivet: Driven red-hot through two plates and hammered into a second head, it only clamps tight once it cools.
facts.ocean_liner: Watertight bulkheads split the hull into compartments — Titanic's simply didn't reach high enough.
facts.elliptical_wing: The lift distribution with the least induced drag of any wing planform — the Spitfire's signature shape.
facts.box: A rigid container, traditionally built from flat wooden panels joined edge to edge and nailed.
facts.veil: A piece of fine, often sheer cloth worn to cover the head or face, traditionally woven in silk.
facts.socrates: Athenian philosopher executed in 399 BCE for impiety and corrupting the youth; wrote nothing himself.
facts.plato: Student of Socrates; founded The Academy in Athens in 387 BCE, Europe's first university.
facts.aristotle: Tutored the young Alexander the Great and founded The Lyceum, teaching logic, biology, and physics.
facts.descartes: French philosopher and mathematician who united algebra and geometry into the coordinate system.
facts.locke: English philosopher who argued the mind at birth is a blank slate, filled only by experience.
facts.kant: German philosopher who argued morality rests on unbreakable, universal rules reason gives itself.
facts.wittgenstein: Austrian philosopher of language and logic who gave away his fortune to teach village schoolchildren.
facts.beauvoir: French existentialist philosopher and author of The Second Sex, a founding text of modern feminism.
facts.confucius: Chinese philosopher and teacher whose sayings on virtue and reciprocity fill the Analects.
facts.gautama_buddha: Born Siddhartha Gautama, a prince who renounced his palace and, on reaching enlightenment, became the Buddha.
facts.avicenna: Persian polymath and physician whose Canon of Medicine was a standard European textbook for 600 years.
facts.plutarch: Greek-born biographer and priest at the Delphic oracle who wrote the paired Lives of Greeks and Romans.
facts.epicurus: Athenian philosopher who taught in a garden school, The Garden, that unusually admitted women as students.
facts.searle: American philosopher who devised the Chinese Room argument against machine understanding in 1980.
facts.turing: British mathematician who laid computing's theoretical foundation and devised a test for machine intelligence.
facts.foot: British philosopher who devised the runaway-tram dilemma known as the trolley problem in 1967.
facts.rawls: American philosopher who devised the 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment for choosing a just society.
facts.aquinas: Dominican friar and theologian who argued from motion to an unmoved first mover he called God.
facts.heidegger: German philosopher whose Being and Time argued the meaning of Being is inseparable from time and mortality.
facts.sartre: French existentialist who argued human existence precedes essence — we exist first, then define ourselves.
facts.camus: French-Algerian philosopher who argued we must imagine Sisyphus happy, embracing the absurdity of existence.
facts.arendt: German-American theorist who covered Eichmann's 1961 trial and coined 'the banality of evil.'
facts.foucault: French philosopher who used the all-seeing prison tower called the Panopticon as a metaphor for modern power.
facts.derrida: French philosopher who coined 'différance,' a difference invisible in speech and legible only in writing.
facts.popper: Austrian-British philosopher who argued a theory counts as scientific only if a single test could disprove it.
facts.kuhn: American philosopher of science who argued science advances through revolutionary paradigm shifts.
facts.chomsky: American linguist and critic who argued mass media manufactures public consent for state and corporate power.
facts.peter_singer: Australian philosopher whose 1975 book Animal Liberation founded the modern animal rights movement.
facts.william_of_ockham: English Franciscan friar remembered for the principle that the simplest sufficient explanation is best.
facts.ayn_rand: Russian-American novelist who founded Objectivism, prizing rational self-interest over altruism.
facts.edward_said: Palestinian-American scholar whose Orientalism argued Western depictions of 'the East' served empire.
facts.habermas: German philosopher who traced the modern public sphere of reasoned debate to 18th-century coffeehouses.
facts.isaiah_berlin: Latvian-British philosopher who distinguished freedom from restraint from freedom to control one's own fate.
facts.adorno: German philosopher who coined 'culture industry' for mass media manufacturing passive, uncritical consumers.
facts.marcuse: German-American philosopher who argued consumer society manufactures false needs to suppress dissent.
facts.levinas: Lithuanian-French philosopher who argued ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter, before any reasoning.
facts.merleau_ponty: French phenomenologist who rejected Descartes' mind-body split, arguing consciousness is always embodied.
facts.quine: American logician who argued translating between languages is fundamentally indeterminate.
facts.barthes: French theorist whose essay 'The Death of the Author' argued a text's meaning outlives its writer's intent.
facts.fanon: Martinican psychiatrist whose Black Skin, White Masks examined colonialism's psychological toll.
facts.arne_naess: Norwegian philosopher who coined 'deep ecology,' urging humans to see themselves as part of nature.
facts.giordano_bruno: Italian friar burned at the stake in 1600 for insisting the universe is infinite, filled with countless suns.
facts.gilbert_ryle: British philosopher who mocked Cartesian dualism as belief in 'the ghost in the machine.'
facts.j_l_austin: J. L. Austin, 1911-1960, who noticed that some sentences do not describe anything — they do something.
facts.rene_girard: French thinker who traced religion and violence to a 'scapegoat mechanism' uniting a group against one victim.
facts.daniel_dennett: American philosopher who argued there is no single place in the brain where consciousness happens.
facts.martha_nussbaum: American philosopher who, with Amartya Sen, developed the 'capabilities approach' to justice and flourishing.
facts.hypatia: Alexandrian mathematician and astronomer who taught astrolabe-making and was murdered by a mob in 415 CE.
facts.sodium_hydroxide: Caustic soda. Dissolving it in water alone gives off enough heat to bring the water to a boil.
facts.potassium_hydroxide: Caustic potash. Its soaps stay soft where sodium hydroxide's go hard.
facts.calcium_hydroxide: Slaked lime, dissolved as limewater — a jar left open clouds within minutes, coated by the CO2 it tests for.
facts.ethane: The second-biggest thing in natural gas after methane, mostly there to be cracked back into ethylene.
facts.hydrogen_peroxide: Kept in dark bottles for a reason: light alone is enough to break it back down into water and oxygen.
facts.silver_nitrate: Darkens skin black over hours as organic matter reduces the silver — the same stain old election inks left on voters.
facts.potassium_acetate: E261. Airports spray it on runways instead of chloride salts — just as effective, far gentler on the concrete.
facts.zinc_chloride: So hygroscopic a jar left open pulls enough water from the air to dissolve itself into a puddle by morning.
facts.hydrochloric_acid: Hydrogen chloride dissolved in water — commercial grades run up to 38%, about as strong as it ships.
facts.sodium_carbonate: Washing soda, Na2CO3 — the alkali glassmakers have used to lower sand's melting point for millennia.
facts.aluminium_sulfate: Al2(SO4)3 — dumped into cloudy water by the tonne, it drags suspended grit down into a settleable clump.
facts.ammonium_phosphate: (NH4)3PO4 and its relatives — most of the world's phosphate fertiliser starts as this salt.
facts.carbon_tetrachloride: CCl4 — a non-flammable solvent banned once its liver toxicity and ozone damage were understood.
facts.magnesium_phosphate: Mg3(PO4)2 and its relatives — magnesium's salts with phosphate, all on the FDA's food-safe list.
facts.sodium_sulfate: Na2SO4 — first isolated in 1625 by Glauber, who named it sal mirabilis, the miraculous salt.
facts.ammonium_bicarbonate: NH4HCO3 — old-world 'hartshorn', a leavener that gasses off completely and leaves no aftertaste.
facts.ammonium_chloride: NH4Cl, sal ammoniac — ninety percent of it becomes nitrogen fertiliser for rice and wheat.
facts.calcium_nitrate: Ca(NO3)2 — pulls water from the air so eagerly it needs sealed storage; first made in Norway, 1905.
facts.barium_nitrate: Ba(NO3)2 — an oxidiser that burns with a hard green flame, and toxic if swallowed.
facts.calcium_acetate: Ca(CH3COO)2, E263 — vinegar poured straight onto limestone or eggshell, made this way for millennia.
facts.phosphoric_acid: H3PO4 — the tang in cola. Ninety percent of the world's output becomes fertiliser instead.
facts.sodium_phosphate: Na3PO4 — strongly alkaline in water, used as everything from a food buffer to a heavy-duty degreaser.
facts.chromium_oxide: Chrome green, and the reason chromium itself does not rust — a film one molecule thick that heals itself.
facts.manganese_dioxide: Half a million tonnes a year go into one job: soaking up electrons inside an ordinary dry-cell battery.
facts.rhubarb: The edible part is only the leaf stalk. The leaf blade itself is poisonous — oxalic acid.
facts.hydrogen_bromide: Hydrogen and bromine, combined between 200 and 400°C, usually over a platinum catalyst.
facts.sodium_citrate: Citric acid neutralised into a calm, food-safe salt — E331, and the anticoagulant in a bag of donated blood.
facts.sodium_nitrite: NaNO2, E250 — the curing salt that turns cured meat pink and holds back botulinum spores.
facts.sulfate: SO4²⁻ — one sulfur, four oxygens, the ion sulfuric acid leaves behind and acid rain deposits.
facts.barium_sulfide: BaS — calcined straight from the elements, and it glows in the dark after exposure to light.
facts.barium_carbonate: Witherite. Soluble enough in stomach acid that it used to be sold as rat poison.
facts.hydrogen_sulfate: HSO4⁻ — sulfuric acid's first proton gone, and sulfate's second still to lose.
facts.permanganate: MnO4⁻, deep purple in solution — the ion a titration is judged by, because its own colour is the endpoint.
facts.silver_phosphate: Ag3PO4 — a yellow precipitate, light-sensitive like silver's other insoluble salts.
facts.silver_oxide: Ag2O — dark brown, and what a silver-oxide button battery actually runs on at the cathode.
facts.ammonium_bromide: NH4Br — a straightforward gas-phase handshake between ammonia and hydrogen bromide.
facts.calcium_phosphate: Ca3(PO4)2 — the anticaking agent in powdered spices, and the mineral half of bone once a hydroxide joins it.
facts.sodium_chromate: Na2CrO4, bright yellow — chromium(III) oxidised and pulled into alkaline solution.
facts.dichromate: Cr2O7²⁻, orange — the same chromium as yellow chromate, just caught on the acid side of a pH swing.
facts.fructose: Fruit sugar — the sweetest common sugar, and glucose's isomer, atom for atom.
facts.potassium_cyanide: KCN — colourless, sugar-like, and the reagent gold mining runs on to pull metal out of crushed ore.
facts.zinc_phosphate: Zn3(PO4)2 — the conversion coating etched onto bare steel before primer goes on.
facts.para_dichlorobenzene: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene — the mothball smell, and benzene with two hydrogens swapped for chlorine.
facts.oxalate: C2O4²⁻ — the ion rhubarb leaves and spinach both carry enough of to matter.
facts.potassium_bicarbonate: KHCO3 — potassium's answer to baking soda, and the base of Purple-K fire-extinguisher powder.
facts.potassium_hypochlorite: KOCl — the original Eau de Javel, before sodium hypochlorite replaced it as the cheaper bleach.
facts.potassium_nitrite: KNO2, E249 — potassium's own curing salt, distinct from potassium nitrate despite the name.
facts.moraine: A glacier works like a conveyor belt: it carries stone for miles and drops it all at the melting end.
facts.breccia: Sharp-edged rock rubble, cemented in place. Nothing wore the corners round, because it never travelled.
facts.arkose: Feldspar-rich sandstone. Feldspar this fresh only survives burial that outraces the rain that would rot it.
facts.graywacke: Sand, mud and rock scraps dumped together by one turbid underwater current, with no time left to sort them.
facts.tillite: Till, buried and hardened. Poorly sorted, striated stones with no layering — a glacier's leftovers, in rock.
