facts.chert: Microcrystalline quartz. Ocean-floor ooze of diatom and radiolarian skeletons, slowly turned to solid stone.
facts.ooid: A grain rolled again and again through shallow, chalky water until it grew its own concentric rind.
facts.banded_iron_formation: Iron oxide and chert, laminated in bands — a record of the exact stretch of time oxygen first filled the sea.
facts.anhydrite: Gypsum with the water baked out. It grabs the water straight back the moment it touches any.
facts.oil_shale: Shale packed with kerogen that never got hot enough to finish cooking into petroleum.
facts.phosphorite: Fish bone and scale, concentrated by upwelling into phosphate-rich rock — fertiliser's raw material.
facts.stoneware: Fired hard enough to hold liquid without a glaze.
facts.necktie: Croatian mercenaries wore knotted neckerchiefs in 1630s France; the French called them cravates.
facts.toes: Fourteen small bones in one foot are just for the toes — two in the big toe, three in each other.
facts.toilet_paper: Perforated so a sheet tears free without scissors — patented in Albany, New York, in 1883.
facts.toilet: An S-shaped pipe traps a plug of standing water that seals the drain against sewer gas. Cumming, 1775.
facts.saliva: About 99% water; the rest is mucus and the amylase that starts breaking down starch in the mouth.
facts.tongue: A muscular hydrostat, like an elephant's trunk — no bones, shaped entirely by its own muscle.
facts.bristle: Coarse hair cut from a boar's back and neck, stiff enough to hold its shape packed in a tuft.
facts.toothbrush: William Addis carved the first mass-produced one from a bone handle and boar bristles in 1780.
facts.toy: Egyptian 'paddle dolls' buried with the dead had hair of black Nile-mud beads threaded on string.
facts.towel: The loop pile that soaks up water is called terry — from Turkish hammam cloth, 17th-century Bursa.
facts.tractor: Bolting an engine onto a plough's running gear let one machine pull what used to take a team of horses.
facts.train: A locomotive coupled to any number of unpowered wagons — the wagons don't move themselves.
facts.triangle: A steel rod bent into a triangle with one corner left open, so it rings without a fixed pitch.
facts.tricycle: A third wheel trades a bicycle's need for balance for standing stability. Farffler's hand-cranked chair, 1680.
facts.stomach: Its own lining constantly makes the mucus that keeps stomach acid from digesting the stomach itself.
facts.umbrella: Folding steel ribs replaced heavy, hard-to-fold wood or whalebone frames. Samuel Fox, 1852.
facts.underwear: Linen underclothes go back as far as flax has been woven — worn next to skin for millennia.
facts.vacuum_cleaner: James Spangler's 1907 motor spun a fan and packed dust into a pillowcase sewn onto the machine.
facts.toy_wagon: Antonio Pasin, an Italian immigrant, hand-built his first pull-wagon in a one-room New York shop, 1917.
facts.washcloth: A terrycloth square about 12 by 12 inches — a towel scaled down to fit one hand.
facts.watch: A coiled mainspring replaced hanging weights, letting a clock's movement finally shrink to pocket size.
facts.whistle: A trapped pea rattling inside the chamber breaks the airstream into a trill a smooth tube can't make.
facts.window: Small triangular nails called glazier's points pin the pane into its frame before the putty seals it.
facts.yoyo: A string looped, not tied, around the axle is what lets it 'sleep' and spin. Flores, 1928.
facts.zipper: Gideon Sundback's interlocking brass teeth, patented 1917, finally made the fastener reliable.
facts.iron_ii_sulfate: FeSO4, pale green crystals also called copperas or green vitriol — dissolve iron in acid instead of burning it in chlorine, and you get the +2 salt instead of the +3 one.
facts.hydrogen_cyanide: HCN — a gas with a faint bitter-almond smell, except that about half of people carry a genetic trait that means they can't smell it at all.
facts.methyl_formate: The simplest ester there is, HCOOCH3 — light enough to boil at just 32°C, and industry's usual route in to formic acid.
facts.sodium_chlorate: NaClO3, chlorine pushed into two different oxidation states in the same reaction. It's potent enough as a total weedkiller that several countries now restrict who can buy it.
facts.chlorine_dioxide: ClO2, an unstable yellow-green gas that can't be shipped or stored — anyone who uses it industrially has to make it fresh, on site, as needed.
facts.sodium_perchlorate: NaClO4, chlorine pushed all the way to its highest possible oxidation state, +7. Its ammonium cousin is the oxidiser packed into solid rocket boosters.
facts.barium_chlorate: Ba(ClO3)2 burns with a deep green firework flame — the same barium that shows up on an X-ray also colours the light when it burns.
facts.barium_chlorite: Ba(ClO2)2 — chlorine's rarest common oxidation state, +3, and really only useful as the one practical door into chlorous acid.
facts.nitrous_acid: HNO2 — too unstable to bottle. It only exists in cold, dilute solution before it falls apart into nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide and water.
facts.hypochlorous_acid: HOCl — the molecule actually doing the disinfecting in chlorinated water and in bleach. Your own white blood cells make it too, to kill bacteria.
facts.chlorous_acid: HClO2, the least stable of chlorine's four common oxoacids and the only one with no industrial use of its own — its salts, the chlorites, are what people actually want.
facts.chloric_acid: HClO3 stays stable only in solution below about 30% strength; push it more concentrated than that and it starts decomposing on its own.
facts.perchloric_acid: HClO4 — one of the strongest acids there is, and hot concentrated solutions of it are such a powerful oxidiser that labs handle it only inside a dedicated, water-washed fume hood.
facts.phosphorous_acid: H3PO3 — despite the name, only two of its three hydrogens are acidic. The third is bonded straight to the phosphorus atom and never lets go.
facts.oxalic_acid: Two carboxyl groups bonded straight to each other with no carbon chain between — the simplest dicarboxylic acid there is, and the same compound that makes rhubarb leaves dangerous.
facts.boric_acid: B(OH)3 — mild enough to have been used as an eyewash, yet sold in the same aisle as roach powder. The dose and the target make all the difference.
facts.silicic_acid: What quartz slowly becomes in water: SiO2 + H2O ⇌ H2SiO3, a reaction Berzelius worked out in the early 1800s and still how silicon ends up dissolved in every river and ocean.
facts.ammonium_hydroxide: What household ammonia actually is — ammonia gas dissolved in water, not a hydroxide compound anyone has ever isolated pure.
facts.magnesium_hydroxide: Mg(OH)2 suspended in water is milk of magnesia; the mineral form of the same exact compound is called brucite.
facts.barium_hydroxide: Ba(OH)2 — one of the few strong bases that isn't an alkali metal hydroxide, made simply by dropping barium oxide into water.
facts.aluminum_hydroxide: Al(OH)3 is amphoteric — it can react as either an acid or a base — and water-treatment plants exploit exactly that to drag suspended dirt out of drinking water.
facts.ferrous_hydroxide: Fe(OH)2 is a pale green solid that doesn't stay pale green for long — open air oxidises it to the reddish-brown +3 hydroxide within minutes.
facts.ferric_hydroxide: What's usually meant by ‘ferric hydroxide’ is really iron(III) oxide-hydroxide, a reddish-brown gel — and the same compound rust eventually becomes.
facts.zinc_hydroxide: Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric like aluminium's hydroxide: too much of the same lye that precipitates it will turn around and redissolve it as zincate.
facts.lithium_hydroxide: LiOH scrubs carbon dioxide more efficiently pound for pound than any other alkali hydroxide, which is why it's what's stocked on a spacecraft, not sodium hydroxide.
facts.hydroiodic_acid: The strongest of the hydrohalic acids: iodine holds on to its hydrogen more weakly than any other halogen does, so in water it lets go of it most completely.
facts.formic_acid: Named for the Latin for ant — first isolated in 1671 by distilling a large pile of crushed ants, and it's still exactly what a red ant's sting injects.
facts.hydrofluoric_acid: Diluted in water it barely stings on contact — which is exactly what makes it so dangerous: skin damage from a splash can take hours to become obvious.
facts.hydrocyanic_acid: Prussic acid, to the Victorians — a dilute water solution of hydrogen cyanide, lethal at a dose small enough that some people can smell it coming and half can't smell it at all.
facts.methylamine: The simplest amine there is, and it smells distinctly of rotting fish — the smell ammonia takes on once carbon gets involved.
facts.pyridine: A six-membered ring like benzene, but with one carbon swapped for nitrogen — and unlike benzene, it mixes with water in any proportion.
facts.nickel_nitrate: Green crystals from a green solution — nickel salts almost always are. Dissolve the oxide in nitric acid and this is what comes out.
facts.sodium_dichromate: Orange, corrosive, and a confirmed carcinogen -- the hexavalent chromium chemistry behind Hinkley, California's Erin Brockovich case.
facts.tartaric_acid: Crystallises out of wine barrels as 'wine stone' — cream of tartar's parent acid.
facts.zinc_iodide: Zinc and iodine won't touch each other dry at room temperature — a drop of water as catalyst is enough to set the reaction boiling.
facts.aluminum_bromide: Aluminium foil dropped into liquid bromine ignites on contact — the same exothermic trick that makes aluminium chloride.
facts.barium_peroxide: Heat barium oxide in air to 500C and it grabs a second oxygen; past 820C it lets go again.
facts.sodium_percarbonate: Soda ash holding a molecule of hydrogen peroxide -- it lets go the moment it hits water, the trick behind oxygen bleach.
facts.nickel_acetate: Nickel's oxide dissolved in vinegar's acid — the same green salt whether it starts from the oxide, the hydroxide or the carbonate.
facts.sodium_sulfite: Sulfur dioxide caught by soda ash before it can escape — the industrial route runs through carbonate rather than the lab's caustic soda.
facts.sodium_thiosulfate: Photographers call it hypo — it dissolves the unexposed silver halide right off a print, fixing the image in place.
facts.acetaldehyde: Your own liver makes this from every drink you take — it's a big part of why a hangover feels like poisoning.
facts.mannitol: Brown seaweed stores up to a fifth of its dry weight as this sugar alcohol — most of the world's supply is still pressed straight out of it.
facts.styrene: Named for storax, the sweetgum resin an apothecary first isolated it from in 1839 — he also watched it slowly turn to hard rubber sitting in a jar.
facts.polystyrene: Eduard Simon's 1839 jar of styrene hardened on its own — air, light and time were the entire recipe for the world's first sample of this.
facts.tetrachloroethylene: Perc, the dry-cleaner's solvent -- chlorine run over hydrocarbons at high heat, and a probable carcinogen.
facts.potassium_iodate: Iodine disproportionates in hot potassium hydroxide — part climbs to iodate, part falls back to iodide, and the iodate is what fortifies salt.
facts.lead_acetate: 'Sugar of lead' — sweet enough that Romans reduced wine in lead pots for the taste, and it poisoned them for exactly that reason.
facts.potassium_thiocyanate: Fuse potassium cyanide with sulfur and the cyanide's lethal reputation mostly stays behind — thiocyanate is a far gentler ion.
facts.maltose: Named for malt, where it was found — beta-amylase clips starch two glucose units at a time and this is what comes off.
facts.dinitrogen_pentoxide: The cleanest lab route skips heat entirely: ozone oxidises nitrogen dioxide straight to this — which then turns around and destroys more ozone.
facts.ferrocyanide: Six cyanide ions clamped so tightly around one iron atom that the complex can barely release any — a cage that traps the danger along with the ion.
facts.potassium_ferrocyanide: Once made by fusing scrap iron with burnt hooves and horn; today built from cyanide and iron instead, then given its potassium.
facts.xenon_difluoride: Seal xenon and fluorine gas in a glass bulb and leave it in sunlight -- even a cloudy day works. No furnace needed.
facts.lead_iodide: The 'golden rain' demonstration: mix dissolved lead and iodide and hexagonal gold crystals fall out as it cools.
facts.bug: A true bug (Hemiptera) skips the pupa stage — its nymph hatches already looking like a wingless adult.
facts.bus: Daimler's 1898 double-decker, one of the first motor buses, put 20 passengers on a car's own drivetrain.
facts.button: Buttons were sewn on as ornaments for centuries before the buttonhole gave them a job to do.
facts.cd: 1.2mm of injection-moulded polycarbonate under an aluminium layer thinner than foil, read by a laser.
facts.cereal: Kellogg patented the toasted-flake process in 1891 and had Corn Flakes on shelves under that name by 1895.
facts.chair: Ancient Egyptian chairs were carved wood — the higher your rank, the taller the one you sat in.
facts.circle: Every point on it sits exactly one radius from the centre — the one rule that defines the whole shape.
facts.clown: Joseph Grimaldi painted his face white in the early 1800s, and most clowns still follow the template he set.
facts.comb: Tortoiseshell combs were once common enough that the trade helped push the hawksbill turtle toward extinction.
facts.cookie: Ruth Wakefield's 1930s Toll House recipe expected chopped chocolate to melt into the dough. It held its shape.
facts.cracker: Jonathan Dodgson Carr's 1836 'water biscuit' rolled the same ship's hardtack dough far thinner and saltier.
facts.crayon: Encaustic painters in ancient Egypt bound pigment into hot beeswax millennia before the first wax crayon.
facts.crown: Soft enough to hammer cold and shape without cracking — which is why gold turns up in crowns worldwide.
facts.cup: Most cheap, mass-produced glassware from the mid-1800s on was pressed into a mould, never blown.
facts.cupcake: The name is literal: early cupcakes were baked one to a pottery cup instead of one big cake to a pan.
facts.curtain: England's earliest window coverings were leather panels threaded on iron rods, before wool took over.
facts.diaper: The word named a woven diamond-pattern cloth for three centuries before it ever meant a baby garment.
facts.dinosaur: The first scientifically recognised dinosaur eggs turned up in Mongolia in 1923, confirming a reptile hunch.
facts.door: Before hinges, a door pivoted on a wooden peg turning in a stone socket worn smooth by centuries of swinging.
facts.dolphin: A toothed whale that hunts by sound — clicks focused through a fat-filled 'melon' in the forehead.
facts.doughnut: Deep-fried instead of baked — the hot oil is what browns the crust and cooks the dough through in minutes.
facts.dress: One piece, not two: a bodice stitched to a skirt so the whole garment hangs from the torso together.
facts.dresser: A table built for one job, the toilette, with a mirror bolted or folded into it since the mid-1700s.
facts.drum: A pot with a skin stretched over the mouth — goblet drums like it turn up in Sumerian finds from 1100 BCE.
facts.ear: A cartilage funnel out front, and hair cells deep inside that turn sound into an actual electrical signal.
facts.greasepaint: Zinc-white pigment bound in lard — Carl Baudin's 19th-century stage recipe still underlies clown makeup.
facts.acetone: Fermented, not just distilled — a WWI-era bacterium turned sugar into the acetone cordite production needed.
facts.bisphenol_a: Two phenols and one acetone, acid-catalysed together — the 'A' in the name is literally for acetone.
facts.phosgene: The industrial reagent behind a lot of ordinary plastic is also the deadliest gas of the First World War.
facts.polycarbonate: About a billion kilograms of it a year, almost all made by linking BPA into chains with phosgene.
facts.thymol: Thyme's own essential oil, steam-distilled out — once a hookworm treatment, now in mouthwash.
facts.bromothymol_blue: A pH indicator: yellow below 6.0, green near neutral, blue above 7.6.
facts.ammonium_iodide: Ammonia's salt of hydroiodic acid — taken as a dietary supplement when iodine runs short.
facts.ammonium_nitrite: So unstable it is never stored pure — it decomposes to nitrogen gas and water at room temperature.
facts.bromate: BrO3-, a suspected carcinogen strict enough to have forced a UK recall of bottled water.
facts.dinitrogen_trioxide: N2O3, deep blue as a liquid or solid — but stable only below -21°C before it falls back apart.
facts.ethylene_oxide: Reactive enough to sterilise a hospital's plastic syringes — carcinogenic for the same reason.
facts.ethylene_glycol: Sweet enough to poison a pet that finds it first — the antifreeze that drops water's freezing point by 45°C.
facts.nickel_sulfate: Turquoise crystals, and the single most common cause of a positive nickel-allergy patch test.
facts.iodide: Iodine reduced by one electron — the form the human thyroid actually takes it up in.
facts.potassium_sulfite: E225. First isolated in the early 1700s, and known for a while as Stahl's sulphureous salt.
facts.silver_carbonate: Precipitates colourless and turns yellow within minutes — nothing about it stays as first made.
facts.sodium_amide: A base strong enough to pull a proton straight off an alkyne — and violent with water.
facts.sodium_nitride: Falls back apart into sodium metal and nitrogen gas almost as readily as it is made.
facts.sodium_cyanide: The salt that dissolves gold straight out of crushed ore — and a dose under a gram can be fatal.
facts.strontium_nitrate: Burns pure enough to give fireworks and road flares their deep, characteristic red.
facts.bleach: Chlorine gas run into cold lye — the industrial route behind nearly every bottle sold as bleach.
facts.aluminum_fluoride: Stirred into molten alumina, it drops the smelting bath's melting point by over 1,000°C.
facts.butanoic_acid: Rancid butter's exact smell — dogs catch it at 10 parts per billion, far below what people notice.
facts.lithium_carbonate: Tarnish lithium leaves in damp air — and, separately, a mood stabiliser shown to cut suicide risk by 87%.
facts.lithium_phosphate: What precipitates out feeds straight into lithium iron phosphate battery cathodes.
facts.hypobromous_acid: The compound that actually does the disinfecting in a bromine-treated hot tub.
facts.hypoiodous_acid: As hypoiodite, the oxidiser your own white blood cells make to use iodine as a weapon on pathogens.
facts.rhyolite: Granite's chemistry, chilled fast at the surface — the most silica-rich lava there is.
facts.andesite: Named for the Andes. Its silica content is close to the average of Earth's whole continental crust.
facts.dacite: The rock that domed up in Mount St. Helens's crater after 1980: lava too viscous to flow far.
facts.diorite: Granite and gabbro's compositional midpoint -- a coarse-grained igneous rock the Ancient Egyptians prized for hard, dark statuary that granite tools alone could barely shape.
facts.gabbro: Basalt's slow-cooled twin: same melt, same minerals, just given time to grow visible crystals.
facts.syenite: Almost granite, but the melt ran out of free silica before quartz could form. Named for Syene, old Aswan.
facts.peridotite: Over 40% olivine — the commonest rock in Earth's mantle, and diamond's ride up from in kimberlite.
facts.dunite: Over 90% olivine, peridotite taken almost as far as it goes. Named in 1859 for Dun Mountain, New Zealand.
facts.komatiite: Lava so hot — up to 1,600°C — it flowed like water. Nearly all of it is Archean, laid down when Earth's mantle ran hotter.
facts.anorthosite: 90–100% plagioclase feldspar, floated together because it's lighter than the melt around it. The Moon's highlands are the same rock.
facts.pegmatite: Granite's minerals given a watery, low-viscosity residue to grow in. A pegmatite beryl crystal from Madagascar reached 18 metres.
facts.perlite: Obsidian that absorbed water over geologic time. Flash-heated past 850°C, the trapped water turns to steam and it puffs up to 16x its size.
facts.tuff: Compacted volcanic ash, soft enough to carve. Rome's Servian Wall and every moai on Easter Island are cut from it.
facts.xenolith: A chunk of older rock, swallowed whole by rising magma before it could melt — a free sample of rock from miles underground.
facts.porphyry: Big crystals frozen mid-growth in a much finer matrix. Rome reserved a deep purple variety, quarried in Egypt, for emperors alone.
facts.potassium_chlorate: KClO3. A powerful oxidizer — the sensitizer packed into a match head, not the strip it's struck against.
facts.hypochlorite: ClO⁻. Chlorine dumped into cold lye disproportionates into this and plain chloride, all in one step.
facts.hydrazine: N2H4. Reacts with certain oxidizers on contact, no spark needed — why spacecraft thrusters run on it.
facts.acetamide: Vinegar's acid with an amide swapped in for the -OH. Molten, it dissolves almost anything.
facts.sodium_silicate: Water glass. Sand fused with an alkali gives a syrupy solution that bonds cardboard and detergent granules.
facts.potassium_chromate: K2CrO4, bright yellow. One roasting step turns chromium's harmless green oxide hexavalent.
facts.zinc_sulfate: ZnSO4. A dietary supplement, a fungicide and a textile mordant, all the same white zinc salt.
facts.chromic_acid: H2CrO4 in solution. Acidify a chromate far enough and it protonates all the way to this.
facts.methyl_acetate: The smallest common ester of acetic acid — fruity, fast-evaporating nail polish remover base.
facts.dimethyl_sulfide: The sulfur smell of the sea and of boiled cabbage. Algae make it by the megatonne.
facts.dimethyl_sulfoxide: DMSO. Crosses skin so readily that whatever is dissolved in it comes along for the ride.
facts.hexane: C6H14. Boils at 69°C, the window refiners cut it out of crude oil in to leach oil from soybeans.
facts.eugenol: 72 to 90 percent of clove oil is this one molecule — most of why cloves smell the way they do.
facts.potassium_bitartrate: Cream of tartar. Crystallizes out of grape juice as it ferments — "wine diamonds" in the cask.
facts.sodium_potassium_tartrate: Rochelle salt — one of the first materials found to be piezoelectric, making its own voltage.
facts.hexamine: Methenamine. Burns clean, no soot or puddled fuel — why camp stoves use little tablets of it.
facts.phosphorus_pentachloride: PCl5. Reacts violently with water, tearing itself back apart into phosphoric acid and hydrochloric acid.
facts.potassium_oxide: K2O. Fertilizer labels report potassium content as if it were all this, though barely any is.
facts.potassium_phosphate: E340. A sodium-free stand-in for trisodium phosphate, buffering cereal, sauce and cheese pH.
facts.silver_acetate: Silver paired with vinegar's acid. In gum or lozenges, it turns smoke metallic-tasting to deter smokers.
facts.ankle: A hinge where the shin bones meet the talus — the only true mortise-and-tenon joint in the body.
facts.arm: Humerus above the elbow, radius and ulna below, muscle wrapped around all three.
facts.baby: Newborn to about age one — 'infant', before the word has to share the job with anything else.
facts.bag: Cloth or hide folded at the edges and cinched shut with a cord of the same fibre.
facts.bagel: Boiled 60 to 90 seconds before it ever sees an oven. That's the whole trick.
facts.backpack: A bag that traded its drawstring for two straps and moved the load onto the shoulders.
facts.balloon: Michael Faraday made the first rubber ones in 1824 — to hold hydrogen for lectures, not parties.
facts.ball: Mesoamerican players whipped latex with morning-glory vine sap — sticky sap, turned into real bounce.
facts.barn: Old English for 'barley house'. The job never changed: keep the harvest dry.
facts.baseball_bat: Turned on a lathe from one solid billet — ash for a century, maple since 1997.
facts.bathtub: Kohler's foundry enamelled cast-iron horse troughs after an 1880 fire. Flip the ears into a rim.
facts.bed: Medieval mattresses were wool, feathers or hair stuffed onto a wood frame, off the drafty floor.
facts.belt: Leather bends, folds and cinches tight without tearing — why it beat cloth as the standard strap.
facts.bird: Feathers and a toothless, horn-covered beak, on every one of the roughly 11,000 living species.
facts.blanket: Wool is the classic fill — thick, warm cloth on its own, long before cotton or synthetics joined in.
facts.building_block: Birch takes a fine, splinter-free polish once it's sanded — safe corners for a toddler's hands.
facts.boot: The only real difference from a shoe is height: enough leather to cover the ankle, sometimes the knee.
facts.bowl: A calabash gourd, dried hard and split in half. Most of the world used exactly this before pottery.
facts.bridge: A clapper bridge is nothing but a flat slab of stone laid across two piers — engineering by omission.
facts.broom: A besom: twigs bound to a handle. English kept the name long after brooms stopped being the plant.
facts.brush: Fibres tied to a handle — split palm leaf in ancient Egypt, plant fibre or animal hair ever since.
facts.bubble: Soap cuts water's surface tension enough for a puff of air to stretch it a micrometre thin.
facts.bucket: A cooper's trade scaled down: staves bent into a cylinder, cinched tight with a metal hoop.
facts.dwarf_planet: Round under its own gravity like a planet, but it hasn't cleared its neighbourhood — the 2006 line.
facts.kuiper_belt: A disc of icy bodies beyond Neptune, running from about 30 out to 50 astronomical units.
facts.oort_cloud: A shell of icy leftovers flung outward by the giant planets, reaching perhaps 100,000 AU from the Sun.
facts.great_dark_spot: A storm on Neptune the size of Earth, photographed by Voyager 2 in 1989 — and gone by 1994.
facts.tidal_locking: Why the Moon always shows Earth the same face — nobody saw the far side until 1959.
facts.solar_wind: Charged particles streaming off the Sun's corona, stripping thin atmospheres like Mars's away.
facts.lima_bean: Phaseolus lunatus, a species apart from the common bean — domesticated in the Peruvian Andes around 2000 BC.
facts.black_eyed_pea: Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea — domesticated in Africa and bred to thrive in soil up to 85% sand.
facts.navy_bean: A small white cultivar of the common bean, named for the US Navy's use of it as a sailor's ration.
facts.pine_nut: Not cracked from a shell like other nuts — shaken loose from a cone dried until it splits open.
facts.brazil_nut: Rarely farmed — plantation trees seldom fruit, since few bee genera can pollinate the flower.
facts.almond_butter: Almonds, crushed to a spreadable paste the same way peanuts are for peanut butter.
facts.marzipan: Ground almonds worked with sugar until pliable enough to shape by hand — documented in Toledo back to 1512.
facts.pumpkin_seed: Sold hulled as pepitas, or whole in a white husk — some cultivars are bred huskless from the start.
facts.soy_milk: Soaked soybeans, ground with water, boiled 15 to 20 minutes, then strained — the liquid tofu is curdled from.
facts.tempeh: Whole soybeans, not curdled like tofu — a mould's mycelium binds the beans into a cake in about a day.
facts.edamame: Soybeans picked green, 35 to 40 days after the plant flowers — sweeter than they'll ever be once dried.
facts.green_bean: The same species as kidney and pinto beans, picked immature and eaten pod and all — a fresh legume.
facts.falafel: Ground raw, not cooked first — cooked chickpeas fall apart in the fryer instead of holding together.
facts.refried_beans: Frijoles refritos — ‘well fried,’ not fried twice. Mashed pinto beans, fried in fat until they hold together.
facts.dal: Names both the raw split pulse and the dish — lentils cooked down soft, a staple across South Asia.
facts.hoppin_john: Black-eyed peas and rice, eaten across the US South on New Year's Day — the peas stand in for coins.
facts.baked_beans: Colonial New England swapped molasses and salt pork into a Native bean-pit method once run on bear fat.
facts.propylene: The propene molecule — steam-cracked from petroleum alongside ethylene, its own biggest use is polypropylene.
facts.butadiene: A four-carbon diene pulled from the same steam-cracker stream as ethylene — the monomer synthetic rubber runs on.
facts.acrylonitrile: CH2=CHCN. Ammoxidized from propylene by the Sohio process — the nitrile in nitrile rubber and in PAN fiber.
facts.nitrile_rubber: A butadiene-acrylonitrile copolymer, oil-resistant enough to be the standard glove and fuel-line rubber.
facts.chloromethane: CH3Cl, also called methyl chloride — hydrochlorinated from methanol, and the feedstock silicone starts from.
facts.dimethyldichlorosilane: Me2SiCl2 — the direct-process product that almost every industrial silicone is hydrolyzed from.
facts.silicone: A silicon-oxygen backbone with organic side groups — polydimethylsiloxane, stable from caulk to breast implants.
facts.aniline: C6H5NH2. Made from nitrobenzene or, less commonly, straight from phenol and ammonia.
facts.isocyanate: The R-N=C=O group, built by phosgenating an amine — the reactive half of every polyurethane.
facts.polyol: A multi-hydroxyl molecule built by ring-opening an alkylene oxide onto a starter alcohol like glycerol.
facts.polyurethane: A diisocyanate and a polyol, stitched together into carbamate links — foam cushions to skateboard wheels.
facts.inconel_625: A nickel-chromium-molybdenum superalloy that keeps its strength red-hot — jet engines, chemical plant, seabed risers.
facts.borosilicate_glass: Silica and boric oxide melted together — the low-expansion glass that survives a hot pan going into cold water.
facts.silicon_carbide: SiC — Acheson's 1893 furnace product, almost as hard as diamond and sold as an abrasive under the name carborundum.
facts.zirconia: Zirconium dioxide — ceramic-hard, cut as a diamond simulant, and stable enough for dental crowns and oxygen sensors.
facts.polyacrylonitrile: Free-radically polymerized from acrylonitrile — spun into filament yarn as the precursor for 90% of carbon fiber.
facts.carbon_fiber: PAN fiber stabilized in air and then carbonized past 1,000°C, driving off everything that isn't carbon.
facts.epichlorohydrin: A chlorinated epoxide — made from propylene or, in Dow's newer process, straight from glycerol and HCl.
facts.epoxy_resin: Bisphenol A stepped together with epichlorohydrin into DGEBA — the resin behind most structural adhesives.
facts.cfrp: Carbon fiber laid into a resin matrix, usually epoxy — strong along the fiber, and a fraction of steel's weight.
facts.glass_fiber: Molten glass drawn through a spinneret's tiny holes into continuous filament — fine enough to weave.
facts.gfrp: Glass fiber set into a plastic matrix — epoxy, polyester or vinyl ester — cheap, stiff, and everywhere from boat hulls to bathtubs.
facts.wood_flour: Sawdust and wood waste ground fine enough to feel like sand — the filler in wood-plastic decking.
facts.wood_plastic_composite: Wood flour compounded into a thermoplastic, usually polyethylene — decking that won't rot or splinter.
facts.pom_acetal: Polyoxymethylene — formaldehyde strung into long -CH2O- chains, stiff and low-friction enough to replace metal gears.
facts.pps: [C6H4S]n — a benzene ring and a sulfur atom, repeated, and one of the few plastics that shrugs off 200°C.
facts.epdm: An ethylene-propylene-diene terpolymer that resists ozone and weather better than almost any other rubber.
facts.chervil: A parsley relative with a faint anise taste — one of the four French fines herbes.
facts.lemongrass: A tropical grass, not a citrus — its lemon smell is geraniol and citronellol, straight from the leaf oil.
facts.savory: A mint-family annual, prized with beans across Persian, Georgian and Balkan kitchens.
facts.anise: Carrot's own family, not star anise's — the two plants share only a flavour compound, by coincidence.
facts.shallot: An onion cultivar that grows in clustered offsets like garlic, not from one bulb — and tastes milder for it.
facts.scallion: An onion pulled before its bulb ever forms — the same plant, kept for its hollow green stem instead.
facts.garlic_chives: A different Allium species from common chives — flat leaves, and a taste closer to garlic than onion.
facts.white_pepper: The same peppercorn as black pepper, ripe instead of unripe, with the rotted-off skin never dried on.
facts.green_peppercorn: The same vine's unripe fruit, brined before it can darken — sharper and fresher than the dried kind.
facts.cayenne: The same species as sweet paprika, bred and picked for capsaicin instead of colour.
facts.celery_seed: Not a seed but a whole dried fruit, off the same plant grown elsewhere for its stalk.
facts.mace: The lacy red aril wrapped around a nutmeg seed, peeled off and dried into its own spice.
facts.chili_powder: A ground blend of dried chilies with cumin, garlic and onion — not chili pepper alone.
facts.chestnut: Unrelated to the toxic horse chestnut despite the name — its spiny bur splits open once ripe on its own.
facts.sunflower_seed: Striped seeds are the snack type — the solid black-hulled kind goes to the oil press instead.
facts.balsamic_vinegar: Not soured wine at all — boiled-down grape must, aged in wood for a legal minimum of 12 years.
facts.sesame_oil: Pressed from roasted rather than raw seed — what gives toasted sesame oil its deep amber colour.
facts.steak_sauce: A ketchup-style base fortified with extra vinegar and spice — tangier than ketchup by design.
facts.relish: Pickle, chopped small enough to spread rather than slice — same preservation, different knife work.
facts.bouquet_garni: French for 'garnished bouquet' — herbs tied in a bundle so they can be fished back out of the pot.
facts.marinade: Acid, oil and spice in balance — too much acid toughens meat instead of tenderising it.
facts.chloroform: CHCl3 -- once a surgical anaesthetic, now a suspected carcinogen and an ozone-depleting solvent.
facts.chlorodifluoromethane: R-22, the refrigerant gas that cooled most 20th-century air conditioners and freezers.
facts.tetrafluoroethylene: TFE -- the monomer for Teflon, discovered by accident in 1938 when a cylinder of it polymerised on its own.
facts.ptfe: Teflon. A carbon backbone wrapped entirely in fluorine -- almost nothing sticks to it or dissolves it.
facts.hexafluoropropylene: HFP -- TFE's own high-heat byproduct, and the second monomer in most fluoroelastomers.
facts.pfa: Perfluoroalkoxy alkane -- almost pure PTFE chemistry, but able to melt-process instead of only sintering.
facts.fkm: Viton. A fluoroelastomer o-ring seal that shrugs off fuel, oil and heat that would swell ordinary rubber.
facts.ethylidene_chloride: 1,1-Dichloroethane -- a Lewis-acid-catalysed addition of HCl across vinyl chloride's double bond.
facts.trichloroethane_111: Once sold as 'chlorothene', a huge industrial solvent until its ozone damage got it phased out.
facts.chlorodifluoroethane: HCFC-142b -- a refrigerant gas whose whole purpose, industrially, is to be cracked into something else.
facts.vinylidene_fluoride: VDF, CH2=CF2 -- the monomer shared by PVDF plastic and Viton-family fluoroelastomers.
facts.pvdf: Kynar. Half its hydrogens replaced with fluorine, which is enough to make it piezoelectric.
facts.cfc_113: 1,1,2-Trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane -- a Montreal Protocol chemical, once everywhere as a degreaser.
facts.chlorotrifluoroethylene: CTFE -- one chlorine short of tetrafluoroethylene, and the monomer half of ECTFE.
facts.ectfe: Halar. Ethylene and chlorotrifluoroethylene alternating almost perfectly, one after the other, down the chain.
facts.ethylene_dichloride: EDC, 1,2-dichloroethane -- made and cracked again in the same plant, on the way to vinyl chloride.
facts.vinyl_chloride: VCM -- a known human carcinogen, and the monomer that makes up every molecule of PVC.
facts.pvc: Polyvinyl chloride. The vinyl chloride monomer is a genuine carcinogen; the finished plastic is not.
facts.ldpe: Low-density polyethylene -- branched, flexible chains, the plastic of bags and squeeze bottles and film.
facts.uhmwpe: Chains millions of daltons long -- too long to melt cleanly, so it goes into hip joints instead.
facts.pp: Polypropylene -- the second most produced plastic on Earth, and the one hinges best without snapping.
facts.butane: Discovered in crude petroleum in 1864 -- the lightest liquid fraction, condensing at just above 0°C.
facts.polybutadiene: Synthetic rubber, chosen for tire treads for the same bounce natural rubber has and steadier supply.
facts.styrene_acrylonitrile: SAN -- clear and rigid on its own, and the resin half of ABS before rubber gets grafted in.
facts.abs: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene -- the plastic LEGO bricks, keyboard caps and car dashboards are made of.
facts.xylene: A three-carbon step up from toluene -- three isomers, and the para one becomes polyester.
facts.terephthalic_acid: p-Xylene's two methyl groups oxidised to acids -- the feedstock behind nearly all polyester.
facts.pet: Polyethylene terephthalate -- soda bottles and polyester fibre are the same molecule, spun or blown.
facts.hydroquinone: Two hydroxyls on opposite corners of a benzene ring -- a photographic developer and a skin-lightening agent.
facts.nitrobenzene: Smells of almonds, looks pale yellow, and is toxic enough that its main use is becoming something else.
facts.fluoroboric_acid: HBF4 -- boric acid dissolved straight into hydrofluoric acid, four fluorines clamping onto one boron.
facts.benzenediazonium_chloride: An aniline salt so unstable it is explosive dry -- made cold and used within the hour.
facts.benzenediazonium_tetrafluoroborate: Swap the chloride's counterion for tetrafluoroborate and the same unstable salt becomes shock-insensitive.
facts.fluorobenzene: A benzene ring with one hydrogen swapped for fluorine -- the Balz-Schiemann reaction's signature product.
facts.difluorobenzophenone: Two fluorinated benzene rings joined through a ketone -- one of PEEK's two building-block monomers.
facts.peek: Polyetheretherketone -- keeps its strength past 250°C, used in jet engines and spinal implants.
facts.cyclohexanone: A six-carbon ring with one carbon turned into a ketone -- 'KA oil', the doorway to nylon.
facts.hydroxylamine: NH2OH -- explosive as a pure solid, so it is made, used and consumed as a dilute solution instead.
facts.cyclohexanone_oxime: Cyclohexanone's oxygen swapped for a nitrogen -- one rearrangement away from a ring nylon is made of.
facts.caprolactam: A seven-membered ring, waiting to be forced open into the single long chain of nylon 6.
facts.nylon_6: Every unit is the same caprolactam ring, unlike nylon 6,6's two alternating monomers.
facts.potassium_carbonate: K2CO3, potash — named for literally being ash boiled down in a pot, the alkali that came before purified lye.
facts.sodium_oxide: Na2O — sodium's true oxide, easily overshot to the peroxide if there's oxygen to spare.
facts.zinc_nitrate: Zn(NO3)2 — dissolve zinc in nitric acid and this crystallises out, one of six water molecules still attached.
facts.phthalic_anhydride: C6H4(CO)2O — nearly all of it today comes off a xylene flame, not the naphthalene it was first made from.
facts.phenolphthalein: The lab's own mood ring — colourless below pH 8.2, hot pink above it, and that's the entire instrument.
facts.magnesium_nitrate: Mg(NO3)2 — a magnesium salt so eager for water it's used industrially to pull the last of it out of concentrated nitric acid.
facts.ammonium_acetate: NH4CH3CO2 — so hygroscopic it's nearly impossible to keep dry, and it breaks back down toward acetic acid and ammonia if melted.
facts.bicarbonate: HCO3- — carbon dioxide's most common disguise in blood and seawater alike, the form that actually carries most of it around.
facts.chromate: CrO4(2-) — chromium at its most oxidised, +6, the state that turns ore green going in and this colour coming out.
facts.methyl_ethyl_ketone: Butanone, MEK — nail-polish-remover-sharp, and one of the few common solvents that dissolves both polar and non-polar compounds at once.
facts.trichloroacetic_acid: CCl3CO2H — three chlorines pull so much electron density off the acid group that it's a stronger acid than sulfuric, dose for dose.
facts.magnesium_sulfate: MgSO4 — Epsom salt, named for a Surrey spring, and the same compound used in hospital drips to stop premature labour.
facts.sulfur_trioxide: SO3 — the molecule sulfuric acid is built from, and so hungry for water it fumes visibly in ordinary damp air.
facts.aluminum_phosphate: AlPO4 — aluminium and phosphate combine in nearly the same one-to-one ratio silicon and oxygen do in quartz, which is why its frameworks mimic zeolites.
facts.stearic_acid: The straight 18-carbon fatty acid that makes tallow solid at room temperature, and candle wax firm instead of greasy.
facts.dinitrogen_monoxide: N2O — the anaesthetic gas dentists call laughing gas, one nitrogen short of the nitrite it takes two more oxidation steps to reach.
facts.acetonitrile: CH3CN — the smallest nitrile, and mostly a byproduct: burned off from the plant that makes acrylonitrile rather than made on purpose.
facts.potassium_dichromate: K2Cr2O7 — the orange crystal that gave 19th-century chemistry its favourite oxidiser, before hexavalent chromium's cancer risk was understood.
facts.zinc_acetate: Zn(CH3CO2)2 — zinc's salt of vinegar's acid, and the zinc source dropped into throat lozenges and cold remedies.
facts.magnesium_carbonate: MgCO3, magnesite — limestone's magnesium twin, and the mineral a chunk of gym chalk is mostly made of.
facts.propane: Three carbons, sold compressed in the tank by the house. Boils at −42°C, below any winter night.
facts.pentane: Five carbons, and the shortest alkane that's a true liquid at room temperature rather than a compressed gas.
facts.octane: Eight carbons, and fuel quality's own ruler — the 100 on an octane rating is defined against its branched cousin.
facts.benzene: A six-carbon ring so stable Kekulé is said to have dreamed its shape as a snake biting its own tail.
facts.hydrobromic_acid: Hydrogen bromide dissolved in water — a strong acid with a lower profile than its chlorine cousin.
facts.carbonic_acid: What CO2 becomes the instant it meets water — the fizz in soda, and half of blood's pH control.
facts.ammonium_sulfate: 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, and it acidifies alkaline soil as it feeds it — two fertiliser jobs in one salt.
facts.copper_sulfate: Blue vitriol. Painted onto grapevines as Bordeaux mixture since 1885, still farming’s default fungicide.
facts.sulfurous_acid: SO2 dissolved in water — so unstable it has never been isolated pure, only ever as this equilibrium.
facts.galactose: Glucose's mirror-twin, locked to it inside every molecule of milk sugar until digestion pulls them apart.
facts.sodium_nitrate: Chile saltpetre — nitrogen mined from Atacama desert crusts a metre thick, never having had to fix itself.
facts.iodic_acid: HIO3 — corrosive like any acid, and a strong enough oxidiser to be a fire hazard around anything combustible.
facts.camphor: That mothball smell, once drawn only from a tree's wood, before chemists learned to build it from turpentine.
facts.silver_iodide: A handful of grains seeded into a cloud can nudge a snowflake into forming around them instead of dust.
facts.arsenic_trioxide: White arsenic — Victorian fiction's classic poison, and today a treatment for a rare form of leukaemia.
facts.gold_iii_oxide: Gold's rarer oxide, and a reluctant one — heat it past 298°C and it falls back apart into the metal.
facts.gold_sulfide: Gold refusing to stay dissolved: pass the right gas through a gold salt solution and this drops out of it.
facts.turpentine: Pine resin steam-distilled down to a solvent — the smell in old paint tins, before petroleum replaced it.
facts.lactose: Milk's own sugar, crystallised straight out of cheesemaking's leftover whey.
facts.wire: Any ductile metal, pulled cold through a die until it's thin enough to bend by hand.
facts.battery: A zinc can for a shell and a manganese dioxide paste inside — the dry cell that made power portable.
facts.skin: Two layers, two jobs: keratin-packed epidermis for a barrier, collagen-rich dermis underneath for strength.
facts.ligament: The same dense collagen bundle as a tendon — a tendon ties muscle to bone, a ligament ties bone to bone.
facts.earring: Gold hammered thin and bent into a hoop — the oldest known earrings, from Ur, are about 4,500 years old.
facts.elbow: A hinge joint of three bones — humerus, radius, ulna — held together by a ligament on either side.
facts.envelope: Paper cut and folded into a rhombus, kite or cross, its overlapping flap held down with a dab of gum.
facts.eye: The retina isn't just wired to the brain — developmentally it is brain tissue, budded outward before birth.
facts.fence: Wire strands stretched taut between wooden posts — far less timber than a fence built solid.
facts.fingernail: A flattened claw: primate nails evolved from ancestral claws to back a sensitive fingertip pad.
facts.finger: Bones called phalanges — three to a finger, two to a thumb — wrapped in skin at a hand's working end.
facts.fire_truck: A combustion engine bolted to a hose and pump — motorised fire engines started replacing horses around 1897.
facts.flashlight: David Misell's 1899 patent: dry-cell batteries in a paper tube, with a bulb and brass reflector at the end.
facts.fork: Common in Byzantium by the 4th century, still mocked as an Italian affectation in 18th-century England.
facts.garbage_can: A steel bin coated in zinc — the same galvanising that keeps an outdoor nail or bucket from rusting through.
facts.ghost: No sighting has been reproduced under controlled conditions; psychologists point to pareidolia instead.
facts.glasses: First ground in Pisa or Florence around 1290; wire temples over the ears took four more centuries.
facts.glove: Sheepskin turned inside out keeps its own wool fleece attached — a glove and its lining from one hide.
facts.glue: Boiled from hide instead of bone, the same collagen chemistry as gelatin — just dried coarse, not refined.
facts.goal: Football had no goal net until 1889 — before that, a disputed score meant arguing about where the ball went.
facts.hair: Keratin filament grown from a follicle in the skin — only the root is alive, never the shaft you can see.
facts.hanger: One length of wire, bent into a triangle and a hook — most coat hangers today are still just steel wire.
facts.hat: Felted fur or wool, stitched and stretched to shape — a fedora is just a soft felt hat with a creased crown.
facts.head: The skull is a bony case built entirely around the brain it protects, with one hinge left for the jaw.
facts.hoop: Naismith nailed up a peach basket in 1891; by 1906 an open metal rim let the ball just pass through.
facts.hose: Rubber wrapped around a woven fabric core — the reinforcement is what keeps it from bursting under pressure.
facts.spring: Steel wound into a coil, then hardened and tempered so it remembers its shape and snaps back after a bend.
facts.slinky: 98 coils of spring steel — the gauge Richard James found, after a year of testing, that would walk downstairs.
facts.sock: Oldest knitted finds: 11th-century cotton socks from Fustat, near Cairo — knitting stretches to fit a foot.
facts.carbonated_water: Joseph Priestley dissolved CO2 into water above a Leeds brewery vat in 1767, his self-declared 'happiest' find.
facts.soda: Mostly carbonated water: commercial cola syrup is cut roughly one part syrup to five parts carbonated water.
facts.sofa: A wood frame under padding, covered in leather or fabric — the Chesterfield's buttoned look dates to the 1700s.
facts.spider_web: Pure silk protein from spinneret glands — a web is commonly about 20 times the size of the spider that spun it.
facts.spoon: A reindeer-antler spoon from the Magdalenian, some 17,000 years old, carves the idea wood spoons still use.
facts.squirrel: A scatter-hoarder that buries several thousand acorns, seeds and nuts a season, and mostly finds them again.
facts.stairs: Cut straight into rock at Egypt's Red Pyramid around 2575 BC — the steps were the material itself, nothing added.
facts.stick: The smallest branches on a tree are twigs — already its driest, most brittle wood, first to snap off in wind.
facts.sticker: Hide glue and gelatin are one substance under two names — boiled collagen, stiff enough to bind paper down.
facts.stove: The first cast-iron stove was built in 1642 at Lynn, Massachusetts — an iron box, with no grates yet.
facts.postage_stamp: The Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp, went on sale 1 May 1840 — paper gummed with starch paste.
facts.stool: One of the earliest forms of wooden furniture — ancient Greece's diphros even folded flat to travel.
facts.string: One more twist than thread, one fewer than rope — plied against its own twist so it cannot unravel.
facts.suitcase: Early suitcases stretched leather over a rigid wood-or-steel frame, with leather or brass caps at the corners.
facts.sunglasses: Ai Tai, 'dark clouds': flat panes of smoky quartz worn in 12th-century China, said to hide judges' expressions.
facts.sweater: The word dates only to 1882, first a woolen vest worn rowing — unscoured wool keeps lanolin and sheds water.
facts.swimsuit: Before the 1930s, swimsuits were wool — they never hugged the body and turned heavy the moment they got wet.
facts.swing: The simplest playground swing needs nothing but a rope over a branch and a seat tied to the ends.
facts.table: Ancient Egyptian tables, around 2500 BC, were wood and alabaster; medieval trestle tables folded away after meals.
facts.tape: Richard Drew's 1925 masking tape was paper backed with a gentler rubber adhesive, made for autobody painters.
facts.teapot: China's shift from whipped tea to steeped leaves called the teapot into being; the earliest one dates to 1513.
facts.nose: The nose's shape is mostly cartilage, not bone — only the bridge is bony — wrapped in skin that's thinnest at the tip.
facts.olfactory_nerve: Cranial nerve I: fibers rise from the nasal lining through the ethmoid bone's cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb.
facts.optic_nerve: Cranial nerve II carries vision from retina to brain — and is technically CNS tissue, not a true peripheral nerve.
facts.trigeminal_nerve: Cranial nerve V: three branches carry sensation from the whole face, and its motor branch alone powers chewing.
facts.vestibulocochlear_nerve: Cranial nerve VIII fuses hearing and balance in one sheath: a cochlear branch for sound, vestibular for motion.
facts.vagus_nerve: Cranial nerve X, named for 'wandering': its right branch reaches the heart's own pacemaker to slow the beat.
facts.accessory_nerve: Cranial nerve XI drives two muscles: sternocleidomastoid, which turns the head, and trapezius, which shrugs it.
facts.hypoglossal_nerve: Cranial nerve XII: purely motor, it alone drives the tongue's own muscles for speech, chewing, and swallowing.
facts.durian: Named for duri, Malay for thorn. The smell strong enough to get it banned from hotels and transit is organosulfur chemistry — diethyl disulfide, dimethyl sulfide and more, the same family that makes onion and garlic sharp.
facts.lavender: A Mediterranean shrub grown for its flower spikes. Nearly all of its scent is one molecule, linalool — lavender oil is the reference chemists compare other linalool-scented things to.
facts.caraway: Carum carvi, Apiaceae like cumin and dill — so alike to cumin that many languages don't bother separating them. Its root is also a genuine root vegetable, eaten like a parsnip.
facts.elderflower: The flowerhead of Sambucus nigra, picked before it sets fruit and steeped for cordial — the one part of the elder that needs no cooking to be safe.
facts.oyster_leaf: Mertensia maritima, a shingle-beach succulent from the Arctic fringe of the Northern Hemisphere. Chewed raw, it genuinely tastes like an oyster.
facts.fenugreek: A legume, family to peas and beans, grown for both its seed and its leaf. The seed carries sotolon, the same molecule behind curry, maple syrup and aged sherry's burnt-sugar edge.
facts.paracress: Acmella oleracea — toothache plant, buzz buttons, electric daisy. Its own name for the tingling, numbing jolt in the flower bud is spilanthol.
facts.yuzu: A hybrid of mandarin and the wild ichang papeda, and it inherited that parent's cold tolerance — yuzu survives winters down to -7°C that would kill an ordinary orange tree.
facts.wakame: Undaria pinnatifida, the same order as kelp — Laminariales — grown by Japanese and Korean sea-farmers for centuries. Not a plant at all: a brown-algal stramenopile.
facts.capsaicin: Chilli's heat, and it barely dissolves in water — 0.0013 g per 100 mL — which is why milk cuts the burn and water does not.
facts.benzaldehyde: Almond-scented in savoury use, cherry-scented in sweet — the same molecule read differently by context. Water hitting a crushed apricot kernel's amygdalin makes it, along with hydrogen cyanide.
facts.allyl_isothiocyanate: Undetectable until the plant is damaged — an enzyme called myrosinase only meets its target molecule, sinigrin, once cells rupture. Then mustard, wasabi and horseradish all sting the same way.
facts.nootkatone: Present in only trace amounts, but it is grapefruit's single most valuable aroma compound.
facts.nonadienal: (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal, often just called cucumber aldehyde — the compound so tied to the vegetable it doubles as the name.
facts.filbertone: The hazelnut's own character-impact compound — no other nut carries it, which is why nothing else quite smells like one.
facts.isoamyl_acetate: Also called banana oil, and used to flavour banana candy for exactly that reason — it occurs naturally in the ripe fruit itself, among dozens of other aroma molecules.
facts.sotolon: Fenugreek's main flavour compound: at high concentration it reads as curry, diluted it reads as maple syrup, caramel or burnt sugar.
facts.diacetyl: Butter's own smell, made by bacteria as a fermentation byproduct — Leuconostoc and its relatives producing it as they sour cream into cultured buttermilk.
facts.skatole: 3-methylindole — pig manure at full strength, and part of why white pepper occasionally develops a faecal off-note when its retting husk sits in stagnant rather than running water.
facts.linalool: Most of lavender's smell is this one molecule — chemists use lavender oil as the reference standard other linalool-scented things get compared to.
facts.limonene: The major component of citrus peel oil, and most of what you smell the instant you zest an orange.
facts.methional: Heat breaks the amino acid methionine down into this — the same Strecker reaction that gives fried potato its cooked-potato smell, wherever else methionine turns up hot.
facts.celeriac: The same species as celery, Apium graveolens, bred toward the root instead of the stalk.
facts.agave: A genus native to the arid Americas. Blue agave takes seven to fourteen years to mature.
facts.pulque: Agave sap fermented by Zymomonas mobilis, not yeast — a milky drink the Aztecs called metl octli.
facts.tequila: Blue agave hearts are baked to convert their fructans to sugar, fermented, then distilled twice by law.
facts.cognac: Twice-distilled wine, mostly Ugni Blanc grapes, aged at least two years in French oak.
facts.cassia: Cinnamomum cassia, a different tree from true cinnamon — sold as 'cinnamon' in most supermarket jars.
facts.hexanal: An aldehyde smelling of freshly cut grass, released the instant a leaf or green fruit's tissue is damaged.
facts.vanillin: The single molecule behind vanilla's scent — first sold in 1874, synthesized from clove oil, not vanilla.
facts.furaneol: Strawberry furanone, also called pineapple ketone — fruity at low concentration, caramellic at high.
facts.cinnamaldehyde: The oily compound that is, chemically, cinnamon's flavour and smell — straight out of the bark oil.
facts.citral: The lemon smell itself, as a molecule — lemongrass oil runs 65 to 85 percent citral by weight.
facts.allicin: Odourless alliin becomes this the instant a garlic cell wall breaks — the enzyme alliinase does it in seconds.
facts.octenol: Mushroom alcohol, first isolated from crushed matsutake in the 1930s — the reason mushrooms smell like this.
facts.eucalyptol: Also called 1,8-cineole — 70 to 90 percent of eucalyptus oil by weight, and present in rosemary's too.
facts.theobromine: Chocolate's stimulant, not caffeine — mild in humans, far more dangerous to dogs, who clear it more slowly.
facts.galangal: Ginger's own family and a rhizome too, but sharper and more resinous — camphor where ginger is warm.
facts.garlic_powder: Garlic, dehydrated and ground fine — the same clove with the water gone.
facts.onion_powder: Onion, dehydrated and ground fine — the same bulb with the water and the sting gone.
facts.garam_masala: Northern India's best-known spice blend — 'garam' means warming, not spicy-hot.
facts.curry_powder: A British colonial approximation — no South Asian region cooks from one fixed spice mix called 'curry powder'.
facts.five_spice: Built to carry all five flavours Chinese cooking names — sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty — in one jar.
facts.berbere: Ethiopia and Eritrea's base hot spice blend — the flavour underneath doro wat and most other stews.
facts.ras_el_hanout: Arabic for 'head of the shop' — once a merchant's own signature top-shelf mix, not one fixed recipe.
facts.herbes_de_provence: Sold pre-mixed since the 1970s — Provençal cooks once used these herbs individually, not blended.
facts.quatre_epices: French for 'four spices' — a charcuterie seasoning built to warm pâtés and terrines without adding real heat.
facts.zaatar: Both an Eastern Mediterranean herb and the tangy sesame-and-sumac mix named after it.
facts.harissa: Tunisia's national chile paste, now spread across North African and French cooking.
facts.tabil: Tunisian for 'seasoning' — once just ground coriander alone, now a fixed four-ingredient mix.
facts.chermoula: A North African herb-and-spice marinade for fish, made fresh to order rather than jarred and stored.
facts.dukkah: Egyptian for 'to pound' — nuts and seeds crushed together, eaten as a dip, not cooked into a dish.
facts.gomasio: A Japanese table seasoning — just enough salt to season sesame without burying its toasted flavour.
facts.shichimi_togarashi: Japanese 'seven-flavour chile' — a table shake-on built to layer heat, citrus, nuttiness and crunch at once.
facts.thai_curry_paste: The pounded aromatic base under Thai curries — chiles, herbs and roots worked into a paste, not a dry powder.
facts.jerk_seasoning: Jamaica's barbecue seasoning, named for the motion of piercing meat to work the spice in.
facts.seven_spices: Lebanon's everyday warming blend — baharat, Arabic for 'spices', under a regional name.
facts.baharat: Arabic simply for 'spices' — a warming, peppery blend that shifts country to country under the same name.
facts.hawaij: A Yemenite Jewish spice blend stirred into soup; a second, sweeter version flavours coffee and cakes.
facts.advieh: Persian for 'spices' — a rose-and-warm-spice blend, garam masala's distant cousin down the old spice routes.
facts.pickling_spice: A whole-spice mix, never ground, so it can be lifted or strained back out of the brine once its work is done.
facts.fines_herbes: Stirred in at the very end of cooking, unlike a dried bouquet garni — the point is fresh, fragile flavour.
facts.gingerbread_spice_mix: Named for its loudest spice, though it is really a small family of warming spices working together.
facts.speculaas_spice: The spice mix behind Dutch and Belgian speculaas cookies — a legacy of trade with the old Spice Islands.
facts.apple_pie_spice: A mixture of sweet spices used to season American apple pie, in many household versions.
facts.pumpkin_pie_spice: A branded product name before it was a category — now sold well beyond pumpkin pie, in lattes and cereal.
facts.poultry_seasoning: An American spice-cabinet staple built specifically for turkey and chicken, not a general all-purpose blend.
facts.crawfish_boil_spices: A whole-spice mix tied in a bag and simmered in the boiling water itself, not rubbed onto the shellfish.
facts.cajun_seasoning: Louisiana's blackening-and-frying spice mix, built around cayenne heat rather than a dried-chile base.
facts.chesapeake_bay_seasoning: A 1940s Baltimore blend that became the model for the world-famous, still-secret Old Bay Seasoning.
facts.adobo_seasoning: Not the Filipino braising dish of the same name — a dry rub used across Latin American cooking.
facts.barbecue_seasoning_rub: Rubbed onto meat before cooking, unlike a sauce — built to survive hours of smoke and heat.
facts.achiote_paste: Yucatán's red seasoning paste, coloured by annatto seed, worked with citrus juice or vinegar, not oil.
facts.zhoug: Yemen's fiery green condiment, now a fixture of Israeli cooking through its large Yemenite Jewish community.
facts.animism: The belief that souls or spirits exist not only in humans but in animals, plants, rocks, and rivers — summed up by the Ainu saying that even a rock has a spirit.
facts.shamanism: A practice in which a shaman enters trance — via drumming or, in some Siberian and Sami traditions, the fly agaric mushroom — to travel to and negotiate with the spirit world.
facts.ancestor_worship: The belief that dead ancestors continue to exist and can influence, and be influenced by, the living, who owe them ongoing offerings and honor.
facts.the_dreaming: In Australian Aboriginal belief, the 'timeless time' of ongoing creation, in which ancestral beings shaped the land and left it charged with living spiritual power.
facts.human_sacrifice: Ritual killing offered to the gods; Aztec priests cut the heart from a living victim, believing the sun needed a steady offering of human hearts and blood.
facts.ahura_mazda: Zoroastrianism's supreme god, the 'Wise Lord' and sovereign creator of all good, worshipped through the sacred fire kept burning in every temple.
facts.angra_mainyu: Zoroastrianism's destructive spirit, also called Ahriman, the eternal opponent of Ahura Mazda, who is said to have created the serpent-demon Aži Dahāka as an agent of chaos.
facts.zoroaster: Persian prophet who reported a revelation of Ahura Mazda by a riverbank around age 30, composed the Gathas hymns, and founded Zoroastrianism.
facts.zoroastrianism: One of the world's oldest monotheistic faiths, centered on the eternal struggle between the good creator Ahura Mazda and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu.
facts.laozi: Legendary sage credited with the Daode Jing; tradition holds he rode an ox out of China and, at the western border, wrote his wisdom down for a guard before vanishing.
facts.dao: The 'Way' of Daoist philosophy: an enigmatic, unseen process of transformation that underlies and sustains all reality.
facts.wu_wei: Daoism's ideal of 'effortless action' — acting in such silent harmony with the dao that it may seem motionless, rather than striving against the current of things.
facts.daoism: A Chinese religious philosophy founded on Laozi's Daode Jing, holding that the dao sustains and orders the universe and is best followed through wu wei, effortless action.
facts.mahavira: Prince Vardhamana, who renounced his throne and family at 30 to live as a wandering ascetic; after 12 years of extreme austerity he attained enlightenment as Mahavira.
facts.ahimsa: Jainism's vow of nonviolence, held to extend to the smallest organisms in water or air — why strict Jains strain their drinking water and watch where they walk.
facts.tirthankara: A 'ford-builder' who shows others the way across the ocean of rebirth; Jains revere 24 per era, with Mahavira honored as the most recent of this cycle.
facts.jainism: The most ascetic of India's major religions, shaped by Mahavira in the 6th century BCE around ahimsa — nonviolence toward all living things — as its highest duty.
facts.confucianism: A Chinese ethical and religious tradition grown from Confucius's sayings, which his disciples collected and jointly edited into the Analects after his death.
facts.junzi: Confucianism's ideal 'superior man,' who rules and lives by acting virtuously himself, on the belief that pure virtue draws others to follow by simple example.
facts.marduk: Chief god of Babylon; he defeated the primordial sea-dragon Tiamat in battle, was crowned king of the gods, and fashioned the ordered world from her body.
facts.enuma_elish: Babylon's epic of creation, recorded on seven clay tablets, telling how Marduk defeated Tiamat and organized the cosmos — legitimizing Babylonian kingship.
facts.mummification: Egyptian embalmers dried the body for 70 days in natron, a natural salt, before wrapping it in linen — a rite myth credits to the jackal-headed god Anubis, who first embalmed Osiris.
facts.book_of_the_dead: A collection of funerary spells buried with wealthy Egyptians, meant to guide the deceased safely through the underworld and into the afterlife.
facts.shinto: Japan's indigenous religion, venerating kami, the sacred spirits of nature, ancestors, and history, and tracing its roots to the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami.
facts.kami: The sacred spirits Shinto venerates; the sun goddess Amaterasu, most revered of all kami, is enshrined at Ise and represented by the Sacred Mirror.
facts.torii: The gateless gate marking a Shinto shrine's entrance, traditionally built of wood, symbolizing the transition from the ordinary world into sacred ground.
facts.ragnarok: Norse mythology's apocalypse, in which Odin and Loki end up on opposing sides of a final battle between gods and giants that destroys the world before it rises again.
facts.valhalla: Odin's hall for warriors slain in battle, supplied nightly with meat from the boar Sæhrímnir — eaten and whole again by morning — and mead from the goat Heiðrún.
facts.oracle: The Pythia, Apollo's oracle at Delphi, entered a trance — possibly from gases seeping through the rock — to deliver the god's cryptic prophecies to those who sought her.
facts.lares: Roman guardian spirits, often linked to the ancestral dead, honored at a shrine by the household hearth-fire and, in their civic role, at crossroads across the community.
facts.bhagavad_gita: A dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna set within the epic Mahabharata, probably the single most popular scripture in all of Hinduism.
facts.dharma: Right living, or moral duty, which varies by role — a soldier's dharma differs from a farmer's — and which the Bhagavad-Gita's Krishna tells Arjuna he must perform even against his own feelings.
facts.karma: The seed sown by every intentional deed, whose fruit — good or bad — ripens across lifetimes to turn the great wheel of rebirth.
facts.samsara: The endless wheel of birth, death, and rebirth, kept turning by karma — a cycle broken only by moksha, liberation.
facts.atman: One's innermost self, which the Upanishads locate within the heart and hold to be identical to Brahman, ultimate reality itself.
facts.brahman: Ultimate, unchanging reality in Hindu philosophy, declared in the Upanishads' teaching 'tat tvam asi' — 'that thou art' — to be identical with the atman, the innermost self.
facts.moksha: Liberation from the endless round of samsara, achieved by realizing that the atman, one's innermost self, is identical to Brahman, ultimate reality.
facts.vedas: Hinduism's four oldest and most authoritative scriptures — the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda — composed between roughly 1500 and 500 BCE.
facts.upanishads: The Vedas' philosophical final layer, moving from ritual toward the exploration of atman and Brahman; the word itself means 'sitting down near' a teacher.
facts.guru: A teacher who passes on advanced spiritual knowledge to students — the word 'Upanishad' itself means 'sitting down near' the guru who imparts it.
facts.ashrama: Hinduism's four life stages, taking a person from student, learning at a guru's side, to householder, to forest-dweller, and finally wandering ascetic.
facts.yoga: A discipline combining physical postures with breath control to calm the mind until it can perceive the atman, the true self, and so attain liberation.
facts.puja: Hindu ritual worship — the loving offering of light, flowers, water, or food before the image of a deity — open to any devotee, not only priests.
facts.bhakti: Loving devotion to a personal god, which finds its most celebrated expression in the romantic devotion between Krishna and Radha.
facts.adi_shankara: 8th-century Vedic philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on the Upanishads and Brahma Sutras, systematizing what became known as Advaita Vedanta.
facts.advaita_vedanta: Adi Shankara's 'non-dual' school of Hindu philosophy, holding that Brahman alone is ultimately real, while the everyday world of separate, multiple things is not fully real.
facts.shakti: Feminine divine power personified as the Great Goddess, taking forms across Hindu tradition from the gentle Parvati to the fierce Durga and Kali.
facts.moses: As an infant, Moses was hidden among the reeds of the Nile River in a basket, according to the Torah's account of his birth; he grew up to lead the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt.
facts.abraham: In Genesis, God promises the childless, desert-dwelling Abraham that his descendants will be as numerous as the stars in the sky; Jews, Christians, and Muslims all trace their religious ancestry back to him.
facts.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples and told them, 'Do this in remembrance of me' — the origin of the Christian Eucharist, or Holy Communion.
facts.muhammad: Before his first revelation, Muhammad worked as a merchant leading camel caravans on the trade route to Syria for the wealthy widow Khadija, whom he later married.
facts.guru_nanak: A Hindu poet who debated with Hindu and Muslim holy men alike, Guru Nanak vanished into a river for three days and returned declaring, 'There is no Hindu, no Muslim.'
facts.zarathustra: At about age 30, Zoroaster experienced a revelation of Ahura Mazda, the 'Wise Lord,' and described existence as an ongoing battle between truth and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu.
facts.huxley: Known as 'Darwin's Bulldog' for his fierce public defense of evolution, including a famous 1860 debate with Bishop Samuel Wilberforce, biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the word 'agnostic' in 1869.
facts.soul: The words for 'spirit' in Latin (spiritus) and Greek (pneuma) both mean 'breath' or 'wind' — many traditions picture the soul as the breath that animates a body and departs at death.
facts.reincarnation: The belief that after death, the nonmaterial essence of a person begins a new life in a new body — a central tenet of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, shaped by the karma accumulated in past lives.
facts.nirvana: Nirvana literally means 'blowing out' or 'quenching' — early Buddhist texts pictured it as a flame going out once the fires of craving, hatred, and ignorance have burned themselves to nothing.
facts.torah: The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally believed to have been revealed by God to Moses atop Mount Sinai.
facts.talmud: Compiled by rabbis over centuries of debate on how to interpret and apply the Torah, the Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.
facts.tanakh: An acronym for its three sections — Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings) — the Tanakh is the canon of the Hebrew Bible.
facts.quran: Muslims believe the Quran's first verses were revealed to Muhammad by the angel Gabriel in the Cave of Hira, near Mecca, in 610 CE; revelations continued for 23 years.
facts.bible: The Christian Bible unites the Hebrew scriptures as its Old Testament with a New Testament of gospels and letters recounting the life and teachings of Jesus.
facts.guru_granth_sahib: Composed predominantly by six Sikh Gurus and compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, the Guru Granth Sahib was declared the Sikhs' eternal, living Guru by Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.
facts.trinity: The Christian doctrine that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one being; legend credits Saint Patrick with using a three-leaved shamrock to explain it to the Irish.
facts.five_pillars: The five obligatory acts of Islam: declaring the faith (Shahada), praying five times daily (Salat), giving to charity (Zakat), fasting during Ramadan (Sawm), and, if able, a pilgrimage to Mecca (Hajj).
facts.hinduism: Hinduism has no single founder; many of its traditions hold that a single Supreme Reality, Brahman, is expressed through gods such as the Trimurti and taught in the ancient Vedas.
facts.buddhism: Founded on the dharma the Buddha taught after his enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, Buddhism holds that suffering ends by following the Noble Eightfold Path.
facts.judaism: The oldest of the Abrahamic religions, built on God's covenant with Abraham and on the Torah, the law revealed to Moses.
facts.christianity: Centered on Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe to be the Son of God; God is understood as a Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
facts.islam: Founded in 7th-century Arabia when Muhammad began receiving revelations later collected as the Quran, Islam teaches submission to the one God, Allah.
facts.taoism: Traditionally traced to the sage Laozi, Taoism teaches that harmony comes from living according to the Tao ('the Way') and keeping yin and yang in balance.
facts.sikhism: Founded by Guru Nanak in 15th-century Punjab, Sikhism's line of living Gurus ended in 1708, when Guru Gobind Singh named the Guru Granth Sahib itself as his eternal successor.
facts.atheism: The absence of belief in gods; Charles Darwin's 1859 On the Origin of Species offered a natural explanation for life's diversity that many atheists point to as evidence a creator isn't needed.
facts.agnosticism: The view that God's existence can never be proven or disproven; biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the term in 1869, from the Greek for 'not knowable.'
facts.yin_yang: Yin (dark, moist, cold, feminine — traditionally likened to moonlight) and yang (light, dry, warm, masculine — likened to fire and sunlight) are pictured as complementary halves that must stay in balance.
facts.om: Considered the primordial sound of the universe, the sacred syllable Om (or Aum) is chanted across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism alike.
facts.mecca: Islam's holiest city, in Saudi Arabia: birthplace of Muhammad and home to the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine built around the sacred Black Stone at the center of the Grand Mosque.
facts.synagogue: A Jewish house of worship built around an ark that holds its Torah scrolls; full communal prayer traditionally requires a minyan, a quorum of at least ten adults.
facts.mosque: An Islamic place of worship with a mihrab, a niche set into the wall to indicate the direction of Mecca, so that everyone can pray facing the same way.
facts.church: Names both a building used for Christian worship and, more broadly, the entire community of Christian believers gathered around it.
facts.temple: Most everyday Hindu worship happens at home shrines, but grand stone temples such as the Brihadisvara Temple, built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE, host puja, ritual devotional worship, on a monumental scale.
facts.rabbi: A teacher and spiritual leader qualified to interpret Jewish law; the title comes from the Hebrew for 'my master,' and rabbis are the primary voices behind the Talmud's centuries of legal debate.
facts.cubeb: Black pepper's own genus, picked unripe and dried whole with its stalk — the “tail” in tailed pepper.
facts.elecampane: A tall Asteraceae with sunflower-like blooms, grown not for its flower but its bitter, camphor-scented root.
facts.licorice: Glycyrrhiza glabra, a Fabaceae legume grown for its root — 50 times sweeter than sugar, and the source of glycyrrhizin.
facts.myrtle: An evergreen Mediterranean shrub whose blue-black berries flavour the Sardinian liqueur Mirto.
facts.nigella: Ranunculaceae — the same family as poisonous aconite — but nigella's black seed is a food-safe spice from Turkey to India.
facts.quassia: Simaroubaceae bark named for Graman Quassi, the formerly enslaved Surinamese man credited with finding its medicinal use.
facts.safflower: A drought-tolerant Asteraceae thistle bred for oil-rich seed and for petals that yield both a yellow and a red dye.
facts.sichuan_pepper: Zanthoxylum's dried fruit husk — citrus and rue's own family, not pepper's — source of the tingling numbness sanshool.
facts.capers: Capparis spinosa's flower buds, hand-picked each morning before they open and pickled in salt or vinegar.
facts.java_galangal: Alpinia galanga, greater galangal — the same genus as lesser galangal but a far bigger plant, grown across tropical Java.
facts.asafoetida: A Ferula gum-resin from Afghanistan and Iran, scored from the taproot and dried into a garlic-strong lump.
facts.grains_of_paradise: Aframomum melegueta — ginger's own family, the one cardamom belongs to — a pepper substitute from West African wetlands.
facts.carvone: Caraway's own S-enantiomer smells of rye; the same molecule's mirror image, R-carvone, is spearmint.
facts.glycyrrhizin: 50 times sweeter than sugar — and, in enough of it for long enough, the reason licorice root can raise blood pressure.
facts.sanshool: Sichuan pepper's own tingle — closer to a mild electric buzz than to chili or black pepper's heat.
facts.carthamin: Safflower's own alcohol-soluble red pigment, used as a natural rouge and lip colour since antiquity.
facts.cubeb_oil: Steam-distilled from cubeb berries — a Victorian antiseptic sold specifically against gonorrhoea.
facts.black_seed_oil: Cold-pressed nigella seed, sold today for its thymoquinone — still “under basic research,” not an established medicine.
facts.quassin: Quassia bark's intensely bitter compound — flavoured bitters and beer for centuries, studied today as an insecticide.
facts.alantolactone: Elecampane root's own sesquiterpene lactone, part of why herbalists still reach for it as an expectorant.
facts.monotheism: Belief in a single, all-powerful God, as held by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
facts.polytheism: Belief in and worship of multiple gods, each often linked to a different domain of life.
facts.syncretism: The blending of beliefs and practices from different religious traditions into a new, combined form.
facts.incarnation: The idea that a deity can take on bodily, often human, form.
facts.messiah: Hebrew for "anointed one"; a figure expected by Jewish tradition to deliver Israel.
facts.covenant: In Judaism, the sacred agreement between God and Israel, given through Moses.
facts.ancestor_veneration: Ritual honoring and offerings made to deceased forebears, believed to still watch over the living.
facts.filial_piety: The Confucian virtue of respecting, obeying, and caring for one's parents and elders.
facts.asceticism: A disciplined life of self-denial and renunciation practiced for spiritual purposes.
facts.pilgrimage: A journey to a sacred place, undertaken for devotion, in nearly every major religion.
facts.mantra: A sacred sound, word, or phrase repeated in prayer or meditation.
facts.incense: Aromatic material burned as an offering or for ritual purification across many religions.
facts.cross: Two beams at right angles, and the central symbol of Christianity.
facts.tomatillo: A nightshade wrapped in its own papery lantern — the calyx husk it ripens inside. Aztec and Maya cooks used it before the tomato ever reached their kitchens.
facts.physalis: A marble-sized orange berry sealed inside its own inflated paper husk — packaging good enough to keep the fruit fresh for over a month at room temperature.
