facts.calamansi: A kumquat-mandarin hybrid small enough to be mistaken for a lime. The Philippines alone exports up to 190,000 tonnes of its juice a year.
facts.yerba_mate: A holly, not a tea plant. Its branches are dried over a wood fire, which is where mate's smoky note comes from, and its caffeine content sits between tea's and coffee's.
facts.bergamot: Too bitter to eat — grown almost entirely for its peel oil, and a hundred bergamot oranges yield only about 85 grams of it. One Italian province supplies nearly all the world's.
facts.jasmine: Blooms for one night only, releasing its scent for 12 to 20 hours before closing for good — pickers take only unopened white buds, since green ones never develop the fragrance.
facts.plantain: A sterile triploid hybrid of two wild bananas, bred for starch instead of sugar, which is why it's always cooked and never eaten raw.
facts.black_cardamom: Dried over an open flame instead of in the sun, which is why it tastes of campfire smoke instead of green cardamom's mint and lemon. Nepal grows more of it than anywhere else.
facts.butternut_squash: A 1944 invention, not an old heirloom — Massachusetts grower Charles Leggett crossed gooseneck and Hubbard squash to make it, and botanically it's classed as a berry.
facts.nasturtium: Every part above ground is edible, peppery like watercress — and its round leaves are so water-repellent that rain beads up and rolls clean off.
facts.perilla: Called shiso in Japan, deulkkae in Korea and zisu in China — a mint-family leaf that's also a livestock hazard: cattle that graze on it can develop fatal respiratory distress.
facts.absinthe_wormwood: Chernobyl is named for it — Old Slavic for 'black grass' — and its bitter compound, thujone, has never actually been proven to be what made 19th-century absinthe dangerous.
facts.doenjang: Korea's own miso, but not built on koji — its meju bricks grow a wild mould in open air for weeks before they ever touch brine.
facts.gochujang: Korea's chilli didn't arrive until the 1500s, carried in by Portuguese traders — yet the fermented pepper paste it made possible has its own centuries-old home town: Sunchang.
facts.geraniol: Bees paint it on flowers to mark them already-visited, and dab it at the hive entrance so stragglers can find their way home.
facts.beta_ionone: The scent of violets, made by snapping beta-carotene in half. Roughly a quarter of people carry a gene variant that makes them smell vinegar instead of flowers.
facts.ethyl_hexanoate: The pineapple-and-apple-peel note inside a wedge of blue cheese — the same ester that turns up in beer and port, part of why cheese pairs so well with both.
facts.dimethyl_trisulfide: Detectable at one part per trillion, foul enough to draw blowflies to a corpse — and the same molecule that gives black truffle and blue cheese part of their pungent kick.
facts.sufism: Islam's mystical tradition, seeking union with God through practices like dhikr and ecstatic whirling dance.
facts.ahmadiyya: Islamic reform movement founded 1889 in Punjab by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, who claimed to be the Mahdi.
facts.shia_islam: Second-largest Islamic branch, holding that Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, was his rightful successor.
facts.sunni_islam: Islam's largest branch (85-90% of Muslims), following Muhammad's sunnah and consensus-chosen caliphs.
facts.sharia: Islamic legal and ethical code from the Qur'an and Sunnah; its name literally means 'path to water.'
facts.jihad: Islamic duty to strive in God's way -- the inner 'greater jihad' against one's own vices, or armed struggle.
facts.wahhabism: Conservative Sunni revivalist movement founded in 18th-century Najd, allied since 1744 with the Saudi dynasty.
facts.salafism: Sunni revivalist movement (from 'salaf,' predecessors) urging return to early Islam's first generations.
facts.nation_of_islam: African American religious-political movement founded in Detroit, 1930, by Wallace Fard Muhammad.
facts.druze: Small esoteric faith split from Ismaili Islam near Cairo, c.1017 CE, teaching reincarnation of the soul.
facts.bahai_faith: Monotheistic faith founded by Baha'u'llah in 19th-century Persia, teaching unity of God and humanity.
facts.rastafari: Afro-Jamaican movement from the 1930s that reveres Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie I as a divine figure.
facts.santeria: Syncretic Cuban religion, 19th century, blending Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saint veneration.
facts.haitian_vodou: Syncretic Haitian religion blending West and Central African traditions with Catholicism; its spirits are lwa.
facts.cargo_cult: 20th-century Pacific Islander movements believing Western manufactured goods were spirit-sent 'cargo.'
facts.scientology: Belief system L. Ron Hubbard developed from his 1950 book Dianetics, centered on 'auditing' sessions.
facts.unification_church: New religious movement founded 1954 in Seoul by Sun Myung Moon, known for mass wedding 'Blessing' rites.
facts.wicca: Modern Pagan religion popularized in 1950s England by Gerald Gardner, venerating a Horned God and Goddess.
facts.unitarian_universalism: Creedless US faith formed in 1961 from the Unitarian and Universalist churches; symbol is the flaming chalice.
facts.hare_krishna: A devotional movement built around chanting the names of Krishna.
facts.falun_dafa: A qigong movement founded in China in 1992, combining slow exercises with a moral teaching.
facts.tenrikyo: Japanese new religion founded 1838 by Nakayama Miki, who recorded revelations in the sacred Ofudesaki.
facts.cao_dai: Syncretic Vietnamese religion founded 1926, uniting Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian, and Catholic elements.
facts.jehovahs_witnesses: Christian movement from 1870s Pittsburgh, known for door-to-door evangelism and refusing blood transfusions.
facts.mormonism: Faith founded 1830 in New York by Joseph Smith, based on the Book of Mormon translated from golden plates.
facts.quakers: Religious Society of Friends, founded mid-1600s England by George Fox, worshipping largely in silence.
facts.amish: Traditionalist Christians who split from the Mennonites in 1693, rejecting modern technology.
facts.mennonites: Anabaptist Christians named for reformer Menno Simons, baptizing only adult believers, not infants.
facts.shakers: Celibate US religious sect founded by Ann Lee, c.1747, famed for plain furniture and ecstatic worship.
facts.seventh_day_adventist: Christian denomination established 1863 in Michigan, observing Saturday Sabbath and vegetarian diet.
facts.pentecostalism: Christian movement from the 1906 Azusa Street Revival, emphasizing speaking in tongues.
facts.christian_science: Church founded 1879 in Boston by Mary Baker Eddy, relying on prayer rather than medicine for healing.
facts.salvation_army: Christian charity founded 1865 in London by William Booth, with military ranks and Christmas kettles.
facts.anglicanism: Church of England, founded 1534 when Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy broke from Rome.
facts.lutheranism: Protestant tradition begun 1517 by Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against indulgences.
facts.presbyterianism: Reformed Protestant tradition from Calvin and Knox, governed by elected elders, or 'presbyters.'
facts.methodism: Revival movement within Anglicanism founded by John Wesley, whose 1738 conversion sparked its growth.
facts.baptists: Protestant tradition from 1609, practicing believer's baptism by full immersion, not infant baptism.
facts.reform_judaism: Modernizing Jewish movement from early 19th-century Germany, emphasizing ethics over ritual observance.
facts.orthodox_judaism: Traditionalist Jewish movement that crystallized in the 1818-21 Hamburg Temple dispute.
facts.hasidic_judaism: Mystical Jewish revival founded c.1740 by the Baal Shem Tov, emphasizing joyful, ecstatic devotion.
facts.conservative_judaism: US Jewish movement centered on the Jewish Theological Seminary, a middle path between Reform and Orthodox.
facts.kabbalah: Jewish mysticism whose text, the Zohar, appeared in 13th-century Spain, describing ten divine sefirot.
facts.vaishnavism: Largest Hindu devotional tradition, revering Vishnu and his avatars Rama and Krishna as supreme.
facts.shaivism: The tradition that takes Shiva as the supreme reality rather than one god among many.
facts.shaktism: Hindu tradition worshipping the Goddess, Devi or Shakti, as ultimate reality, since Vedic times.
facts.arya_samaj: Hindu reform movement founded 1875 in Bombay by Swami Dayananda Saraswati, opposing idol worship.
facts.transcendental_meditation: Mantra-based meditation brought West in 1955 by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, popularized by the Beatles.
facts.theravada_buddhism: Oldest surviving Buddhist school, based on the Pali Canon, dominant in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
facts.mahayana_buddhism: Buddhist tradition emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal, dominant in China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan.
facts.zen_buddhism: Meditation-focused Buddhist school, from China's Chan, brought to Japan; centers on seated zazen.
facts.tibetan_buddhism: Buddhism of the Tibetan Empire, 7th-9th centuries, led by reincarnating lamas like the Dalai Lama.
facts.pure_land_buddhism: Chinese Buddhist tradition devoted to Amitabha Buddha, whose Pure Land paradise is reached by faith.
facts.nichiren_buddhism: Japanese Buddhist school founded by the 13th-century monk Nichiren, centered on the Lotus Sutra.
facts.soka_gakkai: Lay Buddhist movement founded 1930 in Japan by educators Makiguchi and Toda, rooted in Nichiren Buddhism.
facts.cuneiform: Sumerian wedge-shaped script pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus, from Uruk around 3300 BCE.
facts.hammurabi_code: Hammurabi's laws, cut in cuneiform onto a 7.5-foot basalt stele -- 'an eye for an eye' among ~300 clauses.
facts.indus_valley: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro: standardized fired-brick cities sharing one system of weights, with no found king.
facts.oracle_bone: Shang diviners cracked heated turtle shells and ox bones, then carved the question beside the crack.
facts.shang_dynasty: China's earliest dynasty confirmed by its own writing, casting bronze vessels for ritual, not daily use.
facts.minoan: Bronze Age Crete: masted ships carried trade to Egypt and Syria; palace at Knossos anchored the Aegean.
facts.mycenaean: Mainland Greeks who took Minoan Crete and adapted Linear A into Linear B, the earliest written Greek.
facts.bronze_age_collapse: Mycenaean Greece, the Hittite Empire, and Ugarit fell within decades, as iron began spreading in.
facts.phoenician_alphabet: Phoenician traders' phonetic script spread round the Mediterranean, ancestor of Greek, then Latin.
facts.assyrian_empire: Ruled from Nineveh in cuneiform; Ashurbanipal's library held 30,000+ tablets, including Gilgamesh.
facts.cyrus_the_great: Founder of Persia's Achaemenid Empire; took Babylon in 539 BCE nearly without a fight, freeing its exiles.
facts.battle_of_marathon: Outnumbered roughly 2 to 1, Athenian hoplites broke Darius I's invading Persians at Marathon.
facts.alexander_the_great: Broke Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, conquering the Persian Empire Cyrus founded two centuries before.
facts.qin_shi_huang: China's First Emperor, buried near Xi'an behind thousands of individually crafted terracotta soldiers.
facts.ashoka: Maurya emperor who, remorseful after conquering Kalinga, carved Buddhist edicts onto rocks and pillars.
facts.carthage: Phoenician colony on the North African coast, its name meaning 'new city' -- in legend founded by Dido.
facts.hannibal: Carthaginian general who led 38,000 troops and 38 war elephants across the Alps; almost none survived.
facts.julius_caesar: Led his legion across the Rubicon in defiance of the Senate, igniting Rome's civil war.
facts.cleopatra: Last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy after his empire split apart.
facts.augustus: Caesar's heir Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium and became Rome's first emperor.
facts.silk_road: Camel caravans carried China's silk to Rome, where the Senate banned it in vain as decadent.
facts.kush: Nubian kingdom whose King Piye conquered Egypt to found its 25th Dynasty; later capital Meroe smelted iron.
facts.gandhi: Led India's independence movement through nonviolent civil disobedience, or satyagraha.
facts.four_noble_truths: The Buddha's first sermon: suffering exists, it has a cause, it can end, and a path leads there.
facts.noble_eightfold_path: Eight practices of wisdom, ethics, and discipline — Buddhism's Fourth Noble Truth.
facts.middle_way: The Buddha's path of moderation between luxury and extreme self-denial.
facts.bodhisattva: In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who delays their own nirvana to help all others reach it.
facts.dalai_lama: Leader of Tibetan Buddhism's Gelug school, held to be compassion reborn in human form.
facts.ten_commandments: The core laws of the covenant at Sinai, inscribed on stone tablets given to Moses.
facts.diaspora: Jewish communities dispersed across the world after repeated exile from their homeland.
facts.maimonides: 12th-century philosopher and physician who argued God's oneness allows no parts or attributes.
facts.nicene_creed: The Christian statement of belief adopted at Nicaea in 325 CE and expanded in 381 CE.
facts.eucharist: Christian ritual reenacting Jesus's Last Supper, sharing bread and wine as his body and blood.
facts.baptism: Christian rite of initiation through ritual washing with water, following Jesus's own baptism.
facts.monasticism: Christians withdrawing from ordinary life to devote themselves to prayer, discipline, and study.
facts.protestant_reformation: The 16th-century split from the Catholic Church sparked by Luther's protest against indulgences.
facts.chain: Iron rings forged and closed while hot, then linked before they cool. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
facts.key: A sliver of metal cut to match one lock's internal wards, so only its owner — not a thief — can open a door.
facts.prometheus: Titan who fashioned humanity from clay and stole fire from the gods; chained to a rock, an eagle ate his regrowing liver daily.
facts.epimetheus: Prometheus's foolish brother — his name means "afterthought" — who ignored every warning and married Pandora anyway.
facts.pandora: The first woman, molded from clay by Hephaestus and given every grace by the gods, along with a jar she could not resist opening.
facts.pandoras_box: The jar Pandora opened despite every warning, loosing every evil into the world — only Hope stayed trapped inside.
facts.atlas: Titan condemned by Zeus to hold up the heavens forever, punishment for leading the Titans against the Olympians.
facts.deucalion: Prometheus's son, who built a chest to survive Zeus's flood, then repopulated the earth by throwing stones over his shoulder.
facts.pyrrha: Deucalion's wife and fellow flood survivor, whose stones thrown over her shoulder became the first women.
facts.daedalus: Athenian inventor who built Crete's Labyrinth, then fashioned feather-and-wax wings to fly himself and his son off the island.
facts.icarus: Daedalus's son, who ignored his father's warning, flew too near the sun on wax wings, and fell into the sea now named for him.
facts.phaethon: Son of the sun god Helios, who begged to drive his father's chariot for a day and was struck from the sky by Zeus to save the earth.
facts.labyrinth: The maze Daedalus built on Crete at King Minos's order, its passages winding so nothing inside could ever find its way out.
facts.minotaur: Half-man, half-bull son of Queen Pasiphaë and a bull sent by Poseidon, imprisoned by King Minos inside the Labyrinth.
facts.theseus: Athenian prince who volunteered as tribute to Crete and killed the Minotaur, escaping the Labyrinth with Ariadne's thread.
facts.ariadne: Cretan princess whose ball of thread saved Theseus from the Labyrinth; abandoned on Naxos, she married the god Dionysus instead.
facts.perseus: Son of Zeus, conceived as a shower of gold, who beheaded the Gorgon Medusa using a mirrored shield to avoid her petrifying gaze.
facts.medusa: The one mortal Gorgon, her hair living snakes and her gaze turning onlookers to stone, until Perseus struck off her head.
facts.pegasus: The winged horse that sprang fully grown from Medusa's neck the instant Perseus beheaded her.
facts.andromeda: Aethiopian princess chained to a sea cliff as a monster's sacrifice for her mother's boast, until Perseus swept down to save her.
facts.golden_fleece: The fleece of a winged golden ram, hung in a sacred Colchian grove and watched over by a dragon that never slept.
facts.jason: Rightful heir to Iolcos, who sailed the Argo to Colchis and won the Golden Fleece — only with the sorceress Medea's help.
facts.medea: Colchian sorceress whose narcotic herbs lulled the Golden Fleece's dragon to sleep; Jason's later betrayal turned her fury lethal.
facts.sphinx: Thebes's riddling monster — a woman's head, a lion's body, an eagle's wings — that strangled every traveler who answered wrong.
facts.oedipus: Theban king who fulfilled a prophecy of patricide and incest without knowing it, after answering the Sphinx's riddle about man.
facts.orpheus: Greek mythology's greatest musician, whose lyre-song nearly won his dead wife Eurydice back from the underworld.
facts.eurydice: Orpheus's bride, killed by a snakebite and lost forever when he glanced back at her one step before reaching daylight.
facts.midas: Phrygian king granted the golden touch by Dionysus — a blessing that turned his food, wine, and embrace into a curse.
facts.echo_nymph: Nymph cursed by Hera to only repeat others' last words, punishment for distracting the goddess while Zeus roamed unseen.
facts.narcissus: Beautiful youth who spurned the nymph Echo's love, then wasted away staring at his own reflection in a woodland pool.
facts.arachne: Lydian weaver so skilled she challenged Athena herself; struck down for it, she was reborn as the world's first spider.
facts.atlantis: Plato's fictional island empire, "larger than Libya and Asia," swallowed by the sea in a single day and night for its arrogance.
facts.psyche: Mortal princess so beautiful people worshipped her over Venus; her secret husband was Cupid, and her trials led her to godhood.
facts.janus: Roman god of doorways and beginnings, shown with two faces looking opposite ways at once — no Greek god has ever matched him.
facts.vesta: Roman virgin goddess of the hearth; her eternal flame, tended by the Vestal Virgins in the Forum, was never allowed to go out.
facts.hestia: Eldest child of Kronos, first swallowed and last disgorged; Greek goddess of the hearth fire at the center of every home.
facts.romulus: Twin son of Mars, suckled by a she-wolf after being left to die as an infant; he founded Rome on the Palatine Hill in 753 BCE.
facts.remus: Romulus's twin, also raised by the she-wolf; killed after mocking the walls of Rome's first, unfinished city.
facts.aeneas: Trojan prince, son of the goddess Venus, who carried his father from burning Troy and became — in Virgil's telling — Rome's ancestor.
facts.numa: Sabine second king of Rome, who met nightly with the nymph Egeria and founded the Vestal cult, the priesthoods, and the calendar.
facts.cybele: Anatolian "Great Mother" goddess, worshipped in Phrygia since the Bronze Age, brought to Rome in 204 BCE as a black meteoric stone.
facts.attis: Cybele's devoted companion, who castrated himself beneath a pine tree in a fit of grief-madness and was reborn each spring.
facts.mithras: Center of a secretive Roman soldiers' cult, worshipped underground for slaying the cosmic bull whose blood renewed the world.
facts.pygmalion: Cypriot sculptor who fell in love with his own ivory statue; Venus answered his prayer by bringing her to life as Galatea.
facts.sibyl_of_cumae: Apollo's ancient prophetess, granted a lifespan measured in grains of dust but not eternal youth; she guided Aeneas through the Underworld.
facts.medina: Yathrib's feuding tribes invited Muhammad to mediate in 622; his migration there began the Islamic calendar.
facts.umayyad_caliphate: Founded at Damascus in 661 by Mu'awiyah after the civil war that followed Caliph Ali's assassination.
facts.abbasid_caliphate: Overthrew the Umayyads in the 750 revolution, claiming descent from Muhammad's uncle Abbas.
facts.baghdad: Founded on the Tigris in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur; its House of Wisdom made it a center of learning.
facts.seljuk_turks: Turkic sultan Tugrul Beg took Baghdad in 1055, reducing the Abbasid caliph to a figurehead.
facts.byzantine_empire: The eastern Roman Empire that outlived Rome; in 552 its monks broke China's monopoly on silk.
facts.crusades: Launched in 1095 after Byzantine Emperor Alexius I begged Pope Urban II for help against the Seljuks.
facts.cannon: Cast in bronze in China by the 13th century; the 1298 Xanadu Gun is the earliest known survivor.
facts.ottoman_empire: Mehmed II's cannons breached Constantinople's walls in 1453, ending Byzantium.
facts.genghis_khan: Born Temüjin; united the Mongol clans at a 1206 assembly and took the title Genghis Khan.
facts.mongol_empire: Genghis Khan's conquests unified Central Asia, and the Pax Mongolica reopened the Silk Road.
facts.black_death: Mongol siege of Genoese Caffa in 1346 let plague reach ships that carried it to Sicily by 1347.
facts.kublai_khan: Genghis Khan's grandson; completed the conquest of Song China and founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271.
facts.yuan_dynasty: Kublai Khan's Mongol dynasty in China, which issued jiaochao — an early nationwide paper currency.
facts.ming_dynasty: Peasant rebel Zhu Yuanzhang overthrew the Yuan in 1368, rising through the Red Turban Rebellion.
facts.forbidden_city: Built 1406-1420 by the Ming Yongle Emperor from precious zhennan timber and specially baked brick.
facts.zheng_he: Ming eunuch admiral sent on seven treasure-fleet voyages, reaching East Africa by 1433.
facts.qing_dynasty: Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to Manchu forces in 1644, founding the Qing.
facts.samurai: Japan's warrior class, originally mounted horse-archers from wealthy landholding families.
facts.katana: Forged by folding and differentially tempering steel; the Tokugawa made it the samurai's badge.
facts.kamakura_shogunate: Minamoto Yoritomo's naval win at Dan-no-ura in 1185 led to Japan's first military government in 1192.
facts.delhi_sultanate: Founded in 1206 by the former slave Qutb-ud-din Aibak after Muhammad of Ghor's conquest of North India.
facts.tamerlane: Styling himself Genghis Khan's heir, he built a Central Asian empire and sacked Delhi in 1398.
facts.mughal_empire: Babur, descended from Tamerlane and Genghis Khan, used cannon to smash the Delhi Sultanate in 1526.
facts.khmer_empire: Founded by Jayavarman II in 802; its rice wealth came from a hydraulic network off the Tonlé Sap.
facts.angkor_wat: Built 1122-1150 under Suryavarman II, its towers designed to represent Mount Meru, home of the gods.
facts.mali_empire: Sundiata Keita founded it after the 1235 Battle of Kirina, taxing salt and gold across West Africa.
facts.mansa_musa: His 1324-25 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly gave away enough gold to depress its price in Cairo for years.
facts.aztec_empire: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, building an empire on chinampa maize farming and obsidian arms.
facts.tenochtitlan: The Aztec capital, built on a Lake Texcoco island and linked to the mainland by removable causeways.
facts.inca_empire: Centered on Cuzco high in the Andes; expanded explosively from 1438 under the ruler Pachacuti.
facts.machu_picchu: A royal estate built for Pachacuti around 1450 on a mountain ridge, abandoned near the Spanish conquest.
facts.hernan_cortes: Landed in 1519 with 500 men, 13 horses, and Tlaxcalan allies; took Tenochtitlan by siege in 1521.
facts.francisco_pizarro: Captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532; had him executed after a gold ransom in 1533.
facts.smallpox_epidemic: Arrived with Spanish forces in 1520 and killed thousands in Tenochtitlan, crippling Aztec resistance.
facts.martin_luther: Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor who protested indulgence sales in his 1517 95 Theses.
facts.hundred_years_war: Fought 1337-1453 over the French throne; cannon debuted at Crécy and decided it at Castillon.
facts.joan_of_arc: Broke the siege of Orléans in 1429; captured and burned at the stake as a heretic in 1431.
facts.sumer: City-states between the Tigris and Euphrates that gave the world its first cities, from 3000 BCE.
facts.akkadian_empire: Sargon's conquest of Sumer around 2334 BCE built history's first empire.
facts.hittites: Anatolian kingdom that fought Egypt to a standstill, then sealed history's earliest surviving treaty.
facts.minoan_crete: Crete's sea-trading palace culture, famous for the bull-leaping frescoes of Knossos.
facts.mycenaeans: Took Knossos from the Minoans and turned their script into the first written Greek.
facts.mohenjo_daro: A grid city of fired brick from about 2500 BCE with over 700 wells — one for every three houses — and drains running along the streets. Nobody knows why it was left.
facts.olmecs: Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization, famous for colossal carved basalt heads.
facts.chavin_culture: Spread a shared Andean religion of fanged jaguar gods, with no armies at all.
facts.achaemenid_empire: Cyrus's conquests built the largest empire the world had yet seen.
facts.persepolis: Darius's ceremonial capital, its Apadana built to host thousands -- burned by Alexander.
facts.hellenistic_culture: Alexander's generals split his empire into rival Greek-ruled kingdoms.
facts.roman_republic: Rome expelled its kings in 509 BCE and wrote its first laws onto bronze.
facts.punic_wars: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants and nearly destroyed Rome.
facts.fall_of_rome: Huns pushed the Goths into Rome, who sacked it -- ending 500 years of empire.
facts.celts: Iron Age Europe's ironworking, chariot-fighting, hillfort-building warrior culture.
facts.scythians: Steppe archers who buried their dead in gold-heavy kurgan mounds.
facts.huns: Broke the steppe empire that had displaced the Scythians, then turned on Rome.
facts.mauryan_empire: Chandragupta traded 500 war elephants to Alexander's former general for land.
facts.gupta_empire: Chandragupta I's dynasty, ruling from the old Mauryan capital of Pataliputra.
facts.terracotta_army: 8,000 unique clay soldiers guarding the First Emperor's tomb, found by well-diggers.
facts.han_dynasty: Wudi's campaigns opened the Silk Road, carrying Chinese silk as far as Rome.
facts.teotihuacan: The Americas' largest ancient city, built on a monopoly of obsidian trade.
facts.zapotec_civilization: Built Monte Albán on neutral mountaintop ground between three rival valleys.
facts.maya_civilization: City-states like Tikal, built on maize, with kings enthroned on jaguar pelts.
facts.athenian_democracy: Cleisthenes's Council of 500, and a vote of exile scratched onto broken pottery.
facts.sparta: Twin kings and a helot-farmed economy freed Spartan boys for lifelong war training.
facts.greco_persian_wars: 300 Spartans held Thermopylae for three days against Xerxes's Achaemenid army.
facts.peloponnesian_war: 27 years of Athens against Sparta, ending with the Athenian fleet trapped ashore.
facts.thales_of_miletus: Greek philosopher, c.624–546 BCE, credited as the first in the West to seek a rational rather than religious answer to what the cosmos is made of.
facts.pythagoras: Greek thinker, c.570–495 BCE, who taught that number and mathematical ratio underlie the structure of the whole cosmos.
facts.heraclitus: Greek philosopher, c.535–475 BCE, who held that the cosmos is in constant flux, held together only by tension between opposites.
facts.parmenides: Greek philosopher, c.515–445 BCE, who argued through pure logic that reality is a single, unchanging, indivisible whole.
facts.protagoras: Greek Sophist, c.490–420 BCE, who taught that truth is relative to the individual: 'man is the measure of all things.'
facts.democritus: Greek philosopher, c.460–371 BCE, who with Leucippus held that only atoms and the void between them truly exist.
facts.mozi: Chinese philosopher, c.470–391 BCE, who founded Mohism, teaching impartial, universal love (jian ai) for all people equally.
facts.diogenes_of_sinope: Greek founder of Cynicism, c.404–323 BCE, who lived by choice in a large storage jar and owned almost nothing.
facts.zeno_of_citium: Phoenician-Greek philosopher, c.332–265 BCE, who founded Stoicism in Athens after a shipwreck cost him his cargo.
facts.stoicism: School founded by Zeno of Citium holding that the goal of life is to live in agreement with nature, mastering only what reason controls.
facts.socratic_method: Socrates's technique of pressing a partner with question after question until their claimed knowledge collapses into contradiction.
facts.augustine_of_hippo: Christian philosopher, 354–430 CE, who argued evil is not a thing God made but a privation, an absence of good.
facts.boethius: Roman philosopher, c.480–525 CE, who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution on a charge of treason.
facts.anselm: Archbishop of Canterbury, 1033–1109, who devised the Ontological Argument: God, the greatest conceivable being, must exist in reality.
facts.averroes: Andalusian judge and philosopher, 1126–1198, who argued philosophy and Islamic revelation cannot truly contradict, since both pursue truth.
facts.rumi: Jalal al-Din Rumi, 1207-1273, the Persian poet whose work is the most read poetry in the world outside its own language.
facts.erasmus: Dutch humanist, 1466–1536, whose satire In Praise of Folly gives a mock speech in which Folly praises naivety over intellectual pride.
facts.machiavelli: Florentine political philosopher, 1469–1527, whose The Prince argues a ruler needs the ferocity of a lion and the cunning of a fox.
facts.montaigne: French philosopher, 1533–1592, who retired to a tower to write his Essays, arguing the pursuit of fame corrodes true tranquility.
facts.francis_bacon: English philosopher, 1561–1626, credited with 'knowledge is power' and the empirical, observation-based scientific method.
facts.hobbes: Thomas Hobbes, 1588-1679, who argued the state is a bargain people make against each other.
facts.pascal: French mathematician and philosopher whose 1654 letters with Fermat founded probability theory.
facts.spinoza: Dutch-Jewish rationalist excommunicated in 1656; argued God and Nature are one substance.
facts.leibniz: German polymath who argued reality is built from monads, substances that mirror the universe.
facts.berkeley: Irish idealist philosopher who held that objects exist only insofar as they are perceived.
facts.voltaire: French Enlightenment writer who mocked Leibniz's optimism in Candide after the Lisbon earthquake.
facts.hume: Scottish empiricist who argued causation is never perceived directly, only inferred from habit.
facts.rousseau: Genevan philosopher whose Social Contract (1762) argued government must express the general will.
facts.adam_smith: Scottish economist whose Wealth of Nations (1776) founded modern free-market economics.
facts.burke: Irish statesman whose Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) founded modern conservatism.
facts.bentham: English philosopher who founded utilitarianism: the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
facts.wollstonecraft: English writer whose Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued for women's education.
facts.hegel: German idealist who argued reality unfolds through contradiction resolving into higher unity.
facts.schopenhauer: German philosopher who argued a blind, striving Will underlies all appearance and causes suffering.
facts.feuerbach: German philosopher whose Essence of Christianity (1841) argued theology is really anthropology.
facts.mill: English philosopher whose On Liberty (1859) argued freedom may only be limited to prevent harm.
facts.kierkegaard: Danish philosopher, father of existentialism, who wrote most major works under pseudonyms.
facts.thoreau: American writer who lived alone at Walden Pond and argued for civil disobedience.
facts.peirce: American philosopher and logician who founded pragmatism with his pragmatic maxim.
facts.james: American philosopher and psychologist who developed pragmatism and coined 'stream of consciousness.'
facts.nietzsche: German philosopher who proclaimed 'God is dead' and called for humanity to be surpassed.
facts.saussure: Swiss linguist who founded semiotics, arguing a word's link to its meaning is arbitrary.
facts.husserl: German philosopher who founded phenomenology, seeking certainty by 'bracketing' every assumption.
facts.bergson: French philosopher who argued an élan vital, a vital impetus, drives creative evolution.
facts.dewey: American philosopher who argued we only think when we are confronted with problems.
facts.santayana: Spanish-American philosopher: 'those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.'
facts.unamuno: Spanish philosopher whose Tragic Sense of Life (1913) grounded existence in awareness of death.
facts.du_bois: American sociologist and first Black Harvard PhD; named 'double consciousness' and the color line.
facts.russell: British philosopher, co-founder of analytic philosophy, who argued for working less and living fuller.
facts.chernobog: Named by a 12th-century monk as the 'bad god' Slavs invoked over a shared bowl -- blamed for every misfortune.
facts.belobog: The 'White God' has no ancient source -- first appearing in the 1500s, invented as Chernobog's opposite.
facts.baba_yaga: A witch of Slavic folklore who lives in a hut on chicken legs and travels by wooden mortar and pestle.
facts.dievas: The Baltic sky god of light -- said to walk the earth disguised as a beggar, testing people's kindness.
facts.rainbow_serpent: Known by dozens of names across Aboriginal Australia, it carved mountains and lives in the waterholes it made.
facts.baiame: Sky father of southeastern Aboriginal Australia, who came down and shaped its rivers, mountains and forests.
facts.taaroa: Tahitian creator god who broke out of a cosmic shell alone and built the sky and earth from its two halves.
facts.tane: God of forests and birds who forced his sky father and earth mother apart, letting light into the world.
facts.rangi: The Maori sky father, held in an embrace with earth mother Papa so tight their children grew up in darkness.
facts.papa: The Maori earth mother -- the ground itself, wife to sky father Rangi until their son forced them apart.
facts.tawhirimatea: The only child of Rangi and Papa who protested their separation, and answered it with an army of storms.
facts.tu: Maori god of war, the only brother who stood against Tawhirimatea's storm rather than flee.
facts.maui: Polynesian trickster hero who fished up islands with a magic hook and lassoed the sun to slow it down.
facts.makemake: Creator god of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, carved into the island's rock as a face with huge eyes.
facts.haua: Goddess who shared Makemake's place at the heart of Rapa Nui's birdman cult and its seabird rites.
facts.spider_woman: Hopi and Navajo Spider Grandmother, credited with bringing the spindle, the loom, and weaving to the people.
facts.raven_spirit: The Haida credit this shapeshifting trickster with finding the first humans hidden inside a clam shell.
facts.sedna: The Inuit sea goddess, who holds the animals people hunt and withholds them when wronged.
facts.iktomi: Lakota trickster, first-born son of Inyan the Rock, turned into a spider as punishment for his cunning.
facts.nanabozho: Ojibwe trickster called Michabo, 'the Great Hare who created the Earth,' credited with inventing fishing.
facts.kiviuq: An Inuit hero said to travel eternally by kayak and sled across the Arctic, from Alaska to Greenland.
facts.inua: The spirit the Inuit believe lives in every person, animal, lake and mountain -- one life-force per kind.
facts.viracocha: Andean creator god who rose from Lake Titicaca in darkness and made humankind by breathing into stones.
facts.ngai: Creator god of the Kikuyu, Maasai and neighboring peoples, addressed as 'possessor of brightness.'
facts.amma: Dogon sky god whose union with the earth goddess was blocked by a termite mound standing in her place.
facts.nommo: The first living beings Amma made -- hermaphroditic water spirits with a human body and a fish's tail.
facts.legba: Guardian of the crossroads in Haitian Vodou, tracing back to Yoruba and Fon gods carried over the Atlantic.
facts.cicero: Exposed the Catiline conspiracy to overthrow the Republic with four fiery Senate speeches.
facts.charlemagne: Crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800, reviving the title in the West.
facts.william_the_conqueror: Won the English crown at Hastings in 1066, then surveyed his new kingdom in the Domesday Book.
facts.leonardo_da_vinci: Painted The Last Supper and the Mona Lisa, and filled notebooks with anatomy and invention sketches.
facts.michelangelo: Carved David from a single marble block, then spent four years frescoing the Sistine ceiling.
facts.henry_viii: Broke from Rome to divorce his first wife; married six times, beheading two of them.
facts.elizabeth_i: Presided over the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 during her 44-year reign.
facts.nicolaus_copernicus: Placed the Sun, not Earth, at the center of the universe in a book published as he lay dying.
facts.galileo_galilei: Turned a telescope on Jupiter and was later tried by the Inquisition for saying Earth moves.
facts.isaac_newton: United gravity and planetary motion in the Principia after reportedly watching an apple fall.
facts.louis_xiv: France's 'Sun King' ruled for 72 years and built the Palace of Versailles.
facts.oliver_cromwell: Led Parliament's cavalry to victory in the Civil War, then signed the king's death warrant.
facts.george_washington: Crossed the icy Delaware for a surprise victory, then stepped down after two presidential terms.
facts.thomas_jefferson: Drafted the Declaration of Independence, then doubled the nation's size via the Louisiana Purchase.
facts.benjamin_franklin: Flew a kite in a thunderstorm to prove lightning is electric, then signed all three founding documents.
facts.napoleon: Crowned himself Emperor in 1804, then met final defeat at Waterloo eleven years later.
facts.karl_marx: Co-wrote The Communist Manifesto, then spent decades in London writing Das Kapital.
facts.charles_darwin: Collected Galápagos finches on a five-year voyage, then explained their variety through natural selection.
facts.otto_von_bismarck: Vowed to settle great questions with 'iron and blood,' then unified Germany within a decade.
facts.mohandas_gandhi: Walked 240 miles to the sea to make illegal salt, leading India's independence movement.
facts.william_shakespeare: Wrote Hamlet for the Globe Theatre, which later burned down when a stage cannon misfired.
facts.johann_sebastian_bach: Directed Leipzig's church music for 27 years and once improvised a fugue for a king on the spot.
facts.uruk: The world's first true city, on the Euphrates around 3200 BC -- temples and walls of sun-dried mud brick.
facts.gilgamesh: The world's oldest surviving narrative literature -- a Sumerian king's quest for immortality, in cuneiform.
facts.sargon_of_akkad: Conquered Uruk and the Sumerian city-states around 2334 BC to found history's first known empire.
facts.battle_of_kadesh: Ramesses II's Egyptians clashed with the Hittites in 1274 BC in the largest chariot battle ever fought.
facts.egyptian_hittite_treaty: Sealed in silver 15 years after Kadesh -- the oldest peace treaty with both sides' copies still surviving.
facts.fall_of_western_rome: The Germanic king Odoacer deposed Rome's last western emperor in 476 AD, ending the empire.
facts.battle_of_hastings: William of Normandy's ship-borne cavalry defeated King Harold's army in a day, 14 October 1066.
facts.domesday_book: William the Conqueror's survey of nearly every landholder in England, completed in 1086.
facts.magna_carta: Sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215 under baronial revolt -- the first charter to bind the king to law.
facts.marco_polo: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant who set off along the Silk Road in 1271 to reach Kublai Khan's court.
facts.fall_of_constantinople: Ottoman cannons breached 800-year-old walls, taking Constantinople in 1453 and ending Byzantium.
facts.liquorice: A legume root, not a herb — three to five years underground before it's dug up, cleaned, and dried.
facts.caryophyllene: One of the few plant compounds confirmed to directly activate a cannabinoid receptor (CB2) — and it's in cinnamon, cloves, and black pepper, all classed safe to eat by the FDA.
facts.coumarin: Smells of sweet hay and fresh-cut grass, and builds up in the liver at high, sustained doses — the reason cassia and true cinnamon carry different safe limits.
facts.anethole: About 13 times sweeter than table sugar to the tongue, and made independently by three unrelated plant families — aniseed, star anise, and fennel all converged on the same molecule.
facts.shikimic_acid: The starting molecule for synthesizing the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — a 2005 shortage of it, drawn almost entirely from star anise pods, tightened world Tamiflu supply during a flu scare.
facts.myristicin: Nutmeg's own defensive chemical, and a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that clears certain neurotransmitters — a high-quality seed can carry up to 13mg of it per gram.
facts.sabinene: A woody, peppery terpene shared by nutmeg's seed and mace, its own seed coat — one reason the two spices from the same fruit still taste distinct.
facts.safrole: The sweet-shop smell in old-fashioned root beer, and a liver carcinogen in rodents at high dose — the US banned it as a food additive in 1960.
facts.cineole: Cardamom's medicinal, cooling edge — up to 70 percent of some cardamom oils — and the same molecule that makes up most of eucalyptus oil itself.
facts.cuminaldehyde: The molecule responsible for cumin's whole identity — spicy, green, a little sweaty — and the reason cumin doesn't smell like any of its carrot-family relatives.
facts.fenchone: A bitter, camphor-toned compound sitting beneath fennel's aniseed sweetness — structurally in the same family as camphor itself.
facts.mastic: Resin scored from a Chios shrub's bark, hardening into brittle amber tears over two to three weeks. The word 'masticate' comes from chewing it.
facts.rose_petal: Dried buds and petals of the damask rose, the species behind most rose flavouring in Western and Middle Eastern kitchens.
facts.ajwain: A parsley-family seed whose oil is mostly thymol — the compound that makes thyme taste like thyme.
facts.barberry: A thorny shrub's tart berries, dried and sold across Iran as zereshk — the thorns are exactly why they are still mostly hand-harvested.
facts.amchoor: Unripe green mangoes, peeled, sliced, and sun-dried, then ground — the sourness comes mostly from citric acid, the same acid that makes lemon juice sharp.
facts.lemon_myrtle: An Australian tree whose leaf oil runs 90 to 98 percent citral, a higher concentration than lemongrass and the most citral-rich natural source known.
facts.grains_of_selim: Dried pods of a West African evergreen tree in the same family as custard apple and soursop — in Senegal the unripe pods are smoked before drying.
facts.dried_lime: A whole lime left drying mostly out in the sun until it hardens black — the sun exposure is what actually darkens it, not the boiling step some recipes add first.
facts.wattle: Roasted, ground acacia seed with a coffee, chocolate and hazelnut flavour — specialised seed-grinding tools for it date back at least 1,000 years in Australia.
facts.anardana: Whole pomegranate seeds and pulp, sun-dried to reddish brown — used across North India as a souring agent the way lemon is used elsewhere.
facts.germacrene: Annatto seed's single most abundant flavour compound at nearly 18 percent of the essential oil — the reason the spice smells faintly of pine and wood despite being famous only for its red dye.
facts.pinene: The scent molecule behind pine resin and turpentine — mastic gum has been measured at up to 79 percent alpha-pinene, more concentrated than the pine trees it smells like.
facts.thymoquinone: Nigella seed's main aromatic compound — also what thyme and oregano's own thymol slowly oxidises into.
facts.nigellone: Two thymoquinone molecules fused together by sunlight during oil extraction — discovered early enough that it kept its own name instead of its chemical one, dithymoquinone.
facts.paradol: Grains of paradise's slow-building pepper heat — structurally a close cousin of ginger's own gingerol.
facts.picrocrocin: Saffron's bitter-tasting compound, up to 4 percent of the dried spice's weight — bound to a sugar molecule until drying breaks the two apart.
facts.safranal: Saffron's aroma, freed only once heat and enzymes split picrocrocin apart during drying — it can make up 70 percent of the dried spice's volatile oil.
facts.sedanolide: One of two compounds — alongside butylphthalide — credited with celery's entire smell and taste.
facts.phenylethanethiol: Curry leaf's most distinctive odour molecule — sulphurous and meaty, sitting in the same leaf oil as the citrus-scented linalool it shares nothing in common with.
facts.pentylfuran: Poppy seed's primary flavour compound — a furan ring with a five-carbon tail, and most of what a raw poppy seed actually tastes of.
facts.turmerone: A sesquiterpene from turmeric's essential oil, entirely separate from curcumin — turmeric's colour and its characteristic smell come from two different molecules.
facts.ocimene: One of the terpenes found in dried unripe mango, alongside myrcene and limonene — part of why amchoor smells faintly floral under all that sourness.
facts.panch_phoran: Bengal's whole five-seed blend — fenugreek, cumin, nigella, black mustard, and fennel — used unground, unlike almost every other spice mix.
facts.chaat_masala: North India's tangy street-food seasoning, built around amchoor and black salt rather than any single heat source.
facts.bok_globule: A small, dark, cold pocket of dust and gas — first described by Bart Bok in 1947 — that usually collapses into a double or multiple star system rather than one star alone.
facts.cometary_globule: A Bok globule with one side stripped away by a nearby hot star's ultraviolet light, left with a bright rim and a trailing dark tail.
facts.herbig_haro_object: A glowing knot where a young star's jet slams into surrounding gas at hundreds of kilometres a second — over a thousand are now catalogued, each lasting only tens of thousands of years.
facts.t_tauri_star: A pre-main-sequence star under 10 million years old and under 2 solar masses, still contracting toward the main sequence — named for the prototype star in Taurus.
facts.herbig_ae_be_star: The heavier, hotter counterpart to a T Tauri star — 2 to 8 solar masses, still wrapped in its birth disc, first identified by George Herbig in 1960.
facts.fu_orionis_star: A young star caught mid-outburst as its own disc suddenly dumps material onto it, brightening by several magnitudes for decades at a time — the average young star does this 10 to 20 times.
facts.actin_filament: A helical polymer of ATP-bound actin subunits, 7 nm across, that grows faster at one end than the other — the asymmetry is what lets a motor protein read a direction.
facts.myosin: A two-headed motor protein whose tails bundle into thick filaments and whose heads walk along actin, one ATP hydrolyzed per step.
facts.intermediate_filament: A 10 nm rope, midway in width between actin and microtubules, built purely for toughness — it has no polarity and drives no motor.
facts.integrin: A transmembrane receptor with one foot in the matrix outside the cell and one hand on the actin cytoskeleton inside — a literal handshake with its surroundings.
facts.muscle_contraction: Thick and thin filaments never shorten themselves — they slide past each other, millions of tiny myosin strokes firing at once.
facts.cell_migration: Crawling is push and grip: actin polymerization extends the front edge, integrins anchor it to the ground, and the cell body follows.
facts.g_protein_coupled_receptor: Seven passes through the membrane and one job: turn an outside signal into an inside shape-change that swaps GDP for GTP on a G protein.
facts.receptor_tyrosine_kinase: Ligand binding pairs two receptors up, and each spends ATP phosphorylating the other's tail — a handshake that builds its own docking sites.
facts.adenylyl_cyclase: The enzyme a hormone reaches through a G protein to turn ordinary ATP into a completely different kind of message.
facts.cyclic_amp: ATP with its tail looped back to bite its own phosphate — that loop is what turns fuel into a signal.
facts.protein_kinase_a: Cyclic AMP doesn't do the phosphorylating itself — it just pulls the pin that releases PKA's catalytic half.
facts.phospholipase_c: One enzyme, one cut through a membrane lipid, and two different second messengers come out of the same reaction.
facts.inositol_trisphosphate: The water-soluble half of a split membrane lipid, carrying three phosphates — light enough to swim through the cytosol to the ER.
facts.diacylglycerol: The greasy half of the same split lipid — too fat-soluble to leave the membrane, so it waits there for calcium to arrive.
facts.protein_kinase_c: Needs two second messengers at once, a lipid and a calcium spike, before it will touch a substrate.
facts.ras_protein: GTP-bound means on, GDP-bound means off — Ras is a molecular switch, and its stuck-on mutants drive up to 90% of some cancers.
facts.mapk_cascade: Three kinases in a row, each one switching on the next, turn a single Ras signal into a wave that reaches the nucleus.
facts.cortisol: A stress hormone built from cholesterol, small and greasy enough to walk straight through a cell membrane instead of knocking on it.
facts.nuclear_receptor: A receptor that skips the relay entirely — it binds its hormone and the DNA it regulates in the very same protein.
facts.continent: Continental crust is thick but light, so it floats higher than the seafloor — billions of years old in places.
facts.ocean: One of five basins holding 97% of Earth's water, still widening where mid-ocean ridges add new seafloor.
facts.peninsula: Land joined to the mainland on one side only, water on the rest — often via a narrow isthmus.
facts.archipelago: A chain or cluster of islands, like Hawaii or the Azores — most often volcanic in origin.
facts.strait: A narrow channel joining two seas; Gibraltar's separates Europe from Africa.
facts.isthmus: A narrow land bridge between two larger landmasses, sea on both sides — the mirror of a strait.
facts.equator: The imaginary line at 0° latitude, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
facts.hemisphere: Half of Earth's surface — the Equator splits north from south, a meridian splits east from west.
facts.latitude: Circles parallel to the Equator, 0° there to 90° at either pole — north-south position.
facts.longitude: Meridians running pole to pole, perpendicular to latitude — east-west position.
facts.prime_meridian: The longitude fixed at 0° by international agreement in 1884, running through Greenwich, England.
facts.time_zone: A region sharing one standard time, its offset from UTC set relative to the Prime Meridian.
facts.tropic_of_cancer: Latitude 23.4°N — the northernmost point where the Sun sits directly overhead, on the June solstice.
facts.tropic_of_capricorn: Latitude 23.4°S — the southernmost point where the Sun sits directly overhead, on the December solstice.
facts.steppe: Dry, treeless, temperate grassland — too dry for forest, not dry enough to be desert.
facts.savanna: Tropical grassy woodland, trees spaced too far apart for the canopy to close — a fifth of Earth's land.
facts.border: The line where one state's sovereign territory ends and another's begins — natural or drawn.
facts.country: A political entity or its territory — sovereign state, dependent territory, or something between.
facts.nation_state: A sovereign, bordered state whose population shares a common national identity.
facts.capital_city: The city holding a country's seat of government — not always its largest.
facts.population_density: People per unit of land area — Monaco packs in over 18,000/km²; Mongolia has about two.
facts.supply_chain: The network of facilities that turns raw materials into finished products and moves them on to customers.
facts.logistics: Moving goods from origin to consumption — a word the military took from the French for lodgings.
facts.supply_chain_management: Procurement, operations, logistics and marketing, from raw material to customer, run as one system.
facts.sales_forecasting: Using past sales figures to predict short- or long-term performance for financial planning.
facts.demand_planning: Predicting future customer demand so a business holds the right inventory, not too much or too little.
facts.sales_and_operations_planning: A monthly process, credited to consultant Richard Ling in the 1980s, that balances demand against supply.
facts.warehouse: A building for storing goods, used by manufacturers, importers, wholesalers and transport firms alike.
facts.inventory: The goods and materials a business holds on hand for resale, production or use.
facts.inventory_management: Tracking stock with software; retail barcode scanning began in 1974, computerized records in the 1980s.
facts.safety_stock: Extra inventory held on purpose, as insurance against uncertain demand, supply or forecasts.
facts.economic_order_quantity: The order size that minimizes total holding and ordering costs — a formula Ford W. Harris derived in 1913.
facts.bullwhip_effect: Small swings in retail demand get amplified into big swings in orders further up a supply chain.
facts.just_in_time: Receiving goods only as needed, to cut cost and waste — Toyota modeled it on supermarket restocking.
facts.kanban: 'Signboard' in Japanese — a card that authorizes production only after the next step pulls from it.
facts.lean_manufacturing: Produce only what's needed, fix problems immediately, let workers improve the process — named 'Lean' in 1988.
facts.material_requirements_planning: A production and inventory scheduling system Joseph Orlicky developed in 1964.
facts.enterprise_resource_planning: Integrated business-process software; research firm Gartner coined the acronym 'ERP' in the 1990s.
facts.vendor_managed_inventory: The supplier, not the buyer, decides how much stock to ship and hold — a model Walmart and P&G made famous.
facts.distribution_requirements_planning: Applies MRP-style time-phased planning to a distribution network, tracking parameters like safety stock.
facts.fire_lance: A bamboo tube of gunpowder and slow match lashed to a spear — the ancestor of every gun.
facts.composite_bow: Horn belly for compression, sinew backing for tension, wood core between — far more pull per draw.
facts.chariot: A cart built light around spoked wheels, so horses could pull it fast enough for war.
facts.war_elephant: An elephant armored in iron plate and scale, sent to trample ranks and break cavalry charges.
facts.horse_archer: A rider firing a compact recurve bow at a gallop — the steppe's answer to heavy infantry.
facts.stirrup: A foot loop hung from the saddle; a rigid paired version let riders fight without falling off.
facts.greek_fire: A petroleum-based incendiary sprayed from a shipboard siphon; the Byzantines never revealed the recipe.
facts.flintlock_musket: Flint struck steel to spark the priming pan — cheaper and steadier than a smoldering match cord.
facts.machine_gun: Hiram Maxim's recoil-operated, water-cooled gun fired 600 rounds a minute, one crew for sixty riflemen.
facts.torpedo: A self-propelled, compressed-air-driven shell of steel or bronze that runs to its target underwater.
facts.zeppelin: A rigid, aluminum-framed airship lifted by hydrogen gas cells; Germany used them to bomb Britain.
facts.ak47: A steel-bodied rifle that bleeds propellant gas to cycle its own bolt, built to run caked in mud.
facts.atomic_bomb: A weapon of nuclear fission; the Manhattan Project bred its plutonium fuel inside a reactor.
facts.poison_gas: Chlorine drifting downwind from opened cylinders — chemical warfare's first mass battlefield use.
facts.sodium_channel: A membrane protein selective for sodium ions, opening on depolarization to drive the action potential's rise.
facts.potassium_channel: Opens just after a sodium channel does, letting potassium leave and pulling the voltage back down.
facts.refractory_period: The brief window after a spike when a sodium channel sits inactivated and a second one can't fire.
facts.node_of_ranvier: The bare gap between two segments of myelin, where the axon is exposed and sodium channels cluster densely.
facts.saltatory_conduction: The impulse jumps from one exposed node to the next in a myelinated axon, far faster than a bare one allows.
facts.schwann_cell: The peripheral nervous system's myelin-maker — the PNS counterpart to the oligodendrocyte, one axon each.
facts.mechanoreceptor: A sensory nerve ending built to fire when pressed, stretched, or deformed rather than by light or chemicals.
facts.nociceptor: A sensory ending tuned to potentially damaging stimuli, in skin and just as often deep in muscle and joints.
facts.pacinian_corpuscle: A mechanoreceptor wrapped in 20 to 70 onion-like layers, buried deep in skin to catch vibration and pressure.
facts.muscle_spindle: A stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptor inside the muscle itself, reporting how long the muscle currently is.
facts.retina: Technically brain tissue, budded outward before birth — the only piece of CNS visible without surgery.
facts.photoreceptor: Rods and cones share a mechanism: an opsin pigment absorbs a photon and changes shape, starting the signal.
facts.cornea: The eye's clear front window, built from ~200 stacked layers of collagen fibers spaced to not scatter light.
facts.lens: Over 90% protein by weight — crystallins, packed dense enough to bend light with no blood supply of its own.
facts.iris: A pigmented ring of muscle around the pupil — one set of fibers narrows it, another set widens it.
facts.oculomotor_nerve: Cranial nerve III: moves the eyeball with one set of fibers, shrinks the pupil with another.
facts.hair_cell: Stereocilia-tufted cells turning motion into signal — the same design serves both hearing and balance.
facts.cochlea: A fluid-filled spiral making almost three full turns, lined with hair cells to catch sound at every pitch.
facts.tympanic_membrane: A thin cone of tissue turning air-pressure changes into vibration, passed on to three tiny bones.
facts.vestibular_system: The inner ear's other job besides hearing — sensing balance and orientation, via the same cranial nerve.
facts.glossopharyngeal_nerve: Cranial nerve IX: taste from the tongue's back third, and the order that starts the parotid gland salivating.
facts.taste_bud: Taste receptor cells clustered on the tongue — the ones at the very back use a different cranial nerve.
facts.olfactory_epithelium: The nasal lining is a sense organ itself — its receptor neurons' axons bundle straight into a cranial nerve.
facts.motor_neuron: A neuron whose cell body sits in the spinal cord's ventral horn, its axon running out to control a muscle.
facts.reflex_arc: The simplest circuit in the body: a stretched muscle spindle synapses onto a motor neuron, no brain required.
facts.basal_ganglia: Nuclei buried inside the cerebral hemispheres, shaping voluntary movement from beneath the cortex.
facts.substantia_nigra: A basal-ganglia nucleus that makes dopamine; losing enough of these neurons causes Parkinson's disease.
facts.epinephrine: One methyl group away from noradrenaline — the same fight-or-flight chemical, tuned by a single enzyme step.
facts.endorphin: The body's own painkiller: binds the same receptors opioid drugs do, at the nerve endings that report pain.
facts.eeg: Scalp electrodes eavesdropping on the cortex — mostly picking up summed postsynaptic potentials, not spikes.
facts.alpha_wave: An 8-to-13-hertz rhythm on a relaxed, eyes-closed EEG, thought to arise from a thalamic pacemaker circuit.
facts.rem_sleep: The dreaming stage, run on acetylcholine — the same neurotransmitter active in waking, with noradrenaline off.
facts.wernicke_area: The temporal lobe's language-comprehension hub, wired to the ear's own cranial nerve to hear what it parses.
facts.broca_area: The frontal lobe's speech hub, linked to Wernicke's comprehension area by one dedicated fiber tract.
facts.sword: A straight double-edged blade with a crossguard, standard among Norman knights from the 11th century.
facts.dagger: A short, sharply tapered double-edged blade -- a sword scaled down to a size worn at the belt.
facts.misericorde: A long, narrow dagger known from the 12th century -- thin enough to slide through a visor or armor joint.
facts.longsword: An 80-110 cm double-edged blade with a two-handed grip, built to thrust through gaps in plate armor.
facts.gambeson: A quilted jacket of stitched wool or linen padding -- armor by itself, or worn under mail to cushion it.
facts.chain_mail: Wire rings, each riveted shut and linked through four others -- a hauberk worn in Europe for 1,900 years.
facts.shield: Light wood boards faced with leather, centered on a riveted metal boss that guards the holding hand.
facts.kite_shield: Almond-shaped and elongated to a point, covering a mounted rider's leg where a round shield could not.
facts.plate_armor: Well-tempered steel plates, articulated joint by joint -- complete suits existed in Europe by about 1420.
facts.halberd: An axe blade, a spike, and a hook for pulling riders down, all mounted on one long shaft.
facts.pike: A spearhead on a shaft 3 to 7 meters long, reinforced with metal strips -- a wall against cavalry.
facts.war_hammer: A blunt hammer face balanced by a spike on the reverse -- stun with one side, then punch with the other.
facts.poleaxe: An axe blade, a hammer, and a spearhead on one ash shaft -- three chances to find a gap in plate armor.
facts.war_mace: A flanged steel head riveted to a tapered handle -- ridges that focus a blow's force enough to dent plate.
facts.flail: An iron-shod striking head swinging off a wooden shaft on a chain -- a threshing tool turned to war.
facts.crossbow: A bow locked crosswise onto a wooden stock, cocked and released by a trigger -- common in Europe by 1100.
facts.longbow: A six-foot bow made specifically of yew -- the weapon behind English victories at Crecy and Agincourt.
facts.battering_ram: An iron- or steel-capped log slung on chains inside a wheeled frame, swung again and again at a gate.
facts.siege_tower: A wheeled wooden tower faced in iron or wet hide against fire, rolled to a wall to drop a gangplank.
facts.katar: A South Indian push-dagger with an H-shaped grip so a punching thrust lands the whole arm's weight.
facts.kris: A Javanese dagger pattern-welded from layered iron and nickel-rich iron, sometimes meteoric.
facts.shotel: An Ethiopian sword curved into a near semicircle, built to hook around an opponent's shield.
facts.takouba: A meter-long, straight double-edged sword carried across the Sahel by Tuareg, Hausa and Fulani.
facts.tulwar: A curved single-edged saber of the Indian subcontinent, known by its all-metal disc-pommel hilt.
facts.flyssa: A narrow single-edged Algerian blade of the Kabyle Iflissen, pommel capped in an animal head.
facts.iklwa: Shaka's short Zulu stabbing spear, its shaft cut down and its blade widened for close combat.
facts.shamshir: A Persian saber curved into a radical arc; the name literally means 'lion's fang.'
facts.yataghan: An Ottoman forward-curving blade with no guard, its hilt flared into two 'ears' at the pommel.
facts.repeating_crossbow: A Chinese crossbow with a gravity-fed magazine of bolts, worked by one lever for rapid fire.
facts.sling: A pouch on two cords, whirled overhead and released to hurl a stone farther than a bare throw.
facts.macuahuitl: An Aztec wooden sword lined with obsidian blades sharper than steel, but brittle against armor.
facts.vexillum: Cloth hung from a horizontal crossbar on a spear, carried by Roman cavalry -- root of the word 'vexillology'.
facts.saltire: A diagonal cross. Andrew, by tradition, was crucified on one -- giving Scotland's flag its white saltire.
facts.oriflamme: France's medieval royal battle standard: a blood-red banner on a gilded lance. Its name means 'golden flame.'
facts.ensign: A national flag flown by a ship. Britain keeps three: White for the Navy, Blue for government, Red for trade.
facts.tricolour: Three solid colour bands. France's blue-white-red, fixed in 1794, became a liberty-movement template.
facts.union_flag: James I's 1606 flag overlaid Scotland's saltire on England's red cross -- Ireland's cross joined only in 1801.
facts.dannebrog: Denmark's flag, said to have fallen from the sky in 1219. Official since 1625, the oldest one still flown.
facts.flag_norway: Added a blue cross to Denmark's pattern in 1821, to match the French, Dutch, and American 'flags of freedom.'
facts.flag_sweden: Blue and gold trace to Sweden's Three Crowns coat of arms, in use since at least 1364.
facts.flag_finland: Adopted at independence in 1918: blue for Finland's thousands of lakes, white for winter snow.
facts.flag_iceland: Blue for mountains and sea, white for ice, red for fire. Finalised 1915, official with the 1944 republic.
facts.flag_germany: Black, red, and gold trace to the Lützow Free Corps' Napoleonic-era uniforms -- Germany's colours since 1848.
facts.flag_poland: White and red come from the coat of arms' White Eagle on red -- national colours by 1831, flag by 1919.
facts.flag_argentina: Light blue and white from the 1810 May Revolution cockade; the gold Sun of May was added in 1818.
facts.flag_uruguay: Nine stripes for Uruguay's original nine departments, under a Sun of May shared with Argentina. Adopted 1828.
facts.flag_brazil: 27 stars map the sky over Rio on 15 Nov 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed -- one per federal unit.
facts.flag_chile: A lone white star for Venus over Andes-snow white and sky blue. Adopted 1817, decades before Texas's version.
facts.wiphala: A 49-square rainbow checkerboard used by Andean Quechua and Aymara -- Bolivia's official co-flag since 2009.
facts.flag_venezuela: Francisco de Miranda's yellow-blue-red tricolour, first flown 12 March 1806 at Jacmel, Haiti.
facts.flag_costa_rica: The coat of arms shows three volcanoes between two oceans, ringed by seven stars for seven provinces.
facts.flag_el_salvador: Five volcanoes for the five states of the old Central American federation, under a biblical rainbow of peace.
facts.flag_panama: A blue star for the Conservative party and a red star for the Liberal party, designed in 1903.
facts.flag_jamaica: A gold saltire quarters green and black: 'hardships there are, but the land is green and the sun shineth.'
facts.flag_cuba: A Masonic red triangle behind a white 'Lone Star,' first raised by rebels at Cardenas on 19 May 1850.
facts.flag_mexico: The coat of arms' eagle devouring a serpent on a cactus is the Aztec omen that marked Tenochtitlan's site.
facts.flag_canada: An 11-point maple leaf, adopted 15 Feb 1965 -- the point count chosen for staying sharp in wind-tunnel tests.
facts.flag_united_states: 13 stripes for the original colonies, 50 stars for the states -- current design flown since July 1960.
facts.immortals: Persia's elite 10,000-man guard, kept at exactly that number by instantly replacing any casualty.
facts.hoplite: Greek citizen-soldiers who fought shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx behind a bronze-faced shield.
facts.sarissa: Philip II's 5-7 meter Macedonian pike, longer than the Greek dory, that let phalanx rows overlap.
facts.gladius: Rome's short stabbing sword, adopted from Celtiberian designs during the Punic Wars.
facts.pilum: A Roman javelin with a soft iron shank that bent on impact, jamming an enemy's shield.
facts.lorica_segmentata: Roman body armor of overlapping iron bands, buckled over a padded tunic from the 1st century AD.
facts.testudo: Roman legionaries locked shields into a moving wall and roof, shrugging off missiles during a siege.
facts.cataphract: Cavalry armored from head to hoof -- rider and horse both -- charging home with heavy lances.
facts.varangian_guard: Byzantine emperors' bodyguard, deliberately recruited from Norse and later Anglo-Saxon outsiders.
facts.berserker: Norse warriors said to fight in a trance-like fury; a 9th-century poem calls them 'wolf-skin men.'
facts.housecarl: Paid professional soldiers of Scandinavian kings; Harold's housecarls held the line at Hastings.
facts.knight: A mounted, armored warrior who owed a lord roughly 40 days of yearly service in exchange for land.
facts.trebuchet: A pivoting siege beam that hurled stones at castle walls; Chinese crews once pulled its ropes by hand.
facts.chainmail: Interlocking iron rings woven into mesh armor, first made by the Celts around the 3rd century BC.
facts.rapier: A slender 16th-century thrusting sword born in Spain and Italy for civilian dueling, not the battlefield.
facts.scimitar: A light, curved slashing sword built for mounted warfare across Persia, Arabia and the Ottoman world.
facts.janissary: Ottoman infantry levied as Christian boys from the Balkans; among Europe's first troops issued firearms.
facts.landsknecht: German Renaissance mercenary pikemen, known for outlandish slashed-and-puffed dress.
facts.winged_hussar: Polish heavy cavalry, active 1503-1702, famed for lance charges and feathered wings on their backs.
facts.naginata: A Japanese polearm with a curved blade, prized for dismounting cavalry and later favored by noblewomen.
facts.parthian_shot: Firing backward at a full gallop while feigning retreat -- the Parthians' signature cavalry trick.
facts.milgram_obedience_experiments: Experiments Stanley Milgram ran at Yale from 1961, testing how far people would go in obeying orders to harm someone else.
facts.asch_conformity_experiments: Experiments Solomon Asch ran from 1951, testing whether people would echo an answer they knew was wrong to match a unanimous group.
facts.narcissism: Personality trait of grandiosity, a constant need for admiration, and low empathy, from an ordinary style to narcissistic personality disorder.
facts.machiavellianism: Personality trait for a cynical, manipulative style: deceiving and exploiting others, with little regard for conventional morality.
facts.psychopathy: Personality construct of shallow emotion, low empathy and remorse, and impulsive antisocial behavior, often masked by charm.
facts.dark_triad: Construct grouping narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy as three distinct, overlapping traits sharing a callous, manipulative style.
facts.d_factor: Proposed common core beneath dark traits: a general tendency to maximize one's own gain at others' expense, dressed in self-justifying beliefs.
facts.cognitive_dissonance: Discomfort felt when holding two contradictory beliefs, or when belief and behavior don't match, that motivates changing one of them.
facts.classical_conditioning: Learning process where a neutral stimulus, paired repeatedly with a meaningful one, comes to trigger that stimulus's own response.
facts.principles_of_persuasion: Six patterns Robert Cialdini identified as reliably raising compliance: reciprocity, consistency, social proof, liking, authority, scarcity.
facts.foot_in_the_door_technique: Compliance pattern where agreeing to a small request raises the odds of later agreeing to a larger, related one.
facts.door_in_the_face_technique: Compliance pattern where refusing an extreme request raises the odds of accepting a smaller one that follows it.
facts.groupthink: Pattern where a group's push for harmony overrides real appraisal of alternatives, steering it toward a bad decision.
facts.neuro_linguistic_programming: Techniques and a communication theory introduced by Richard Bandler and John Grinder in the 1970s; controlled studies have found no scientific support for its central claims.
facts.milton_erickson: American psychiatrist, 1901–1980, founder of the indirect, conversational style of clinical hypnosis known as Ericksonian hypnosis.
facts.bradley_ifv: An aluminum-armored troop carrier armed like a tank, carrying a 25mm cannon and TOW missiles since 1981.
facts.black_hawk: Two General Electric T700 turboshaft engines replace the single engine of the Huey it succeeded in 1979.
facts.ch47_chinook: Two counter-rotating rotors cancel each other's torque, so the Chinook needs no tail rotor at all.
facts.apache_helicopter: Its AN/APG-78 'Longbow' radar, mounted above the rotor, tracks up to 128 targets at once.
facts.kiowa_warrior: A sensor ball above the rotor — crews call it the beach ball — packs a camera, thermal imager and laser designator.
facts.m109_paladin: A 155mm howitzer on a tracked, diesel-powered chassis that moves under its own power instead of being towed.
facts.mlrs: One launcher firing all twelve rockets blankets a square kilometer — troops nicknamed it the 'grid square removal system.'
facts.himars: The same launcher as the M270 MLRS, but with one rocket pod on a wheeled truck instead of tracks.
facts.patriot_missile: Its AN/MPQ-53 phased-array radar tracks both target and missile, radioing steering corrections back in flight.
facts.javelin_missile: Its onboard infrared seeker locks on before launch, so the gunner can take cover immediately — no wire or laser needed.
facts.tow_missile: Two hair-thin wires spool out behind it, carrying the gunner's steering commands to the target.
facts.hellfire_missile: It homes in on a laser spot someone else paints on the target, rather than carrying its own radar or camera.
facts.hmmwv: Portal-axle hubs raise the drivetrain above the wheel centers, nearly doubling an SUV's ground clearance.
facts.stryker_vehicle: An 8x8 wheeled armored vehicle trades off-road ability and armor for road speed and easy maintenance.
facts.mrap_vehicle: A V-shaped hull, first built for South Africa's Casspir in 1979, throws a mine blast sideways instead of straight up.
facts.m16_rifle: Its aluminum-alloy receiver made it far lighter than the steel-and-walnut rifles it replaced in 1964.
facts.m4_carbine: A shortened M16: 80% of parts interchange, but a 14.5-inch barrel makes it far easier to handle indoors.
facts.m249_saw: Adapted from Belgium's FN Minimi, its belt feed fires the M16's own round in bursts no magazine could sustain.
facts.m2_browning: Designed by John Browning around 1918, it's been in continuous U.S. service since 1933 — longer than any firearm but his own M1911.
facts.amyloid_precursor_protein: A membrane protein encoded on chromosome 21, clipped by secretase enzymes into fragments including amyloid-beta.
facts.amyloid_beta: A 36-to-43-amino-acid peptide cut from APP; the main component of the amyloid plaques found in Alzheimer's brains.
facts.amyloid_plaque: Extracellular deposits of misfolded amyloid-beta in the brain's grey matter — one of Alzheimer's two hallmark lesions.
facts.tau_protein: A protein that normally stabilizes the microtubule tracks running down a neuron's axon.
facts.neurofibrillary_tangle: Intracellular tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, twisted into paired helical filaments — Alzheimer's other hallmark lesion.
facts.alpha_synuclein: A presynaptic protein that regulates synaptic vesicle recycling; its misfolded form builds Lewy bodies.
facts.lewy_body: A round inclusion of misfolded alpha-synuclein inside a neuron, first described in 1902.
facts.apolipoprotein_e: A fat-transport protein whose ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.
facts.neurodegeneration: The progressive loss of neurons' structure and function, ending in cell death — the process behind every dementia.
facts.dementia: A syndrome of progressive cognitive decline severe enough to interfere with daily life — not one disease, but many.
facts.alzheimers_disease: The most common cause of dementia, marked by amyloid plaques and tau tangles; first described in 1906.
facts.vascular_dementia: The second most common form of dementia, caused by strokes or other damage that restricts blood flow to the brain.
facts.lewy_body_dementia: Dementia marked by fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder.
facts.frontotemporal_dementia: A family of disorders degenerating the frontal and temporal lobes, changing personality and language before memory.
facts.alois_alzheimer: German psychiatrist and neuropathologist (1864–1915) who first described the disease that bears his name.
facts.friedrich_lewy: German-American neurologist (1885–1950) who identified the brain inclusions later named Lewy bodies.
facts.arnold_pick: Czech-German psychiatrist (1851–1924) whose 1892 case report first described what became frontotemporal dementia.
facts.auguste_deter: Alzheimer's first documented patient; her 1906 autopsy revealed the plaques and tangles that define the disease.
facts.otto_kernberg: Vienna-born psychiatrist who fled Nazi Austria for Chile in 1939 and later built the object relations model of personality disorders.
facts.marsha_linehan: Psychologist whose 1993 book, decades after her own adolescent hospitalization, introduced dialectical behavior therapy.
facts.john_gunderson: Harvard psychiatrist whose 1975 paper helped define borderline personality disorder as a distinct diagnosis.
facts.peter_fonagy: Psychologist who, with Anthony Bateman, built mentalization-based treatment from attachment theory's caregiver-mirroring research.
facts.jeffrey_young: Psychologist trained under Aaron Beck who founded schema therapy, extending CBT to personality disorders.
facts.theodore_millon: Psychologist who founded the Journal of Personality Disorders and built a biosocial theory of personality pathology.
facts.robert_cloninger: Psychiatrist-geneticist who modeled personality as four temperament dimensions plus three character dimensions.
facts.mary_zanarini: Harvard researcher who has followed roughly 300 hospitalized borderline personality disorder patients for decades.
facts.thomas_widiger: Clinical psychologist on the DSM-III-R advisory committee and DSM-IV's first research coordinator.
facts.object_relations_theory: Psychoanalytic theory holding that early caregiving relationships form lasting internalized images of self and others.
facts.splitting_defense_mechanism: Defense mechanism of experiencing people as wholly good or wholly bad, with no stable middle ground.
facts.transference_focused_psychotherapy: Structured psychodynamic therapy working through a patient's contradictory feelings as they surface toward the therapist.
facts.dialectical_behavior_therapy: Therapy pairing CBT technique with mindfulness and acceptance skills drawn from Zen practice.
facts.mentalization_based_treatment: Therapy building the capacity to read mental states, one's own and others', often impaired by disorganized attachment.
facts.schema_therapy: Integrative therapy targeting 'early maladaptive schemas' — self-defeating patterns formed in childhood.
facts.good_psychiatric_management: Less-intensive borderline personality disorder treatment that began as a drug-trial control condition.
facts.alternative_dsm5_model_for_personality_d: DSM-5 model rating personality on continuous trait and functioning scales instead of categories alone.
facts.temperament_and_character_inventory: 240-item questionnaire from Cloninger's model, scoring seven temperament and character dimensions.
facts.mclean_study_of_adult_development: Decades-long study that overturned the assumption that borderline personality disorder rarely improves.
