facts.procyon: Canis Minor's brightest star, Greek for 'before the dog' — it rises just ahead of Sirius from most northern latitudes.
facts.aldebaran: Taurus's brightest star, a red giant 45 times the Sun's width marking the bull's eye — Arabic for 'the follower' of the Pleiades.
facts.regulus: Leo's brightest star, Latin for 'the little king' — it sits so near the ecliptic that the Moon and planets cross in front of it.
facts.antares: Scorpius's brightest star, a red supergiant 680 times the Sun's radius — Greek for 'rival of Mars,' after its ember-red glow.
facts.capella: Auriga's brightest star, 'the goat star' — named for Amalthea, the mythical she-goat that nursed the infant Zeus.
facts.castor: One of Gemini's twin stars, named for the mortal horseman of Greek myth — Homer called him 'the horse breaker.'
facts.pollux: Gemini's other twin star, named for the immortal son of Zeus — a champion boxer who beat a king in the ring.
facts.polaris: The current North Star, under a degree from the north celestial pole, at the tip of Ursa Minor's tail.
facts.ursa_major: The Great Bear, third-largest of the 88 constellations — Callisto, turned into a bear, swept into the sky by Zeus.
facts.ursa_minor: The Little Bear, home to Polaris at the tip of its tail — ancient Phoenician sailors steered by it, not the larger bear.
facts.cassiopeia: The vain queen's constellation, a W of five bright stars — Poseidon condemned her to circle the pole, upside-down half the time.
facts.cepheus: Andromeda's father and Cassiopeia's husband, King of Aethiopia — five stars tracing a child's drawing of a house.
facts.orion: The hunter, one of the sky's most recognizable figures — his three-star belt points the way to half a dozen neighboring stars.
facts.canis_major: The Greater Dog, Orion's hunting companion — home to Sirius, found by extending Orion's Belt southeast.
facts.canis_minor: The Lesser Dog — just two bright stars, but Procyon, its lead star, always rises moments before the Dog Star itself.
facts.scorpius: The scorpion that killed Orion — placed on the sky's opposite side, so the hunter forever flees as it rises.
facts.ophiuchus: The Serpent Bearer, depicted grappling a snake while treading on Scorpius — sometimes miscalled a '13th zodiac sign.'
facts.serpens: The only one of the 88 constellations split into two disconnected halves, divided by Ophiuchus, who holds it.
facts.cygnus: The swan, its brightest star Deneb marking the tail — ancient myths disagree on whose transformation it commemorates.
facts.lyra: The lyre of Orpheus, placed in the sky by Zeus after the musician's death — its music had nearly won his wife back from Hades.
facts.aquila: The eagle, its brightest star Altair marking the bird's head — Arabic for 'the flying eagle.'
facts.canes_venatici: The Hunting Dogs, a 1687 invention of Johannes Hevelius born from a translation error — Ptolemy's 'club' became 'dogs.'
facts.bootes: The herdsman, appearing to drive the Great Bear around the pole — home to Arcturus, the brightest northern star.
facts.corona_borealis: The Northern Crown, a half-circle of stars — Ariadne's wedding gift from Dionysus, set in the heavens to mark their marriage.
facts.auriga: The charioteer, cradling the she-goat Amalthea and her Kids — Capella marks the goat that nursed the infant Zeus.
facts.big_dipper: Seven stars of Ursa Major forming a ladle, not a constellation of its own — two of them point straight at Polaris.
facts.winter_triangle: Sirius, Betelgeuse, and Procyon, one from each of three neighboring constellations — an almost-equilateral triangle.
facts.summer_triangle: Vega, Deneb, and Altair, the brightest star of Lyra, Cygnus, and Aquila — each a corner of the same wide triangle.
facts.cigar_galaxy: A starburst galaxy near Ursa Major forging stars ten times faster than the Milky Way, stretched cigar-thin by a neighbor's pull.
facts.whirlpool_galaxy: The first galaxy ever recognized as spiral-shaped, its arms stirred by a smaller companion galaxy merging into it.
facts.ring_nebula: A dying sun-like star's outer layers, shed into a glowing ring around the white dwarf core left behind.
facts.gnomon: A vertical rod that tells time and season by its shadow — the working part of every sundial.
facts.sundial: The earliest known sundials are Egyptian and Babylonian shadow clocks, dated to around 1500 BCE.
facts.water_clock: Kept time by a steady drip when the sun wasn't visible -- by night, or under cloud.
facts.armillary_sphere: Nested rings modelling the sky's great circles -- equator, ecliptic, meridians -- around a central Earth.
facts.antikythera_mechanism: At least 30 meshing bronze gears turned by hand, predicting eclipses and planetary positions decades out.
facts.astrolabe: A flat brass model of the sky that tells time, finds latitude, and casts a horoscope from one reading.
facts.merkhet: A plumb line on a wooden bar -- Egypt's simplest tool for finding north and telling the hour by starlight.
facts.eratosthenes: Chief librarian at Alexandria who measured Earth's circumference from two shadows, to within a few percent.
facts.hipparchus: Catalogued roughly 850 stars, then found by comparing older records that the equinoxes slowly creep.
facts.claudius_ptolemy: His Earth-centered Almagest, circles turning on circles, stood as astronomy's last word for over 1,400 years.
facts.eudoxus_of_cnidus: Nested 27 invisible spheres around the Earth, around 370 BCE, to reproduce every planet's looping path.
facts.aristarchus_of_samos: Proposed the Sun stood still and Earth moved around it -- some 1,800 years before Copernicus dared the same.
facts.zhang_heng: Han-dynasty polymath who set his armillary sphere turning on its own, driven by a water clock, around 125 CE.
facts.nabta_playa: A ring of megaliths in Egypt's desert, raised around 4800 BCE, its gates facing summer solstice sunrise.
facts.eclipse: The Moon crossing directly between Sun and Earth, or Earth's shadow falling across the Moon.
facts.saros_cycle: 223 lunar months, about 18 years and 11 days, after which nearly the same eclipse comes round again.
facts.ionic_bond: Na+ and Cl- locked by opposite charge — melting the crystal apart takes 801°C.
facts.covalent_bond: Shared electrons, not traded ones. Diamond is one giant covalent molecule.
facts.hydrogen_bond: Weak, fast, and constant — each water molecule holds about 3.6 of them at once.
facts.van_der_waals_force: The faintest attraction in chemistry — too weak to liquefy helium without deep cold.
facts.hydrophobic_effect: Water pushes oily molecules together — it isn't the oil doing the reaching.
facts.nadh: NAD+ carrying two electrons it picked up while a nutrient was being oxidised.
facts.quaternary_structure: Separately folded chains assembled into one machine — hemoglobin's four subunits.
facts.protein_domain: A 50-to-250-residue stretch that folds into its own shape wherever it ends up.
facts.actin: 1 to 5 percent of a cell's protein by weight — one of the cytoskeleton's three filaments.
facts.kinesin: Walks hand-over-hand toward a microtubule's plus end, cargo in tow.
facts.dynein: Walks the other way — toward a microtubule's minus end, back to the cell's centre.
facts.motor_protein: Spends one ATP hydrolysis per step to walk a filament, not just to fold.
facts.antibody: Y-shaped, and the immune system can build roughly 10 billion different versions.
facts.lysozyme: Fleming named it in 1922 — an enzyme that bursts bacteria by cutting their wall.
facts.histone: Small, positively charged, rich in lysine and arginine — DNA's own spool.
facts.nucleosome: 146 base pairs of DNA wound 1.65 times around eight histone proteins.
facts.telomere: TTAGGG, repeated, capping a chromosome — and a little shorter after every division.
facts.telomerase: Rebuilds the chromosome-end repeats most cells let shrink. Nobel Prize, 2009.
facts.mismatch_repair: Catches base-pairing errors that slipped past DNA polymerase's own proofreading.
facts.g_protein: On when it holds GTP, off once its own enzyme activity clips that to GDP.
facts.gtp: ATP's cousin with guanine instead of adenine — fuel and a signal both.
facts.phosphorylation: A phosphate tag that flips a protein's shape, and its job, on or off.
facts.allosteric_regulation: One binding site changes another — hemoglobin's four seats talk to each other.
facts.five_themes_of_geography: Location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, region — the NCGE/AAG's 1984 teaching framework.
facts.antarctica: The only continent no country owns — an international treaty holds every territorial claim in abeyance.
facts.arctic: The smallest, shallowest of the five oceans, and the only one covered in drifting sea ice most of the year.
facts.china: Capital Beijing. Sericulture began here 8,500 years ago; China guarded the silk monopoly for a thousand more.
facts.japan: Capital Tokyo. An archipelago of four main islands and 14,000+ smaller ones, set on the Pacific Ring of Fire.
facts.india: Capital New Delhi. Independent since 15 August 1947, when British India split into India and Pakistan.
facts.mongolia: Capital Ulaanbaatar. Nomadic life on the steppe has centred on the felt-covered ger for thousands of years.
facts.kazakhstan: The Botai, in northern Kazakhstan, left the earliest strong evidence of horse domestication, c. 3500 BCE.
facts.nepal: Capital Kathmandu. Everest sits on its China border, and Nepal holds parts of all 14 of the world's 8,000m peaks.
facts.sri_lanka: Formerly Ceylon, and still the source of 'true cinnamon' — Cinnamomum verum, named Ceylon cinnamon after it.
facts.maldives: Capital Malé. The world's lowest-lying country, its 1,192 coral islands averaging just 1.5 m above the sea.
facts.indonesia: Capital Jakarta. More than 17,000 islands make it the world's largest archipelagic state.
facts.philippines: The golden South Sea pearl, farmed here, was declared the Philippines' national gem in 1996.
facts.thailand: Capital Bangkok. Briefly the world's top rice exporter in 2011, and consistently among the top three since.
facts.cambodia: Angkor Wat, built here by the Khmer Empire from 1113-1150 CE, is the largest religious monument on Earth.
facts.laos: Capital Vientiane. Prince Fa Ngum founded its precolonial kingdom, Lan Xang — 'a million elephants' — in the 1300s.
facts.vietnam: Capital Hanoi. Reunified as one state on 2 July 1976, a year after the Vietnam War ended.
facts.malaysia: Capital Kuala Lumpur. Its share of Borneo carries a rainforest estimated at 140 million years old.
facts.singapore: Independent 9 August 1965 — not by choice, but by a 126-0 vote expelling it from the Federation of Malaysia.
facts.taiwan: Capital Taipei. Its tea shops gave the world bubble tea in the 1980s, tapioca pearls dropped into cold tea.
facts.brunei: Capital Bandar Seri Begawan. A 1929 oil strike turned a small Bornean sultanate into one of the richest states.
facts.north_korea: Capital Pyongyang. Its border with the South, fixed by the 1953 armistice, is among the most militarised on Earth.
facts.south_korea: Capital Seoul. Along with China and Russia, one of the world's three major sources of cultivated ginseng.
facts.afghanistan: Capital Kabul. Grew over 90% of the world's illicit opium for two decades, until cultivation fell 95% in 2023.
facts.uzbekistan: Soviet cotton irrigation — Uzbekistan was top exporter by 1988 — shrank the Aral Sea 60% in under 40 years.
facts.pakistan: Independent 14 August 1947. Its capital moved from Karachi to purpose-built Islamabad, completed in 1967.
facts.bangladesh: 80% of the country lies within the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, the largest river delta in the world.
facts.australia: The Great Barrier Reef off its northeast coast is the largest coral reef system on Earth, visible from space.
facts.new_zealand: Home to the flightless kiwi, the bird whose name New Zealanders themselves have worn ever since.
facts.papua_new_guinea: Shares New Guinea, the world's 2nd-largest island, with Indonesia — and speaks 840 languages, more than anywhere.
facts.fiji: Capital Suva. Taveuni's Rainbow Reef has earned Fiji's waters the name 'soft coral capital of the world.'
facts.samoa: Jumped the International Date Line in Dec 2011, skipping 30 December to trade with Australia in real time.
facts.reflecting_telescope: Newton's 1668 design swapped the lens for a curved mirror, killing the color-fringing that plagued refractors.
facts.sextant: Two mirrors double the measured angle, so a 60° arc can read up to 120° of sky.
facts.adaptive_optics: A laser fakes a star in the sky so a mirror can flex fast enough to cancel the atmosphere's twinkle.
facts.coronagraph: An occulting disk in the telescope blots out a star's glare so instruments can see what's hiding beside it.
facts.spectrograph: Same prism as a spectroscope, but a camera behind it instead of an eye — the spectrum gets recorded.
facts.interferometer: Link two telescopes and their combined light resolves detail as fine as the gap between them.
facts.hubble_space_telescope: A reflecting telescope orbiting above the blur of Earth's atmosphere, riding up on Discovery in 1990.
facts.james_webb_space_telescope: 18 hexagonal beryllium mirrors, gold-plated to reflect the infrared light the telescope was built to see.
facts.voyager_program: Powered by decaying plutonium, not sunlight — why it still transmits from interstellar space 45+ years on.
facts.sputnik_1: A 58cm metal sphere that did nothing but broadcast a radio beep — and started the Space Race doing it.
facts.apollo_11: Two astronauts walked on the Moon while a third circled alone overhead in the command module.
facts.international_space_station: Continuously crewed since November 2000 — the longest unbroken human presence off Earth.
facts.curiosity_rover: Its ChemCam fires a laser at rock from 7m away and reads the flash of vaporized plasma to tell what it is.
facts.new_horizons: A spare part built for the Cassini mission — its plutonium power generator — carried it past Pluto in 2015.
facts.cassini_huygens: Launched to Saturn in 1997, it dropped a probe onto Titan in 2005 — the only landing ever made past Mars.
facts.alpha_centauri: Three stars, one system, and the nearest neighbors our Sun has — the closest just 4.2 light-years off.
facts.proxima_centauri: The single closest star to the Sun — and it has a roughly Earth-mass planet sitting in its habitable zone.
facts.virgo_cluster: Not close enough to hold onto us, but massive enough to slow our galaxy's drift away by about a tenth.
facts.halleys_comet: Edmond Halley used Newton's laws to prove this comet keeps returning — and predicted the exact year it would.
facts.parallax: Wait six months for Earth to cross its orbit, and a nearby star visibly shifts against the background sky.
facts.settlement: A permanent home base, no longer struck and carried onward after the harvest.
facts.cultural_hearth: The place a cultural trait or practice is first invented, from which it then spreads outward.
facts.distance_decay: Interaction between two places fades the farther apart they are — Tobler's First Law of Geography.
facts.culture_region: An area unified by one shared cultural trait, strongest at its core and fading toward its edge.
facts.contagious_diffusion: A practice spreading outward person to person, like a disease, with no regard for city size.
facts.hierarchical_diffusion: An innovation leapfrogging straight to the biggest cities first, only later reaching small towns.
facts.stimulus_diffusion: The core of a practice spreads, but gets reshaped to fit each new place it lands in.
facts.relocation_diffusion: A practice carried to a new place in person, by someone who actually moved there.
facts.migration: A permanent change of home, whether across town or across an ocean.
facts.push_factor: A hardship at home — war, drought, no jobs — that drives people to migrate away.
facts.pull_factor: An opportunity elsewhere — jobs, safety, freedom — that draws migrants toward it.
facts.urbanization: The rising share of a population living in cities rather than the countryside.
facts.unitary_state: A country where the central government holds supreme power over every region.
facts.federalism: Power split geographically between a central government and self-governing regions.
facts.separatist_movement: An organized push by a minority group to fully break away from the larger country.
facts.self_determination: The principle that a people has the right to choose its own political status.
facts.census: An official count of everyone living in a territory, ideally taken once a decade.
facts.electoral_district: A slice of territory whose voters elect their own representative to a legislature.
facts.gerrymandering: Drawing electoral district lines to favor one party — named for an 1812 salamander-shaped map.
facts.primary_sector: The part of an economy that extracts raw material straight from land or sea.
facts.secondary_sector: The part of an economy that manufactures raw material into a finished product.
facts.tertiary_sector: The service economy — retail, healthcare, transport — now most of US employment.
facts.quaternary_sector: The knowledge economy split off from services around 1970: software, R&D, finance.
facts.factors_of_production: Land, labor and capital: the classic inputs every business must pay for.
facts.comparative_advantage: The principle that a place should make what it produces most efficiently, and trade for the rest.
facts.footloose_industry: A factory so cheap to relocate it can chase wherever labor is cheapest.
facts.gini_coefficient: A single number from 0 to 1 measuring how unequally income is shared across a population.
facts.break_of_bulk: The point where cargo switches transport modes and must be unloaded and reloaded by hand.
facts.agglomeration: The economic payoff of clustering close together — the basic reason cities exist at all.
facts.central_place_theory: Christaller's model of how villages, towns and cities space themselves evenly across a plain.
facts.suburbanization: The mid-20th-century population shift from city centers into car-dependent suburbs.
facts.redlining: Government maps that outlined minority neighborhoods and marked them too risky for loans.
facts.white_flight: The mass departure of white residents as a neighborhood or city grows more diverse.
facts.gentrification: Wealthier newcomers moving into a once-abandoned inner-city area, raising rents as they arrive.
facts.urban_sprawl: Low-density development leapfrogging outward from a city with little planning.
facts.edge_city: A suburban node with more office space than downtown, that didn't exist before the 1960s.
facts.ghetto: A district where one ethnic or religious group is confined, a term dating to 16th-century Venice.
facts.restriction_enzyme: An enzyme that cuts DNA at one exact sequence — a bacterium's chemical scissors against invading viruses.
facts.cloning_vector: A plasmid cut open at one site, ready to accept and carry a foreign piece of DNA.
facts.recombinant_dna: DNA stitched together from two different sources into one molecule.
facts.transformation: A bacterium taking up foreign DNA from its surroundings and replicating it as its own.
facts.taq_polymerase: A DNA polymerase from a hot-spring bacterium, stable enough to survive PCR's near-boiling step.
facts.pcr: Repeated heating and cooling that doubles a target DNA sequence millions of times over.
facts.gel_electrophoresis: An electric field pulling DNA through a gel's mesh, sorting fragments from small to large.
facts.hybridization: Heat splits a DNA double strand apart; cooling lets matching sequences find each other again.
facts.southern_blot: DNA sorted by gel, blotted onto a membrane, then probed to find one sequence in the mix.
facts.sahara: The world's largest hot desert, roughly the size of the contiguous US, across North Africa.
facts.nile: At 6,650 km, among Earth's longest rivers; its yearly flood built Ancient Egypt's farmland.
facts.amazon_river: Carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined, draining the Amazon rainforest.
facts.andes: The world's longest continental mountain range -- 8,900 km along South America's Pacific edge.
facts.alps: Europe's youngest, highest range, thrust up where the African and Eurasian plates collided.
facts.mediterranean_sea: Nearly landlocked; it reaches the Atlantic only through the 14-km-wide Strait of Gibraltar.
facts.argentina: Stretches from the Andes to the Atlantic; independence declared 1816 at the Congress of Tucuman.
facts.brazil: Holds most of the Amazon basin and rainforest; the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas.
facts.chile: A ribbon of land between the Andes and the Pacific -- over 4,300 km long, rarely 350 km wide.
facts.peru: Once the heart of the Inca Empire, whose ruins at Machu Picchu still crown the Andes.
facts.colombia: One of only two South American countries with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
facts.venezuela: Home to the world's largest known oil reserves, which have shaped its economy for a century.
facts.bolivia: The largest landlocked country in the Southern Hemisphere; a third of it lies in the Andes.
facts.ecuador: Named for the equator itself, which its capital Quito sits almost exactly on.
facts.paraguay: Landlocked and split into two regions by the Paraguay River, which flows past its capital.
facts.uruguay: The only South American country lying entirely south of the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.nigeria: Africa's most populous country, from northern savanna to southern coastal rainforest.
facts.egypt: Ancient civilization arose along the Nile's fertile floodplain, cutting through the Sahara.
facts.south_africa: Where the Atlantic meets the Indian Ocean; uniquely among nations it has three capitals.
facts.kenya: Named for Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest peak, whose slopes the equator crosses.
facts.ethiopia: One of only two African countries never colonized; fossils here rank among the oldest human ancestors.
facts.morocco: Separated from Spain by just 14 km at the Strait of Gibraltar.
facts.algeria: Africa's largest country by area; the Sahara covers most of its territory.
facts.ghana: The first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, on 6 March 1957.
facts.tanzania: Home to Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, and the Serengeti's migrating herds.
facts.senegal: Its capital Dakar sits on the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
facts.democratic_republic_of_the_congo: Centered on the Congo, the world's deepest river, under Earth's second-largest rainforest.
facts.madagascar: The world's fourth-largest island; over 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else.
facts.france: The 1789 Revolution overthrew the monarchy and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
facts.germany: Unified into a single empire in 1871 under Prussian leadership, with Berlin as capital.
facts.italy: Unified as a kingdom in 1861 on the peninsula that was once the heart of the Roman Republic.
facts.spain: Spans most of the Iberian Peninsula, which it shares only with Portugal.
facts.portugal: Borders barely changed since 1297, making it one of Europe's oldest stable nation-states.
facts.united_kingdom: Great Britain, part of Ireland, and thousands of smaller islands -- an archipelago nation.
facts.netherlands: More than a quarter of the country lies below sea level, reclaimed from the sea since the 1300s.
facts.switzerland: The Alps cover most of this landlocked country, neutral and war-free since 1815.
facts.poland: Named for its flat terrain along the North European Plain -- from 'pole,' open field.
facts.russia: The largest country on Earth by area, so vast it spans eleven time zones.
facts.greece: Birthplace of Athenian democracy, scattered across thousands of Mediterranean islands.
facts.sweden: Stretches roughly 1,600 km along the Scandinavian Peninsula, from 55N to 69N latitude.
facts.glycolysis: Ten enzyme steps split one glucose into two pyruvate, right in the cytosol, no oxygen required. Net gain: two ATP, two NADH.
facts.pyruvate: Glycolysis's three-carbon output, sitting at a metabolic fork: burn it for more ATP with oxygen, or ferment it to lactate without.
facts.krebs_cycle: Pyruvate's carbons get stripped away one by one in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO2 and stacking up NADH and FADH2 to spend later.
facts.electron_transport_chain: A relay of protein complexes in the mitochondrion's inner membrane passes electrons down an energy staircase to oxygen, pumping protons across as it goes.
facts.atp_synthase: A molecular turbine: protons flowing back down the gradient the electron transport chain built spin its rotor, and each turn bolts a phosphate onto ADP.
facts.cellular_respiration: Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain running in sequence — about 30 to 32 ATP squeezed from one glucose molecule with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
facts.homeostasis: Steady internal conditions held constant by active correction — blood sugar spikes, the pancreas releases insulin, and the level comes back down.
facts.diabetes: Insulin production fails or cells stop responding to it, and glucose piles up in the blood instead of getting taken up for fuel.
facts.apoptosis: Programmed cell death: mitochondria release cytochrome c, an apoptosome assembles, and a cascade of caspase enzymes dismantles the cell from the inside out.
facts.cell_cycle: G1, S, G2, then M: growth, DNA replication, more growth, then division — checkpoints at each border refuse to let a damaged cell proceed.
facts.carbohydrate: Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen roughly one-two-one. Starch and cellulose are both just glucose chained together — wired two different ways.
facts.nucleic_acid: DNA and RNA — both built from repeating nucleotides, each one a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base.
facts.centrosome: Two centrioles at right angles, wrapped in pericentriolar material — the cell's main microtubule organizing center, doubling before mitosis so each pole gets one.
facts.operon: A cluster of genes run by one shared promoter, switched on or off together — E. coli's lac operon turns on only when there's lactose around to digest.
facts.transcription_factor: A protein built to grab one specific DNA sequence, usually near a gene's start, and turn that gene's transcription up or down.
facts.oncogene: A mutated or overactive version of a normal growth gene — push the cell cycle's accelerator hard enough and a tumor is what you get.
facts.nondisjunction: Chromosomes fail to separate cleanly during meiosis, leaving one gamete with an extra copy and another one short — trisomy 21 is the most common survivable result.
facts.horizontal_gene_transfer: Bacteria hand a plasmid straight to a neighbor through direct contact, no reproduction required — the main route antibiotic resistance spreads between species.
facts.endosymbiosis: Mitochondria keep their own circular DNA and divide by binary fission — strong evidence they were once free-living bacteria engulfed over a billion years ago.
facts.tonicity: Whether the outside of a cell is saltier (hypertonic), more dilute (hypotonic), or matched (isotonic) — tonicity decides which way osmosis pushes the water.
facts.turgor_pressure: Water pushes the plant cell's membrane hard against its rigid wall from the inside — the pressure that keeps a plant upright without a single bone.
facts.pinocytosis: Cell drinking: the membrane dimples around a droplet of fluid and pinches off as a vesicle, taking in whatever happens to be dissolved in it — no target required.
facts.quorum_sensing: A bacterial population senses its own chemical signal building up; once it crosses a threshold, every cell switches behavior at once.
facts.genotype: The specific alleles an organism actually carries — its genetic parts list, as opposed to what those parts end up building.
facts.phenotype: What a genotype actually becomes once development and environment get involved — the traits you can see, measure, or catch a disease from.
facts.auxin: A plant hormone made at the shoot tip. Darwin showed in 1881 that the tip senses light while the bend happens lower down; Frits Went isolated the chemical itself decades later.
facts.phototropism: Auxin builds up on a stem's shaded side, making those cells stretch more than the sunlit side — the whole stem curves toward the light.
facts.ireland: Britain ceded Dublin Castle, its seat of rule here for 700 years, to the new state in 1922.
facts.austria: Full sovereignty was restored 15 May 1955, when Allied powers signed a treaty at Vienna's Belvedere Palace.
facts.turkiye: In 2022 its government asked the world to use 'Türkiye' instead of 'Turkey', partly to avoid the bird's name.
facts.israel: Independence was declared 14 May 1948; its Star of David was adopted by Zionists in Basel in 1897.
facts.lebanon: Became a republic when French Mandate rule ended in 1943, choosing the ancient cedar as its emblem.
facts.saudi_arabia: Ibn Saud's 1902 raid retaking Riyadh's Masmak fort began the conquest that unified the kingdom by 1932.
facts.iran: Its Lion and Sun emblem, official since the Safavid era, was dropped after the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
facts.flag_of_netherlands: Started orange-white-blue for William of Orange; orange faded to red, fixed by decree in 1937.
facts.flag_of_ireland: Green for Catholics, orange for Protestants, white between for peace; standardized in 1848.
facts.flag_of_switzerland: White couped cross on red, from the war flag of Schwyz; one of only two square national flags.
facts.flag_of_austria: Red-white-red, recorded on a 1230 abbey seal, is among the oldest state symbols still flown.
facts.flag_of_greece: Nine stripes spell 'Freedom or Death' in syllables; the cross recalls Greek Orthodox Christianity.
facts.flag_of_turkiye: The star and crescent flew on Ottoman flags by the 1840s; the Republic kept it unchanged in 1923.
facts.flag_of_israel: Blue stripes echo the tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl; the flag was adopted 28 October 1948.
facts.flag_of_lebanon: A cedar tree on red-white stripes, adopted 7 December 1943, days before independence.
facts.flag_of_saudi_arabia: Bears the Shahada above a sword, printed identically on both sides so the text always reads right.
facts.flag_of_iran: 'Allahu Akbar' repeats 22 times along its bands, marking the date of the 1979 revolution.
facts.flag_of_japan: The Hinomaru sun-disc is centuries old, but only became Japan's legal flag by statute in 1999.
facts.flag_of_south_korea: Red-blue taegeuk for cosmic balance, with four trigrams; first flown under Joseon in 1883.
facts.flag_of_china: Four small stars for the people's classes orbit one large star for the Communist Party.
facts.flag_of_indonesia: Nearly identical to Monaco's flag; Monaco's later objection to the resemblance was ignored.
facts.flag_of_australia: Its Commonwealth Star gained a seventh point in 1908, for the Territory of Papua.
facts.flag_of_new_zealand: Four red Southern Cross stars on a Blue Ensign; voters chose to keep it in a 2016 referendum.
facts.flag_of_papua_new_guinea: Designed by 15-year-old Susan Karike; adopted 1971, sharing the Southern Cross with Australia.
facts.metonic_cycle: Almost exactly 19 years and 235 lunar months, after which the Moon's phases fall on the same calendar dates again.
facts.tumor_suppressor_gene: The real stop signal: halts a damaged cell, or forces it to self-destruct. p53 is disabled in a third of cancers.
facts.tumor: An uncoordinated mass of tissue growth. Most stay contained — invading nearby tissue is what makes one cancer.
facts.metastasis: Cancer cells breaking off to colonize a distant organ — over 90% of cancer deaths trace to this.
facts.glioma: Grows from the brain's glial support cells, not its neurons — about 80% of malignant brain tumors.
facts.melanoma: Grows from melanocytes, the skin's pigment cells. Caused mainly by UV — the deadliest skin cancer.
facts.leukemia: Begins in bone marrow and floods the bloodstream with abnormal cells, instead of forming one solid mass.
facts.nitrification: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonium to nitrite, and Nitrobacter finishes the job by oxidizing nitrite to nitrate.
facts.denitrification: Bacteria reduce nitrate back to nitrogen gas once oxygen runs out — the nitrogen cycle's only way back to air.
facts.nitrogen_cycle: Fixation, nitrification and denitrification move one element between air, soil and every living cell.
facts.carbon_cycle: Photosynthesis pulls CO2 from the air; respiration, decay and methanogenesis put it back in other forms.
facts.sulfur_cycle: Bacteria oxidize hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, and others reduce sulfate back to hydrogen sulfide.
facts.methanogen: An archaeon that combines CO2 and hydrogen for energy; methane is the only waste product it can make.
facts.extremophile: Life that doesn't merely survive extreme heat, cold, acid, pressure or salt — it needs the extreme to grow.
facts.thermophile: An organism whose growth optimum sits between 41°C and 122°C — hot springs and geysers are full of them.
facts.halophile: Needs salt to grow, not just tolerates it — some strains require water several times saltier than the sea.
facts.eutrophication: Nutrient overload: algae bloom on the surplus, then die and rot, and the rotting uses up the water's oxygen.
facts.biomagnification: A pollutant too stable to break down concentrates further at every step up the food chain.
facts.wastewater: Everything that flows from a drain, plus whatever else households, industry or storms send after it.
facts.primary_treatment: The physical stage: screens catch trash, then gravity settles most of the solids out in a couple of hours.
facts.activated_sludge: Aerobic bacteria clump into flocs in an aeration tank, and part of every batch reseeds the next one.
facts.trickling_filter: Wastewater trickles over a bed of rock or plastic coated in a living biofilm a few millimetres thick.
facts.secondary_treatment: The biological stage: microbes finish what settling couldn't, converting dissolved waste to cells and CO2.
facts.anaerobic_digestion: Sludge fed to anaerobic microbes in sequence — acids first, then acetate, then methanogens finish it as gas.
facts.septic_system: A tank does the anaerobic work solids need; a soil drain field does the aerobic work the liquid needs next.
facts.indicator_organism: Testing every pathogen in water isn't practical, so labs test for E. coli as a stand-in for all of them.
facts.water_treatment: Coagulate, settle, filter, then disinfect — four stages turning raw river water into safe tap water.
facts.bioremediation: Using microbes already living in a polluted site — sometimes sped with nutrients — to break it down in place.
facts.water_activity: Pure water rates 1.0; jam sits near 0.85 since its water is chemically bound to sugar, not free for microbes.
facts.food_spoilage: Not the same as foodborne illness: spoilage bacteria make food taste and smell bad without being dangerous.
facts.clostridium_botulinum: An anaerobic, endospore-forming soil bacterium whose toxin is the most potent one known — nanograms can kill.
facts.staphylococcus_aureus: Lives harmlessly on human skin and in the nose, but the toxin it makes in food survives cooking.
facts.listeria_monocytogenes: One of the few foodborne pathogens that keeps growing in the refrigerator, dividing even down near 0°C.
facts.campylobacter: The most common bacterial cause of foodborne illness in the US, and most of it traces back to poultry.
facts.aflatoxin: A carcinogen made by Aspergillus flavus on stored peanuts and grain; the FDA limits it strictly by law.
facts.pasteurization: Heat a food just enough to kill the microbes troubling it, not enough to cook it or ruin its flavour.
facts.food_irradiation: Ionizing radiation kills microbes by breaking their DNA, without heating the food — 'cold pasteurization.'
facts.sake: Koji's mould enzymes turn rice starch to sugar and yeast ferments that sugar to alcohol — both at once.
facts.single_cell_protein: Growing yeast or bacteria on an industry's leftover waste, then eating the microbial biomass as protein.
facts.attenuated_vaccine: A live pathogen weakened by growth in a foreign host until it can no longer cause disease at home.
facts.inactivated_vaccine: Killed by heat or chemicals — unable to replicate, but intact enough to still teach the immune system.
facts.toxoid: A bacterial toxin disarmed by formaldehyde — poison gone, shape the immune system still learns intact.
facts.subunit_vaccine: Only the antigenic fragment of a pathogen, not the whole organism — nothing left alive to cause disease.
facts.conjugate_vaccine: A bacterial sugar antigen bolted to a carrier protein so a young immune system finally notices it.
facts.mrna_vaccine: Genetic instructions, not the pathogen itself — host cells read the mRNA and build the antigen on their own.
facts.adjuvant: Added to a vaccine to make the immune system take a weak antigen more seriously.
facts.hybridoma: An antibody-making B cell fused to an immortal cancer cell — one cell, one target, dividing forever.
facts.monoclonal_antibody: Every molecule identical — descended from one B cell, so every copy has the same shape, same target.
facts.elisa: An enzyme-tagged antibody turns a colourless liquid visibly colored wherever its target is present.
facts.incidence: The count of brand-new cases of a disease in a population over a set stretch of time.
facts.prevalence: Every existing case of a disease at one moment — old cases and new ones both, all counted together.
facts.pandemic: An epidemic that has crossed borders and continents, no longer confined to one region.
facts.endemic_disease: Constantly present in a population at a fairly steady baseline, neither spiking nor vanishing.
facts.epidemic: A sharp, unusual rise in a disease's incidence above its normal baseline in one population.
facts.herd_immunity: Once enough of a population is immune, a pathogen can't find hosts fast enough to keep spreading.
facts.basic_reproduction_number: R0 — how many new infections one case causes, on average, in a population with no immunity at all.
facts.zoonotic_disease: An infection that jumps from a non-human animal into humans — roughly 75% of emerging diseases start this way.
facts.vector: A living carrier of a pathogen from one host to another — sometimes just a ride, sometimes a second home.
facts.fomite: A doorknob, a glass, a railing — an inanimate object carrying infection between people who never touched.
facts.john_snow: London physician who traced 1854's cholera to a single water pump, a decade before germ theory existed.
facts.nosocomial_infection: An infection picked up during treatment in a healthcare facility, not the illness the patient arrived with.
facts.notifiable_disease: A disease physicians are legally required to report, so health authorities can spot an outbreak forming.
facts.beta_lactamase: A bacterial enzyme that snaps open the ring at the heart of every penicillin-family drug, destroying it.
facts.cephalosporin: A beta-lactam antibiotic family bred to dodge the enzymes that destroy natural penicillins.
facts.vancomycin: Binds the cell-wall building block itself, not an enzyme — medicine's antibiotic of last resort.
facts.tetracycline: Jams the ribosome's 30S subunit so incoming tRNA can't dock — pumped into bacterial cells, not animal ones.
facts.macrolide: Binds the ribosome's 50S subunit, stopping the growing protein chain — standard swap for penicillin allergy.
facts.sulfonamide: A structural mimic of PABA that jams folate synthesis — bacteria need to make their own, human cells don't.
facts.fluoroquinolone: Jams DNA gyrase mid-unwind, stopping bacterial DNA from replicating or being read.
facts.mrsa: Staph aureus with an altered cell-wall protein that keeps working even with methicillin bound everywhere else.
facts.azole: Blocks the enzyme that finishes building ergosterol, the molecule holding a fungal cell membrane together.
facts.protease_inhibitor: Jams the enzyme that cuts HIV's one long protein chain into working pieces — the virus keeps assembling junk.
facts.chloroquine: Concentrates in Plasmodium-infected blood cells, blocking disposal of digested hemoglobin's toxic waste.
facts.paul_ehrlich: Coined the 'magic bullet' idea — a chemical that kills a pathogen and leaves the patient untouched.
facts.oseltamivir: Blocks neuraminidase, the enzyme new flu particles need to cut themselves free of the cell that made them.
facts.endospore: A bacterium's dormant, armoured backup copy of itself. Some have woken up after 25 million years.
facts.growth_curve: Lag, then exponential doubling, then a stationary plateau, then death — a closed culture's whole biography.
facts.sterilization: Not mostly dead — completely. The one microbial control standard tough enough to also take out endospores.
facts.autoclave: Steam under pressure hits 121°C, hot enough to kill even endospores.
facts.disinfectant: Kills most microbes on a countertop, not a body. Endospores may still walk away.
facts.antiseptic: The disinfectant gentle enough to put on skin instead of just a countertop.
facts.hepa_filter: Certified to trap 99.97% of particles at 0.3 micrometres — the size that slips past filters easiest.
facts.germicidal_uv: UV-C at 254 nanometres welds a microbe's own DNA bases together in pairs they were never meant to share.
facts.lyophilization: Freeze it, then drop the pressure until the ice skips melting and sublimates straight to vapour.
facts.triclosan: Once in 3 of every 4 liquid soaps sold in the US — banned from them by the FDA in 2016.
facts.coenzyme: An enzyme's reusable organic sidekick, usually cut straight from a vitamin.
facts.cofactor: Not every enzyme works alone. Some need a bound metal ion or organic helper just to hold their shape.
facts.competitive_inhibition: A sulfa drug fits a bacterial enzyme's active site because it is built to resemble the real substrate, PABA.
facts.iron_bacteria: Lives on oxidizing dissolved iron, leaving reddish-brown slime in wells, streambeds and pipes.
facts.anaerobic_respiration: Still runs an electron transport chain, just not with oxygen at the end — nitrate or sulfate stands in.
facts.photosystem_i: Named first, works second — it re-boosts spent electrons high enough to finally make NADPH.
facts.carbon_fixation: Turning CO2 into something with a carbon skeleton. About 250 billion tonnes of it happens every year.
facts.calvin_cycle: Fixes carbon, spends ATP and NADPH to reduce it, then rebuilds its own starting material to run again.
facts.rubisco: Probably the most abundant enzyme on Earth — up to half of all soluble protein in a leaf is this one molecule.
facts.beta_oxidation: A fatty acid chain gets chewed down two carbons at a time, each bite handed off as a fresh acetyl-CoA.
facts.cellulase: Almost nothing alive makes this enzyme — a problem, since cellulose is Earth's most abundant organic polymer.
facts.ion: An atom that has gained or lost an electron. Hydrogen gaining one becomes hydride, H⁻; losing its only one leaves a bare proton.
facts.purine: The double-ring nucleobases, adenine and guanine — the bulkier half of DNA and RNA's four-letter alphabet.
facts.pyrimidine: The single-ring nucleobases — cytosine, thymine, and uracil — the smaller half of the genetic alphabet.
facts.sucrose: Table sugar: one glucose and one fructose locked together by a glycosidic bond.
facts.chitin: A tough polymer of nitrogen-bearing glucose units — fungal cell walls, insect and crustacean shells.
facts.triglyceride: Glycerol with three fatty-acid tails, each attached by an ester bond that releases a water molecule.
facts.saturated_fat: A fat with no carbon=carbon double bonds — every carbon holds its maximum hydrogen and packs solid at room temperature.
facts.unsaturated_fat: A fat with at least one carbon=carbon double bond — the kink stops it packing tightly, so it stays liquid as oil.
facts.steroid: Four fused carbon rings — the shared skeleton of cholesterol, testosterone, and cortisone alike.
facts.sterol: A steroid with a hydroxyl group on its ring — cholesterol in animal membranes, ergosterol doing the same job in fungi.
facts.lipoprotein: A protein shell around a fat cargo — the only way something as water-fearing as cholesterol travels through blood.
facts.adp: Adenosine with two phosphates instead of three — what's left of ATP after the cell spends its last one.
facts.denaturation: Heat or extreme pH unravels a protein's shape without breaking a single peptide bond — cooked, not digested.
facts.buffer: A weak acid paired with its conjugate base, holding pH nearly steady even as acid or base is added.
facts.germ_theory: The idea that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease — it displaced miasma theory by the 1880s.
facts.koch_postulates: Four criteria for proving a microbe causes a disease: present in every case, grown pure, reproduces disease, recovered unchanged.
facts.louis_pasteur: French chemist, 1822–1895, who proved germ theory, invented pasteurization, and produced the first rabies vaccine.
facts.robert_koch: German physician, 1843–1910, who identified the anthrax bacterium in 1876 and the tuberculosis bacterium in 1882.
facts.van_leeuwenhoek: Dutch draper who ground his own glass lenses to about 275x and in 1676 was first to see a living bacterium.
facts.prion: A misfolded protein that forces normal copies of itself to misfold too — no DNA or RNA involved, and the disease still spreads.
facts.helicobacter_pylori: A spiral bacterium that neutralizes stomach acid with its own urease enzyme — and turned out to cause most peptic ulcers.
facts.light_microscope: Two glass lens systems in series, magnifying to about 1000x before visible light's own wavelength blurs any more detail.
facts.transmission_electron_microscope: An electron beam through a wafer-thin specimen resolves single columns of atoms — a thousand times finer than light allows.
facts.scanning_electron_microscope: Scans a beam across a metal-coated surface and reads the scattered electrons back — a 3D-looking image down to 0.4 nanometers.
facts.phase_contrast_microscope: Converts the invisible phase shifts light makes in a transparent cell into visible brightness — no stain, no dead cells.
facts.fluorescence_microscope: Shines one wavelength at a specimen and captures only the longer wavelength it fluoresces back — labeled structures glow.
facts.confocal_microscope: A laser and a pinhole that rejects light from outside the focal plane — stack the slices and reconstruct a 3D image.
facts.gram_stain: Crystal violet, then iodine, then alcohol, then safranin — thick-walled cells stay purple, thin-walled ones wash out pink.
facts.acid_fast_stain: Carbolfuchsin steamed into a waxy mycolic-acid wall, rinsed with acid-alcohol strong enough to strip a plain Gram stain.
facts.negative_stain: An acidic dye colors the background, not the cell — both are negatively charged and repel, leaving a pale silhouette.
facts.endospore_stain: Malachite green steamed through a spore coat nothing else penetrates — spores stay green, safranin turns the rest red.
facts.peptidoglycan: Alternating sugar rings cross-linked by short amino acid chains into a mesh — the load-bearing wall unique to bacteria.
facts.teichoic_acid: Glycerol-phosphate polymers threaded through a Gram-positive wall, gripping magnesium and calcium ions.
facts.lipopolysaccharide: Lipid A anchoring a core sugar and a variable O-antigen chain — the outer coat of Gram-negative bacteria, and their endotoxin.
facts.outer_membrane: A second, asymmetric membrane found only in Gram-negative bacteria — phospholipid inside, lipopolysaccharide facing out.
facts.periplasm: The gel-filled gap between a Gram-negative cell's two membranes — up to 40% of its volume, packed with enzymes.
facts.porin: Barrel-shaped protein channels through the outer membrane, letting molecules under about 600 daltons pass and nothing bigger.
facts.mycoplasma: A bacterium with no cell wall at all, among the smallest free-living cells — and naturally immune to penicillin.
facts.coccus: A spherical bacterium, dividing into the pairs, chains, or grape-like clusters that name Strepto- and Staphylococcus.
facts.spirochete: A corkscrew-shaped bacterium that moves with flagella wound inside its own periplasm instead of trailing outside the cell.
facts.proton_motive_force: A proton gradient built across a membrane — stored energy driving ATP synthase, transport proteins, and the flagellum alike.
facts.bacterial_flagellum: A protein propeller run by a rotary motor in the cell envelope — powered by proton flow, not ATP, up to 100,000 rpm.
facts.chemotaxis: Counterclockwise flagella bundle into a smooth run; clockwise, they fly apart into a tumble — attractants just lengthen the runs.
facts.pilus: A thin protein filament, 3–10 nanometers across, for gripping surfaces or — as the sex pilus — pulling two bacteria together.
facts.conjugation: A sex pilus reels a recipient in, then a plasmid crosses the bridge as a single strand — the fastest way resistance spreads.
facts.transduction: A bacteriophage mispackages bacterial DNA instead of its own and delivers it into the next cell it infects.
facts.nucleoid: The unbound tangle where a bacterium's DNA sits — compacted a thousandfold, with no membrane around it at all.
facts.capsule: A gelatinous polysaccharide coat outside the wall, thick enough to stop a phagocyte from getting a grip.
facts.poly_hydroxybutyrate: A carbon-storage granule bacteria stockpile when food is abundant but another nutrient is scarce — today, a compostable plastic.
facts.peroxisome: A tiny organelle that dismantles fatty acids and disarms hydrogen peroxide with its own catalase enzyme.
facts.aquaporin: A membrane channel built for one job — passing about a billion water molecules a second while blocking every ion.
facts.epidermis: Keratin-filled dead cells at the surface, replaced about every 48 days — the body's real barrier.
facts.dermis: Collagen and elastic fibers beneath the epidermis, threaded with blood vessels and nerve endings.
facts.plant_epidermis: One cell layer covering a leaf's surface. Almost no chloroplasts — except in its own guard cells.
facts.plant_cuticle: A waxy film the epidermis secretes over itself — the reason water beads on a leaf instead of soaking in.
facts.three_domain_system: Woese split all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eucarya in 1990, using ribosomal RNA alone.
facts.bergeys_manual: The reference microbiologists check first: every characterized bacterial species, catalogued since 1923.
facts.binomial_nomenclature: Two italicized Latin words, genus then species — Linnaeus's fix for a world of clashing common names.
facts.carl_woese: Compared ribosomal RNA across life and found a whole missing domain hiding in plain sight: Archaea.
facts.phylogenetic_tree: Branches trace divergence, nodes mark a common ancestor — Darwin's only diagram in Origin of Species.
facts.extreme_halophile: Needs at least 2 molar salt and often grows in fully saturated brine — home is the Dead Sea, not the sea.
facts.hyperthermophile: Thrives above 80°C; the record holder grows at 122°C, hotter than any home oven reaches.
facts.nitrogen_fixation: Nitrogenase yanks N2 apart into usable ammonia — and stops working the instant oxygen touches it.
facts.heterocyst: A thick-walled cell some cyanobacteria build just to fix nitrogen inside an oxygen-free bubble.
facts.rickettsia: Can't survive outside a living cell; ticks and lice inject it, and spotted fever follows.
facts.chlamydia_bacterium: Lives only inside host cells, alternating an infectious spore-like form with a growing one.
facts.myxobacteria: Hunts in swarms nicknamed 'wolf packs,' then starves into a fruiting body built of its own cells.
facts.deinococcus_radiodurans: Shrugs off 5,000 grays of gamma radiation — roughly a thousand times the dose that kills a human.
facts.thermus_aquaticus: Found thriving in a scalding Yellowstone spring; its heat-proof enzyme now runs every PCR machine.
facts.bdellovibrio: Rams another bacterium at 100 body-lengths a second, then eats it alive from inside its own wall.
facts.clostridium: Anaerobic and spore-forming, behind three of history's nastiest toxins: tetanus, botulism, gas gangrene.
facts.bacillus_anthracis: Its spores can wait in soil or wool for decades, then cause anthrax the moment they're inhaled.
facts.mycobacterium_tuberculosis: A waxy cell wall shrugs off Gram stain entirely — only an acid-fast dye reveals it in the lungs.
facts.pseudomonas_aeruginosa: Smells faintly of grapes, glows blue-green, and sits on the WHO's own list of resistance threats.
facts.legionella: Normally lives inside amoebae in water pipes; a 1976 hotel outbreak in Philadelphia gave it its name.
facts.chytrid: The only fungus with a swimming spore — one species has driven whole frog populations extinct.
facts.zygomycete: Black bread mold in a nutshell: sporangia bursting with spores, plus a tough dormant zygospore.
facts.ascomycete: Sac fungi, over 64,000 species strong — includes the mold that gave the world penicillin.
facts.basidiomycete: Club fungi: every mushroom, plus the rusts and smuts that quietly wreck grain harvests.
facts.apicomplexan: Nearly every species is a parasite, armed with an apical complex built to drill into a host cell.
facts.oomycete: Looks like a fungus, isn't one — its cellulose walls helped trigger the Irish Potato Famine.
facts.trypanosoma: Swaps its surface coat again and again to dodge the immune system — the trick behind sleeping sickness.
facts.leishmania: Rides in a sandfly's gut as a whip-tailed cell, then hides inside human immune cells once bitten in.
facts.naegleria_fowleri: Warm-freshwater amoeba that enters through the nose; the resulting brain infection kills over 97%.
facts.nematode: Roundworms may be the most numerous animals on Earth; one species mapped its every single neuron.
facts.tapeworm: Has no gut of its own — it just soaks up the host's pre-digested food through its entire skin.
facts.trematode: A flatworm with two suckers that needs a snail, then a vertebrate, in sequence, to complete its life.
facts.proto_oncogene: The normal growth gene every cell carries — one mutation away from becoming an oncogene.
facts.mimivirus: Once mistaken for a purple-staining bacterium; its genome tops a million base pairs, rivaling real cells.
facts.plaque_assay: Each clear ring in a bacterial lawn is one phage's descendants — count rings, know the virus titer.
facts.restriction_modification_system: Shreds any incoming phage DNA on sight, while methyl tags keep the bacterium's own DNA safe from itself.
facts.cytokine: Stanley Cohen coined the term in 1974, after showing production wasn't limited to immune cells.
facts.interferon: Discovered in 1957 by Isaacs and Lindenmann: a virus-infected cell's chemical warning to its neighbors.
facts.complement_system: About 50 blood proteins, three separate pathways in, but always the same three jobs on the invader.
facts.dendritic_cell: Named in 1973 by Ralph Steinman, who won a 2011 Nobel for showing it bridges innate and adaptive immunity.
facts.toll_like_receptor: Named for a 1985 exclamation — “Das ist ja toll!” — at a mutant fruit fly with the same broken gene.
facts.natural_killer_cell: Carries no antigen receptor at all — it kills any cell that fails to show a normal MHC class I badge.
facts.mast_cell: Loaded with histamine and heparin; emptying every granule at once is what anaphylaxis actually is.
facts.inflammation: Redness, heat, swelling and pain — Celsus wrote down all four around the time of Christ.
facts.fever: The hypothalamus's thermostat gets reset upward; 38.3°C is the line doctors call a fever.
facts.antigen: Short for “antibody generator” — though plenty of antigens never actually trigger one.
facts.epitope: The one small patch of an antigen an antibody actually touches — the rest is just scaffolding.
facts.b_cell: Named for the bursa of Fabricius, a bird organ — even though human B cells mature in bone marrow.
facts.t_cell: Named simply for the thymus, the organ where it learns to recognize a fragment riding on MHC.
facts.helper_t_cell: Carries the CD4 marker HIV also grabs onto — exactly why the virus targets this cell first.
facts.cytotoxic_t_cell: Carries the CD8 marker and delivers perforin and granzymes — a chemical order to self-destruct.
facts.plasma_cell: A B cell's factory form: several thousand identical antibody molecules leave it every second.
facts.memory_cell: Can sit quiet in the blood for decades, then outrace a naive cell the moment its antigen returns.
facts.mhc_class_i: Every nucleated cell wears one, showing cytoplasmic protein fragments to any passing cytotoxic T cell.
facts.mhc_class_ii: Only a few cell types make this one — dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells — to brief helper T cells.
facts.clonal_selection: Burnet's 1957 theory: an antigen picks out — doesn't teach — the one lymphocyte that already matches it.
facts.igm: A five-unit pentamer, first responder of the primary response, too big to ever leave the bloodstream.
facts.igg: Three in every four antibodies in your blood, and the only class that crosses the placenta.
facts.iga: More of this is made than every other antibody class combined — most never even reaches the blood.
facts.ige: Under 0.0001% of your antibodies, bound tight to mast cells, and enough to trigger anaphylactic shock.
facts.normal_microbiota: Roughly 10,000 microbial species have been catalogued living across the healthy human body.
facts.adhesin: Often just one minor protein riding the tip of a pilus — it decides which host cell a bacterium can grab.
facts.exotoxin: A secreted bacterial protein, sometimes potent enough that heat alone turns it into a safe vaccine.
facts.endotoxin: Lipid A, the toxic core of a Gram-negative cell's own outer membrane, released only when the cell dies.
facts.virulence_factor: Adhesins, capsules, enzymes, toxins — whatever trait actually lets a microbe make a healthy host sick.
facts.opportunistic_pathogen: Candida albicans lives in you harmlessly for years, until something tips its numbers out of balance.
facts.hypersensitivity: Gell and Coombs sorted every kind of damaging immune overreaction into just four types, in 1963.
facts.allergy: Cow's milk, soy, egg, wheat, peanut, tree nut, fish and shellfish cause 90% of food allergies.
facts.anaphylaxis: Richet's 1902 coinage means the opposite of protection — and the Nobel committee agreed in 1913.
facts.autoimmune_disease: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system's own T cells are what destroy the insulin-making cells.
facts.immunodeficiency: AIDS has one hard number attached to it: a CD4+ T cell count below 200 per microliter of blood.
facts.transplant_rejection: T cells reading a donor organ's HLA proteins as foreign is exactly what immunosuppressants exist to blunt.
facts.promoter: DNA just upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase, sigma factor in hand, docks to start transcription.
facts.transcription_terminator: A GC-rich hairpin, or the Rho protein pulling along the mRNA, knocks RNA polymerase off the DNA.
facts.operator: Sits between the promoter and an operon's genes; a repressor parked here blocks RNA polymerase.
facts.repressor: A protein that clamps an operator shut; the lac repressor lets go the moment allolactose binds it.
facts.sigma_factor: Swapping RNA polymerase's sigma subunit retargets it — E. coli's sigma-32 turns on heat-shock genes.
facts.two_component_system: A membrane sensor autophosphorylates on cue, then hands the phosphate to a partner that flips genes on.
facts.rna_interference: Small RNA loaded into RISC finds and shreds a matching mRNA; Fire and Mello won the 2006 Nobel for it.
facts.open_reading_frame: DNA from a start codon to a stop codon with none between; long runs get flagged as candidate genes.
facts.bioinformatics: BLAST checks a new sequence against a database of hundreds of billions of nucleotides to guess its job.
facts.metagenomics: Sequencing soil or seawater DNA directly finds microbes culturing misses; under 1% of species grow in a dish.
facts.catabolite_repression: Glucose keeps E. coli's lac operon off despite lactose; cAMP and CAP switch it on once glucose runs out.
facts.antigenic_variation: N. gonorrhoeae swaps which pilin gene it expresses, altering its surface protein so old antibodies miss it.
facts.phase_variation: E. coli pili genes flip on and off by inverting a promoter inside them — no new mutation needed.
facts.auxotroph: A microbe that lost the ability to make a compound, like an amino acid, and needs it supplied to grow.
facts.thymine_dimer: UV light fuses two adjacent thymine bases on a DNA strand, kinking the helix and blocking replication.
facts.photoreactivation: An enzyme, absent in humans, uses visible light to break a UV thymine dimer's bonds, undoing the damage.
facts.excision_repair: Snips out a DNA segment with a lesion like a thymine dimer; polymerase and ligase refill and seal the gap.
facts.sos_repair: A bacterial last resort: an error-prone polymerase copies past DNA damage, trading accuracy for survival.
facts.ames_test: Screens chemicals for mutagenicity using a histidine-starved Salmonella strain that reverts back to growth.
facts.transposon: A DNA segment that jumps to a new spot in the genome, often disrupting whatever gene it lands in.
facts.f_plasmid: Carries the genes for its own pilus and transfer; spliced into the chromosome it makes an Hfr cell.
facts.r_plasmid: A resistance plasmid stacking genes for several antibiotics at once, often ten on one loop of DNA.
facts.genomic_island: A stretch of chromosome over 10 kilobases whose GC content betrays that it came from another species.
facts.replica_plating: Stamping a velvet-pressed copy of a colony plate onto fresh media to spot mutants without poisoning them.
facts.dna_library: A whole genome, cut into fragments by restriction enzymes and cloned one fragment per host cell.
facts.cdna: DNA copied from mature mRNA, so it skips introns entirely — bacteria can read it without splicing.
facts.selectable_marker: A resistance gene on a vector that lets only successfully transformed cells survive antibiotic selection.
facts.gfp: A jellyfish protein that glows green under blue light, fused to genes to reveal exactly when they switch on.
facts.colony_blotting: Colonies pressed onto a membrane, lysed in place, then probed to find which ones carry a target gene.
facts.dna_probe: A labeled single strand of DNA that seeks out and binds its exact complementary sequence.
facts.fish_probe: A glowing probe that lights up a target sequence right inside an intact cell on a microscope slide.
facts.dna_microarray: A chip dotted with thousands of DNA probes that lights up to show every gene a cell was expressing at once.
facts.transgenic_plant: A plant carrying a gene inserted from another species, often delivered by a bacterium's own plasmid.
facts.bt_toxin: An insect gut-rupturing protein made by a sporulating soil bacterium; engineered into crops as a built-in pesticide.
facts.golden_rice: Rice engineered to make beta-carotene in its grain, fighting vitamin A deficiency where rice is a staple.
facts.ti_plasmid: A soil bacterium's plasmid that inserts its T-DNA into a plant's chromosome, causing crown gall tumors.
facts.electroporation: A brief electric pulse punches temporary pores in a cell membrane, letting DNA slip inside.
facts.streptococcus_pyogenes: Clears a wide zone on blood agar — it lyses red blood cells completely, not just partially.
facts.strep_throat: Streptococcal pharyngitis: S. pyogenes in the throat, spread on the coughs and sneezes of someone already infected.
facts.corynebacterium_diphtheriae: Club-shaped rods lined up like a wooden fence. Most often enters through the nose, tonsils, or throat.
facts.diphtheria: A grey pseudomembrane clogs the tonsils while its toxin rides the blood to the heart, kidneys, and nerves.
facts.streptococcus_pneumoniae: An encapsulated diplococcus, cells found in pairs, and the top cause of pneumonia in children and the elderly.
facts.pneumococcal_pneumonia: The most common bacterial pneumonia in adults. Fluid fills the lung's own tiny air sacs and blocks oxygen from crossing in.
facts.bordetella_pertussis: A tiny, encapsulated coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated cells lining the airway with proteins built for exactly that.
facts.whooping_cough: Pertussis: paroxysms of coughing end in a sharp, high-pitched gasp as the next breath forces its way back in.
facts.tuberculosis: Initially infects the lungs. Most infections stay silent for years, latent rather than active, before a few progress.
facts.rhinovirus: Grows best at 33°C, noticeably colder than the body's core — exactly why it sets up in the nose and not deeper down.
facts.common_cold: Rhinoviruses cause up to 40% of colds on their own — over 100 known types of just that one genus.
facts.folliculitis: Infection and inflammation of a hair follicle. Most boils and carbuncles trace back to S. aureus.
facts.staphylococcal_scalded_skin_syndrome: An exfoliative toxin cleaves the protein holding two skin layers together, and the skin separates like a scald.
facts.impetigo: A contagious infection of the skin's outer layer, typically Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
facts.rickettsia_rickettsii: Rides into the blood on a tick's saliva, then invades the cells lining small and medium blood vessels.
facts.rocky_mountain_spotted_fever: A rash of small spots of bleeding starts at the wrists and ankles, then works its way toward the trunk.
facts.measles_virus: An enveloped RNA virus with no known animal reservoir. Humans are its only natural host.
facts.measles: Nine in ten non-immune people sharing a home with a case will catch it — among the most contagious diseases known.
facts.rubella_virus: An enveloped RNA virus in its own genus, Rubivirus. Found in the blood five to seven days after infection.
facts.rubella: German measles: a pink, lighter rash than measles proper. Crossing the placenta in pregnancy is the real danger.
facts.dermatophyte: A group of fungi that feed on keratin itself, which is why they only ever colonize skin, hair, and nails.
facts.ringworm: Tinea: a red, itchy, scaly, circular rash, from the Latin for worm. No worm is actually involved.
facts.wart: Human papillomavirus infecting skin through the smallest of breaks — a wound is the virus's actual entrance.
facts.clostridium_tetani: An anaerobe that cannot grow around oxygen at all. Its toxin travels the nerves it reaches, not the blood.
facts.tetanus: Lockjaw starts it: the toxin blocks the nerve signals that normally tell a muscle to relax, not just contract.
facts.clostridium_perfringens: The shortest reported generation time of any known organism — 6.3 minutes — an anaerobic spore-former.
facts.gas_gangrene: Myonecrosis: muscle tissue dies outright, gas collects in it, and it can turn to shock within hours.
facts.pseudomonas_infection: The single most common cause of infection in burn injuries — needs only a breach to get in.
facts.actinomyces_israelii: A normal colonizer of the mouth, vagina, and colon — harmless as long as it stays in those anoxic pockets.
facts.actinomycosis: Slow, spreading tissue infection after trauma opens a way in — dental work, a broken jaw, a bite.
facts.bartonella_henselae: Carried by domestic and feral cats, passed on by their scratches, bites, and the fleas that ride them.
facts.cat_scratch_disease: Most often passed on by a scratch or bite from a kitten rather than an adult cat.
facts.streptobacillus_moniliformis: Nearly every wild and domestic rat carries it, almost always without symptoms of its own.
facts.rat_bite_fever: High fevers, shivering, headache, and joint pain, days after a bite or scratch from a colonized rodent.
facts.peptic_ulcer: One in five to one in ten people infected go on to develop an ulcer; most never notice a thing.
facts.mumps_virus: An enveloped RNA paramyxovirus. Humans are its only host, and it travels on respiratory secretions and saliva.
facts.mumps: Parotitis — painful swelling of the salivary glands in front of the ears — is the single most common symptom.
facts.hepatitis_a_virus: A non-enveloped RNA picornavirus, fecal-oral in spread — water or food fouled by infected feces.
facts.hepatitis_a: Usually resolves completely on its own, with no ongoing liver disease left behind once it's over.
facts.clostridioides_difficile: Held in check by a healthy gut microbiome. Let an antibiotic clear out the competition and it grows unopposed.
facts.c_diff_infection: Ranges from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening colon inflammation — a pseudomembrane can even form.
facts.norovirus: As few as ten virions are enough to start an infection — among the most contagious viruses known.
facts.norovirus_gastroenteritis: Spread by the fecal-oral route — through contaminated food or water, or straight person to person.
facts.cyclospora_cayetanensis: Oocysts shed in feces aren't infectious yet — sporulation takes one to several weeks outdoors first.
facts.cyclosporiasis: A diarrheal disease rarely spread person-to-person, because the parasite needs weeks outdoors first.
facts.cryptosporidiosis: Infects the small intestine's brush border, producing watery diarrhea — sometimes with a cough alongside it.
facts.typhoid_fever: Unlike other Salmonella strains, this one is a human-only pathogen — no animal reservoir carries it at all.
facts.urethra: A short mucosa-lined tube from bladder to skin surface — about 4 cm in women, roughly 20 cm in men.
facts.vagina: A muscular, mucosa-lined canal kept acidic, pH 3.8–4.5, by resident Lactobacillus fermenting glycogen.
facts.leptospira_interrogans: A hook-ended spirochete living in the kidneys of carrier rodents, shed continuously in their urine.
facts.gardnerella_vaginalis: A small gram-variable rod that signals a vagina's shift away from its normal Lactobacillus.
facts.neisseria_gonorrhoeae: A coffee-bean-shaped diplococcus whose pilin genes reshuffle into over a hundred antigenic variants.
facts.chlamydia_trachomatis: An obligate intracellular bacterium, alternating an infectious form with a dividing form inside the host cell.
facts.treponema_pallidum: A corkscrew-shaped spirochete too thin to Gram-stain — visible only by dark-field microscopy.
facts.haemophilus_ducreyi: True to its genus name, 'blood-loving' — it grows only on blood-enriched chocolate agar.
facts.tampon: A compressed core of cotton, rayon, or both; the most absorbent 1970s blends soaked up nearly 20x their weight.
facts.cystitis: Bladder infection, usually uropathogenic E. coli climbing the urethra and attaching to bladder cells.
facts.pyelonephritis: A bladder infection that climbed the ureters into the kidneys — 1 to 2 women per 1,000 get it yearly.
facts.leptospirosis: A biphasic zoonosis from water fouled by infected urine — about a million cases and 58,900 deaths yearly.
facts.bacterial_vaginosis: The most common vaginal condition in reproductive-age women — thin discharge, strong fishy odor, no inflammation.
facts.vulvovaginal_candidiasis: Candida albicans overgrowth causing itching and thick white discharge; about 75% of women get it once.
facts.toxic_shock_syndrome: A Staphylococcus aureus superantigen touching off a cytokine storm and a dangerous blood-pressure crash.
facts.gonorrhea: Often silent — about half of infected women show no symptoms — yet it can still scar the fallopian tubes.
facts.chlamydia: The most-reported bacterial STI in the US; about 70% of infected women never notice a symptom.
facts.syphilis: 'The great imitator' — a painless chancre, then a rash, then years of silence before possible late damage.
facts.chancroid: Painful soft genital ulcers, unlike syphilis's painless chancre, with tender, pus-filled groin nodes.
facts.botulism: Clostridium botulinum's toxin blocks the neuromuscular junction's go signal — the opposite of tetanus.
facts.meningitis: Inflammation of the meninges, from infection — bacterial cases are far deadlier than viral ones.
facts.meningococcemia: Neisseria meningitidis in the bloodstream, releasing endotoxin at up to 1,000 times normal levels.
facts.poliomyelitis: In under 1% of infections, poliovirus destroys motor neurons, causing lopsided flaccid paralysis.
facts.arbovirus: A virus amplified in a wild bird or rodent host, then carried between them by a biting mosquito or tick.
facts.west_nile_virus: Introduced to North America in 1999; birds are its real host, humans an accidental dead end.
facts.encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain itself, not just its coverings — likelier than meningitis to kill or disable.
facts.rabies_encephalitis: Once rabies virus reaches the brain by riding motor-neuron transport backward, death is over 99% certain.
facts.lymph_node: Bean-shaped and strung along the lymph vessels — packed with B and T cells that filter what drains in.
facts.spleen: Fist-sized, behind the stomach — red pulp filters worn blood cells, white pulp mounts immune responses.
facts.lymphocyte: A white blood cell born in bone marrow — as a B cell, T cell, or NK cell, each with a different job in immunity.
facts.yersinia_pestis: Grows in a flea's gut until it blocks the foregut, so the starving flea keeps biting and regurgitating bacteria.
facts.plague: Called the Black Death — bacteria dumped into a flea bite reach a lymph node and swell it into a tender bubo.
facts.francisella_tularensis: So infectious that a lab exposure alone can cause tularemia — a handful of organisms is enough by some routes.
facts.tularemia: An ulcer marks where it got in, and the lymph node draining that spot swells and turns tender within days.
facts.brucella: Each species keeps mainly to one host — melitensis in goats and sheep, abortus in cattle, suis in pigs.
facts.brucellosis: Undulant fever — from raw milk or a slaughterhouse cut, temperature spikes and fades in waves for weeks.
facts.sepsis: The body's own inflammatory response to infection does the damage here, not the microbe alone.
facts.septic_shock: Sepsis whose blood pressure won't hold even with fluids — roughly 4 in 10 who reach this stage do not survive.
facts.infective_endocarditis: Bacteria seed a clot already sitting on a damaged heart valve — a valve with no blood supply to fight back.
facts.epstein_barr_virus: A herpesvirus that infects the throat, then quietly settles into B cells for good — most adults carry it.
facts.infectious_mononucleosis: Kissing disease — weeks of fatigue and fever from a virus spread almost entirely through saliva.
facts.yellow_fever_virus: A flavivirus that cycles between Aedes mosquitoes and forest monkeys long before it ever reaches a person.
facts.yellow_fever: Named for the jaundice it causes — in severe cases, black vomit and bleeding, fatal up to half the time.
facts.acute_retroviral_syndrome: Fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes 2 to 4 weeks after HIV exposure, as the virus floods the bloodstream.
facts.clinical_latency: HIV keeps replicating for years while CD4+ T cell counts slowly fall, even with no symptoms yet.
facts.aids: Diagnosed once the CD4+ T cell count drops below 200 cells per microliter, or a defining opportunistic disease appears.
facts.needle_borne_hiv_transmission: A needlestick from HIV-positive blood infects a health worker about 0.3% of the time, far below hepatitis B's roughly 10%.
facts.perinatal_hiv_transmission: Untreated, HIV passes from mother to child around birth or through breastfeeding in a fifth to a third of cases; treatment cuts that below 5%.
facts.human_herpesvirus_8: Identified in Kaposi's sarcoma tissue in 1994, this double-stranded DNA herpesvirus usually persists for life without symptoms.
facts.kaposis_sarcoma: Purple-to-black nodules from HHV-8-infected blood vessel cells; it became an AIDS-defining illness once the epidemic began.
facts.pneumocystis_jirovecii: A fungus so adapted to mammal lungs it has never been grown outside one; healthy people carry it without knowing.
facts.pneumocystis_pneumonia: Once the most common AIDS-defining illness in the US; risk climbs sharply once CD4+ counts fall under 200 per microliter.
facts.toxoplasmic_encephalitis: Latent Toxoplasma cysts reactivate in the brain once immunity collapses, an AIDS-defining condition.
facts.cytomegalovirus: A herpesvirus with the largest genome of any known human herpesvirus; infected cells swell with an 'owl's eye' nucleus.
facts.cmv_retinitis: Reactivated cytomegalovirus infects the retina in 15% to 40% of people with AIDS, once a leading cause of AIDS-related blindness.
facts.hiv_wasting_syndrome: Cachexia from chronic, uncontrolled HIV infection; it was the presenting sign of AIDS in about a fifth of early cases.
facts.zidovudine: AZT: a thymidine look-alike missing the 3' hydroxyl group reverse transcriptase needs to extend the DNA chain, so it just stops.
facts.haart: Combining antiretrovirals from different drug classes suppresses HIV for years — it lowers viral load but never clears the provirus.
facts.big_bang: The universe expanding from an initial hot, dense state, 13.8 billion years ago.
facts.universe: All space, time, matter and energy — 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter, under 5% ordinary matter.
facts.microbe: An organism too small to see unaided — most of the tree of life, by species count and by mass.
facts.pathogen: A microbe that causes disease — most microbes don't, which is why this needed its own word.
facts.infection: A pathogen established and multiplying in a host — the event, before any symptom shows.
facts.disease: The harm an infection does made visible — the same infection can stay silent or become this.
facts.iceland: Capital Reykjavík. The only large island sitting astride a mid-ocean ridge at sea level, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between the North American and Eurasian plates.
facts.norway: Capital Oslo. Its coast measures about 29,000 km with its roughly 1,200 fjords counted in, but only about 2,500 km without them.
facts.finland: Capital Helsinki. Over 180,000 lakes have been recorded within its borders, and in 1906 it became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage.
facts.estonia: Capital Tallinn. Estonian is a Finnic language, not Indo-European, and the country takes in more than 2,300 Baltic islands and islets.
facts.lithuania: Capital Vilnius. On 11 March 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to declare the restoration of its independence.
facts.latvia: Capital Riga. It first declared independence from the Russian Empire on 18 November 1918 and restored it on 21 August 1991.
facts.denmark: Capital Copenhagen. Its highest natural point, Møllehøj, reaches only 170.86 m — the country is the Jutland peninsula plus an archipelago of 406 islands.
facts.belgium: Capital Brussels. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and Brussels is now the de facto capital of the European Union.
facts.luxembourg: Capital Luxembourg City. The world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy, and in 2020 the first country anywhere to make all public transport free.
facts.liechtenstein: Capital Vaduz. One of only two doubly landlocked countries on Earth — landlocked, and ringed entirely by other landlocked states.
facts.andorra: Capital Andorra la Vella, at 1,023 m the highest capital city in Europe. The country is a co-principality with two heads of state.
facts.san_marino: Capital City of San Marino. Traditionally founded in AD 301, it claims to be the oldest extant sovereign state and the oldest constitutional republic.
facts.monaco: A city-state whose capital is itself. At 2.08 km² it is the second-smallest sovereign state after Vatican City, and the most densely populated country in the world.
facts.malta: Capital Valletta. Its megalithic temples, begun around 3500 BC, are among the oldest free-standing structures in the world.
