facts.genus: The rank above species, and the first word of every binomial: Panthera leo and Panthera onca are a lion and a jaguar filed under one name.
facts.phylum: The rank below kingdom and above class — Animalia holds about 32 of them, Plantae about 14, Fungi about eight.
facts.kingdom: Linnaeus made it the top rank in 1735; domain was slotted in above it in 1990, leaving kingdom second, and divided into phyla.
facts.biological_domain: The highest rank of all, proposed by Woese, Kandler and Wheelis in 1990 to hold just three groups: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
facts.zoology: The scientific study of animals — structure, embryology, classification, habits, distribution — which begins formally with Aristotle.
facts.ethology: The branch of zoology that studies animal behaviour in the field as much as the lab; its founders Lorenz, Tinbergen and von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.
facts.homo_sapiens: Our own species, emerging in Africa around 300,000 years ago — Linnaeus coined the name in 1758 and is himself the designated type specimen.
facts.ardipithecus: An Ethiopian hominin genus of two named species — A. kadabba at 5.6 million years, A. ramidus at 4.4 — both still carrying an ape's grasping, divergent big toe.
facts.bipedalism: Moving on the two rear limbs — invented independently by theropod dinosaurs and their bird descendants, by kangaroos and hopping mice, and by hominins.
facts.gene_pool: Every allele carried by a population — Serebrovsky named it the genofond in the 1920s, and Dobzhansky translated it into English as 'gene pool'.
facts.fermentation: Catabolism with the oxygen switched off: roughly 2 ATP per glucose instead of 32, and the carbon that cannot be burned walks out as ethanol or lactate.
facts.gluten: Glutenin and gliadin are 75–85% of bread wheat's protein, but they are not gluten until water and kneading cross-link them by disulfide bonds into one elastic net.
facts.maillard_reaction: Amino acids meeting reducing sugars, running fast from about 140 °C and building the melanoidins that brown a crust — Louis Camille Maillard found it in 1912 while trying to synthesise proteins.
facts.umami: Ikeda named it in 1908 from kombu broth, but the TAS1R1+TAS1R3 receptor that senses it was not found until 2000 — and glutamate with inosinate tastes stronger than the two added up.
facts.emulsion: Droplets of one immiscible liquid held inside another by an amphiphile — thermodynamically doomed the entire time, which is why mayonnaise eventually breaks.
facts.caramelization: Pure sugar pyrolysis with no protein anywhere in it: fructose gives way at 105 °C and sucrose holds out to 170 °C, and the butter smell coming off is diacetyl.
facts.fat: One glycerol carrying three fatty acids, at 9 kcal a gram — more than double sugar or protein — and the only vehicle vitamins A, D, E and K travel in.
facts.roux: Equal weights of flour and fat cooked out together; take it darker for flavour and you lose thickening — a chocolate roux does about a quarter the work of a white one.
facts.sauce: From Latin salsus, 'salted'. Escoffier's Guide culinaire fixed five mothers — espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate, hollandaise — and everything else is a daughter of one of them.
facts.vegetable: A kitchen category, not a botanical one: in Nix v. Hedden (1893) the US Supreme Court taxed the tomato as a vegetable while conceding it is botanically a fruit.
facts.spice: The line against herbs is anatomical: seed, fruit, bark, root or flower bud makes a spice — pepper, cinnamon, ginger, clove — while leaves and stems make a herb.
facts.seasoning: Salt, acid and spice added late or at the table — done properly you cannot taste the seasoning at all, only the ingredient it is sharpening.
facts.condiment: From Latin condire, 'to pickle or season' — it arrives after the cooking so the eater, not the cook, sets the dose. Rome's was garum.
facts.nutrition: The short list a human body cannot build for itself: 9 amino acids, 2 fatty acids, 13 vitamins, 14 minerals and choline. Everything else it makes.
facts.leavening: Three ways to inflate a dough — yeast, an acid-base fizz, or air beaten in — and all three fail unless gluten and gelatinising starch hold the bubble until it sets.
facts.gravy: Built from the juices a roast sheds and leaves welded to the pan, then thickened; the word is in English cookery by the 14th century, from Old French grané.
facts.dairy: Milk from cattle, buffalo, goats or sheep, worked into cheese, butter and yoghurt — Anatolian potsherds put the practice in the seventh millennium BC, long before adults could digest it.
facts.distillation: Not a reaction at all — boil, condense, repeat along a volatility gap. With ethanol the gap shuts at 95.6% by mass and the azeotrope stops you dead.
facts.food_drying: The oldest preservation trick there is, about 12,000 BC in the Middle East: take the water activity low enough and bacteria, yeasts and moulds simply cannot grow.
facts.curing: Near 20% salt to draw water out of any microbe by osmosis, then nitrite to hold back Clostridium botulinum — and the pink is nitric oxide bound to myoglobin, not blood.
facts.smoking_process: Cold smoke sits at 20–30 °C and never cooks anything; what preserves is chemistry — phenols, formaldehyde and acetic acid at around pH 2.5, with guaiacol supplying the taste.
facts.pickling_process: Two routes to the same number: lactic bacteria making the acid themselves in 20–40 g of salt per litre, or vinegar poured straight on. Either way, pH 4.6 or under.
facts.mouthfeel: The part of flavour the mouth reports as physics rather than chemistry — viscosity, grain, crunch, the oily film left behind — and viscosity alone changes how full you feel.
facts.food_safety: Between 5 and 60 °C is the danger zone; the WHO counts about 600 million foodborne illnesses and 420,000 deaths a year, and its whole programme fits on five keys.
facts.brewing: Mash the malt at 60–70 °C so amylase can cut its starch into maltose, boil with hops, pitch yeast — Natufians at Raqefet Cave were running a version of it 13,000 years ago.
facts.searing: The surface has to be dry to get past 150 °C, and it does not seal in juices — Justus von Liebig's 1850 claim was already failing tests in the 1930s, and Harold McGee buried it.
facts.braising: Brown it dry, then simmer it covered in a little liquid; the tenderness is collagen melting into gelatin and lubricating the fibres, not water getting in.
facts.culture_medium: Nutrient broth set with agar. Gelatin melted at incubation heat and microbes ate it; agar does neither, so the colonies stay put.
facts.nucleoside: A sugar joined to a base and nothing else. Add one phosphate group and it becomes a nucleotide — that group is the whole difference.
facts.double_helix: Two antiparallel strands wound around a shared axis, bases paired inward like rungs. Watson and Crick published the model in Nature on 25 April 1953.
facts.rosalind_franklin: Her X-ray diffraction work on DNA produced the image that showed it was helical. She died in 1958, four years before the Nobel her data underpinned.
facts.war: Armed conflict between organised forces under a command able to sustain operations; the cemetery at Jebel Sahaba in Sudan, about 13,400 years old, held 64 burials, and stone projectile points were found in the bodies of 21 of them.
facts.soldier: The word runs back through Old French soudeour, 'one paid a wage', to the solidus, the late Roman gold coin — a soldier was defined from the start by being paid.
facts.army: A land force organised under command: a modern field army holds three or four corps, each of two or more divisions, down to battalions of 500 to 750 soldiers.
facts.navy: A state's fleet kept for war: Athens voted a silver strike at Laurion into triremes from 483 BC, and that fleet broke the Persian navy in the straits of Salamis three years later.
facts.air_force: A branch that fights in the air rather than a scouting wing of an army: Britain merged the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service into the Royal Air Force on 1 April 1918, fifteen years after the first powered flight.
facts.infantry: Troops who fight on foot, the largest part of almost every army in history; the word reached English in the 1570s from Italian infanteria, men reckoned too junior for the cavalry.
facts.cavalry: Troops who fight mounted, trading numbers for height, speed and mass — and largely converted to tanks and motorised infantry between the world wars.
facts.artillery_branch: The guns as a service of their own, with trained officers instead of hired mechanics: artillery caused the majority of combat deaths in the Napoleonic Wars and both world wars.
facts.phalanx: A block of spearmen eight or more ranks deep, each shield covering its owner's left side and his neighbour's right — which left the rightmost file of the line half-exposed.
facts.legion: Rome's infantry formation: 4,200 foot and 300 horse in the manipular Republic, later about 5,200 men in ten cohorts.
facts.fortification: From Latin fortis and facere, to make strong: works built to hold ground — Solnitsata in Bulgaria had stone walls 1.4 m thick by about 4700 BC.
facts.city_wall: A town's enclosing defence and usually its first great public work; Jericho had one by the 8th millennium BC, and such walls doubled as toll gates that funnelled all trade through a few watched entrances.
facts.keep: The fortified tower inside a castle, both the lord's residence and the last refuge if the outer walls fell — the White Tower's rag-stone walls run about 7.3 m thick.
facts.motte_and_bailey: A timber tower on a piled-earth mound with a ditched courtyard below: it needed almost no skilled labour, and about 741 were thrown up across England and Wales after 1066.
facts.portcullis: A latticed grille of wood and metal dropped down grooves cut into the gateway jambs; gatehouses often carried two, to trap attackers in the passage between them.
facts.bastion_fort: Low, thick ramparts sunk behind a ditch, with diamond-shaped bastions at the corners so no stretch of wall lay out of another's fire — worked out in Italy around 1500 once cannon had made high walls indefensible.
facts.siege: The blockade of a city or fortress meant to take it by attrition or prepared assault; the encirclement of Leningrad lasted 872 days, from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944, and killed over a million civilians, most by starvation.
facts.blockade: Force used to cut a whole region off from supply rather than to capture it — and unlawful under modern international law where the purpose is to starve civilians.
facts.attrition: Wearing an opponent down by continuous losses instead of by manoeuvre; at Verdun in 1916 Falkenhayn set out to bleed the French army, and the ten-month battle produced over 700,000 casualties.
facts.conscription: Compulsory military service by law: the Jourdan Law of 1798 held that every Frenchman owed himself to the defence of the nation, and more than 2.6 million men were inducted between 1800 and 1813.
facts.standing_army: Full-time troops kept and paid in peacetime; Tiglath-Pileser III disbanded Assyria's militias for paid professionals around 745 BC, and Charles VII raised the first Christian standing army in the 1430s.
facts.mercenary: A soldier who fights for private gain rather than allegiance; the 1977 Geneva Protocol denies mercenaries combatant status, so a captured one has fewer protections than a captured soldier.
facts.guerrilla_warfare: Small irregular bands using ambush, raid and sabotage instead of pitched battle; the Spanish word means 'little war', and Wellesley carried it into English in 1809.
facts.total_war: War in which a whole economy and population are mobilised and the enemy's civilians are counted as legitimate targets — Ludendorff gave it its name in Der totale Krieg in 1935, four years before the war that fit it best.
facts.gravity: By far the weakest of the four forces — two electrons repel electrically 4×10^42 times harder than they attract — yet it alone builds the universe.
facts.orbit: Newton's cannonball: fire it fast enough and the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, so it never lands.
facts.solar_system: Collapsed out of a molecular cloud at least 4.568 billion years ago, and the Sun kept 99.86% of the mass for itself.
facts.escape_velocity: √(2GM/d): 11.186 km/s off Earth, 2.38 off the Moon, 617.7 off the Sun — and it does not depend on what is escaping.
facts.astronomical_unit: Fixed by the IAU in 2012 at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres — sunlight crosses it in 499 seconds.
facts.light_year: 9,460,730,472,580.8 km — the distance light covers in a Julian year of exactly 365.25 days. A length, not a time.
facts.parsec: The distance at which one AU subtends one arcsecond: 3.26 light-years. Herbert Hall Turner coined the name in 1913.
facts.main_sequence: The band where core hydrogen burns, and where a star spends roughly 90% of its life — the Sun has 6.5 billion years left on it.
facts.red_dwarf: Three-quarters of the Milky Way's fusing stars, not one visible to the naked eye, and none has ever died — they last trillions of years.
facts.planetary_nebula: Nothing to do with planets — Herschel's 1780s misnomer for the roughly 10,000-year glow of gas a dying star sheds.
facts.supernova_remnant: Ejecta at up to 10% of light speed ploughing into interstellar gas — and the main source of the galaxy's cosmic rays.
facts.binary_star: About a third of Milky Way systems, and the only way to weigh a star directly — everything else is inferred from these.
facts.stellar_classification: O B A F G K M, hottest to coolest — Annie Jump Cannon's ordering of the Harvard spectra, on which the Sun comes out G2V.
facts.apparent_magnitude: Backwards and logarithmic: Pogson fixed it in 1856 so five steps is exactly 100× in brightness, and good eyes reach about +6.5.
facts.asteroid_belt: 2.06 to 3.27 AU, and it has lost 99.9% of its original mass — everything left adds up to 3% of the Moon.
facts.meteoroid: The IAU's 2017 size band: 30 micrometres to one metre. Smaller is a micrometeoroid, larger is an asteroid.
facts.meteor: The streak is ram-pressure heating, not friction, between about 120 and 50 km up — 25 million enter the air each day.
facts.heliosphere: The bubble the solar wind inflates against interstellar space — Voyager 1 crossed out of it at 121 AU on 25 August 2012.
facts.magnetosphere: Earth's field holds the solar wind off at 5–10 Earth radii on the day side and trails a magnetotail over 6.3 million km long.
facts.aurora: Atomic oxygen struck by precipitating electrons glows green at 557.7 nm near 100 km up, and red at 630 nm above 150.
facts.sunspot: Magnetic flux strangling convection: the umbra sits at 3,000–4,500 K against a 5,780 K photosphere, so it is dark only by contrast.
facts.coronal_mass_ejection: Around 1.6 billion tonnes of coronal plasma thrown out at an average 489 km/s — one of these blacked out Quebec on 13 March 1989.
facts.solar_eclipse: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and 400 times farther off, so the discs match — totality never exceeds 7 min 32 s.
facts.lunar_eclipse: Sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere loses its blue to Rayleigh scattering, so the shadowed Moon runs red for up to 107 minutes.
facts.hubbles_law: v = H₀D. Lemaître derived it in 1927, Hubble published in 1929, and the constant still won't agree: 67.7 against 73 km/s/Mpc.
facts.cosmic_inflation: Alan Guth's January 1981 fix — distances doubling every 10⁻³⁷ seconds, which is why opposite sides of the sky match in temperature.
facts.observable_universe: 93 billion light-years across though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old — expansion carried the edge out to 46.5 billion.
facts.event_horizon: The boundary where escape velocity reaches the speed of light — about 3 km out for one solar mass, and one-way in every direction.
facts.gravitational_wave: Einstein predicted them in June 1916; LIGO first caught one on 14 September 2015, as a stretch of a thousandth of a proton's width.
facts.gravitational_lensing: Mass bends light — 1.75 arcseconds past the Sun's limb, twice the Newtonian figure, which is what the 1919 eclipse settled.
facts.antibiotic: Waksman and his collaborators first used the word in 1942 for a substance one microbe makes to stop another — and not one of them works on a virus or a fungus.
facts.antiviral: A virus replicates using your own cells, so there is barely anything to poison that isn't you — aciclovir's trick is to jam the viral DNA polymerase and terminate the chain.
facts.antifungal: A fungus is a eukaryote like you; the one usable difference is that its membrane is built on ergosterol where yours uses cholesterol.
facts.macrophage: One cell type under many names — Kupffer cells in the liver, microglia in the brain, alveolar macrophages in the lung — patrolling tissue by amoeboid movement.
facts.neutrophil: 40 to 70% of your white blood cells, dead within 5 to 135 hours, and able to kill by flinging its own chromatin out as a sticky net.
facts.innate_immunity: It reads molecular patterns shared broadly across pathogens but absent from you — and it is the only immune system plants, fungi, prokaryotes and invertebrates have.
facts.adaptive_immunity: Found only in jawed vertebrates: V(D)J recombination shuffles a small family of genes into a receptor for almost anything, before the body has met a single thing.
facts.pus: Mostly dead neutrophils, killed by bacterial leukocidins and cleared by macrophages — and it goes green when myeloperoxidase, an intensely green antibacterial protein, is in it.
facts.abscess: Pus collected into a pocket inside the tissue — the standard treatment is still to cut it open and drain it, and in most uncomplicated cases adding antibiotics shows no benefit at all.
facts.bone_marrow: About 5% of your body mass, releasing roughly 500 billion new blood cells into circulation every day.
facts.thymus: Grows to 20–50 grams by puberty and then turns to fat — but first it kills, by apoptosis, every T cell whose receptor reacts against the body's own proteins.
facts.parasite: Not a lineage but a living: the roll call runs from malaria's protozoan through hookworms, lice and vampire bats to ringworm fungi and flowering plants like mistletoe.
facts.toxin: Ludwig Brieger's word for a poison a living cell makes — the range runs from a bee sting to botulinum toxin, fatal at doses too small to see.
facts.antitoxin: An antibody grown in an animal against one specific toxin — Behring and Kitasato published serum therapy on 4 December 1890, and The Lancet called diphtheria antitoxin the century's greatest advance in treating acute infection.
facts.passive_immunity: Borrowed antibodies, not your own — protection that starts immediately and is gone in a few weeks to three or four months, because nothing was ever learned.
facts.opsonization: Wright and Douglas named it in 1904 from opsono, "I prepare victuals for" — a coating that makes a microbe appetising to a phagocyte.
facts.airborne_transmission: The old 5 μm line between "airborne" and "droplet" has been abandoned: exhaled particles form a continuum, and only those above about 100 μm reliably fall within 2 metres.
facts.contagion: Once it meant a disease passed only by direct physical contact; the working test now is whether isolating the sick actually slows it down.
facts.quarantine: Ragusa held arrivals 30 days from 1377 — a trentine; Venice stretched it to 40 in 1448, and quaranta gave the practice its name.
facts.outbreak: Cases in excess of what that place and that season normally produce — the count that matters is the baseline you were expecting, not the count itself.
facts.contact_tracing: Smallpox was not finished off by blanket vaccination but by finding every infected person's contacts, isolating them, and immunising the ring around them.
facts.epidemiology: Literally "the study of what is upon the people" — epi, demos, logos — and it works on populations, never on one patient.
facts.incubation_period: The gap between exposure and the first symptom, while the organism multiplies toward the threshold that produces one — and depending on the disease, you may be contagious the whole time.
facts.petri_dish: Koch published a precursor dish in 1881; his assistant Julius Richard Petri made the final modification in 1887, and it has not needed changing since.
facts.pure_culture: Axenic — one species and nothing else, usually clones of a single cell, because the streak plate spread the sample thin enough that each colony grew from one.
facts.aseptic_technique: The goal is to eliminate infection, not to achieve sterility — keep the microbes out of the field rather than fight them once they are in it.
facts.edward_jenner: On 14 May 1796 he cut cowpox pus into the arm of James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son, then gave him smallpox on 1 July and nothing happened.
facts.alexander_fleming: He named lysozyme in 1922 after his own nasal mucus cleared a plate; back from holiday on 3 September 1928 he found a staph plate spoiled by mould and said "That's funny".
facts.joseph_lister: On 12 August 1865 he packed 11-year-old James Greenlees's compound fracture with lint soaked in carbolic acid; four days later there was still no infection.
facts.ignaz_semmelweis: Vienna's First Clinic lost 18.3% of its mothers in April 1847; he made the doctors wash in chlorinated lime from mid-May, and July's figure was 1.2%.
facts.genome: All of it, coding or not: 3.1 billion bases spread over 24 distinct chromosome molecules in a human, and 98% of that never becomes protein.
facts.prokaryote: A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles at all — Bacteria and Archaea, mostly 1 to 10 micrometres, doing their chemistry straight across the cell membrane.
facts.symbiosis: De Bary's 1878 phrase for the living together of unlike organisms — the arrangement, not the verdict, so mutualism, commensalism and parasitism all count.
facts.eusociality: Three tests, all required: reproductive division of labour, overlapping generations, and cooperative care of the brood. Every termite species passes; so does one rodent.
facts.kin_selection: Hamilton's 1964 rule: help a relative when rB exceeds C. Haldane had already made the joke in 1955 — he would die for two brothers or eight cousins.
facts.clade: An ancestor and every last one of its descendants, no branch left out — which is why 'reptile' and 'fish' are not clades. Julian Huxley coined it in 1957.
facts.heredity: Traits passed on as discrete units rather than blended — blending would flatten a population to uniformity in a few generations and leave selection nothing to act on.
facts.mendelian_inheritance: Three laws out of some 28,000 pea plants — dominance, segregation, independent assortment — published in 1866, ignored, and rediscovered by three men independently in 1900.
facts.recessive_allele: It only shows when both copies match. One dominant copy hides it completely, and the carrier never finds out.
facts.heterozygous: Two different alleles at one locus, Rr. The dominant one is what you see; the other rides along silently and gets passed on anyway.
facts.homozygous: Both copies identical, PP or pp — and a recessive trait like Mendel's wrinkled pea turns up in the pp quarter of a cross and nowhere else.
facts.heterozygote_advantage: One sickle-cell allele makes infected red cells sickle and get cleared, which limits malaria; two cause the anaemia. That trade keeps a lethal allele common.
facts.genetic_code: 64 codons for 20 amino acids plus stop, so most amino acids have several spellings. Nirenberg and Matthaei read the first entry in 1961: poly-U gave phenylalanine.
facts.central_dogma: Crick's 1957 claim was about direction, not sequence of steps: once information has passed into protein, it cannot get out again.
facts.gene_expression: Every cell in you carries the same genome; what makes a neuron a neuron is which genes are switched on and how hard.
facts.epigenetics: Waddington's 1942 word, from his landscape of marbles rolling into valleys: changes in which genes run that survive cell division without touching a single base.
facts.dna_methylation: A methyl group parked on carbon 5 of a cytosine. About 75% of CpG sites carry one in mammalian somatic cells, and a methylated promoter goes quiet.
facts.crossing_over: Morgan named it in 1912 for the swap he could only infer; Creighton and McClintock caught it physically in 1931, at the X-shaped chiasmata.
facts.sex_chromosome: The X carries about 1,500 genes and the Y about 78 — and just one of those, SRY, is the switch. Nettie Stevens and E. B. Wilson spotted the pair in 1905.
facts.centromere: The constriction that pinches a chromosome into a short arm and a long one — and the only place a kinetochore will build, because only there does histone CENP-A replace H3.
facts.karyotype: Every chromosome stained and lined up in pairs: 46 in a human, a count only settled by Tjio and Levan in 1956, with G-banding resolving 300 to 400 bands.
facts.exaptation: Gould and Vrba's 1982 replacement for 'preadaptation', which had made evolution sound like it was aiming at something: a part that simply changed jobs.
facts.neoteny: Growing up without growing out of it. Kollmann coined the word in 1885 after the axolotl, and domesticated animals drift the same way.
facts.sexual_dimorphism: Two body plans in one species, and not always the way you expect — in eclectus parrots it is the female who is scarlet and the male who hides in green.
facts.great_oxidation_event: From about 2.46 to 2.06 billion years ago, cyanobacterial oxygen filled the air to roughly a tenth of today's level — and the sulfur isotopes read as a biosphere cut by over 80%.
facts.snowball_earth: Ice all the way to the equator, twice in the Cryogenian — Sturtian 717 to 660 Ma, Marinoan 650 to 635 Ma. Kirschvink named it in 1992.
facts.trilobite: Over 22,000 described species across 270 million years — and every lens in their eyes was a single crystal of calcite, up to 15,000 of them under one cornea.
facts.permian_triassic_extinction: 251.9 Ma, and 81% of marine species gone in perhaps 60,000 years while the Siberian Traps flooded basalt across a continent — the only mass extinction insects have ever suffered.
facts.stromatolite: Layer on layer of microbial mat cementing sediment into a mound, a metre high or more. They peaked about 1.25 billion years ago, then grazers arrived.
facts.rna_world: One molecule holding the message and doing the chemistry, before DNA or protein. Walter Gilbert named it in 1986; the ribosome's catalytic core is still RNA.
facts.hearing: Each pitch shakes its own spot on the basilar membrane — high notes at the cochlea's base, low at its apex — and the brain reads that map, from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
facts.deafness: Diagnosed when an ear cannot detect 25 decibels; profound loss starts above 90 dB, and some 1.33 billion people — a tenth of everyone alive — have some degree of it.
facts.latte: Espresso lost in steamed milk, served in a 230 ml glass with no thick foam layer — 'caffè latte' is attested in English by 1847, decades before the espresso machine.
facts.cappuccino: Equal thirds espresso, steamed milk and foam in a 150-180 ml cup, named not for a hood but for the brown of the Capuchin friars' habits.
facts.masala_chai: Black tea boiled with milk, sugar and spice — the Indian Tea Association, which pushed tea breaks on mills and mines in the early 1900s, at first thought the added spice and milk wasteful.
facts.mont_blanc: The Alps' highest summit, 4,807.3 m in 2025 and a metre lower in the 2023 drought year; first climbed 8 August 1786 by Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard.
facts.soviet_union: Founded 30 December 1922 by treaty as a federal union of national republics under one party, and dissolved on 26 December 1991.
facts.atmosphere: Gas a world holds down with its own gravity: Earth's dry air is 78.08% nitrogen and 20.95% oxygen, pressing 101,325 pascals at sea level.
facts.eruption: Dissolved gas coming out of solution as magma decompresses; the explosivity index runs 0 to 8 and each step is ten times the last, but most eruptions never get past 2.
facts.seismograph: A hanging mass too lazy to move while its frame shakes with the ground — the gap between the two is the whole measurement.
facts.joust: Two riders closing along either side of a tilt barrier with blunt-tipped wooden lances built to shatter; the armour made for it could reach 50 kg, heavier than armour for war.
facts.siege_of_jerusalem: Five weeks from 7 June to 15 July 1099, decided by two wheeled towers and an iron-headed ram built from ship timber, and followed by a massacre of the city's Muslims and Jews.
facts.bellerophon: Athena handed him a golden bridle in a dream so he could take Pegasus at Corinth's Pirene spring; he killed the Chimera with a lead-tipped spear, then fell when Zeus set a gadfly on the horse.
facts.fenrir: Loki's wolf son snapped two iron fetters and was held only by the soft ribbon Gleipnir — and Týr paid for the trick with the hand he had left in the wolf's mouth.
facts.norns: Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld draw water and clay from the well at Yggdrasil's root and daub the world tree every day so it will not rot.
facts.rabbi_loew: Judah Loew ben Bezalel, the Maharal, took up his Prague post in 1573 and died there in 1609 — the golem story only attached to him much later, first in print in 1834.
facts.prague: Capital on the Vltava where Charles IV founded Central Europe's oldest university in 1347; the 'city of a hundred spires' actually carries about five hundred.
facts.cauldron: A big pot for boiling over an open fire — the Battersea cauldron is about 2,800 years old, and the word runs back through Norman French caudron to the Latin for 'hot'.
facts.phonograph_record: One modulated spiral groove running inward from the rim — shellac at 78 rpm until Columbia's 1948 LP put 22 minutes a side onto 33⅓.
facts.qwerty: Sholes started from a piano-like alphabetical keyboard and spent five years shuffling it into this order by 1870; the tidy typebar-jamming explanation everyone repeats is disputed.
facts.wireless_telegraphy: Morse dots and dashes carried on damped spark-gap waves instead of copper — broad, interference-prone, and across the Atlantic by 1901.
facts.space_race: The US announced satellite plans on 29 July 1955 and the USSR answered five days later; the contest ran to a handshake in orbit in July 1975.
facts.pesto: From the Genoese pestâ, 'to pound' — garlic and pine nuts crushed to a cream in a marble mortar first, basil and coarse salt next, cheese last, oil only to loosen.
facts.mole_sauce: From Nahuatl mōlli, simply 'sauce'; mole poblano averages twenty ingredients and Oaxaca's run past thirty, and both Puebla and Oaxaca claim to have invented it.
facts.marinara: Alla marinara means sailor's style, not seafood — in Italy it is tomatoes, basil, olive oil, garlic and oregano, and the fish stays out.
facts.hemp: Legally it is Cannabis sativa carrying 0.3% delta-9 THC or less on a dry-weight basis — the same species above that line is a controlled drug.
facts.canola: Rapeseed oil once ran to 54% erucic acid, which damages heart muscle; canola is the cultivar group bred under 2%, trademarked by the Canola Council of Canada in 1978.
facts.clover: Domesticated in Spain around 1000 CE, and it was clover in the rotation that replaced the fixed nitrogen European cities ate and never sent back.
facts.chia: A 1–2 mm seed that soaks up twelve times its own weight in liquid and sheathes itself in mucilage; the seed is 25–30% oil, 55% of that omega-3.
facts.jojoba: Its seed is about 54% liquid wax, not oil — straight-chain C36–C46 esters, chemically closer to whale oil than to any vegetable triglyceride.
facts.kenaf: A hibiscus grown for two fibres at once: bast is 40% of the stem and woody core the other 60%, and pulping the whole stalk gives paper of hardwood quality.
facts.jute: Bangladesh calls it the golden fibre — bast strands one to four metres long, retted out of the stem in standing monsoon water.
facts.sisal: One agave gives 200–250 usable leaves over a 7–10 year life, each holding about 1,000 fibres — and the fibre is only 4% of the plant's weight.
facts.abaca: A Philippine banana harvested for its leaf sheaths, not its fruit; stronger than hemp and salt-resistant, it made ships' Manila rope and now makes tea bags and banknotes.
facts.ramie: Six thousand years old and still awkward — alone among bast crops it will not simply ret, and degumming it chemically costs up to a quarter of the fibre's weight.
facts.woad: A mustard-family plant yielding the very same indigo molecule as true indigo, only far less of it — which is why Vasco da Gama's 1498 sea route to India ruined Europe's woad towns.
facts.hop: Only female plants are grown; the lupulin inside their cones holds humulones that are barely bitter until a boil isomerises them into iso-alpha acids.
facts.sugarsnap_pea: Calvin Lamborn crossed a shelling-pea mutant found in 1952 with a snow pea and released the result in 1979 as Sugar Snap; the pod has no membrane, so it never splits open.
facts.mung_bean: Germinates in four to five days, and the sprout is picked at the moment the seed splits and the white root shows — before the plant ever makes a leaf.
facts.fava_bean: Rich in levodopa, and carrying the glycoside vicine — which in people with G6PD deficiency sets off favism, a haemolytic crisis brought on by a plate of beans.
facts.lupin: The seeds are edible only once their bitter alkaloids are brined out — and Australia, where the plant is not native, grows 85% of the world's commercial crop.
facts.poppy_seed: About 3,300 seeds to the gram, and harvesting them well is the opposite of harvesting opium: seed wants a dry ripe pod, latex wants a green one.
facts.amaranth: A C4 pseudocereal whose oil is about 5% squalene, sold as the plant-based stand-in for shark liver oil in cosmetics and supplements.
facts.emmer: The wild spikelet plants itself: its awns spread apart in night humidity and clamp shut by day, and silica hairs act as barbs so it can only travel downward into the soil.
facts.spelt: A hexaploid hulled wheat, most likely a hybrid of emmer with a bread-wheat type, whose grain stays sealed inside its husk even after threshing.
facts.kamut: Khorasan wheat, its kernels twice the size of modern wheat at up to 60 g per thousand — and 'Kamut' is a trademark, held by a Montana company that requires organic growing.
facts.einkorn: German for 'single grain', because each spikelet holds exactly one; diploid, 14 chromosomes, and among the very first wheats farmed.
facts.triticale: Wheat mother, rye father — the cross comes out sterile, and only colchicine doubling its chromosomes makes it breed; the first commercial variety appeared in 1970.
facts.fonio: A Digitaria crabgrass with the smallest seed of any millet and a root over a metre deep; Guinea alone grew more than 75% of the world crop in 2019.
facts.teff: Its Amharic name is thought to mean 'lost' — the seed is under a millimetre across — and Ethiopia grew more than 90% of the world's crop in 2016.
facts.wild_rice: Not rice at all but four species of Zizania, aquatic grasses standing in shallow lake water with only the flowering head above the surface; the Ojibwe name manoomin means 'good grain'.
facts.cinnamon_crop: Cinnamomum verum would reach 15 m but is coppiced to a 3 m bush, first cut at three years old and kept peeling for 40 to 50 more.
facts.clove_crop: An 8–12 m evergreen of the Maluku Islands whose buds are picked at 1.5–2 cm, the moment they turn bright red and before a single petal opens.
facts.nutmeg_crop: Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and one fruit yields two different spices — nutmeg from the seed, mace from the crimson aril wrapped round it.
facts.turmeric_crop: Commercial turmeric powder averages 3.14% curcumin by weight; curry powder, where turmeric is only one ingredient among many, averages 0.29%.
facts.chilli_pepper: Five domesticated species of Capsicum, a nightshade genus 17 million years in the making, and already in Mexican pottery by 3000 BC.
facts.fennel_crop: A 2.1 m carrot-family perennial whose fruits carry trans-anethole and fenchone; with anise it is one of absinthe's primary ingredients.
facts.star_anise_crop: An evergreen of South China and northern Vietnam whose eight woody carpels are picked just before ripening; until 2012 Roche took up to 90% of the world crop to make Tamiflu.
facts.dill_crop: One Greek word once meant both dill and anise; Latin split it into anethum and anisum, and Anethum is still dill's genus name.
facts.saffron_crocus: A sterile triploid clone — three sets of eight chromosomes, 24 in all, and no viable seed — so every saffron crocus alive was split off a corm by hand.
facts.spearmint_crop: Mentha spicata: square-stemmed, spike-flowered, and one of peppermint's two parents — unlike its sterile hybrid child it still sets seed.
facts.peppermint_crop: Spotted in a Hertfordshire field and published by John Ray in 1696; Linnaeus made it a species in 1753, but it is a hybrid of watermint and spearmint.
facts.tea_tea: Camellia sinensis would grow 20 m tall, but a plantation keeps it clipped to a flat-topped metre so pickers can take nothing but the bud and top leaves.
facts.coffee_crop: Two of Coffea's 120-odd species carry the whole trade — arabica about 55% of world production, robusta about 45% — and a tree takes three to five years to fruit, then bears for fifty.
facts.honeydew_melon: The Inodorus group of Cucumis melo: smooth-rinded and, as the name says, without the musk of a cantaloupe — 90% water, and judged ripe by rind colour rather than size.
facts.kiwifruit: Renamed from Chinese gooseberry in 1959 for the American market; China now grows 55% of the world's crop, more than New Zealand ever did.
facts.date_palm: Runs to 30 m and past 100 years of age, is male or female but never both, and has been farmed in Arabia since the 6th millennium BCE.
facts.passionfruit: Missionaries in Brazil named it around 1700 for the flower, not the fruit — five wounds of the crucifixion read into a vine's blossom, whose fruit is a pepo, a botanical berry.
facts.mangosteen: The inedible purple rind is so loaded with tannins and xanthones that it has been used to tan leather in China.
facts.elderberry: Only the flowers and the ripe berries are safe: everything else on Sambucus nigra, ripe seeds included, carries the cyanogenic glycoside sambunigrin.
facts.boysenberry: A four-way cross of raspberry, blackberry, dewberry and loganberry, traced in the late 1920s to vines Rudolph Boysen had abandoned on a farm in Anaheim.
facts.currant: Ribes bushes are the alternate host white pine blister rust needs, so the United States banned currant growing for most of the 20th century — the federal ban went in 1966 and some state bans still stand.
facts.gooseberry: Same genus as the currant, and the French name is groseille à maquereau — mackerel berry — after the old sauce its sourness was cooked into.
facts.kumquat: The one citrus eaten whole and backwards — the rind is the sweet part, the pulp inside is the sour one — from the Cantonese gām gwāt, 'golden orange'.
facts.quince: Hard, tart and astringent raw, with gritty stone cells right through a fruit that can reach a kilogram, and seeds whose nitriles release hydrogen cyanide in the stomach.
facts.cherimoya: Every flower opens female and turns male within hours, so nothing can pollinate itself — small nitidulid sap beetles do the carrying.
facts.jujube: Its leaves hold ziziphin, which switches off the ability to taste sweetness, and the dried fruit sells as 'red date' with no date palm anywhere in it.
facts.saskatoon_berry: Not a berry but a 5-15 mm purple pome, named from the Cree misâskwatômina, and dried into pemmican as both flavour and preservative.
facts.feijoa: Its perfume is methyl benzoate, and the plant will not set fruit without at least 50 hours of winter chilling.
facts.blood_orange: Anthocyanins are rare in citrus; the crimson only develops when the fruit ripens through cold nights, and it keeps deepening in cold storage after picking.
facts.meyer_lemon: Not a lemon: a citron crossed with a mandarin-pomelo hybrid, collected in China and brought to the USDA in 1908 by the plant explorer Frank N. Meyer.
facts.finger_lime: Its juice vesicles come out as loose spheres that burst between the teeth, which is why it sells as lime caviar.
facts.aonla: Called Indian gooseberry but related to no gooseberry at all — a Phyllanthus tree fruit whose bitterness is ellagitannin, emblicanin A alone making up 37%.
facts.medlar: Inedible until it half-rots: a hard frost starts bletting, breaking the cell walls down until the brown flesh can be spooned straight out of the skin.
facts.pawpaw: A custard-fleshed Annonaceae tree that survives eastern US winters, pollinated by beetles drawn to maroon flowers that smell yeasty.
facts.huckleberry: Never domesticated — Idaho's state fruit is still picked wild, resprouts from buried rhizomes after fire, and feeds black and grizzly bears.
facts.lingonberry: It keeps its leaves through winter, tolerates about -45 °C, and runs right across boreal forest and Arctic tundra under insulating snow.
facts.juniper_berry: Not a berry but a female cone whose scales stay fleshy and fuse into a ball called a galbulus — one of the very few spices that come from a conifer.
facts.sea_buckthorn: Its roots partner with nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria, so it colonises bare ground, and the orange fruit runs about 400 mg of vitamin C per 100 g.
facts.parsnip: Frost turns part of the root's starch to sugar, which is why it is left in the ground over winter — but the leaf sap's furanocoumarins blister skin in sunlight.
facts.jerusalem_artichoke: Neither from Jerusalem nor an artichoke: a North American sunflower whose tubers store 8 to 13% inulin, which human digestion cannot touch.
facts.sweetcorn: A recessive mutation stalls the conversion of sugar to starch in the kernel, so it has to be picked at the milk stage — ripening would spend the sugar.
facts.bok_choy: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, which never forms a head; the name is Cantonese baak choi, 'white vegetable', for the pale thick leaf stalks.
facts.endive: A Cichorium crop grown three ways at once: for bitter salad leaves, for roots roasted as a coffee substitute, and for chicons blanched in the dark.
facts.radicchio: The red and white only appear once the light is taken away: plants are lifted and stood in water in dark sheds until chlorophyll stops forming.
facts.swiss_chard: The same species as beetroot and sugar beet, bred for leaf and stalk instead of root — which is why it is also called leaf beet.
facts.collard_green: Brassica oleracea in the headless Acephala group with kale, on an upright stalk often over two feet and up to six in Portuguese cultivars.
facts.mustard_green: The leaves of Brassica juncea — the brown mustard whose seeds make the condiment — and sharper than any Brassica oleracea green they get mixed with.
facts.horseradish: The intact root smells of almost nothing; cut it and myrosinase turns sinigrin into allyl isothiocyanate, which goes for the sinuses rather than the tongue.
facts.yam: Dioscorea vines, not sweet potatoes: some 870 species, tubers running 1.5 m down, and the source of the diosgenin used to synthesise progesterone and cortisone.
facts.taro: Toxic raw: the corm's cells are packed with needle-shaped calcium oxalate raphides, which cooking or an overnight soak in cold water defuses.
facts.jicama: A pea-family vine grown for one crisp taproot while the rest of it is poison — the seeds, flowers and pods are heavy with rotenone.
facts.kohlrabi: German Kohl plus Rübe, cabbage plus turnip — but the swollen part is a stem sitting above ground, not a root, and the group name means 'roundish'.
facts.fennel_bulb: Not a root but a stack of swollen leaf bases — 90% water, milder and sweeter than the herb, and mislabelled 'anise' in half the supermarkets in North America.
facts.bamboo_shoot: Raw shoots carry the same cyanogenic glycosides as cassava and must be boiled — giant pandas eat them raw and survive on gut microbes enriched in cyanide-degrading genes.
facts.lotus_root: A rhizome 31.2% starch with almost no taste of its own — Japan grows its own and still imports 18,000 tonnes a year, 15,000 of them from China.
facts.rutabaga: An accidental hybrid that doubled its chromosomes to 2n=38, first recorded by Gaspard Bauhin in 1620 growing wild in Sweden — hence 'swede'.
facts.daikon_radish: A winter radish grown as a long white taproot, and sometimes left unharvested on purpose — rotting in place, it loosens compacted soil and pulls nutrients back up.
facts.water_chestnut: Not a nut but the corm of a flooded-paddy sedge — oligomers of ferulic acid cross-link its cell walls, so it stays crisp even boiled or canned.
facts.chayote: A Mesoamerican gourd holding one flat stone up to 10 cm long — and unusually, its tubers, shoots and leaves are eaten too.
facts.spaghetti_squash: Raw, the flesh is solid like any squash; cooked, it falls away from the rind in strands — and the orange cultivars carry the most carotene.
facts.acorn_squash: Cucurbita pepo var. turbinata — the same species as zucchini and crookneck, just left on the vine until the ridged rind hardens, which is what makes it a winter squash.
facts.snow_pea: An edible-pod pea described in 1825 as having compressed, non-leathery pods — flat and thin-walled, where the snap pea's are round and thick.
facts.yardlong_bean: The pods run 35 to 75 cm — about half a yard, not the one the name promises — and the plant is a cowpea, a different genus from the common bean.
facts.fiddlehead_fern: The still-coiled frond of an ostrich fern, on sale for only a few weeks each spring — boil it 15 minutes, after the CDC traced food-borne illness to undercooked ones in the early 1990s.
facts.sea_kale: William Curtis published on forcing it under blanching pots in 1799; by Mrs Beeton's day a basket of the blanched shoots cost ninepence, among the dearest vegetables in Britain.
facts.samphire: Also called glasswort, because its ashes were burned for the soda ash that made glass and soap — until the Leblanc process replaced plant sources in the early 1800s.
facts.napa_cabbage: A 1 to 3 kg barrel of leaves from near Beijing and the cabbage inside baechu-kimchi — Korean state breeding of it began in 1906, aimed squarely at yield.
facts.tatsoi: Spoon-shaped leaves in a flat ground-hugging rosette, ready in 45 to 50 days and hardy to −10 °C — it is often cut from under the snow.
facts.komatsuna: Japanese mustard spinach: a Brassica rapa leaf variety with mature blades about 30 cm long, grown commercially in Japan and Taiwan and fed to livestock besides.
facts.malabar_spinach: A soft-stemmed vine reaching 10 m whose leaves are 93% water and mucilaginous enough to thicken a soup — its red cultivar once dyed cosmetics and sealing wax in China.
facts.new_zealand_spinach: For two centuries the only cultivated vegetable to have come out of Australia and New Zealand — blanch the leaves one minute first to strip the oxalates.
facts.chaya: Simmer it 20 minutes and never in aluminium — raw chaya leaves hold cyanogenic glycosides like cassava's, and the toxins react with aluminium cookware.
facts.alfalfa_sprout: Ready in three to five days at 5 to 8 cm — and both seed and sprout carry L-canavanine, which has produced a lupus-like disease in primates.
facts.mung_bean_sprout: Caught in the four-to-five-day window after the seed splits and a soft white root pushes out — leave it longer and it puts up a green stem and stops being a sprout.
facts.microgreen: Not a sprout: it is grown in a medium and cut above the soil line at 1 to 3 inches, once the cotyledons are open and one pair of true leaves has started.
facts.portobello_mushroom: The same Agaricus bisporus sold as a white button, simply grown on — the cap opens out to 10–15 cm, browns, and the gills go dark.
facts.teak_tree: A mint-family tree whose own oils leave the timber termite-proof and durable with no oil or varnish at all — Myanmar's forests hold nearly half the world's naturally occurring teak.
facts.mahogany_tree: Philip II used it for joinery at El Escorial from 1584 and Havana made it a royal monopoly in 1622; in 2003 big-leaf mahogany became the first high-volume tropical timber on CITES Appendix II.
facts.walnut_tree: Its roots and hulls leak hydrojuglone that oxidises in soil to juglone — apples, tomatoes, pines and birches planted beneath a black walnut yellow and wilt.
facts.cherry_wood_tree: Black cherry's wilted leaves release hydrogen cyanide and are a leading cause of livestock poisoning — while the same tree yields perhaps the premier cabinet timber of the United States.
facts.ash_tree: An olive-family tree, 45 to 65 species, whose elastic wood becomes tool handles and drum shells — and which the emerald ash borer has killed by the tens of millions across 22 US states.
facts.ebony_tree: Heartwood up to 1,200 kg/m³ — twice as hard as oak and dense enough to sink in water — which is why it ends up as piano keys and violin fingerboards.
facts.sandalwood_tree: A thief with roots: haustoria tap up to 300 other species for phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, and the heartwood yields an oil about 90% santalol against 39% in the Australian species.
facts.frankincense_tree: A shallow cut in the trunk bleeds a milky sap that hardens in air into tears collected by hand — the tree died out in Israel and was replanted there in 2012, 1,500 years later.
facts.myrrh_tree: A thorny tree of arid Somalia and Arabia whose dried sap has been in use over 3,000 years — ancient Egypt embalmed with it, and Somalia is still the largest producer.
facts.cork_oak_tree: Once past 25 years old it can be stripped of bark every 9 to 12 years for up to two centuries without harm — and as plastic closures displace cork, its woodlands and the Iberian lynx in them are at risk.
facts.cinchona_tree: Called the fever tree: bark of Cinchona ledgeriana grown in Dutch Java ran 8 to 13% quinine, and nothing else worked against malaria until quinine was synthesised in 1944.
facts.neem_tree: Its seeds hold 0.2 to 0.8 percent azadirachtin by weight, a compound that blocks the insect moulting hormone ecdysone and deters over 600 pest species while barely troubling mammals.
facts.camphor_tree: Camphor was condensed straight out of steam driven through its pulverised wood, a trade lucrative enough that a British naval force bombarded Anping in 1868 to break Taiwan's camphor monopoly.
facts.olive_wood_tree: Hard, dense and strongly patterned, it takes a high polish for bowls and carving, but weather and insect damage rule it out of doors entirely.
facts.agarwood_tree: Aquilaria heartwood is pale and scentless until a Phaeoacremonium mould infects it; the dark resin the tree floods into the wound is oud, one of the costliest raw materials on Earth.
facts.argan_tree: Goats climb up into its thorny branches for the fruit and spit out the nuts, which then have to be cracked by hand between two stones, the slowest step in making argan oil.
facts.shea_tree: Its kernel fat runs 20 to 50 percent stearic acid, which is why shea butter stays solid at room temperature; the tree's old genus name, Butyrospermum, meant 'butter seed'.
facts.spruce_tree: The default soundboard wood for stringed instruments, with long fibres stiff along the grain; the Paneveggio 'Violin Forest' in the Dolomites has been cut for instrument makers for centuries.
facts.fir_tree: Told from the rest of the pine family by needles set singly on round bases, and by cones that stand upright like candles and fall apart on the branch instead of dropping whole.
facts.cypress_tree: Bald cypress heartwood resists rot so thoroughly that swamp-cut timber went into caskets, shingles and fence posts; one tree on North Carolina's Black River rings back to 605 BC.
facts.rosewood_tree: True rosewood is Dalbergia, a genus in the pea family, and CITES now lists every species after rosewood became the most trafficked wild product in the world.
facts.mulberry_tree: The leaf Bombyx mori silkworms are reared on, cultivated in China for more than 4,700 years, and its flowers release pollen at over half the speed of sound.
facts.almond_tree: Wild almonds are lethally bitter; a point mutation in one bHLH transcription factor shut off two cytochrome P450 genes and produced the sweet kernel the entire crop rests on.
facts.pecan_tree: A hickory of the Mississippi bottomlands and one of the last major crops to be domesticated: wild nuts were gathered for centuries, but commercial orchards only began in the 1880s.
facts.cashew_tree: Its seed shell is loaded with anacardic acid, chemical kin to poison ivy's urushiol; heat decarboxylates it into cardanol, sold as an industrial resin and a termite-proofing for timber.
facts.chestnut_tree: Its wood carries roughly 13 percent tannin, enough that poles coppiced on a 12 to 30 year rotation survive years of ground contact with no treatment at all.
facts.hazelnut_tree: Cut back to the stump every few years it throws up straight rods, and those coppice wands were the raw material of wattle-and-daub walls and English hedgerow fencing.
facts.alder_tree: It barely rots once submerged, which is why most of Venice stands on alder piles, and its roots carry nodules of nitrogen-fixing Frankia alni that can reach the size of a fist.
facts.lime_tree: Pale, soft and almost grainless, its timber is the classic European carving wood, the material of Riemenschneider's altarpieces and Grinling Gibbons's foliage.
facts.peat_moss: Sphagnum's dead hyaline cells hold 16 to 26 times the plant's dry weight in water, and it sours its own bog by taking up calcium and magnesium and releasing hydrogen ions.
facts.spanish_moss: Neither Spanish nor a moss but a rootless bromeliad, a pineapple relative living on rain and dust; over 10,000 tons were processed in 1939 to pad car seats and mattresses.
facts.papyrus_reed: A sedge with triangular stems whose pith was cut into strips, laid in two crossed layers and hammered damp into a sheet, while its buoyant culms were bundled into boats.
facts.cattail_reed: The US Navy stuffed life vests with its seed down when kapok ran short in the Second World War; the down was still buoyant after 100 hours submerged.
facts.rattan_palm: A climbing palm, and a monocot with no secondary growth, so a cane stays 2 to 5 cm across along its whole length, which can run hundreds of metres through the canopy.
facts.raffia_palm: Raphia regalis grows the longest leaves of any plant, pinnate fronds up to 25 metres long, and raffia fibre is the membrane peeled off their undersides.
facts.coir: One of the few natural fibres saltwater will not rot: lignified cells from the coconut husk, loosened by up to ten months of retting and then beaten free with iron rods.
facts.sorghum_broomcorn: Sorghum grown for its stiff panicle rather than its grain, after Levi Dickenson of Hadley, Massachusetts tied a broom from the tassels in 1797 and could not keep up with the orders.
facts.gum_arabic_tree: Strip its bark and the acacia seals the wound with a glycoprotein gum; about 70 percent of the world's supply comes from Sudan, where over five million people depend on the trade.
facts.guayule_shrub: A Chihuahuan Desert shrub whose latex contains none of the proteins behind Type 1 latex allergy; Bridgestone announced the first all-guayule tyres in 2015.
facts.canaigre_dock: Tanner's dock: a wild rhubarb relative of the American southwest, cultivated for tannin-rich roots that also give a warm medium-brown dye.
facts.sweet_gale: Bog myrtle, the bittering herb of gruit, the pre-hop beer seasoning that Henry IV licensed out in the 11th century as a de facto beer tax.
facts.serpentinite: Mafic and ultramafic rock hydrated by seawater forced deep below the ocean floor, at mid-ocean ridges and in the forearc mantle of subduction zones.
facts.asbestos: Six regulated minerals in two groups: chrysotile, the only serpentine one, and five amphiboles. Around 255,000 people a year are thought to die of diseases it causes.
facts.mesothelioma: A cancer of the lung lining, with a latency of about twenty years from exposure and a life expectancy often under twelve months from diagnosis.
facts.equus: The one surviving horse genus — seven species of horse, ass and zebra. It arose in North America around 4 million years ago, spread into the Old World, and then died out in the Americas about 12,000 years ago; horses only came back in 1519.
facts.wild_dromedary: The wild camel of the southeast Arabian coast that domestic dromedaries were taken from, and were still being bred back to long afterwards. It had a narrow range and died out about 2,000 years after the first domestication.
facts.mongoose: Herpestidae: 34 living species in 14 genera, across southern Europe, Africa and Asia. They are one of at least four mammal groups carrying a mutation in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that blocks snake venom — and the only one that does it by glycosylation.
facts.myriapod: Four living classes — centipedes, millipedes, symphylans and pauropods — about 13,000 species, every one of them terrestrial. Their oldest body fossils are about 427 million years old.
facts.sauropod: Hollow, air-filled bones are a feature of all of them, which is how the necks got so long: some carried as many as 19 cervical vertebrae where almost every mammal is limited to seven.
facts.african_wild_ass: Equus africanus, of the deserts and arid country of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia — the wild ancestor of every donkey, and now down to a few hundred animals in the wild.
facts.wild_boar: Sus scrofa, ancestor of nearly every pig breed and one of the widest-ranging mammals alive, from North Africa to Korea and the Sunda Islands. European males run 75 to 100 kg; in northeastern Asia they reach 270.
facts.pipefish: A straight-bodied member of the seahorse family Syngnathidae, armoured in bony plating and feeding through a tube snout. The male carries the eggs, supplying them with nutrients and oxygen through a placenta-like connection.
facts.mackerel: Scombridae, the family that also holds the tunas and bonitos — slim, deeply forked in the tail, with rows of finlets and fins that fold into grooves for streamlining. The vertical stripes work as schooling marks; an Atlantic mackerel cruises at about 0.98 m/s and bursts at 5.5.
facts.fern: Over 10,500 living species of vascular plant that reproduce by spores and have neither seeds nor flowers; the fern crown group goes back about 423 million years.
facts.okapi: The giraffe's only living relative: 1.5 m at the shoulder, 200–350 kg, striped behind like a zebra, and found only north and east of the Congo River.
facts.pterosaur: Flying reptiles of the Mesozoic, 228 to 66 million years ago, on a wing of skin and muscle stretched to one enormously lengthened fourth finger — wingspans from 0.4 m to 10–11 m. Not dinosaurs, but close kin.
facts.areca_palm: Native to the Philippines, growing straight to 20 m on a trunk 10–15 cm across, and carried through the tropics by Austronesian voyagers since at least 1500 BCE for one seed crop.
facts.wild_coca: Erythroxylum gracilipes, the wild shrub from which all four cultivated cocas were domesticated, two or three separate times during the Holocene.
facts.wild_tobacco: Nicotiana sylvestris, of the Andes of Argentina and Bolivia — one of the two wild parents of the cultivated tobacco plant.
facts.wild_turkey: The ancestor of the domestic bird. A tom weighs 5–11 kg and stands 100–125 cm long, and the flock heads for the trees at twilight to roost well off the ground.
facts.mallard: The wild dabbling duck almost every domestic breed descends from — 50 to 65 cm long, and still more than 17 million mature birds strong.
facts.mouflon: The Asiatic wild sheep, Ovis gmelini, behind every domestic breed; a mature ram's horns curve almost a full revolution, up to 85 cm.
facts.bezoar_ibex: Capra aegagrus, the wild goat the domestic one came from — now held to the Zagros Mountains, formerly widespread across Anatolia.
facts.junglefowl: The wild forest bird every chicken descends from, still living from Pakistan east to Vietnam and south into Indonesia.
facts.wild_water_buffalo: Bubalus arnee, ancestor of some 208 million domestic buffalo, is down to fewer than 4,000 mature wild animals, mostly in Assam and Nepal.
facts.grasshopper: About 11,000 species of chewing herbivore in the suborder Caelifera, a lineage reaching back to the early Triassic 250 million years ago.
facts.ape: The family Hominidae: eight living species in four genera, the orangutans, the gorillas, the chimpanzee and bonobo, and ourselves.
facts.beetle: About 400,000 described species, a quarter of all known animals, each with its front wings hardened into cases over the flying pair.
facts.crocodilian: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials; with the birds, the only survivors of the archosaurs.
facts.theropod: Hollow-boned, three-toed and ancestrally carnivorous dinosaurs, first appearing 231.4 million years ago; birds came out of the small feathered ones, so about 11,000 species are still alive.
facts.lagomorph: Rabbits, hares and pikas, and not rodents: they carry four upper incisors instead of two, with a small peg pair tucked behind the front ones.
facts.perissodactyl: About 17 living species, horses, rhinos and tapirs, bearing weight on the third toe and fermenting plants in the intestine rather than a chambered stomach.
facts.isopod: Crustaceans with seven pairs of thoracic legs and five pairs of branching abdominal appendages used for breathing; the female broods her young in a pouch called a marsupium.
facts.spurge: Euphorbiaceae, a cosmopolitan family richest in the tropics; it holds cassava and the rubber tree, and succulents that look like cacti purely through convergent evolution.
facts.scorpionfish: A family of mostly marine fish carrying a sting in sharp spines coated with venomous mucus, widespread in warm seas and richest in the Indo-Pacific.
facts.requiem_shark: Carcharhinidae: migratory sharks of warm seas, from the 69 cm Australian sharpnose to the 4 m oceanic whitetip, every one of them bearing young fully developed.
facts.greylag_goose: Anser anser, the wild goose most domestic breeds descend from - 74 to 91 cm long and around 3.3 kg, and the bird Konrad Lorenz used for his imprinting studies.
facts.wild_silk_moth: Bombyx mandarina, the wild moth of inland China, Korea and Japan that every domesticated silkworm descends from - and unlike its domestic descendant, the males still fly.
facts.africa: The fragment of Pangaea that moved least. It sat near the supercontinent's centre and is still close to where it was, which is why the other continents are described as having rifted away from it rather than the other way round.
facts.south_america: Rifted from Africa to open the South Atlantic: the split began around 190 million years ago at Falkland latitudes, seafloor spreading took over about 130 to 135 million years ago, and the ocean was fully open by roughly 83 million years ago.
facts.asia: The eastern bulk of Laurasia, which was the northern half of Pangaea from about 335 to 175 million years ago. It grew by collision, welding on one continental block and island arc after another.
facts.europe: Not a separate landmass but the western end of one, divided from Asia by convention along the Urals. The range is the suture of a real collision, and it has never undergone the extensional collapse that flattens most mountains of its age.
facts.north_america: Separated from Eurasia when the North Atlantic opened about 56 million years ago, the same moment Greenland became a plate of its own across the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay rift.
facts.carcinogen: Any agent that raises the incidence of cancer. The IARC has looked at about 1,060 of them and put 135 in Group 1 — carcinogenic to humans.
facts.mutagen: An agent that pushes the mutation rate above its natural background. Muller showed in 1927 that X-rays do it — the first proof that mutation could be caused rather than waited for.
facts.teratogen: An agent that deforms how an embryo is built rather than what it inherits — the defect is not passed on. Teratogens are held responsible for 2 to 3% of developmental defects in US newborns.
facts.birth_defect: An abnormal condition present at birth, either structural or functional. About 3% of US newborns have one, and roughly 65% of cases have no identifiable cause at all.
facts.chromosomal_aberration: Damage on a scale a point mutation never reaches: a stretch of chromosome deleted, doubled, flipped end for end, or moved onto a different chromosome. One live birth in 160 carries a chromosome abnormality of some kind.
facts.organogenesis: The stretch after gastrulation when three germ layers turn into organs — in humans the internal organs start between weeks three and eight after fertilisation.
facts.angiosarcoma: A cancer of the endothelial cells lining blood and lymph vessels. About one case per million people a year — 1 to 2% of soft-tissue sarcomas, which are themselves under 1% of adult cancer.
facts.free_radical: An atom or molecule carrying an unpaired valence electron, which is the whole reason it is so reactive. Gomberg found the first one, triphenylmethyl, in 1900; ordinary oxygen is a diradical.
facts.hydroxyl_radical: •OH — hydroxide minus an electron, and about the most reactive thing a cell has to cope with. Its half-life in tissue is around a nanosecond, and no enzyme disposes of it the way one does for superoxide.
facts.polycyclic_aromatic_hydrocarbon: Benzene rings fused edge to edge into a flat, uncharged sheet. Most of it is made by burning things incompletely: wood and other biofuels alone contribute more than half of annual global emissions.
facts.naphthalene: C10H8: two fused rings, the smallest PAH there is. It melts at 80 °C, the nose picks it up at 0.08 ppm, and it is the main ingredient of traditional mothballs.
facts.anthracene: Three rings in a straight line, C14H10. Colourless in daylight, it fluoresces blue under ultraviolet with a peak at 400–500 nm, which is why particle physicists use it as a scintillator.
facts.phenanthrene: The same fourteen carbons as anthracene with the third ring hung at an angle instead of in line. Its bent skeleton is the core of morphinan, and so of morphine and codeine.
facts.benzanthracene: C18H12, four rings, produced whenever organic matter burns incompletely. It is one of the carcinogenic constituents of tobacco smoke, and IARC lists it in Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans.
facts.dibenzanthracene: Five fused rings, C22H14. In 1929 Ernest Kennaway found it was the first pure compound with evidence of cancer-causing activity, and in 1930 he and Izrael Hieger showed single PAHs raise tumours on mouse skin.
facts.benzo_a_pyrene: A benzene ring fused to pyrene, C20H12. In 1933 it became the first single compound picked out of an environmental mixture — coal tar — and shown to cause cancer.
facts.soot: Impure carbon left over from incomplete combustion: clumps of nanoparticles 6 to 30 nm across, carrying polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and sometimes heavy metals such as mercury.
facts.tobacco_smoke: Sidestream smoke — the stream that leaves the burning cone between puffs — carries more than 4,000 chemicals, 69 of them known carcinogens, and is about four times more toxic than the smoke a smoker draws.
facts.chlorinated_hydrocarbon: Any carbon compound carrying a chlorine — chloroform, DDT, PCBs, vinyl chloride. The carbon–chlorine bond is strong and greasy, so the molecule lasts and it collects in fat.
facts.beta_propiolactone: A four-membered ring strained enough to alkylate nucleic acid, which is how it kills a virus for a vaccine — and why it is not used more widely than that.
facts.ethyleneimine: Aziridine: a nitrogen forced into a three-membered ring, boiling at 56 °C. The strain in that ring is what opens it against DNA.
facts.nitrosamine: R2N–N=O. Nitrite in acid becomes nitrous acid, and nitrous acid nitrosates any secondary amine it meets — which is why these turn up wherever curing salt meets protein.
facts.aflatoxin_b1: The B is for the blue it fluoresces under ultraviolet light; the G-group toxins glow green. Of the four, B1 is the most toxic.
facts.thalidomide: Chemie Grünenthal sold it from 1957 in West Germany as Contergan, a sedative mild enough to be given for morning sickness. It was taken off the market in November 1961.
facts.methylmercury: CH3Hg+ — one carbon stuck to a mercury atom, which is the difference between a metal that mostly passes through and one that does not. Its half-life in human blood is about 50 days.
facts.benzoic_acid: E210, named for gum benzoin, whose dry distillation Nostradamus described in 1556. Ripe cranberries and bilberries still carry 0.03–0.13% of it free.
facts.bha: E320, in food since about 1947. Two isomers sold as one antioxidant: the ring stabilises a free radical and sequesters it, so the chain reaction that turns fat rancid never gets going.
facts.bht: E321 — 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol. It hands a hydrogen atom to a peroxy radical, turning it into a hydroperoxide and breaking the autoxidation chain.
facts.cream_cheese: At least 33% milkfat, no more than 55% water, and up to 0.5% of gum to stop it weeping.
facts.soft_serve: Drawn at −4 °C, a third of it air, and 3–6% milkfat where ice cream runs 10 to 18.
facts.gluten_free_bread: Gluten is 75–85% of the protein in bread wheat, and the reason bread rises. This loaf has none.
facts.carrageen_moss_pudding: The Irish milk pudding that named the additive: carraigín, 'little rock', 55% carrageenan dry.
facts.spherified_pearl: Liquid inside a skin of gel. Unilever documented it in the 1950s; elBulli's kitchen made it famous.
facts.oat_milk: Oat starch, 50–60% of the grain, cut short by amylase. US sales: $4.4m in 2017, $213m in 2020.
facts.fracking_fluid: Shale oil and gas take about 90% of the guar gum India and Pakistan grow, to carry sand into rock.
facts.processed_cheese: Cheese melted with an emulsifying salt so it will melt again. US rules cap that salt at 3% by weight.
facts.coffee_creamer: The pot that whitens coffee without curdling. Carnation had it in 1958 and sold it from 1961.
facts.yellow_mustard: George J. French sold it from 1904 as 'cream salad mustard' — mild seed, heavy vinegar, turmeric yellow.
facts.strawberry_yoghurt: Chilled, short-lived and pink, which is the one thing the cooked fruit in it cannot supply on its own.
facts.cola: Named for the kola nut, coloured by caramel, and acidified with phosphoric acid.
facts.jelly: Gelatin, sugar and water. It sets around 15 °C, melts again in the mouth, and sets colourless.
facts.sweet_wine: Bottled with its sugar unfermented. The sorbate that holds it there is reckoned safe to 1.75 g a day.
facts.cordial: A concentrate for diluting, one part to four or five, and about 30% juice on average.
facts.whitfields_ointment: 6% benzoic acid and 3% salicylic acid in petrolatum, named for the dermatologist Arthur Whitfield.
facts.dried_apricot: Sulfured, it stays orange on the shelf. The same fruit dried without sulfite goes the brown of leather.
facts.corned_beef: Named for the coarse 'corns' of salt in the brine. Brazil now cans about 80% of the world's supply.
facts.canned_heat: Alcohol held in a gel and sold in a tin. One lit under a chafing dish burns for about twenty minutes.
facts.runway_deicer: Potassium acetate in water, sprayed on airfield pavement. The same salt is the food additive E261.
facts.surimi: Washed fish mince. Freezing wrecked its gel until Nishitani Yosuke froze it with sugars in 1969.
facts.sugar_free_gum: Sugar alcohols run 40 to 50% of a stick by weight. The sweetener is most of the gum.
facts.diet_soda: Coca-Cola launched Diet Coke in July 1982, a year before aspartame was cleared for fizzy drinks.
facts.tabletop_sweetener: About 1.1% sweetener and the rest bulk, so a spoon of it measures like a spoon of sugar.
facts.instant_mashed_potato: Cooked mash dried on a hot drum into a sheet. Two USDA researchers patented the flake in 1954.
facts.shortening: Procter & Gamble launched Crisco in June 1911 — the name is short for crystallized cottonseed oil.
facts.indium: Half of all indium ends up as indium tin oxide — the transparent conductor on a flat screen.
facts.thallium: Named for the green line in its spectrum. Soluble, tasteless, and absorbed straight through skin.
facts.nihonium: The first element named in Asia — Nihon, for Japan, and for the Riken lab that caught three atoms.
facts.flerovium: Named for Georgy Flerov, who found spontaneous fission in 1940 and founded the Dubna laboratory.
facts.moscovium: Named for the Moscow region, home of Dubna — four atoms in 2003, gone in a tenth of a second.
facts.livermorium: Named for the Livermore lab, which tried the very reaction in 1977 and found nothing at all.
facts.praseodymium: The other half of didymium, the element that wasn't. Named for the leek-green colour of its salts.
facts.terbium: Mosander found it in yttria in 1843; its name and erbium's were swapped later and never swapped back.
facts.dysprosium: Named dysprositos, 'hard to get at' — it took Boisbaudran more than thirty goes to get the oxide out.
facts.holmium: Cleve split erbia and got two oxides: brown holmia, named for Stockholm, and green thulia.
facts.erbium: Ytterby again: Mosander pulled erbia out of yttria in 1843, and the Er3+ ion turns a solution pink.
facts.thulium: The rarest lanthanide but promethium. Charles James needed 15,000 crystallisations to get it pure.
facts.ytterbium: Marignac found it hiding inside erbia in 1878; in 1907 something else turned out to be hiding in it.
facts.lutetium: The last rare earth out and the dearest: about $10,000 a kilogram, roughly a quarter the price of gold.
facts.francium: The last element found in nature rather than made. About 28 grams exist in the whole crust at once.
facts.einsteinium: Found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb, on filter papers flown through the cloud.
facts.fermium: Fermium-257 is the heaviest nuclide neutron capture can reach. Past it, everything fissions at once.
facts.mendelevium: The first element ever made one atom at a time — seventeen atoms of it, in 1955.
facts.nobelium: Claimed by Sweden, Britain, America and the USSR. Dubna's 1966 report was the first that held up.
facts.lawrencium: Named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron — and made on a linear accelerator instead.
facts.torsion: The 180° twist every gastropod larva makes, swinging its mantle cavity and anus round over its head.
facts.gastropod: Snails and slugs: 65,000 to 80,000 species, the second-largest animal class, and every one twists.
facts.cephalopod: About 800 living species, and the only mollusks that closed the circulatory system — a squid has 3 hearts.
facts.bivalve: Two hinged valves, no head and no radula — about 9,200 species that feed and breathe on the same gills.
facts.clam: Not a taxon but a habit: a bivalve with two equal valves that burrows on a powerful muscular foot.
facts.squid: Eight arms, two tentacles, and the ancestral shell reduced to a chitin blade buried in its own back.
facts.jellyfish: Not a species but a life stage — the free-swimming medusa phase of certain members of Medusozoa.
facts.worm: A shape, not a lineage — flatworms, roundworms and annelids are no closer kin than a fish is to a fly.
facts.flatworm: About 18,600 species with no body cavity and no blood — oxygen has to reach every cell by diffusion.
facts.protist: Defined by exclusion: a eukaryote that is not an animal, plant or fungus. No one trait unites them.
facts.organism: Any living thing that functions as one individual — and biology still argues where one individual ends.
facts.life: Carl Sagan's working definition, adopted by NASA: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of evolving.
facts.eggshell: 95 to 97% calcium carbonate in a protein matrix; without the protein it would be too brittle to hold.
facts.carapace: A turtle's ribs and spine ossified into one bony box under keratin scutes — it can never leave it.
facts.solid: Definite shape and definite volume: atoms packed so tightly they can only vibrate in place.
facts.liquid: Keeps its volume, not its shape. Only two elements are liquid at room temperature: mercury and bromine.
facts.gas: Neither shape nor volume of its own. It keeps expanding until the container runs out.
facts.melting: Solid to liquid. The temperature stops rising while the lattice comes apart — that is latent heat.
facts.freezing: Liquid to solid, giving heat back as it goes. Pure water can supercool to −40°C before it yields.
facts.vaporization: Liquid to gas. At the surface it is evaporation; once bubbles form inside, it is boiling.
facts.condensation: Gas back to liquid at the dew point. Every cloud and every fogged window is this.
facts.sublimation: Solid straight to gas, skipping the liquid. Dry ice does it at −78.5°C; mothballs do it on a shelf.
facts.deposition: Gas straight to solid, no liquid between. Frost grows this way, and so do snow crystals.
facts.ionization: Knock electrons off atoms and the gas becomes a plasma that conducts and answers to magnets.
facts.matter: Anything with mass that takes up space — and under 5% of the universe. The rest is dark.
facts.antimatter: Same mass, opposite charge. Only ever made in pairs, and nobody knows why so little survived.
facts.spin: Intrinsic angular momentum, quantised in halves of ħ. Nothing is actually spinning.
facts.fermion: Half-integer spin, one to a quantum state. The twenty-four of them are what matter is made of.
facts.boson: Whole-integer spin, and any number can share one state. Five are elementary; they carry the forces.
facts.pauli_exclusion_principle: No two identical fermions in one state. It is why atoms have shells and why matter is rigid.
facts.fundamental_force: Four interactions that reduce to nothing simpler. Gravity is the weakest by an absurd margin.
facts.strong_force: About 100 times electromagnetism at a femtometre, and it does not fade with distance.
facts.weak_force: The only force that changes a quark's flavour, and the only one that tells left from right.
facts.electromagnetism: Infinite range, carried by the photon, and the force behind all of chemistry and every push.
facts.hadron: Quarks bound by the strong force. Of all of them, only the free proton is stable.
facts.baryon: Three quarks, so half-integer spin: a fermion. Protons and neutrons are almost all the mass you touch.
facts.meson: A quark and an antiquark, so whole spin: a boson. The longest-lived last tenths of a nanosecond.
facts.quark: Charge in thirds, and never seen alone. Six flavours, every one held captive by gluons.
facts.strange_quark: Charge −1/3, about 95 MeV. Named for the oddly long-lived particles found in cosmic rays in 1947.
facts.charm_quark: Charge +2/3, 1.27 GeV. Two labs published its signature on the same day in November 1974.
facts.bottom_quark: Charge −1/3, about 4.18 GeV. It decays reluctantly, which is what makes b-tagging possible.
facts.top_quark: About 173 GeV — the heaviest particle known, and the only quark that dies before it can hadronise.
facts.lepton: A fermion that ignores the strong force, so it travels alone. Six of them, in three generations.
facts.muon: An electron 207 times over, living 2.2 microseconds. Around 10,000 hit each square metre a minute.
facts.tau: 1777 MeV, heavier than a proton — the only lepton massive enough to decay into hadrons.
facts.neutrino: No charge, almost no mass, and it barely notices matter. Three flavours, and it swaps between them.
