facts.electron_neutrino: First generation. About 65 billion from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you each second.
facts.muon_neutrino: Second generation. A 1962 beam of them made only muons — proof neutrinos come in more than one kind.
facts.tau_neutrino: Third generation, and the last Standard Model fermion to be seen directly, in July 2000.
facts.gluon: Massless, eight kinds, and it carries the colour charge it acts on — so gluons pull on each other.
facts.w_boson: 80.4 GeV of carrier for the weak force — heavy enough that the force barely crosses a proton.
facts.z_boson: 91.19 GeV and no charge. It lets a neutrino bounce off matter and stay a neutrino.
facts.higgs_boson: 125 GeV, zero spin — the first elementary scalar particle ever found, on 4 July 2012.
facts.standard_model: Twelve fermions, five bosons, three forces. Fifty years unbeaten, and it still has no gravity.
facts.oxide: Oxygen bonded to another element at oxidation state −2. Most of the Earth's crust is oxides.
facts.periodic_table: 118 elements in proton order. Columns share their outer electrons, so they share their chemistry.
facts.metallic_bond: Electrons pooled by every atom at once. That shared sea is the shine, the wire and the bend.
facts.transition_metal: Groups 3 to 12, with a part-filled d shell: many oxidation states, coloured salts, and catalysis.
facts.alkaline_earth_metal: Group 2, two outer s electrons. Named for their oxides — fireproof 'earths' that turn water alkaline.
facts.lanthanide: Fifteen metals filling the 4f shell, so alike that telling them apart needs solvent extraction.
facts.actinide: Fifteen elements filling 5f, every one radioactive. Only thorium and uranium remain in quantity.
facts.kiln: A thermally insulated chamber — a kind of oven — reaching temperatures an open fire never will.
facts.oven: A hollow chamber and a controlled way of heating it. In use since antiquity, for far more than food.
facts.kettle: A vessel specialised for exactly one job: boiling water. Lid, spout, handle.
facts.toaster: Radiant heat from nichrome ribbon. The browning is the Maillard reaction.
facts.freezer: A refrigerator held below the freezing point of water — around -18 °C.
facts.blender: A container with a blade at the bottom and a motor in the base.
facts.jar: Glass body, threaded band, separate flat lid pressed onto the rim. Patented 1858.
facts.tin_can: Steel that would rust, wearing a coat of tin that will not.
facts.basket: Pliable stems woven into a rigid shape, with no frame, no thread and no glue.
facts.sink: A bowl-shaped plumbing fixture: a basin with water coming in and a drain taking it out.
facts.tap: A washer screwed down onto a seat to stop the flow. Patented in Rotherham in 1845.
facts.plate: A broad, mainly flat vessel with a lip. Rounder and deeper, and it is a bowl instead.
facts.mug: A cup with a handle, holding 250 to 350 ml — more than a teacup, less than a tankard.
facts.house: A dwelling, from a rudimentary hut upward. The social unit inside it is a household.
facts.wall: Masonry, concrete, adobe or rammed earth, stood up to divide one space from another.
facts.roof: Layered so it sheds water outward. Densely packed thatch traps air and insulates too.
facts.floor: Boards laid across the joists at right angles — originally structural, not decorative.
facts.room: Any enclosed space in a structure, bounded by walls, entered only through a door.
facts.chimney: Vertical so the gases draw themselves up. That pull is called the stack effect.
facts.lock: In use for over 6,000 years. The Yale pin tumbler is a developed Egyptian wooden lock.
facts.shelf: A flat horizontal plane for storing things on. From Old English scylfe.
facts.cupboard: It began literally as a cup board: open tiers for displaying plates, cups and saucers.
facts.carpet: Rug once meant a coarse coverlet; it only came to mean a floor mat around 1808.
facts.saw: Teeth bent alternately left and right, so the cut is wider than the blade and it never binds.
facts.drill: Makes round holes or drives fasteners. Patented as an electric tool in Melbourne in 1889.
facts.screw: An externally helical threaded fastener, and one of the six classical simple machines.
facts.screwdriver: Classified entirely by its tip, because the tip has to match the screw head.
facts.wrench: Called a spanner in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.
facts.axe: Hafted axes go back at least 46,000 years, in northern Australia.
facts.shovel: A broad blade for digging and lifting. The seam at its back is folded into a socket.
facts.ladder: One is painted on a Mesolithic wall in the Spider Caves, Valencia, 10,000 years ago.
facts.workbench: A table that holds the work still, so both of your hands are free to work it.
facts.tape_measure: A ribbon stiff enough to stand out straight, springy enough to roll itself back up.
facts.gear: A toothed wheel. Its teeth engage another's, and two meshed gears are a gear train.
facts.shirt: The world's oldest preserved garment is a linen shirt from a tomb at Tarkhan, Egypt.
facts.trousers: The oldest known pair, from Turpan, is wool with straight legs and a wide crotch.
facts.wallet: The word first meant a knapsack. It only came to mean a flat case in the 1600s.
facts.razor: The oldest razor-like object found is 20,000 years older than the Bronze Age.
facts.banknote: A promise, not a thing: the issuing bank was legally bound to redeem it in coin.
facts.pen: Early pens held only a bead of ink in a nib, and had to be dipped again every few words.
facts.pencil: The core is graphite powder held together by clay. More clay, harder and paler the line.
facts.eraser: Before rubber, you rubbed pencil off paper with tablets of wax — or with breadcrumbs.
facts.scissors: Two blades whose edges slide past each other. It cuts and shears at the same time.
facts.newspaper: A book is finished. A newspaper is only ever the latest one, and is obsolete by morning.
facts.map: A portolan chart has no latitude or longitude at all — only coastlines and bearings.
facts.road: A prepared surface whose job is transport. A street's job is the people beside it.
facts.street: A public thoroughfare lined with buildings — one of the few easements everyone shares.
facts.town: Domesday listed 50 markets in England in 1086. Some 2,000 more opened by 1349.
facts.market: A souk, a bazaar, a mercado, a tianguis, a palengke. Everywhere, the same idea.
facts.shop: Retail sells to the person who will use the thing. Wholesale sells to whoever resells it.
facts.school: Early public schools were one room, where a single teacher took seven grades at once.
facts.hospital: The word means a place of hospitality, and that is what these were long before medicine.
facts.bicycle: The shape has barely changed since the first chain-driven safety bicycle of about 1885.
facts.truck: Body-on-frame, with the cab built separate from whatever it is carrying behind.
facts.drone: Two rotors turn clockwise and two anticlockwise, so the torques cancel and it does not spin.
facts.acetabulum: The muscular sucking cup of a fluke or a tapeworm. A fluke has two; a tapeworm's head has four.
facts.scolex: A tapeworm's holdfast, under 2 mm long, on a body that can run to 20 metres behind it.
facts.rostellum: A fleshy, retractable knob on some tapeworm heads, ringed with hooks. Taenia saginata has none.
facts.proglottid: One segment of a tapeworm, and a whole reproductive animal in itself: both sexes, in every one.
facts.tegument: The body surface of a fluke or tapeworm: it absorbs the food and passes out the waste.
facts.oncosphere: The first tapeworm larva: six tiny hooklets and almost nothing else, built to cut through a gut wall.
facts.cysticercus: A fluid-filled bladder in muscle with a tapeworm's head folded inside it, waiting to be eaten.
facts.hydatid_cyst: One Echinococcus larva, grown for years into a fluid cyst budding thousands of tapeworm heads inside.
facts.gynecophoral_canal: A groove down a male blood fluke's belly. The female lies in it for the rest of both their lives.
facts.miracidium: The first fluke larva, rowed along by cilia, with hours to find the one snail species it can enter.
facts.cercaria: The fluke larva that leaves the snail, tail-first. Hundreds come out of every one that went in.
facts.metacercaria: A cercaria that dropped its tail and walled itself up, waiting on a leaf or inside a fish to be eaten.
facts.cuticle: A roundworm's tough outer coat, resistant to digestion — and shed four times as the larva grows.
facts.buccal_capsule: The hard-lined mouth cavity of a roundworm — a hookworm's is armed with cutting plates or teeth.
facts.polar_plug: A clear knob at each end of a whipworm egg. Nothing else in a stool sample is shaped like that.
facts.nurse_cell: A muscle cell a Trichinella larva has rebuilt into a walled room, and then moved into.
facts.microfilaria: The live embryo a filarial worm releases into the blood; some surface only between 10pm and 4am.
facts.flagellate: A protozoan that swims by whipping one or more flagella. Giardia has four pairs of them.
facts.sucking_disc: Giardia's dished underside. It clamps the cell to the gut lining and will not let go.
facts.undulating_membrane: A flagellum bound down along a cell's flank, so its beat ripples the whole side of the body.
facts.axostyle: A stiff rod of microtubules down the middle of a trichomonad, projecting out through the tail end.
facts.kinetoplast: Thousands of DNA circles catenated into one disc, packed inside a single giant mitochondrion.
facts.apical_complex: A drill at one end of a cell: polar rings, microtubules, and glands that open on the way in.
facts.hemozoin: Malaria pigment: heme crystallised into an inert, iron-rich grain the parasite cannot be poisoned by.
facts.trichuris_trichiura: Threaded head-first into the gut lining and feeding on tissue fluid, not blood. Around 35 to 50 mm.
facts.strongyloides_stercoralis: The only intestinal roundworm that passes larvae, not eggs — and it can reinfect you without leaving.
facts.dracunculus_medinensis: The largest roundworm to parasitise people: a female close to a metre long, leaving through a blister.
facts.onchocerca_volvulus: Adults sit coiled in fibrous nodules under the skin. It is the wandering young that cause the blindness.
facts.echinococcus_granulosus: An adult only 3 to 6 mm long with three segments. Almost all its bulk is the cyst, in another animal.
facts.diphyllobothrium_latum: Can reach 20 metres in one gut, and take up to all the vitamin B12 in the meals passing it.
facts.fasciola_hepatica: A leaf-shaped fluke that ends up in the bile ducts of a sheep — or of whoever ate the same salad.
facts.paragonimus_westermani: Lives encysted in pairs inside the lungs, and the cough it causes is regularly mistaken for TB.
facts.balantidium_coli: The only ciliate known to make people ill, and the largest protozoan that infects them.
facts.trypanosoma_brucei: It lives outside cells, in the blood, and stays there by changing its coat faster than antibodies form.
facts.trypanosoma_cruzi: C-shaped in a blood smear, then hidden in heart muscle for decades before the damage shows.
facts.tsetse_fly: Both sexes live on blood, and can drink a meal weighing as much as they do.
facts.sandfly: About 3 mm long and covered in hair, which is part of why the bite is often not noticed.
facts.black_fly: Its larvae need fast running water, which is why the blindness it spreads follows the rivers.
facts.triatomine_bug: It does not inject the parasite. It defecates while feeding, and the bite gets rubbed into the wound.
facts.praziquantel: Floods a fluke or tapeworm with calcium until its muscles lock, and strips its skin at the same time.
facts.albendazole: Blocks the worm from building microtubules, so it cannot take up glucose and starves on its reserves.
facts.mebendazole: Same target as albendazole, on the colchicine site of the worm's own beta-tubulin.
facts.ivermectin: From a Streptomyces found in Japanese soil; it opens chloride channels invertebrates have and we do not.
facts.metronidazole: Harmless until something with no oxygen in its metabolism reduces it. Then it is not harmless at all.
facts.niclosamide: Works on tapeworms and nothing else — not flukes, not roundworms — because it is never absorbed.
facts.diethylcarbamazine: It does not kill the adult worm. It makes the young ones visible to an immune system that was ignoring them.
facts.pyrantel_pamoate: Contracts a worm so hard it cannot hold on, and it is carried out of the gut still alive.
facts.nitazoxanide: The one drug licensed for cryptosporidiosis, aimed at an enzyme of oxygen-free metabolism we lack.
facts.quinine: Isolated from cinchona bark in 1820, after three centuries of the bark itself being the only treatment.
facts.taeniasis: Usually silent. Often the first sign is a segment of the worm leaving on its own.
facts.cysticercosis: Caught from the eggs, not the meat — so the person, not the pig, becomes the intermediate host.
facts.neurocysticercosis: Tapeworm larvae in the brain. In much of the world it is the commonest cause of adult-onset epilepsy.
facts.ascariasis: The larvae take a detour through the liver and lungs, get coughed up, and are swallowed a second time.
facts.hookworm_disease: It does not have to be swallowed. The larvae come up through the skin of a bare foot.
facts.trichuriasis: Heavy infections in children can pull the rectum inside out. Light ones show nothing at all.
facts.enterobiasis: The commonest worm infection in Western Europe and the United States, and it spreads on fingers.
facts.strongyloidiasis: Because it can reinfect its host without leaving, it has been found still running after decades.
facts.onchocerciasis: Second only to trachoma as an infectious cause of blindness. The adult worm is not what blinds you.
facts.dracunculiasis: Caught by drinking water with an infected water flea in it. Cases fell from 3.5 million to a handful.
facts.echinococcosis: A dog's tapeworm eggs, in the wrong host. The cyst can grow silently for years before anything shows.
facts.fascioliasis: A sheep's disease that people catch from the plant, not the animal. Called liver rot in livestock.
facts.clonorchiasis: Thirty years in one set of bile ducts, and a recognised risk factor for bile-duct cancer.
facts.paragonimiasis: A bloody cough from a fluke in the lung, treated as tuberculosis more often than anyone would like.
facts.diphyllobothriasis: From raw freshwater fish. Rarely, the worm takes enough B12 to cause anaemia on its own.
facts.leishmaniasis: Three diseases from one genus: a self-healing sore, a disfiguring ulcer, or an infection of the organs.
facts.sleeping_sickness: Named for the last stage, once the parasite has crossed into the brain and wrecked the sleep cycle.
facts.chagas_disease: Silent for twenty or thirty years, then up to a third of infections damage the heart.
facts.balantidiasis: The only human disease caused by a ciliate, and it tracks living closely with pigs.
facts.trichomoniasis: The commonest non-viral sexually transmitted infection, and men usually carry it without symptoms.
facts.switch: A gap in a circuit you can open and close. Contacts touching or not — there is no third state.
facts.relay: An electrically operated switch: a coil pulls the contacts shut, so one circuit works another.
facts.logic: The study of which conclusions follow from which premises, judged by the shape of the argument alone.
facts.algebra: Arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers, so one statement covers every case at once.
facts.boolean_algebra: Algebra whose variables take only true and false, with the operations and, or and not.
facts.truth_table: One row per combination of true and false for the inputs. Two inputs need four rows.
facts.logic_gate: A circuit performing one Boolean operation on binary inputs, giving a single binary output.
facts.not_gate: The inverter. Its output is always the opposite of its input.
facts.or_gate: True when either input is true. Two diodes into one shared resistor will do it.
facts.and_gate: True only when both inputs are true — logical conjunction, built as a circuit.
facts.nand_gate: AND with the answer inverted. Every other gate can be built from these alone.
facts.xor_gate: True when the inputs differ. It is the sum of two bits, ignoring the carry.
facts.multiplexer: A data selector: select lines choose one of several inputs and pass it to the single output.
facts.flip_flop: Two stable states, so it holds one bit after you stop pushing. The basic element of sequential logic.
facts.half_adder: Adds two bits: XOR gives the sum digit, AND gives the carry.
facts.adder: A circuit that adds binary numbers, carrying from each column into the next.
facts.alu: One circuit doing arithmetic or bitwise operations on binary integers, picked by an opcode.
facts.bit: The basic unit of information: one of two values. A contraction of 'binary digit'.
facts.byte: Eight bits — historically the number needed to encode one character of text.
facts.hexadecimal: Base 16, written 0-9 then A-F. One digit per four bits, so a byte is exactly two of them.
facts.ascii: 128 code points — 95 printable, 33 control — each stored as a seven-bit number.
facts.unicode: One number per character for every writing system that can be digitised.
facts.register: A handful of bits the processor reaches instantly — the fastest storage a machine has.
facts.random_access_memory: One transistor and one capacitor per bit. The charge drains away, so every cell must be refreshed.
facts.read_only_memory: A pattern fixed when the chip is made. It cannot be rewritten and survives the power going off.
facts.cache: A small fast memory beside the core holding copies of whatever was used lately.
facts.clock_signal: A square wave at a constant frequency, used like a metronome so the whole circuit steps together.
facts.data_bus: A shared bundle of wires that components take turns driving, instead of a wire between every pair.
facts.instruction: A number that names an operation. Read it, do that one thing, move on.
facts.machine_code: Instructions as bare numbers — the only language a processor reads directly.
facts.cpu: Fetch an instruction, do what it says, fetch the next. Arithmetic, logic and control in one unit.
facts.assembly_language: One line per machine instruction, but with names instead of numbers. ADD, not 00000101.
facts.compiler: Software that translates a high-level language into the low-level code a processor executes.
facts.programming_language: An engineered language for writing programs people can read and machines can run.
facts.operating_system: The program that manages the hardware and runs the others.
facts.file: A named collection of bytes treated as one unit — asked for by name, not by position.
facts.filesystem: The directory of names against blocks, so files can be found without tracking the medium.
facts.database: Data held as relations — tables of rows — with a language for asking questions of them.
facts.punched_card: Stiff paper storing information as the presence or absence of a hole at a fixed position.
facts.jacquard_loom: A loom driven by a laced chain of punched cards, one card per row of the design.
facts.tabulating_machine: Hollerith's electromechanical counter for punched cards, built for the 1890 US census.
facts.turing_machine: An endless tape of symbols, a head that reads and writes one at a time, and a table of rules.
facts.moores_law: Transistors per chip have doubled roughly every two years. An observation, not a law of nature.
facts.pixel: The smallest addressable element of a raster image. The word was first published in 1965.
facts.bitmap: A grid of pixels held in memory. A framebuffer is exactly this, scanned out to a display.
facts.font: A file of glyphs, taking over the job of a case of metal type.
facts.jpeg: Lossy image compression, about 10:1, by discarding detail the eye is least likely to miss.
facts.floating_point: A number as a significand times a power of the base, so the point moves with the exponent.
facts.checksum: A short value computed from a block of data and sent with it, to detect damage.
facts.hamming_code: Check bits arranged so a single wrong bit is not just detected but located.
facts.computer_network: Computers exchanging data over links by agreed protocols, each found by its network address.
facts.packet: A short formatted unit of data with a header saying where it is going.
facts.network_protocol: The agreed rules of format, meaning, timing and error recovery that let two machines talk.
facts.ip_address: The number identifying a machine on the network and saying where it is. IPv4 uses 32 bits.
facts.tcp: Numbers, checks and re-requests every byte, turning unreliable packets into an ordered stream.
facts.domain_name_system: A distributed directory turning memorable names into the numeric addresses the network uses.
facts.url: One line naming a protocol, a machine and a path — an address for a single resource.
facts.http: Request and response: a client asks for a resource by URL, a server answers.
facts.html: Tags inside plain text marking what is a heading, a paragraph, or a link.
facts.web_browser: Fetches a page's files from a server and renders them on screen.
facts.server: A computer whose job is answering other computers' requests — the far half of client-server.
facts.ethernet: The wired local-network standard, commercially introduced in 1980 and standardised in 1983.
facts.modem: Turns bits into tones a phone line will carry, and back again.
facts.cipher: A defined procedure for turning a message unreadable and back, controlled by a key.
facts.encryption: Plaintext turned into ciphertext, so only a holder of the key can read it.
facts.prime_number: A whole number above 1 with no smaller factors. Every other number is a product of these.
facts.public_key: A pair of related keys: publish one, keep the other. What one locks, only the other opens.
facts.hash_function: Any input mapped to a fixed-size fingerprint: quick forwards, infeasible backwards.
facts.digital_signature: Proof that a message came from one holder of a private key and was not altered after.
facts.keyboard: The typewriter's layout with a switch under every key, so a keystroke becomes a number.
facts.information_theory: The mathematics of measuring, storing and sending information. Shannon, in the 1940s.
facts.resin: A terpene secretion a conifer pushes into its own wounds. Not sap, not latex — and it sets hard.
facts.thorn: A modified shoot, lignified to a point. A spine is a modified leaf; a prickle is only skin.
facts.berry: One flower, one ovary, seeds loose in the flesh. A stone in there would make it a drupe instead.
facts.aerenchyma: Parenchyma that kills off its own cells to leave air channels — a snorkel from shoot to drowned root.
facts.isoprene: C5H8, 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene. Vegetation breathes out about 600 million tonnes of it a year.
facts.polyisoprene: Isoprene chained up. In the cis-1,4 arrangement it is natural rubber — 99.9% of what a tapped tree gives.
facts.synthetic_rubber: Elastomer polymerised from petroleum instead of tapped from a tree. Two thirds of US rubber.
facts.carbon_black: Petroleum burned in too little air, on purpose. 70% of it goes into tires, and it is why they are black.
facts.tire: Vulcanised rubber packed with carbon black and forced onto a wheel rim. Over 2 billion made a year.
facts.empire: A state that rules many peoples and territories from one centre, as subjects rather than citizens.
facts.treaty: A written agreement between states, binding in international law. The oldest surviving is 3,300 years old.
facts.sovereignty: Supreme authority over a territory, answerable to no higher power. Dated by convention to 1648.
facts.independence: A territory becoming a sovereign state in its own right — self-determination actually exercised.
facts.revolution: A rapid, forced remaking of a state's institutions, driven from outside them by mass action.
facts.constitution: The founding law setting out how a state is governed. Around 800 have been adopted since 1789.
facts.republic: A state whose head of state is not born to the job. About 159 of 206 states use the word.
facts.referendum: A direct vote of the whole electorate on one question, not on who should decide it.
facts.colonialism: One state ruling a distant territory and its people, usually reached across an ocean.
facts.decolonisation: The unwinding of colonial rule. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies became states.
facts.partition: One territory cut into two or more states, the new border and the new states arriving together.
facts.unification: Separate polities merged into one state, usually on a claim of shared language or nation.
facts.city_state: A city that is the whole of its own country. Three sovereign ones survive today.
facts.co_principality: A state with two heads of state at once. Andorra's pair date from a feudal pact of 1278.
facts.british_empire: At its 1920 peak it covered 24% of the world's land — the largest empire in history.
facts.austria_hungary: The dual monarchy of 1867–1918: one monarch, two parliaments, three shared ministries.
facts.czechoslovakia: Proclaimed 28 October 1918 from the wreck of Austria-Hungary; wound up by agreement in 1993.
facts.yugoslavia: The South Slav kingdom of 1918, renamed Yugoslavia in 1929 and broken up between 1991 and 2006.
facts.basidium: A club-shaped cell that buds four spores on horns, then flicks each one off at about 10,000 g.
facts.elasmobranch: Sharks, rays and skates together. Their skeletons stay cartilage for life rather than turning to bone, they have five to seven gill slits opening straight to the outside instead of under a bony cover, and their teeth sit in rows that move forward as the front ones are shed.
facts.ray: A flattened elasmobranch whose pectoral fins are fused to the sides of the head, forming the disc it swims with. Its gill slits open on the underside rather than the flank, which is the quickest way to tell a ray from a shark.
facts.plank: A flat length of timber sawn from a log. Almost everything wooden that is not carved starts as one.
facts.blade: The working part of any cutting tool: a piece of hard metal with one edge ground thin enough to part what it is pushed through.
facts.handle: The part shaped to be held. It sets how much force reaches the tool and keeps the hand away from the working end.
facts.pole: A long round shaft stood upright. Most street furniture is something bolted to the top of one.
facts.pigment: A coloured solid ground fine enough to stay suspended rather than dissolve. It colours by being there, which is why a pigment can outlast the thing it is painted on.
facts.paint: Pigment carried in something that dries. The carrier spreads the colour thin and then hardens, locking it to the surface.
facts.cable: Wire wrapped in something that does not conduct, so the current stays inside it and the outside is safe to touch.
facts.sheet_metal: Metal worked flat and thin. Thin enough to cut and bend cold, stiff enough to hold a shape once folded.
facts.mesh: An open grid of wire. It holds things back while letting air, water and light through.
facts.drain: The opening at the edge of a road that takes rainwater off it and into a pipe below.
facts.pavement: The raised, made-up strip beside a road for walking on.
facts.kerb: The stone edge between pavement and road. It holds the pavement in and steers water along the gutter to the drain.
facts.traffic_light: Three coloured lamps on a pole that take it in turns to give right of way.
facts.streetlight: A lamp on a pole, lighting the road rather than any building.
facts.bollard: A short post set in the ground to stop vehicles going somewhere, while letting people walk past.
facts.pedestrian_crossing: A marked strip of road where people on foot have priority over traffic.
facts.road_sign: A painted metal plate carrying an instruction, in a shape and colour meant to be read before it can be spelled out.
facts.manhole: A covered shaft giving access to the pipes and cables under a street.
facts.litter_bin: An open container fixed in a public place for rubbish.
facts.postbox: A cast-iron box in the street that takes prepaid letters for collection.
facts.saucepan: A straight-sided pan with one long handle, for cooking liquid on a hob.
facts.colander: A bowl punched full of holes, for draining what has been boiled.
facts.sieve: A mesh stretched on a rim. What passes through is decided by the size of the holes and nothing else.
facts.whisk: Loops of wire on a handle, for beating air into something.
facts.grater: A metal sheet worked so that every hole in it is a small blade.
facts.peeler: A blade with a slot in it, set so it can rock, for taking the skin off a vegetable and little else.
facts.chopping_board: A slab of wood to cut on, so the knife meets something softer than itself.
facts.corkscrew: A helix of steel on a handle, for pulling a cork out whole.
facts.ladle: A deep bowl on a long handle, for lifting liquid out of a deeper pot.
facts.spatula: A flat flexible blade for lifting, turning and scraping.
facts.rolling_pin: A heavy wooden cylinder for pressing dough out flat and even.
facts.clock: A machine that counts something regular and shows the total. Every clock is that: an oscillator, a way of counting its swings, and a face.
facts.cardboard: Paper made thick and stiff. Corrugated board is a fluted sheet glued between two flat ones, which is why an empty box holds its shape.
facts.ruler: A straight edge with a scale marked along it, for drawing a line or measuring one.
facts.stapler: A device that drives a wire staple through a stack of paper and folds its legs over on the far side.
facts.paperclip: A single piece of wire bent back on itself twice, holding paper by springing against it.
facts.notebook: Paper bound along one edge so it stays in order and opens where you left it.
facts.rubber_stamp: A raised rubber relief that prints the same mark every time it is pressed.
facts.highlighter: A pen whose ink is transparent, so it marks a line of text without hiding it.
facts.folder: A sheet of card folded once, to keep loose papers together and the right way up.
facts.binder: A stiff cover with rings through it, so pages can be added and taken out without unbinding anything.
facts.pliers: Two levers crossed on a pivot, with jaws at the short end and handles at the long one.
facts.sandpaper: Hard grains glued to a backing, so that a sheet of paper can cut.
facts.spirit_level: A sealed glass vial, almost full of liquid, with one bubble left in it.
facts.clamp: A screw that pulls two jaws together and holds them there without a hand.
facts.vice: A clamp bolted to a bench, so the work is held and both hands are free.
facts.crowbar: A steel bar with one end flattened into a wedge and bent, for levering things apart.
facts.drawer: A box that slides out of the thing it lives in, so what is at the back can be reached without unpacking the front.
facts.desk: A table meant for working at, with the things needed for the work kept in it.
facts.wardrobe: A cupboard tall enough to hang clothes at full length instead of folding them.
facts.mattress: A padded layer to lie on, thick enough that the body's weight is spread rather than borne at the hips and shoulders.
facts.pillow: A soft bag for the head, filling the gap between the shoulder and the mattress.
facts.mop: Absorbent strands on the end of a pole, for washing a floor while standing up.
facts.tower: A building far taller than it is wide, built for the height itself rather than for the floor space.
facts.laptop: A computer with its screen, keyboard and power supply folded into one case you can carry.
facts.printer: A machine that puts what is on a screen onto paper.
facts.monitor: A screen for looking at what a computer is doing.
facts.speaker: A device that turns a changing electric current into sound.
facts.headphones: Two small speakers held at the ears.
facts.charger: A device that pushes energy back into a battery.
facts.tram: A passenger vehicle running on rails laid in the surface of a street.
facts.van: A road vehicle built around its cargo space rather than its passengers.
facts.motorcycle: A bicycle with an engine, and everything that had to change once it had one.
facts.scooter: A board with small wheels and an upright handle, pushed along by foot.
facts.office: A building, or part of one, given over to work done sitting down.
facts.library: A building holding books arranged so that a stranger can find one.
facts.crate: An open box of nailed boards, for moving heavy things.
facts.purse: A small closed pouch for carrying money.
facts.coat: An outer garment worn over everything else, mainly for warmth.
facts.jacket: A short coat, ending at the hip rather than the knee.
facts.day: One turn of the Earth, measured against the Sun. Everything alive keeps time to it.
facts.month: One cycle of the Moon's phases, and the reason nearly every calendar has a middle unit between the day and the year.
facts.year: One circuit of the Sun. Twelve lunar months come to 354 days and a solar year to 365, and every calendar in history is an attempt to reconcile the two.
facts.calendar: An agreed scheme for naming days ahead of time, so that people who are not together can arrange to be.
facts.counting: Matching things one-to-one against something else, so a quantity can be held without holding the things.
facts.writing: Marks that record language itself, so that speech outlives the moment and the speaker.
facts.number: A count separated from the things counted, and written down as a thing in its own right.
facts.zero: A number for none, and a mark that holds an empty place so that 105 is not 15.
facts.geometry: The mathematics of shape, distance and space.
facts.agriculture: Growing food on purpose instead of finding it. Everything else people built rests on it.
facts.city: A settlement too large to feed itself, living on food grown elsewhere.
facts.law: Rules a society will enforce, set down so that they are the same for the person applying them as for the person they are applied to.
facts.memory: Holding something after it has gone, and being able to bring it back.
facts.history: The recorded past, as distinct from the past itself.
facts.light: Electromagnetic radiation in the narrow band the eye can see, roughly 380 to 700 nanometres.
facts.mass: How much matter something is, measured two entirely different ways that always agree.
facts.energy: The capacity to do work, and the one thing in physics that is never created or destroyed, only moved and changed in form.
facts.time: What clocks measure, and the dimension along which cause reaches effect.
facts.distance: How far apart two things are.
facts.speed: Distance covered divided by the time it took.
facts.acceleration: The rate at which speed changes.
facts.force: A push or a pull, measured by the acceleration it gives a given mass.
facts.momentum: Mass times speed — how hard something is to stop.
facts.work: Force applied along the distance something actually moves.
facts.power: Work divided by the time taken to do it. Not how much, but how fast.
facts.temperature: How fast, on average, the particles in something are moving.
facts.entropy: A measure of how many ways the parts of something could be arranged and still look the same.
facts.trade: Giving what you have too much of for what you have none of.
facts.money: A thing everyone will accept, so that trade no longer needs both sides to want what the other has.
facts.debt: A payment moved into the future, and the claim on it that exists meanwhile.
facts.tax: A payment the state requires rather than requests.
facts.government: Whoever gets to make and enforce the rules, and the machinery they do it with.
facts.democracy: Government in which the decisions belong to the governed.
facts.monarchy: Government by one person, usually for life, usually inherited.
facts.contract: A promise the law will enforce.
facts.family: The people you are raised by and raised with.
facts.society: People who depend on each other while mostly not knowing each other.
facts.nation: A people who consider themselves one, and usually want a state to match.
facts.property: The right to exclude other people from a thing.
facts.ship: A vessel big enough to cross open ocean and carry cargo or people at scale.
facts.crocodile: A large semi-aquatic ambush predator, and an archosaur — closer kin to birds than to lizards.
facts.otter: A river-hunting mustelid, built long and low with webbed feet and a rudder of a tail.
facts.blue_whale: The largest animal that has ever lived, up to about 30 metres and 150 tonnes.
facts.emu: A tall flightless bird of Australia, second only to the ostrich in height.
facts.skunk: A small American mammal that defends itself chemically rather than by running.
facts.seaweed: Large marine algae, anchored to rock rather than rooted in soil.
facts.kite: A tethered wing, held up by the wind because the line stops it drifting downwind.
facts.whisky: A spirit distilled from fermented grain and aged in wood.
facts.swamp: Wetland with trees standing in it, as distinct from marsh, which has none.
facts.oasis: Water at the surface in a desert, and everything that gathers around it.
facts.snowflake: A single ice crystal grown in cloud, six-sided because of how water molecules bond.
facts.robot: A machine that senses, decides and acts without a person in the loop.
facts.statue: A figure carved or cast at full size, made to stand and to last.
facts.pyramid: A tomb built as a square-based pyramid, the most stable large shape you can pile up.
facts.sushi: Vinegared rice served with fish, vegetables or egg, often wrapped in seaweed.
facts.polio: A gut infection that in a small fraction of cases reaches the nerves of the spinal cord and paralyses what they served.
facts.influenza: A respiratory infection that returns every year in a slightly different form, and occasionally in a very different one.
facts.rabies: A viral infection that travels up the nerves to the brain, and is almost always fatal once it arrives.
facts.scurvy: The disease of long voyages: collagen cannot be built without vitamin C, so old wounds reopen, gums bleed and teeth loosen.
facts.rickets: Soft, bending bones in a growing child, from too little vitamin D to lay calcium into them.
facts.cholera: A gut infection whose toxin makes the intestine pour out water, so fast that death is from dehydration rather than from the bacterium.
facts.oral_rehydration_therapy: Salt and sugar in the right proportions in clean water, which stops most cholera deaths.
facts.vitamin_c: The vitamin most animals make for themselves and we cannot, because the gene for the last enzyme is broken in us.
facts.vibrio_cholerae: A comma-shaped marine bacterium that lives in brackish water on the shells of copepods, and only sometimes in people.
facts.timber: Wood cut and seasoned for building, as distinct from the tree it came from.
facts.beam: A horizontal member carrying a load across a gap to the supports at each end.
facts.joist: One of the parallel beams that carry a floor or a ceiling between walls.
facts.gravel: Loose rounded stone between about 2 and 60 millimetres, sorted and rounded by moving water.
facts.foundation: The part of a building below ground, spreading its weight over enough soil to carry it.
facts.lintel: The beam over a door or window, carrying the wall above the hole.
facts.plaster: A paste spread on a wall that sets hard and flat.
facts.plasterboard: A sheet of gypsum plaster between two paper liners, nailed up instead of spread on.
facts.mortar_lime: The older mortar: lime and sand, which sets slowly by taking carbon dioxide back out of the air.
facts.insulation: Material that slows heat leaving a building, mostly by holding air still.
facts.ceiling: The overhead surface of a room, hung below the floor above it.
facts.floorboard: A board laid across joists to make a floor.
facts.gutter: A channel at the eaves catching what runs off the roof.
facts.hinge: A joint that allows rotation about one fixed line and nothing else.
facts.radiator: A panel of hot water in a room, warming it mostly by convection despite the name.
facts.scaffold: A temporary frame that puts a working platform beside a building.
facts.cylinder: The bore a piston runs in, and the sealed volume the working stroke happens inside.
facts.engine: A machine that turns fuel into rotation.
facts.crank: The bend in a shaft that turns a push along a line into a turn around a centre.
facts.lever: A rigid bar turning about a fixed point, trading distance for force.
facts.fulcrum: The fixed point a lever turns about.
facts.rod: A long straight bar of solid metal, the stock most other parts start as.
facts.flywheel: A heavy wheel that stores rotation and gives it back, smoothing an intermittent push into steady turning.
facts.boiler: A closed vessel where fire turns water into steam under pressure.
facts.valve: A part that opens and closes a passage, letting flow go one way or none.
facts.pump: A machine that moves fluid from where it is to where it is not.
facts.bearing: What a shaft turns in, arranged so the surfaces roll rather than rub.
facts.brake: A device that turns motion into heat in order to stop something.
facts.friction: The force resisting one surface sliding over another.
facts.surface: The boundary where a thing stops and everything else begins.
facts.area: How much surface something has, in units of length squared.
facts.petrol: The fraction of crude oil that boils between about 40 and 200 degrees, light enough to vaporise in an engine.
facts.gearbox: A set of gear ratios between engine and wheels, so one engine speed can serve many road speeds.
facts.clutch: The joint that lets a running engine be connected to and disconnected from the wheels.
facts.driveshaft: The turning shaft carrying power from the gearbox to the wheels.
facts.differential: The gearset that lets driven wheels turn at different speeds while both still pull.
facts.spark_plug: The part that fires the mixture, and the reason a petrol engine is called spark-ignition.
facts.alternator: The engine-driven generator that keeps a car's battery charged.
facts.exhaust: The pipe carrying burnt gas away from the engine, and everything fitted along it.
facts.catalytic_converter: A honeycomb coated in precious metal that finishes the reactions the engine did not.
facts.steering_wheel: The wheel the driver turns, and the linkage that turns the road wheels less than it does.
facts.dashboard: The panel of instruments in front of the driver.
facts.dial: A face with a scale and a pointer, showing a quantity as a position.
facts.speedometer: The instrument showing how fast a vehicle is going.
facts.headlight: A lamp with a mirror behind it, throwing light forward along the road rather than everywhere.
facts.seat: Something shaped to hold a body at rest, taking its weight through the hips rather than the spine.
facts.foam: A solid or liquid full of gas bubbles, which is how it becomes light and soft at once.
facts.syringe: A barrel, a plunger and a hollow needle, for putting a measured dose under the skin or drawing one out.
facts.suture: A stitch closing a wound so the edges heal to each other rather than filling in from the bottom.
facts.bandage: A covering held over a wound, to keep it clean, keep it together and take up what comes out of it.
facts.wound: A break in the skin, and the body's most practised emergency.
facts.forceps: Hinged tongs for gripping what fingers cannot reach or should not touch.
facts.anaesthetic: A drug that removes the sensation of pain, and usually consciousness with it.
facts.surgery: Treatment by opening the body and working inside it.
facts.nurse: The person who watches a patient over hours and days, which is most of what care actually is.
facts.doctor: The person who decides what is wrong and what to do about it.
facts.diagnosis: Working out which disease is producing what you can see.
facts.symptom: What the patient notices, as distinct from what the examiner finds.
facts.ambulance: A vehicle that brings treatment to the patient and the patient to the hospital.
facts.escapement: The part of a clock that lets the gear train advance one step per swing, and pushes the swing along as it goes.
facts.pendulum: A weight on a rod, swinging at a period set by its length and almost nothing else.
facts.hilt: Everything on a sword that is not the blade: the guard, the grip and the pommel.
facts.scabbard: The sheath a blade lives in.
facts.aperture: The adjustable hole a lens looks through, setting how much light gets in and how much is in focus.
facts.shutter: The gate that decides for how long light is allowed to fall.
facts.wax: A soft solid that melts at low heat and repels water, made by bees and later from petroleum.
facts.wick: A twist of fibre that carries liquid fuel up to a flame by capillary action.
facts.sole: The part of a shoe between the foot and the ground, and the part that wears out.
facts.heel: The raised block under the back of a shoe.
facts.lace: A cord threaded through holes, pulling a shoe tight around the foot.
facts.eyelet: A reinforced hole, so a cord can pull hard on fabric without tearing it.
facts.cord: Several strands twisted together, which is far stronger than the same fibre laid straight.
facts.twist: Turning strands about each other so that friction holds them together.
facts.fret: A raised bar across a fingerboard, fixing exactly where a string is stopped.
facts.neck: The long arm of a stringed instrument, carrying the fingerboard and taking the pull of the strings.
facts.varnish: A clear finish that hardens on a surface, protecting it while leaving it visible.
facts.furnace: An enclosure built to hold fire hot enough to change what is put in it.
facts.soda_ash: Sodium carbonate, the flux that lets glass be made at a workable temperature.
facts.putty: A soft paste that sets slowly, used to bed glass into a frame.
facts.frame: A skeleton of members carrying load, with nothing filling the spaces between them.
facts.spoke: One of the wires between the hub and the rim of a wheel.
facts.rim: The outer hoop of a wheel, holding the tyre and taking the pull of every spoke.
facts.hub: The centre of a wheel, holding the bearings the whole thing turns on.
facts.tyre: The compliant ring between a wheel and the road.
facts.inner_tube: An airtight ring inside a tyre, holding the pressure the tyre only shapes.
facts.sprocket: A toothed wheel made to engage a chain rather than another gear.
facts.pedal: The platform a foot pushes, on a bearing so it stays level as the crank goes round.
facts.handlebar: The bar the rider steers and leans on.
facts.spade: A flat blade on a shaft, for cutting into ground and lifting it.
facts.rake: A row of teeth on a handle, for gathering loose material without lifting the ground with it.
facts.tine: One prong of a fork, rake or harrow.
facts.trowel: A small flat blade for lifting and spreading mortar or soil.
facts.blowpipe: A hollow iron tube for gathering molten glass and inflating it.
facts.film: A flexible strip carrying a light-sensitive layer.
facts.binding: Whatever holds the pages of a book together and to its cover.
facts.rebar: Steel bars cast into concrete to carry the loads concrete cannot.
facts.rafter: One of the sloping members carrying a roof from ridge to wall.
facts.ridge: The horizontal line where two roof slopes meet at the top.
facts.batten: A thin strip nailed across rafters, giving tiles something to hook on to.
facts.roof_tile: A fired clay plate, overlapped in courses so water runs off and never in.
facts.flashing: Sheet metal worked into the joint where a roof meets something else.
facts.downpipe: The vertical pipe taking water from the gutter to the ground or the drain.
facts.render: A coat of mortar spread over masonry, for weather and for looks.
facts.primer: The first coat, which is for sticking rather than for colour.
facts.sealant: A flexible filler for the joints between things that move at different rates.
facts.screed: A thin levelling layer poured over a structural floor.
facts.underlay: A soft layer between a floor and its covering.
facts.block: A cast concrete unit, larger than a brick and laid the same way.
facts.sill: The ledge under a window, throwing rainwater clear of the wall below.
facts.pane: A single sheet of glass in a frame.
facts.latch: A catch that holds a door shut without locking it.
facts.silica: Silicon dioxide — the mineral that most sand, most rock and all ordinary glass is made of.
facts.bolt: A threaded rod with a head, clamping through a hole rather than gripping the material.
facts.tang: The unsharpened part of a blade that runs back into the handle.
facts.guard: The crosspiece between grip and blade.
facts.grip: The part actually held, wrapped so the hand does not slip on it.
facts.pommel: The weight at the end of a hilt.
facts.whetstone: A fine abrasive block for putting an edge back on a blade.
facts.quenching: Cooling hot steel fast enough to trap it in a hard, brittle state.
facts.glaze: A layer of glass fused onto pottery, making a porous body watertight.
facts.slip: Clay thinned to a cream, for casting, joining and decorating.
facts.firing: Heating clay until it changes irreversibly into ceramic.
facts.harrow: A frame of tines dragged over ploughed ground to break the clods.
facts.irrigation: Bringing water to a crop rather than waiting for it to fall.
facts.fertiliser: Anything added to soil to replace what a crop takes out of it.
facts.silo: A tall sealed store keeping grain or fodder without it spoiling.
facts.livestock: Animals kept for what they produce or become.
facts.stud: One of the upright timbers in a framed wall.
facts.door_frame: The lining fixed in the opening, that a door is hung from.
facts.window_frame: The surround holding glass in a wall.
facts.water_tank: A stored volume of water, high enough that gravity does the delivering.
facts.fan: Angled blades spun to push air along.
facts.press: A machine that applies steady, very large force over a small distance.
facts.circuit_board: A rigid sheet with copper tracks etched on it, replacing wiring with printing.
facts.resistor: A component that deliberately makes it harder for current to flow.
facts.heat_sink: A finned block of metal carrying heat away from something that must stay cool.
facts.fin: A thin projecting plate, put on something to multiply its surface.
facts.case: A rigid container shaped to what it protects.
facts.weight: The force gravity exerts on a mass.
facts.mainspring: The coiled ribbon of steel that stores the energy a clock runs on.
facts.balance_wheel: A weighted wheel oscillating against a spring, keeping time in anything that has to be carried.
facts.hoe: A blade set across a handle, for cutting weeds off at the root without turning the soil.
facts.watering_can: A vessel with a spout and a perforated head, delivering rain rather than a stream.
facts.mulch: A layer spread on soil rather than dug into it.
facts.hops: The flower that makes beer bitter and keeps it.
facts.mash: Crushed malt steeped in hot water, where starch becomes sugar.
facts.cask: A wooden barrel for storing and moving liquid.
facts.antenna: A conductor shaped so that a passing radio wave makes a current in it, or the reverse.
facts.microphone: A device turning sound into a matching electrical signal.
facts.fuel_tank: The vessel a vehicle carries its own fuel in.
facts.camshaft: The shaft of lobes that opens each valve at exactly the right moment.
facts.carburettor: The part that mixed fuel into the air before injection replaced it.
facts.starter_motor: The electric motor that turns an engine over until it can run itself.
facts.brake_disc: The disc a brake grips, turning motion into heat.
facts.suspension: What lets a wheel move up and down without the body doing the same.
facts.shock_absorber: The damper that stops a spring bouncing.
facts.chassis: The structural frame everything else on a vehicle is attached to.
facts.windscreen: The front window of a vehicle, and a structural part of it.
facts.wiper: A rubber blade sweeping water off glass.
facts.seatbelt: A woven strap that spreads a sudden stop across the strongest parts of the body.
facts.muffler: The chamber that quietens an exhaust.
facts.fretboard: The surface a string is pressed against, carrying the frets.
facts.tuning_peg: The geared post a string is wound on and tensioned by.
facts.motherboard: The main board everything in a computer plugs into.
facts.hard_drive: Spinning platters storing bits as magnetised patches.
facts.power_supply: The unit turning mains electricity into the steady low voltages a machine needs.
facts.computer_mouse: A device that turns hand movement on a surface into movement on a screen.
facts.dye: A colour that dissolves and bonds to a fibre, rather than sitting on it.
facts.viewfinder: The window showing what the lens is about to record.
facts.focus_ring: The collar that moves a lens to bring one distance sharp.
facts.leg: An upright support holding something at a working height.
facts.backrest: The part of a seat supporting the spine.
facts.upholstery: The padding and covering over a seat frame.
facts.cover: The stiff outside of a book, protecting the pages and naming them.
facts.page: One leaf of a book, printed on both sides.
facts.spine: The bound edge of a book, and the only part visible on a shelf.
facts.firebox: The chamber in a locomotive where the fire actually burns.
facts.carriage: A wheeled vehicle body, drawn or hauled rather than driven.
facts.signal: A fixed indication telling a driver whether the line ahead is clear.
facts.saponification: The reaction that splits fat with alkali and makes soap.
facts.perfume: Scent carried in something that evaporates and takes it with it.
facts.rag: Worn-out cloth, and for centuries the raw material of paper.
facts.annealing: Cooling glass or metal slowly enough that it does not tear itself apart.
facts.flux: Something added to lower the temperature at which another thing melts.
facts.ward: A hospital room of several beds, watched as one.
facts.flap: A hinged section of wing, lowered to make it lift more at low speed.
facts.cockpit: The compartment the aircraft is flown from.
facts.cabin: The enclosed, pressurised space people travel in.
facts.altimeter: An instrument reading height from air pressure.
facts.altitude: Height above a reference, which has to be chosen and stated.
facts.insole: The layer inside a shoe, between the foot and the sole.
facts.last: The foot-shaped form a shoe is built around.
facts.soundhole: The opening in the body of a stringed instrument.
facts.fragrance: A volatile compound made to be smelled.
facts.pruning_shears: Two blades on a pivot with a spring, for cutting a living stem cleanly.
facts.brake_pad: The friction material pressed against a disc.
facts.reflector: A surface returning light straight back toward whatever lit it.
facts.grease: Oil held in a soap thickener so it stays where it is put.
facts.operating_theatre: The room surgery is done in, built for cleanliness and light above all.
facts.touchscreen: A display that senses where it is touched.
facts.fuse_box: Where a building's circuits are divided and protected.
facts.soil_pipe: The large vertical pipe carrying waste from a building to the sewer.
facts.fireplace: A hearth built into a wall, with a flue above it.
facts.body_panel: A pressed steel skin over a vehicle's structure.
facts.glazing_bar: The slim timber divider between panes in a window.
facts.crop: A plant grown deliberately, in quantity, for use.
facts.fork_garden: Several stout tines on a handle, for lifting and breaking soil rather than cutting it.
facts.worktop: The working surface of a kitchen, at a height set by the person and not the room.
facts.damp_proof_course: A waterproof layer built into a wall near the ground.
facts.cavity_wall_tie: A metal tie holding the two leaves of a cavity wall together across the gap.
facts.roofing_felt: A bitumen-soaked sheet laid under tiles as a second line of defence.
facts.socket: The fixed outlet a plug is pushed into.
facts.track_gauge: The distance between the inner faces of the rails.
facts.indicator: The flashing lamp that tells other people what a driver intends.
facts.sim_card: The small card holding the identity a phone uses on a network.
facts.hand: The end of the arm, and the reason so much of the brain is given over to touch.
facts.cave: A natural space underground, large enough to enter.
facts.size: A sealing coat applied before another, so the next layer sits on the surface instead of soaking in.
facts.soundboard: The thin top plate of a stringed instrument, and the part that actually makes the sound.
facts.mind: Everything the brain is doing that can be described without mentioning the brain — thinking, wanting, noticing, remembering.
facts.meditation: Training attention deliberately, usually by holding it on one thing and noticing when it has wandered.
facts.building: An enclosed structure people go inside, and the umbrella the corpus was missing under house, office, library, tower and hospital.
facts.arch: A curved span made of wedge-shaped blocks, standing entirely in compression.
facts.column: An upright taking a load straight down its own length.
facts.vault: A roof made by running an arch along, or crossing two of them.
facts.buttress: Masonry set against a wall to take the sideways push of what it carries.
facts.spire: A tall tapering point on a tower.
facts.stained_glass: Coloured glass held in lead, telling a story in a window.
facts.altar: The table a religious rite is performed at, and usually the reason the building is oriented as it is.
facts.shaft: A vertical hole sunk to reach something below, propped so it stays open.
facts.millstone: A pair of dressed stones, the upper turning on the lower, that grind grain to flour.
facts.harbour: Sheltered water where a ship can lie still enough to be loaded.
facts.anchor: A weight with flukes, dropped to hold a vessel against wind and current.
facts.lighthouse: A tower showing a light with a pattern of its own, so it can be told from every other light.
facts.crane: A machine for lifting a load and putting it somewhere else.
facts.cargo: Goods carried for someone else, and the reason ships exist.
facts.stage: A raised floor that separates performers from watchers.
facts.mask: A covering for the face that replaces one identity with another.
facts.actor: Someone who performs as someone else, in front of people who know it.
facts.eyepiece: The lens you actually look into, magnifying the image the main lens made.
facts.tube: A hollow cylinder — stiff for its weight, and a container for a path.
facts.theatre: A building arranged so that many people can watch the same thing at once.
facts.transmitter: The half of radio that makes the wave.
facts.receiver: The half of radio that picks one wave out of all of them.
facts.tuner: A circuit that resonates at one frequency and ignores the rest.
facts.inductor: A coil that resists a change in the current through it.
facts.coil: Wire wound in turns, so that each turn's magnetic field adds to the others'.
facts.frequency: How many times something repeats in a second.
facts.survey: Measuring land accurately enough to describe it on paper.
facts.projection: A rule for flattening a curved surface onto a flat one.
facts.contour: A line joining points of equal height.
facts.pier: The masonry support a bridge span lands on, standing in the water it crosses.
facts.deck: The flat surface of a bridge or ship — the part actually used.
facts.truss: A frame of triangles carrying a span with far less material than a beam.
facts.tunnel: A passage driven through ground rather than over it.
facts.pickaxe: A pointed iron head on a handle, for breaking rock the point can be driven into.
facts.cart: A wheeled container pulled or pushed.
facts.winch: A drum turned by a handle, winding rope in under load.
facts.screen: A surface made to emit light in a controlled pattern.
facts.phosphor: A substance that glows when something strikes it.
facts.gate: The deliberate weak point in a barrier, and therefore the strongest part of it.
facts.well: A shaft sunk to the water table, and the reason a settlement can be where it is.
facts.quay: A solid stone-faced edge to the water, built so a ship can lie against it and be worked straight onto land.
facts.jetty: A structure run out from the shore into the water, so that deep water can be reached without dredging the whole bank.
facts.dock: An enclosed basin whose gates hold the water in, so ships inside stay afloat whatever the tide outside is doing.
facts.breakwater: A wall built out into open water for no other reason than to have the waves break on it instead of on what lies behind.
facts.abutment: The structure at each end of a bridge that takes both its weight and its outward push, and hands them to the ground.
facts.span: The clear distance carried between two supports, and the thing every bridge is really measured by.
facts.weir: A low wall across a river that the water runs over rather than through, holding the level up behind it.
facts.channel: A cut made to carry water where it is wanted rather than where it would go.
facts.millrace: The channel that takes water from behind the weir to the wheel, and the tailrace that takes it away again.
facts.battlement: A parapet cut into alternating solid blocks and gaps, so a defender can shelter and shoot from the same place.
facts.arrow_slit: A narrow vertical opening in a wall, wide enough to shoot out of and hard to shoot into.
facts.courtyard: The open ground enclosed between the curtain wall and the buildings inside it.
facts.crypt: A vaulted chamber under the floor of a church, usually holding a burial.
facts.nave: The long central body of a church, between the rows of columns and open to the congregation.
facts.sail: A sheet of canvas roped at its edges, set to take the wind's push and hand it to whatever it is fastened to.
facts.hopper: A bin with sloping sides narrowing to a hole, so what is put in feeds itself out at a steady rate.
facts.tail_vane: A small wind wheel set crossways to the main sails and geared to the cap, turning the mill to face the wind and then stopping.
facts.anvil: A heavy block that gives the hammer back to the work instead of swallowing the blow.
facts.tongs: Two levers crossed on a pivot, so a squeeze at the long end becomes a grip at the short.
facts.vat: A large open vessel of staves drawn tight by bands, made to hold a liquid for a long time.
facts.condenser: The finned pipe on the back of a fridge, where squeezed gas gives up its heat and turns back into liquid.
facts.evaporator: The pipe inside the cold cabinet, where the liquid is let go to a low pressure and boils.
facts.piano_action: The linkage between a key and its hammer, which throws the hammer at the string and lets it fall back free.
facts.cast_iron: Iron carrying two to four per cent carbon: too brittle to forge, and so fluid when molten that it takes any mould.
facts.damper: A felt pad resting on the string, lifted while the key is held and dropped the moment it is released.
facts.lid: A cover hinged along one edge, so it can be opened without being put down anywhere.
facts.horsehair: Hair from the tail or mane, long, strong, and covered in microscopic scales.
facts.rosin: The brittle amber solid left behind when the turpentine is boiled out of pine resin.
facts.fingerboard: A hard board glued along the neck, which the string is pressed against rather than onto the neck itself.
facts.tripod: Three legs meeting at a head — the fewest that stand, and the most that stand without rocking.
facts.grinding: Two discs of glass rubbed face to face with wet abrasive between them until each takes a true curve.
facts.silvering: Silver brought out of solution onto clean glass as a film a few hundred atoms thick.
facts.kneading: Working dough until it stops tearing and starts stretching.
facts.peel: A thin flat board on a long handle, for putting bread into an oven and taking it out.
facts.easel: A standing frame that holds the work upright at the height of the eye.
facts.palette: A thin sealed hardwood board with a hole for the thumb, where the colours are laid out and mixed.
facts.costume: Cloth cut and made up to say who someone is before they have said anything.
facts.rehearsal: The play run through without an audience, until it can be done without thought.
facts.platen: The flat plate that comes down on the paper and presses every letter at once.
facts.wafer: A thin disc sawn from a single silicon crystal grown as one unbroken lattice from end to end.
facts.doping: Driving foreign atoms into chosen regions of a finished wafer — one for every ten million or so of its own.
facts.lithography: The pattern is printed onto the wafer rather than drawn on it, all of it in one exposure.
facts.grid: Two families of lines crossing at right angles, so that any point on the world has exactly one pair of numbers.
facts.legend: The panel that says what each mark on the map stands for.
facts.journalist: Someone whose whole occupation is finding out what happened and writing it down in time.
facts.editor: Someone whose job is not to write but to decide what runs, how long it is, and where it goes.
facts.headline: The few words set large at the top, written not by the reporter but by the desk.
facts.advertisement: Space in the paper sold to someone who wants your attention.
facts.clerk: Someone kept to write the same kind of thing down, accurately, every day.
facts.deposit: Money handed to someone else to keep, in exchange for the right to ask for it back.
facts.interest: What is paid for the use of money, and it is priced by how long it is used for.
facts.credit: A bank does not keep the deposits in the vault. It lends most of them out.
facts.conductor: One person whose only instrument is everyone else.
facts.type: Each letter cast as a separate block, from a hand mould that makes identical copies in minutes.
facts.composing_stick: A small metal tray held in the left hand, into which type is set letter by letter.
facts.canary: A small seed-eating finch of the Atlantic islands, kept for four hundred years for its song.
facts.modulation: Varying a steady high carrier wave so that it carries something that is not steady.
facts.soundpost: A short spruce rod wedged upright between the belly and the back, just behind one foot of the bridge.
facts.gangrene: Tissue dying because its blood supply has failed, and then being fermented by what got into it.
facts.dysentery: Diarrhoea with blood in it, which is a different thing from ordinary diarrhoea and means the gut wall itself is being destroyed.
facts.phytophthora_infestans: Not a fungus, despite everything about it. An oomycete — closer to brown algae than to a mushroom.
facts.puccinia_graminis: Wheat stem rust, and it needs two unrelated host plants to complete its life cycle.
facts.hemileia_vastatrix: Coffee leaf rust, which ended coffee growing in Ceylon within twenty years and is why Britain drinks tea.
facts.magnaporthe_oryzae: Rice blast, and it gets in by generating a pressure no other cell is known to reach.
facts.fusarium_oxysporum: Panama disease. It killed the Gros Michel banana commercially, and its next race is now working through the one that replaced it.
facts.botrytis_cinerea: Grey mould, which ruins a crop — except when it does the opposite and makes the best sweet wines there are.
facts.erysiphe: Powdery mildew — the white dust on a leaf, and it is the fungus itself, not a deposit.
facts.plasmopara_viticola: Downy mildew of the grape, brought to Europe from America in the 1870s on vines imported to resist something else.
facts.claviceps_purpurea: Ergot: the fungus replaces the grain with a hard black body of its own, full of alkaloids.
facts.ustilago_maydis: Corn smut, which is a disease in Iowa and a delicacy in Mexico.
facts.venturia_inaequalis: Apple scab, which overwinters in the fallen leaves rather than on the tree.
facts.ophiostoma_ulmi: Dutch elm disease — a fungus that cannot travel and a beetle that can.
facts.cryphonectria_parasitica: Chestnut blight, which removed roughly four billion trees from the eastern American forest in fifty years.
facts.hymenoscyphus_fraxineus: Ash dieback, harmless on its Asian host and lethal on the European one.
facts.xylella_fastidiosa: A bacterium that lives only in the xylem, and blocks it.
facts.erwinia_amylovora: Fireblight — the first plant disease ever shown to be caused by a bacterium.
facts.agrobacterium_tumefaciens: A bacterium that inserts its own DNA into a plant's chromosomes and makes the plant build it a home.
facts.plasmodiophora_brassicae: Clubroot: neither fungus nor bacterium, but a soil-dwelling protist.
facts.rhizoctonia_solani: Damping off: the seedling germinates, emerges, and then falls over at soil level.
facts.verticillium_dahliae: A wilt that often takes one side of the plant and leaves the other alone.
facts.pseudomonas_syringae: A plant bacterium carrying a protein that makes water freeze at a temperature it otherwise would not.
facts.potato_virus_y: The most damaging virus of the potato, and it is carried on the aphid's mouthparts rather than inside it.
facts.barley_yellow_dwarf_virus: The most widespread virus of cereals anywhere, and it never leaves the phloem.
facts.candidatus_liberibacter: A bacterium nobody has ever grown in a dish, which is what the Candidatus in its name means.
facts.potato_blight: The leaves go black in days and the tubers rot in the ground and in the store.
facts.stem_rust: Reddish pustules that break through the stem and steal what the grain was going to be.
facts.coffee_rust: Orange powder on the underside of the leaf, and the leaf falls.
facts.rice_blast: Diamond-shaped lesions on the leaf, and a neck rot that empties the panicle.
facts.panama_disease: The banana wilts with its roots in wet soil, because the plumbing is blocked rather than the water absent.
facts.grey_mould: A dusty grey felt over soft fruit, and the whole crop goes in a few damp days.
facts.noble_rot: The same fungus as grey mould, in different weather, making Sauternes and Tokaji.
facts.powdery_mildew: White dust on the upper leaf, and it will not rub off because it is alive.
facts.downy_mildew: Oily yellow patches on top of the leaf and a white down underneath, following rain.
facts.ergotism: St Anthony's Fire: burning limbs, gangrene, convulsions and hallucinations, from bread.
facts.corn_smut: The kernel swells into a grey gall full of black spores. In Mexico it is picked and sold.
facts.apple_scab: Olive-brown blotches on leaf and fruit, and the fruit cracks as it grows under them.
facts.dutch_elm_disease: Britain lost something like twenty-five million elms, and the landscape they made does not exist any more.
facts.chestnut_blight: Roughly four billion American chestnuts, a quarter of the eastern forest canopy, gone in fifty years.
facts.ash_dieback: Black lesions where leaf meets twig, and the crown thins from the top down.
facts.citrus_greening: Fruit that stays green at the bottom, tastes bitter, and drops before it ripens.
facts.fireblight: Shoots blacken and hook over at the tip, so the tree looks as though it has been scorched.
facts.crown_gall: A tumour at the base of the stem, built by the plant, to the bacterium's instructions.
facts.clubroot: The roots swell into useless clubs and the plant wilts in full sun with wet soil underneath.
facts.damping_off: The seedling comes up healthy and then falls over, pinched through at soil level.
facts.verticillium_wilt: Half the leaf yellow and half still green, and often one whole side of the plant.
facts.foot_and_mouth_virus: One of the most contagious animal viruses there is, and it rarely kills an adult beast.
facts.rinderpest_virus: The second disease ever driven to extinction, after smallpox, and the only animal one.
facts.african_swine_fever_virus: No vaccine that works, no treatment, and near-total mortality in domestic pigs.
facts.avian_influenza: The reservoir of every influenza pandemic, sitting harmlessly in wild ducks.
facts.newcastle_disease_virus: A poultry virus that kills whole flocks, and is in trials against tumours in people.
facts.bluetongue_virus: Carried by a biting midge, which is why its range is set by climate rather than by trade.
facts.canine_parvovirus: A virus that did not exist before about 1976 and was worldwide within two years.
facts.myxoma_virus: Released deliberately in Australia in 1950, and the best-documented case of a pathogen and its host evolving against each other.
facts.batrachochytrium: A fungus that has driven more vertebrate species to extinction than any other single pathogen known.
facts.white_nose_fungus: A cold-loving fungus that grows on hibernating bats at temperatures where nothing can fight it.
facts.varroa_mite: A mite the size of a dinner plate on a person, feeding on the bee's fat body and carrying viruses in.
facts.paenibacillus_larvae: American foulbrood: the reason beekeepers burn hives rather than treat them.
facts.nosema: A microsporidian — a fungus that has thrown away its own mitochondria and steals ATP from its host.
facts.dirofilaria_immitis: Heartworm: a nematode up to thirty centimetres long living in the pulmonary artery.
facts.sarcoptes_scabiei: A mite that tunnels in the skin, and the same species causes scabies in people and mange in animals.
facts.theileria: The only eukaryotic parasite known to transform a host cell into something like a cancer.
facts.babesia: A tick-borne parasite of red blood cells, and the cause of Texas cattle fever.
facts.mite: Eight legs, usually under a millimetre, and there are more of them in a handful of soil than almost anything else.
facts.midge: A biting fly small enough to pass through mosquito netting, and it carries bluetongue.
facts.variola: Smallpox: the only human disease ever eradicated, and it had no animal reservoir to hide in.
facts.sars_cov_2: A coronavirus that spreads before people feel ill, which is what made it uncontainable.
facts.coronavirus: Named for the crown of spikes around it, and it carries the largest genome of any RNA virus.
facts.ebola_virus: A filovirus that spreads only by contact with the very ill or the newly dead.
facts.marburg_virus: The first filovirus ever identified, and it was found in a European laboratory in 1967.
facts.lassa_virus: Carried by one species of rat that lives in houses across West Africa, and shed in its urine.
facts.nipah_virus: It reached people through pigs the first time, and through date palm sap the second.
facts.hantavirus: Breathed in from dried rodent urine and droppings, and person-to-person spread is essentially absent.
facts.dengue_virus: Four types, and surviving one makes the next one worse rather than better.
facts.zika_virus: Known since 1947 and considered trivial until 2015, when it was found to cross the placenta.
facts.chikungunya_virus: The name means 'that which bends up', for the posture of someone with the joint pain.
facts.hepatitis_b: A DNA virus that copies itself through an RNA intermediate, like a retrovirus running backwards.
facts.hepatitis_c: Found in 1989 by cloning the genome of something nobody had ever seen, and curable since 2014.
facts.herpes_simplex: It retreats into a nerve cell body and waits there for the rest of your life.
facts.varicella_zoster: One virus, two diseases, decades apart — and the second one is the first one coming back.
facts.chickenpox: Not related to smallpox at all, despite two centuries of the two being confused.
facts.rotavirus: Before the vaccine it killed around half a million children a year, and it infects essentially everyone.
facts.mycobacterium_leprae: It has lost about a third of its own genes and cannot be grown in any culture medium.
facts.borrelia_burgdorferi: Lyme disease, and its genome is split across a chromosome and more than twenty plasmids.
facts.shigella: Genetically it is Escherichia coli, and it is kept as a separate genus for historical reasons only.
facts.candida_albicans: A yeast most people carry harmlessly, which turns invasive by changing its shape.
facts.aspergillus_fumigatus: Everyone breathes in hundreds of its spores a day, and almost nobody is harmed.
facts.cryptococcus_neoformans: A yeast with a thick sugar capsule, found in pigeon droppings and in old tree hollows.
facts.schistosoma_mansoni: A fluke whose male and female live permanently paired, the female held in a groove along his body.
facts.necator_americanus: Hookworm: it enters through the sole of a bare foot and ends up in the small intestine.
facts.canine_distemper_virus: A close relative of measles and rinderpest, and it does not stay in dogs.
facts.feline_leukaemia_virus: A retrovirus that inserts itself into the cat's own chromosomes, and sometimes lands in the wrong place.
facts.pain: A signal, not a substance — and the only symptom that is entirely private to the person having it.
facts.anaemia: Not too little blood, but too little of the thing in it that carries oxygen.
facts.thyroid: A butterfly-shaped gland that sets the speed at which the whole body runs.
facts.goitre: The gland swelling because it is being told to work harder and lacks the one ingredient it needs.
facts.heart_attack: The heart muscle starving because one of the vessels feeding it has closed.
facts.heart_failure: Not the heart stopping, but the heart no longer keeping up with what is asked of it.
facts.stroke: Brain tissue dying because its blood supply stopped, or because a vessel burst into it.
facts.asthma: The airway narrowing from the inside, and it is reversible, which is what separates it from everything else.
facts.arthritis: Two quite different diseases share the name, and telling them apart decides everything.
facts.osteoporosis: Bone is being replaced all your life, and this is what happens when the replacing falls behind.
facts.cataract: The lens clouding because its proteins, which are never replaced, have clumped.
facts.ulcer: For a century the cause was thought to be stress and spice. It is mostly a bacterium.
facts.haemophilia: One missing clotting protein, and the gene for it sits on the X chromosome.
facts.gout: Uric acid crystallising in a joint, and it picks the coldest one — usually the big toe.
facts.lead_poisoning: Lead has no biological role at all, and the body mistakes it for calcium.
facts.carbon_monoxide_poisoning: It binds the same site as oxygen, about two hundred times more tightly, and it has no smell.
facts.dehydration: Losing water is survivable for a while. Losing water and salt together is what kills.
facts.hypothermia: The body has a very narrow range it works in, and two degrees below it the shivering stops.
facts.altitude_sickness: The air is the same mixture all the way up. There is simply less of it pressing down.
facts.pellagra: The four Ds — dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death — from a diet built on maize.
facts.beriberi: It arrived with the machine that polished rice, and nobody connected the two for decades.
facts.night_blindness: The first thing to fail when vitamin A runs short, because the eye spends it fastest.
facts.kwashiorkor: A swollen belly on a starving child, and the swelling is why it was misread for so long.
facts.childbirth: The only routine event in medicine where two patients share one body and their interests can differ.
facts.labour: Contractions that build on themselves, because the thing that causes them is released by them.
facts.vitamin_b1: Thiamine: the first vitamin to be identified, and the reason the word exists at all.
facts.bran: The outer layer milled off to make white flour, and it carries most of what was worth eating.
facts.hypothyroidism: The gland running slow, and everything downstream of it running slow too.
