facts.bradycardia: A heart beating too slowly to keep the brain supplied.
facts.stator: The half that stays still, and in a generator it is usually where the useful current is made.
facts.anode: The electrode where oxidation happens — and which end that is depends on which way the current is going.
facts.cathode: The electrode where reduction happens, and the one metal is deposited onto.
facts.electrode: The point where a circuit stops being wire and starts being chemistry.
facts.electrolyte: A liquid that carries ions but not electrons, which is exactly what a battery needs between its plates.
facts.terminal: Where the device stops and your wiring starts, and most electrical faults are here.
facts.casing: The part whose whole job is that nothing inside it is your problem.
facts.commutator: A rotary switch that reverses the connection twice per turn, so the torque never changes sign.
facts.armature: The winding that moves through the field — or the field that moves past the winding.
facts.insulator: Not the absence of conduction but the deliberate maintenance of it, over decades, in weather.
facts.bushing: The way a live conductor gets through an earthed metal wall without arcing to it.
facts.loudspeaker: A coil in a magnetic field, glued to a cone, and it is a microphone run backwards.
facts.warp: The threads that run the length of the cloth, held under tension for the whole weaving.
facts.weft: The thread that crosses, and the only one that actually has to travel.
facts.heddle: A loop that one warp thread passes through, so that lifting it lifts that thread and no other.
facts.shed: The triangular gap opened between raised and lowered warp threads, and it exists for about a second.
facts.shuttle: A boat-shaped case carrying the weft, thrown from one side to the other.
facts.bobbin: A spool sized to fit inside whatever has to carry it.
facts.cam: A shaped disc that turns rotation into a pushing that follows whatever profile you cut.
facts.feed_dog: The toothed bar under the needle plate that moves the cloth along, a stitch at a time.
facts.tension_disc: Two plates squeezed by a spring, with the thread running between them.
facts.pivot: The point a thing turns on, and in an instrument it is sharpened almost to nothing.
facts.jewel: A synthetic sapphire with a hole in it, used as a bearing because it will not wear.
facts.gimbal: Rings pivoted at right angles, so that whatever they carry stays level while the ship rolls.
facts.ring: A closed curve of material, and the shape that carries a pull evenly all the way round.
facts.vacuum: Not nothing — just less than there was, and the difference is what does the work.
facts.cistern: A reservoir that holds a head of water so the supply is steady rather than intermittent.
facts.mouldboard: The curved plate that lifts the cut slice and turns it over, and the curve is the whole invention.
facts.share: The wedge that cuts the furrow horizontally, and the part that wears out first.
facts.wedge: One of the six simple machines, and the only one you hit.
facts.nozzle: A narrowing that trades pressure for speed, and past a certain point it must widen again.
facts.governor: Two weights that fly outward as the engine speeds up, and close the steam as they do.
facts.flyweight: A weight on an arm, thrown outward by rotation, and its position reports the speed.
facts.rind: The skin a cheese grows, and it is not a wrapper — it is the outside of the cheese behaving differently.
facts.filter: A barrier chosen so that what you want goes through and what you do not stays behind.
facts.kernel: The part of an operating system that is always resident, and the only part allowed to touch the hardware.
facts.scheduler: Decides which program runs next, and it does this thousands of times a second.
facts.device_driver: The translation between what the operating system asks for and what one particular piece of hardware wants.
facts.interrupt: A device saying 'now' loudly enough that the processor stops what it was doing.
facts.process: A running program, together with everything it thinks is its own.
facts.signature: A single sheet folded down to make several leaves, and books are built from these rather than from pages.
facts.horizon: The line where you stop being able to see, and its distance tells you how high you are.
facts.morse_code: The commonest letters get the shortest signals, which is why E is one dot.
facts.exchange: Wiring every telephone to every other needs a wire for each pair. An exchange needs one wire each.
facts.valley: The river makes it. The mountains are just what is left standing either side.
facts.gorge: A valley cut faster than its walls can fall in, which is what makes it narrow.
facts.cliff: Not carved so much as continually broken off at the bottom.
facts.scree: The pile of broken rock at the foot of a slope, and it always settles at about the same angle.
facts.snowline: The height above which snow lasts the summer, and it is a line you can see.
facts.treeline: The height above which trees stop, and it is temperature rather than cold that sets it.
facts.erosion: The whole landscape is temporary, and this is the rate.
facts.crater: Always round, whatever angle the thing arrived at, because it is an explosion and not a dent.
facts.hot_spring: Rain that fell years ago, went down far enough to be heated, and found a way back up.
facts.sunset: The blue light has been scattered out of the beam before it reaches you, and only the red is left.
facts.hearth: A fire given a permanent place, and that is the moment a shelter becomes a house.
facts.molasses: What is left after the sugar has been crystallised out, and it holds most of what was not sugar.
facts.rum: Distilled from the waste of sugar making, which is why it belongs to the Caribbean and not to a grain country.
facts.cologne: Named after the city, and it is defined by being weak — two to five per cent oil, where perfume is twenty.
facts.currency: Money that a particular authority says is money, and its value rests on that saying.
facts.banknote_pound: The oldest currency still in use, and the name was once literally a pound of silver.
facts.dollar: The name comes from a Bohemian valley, and it is now the currency of about twenty countries.
facts.poodle: A working water dog, and the haircut everyone laughs at was cut for a reason.
facts.labradoodle: Bred in Australia in 1989 to be a guide dog someone with an allergy could keep.
facts.cassowary: The most dangerous bird alive, and the claw that does it is on the inner toe.
facts.ratite: Flightless birds with no keel on the breastbone, and they did not lose flight once.
facts.mustelid: Long body, short legs, and a scent gland that is the family signature.
facts.weasel: The smallest carnivore there is, and small enough to follow a vole underground.
facts.badger: A mustelid that went the other way: heavy, powerful, and built to dig rather than to follow.
facts.system: Parts whose behaviour together is not in any of them separately.
facts.cycle: A process whose end is its own beginning, which is why it can run forever on nothing but energy passing through.
facts.theory: In science it is the strongest thing there is, and in ordinary speech it means a guess. That gap causes most public arguments about science.
facts.evidence: An observation only becomes evidence in relation to a claim — the same fact can support one and refute another.
facts.observation: Looking at something without changing it, which is harder than it sounds and sometimes impossible.
facts.measurement: Comparing a thing to an agreed unit, and the agreement is the hard part.
facts.standard: Something everyone agrees to do the same way, and its whole value is that nobody defects.
facts.agreement: Two parties choosing to be predictable to each other, which is what makes anything past barter possible.
facts.trust: Acting on an expectation you cannot verify, and it is cheaper than verifying.
facts.selection: Not a force and not a chooser. Just the arithmetic of what leaves more descendants.
facts.variation: The differences within a species, and without it nothing can evolve at all.
facts.population: The unit evolution actually acts on. An individual cannot evolve.
facts.bond: Atoms sharing or handing over electrons, and everything chemistry does is this.
facts.gland: An organ whose whole job is to make something and release it.
facts.lobe: A part of an organ marked off by a groove, and in the brain the grooves came before the names.
facts.fissure: A deep groove, and in a brain it is what lets a large sheet fit in a small box.
facts.fold: Doubling something over, which multiplies its area in a given space and its stiffness along the crease.
facts.structure: The arrangement that decides what a thing can carry, and it usually matters more than what it is made of.
facts.form: What a thing is, as distinct from what it is made of — the oldest distinction in philosophy and still the useful one.
facts.load: What a structure has to carry, and the temporary ones usually decide the design.
facts.code: An agreed mapping between symbols and meanings, and it does not have to be secret.
facts.symbol: A mark that stands for something by agreement rather than by resemblance.
facts.meaning: What a sign points to, and it lives in the reader rather than in the mark.
facts.mark: The oldest technology for making something outlast the moment it was made in.
facts.machine: Something that changes a force's size or direction, and there are only six of them underneath.
facts.motor: A generator run backwards, and the same machine will do either.
facts.giant: What a star becomes when it runs out of hydrogen in its core, and it gets bigger by cooling.
facts.dwarf: What is left when a star has nothing to burn and nothing holding it up but the electrons themselves.
facts.helix: A circle that is also travelling, and the shape a chain takes when every link turns by the same angle.
facts.axis: The line a thing turns about, and it is the one part that does not move.
facts.rotation: Turning about a line rather than moving along one, and it conserves its own quantity.
facts.zone: A band where conditions are similar enough that the same things live or happen throughout it.
facts.region: An area treated as one thing, and what makes it one is a decision.
facts.boundary: Where one thing stops being itself, and it is nearly always a gradient someone has drawn a line across.
facts.edge: Where a surface ends, and in ecology it is where most of the life is.
facts.perception: Not a recording of the world but the brain's best guess at what would explain the signals.
facts.consciousness: The only thing anyone has direct evidence of, and the only thing nobody can demonstrate to anyone else.
facts.attention: Not looking harder — deciding what to leave out.
facts.emotion: The body changes first and the feeling names it afterwards, which is the opposite of how it seems.
facts.fear: It takes a fast road that reaches the body before you know what you saw.
facts.anger: The one negative emotion that makes people approach rather than withdraw.
facts.happiness: Wanting and liking are different systems, and only one of them is happiness.
facts.love: Three separate systems that evolved for different jobs and do not have to point at the same person.
facts.attachment: An infant's tie to whoever comes when it cries, formed in the first year and audible in adults decades later.
facts.grief: The cost of attachment, and it arrives in the shape of the thing that is gone.
facts.dream: The brain runs while the body is switched off at the spine, which is why you can fly and not fall out of bed.
facts.sleep: Every animal with a nervous system does it, and it costs so much that it must be paying for something.
facts.thought: Much of it is not in words, which is why the right word is so hard to find.
facts.reason: It arrives at conclusions the arguer already held far more often than it arrives anywhere new.
facts.learning: The synapse changes, and the change is the memory.
facts.repetition: Spacing it out beats massing it together, and this has been known and ignored since 1885.
facts.intelligence: Whatever it is, it is not one thing, and the argument about that is the whole history of the subject.
facts.problem: A gap between where you are and where you want to be, plus not knowing the way.
facts.want: Wanting is not the same system as liking, and it is the one that keeps you going.
facts.need: What an organism must have or fail, which is a much shorter list than what it wants.
facts.belief: Holding something to be so, and it is what you act on rather than what you say.
facts.knowledge: Justified true belief — and Gettier showed in three pages in 1963 that this is not enough.
facts.philosophy: The discipline that keeps losing its subjects, and that is what it is for.
facts.question: A shape in the language for the gap where an answer would go.
facts.ethics: The question of what to do, which cannot be answered by finding out what is the case.
facts.art: A made thing whose purpose is to be attended to, and every attempt to define it more tightly has failed.
facts.colour: Not a property of things. A property of the conversation between a surface, a light and three kinds of cell.
facts.story: Events put in an order that implies why, which is not the order they happened in.
facts.myth: A story a culture treats as explaining why things are as they are, rather than as something that once happened.
facts.ritual: Actions whose form matters more than their effect, done the same way because that is the way.
facts.festival: A date the whole community stops on, and almost all of them sit on the farming year.
facts.dance: Movement made to be watched and to be synchronised with, and the synchronising is the older function.
facts.song: Words and pitch together, and it is easier to remember than either alone.
facts.poetry: Language arranged so the form carries meaning too, and the constraint is what does the work.
facts.instrument: Something that turns a small motion into a loud sound, which is a problem of matching rather than of amplifying.
facts.resonator: A body that answers at one pitch and ignores the rest.
facts.painting: Pigment held in a binder on a surface, and the binder decides almost everything about it.
facts.sculpture: Carving is subtractive and cannot be undone, which is why so much of it was worked out in clay first.
facts.architecture: Building with the load in mind, and for most of history the mathematics followed the buildings rather than led them.
facts.tradition: Information passed by copying rather than by inheritance, which lets it change far faster than genes.
facts.generation: The interval between a parent and a child, and it sets the clock for everything inherited.
facts.play: Practising things that matter, at a time when getting them wrong is cheap.
facts.sport: A contest with agreed constraints, and the constraints are what make it worth watching.
facts.rule: A constraint accepted in advance, which is what makes the outcome mean something.
facts.humour: Something is set up to go one way and goes another, safely, and the laugh is the release.
facts.surprise: The size of the gap between what was predicted and what arrived, and the brain is built to measure it.
facts.expectation: The brain runs slightly ahead of the world, and what you perceive is mostly the prediction.
facts.pattern: A regularity that lets you say what comes next, which is the only reason it is worth finding.
facts.fashion: Change for its own sake, and the speed of the change is the signal rather than the clothes.
facts.ratio: One quantity against another, and it is the first thing that stops depending on the units.
facts.division: Sharing out, and the one arithmetic operation with a forbidden case.
facts.part: Something considered separately from what it belongs to, and the separating is a decision.
facts.whole: What the parts add up to, and it usually has properties none of them has.
facts.fraction: A number between the whole ones, and admitting they exist took a very long time.
facts.limit: What a thing gets arbitrarily close to without ever having to arrive.
facts.infinity: Not one size. Cantor showed there are infinitely many infinities, and some are strictly bigger.
facts.change: The only thing measurable without a second object to compare against.
facts.difference: The first thing any measurement produces, and often the only thing that is real.
facts.calculus: The mathematics of things that are changing, invented twice at once and argued over for a century.
facts.axiom: A starting point assumed rather than shown, because something has to be.
facts.proof: A chain from things agreed to a thing not yet agreed, where every link can be checked on its own.
facts.theorem: A statement shown to follow, and it stays shown.
facts.contradiction: A statement and its denial both held, and it is fatal because everything follows from it.
facts.paradox: An argument that looks sound and reaches something that cannot be, which means an assumption is wrong.
facts.equation: A claim that two descriptions pick out the same thing, which is why it can be rearranged.
facts.function: A rule giving exactly one output for each input, and the 'exactly one' is the whole definition.
facts.event: Something happening at a place and a time, which is the smallest thing physics will discuss.
facts.outcome: One of the ways a thing could have turned out, and listing them properly is most of the work.
facts.chance: Either the world is not determined, or we do not know enough. The mathematics is the same either way.
facts.probability: It began as a way of splitting the stake in an interrupted gambling game.
facts.sample: A part chosen to stand for the whole, and how it was chosen matters more than how big it is.
facts.statistics: Reasoning from a part to the whole, which is always a bet.
facts.average: A single number standing for many, and it can describe a set containing nothing like it.
facts.symmetry: A change that makes no difference, and every conservation law is one.
facts.pi: The same number for every circle there has ever been, and it never ends or repeats.
facts.season: Caused by the tilt, not the distance. Earth is closest to the Sun in January.
facts.era: A stretch of time named after the fact, by people deciding where the joins were.
facts.past: Fixed, and known only through what happened to survive.
facts.future: Not yet fixed, and the only part of time anything can be done about.
facts.prehistory: Everything before writing, which is over ninety-five per cent of it.
facts.bronze_age: Named for an alloy whose two metals are almost never found in the same place.
facts.iron_age: Iron is a worse metal than bronze until you can work it, and far commoner once you can.
facts.antiquity: The period with written records and no continuous institutions reaching us, which is why it needed rediscovering.
facts.middle_ages: Named by people who thought of it as the gap between two better times, which is a judgement rather than a period.
facts.renaissance: A rediscovery, and the press is why this one did not fade like the earlier ones.
facts.modernity: The period that thinks of itself as new, which is itself the novelty.
facts.archaeology: Reading the ground, in which depth is time and disturbance is the enemy.
facts.industry: Making things by machine rather than by hand, and the change was in the power rather than the tools.
facts.fuel: Anything holding chemical energy loosely enough to be released on purpose.
facts.natural_gas: Mostly methane, and for a century it was burnt off at the wellhead as a nuisance.
facts.refinery: One input and a dozen products, separated by nothing more than boiling point.
facts.mining: Taking rock out of the ground for the small part of it that is wanted.
facts.solar_power: A photon knocks an electron loose and the junction decides which way it goes.
facts.sunlight: Eight minutes old when it arrives, and the energy in it left the core about a hundred thousand years before that.
facts.wind_power: No turbine can take more than about 59% of the wind's energy, and that is a theorem.
facts.hydroelectricity: The only large-scale way of storing grid electricity that anyone actually uses.
facts.dam: It holds back water with its own weight, and the pressure it must resist depends on depth rather than on how much is behind it.
facts.nuclear_power: The energy comes from mass that is simply gone, and the amount is set by the most famous equation there is.
facts.fission: A nucleus split by being hit, and it throws out more of what hit it — which is the chain.
facts.waste: A category rather than a substance: it is whatever the process was not for.
facts.recycling: Some materials come back as themselves and some come back worse, and the difference is not about effort.
facts.pollution: The dose and the place, not the substance. Everything is a pollutant somewhere.
facts.tribe: The largest group in which everyone still knows everyone, and that ceiling is roughly 150 people.
facts.justice: Treating like cases alike, which sounds empty until you try to say which cases are alike.
facts.slavery: Owning a person as property, and almost every society practised it until very recently.
facts.class: A division that survives the individuals in it, which is what makes it a class rather than a rank.
facts.peace: Not the absence of war but the presence of something that settles disputes instead.
facts.skeleton: Living tissue with its own blood supply, being rebuilt continuously, and about a fifth of it is replaced each year.
facts.intestine: Seven metres of it, folded into an area of about thirty square metres, which is why it fits.
facts.hormone: A message sent to the whole body, and only the cells with the receptor hear it.
facts.circulation: Harvey worked it out by arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in an hour than the body contains.
facts.breathing: Driven by carbon dioxide rather than by oxygen, which is why you cannot hold your breath to harm.
facts.birth: The moment the lungs take over from the placenta, and the circulation rearranges itself in seconds.
facts.death: Not one event. Different tissues stop at different times, and where the line is drawn has changed with what medicine can do.
facts.ageing: A cell can divide only about fifty times, and the counter is on the end of the chromosome.
facts.genetics: Mendel's paper sat unread for 34 years, and the mechanism he inferred was found long after he died.
facts.respiration: The same reaction as burning, run in about thirty small steps so the energy comes out in usable pieces.
facts.reproduction: Sex costs half your genes in every offspring, and almost everything complex does it anyway.
facts.predation: It shapes both sides, and the prey is usually running for its life while the predator is running for its dinner.
facts.decomposition: Without it every atom life ever used would still be locked in a corpse.
facts.space: Not a container things sit in. It is a relation between things, and it can stretch.
facts.spacetime: One thing, not two, and different observers slice it differently.
facts.velocity: Speed with a direction, and it only exists relative to something else.
facts.pressure: Force spread over area, which is why a drawing pin works and a bed of nails does not hurt.
facts.heat: Energy in transit because of a temperature difference. A thing does not contain heat.
facts.thermodynamics: Four laws, and the second one is the reason anything happens in a direction.
facts.relativity: It starts from one stubborn fact: everyone measures light at the same speed, however they are moving.
facts.quantum_mechanics: It predicts what fraction of many identical experiments give each result, and refuses to say more.
facts.uncertainty_principle: Not a limit on instruments. A particle does not have a precise position and momentum at once.
facts.rock: An aggregate of minerals, and there are only three ways to make one.
facts.igneous_rock: The crystal size tells you how fast it cooled, and nothing else needs to be known.
facts.sedimentary_rock: The only rock that keeps a record, because it is the only one made without destroying what came before.
facts.metamorphic_rock: Changed by heat and pressure without ever melting, which is the whole definition.
facts.sediment: Sorted by the water that carried it, so grain size records how fast the current was.
facts.silt: Between sand and clay, and it is what makes a floodplain worth farming.
facts.weathering: Breaking rock where it stands, which is different from carrying it away.
facts.reduction: Gaining electrons, and it cannot happen without something else losing them.
facts.solvent: Like dissolves like, and that one rule decides most of what mixes with what.
facts.valence: How many bonds an atom makes, and it is set by how far its outer shell is from full.
facts.organic_chemistry: It was named for the belief that these compounds needed a living thing to make them, which was disproved in 1828.
facts.isomer: The same atoms in the same numbers, arranged differently, and behaving nothing alike.
facts.boiling: It happens when the vapour pressure inside equals the pressure outside, which is why altitude changes the number.
facts.plain: Flat because something levelled it, and usually that something was water.
facts.forest: It makes its own rain, and past a certain size cutting it stops that.
facts.grassland: Kept treeless by fire and grazing, not by climate. Most of it could be forest.
facts.wetland: Waterlogged ground, and the waterlogging is what makes it store carbon instead of releasing it.
facts.coast: The only landscape rebuilt twice a day, and it is a system rather than a line.
facts.prairie: Two metres of the best soil on Earth, made by grass roots dying and being replaced for ten thousand years.
facts.lake: Geologically temporary. Every one of them is filling in, and most last only thousands of years.
facts.groundwater: There is about a hundred times more fresh water below ground than in all the rivers and lakes together.
facts.weather: The atmosphere redistributing heat from the equator to the poles, and everything else is detail.
facts.climate: Weather is what happens; climate is the distribution it is drawn from.
facts.drought: Defined against expectation, so a wet country can have one on rainfall a dry one would call normal.
facts.greenhouse_effect: Without it the Earth would average about minus eighteen degrees. The question has never been whether it exists.
facts.smelting: Not melting. It is a chemical reaction that takes the oxygen off the metal.
facts.casting: Every casting shrinks as it cools, so the pattern must be made larger than the thing wanted.
facts.forging: It does not just shape the metal, it aligns the grain, which is why a forged part is stronger than a machined one.
facts.welding: Making two pieces into one piece, which is different from sticking them together.
facts.weaving: Two sets of thread at right angles, and the cloth's whole behaviour comes from the angle you pull it at.
facts.dyeing: Most dyes will not stay on the fibre without a mordant, which is a metal salt that binds to both.
facts.tanning: Skin rots and leather does not, because the tannin cross-links the collagen so bacteria cannot break it.
facts.food: The only thing an animal must take from outside to rebuild itself with, and it is both fuel and parts.
facts.cooking: It externalises digestion, and it may be why the human gut is short and the brain is large.
facts.baking: Dry heat from all sides, and the crust forms first and then holds the shape.
facts.roasting: The browning is not caramelisation. It is protein and sugar reacting together, and it makes hundreds of new compounds.
facts.preservation: Every method does one of four things: take the water, take the oxygen, take the temperature, or take the pH.
facts.famine: Rarely a shortage of food. Almost always a collapse in who can get hold of it.
facts.aqueduct: Gravity does all the work, and the fall must be gentle and unbroken over tens of kilometres.
facts.sewer: London built one because of the smell, and it stopped the cholera by accident.
facts.village: Small enough that everyone is known, which is a form of enforcement as much as of company.
facts.farm: It is an argument with succession: every field would rather be a forest.
facts.railway: Steel on steel has almost no grip, which is the point and also the problem.
facts.canoe: The first boats were hollowed logs, and stability came at the cost of speed from the start.
facts.raft: It does not need to be watertight, which is why it is the oldest craft there is.
facts.rocket: It pushes against nothing. It throws mass backwards, and the reaction is the thrust.
facts.navigation: Latitude is easy and longitude is a clock problem, and that took four hundred years to accept.
facts.radioactivity: Nothing you do to an atom changes when it will decay. Heat, pressure and chemistry make no difference.
facts.fusion: Easy in a star and hard everywhere else, because a star has gravity holding it together and we do not.
facts.superconductivity: Not very low resistance. Exactly zero, and a current started in a loop will run for years.
facts.tool: Using one is common in animals. Making one to make another is nearly ours alone.
facts.pulley: Each extra line halves the force and doubles the distance, and the total work is unchanged.
facts.mechanism: Parts arranged so that one motion determines another, which is what makes it a mechanism rather than a heap.
facts.program: Instructions stored in the same memory as the data, which is what made a computer general.
facts.network: Its value rises faster than its size, which is why the second telephone was worth more than the first.
facts.artificial_intelligence: The goalposts move: once something works it stops counting as intelligence.
facts.topology: What survives stretching. A cup and a doughnut are the same, and the hole is why.
facts.medicine: For most of its history it did more harm than good, and the turn came within living memory.
facts.drug: The dose makes the poison, and there is nothing that is not a poison at some dose.
facts.dose: The gap between the dose that works and the dose that harms is called the therapeutic index, and for some drugs it is very narrow.
facts.hygiene: Semmelweis showed hand-washing cut deaths from 18% to 2%, and was driven out of the profession for it.
facts.vitamin: Thirteen substances with nothing chemically in common. What unites them is only that we cannot make them.
facts.malnutrition: It includes having too much as well as too little, and both can be in the same person.
facts.mental_illness: Diagnosed almost entirely by description rather than by test, which is unusual in modern medicine.
facts.sedan: Three boxes: engine, people, luggage — and the luggage box is sealed off from the cabin.
facts.hatchback: Two boxes. The luggage space is inside the cabin and the back window lifts with the door.
facts.suv: It began as a car body on a truck's ladder frame, which is why the early ones handled as they did.
facts.pickup: An open bed behind a closed cab, and the bed is structurally separate from it.
facts.coupe: Two doors, and the name comes from a cut-down horse carriage — coupé means cut.
facts.convertible: Removing the roof removes most of the structure, so the floor has to be rebuilt.
facts.estate_car: The roofline runs flat all the way to the tail instead of dropping.
facts.limousine: Named after a region of France, for a cloak, because of the driver's hood.
facts.jeep: Designed to a US Army specification in 1940 that gave the bidders 49 days.
facts.taxi: Named after the taximeter, which is the actual innovation — the vehicle was already there.
facts.bulldozer: The tracks matter more than the blade: they spread the weight so it does not sink into what it is pushing.
facts.fire_engine: It carries a pump rather than much water. The water comes from the hydrant it parks beside.
facts.toyota: It began as a loom company, and the car business was funded by selling a weaving patent.
facts.ford: The moving line cut assembly of a Model T from twelve hours to ninety-three minutes.
facts.volkswagen: Founded by the German state in 1937 to build one specific cheap car, and it nearly died in 1945.
facts.ferrari: The road cars exist to fund the racing team, which is the opposite of every other manufacturer.
facts.tesla: Named after Nikola Tesla, and the first car was a Lotus Elise with the engine taken out.
facts.mercedes: Named after a customer's eleven-year-old daughter.
facts.bmw: It made aircraft engines first, and the roundel is the Bavarian flag rather than a propeller.
facts.honda: Started by bolting surplus army generator engines onto bicycles in 1946.
facts.race: The rules exist to make the comparison mean something, which is why they are always argued about.
facts.beauty: Some of it is agreed across every culture ever tested, and some of it is entirely local.
facts.disorder: A pattern of difficulty, named because it recurs — not because a cause is known.
facts.syndrome: Symptoms that travel together, which is a clue that one thing is behind them.
facts.therapy: About half the benefit across every school of it comes from things all schools share.
facts.treatment: It has to be compared against doing nothing, because a great many things get better anyway.
facts.patient: The word means one who suffers, and until recently it also meant one who waits.
facts.effect: What follows, and separating it from what merely accompanies is most of science.
facts.cause: Almost nothing has one. What is called the cause is the part that was unusual.
facts.factor: One of the things a result depends on, and the interesting ones are those that limit it.
facts.variable: Something that could have been otherwise, which is what makes it worth measuring.
facts.culture_biology: Growing an organism deliberately, and about 99% of bacteria will not do it.
facts.powder: Grinding does not change the substance. It changes the surface, and the surface is what reacts.
facts.paste: Enough liquid to move and not enough to flow, which is a narrow band.
facts.cluster: Things found together more often than chance allows, which is a claim about the expected rate.
facts.group: Members and a boundary, and the boundary is usually doing more work than the members.
facts.disc: Spinning material flattens into one, whatever it started as, because only the spin axis survives collapse.
facts.stain: Cells are nearly transparent, so almost nothing in microbiology could be seen before dyes.
facts.microscope: Two lenses beat one, and the limit is not the glass but the wavelength of light.
facts.stand: Something whose only job is to hold another thing still.
facts.dynasty: Power inherited rather than chosen, and its problem is always the succession.
facts.sector: Primary takes from nature, secondary makes, tertiary serves — and countries move through them in order.
facts.economy: The study of what people do when they cannot have everything, which is always.
facts.conflict: Two parties wanting things that cannot both happen, which is not the same as disliking each other.
facts.missile: The difference from a rocket is that it corrects itself on the way.
facts.guidance: Measure the error, act to reduce it, repeat — and almost everything that steers itself does exactly this.
facts.feedback: Sending part of the output back to the input, and the sign of it decides everything.
facts.output: What comes out, and what counts as it is a decision about where you drew the boundary.
facts.result: What actually happened, as against what could have.
facts.molten_gold: Gold melts at 1064°C and comes back exactly as it was, every time.
facts.molten_bronze: It melts around 950°C — lower than either metal it is made of.
facts.travertine: Freshwater limestone, laid down where groundwater loses its carbon dioxide at the surface. It is one of the few rocks you can watch being made.
facts.velebit: Croatia's longest range, 145 km from Senj to the source of the Zrmanja, and karst the whole way. Its highest point is Vaganski vrh at 1,758 m.
facts.senj: A harbour at the seaward end of the Vratnik pass, inhabited for more than 3,000 years because it is where the road over the Velebit reaches the Adriatic.
facts.uskok: Christian refugees from Ottoman Bosnia, resettled at Senj to hold the Habsburg frontier. Venice called them pirates; the Uskok War ended in 1617 with their expulsion.
facts.nehaj: Eighteen metres tall, twenty-three wide, walls two to three metres thick, five towers and eleven cannon openings — finished in 1558 and built out of the town it was defending.
facts.plitvice: Sixteen lakes in a staircase, dropping 133 m from the first to the last over barriers that are still growing by up to 13 mm a year.
facts.sticky_rice_mortar: Lime mortar with boiled sticky rice in it. The starch controls how the lime crystallises, and the result outlasts lime alone by centuries.
facts.shona: The people whose ancestors built Great Zimbabwe, and whose descendants were told for most of a century that they had not.
facts.lalibela: Eleven churches cut downward into scoriaceous basalt — not built up but excavated out, four of them free-standing in their own trenches.
facts.great_zimbabwe: Dry-stone granite with no mortar anywhere in it. The Great Enclosure wall runs about 250 m and stands 11 m high, laid course by course without a binder.
facts.olduvai_gorge: Thirty miles of gorge cut 90 m down through lake beds, so the last two million years lie exposed in order. Volcanic ash from Olmoti and Kerimasi sealed each layer as it formed.
facts.aksum_obelisk: Twenty-four metres and 160 tonnes of phonolite, carved as a multi-storey building with false doors and windows. Italy took it in 1937 and flew it home in three pieces in 2005.
facts.twyfelfontein: More than 5,000 engravings chiselled through the dark desert varnish on sandstone, so the picture is simply the paler rock underneath.
facts.kilwa_kisiwani: A Swahili city built of coral limestone that took the Sofala gold trade in the 13th century and shipped ivory, incense and cloth to Arabia, India and China.
facts.mapungubwe: A kingdom of 5,000 people by 1250, trading gold and ivory for Indian glass beads. Its golden rhinoceros is gold foil over wood, and apartheid governments tried to bury the whole find.
facts.ngorongoro: The largest intact unflooded caldera on Earth: a volcano perhaps 5,000 m high that fell into itself two to three million years ago, leaving a 260 km² floor 610 m below the rim.
facts.desert_varnish: A dark manganese and iron coating that builds on desert rock over thousands of years, thinner than a sheet of paper. Scratch through it and the pale rock beneath is your line.
facts.anangu: The Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara people of the central Australian desert, to whom Uluru is sacred and who hold its title.
facts.gunditjmara: The people of western Victoria who dammed a lava flow to farm eels, six and a half thousand years ago.
facts.rapa_nui_people: The Polynesian people of Easter Island, who carved more than nine hundred moai between about 1250 and 1500.
facts.uluru: A single mass of coarse arkose standing 348 m above the plain with a 9.4 km perimeter, and far more of it underground than above.
facts.budj_bim: Basalt weirs, dams and channels built to hold and harvest short-finned eels. One trap at Lake Condah carbon-dates to 6,600 years — older than the pyramids and still a working idea.
facts.moai: More than nine hundred figures, nearly all cut from compressed volcanic ash at one quarry, averaging 4 m and 12.5 tonnes. The largest raised weighed 86 tonnes.
facts.nan_madol: Ninety-two artificial islets stacked out of natural basalt columns on a reef flat, laid like logs. Megalithic building began about 1180.
facts.sydney_opera_house: Its shells were unbuildable until Jørn Utzon cut every one from the surface of a single sphere, so the same precast rib could be repeated instead of individually formed.
facts.great_barrier_reef: The largest structure built by living things: 2,300 km of coral, visible from orbit and made entirely of the skeletons of animals a few millimetres across.
facts.columnar_basalt: Lava that cracks into hexagons as it cools and contracts, splitting downward into columns. Nature supplies the pillar already quarried.
facts.megalith: A stone too big to carry, moved anyway. The whole technology is levers, rollers, ramps and a great many people who all turned up.
facts.corbel_vault: Each course laid a little further in than the one below until the two sides meet. No arch, no keystone, no mortar — and Newgrange's has stood for five thousand years.
facts.skara_brae: Ten stone houses on Orkney with stone beds, stone dressers and a central hearth, built where there were no trees. A storm in 1850 stripped the dune off them.
facts.newgrange: A passage tomb of about 3100 BC with an opening above the door that lets the midwinter sunrise run 19 m to the back chamber for roughly seventeen minutes.
facts.lascaux: Nearly 6,000 figures in iron and manganese pigment, blown through a tube or blotted on, 17,000 to 22,000 years old. Twelve hundred visitors a day damaged them in fifteen years.
facts.iron_bridge: The first cast-iron bridge, opened 1781: 30.6 m of span and 384 tonnes of iron, jointed with mortises, tenons and dovetails because the only people who knew how to join a frame were carpenters.
facts.wieliczka: 287 km of galleries down to 327 m, worked from the 13th century to 1996, with four chapels and a chandelier carved out of the rock salt by the miners.
facts.rock_salt: Halite left behind by a sea that dried up. It is soft enough to carve and strong enough to hold a roof, which is why salt mines have chapels in them.
facts.neolithic: The stretch in which people started farming, staying put and building in stone. Everything monumental before metal belongs to it.
facts.abraham_darby: Third of the Coalbrookdale Darbys. His grandfather worked out how to smelt iron with coke instead of charcoal; he spent the family fortune casting the first iron bridge.
facts.jorn_utzon: Won Sydney with a drawing nobody could cost, then spent years finding the geometry that made it buildable — and resigned before it opened.
facts.nabataean: Desert traders who got rich on incense and then spent it on water: dams, conduits and cisterns that turned a canyon into a city of 20,000.
facts.gobekli_tepe: Limestone enclosures raised from about 9500 BCE by people who had not yet taken up farming. Monumental building came before the crop, not after it.
facts.petra: Facades cut into sandstone, reached through a natural cleft only three or four metres wide. Al-Khazneh is 24 m across and 37 m high, carved top-down out of the cliff.
facts.borobudur: Nine stacked platforms of andesite — six square, three round — carrying 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddhas. Seen from above it is a mandala; walked, it is a path.
facts.nazca_lines: Over 1,300 km of line made by lifting rust-coated pebbles off pale subsoil. A hummingbird 93 m long, a condor 134 m, all still there because it never rains.
facts.geoglyph: A drawing made by moving what is already on the ground. Nothing is added, so the picture lasts exactly as long as the ground does.
facts.stupa: A solid dome over a relic, with no interior to enter. You do not go in; you walk around it, and the walking is the point.
facts.hunter_gatherer: How everyone lived for the first ninety-five per cent of the species. Göbekli Tepe is the evidence that they built monuments too.
facts.djenne_mosque: The largest mud-brick building in the world, replastered every year by the whole town. The palm sticks bristling out of its walls are the scaffolding, left permanently in place.
facts.toron: Bundles of palm stick left projecting about 60 cm from a mud wall. They are decoration and permanent scaffolding at once — the building comes with the means of its own repair.
facts.citadelle_laferriere: Built 900 m up a Haitian mountain after independence, with 365 cannon and stores for 5,000 men for a year, against a French invasion that never came. It cost up to 20,000 lives to build.
facts.registan: Three madrasahs round a square in Samarkand. One has tigers with the sun on their backs in its tilework — living creatures, in a tradition that mostly refuses them.
facts.madrasah: A college built round a courtyard: lecture rooms, a mosque and cells to sleep in, all facing inward. Ulugh Beg taught astronomy in his.
facts.tilework: Glazed ceramic cut and set into pattern. It survives sun and frost that would strip paint, which is why the great buildings of Central Asia are still the colour they were built.
facts.mason: The trade that turns a heap of stone into a wall that stands. In Djenné the masons' guild is hereditary, and the mosque is replastered under its direction every year.
facts.guild: A trade that controls who may practise it, what it costs, and who teaches the next lot. It is how a skill survives longer than the people who have it.
facts.turf: Soil held together by living grass roots, cut in blocks. Where there are no trees and no stone it is the wall, the roof and the insulation at once.
facts.kuk_swamp: Drainage ditches dug about 9,000 years ago in the New Guinea highlands to farm taro, and bananas by 6,900. Agriculture was invented here independently, on its own schedule.
facts.great_bath: Twelve metres by seven and 2.4 deep, lined with bitumen to hold water. The oldest public water tank anyone has found, and nobody can say what it was for.
facts.cahokia: A city of up to 15,000 on the Mississippi around 1100, with about 120 earthworks. Monks Mound is 30 m high and holds 622,000 cubic metres of earth, carried basket by basket.
facts.earthwork: A structure made by moving soil. It needs no material anyone has to make, and no tool but a basket — which is why the largest pre-industrial structures in the Americas are earth.
facts.talud_tablero: A sloping face with a framed rectangular panel sitting on it. Teotihuacan's signature, and the way archaeologists trace its influence across Mesoamerica.
facts.farmer: The first job that meant staying in one place, and the one nearly everybody did for ten thousand years.
facts.flying_buttress: A half-arch standing outside the wall, catching the vault's outward push and carrying it to the ground. The wall stops holding the roof up, so the wall can be glass.
facts.gothic: Pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress, working together. Each one alone is a detail; the three at once let a stone building be mostly window.
facts.cathedral: Not a size but a job: the church that holds a bishop's chair. Most take a century or more, so the people who start one are not the people who finish it.
facts.chartres: Rebuilt after the 1194 fire in about twenty-five years, which was extraordinary, and it still has 167 windows of its original glass — most cathedrals lost theirs.
facts.mont_saint_michel: A granite outcrop 92 m high in a bay with a 14 m tidal range, so it is an island twice a day. A causeway built in 1879 stopped the scouring and silted the bay up; a dam and a new bridge undid it.
facts.mbanza_kongo: Capital of the Kingdom of Kongo from about 1390 to 1915, on a mountain at a junction of trade routes. Around 1620 the city and its hinterland held some 130,000 people.
facts.monk: Someone who has given up ordinary life for a rule. Monasteries kept literacy, brewing, herbal medicine and bookkeeping going through centuries when nobody else was doing them at scale.
facts.emperor: A ruler of rulers. Diocletian is the only Roman one who retired, and he built somewhere to retire to first.
facts.amphitheatre: A theatre doubled — seats all the way round instead of a half-circle. The word means exactly that, and the shape exists because the show is in the middle rather than at one end.
facts.diocletians_palace: A retirement palace of Brač limestone finished about 305. When Salona was destroyed its refugees moved inside the walls and never left — about 3,000 people still live in it.
facts.dubrovnik_walls: 1,940 m of uninterrupted circuit up to 25 m high, six metres thick on the landward side and as little as 1.5 on the sea. Three round towers, fourteen square, and more than 120 cannon.
facts.pula_arena: The only Roman amphitheatre with its entire outer wall still standing — 132.5 m by 105.1, four storeys, and four towers each holding two cisterns.
facts.lager_yeast: A hybrid of brewing yeast and a cold-tolerant wild species from Patagonia. It works below 10 °C and settles to the bottom, which is the whole difference between an ale and a lager.
facts.dextrin: Starch broken into shorter chains by dry heat. It is why toasted flour thickens less than raw flour and tastes of something.
facts.silage: Green fodder pickled in its own lactic acid under an airtight cover. It keeps a summer's grass edible through a winter.
facts.dried_chilli: Drying concentrates the capsaicin and lets Maillard reactions run slowly, which is why a dried chilli tastes of raisin and tobacco and a fresh one does not.
facts.crystallised_honey: Honey is supersaturated glucose, so it wants to crystallise. Set honey is not spoiled honey; it is honey doing what the chemistry says it should.
facts.pagoda: A stupa redrawn in timber, storey by storey. The floors are not tied to the central pillar, so in an earthquake they slide against each other instead of snapping.
facts.horyuji: The oldest wooden buildings standing anywhere. Ring-counting puts the felling of the pagoda's central pillar at 594, which is a date read off the timber itself rather than off a document.
facts.giants_causeway: About 40,000 basalt columns, mostly six-sided, the tallest around 12 m. They are cooling cracks — the same pattern dried mud makes, propagated downward through a lava flow.
facts.stonehenge: Sarsen uprights with lintels held on by mortise and tenon, cut in stone — carpentry joints in rock, by people with no metal.
facts.hadrians_wall: 117 km across Britain, built from AD 122 by three legions in about six years. A milecastle every Roman mile and a turret every third of one, so nothing crossed unseen.
facts.dendrochronology: Tree rings vary with the weather, and the pattern is the same across a region. Match a beam's rings to a master sequence and you get the year the tree was felled, not an estimate.
facts.alcove: Where a band of shale sits inside sandstone, water seeps along it and undercuts the cliff. The overhang is not a cave — it is a seep line that ate its way in.
facts.ancestral_puebloan: Farmers of the Colorado Plateau who built in stone under cliff overhangs, and left after a drought that ran from 1276 to 1299.
facts.mesa_verde: Six hundred cliff dwellings of hard sandstone laid in adobe mortar, tucked under seep-cut overhangs. Occupied for seven centuries and empty by about 1285.
facts.teutonic_order: A crusading order that ended up running a state on the Baltic. It built in brick because the north German plain has no building stone at all.
facts.malbork: The largest brick complex in Europe, 21 hectares inside its outer walls, built over 132 years. More than half of it was destroyed in 1945 and it has been under restoration since 1962.
facts.palace: Where power lives rather than where it defends itself. The distinction matters: a palace is built to be seen into, a fortress to be kept out of.
facts.cenote: A sinkhole into the water table. The Yucatán has no rivers at all — the limestone drains everything underground — so a cenote is the only water there is.
facts.chichen_itza: El Castillo has 91 steps on each of four faces and one at the top: 365. Around the equinoxes the northwest corner throws triangular shadows down the north balustrade that read as a serpent.
facts.inselberg: An island mountain: the hard plug of an old volcano left standing when everything softer around it eroded away. Uluru and Sigiriya are both this.
facts.sigiriya: A palace on a granite plug 180 m high, built 477–495 CE, entered through a gateway shaped as a lion. Its polished plaster mirror wall carries over 1,500 verses left by visitors from the 8th century on.
facts.dome: An arch spun about its own axis, so every line through it is an arch. It carries itself in compression and needs no beam, which is why it can span what nothing else can.
facts.pendentive: A curved triangle that lets a round dome sit on a square room. Without it a dome needs a round wall under it, and rooms are not round.
facts.hagia_sophia: Built in five years and ten months, from February 532. Its first dome came down in 558; the replacement is ribbed, 33 m across and raised 6.25 m higher, and it has stood ever since.
facts.sacsayhuaman: Limestone blocks of up to 200 tonnes fitted so closely a sheet of paper will not go between them, with no mortar anywhere. The largest came about 35 km.
facts.wrought_iron: Iron with almost no carbon and a grain of slag stringers running through it. It bends rather than snapping, and it rusts slowly, which is why Victorian ironwork is still standing.
facts.eiffel_tower: 7,300 tonnes of puddled iron in 18,038 parts, held by 2.5 million rivets. The curve of the legs is not decoration: it is the shape that balances wind load at every height.
facts.maze: A plan whose purpose is to cost you time. At Himeji the keep is 130 m from the gate and the path to it is 325.
facts.himeji: Eighty-three buildings, white with fire-resistant lime plaster over every timber surface. Himeji was firebombed in 1945 and the castle came through; one bomb landed on the top floor and did not go off.
facts.pont_du_gard: 48.8 m high and 274 m long, laid dry — no mortar, no clamps, 50,400 tonnes of limestone held by friction and its own weight. It falls 2.5 cm across its whole span.
facts.surveying: Measuring the ground accurately enough to build across it. A Roman aqueduct falling one metre in three thousand is a survey error budget, not a construction one.
facts.potala: Stone walls three metres thick and five at the base, battered inward, with copper poured into the foundations against earthquakes. The shell went up in three years and the inside took forty-five.
facts.benin_moat: A ditch and rampart around Benin City, about 12 km long, reaching 17 m from the bottom of the ditch to the top of the bank. The inner Iya dates to about 1460.
facts.merv: Not one city but several walled cities side by side, each built fresh on empty ground by a different era. By 1150 it may have been the largest city in the world.
facts.grog: Fired clay ground up and mixed back into raw clay. It has already shrunk as far as it will, so the pot shrinks less and cracks less as it dries.
facts.conchoidal_flake: Struck from glassy stone, a flake comes off in a shell-shaped curve with an edge a few molecules thick. Nothing manufactured was sharper until the twentieth century.
facts.silica_sand: Quartz ground down and nothing else. Quartz has no cleavage planes, so it wears round instead of splitting — which is why the world's beaches are quartz and not feldspar.
facts.crushed_ice: The same ice with far more surface. It chills a drink faster and dilutes it faster, and you cannot have one without the other.
facts.tower_karst: Limestone dissolved away until only steep isolated towers are left, typically six times taller than they are wide. It needs heavy rain and warmth, which is why it is a tropical landform.
facts.ha_long_bay: Some 1,600 limestone towers standing in the sea, 20 million years in the making. The sea then cut notches at its own level into every one of them, at the same height.
facts.reservoir: Water held against a dry season. Whoever controls one controls the year, which is why they are so often built where the temple is.
facts.tikal: A city with no river, no lake and no cenote — it ran entirely on rainwater held in plastered reservoirs. Temple IV stands 70 m from the plaza floor to the top of its roof comb.
facts.bagan: More than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries raised on one plain in two centuries. About 2,200 survive; the 1975 earthquake took many and 2016 damaged nearly 400 more.
facts.shicra: A loose reed bag of rubble, stacked to build a platform. It flexes in an earthquake instead of cracking, and because each bag is woven from a dated plant it tells you exactly when the wall went up.
facts.caral: The oldest urban centre in the Americas, occupied from about 2600 BC. No pottery, no battlements, no weapons and no mutilated bodies — a city built before either of those things.
facts.concentric_castle: A ring of wall inside a ring of wall, the inner one taller, so both can shoot at once and taking the outer gains you a killing ground rather than the castle.
facts.krak_des_chevaliers: Held 2,000 men and was never stormed. Baibars took it in 1271 with a forged letter from the Grand Master telling the garrison to surrender, after 36 days.
facts.balance: It compares two masses rather than measuring one, so it gives the same answer on a mountain, at sea level or on the Moon. A spring scale does not.
facts.quenching_trough: The water beside the anvil. Dropping hot steel into it freezes the crystal structure mid-change, which is what makes it hard — and brittle until it is tempered.
facts.drying: Taking water out slowly enough that what is left does not warp. It is the longest step in papermaking, in timber, in brick and in pasta, and the one that is always rushed.
facts.pietra_dura: Stone cut to a drawn shape and set flush into stone, so the picture is level with the surface and has no paint in it. It cannot fade, because nothing about it is a pigment.
facts.taj_mahal: Its four minarets lean very slightly outward, so that if one ever falls it falls away from the tomb. Twenty-eight kinds of stone are inlaid into the marble, from Afghanistan, Tibet, Sri Lanka and China.
facts.suspension_bridge: The deck hangs from a cable, so the span carries itself in tension. Nothing underneath has to hold it up, which is why it can cross what a pier cannot stand in.
facts.caisson: An upturned box pumped full of compressed air so men can dig underwater inside it. Coming up too fast dissolves nitrogen out of the blood as bubbles, which is how decompression sickness got its other name.
facts.great_house: A Chacoan great house is hundreds of rooms in one planned structure, four storeys in places, and mostly not lived in. Nobody is sure what they were for.
facts.chaco_canyon: Roads up to 97 km long, nine metres wide and dead straight regardless of terrain, in a culture with no wheel and no draught animal. 200,000 conifers were carried in on foot from up to 110 km away.
facts.brooklyn_bridge: Its designer died of tetanus before it began and his son was paralysed by caisson disease building it, so Emily Warren Roebling ran the site for eleven years.
facts.log_building: Horizontal logs notched at the corners so their own weight locks them. It needs an axe and nothing else — no saw, no nail, no mortar — which is why it is the northern forest's building method everywhere at once.
facts.shingle: A thin split board laid overlapping. Split rather than sawn, so the grain runs unbroken end to end and water follows it off instead of soaking in.
facts.kizhi_pogost: Twenty-two domes, 37 m high, of notched pine logs and not one nail in the structure — but about 180,000 of them holding its 60,000 aspen shingles. The famous claim is half true, and the half that is false is the roof.
facts.onion_dome: Wider than the drum it sits on and drawn to a point. It sheds snow, which a hemisphere does not, and the timber frame under the sheathing carries no load from above.
facts.saint_basils: Nine chapels on one foundation, eight around a central one. It was gilded when built; the colours came in between the 1680s and 1848, so nobody in the sixteenth century ever saw it as it looks now.
facts.brimstone_hill: Designed by British engineers and built and maintained by enslaved Africans, on a hill 972 feet above the sea. Guns went up in 1689; by 1736 it carried 49 of them.
facts.sterkfontein: Mrs Ples, found in 1947, dates to between 2.05 and 2.01 million years. Little Foot's date has moved from about 2.6 to about 3.4 million, which rearranges who descended from whom.
facts.patina: The green skin on old copper is a mixture of copper carbonates and sulfates, and it is airtight. Unlike rust it stops the corrosion it came from, which is why a copper roof lasts centuries.
facts.linseed_oil: It does not dry by evaporating — it takes oxygen out of the air and cross-links into a solid film. That reaction gives off heat, which is why a pile of oily rags can set itself alight.
facts.lachrymatory_factor: Cutting an onion releases an enzyme that builds a small sulfur compound in the air. It reaches your eye, meets water, and turns into sulfuric acid, which is the whole reason you cry.
facts.verdigris: Copper acetate: the green pigment made by leaving copper in vinegar fumes. It was the brightest green available for a thousand years and it eats through the paper it is painted on.
facts.galleon: Built to carry cargo across an ocean and fight at the end of it. Spain sailed them in convoy because one ship alone was a prize and forty together were a problem.
facts.old_havana: Founded 1519 on a bay deep enough to hold a treasure fleet. A French corsair burned it in 1555, and the first fortress went up three years later.
facts.fynbos: A fire-dependent shrubland on soil so poor almost nothing else grows. Table Mountain and the Back Table hold about 1,500 plant species in 57 km² — as many as the whole United Kingdom.
facts.table_mountain: Flat on top because it is the floor of an old valley: a syncline of quartzitic sandstone, 450 to 510 million years old, left standing when everything softer around it went.
facts.prison: Holding people as the punishment itself, rather than while they wait for one, is a fairly recent idea. Before it, a gaol was mostly somewhere to keep you until the sentence happened.
facts.apartheid: South Africa's system of racial separation in law, from 1948 to the early 1990s. It was not custom or prejudice alone but statute — registration, pass laws and separate areas, written down and enforced.
facts.robben_island: A prison from the late seventeenth century until 1996. Nelson Mandela was held there for 18 of his 27 years, and it became a World Heritage Site three years after it closed.
facts.muqarnas: Tiers of small niches stacked into a vault, each one holding the next. It carries almost nothing — the structure is behind it — so the ceiling reads as a honeycomb hanging in the air.
facts.alhambra: Begun 1238 under the first Nasrid sultan and finished as a palace-city once a canal brought mountain water up onto the plateau. It was surrendered in 1492 without being attacked.
facts.rock_cut_architecture: Building by removing. There is no foundation, no joint and no possibility of correction — a column is whatever was left standing when the cutting stopped.
facts.ajanta_caves: Thirty cave monuments cut into a basalt cliff, holding the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting. A British officer out hunting tigers was shown the entrance to one in 1819.
facts.leptis_magna: A Punic port that became Rome's third largest in the Mediterranean, because an emperor was born there. Abandoned, it was buried by dunes — which is why so much of it is still standing.
facts.ember: Charcoal burning without a flame, because the volatiles have already gone. It glows rather than flickers, and it is hotter than the fire it came from.
facts.blast: Air pushed into a fire rather than drawn in. It is the whole difference between a fire that cooks and a fire that smelts — above about 1,200 °C nothing happens without it.
facts.mogao_caves: Nearly 500 painted cave temples above a desert oasis, with 46,000 m² of wall painting. One of them was walled up early in the 11th century with some 50,000 manuscripts inside and not opened again until 1900.
facts.mount_fuji: Four volcanoes stacked on the same spot, the newest about 10,000 years old. It has not erupted since 1707 and is not extinct — only quiet.
facts.rolled_oats: Steamed and pressed flat between rollers. Flattening breaks the cell walls, which is why rolled oats cook in minutes and whole groats take an hour.
facts.natto: Soybeans fermented by a hay bacillus that lives on rice straw. It makes long threads of polyglutamic acid, which is the stringiness, and enough vitamin K2 to interfere with warfarin.
facts.firn: Snow that has survived a summer and been packed by the snow above it. Halfway to ice: the crystals have fused but air still gets through, and one more year of burial closes it.
facts.rock_candy: Sugar coming out of a supersaturated syrup onto a string, one molecule at a time in the same orientation. It is a crystal you can grow on a kitchen shelf and eat.
facts.clotted_cream: Cream held just below simmering for hours until the fat rises and sets into a crust. Nothing is added and nothing ferments — it is only heat, time and patience.
facts.phonolite: Fine-grained alkaline lava, too poor in silica to make quartz. Thin slabs ring when struck, which is where the name comes from.
facts.meroe_pyramids: Steep, narrow and small: 6 to 30 m tall and raked to about 70°, where an Egyptian pyramid of the same height sat on a footprint five times larger.
facts.catalhoyuk: A town with no streets. Houses packed wall to wall were entered through the roof, so the rooftops were the streets and a ladder was the front door.
facts.segovia_aqueduct: 167 arches of unmortared granite, 28.5 m at the tallest point. Nothing holds it up but its own weight.
facts.banaue_terraces: Rice cut into a mountainside 1,500 m up, walled with stone and rammed earth and watered by canals from the rainforest above.
facts.ziggurat_of_ur: A solid mass of mud brick, faced in burnt brick set in bitumen. The core is what it is made of; the facing is why any of it is still there.
facts.animal_scale: A reptile scale is not a separate plate. It is a fold of the skin with a thickened keratin layer on top, which is why a snake sheds the whole covering in one piece.
facts.wing_scale: A modified bristle, flattened to a blade on a stalk. Lepidoptera means scale-wing, and the scales are the order.
facts.set_math: A collection considered as one object. "Any collection you can describe" turned out to be a contradiction, so which collections exist is now settled by axiom.
facts.wave_physics: Energy moves; the medium does not. A cork on the sea goes up and down while the wave goes past it.
facts.osteoderm: Bone that grows inside the skin instead of from the skeleton. Crocodile scutes, an armadillo’s shell and a Stegosaurus’s plates are the same trick, arrived at separately.
facts.cone_solid: A surface ruled by straight lines, which is why it can be rolled from a flat sheet and a sphere cannot.
facts.benin_walls: Not a wall but a ditch with its own spoil banked behind it — and not one line but thousands, dividing a whole landscape into enclosures.
facts.tiwanaku: A city on the altiplano beside Lake Titicaca, whose largest single stone block weighs an estimated 131 tonnes.
facts.longmen_grottoes: 2,345 caves cut into limestone cliffs over six centuries. The statues run from 25 mm to 17 m.
facts.ellora_caves: The Kailasa temple was cut downward out of one rock: 85,000 m³ removed, and nothing added.
facts.prambanan: Interlocking andesite blocks, no mortar. It fell in a 16th-century earthquake and was put back together stone by original stone.
facts.jelling_stones: The larger one carries the first written use of the name Denmark by a Dane — a king announcing a country and a religion in the same sentence.
facts.bison: Tens of millions of them made the prairie, grazing hard and moving on before the grass was killed. Shot down to a few hundred by 1889.
facts.taputapuatea: The marae other maraes were founded from — a new one was consecrated with a stone carried from here, so the link across the Pacific was a physical object.
facts.latte_stone: A pillar and a hemispherical cap, set in parallel rows: the foundation of a raised house, and the only megalithic tradition in the Marianas.
facts.el_morro: Two and a half centuries of building on one headland, ending with walls up to 12 m thick standing 43 m above the Atlantic.
facts.head_smashed_in: Twelve metres of bone below an eleven-metre cliff. The structure is not the cliff — it is the drive lanes, hundreds of cairns long, that got the herd there.
facts.gur_e_amir: Timur’s tomb, under a ribbed azure dome 15 m across. Opened in June 1941, two days before the German invasion.
facts.lope_okanda: Over 1,600 petroglyphs on the edge between rainforest and savanna, cut about the time iron-working reached the valley.
facts.roi_mata_domain: A grave found in 1967 by taking the oral tradition seriously enough to dig where it said, and finding a chief with more than 25 of his retinue around him.
facts.zollverein: A colliery built to be looked at: cubic reinforced concrete and steel trusses, and a winding tower that became the symbol of German heavy industry.
facts.konark: A temple built as the sun god’s chariot, with 24 carved stone wheels and seven horses. The tower over the sanctum fell in 1837.
facts.bialowieza: Almost half the wood in it is dead — ten times a managed forest — and half of its 12,000 species need the rotting logs.
facts.amsterdam_canals: Three concentric canals dug in one plan in the 17th century, and the city has been the shape of that plan ever since.
facts.canal_lock: A boat lift with no machinery. Shut both gates, let water in or out, and the boat rides up or down on it.
facts.panama_canal: Not a cut through the isthmus but a staircase over it: ships are lifted 26 m to a lake and let down the other side.
facts.sanchi_stupa: A brick dome over relics, later doubled in size and cased in stone. The gateways came two centuries after the building.
facts.kalyan_minaret: Fired brick in gypsum mortar, 45.6 m of it, standing since 1127. Genghis Khan had it spared while the city around it came down.
facts.carcassonne: Two concentric walls and 52 towers — and a 19th-century restoration that roofed it in slate from a region with no slate in it.
facts.rila_monastery: Burned to the ground in 1833 and rebuilt by public subscription — striped arcades, 300 chambers, and frescoes finished in 1846.
facts.sungbo_eredo: More than 160 km of ditch and bank in laterite, ringing a kingdom, with 20 m from ditch floor to bank rim.
facts.volcanic_ash: Not smoke — rock. Magma torn into fragments under 2 mm across, which is why it settles as a blanket and stays where it lands.
facts.joya_de_ceren: A Maya farming village under ten metres of ash, with the crops still in the ground and nobody in the houses. They had time to leave.
facts.monte_alban: A mountain top flattened by hand, 400 m above the valley and 500 years before Christ, then built on for a millennium.
facts.fasil_ghebbi: Brown basalt trimmed in wine-coloured tuff — Portuguese, Indian and Arab building put together by Ethiopian emperors behind one wall.
facts.bikini_atoll: Twenty-three devices, about 77 megatons, and a fleet on the lagoon floor. Listed by UNESCO for exactly that.
facts.levuka: Fiji’s first colonial capital, kept as it was because the hills behind it left no room to grow and the government left instead.
facts.sangha_trinational: One forest, three countries, and the clearings in it — the bais — are where the elephants can be counted at all.
facts.pantheon: Still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, nineteen centuries on. It gets lighter as it goes up, on purpose.
facts.parthenon: Almost nothing in it is straight. The floor bulges 10.3 cm over 70 m and the columns lean inward, so that it looks straight.
facts.knossos: Lit from above rather than from the sides, so rooms deep inside a dense building still get daylight and air.
facts.meteora: Twenty-four monasteries on top of conglomerate pillars, reached for three centuries only by rope, basket and removable ladder.
facts.pompeii: The bodies rotted and left holes. Fiorelli poured plaster into the holes, and got the people back.
facts.etna: Its own height is not a fixed number: 3,403 m in September 2024, and it changes with every summit eruption.
facts.dome_of_the_rock: An octagon built around one rock, finished in 691–2. The dome is wooden, and the one standing now replaced the original after it fell in 1015.
facts.masada: A desert plateau made habitable by cisterns holding 40,000 m³ — and taken in the end by a ramp 114 m high.
facts.cappadocia: Soft volcanic rock under a hard cap: the cap protects a column while everything around it goes, and then people cut houses into what is left.
facts.grand_canyon: 446 km long and over 1,850 m deep, cut in about five million years through rock two billion years old.
facts.salar_de_uyuni: 10,582 km² of salt whose elevation varies by less than a metre — flat enough that satellites are calibrated against it.
facts.urnes_stave_church: Standing on staves rather than sills, from about 1132 — and carved on the north portal in the last Viking animal style.
facts.harappa: 23,500 people in flat-roofed brick houses on a near-orthogonal plan, with drains. Then the Lahore–Multan railway used it for ballast.
facts.hoover_dam: Poured in blocks with 937 km of pipe inside them, because left to itself the concrete would have taken 125 years to cool.
facts.grand_canal: 1,776 km of canal with a summit 42 m up, and the pound lock — invented for it in 984 — is what let boats get over the top.
facts.suomenlinna: A star fort bent onto six rocky islands, called the Gibraltar of the North, surrendered after two months.
facts.todai_ji: 500 tonnes of bronze inside what was, until 1998, the largest wooden building in the world — and the hall is 30% smaller than the one before it.
facts.qhapaq_nan: About 40,000 km of road with no wheel on it anywhere, and fibre bridges that had to be rebuilt every two years.
facts.cologne_cathedral: Begun 1248, abandoned around 1560, finished in 1880 to the medieval drawings that had survived the gap — 632 years, and it was the tallest building on Earth for four of them.
facts.notre_dame: The weight of the roof is carried outside the building, which is what lets the walls be thin and the windows large. The roof itself burned in 2019.
facts.yellowstone: The first national park, and the reason it is worth protecting is a magma chamber: at least 1,283 geysers and 10,000 hydrothermal features over one caldera.
facts.iguazu_falls: Three layers of basalt make a two-step staircase 2.7 km wide, and about half the river goes down one throat in it.
facts.angel_falls: A plunge of 807 m off the edge of a table mountain — far enough that in the dry season the water is mist before it lands.
facts.seokguram: An artificial granite dome assembled with stone rivets and no mortar, which let it breathe — until a concrete restoration stopped it.
facts.port_arthur: A prison whose outer wall is the sea. The only way off the peninsula was a 30-metre neck, fenced, and lined with dogs.
facts.kakadu_rock_art: More than 5,000 recorded sites, some paintings up to 20,000 years old, on ground occupied continuously for around 60,000.
facts.tash_rabat: Thirty-one domed stone rooms at 3,200 m, each lit through a hole at the top of its own dome.
facts.larabanga_mosque: Eight metres square, twelve conical buttresses, and timbers laid through the walls — adobe needs help, and this is what the help looks like.
facts.volubilis: Fifty-eight olive-pressing complexes in one Roman town, and its stone later went into Meknes.
facts.ayutthaya: A capital on an island made by three rivers, which is a moat you do not have to dig — until a siege lasts fourteen months.
facts.baalbek: The largest ancient block known is still lying in the quarry: 19.6 m long and an estimated 1,650 tonnes, never moved.
facts.aral_sea: The fourth-largest lake on Earth in 1960, and a tenth of that by 2007. Nothing was done to the lake — the work was all done to the two rivers.
facts.sagrada_familia: Gaudí found his arches by hanging weighted strings upside down: a chain in tension, inverted, is a line in pure compression.
facts.hwaseong: Built 1794–96 with pulleys and paid labour, and written up afterwards in ten volumes — including the wages.
facts.sundarbans: A forest standing in salt and airless mud, breathing through roots that grow upward — and a sea wall for millions of people.
facts.cueva_de_las_manos: Over 2,000 hands, 829 left to 31 right — because you hold the pipe in the hand you are better with and stencil the other one.

0.w: Rain, frost and lichen break stone into grains over centuries. Mix in dead plants and you have soil — roughly 45% mineral, 5% once-living.

1.w: Sand is only rock ground small: grains between 0.06 and 2 mm. Most of it is quartz, because quartz outlasts everything else.

2.w: Strike two stones and you shear off fragments hot enough to glow. Cutting tools are far older, but this is how every fire began for a million years.

3.w: Flint breaks in smooth conchoidal curves, so almost every fracture leaves a working edge. Obsidian breaks the same way and finer still — fine enough that surgeons occasionally still use it.

4.w: Water fills the gaps between soil grains and lets them slide. Mud is soil that has lost its grip.

5.w: The finest particles settle out last: clay, flat sheets of aluminium silicate under 0.002 mm across. Wet, the sheets slip over each other — that is why clay is plastic.

6.w: Straw stops drying mud from cracking as it shrinks. The same trick holds plaster and cob walls together.

7.w: Sun-dried mud brick built Jericho, Babylon and much of the American Southwest. No fuel required — only weeks of dry weather.

8.w: Around 600 °C the water chemically bound inside the clay is driven out, and higher still the particles fuse. Either way it is irreversible: a fired pot will never be mud again.

9.w: Silica melts at about 1700 °C, which no early furnace could reach. Wood-ash potash drops that to roughly 1000 °C, and glass becomes possible.

10.w: Flood a shallow pan, let the sun take the water, sweep up what stays. Seawater is 3.5% salt by weight.

11.w: Salt water pulls water out of any cell it touches. That is the whole principle of preserving in brine — the microbes dry out before the food does.

12.w: Water is one of very few substances that expands as it freezes. Ice floats, so lakes freeze from the top and life survives underneath.

13.w: Turning 1 litre of water to steam takes five times more energy than heating it from freezing to boiling. That hidden energy is why steam scalds.

14.w: A spark only needs something dry and thin enough to catch. Control of fire predates our own species — Homo erectus was carrying it into caves well over a million years ago.

15.w: Heat wood without air and the water and tar bake off, leaving almost pure carbon. Charcoal burns far hotter than the wood it came from.

16.w: Ash is what will not burn: the minerals the tree drew out of the soil, mostly potassium and calcium salts.

17.w: Water leached through wood ash dissolves potassium carbonate. The solution is caustic enough to dissolve fat — and skin.

18.w: Castile soap is olive oil and lye, nothing else. The lye splits the fat into glycerol and soap, and is entirely used up doing it.

19.w: A tree is a plant that solved a problem: build a trunk of dead wood and you can hold your leaves above everyone else's.

20.w: Vachellia tortilis, the classic African acacia, is native to savanna and Sahel and tolerates drought, extreme heat and sandy, stony soil that would defeat most trees.

21.w: Wood is cellulose fibres set in lignin — nature's fibreglass. Along the grain it rivals steel for strength per kilogram.

22.w: Dried stalks: the part of a crop with no food value left, and the best tinder, thatch and bedding humans ever had for free.
