950.w: Hydrogen peroxide oxidises the selenol of a selenocysteine residue, and glutathione then reduces it back. Selenium is there because its Se-H is far more acidic than a thiol — pKa 5.43 against roughly 8.3 — so it is already reactive.

951.w: Molybdenum rides on a pterin cofactor in the mitochondrial intermembrane space. It hands one oxygen atom to sulfite, making sulfate, and drops from Mo(VI) to Mo(IV) doing it. That is how sulfur from cysteine and methionine leaves.

952.w: 2 H+ + 2 O2- → O2 + H2O2, and it runs diffusion-limited — as fast as two molecules can find each other. Different lineages built the same trick around copper and zinc, manganese, iron or nickel.

953.w: Three sodium out, two potassium in, one ATP spent. One net positive charge leaves each cycle, so the pump is electrogenic — the resting membrane potential of every cell you have is this transaction, repeated.

954.w: Sodium channels open and sodium floods in; potassium channels open behind them and potassium leaves. Remarkably few ions actually cross — the concentrations inside and out barely change — and the voltage swings all the way regardless.

955.w: Beta-carotene 15,15'-dioxygenase cuts a beta-carotene down the middle: beta-carotene + O2 gives two retinal. One pigment molecule out of a carrot becomes two of the molecule an eye actually runs on.

956.w: 11-cis-retinal is bound covalently to a lysine in opsin's seventh helix through a Schiff base. One photon isomerises it to all-trans, and that straightening is the receptor switching on. Everything downstream of seeing starts there.

957.w: Magnesium burns at about 3,100 °C with a brilliant white light strong in ultraviolet, and what falls out of it is a white powder. Early photographers set light to the metal to light a room.

958.w: Calcium is reactive enough that finely divided it catches fire in air on its own, taking oxygen and nitrogen at once. The oxide left behind is quicklime — the same compound a limekiln drives out of limestone, reached from the other side.

959.w: Zinc burns in air with a bright bluish-green flame and the fume coming off it settles as a white powder. Alchemists burned the metal on purpose to collect it and called what they got philosopher's wool.

960.w: Between about 300 and 800 °C copper takes oxygen straight out of the air and goes black. Potters use that black powder deliberately: fired into a glaze it comes back blue, green or red depending on what the kiln does.

961.w: Dry oxygen leaves iron almost alone — it is the moisture in ordinary air that lets the reaction run. And rust is flaky and friable, so unlike aluminium's oxide it gives the iron underneath no protection whatsoever.

962.w: Molten lead under a forced draught of air at around 450 °C turns to litharge. Below 486 °C it comes out red and tetragonal, above it yellow and orthorhombic — the same compound, two ways of stacking it.

963.w: Mercury held in oxygen at roughly 350 °C turns to a red powder. Heat the powder harder and it hands the oxygen back — which is how Priestley found the gas in 1774, some years before anyone had a name for it.

964.w: Aluminium is very reactive with oxygen. A film of oxide about 5 nanometres thick forms on any fresh surface almost instantly and then stops the reaction dead. The metal's famous inertness is the film, not the metal.

965.w: Copper and sulfur combine directly, faster the finer the copper and the hotter it gets, into the black solid that occurs in the ground as chalcocite — the mineral most of the world's copper is roasted out of.

966.w: Zinc and sulfur ignited together combine in a single flash. Add a few parts per million of another metal and the product glows when something hits it — this was the screen that flickered under Rutherford's alpha particles.

967.w: Molten lead combines directly with sulfur. What it makes is galena, the main lead-bearing mineral and the rock nearly all the world's lead has been roasted out of — and it is mostly found sitting alongside zinc ores.

968.w: Silver does not react with air even at red heat, but it reacts with sulfur readily. So the black on old silver is not an oxide at all — it is silver sulfide, built out of the trace sulfur compounds drifting past it.

969.w: Ground together, mercury and sulfur make a black compound the alchemists called aethiops mineralis. Heated in a flask it vaporises and recondenses red — the vermilion Jabir ibn Hayyan wrote down in the early 9th century.

970.w: Each sodium atom hands one electron to a chlorine atom. Both end up charged, both end up stable, and they stack one-to-one into a lattice. A metal that catches fire in water and a green poison gas, making the one rock people eat.

971.w: The salt that is not table salt. Most of it goes onto fields as potash, because potassium is the nutrient that runs out first for a great many plants; the rest goes into low-sodium salt, cut with the ordinary kind to hide the taste.

972.w: A few parts per million of this in table salt is the whole of what 'iodised' means. It is the commonest additive used for it, and a public-health measure against iodine deficiency in populations that get little seafood.

973.w: In trace amounts in drinking water and in toothpaste, this is what hardens a tooth. The fluoride works itself into the enamel as fluorapatite — a mineral that is already a naturally occurring component of enamel.

974.w: Hydrogen and chlorine combine straight into hydrogen chloride, and blue light on its own is enough to set it going. Dissolve the gas in water and it comes apart completely into hydronium and chloride: that is hydrochloric acid.

975.w: Tungsten powder and carbon held between 1,400 and 2,000 °C combine into a compound about 9 to 9.5 on Mohs — as hard as corundum, approaching diamond. It is what the tip of the tool that cuts the steel is made of.

976.w: Quicklime and coke in an electric arc furnace at about 2,200 °C give calcium carbide and carbon monoxide. The reaction takes energy in rather than giving it out, which is why it had to wait for the electric furnace — 1892.

977.w: Water landing on calcium carbide gives acetylene and slaked lime and nothing else is needed — Wöhler found that in 1862. Burnt with oxygen the gas passes 3,300 °C, the hottest flame any common pair of gases makes.

978.w: Held at 1,200 °C in nitrogen, titanium turns into its nitride. The powder is brown, but laid down as a thin coating it looks gold — that is the gold film on a drill bit, and it is there for edge retention, not for looks.

979.w: A magnesium fire does not stop when the oxygen does. It goes on burning in pure nitrogen, making the nitride, and it goes on burning in carbon dioxide too, stripping the oxygen out of it and leaving loose carbon behind.

980.w: Force air in and the carbon gets all the oxygen it can use, so every atom of it ends up in carbon dioxide. This is the complete burn — same fuel, different product, and nothing decides which but the air supply.

981.w: Take the air away and the same carbon burns short. With too little oxygen to reach carbon dioxide, what comes off instead is carbon monoxide — colourless, odourless, and the commonest fatal air poisoning in many countries.

982.w: Burning sulfur gives a colourless gas that smells of a struck match. Volcanic eruptions are the largest source of it on Earth, and the Romans found that burning sulfur inside an empty wine vessel kept the next wine sweet.

983.w: Hydrogen over molten sulfur at about 450 °C gives the rotten-egg gas. It is pungent at first and then it is not: at 100 to 150 ppm the olfactory nerve is paralysed within a few breaths and the warning simply goes away.

984.w: A lightning channel carries enough energy to break nitrogen's triple bond, and the freed atoms grab oxygen instead. Every strike fixes a little of the air into something that can eventually reach a root.

985.w: Ammonia burning in oxygen at about 900 °C over a platinum gauze comes out as nitric oxide. It is the first step of the Ostwald process, and it arrives at the same molecule a lightning strike makes, by an entirely different road.

986.w: Nitric oxide is colourless and does not stay colourless. Exposed to oxygen it picks up one more atom and turns reddish-brown with a sharp, acrid smell. That brown is what sits over a city in a photochemical smog.

987.w: Nitrogen dioxide dissolving into rain gives nitrous and nitric acid, and where that rain soaks in, those become nitrate. Nitrate is the form a root can actually take nitrogen up in — the far end of a road that began with a lightning strike.

988.w: One phosphorus with four oxygens around it in a tetrahedron, carrying three negative charges. It is the bridge in the DNA backbone, the bond ATP spends and the head of every phospholipid — one group doing three jobs.

989.w: Ribose is not built from scratch. The pentose phosphate pathway takes glucose 6-phosphate, strips a carbon off it, and hands back ribose 5-phosphate — the sugar every nucleotide is assembled on.

990.w: Ribonucleotide reductase takes one oxygen off the sugar at the 2' position and changes nothing else. That single missing hydroxyl is the entire chemical difference between RNA and DNA.

991.w: ATP is adenosine triphosphate: adenine, a ribose and three phosphates. Take the phosphates and the sugar away and what is left is one of the four letters of the genetic code. The cell pays with the same part it writes with.

992.w: Purine rings are not made and then attached — they are built directly on ribose 5-phosphate, and glycine goes in whole, both its carbons and its nitrogen. Ten steps later comes inosine monophosphate, which forks to adenine or guanine.

993.w: Pyrimidine rings are built first and joined to a sugar afterwards — the reverse of how purines are made. Ammonia and bicarbonate make carbamoyl phosphate, that meets aspartate, the ring closes, and the first finished pyrimidine is uracil's.

994.w: Cytosine is made from uracil rather than alongside it. CTP synthase takes the finished uracil nucleotide and swaps an oxygen for an amino group; the nitrogen arrives as ammonia, released inside the enzyme from glutamine.

995.w: Cytosine is not stable. A water molecule takes its amino group off and leaves uracil — a letter DNA is not supposed to contain. Cells carry uracil glycosylase, an enzyme whose whole job is cutting that mistake back out.

996.w: Thymine is 5-methyluracil and nothing more: uracil with one methyl group added at carbon 5. DNA uses the methylated version, RNA does not bother, and that one carbon is the difference between the two alphabets.

997.w: A pairs with T across two hydrogen bonds, and only with T — the shapes and hydrogen-bond pattern do not fit any other way. That constraint is exactly why Chargaff found, by measurement alone, that A always equals T in any sample of DNA.

998.w: G pairs with C across three hydrogen bonds rather than two, so a run of them is harder to prise apart: GC-rich DNA takes a higher temperature to melt than AT-rich DNA does.

999.w: Stack the pairs and you have the double helix Watson and Crick described in 1953: two antiparallel strands, backbone outside, pairs lying flat as rungs about 2 nanometres apart, one full turn every 3.4 nanometres.

1000.w: Adenine joined to ribose is adenosine — a nucleoside, sugar plus base and nothing more. It is not yet a nucleotide: that needs a phosphate group attached to the sugar.

1001.w: The same chain as DNA with two swaps: ribose for deoxyribose, uracil for thymine. And usually one strand instead of two, which lets it fold back on itself into shapes DNA cannot make.

1002.w: Take the 2' hydroxyl off the sugar and RNA becomes DNA. That hydroxyl is what makes RNA chemically labile, and its absence is what lets the chain flex into the double helix.

1003.w: A tRNA is 76 to 90 nucleotides folded into a clover: a three-base anticodon at one end, an amino acid bolted to the 3' end by an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase. It is the only thing that knows which codon means which amino acid.

1004.w: Take a ribosome apart and roughly 60% of it by mass is RNA. The peptidyl transferase centre — the spot where the peptide bond is actually made — is formed by nucleotides from the 23S rRNA and contains no protein at all.

1005.w: About 60% RNA and 40% protein. The proteins stabilise and position the RNA; the reaction that joins one amino acid to the next is run by the RNA, which is why a ribosome counts as a ribozyme.

1006.w: The anticodon on the tRNA base-pairs with the codon on the mRNA, three letters at a time, and the amino acid it was carrying is added to the growing chain. Nothing in the cell reads the code except this pairing.

1007.w: An RNA strand folds back on itself, and some folds come out with a catalytic pocket. Cech and Altman shared the 1989 Nobel in chemistry for the discovery of catalytic properties of RNA — before that, enzymes were assumed to be protein.

1008.w: A glycerol with two fatty acid tails and a phosphate head. One end wants water and the other refuses it, and that split is the only reason anything alive has an inside.

1009.w: Drop them in water and they sort themselves out: tails huddle away from the water, heads face it, the sheet closes into a hollow sphere. No enzyme, no template, no energy put in — just tails avoiding water.

1010.w: Cholesterol is an animal molecule — plants make only traces and build phytosterols instead. And most of yours is not eaten: a man synthesises about a gram a day against roughly 300 mg on the plate.

1011.w: Cholesterol wedges in between the phospholipids and modulates membrane fluidity over the range of physiological temperatures — stiffening the sheet when it is warm, stopping it setting when it is cold.

1012.w: One carbon holding four hydrogens at the corners of a tetrahedron — the simplest alkane there is. Weight for weight it traps about eighty times as much heat as carbon dioxide over twenty years.

1013.w: Oparin in 1924 and Haldane in 1929 proposed that the early ocean built up organic matter from inorganic gases, and Haldane supplied the word soup. The gases they named are probably not the ones the early Earth actually had.

1014.w: Miller's 1952 flask held methane, ammonia and hydrogen over water in a 2:2:1 ratio, with a spark passed through to simulate lightning. After a week of continuous operation the solution was deep red and turbid, and it held amino acids.

1015.w: A bilayer sac with self-copying chemistry inside it is the smallest thing anyone can call a candidate for early life. Vesicles form on their own and ribozymes catalyse on their own — but a functional protocell that evolves has not yet been made in a lab.

1016.w: Cytoplasm is about 80% water and usually colourless, but it is not a solution in the ordinary sense. It is so crowded with protein and fibre that the things dissolved in it do not behave as they would in dilute water.

1017.w: No nucleus, and rarely any membrane-bound organelle: a single circular bacterial chromosome of DNA located in the cytoplasm, with the machinery loose around it. There are roughly 2×10^30 of them alive on Earth.

1018.w: Archaea look like bacteria and are not. Woese and Fox classified them separately in 1977 on their ribosomal RNA genes alone — before that sequencing, nobody had a reason to think there was a third domain of life.

1019.w: Methanogenesis is a form of anaerobic respiration only known to be conducted by some members of the domain Archaea. Nothing else alive makes methane — not a plant, not an animal, not a bacterium.

1020.w: A genome and a protein coat, and nothing else — no ribosomes, no metabolism, no way to copy itself. It can only replicate inside the living cells of an organism, which is why viruses get called organisms at the edge of life.

1021.w: One cell grows to a set size and divides into two parts, each with the potential to grow to the size of the original. No partner, no gametes, no shuffling. E. coli does it about every 20 minutes at 37 °C.

1022.w: Two cells where there was one, and both of them are the parent. Doubling on a fixed clock is what makes bacterial growth exponential rather than merely fast — the numbers, not the speed, are the point.

1023.w: Yeast does not split down the middle. Saccharomyces cerevisiae divides asymmetrically by budding: a small bulb-like projection swells out of the mother cell and pinches off, leaving a large mother and a small daughter.

1024.w: The bud detaches and is a clone — genetically identical to the parent organism, mutations excepted. A hydra does the same thing at animal scale, growing a whole small hydra off one side and letting it walk away.

1025.w: Cut a stem off and it does not simply die; it answers the wound. Root primordia form from cambial cells in the stem, and the severed piece grows a root system of its own.

1026.w: It is possible to root cuttings in water — a glass on a windowsill will do it, so long as the water is changed often enough to keep bacteria down. The offspring are practically clones of their parent plants.

1027.w: Plant a potato and you get potatoes, with no flower and no seed anywhere in it. And a potato is not a root: it is a stolon whose tip thickened, with all the parts of a normal stem. The eyes are the nodes.

1028.w: Every eye is a bud with a leaf scar beside it, and given warmth it shoots. The tuber is produced in one growing season and used to perennate the plant and as a means of propagation — one year's plant feeding the next year's.

1029.w: A stolon is a stem that grows along the soil surface and forms adventitious roots at the nodes, and new plants from the buds. A strawberry bed can fill a plot without a single seed being set.

1030.w: Where the runner touches down it roots, hormones from those roots trigger a shoot, and the tie back to the parent eventually withers. What is left standing is a separate plant carrying an identical genome.

1031.w: Pulp is a fibrous lignocellulosic material prepared by isolating the cellulose fibres of wood, fibre crops, waste paper or rags. Wood is only about 40 to 45% cellulose — pulping is mostly the business of removing the rest.

1032.w: No animal makes cellulase — not one. Termites keep flagellate protozoa in the hindgut to produce it for them, and the β bonds only come apart into glucose once something else has supplied the enzyme.

1033.w: Animals store glucose as glycogen: the same α bonds as starch but far more branched, so many ends can be cut at once. A 70 kg adult carries roughly 100 to 120 g in the liver and about 400 g in the muscles.

1034.w: Liver glycogen goes back out into the blood; muscle glycogen never does. Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, so the glycogen they store is available solely for internal use and is not shared with other cells.

1035.w: Where water is scarce, opening the pores by day is fatal. A cactus keeps its stomata shut through the day and opens them at night instead — 99% of the 1,700 cactus species run photosynthesis that way round.

1036.w: The night's carbon dioxide is parked as four-carbon malic acid in the cell vacuoles. Come daylight the malate goes to the chloroplasts, turns back into CO2, and feeds the Calvin cycle behind closed pores.

1037.w: A guard cell opens the pore by taking potassium in. Water follows by osmosis, the cell swells, and the pair bow apart. Plants cannot take in carbon dioxide without losing water vapour through the same hole.

1038.w: Water is not pushed up a tree, it is pulled. Evaporation at the leaves puts the whole column under negative pressure, and hydrogen bonds between water molecules hold it together. The cells doing it are dead.

1039.w: The other pipe, and it runs the other way. Sugar made in the leaf is loaded into cells that are still alive, and positive pressure pushes the sap to wherever it is being spent — a root, a fruit, a new shoot.

1040.w: Xylem sap runs up from the roots carrying water and minerals; phloem sap runs down carrying sucrose. Latex and resin are neither of them — separate substances, separately made, doing a different job.

1041.w: Bark is not a skin. It is everything outside the growing layer, and the innermost part of it is the living phloem. Cut a ring of bark the whole way round and the roots are starved: the tree dies.

1042.w: The cork oak grows a bark thick enough to strip without killing the tree, and then grows it back. The cells inside are dead and full of gas, which is why cork floats, springs back, and keeps water out.

1043.w: Cellulose fibres on their own would buckle. Lignin is the water-hating polymer set between them — 20 to 35% of dry wood — and it is why a trunk stands up, why the water pipes hold, and why wood resists rot.

1044.w: Paper needs the lignin gone: it is coloured, it yellows in air, and it weakens the sheet. Lye and sulfide at 170 °C break the bonds tying it to the fibres, and about half the dry wood is left as pulp.

1045.w: Some 500 oaks, and every one loads leaf, acorn and bark with tannic acid against fungi and insects. It is why acorns must be leached before people can eat them, and why oak bark tanned the Old World's leather.

1046.w: Hardwood means wood from a flowering tree, and the giveaway under a lens is pores — vessels, wide tubes carrying water. It does not mean hard. Balsa is a hardwood and is softer than most softwoods.

1047.w: A conifer has no vessels at all. Water and support both go through tracheids, narrow cells doing the two jobs at once. Yew is a softwood, and it is harder than a good many hardwoods.

1048.w: Tree-sized, and still a grass. A culm comes out of the ground already at its final diameter and reaches full height in a single season — some species 91 cm in a day, close to 40 mm an hour.

1049.w: A husk built to float: thick, fibrous, sharply ridged. Coconuts really do colonise beaches this way — but drift models say they could not have crossed the Pacific unaided. Austronesian sailors carried them.

1050.w: The water is the endosperm, still liquid. Layers of it settle onto the shell wall and set as the white flesh — so the drink and the meat are the same tissue caught at two different ages.

1051.w: The fibre in linen, hemp and jute is phloem fibre out of the stem. Retting frees it — micro-organisms rot away the pectin gluing the bundles on. Leaf fibres, like sisal, come out hard and stiff instead.

1052.w: The same sucrose as cane, out of a temperate taproot instead of a tropical stalk. The leaves make it and the root banks it: 12 to 21% by weight, bred up from 8% over two hundred years.

1053.w: Cane is crushed and the juice pressed out of it. Beet is sliced into strips called cossettes and the sucrose is drawn out of the cells into water instead. Two plants, two methods, and the sugar is identical.

1054.w: Tapping is a shallow cut on a spiral. The latex vessels sit in the bark, mostly outside the phloem, and the cut goes just deep enough to open them without touching the growing wood, so the tree carries on.

1055.w: Same family as the fig, Moraceae, and the same trick: what looks like one fruit is many. A mulberry is a multiple fruit two to three centimetres long, built from a whole cluster of separate flowers.

1056.w: The bitter compound in willow bark. The gut turns it into salicylic acid, which is the part that works. Bayer acetylated that in 1897 to make something less punishing on the stomach, and called it aspirin.

1057.w: Autumn-sown wheat will not flower until it has had a long spell of cold — weeks somewhere between 1 and 7 °C. The cold switches off a repressor protein, FLC, and the plant carries the memory of that winter forward.

1058.w: Named after a rice disease. Gibberella fujikuroi floods a seedling with a surplus of growth hormone until it goes long, weak and pale — bakanae, the foolish seedling. The plant's own version drives stem growth.

1059.w: Gibberellin is what drives the stem up, so wheat bred to make less of it stays short. Short straw does not go top-heavy and fall over under heavy fertiliser, and it puts the difference into grain instead.

1060.w: Apples do not come true from seed — one tree's fruit can vary in size, colour and flavour. So every named variety is a cutting joined to a rootstock, cambium pressed to cambium; the top stays itself, the root sets the size.

1061.w: A short-day plant is really a long-night plant. Red light through the day flips phytochrome to its active form — and a few minutes of light in the middle of the night is enough to stop the plant flowering.

1062.w: A biennial: a flat rosette the first year, a spire the second, then it dies. It colonises ground that has been cleared or burnt, and bees climb right inside the tube. Leaves, flowers and seeds are all poisonous.

1063.w: It jams the sodium-potassium pump in heart muscle. Sodium builds up inside the cell, calcium follows it in, and every beat pulls harder. The margin between the dose that works and the dose that poisons is famously narrow.

1064.w: Bell pepper, paprika, jalapeño and cayenne are not different plants. They are cultivars of one species, Capsicum annuum, and what separates them is how much capsaicin they hold — from none at all to a very great deal.

1065.w: The same species as cayenne, bred the other way. On the Scoville scale a bell pepper is 0 and a pimiento 0 to 500, while a cayenne runs 25,000 to 50,000. The scale counts capsaicinoids and nothing else.

1066.w: The two things pectin is actually made from: dried citrus peel is 85% of world production and apple pomace 14%, both of them left over from juicing. In the fruit it is the glue of the middle lamella, holding cell to cell.

1067.w: Sheep secrete lanolin from the glands that oil their skin, and it waterproofs the fleece from outside. Wash raw wool in hot water and the grease comes out with the dirt — that is where every tub of it starts.

1068.w: Rendering: heat dries the material and lets the fat separate from bone and protein. Suet run this way comes out hard at room temperature and keeps for months, which raw fat does not.

1069.w: The lye is consumed doing the work: it hydrolyses the triglyceride into glycerol and the fatty-acid salts that are the soap. Soda lye gives a firm bar, potash lye a soft or liquid one.

1070.w: The cheap candle. Beeswax burns without smoke or smell and almost nobody could afford it, so households burned tallow instead and put up with what tallow does to a room.

1071.w: A horn is a keratin sheath — hair and hoof protein — grown over a core of living bone. It is permanent, and that is the entire difference from an antler: horn is never shed.

1072.w: Horn is thermoplastic. Heat it just past the boiling point of water and it softens enough to press in a die; cut into strips it made the semi-transparent windows people glazed lanterns with before glass was cheap.

1073.w: Neolithic miners sank shafts through chalk to reach flint seams using picks made from red deer antler. Grime's Graves has at least 433 shafts, and the pits excavated up to 2008 averaged 142.5 antler picks each.

1074.w: Down is the layer underneath, and its barbules have no hooks — they float free of each other instead of locking up. Nothing there to make a flight surface, everything to trap air, and that is the whole of why it is warm.

1075.w: The mantle wraps an intruder in the same nacre it lines the shell with, layer on layer. The intruder is usually organic — a parasite, or displaced mantle tissue. A grain of sand rarely does it, whatever the story says.

1076.w: The shell's inner lining: aragonite tablets about 0.5 µm thick stacked between sheets of protein. That thickness is close to the wavelength of visible light, so the layers interfere and the colour you see is structure, not pigment.

1077.w: Sticklac is heated in canvas tubes until the resin liquefies and seeps through, leaving bark and insects behind. Dried and broken into flakes it is shellac — a varnish once alcohol dissolves it, and once the substance of records.

1078.w: The dye is crushed out of the dried insect and complexed with aluminium; that complex is carmine. It colours yoghurt, sweets, meat and fruit juice — and it is insect protein, which is why it is a real allergen.

1079.w: A dye this bright still needs a mordant to stay put. The mordant forms a coordination complex with the dye and that complex attaches to the fibre — heavier, and bonded, so the colour survives washing.

1080.w: Rennet comes from the lining of the abomasum, the fourth stomach chamber of a calf still nursing. Each ruminant makes a rennet tuned to its own species' milk, so the calf's own gut clots what it drinks and holds it there longer.

1081.w: Chymosin cuts kappa-casein at one bond, between residues 105 and 106. That takes off the water-loving tail holding the micelles apart, and the water-hating remains link into a 3D net that traps the liquid. Acid curdling is a different thing.

1082.w: Cutting the set gel lets it contract and press out the whey — syneresis. How small the cut is decides how much drains, and how much drains decides whether the cheese ends up soft or firm.

1083.w: Rennet never clotted the whey proteins, so they are still dissolved in what drained away. Heat close to boiling denatures them and they flocculate into a fine curd. Ricotta means recooked, and that is exactly what it is.

1084.w: A gas-filled organ inside a bony fish, trimmed to match the density of the water so the animal can hold a depth without swimming to stay there. It is the same organ as a lung — the two are homologous.

1085.w: Dried swim bladder is almost pure collagen. Stir it into a cask and it flocculates the live yeast still hanging in the beer into a jelly that settles out — which is how a pint is made clear without filtering it.

1086.w: Salmon feed for years at sea and come back to the river they hatched in — magnetoreception to find the coast, then smell to find the mouth. Roe is the ripe egg mass they spawn there; one redd can hold five thousand eggs.

1087.w: Ambergris starts as a bile-duct secretion in a sperm whale's intestine, probably to get squid beaks through it — beaks turn up inside the lumps. Passed out at sea it floats for years, and only after that weathering does the faecal smell turn sweet.

1088.w: Baleen is keratin — fingernail protein — in bristled plates across the upper jaw. The whale takes a mouthful of sea and pushes it out through the rack, keeping whatever will not go through. It is called whalebone, and it is not bone.

1089.w: An ox is cattle trained to draught, and castrated first: without testosterone the animal is docile enough to work alongside. They are yoked in pairs — light loads take one pair, heavy work simply adds more.

1090.w: A mouldboard in heavy ground needs steady pull rather than speed, and that is what an ox is for: ploughing, hauling carts and wagons, and threshing grain by walking on it.

1091.w: What the animal did not keep. Dung puts organic matter and nutrients back — nitrogen above all — for the soil's bacteria and fungi to work on, and it improves the soil's structure so it holds more water and more nutrients.

1092.w: Composting wants a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio near 25 to 1. Dung is the nitrogen, straw is the carbon, and get the balance right and the heap heats itself to somewhere around 54–71 °C on the work of its own bacteria.

1093.w: Lime loosens the hair so the skin can be scraped bare, and then it is dried stretched on a frame rather than tanned. That is the whole difference from leather — and it is why parchment buckles when the humidity moves.

1094.w: Parchment takes ink on both sides and outlasts papyrus, which is what made a bound codex worth making. It also never settles: parchment books needed wooden boards and clasps to hold the leaves flat against changes in damp.

1095.w: The tendon that ties one to the other: collagen fibres bundled into fascicles all running the same way, which is why it takes an enormous pull along its length. Dried and split it makes cordage that shrinks tight as it dries, so it needs no knot.

1096.w: A tusk is an incisor that never stopped growing, and it is dentine, not bone — 35 on the Vickers scale, harder than bone is. Polished, its mineralised collagen shows a checkerboard called the Schreger pattern, and that is what identification looks for.

1097.w: Worker bees secrete it from glands in their heads. A larva fed large amounts of it becomes a queen; a larva with identical DNA raised on ordinary food becomes a worker, and the two adults end up strongly different animals.

1098.w: Thermophilus means heat-liking, from thermē, heat, and philus, to like. Its best growth is 35–42 °C, and its yoghurt partner L. d. bulgaricus prefers it hotter still, 43–46 °C. Warm milk decides which bacteria you get.

1099.w: Stamen Grigorov found it in Bulgarian yoghurt in 1905, and it still carries the country's name. It is not only a milk organism: the strain GLB44 was extracted from the leaves of a snowdrop.

1100.w: The two are synergistic: S. thermophilus probably supplies L. d. bulgaricus with the folic and formic acid it needs to build purines. Their optima differ — 35–42 °C against 43–46 °C — so warm milk suits both at once.

1101.w: 72 °C for fifteen seconds, or 63 °C for half an hour — two equivalences confirmed by 1943 against the heat-resistant milk pathogens. It is not sterilisation: most bacterial spores come through it intact.

1102.w: Milk held between 30 and 45 °C for four to twelve hours. The bacteria ferment the lactose to lactic acid, the falling pH partially coagulates the casein, and what was a liquid is a soft solid.

1103.w: Freeze-drying is the preferred way to keep the cells viable away from milk, and not all of them survive it. What comes through is a culture that starts the next batch, instead of one that has to be caught again.

1104.w: Backslopping: a spoonful of the last batch begins the next. It bypasses the first and second waves of bacteria entirely — and those waves are where much of the flavour was being made.

1105.w: Glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pi → 2 lactate + 2 ATP. Homofermentative bacteria stop there — no gas, no alcohol. Yeast given the same glucose gives off carbon dioxide instead; the sugar is identical, the organism is not.

1106.w: Acidophilus is Neo-Latin for acid-loving, and it is not decoration: the species grows most readily below pH 5, at an optimum of 37 °C. It is found in the human gut and mouth — body temperature, not milk temperature.

1107.w: Take the air away and the anaerobes are what is left. Bifidobacterium is often branched — Y-shaped, bifid, which is where the name came from in 1899 — and it is the commonest bacterium in an infant's gut.

1108.w: It is not a starter. It is somewhat heat resistant, grows well in cheese as the cheese ripens, and is strongly proteolytic — taking apart the proteins the starter organisms left behind.

1109.w: Grass cut and packed airtight is silage. Within 48 hours L. plantarum dominates everything else in it, producing lactic and acetic acid that diminish its own competition. It still grows at pH 3.4.

1110.w: Nothing is added: it is already living on the skins of fleshy fruit and vegetables. It is heterolactic, so from glucose it makes ethanol and CO₂ as well as lactate — the gas is the sign it has started.

1111.w: Phase two of three. The first bacteria acidify the brine until it is too sour for themselves, and Leuconostoc species take dominance — souring it further, and giving off the gas that fills the crock.

1112.w: Phase three, and a handover. The acid Leuconostoc made is too much for Leuconostoc. L. plantarum is untroubled by it, ferments whatever sugars are left, and lowers the pH further still.

1113.w: The cheese bacterium began as a plant bacterium. Dairy strains are thought to descend from plant strains that lost or turned down the genes of no benefit in milk — genome erosion, and it has been reproduced in the lab.

1114.w: It uses enzymes to make ATP from lactose, and lactic acid is the by-product. That acid curdles the milk and the curds separate. Brie, camembert, cheddar, colby, gruyère, parmesan and roquefort all start here.

1115.w: Souring the cream first is not for flavour. Fat from cream at a lower pH coalesces more readily, so it churns to butter sooner. Buttermilk is what is left behind in the churn: sharp, and under 0.5 per cent fat.

1116.w: Nobody adds them. Acetic acid bacteria are airborne and ubiquitous, active wherever sugars are fermenting to ethanol, and often carried in by fruit flies. Every one of them is an obligate aerobe.

1117.w: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. This is an oxidation, not a fermentation in the airless sense, so it needs oxygen: dilute alcohol left in a warm, airy place turns over a few months.

1118.w: Vinegar is that one acid, diluted, and nothing cleverer. Traditional vinegars for eating run 4.5 to 7 per cent acidity, which puts the pH somewhere between 2.38 and 3.76.

1119.w: Not one organism but a community, and it builds its own housing: a biofilm of kefiran, a polysaccharide of glucose and galactose in equal parts, with lactobacilli, yeasts and acetic acid bacteria living in it.

1120.w: Grains at two to five per cent of the milk, twelve to twenty-four hours at 20–25 °C. The bacteria make the acid and the yeasts make the gas and a little alcohol, which is why kefir is fizzy and yoghurt is not.

1121.w: Cold does not stop this mould, it selects for it. P. roqueforti tolerates cold, low oxygen, and both alkali and weaker acid preservatives — which is exactly what lets it thrive in a dairy, and inside a cheese.

1122.w: Sprayed on the outside rather than mixed in: a suspension of P. camemberti on the surface, then three weeks minimum of ripening working inward from the rind. Blue cheese is the reverse — P. roqueforti, in the interior.

1123.w: One species out of more than three hundred. Penicillium chrysogenum, long called P. notatum, is the original industrial source and still the present-day one. The rest of the genus is doing other things.

1124.w: Rice koji is grain fermented with the hyphae of Aspergillus oryzae. Genome analysis suggests it is a domesticated Aspergillus flavus: the aflatoxin gene cluster is still in there, and it no longer functions.

1125.w: The mould does the demolition. Its peptidases cut soy protein into free amino acids, glutamic acid among them, and they are salt-tolerant — so the salt that keeps everything else out of the paste does not stop them.

1126.w: Wool is what cutting a sheep normally means. Mutton is the other outcome: a sheep with more than two permanent incisors in wear, past two years old, tougher than lamb, and darker, because colour tracks age.

1127.w: A ewe carries about five months and labour takes one to three hours. Most breeds give a single lamb or twins, and a few lines throw triplets or more.

1128.w: Nothing but time separates them: lamb in the first year, hogget in the second, mutton after that. The line is not drawn on a calendar but in the mouth — how many permanent incisor teeth have come into wear.

1129.w: Venison is Latin venari, to hunt, arriving through Norman French in the 11th century with the Royal Forests. It first meant the meat of anything hunted — hare, wild boar, ibex — and only later narrowed to deer.

1130.w: Barding: bacon laid over a lean roast, especially game like venison and pheasant. The pork fat insulates the joint and bastes it from outside as it renders, which is what venison cannot do for itself.

1131.w: To keep milking, a dairy cow has to be bred and produce a calf. The heifers may replace their mothers in the herd; the male calves are sold on for veal or beef.

1132.w: Veal is the meat of calves rather than of grown cattle, and most of it comes from male calves of dairy breeds that will never milk and are not wanted for breeding. It is a way of adding value to them.

1133.w: The flavour comes out of marrow, cartilage and connective tissue: their collagen converts to gelatin, which is what thickens the liquid. Brown stock is usually beef or veal, roasted before it is simmered.

1134.w: Suet is the hard fat around the loins and kidneys of beef, lamb or mutton. Melted, simmered a long while, strained and cooled, it becomes tallow — which is most of what suet was ever for.

1135.w: Slow moist heat does not add moisture to meat, despite the common belief. The juiciness comes from connective tissue and collagen breaking down and lubricating the fibres, which is why the toughest cuts stew best.

1136.w: Bacon is salt-cured pork, typically from the belly or the less fatty parts of the back. Smoking is usual but optional: it is the cure that makes it bacon, and the cure is what let it keep before refrigeration.

1137.w: Gammon is the hind leg cured in brine and still raw — strictly the bottom end of a whole side of bacon, where ham is the back leg cured on its own. Outside Britain and Ireland the distinction is mostly not made.

1138.w: Potassium nitrate and sodium nitrite bond to the meat's myoglobin and stand in for oxygen, holding it red where a plain roast turns grey. Curing salt is dyed pink so nobody mistakes it for table salt; it is not naturally pink.

1139.w: Poultry spans two branches at once: the landfowl, chicken and turkey, and the waterfowl, duck and goose. What it excludes is any wild bird taken by hunting — that is game. The word came from Old French pouletrie.

1140.w: Game is not a species but a status: wild animals hunted for meat, sport or trophies. The gamey taste is put down to what the animal ate for itself, which usually leaves it with less fat than a farmed one carries.

1141.w: The legs and neck do the most work and are the toughest; meat gets more tender the further it lies from hoof and horn. A steak comes off the loin, in the middle, which holds the animal up and little else.

1142.w: Fifteen to twenty-eight days near freezing. The beef's own enzymes break down the connective tissue in the muscle, and moisture evaporates as it hangs — a third or more of the weight goes, and the flavour left behind is concentrated.

1143.w: An ox is cattle kept for work, and work is what makes meat tough. The legs and the neck do the most of it and are the toughest cuts on any carcass.

1144.w: Ceratonia siliqua is a legume that grows as an evergreen tree, and its fruit is a pod. It is a xerophyte: 250 to 500 mm of rain a year is enough for it to live on, which is why it is a Mediterranean tree.

1145.w: The pods are kibbled to free the seeds, the skins come off with acid or heat, and the brittle germ is broken up and sieved away. What is left is the endosperm — 42 to 46% of the seed — milled to powder.

1146.w: Guar is a legume, Cyamopsis tetragonoloba, and the gum is the endosperm of its seed with the husk ground away. It has about eight times cornstarch's water-thickening ability, so very little of it is needed.

1147.w: Xanthomonas campestris is the black rot of cabbages and broccoli. Fed glucose in a stirred, aerated tank it secretes the gum outside its own cells, and alcohol drops it out of the broth as a powder.

1148.w: Most red algae are marine and most of those are attached to rock rather than drifting. The red is phycobiliproteins working as accessory pigments — the same job chlorophyll does, on light chlorophyll misses.

1149.w: Hot alkali — 5 to 8% potassium hydroxide — takes the cellulose out and leaves the carrageenan. The kappa form then gels with potassium ions and binds to dairy protein, which is most of what it is used for.

1150.w: The outer cell wall of a red alga is agarose and agaropectin, and boiling water takes them straight out of it. The gel that results sets at 32 to 42 °C but will not melt again below 85.

1151.w: Walther Hesse's gelatin plates kept liquefying in Robert Koch's laboratory until his wife Fanny suggested agar in 1881, knowing from her own kitchen that it holds at warm temperatures. Koch's 1882 tuberculosis paper used agar without crediting her.

1152.w: Acid first turns the seaweed's alginate salts into insoluble alginic acid; alkali near pH 9–10, usually soda, converts that back to sodium alginate, which dissolves and can then be precipitated back out.

1153.w: Almost no citric acid is squeezed out of fruit. James Currie found in 1917 that Aspergillus niger fed sugar would pour it out, Pfizer industrialised that two years later, and mould fermentation is still the route.

1154.w: Scheele crystallised the first citric acid out of lemon juice in 1784, and lemons and limes do carry up to 8% of their dry weight as it. It is the same molecule the mould makes. Origin is not composition.

1155.w: Acetic acid neutralised with sodium hydroxide, and that is the whole preparation: CH3CO2H + NaOH → CH3CO2Na + H2O. A corrosive liquid becomes a stable solid that holds a food at a mildly acidic pH.

1156.w: Glutamate is the part that tastes savoury; the sodium is there to make it dissolve. The same glutamate is already in tomatoes and in cheese, in the free acid form, doing the same thing.

1157.w: Kikunae Ikeda boiled kombu down in 1908, crystallised glutamic acid out of it and named the taste umami. Most MSG is now fermented from sugar by Corynebacterium, with the sodium added afterwards.

1158.w: Inosinate is not an invention. Meat and fish carry 80 to 800 mg of it per 100 g already; the additive is its disodium salt, now mostly fermented from sugar rather than extracted from animals.

1159.w: Guanosine monophosphate's disodium salt, made at scale by fermenting sugar with Corynebacterium stationis and E. coli. It is expensive, so it is almost never used unless glutamate is present too.

1160.w: E635 is the two of them mixed, and the point is synergy rather than flavour of its own: 98% monosodium glutamate with 2% E635 has four times the flavour-enhancing power of MSG alone.

1161.w: This pair is what a stock cube is doing. MSG with disodium ribonucleotides is standard in bouillon cubes, soups, ramen and gravy — savour arriving without anything having been simmered.

1162.w: Starch boiled to a paste and then cut with acid and enzymes into glucose chains three to seventeen units long. How far the cutting goes is the whole specification — past dextrose equivalent 20 it is glucose syrup.

1163.w: Soy protein cooked in 15 to 20% hydrochloric acid at 90 to 120 °C for up to eight hours comes apart into its amino acids, then is neutralised back to pH 5–6. Berzelius got a bouillon taste this way in 1831.

1164.w: The other route uses proteases instead of acid, and the common mixture is taken from Aspergillus oryzae — the soy sauce mould. Add a glutaminase as well and glutamine turns into glutamate, which is the savoury part.

1165.w: Quartz sand vaporised in a 3,000 °C arc condenses as microscopic droplets of amorphous silica welded into branched chains. The powder is almost all surface, and that is what keeps a spice from caking.

1166.w: The commonest carotenoid in plants, richest in carrots, pumpkin, spinach and sweet potato. One molecule of it is cleaved in the gut into two of vitamin A, which is what provitamin A means.

1167.w: The pigment of Bixa orellana sits in a reddish waxy coating on the outside of the seed, and it is fat-soluble, so hot oil or lard lifts it straight off. Saponified, the same bixin becomes water-soluble norbixin.

1168.w: Curcuma longa is a perennial of the ginger family that wants 20 to 30 °C and heavy annual rain, and what is dug up is the rhizome. It cannot seed itself into new ground: every plant is a piece of another one.

1169.w: Curcumin is hydrophobic — poorly soluble in water, easily soluble in organic solvents — so water will not take it out of the rhizome. Vogel and Pelletier reported the first isolation in 1815.

1170.w: Red beet holds 300 to 600 mg of betanin per kilogram. Its colour is a pH reading: bright bluish-red at pH 4 to 5, blue-violet as that rises, and hydrolysed to yellow-brown once it goes alkaline.

1171.w: Carbohydrate heated with acids, alkalis or salts until it browns, and more fully oxidised than a caramel sweet. Ammonium compounds make the class III and IV colours, which are the dark ones in cola and beer.

1172.w: An azo dye is built by treating an aromatic amine with nitrous acid, made in the flask from sodium nitrite, then coupling the diazonium salt onto a second ring. The rings come from coal and oil. Nothing here grew.

1173.w: Hofmann distilled sorbic acid out of rowanberry oil in 1859 and it is named for the tree. Virtually all supply is now synthetic. The salt stops moulds and yeasts, and only below about pH 6.5.

1174.w: Benzoic acid is made by partial oxidation of toluene over a cobalt or manganese catalyst, and toluene is a by-product of coking coal and of refining oil. Gum benzoin, which named it, was its only source for centuries.

1175.w: Sulfur dioxide run into sodium hydroxide gives the sulfite; more of the gas turns that into metabisulfite, which crystallises out on cooling. In wine it arrests fermentation and blocks oxidation and bacteria.

1176.w: Saltpetre cures nothing by itself; something has to reduce it first. Ferment a nitrate-rich juice — celery is the usual one — and the microbes produce nitrite at levels sufficient for commercial meat curing.

1177.w: Nitrite gives up nitric oxide, which binds the iron at the centre of myoglobin's heme: nitrosomyoglobin raw, nitrosohemochrome pink once cooked. Two to fourteen parts per million is enough to turn the colour.

1178.w: A vegetable oil is liquid because its fatty acids carry double bonds. Hydrogen added across those bonds over a nickel catalyst removes them and the fat sets solid. Normann was granted the patent in 1902.

1179.w: The reaction was deliberately stopped part-way to hit a melting point, and the catalyst flipped much of the double bonds left over from cis to trans. At 20 psi the product was about 40% trans fatty acid by weight.

1180.w: Lipase takes fatty acids off a triglyceride, and what is left with one tail is a monoglyceride — a glycerol head that water will accept on one end and oil on the other. Industry makes them by adding glycerol instead.

1181.w: Théodore Gobley pulled it out of egg yolk in 1845 and named it from lekithos, the Greek for yolk. It is not one molecule but a mixture of phospholipids, each with an end that wants water and an end that refuses it.

1182.w: Crude soybean oil carries phospholipids dissolved in it. Stir water in and they hydrate, drop out as gums and are spun off — water degumming, and it is where most commercial lecithin comes from.

1183.w: The yolk in mayonnaise is only there for this. Lecithin lines up at the boundary of every oil droplet, water-loving end outward, and the oil cannot find its way back together.

1184.w: Reducing glucose turns the aldehyde at the end of the chain into an alcohol, and the result is a sugar alcohol about half as sweet as sucrose. It is named for Sorbus, the rowan, where it also occurs.

1185.w: Xylan is pulled out of woody biomass, acid splits it to xylose, and the xylose is hydrogenated over Raney nickel — the same trick as sorbitol, one carbon shorter. Hence the other name for it, birch sugar.

1186.w: A methyl ester of the aspartic acid–phenylalanine dipeptide: two ordinary amino acids joined and capped. It is about 200 times as sweet as sucrose, so the amount needed carries almost no energy at all.

1187.w: A flower above ground, a fruit below it. After fertilisation a stalk called a peg grows down from the base of the ovary and pushes into the soil, and the pod ripens there. Light sandy loam is the ground loose enough to let the peg through.

1188.w: The fruit is a capsule that bursts when the seed is ripe — dehiscence, the same shattering cereals were bred out of ten thousand years ago. An indehiscent sesame mutant turned up in 1943 and breeders have chased it since. It still limits the crop.

1189.w: Most planted almond varieties cannot fertilise themselves, so an orchard must mix varieties and rely on insects to carry pollen between them. California's bloom is the largest managed pollination event on Earth: over a million hives each February.

1190.w: Flesh outside, one seed inside a woody shell that the flower's own ovary wall built. Olive, cherry, coffee, mango and coconut are all this shape — the coconut's husk is only a drupe's flesh gone dry and fibrous.

1191.w: The stone is the flower's own ovary wall, gone woody with lignin — the same stuff as timber. Some other fleshy fruits have a stony case around the seed, but it grows from the seed coat, and those are not drupes.

1192.w: Mangifera indica sits in Anacardiaceae beside cashew, pistachio and sumac. It is also an evolutionary anachronism: the animal big enough to swallow that stone and carry it off is extinct, so the tree depends on us.

1193.w: Peeling is where people get caught. Urushiol is a catechol oil found across the cashew family — poison ivy, poison oak, and mango leaves, stems, sap and skin. It is too small to be seen alone, so it binds a skin protein first.

1194.w: Rhus coriaria's fruits are drupes, dried and milled whole — skin, flesh and stone — into a crimson powder. The sourness is malic acid, the same acid a cactus makes in the dark. Rome had it long before it had lemons.

1195.w: The hard shell is the stone and the kernel inside it is the seed, but the green husk around the lot is an involucre — leaf tissue, not ovary wall. That one detail is why a walnut is called a drupe-like nut and not a drupe.

1196.w: Walnut roots, leaves, husks and bark leak juglone into the ground, and it stunts or kills what tries to grow there. In 1926 walnut trees standing in an alfalfa field killed the alfalfa and left the grass untouched.

1197.w: Piper nigrum is a climbing vine and the peppercorn is its fruit. The green drupes are boiled briefly; the heat bursts the cell walls and frees enzymes that brown the skin as it dries. White pepper is the same fruit, ripe, skin rotted off.

1198.w: White pepper is the same vine's fruit with the fruit taken off. Ripe red berries are soaked about a week until the flesh rots and rubs away, and the naked seed is dried. Take the skin off and the citrus and pine notes go with it.

1199.w: Piperine and capsaicin both open TRPV1, the nerve channel that also reports scalding — which is why both read as heat. The plants are unrelated; Europeans called chillies pepper by mistake. By weight piperine is about 1% as hot.

1200.w: Bell, jalapeño, cayenne and paprika are all Capsicum annuum: one species carrying both the sweet pepper and the hot one. Jalapeños are picked green for market; left on the bush they turn red and get hotter.

1201.w: Not a plant, a process. Ripe red jalapeños are smoked over pecan wood at 65–75 °C for six days and go from 88% water to 6%. Ten pounds in, one pound out. The Aztecs were doing this before the Spanish arrived.

1202.w: Traditionally done in an open oven in the field, and the wood chooses the flavour. Some producers now use large gas dryers and artificial smoke flavouring instead, which is quicker and makes a less flavourful chipotle.

1203.w: Cuminum cyminum is an umbellifer, family to carrot, celery, parsley and dill. What is sold as a cumin seed is the dried fruit, holding two mericarps with one seed each. It looks so like caraway that many languages do not separate them.

1204.w: The warm smell is one compound, cuminaldehyde, in an oil the plant makes for itself. Toasting the seed does not just strengthen that — it builds pyrazines that were not there before, which is why toasted cumin smells different.

1205.w: Two species of one genus, and the names cross over. Sweet marjoram is Origanum majorana; oregano is Origanum vulgare and is also called wild marjoram. Most pots sold as Italian oregano are O. × majoricum, a cross of the two.

1206.w: Apium graveolens is an umbellifer, family to carrot, parsley and cumin, and it grows wild in marshes. Pull a stalk apart and the strings that come away are bundles of collenchyma cells sitting outside the vascular bundles.

1207.w: One wild species bred three ways. Stalk celery is grown for the petiole, leaf celery for the leaves, and celeriac for a swollen hypocotyl — the same plant, pushed in three directions until they no longer look related.

1208.w: Celery powder and salt is the uncured cure. Celery carries nitrate on its own, it ends as the same nitrite the pink salt would have supplied, and the USDA still lets the pack say no nitrites added.

1209.w: Britain's lemons came from the Mediterranean and war cut them off, so the ration became West Indian lime from its own colonies. Limes are much weaker antiscorbutics, and the juice sat in light and ran through copper pipe. Scurvy returned.

1210.w: There is no wild lime either. The Key lime is a natural hybrid of the citron and a wild papeda, Citrus micrantha; cross that with a lemon and you get the Persian lime, which is nearly seedless and most of the world crop.

1211.w: Citrus hystrix is grown for its leaves. Each looks like two joined end to end: the blade, plus a leaf-shaped winged petiole behind it. The smell is almost one molecule — citronellal is up to 80% of the leaf oil.

1212.w: The test is nodes. A rhizome is a stem creeping horizontally underground, sending roots down from its nodes and shoots up from them. A root has no nodes and ends in a cap. A stem tuber is a rhizome swollen for storage.

1213.w: Zingiber officinale is a rhizome in the same family as turmeric, cardamom and galangal. It is a true cultigen and does not exist in the wild, so it is grown only by planting pieces of last year's rhizome.

1214.w: A monsoon crop. It goes in the ground between March and June as the rains start, and where the rain stops in September it has to be watered at least every fortnight until November or the rhizome comes up small.

1215.w: [6]-gingerol is the pungent yellow oil in fresh ginger, and it works the way capsaicin and piperine do — on the heat receptors of the tongue. It is unstable: dry the ginger and it loses water and becomes something else.

1216.w: Heat or storage pulls a water molecule out of gingerol, and what is left is about twice as pungent. Shogaol sits at 160,000 Scoville: hotter than piperine, a hundred times cooler than capsaicin. Dried ginger is a different spice.

1217.w: A grape is built to keep its water in. Wax in the skin's cuticle blocks the water trying to get out, and the whole outer layer is adapted to prevent loss — so drying one means defeating the fruit's own waterproofing.

1218.w: Held near 65 °C in a tunnel dryer, water leaves faster than the sugars can caramelise. The traditional sun-dried raisin takes weeks and darkens; the machine-dried one takes hours and does not.

1219.w: Lens culinaris: two seeds to a pod, each a flat disc thicker in the middle. The Latin for that seed was lens, and opticians took the word for a piece of glass ground to the same shape. Like other legumes it fixes its own nitrogen.

1220.w: A pea seed is two cotyledons packed face to face. Dry it, rub the skin off, and it comes apart at that seam on its own. Mendel's green against yellow was the colour of exactly this tissue, and green is the recessive one.

1221.w: Farro names three species, not one: einkorn, emmer and spelt. What they share is the hull — they hold their husks so tightly that threshing will not free the grain, so it has to be pounded off. Italy usually means emmer.

1222.w: What looks like one flower is a head of hundreds. Each floret sits 137.5° round from the last, so the spirals running each way count out as two successive Fibonacci numbers — 89 and 144 in a very large head.

1223.w: The bud does track the sun: it faces east at dawn, swings west through the day and turns back overnight, on a circadian rhythm that keeps running under cloud. Then growth stops, and the head stays facing east for good.

1224.w: Pressing is the old way and most oil is not made that way. Seeds are washed with hexane, the solvent boiled off near 149 °C, then the oil is steamed under vacuum at about 232 °C until it has no smell or taste left to give it away.

1225.w: Sunflower seed comes in two kinds and only one is for oil: oilseed varieties are pressed, confectionery ones are eaten whole. Sunflower is the fourth most used vegetable oil in the world.

1226.w: The compounds that make a herb smell dissolve in fat, not water, so any neutral oil will carry them. A deodorised one carries them without adding a flavour of its own — which is most of what deodorising is for.

1227.w: Retinal is the aldehyde and retinol the alcohol, one reduction apart, and the body runs it both ways as needed. Retinol is the form that is kept: the liver stores it as an ester and releases the alcohol when a tissue asks.

1228.w: Carotene is the safe way in. The body cleaves it to vitamin A only as fast as it needs to and stops when it has enough, so carotene cannot poison you — the ready-made animal form can, and polar bear liver famously does.

1229.w: UVB light strikes 7-dehydrocholesterol in the deeper skin and what comes out is cholecalciferol. It is a secosteroid hormone, not a vitamin — it got the name in 1922 for being the fourth found. Roughly 80% of yours is made this way.

1230.w: Koji-covered soybeans and roasted wheat go into 17–20% brine and sit for 90 to 180 days. Only salt-tolerant microbes survive that; the mould's enzymes cut protein into free amino acids, and the brown is those meeting the sugars.

1231.w: The other soy sauce is never brewed. Acid takes soy protein apart in hours instead of months, and the result is salted and coloured to match. La Choy was selling it in the United States from 1933.

1232.w: Not a coating. The fruit is steeped in syrups of rising strength for weeks, and osmotic pressure pulls its water out and drives sugar in until the flesh is saturated and nothing that spoils food can live in it.

1233.w: Nothing to do with the fruit. A cut is made in the flower stalk and sap runs from it into a container; the sap is about 80% water and is boiled down in a wok. The brown is caramelisation, and it is no better for you than sugar.

1234.w: Parsley wants moist, well-drained soil and full sun, and is oddly slow to start — it takes four to six weeks just to germinate.

1235.w: Sage tolerates poor soil but not wet feet — a cold winter in badly drained ground can kill it outright, which is why it wants stony, free-draining beds.

1236.w: Ros marinus, 'dew of the sea' — native to Mediterranean coasts, and able to withstand a severe lack of water for lengthy periods.

1237.w: A tender plant, sensitive to cold, that grows best in hot, dry conditions and needs protection from frost — the clove note in some cultivars is pure eugenol.

1238.w: Burnt as incense in Greek temples in the belief it gave courage — the smell is mostly thymol, historically used itself as an antibiotic and antiseptic.

1239.w: Peppermint is a sterile hybrid of watermint and spearmint, so it spreads by runners rather than seed, and wants a steady supply of water without ever waterlogging.

1240.w: Dracunculus, 'little dragon', named for its coiled roots. French tarragon's flowers are sterile, so it is propagated only by dividing the root, never by seed.

1241.w: Needs a summer of strong sun and rich, well-drained soil — even partial shade cuts the yield substantially. Carvone is one of the oils behind its smell.

1242.w: Small white or pale pink umbel flowers, asymmetrical, with outer petals longer than inner. Let them ripen to seed and you get a different spice with a different name: coriander seed.

1243.w: Grows from small conical bulbs, 2 to 3 centimetres long, packed into dense clusters — the hollow, grass-like leaves above them are what gets snipped for the kitchen.

1244.w: Unlike almost every other kitchen herb, this one comes off a woody evergreen tree — which is why the leaf stays stiff even after cooking and has to be fished back out before serving.

1245.w: Its leaves pack in extra aromatic oil right at the end of the growing season, exactly when the plant is usually cut for drying — which is why dried oregano can taste stronger than fresh.

1246.w: Umetaro Suzuki isolated the antineuritic factor from rice bran in 1910 — the outer layer polishing strips away, and the exact deficiency Christiaan Eijkman had traced to polished rice in 1897.

1247.w: First isolated as 'lactochrome' from cows' milk whey in 1879, later renamed lactoflavin and then riboflavin — the same yellow-green fluorescent pigment that colours whey today.

1248.w: Conversion is fixed and wasteful: 60 milligrams of tryptophan makes 1 milligram of niacin. Corn-dependent diets caused pellagra because corn's own niacin is poorly bioavailable and its protein runs short on the tryptophan that would make up the gap.

1249.w: First isolated by extraction from spinach leaves in 1941, a decade after Lucy Wills identified the missing nutrient behind a pregnancy-related anaemia. Its name comes from folium, Latin for leaf.

1250.w: Plants synthesise pyridoxine partly as their own defence against UV-B radiation in sunlight — a pathway animals never evolved, which is why every animal that has it got it from something that photosynthesises.

1251.w: Discovered in 1922 as the unnamed dietary factor rats needed to carry a pregnancy to term — hence tocopherol, Greek for 'to bear a child'. Wheat germ oil is the richest known source.

1252.w: Allura Red AC couples diazotized cresidinesulfonic acid onto 2-naphthol-6-sulfonic acid — both sulfonated aromatic rings from coal tar. Invented in 1971 to replace amaranth, the red dye the FDA itself banned for carcinogenicity five years later.

1253.w: Tartrazine couples diazotized sulfanilic acid onto a sulfonated pyrazolone ring, whose extra nitrogen sets it apart from its naphthalene-ring rack-mates. Ammonia stands in for that ring nitrogen — the game has no hydrazine element for the real reagent.

1254.w: Sunset Yellow FCF's own preferred name is Disodium 6-hydroxy-5-[(4-sulfophenyl)azo]-2-naphthalenesulfonate — a disodium salt from the moment it is named. Petroleum-derived, and often mixed with amaranth to fake the brown of chocolate.

1255.w: Brilliant Blue FCF isn't an azo dye like its rack-mates — no diazonium coupling. It's made by condensing a sulfonated benzaldehyde with an aniline compound, then oxidising the result. The game has no separate aniline element, so this collapses to one verb.

1256.w: Acacia is tapped for gum by stripping bits off the bark, from which gum then exudes — no pressing or extraction, just an open wound left to weep.

1257.w: Its bacterium, Sphingomonas elodea, was first isolated from lily plant tissue in a Pennsylvania pond in 1978 — a wild find turned into a commercial fermentation product.

1258.w: The rhizome is beaten to a pulp and washed; the milky liquid is sieved, and the pure starch — insoluble in water — settles out at the bottom.

1259.w: Traditionally raised by cutting shii and other deciduous trees, then setting the logs beside trees already colonised by shiitake spores — log cultivation still practiced today.

1260.w: Hen-of-the-woods grows at the base of old growth oaks or maples, and is a perennial fungus that often returns to the same spot for years running, not a one-off annual growth.

1261.w: Spirulina is, quite literally, the dried biomass of cyanobacteria — the Kanembu people of Lake Chad have long dried it into cakes called dihe, still sold in local markets today.

1262.w: Michel Eugène Chevreul isolated it from a water-extract of skeletal muscle in 1832, and named the crystals after kreas, Greek for meat.

1263.w: Nitric oxide synthase oxidises arginine and releases nitric oxide as it goes — citrulline is the amino acid left over, the byproduct of the same reaction.

1264.w: Discovered in 1949 as a constituent of green tea and isolated the next year from gyokuro leaves. It makes up roughly one to two percent of dry tea leaf.

1265.w: Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge isolated it from coffee beans Goethe gave him in 1819: "soon thereafter I discovered therein caffeine, which became so famous on account of its high nitrogen content."

1266.w: Alpha-GPC is made by deacylating phosphatidylcholine and can be derived from purified soy lecithin — strip the two fatty acid tails and the glycerophosphocholine head is what remains.

1267.w: Citrus is believed to build it by the same route animals use for adrenaline: tyrosine to tyramine to N-methyltyramine to synephrine, one methyl group short of the finish.

1268.w: It absorbs silicon from the soil, rare among herbs, and its stems are coated in abrasive silicates — once used to polish pewter and wood, hence the old name 'pewterwort'.

1269.w: Named for its jagged leaves — French dent de lion, lion's tooth — and grown from an unbranched taproot that can be roasted into a caffeine-free coffee substitute.

1270.w: Succulence lets it survive low-rainfall ground; its thick leaves store water in a gel core, wrapped in an outer layer holding the toxic compound aloin.

1271.w: Native to mountainous ground in the Russian Far East, Northeast China and Korea. The root is usually harvested at five or six years old.

1272.w: About a quarter of the seed's weight is mucilage, obtained by milling away the outer husk layer — this game's closest available action is cutting it free.

1273.w: Made by letting a fungal beta-fructosidase enzyme act on ordinary sucrose — the transfructosylation route to fructooligosaccharides, alongside inulin breakdown.

1274.w: Pineapple doesn't grow from seed commercially: the plant normally propagates from the leafy offset produced at the top of a ripe fruit, or from a side shoot, cut free and rooted.

1275.w: Spinach is dioecious — separate male and female plants — and its small green flowers are wind-pollinated rather than carried by bees or other insects.

1276.w: Acai comes from a palm native to the swamps and floodplains of eastern Amazonia, its small black-purple drupes borne in branched clusters of 500 to 900 fruit.

1277.w: Botanically the pomegranate is a berry, the ripened ovary of a single flower, and an unusually seedy one: a single fruit can hold 200 to about 1,400 seeds.

1278.w: Goji is a nightshade too — Lycium barbarum sits in the family Solanaceae alongside tomato and potato — but it grows as a woody shrub, not a vine.

1279.w: The papaya is a large herbaceous plant, usually a single stem 5 to 10 metres tall, its huge lobed leaves (up to 70cm across) confined to the very top.

1280.w: Broccoli is Brassica oleracea, the same species behind cabbage, but bred for its large flowering head, stalk and small leaves rather than a wrapped leaf ball.

1281.w: Alfalfa is a legume that fixes nitrogen through root nodules — a symbiosis with the bacterium Sinorhizobium meliloti living inside them.

1282.w: First crystallized out of egg yolk in 1936, in a paper literally titled 'preparation of crystallized biotin from egg yolk.' Raw egg white blocks it instead: avidin binds it so tightly it can't be absorbed, a deficiency now called egg-white injury.

1283.w: First isolated from a cow's vitreous humor in 1934, then from pig skin, human skin and rooster's comb — comb remains the most common animal source today, a byproduct of the meat industry rather than a purpose-raised one.

1284.w: Made by chlorinating ordinary sucrose, replacing three hydroxyl groups with chlorine atoms — about 600 times as sweet as the sugar it started from. Discovered in 1975 when 'test it' was reportedly misheard as 'taste it.'

1285.w: Stevia rebaudiana prefers sandy-like soil and cannot survive frost, native to the warm, humid growing conditions of Paraguay and Brazil — European growers still raise it under glass for exactly that reason.

1286.w: Fish or shellfish are mixed with salt at 10-30% and sealed in a closed container for up to two years — brief fermentation tastes fishier, extended fermentation turns nuttier and richer.

1287.w: Charge a lithium-ion cell and the lithium migrates to the graphite anode and slides in between its carbon sheets. Fully loaded the ratio is one lithium to six carbons — LiC6 — with a theoretical capacity of 372 mAh per gram.

1288.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides — all soluble in water except one: lithium fluoride, also the only common crystal that lets short-wavelength ultraviolet light straight through.

1289.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Lithium chloride is so eager for water it is used to dry air streams, and as a flux for brazing aluminium.

1290.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Lithium iodide is the standard electrolyte inside artificial pacemakers, chosen for the long cycle life it gives the cell.

1291.w: 6 Li + N2 → 2 Li3N, straight from the elements — lithium is the only alkali metal that forms a stable nitride this way. Sodium, potassium and the rest simply do not react with nitrogen gas at all.

1292.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Sodium bromide was the standard sedative and anticonvulsant of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, before anyone understood why.

1293.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Doped with a trace of thallium, sodium iodide scintillates under radiation and became the crystal at the core of the first particle detectors.

1294.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. After hydrogen fluoride itself, potassium fluoride is chemistry's main working source of a free fluoride ion.

1295.w: Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Spun fast enough, caesium chloride's own high density builds a gradient in the tube — the method that first separated DNA fragments by weight.

1296.w: Iron needs only 10.5% chromium mixed through it to stop rusting. The chromium reacts with air to grow a microscopically thin, invisible oxide skin that heals itself the instant it is scratched.

1297.w: A few percent beryllium worked into copper makes an alloy strong enough for tools, but nonmagnetic and non-sparking — which is why it is chosen for wrenches used anywhere a stray spark could ignite gas.

1298.w: A ductile alloy of the two metals that becomes a superconductor when chilled near absolute zero. Wound into coil it is the wire inside the great majority of MRI machines' magnets.

1299.w: Gold alloyed with copper turns pink rather than yellow — the whole of rose gold's colour is copper mixed through the gold, nothing more exotic than that.

1300.w: Pure lead sags under its own weight. Alloyed with 8 to 12 percent antimony it stiffens into a metal rigid enough for a battery grid — and antimony barely shrinks as it cools, which keeps a cast sharp.

1301.w: Titanium alloyed with aluminium (and, in the real alloy, a little vanadium this recipe cannot carry) is Ti-6Al-4V — strong, corrosion-resistant and light, and the single most-used titanium alloy in aircraft and rockets.

1302.w: 2 Fe + 3 Cl2 → 2 FeCl3, iron burning directly in chlorine gas at a few hundred degrees. The compound clumps dirt out of water as a coagulant and eats bare copper straight off a circuit board.

1303.w: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so a zinc coating corrodes first, on purpose — a sacrificial anode that keeps protecting the iron underneath even after the coating itself is scratched through.

1304.w: All four silver halides can be made by the direct reaction of their elements. Silver chloride darkens the instant light hits it, disintegrating into metallic silver — the fact photography was built on from its very beginning.

1305.w: Gold amalgamates with mercury readily and quickly, forming compounds from AuHg2 up to Au8Hg. Ore washed over mercury-coated sheets let miners catch gold flour too fine for any pan to hold.

1306.w: Liquid mercury mixed with particles of silver, copper and tin stays workable for a few minutes and then sets hard — the alloy that has filled cavities in teeth for close to two centuries.

1307.w: Xe + 2 F2 → XeF4, sealed in a nickel vessel at 400 °C — first made in 1962, proof that a noble gas could bond at all. Almost every other xenon compound traces back to a fluoride made this same way.

1308.w: Burned in air above 100 °C, lithium metal combines with oxygen into lithium oxide, alongside a little of its peroxide. Stirred into a glaze it acts as a flux and shifts copper toward blue, cobalt toward pink.

1309.w: Sodium ignited in excess oxygen does not stop at a simple oxide — it overshoots straight to the peroxide. The same compound that once bleached wood pulp for paper can also regenerate breathable oxygen in a sealed submarine.

1310.w: Molten potassium burned in excess oxygen overshoots further still, to the superoxide KO2. It scrubs carbon dioxide and water vapour from sealed air while handing back oxygen — the working chemistry inside a rebreather.

1311.w: Titanium reacts with oxygen at 1,200 °C in air, or at 610 °C in pure oxygen, forming titanium dioxide. First mass-produced in 1916, it is the most widely used white pigment there is, prized for its brightness alone.

1312.w: Chromium metal in air passivates instantly, growing a thin protective skin of chromium oxide with the same crystal structure as corundum. The same green compound is sold as a pigment, chrome green.

1313.w: Heated above 400 °C, nickel powder reacts with oxygen to give nickel oxide — green as a pure crystal, black the moment it is not quite stoichiometric. It served as an electrode in the earliest nickel-iron batteries.

1314.w: Manganese tarnishes and oxidises in air the way iron rusts in wet water. Its dioxide, more often mined than grown from the metal, is what soaks up electrons inside an ordinary alkaline or zinc-carbon dry cell.

1315.w: Burn tin metal in air and it becomes tin dioxide directly. Suspended in a glaze the compound scatters light rather than passing it, which is what makes an old tin-glazed pot opaque white instead of clear.

1316.w: Palladium readily adsorbs hydrogen at room temperature, splitting the H-H bond and packing atoms into its own lattice. At standard pressure a block of it can hold nine hundred times its own volume of the gas.

1317.w: A potential of several thousand volts ionizes the gas straight through the tube, no filament needed. Pure neon gives off the popular orange light every classic neon sign is actually built from.

1318.w: All four silver halides can be made by the direct reaction of their elements. Silver bromide is soft, pale yellow and unusually light-sensitive — it became the basis of modern photographic film.

1319.w: Blended with silicon dioxide as 'silica-germania,' germanium dioxide raises glass's refractive index without raising its viscosity — precisely the control a fiber-optic cable's light-guiding core needs.

1320.w: Bismuth and tellurium powders sealed together under vacuum and heated to 800 °C fuse into bismuth telluride, the working crystal inside every solid-state Peltier cooler and portable thermoelectric generator.

1321.w: Vanadium alloyed into iron gives ferrovanadium, the additive steelmakers use as a universal hardener and strengthener — it toughens steel and makes it markedly more resistant to heat and torsion.

1322.w: A nickel oxide-hydroxide plate and a metallic cadmium plate, separated in an alkaline electrolyte, make a nickel-cadmium cell — a rechargeable battery that predates lithium-ion by decades.

1323.w: Platinum gauze alloyed with 10% rhodium is the catalyst ammonia burns across at 900 °C in the Ostwald process, the step that turns fixed nitrogen into nitric oxide — rhodium is what keeps the gauze from wearing through.
