1735.w: A kora's body is a large calabash gourd cut in half and covered with cow skin as a resonator, carrying 21 strings over a long hardwood neck.

1736.w: A piano's steel strings can pull with up to 20 tons of combined tension, enough that the frame holding them is cast iron rather than wood; pressing a key swings a wool-felt-covered hammer to strike them.

1737.w: A flute is a tube, often bamboo, with finger holes cut along its length; covering and uncovering them changes the effective length of the vibrating air column, and that changes the pitch.

1738.w: A pan flute is several bamboo tubes of different lengths, each stopped at the bottom and sounding one note, tied together side by side with woven cord — unlike a flute, it has no finger holes at all.

1739.w: A trumpet is brass tubing, shaped and bent twice into a rounded loop; sound starts when the player buzzes their lips into the cupped mouthpiece, setting up a standing wave in the air column.

1740.w: A traditional didgeridoo comes from a eucalyptus branch termites have already hollowed from the inside — they eat the dead heartwood, since a chemical in the living sapwood repels them.

1741.w: A bagpipe's bag is an airtight reservoir, traditionally a whole goat-, sheep- or cowskin, that the player's arm keeps squeezed — feeding a steady stream of air to the reed pipes so the sound never pauses for breath.

1742.w: A ram's horn is keratin around a bony core; heat softens the keratin enough to flatten and straighten it into a shofar, which is then hollowed from tip to base.

1743.w: A theremin's two metal antennas are wired into an oscillating circuit; a player's hand acts as the other plate of a capacitor, and its distance from an antenna shifts the circuit's frequency and volume — played without ever being touched.

1744.w: A pickup is a magnet wrapped in a coil of copper wire; a vibrating steel string moves the magnet's field, and that induces a matching electrical current in the coil, sent on to an amplifier.

1745.w: Rather than amplifying an existing vibration, a synthesizer's oscillator generates an electrical current oscillating into a waveform from scratch; Robert Moog's 1964 transistor-based voltage-controlled oscillator became the standard circuit for doing it.

1746.w: Arundo donax, the giant cane used for almost all woodwind reeds, grows in dense stands along riverbanks; mature stalks are harvested and dried in the sun for weeks before use.

1747.w: A single reed is a thin blade cut and shaved from one stalk of cane, roughly rectangular with a tip rounded to match the mouthpiece; clamped on by a ligature, it beats against the mouthpiece itself.

1748.w: A double reed is two thin blades of cane tied together with wire onto a small metal staple, the lower half of the staple wrapped in cork for an airtight seal into the instrument — no mouthpiece at all; the two blades beat against each other.

1749.w: A clarinet's single reed of cane beats against the mouthpiece; its body is a cylindrical wood bore, traditionally African blackwood, which gives the instrument its dark, covered tone.

1750.w: A saxophone uses the same single cane reed as a clarinet, but its body is sheet brass rolled into a conical bore; Adolphe Sax patented the family of instruments in 1846.

1751.w: An oboe's double reed has no mouthpiece — its two cane blades beat against each other — feeding into a narrow conical wood bore, traditionally African blackwood, that gives the oboe its bright, penetrating tone.

1752.w: A bassoon uses the same double reed as an oboe, but on a conical bore 2.54 m long — grown from hardwood, usually maple — that has to fold back on itself so the finished instrument stands just 1.34 m tall.

1753.w: A free reed is a thin tongue cut from brass and fitted into a frame slot just barely wider than itself, so it can swing freely back and forth through the slot without ever touching its edges — unlike a cane reed beating against a mouthpiece.

1754.w: Bellows are a pleated, airtight chamber of flexible material — cloth and cardboard reinforced with leather — that draws in air as it expands and forces out a jet of it when squeezed shut.

1755.w: A harmonica's free reeds, usually brass, are mounted to a wood comb — reeds on the inner side sound on the blow, reeds on the outer side sound on the draw — and it's played by breath alone, with no bellows at all.

1756.w: An accordion's hand-squeezed bellows of cloth and leather drive air across banks of free reeds, usually brass or steel; Cyrill Demian patented the name in Vienna in 1829.

1757.w: A reed organ has no pipes at all: foot-pumped bellows drive air over banks of free reeds, thin metal strips vibrating in a frame, to sound its keys — the same free-reed principle Alexandre Debain patented as the harmonium in 1840.

1758.w: A leaf's chloroplasts make sugar from sunlight without eating anything else — plants and algae are producers because they manufacture their own food by photosynthesis, the base every food chain runs on.

1759.w: Animals that eat producers like plants are called herbivores — deer graze grass directly, making them primary consumers, the food chain's first animal step above the producer itself.

1760.w: Wolves prey mostly on large herbivores like deer — primary consumers, which eat plants — which makes a wolf a secondary consumer, one step further up the same food chain than its prey.

1761.w: Fungi feed on waste and dead matter, converting it into inorganic chemicals that can be recycled as mineral nutrients for plants to use again — the recycling step no food chain can skip.

1762.w: Trophic level is simply an organism's position in a food web — a producer occupies the first rung, and the herbivore that eats it sits one rung higher on the exact same ladder.

1763.w: A linear network of links, typically starting with a producer and running up through consumer after consumer to whatever eats last — the simplest possible picture of who-eats-whom.

1764.w: A real ecosystem is never just one food chain — a food web is the natural interconnection of many food chains, a full graph of what eats what across a whole community at once.

1765.w: A predator at the top of a food chain with few or no natural predators of its own, if any — the last link in the chain, not simply another consumer somewhere along the way.

1766.w: Suppressing a whole trophic level ripples down every level beneath it — Yellowstone's wolves are the textbook case, though the ecosystem as a whole never fully reverted to how it was before they were wiped out.

1767.w: North Pacific coastlines without sea otters often turn into urchin barrens instead — abundant sea urchins and no kelp forest, because nothing is left eating the urchins that graze the kelp.

1768.w: A species whose effect on its ecosystem is disproportionate to its own numbers: hunt sea otters to near-extinction and the kelp forests they protected largely disappear soon after.

1769.w: Each side is genuinely better off: the anemone's sting protects the clownfish from predators that cannot tolerate it, and in return the clownfish drives off butterflyfish that would eat the anemone.

1770.w: One species benefits and the other is essentially unaffected: a whale barnacle embedded in the skin gets a free ride and a feeding platform, an arrangement generally reckoned to cost the whale nothing.

1771.w: One organism feeds off another and gives nothing back: a flea is an ectoparasite living on the host's surface, hematophagic and feeding on its blood — real, one-sided harm, not an exchange.

1772.w: The first colonisers of bare ground before there is any soil to work with — the stages of primary succession explicitly begin with pioneer species such as lichens and mosses.

1773.w: Ecological succession is how species composition in a community changes over time — pioneers give way to grasses, then shrubs, then trees, one wave of colonisers replaced by the next.

1774.w: A climax community is the final, stable stage of succession — self-perpetuating and in equilibrium with the habitat, the community, like a mature oak forest, that stops replacing itself.

1775.w: Permafrost keeps the subsoil permanently frozen, so tree growth is hindered by the cold and short seasons — nothing taller than dwarf shrubs, grasses, moss and lichen actually roots there.

1776.w: A desert is defined by dryness, generally under 250 mm of rain a year, and a cactus survives it by dispensing with leaves entirely, storing water instead in a modified, swollen trunk.

1777.w: The world's largest land biome: coniferous forest of mostly pine, spruce and larch across the subarctic, where a long, cold winter with heavy snow is the dominant feature of the year.

1778.w: Needs no less than 1.68 m of rain a year, and enough leaf canopy overhead that the forest floor below receives only about 2% of the sunlight that falls on the top of the trees.

1779.w: Growth is controlled not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one — the textbook case is sunlight in a rainforest, where the canopy takes nearly all of it before it reaches the floor.

1780.w: The maximum population an environment can sustain, given its food, water and space — push a population above that threshold and it typically decreases again, capped by whatever runs out first.

1781.w: Earth's outermost shell is broken into semirigid tectonic plates built from both kinds of crust — basalt flooring nearly every ocean and granite forming the continents riding on top of it.

1782.w: Where two plates are pulled apart, magma from the mantle rises into the gap and freezes into new crust — mostly beneath the oceans, along a divergent boundary.

1783.w: Where two plates converge, their leading edges either crumple upward into mountains or, if one is thinner and denser, get shoved beneath the other — a convergent boundary either way.

1784.w: Two plates sliding horizontally past one another neither build crust nor destroy it — California's San Andreas Fault, about 1,210 km of it, between the Pacific and North American plates, is the textbook transform boundary.

1785.w: Stress builds for years along a locked fault like the San Andreas until it slips all at once, releasing the strain as seismic waves — an earthquake.

1786.w: Beneath the oceans a divergent boundary wells up fresh basalt as the plates part, building a continuous seam of new seafloor that circles the planet for about 65,000 km — the mid-ocean ridge system.

1787.w: Two slabs of continental crust collide and neither can sink beneath the other, so the crust between them thickens and compression pushes it upward — the Himalayas have been rising this way for 65 million years.

1788.w: Where a convergent boundary joins two slabs of continental crust like granite, neither can sink beneath the other, so compression thickens and folds the crust upward — the mechanism that has been raising the Himalayas for 65 million years.

1789.w: Where a slab of oceanic crust flexes downward and begins diving beneath another plate, the seafloor above the bend sags into a long, narrow trench — the Mariana reaches 10,994 metres down.

1790.w: Where a convergent boundary meets oceanic crust like basalt, the thinner, denser plate is forced down in subduction, and the seafloor above the bend sags into a trench.

1791.w: Above a trench, the down-going plate lets go of water that lowers the mantle's melting point above it. That magma rises, and erupting again and again in alternating layers of lava and ash builds the cone.

1792.w: Stretched continental crust thins and cracks along two parallel faults, and the block between them drops to leave a valley — the mechanism opening East Africa's rift right now, at 8-9 mm a year.

1793.w: On continents, the same pulling-apart that widens ocean basins elsewhere stretches and cracks granite crust until the block between two faults drops — the mechanism opening East Africa's rift today.

1794.w: Magma rising from the mantle beneath a broad, flat slab of crust swells the ground upward without folding it — a plateau, raised whole rather than crumpled like a mountain range.

1795.w: The Colorado River cut its channel through layer after layer of rock while the Colorado Plateau it was crossing was itself being lifted 5,000-10,000 feet — the two together are why the Grand Canyon is so deep.

1796.w: Each time a river tops its banks it drops a thin veneer of sediment on the land beside it, coarsest nearest the channel. Flood after flood, that layering builds the flat ground of the floodplain.

1797.w: Water runs faster on the outside of any bend, eroding it, and slower on the inside, dropping sand there instead. Bend by bend the channel migrates back and forth across its own floodplain.

1798.w: Erosion of the two banks either side of a meander's neck, or one strong flood, finally cuts straight through it. The river takes the new shortcut, and sediment seals the old loop off as its own lake.

1799.w: A river's sediment load rides all the way to where the current stops. In standing water the flow spreads out and slows, loses the capacity to carry that load, and drops it — building the delta outward.

1800.w: A river crossing from resistant rock onto softer rock beneath erodes the soft layer faster and undercuts the hard cap above it. The unsupported ledge keeps breaking off, so the drop grows a little every year.

1801.w: Waves attacking the foot of coastal rock cut a notch by constant abrasion. The notch grows until the overhang above it collapses under its own weight, and the cliff retreats a step inland.

1802.w: Waves force their way into an existing crack — a fault or a joint — in the cliff face, and the water trapped in that confined space hits it with far more force than open water ever could, widening it into a cave.

1803.w: Kept up long enough, the same erosion that hollowed the cave eventually breaks all the way through the headland behind it. Where the cave used to end in rock, there is now an opening straight through.

1804.w: An arch has no support underneath its roof, only either side of it, and erosion never stops working on it. Eventually the roof collapses, and the harder rock that was the arch's pillar is left standing alone.

1805.w: The moon's pull raises a tide that pushes into a river mouth twice a day. Where that salt water measurably dilutes with the river's fresh water rather than staying apart, the mixing zone is an estuary.

1806.w: A ridge of sand piled by wind along a shoreline can grow into a barrier separating a strip of shallow water from the open sea behind it, connected only by a narrow inlet or two.

1807.w: Where snowfall outpaces melting for centuries, each year's layer presses the one below into denser and denser ice. Once that ice is thick enough it starts to flow downhill under its own weight.

1808.w: A glacier picks up rock shed from the valley walls above it and, like a conveyor belt, carries that debris from the top of the ice down to wherever the glacier finally melts and drops it.

1809.w: A chunk of a glacier's leading edge breaks — calves — away from the rest of the ice and floats off on its own. The largest icebergs on record calved from the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica.

1810.w: A glacier grinds a U-shaped valley far below present sea level as it advances. When it retreats and the ocean rises to meet the empty trough, the flooded valley is a fjord.

1811.w: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from soil and air and turns faintly acidic. That acid dissolves limestone wherever it seeps through a crack, and the crack widens into a cave over centuries.

1812.w: Dissolution keeps hollowing the rock below a cavern's roof, and the surface stays intact right up until it no longer has enough support. Then it collapses all at once, opening a sinkhole.

1813.w: Weather eats back a plateau's edge unevenly: a hard caprock resists while the softer rock beneath it is sapped away, and the margin retreats until an isolated flat-topped block of the old plateau is left standing.

1814.w: The same retreat that made the mesa keeps going. Once the protective caprock has caved away to the point where only a little remains, the same landform under a smaller cap is called a butte instead.

1815.w: A major eruption can empty enough of the magma chamber beneath a volcano that the walls and roof above it can no longer support their own weight, and the summit collapses down into the space left behind.

1816.w: Groundwater sinks to where magma-heated rock waits about 2,000 metres down. The water above holds the pressure too high for the superheated water below to boil — until it flashes to steam all at once and erupts.

1817.w: Golden eagles take rabbits, hares and marmots more than anything else, diving at up to 320 km/h to catch them in open country.

1818.w: It hunts open and semi-open ground from a nest built on a cliff face, avoiding dense forest almost entirely.

1819.w: Unlike any other big cat, the jaguar regularly preys on turtles -- its bite is strong enough to crack straight through the shell.

1820.w: A powerful swimmer that hunts in water more than a tiger does, taking anacondas and caimans along Central and South American rivers.

1821.w: Turquoise is a hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium, CuAl6(PO4)4(OH)8.4H2O -- the copper is what gives it its blue.

1822.w: Aluminium and phosphate make up most of its structure by weight; copper is the minor ingredient that supplies all of the colour.

1823.w: Quetzalcoatl's own name is Nahuatl for 'quetzal-feathered serpent' -- precious plumage fused to a snake's body, worshipped across Mesoamerica for over a thousand years.

1824.w: Known as the giver of maize to mankind, and worshipped as the wind itself in his Ehecatl aspect -- one god wearing two faces of the same generosity.

1825.w: His name means Smoking Mirror. Aztec priests read the future in obsidian mirrors, just like the one he is shown holding in the codices.

1826.w: God of the night sky -- moon, stars and jaguars all his domain -- he ruled the first, dim half-sun until Quetzalcoatl knocked him down and he fell to earth as a jaguar.

1827.w: He told the wandering Aztecs to build their city wherever they found an eagle perched on a cactus -- the omen they found at Lake Texcoco, founding Tenochtitlan there.

1828.w: Conceived when a ball of feathers touched his mother Coatlicue as she swept a temple floor, he was born fully grown and already armed for war.

1829.w: Rain and lightning were one motif to the Aztecs: bolts were drawn as fiery serpents, and Tlaloc is shown flanked by snakes as often as by storm clouds.

1830.w: The rain god of goggle eyes and fangs appears in art alongside jaguars, serpents and butterflies -- the creatures of the wet, green world he governed.

1831.w: Her name means 'Serpent Skirt.' The stone statue found beneath Mexico City's main square wears a skirt woven from writhing snakes.

1832.w: Her necklace is human hands, hearts and a skull; her face, on the same statue, is two serpents meeting where her head was struck off.

1833.w: Sun god of the fifth age specifically, and he demanded sacrifice to keep moving across the sky.

1834.w: The Aztecs believed Tonatiuh's daily crossing of the sky consumed him, and that the debt had to be repaid in sacrifice to keep the sun moving.

1835.w: His whole body is drawn as bone -- a toothy skull for a face, bared ribs, a necklace strung with human eyeballs.

1836.w: Called the Turquoise Lord: to Aztec priests turquoise was fire's own stone, so masks of Xiuhtecuhtli were laid in a mosaic of it.

1837.w: Households kept a small fire burning at all times in his honour -- warmth against cold, light against dark, food against famine, in one god.

1838.w: One tradition names the flower goddess Xochiquetzal as his mother -- the young maize god born of blossoms as much as of earth.

1839.w: The Florentine Codex instead names him son of the earth goddess Tlazolteotl and the solar lord Piltzintecuhtli.

1840.w: Xolotl was Quetzalcoatl's own twin, the dark half of the same pair -- dog-headed where his brother wore feathers.

1841.w: Every night he escorted the sun through the underworld and back, guarding it on the one journey it could not survive alone.

1842.w: Twice a year, sunlight and the shadow of El Castillo's stepped edges combine to crawl a serpent of light down the pyramid at Chichen Itza to meet its carved stone head.

1843.w: Chief among the Maya creator gods and credited with shaping humankind, his transformation into the Principal Bird Deity is one of his oldest depictions.

1844.w: A colonial-era source credits him with inventing the priestly art of writing -- the deity behind the very books the Maya kept.

1845.w: Called 'the aged jaguar goddess,' she governed fertility, medicine and the water Mesoamerican life depended on.

1846.w: Consort to the creator god Itzamna, she was said to have borne him thirteen sons and was invoked by name over every childbirth.

1847.w: Long-nosed and fanged, Chaac strikes storm clouds with a lightning axe -- the bolt that starts the rain the Maya's fields depended on.

1848.w: The Ch'a Cháak ceremony still asks Chaac for rain with an offering of turkey blood poured onto the fields.

1849.w: Patron of cacao among the Maya; his name may mean 'black star,' tying him to Polaris, the star merchants steered by.

1850.w: Merchants travelling under his protection stacked stones and burned incense to him each night on the road.

1851.w: The K'iche' creation story tried earth, mud and wood first, before the gods finally shaped people successfully out of maize dough.

1852.w: Recorded from oral memory around 1550, in the same tradition of writing the Maya credited to a god.

1853.w: Hunahpu and Xbalanque inherited their dead father's rubber ball and gear, and their ballgame against Xibalba drives the Popol Vuh's central story.

1854.w: Having tricked and defeated the lords of the underworld, the twins are described in the text itself as two stalks of maize.

1855.w: Getting to the Xibalban court meant crossing rivers of blood, pus and scorpions before ever reaching the ballcourt where the Hero Twins were forced to play.

1856.w: Among its six trial chambers was the Jaguar House, and the road there crossed rivers where scorpions swarmed alongside the blood and pus.

1857.w: Xolotl guided the dead across a river of blood crawling with jaguars and snakes, one obstacle among several on the four-year descent through Mictlan.

1858.w: Its lowest of nine levels is ruled by Mictlantecuhtli from a windowless house -- a skeleton god presiding over exactly what is left.

1859.w: The current Aztec cosmic age, born when two gods threw themselves into a divine bonfire and became the sun and the moon.

1860.w: Four earlier suns had already failed -- among them ages ruled by Tezcatlipoca and by Tlaloc -- before this fifth one ever began.

1861.w: For decades the carved face at its centre was read as Tonatiuh; many scholars now argue it is instead the earth monster Tlaltecuhtli.

1862.w: A 3.6-metre basalt disc carved under Moctezuma II, its rings record the four cosmic ages that failed before this, the fifth.

1863.w: Aztec tradition holds that Quetzalcoatl brought the cacao plant down from a sacred mountain and taught women how to prepare it as a drink.

1864.w: Linnaeus later named the plant Theobroma -- Greek for 'food of the gods' -- echoing exactly this belief, held on both sides of the Maya-Aztec divide.

1865.w: Big low-grade deposits like hematite are exactly what open-pit mining is built for: dug in stepped benches, with haul roads spiralling up the walls so wheeled trucks can carry blasted rock out — up to a million tons a day from the largest pits.

1866.w: Strip mining works a shallow, flat seam like coal one long trench at a time: the overburden — soil and rock above the seam — dug from each new strip is dumped into the void the previous strip left, and the operation walks down the seam.

1867.w: Mountaintop removal takes strip mining to its most drastic form: explosives blast up to 120 metres off an Appalachian summit to reach thin coal seams beneath, and the shattered rock is dumped into the valley next door as valley fill.

1868.w: Hydraulic mining points pressurised water at a bank of loose sand and gravel and blasts it apart on purpose — an engineered flood — then sluices the debris through, letting anything dense enough to sink stay behind.

1869.w: Room-and-pillar mining leaves blocks of coal standing as pillars to hold the roof up while rooms are dug out between them, the ceiling braced further with timber props — one of the oldest ways to work a seam underground.

1870.w: A longwall panel starts as gate roads driven the room-and-pillar way; a shearer then cuts the face while hydraulic supports advance and let the roof collapse behind — about 80% of the coal comes out, against 60% for room-and-pillar.

1871.w: Block caving works the same huge, low-grade ore body an open pit would, once it's too deep to strip: undercut the base and gravity fractures the column into tunnels below. Palabora's copper mine went from open pit to block cave in 2002.

1872.w: Bauxite is what a rock like granite becomes after ages of weathering under intense tropical rainfall: everything but aluminium washes away, leaving bauxite so close to the surface it's almost always strip mined, not dug from a pit.

1873.w: Bauxite is virtually the only ore aluminium comes from, and it's split apart the same way any aluminium ore is — in a Hall–Héroult electrolysis cell, the 1886 process that finally made the metal cheap enough for everyday use.

1874.w: Spodumene, a lithium aluminium silicate, crystallises in granite pegmatites — Greenbushes in Western Australia, the world's biggest hard-rock lithium deposit, is a single enormous open-pit mine dug into one.

1875.w: Spodumene locks its lithium into a crystal structure acid alone can't touch. Roasting the ore first converts it to more reactive β-spodumene, and only then does dissolving it in acid actually free the lithium.

1876.w: Mountain Pass, California's only working rare-earth mine, digs its ore from a 1.4-billion-year-old carbonatite as a single open pit — almost all the rare-earth content in that ore rides in one mineral, bastnäsite.

1877.w: Bastnäsite gives up its rare earths to acid, not lye: the ore is roasted, then dissolved in hydrochloric acid down to a pH under 5 — a different chemistry from monazite's caustic crack, but the same rare-earth mixture at the end.

1878.w: Most of the world's tin isn't dug from hard rock at all — cassiterite survives weathering and piles up in river gravel, and placer mining is how Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia have supplied most of the world's tin for generations.

1879.w: Monazite is dense enough to survive weathering whole, and placer mining — the same density trick that concentrates gold — piles it up in beach and river sand alongside other heavy minerals like zircon.

1880.w: Missouri's Viburnum Trend, some of the purest lead ore on Earth, is worked entirely by room-and-pillar mining: crews blast dolomite rock loaded with galena, leaving pillars standing to hold the roof up.

1881.w: The same Viburnum Trend room-and-pillar mines that produce Missouri's lead also produce its zinc — crews blast dolomite rock loaded with sphalerite, zinc sulfide, sitting right alongside the galena that gives up the lead.

1882.w: Cheetahs hunt by daylight across open grassland, using explosive speed to run down fast, small prey — hares among them, killed with a single bite once run down.

1883.w: Earthworms can supply over 60% of a fox's calories in some months. It hunts them mainly by ear, walking pasture and lawns on warm, damp nights when worms surface.

1884.w: Historically confined to open plains, coyotes hunt in loose bands to bring down prey too large to take alone — like deer — a habit noted since Lewis and Clark's 1805 expedition.

1885.w: A specialised pack hunter of the open savanna. Certain packs are known to specialise in bringing down adult zebra weighing up to 240 kg — many times their own size.

1886.w: An ophiophagous apex predator: its diet 'consists primarily of other snakes and lizards,' including venomous species and monitor lizards.

1887.w: A bulb is a bud wrapped in fat leaf bases — a whole plant packed with next season's food, sitting underground.

1888.w: A potato is not a root. It is a swollen underground stem, storing starch for next year's shoots — which is why it has eyes.

1889.w: Many bulbs need a cold spell before they will flower — vernalisation. Without a winter, they simply sit.

1890.w: Earth up the stems with straw and the buried part makes more tubers. The potato grows in the dark, not in the soil's nutrients.

1891.w: Mechanical stress from wind suppresses a stem's internode elongation and thickens it instead — plants build a shorter, sturdier stem in direct response to being pushed around.

1892.w: A node is the point of attachment of a leaf on a stem — a small growth zone that can also produce buds, branches, or extra roots.

1893.w: An internode is the stretch of stem between two nodes. It elongates to space the leaves apart, while the compact node itself barely grows at all.

1894.w: The bud capping a stem's growing tip, past its last internode. While active it produces auxin that suppresses the buds below — apical dominance — so removing it makes a plant branch instead of just growing taller.

1895.w: An axillary bud sits in the axil where a leaf meets the stem, right at a node — dormant while the terminal bud dominates, but able to grow into a side branch.

1896.w: Cut the leaf away and the abscission layer at the node seals over, leaving a corky leaf scar — the exact mark of where the leaf used to attach.

1897.w: As a stem thickens, bark replaces the smooth skin outside it — but that skin still needs to breathe, so lenticels form: loosely packed cork cells that let gases through.

1898.w: A growing root tip is shielded by its root cap — a layer of cells that takes the abrasion of pushing through soil and is constantly shed and replaced, helping the root penetrate.

1899.w: Just behind the root cap sits the apical meristem: a knot of ceaselessly dividing cells that produces every new cell the root will ever have.

1900.w: Cells born in the meristem stop dividing and stretch lengthwise in the elongation zone — that expansion, not more division, is what actually pushes the root tip forward.

1901.w: Once a cell finishes elongating it matures, and in this zone many grow a root hair — a fine tubular outgrowth that multiplies the root's surface for taking up water and minerals.

1902.w: As a seed sprouts, its embryonic seed-leaf — the cotyledon — is often the first green tissue to unfurl, still carrying the food reserve that fed germination.

1903.w: Ceiba pentandra grows wide plank buttresses instead of a deep taproot, spreading sideways through the thin, nutrient-rich humus layer of rainforest soil that a taproot would simply miss.

1904.w: Buttress roots are large, wide roots on all sides of a shallowly rooted tropical tree — support that substitutes for a deep taproot in thin, waterlogged rainforest soil.

1905.w: In maize, adventitious roots emerge from stem nodes above the ground and arch down into the soil — brace roots that physically prop up a tall, top-heavy stalk.

1906.w: English ivy climbs trees and walls by growing as a vine, gripping the surface with clinging roots along the shaded side of each shoot rather than rooting in soil there.

1907.w: Ivy's clinging roots are covered in root hairs that secrete an adhesive and reshape themselves around the surface — a permanent structural grip, not a nutrient-seeking one.

1908.w: Many epiphytic orchids grow with no soil at all: spongy, velamen-covered roots hang in open air, turn green with chlorophyll, and both catch rainwater and photosynthesize.

1909.w: In waterlogged mud, some mangrove roots grow upward into pneumatophores studded with porous lenticels leading to spongy aerenchyma that carries oxygen down to the buried roots.

1910.w: Type metal is hard lead with tin stirred in: Gutenberg's own mix was lead, tin and antimony, cast one letter per piece in a hand mould so a page could be assembled and reused instead of carved from a single block. It stayed standard for 550 years.

1911.w: Gutenberg developed an oil-based ink that stuck to metal type instead of beading like the water-based ink scribes used; a lever-driven screw then pressed the inked type against the paper.

1912.w: A convex glass lens set in a wooden tube bends distant light to a focus; a concave glass eyepiece spreads it back out, magnifying the view without flipping it. Lippershey filed the first patent in 1608, Galileo built his own in 1609.

1913.w: Newcomen's engine cooled its cylinder every stroke to condense the steam, then reheated it before the next. Watt's separate condenser, 1769, does the condensing elsewhere, so the iron cylinder stays hot throughout.

1914.w: A glass tube of mercury, sealed at one end and stood in a dish of mercury, leaves a vacuum at the closed top. Torricelli, 1643: it is the weight of the air on the open dish that holds the column up, not the vacuum pulling.

1915.w: A pendulum's swing takes the same time regardless of how wide it swings, so Huygens, 1656, coupled one to an escapement: each swing releases an iron-toothed wheel by exactly one tooth, pacing the whole clock.

1916.w: A cylinder of iron teeth pulls cotton fiber through slots in a metal plate too narrow for the seeds to follow; a second brushed cylinder wipes the fiber off before it can jam the teeth. Whitney, 1793.

1917.w: Howe's iron needle carries its eye near the point instead of the back, so it can push a loop of thread through the cloth from above; a shuttle underneath passes a second thread through that loop, locking the stitch. 1845.

1918.w: Otis hung the platform from a steel spring under the hoisting rope's tension. Let the rope go slack — as it would if it broke — and the spring drives two pawls out to lock into ratchet teeth on the iron guide rails. 1852.

1919.w: A key at one station switches the current in a wire circuit on and off; at the far end, that current switches an electromagnet, moving an armature that clicks or embosses the dots and dashes of the message. Morse, 1837–1844.

1920.w: Bell's telephone used permanent magnets with iron diaphragms: sound vibrates the iron disc near the magnet's coil, inducing a fluctuating current shaped like the sound itself, which a second diaphragm turns back into sound.

1921.w: A transformer charges a capacitor; discharged across a gap, the current oscillates back and forth and radiates from a wire antenna as a radio wave. Marconi built the first practical version around 1896.

1922.w: Fleming built his 'oscillation valve' specifically to rectify a radio-frequency current: a heated filament boils electrons into a vacuum, and they cross to the plate only when it is positive, never the other way. 1904.

1923.w: An iron diaphragm-and-needle assembly indents hill-and-dale grooves into tinfoil wrapped around a rotating, threaded cylinder as sound vibrates it; tracing the groove afterward vibrates the diaphragm again, faintly reproducing the sound.

1924.w: High voltage across electrodes sealed in an evacuated glass tube drives cathode rays that strike the far wall and throw off penetrating radiation. Röntgen photographed his wife's hand with it in 1895 — she saw her own skeleton.

1925.w: Light through a small hole in one wall of a box lands inverted and reversed on the far wall. Della Porta suggested catching that image on a sheet of paper as a drawing aid, centuries before any lens improved it.

1926.w: Silver fumed with iodine vapor forms a coating of silver iodide — a compound so light-sensitive that exposure alone converts some of its ions back to visible metallic silver.

1927.w: Daguerre's camera projects the scene onto the light-sensitized plate; where light struck hardest, the most silver darkens. Mercury vapor then develops that faint, invisible result into a picture anyone can see. 1839.

1928.w: Sulfuric acid dehydrates two ethanol molecules into one molecule of ether — a reaction known since the 13th century. Morton demonstrated inhaling its vapor for painless surgery in Boston, October 16, 1846.

1929.w: Kilby's 1958 chip put every component of a circuit — not just the transistors — onto one block of semiconductor, wired together instead of joined by hand. Noyce's silicon version, 1959, is what modern chips still follow.

1930.w: Faggin's Intel 4004, 1971, packed 2,300 transistors onto one integrated circuit — instruction decoding, computation, result routing and register storage, an entire CPU's worth of components, all on the same chip.

1931.w: Otto's engine, 1876, was the first to compress the fuel-air mixture — coal gas and air — inside an iron cylinder before igniting it, for far higher efficiency than any engine that just burned the mixture unpressurized.

1932.w: The Flyer's wings, cambered 1-in-20 to generate lift, were covered in cotton muslin; wing-warping twisted the tips to steer; a chain drive off their own 12-horsepower engine spun the propellers. Kitty Hawk, December 17 1903.

1933.w: Press a key and an iron typebar swings up, its letter molded in reverse on the striking head, and hits an inked ribbon against the paper on the platen, printing the letter right-reading. Sholes and Glidden, patented 1868.

1934.w: Its lower jaws were built for slicing, not crushing — compressed, serrated teeth that cut through flesh and hide and manipulated prey with the front of the mouth, unlike a tyrannosaur's bone-breaking bite.

1935.w: Before an open pit's bench is blasted, a rotary rig with tungsten-carbide-tipped bits bores rows of holes across it — up to 27cm wide and over 40 metres deep, the pattern every blast round is built from.

1936.w: Draglines strip the overburden off a coal seam, and almost all large ones run on grid electricity delivered by a trailing cable rather than diesel — Big Muskie's ran at 13,800 volts, stripping 8,000 cubic yards an hour.

1937.w: A diesel engine turns a generator instead of a gearbox; the electricity it makes feeds motors that turn the wheels. It skips the mechanical transmission entirely, which is why locomotives and giant mining trucks both use it.

1938.w: The haul roads spiralling up an open pit's walls exist for one machine. BelAZ's 75710 hauls 450 tonnes on eight tyres 4 metres across, each rear wheel turned by its own electric motor fed by an onboard diesel-electric drivetrain.

1939.w: A continuous miner's rotating steel drum, fitted with tungsten-carbide picks, scrapes up to 14 tons of coal a minute straight off the seam — no separate drilling or blasting, the way older room-and-pillar work needed.

1940.w: Tungsten carbide is literally what a longwall shearer's picks are made of, one of the material's standard mining uses alongside rock-drill bits and plough chisels. The drums shear coal off the face as hydraulic supports advance behind them.

1941.w: Diesel-electric transmission reached railways before it reached mining trucks: a locomotive's engine turns a generator, and traction motors geared to the wheels supply the torque — the drivetrain of nearly every modern freight locomotive.

1942.w: Every haul truck dumps its load straight into a primary crusher — a gyratory or jaw crusher, essentially a moving steel jaw, that breaks head-sized boulders down to fist-sized chunks before anything else happens to the ore.

1943.w: Crushed ore still isn't fine enough for flotation. A ball mill takes over: a rotating steel drum tumbling with forged steel grinding balls reduces it further, to sand- and silt-sized grains, before the ore can go anywhere else.

1944.w: Ground ore becomes a slurry; blow air through it with a reagent that makes the valuable grains hydrophobic, and they stick to the rising bubbles and float off as a froth. Froth flotation is the main way sulfide ores are recovered.

1945.w: Flotation only wants the sliver of the rock that's valuable mineral. Almost everything else — roughly 99% of what the ball mill ground, still wet — leaves as tailings, pumped to a dam built to hold the slurry back.

1946.w: A conveyor belt is a closed loop of reinforced rubber slung between rotating pulleys — cheaper per tonne-kilometre than trucking, which is why crushed ore usually rides a belt for the rest of its trip through a plant.

1947.w: Crushed ore rides a conveyor out to open stockpiles, where truckloads of different grades get blended into one consistent pile — buffering the swings in ore grade the mill or the ship both need smoothed out.

1948.w: Stockpiled ore is loaded into hopper cars and hauled out as a dedicated unit train. BHP's Pilbara train set the world record for longest and heaviest ever: 7.35km long, 682 cars, 99,734 tonnes, hauled by eight locomotives.

1949.w: A shiploader — a travelling conveyor on a gantry — is what actually gets stockpiled ore into a waiting hold. Capesize ships, up to 400,000 tonnes deadweight and too big for the Suez or Panama Canal, carry about 75% of the world's seaborne iron ore.

1950.w: Pilbara ore railways run to one kind of destination: a dedicated bulk-export terminal. Port Hedland, the world's biggest bulk export port by tonnage, shipped 531.5 million tonnes of iron ore in a single year.

1951.w: Grey cast iron self-lubricates: graphite flakes already in its microstructure reduce galling and wear on their own, which is why piston rings — most of them cast iron — can seal a moving cylinder without a separate lubricant film.

1952.w: A wheelset is two wheels mounted rigidly on one steel axle so they always rotate together — the axle is what actually turns; the wheel is just the part that touches the rail.

1953.w: A bogie is the frame under a rail car to which axles are attached through bearings; the whole frame pivots so a pair of wheelsets can swivel together and steer the car around a curve without the axles themselves bending.

1954.w: Steam pushes the piston; a connecting rod carries that push to a crank pin fixed on the driving wheel itself, turning straight-line force into rotation one stroke at a time.

1955.w: The diesel engine never drives the wheels directly. It spins a generator, and the current from that generator powers electric traction motors mounted right on the bogie — diesel-electric transmission, standard since the 1930s.

1956.w: No onboard engine at all: current is drawn straight from an overhead wire or third rail and fed to the traction motors — the real difference from a diesel-electric, which only generates its own current.

1957.w: An unpowered steel-framed car riding on bogies at each end, fitted with standardised couplers and air-brake hoses so different wagon types can all be assembled into the same train.

1958.w: A sloped floor and bottom gates let a hopper car dump loose bulk cargo — coal, ore, grain — without a shovel; the type developed alongside automated coal loading and unloading.

1959.w: A cylindrical pressure vessel for liquid or gas cargo, bolted to the underframe; some interiors are lined in glass or other coatings so corrosive contents never touch the steel shell.

1960.w: No sides or roof, just an open deck for loads too big or heavy for a boxcar — the deck can be wood or steel, and heavy-duty flatcars use a steel-plated one.

1961.w: The original enclosed freight car: a wood-sided box on wheels with sliding doors, built to keep general merchandise dry — all-steel sides only became standard decades later.

1962.w: Cabooses started life as flatcars or modified boxcars with a cabin added; the glass-windowed cupola on the roof let the crew watch their own train for shifting loads and overheating axles.

1963.w: Push two cars together and the knuckle pivots shut and locks itself, no one standing between them — Eli Janney's forged-steel knuckle coupler, patented April 1873, replacing the link-and-pin worked by hand.

1964.w: Bearing steel is iron with about 1% carbon and 1.5% chromium, hardened until the rollers packed between the races can carry an axle's full load while barely sliding at all.

1965.w: The simplest bearing has no rolling parts: the axle just slides inside a sleeve. Graphite packed into that sliding surface was how 19th-century axleboxes were lubricated before rollers took over.

1966.w: Compressed air runs the length of the train and presses a shoe against each wheel; break the train apart and the line loses pressure — which is exactly what makes the brakes clamp on, not release.

1967.w: A track circuit runs current straight through the rails themselves, and a train's own axles short it — that trips a signal, genuinely different from a road signal, which runs on a fixed timer, not on where the traffic actually is.

1968.w: All modern rails are hot-rolled steel: reheated and passed through grooved rollers until the bar takes the asymmetric I-beam profile that resists wear at the head and bolts down at the foot.

1969.w: A bloomery never melts the iron: at about 1200°C the ore is reduced to a spongy mass and the slag runs out, leaving metal that has to be hammered. Actually melting iron needs 1538°C, which is why cast iron waited for the blast furnace.

1970.w: Creosote is a coal-tar distillate, and it is still the most common preservative for wooden railway ties — soaked in, it keeps the crosstie from rotting under a century of weather.

1971.w: A prestressed concrete tie is cast around steel wires stretched taut before the pour; once the concrete cures and the wires relax, they squeeze it into permanent compression that resists cracking under load.

1972.w: Ballast has to be sharp, angular and hard enough to interlock and stay put under a rolling load — quartzite is one of the rock types railways crush for exactly that durability.

1973.w: Ballast has to be sharp, angular and hard enough to interlock and stay put under load — gneiss is one of the parent rock types different railways crush into ballast for that same durability.

1974.w: The oldest switches are forged rail and rod, thrown by a lever in a signal box and moved entirely by hand — the tapered points swing across to send the train onto one track or the other.

1975.w: Modern switches move the rail itself with a remote point machine — an electric motor, or a pneumatic or hydraulic actuator — strong enough to throw points too stiff to move by hand.

1976.w: Not a station — a ladder of switches routes each wagon off the arrival track onto its own classification track, sorting one jumbled train into the separate trains it needs to become.

1977.w: A capacitor is two conductors with an insulating gap between them — glass, ceramic, paper, and oxide layers all serve as that dielectric, with copper as the plates.

1978.w: A MEMS accelerometer is a proof mass on silicon springs, wired as one plate of a capacitor; acceleration deflects the mass, changing the capacitance against a fixed plate, and that shift is read as motion.

1979.w: Silicon absorbs photons from 190 to 1100 nanometres, well into the infrared — why a plain silicon photodiode, not a special sensor, is what receives an infrared remote control's beam.

1980.w: The iPod's Click Wheel senses touch by capacitive sensing: a ring of copper electrodes under its plastic cover forms a capacitor, and a finger's own capacitance tells the controller where it is resting.

1981.w: A floating-gate transistor's extra gate is electrically isolated by an insulating oxide layer, so electrons placed there stay trapped — a stored bit that survives with the power off.

1982.w: The fifth-generation iPod paired flash memory for offline music storage with the touch-sensitive Click Wheel for navigation, once Apple's design moved on from a spinning hard drive.

1983.w: A piezoelectric sensor — the effect quartz shows under pressure — sits under the shoe's insole and radios a packet to the iPod once a second while the wearer walks or runs, and for ten seconds after.

1984.w: EVA foam is what shoemakers call an expanded rubber or foam rubber, blown under heat into a mass of closed gas cells — Nike sells its own compression-moulded version, Phylon, for running-shoe midsoles.

1985.w: A foam midsole cushions between a rubber outsole and the foot. Pronation, the foot's natural inward roll on landing, is normal and necessary — shoe support only changes how much of it happens.

1986.w: A polarizing filter is plastic film with iodine chains stretched straight through it: light vibrating along the chains is absorbed, the perpendicular light passes. In an LCD that film rides on glass.

1987.w: Friedrich Reinitzer heated cholesteryl benzoate in 1888 and found it did not melt like other compounds: at 145.5°C it turned into a cloudy liquid, and only at 178.5°C did that liquid clear.

1988.w: A thin-film transistor is grown on a non-conducting substrate such as glass rather than cut from a wafer — which is how an LCD gives every pixel its own transistor without going opaque.

1989.w: The whole benefit of TFT technology is a separate transistor for each pixel, so every liquid crystal in the panel twists open or shut on its own, independent of its neighbours.

1990.w: Each pixel sits between two crossed polarizing filters. Voltage untwists the liquid crystal between them, rotating light through to the second filter, and colour filters split it into red, green, blue.

1991.w: IMAX 3-D films are shot with two cameras joined by a beam-splitter mirror, their lenses closer than the camera bodies allow; projection then sends each eye's film through a polarizing filter set at right angles to the other, sorted by matching glasses.

1992.w: A laser diode's crystal is cleaved to perfectly smooth, parallel edges that form a resonant cavity; light bounces between those mirror-facets and is amplified until the diode begins to lase.

1993.w: A laser diode reads a spiral of pits stamped into a thin aluminum reflective layer: light off a pit's peak returns half a wavelength out of phase with light off the land beside it, and a photodiode reads that flicker as data.

1994.w: A CCD pixel is a metal-oxide-semiconductor capacitor: light frees electrons the way a photodiode does, and the capacitor traps that charge, building up proportional to the light received.

1995.w: A control circuit shifts each photosite's charge to its neighbour like a bucket brigade until the last one reaches a transistor amplifier, which converts the arriving charge into a voltage.

1996.w: Light striking the CCD sensor becomes an analog current; an analog-to-digital converter samples that current and outputs a digital number for every photosite, making the picture a file, not a voltage trace.

1997.w: Magnetic tape coats a strip of plastic film with magnetizable particles like magnetite; a recording head fed by the signal's current imprints that coating with a matching pattern of magnetism.

1998.w: A tape head is an electromagnet: a ring of magnetic material with a narrow gap and a coil wound around it — fully reversible, so the same gap that magnetizes the tape recording it reads the pattern back on playback.

1999.w: Electrons boiling off a heated cathode are bent into spirals by a magnet's field, sweeping past cavities cut into a solid copper block and exciting them into microwave oscillation.

2000.w: A magnetron's alternating field makes polar molecules — not only water — keep rotating to face it, about 2.45 billion times a second; that molecular friction heats the food, not surface radiant heat.

2001.w: A flatbed scanner shines light onto the original and reads the intensity and colour reflected back, a line at a time; mirrors and a lens direct that light onto the moving CCD array.

2002.w: A barcode reader swaps a flatbed scanner's CCD array for a single sweeping laser diode spot: a rotating mirror sweeps the beam across the bars up to 1,200 times a second, and a photodetector reads the reflected brightness to decode it.

2003.w: A capacitive fingerprint sensor is a grid of tiny capacitors, and current between them forms the image; a human fingertip's ridges sit closer to the sensor than the valleys between them do, so they read differently.

2004.w: The Wii Remote points using an array of photodiodes — a PixArt optical sensor — that tracks the Sensor Bar's ten infrared LEDs by triangulation, while a separate MEMS accelerometer senses acceleration along three axes.

2005.w: Liquid helium chills the niobium-titanium coil below its critical temperature, where it loses all electrical resistance. Current started flowing in the closed loop then persists on its own for months, sustaining the field.

2006.w: The magnet aligns the spin of hydrogen nuclei, abundant in the body's water and fat. A radio pulse tips them out of alignment, and the signal they emit relaxing back becomes a cross-sectional image — no X-rays involved.

2007.w: Fludeoxyglucose substitutes the positron-emitting isotope fluorine-18 for the hydroxyl group at glucose's C-2 position. Cells take it up exactly like ordinary sugar, so it concentrates wherever metabolism runs hottest.

2008.w: Fluorine-18 is unstable. It decays by converting a proton to a neutron and ejecting a positron — the antimatter counterpart of an electron — which travels only millimetres through tissue before meeting one.

2009.w: The positron meets an ordinary electron in nearby tissue. The two annihilate, and their combined mass converts entirely into two gamma-ray photons of 511 keV each, launched in exactly opposite directions.

2010.w: The two annihilation photons fly off 180 degrees apart. A ring of detectors times pairs arriving within nanoseconds of each other, and the line between the two hits locates where the tracer decayed.

2011.w: An alternating voltage across a piezoelectric crystal like quartz makes it expand and contract at the driving frequency — the piezoelectric effect run in reverse — launching a beam of sound past human hearing.

2012.w: Pulsing the current oscillates the transducer's crystal, launching packets of ultrasonic pressure waves at 1.5 to 20 megahertz into the body — the same piezoelectric vibration, aimed outward.

2013.w: Each boundary the wave meets — skin, muscle, amniotic fluid — reflects part of it back toward the probe. The timing of that echo gives depth, and its strength hints at what tissue produced it.

2014.w: A motor sweeps the transducer's beam through an arc many times a second. Each sweep of echoes builds one 3-D slice, and stringing thousands together in real time adds a fourth dimension: time itself.

2015.w: In intracytoplasmic sperm injection, a single immobilised sperm is drawn into a glass micropipette fine enough to pierce an egg's membrane directly, bypassing the swim natural fertilisation depends on.

2016.w: The loaded needle is pushed through the zona pellucida and the sperm released straight into the ovum's cytoplasm — the technique used whenever sperm cannot fertilise an egg unassisted.

2017.w: Nerve tissue is specialised to carry an electrical impulse — the action potential — down its length, in the fastest myelinated human fibres at up to 120 metres per second.

2018.w: Surgeons reroute a residual arm nerve into a chest or thigh muscle no longer needed for its own job. When the brain still sends the command to close a missing hand, that nerve fires into the muscle, producing a detectable twitch.

2019.w: A sensor on the skin reads the myoelectric twitch and a controller decodes which motion it stands for, drawing current to drive motors at the wrist and elbow — intuitive control from a limb that is gone.

2020.w: The surgeon's hand movements at a console are scaled down and electronically filtered to remove tremor before current drives motors in robotic arms holding the instruments, watched through a magnified 3-D view.

2021.w: A titanium-and-polyurethane pump uses a motor-driven rotor, spinning several thousand times a minute, to shuttle fluid between two chambers — alternately filling one side with blood while it empties the other.

2022.w: A coil outside the body sends power through intact skin by electromagnetic induction to an internal coil, recharging the implant's batteries without any wire or tube breaking the skin — the usual route for infection.

2023.w: The earliest reinforced concrete, patented by Joseph Monier in 1867, embedded iron mesh in wet concrete so the two shared the load; steel later replaced iron for its greater tensile strength, but the same principle — concrete carrying compression, metal carrying tension — has held ever since.

2024.w: Hung on the finished frame, a curtain wall carries no load beyond its own weight — which is exactly what lets it be built from something as light as glass panels instead of load-bearing masonry.

2025.w: A reinforced-concrete and steel frame, anchored in a core that houses the elevators and stairs, carries the entire structural load; the curtain wall hung over it is doing nothing but keeping the weather out.

2026.w: A flash of light pumps chromium ions in a ruby rod to an excited state. As they drop back down together, they release identical photons in phase — stimulated emission, the process the acronym LASER names.

2027.w: A silver-halide photographic emulsion, its grains far finer than ordinary film, coats a glass plate — fine enough to resolve the microscopic interference fringes two coherent beams of light leave behind.

2028.w: A split beam sends an object beam off the subject and a reference beam straight to the plate. Where the two coherent beams cross, they interfere, and the plate records that pattern — a light wave's phase, reconstructed later by the same reference beam.

2029.w: A laser vaporises graphite rods in an atmosphere of helium gas. The carbon vapour condenses into cage-like molecules of exactly 60 atoms, closed into a hollow sphere shaped like a soccer ball — a Nobel-winning 1985 discovery.

2030.w: Peel a single atom-thick sheet of graphite's honeycomb lattice and roll it into a seamless cylinder a few nanometres across, and the way that sheet was rolled determines whether the tube conducts like a metal or a semiconductor.

2031.w: A tungsten wire is electrochemically etched, drawn slowly out of the acid bath as it thins, until it narrows to a point that ends, ideally, in a single atom.

2032.w: Held about a nanometre from a conductive surface with a small bias voltage applied, electrons quantum-mechanically tunnel across the vacuum gap they classically lack the energy to cross — a current so distance-sensitive it maps atoms.

2033.w: Superconducting dipole magnets, cooled to 1.9 K, bend two beams of protons around a 27-kilometre ring and steer them into a head-on collision at nearly the speed of light — recreating energies not seen since a fraction of a second after the Big Bang.

2034.w: Hand cards are wooden paddles set with fine wire teeth that break up locked clumps of fibre and comb them straight and parallel to each other, ready to spin.

2035.w: A wool card's wire teeth disentangle, clean and intermix raw wool's fibres into a continuous web, aligning them and combing out the vegetable-matter contaminants still caught in the fleece.

2036.w: Wool fibres are covered in microscopic scales; heat, moisture and agitation make those scales open and latch onto their neighbours, matting the fibres into felt without any spinning or weaving.

2037.w: Carding produces a continuous, aligned web of fibre suitable for spinning — the same drawing-and-twisting act that turns any prepared fibre into thread, just starting from fibres that already run one way.

2038.w: Reeled silk filament is too fine and weak on its own — throwing cleans it, adds a twist and winds it onto bobbins, turning raw filament into thread strong enough to serve as warp or weft.

2039.w: A spindle twists fibre into yarn as it spins, and a whorl — a weight of wood, stone, clay or bone fixed partway down the shaft — keeps it spinning longer; whorls turn up in the archaeological record from 12,000 years ago.

2040.w: The first mechanised spinning mounted the spindle horizontally so it could be spun by a cord encircling a large, hand-turned wheel — the wheel driving the spindle instead of a hand doing it, more than ten times as fast as spinning by hand alone.

2041.w: A loom's whole job is to hold warp threads under tension so weft threads can be woven through them; the earliest kind, the warp-weighted loom, may date to the Neolithic and used hanging stone or clay weights to do exactly that.

2042.w: John Kay's 1733 flying shuttle ran along the loom on cords and pickers mounted on wheels, letting a single weaver throw it from side to side alone — roughly doubling weaving productivity and the width of cloth one person could weave.

2043.w: A knitting needle's shaft holds a fabric's live loops while its tapered end draws a fresh loop of yarn through each one; antique needles were carved from bone or ivory, and modern ones are typically wood, bamboo or steel.

2044.w: A pair of knitting needles interloops one meandering strand of thread into a row of connected loops, unlike weaving's straight, right-angled warp and weft — the oldest knitted finds are 11th-century cotton socks from Fustat, near Cairo.

2045.w: Indigofera tinctoria is a shrub in the bean family, native from West Africa to Southeast Asia, grown as a field crop specifically for its leaves — one of the original plant sources of indigo dye.

2046.w: Fresh indigo leaves are soaked and pressed in a vat; fermentation hydrolyses the indican inside them, and after 12 to 15 hours the result is leucoindigo — a yellow compound that, unlike indigo itself, actually dissolves in water.

2047.w: Rubia tinctorum is grown in soil for its roots, which run over a metre long and up to 12mm thick — the source of the red dyes known as rose madder and Turkey red.

2048.w: Crushing the dried madder root releases alizarin, an anthraquinone-group pigment and the actual chemical compound behind the root's red colour.

2049.w: Aluminium sulfate, the base of alum, is obtained by treating minerals like bauxite with sulfuric acid — and alum itself was the most common mordant used by the dye industry, especially in the Islamic world, in the Middle Ages.

2050.w: A mordant like alum forms a coordination complex with a dye molecule, and that complex — not the loose dye alone — is what attaches permanently to the fibre; alizarin bound to alum this way is the pigment historically called rose madder.

2051.w: Rose madder is alizarin already bonded to its mordant, so working it into cloth bonds the dye straight to the fibre instead of leaving it to wash back out later.

2052.w: Leucoindigo soaks into cloth's fibres while still dissolved, and the moment the dyed cloth is pulled out into the air it reoxidises back into insoluble blue indigo, trapped in the fibre for good.

2053.w: Piece dyeing colours the woven fabric itself, and garment dyeing waits until after cutting and sewing — either way, dyed cloth gets cut and stitched into clothing exactly like plain cloth does.

2054.w: A quartz crystal's natural vibration is tuned until it matches caesium-133's fixed atomic transition frequency — that resonance, not the quartz, is what actually defines the second.

2055.w: Rubidium standards work the same way as caesium clocks — a quartz oscillator locked to an atom's resonance — but rubidium's transition is easier to probe, making the clock smaller and cheaper.

2056.w: A satellite is a radio transceiver with nothing to plug into, so solar cells are what keep its transmitter powered through orbits that pass in and out of Earth's shadow.

2057.w: Telstar, the first active communications satellite, amplified its signal with vacuum tubes rather than transistors, and ran entirely on solar cells with no ground power line to draw on.

2058.w: GPS satellites are communications satellites that also carry atomic clocks, because the whole positioning system works by timing a radio signal's travel time to within nanoseconds.

2059.w: A GPS receiver's microprocessor times signals arriving from at least four gps satellites and solves by trilateration for the one position where all the measured distances agree.

2060.w: A cellular phone is a telephone's microphone and earpiece wired to a radio transceiver instead of a copper line, handing off from one tower's antenna to the next as the caller moves.

2061.w: The first commercial cellular phone, Motorola's DynaTAC, built its radio transceiver from transistor circuitry rather than vacuum tubes, which is what finally made a handset small enough to carry.

2062.w: A smartphone bolts a general-purpose microprocessor onto a cellular phone's radio, so the device runs software instead of only carrying a voice call.

2063.w: The stored-program design needs both: a microprocessor to execute instructions and memory to hold the program and data it is working on. Neither alone is a computer.

2064.w: Early computers like UNIVAC I paired their processing circuitry with magnetic tape as working storage, decades before flash memory existed.

2065.w: A router is a small dedicated computer: its microprocessor reads each packet's destination address and switches it out the correct wire, one hop closer, using the TCP/IP protocol.

2066.w: ARPANET's first routers, the Interface Message Processors, switched packets using integrated circuits years before single-chip microprocessors existed — the job just needs logic that can read an address.

2067.w: The Internet is not one machine — it is what you get when routers keep forwarding computers' data packets from network to network by address until each one arrives.

2068.w: Motion-picture film is a flexible cellulose base coated with the same silver-bromide emulsion used in still photography — light-sensitive chemistry on a strip instead of a plate.

2069.w: A movie camera is a camera obscura fitted with a lens and a claw mechanism that advances a strip of film one frame at a time, holding each frame still while the shutter is open.

2070.w: A projector shines a bright bulb through the same sprocketed film a camera exposed; an intermittent mechanism holds each frame still just long enough for the lens to cast it on the screen.

2071.w: Twenty-four frames a second, run past a lamp at the same rate. Not persistence of vision — that is the usual story and was disputed before cinema existed. The effect is stroboscopic, explained by Simon Stampfer in 1833.

2072.w: A television is a radio receiver tuned to a video channel instead of an audio one, feeding the picture it decodes to a screen — LCDs replaced the cathode-ray tube but not that basic job.

2073.w: Ionizing radiation like gamma rays breaks DNA strands directly; when the repair machinery patches the break imperfectly, the sequence comes back changed — a mutation.

2074.w: The UV component of sunlight fuses two adjacent thymine bases into a dimer that DNA polymerase can misread when it copies past the kink, which is how sun-damaged skin picks up new mutations.

2075.w: A mutation that raises the odds of surviving to reproduce gets passed on more often than the alleles competing with it — run that quietly for enough generations and that's the whole mechanism of natural selection.

2076.w: One copy of the sickle-cell mutation distorts red blood cells just enough to starve the malaria parasite of a hospitable cell, so carriers in malaria regions survive at higher rates — natural selection favouring a single mutant allele.

2077.w: Natural selection acting generation after generation is the mechanism Darwin identified: keep it running long enough on a population and its traits drift into something new.

2078.w: The tree of life's root sits in an RNA world before DNA existed — a soup of self-copying RNA molecules is the leading hypothesis for the chemistry of the last common ancestor every branch evolved from.

2079.w: A protocell, a membrane-bound sac of replicating chemistry, is the structural starting point every branch of the tree of life is thought to share, however far evolution has carried what grows from it since.

2080.w: Organizing everything descended from life's shared ancestry needed a system: Linnaeus's 1758 Systema Naturae, published as a book, ranked all life into a nested hierarchy — kingdom down to genus and species — named with two-part Latin binomials.

2081.w: A tree of life diagrams evolution's branching pattern using taxonomy's classified groups, showing how each one relates back through common descent — Darwin sketched the first version in 1837.

2082.w: Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived traits — mutations since a common ancestor — rather than overall resemblance; rebuilding the tree of life this way revealed the whale's closest living kin is the hippopotamus.

2083.w: A mutation inside a gene's sequence creates a new version of it — a new allele — while copies of that gene elsewhere in the population stay as they were.

2084.w: Humans carry two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Line up the same gene on both copies and it often reads slightly differently between them — two alleles of one gene.

2085.w: Every new mutation is one more variant added to a population's shared pool of alleles; enough of them accumulated across a population is what geneticists call its genetic diversity.

2086.w: Balancing selection is natural selection actively preserving variation instead of erasing it — the same force that keeps one copy of the sickle-cell allele common in malaria regions without ever letting it take over.

2087.w: The most common CF-causing mutation deletes three DNA bases from the CFTR gene, removing one amino acid from the chloride-channel protein it codes for; the misfolded channel is destroyed before it reaches the cell surface.

2088.w: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive: it takes two mutated CFTR alleles, one inherited from each parent, before the chloride channel fails everywhere — one faulty allele paired with a working one causes no disease.

2089.w: A single-base mutation in the beta-globin gene swaps one amino acid in hemoglobin; the altered protein polymerizes into rigid rods when oxygen runs low, bending red blood cells into the sickle shape that names the disease.

2090.w: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: only when both the egg and the sperm carry the mutated beta-globin allele does the child inherit two copies and develop full disease — one copy alone gives sickle cell trait, not the disease.

2091.w: Mutations that pile up in the genes controlling cell division let a cell divide without limit; the extra cells form a mass called a tumor, and cancer is what happens when it invades surrounding tissue.

2092.w: Cancer is fundamentally a disease of mitosis gone wrong — mutations disable the checkpoints that normally stop a damaged cell from dividing, so division runs on unchecked.

2093.w: A virus is disabled so it can't cause disease, then loaded with a working copy of a gene the patient's own version can't make properly; when it infects the patient's cells, they start reading the healthy gene instead.

2094.w: Sickle cell disease was one of the first diseases cured by gene editing: a 2023-approved CRISPR therapy edits a patient's own bone-marrow stem cells to switch fetal hemoglobin back on, compensating for the faulty adult hemoglobin.

2095.w: CRISPR began as a bacterial immune system: bacteria store snippets of virus DNA and use a Cas enzyme, guided by matching RNA, to slice up any virus DNA that matches on a future infection.

2096.w: The lab tool is just two parts: a short guide RNA that finds the matching DNA sequence by base-pairing, and the Cas9 enzyme it drags along to cut the DNA there. Swap the guide RNA and the whole system retargets.

2097.w: A rooted cutting isn't a hypothesis about cloning, it's cloning already done — left to grow, it becomes a mature plant carrying the exact same DNA as the one the stem was cut from.

2098.w: Somatic cell nuclear transfer: an egg cell has its own nucleus destroyed and replaced with a donor's, so the embryo that grows carries only the donor's DNA. This is how Dolly the sheep was made in 1996.

2099.w: Left to develop, an unfertilized egg that divides by parthenogenesis grows into an offspring with DNA identical to its mother's — nature's own version of cloning, no lab required.

2100.w: In parthenogenesis an egg cell divides and develops into an embryo without ever being fertilized by sperm — aphid mothers produce daughters this way by mitosis alone, each one a genetic clone of her.

2101.w: The leading woolly-mammoth revival plan edits mammoth genes for shaggy hair and cold tolerance, recovered from frozen remains, directly into the genome of the Asian elephant, the mammoth's closest living relative.

2102.w: Cloning is the other real de-extinction route: in 2003 the extinct Pyrenean ibex was briefly revived by cloning a preserved cell into a goat's egg, the same nuclear-transfer approach proposed for reviving the mammoth in an elephant egg.

2103.w: Sanger sequencing hijacks the enzyme that copies a chromosome, DNA polymerase, mixing in a small fraction of modified bases that stop the chain wherever they're inserted — sorting the stopped fragments by length reads out the sequence.

2104.w: Nanopore sequencing threads a single strand of a gene's DNA through a pore in a membrane and reads the sequence directly from the distinctive dip in electrical current each base causes as it passes — no copying step required.

2105.w: Mitochondria carry their own small loop of DNA, separate from the DNA in the nucleus — a leftover from the free-living bacterium a cell engulfed roughly two billion years ago.

2106.w: Almost none of a father's mitochondria survive fertilization; the egg's own mitochondria are what pass to the embryo, which is why mitochondrial DNA traces a single unbroken maternal line back through history.

2107.w: As few as five skin cells left at a scene hold enough DNA to sequence certain repeat regions and produce a profile — a set of DNA markers specific enough to match one person out of a population, or clear everyone else.

2108.w: Comparing mitochondrial DNA sequences let geneticists match a skeleton dug up from a parking lot to two living relatives of Richard III of England through an unbroken maternal line — identification made from bone buried since 1485.

2109.w: The spar is the beam running the length of the wing, carrying almost all its bending load. Modern spars are aluminium alloy, machined or extruded to a tapered shape rather than carved from solid spruce, the way early builders made them.

2110.w: A cambered wing turns air down; by Newton's third law the air pushes back. Bernoulli's pressure drop describes the same event, not a rival theory — unlike the false 'equal transit time' myth. Ribs on the spar hold the curve; canvas carries none of the load.

2111.w: Early fuselages were an open truss of welded steel tubing, with canvas stretched over it for aerodynamics only — the canvas carried none of the structural load, the steel frame carried all of it.

2112.w: A monocoque fuselage drops the internal frame and lets the aluminium skin itself be the primary structure — worked and formed at the same forge that shapes any other sheet metal, it is stressed skin, not just a cover.

2113.w: The tailplane is a small fixed aerofoil at the rear of the fuselage, built from the same aluminium sheet as the wing but far smaller, giving a steady pitching force that balances the wing's own lift and keeps the aircraft flying level.

2114.w: Hinged in steel at the wing's trailing edge, the aileron increases lift on one wing while decreasing it on the other, rolling the aircraft — it replaced the Wright brothers' wing-warping, which twisted the whole wing instead, by about 1915.

2115.w: A steel-hinged panel on the fixed fin at the tail of the fuselage, the rudder swings the nose left or right — yaw control borrowed directly from a ship's rudder, and the earliest control surface aircraft designers built.

2116.w: A steel-hinged panel on the tailplane's own trailing edge, the elevator changes the tailplane's lift and pitches the nose up or down — pitch control, the third and last of the three flight-control axes.

2117.w: The wheel rides on an oleo strut: a telescoping tube where compressed gas acts as a spring, but it is oil forced through a narrow metering orifice as the strut compresses that actually damps the shock of touchdown.

2118.w: The Wright brothers realised a propeller is really a wing, spun on a hub that turns like any wheel instead of pushed straight through air — their carved wooden blades, twisted along their length like a wing tapers, reached about 82% efficiency.

2119.w: Modern propeller blades are cast or forged aluminium alloy, keeping the same twisted airfoil shape, bolted to a hub that spins on the engine's shaft like any other wheel.

2120.w: Petroleum forms mostly from marine algae and plankton that settled into seafloor mud, were sealed off from oxygen, buried deeper by more sediment, and slowly cooked by heat and pressure into crude oil over millions of years.

2121.w: Fractional distillation separates petroleum by boiling point. Kerosene, the cut used as jet fuel, boils off between about 175 and 325°C — lighter than diesel, heavier than the petrol cut below it.

2122.w: A compressor is rows of titanium alloy blades on a spinning wheel-like disc, alternating with fixed ones, each stage squeezing the air a little more — titanium works here because the air is still cool enough for it to keep its strength.

2123.w: Jet fuel sprays continuously into the compressor's stream of compressed air and burns in a steady, unbroken flame — a jet engine never stops combustion the way a piston engine's cylinders do, stroke by stroke.

2124.w: The turbine sits right behind the combustor's flame, in gas that can reach 1,370°C — too hot for the compressor's titanium, so turbine blades are cast from nickel-based superalloy instead, and geared straight back to spin the compressor.

2125.w: The turbine and compressor share one shaft: hot gas spinning the turbine is what turns the compressor at the front, the two halves of a turbojet mechanically locked together rather than connected by any belt or gearbox.

2126.w: A turbofan bolts a large ducted fan — mechanically a shrouded propeller — onto the front of a jet engine's core. Most of the incoming air bypasses the hot core entirely, and that cool bypass air alone supplies 30 to 70% of the engine's total thrust.

2127.w: A glider is an airframe of wing and fuselage with no engine at all: it trades altitude for forward speed in a shallow, continuous descent, and a pilot stays up for hours by finding air itself rising faster than the glider sinks.

2128.w: Fire heats the air inside a canvas envelope until it's less dense than the cool air outside, so the whole balloon floats the way a bubble rises in water. The Montgolfier brothers flew the first manned flight this way on 21 November 1783.

2129.w: Unlike a plain hot air balloon, which only drifts with the wind, an airship adds engines and steering, swapping hot air for a dedicated lifting gas. Early rigid airships used hydrogen, cheap and buoyant but flammable — Zeppelin's LZ1 flew on it in 1900.

2130.w: After the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg burned in 1937, airships swapped their hot air balloon ancestor's flame for a sealed envelope of helium — non-flammable, if scarcer and less buoyant — while keeping the engines that make an airship steerable, not adrift.
