2131.w: A rotor blade is an airfoil exactly like a wing's, long and narrow — mounted instead on a hub that spins like a wheel on a shaft, so it generates its own airspeed rather than needing the whole aircraft to move forward first.

2132.w: A spinning rotor lifts the fuselage straight up with no runway, but spinning it also twists the fuselage the other way by simple reaction — why Igor Sikorsky's VS-300, developed from 1939, added a second small rotor at the tail purely to cancel that torque.

2133.w: A wide canopy multiplies the drag of a falling body, so a jumper settles to a survivable speed instead of freefall's terminal velocity; rope lines gather the canopy's pull to a harness. Garnerin made the first descent under a frameless silk parachute in 1797.

2134.w: A fuselage carried aloft by turbofans instead of propellers is what makes a jet airliner: the de Havilland Comet, first flown in 1949 and flying fare-paying passengers by 1952, was the world's first, powered by four turbojet engines in its wing roots.

2135.w: Runway concrete doesn't need steel reinforcement the way a bridge deck does — plain concrete resists the compressive load a landing gear applies well enough alone, which is why most runways go unreinforced except at the expansion joints.

2136.w: Aircraft need a roof with no column in the way of their wingspan, so the US Navy's WWII hangars — some of the largest freestanding timber structures ever built — spanned the width in wide wooden trusses, set on a poured concrete floor built to bear the load.

2137.w: A taxiway is paved like a runway but marked differently — one continuous yellow centreline instead of the runway's white markings, lit blue rather than white at night — because it's where aircraft move on their own engines between the runway and the hangar.

2138.w: Controllers work from a glass-walled cab tall enough to see the whole airfield in every direction, but they sequence aircraft on the runways and taxiways below entirely by two-way radio — the world's first control tower opened at Croydon Airport in 1920.

2139.w: An airport is the whole system, not one building: a control tower sequences traffic by radio while taxiways link runways to hangars and terminals — the same layout logic a rail yard uses to sort wagons, just built for aircraft.

2140.w: Helicase is a motor protein that burns ATP to break the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, prying the double helix apart at a replication fork so each strand can be copied separately.

2141.w: Primase is an RNA polymerase that lays a short RNA primer onto the single-stranded DNA helicase has just exposed — DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3' end, so replication cannot start without one.

2142.w: DNA polymerase extends the RNA primer primase lays down, adding free nucleotides to its exposed 3' end one at a time and pairing each one against the template strand.

2143.w: DNA polymerase can only build in the 5' to 3' direction, so on the lagging strand it works in short bursts behind the moving helicase, leaving a series of short, disconnected pieces called Okazaki fragments.

2144.w: Ligase is the enzyme that seals the nicks left between neighbouring Okazaki fragments, forming the final phosphodiester bond that joins them into one continuous lagging strand.

2145.w: Leading-strand synthesis runs continuous while the lagging strand is built in fragments and ligase seals the last nicks — together they make replication semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one original strand and one freshly made one.

2146.w: RNA polymerase binds a promoter sequence in the DNA, prises the two strands apart, and builds a strand of RNA against the exposed template — the enzyme that turns any gene in that chromatin into a working molecule.

2147.w: Transcription is RNA polymerase reading one strand of a gene 5' to 3' and building a complementary strand of messenger RNA — the first of the two steps, transcription and translation, that turn a gene into a protein.

2148.w: A codon is a run of three consecutive bases on a messenger RNA strand. Four possible bases in each of three positions gives 64 codons, 61 of which each specify one particular amino acid.

2149.w: A tRNA's anticodon is the three-base loop at the opposite end from its amino acid attachment site. It base-pairs with a matching codon on the mRNA — the physical step that matches the right amino acid to the right instruction.

2150.w: Translation is the ribosome reading an mRNA strand three bases at a time, matching each codon to the tRNA anticodon that base-pairs with it, and linking the amino acids those tRNAs carry into a growing polypeptide chain.

2151.w: An intron is a non-coding stretch transcribed from a gene into the initial RNA transcript but cut out before the mature messenger RNA leaves the nucleus — in humans, introns make up far more of that first transcript than the exons that remain.

2152.w: Exons are the segments of a gene's RNA transcript that remain once splicing removes the introns between them; stitched end to end, they are what becomes the mature messenger RNA that leaves the nucleus.

2153.w: Splicing is carried out by the spliceosome, a large RNA-protein complex that cuts the introns out of a pre-mRNA transcript and joins the remaining exons together to make the mature messenger RNA.

2154.w: A point mutation swaps one base pair for another. Depending on which base changes and where in a codon, the effect is silent (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid), or nonsense (a premature stop signal).

2155.w: Insert or delete a run of bases that isn't a multiple of three and every codon downstream shifts by one letter, scrambling the amino acid sequence read from that point on — a frameshift mutation.

2156.w: Modern geological mapping drapes satellite imagery over a mountain's exposed rock and combines it with GPS-positioned field data, plotting rock types and structures onto a map before anyone decides where to drill.

2157.w: Laid over the same geological mapping, a magnetic field survey flags anomalies — some mineral deposits raise or lower the abundance of magnetic minerals enough to register — and where those anomalies sit on the mapped structures is exactly where target generation points the drill next.

2158.w: Once target generation narrows the search to one anomaly, a bit set with industrial diamonds — the soft metal around them wearing away to expose fresh diamonds as it cuts — bores down to bring up an intact rock core from exactly that spot.

2159.w: Every core exploration drilling brings up gets assayed and logged, and a computer turns hundreds of those point samples into a 3D block model — thousands of identically sized blocks, each assigned its own grade — which is how a deposit's tonnage and grade actually get calculated.

2160.w: A feasibility study prices a specific mining method — open-pit mining here — against resource estimation's own block model of tonnage and grade; scoping, pre-feasibility and definitive studies get progressively more precise before anyone commits capital to digging.

2161.w: The same block model from resource estimation can instead be priced against going underground — room-and-pillar mining here — when a deposit sits too deep or too steep for open-pit stripping to reach it economically.

2162.w: Once a feasibility study clears a deposit for development, one of the first things built is the haul road itself — a subbase of compacted stone and crushed rock engineered around the haul truck fleet's own weight, width and turning circle, not built to any ordinary road standard.

2163.w: The same green light from a feasibility study pays for the rest of a mine's infrastructure before any ore moves — a power plant, water-management ponds, and a camp built around the mine to house the workforce — concrete under nearly every foundation of it.

2164.w: Before an open pit can reach the ore itself, the overburden — soil and rock with no value that simply happens to sit on top of the deposit — has to be pre-stripped and moved out of the way first; how many tonnes of it that takes for every tonne of ore recovered is the mine's strip ratio, and it alone can decide whether a pit is worth digging.

2165.w: An open pit is dug in stepped benches, not a single hole, and each bench carries its own segment of haul road spiralling up the wall so trucks can climb one level at a time — the bench is the actual unit an open pit gets mined in.

2166.w: The Ostwald process burns ammonia in oxygen over a hot platinum catalyst, oxidises the result further, and absorbs it in water — nitric acid, made this way, is nearly all of the world's supply.

2167.w: Ammonia neutralises nitric acid in a straightforward acid-base reaction, HNO3 + NH3 → NH4NO3, and evaporating off the water leaves solid ammonium nitrate — a powerful oxidiser that doesn't burn on its own but accelerates almost anything else that does.

2168.w: ANFO is nothing more than ammonium nitrate prills soaked with about 6% fuel oil, a petroleum product — cheap and easy enough to mix right at the borehole that the mining industry now accounts for most of the explosive tonnage used this way.

2169.w: The rows of holes a drilling rig bores across a bench get loaded with ANFO and detonated in a timed sequence, and that is blasting — the step that actually fractures rock too solid for any bucket or blade to just dig into.

2170.w: Once blasting fragments the rock, a hydraulic excavator's bucket — driven by hydraulic pumps rather than the cables and gears older shovels used — claws into the broken pile and swings each load up into a waiting truck; that's the actual 'load' half of load-and-haul.

2171.w: What an excavator loads and a haul truck hauls out, before it has been crushed, sorted or processed in any way, is run-of-mine ore — raw material exactly as it exists in the mine.

2172.w: The same excavator that loads ore also loads the barren rock a blast fragments alongside it — granite and other country rock with no value — and that material is displaced during mining without ever being processed; it's waste rock.

2173.w: Waste rock has nowhere useful to go, so the same haul trucks that carry ore to the crusher carry it instead to a waste dump — also called a spoil tip or mine dump — a deliberately engineered pile, not just wherever a truck happens to tip its load.

2174.w: Overburden stripped off before mining even starts gets hauled by the same trucks to the same waste dump as the mine's ordinary waste rock — a spoil tip is built from both, whichever stage of the pit produced it.

2175.w: Fire assay mixes crushed ore with a flux containing lead oxide; carbon in the flux reduces that to metallic lead, which alloys with any gold or silver present as everything melts and sinks together into a button, while the barren rock floats off as slag — accurate to one part in ten thousand on the bead of gold that's left.

2176.w: Grade control continuously assays samples of run-of-mine ore against the cut-off grade — the minimum grade worth processing at all — catching dilution, barren wall rock that blasting inevitably mixes into the ore, before diluted material reaches the mill instead of the dump.

2177.w: Once grade control has confirmed a load is genuinely ore, above cut-off, it goes to the same steel-jawed primary crusher every other load does — grading happens before crushing, not after, so nothing gets ground down for nothing.

2178.w: A magnet pulls the strongly ferromagnetic grains straight out of a ball mill's ground-ore stream — magnetite needs just one kilogauss of field strength to respond — while the non-magnetic gangue simply carries on past.

2179.w: Ground ore from a ball mill, slurried in water and run down a spiral trough, sorts itself by density alone — heavier grains sink and migrate to the centre of the spiral while lighter waste rides the outside edge, no chemicals needed.

2180.w: Comminution already reduced this copper sulfide to sand-sized grains before it ever reached the flotation cell; the sulfide grains stick to the rising air bubbles and are skimmed off as concentrate, running many times richer in copper than the ore it started as.

2181.w: Magnetite is strongly ferromagnetic on its own, no roasting needed first, so magnetic separation alone turns it into a concentrate running well over 60% iron — the ore this method was practically built for.

2182.w: Rutile is one of the dense heavy minerals — titanium dioxide sitting alongside ilmenite and zircon in beach and river sands — that gravity separation is built to pull out, a spiral trough sorting it from ordinary quartz sand by density alone into a heavy-mineral concentrate.

2183.w: The cyanide ion is nothing more than one carbon atom triple-bonded to one nitrogen atom, CN⁻ — simple enough that it also forms naturally in interstellar clouds and comets, not just industrially.

2184.w: Cyanide leaches straight through a ball mill's ground ore, dissolving any gold present into a soluble complex — 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O → 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH — and what's recovered from that solution on-site is doré, an unrefined bar at least 70% gold and silver by weight, not yet pure metal.

2185.w: The Miller process bubbles chlorine gas through molten doré; every base-metal contaminant reacts with the chlorine and boils off as a chloride vapour while the gold itself is untouched at that temperature, leaving 99.5% pure gold behind.

2186.w: Dilute sulfuric acid sprayed over a stockpile of crushed low-grade copper ore, heaped on a lined pad, percolates all the way through and dissolves the copper out as it goes — recovering roughly 60-70% of the copper in the ore, lower than a mill manages, but cheap enough on ore that low-grade to be worth it anyway.

2187.w: Run a current through heap leach's copper-bearing solution and the dissolved copper plates straight onto a cathode — electrowinning, the 'EW' half of solvent-extraction/electrowinning, recovers copper this way without the solution ever touching a smelter.

2188.w: Smelting concentrate in a furnace melts the sulfide grains together into copper matte, a 30-70% copper mixture still carrying most of its iron sulfide — the impurities haven't been burned off yet.

2189.w: Blowing air through molten matte oxidises the iron sulfide to slag and burns the remaining sulfur off as sulfur dioxide gas — the escaping gas is what leaves blister copper's surface pitted, and the metal that's left is about 98% pure.

2190.w: Blister copper is still only 98% pure, so it's cast as an anode and put through electrolysis: current dissolves the impure copper off the anode and plates 99.99% pure copper onto the cathode on the other side, the last impurities dropping away as anode slime.

2191.w: A tailings dam is usually raised in stages using the tailings themselves as fill once the starter embankment is up, but that first embankment and any engineered barrier layer need concrete and rockfill — designed, unlike almost anything else a mine builds, to hold its contents forever.

2192.w: Not every mine produces enough concentrate to justify a unit train — Zimbabwe alone trucked roughly 1.13 million tons of spodumene concentrate to ports in Mozambique and South Africa in 2025 over ordinary roads, connected all the way back to the haul road built at the mine, before a dedicated rail line existed to replace it.

2193.w: Concentrate mixed with water into a slurry can be pumped through an ordinary pipe instead of railed or trucked — Tasmania's Savage River pipeline has carried iron concentrate slurry this way since 1967, 85km including one span 167 metres above the river.

2194.w: At the terminal, a rotary car dumper clamps a loaded hopper car — without even uncoupling it from the rest of the train, in the modern rotary-coupler design — and rotates the whole car to empty it in one motion; a 1909 dumper could already empty five cars a minute.

2195.w: What a car dumper empties gets stockpiled again, into yards built far bigger than the mine's own stockpile ever needed to be — blending trainload after trainload of variable-grade ore into one consistent grade a ship can load from without stopping. The alternative is a ship idling at berth past its allotted time, racking up demurrage, a per-day penalty charged for exactly that delay.

2196.w: A stacker lays incoming ore onto the port stockpile in the first place, and its own reclaiming arm — often the same travelling gantry, riding the same conveyor-belt technology moving ore everywhere else in the chain — later pulls material back off, blending the stacked product as it goes so throughput to the ship stays continuous.

2197.w: A ship loader is the stacker-reclaimer's own conveyor extended out on a boom that swings and luffs to reach every part of a ship's hold as it fills and its draught deepens — the last machine in the chain before the cargo is actually on board.

2198.w: Only once a ship loader has actually loaded a waiting vessel out on the sea does ore become cargo instead of stockpile — and the moment the last tonne crosses the ship's rail, the cargo is FOB: the exporter's responsibility ends and the buyer's begins.

2199.w: Concentrate rides the same conveyor belt crushed bulk ore does out to the yard, but instead of being screened for size like iron ore, it gets stockpiled to blend flotation or leach batches from different shifts into one uniform grade before anything moves further down the chain.

2200.w: A blast-hole rig doesn't drill just anywhere in an open pit — it works one bench at a time, boring rows of tungsten-carbide-tipped holes up to 27cm across and 40+ metres deep straight across that bench's own surface.

2201.w: Road freight reaches the same bulk terminal a unit train does — plenty of ports load ships from truck-delivered concentrate as well as railed ore, especially where no dedicated line exists yet, the truck fleet's own last stop before the sea.

2202.w: A slurry pipeline can end at a port terminal just as a railway does — filter presses strip the water back out of the concentrate on arrival, and from there it's stockpiled and shipped exactly like anything that came in by rail, ready for the sea.

2203.w: Yoruba tradition holds that thunderstones -- stones believed formed where lightning strikes -- are hurled to earth by Shango, the orisha of thunder.

2204.w: One account of Shango's power has him breathing fire and smoke through his own nostrils -- the same fire that legend says brought down his palace and ended his reign as Alaafin of Oyo.

2205.w: Obatala is said to have descended from the sky on a chain to knead the first humans out of mud -- clay and water together, per the Yoruba creation account.

2206.w: Obatala drank himself senseless on palm wine before finishing his work, marring the humans he shaped -- ever after he wore only white cloth and swore off wine for good.

2207.w: Yoruba belief holds that the orisha are spirits sent by the supreme god Olorun (Olodumare) to help humanity thrive and prosper on earth.

2208.w: Obatala and Shango are two of the four hundred and one orisha Yoruba tradition counts in all -- a pantheon carried across the Atlantic and still honored, syncretized with Catholic saints, from Cuba to Brazil.

2209.w: Yoruba and Candomble temples keep a shrine to Eshu just outside the entrance gate -- traditionally nothing more than a simple mound of red clay, guarding the threshold humans cross.

2210.w: In every offering a human makes to an orisha, a portion is set aside for Eshu first -- he is the messenger who carries sacrifices and complaints between the two worlds.

2211.w: Cuban Santeria images of Elegua are built of cement studded with cowrie shells, and often set to sit within a small clay dish on the household altar.

2212.w: Santeria tradition holds that Elegua is Eshu's own brother -- a separate, more dangerous and aggressive figure who must personally approve any ceremony humans hold before it can begin.

2213.w: The supreme sky god, worshipped only indirectly, through the orisha he sends in his place.

2214.w: Called Olorun Elemi, 'Owner of Breath,' the god is credited with every breath a human draws -- yet he keeps no shrine and receives no direct worship of his own.

2215.w: In Yorubaland, Yemoja is above all a river goddess of the Ogun River -- legend holds her own waters breaking loosed the flood that carved out every river and stream.

2216.w: Carried across the Atlantic by enslaved Yoruba believers, Yemoja became goddess of the open sea rather than a single river -- but stayed, as ever, mother to humankind.

2217.w: One of Anansi's own trials, set by the sky god Nyame, was capturing the python Onini -- the spider's cunning pitted against a snake many times his size.

2218.w: Anansi completed every trial the sky god Nyame set him and won ownership of Nyame's own stories outright -- which is why they are still told today as Anansi, or Spider, stories.

2219.w: Oya is patroness of the Niger River and is believed able to shapeshift into a buffalo -- an animal her own priests are forbidden from ever killing.

2220.w: Oya won her rule over the dead by dancing for Babalu-Aye, the god of disease -- moved by her courage and compassion, he granted the storm orisha dominion over the ancestral spirits.

2221.w: Babalu-Aye's whole body is traditionally wrapped in palm straw, and dogs are kept as his sacred companions -- said to sniff out the sickness only he can cure or cause.

2222.w: Diviners read Babalu-Aye's presence in Metanla, the sign cast with thirteen cowrie shells -- humans turn to him alone for cures to the epidemic diseases he can also inflict.

2223.w: Efik tradition calls him both Abassi Anyong, dweller of the sky, and Abassi Isong, dweller of the earth -- the reluctant creator who let the first humans live on earth at all.

2224.w: Abassi forbade the first humans from farming their own field or having children of their own -- when they broke both rules anyway, his wife Atai sent death into the world to keep them in check.

2225.w: Alone in the dark over water, he was sick, and brought up the sun, the moon, the stars and every animal in turn.

2226.w: Among the nine creatures Bumba is said to have vomited up next were the leopard and the goat, followed at last by humankind itself.

2227.w: Lotus seeds are extraordinarily durable — one recovered from a dry lakebed and dated to about 1,300 years old still germinated in mud in 1994.

2228.w: Its roots (rhizomes) anchor and spread through the mud of slow rivers and ponds, beneath blossoms that stay clean above the waterline.

2229.w: Mute swans favor slow-flowing rivers and larger lakes, and are one of the heaviest birds still capable of flight.

2230.w: They reach submerged plants with their long necks and graze on land too, taking the occasional fish or frog.

2231.w: Traditionally built from hollowed wood and a gourd resonator, the veena is strung with melody and drone strings alike.

2232.w: A large sea snail's shell, its spire tip cut off so it can be blown as a trumpet — one of Hinduism's eight auspicious symbols.

2233.w: Blowing air across the cut spire of this marine gastropod's shell produces the deep note used to open rituals.

2234.w: In Ancient Greece the trident was used as a harpoon for tuna and other large fish, its barbed tines trapping the catch.

2235.w: Roman gladiators called retiarii fought with a trident and a net, pitted against an opponent called a secutor.

2236.w: House mice thrive in open fields and farmland as readily as indoors, feeding on whatever crops and stores go unattended.

2237.w: Living commensally alongside people, house mice retreat into buildings for warmth and stored food each autumn and winter.

2238.w: Many monkey species are arboreal, tree-dwelling foragers whose varied diet includes fruit such as bananas.

2239.w: The Old and New World monkey families together add up to well over 200 species, many of them fruit-eating and tree-dwelling.

2240.w: Brahma is seated on a lotus, and his vahana is a hamsa — a swan, goose or crane — that carries him wherever he goes.

2241.w: His four heads each represent and recite one of the four Vedas, while a hamsa serves as his vahana.

2242.w: Two of Vishnu's traditional held objects: the Panchajanya conch and the Padma lotus, alongside his mace and discus.

2243.w: Vishnu reclines on the coils of the serpent Shesha, afloat on the cosmic ocean of milk, with Lakshmi at his side.

2244.w: Shiva carries the trishula trident and covers his body in ash (vibhuti), a reminder that material existence is impermanent.

2245.w: He wears the serpent Vasuki garlanded around his neck and the crescent moon set in his matted hair.

2246.w: Saraswati plays the veena, her signature instrument, with a hamsa (swan) shown resting at her feet.

2247.w: She carries a book as goddess of learning, and in the earliest Vedic hymns was herself the Saraswati river personified.

2248.w: Lakshmi is shown seated on a lotus with gold coins pouring from one of her four hands, symbolizing fortune.

2249.w: In her Gajalakshmi form she stands on a lotus flanked by elephants, which represent water, rain and fertility.

2250.w: Parvati is the daughter of Himavan, king of the Himalayas, and the tiger is named among her mounts.

2251.w: Born of that same Himalayan lineage, she is also shown mounted on a lion, the other of her two named vahanas.

2252.w: Durga slew the shapeshifting buffalo demon Mahishasura with her trident, ending his reign of terror.

2253.w: Riding her lion into battle, she wielded the trident among the many weapons the gods had gifted her.

2254.w: Garlanded with skulls and rampaging out of control, Kali was only calmed when she found herself standing on Shiva's chest.

2255.w: Ganesha's elephant head sits atop a body carried everywhere by his vahana, the mouse Mushika.

2256.w: Tradition credits him with breaking off his own tusk to use as a pen, transcribing the Mahabharata for the sage Vyasa.

2257.w: When Lakshmana lay dying, Hanuman flew off and carried back an entire Himalayan mountain of healing herbs.

2258.w: Captured and set alight in Lanka, Hanuman shrank his burning tail free and burned the city rooftop by rooftop.

2259.w: Indra wields the thunderbolt vajra and rides Airavata, his white elephant, as king of the devas.

2260.w: As the Vedic god of storms and rains, he governs the weather from atop Airavata, his elephant mount.

2261.w: Agni's vahana is the ram, and a dramatic halo of flames leaps upward from his crown.

2262.w: Vedic doctrine places him at three levels at once: fire on earth, lightning in the atmosphere, the sun in the sky.

2263.w: The Konark Sun Temple recreates Surya's chariot in stone, its twelve carved wheels drawn by seven horses.

2264.w: Surya's chariot is pulled by seven horses, read as the seven colours of visible light or the seven days of the week.

2265.w: Vayu fathered Hanuman, who carries the epithet Pavanaputra — son of Pavana, one of Vayu's own names.

2266.w: The Upanishads praise him as prana, the life-breath of the world sustaining every human body.

2267.w: Cathode copper is already 99.99% pure. Melting it at copper's 1085 °C and casting it into rod, billet and ingot is the step that turns a traded commodity into something a factory can use.

2268.w: An axon is a neuron's single, thread-like extension, built to carry the ionic current of an action potential away from the cell body toward the next cell — sometimes over a metre in a human leg.

2269.w: Dendrites are branching, membrane-bound extensions of a neuron's cell body, thickly studded with receptor proteins that detect neurotransmitters released by neighbouring cells.

2270.w: Most neurons share the same basic architecture: a cell body flanked by branching dendrites that collect incoming signals, and a single axon that carries the outgoing impulse on to the next cell.

2271.w: Roughly half of the brain's approximately 160 billion cells are neurons; the other half are glia, a separate population of cells that individually support, feed, and insulate the neurons around them.

2272.w: Astrocytes are star-shaped glia whose end-feet wrap around brain capillaries and tighten the junctions between the vessel wall's cells, controlling what can cross from blood into brain tissue.

2273.w: Oligodendrocytes are glial cells built to manufacture myelin — a phospholipid-rich membrane — and extend it out to wrap nearby axons.

2274.w: An oligodendrocyte extends flattened processes that spiral repeatedly around a nearby axon, laying down concentric wraps of fatty membrane that insulate it and speed the signal along.

2275.w: A synapse is the junction where one neuron's axon terminal meets another neuron's dendrite — not a physical fusion, but a gap of about 20 nanometres that a chemical messenger has to cross.

2276.w: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal at a synapse, it depolarizes the membrane and opens voltage-gated channels, letting calcium flood in and trigger vesicles to dump their contents — neurotransmitters — into the synaptic cleft.

2277.w: Choline is the amine head-group of phosphatidylcholine, the most abundant phospholipid in a cell membrane; hydrolyzing the membrane's phospholipid releases free choline.

2278.w: The enzyme choline acetyltransferase attaches an acetyl group to choline, producing acetylcholine — the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction and throughout the autonomic nervous system.

2279.w: Dopamine is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine in two enzymatic steps. Reuptake of it back into the sending neuron is exactly what cocaine blocks, raising its concentration at the receiving neuron's receptors.

2280.w: Serotonin is synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan in two enzymatic steps — the biochemical basis for linking tryptophan-rich food to mood.

2281.w: The same amino acid that builds proteins as glutamic acid does a second job once packaged into a synaptic vesicle and released: it is, by a wide margin, the brain's most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter.

2282.w: GABA is made from glutamate — the brain's chief excitatory neurotransmitter — by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase, which removes one carboxyl group. The molecule sits one enzymatic step from its own functional opposite.

2283.w: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is made from dopamine in one step: the enzyme dopamine β-hydroxylase adds a hydroxyl group built from a molecular oxygen atom, using ascorbic acid as a co-factor.

2284.w: White matter is made of long-range axons wrapped in fatty myelin — the myelin's own lipid content is what gives the tissue its pale colour next to the darker gray matter.

2285.w: Gray matter is tissue densely packed with neuron cell bodies and the synapses between them, unlike white matter's long insulated fibers — it forms the brain's thin outer layer and its deeper nuclei alike.

2286.w: The cerebral cortex is a folded sheet of gray matter — neuron cell bodies at the surface — sitting over tracts of white matter that carry signals to and from the rest of the brain.

2287.w: The spinal cord's outer region is white-matter nerve tracts carrying signals up and down its length, wrapped around a butterfly-shaped core of gray matter that handles local reflexes.

2288.w: The brain stem is dense with the white-matter tracts relaying signals between forebrain and body, and its lowest part, the medulla, narrows and merges directly into the top of the spinal cord.

2289.w: The thalamus sits between the cerebral cortex and the lower brain, formed from bundles of nerve tracts that send and receive signals in both directions — every sense but smell is routed through it to reach the cortex.

2290.w: The hypothalamus is a small cluster of gray-matter nuclei sitting just below the forward part of the thalamus, the main interface between the nervous system and the body's hormones.

2291.w: The pituitary's posterior lobe develops as a literal extension of the hypothalamus: hypothalamic neurons project their axons down the pituitary stalk and release hormones straight from the nerve terminals.

2292.w: The hippocampus is a fold of gray matter connected by the fornix, a nerve tract, to the thalamus and the lower brain — including the hypothalamus — beneath it.

2293.w: The amygdala is a gray-matter nucleus sitting immediately next to the hippocampus in the medial temporal lobe, most associated with attaching fear to a stimulus.

2294.w: The corpus callosum is a dense band of white-matter nerve tracts connecting the cerebral cortex of one hemisphere to the other, the brain's single largest point of connection between the two sides.

2295.w: The cerebrum's two hemispheres, each covered by cerebral cortex, are separated by the longitudinal fissure but still share an extensive connection through the corpus callosum.

2296.w: The cerebellum's outer layer is gray matter packed with more neurons than the rest of the brain combined, and it connects to the brain stem through thick fiber bundles called peduncles.

2297.w: The hindbrain is made up of the cerebellum, at the lower rear of the brain, and the brain stem that connects it onward to the spinal cord — the most evolutionarily primitive part of the brain.

2298.w: The brain divides into the forebrain — dominated by the cerebrum, nearly 90 percent of its weight — and the smaller midbrain and hindbrain below it, which run the basic functions that keep a body alive.

2299.w: The frontal lobe holds the primary motor cortex, the origin of the corticospinal tract — a white-matter pathway that descends all the way to the spinal cord to drive voluntary movement of the limbs and trunk.

2300.w: Touch and body-position signals climb through the spinal cord to a nucleus of the thalamus, which relays them on to the parietal lobe's somatosensory cortex — where the parietal lobe assembles its map of the body.

2301.w: The amygdala sits medially within the temporal lobe, whose surrounding cortex handles the language and emotion processing that the amygdala's own neighbourhood reflects.

2302.w: Vision's signal reaches the occipital lobe by way of the optic radiation, a white-matter tract whose axons are wrapped in the same myelin sheaths that speed every other long-range signal in the brain.

2303.w: The brain never touches the skull directly — it's wrapped in three membrane layers, the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater, which together are called the meninges.

2304.w: Cerebrospinal fluid, mostly water, is produced by the choroid plexus inside the brain's own ventricles and completely replaced three to four times a day, cushioning the brain and spinal cord.

2305.w: The blood-brain barrier is formed where astrocyte end-feet ensheath a brain capillary's endothelial cells, tightening the junctions of the vessel wall's own membrane and controlling what can cross into brain tissue.

2306.w: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves connect directly to the brain rather than routing through the spinal cord — ten of the twelve pairs plug into nuclei inside the brain stem itself.

2307.w: Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves branch out from the spinal cord, one above each vertebra, each splitting into a sensory branch carrying data up and a motor branch carrying commands back out.

2308.w: The peripheral nervous system is built from the two categories of nerve that branch out from the central nervous system to reach the rest of the body: the spinal nerves and the cranial nerves.

2309.w: The two main parts of the nervous system are the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system. The central nervous system is made up of the brain and the spinal cord.

2310.w: The nervous system is built from its two main parts working together: the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system that branches out from it to reach the entire body.

2311.w: The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary branch of the peripheral nervous system, coordinated by the hypothalamus, which functions as its main control and regulation center.

2312.w: Sympathetic nerves emerge from the spinal cord in the chest and abdominal regions and connect to a chain of ganglia running down either side of the spine, driving the fight-or-flight response.

2313.w: The parasympathetic system is chiefly carried by the cranial nerves — especially the vagus nerve — and works to reduce energy use, returning the body to a rest-and-digest state.

2314.w: A widely accepted theory holds that the frontal lobe's prefrontal cortex stores short-term memory as a held pattern of ongoing synaptic activity, one that decays within seconds unless something reinforces it.

2315.w: A newly formed memory is first encoded in the hippocampus, then gradually reorganized across the cortex's own networks — the hippocampus's short-term trace becomes a long-term memory only after that transfer completes.

2316.w: Repeated communication across a synapse strengthens it — more receptors accumulate at the connection — while a synapse that goes unused weakens and fades; given enough time, this reshapes the brain's whole network around what actually gets used.

2317.w: Neurogenesis is the creation of new neurons from neural stem cells; in adult mammals it continues in the hippocampus, feeding into learning and memory, though whether it happens at any meaningful rate in adult humans is still genuinely contested.

2318.w: The oldest boat hulls were logs or planks bound together with rope or cord -- buoyant long before anyone added a sail or an engine.

2319.w: Since prehistoric times, wood tar has waterproofed boat hulls, sails and roofs -- a coating still used on traditional wooden boats today.

2320.w: Spends the day cooling in the shallows the Nile's flood leaves behind, then travels miles at night to graze on grasses before returning to the water by dawn.

2321.w: Its skin secretes a reddish oily substance nicknamed 'blood sweat' -- neither blood nor sweat, but a natural sunscreen that protects it through hours submerged in the river.

2322.w: In Egypt it ranges from the Nile shoreline at Lake Nasser out into agricultural land and desert margins alike -- at home on both sides of the river's edge.

2323.w: Wades shallow Nile wetlands and mudflats hunting snails, worms and insects with its long curved bill.

2324.w: Once mummified as a votive offering to Thoth by the millions -- an estimated eight million birds entombed -- yet the species had vanished from Egypt itself by the 1850s.

2325.w: Ranges North Africa's deserts and savannas at up to 1.4 metres long; unlike some African cobras, it delivers its venom by a direct bite rather than a spray.

2326.w: Prefers toads above all, but also preys on small mammals, birds and eggs, and often slips into villages hunting the rats that follow people.

2327.w: Packed with mitochondria for a constant supply of energy, cardiac muscle burns oxygen non-stop and almost never fatigues.

2328.w: Its own natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, creates an electrical signal that travels through the heart and makes the muscle contract -- no outside signal required.

2329.w: Ra crossed the sky by day in the falcon-headed Mandjet barque, then switched to the ram-headed Mesektet barque to sail the underworld through the hours of night.

2330.w: Khepri, the scarab beetle who rolls the sun up like a ball of dung, was seen as Ra's own morning manifestation.

2331.w: Egyptians shaped 'Osiris beds' in his own likeness, filled them with soil and sowed them with grain -- the sprouting seed, fed by the Nile's flood, was Osiris rising from the dead.

2332.w: Set tricked Osiris into lying in a chest, then sealed it with lead and threw it into the Nile to drown him.

2333.w: Isis took the form of a kite and fanned breath and life back into Osiris's body with her wings, conceiving Horus from his restored corpse.

2334.w: She molded a snake that bit the aging Ra himself, sickening him with venom only she could cure -- and cured him only once he whispered her his true, secret name.

2335.w: Born falcon-headed, Horus was raised by his mother Isis in hiding among the papyrus marshes of the Nile Delta, safe from his murderous uncle Set.

2336.w: Set tore out Horus's eye during their battle for the throne; Thoth reassembled it whole, and the restored Eye of Horus became Egypt's most powerful protective symbol.

2337.w: Set was lord of the 'Red Land,' Egypt's desert of storms and disorder, the balance to Horus's rule over the fertile 'Black Land.'

2338.w: Set ruled the desert red land as Horus ruled the fertile black land -- two gods, defeated and victor, dividing Egypt between chaos and order.

2339.w: Jackal-headed Anubis, god of embalming, was the deity who prepared and guided Osiris's own body toward the afterlife.

2340.w: Anubis weighed the heart of the dead against ma'at, shown as an ostrich feather -- a heart too heavy with sin was devoured, one lighter than the feather passed into paradise.

2341.w: Depicted with the head of an ibis, Thoth was god of the moon, wisdom, writing and hieroglyphs, the record-keeper of the gods.

2342.w: As A'an, god of equilibrium, Thoth also took the form of a dog-faced baboon -- and either way, he was credited with inventing the written word.

2343.w: Bastet was worshipped as the daughter of Ra, her cat form beloved throughout Egypt as a protector against disease and evil spirits.

2344.w: More than 300,000 mummified cats were unearthed at her temple in Bubastis, whose annual festival by the Nile once drew some 700,000 pilgrims a year.

2345.w: Sobek was worshipped in crocodile form as lord of the Nile's waters and marshes, his temples keeping live sacred crocodiles that were mummified when they died.

2346.w: Sobek's link to the sun god deepened over time into Sobek-Ra, fusing the crocodile lord of the marshes with Egypt's own supreme solar deity.

2347.w: Ra dyed beer red and flooded the land with it to stop the rampaging lioness Sekhmet from destroying humanity; she drank it mistaking it for blood, and woke again as the gentle Hathor.

2348.w: Called 'Mistress of the Sky' and 'Mistress of the Stars,' Hathor was also imagined as the great celestial cow who birthed the sun god and carried him between her horns.

2349.w: As the vengeful Eye of Ra, his own daughter, Sekhmet took lioness form and was sent to destroy the humans who had conspired against her father's rule.

2350.w: Sekhmet was said to breathe fire, the desert's hot winds likened to her own breath -- the same goddess invoked both to bring plague and to heal it.

2351.w: Nephthys completed the four children of Geb and Nut: sister to Isis, and sister-wife to Set.

2352.w: When Set murdered and dismembered Osiris, it was Nephthys who helped her sister Isis gather the scattered pieces of his body and mourn him.

2353.w: Thoth gambled with the moon itself and won five days' worth of its light -- extra days outside the calendar year, in which Nut was finally free to give birth to Osiris, Set, Isis and Nephthys.

2354.w: Nut personified the star-filled sky, arched on her fingertips and toes above her husband Geb, who was the earth stretched out beneath her.

2355.w: Geb was the earth itself, whose ground let crops grow and whose own laughter, the Egyptians believed, was the cause of earthquakes.

2356.w: Husband to the sky goddess Nut, Geb embraced her so closely that their son Shu had to force his way between earth and sky to hold them apart.

2357.w: Shu, whose name means 'emptiness,' was shown with an ostrich feather on his head -- a symbol of the lightness of the air and light he embodied.

2358.w: Fog and clouds were called Shu's own bones -- the primordial god of air given the sky's own weather as his body.

2359.w: From his post at Elephantine, ram-headed Khnum was believed to regulate the Nile's own inundation, guarding the river's First Cataract at its source.

2360.w: In the Memphite Triad, Ptah -- patron of the sculptors and craftsmen who shaped stone -- was husband to Sekhmet and father to Nefertem.

2361.w: Egyptian theology held that Ptah conceived the entire world in his heart and spoke it into being with his tongue -- a craftsman who thought a universe into stone and everything else.

2362.w: Amun merged with Ra to become Amun-Ra, Egypt's supreme creator god -- and took on the ram as his sacred animal through his identification with a Kushite ram deity.

2363.w: His name means 'the hidden one' -- so hidden the Pyramid Texts call him 'the great god whose name is unknown' -- yet he began as a humble Theban god of crops and fertility.

2364.w: Crowned with an ostrich feather, Ma'at personified truth and order, and was said to regulate the stars, the seasons, and the actions of gods and mortals alike.

2365.w: In Osiris's own hall of judgment, the heart of the dead was weighed against Ma'at's feather -- the measure of whether a soul could reach paradise.

2366.w: Khonsu, whose name means 'traveller' for the moon's nightly journey across the sky, completed the Theban Triad as the son of Amun and Mut.

2367.w: Khonsu's reputation as a healer spread beyond Egypt itself -- a stela records a foreign princess cured the instant his image arrived, and Ptolemy IV called himself 'Beloved of Khonsu, who drives away evil spirits.'

2368.w: Shown pregnant herself, hippopotamus-formed Taweret was invoked throughout pregnancy and childbirth as protector of mother and child.

2369.w: Despite her fearsome hippopotamus shape, later myth placed Taweret firmly on the side of order, joining Horus's own forces against Set.

2370.w: In one myth, seven scorpions -- each an emanation of Serket herself -- guarded the pregnant Isis and her unborn child from harm.

2371.w: Serket was carved alongside Isis, Nephthys and Neith on Tutankhamun's own gilded canopic shrine, each of the four goddesses standing guard with arms outstretched.

2372.w: With the help of Isis, cobra-goddess Wadjet nursed and protected the infant Horus in the swamps of the Nile Delta, hidden from his murderous uncle Set.

2373.w: Coiled upon the head of Ra as his protector, Wadjet's rearing cobra form became the uraeus, the serpent worn on every pharaoh's crown.

2374.w: Apep, the 'World-Encircler,' was a giant serpent that rose against Ra's own sun barque every night as it crossed the underworld, held off by Ra's crew of defenders.

2375.w: Temple priests performed the annual Ritual of Overthrowing Apophis, building an effigy of the serpent and burning it to hold off his evil for another year.

2376.w: Ravens trail wolf packs as kleptoparasites, scavenging carcasses through the winter -- and have even been seen leading wolves to prey.

2377.w: Among the highest-flying birds on record, common ravens have been counted as high as 6,350 m on Mount Everest.

2378.w: The 300,000-year-old Schoningen spears were wood alone; flint blades came later, bound to the shaft with cord, sinew or resin.

2379.w: Bronze Age spearheads were cast in the metal, then bound or socketed onto a wooden shaft -- sharper and tougher than any flaked stone tip.

2380.w: The first hammers with handles were a stone head lashed to a wooden haft with strips of leather or sinew, in use by about 30,000 BCE.

2381.w: A forged iron head later replaced the stone one, hafted the same way and often leather-wrapped at the grip.

2382.w: Runestones -- memorial boulders raised across Scandinavia -- were carved with iron tools into letterforms built to be cut, not written.

2383.w: Runes were also carved with an iron point into everyday bone and antler objects -- combs, pins, sticks -- not just monumental stone.

2384.w: His ravens Huginn and Muninn fly out at dawn and tell him everything they see and hear by evening; he carries the spear Gungnir into battle.

2385.w: He drank the Mead of Poetry dry inside the giant Suttungr's mountain, then fled in eagle form -- later spitting it out to gift poets among gods and men.

2386.w: He slaughters and eats his two goats, Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr, each night, then blesses their skins and bones with Mjolnir to raise them again by morning.

2387.w: In the form of a mare, Loki was pursued and mounted by the stallion Svadilfari, and gave birth to the eight-legged horse Sleipnir.

2388.w: With the giantess Angrboda he fathered three monstrous children: the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jormungandr, and the being Hel.

2389.w: She rides a chariot pulled by two cats and owns the golden necklace Brisingamen, said to be earned by spending a night with each of the four dwarves who forged it.

2390.w: Owns a cloak of falcon feathers that lets its wearer shift into falcon shape -- Loki borrows it more than once, including to fly off and rescue Idun.

2391.w: The three stars of Orion's Belt were known in Scandinavian tradition as 'Frigg's Distaff' (friggerock), her spinning tool set among the stars.

2392.w: She made every weapon and even wood itself swear never to hurt her son Baldr -- but thought the young mistletoe too harmless to bother asking.

2393.w: Son of Odin and Frigg, said to be so bright and beautiful that light shone from him.

2394.w: Frigg had won an oath from every object in the world not to harm Baldr -- except the mistletoe, which Loki shaped into a weapon and used to kill him.

2395.w: Stands guard where the rainbow bridge Bifrost meets the sky, and will blow his horn Gjallarhorn -- heard in all nine worlds -- to open Ragnarok.

2396.w: To get the fetter Gleipnir -- thin as a silken ribbon, yet stronger than any iron chain -- onto Fenrir, the gods needed Tyr to place his hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge.

2397.w: When Fenrir realized he had been tricked, he bit off Tyr's hand at what is still called 'the wolf-joint' -- the wrist.

2398.w: The Vanir sea god, and father of Freyr and Freyja — which is how the pantheon places him.

2399.w: As a condition of peace with her, Loki made her laugh by tying a cord between a nanny goat's beard and his own body and tugging until both squealed.

2400.w: The giantess of winter and skiing, and the mountain marriage to Njord that failed within nights over which of them had to live by the sea.

2401.w: Her golden hair, cut off by Loki as a prank and replaced with real forged gold, has long been read by scholars as standing for fields of golden wheat.

2402.w: The dwarven Sons of Ivaldi forged both her golden hair and Odin's spear Gungnir in the same commission.

2403.w: The Poetic Edda's Sigrdrifumal lists runes carved 'on the bear's paw and on Bragi's tongue,' among the charms every person ought to know.

2404.w: In skaldic poems he greets fallen kings arriving in Valhalla, welcoming the newly dead with mead and verse.

2405.w: The giant Thjazi, disguised as an eagle, lured her out of Asgard and abducted her along with the apples she carried -- and without them, the gods began to age.

2406.w: Keeps the apples the gods bite into as they grow old to become young again, a cycle said to continue right up until Ragnarok.

2407.w: Daughter of Loki, appointed by Odin to govern a realm called Hel, set within the icy world of Niflheim.

2408.w: One of three monstrous children born to Loki -- her brother the serpent Jormungandr among them -- she alone was given power over the ordinary dead, those who die of sickness or age rather than battle.

2409.w: His thick shoe, cobbled from every scrap of leather people ever trimmed from their own shoes, lets him pin the wolf Fenrir's jaw and tear it apart at Ragnarok.

2410.w: Son of Odin and nearly as strong as Thor, known as 'Vidar the Silent' -- he survives Ragnarok to avenge his father's death.

2411.w: Rides the dwarf-made boar Gullinbursti, whose golden bristles glow bright enough to light his master's way in the dark.

2412.w: Rules over the rain and the shining of the sun, and with them the fruit of the earth -- the Prose Edda says it is good to call on him for peace and fruitful seasons.

2413.w: Ossicones start forming in late gestation as small, unfused bone cores under the skin — the giraffe family's real alternative to horns or antlers, which only fuse to the skull at sexual maturity.

2414.w: A tooth is built on a bony root, but enamel itself is almost pure mineral — 96% hydroxyapatite by weight — which is what makes it the hardest tissue a body makes.

2415.w: An elephant's trunk is a fusion of the nose and upper lip that happens in early fetal development — the finished organ has no bone in it at all, just up to 150,000 separate muscle fascicles.

2416.w: Brown bears are the only living bears with a hump at the top of the shoulder, and it is made entirely of muscle — grown to add force for digging and for building a den before hibernation.

2417.w: A sagittal crest is a ridge of bone running along the skull's midline, serving mainly to anchor the temporalis — one of the main chewing muscles — as it grows larger with age.

2418.w: A lion's mane is keratin, the same protein as any hair, but only males grow one — starting at adolescence as testosterone rises and not reaching full size until around age four.

2419.w: A claw is a hard keratin sheath — the same protein as hair, horn, and hoof — capping the last bone of a toe, itself built on the collagen scaffold that any bone needs.

2420.w: A koala's cecum — the fermentation chamber off its gut — runs about 200 cm long, proportionally the largest of any animal its size, built to break down eucalyptus leaf its small intestine can't get enough from alone.

2421.w: A marsupial pouch is a fold of skin holding several nursing teats. Marsupials give birth early, at a stage equivalent to an 8- to 12-week human fetus, and finish developing in the pouch instead of the womb.

2422.w: A red blood cell is a cell built around hemoglobin, with no nucleus to spare the room — round in almost every mammal, but oval in the dromedary camel alone.

2423.w: A knuckle is where finger bones meet. Chimpanzees and gorillas lock this joint rigid and carry their weight on the back of the middle finger bones — knuckle-walking, which evolved independently in each.

2424.w: A horse's hoof is keratin — the same protein as hair and horn — grown into a hard wall around the one enlarged toe bone that, after 55 million years of evolution, is all that is left to carry its weight.

2425.w: A kangaroo can freeze a blastocyst's development entirely — embryonic diapause — until the joey already in the pouch is ready to leave; that joey was born the size of a lima bean and climbed there itself.

2426.w: Two membranes, not one, wrap the nucleus — an inner and an outer layer, with the outer one physically continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and perforated by pores that let material cross to the cytoplasm.

2427.w: The ER's membrane is physically continuous with the outer nuclear envelope — its tubules and flattened sacs are, structurally, the envelope extended outward through the cytoplasm.

2428.w: What makes ER "rough" is ribosomes docked on its cytoplasmic face, translating mRNA straight into the ER lumen — the surface studded with protein-manufacturing ribosomes is the entire reason for the name.

2429.w: Strip the ribosomes off the ER and what's left is smooth ER, its membrane devoted to building lipids and phospholipids rather than protein — plus detoxification and steroid hormone production.

2430.w: The nucleolus assembles around the genes transcribed into ribosomal RNA, and it's the largest structure inside the nucleus precisely because that's where ribosomal subunits are built before being shipped out to the cytoplasm.

2431.w: Vesicles budding from the rough ER fuse onto the Golgi's receiving face, and what comes out is different: the Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts that cargo before shipping it onward from its opposite face in fresh vesicles.

2432.w: Hydrolytic enzymes made in the ER are modified in the Golgi apparatus and packaged into vesicles that bud off its far face — a lysosome is that vesicle, an acid-filled enzyme bag on permanent standby to digest whatever it's sent.

2433.w: A vacuole starts as smaller membrane vesicles that fuse together and fill with fluid — in a mature plant cell the resulting central vacuole can occupy more than 30%, sometimes as much as 80%, of the entire cell's volume.

2434.w: Microtubules are only one of three filament systems — alongside actin microfilaments and intermediate filaments built from other structural proteins — that interlink into the cytoskeleton, giving the cell its shape and positioning its organelles.

2435.w: A centriole is built from nine sets of microtubule triplets arranged in a short cylinder; animal cells keep a bound pair near the nucleus, and that pair organizes the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart at division.

2436.w: A centriole that migrates to the cell surface becomes a basal body, and the axoneme it templates grows out over time as a cilium — a short hair-like projection whose nine-plus-two microtubule core beats to move fluid, or, in a Paramecium, the whole cell.

2437.w: A flagellum shares the exact nine-plus-two microtubule axoneme of a cilium, built on the same basal-body centriole, but with extra microtubule length added to the core — which is why a cell gets one long lashing tail instead of a fringe of short beating hairs.

2438.w: The cell wall is a structural layer of cellulose fibres deposited immediately outside the cell membrane, giving the cell its fixed shape and letting it resist the internal pressure that would otherwise burst a wall-less cell by osmosis.

2439.w: Resistance to an antibiotic often doesn't live on a bacterium's own chromosome at all — it rides on a plasmid, a small circular DNA molecule that replicates independently of the chromosome and that conjugation can hand to a neighbouring cell, spreading the resistance as it goes.

2440.w: Diffusion needs nothing but a concentration difference: oxygen gas is reliably scarcer inside a respiring cell than outside it, so it crosses the membrane spontaneously, net movement running from high concentration to low until the gradient is gone.

2441.w: A plant vacuole keeps its cell turgid by osmosis: water crosses the tonoplast membrane toward the more solute-concentrated sap inside, pressing the vacuole outward against the cell wall.

2442.w: Active transport pushes molecules from low concentration to high, against the gradient diffusion would take them down, and that never happens for free — the sodium-potassium pump is the textbook example, spending one ATP per cycle to force the traffic uphill.

2443.w: In endocytosis a patch of membrane wraps around material outside the cell and buds off inward, so what was extracellular ends up sealed inside a newly formed vesicle — the membrane doing the same trick that built the vesicle to begin with.

2444.w: Exocytosis is the Golgi apparatus finishing the job it started: a secretory vesicle it packaged from its shipping face travels to the plasma membrane, fuses with it, and empties its contents into the space outside the cell.

2445.w: Phagocytosis is endocytosis scaled up for solid targets: a white blood cell folds its plasma membrane around a whole bacterium, sealing it into a phagosome — the professional-phagocyte version of the trick every endocytosing cell already does in miniature.

2446.w: A neuron keeps every organelle a generic cell has, but rebuilds its cytoskeleton into a distinctive shape — profusely branching dendrites that receive signals near the cell body, and a single axon that can run a metre or more to carry the impulse away.

2447.w: A muscle cell packs its actin cytoskeleton into thousands of repeating sarcomeres, and unlike an ordinary cell it spends ATP directly, cycle after cycle, to force those filaments to slide past one another and shorten the whole cell.

2448.w: A red blood cell expels its nucleus and organelles during development, leaving almost nothing but membrane and cytoplasm — the lack of a nucleus and mitochondria makes room for the maximum possible load of oxygen-carrying hemoglobin.

2449.w: A white blood cell carries the same organelles as any cell, but keeps its lysosomes primed: once it engulfs a bacterium by phagocytosis, sealing it in a phagosome, those enzyme-filled sacs fuse with it within about a minute and digest what's trapped inside.

2450.w: Guard cells come in mirror-image pairs flanking a stomatal pore, and — unlike the ordinary epidermal cells they're derived from and otherwise resemble — keep unusually many chloroplasts; pumping potassium in drops their water potential and osmosis does the rest, swelling them apart.

2451.w: Palisade cells stack as long cylinders just beneath a leaf's upper epidermis, carrying a high concentration of chloroplasts that make them the primary site of photosynthesis in the leaf, while each cell's large vacuole squeezes the chloroplast-rich cytoplasm into a thin layer near the light.

2452.w: A goblet cell is named for its shape: mucin granules accumulate near its open surface with the Golgi apparatus sitting right between them and the nucleus, packaging the mucin as it's secreted and stretching the cell into a goblet outline.

2453.w: Goblet cells secrete mucins into the water around them, and the result — mucus, a gel that's 90 to 95% water — traps inhaled dust, bacteria and viruses before they can reach the tissue underneath.

2454.w: A ciliated cell studs its exposed surface with cilia that all beat in the same direction; lining the trachea, they perform mucociliary clearance, sweeping the mucus blanket — and everything trapped in it — continuously up and out of the airway.

2455.w: Wrapping chromatin in a nuclear envelope is what makes a nucleus: the same double membrane that's continuous with the ER also keeps the genome behind a wall, with transcription on one side and translation on the other.

2456.w: A ribosome's two subunits are assembled inside the nucleolus around newly transcribed ribosomal RNA and imported protein, then exported through the nuclear pores to the cytoplasm as finished, functional machines.

2457.w: The Golgi apparatus doesn't just receive cargo, it ships it: at its far face, membrane pinches off around sorted, packaged contents to form a new transport vesicle bound for the plasma membrane or elsewhere in the cell.

2458.w: A sperm cell is essentially a haploid nucleus mounted on an engine: mitochondria packed into the mid-piece generate the energy that powers the flagellum lashing the tail, driving the cell forward.

2459.w: A nerve is neurons bundled together: many individual axons, each specialised to carry an electrical impulse, run side by side wrapped in connective tissue to link distant parts of the body to the spinal cord and brain.

2460.w: Muscle tissue is built from muscle cells packed side by side, each one already full of the same actin filaments sliding past myosin — group enough of them together and their individual contractions add up to a tissue that can move a joint.

2461.w: A stoma is not a single cell but the pore between two: guard cells are produced in mirror-image pairs with a gap between them, and that gap — which the pair opens and closes together — is the stoma itself.

2462.w: A leaf packs its palisade mesophyll — vertically elongated cells just under the upper surface, doing most of the photosynthesis — right alongside veins of xylem and phloem, so the water xylem delivers and the sugar phloem carries out never have far to travel.

2463.w: Blood is blood cells suspended in plasma: red blood cells carry hemoglobin to ferry oxygen, while white blood cells patrol for infection — two completely different jobs, sharing the same fluid.

2464.w: The same sharing, three times over — three shared pairs, a triple bond. N2 is the form nitrogen actually takes at ordinary temperature, not the lone atom, and that triple bond is why free nitrogen is so chemically inert.

2465.w: Dry air is 78% nitrogen gas and 21% oxygen gas by volume — the two real molecules doing almost all of the work, mixed in roughly the proportion they actually occur in the lower atmosphere.

2466.w: The most widely distributed member of the dog family hunts rabbits and rodents across open farmland as readily as forest edges.

2467.w: A notorious raider of henhouses wherever people keep poultry -- one of the oldest, most documented conflicts between foxes and farmers.

2468.w: A flexed wood stave backed with sinew, which stores energy in tension; releasing the string converts that stored energy into an arrow's flight.

2469.w: The traditional Japanese yumi is a tall, asymmetric bow whose stave is built from laminated bamboo and wood, a technique centuries old.

2470.w: In the shime-daiko style, cowhide heads are stretched over iron rings and tensioned by rope laced across the shell, tuning the drum tighter.

2471.w: He churned the sea with a spear and the islands of Japan formed from the brine that dripped back off it.

2472.w: Fleeing Izanami's decaying corpse in the underworld Yomi, he purified himself in a river; Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo were all born from that washing.

2473.w: She died bearing the fire god, and everything after — Yomi, the rotting, the pursuit, the sealed rock — follows from that one birth.

2474.w: Sealed behind the boulder Izanagi used to block Yomi's entrance, she vowed to kill a thousand of the living every day; he vowed fifteen hundred would be born in return.

2475.w: Born when Izanagi washed his left eye clean, in the purification ritual after his return from the underworld Yomi -- the sun goddess of that eye.

2476.w: After Susanoo's rampage she hid inside Ame-no-Iwato; Ame-no-Uzume's bawdy dance made the assembled gods laugh so hard that Amaterasu peeked out to look.

2477.w: Born when Izanagi washed his nose clean, in the same ritual that produced his sisters Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi -- the storm god of that washing.

2478.w: He got the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi drunk on sake set out in eight vats, then slew it in its sleep, finding the sword Kusanagi in its tail.

2479.w: Born when Izanagi washed his right eye clean, in that same purification ritual -- the moon god of that eye, brother to Amaterasu and Susanoo.

2480.w: Disgusted that Uke Mochi had conjured her feast by spitting, coughing and defecating it from her own body, he killed her -- so Amaterasu vowed never to face him again.

2481.w: The fire of his own birth burned his mother Izanami to death -- the fire god born of that same fire.

2482.w: His father Izanagi beheaded him with a sword in revenge and cut his body into eight pieces, which became eight volcanoes.

2483.w: White foxes, kitsune, serve as this kami's divine messengers at the thousands of vermilion torii gates built in Inari's honor across Japan.

2484.w: Presides over rice, tea, sake and agriculture together -- sake itself is rice wine, brewed under this kami's own domain.

2485.w: His palace, Ryugu-jo, is built of red and white coral beneath the sea.

2486.w: In the tale of Urashima Taro, a sea turtle he sent carried a fisherman down to his undersea palace, where the fisherman met Ryujin's daughter Otohime.

2487.w: One of the eldest Shinto gods: at the world's creation he opened his bag and blew away the thick mist, letting Amaterasu's sunlight finally reach the earth.

2488.w: Stands atop the clouds beating rings of taiko drums marked with the tomoe symbol to create the sound of thunder.

2489.w: His companion Raiju, a thunder-beast usually shown as a wolf or dog, crackles with lightning at his side.

2490.w: His shintai, the sacred object enshrined in his honor, is traditionally a stirrup or a bow -- mounted archery fell under his protection.

2491.w: Patron kami of Japan's warriors: the Minamoto samurai clan took him as their guardian, and the warrior Minamoto no Yoshiie was even nicknamed 'Hachiman Taro.'

2492.w: Legend says the ox pulling his funeral cart refused to go further, marking his shrine's site; a plum tree by his window in Kyoto is said to have flown to be with him in exile.

2493.w: After his exile and death, the court blamed a deadly lightning storm on his vengeful spirit and enshrined him as a god to appease it; today students pray to him before exams.

2494.w: She conjured a feast by facing the ocean and spitting out fish, then a rice paddy for a bowl of rice -- a method Tsukuyomi found so disgusting he killed her for it.

2495.w: After her death, crops and animals sprang from her corpse -- millet from her forehead, silkworms from her eyebrows among them.

2496.w: The star god, and the only deity who refused to submit when the heavenly gods took the earth.

2497.w: His defiance ended only when the heavenly gods sent the weaver god Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto, who finally won the star god's submission.

2498.w: The name means 'heavenly rock cave door'; after Susanoo's rampage ruined her domain, Amaterasu retreated inside it, plunging heaven and earth into darkness.

2499.w: Once Amaterasu was lured back out, the cave's entrance was sealed shut behind her with a shimenawa, a sacred straw rope, in the mountain where the cave itself is traditionally located.

2500.w: She overturned a tub and danced boisterously atop it outside Ame-no-Iwato, exposing herself and making the assembled gods roar with laughter until Amaterasu peeked out.

2501.w: Escorting Ninigi's descent to earth, she boldly confronted the guardian Sarutahiko blocking the way; the two fell in love and married, founding the Sarume clan of ritual dancers.

2502.w: His eyes were said to shine red like mirrors; he guarded the heavenly crossroads where the gods descended from the sky to earth.

2503.w: While fishing in a river near Ise, a giant clam trapped his hand and he drowned.

2504.w: Undersea volcanic eruptions pile up layer after layer of cooled lava until the peak breaches the ocean surface — the way the Hawaiian Islands, and Darwin's own Galápagos, both formed.

2505.w: Buried in sediment and left long enough, a bone's minerals are gradually replaced by rock, atom by atom, until it turns to stone — the slow process that makes a fossil.

2506.w: Left to run across generations with no help from fitness, an allele's frequency drifts up or down by chance alone — genetic drift, strongest of all in small populations.

2507.w: Wind carrying one population's pollen into another population's flowers carries their alleles along with it — gene flow, the movement of genetic variants between populations.

2508.w: New mutations and alleles arriving with migrants both add fresh variants to a population's gene pool — mutation and gene flow are evolution's two sources of new genetic diversity.

2509.w: Natural selection acting on a population's genetic diversity, generation after generation, leaves behind adaptation: traits well-suited to survive and reproduce in that environment.

2510.w: Peahens choosing mates with the most elaborate tail feathers pulled that ornament past what pure survival would ever favour — sexual selection acting on a population's genetic diversity.

2511.w: Breeders repeatedly choosing which individuals in a population reproduce — from fancy pigeon breeds to today's dog breeds — is the same mechanism as natural selection, with a person as the filter.

2512.w: Marooned on an island in numbers too small for gene flow back to the mainland, a population's genetic drift pulls its gene pool apart from its relatives until the two can no longer interbreed.

2513.w: A population that has both adapted to its own conditions and become reproductively isolated from its relatives has crossed the line into a new species.

2514.w: One finch species blown off course to the Galápagos speciated again and again across the islands' separate niches, radiating into thirteen species with thirteen different beaks.

2515.w: With the dinosaurs gone after the mass extinction 65 million years ago, mammals drew on their existing genetic diversity to radiate rapidly into the niches left empty, growing larger and more varied.

2516.w: A bat's wing, a whale's flipper, and a human hand all share the same five-fingered bone plan, inherited from a shared four-limbed common ancestor and reshaped for different jobs — homology.

2517.w: Once natural selection stops favouring a homologous structure — a horse's side toes, a snake's hip bones — it shrinks over generations to a nonfunctional vestige built from the same ancestral parts.

2518.w: Enough fossils, laid down in order through successive rock strata, become the fossil record — the closest thing evolution has to a paper trail, chronicling life's change across billions of years.

2519.w: Archaeopteryx carries teeth and a bony tail from its reptile ancestry alongside true flight feathers — a fossil bridging two groups so cleanly it is the textbook transitional fossil.

2520.w: Darwin coined the phrase in 1859, about the platypus and the South American lungfish. It got attached to the coelacanth eighty years later, and to a great deal else since — usually to mean a lineage that has not changed, which is not what he meant.

2521.w: When limiting factors squeeze a population below the numbers its environment's carrying capacity would otherwise allow, and it can't recover, the species goes extinct.

2522.w: Mass extinction shows up in the fossil record as a sudden, global loss of a huge share of species at once — 90 percent at the end of the Permian, the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

2523.w: When industrial soot darkened English tree bark through the nineteenth century, dark peppered moths survived being spotted by birds far better than the pale form did — camouflage evolving in real time.

2524.w: A large pheasant relative of the domestic fowl, native to South Asia and Sri Lanka.

2525.w: Males spread their iridescent, eye-marked tail feathers -- the train -- in a courtship display to attract females.

2526.w: Comb-like serrations on the leading edge of its flight feathers break up turbulence, letting it hunt by night in near silence.

2527.w: Exceptional low-light vision and near-silent flight make many owls effective night hunters of small mammals.

2528.w: Many ancient helmets combined a bronze bowl, like the crested Corinthian design, with a snug leather liner underneath.

2529.w: The classic form of the ancient Greek lyre used a hollowed tortoise shell as its soundbox, strung with gut strings.

2530.w: The classic lyre (chelys) used a tortoise-shell soundbox with sinew or gut strings stretched across it — the kithara later swapped in a wooden soundbox instead.

2531.w: The scarlet corn poppy, Papaver rhoeas, grows wild as a weed among barley and wheat fields.

2532.w: Poppy seeds can lie dormant in undisturbed soil for decades; rain onto freshly churned earth triggered the mass blooms across WWI battlefields that made it a symbol of remembrance.

2533.w: Fletching -- feathers fixed to the shaft's tail -- spins and stabilises an arrow in flight.

2534.w: Copper was among the first metals shaped into arrowheads, before harder bronze and iron took over.

2535.w: Ancient writers gave him a mane of snakes and a serpent for a tail -- a monstrous dog Hesiod even made fifty-headed, though three heads became the standard image.

2536.w: Offspring of the serpent-woman Echidna and the monster Typhon, who ancient tradition says lies imprisoned beneath Mount Etna's fire.

2537.w: The Cyclopes forged his thunderbolt for him out of gratitude at being freed, and it became his signature weapon; the eagle was his sacred bird and the shape he took to sweep up Ganymede.

2538.w: At Dodona, an oracle second only to Delphi in prestige, his priests and priestesses read the future in the rustling of a sacred oak's leaves.

2539.w: Her Homeric epithet Boopis, 'cow-eyed,' recalls her archaic cattle-cult roots; the pomegranate she carries is an emblem of the sacred marriage that bound her to Zeus.

2540.w: Her chariot, in later art, was drawn by peacocks; she was also one of three goddesses who contested Paris's golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' -- the dispute that lit the Trojan War.

2541.w: His epithet Hippios, 'of horses,' recalls the myth that he struck a rock with his trident to create the very first horse, Skyphios.

2542.w: He sent King Minos a pure white bull as a sign of favor; when Minos refused to sacrifice it, Poseidon's revenge -- cursing Pasiphae -- produced the Minotaur.

2543.w: Guarded by his three-headed dog Cerberus, and known by the euphemism Plouton, 'the rich one,' for the earth's buried wealth -- the dead paid a single coin, Charon's obol, to cross into his realm.

2544.w: The Cyclopes forged him a helm that made its wearer invisible, which he wore to fight unseen alongside Zeus and Poseidon in the war against the Titans.

2545.w: She won the patronage of Athens from Poseidon by gifting the city its first olive tree; the little owl, glaukopis, became her sacred bird and the city's own civic emblem.

2546.w: Shown in a crested helmet, she carried an aegis bearing the severed, snake-haired head of the Gorgon Medusa.

2547.w: The nymph Daphne became a laurel tree fleeing him, and his arrow killed the serpent Python at Delphi -- the laurel became his tree, and Delphi his most famous oracle.

2548.w: His lyre beat the satyr Marsyas's double-piped aulos in a contest judged by the Muses; for his hubris in challenging a god, Apollo had Marsyas flayed alive.

2549.w: When the hunter Actaeon glimpsed her bathing, she turned him into a stag -- and his own hounds, not recognising their master, tore him apart.

2550.w: Her name may derive from arktos, 'bear': at Brauron, girls performed the arkteia, 'acting the bear,' in her honor before marriage.

2551.w: At Sparta he was offered an ox in thanks for a victory won by stratagem, or a rooster for a victory won by open onslaught.

2552.w: His sacred dragon guarded a spring at Thebes; when Cadmus killed it and sowed its teeth like seed, armed warriors -- the Spartoi -- sprang from the ground, and Ares made Cadmus serve him eight years in penance.

2553.w: Cronus cast Uranus's severed flesh into the sea; where it fell, the foam bore her -- her very name means 'foam-arisen.'

2554.w: Paris awarded her the golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' over Hera and Athena -- the judgment that lit the Trojan War.

2555.w: His winged sandals, the talaria, gave him speed; his caduceus, a herald's staff twined with two serpents, is his badge of office.

2556.w: As a newborn he stole Apollo's cattle, then made peace by inventing the lyre from a tortoise shell and cow-gut strings, trading it to Apollo for the herd.

2557.w: His mortal mother Semele was incinerated by Zeus's lightning; Zeus sewed the unborn wine-god into his own thigh to finish his gestation, hence his epithet 'twice-born.'

2558.w: His thyrsus staff was wound with ivy, and later art shows his chariot drawn by leopards or panthers amid the ecstatic revels of his followers, the Maenads.

2559.w: Her emblem, the scarlet poppy, grows wild among the barley she blesses as goddess of the grain harvest.

2560.w: She taught the youth Triptolemus the art of agriculture and gave him a chariot drawn by serpents, in which he flew across the world sowing wheat.

2561.w: Hades tricked her into eating pomegranate seeds before releasing her, binding her to the underworld for part of every year after.

2562.w: Abducted while picking flowers in the fields of Nysa, she is daughter to Demeter, whose grief at the loss brings winter each year she is away.

2563.w: His workshop lay beneath Mount Etna -- his epithet Aitnaios means 'of Etna' -- where twenty bellows worked at his command.

2564.w: Given a flint sickle by his mother Gaia, he castrated his own father Uranus, the sky, and seized the throne of the cosmos.

2565.w: He swallowed each of his children at birth, until Rhea tricked him with a stone wrapped in swaddling cloth in place of baby Zeus; an old harvest-god besides, he gave his name to the harvest month Kronion.
