2566.w: The Earth personified, and the mother of the Titans. A primordial is placed by what it bore, not by what it is made of — nothing made Gaia.

2567.w: She fashioned the flint sickle her son Cronus used to castrate Uranus, and bore the Mountains, the Ourea, by herself.

2568.w: Gaia bore him and then took him as husband: he is the sky, and he is her son. That relation is what his castration by Cronus ends.

2569.w: Cronus castrated him with Gaia's flint sickle and cast the severed flesh into the sea, ending his reign; from the foam where it fell, Aphrodite was born.

2570.w: A Titaness whose whole story is her marriage to Cronus and the stone she wrapped in cloth and handed him instead of Zeus.

2571.w: Later identified with the Anatolian goddess Cybele, she is shown enthroned on a chariot drawn by a pair of lions.

2572.w: His gold-tipped arrows kindled love on the spot; a second kind, tipped with lead, drove love away, according to Ovid.

2573.w: Later tradition makes him the winged son of Aphrodite, always shown at her side.

2574.w: The winged goddess of victory crowned champions with a laurel wreath.

2575.w: Daughter of the river Styx, she was among the first to side with Zeus in the war against the Titans, and he kept her by his side ever after.

2576.w: He drives a golden chariot pulled by four fire-named horses -- Pyrois, Aeos, Aethon and Phlegon -- across the sky each day.

2577.w: When Odysseus's starving crew ate his sacred cattle on Thrinacia against every warning, Zeus destroyed their ship with lightning in punishment.

2578.w: In some accounts her chariot is drawn not by horses but by a pair of oxen, crossing the night sky.

2579.w: The moon personified within one named tradition. Roman Luna is the same body under another culture's name, which is why the tradition has to be part of it.

2580.w: Her chariot team, named Firebright and Daybright in the Odyssey, carried her across the sky ahead of the sun each dawn.

2581.w: She won immortality for her mortal lover, the Trojan prince Tithonus, but forgot to ask for eternal youth -- he withered with endless age until she turned him into a cicada.

2582.w: His own legs and horns are a goat's; his signature pipes were cut from reeds that were once the nymph Syrinx, transformed while fleeing his advances.

2583.w: Patron of shepherds and flocks across the wild highlands of Arcadia, his sudden shout in lonely places is said to be the origin of the word 'panic.'

2584.w: His lightless cave, deep in a silent mountain, is ringed with poppies and other soporific plants.

2585.w: The winged god of sleep once lulled Zeus himself at Hera's request, so she could raise a storm against Heracles -- and woke to an enraged Zeus hunting for him.

2586.w: He wore the pelt of the invincible Nemean Lion he had strangled, and later cut down the many-headed Hydra, which grew two heads for every one severed.

2587.w: For his sixth labor he diverted the rivers Alpheius and Peneus through the Augean stables, washing out decades of filth in a single day.

2588.w: Odysseus devised the hollow wooden horse -- built by Epeius 'through Pallas's [Athena's] divine art' -- that let Greek soldiers slip into Troy hidden inside it.

2589.w: He sharpened an olive-wood stake and hardened it in the fire to blind the drunken Cyclops Polyphemus, then escaped by calling himself 'Nobody.'

2590.w: The large intestine is the cecum, colon, rectum and anal canal end to end — together they reclaim water and salt from what digestion left behind, rather than absorbing nutrients, which the small intestine already finished doing.

2591.w: The colon picks up where the cecum ends and runs ascending, transverse, descending, then sigmoid, turning at the hepatic and splenic flexures; it extracts water and salt and is where gut microbiota ferment what the small intestine couldn't absorb.

2592.w: The colon's segmented pouches were long explained by its muscle bands (teniae coli) running shorter than the tube itself — the more commonly accepted explanation now is that enteric nervous system activity drives the puckering instead.

2593.w: Five centimetres above the rectum the colon's three muscle bands blend into one continuous sheath — the sacculated haustra disappear with them, leaving a smooth reservoir, the rectal ampulla, that stores feces until release.

2594.w: A blind-ended tube off the cecum, no longer written off as vestigial since the early 2000s: its wall is packed with gut-associated lymphoid tissue standing immune watch, and a 2007 Duke hypothesis says it shelters gut bacteria through illness or antibiotics.

2595.w: Circular muscle relaxes ahead of the load and contracts behind it while longitudinal muscle pushes forward, coordinated by the gut's own neurons — though the large intestine mostly skips it, relying instead on a few mass-action contractions a day.

2596.w: The large intestine holds the largest bacterial ecosystem in the human body, and research finds the relationship isn't simple tenancy — it's mutualistic, not merely commensal, with host and microbes each depending on the other.

2597.w: Bacteria in the gut flora — E. coli among them, resident in the large intestine — convert vitamin K1 into K2 forms and can synthesize their own, supplying part of the body's vitamin K even though most still comes from the diet.

2598.w: A beak is hollow bird bone reinforced internally with bony struts, wrapped in a thin keratin sheath called the rhamphotheca -- the same covering material a claw or horn is made of, just grown over a jaw instead of a toe.

2599.w: A raptor's talon is a claw driven by strong leg and foot muscles: birds of prey have strong feet with sharp talons for grasping or killing prey, and curved beaks reserved for tearing flesh afterward.

2600.w: Air sacs are thin-walled tissue sacs that act as bellows: air passes through a bird's lungs in one direction during both inhalation and exhalation, with almost no mixing of fresh and spent air — unlike a mammal's in-and-out breathing.

2601.w: A pneumatic bone has its marrow replaced with air, reinforced by internal struts for strength. Branches of the air sac system invade and inflate many of a bird's bones directly, from the sternum to the wing bones.

2602.w: The keel is an extension of the sternum running along its midline, giving the pectoralis and supracoracoideus flight muscles the leverage to work. Flightless ratites are named for having only a subtle keel, or none at all.

2603.w: The pectoralis powers the downstroke; the supracoracoideus, pulling through a pulley-like tendon over the shoulder, powers the upstroke — both anchored to the keel for leverage.

2604.w: Remiges and rectrices are long, stiff, asymmetrically shaped feathers — the leading edge narrower than the trailing edge — that grow specifically along the wing and tail to carry the aerodynamic load of flight.

2605.w: A hummingbird's shoulder joint lets the whole wing rotate, giving it helicopter-like flight in any direction — the only bird family that can truly hover and fly backward, feeding on nectar as it does.

2606.w: A penguin's wings have the same bone structure as a flying bird's, but shorter and stouter, built to serve as flippers for 'flying' underwater through the sea — useless for flight in the air.

2607.w: A flamingo's bill is lined with hairy, comb-like structures called lamellae and used uniquely upside-down, letting it separate mud and silt from the brine shrimp and algae it filters out to eat.

2608.w: A sheet of tendon locks an albatross's wing when fully extended, letting it stay outstretched on the wind without any muscle expenditure — the mechanism behind gliding near 1,000 km a day with barely a wingbeat.

2609.w: An ostrich is didactyl — just two toes on each foot where most birds have four — with the larger inner toe carrying a hoof-like nail across open field at up to 70 km/h, the fastest land speed of any bipedal animal.

2610.w: A kiwi is the only bird with nostrils at the very tip of its beak, letting it smell earthworms underground that it cannot see or feel. Its egg can weigh up to a fifth of the female's own body mass.

2611.w: A toco toucan's bill is the largest relative to body size of any bird — up to half its surface area — hollow and light, reaching fruit in the tree canopy while shedding several times the bird's resting body heat through it.

2612.w: A woodpecker's long hyoid bone winds around outside the skull and cushions the brain; modelling shows 99.7% of a peck's impact energy is stored as strain elsewhere in the body, hardly any reaching the brain as the beak drills into wood.

2613.w: A heron's neck has 20 or 21 modified cervical vertebrae that let it fold into a tight S-shape. From a crouch by the river it tracks prey through the water's refraction, then the S releases to spear it with the bill.

2614.w: A cormorant dives from the river to hunt fish underwater, then perches with its wings held open. A detailed study on the great cormorant concluded there is little doubt this spread-wing posture serves to dry the plumage.

2615.w: A parrot's upper mandible is not fused to the skull, moving independently and adding to its tremendous bite force — paired with zygodactyl feet, two toes forward and two back, for climbing and handling food.

2616.w: A common swift's legs are so short they're used mainly for clinging to vertical surfaces; except when nesting it lives its life in the sky, drinking, feeding, and often mating and sleeping on the wing — some individuals go ten months without landing.

2617.w: Cartilage is tightly packed collagen fibres running through soft tissue, with no blood vessels of its own — flexible padding wherever a joint needs to bend rather than lock.

2618.w: A whisker is keratin hair grown from a follicle wrapped in a blood sinus and fed by 100–200 sensory nerve endings — enough for a cat to judge whether a gap is wide enough to pass through, unseen.

2619.w: Unlike a human collarbone jointed at both ends, a cat's clavicle is a small bone floating free in the shoulder, held by collagen-rich connective tissue rather than a joint — so there's no fixed shoulder width to squeeze past.

2620.w: At rest, a cat's claw sheathes back inside a fold of skin and fur (tissue) around the toe pad, keeping its point sharp; flexor tendons bare it in an instant to hunt, climb, or knead.

2621.w: The tapetum lucidum is a layer of riboflavin- and zinc-rich cells sitting directly behind the nerve tissue of the retina, bouncing light the photoreceptors missed back through them a second time — reflectance nearly 130 times a human eye's.

2622.w: A falling cat reads up from down with its vestibular apparatus (nerve) and its eyes, then twists front half and rear half separately to land feet-first — a trick only a flexible spine and a jointless, free-floating collarbone make possible.

2623.w: A small cat's hyoid bone is fully ossified, letting its larynx rhythmically open and close as breath (wind) crosses it, generating the purr on both the in- and out-breath; a big cat's hyoid stays gristly, and it roars instead.

2624.w: A cat's tongue is muscle covered in filiform papillae, backward-facing keratin-stiffened spines about 0.5 mm long — hooks that rasp meat off a bone and comb loose fur out of a coat in the same stroke.

2625.w: The vomeronasal organ is a crescent of nerve-rich mucosal tissue in the roof of the mouth, wired to the brain by its own nerve pathway rather than the main smell nerve — cats draw scent onto it with the open-mouthed flehmen grimace to read pheromones.

2626.w: Two rings of nerve-controlled muscle cells in the iris — a sphincter and a dilator — snap a domestic cat's pupil down to a vertical slit in bright light; a Siberian tiger's pupil stays circular at every light level.

2627.w: Nerve-rich whiskers measure a gap's width in the dark, and a jointless, free-floating collarbone lets the rest of the body follow anywhere the head fits — together, why a cat can vanish through spaces that look far too small.

2628.w: Claws sheathed at rest so they never dull on the ground, and a tapetum lucidum reflecting unused light back through the retina so the eye needs only a sixth of the light a human's does — a hunter built to work claws-out, after dark.

2629.w: The Manx's taillessness traces to a dominant mutation in the brachyury (T-box) gene that shortens the developing spine; a kitten inheriting it from both parents doesn't survive to birth, so every living tailless Manx carries only one copy.

2630.w: The Devon Rex's curly coat looked identical to the Cornish Rex's, so breeders test-crossed the two — and got straight-coated kittens, proving the curl gene sits at a different locus in each breed rather than being the same mutation twice.

2631.w: A dominant mutation in TRPV4, a gene for cartilage and bone formation, folds the Scottish Fold's ear forward — but the same mutation runs through every cartilage in the body, causing a degenerative joint disease even with just one copy.

2632.w: Twice a day the sea rises and falls along the shore, a tide raised mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling the ocean into a bulge, with the Sun adding a smaller pull of its own.

2633.w: Between the highest and lowest reach of the tide lies a band that floods and drains twice a day. On a rocky shore it runs from barnacles at the top, down through wrack seaweeds, to the kelp only the lowest tides uncover.

2634.w: Water left behind in a rocky hollow when the tide retreats becomes its own miniature sea, where temperature, saltiness, and oxygen can swing wildly until the tide returns to refresh it.

2635.w: Despite the shell, a barnacle is a crustacean, not a mollusk: it cements its head to the rock for life and beats six pairs of feathery legs, called cirri, to kick passing food into its mouth.

2636.w: A hermit crab has no shell of its own, it backs its soft, curled abdomen into the empty shell of a dead sea snail, and moves to a bigger one every time it outgrows the last.

2637.w: Unlike its low-shore kelp relatives, bladder wrack keeps its fronds near the surface using paired air bladders blown up along each frond, buoyancy that lets it dominate the middle shore instead.

2638.w: Sea lettuce is a green alga only two cells thick, simple enough to grow from full-strength seawater down into the brackish water of an estuary, where thicker seaweeds can't cope with the changing salt.

2639.w: A porcelain crab is a filter feeder more closely related to hermit crabs than to true crabs; sharp spines on its legs grip slick kelp holdfasts so it can slide its flattened body into their hollows.

2640.w: Amphibians never evolved the amniotic membrane that keeps a reptile or bird egg from drying out; an ovum wrapped only in jelly has no shell, and must stay in water or moisture to survive.

2641.w: A frog's grip during mating triggers her to release eggs "wrapped in jelly, as spawn" — a swollen gel coat, not a shell, that only forms once it takes up water.

2642.w: Frog eggs hatch into fully aquatic larvae called tadpoles, which have tails and gills weeks before any leg appears.

2643.w: When first hatched, tadpoles grow external gills that are eventually covered by skin, forming a chamber with internal gills beneath — both stages pull oxygen straight from the water.

2644.w: As thyroid hormone drives metamorphosis, a tadpole's gills and gill sac disappear while its lungs develop rapidly to take over gas exchange in air.

2645.w: Metamorphosis in amphibians is regulated by thyroxine concentration in the blood, which stimulates the transformation from a gilled tadpole into an air-breathing adult.

2646.w: An axolotl normally lacks enough thyroid-stimulating hormone to change; dosing one with iodine or thyroid hormone reliably triggers the same transformation into a land-going salamander anyway.

2647.w: Amphibian skin contains little keratin and lacks scales; glands keep its surface constantly wet with mucus so gas can diffuse across it.

2648.w: Salamanders and frogs moult their skin regularly and often eat it — the whole keratinised outer layer replaced at once, not worn down gradually like reptile scales.

2649.w: Plethodontid salamanders, the largest amphibian family, lack lungs entirely and conduct all their respiration through their skin and the tissues lining their mouths.

2650.w: To enable sufficient cutaneous respiration, the surface of an amphibian's highly vascularised skin must stay moist enough for oxygen to diffuse across it fast enough to matter.

2651.w: With their complex reproductive needs and permeable skins, amphibians are often used as ecological indicators of habitat conditions — canaries for a whole pond.

2652.w: Most amphibian larvae, and some fully aquatic adults, keep a mechanosensitive lateral line system that senses movement and pressure changes in the water around them.

2653.w: The lateral line is a system of sensory organs found in fish that detects movement, vibration, and pressure gradients in the surrounding water — the same system aquatic amphibian larvae keep.

2654.w: Entirely aquatic and functionally lungless, the Japanese giant salamander absorbs oxygen through skin folded to increase its surface area, restricted to the clear, cool, fast-flowing mountain streams that supply enough of it.

2655.w: Surinam toad eggs are pressed into the female's swollen back skin, which closes into individual pockets; the embryos develop right through to the toadlet stage inside, never becoming free-swimming tadpoles.

2656.w: Poison-dart frogs do not produce their toxin themselves; they are believed to gain it from the toxin-carrying insects they eat, then secrete it through the skin. Captive-bred frogs raised without that diet make none.

2657.w: The olm lives in the underground rivers of the Dinaric Alps' limestone karst; permanent darkness left it blind and depigmented, and unlike the axolotl, its tissues stay unresponsive to thyroxine, so it never metamorphoses.

2658.w: Unlike most other salamanders, sirens keep external gills bunched on the neck as both larvae and adults, while also remaining obligate air-breathers with well-developed lungs.

2659.w: Bauxite carries gallium as a trace impurity, and refining it into aluminium by the Bayer process — dissolving it in hot lye — concentrates that gallium in the leftover liquor, which is where almost all of the world's supply is recovered from.

2660.w: Zinc's own ore, zinc sulfide, carries enough trace gallium that leaching it out is a real secondary commercial source — smaller than bauxite refining, but a genuine byproduct stream of its own.

2661.w: Carbon dioxide freezes at -78.5°C, and at ordinary atmospheric pressure it has no liquid phase to pass through on the way — its triple point sits above 5 atmospheres, so chilling the gas takes it straight to solid.

2662.w: Warmed dry ice skips liquid entirely and sublimates straight back to carbon dioxide gas — the visible fog around it is ordinary water vapour condensing in the cold, not the invisible carbon dioxide itself.

2663.w: Musca domestica lives in close association with people and their livestock, and its larvae develop in the manure and other decaying organic matter that association produces.

2664.w: Rattus norvegicus is a commensal pest of grain stores and farm middens, thriving wherever people stockpile grain or keep livestock manure close by.

2665.w: An omnivorous scavenger of human leftovers, the brown rat spread out of northern China along trade and migration routes and now lives almost everywhere people do.

2666.w: Feral pigeons descend from domestic rock doves that escaped captivity, and they still lay their eggs on bare building ledges the way their ancestors nested on sea cliffs.

2667.w: A newly hatched squab is fed crop milk, a fat- and protein-rich secretion from its parents' crop lining, not the seeds and grain the adults eat once it is grown.

2668.w: Cornu aspersum grazes garden leaves and is a hermaphrodite: a mating pair each fire a calcite 'love dart' into the other before exchanging sperm.

2669.w: To survive cold or drought it seals its shell's opening with a dried mucus membrane called an epiphragm, tough enough to hold up through temperatures down to -5°C.

2670.w: Bufo bufo shelters by day under log piles and leaf litter in damp woodland, and unlike a frog it walks on all four legs rather than hopping.

2671.w: More than 80% of common toads return every spring to breed in the exact pond where they themselves hatched, finding their way back even from kilometres away.

2672.w: Chlorophyta carry chlorophyll a and b and store surplus sugar as starch inside the chloroplast — the same pigment pair and storage strategy land plants use, the strongest evidence the two share a common ancestor.

2673.w: About 90% of green algae species live in fresh water, not the ocean — the opposite of the mostly-marine red algae they are often mistaken for.

2674.w: Traditional niter beds packed manure and straw together for a year or more while soil bacteria oxidised the ammonia into nitrate; leaching that through wood ash swapped in potassium to crystallise out saltpetre.

2675.w: Reacting nitric acid directly with the potash in wood ash crystallises potassium nitrate straight out, replacing a year-long niter bed with an afternoon of chemistry.

2676.w: High-pressure steam splits tallow's fat molecules apart into glycerol and free fatty acids — industrial 'fat splitting' that reaches glycerol without needing lye at all.

2677.w: Reacting tallow's fat with methanol strips off its fatty acids as biodiesel and leaves glycerol behind as the byproduct — the same splitting reaction, run for fuel instead of soap.

2678.w: Toluene is a byproduct of coking coal into coal tar, and steam-distilling that tar was how it was first separated out and named, after the aromatic tolu balsam it chemically resembles.

2679.w: Almost all toluene made today comes from reforming petroleum naphtha over a platinum catalyst, not coal tar — a byproduct of making higher-octane petrol.

2680.w: Nitrating toluene three times over with nitric and sulfuric acid builds up to 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, first made in 1863 as a yellow dye and not adopted as a military explosive until 1902, once armies valued how insensitive to shock it is.

2681.w: Black powder is roughly 75% potassium nitrate as the oxidiser and 15% charcoal as fuel, with sulfur making up the rest — the earliest known written formula for it appears in the Chinese military text Wujing Zongyao, from 1044.

2682.w: Sulfur is only 10% of black powder by weight, but it lowers the mixture's ignition temperature enough that a spark reliably sets off the potassium nitrate and charcoal around it.

2683.w: Alfred Nobel found that soaking nitroglycerin into kieselguhr, a diatom-shell silica he collected near his factory on the Elbe, made it stable enough to transport and stack safely — patented in 1867.

2684.w: Nitrating glycerol with nitric acid, held near 22°C to stop the reaction running away, is how Ascanio Sobrero first made nitroglycerin in 1846.

2685.w: Surface wind and the air higher in the sky rarely blow at the same speed or from the same direction, and that mismatch between them is wind shear.

2686.w: Enough wind shear over a thunderstorm tilts its rising air into a rotating mesocyclone, and stretching that rotation vertically is what turns a supercell into a tornado.

2687.w: Landfalling hurricanes spawn their own tornadoes too, clustered in the right-front quadrant of the storm as its outer rainbands cross the coast.

2688.w: A megathrust earthquake at a subduction zone shoves the seafloor vertically, and it is that vertical displacement, not the earthquake's shaking, that moves the whole water column above it as a tsunami.

2689.w: Subduction-zone earthquakes at convergent boundaries, where one plate grinds down beneath another, produce the most powerful earthquakes on Earth — the 1960 Chile and 2011 Tōhoku quakes among them.

2690.w: Hydrogen gas condenses to liquid at -252.87°C, just 20 degrees above absolute zero — cold enough that it is used, alongside liquid oxygen, as the highest-performance chemical rocket propellant there is.

2691.w: Nitrogen gas condenses to liquid at -196°C, and because air is 78% nitrogen it is cheap enough to be the everyday cryogen for freezing biological samples and shrink-fitting machine parts.

2692.w: Smashing a proton beam into a target at high enough energy creates a proton and an antiproton together — how the antiproton was first confirmed in 1955 at Berkeley's Bevatron, winning Chamberlain and Segrè the 1959 Nobel Prize.

2693.w: A positron bound to an antiproton is a complete antimatter atom — antihydrogen, first synthesised at CERN in 1995 and first trapped and held for study by the ALPHA experiment in 2010.

2694.w: Pyrope is the magnesium end of the garnet group, Mg3Al2(SiO4)3, and it turns up as grains carried up from the mantle in basalt and kimberlite — the same volcanic lift that brings diamond to the surface.

2695.w: Spessartine is the manganese end of the garnet group, Mn3Al2(SiO4)3, and its classic address is granite pegmatite and manganese-bearing rhyolite — exactly where granite's own leftover fluids concentrate rare elements.

2696.w: Grossular is the calcium-aluminium end of the garnet group, Ca3Al2(SiO4)3, and it grows where metamorphism cooks an impure limestone — marble with just enough aluminium in it to build garnet instead of more calcite.

2697.w: Andradite is the calcium-iron end of the garnet group, Ca3Fe2(SiO4)3, grown in skarn — marble baked and metasomatised by an iron-bearing igneous intrusion at the contact zone.

2698.w: Uvarovite is the calcium-chromium end of the garnet group, Ca3Cr2(SiO4)3, and its only real address is chromium-rich serpentinite — wherever there is enough chromium loose in an ultramafic rock to build it.

2699.w: Heliodor is golden beryl, coloured by iron in its Fe3+ state, and it crystallises in the same granite pegmatites that grow colourless and green beryl — iron is the only difference.

2700.w: Morganite is beryl with manganese standing in for a trace of aluminium: "the pink colour of morganite is attributed to Mn2+ ions," the same trick chromium plays for emerald in the same host crystal.

2701.w: Red beryl gets its colour from manganese too, but grows in volcanic gas cavities inside rhyolite lava rather than a pegmatite — a completely different address for the same beryllium aluminium silicate, which is part of why it is rarer than diamond.

2702.w: Amethyst is quartz with iron impurities sitting in for silicon, turned violet by natural background irradiation acting on those iron centres over geological time.

2703.w: Heat amethyst past a few hundred degrees and its iron colour centres flip from the state that reads purple to the one that reads gold — most citrine on the market started life as amethyst.

2704.w: Rose quartz's pink turned out not to be a dissolved impurity at all: it is caused by microscopic inclusions of a fibrous silicate mineral related to dumortierite, threaded all through the quartz.

2705.w: Smoky quartz forms when aluminium substitutes for a little silicon in the quartz lattice and natural irradiation then activates that site into a colour centre, smoking the crystal brown to black.

2706.w: Aventurine quartz owes its glitter to included flakes of fuchsite mica catching the light — the sparkle is reflection off the mica, not any colour the quartz itself has taken on.

2707.w: Tiger's eye starts as crocidolite, a fibrous blue asbestos, silicified fibre by fibre into quartz; hematite then stains the silicified fibres gold-brown and keeps the silky, chatoyant sheen of the original asbestos.

2708.w: Rutilated quartz grows around needles of rutile, titanium dioxide, that crystallised first and simply got walled in as the quartz kept growing around them.

2709.w: Chalcedony is quartz too fine-grained to see as separate crystals, deposited by silica-bearing groundwater filling cavities and vesicles — basalt's own gas bubbles are a classic address for it.

2710.w: Agate is chalcedony banded by repeated deposition: silica-bearing water fills the same cavity again and again over time, and each pulse lays down one more band.

2711.w: Carnelian and sard are both chalcedony "coloured by impurities of iron oxide" — hematite specifically, dispersed finely enough to leave the stone translucent.

2712.w: Jasper is opaque chalcedony, and its common reddish colour is iron inclusions running right through the stone rather than sitting as a thin translucent stain the way carnelian's do.

2713.w: Chrysoprase is chalcedony that "contains small quantities of nickel" — nickel, not chromium, is what turns this quartz apple-green.

2714.w: Bloodstone, or heliotrope, is "green chalcedony and red jasper that contains inclusions of hematite" — the red flecks are hematite sitting inside the green jasper base, not literal blood.

2715.w: Moss agate is chalcedony with dendritic inclusions — mainly oxides of manganese or iron — branching through a clear or milky base in patterns that only resemble moss.

2716.w: Buried wood, kept from rotting by waterlogging, has its cell walls permineralised as silica — often specifically chalcedony — precipitates out of mineral-laden water and fills every empty space cell by cell.

2717.w: Tourmaline is a boron silicate — boron is the one element every member of the group must have — and it crystallises out of boron-rich fluids in granite pegmatite.

2718.w: Schorl is iron-rich tourmaline, black and by a wide margin the commonest tourmaline there is — roughly 95% of all tourmaline found is schorl.

2719.w: Dravite is tourmaline's magnesium-rich end, brown, first described from the Drave district of Carinthia that gave it its name.

2720.w: Rubellite is tourmaline coloured pink to red by manganese, part of the lithium-bearing elbaite branch of the tourmaline group rather than the iron- or magnesium-rich branches.

2721.w: Indicolite is tourmaline's blue variety, its colour built the same way sapphire's is: an iron ion and a titanium ion sit side by side and trade an electron, absorbing everything but blue.

2722.w: A watermelon tourmaline is one crystal that zoned as it grew: manganese coloured the pink core rubellite, then the chemistry of the growing fluid shifted and iron coloured a green rim around it.

2723.w: Padparadscha needs both colouring acts in the same corundum crystal at once — chromium, the element behind ruby's red, and iron paired with titanium, the pair behind sapphire's blue — landing together on pink-orange.

2724.w: Spinel is magnesium aluminium oxide, MgAl2O4, and it grows alongside corundum in metamorphosed limestone and silica-poor igneous rock — which is exactly why spinel and ruby are so often found together, and were sold as the same gem for centuries.

2725.w: Sodalite, Na8(Al6Si6O24)Cl2, is a feldspathoid — too low in silica to be a true feldspar — that locks salt's own chlorine into cages within an aluminosilicate framework, in silica-poor igneous rock.

2726.w: Hauyne is a sulfate-bearing member of the sodalite group, forming a solid solution with sodalite itself — sulfur is what it has that sodalite does not.

2727.w: Lapis lazuli is not one mineral but a rock, "composed primarily of the minerals lazurite, pyrite, diopside, and calcite" — lazurite is a sodalite-group mineral, and the pyrite is what supplies the gold flecks.

2728.w: Scapolite is what metamorphism makes of calcium-rich feldspar in a marble-hosted rock, trapping chlorine, carbonate or sulfate from the surrounding fluid into its structure as it grows.

2729.w: Zircon is zirconium silicate, ZrSiO4 — a completely different substance from metallic zirconium, even though zircon ore is where that metal is actually mined from.

2730.w: Vesuvianite, also called idocrase, occurs as skarn: limestone baked by contact metamorphism next to an intruding melt, with magnesium among the cations built into its complex silicate structure.

2731.w: Taaffeite is close enough to spinel's own magnesium aluminium oxide, with beryllium worked in, that every known piece was sold and catalogued as spinel until 1945, when one buyer's stone tested wrong.

2732.w: Benitoite is a barium titanium silicate, and it was mistaken for sapphire on discovery — the colour was close, but a hardness test immediately gave it away as something new.

2733.w: Topaz is "a silicate mineral made of aluminum and fluorine," Al2SiO4(F,OH)2 — fluorine locked into the structure is what makes it topaz rather than some other aluminosilicate.

2734.w: Chrysoberyl is an aluminate of beryllium, BeAl2O4: "despite the similarity of their names, chrysoberyl and beryl are two completely different gemstones," though chrysoberyl does share beryllium, aluminium and oxygen with corundum's own aluminium oxide.

2735.w: Alexandrite is chrysoberyl coloured by chromium — the same element behind ruby's red — but chrysoberyl's own crystal field splits the absorption so finely that the stone reads green in daylight and red under incandescent light.

2736.w: Cymophane is cat's-eye chrysoberyl: parallel needle-like inclusions, often rutile, focus reflected light into a single moving band across the cut stone.

2737.w: Andalusite is aluminium silicate, Al2SiO5 — one of three minerals with that exact formula, and the one that is stable at moderate pressure and moderate temperature.

2738.w: Chiastolite is andalusite that grew with dark inclusions of carbon or clay swept to its corners as the crystal formed, leaving a cruciform pattern in cross-section.

2739.w: "At higher temperatures and pressures, andalusite may convert to sillimanite" — the identical formula, Al2SiO5, rearranged into a new crystal structure by more heat.

2740.w: Andalusite, kyanite and sillimanite are all Al2SiO5, sorted only by the pressure and temperature they formed under — kyanite is the polymorph that needs the higher pressure of the three.

2741.w: Enstatite is magnesium silicate pyroxene, MgSiO3, the iron-free end of a solid-solution series that runs all the way to iron-only ferrosilite.

2742.w: Hypersthene is what the enstatite-ferrosilite series is called partway along, once enough iron has mixed in that neither pure end-member name still applies.

2743.w: Iolite, cordierite to a mineralogist, typically occurs in contact or regional metamorphism of pelitic (clay-rich) rock like shale, with magnesium as its dominant cation.

2744.w: Peridot is "a yellow-green transparent variety of olivine, specifically the magnesium rich end member called forsterite" — more magnesium relative to iron is exactly what makes olivine gem-grade.

2745.w: Sinhalite, MgAl(BO4), sits close enough to spinel's own magnesium aluminium oxide, with boron worked in, that for decades every known piece was catalogued as peridot instead.

2746.w: Kunzite is spodumene, the lithium aluminium silicate, coloured lilac to pink by manganese — named for the mineralogist who first described it in 1902.

2747.w: Hiddenite is spodumene coloured emerald-green by chromium — the same element, in the same lithium aluminium silicate host, that colours kunzite pink is swapped out for the one that colours ruby and emerald.

2748.w: Zoisite is a calcium aluminium silicate that grows in calcium-rich schist and amphibolite during metamorphism — colourless on its own, like beryl and corundum before a trace element gets in.

2749.w: Tanzanite is "the blue and violet variety of the mineral zoisite... the color is caused by small amounts of vanadium," and it usually needs heat treatment afterward to burn off a brownish veil and let the blue-violet through.

2750.w: Thulite is zoisite coloured pink by manganese — tanzanite's sibling variety, with manganese standing in for the vanadium that colours tanzanite blue-violet.

2751.w: Moonstone's schiller, adularescence, comes from feldspar that cooled slowly enough to separate into alternating microscopic layers of orthoclase and albite — light diffracts between the layers rather than through one uniform crystal.

2752.w: Labradorite is the calcium-rich end of the plagioclase feldspar series — its own exsolved compositional layering is what splits light into labradorescence's shifting colours.

2753.w: Albite is the sodium end of the plagioclase feldspar series, NaAlSi3O8 — labradorite's opposite number on the same solid-solution scale.

2754.w: Oregon sunstone's glitter comes from "inclusions of red copper... in the form of minute scales" grown inside an albite-type feldspar — other sunstone gets the same schiller from hematite or goethite platelets instead.

2755.w: Amazonite is green-blue microcline, "a variety of the potassium feldspar," KAlSi3O8, with its colour tied to trace lead built into the same triclinic structure.

2756.w: Jadeite, NaAlSi2O6, forms only where subduction squeezes rock at high pressure and low temperature — the pressure that same setting applies to albite, NaAlSi3O8, drives off a silicon dioxide unit and collapses it straight into jadeite.

2757.w: Nephrite is a tremolite-actinolite amphibole, Ca2(Mg,Fe)5Si8O22(OH)2 — the other, unrelated mineral called jade, grown where silica-bearing fluid reacts with a magnesium-calcium carbonate rock like dolomite.

2758.w: Chrysocolla is a hydrous copper silicate that grows where malachite and azurite, copper's carbonates, weather further in the presence of silica-bearing water in the same oxidised zone.

2759.w: Dioptase is hydrous copper silicate, grown in the same oxidised zone above a copper deposit as malachite — silica took the carbonate's place in the reaction.

2760.w: Dolomite is calcium magnesium carbonate — limestone that magnesium-bearing groundwater has partly replaced, swapping in magnesium for roughly half the original calcium.

2761.w: Calcite and aragonite are both CaCO3 — identical formula, different crystal packing — and aragonite is the polymorph that is stable at the higher pressure.

2762.w: Rhodochrosite is manganese carbonate, MnCO3, its rose-red colour coming straight from the manganese ion — the same carbonate chemistry that builds malachite out of copper instead.

2763.w: Bake rhodochrosite with silica present and metamorphism drives off its carbon dioxide, converting the manganese carbonate straight into rhodonite, the manganese silicate — the two are close enough to be mistaken for each other.

2764.w: Smithsonite is zinc carbonate, ZnCO3, precipitated as a secondary mineral where zinc sulfide ore weathers in the oxidised cap above a zinc deposit — the zinc equivalent of malachite's own carbonate chemistry.

2765.w: Cerussite is lead carbonate, PbCO3, formed the same way malachite is — weathering in carbon-dioxide-charged water in the oxidised zone above a lead deposit.

2766.w: Anglesite, lead sulfate, is what galena becomes when it oxidises in air — the lead equivalent of pyrite roasting down to hematite, with sulfate left standing in for the original sulfide.

2767.w: Celestine, strontium sulfate, precipitates straight out of evaporating water exactly the way gypsum does — strontium taking calcium's usual seat in the same reaction.

2768.w: Titanite, also called sphene, is calcium titanium silicate — one of the few common rock-forming minerals built directly around titanium.

2769.w: Epidote grows where hydrothermal fluids alter calcium-rich feldspar, with iron taking up part of the aluminium site and turning the resulting silicate its characteristic pistachio green.

2770.w: Staurolite is unusually aluminium-rich for a silicate, Fe2Al9O6(SiO4)4(O,OH)2, and grows in schist during regional metamorphism alongside almandine garnet and kyanite — often twinned into a natural cross.

2771.w: Danburite, calcium borosilicate, "typically occurs in contact metamorphic rocks" — limestone cooked by an intrusion, with boron-bearing fluid supplying what marble alone does not have.

2772.w: Datolite is a calcium boron silicate that "occurs as a secondary mineral in mafic igneous rocks, often filling vesicles along with zeolites in basalt" — a gas bubble in cooling lava, filled in afterward.

2773.w: Axinite is a calcium aluminium borosilicate that grows at metamorphic contact zones where boron-rich fluid reaches a rock like schist — pyroelectric and piezoelectric, like tourmaline, for the same low-symmetry reason.

2774.w: Dumortierite, an aluminium borosilicate, grows as fibrous crystals in aluminium-rich rock like shale once regional metamorphism and boron-bearing fluid get to it.

2775.w: Prehnite, a calcium aluminium silicate, is a classic secondary mineral of basalt's own gas cavities — grown alongside zeolites and datolite in the same amygdules.

2776.w: Petalite, lithium aluminium silicate, crystallises in the same lithium-bearing granite pegmatites that grow spodumene — one more mineral competing for the same lithium.

2777.w: Euclase is beryl's beryllium aluminium silicate chemistry with a hydroxyl group folded in from hydrothermal water — named for how easily it cleaves, from the Greek for "good fracture."

2778.w: Brazilianite, sodium aluminium phosphate, grows in phosphate-rich granite pegmatite — one of several phosphate minerals competing for space alongside the more familiar silicates.

2779.w: Beryllonite, sodium beryllium phosphate, is pegmatite chemistry with a phosphate framework in place of beryl's usual silicate one, but the same beryllium underneath.

2780.w: Amblygonite, a lithium aluminium fluorophosphate, is one more lithium mineral competing for space in the same granite pegmatites that grow spodumene and petalite.

2781.w: Phosphophyllite, a rare zinc iron phosphate, grows in hydrothermal veins and takes its name from a leaf-like cleavage — phyllon, Greek for leaf.

2782.w: Hambergite, beryllium borate with a hydroxyl group, is one of the few gem minerals built directly out of beryllium and boron together rather than beryllium and silica.

2783.w: Scheelite is calcium tungstate, CaWO4, named for the chemist who discovered tungsten in it — and it is still mined as a tungsten ore today.

2784.w: Cassiterite is tin oxide, SnO2 — the ore the Bronze Age's tin came from, and still the most important tin ore now.

2785.w: Jet is "derived from wood that has changed under extreme pressure," commonly Araucariaceae driftwood buried in marine sediment and compressed for millions of years into something dense enough to carve and polish.

2786.w: Amber is fossilised conifer resin — pine's own sticky sap, buried and left for millions of years until every volatile compound has gone and only the hardened resin remains.

2787.w: Tortoiseshell is keratin, cut from the carapace scutes of mainly the hawksbill sea turtle — exploitation for exactly this trade helped push the species to critically endangered, and it has been banned in most countries since the 1970s.

2788.w: As East African forest gave way to grassland, early hominins spent more time foraging and scavenging bones on the ground -- a shift that favoured walking upright. Australopithecus afarensis, like ‘Lucy’, lived 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago.

2789.w: Around 2.4 million years ago, Australopithecus gave rise to the genus Homo. Its first species, Homo habilis -- ‘handy man’ -- is defined by knapping flint and other stone into the Oldowan industry, the earliest recognized stone tools.

2790.w: By about 1.9 million years ago, Homo erectus had a markedly bigger brain and body than Homo habilis, and struck flint and stone into a new kind of tool, the bifacial Acheulean handaxe. Its humanlike stride made it the first hominin to leave Africa.

2791.w: By around 700,000 years ago, an African population of Homo erectus had evolved into Homo heidelbergensis, a bigger-brained hunter of large game whose people made the 300,000-year-old wooden spears found at Schöningen, Germany.

2792.w: Homo heidelbergensis populations that stayed in Ice Age Europe grew stockier and cold-adapted as glaciers advanced and retreated, becoming Homo neanderthalensis. Neanderthals buried their dead, and later interbred with the Homo sapiens who reached Europe.

2793.w: Sahelanthropus tchadensis, found in Chad and dated to about 7 million years ago, lived in a mosaic of forest and grassland -- among the earliest known hominin candidates, though whether it walked upright remains disputed.

2794.w: Orrorin tugenensis lived in Kenya's Tugen Hills about 6 million years ago in dry evergreen forest, where fossil leaves show fruiting trees grew. Its femur has the forward-rotated head of a biped, among the oldest such evidence in the hominin fossil record.

2795.w: Ardipithecus ramidus lived in Ethiopian woodland, not open savanna, about 4.4 million years ago. It had a divergent, grasping big toe for climbing alongside evidence of bipedal walking, challenging the idea that upright walking began on open grassland.

2796.w: Australopithecus africanus lived at South African cave sites -- Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat -- from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago, descended from an afarensis-like ancestor. It is known from the 1924 Taung Child, the first australopithecine found.

2797.w: Paranthropus boisei lived in East Africa from about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago. Its huge molars, thick enamel, and bony sagittal crest for chewing muscles earned it the nickname 'Nutcracker Man' -- an evolutionary side branch, not a human ancestor.

2798.w: Homo rudolfensis is known mainly from a 1972 skull found near Lake Turkana, Kenya, dated to about 1.9 million years ago. Its brain, at roughly 750 cc, was notably larger than Homo habilis, though some researchers doubt it is a distinct species at all.

2799.w: Homo antecessor lived at Gran Dolina in Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from about 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago. Cut marks on some 80 individuals' bones show its people practiced cannibalism, and it may sit near the root of the Neanderthal-sapiens split.

2800.w: Homo naledi, found in South Africa's Rising Star cave system in 2013, had a chimp-sized brain under 610 cc yet Homo-like hands and feet. Its bones, dated to as recently as 236,000 years ago, lay deep in a chamber some argue was reached to deposit the dead.

2801.w: Homo floresiensis, found on the Indonesian island of Flores, stood about 1.1 metres tall with a brain near chimpanzee size. It likely descended from Homo erectus isolated on the island and shrunk by insular dwarfism, a reduction common among island animals.

2802.w: Denisovans are known mainly from DNA in bone fragments from Siberia's Denisova Cave, identified in 2008. They form a sister lineage to Neanderthals, and their genes persist today in Melanesians and in Tibetans, who inherited a gene for living at high altitude.

2803.w: Australopithecus sediba, found at Malapa Cave, South Africa, and dated to about 1.98 million years ago, mixes an australopithecine-sized brain and climbing arms with a more human-like pelvis and face -- possibly, though contestedly, near the ancestry of Homo.

2804.w: Homo habilis produced the Oldowan industry, the oldest recognized stone-tool tradition, from about 2.9 to 1.7 million years ago: a hammerstone struck against a stone core to knock off sharp flakes for butchering meat and crushing bone.

2805.w: Homo erectus invented the Acheulean industry by at least 1.95 million years ago: flakes struck from both faces of a flint or stone core left a symmetrical, teardrop-shaped edge -- the longest-used tool design in human history.

2806.w: The simplest friction fire-starting method needs no rope or bow: a thin wooden shaft is spun by hand against a wooden hearth board until the hot dust it grinds off glows into an ember.

2807.w: Wind a leather cord around the same spindle used in a hand drill and drive it with a bow instead: longer, easier strokes spin the shaft faster and protect the palms, working in conditions too poor for hand-spinning alone.

2808.w: Ochre is a natural earth pigment: hematite gives it a red streak, mixed through clay and sand. Ground fine, it is the pigment humans have used for painting and body decoration for at least 300,000 years.

2809.w: The animal paintings on the walls of caves like Chauvet (about 35,000 years old), Lascaux (about 17,000), and Altamira (about 15,500) were made with ochre and other mineral pigments, sometimes blown onto the rock through a hollow bone.

2810.w: Small carved female figures -- ‘Venus figurines’ -- were shaped from mammoth ivory, bone, or soft stone using flint tools. Most date from the Gravettian period, 26,000 to 21,000 years ago, and are found from Spain to Russia.

2811.w: A spear-thrower is a wooden shaft with a hook or cup at the end that engages the butt of a dart, extending the throwing arm for far more force. Homo sapiens used them from at least the Upper Paleolithic, about 30,000 years ago.

2812.w: The oldest known spear-thrower, about 17,500 years old, was carved from reindeer antler and found at Combe Saunière in France -- one of many made from bone or antler rather than plain wood.

2813.w: Woolly mammoths grazed the mammoth steppe, the cold, dry tundra-grassland that spread across Ice Age Eurasia and North America -- a six-tonne adult ate roughly 180 kg of grasses and sedges a day.

2814.w: On the treeless East European Plain, both Neanderthals and modern humans built dome-shaped dwellings from mammoth bones -- long bones and skulls for the frame, tusks for the entrance -- weighted down and covered with hide.

2815.w: More than 70 mammoth-bone dwellings have been found on the East European Plain. Some were built by modern humans who entered Europe 30,000 to 40,000 years ago, continuing a practice already established by Neanderthals.

2816.w: Coking: heated past 1,000 °C with the air shut out, coal doesn't burn, it decomposes — water, coal gas and tar drive off, leaving the porous, almost-pure carbon a blast furnace runs on.

2817.w: A blast furnace: ore concentrate, coke and limestone flux go in the top, hot air blows in the bottom, and carbon monoxide off the burning coke reduces the ore — Fe2O3 + 3CO to 2Fe + 3CO2 — while limestone melts the leftover rock into slag.

2818.w: Pig iron fresh from the blast furnace is brittle and full of carbon. Remelted with scrap and its composition adjusted, it becomes cast iron — poured into a mould rather than forged like wrought iron or steel.

2819.w: The basic oxygen process: a lance blows pure oxygen through molten pig iron at supersonic speed, burning off the excess carbon in under 40 minutes — by 2000 this made 60% of the world's steel.

2820.w: Cassiterite is heavy — a specific gravity around 7.0, roughly double ordinary rock — so hydraulic and spiral gravity concentration sort tin ore from waste by weight alone, no chemicals needed.

2821.w: Tin smelting is carbothermic reduction straight to metal, SnO2 + C to Sn + CO2, run in a reverberatory or electric furnace — cassiterite reduces cleanly, with no matte or blister stage in between.

2822.w: The same froth flotation that lifts copper sulfide off its gangue does the same job on sphalerite, zinc sulfide — a xanthate collector is what actually separates it from the galena it's usually found sitting next to.

2823.w: Sodium ethyl xanthate as a collector floats galena, lead sulfide, off the sphalerite it's usually mined alongside — the same froth flotation cell copper's ore runs through, just tuned to a different mineral.

2824.w: Roasting: burn a zinc sulfide concentrate in a stream of air and the chemistry runs directly, 2ZnS + 3O2 to 2ZnO + 2SO2 — around 90% of the zinc converts to oxide, and the sulfur dioxide is captured for sulfuric acid.

2825.w: Roast-leach-electrowin: roasted zinc oxide dissolves in sulfuric acid to a zinc sulfate solution, and current through it plates pure zinc onto the cathode — the same electrowinning that turns copper's leach solution into cathode.

2826.w: Sintering a lead concentrate in a blast of air does the roasting chemistry directly: the sulfide oxidises to a sulfite, which decomposes straight through to lead oxide and sulfur dioxide gas — litharge, ready for the blast furnace.

2827.w: The sinter goes into a blast furnace with coke and a flux; carbon monoxide off the burning coke pulls the last oxygen out of the lead oxide, and the reduced metal taps out the bottom as lead bullion.

2828.w: Crushing the plant releases the tropane alkaloid atropine, along with scopolamine and hyoscyamine, from every tissue.

2829.w: Crushing the seed releases ricin, a ribosome-inactivating protein potent enough that a few milligrams can be lethal.

2830.w: Crushing the resin-rich flower releases THC, the cannabinoid chiefly responsible for cannabis's psychoactive effect.

2831.w: Crushing and chemically processing the leaf concentrates its alkaloid into cocaine, far more potent than chewing the raw leaf.

2832.w: Crushing and curing the leaf concentrates nicotine, an alkaloid absorbed easily through skin and lung alike.

2833.w: Cutting the ripening pod and collecting its dried latex yields raw opium, from which morphine was first isolated in 1803.

2834.w: Crushing the cactus's buttons releases mescaline, a phenethylamine alkaloid structurally closer to amphetamines than to most plant hallucinogens.

2835.w: San Pedro produces the same mescaline as peyote, independently, in a different genus on a different continent's mountains.

2836.w: Crushing the mushroom releases psilocybin, a prodrug the body converts to psilocin, the compound responsible for the hallucinogenic effect.

2837.w: Atmospheric friction and ablation burn a meteoroid as it falls — that streak is a meteor. One that survives intact and reaches the ground is a meteorite; only five to ten are recovered worldwide in a typical year.

2838.w: Meteorites strike at up to tens of km/s. The shock wave compresses rock past a million bar in an instant, excavating a bowl-shaped cavity and leaving shatter cones and shocked quartz in the walls.

2839.w: The Moon has no atmosphere or weather to erase a scar, so nearly every impact it has ever taken stays legible — radiometric dating of Apollo impact-melt rock clusters between 3.8 and 4.1 billion years old.

2840.w: Impact melt thrown clear of the crater cools too fast for any crystal to start. It lands as tektite: over 65% silica, completely glassy, and with less than 0.02% water by weight — far drier than volcanic glass.

2841.w: At the Ries crater the impact melted the sandy Cenozoic cover over the crystalline basement. That glass, tinted green by trace iron, was thrown up to 450 km and fell across Bohemia and Moravia 15 million years ago.

2842.w: Most tektites are simple splash forms. Australites were flung clear of the atmosphere and re-entered it a second time — that second, high-velocity pass re-melted and reshaped them into aerodynamic buttons and flanges.

2843.w: Krishna is traditionally counted as Vishnu's eighth avatar, recognized above all by the bansuri flute he plays.

2844.w: Raised among Vrindavan's cowherds, young Krishna earned the nickname Makhan Chor — ‘butter thief’ — for raiding the village's butter stores.

2845.w: Her own symbol is the Golden Lotus, and devotional art places her among Vrindavan's lotus ponds at Krishna's side.

2846.w: Some scriptures describe her as an avatar of Lakshmi — Vishnu's own consort, taking form again alongside his avatar Krishna.

2847.w: After young Krishna ate a fistful of sand, Yashoda tied him by the waist to a grinding mortar — he dragged it off anyway, uprooting two trees.

2848.w: Unconvinced by his denial that he had eaten dirt, Yashoda looked into the boy’s mouth and saw the entire universe inside it.

2849.w: A voice from the sky prophesied that his sister Devaki's eighth child would kill him — and Krishna, that eighth child, ultimately did.

2850.w: At Sita's swayamvara in Mithila, Rama alone could string — and then snap in two — Shiva's own bow, the Pinaka.

2851.w: Counted as Vishnu's seventh avatar, Rama's own iconography shows him holding the bow Sharanga.

2852.w: Rama's duel with Ravana ended when an arrow bearing the Brahmastra, gifted to him by the sage Agastya, finally killed the ten-headed king.

2853.w: Sita's own name comes from the Sanskrit for ‘furrow’ — tradition holds King Janaka found her while ploughing a field for a royal ritual.

2854.w: After her rescue from Lanka, tradition has Rama ask her to undergo a trial by fire, Agni Pariksha, to attest to her purity.

2855.w: Ruler of the island kingdom of Lanka, Ravana was also an ardent devotee of Shiva, composing the hymn Shiva Tandava Stotra in his praise.

2856.w: His ally Maricha shape-shifted into a bejeweled golden deer at his command, luring Rama away and clearing the way to carry Sita off to his island kingdom.

2857.w: Before leaving to search for Rama, tradition says he drew a protective line in the soil around their forest dwelling — the Lakshmana Rekha Sita was never to cross.

2858.w: Mortally wounded by Indrajit's weapon at Lanka, he was saved only when Hanuman carried back an entire Himalayan mountain of healing herbs.

2859.w: At Kurukshetra, Krishna served as Arjuna’s charioteer and delivered the Bhagavad Gita to steady him before the battle.

2860.w: His own bow, Gandiva, was won during the burning of the Khandava forest at Agni’s request — the bow itself a gift from Varuna.

2861.w: Methane is the main component of natural gas, and it is highly flammable — a spark is enough to ignite it. Historically the leading cause of coal-mining disasters was exactly this: "firedamp", methane seeping out of the coal seam, igniting from a stray spark.

2862.w: A chisel is a hand tool with a wedge-shaped cutting edge, usually steel, driven into the material by a mallet or hammer.

2863.w: Laennec's 1816 stethoscope was a hollow wooden tube; Arthur Leared's 1851 binaural redesign is the ancestor of today's flexible-tubed instrument.

2864.w: A dental drill spins a bur -- a small cutting tip usually made of tungsten carbide or diamond -- fast enough to cut through tooth enamel.

2865.w: A magnetised compass needle, mounted on a low-friction pivot, rotates freely and aligns with the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field.

2866.w: Jan van der Heyden's 1673 Amsterdam fire hose was sewn leather; vulcanised rubber later replaced leather's tendency to burst under pressure.

2867.w: A blackboard is written on with sticks of calcium sulphate or calcium carbonate -- chalk. Most classroom chalk today is the cheaper gypsum kind.

2868.w: Carpenters cut and shape wood with tools including chisels; formal training runs apprentice to journeyman over three to four years in many countries.

2869.w: Electricians install and maintain building wiring; 19th- and early-20th-century cable was commonly insulated with rubber over the copper conductor.

2870.w: Plumbing uses pipes, valves, and fixtures to convey fluids -- potable water supply and waste drainage chief among them -- installed and kept working by plumbers.

2871.w: Astronomers study stars, planets, and galaxies through observation; most now expose a CCD camera through the telescope rather than watch at the eyepiece.

2872.w: Meteorologists collect surface data with basic instruments -- thermometers, barometers, weather vanes -- and track clouds, precipitation, and wind to forecast conditions.

2873.w: A spacesuit's sealed helmet supplies breathable oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, exchanged with the spacecraft or a self-contained Portable Life Support System.

2874.w: Veterinarians combine a stethoscope exam with diagnostic tests and preventive care -- vaccination against illnesses such as distemper or rabies chief among them.

2875.w: A plough loosens and turns the soil, burying weeds and bringing fresh nutrients up, before a field is sown with seed -- planning that sequence is a farm manager's job.

2876.w: A physician examines patients with tools including the stethoscope and X-ray, after four to five years of medical school and a supervised residency.

2877.w: A dentist treats what dental X-rays commonly diagnose -- cavities and other oral problems -- after earning a B.D.S., D.M.D., or D.D.S. degree.

2878.w: A train driver is in charge of a locomotive's speed and handling on the rails; in the US, engineers must be certified and recertified every two to three years.

2879.w: A ship's captain is, under the law, ultimately responsible for its safe navigation, seaworthiness, cargo handling, and crew -- steered in part by a magnetic compass.

2880.w: An Airline Transport Pilot License -- the certificate required to captain an airliner -- sits atop a ladder that starts with a Private Pilot License and 35-plus flight hours.

2881.w: A firefighter's helmet is part of a protective turnout-gear kit, and the fire hose delivers the water; the skills come from a fire academy before active duty.

2882.w: Paramedics administer oxygen and monitor patients in the field; US certification requires 1,500-plus classroom hours and 500-plus clinical hours.

2883.w: Like many skilled trades, chefs typically go through a three- to four-year apprenticeship combining classroom instruction with on-the-job kitchen training.

2884.w: Camera obscura boxes were directly adapted by Niepce, Daguerre, and Talbot to expose the first photographs -- the same box-and-lens principle a digital camera still uses.

2885.w: Jewelry designers work in precious metals -- 24-karat gold was favored in antiquity for being more accessible than silver -- and in cut gemstones such as diamond.

2886.w: Woven textile design produces fabric on a loom by interlacing a vertical warp yarn with a horizontal weft; printed textile design instead works over cloth already dyed.

2887.w: Blackboards, written on with sticks of chalk, became synonymous with education from the 16th century on; teaching itself requires professional training in pedagogy.

2888.w: In 1903 Flinders Petrie dug a small ivory statuette -- the only surviving three-dimensional image of Khufu -- from the sand at Abydos, despite his having built the largest pyramid ever raised.

2889.w: Tura limestone cased its faces and granite hauled some 900 km from Aswan lined the King's Chamber -- together part of the roughly 2.3 million blocks of the only Wonder still standing today.

2890.w: Khufu raised it from the Giza desert plateau around 2600 BC; at 146.6 meters it stood the tallest human-made structure on Earth for over 3,700 years.

2891.w: Before Zeus, Pheidias carved ivory into the flesh of his standing Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon -- a chryselephantine giant nearly 13 meters tall.

2892.w: Gold leaf, cast as removable panels sheathing her robes, let his Athena Parthenos double as a literal city treasury that could be stripped down and reweighed in an emergency.

2893.w: The technique is literally named for its two materials -- khrysos, gold, and elephantinos, ivory -- carved and cast over a hidden wooden armature.

2894.w: Pheidias built the seated Zeus around 435 BC using the same gold-and-ivory technique that had made his Athena famous, on a scale of roughly 12 meters.

2895.w: Ancient descriptions agree on his attributes: a small figure of Nike, goddess of victory, in his right hand, and a scepter topped with an eagle in his left.

2896.w: Nabopolassar took Babylon while Assyria was collapsing and his son inherited an empire and the treasury to rebuild the city with. Everything Nebuchadnezzar is remembered for was paid for by somebody else's fall.

2897.w: Nebuchadnezzar completed Etemenanki, Marduk's great stepped tower begun by his father -- a structure ancient tradition may have folded into the Tower of Babel.

2898.w: Nebuchadnezzar II's north gate, faced in glazed brick: the blue is a copper-bearing glaze fired onto moulded relief, so the aurochs and dragons stand proud of a surface that has kept its colour for 2,600 years.

2899.w: Tradition holds Nebuchadnezzar planted the terraces to console his homesick wife -- but no Babylonian inscription of his, usually boastful about his own building work, ever mentions them.

2900.w: Some historians now argue the 'hanging gardens' actually stood at Nineveh beside Sennacherib's own ziggurat, watered by his documented canals and aqueducts, and were confused with Babylon only later.

2901.w: Croesus was the first ruler to strike coins of standardised, pure gold for general circulation -- the Croeseid -- rather than the natural gold-silver alloy electrum used before him.

2902.w: Croesus, the fabulously wealthy king of Lydia, personally funded much of its reconstruction and donated many of its marble columns after annexing Ephesus.

2903.w: Built to house her cult statue -- shown in Asia Minor as a many-breasted mother goddess -- it became the largest marble temple in the Greek world, and Ephesians worshipped there into the 4th century AD.

2904.w: He confessed under torture that he burned the temple only to make his name immortal; Ephesus banned anyone from ever speaking it and failed -- 'herostratic fame' now names destruction sought purely for notoriety.

2905.w: Pliny the Elder names Sostratus of Cnidus as the lighthouse's architect and says Ptolemy graciously let him inscribe his own name on the great mirrored tower, though the attribution is still disputed.

2906.w: Built of great blocks of light-coloured limestone quarried at Wadi Hammamat, begun on Ptolemy I's orders and finished under Ptolemy II around 280 BC.

2907.w: Raised on the small island of Pharos, it used a mirror mounted at its summit to throw sunlight far out to sea by day, with fire lit for the same purpose at night.

2908.w: Mausolus moved his capital to Halicarnassus and began raising his own tomb there in marble, its monumental staircase eventually ringed by nearly fifty carved marble lions.

2909.w: When Rhodes sent its fleet against her for daring to rule as a woman, Artemisia hid ships in a secret harbor, let the Rhodians land, then sailed out and used their own captured ships to seize the island.

2910.w: Mausolus began the tomb during his own lifetime; after his death Artemisia continued the project, though it was finished only after her own death two years later.

2911.w: Artemisia II built it for Mausolus, her brother and husband, and it is his name that became the word for any grand tomb. Four Greek sculptors took one side each in marble.

2912.w: Chares raised an iron framework first, then fixed bronze plates over it and packed the hollow figure with stone for stability -- an engineering feat, not just a casting.

2913.w: Trained under the sculptor Lysippos, Chares came from Lindos on the island of Rhodes and cast his masterpiece for his own city in bronze.

2914.w: Chares built the roughly 33-meter bronze Helios between 294 and 282 BC, paid for by selling the siege equipment an enemy army abandoned after a failed year-long siege of Rhodes.

2915.w: Rhodian coins already stamped Helios's radiate head before the Colossus rose; one numismatist argues the statue's own face was even modeled on that same coin portrait.

2916.w: A molecular cloud fragment collapses under its own gravity and heats as it compresses, forming an opaque pressure-supported core — a protostar generating light from that infall, not from fusion.

2917.w: The infalling gas runs out and the core keeps contracting and heating until hydrogen fusion ignites at its center — the moment a protostar becomes a true, main-sequence star.

2918.w: Below about 80 Jupiter masses a collapsing core never gets hot enough to sustain hydrogen fusion. Without that furnace lit, the object just cools, drifting down through spectral types for the rest of its life.

2919.w: Stars of 8 solar masses and up run so hot that when core hydrogen runs out they fuse helium smoothly and keep going, swelling into supergiants — 1,000 to over a million times the Sun's luminosity.

2920.w: A supergiant is, almost by definition, destined to end violently: most Type II supernova progenitors are red supergiants, whose cores collapse once they've fused their way to iron.

2921.w: The 1054 CE supernova recorded by Chinese, Arab and Japanese observers blew its outer layers outward; that debris is still expanding today as the Crab Nebula, with a 30.2-times-a-second pulsar at its center.

2922.w: A prism or grating cuts starlight into its component wavelengths — a rainbow spectrum crossed by dark absorption lines that give away a star's chemical makeup, temperature, and motion.

2923.w: As the universe expanded, the hot plasma of its first 380,000 years cleared into free-streaming photons — the same photons, cooled and redshifted by billions of years of expansion, now measure 2.725 kelvin.

2924.w: Jocelyn Bell found the first pulsar on August 6, 1967, in data from a newly built radio telescope — a rotating neutron star whose radio beam sweeps past Earth like a lighthouse.

2925.w: M42 is the nearest large region of massive star formation to Earth, 1,267 light-years off — visible to the naked eye, and directly observed to hold protostars and protoplanetary discs.

2926.w: The Pleiades is an open cluster of over 1,000 young B-type stars 444 light-years away, its brightest seven named for the mythological sisters — the most obvious star cluster to the naked eye.

2927.w: A globular cluster packs hundreds of thousands of stars into a sphere held together by gravity, mostly in a galaxy's outer halo — its coolest white dwarfs dating some clusters to 12.7 billion years old.

2928.w: A galaxy is nothing more or less than stars, gas and dust bound together by gravity — from a couple of hundred billion of them, in a structure like the Milky Way, up to two trillion across the observable universe.

2929.w: The Sun sits about 27,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way, one of 100 to 400 billion stars completing an orbit of the galaxy roughly every 240 million years.

2930.w: Elliptical galaxies are smooth, ellipsoidal and dominated by old, red stars. The giant ones are preferentially found close to the centers of galaxy clusters, where they grew by devouring smaller galaxies.

2931.w: About two-thirds of spiral galaxies carry a straight bar of stars through their core, funneling gas inward — the Milky Way itself is a barred spiral, its bar confirmed by Spitzer Space Telescope data in 2005.

2932.w: A lenticular galaxy is a type intermediate between an elliptical and a spiral: it keeps a large-scale disc like a spiral's, but has no spiral arms and, like an elliptical, has mostly used up its star-forming gas.

2933.w: The Local Group is the galaxy group containing the Milky Way. Its two largest members, the Milky Way and Andromeda, are both spiral galaxies of roughly a trillion solar masses each, among 100-plus known members.

2934.w: A galaxy cluster is hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound together by gravity, along with hot X-ray gas and dark matter — the biggest gravitationally bound structures known in the universe.

2935.w: Superclusters are large groups of galaxy clusters and groups, among the biggest structures known. The Local Group belongs to the Laniakea Supercluster, itself part of the wider Pisces-Cetus complex.

2936.w: Observational evidence indicates that almost every large galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center — ours, Sagittarius A*, has a mass estimated from stellar orbits at about 4 million suns.

2937.w: In a close binary, once the heavier star has become a black hole, gas flowing from its companion spirals inward, rubbing and heating as it goes — hot enough near the black hole to radiate X-rays.

2938.w: An active galactic nucleus is powered by matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center — radiation not produced by starlight, making these the most luminous persistent sources known.

2939.w: A quasar is the most luminous class of active galactic nucleus, powered by accretion onto a supermassive black hole — the brightest known, 3C 273, radiates about 100 times the entire Milky Way's output.

2940.w: Seen in visible light, most Seyfert galaxies look like ordinary spirals — but their compact nuclei are exceptionally luminous, a class Carl Seyfert first described in 1943.

2941.w: Radio galaxies pour out radio emission from jets far beyond their visible structure, and their host galaxies are almost exclusively giant ellipticals, thought to house the most massive black holes.

2942.w: An exoplanet is simply a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz confirmed the first one around a normal star, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995.

2943.w: Henrietta Swan Leavitt found the pattern in 1908, and confirmed it in 1912, examining photographic plates of the Magellanic Clouds: a Cepheid's pulsation period tracks its true luminosity, letting a star's brightness be turned into a distance.

2944.w: A star's spectrum reveals its chemical composition, temperature, density, mass, distance and luminosity — split out by a spectroscope and read through the pattern of dark absorption lines crossing it.

2945.w: When a galaxy's light is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, its spectral lines shift toward the red end of the spectrum — Hubble combined this with distance data in 1929 to show the universe is expanding.

2946.w: In 1998 the High-Z Supernova Search Team measured the redshifts of distant Type Ia supernovae and found the universe's expansion is accelerating — evidence for dark energy, now put at 68% of the cosmos.

2947.w: Vera Rubin found that stars far out in a galaxy orbit its center just as fast as stars near the middle, when gravity from visible matter alone predicts they should slow down — evidence for unseen dark matter.

2948.w: A radio telescope is a large antenna and receiver that detects radio waves — the same objects an optical telescope sees, but at radio wavelengths. Karl Jansky built the first one and found the Milky Way's radio hiss in 1932.

2949.w: In familial ALS, mutations in genes such as SOD1 or C9orf72 damage motor neurons -- the nerve cells carrying signals from brain to muscle -- causing them to die while the mind stays intact.

2950.w: Orcas and other toothed whales emit high-frequency clicks focused through a fatty 'melon,' then read the returning echoes through their jaw to sense prey and obstacles in the dark.

2951.w: The knobby tubercles on a humpback whale's flipper delay stall and cut drag by smoothing how water flows over the edge; copied onto wind-turbine and fan blades, they measurably raise lift and output.

2952.w: San Diego Zoo's Frozen Zoo has stored sperm, eggs, embryos, and living cell cultures from more than 1,300 species and subspecies in liquid nitrogen at -196C since 1972, to support future breeding of endangered animals.

2953.w: Driving an electric current through mercury vapour excites its atoms to radiate strongly in the ultraviolet, mainly at 254 and 185 nanometres -- the mechanism inside every mercury-vapour lamp and black light.

2954.w: Trace europium ions in fluorite absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as visible blue light -- the effect that in 1852 gave the phenomenon of fluorescence its name, after fluorite itself.

2955.w: Dry a silica gel under heat and pressure instead of letting it shrink, and the liquid leaves behind a fragile lattice of the same silica that makes glass, laced with up to 99.8% air -- one of the best thermal insulators known.

2956.w: A quasar is what an active galactic nucleus looks like when a supermassive black hole's own accretion disc is fed a fresh supply of gas -- often stirred up by a galaxy merger -- outshining the entire galaxy's stars combined, up to trillions of times the Sun's brightness.

2957.w: A lightning strike can singe a large branching, fractal scorch pattern into the grass around the point it hits -- a Lichtenberg figure, the same treelike shape Georg Christoph Lichtenberg first produced on charged surfaces in 1777.

2958.w: A fuel cell splits hydrogen into protons and electrons at one electrode; the electrons power a circuit while the protons cross to meet oxygen at the other, combining into water. NASA's Apollo and Shuttle crews drank the water it made.

2959.w: Where the Arabian, Nubian, and Somali plates meet in a triple junction, the same crust-thinning rifting that opens ocean basins elsewhere is happening above sea level -- parts of the Afar Triangle already lie over 100m below sea level.

2960.w: A nocturnal forager covering 2-5 km a night, the aardvark rips into termite mounds and ant nests with stout claws and an unusually reinforced forearm, then sweeps up its meal -- as many as 50,000 insects a night -- on a long, sticky tongue.

2961.w: Each tooth is a cluster of up to 1,500 thin hexagonal tubes of vasodentin with no enamel coating, worn away and regrown continuously -- unique dentition in the only living species of the order Tubulidentata.

2962.w: A beaver stacks logs across a stream and packs them with mud and stone, damming the current into a pond -- an ecosystem-engineering habit that reshapes more landscape than almost any other animal's.

2963.w: Its four chisel incisors grow continuously and never dull: iron compounds stain the enamel orange-red and keep the softer dentine behind it wearing faster, so gnawing wood keeps the edge self-sharpening.

2964.w: Its skin nerve fibers lack the neurotransmitter that normally signals acid pain, an adaptation to the carbon-dioxide-thick air of crowded burrows -- and its body temperature drifts with its surroundings rather than being held constant.

2965.w: The fastest land mammal in the Western Hemisphere, a pronghorn can hit 55 mph (88.5 km/h) in short bursts and still sustain 35 mph (56 km/h) for four miles -- outlasting even a cheetah on endurance.

2966.w: Its speed far exceeds any predator alive in North America today -- evidence it evolved to outrun the extinct American cheetah, and it runs on an oversized heart, lungs, and windpipe built to move huge volumes of air.

2967.w: The fennec fox has the largest ear-to-body ratio of any canid -- up to 10 cm long on a fox that weighs barely a kilogram -- radiating desert heat away from its body while picking up the sound of prey moving underground.

2968.w: Hunting only in full darkness, a vampire bat homes in on a heat-sensitive nerve channel in its nose, tuned to fire at skin-warm temperatures, to find a blood vessel close to the surface before it ever bites.

2969.w: Its saliva carries anticoagulants that keep a wound bleeding long after the bite -- one of them, desmoteplase, has been studied as a stroke drug for its ability to dissolve blood clots.

2970.w: An aye-aye taps a branch up to eight times a second and listens to the echo, a technique called percussive foraging that reveals hollow tunnels chewed by grubs beneath the bark.

2971.w: Once it finds a hollow, the aye-aye gnaws a hole through the wood and fishes the grub out with one thin, bony middle finger on a ball-and-socket joint tipped with a hooked nail -- filling a niche woodpeckers hold elsewhere.

2972.w: Twenty-two fleshy tentacles ringing its nostrils carry over 25,000 Eimer's organs, mechanical touch sensors so fine the star-nosed mole can identify and eat a piece of food in as little as 120 milliseconds -- the fastest forager known.

2973.w: An owl's ear openings sit at different heights on the skull, so a sound reaches each ear a few dozen microseconds apart -- enough for strictly nocturnal hunters like barn owls to pinpoint prey in total darkness by hearing alone.

2974.w: A male satin bowerbird builds a stick bower separate from any nest and decorates it, as he matures, with more and more blue objects -- a display females inspect before choosing a mate.
