2975.w: A countercurrent network of blood vessels around its flippers and windpipe, wrapped in an insulating layer of brown fat, lets a leatherback hold its core 18°C above the surrounding water -- and dive to 1,280 m, deeper than any other reptile.

2976.w: An archerfish shapes a groove in its mouth to fire a water jet that outruns itself and balls up just before impact, almost always hitting an insect on the first shot -- correcting, as it aims, for how light bends where air meets water.

2977.w: Not a true eel, this Amazonian fish stacks about 6,000 electricity-generating cells into a single organ that can discharge over 600 volts -- with a second, low-voltage organ used just to sense its surroundings.

2978.w: It can curl its body around prey to strike it with both poles of its electric organ at once, doubling the shock -- and a leaping eel can deliver a jolt strong enough to drive off an animal as large as a horse.

2979.w: A smashing mantis shrimp's raptorial claw accelerates at over 10,000 g to speeds of 23 m/s, hard enough to crack mollusk shells outright -- and the collapsing cavitation bubble it leaves behind delivers a second, separate hit.

2980.w: Its compound eyes carry 12 to 16 types of photoreceptor, versus four in humans, and can detect circularly polarized light -- a sense not documented in any other animal.

2981.w: Snapping its oversized claw shut fires a jet fast enough to collapse a cavitation bubble in a flash of light -- if the light were purely thermal, it would take a temperature over 5,000 K, hotter than the Sun's surface.

2982.w: The collapsing bubble's snap peaks at 218 decibels underwater, loud enough to stun small fish outright -- and in large colonies, the combined noise can interfere with sonar and submarine detection.

2983.w: A bombardier beetle mixes stored hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide with catalytic enzymes in an internal chamber; the exothermic reaction hits near 100°C and fires out in some 70 pulses a second, aimed by a nozzle that can swivel 270 degrees.

2984.w: Facing drying-out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs and forms a desiccated 'tun,' flooding its cells with protective proteins that let it survive years without water and temperatures from -272°C to 149°C.

2985.w: In a 2007 European Space Agency experiment, dehydrated tardigrades were exposed directly to the vacuum of space for ten days -- the vacuum alone did little harm, though direct solar ultraviolet radiation proved far more lethal.

2986.w: The largest land-living arthropod, weighing up to 4.1 kg, a coconut crab strips a coconut's husk from its germination pores and strikes until one gives way -- and as an adult it abandons the borrowed shell its hermit-crab relatives still carry.

2987.w: Griffon vultures eat only carrion, and their bald heads flush with bare skin to shed heat in the sun instead of growing feathers that would foul with rot.

2988.w: A wingspan up to 2.8 metres lets a griffon vulture soar for hours at barely more than its resting metabolism, ranging from North Africa's deserts into the mountains of Asia.

2989.w: Neith's own hieroglyph is a shield crossed by two bows -- she was Sais's warrior goddess of hunting and archery long before she was called a creator.

2990.w: When the gods split over which nephew should inherit the throne, they wrote to Neith at Sais for a verdict, and she advised that Horus, not Set, should be king.

2991.w: In the 'stretching of the cord' ceremony, Seshat and the pharaoh each held a stake and pulled a cord taut between them to align a new temple's corners to the stars.

2992.w: Seshat was said to be Thoth's own sister, wife or daughter depending on the telling, and myth credited her with inventing writing, which Thoth then taught to humanity.

2993.w: The Book of the Dead has the deceased pray to 'rise like Nefertem from the blue water-lily, to the nostrils of Ra' -- Nefertem himself was that first lotus opening at creation.

2994.w: Nefertem completed the Memphis triad as the son of the creator god Ptah, a beautiful young god shown crowned with the same blue lotus he was born from.

2995.w: Nekhbet and Wadjet were worshipped together as the 'Two Ladies,' vulture and cobra standing for Upper and Lower Egypt on the pharaoh's own crown.

2996.w: Her shrine at Nekheb, in what is now El Kab, is reckoned one of Egypt's earliest temples, founded in the Predynastic period around 3200 BCE.

2997.w: At the Min Festival, priests carried his image out to bless the fields at harvest, and worshippers ate the tall, milky-sapped wild lettuce sacred to him for potency.

2998.w: Min's shrine at Coptos was crowned with real bull horns for his sacred white bull, and New Kingdom images gave him a crown of two tall feather plumes.

2999.w: Images of the cobra goddess stood in kitchens, granaries and cellars, invoked to guard stored grain against mice and insects.

3000.w: Renenutet was sometimes paired with Sobek, whose Nile floodwaters laid down the silt that made her own bountiful harvests possible.

3001.w: Bes and the hippo goddess Taweret were both invoked at childbirth, their images kept close by to protect mother and newborn.

3002.w: Scholars trace Bes's earliest form to a lion rearing up on its hind legs, long before he became the dwarf figure familiar from later household amulets.

3003.w: One tradition described Mut as a great serpent coiled around her own father Ra, rebirthing him each day as her son Khonsu.

3004.w: As Amun's wife at Karnak, Mut wore the vulture headdress with the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt layered on top.

3005.w: The Pyramid Texts say Atum-Ra sneezed, and the moisture of his own breath became Tefnut -- a wet twin born alongside Shu, the air.

3006.w: As a fierce lioness-headed Eye of Ra, Tefnut was Shu's own twin sister and consort, and together the pair parented Geb and Nut.

3007.w: Sokar ruled the Memphis necropolis as a mummified falcon, and his fusion with Osiris as Ptah-Sokar-Osiris made him patron of the resurrected dead.

3008.w: Wepwawet shared jackal iconography and even a cult city with Anubis, and over time myth settled the overlap by making the two wolf gods brothers.

3009.w: Carried on the army's lead standard and armed with mace and bow, Wepwawet was invoked to 'open the way' to the pharaoh's own victory.

3010.w: A sponge has no nerves or organs: choanocytes, collar cells with a whip-like flagellum, pump water through the body's pores, capturing roughly 80% of its food — one of the oldest surviving animal body plans.

3011.w: A comb jelly is a distinct phylum from the jellyfish it resembles. Its eight rows of fused cilia (ctenes) form a natural photonic crystal, splitting light into rainbow bands as it swims — pure optics, not the bioluminescence some species also produce when disturbed.

3012.w: A well-fed Hydra buds a genetic clone off its own body wall roughly every two days, and if cut in half each piece regrows the missing end. Its stem cells divide indefinitely, a case researchers study for clues to negligible senescence — though whether it truly never ages is still debated.

3013.w: A planarian flatworm carries neoblasts, adult stem cells making up a fifth or more of its body, able to become any cell type; a fragment as small as roughly 1/279th of the worm can regenerate a complete animal within about two weeks.

3014.w: A leech is an annelid, close kin to the earthworm in the shared class Clitellata. A blood-feeding species' saliva contains hirudin, an anticoagulant so effective that leeches are still used in microsurgery to keep blood flowing through reattached tissue.

3015.w: A nemertean hunts by firing an eversible proboscis from a separate internal cavity, in venomous species tipped with a barbed stylet. One washed-up bootlace worm was reported at up to 54m, though zoologists warn the measurement is unreliable, with sturdier estimates nearer 30m.

3016.w: A bryozoan colony ("moss animal") is built from thousands of genetically identical zooids, each under a millimetre, feeding through its own lophophore, a ciliated tentacle crown — cooperating so closely the colony acts almost like one larger animal.

3017.w: A lampshell's two valves are dorsal and ventral, not left-right like a bivalve mollusc's, and it feeds through a U-shaped lophophore rather than gills. The clam-like shape evolved independently in Brachiopoda — convergent evolution on an unrelated body plan.

3018.w: A dehydrated tardigrade curls into a tun, metabolism nearly stopped, its cells stabilised by protein-based glassy matrices. It has tolerated temperatures from near absolute zero to 149°C and survived the vacuum of space in a 2007 ESA test, though full solar UV proved lethal to most.

3019.w: Onychophora pairs a soft, worm-like body with clawed, arthropod-like legs, long discussed as a possible bridge between annelid worms and arthropods. It hunts by shooting two oscillating slime jets, usually about a centimetre and rarely to 10cm, weaving prey into a sticky net.

3020.w: Horseshoe crabs mass-spawn on sandy beaches at the highest tides around full and new moons. Their blue, copper-based blood carries amebocytes that clot instantly around bacterial endotoxin — the basis of the LAL test still used to screen vaccines for contamination.

3021.w: A scaphopod lives buried head-down in sand or mud, its curved, tapering shell open at both ends. It hunts with dozens of thread-like tentacles called captacula, reaching into the sediment to pluck out single-celled foraminifera.

3022.w: A slug is a gastropod, the same broad group as the snail, but its external shell has been lost or reduced to an internal plate used mainly for calcium storage — independently, in multiple lineages, making "slug" a body plan rather than one evolutionary group.

3023.w: A foraminiferan is a single amoeba-like cell that secretes a multi-chambered shell, usually of calcium carbonate. Nummulitic limestone, made almost entirely from fossil foraminifera shells, is the actual building stone of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

3024.w: A radiolarian secretes an internal silica skeleton in elaborate, often symmetrical lattices. Accumulated skeletons blanket parts of the ocean floor as siliceous ooze, which can later become the rock chert — and their geometry inspired Ernst Haeckel's famous illustrations.

3025.w: A dinoflagellate swims with two flagella, one wrapped in a groove around the cell. In bioluminescent species, disturbance triggers a luciferin-luciferase reaction in organelles called scintillons, flashing blue light — other dinoflagellate blooms turn the water red and release toxins.

3026.w: A diatom builds a two-part cell wall, or frustule, of silica glass so precisely shaped the larger half overlaps the smaller like a pillbox lid. As a group, diatoms are estimated to generate a fifth to half of the oxygen produced on Earth each year.

3027.w: Euglena's chloroplasts, wrapped in three membranes rather than two, came from engulfing a green alga generations ago. In light it photosynthesises; in the dark it swims by flagellum and absorbs food instead — a genuine straddle of the plant/animal divide.

3028.w: A paramecium is covered in thousands of cilia beating in coordinated waves, an effect often compared to wind rippling a field of grain. The same beating rows sweep bacteria and detritus down an oral groove — though this can burn over half its total energy budget.

3029.w: A stonewort (Charales) is a green alga whose whorled branches often crust over with deposited calcium carbonate, masking the chlorophyll and giving the group its name. Stoneworts sit among the charophyte algae counted as the closest living algal relatives of land plants.

3030.w: Cycads are gymnosperms with a fossil record stretching back some 300 million years, predating flowering plants. Despite bearing seeds, several genera still produce motile sperm — a trait otherwise limited to ferns and mosses — and host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in special roots.

3031.w: Ginkgo biloba is the sole surviving species of the order Ginkgoales, which first appeared over 290 million years ago, and is strikingly resistant to disease, insects and pollution. Six ginkgo trees 1-2km from the 1945 Hiroshima blast survived it, and all six are alive today.

3032.w: A hornwort is a distinct, ancient lineage of non-vascular land plant, its own division apart from mosses and liverworts. Unlike almost every other plant, most hornwort cells carry one large chloroplast, and many species host nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria in internal cavities.

3033.w: A manatee grazes over 60 kinds of freshwater and saltwater plants, up to seven hours a day, eating roughly a tenth of its body weight. Its low metabolic rate and thin fat leave it unable to survive prolonged cold, forcing seasonal migration to warm springs.

3034.w: Unlike its river-tolerant manatee relatives, a dugong lives entirely in the sea, uprooting whole seagrass plants and shaking off sand before eating, leaving furrowed trails on the seabed. Sailors' half-glimpsed sightings are credited as a real source of mermaid folklore.

3035.w: Despite its size, the hyrax belongs to Afrotheria, the same mammalian branch as elephants and sirenians. It has poor internal temperature control, so it basks on sun-warmed rock outcrops; its communal dung middens fossilise into hyraceum, used historically in perfumery.

3036.w: Tenrecs radiated across Madagascar into forms convergently resembling hedgehogs, shrews, moles and otters found nowhere on the island naturally. The lowland streaked tenrec makes sound by rubbing quills together, and tenrecs run unusually low body temperatures for placental mammals.

3037.w: A golden mole has no functional eyes or external ears, and iridescent fur that helps it glide through soil. Grant's golden mole, of Namibia's desert dunes, presses its head to the sand to detect prey through an oversized malleus, an inner-ear bone tuned to seismic vibration.

3038.w: A colugo's patagium, a skin membrane running from shoulder to fingertip to tail-tip, is the most extensive gliding membrane of any mammal, covering 70m or more between rainforest trees in a single glide. Genetics places it nearer primates than any lemur, and it never achieves true flight.

3039.w: A tapir's short, prehensile snout works almost like a limited trunk, flexible enough to grab foliage out of easy reach. It wades into rivers, sinks to the bottom and walks the riverbed to feed, sometimes staying under long enough for fish to pick parasites from its skin.

3040.w: A giant anteater has no teeth and only limited jaw movement; it tears open a nest with one massive foreclaw, then flicks a sticky tongue up to 60cm long roughly 160 times a minute. It may raid 200 nests and eat 35,000 insects a day, digesting them with formic acid from its own prey.

3041.w: A wombat's pouch faces backward, so tunnelling through its own burrow system doesn't fling soil onto its joey. Its droppings emerge as distinct cubes, shaped by alternating stiff and flexible sections of the intestine wall, keeping the scent-marking dung stacked instead of rolling off.

3042.w: All three living mesite species are found only in Madagascar, gleaning insects and seeds from the forest floor. Despite having wings, they are weak, reluctant fliers, using short escape flutters rather than sustained flight — common among birds that evolved without mammalian predators.

3043.w: A sunbittern forages alone along tropical American riverbanks. Startled, it spreads its wings and tail into a sudden fan, revealing large red, yellow and black eyespots on the flight feathers — a defensive illusion meant to look bigger and more dangerous than it is.

3044.w: A turaco's feathers contain turacoverdin and turacin, real copper-based pigments found in no other bird. Almost every other "green" bird gets its colour from feather structure scattering light over yellow pigment, not a genuine green pigment.

3045.w: The hoatzin is the only bird known to rely on foregut fermentation, breaking down leaves with gut microbes in an enlarged crop much like a cow's rumen. Its chicks hatch with claws on their wing digits, letting them climb back up after dropping into water to dodge a predator.

3046.w: A seriema is the nearest living relative of the giant, extinct terror birds (Phorusrhacidae). It hunts snakes, lizards and large insects on foot across South America's open country, killing prey by seizing it in the beak and beating it against the ground.

3047.w: The cuckoo-roller is the sole living species in its own order, Leptosomiformes, found only in Madagascar and the Comoro Islands. Its name reflects a passing resemblance to cuckoos and rollers, not any kinship — genetics places it as an early, isolated branch of its own.

3048.w: The tuatara is the sole survivor of Rhynchocephalia, a reptile order that split from squamates over 240 million years ago. Hatchlings carry a functioning parietal ("third") eye on top of the skull, later covered by scales, and an egg can take well over a year to hatch.

3049.w: Most amphisbaenians ("worm lizards") have lost all four limbs and burrow forward or backward with near-equal ease, bunching ring-like skin against the tunnel wall to push. A blunt tail that vaguely mimics the head gave rise to old folk beliefs in a two-headed serpent.

3050.w: Sunlight heats open ground until bubbles of moist air break free and rise as thermals; cooling as they climb turns the moisture in a cloud into cumulus's puffy, flat-bottomed heaps.

3051.w: Bare desert ground heats faster than almost any other surface, driving the strong afternoon thermals that build fair-weather cumulus fastest and biggest.

3052.w: Cirrus is a high genus of ice-crystal cloud, 6,000 to 20,000 m up, where strong winds aloft comb it into hooked strands nicknamed mare's tails.

3053.w: A stratus deck is essentially fog that never reached the ground: moist air cools to its dew point and condenses into a flat grey sheet under 2,000 m instead of touching down.

3054.w: Lift a bank of morning fog off the ground and it keeps its shape as a layer cloud — one of stratus's two main ways of forming.

3055.w: Kept fed by rising air instead of running out of instability, a cumulus keeps swelling until it reaches the tropopause and spreads into cumulonimbus's flat anvil top.

3056.w: A cold front's lifting is sharp and narrow, forcing cloud straight up into the towering, hail- and lightning-bearing cumulonimbus rather than a wide layer.

3057.w: Warm air gliding up over the retreating cold wedge of a warm front spreads cloud into nimbostratus, the thick dark layer that can rain steadily for days.

3058.w: Enough wind shear tilts a cumulonimbus's rising air into a persistent rotating updraught — a mesocyclone — turning an ordinary storm into a supercell.

3059.w: Farmland heats and cools far faster than the ocean beside it; that seasonal contrast reverses the wind twice a year, driving monsoons like South Asia's.

3060.w: The starkest version of the same imbalance: hot, dry land beside warm ocean sharpens the pressure gradient that drags moist monsoon winds ashore each summer.

3061.w: Wind shear can stretch a supercell's mesocyclone tighter and thinner until it reaches down to touch the ground as a tornado.

3062.w: Air sinking at about 30° latitude spreads out at the surface as a subtropical ridge of high pressure — the same descending, drying air that starves deserts of rain.

3063.w: A mid-latitude depression is built from exactly these two: a warm front and a cold front spiralling in around a shared centre of low pressure, the classic frontal-cyclone shape.

3064.w: Sustained heavy rainfall is one of the standard causes of river flooding, and a slow-moving low-pressure system is exactly what can supply rain steadily enough, for long enough, over the same ground.

3065.w: A warm front is exactly this: an advancing mass of warm, moist air riding up and over the retreating cold air ahead of it, arriving slowly under a wide sheet of cloud.

3066.w: A cold front is dense cold air undercutting the warmer air ahead of it, moving up to twice as fast as a warm front and triggering a much sharper line of storms.

3067.w: Ice pellets, what Americans call sleet, form when raindrops fall through a sub-freezing layer near the ground and refreeze solid before they land — hard enough to bounce.

3068.w: Drizzle is official only below 0.5 mm across — droplets that shallow, misty stratus and stratocumulus clouds produce without the collision-and-growth process that builds heavier rain.

3069.w: Wind spins hemispherical cups mounted on a shaft, because a cup's hollow face catches more drag than its convex back — Robinson's design, 1846.

3070.w: A funnel feeding a graduated cylinder converts rainfall depth straight into a number. Korea's cheugugi, standardised in 1441, was the first version issued nationwide.

3071.w: An asymmetric tail catches more wind than the pointed head, so the whole vane swings to face into the wind. Athens' Tower of the Winds carried a bronze Triton doing exactly this, around 50 BCE.

3072.w: Human hair — pure keratin — lengthens measurably as humidity rises. De Saussure built the first hair hygrometer around a single strand in 1783.

3073.w: Both Köppen's tropical rainforest and tropical monsoon types share the same rule: every month averages 18°C or warmer, and they differ only in how the rain is timed across the year.

3074.w: Warm tropical seas keep even the coolest month above Köppen's 18°C tropical threshold, and it's that same warm water that feeds the monsoon winds blowing off it.

3075.w: Köppen draws the arid line on evaporation, not heat: where potential evaporation driven by strong sun outstrips whatever rain falls, however little, the climate counts as arid.

3076.w: Wind speeds up evaporation from what little moisture the ground holds, widening the same gap between rainfall and evaporative demand that defines an arid climate.

3077.w: Steady seasonal rain across the mid-latitudes is what lets temperate farmland exist at all — Köppen's Class C zone, coldest month between −3°C and 18°C.

3078.w: Thunderstorms breaking up warm spells are a routine feature of temperate summers, the mid-latitude belt between the tropics and the polar circles.

3079.w: Mercury is about 70% metal by mass, giving it the largest core of any planet relative to its size — an iron core filling 57% of its volume, versus 17% for Earth's.

3080.w: Radar observations in 1965 proved Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, was not tidally locked as assumed — it rotates three times for every two orbits, a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance.

3081.w: A 96.5% carbon dioxide atmosphere drives a runaway greenhouse effect, holding Venus's surface at 464°C — hotter than Mercury, despite Venus being nearly twice as far from the Sun.

3082.w: NASA's Magellan spacecraft mapped more than 85,000 volcanoes on Venus; a global resurfacing event 300-600 million years ago left most of its impact craters looking barely worn.

3083.w: Earth is the only body in the solar system known to sustain stable liquid water on its surface, covering 70.8% of it.

3084.w: Earth's atmosphere is unique for its free molecular oxygen — 20.95% of the air — accumulated over billions of years once photosynthesis began harvesting sunlight directly.

3085.w: Iron(III) oxide dust and the mineral goethite coat the Martian surface, giving the Red Planet its rust color.

3086.w: Mars's atmosphere is only about 0.6% as thick as Earth's at sea level, so it holds almost no heat — surface temperatures swing from -153°C to 20°C.

3087.w: Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet, generated by eddy currents deep in its vast layer of electrically conductive metallic hydrogen.

3088.w: Jupiter radiates more heat than it receives from the Sun. The Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism — slow gravitational contraction left over from its formation — still shrinks it by about 1 mm a year.

3089.w: At 0.6871 g/cm3, Saturn is the only planet less dense than water — about 30% less — so a tub big enough to hold it would let it float.

3090.w: A six-sided jet-stream pattern circles Saturn's north pole, its sides each longer than Earth's diameter. First spotted in Voyager images, it was confirmed still there decades later by Cassini.

3091.w: Methane in Uranus's atmosphere absorbs red light and reflects blue and green, giving the planet its aquamarine color.

3092.w: Uranus has the coldest atmosphere of any planet, dropping to 49 K (-224°C), because unlike similar-sized Neptune it radiates almost no internal heat of its own — a mystery still unexplained.

3093.w: Voyager 2 clocked winds on Neptune at 2,100 km/h during its 1989 flyby — the fastest sustained winds of any planet in the solar system.

3094.w: Voyager 2 found a storm as wide as Earth on Neptune in 1989, the Great Dark Spot — then the Hubble Space Telescope found it had vanished by 1994, replaced by a new one elsewhere.

3095.w: Pluto is the largest known object in the Kuiper belt by volume, a frozen planetesimal of rock and ice that never became a planet. New Horizons found a bright, heart-shaped glacier of nitrogen ice on it in 2015.

3096.w: Pluto orbits among the same population of icy trans-Neptunian bodies that supply the solar system's comets. Clyde Tombaugh found it on February 18, 1930, while hunting a hypothesized 'Planet X'.

3097.w: Jupiter's gravity flexes Io so hard, and an orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps the flexing going, that tidal heating melts its interior and drives hundreds of active volcanoes.

3098.w: Sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost from its own volcanic plumes coat Io in yellow, white, and red-brown deposits, the most colorful surface in the solar system.

3099.w: Europa is the smoothest known solid object in the solar system — a young, ice-covered surface with almost no mountains or large craters.

3100.w: Beneath its ice shell, Europa hides a saltwater ocean holding roughly two to three times as much water as every ocean on Earth combined, kept liquid by Jupiter's tidal heating.

3101.w: Ganymede is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field, from convection in a liquid iron core — a field the Galileo spacecraft detected on its first flyby in 1996.

3102.w: Galileo Galilei spotted Ganymede with a homemade telescope in January 1610, along with Io, Europa, and Callisto. It is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger across than Mercury.

3103.w: Callisto's surface is the oldest and most heavily cratered in the solar system, dating back some 4.5 billion years — so saturated with impacts that new craters erase old ones.

3104.w: With no volcanoes, mountains, or tectonic activity, Callisto has had nothing to erase its impact record — its cratered plains have simply sat there, unresurfaced, since the early solar system.

3105.w: Saturn's rings are 99.9% pure water ice, in pieces ranging from dust grains to house-sized chunks, spread into a disc barely a hundred meters thick.

3106.w: One leading model for the rings' origin has an icy moon straying inside Saturn's Roche limit and being torn apart by tides; another has two icy moons colliding — both would explain why the rings are almost pure ice.

3107.w: Giovanni Cassini spotted this 4,800 km gap in Saturn's rings in 1675. Ring particles there orbit twice for every orbit of the moon Mimas, and that 2:1 resonance sweeps the gap clear over time.

3108.w: Titan is the only moon with an atmosphere denser than Earth's — thick, nitrogen-rich air, first found around a moon orbiting anything other than Earth's own planet.

3109.w: Titan is the only place besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface — seas and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed in one of its dry plains on January 14, 2005.

3110.w: Cassini imaged geysers of water vapor and ice erupting from fractures at Enceladus's south pole in 2005, feeding Saturn's E ring — strong evidence of a liquid ocean under the ice.

3111.w: Enceladus's fresh ice reflects almost all the sunlight that hits it, among the highest reflectivity of any body in the solar system — and that keeps its surface at a frigid -198°C.

3112.w: The crater Herschel spans 139 km, a third of Mimas's own diameter, giving the moon a startling resemblance to the Death Star — three years before Star Wars existed to compare it to.

3113.w: Titania, Uranus's largest moon, is roughly half ice and half rock, with a canyon called Messina Chasma running 1,500 km toward its south pole — evidence its interior once expanded and cracked the crust.

3114.w: Oberon, the outermost of Uranus's large moons, is heavily cratered and among the reddest bodies in the system; Voyager 2's single 1986 flyby found an unexplained 11 km peak near its south pole.

3115.w: Miranda's jumbled chevron-shaped terrain and a scarp nearly 20 km high, Verona Rupes, suggest it may once have been shattered by an impact and gravitationally reassembled.

3116.w: Triton is the only large moon in the solar system with a retrograde orbit, circling Neptune backward — a sign it was likely a Kuiper belt dwarf planet captured by Neptune's gravity, not born there.

3117.w: Voyager 2 saw nitrogen-gas geysers erupting through Triton's thin, icy surface in plumes up to 8 km high — sunlight warming buried nitrogen ice until the pressure blows it out.

3118.w: Long assumed a captured asteroid, though its oddly porous interior casts doubt on that — it may instead be debris a giant impact blasted off Mars. Either way, tides drag it inward: a crash or a ring within 30-50 million years.

3119.w: Asaph Hall found Deimos on August 12, 1877, six days before Phobos. Unlike its sibling, Deimos orbits beyond the point where Mars's gravity holds a moon in place, so tides are slowly pushing it away rather than in.

3120.w: Pluto and Charon have tidally locked to each other so completely that each always shows the other the same face, and their shared center of mass lies out in space, outside Pluto itself.

3121.w: Ceres holds about 40% of the entire asteroid belt's mass, and as much as a quarter of that mass is water ice.

3122.w: Ceres is large enough that its own gravity has pulled it into a near-perfect sphere, a state called hydrostatic equilibrium that no other asteroid has reached — the reason the IAU classed it a dwarf planet in 2006.

3123.w: Eris takes about 560 years to complete one orbit of the Sun, out in the scattered disc far beyond Neptune, one of the most distant large bodies known.

3124.w: When Mike Brown's team found Eris in January 2005, it appeared to outweigh Pluto, and NASA briefly called it a tenth planet. The dispute pushed the IAU to define 'planet' for the first time in 2006, demoting both Eris and Pluto to dwarf planets.

3125.w: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm 1.3 times the width of Earth, continuously tracked since 1878 — and it may be the same 'permanent spot' Giovanni Cassini recorded between 1665 and 1713.

3126.w: Viking longships were clinker-built for a fast, shallow-draft hull and rigged with a single square sail woven from rough wool cloth -- around 100 square meters of it per sail.

3127.w: Old Norse vikingr, the root of "Viking," is almost absent from written sources before the 12th century -- it survives from the era itself mostly on a handful of runestones.

3128.w: Norse Greenlanders built a base camp at L'Anse aux Meadows on the island of Newfoundland; a 2021 tree-ring study dated their presence there to exactly 1021 CE, nearly 500 years before Columbus.

3129.w: Malbork Castle in Poland, raised by the Teutonic Order and completed in 1406, is the largest brick castle in the world -- its walls enclose 21 hectares, four times the area of Windsor Castle.

3130.w: A moat is a ditch dug around a fortification, dry or filled with water, that keeps siege towers and battering rams away from the walls and makes tunnelling under them far harder.

3131.w: A castle's drawbridge pivoted at the gatehouse threshold to cross its moat, and could be winched up by ropes or chains to a windlass to seal the entrance during an attack.

3132.w: Rome's amphitheatre is faced in travertine quarried at Tibur and carted twenty miles, held together with iron cramps rather than mortar. When the cramps were robbed out for their metal the facade started coming down, which is why one side is missing.

3133.w: Rome's earliest gladiators were soldier-prisoners and enslaved people condemned to fight in amphitheatres; the first types were named, and armed, after the enemies Rome had just defeated -- the Samnite, Thracian, and Gaul.

3134.w: Ming builders boiled sticky rice into their slaked lime. The amylopectin in the starch controls how the calcium carbonate crystallises, so the mortar sets finer, denser and far tougher than lime alone — an organic-inorganic composite, six centuries early.

3135.w: The Portuguese caravel, perfected under Prince Henry the Navigator, paired a narrow hull -- about 3.5 times as long as it was wide -- with lateen sails that could point closer to the wind than a square-rigger.

3136.w: Two of Columbus's three 1492 ships, the Nina and the Pinta, were caravels (his flagship Santa Maria was a larger carrack); the fleet crossed the Atlantic in about five weeks, and he insisted he had reached Asia.

3137.w: Hardtack is flour, water, and salt baked into a dense, unleavened cracker dry enough to survive months at sea; by 1731, Royal Navy sailors received a pound of it every day.

3138.w: The Hoba meteorite, an 84% iron ataxite a farmer's plough struck near Grootfontein, Namibia, in 1920, is the largest intact meteorite ever found -- over 60 tonnes, never moved because of its mass.

3139.w: Self-tickling doesn't work: the cerebellum predicts the exact sensation of one's own movement and dampens the response, so only another person's touch on the same nerve endings registers as a tickle.

3140.w: A sneeze is a nerve reflex fired when irritants like pollen or dust hit the nasal lining; 2020 high-speed video caught sneeze plumes carrying roughly 40,000 droplets as far as 8 meters.

3141.w: Vacuum distillation boils the lighter fractions — naphtha, gasoline, diesel — out of crude oil. What won't distil below about 500°C is bitumen, the sticky black residue left in the still.

3142.w: A helical blade inside a tube scoops water at the bottom and carries it up as the shaft turns. Archimedes is traditionally credited with it, though the total lack of any evidence for it before his time is disputed among historians.

3143.w: A water clock housed inside an elephant: a floating bowl sinks over thirty minutes, tugs a string, and a see-saw drops a ball into a serpent's mouth to strike the hour. al-Jazari described it in 1206.

3144.w: A wheel sets crankpins moving in a circle while a connecting rod turns that into a straight back-and-forth push. al-Jazari built it into a twin-cylinder water pump in 1206 — the earliest known true crankshaft.

3145.w: Drebbel's submarine was a wooden rowboat frame wrapped in greased leather to seal it, rowed by oarsmen through leather-sealed oar-holes. It stayed under the Thames for three hours in 1620, King James I aboard.

3146.w: Mercury expanding with heat pushes an iron lever that closes a damper, choking the fire until the temperature falls back. Drebbel built one in the 1620s to hold a chicken incubator steady — among the first feedback-controlled devices on record.

3147.w: A grounded iron point gives a stroke a low-resistance path to the ground that doesn't run through the building. Franklin proposed it in 1752, reasoning the charge would bleed off silently before a strike could even happen.

3148.w: Two lenses ground for two distances, each cut in half and set together in one frame — near vision below, far vision above. Franklin is generally credited with the design, though London opticians already knew the trick when he first ordered a pair.

3149.w: Flyweights spun by the engine's own output shaft swing outward as it speeds up, and a linkage from their arms closes the throttle valve. Watt adapted the mechanism, already used to regulate windmills, to his steam engine in 1788.

3150.w: Bitumen of Judea dissolved in lavender oil, coated on a pewter plate and exposed to sunlight for hours, hardens where light strikes it; washing away the rest leaves an image. Niépce's plate, fixed by about 1827, is the earliest surviving photograph.

3151.w: Lister soaked clean cotton towels in undiluted carbolic acid and packed them onto a compound fracture in 1865, then covered the wound in tin foil to keep the dressing from drying out. His infection rates collapsed.

3152.w: Nitroglycerin won't detonate from a plain fuse, so Nobel first triggered it with a small gunpowder charge in 1863, then by 1867 was packing mercury fulminate into the gunpowder itself inside a copper capsule — the detonator that made dynamite usable.

3153.w: Benz's Patent-Motorwagen bolted a single-cylinder four-stroke engine to a three-wheeled carriage with wooden, iron-tyred wheels. Built and sold from 1886, it's widely regarded as the first automobile put into production.

3154.w: Bell wired a coil into a balance circuit and used a telephone receiver to listen for the tone breaking near metal. Built in 1881 to find the bullet in President Garfield's chest, it worked in principle, but a metal-coil bed frame threw off the reading.

3155.w: A primary coil and capacitor discharge across a spark gap into a secondary coil tuned to the same resonant frequency, stepping the voltage up far higher than an ordinary transformer's turns ratio could. Tesla patented the circuit in 1891.

3156.w: Alternating current fed through stator coils creates a magnetic field that rotates in step with the AC oscillations, and that turning field drags an unpowered rotor around behind it — no brushes needed. Tesla demonstrated the motor in 1887, patented in 1888.

3157.w: An engine-driven propeller supplies forward thrust while the rotor overhead spins on its own, powered only by air flowing up through it — unlike a helicopter, whose engine drives the rotor directly. de la Cierva flew the first one in January 1923.

3158.w: The V-2 burned a 75% ethanol/25% water fuel against liquid oxygen, forced through a nozzle built to survive the heat. First flown successfully in October 1942, it became the first artificial object to reach space in 1944 under von Braun's direction.

3159.w: Press a key and current runs through a set of wired, rotating discs to light one of 26 lamps — a different letter each time, since a rotor steps forward with every keystroke. Scherbius patented the design in 1918.

3160.w: The bombe wired together the equivalent of dozens of Enigma rotor sets and ran through possible settings electromechanically, ruling out all but a handful for checking by hand. Turing's design, built on the Polish bomba, reached Bletchley Park in 1939.

3161.w: Mercaptopurine is a purine ring with sulfur substituted where guanine and hypoxanthine carry oxygen, letting it jam the same enzyme those two natural bases use. Elion and Hitchings discovered it in 1953, the first rationally designed chemotherapy for leukemia.

3162.w: A page whose references are links a reader can follow immediately instead of a citation to go look up. Ted Nelson coined the term in 1965 for a computerised version of the cross-references that print already used.

3163.w: Hypertext and the Internet had both existed since the 1960s, but nobody had combined them: Berners-Lee's 1989 CERN proposal described a hypertext database running over the Internet, and by December 1990 he'd built HTTP, HTML, the URL, and the first browser.

3164.w: In 1811 twelve-year-old Mary Anning's brother Joseph found a skull at Lyme Regis; months later she excavated the rest of a 5-metre skeleton, the first ichthyosaur specimen to draw serious scientific attention.

3165.w: Mycobacterium leprae (or the rarer M. lepromatosis) spreads mainly through nasal droplets, not touch — about 95% of people exposed never develop symptoms, and it can take five years or more to show up.

3166.w: Chaulmoogra oil's fatty acids, esterified with ethanol, turn soluble enough to inject. Alice Ball worked this out in 1915-16 at Hawaii — the first effective leprosy treatment before antibiotics — though she died at 24 before publishing it herself.

3167.w: Ge Hong's 4th-century recipe said to steep the plant in cold water, not boil it. Heat wrecks the compound's activity — cold extraction from Artemisia annua isolated artemisinin in 1972, earning Tu Youyou a share of the 2015 Nobel Prize.

3168.w: In his 1809 Philosophie Zoologique, Lamarck proposed that organs strengthen with use and weaken with disuse, and that acquired traits pass to offspring — his own example was a giraffe's neck lengthening, generation by generation, to reach higher leaves.

3169.w: Mixing serum and red cells from different people, Karl Landsteiner found some combinations clumped and some didn't, sorting blood into groups he called A, B, and C in 1900-01. C was later renamed O, and his students found a fourth group, AB, the next year.

3170.w: A returning forager runs a figure eight, waggling along the straight middle stretch. The run's angle from vertical shows the food's angle from the Sun, and the waggle's length shows the distance — a code Karl von Frisch spent decades decoding.

3171.w: Ibn al-Haytham's seven-volume Book of Optics (1011-1021 CE) broke with the old idea that eyes emit rays, arguing instead that vision happens because light enters the eye — and used the camera obscura's inverted image, among other experiments, to make the case.

3172.w: Eight radio observatories on four continents, linked by interferometry into one Earth-sized virtual telescope. Katie Bouman helped build the CHIRP algorithm that reconstructed the image — the first picture of a black hole, M87*, released 10 April 2019.

3173.w: A germinating seed's first green leaves, its cotyledons, turn photosynthetic in the light and power the seedling's climb toward becoming a sapling.

3174.w: Photosynthesis, run on chlorophyll, is what actually funds a seedling's growth into a woody sapling — sunlight is the fuel behind the whole climb.

3175.w: Given years and enough light, a sapling's single woody stem keeps thickening until it is unmistakably a tree — trunk, crown and all.

3176.w: The vascular cambium is the ring of dividing cells sandwiched between xylem and phloem; it builds new xylem inward and new phloem outward every growing season.

3177.w: Cambium cells divide every growing season to lay down new sapwood — the living, water-conducting wood just inside the bark.

3178.w: Sapwood is simply the newest xylem: the living outer wood layer that actively conducts water from root to leaf.

3179.w: As a tree ages, its oldest sapwood undergoes a genetically programmed chemical change and becomes heartwood — no longer conducting water, but more resistant to decay.

3180.w: Heartwood forms when a tree's cambium-built wood is impregnated with extra lignin and resins, converting living sapwood into tough, dead structural timber.

3181.w: A giant sequoia's seed cone takes 18 to 20 months to mature, and can then stay green and sealed shut on the tree for as long as twenty years.

3182.w: Coast redwoods, like their giant sequoia relatives, are conifers that reproduce with small woody seed cones instead of flowers.

3183.w: A tree sheds a leaf by growing a layer of cork cells across the base of its stalk — the abscission layer, which severs the leaf on purpose.

3184.w: A deciduous tree drops its leaves through abscission on a seasonal schedule, rather than holding onto them year-round the way an evergreen does.

3185.w: Many oaks are deciduous, shedding their leaves each autumn through the same corky abscission layer that drops leaves on any other deciduous tree.

3186.w: A samara is a winged seed — a flattened, papery wing that makes it autorotate as it falls, the way a maple's or an ash's does.

3187.w: A catkin is a dangling spike of tiny, petal-less flowers built to shed pollen on the wind rather than lure in an insect.

3188.w: Larches are the rare deciduous conifers: unlike almost every other cone-bearing tree, they drop every needle each autumn.

3189.w: True cedars are resinous evergreen conifers whose aromatic wood is naturally repellent to moths, with barrel-shaped cones that disintegrate scale by scale on the tree.

3190.w: Juniper cone scales fuse into a fleshy, berry-like ball, and it's this 'juniper berry' — not a true berry at all — that flavours gin.

3191.w: Holly keeps its spiny, glossy leaves through winter frost, and its bright red berries are mildly toxic if a person eats them.

3192.w: Magnolia is an ancient genus — its flowers evolved before bees existed, so beetles have always done the pollinating.

3193.w: A maple is known by its winged samara seeds — and by its sap, which in species like the sugar maple is boiled down into maple syrup.

3194.w: Birch bark peels off in thin, papery, horizontal strips, and its flowers hang as long, drooping catkins.

3195.w: Beech trees have smooth, thin grey bark, and their oil-rich nuts — beech mast — once fattened pigs turned loose in the woods each autumn.

3196.w: Dutch elm disease is a fungus spread by elm bark beetles; it has killed the majority of elms across North America and Europe since the 20th century.

3197.w: Eucalyptus leaves are packed with aromatic oil that most animals cannot stomach — koalas are among the few mammals able to tolerate it.

3198.w: A banyan is a strangler fig that spreads by growing aerial roots down from its branches; each one thickens into a new trunk until a single tree looks like a grove.

3199.w: A quaking aspen's leaf stalks are flattened sideways, so they twist and flutter — quake — in even a light wind.

3200.w: In grafting, the rootstock is the lower plant supplying the root system; graft an apple onto a dwarfing rootstock and the tree stays small no matter what size the variety normally grows.

3201.w: The scion is the upper cutting joined onto a rootstock in a graft — it carries the genes for the fruit, and every scion of a variety is a genetic clone.

3202.w: Apples don't breed true from seed — they're extreme genetic heterozygotes, so a seed-grown tree reverts toward something small and sour, much like a wild crabapple.

3203.w: Apricots and other stone fruit need a minimum number of accumulated winter chilling hours before their dormant buds will break properly come spring.

3204.w: Breadfruit is starchy enough to be a Pacific staple food, eaten baked, boiled or fried but never raw.

3205.w: Jackfruit is breadfruit's close relative, same genus Artocarpus, but far bigger — up to 55 kg — with large edible seeds most breadfruit varieties lack.

3206.w: Lychee is native to the forests of southern China, a drupe fruit whose sweet, translucent flesh (the aril) wraps a single inedible seed.

3207.w: Rambutan is lychee's close cousin in the soapberry family — its name is just Malay for 'hair,' after its spiky-haired skin.

3208.w: Longan is the third of the trio with lychee and rambutan in the soapberry family — its Chinese name means 'dragon eye,' for the black seed showing through the flesh.

3209.w: Tamarind is a legume tree, drought-tolerant enough for arid soil, whose pod fruit holds a sour-sweet pulp used to season food from Mexico to India.

3210.w: Dragon fruit grows on a climbing cactus that scales nearby trees for support, its stems never rooting in the ground.

3211.w: Star fruit gets its name from its five ridges — slice it crosswise and every piece is shaped like a star.

3212.w: Soursop is in the same genus as cherimoya and sugar apple, a custard-apple relative with large, spiny green fruit.

3213.w: Unripe akee is toxic — it contains hypoglycin A and must be left to split open naturally on the tree before it is safe to eat. Ripe, it's Jamaica's national fruit.

3214.w: Curry leaves are usually fried in hot oil at the very start of cooking, which is how South Asian cooks release their aroma.

3215.w: Boron carbide is a standard control-rod neutron absorber in both pressurized- and boiling-water reactors — it soaks up neutrons fast enough to choke off the chain reaction.

3216.w: A silver-indium-cadmium alloy, roughly 5% cadmium, is a common control-rod material in pressurized-water reactors — a second real absorber alongside boron carbide.

3217.w: The RBMK design that exploded at Chernobyl is graphite-moderated: graphite slows fission neutrons enough to sustain the chain reaction without needing enriched fuel.

3218.w: Most of the world's power reactors moderate and cool with the same ordinary water — the light-water reactor design, genuinely distinct from a graphite-moderated one.

3219.w: Chernobyl's corium was literally fuel, control rods and structural metal melted together into one radioactive lava once the core lost its coolant.

3220.w: Past about 2,700°C the uranium oxide fuel itself melts and the core structure collapses into the same lava-like corium, mostly heated by the fission products' own decay.

3221.w: A reactor never spins a generator directly — it boils water (or heats it under pressure), and it's that steam driving an ordinary turbine that makes the electricity.

3222.w: Space Shuttle tiles were fired from essentially pure quartz sand into a silica-fiber ceramic so porous it's 90% empty space, yet it held off 1,260°C on re-entry.

3223.w: Hydraulic cylinders press the machine's steel shield against the tunnel lining and shove the rotating cutterhead into the rock face — the real thrust mechanism of a TBM.

3224.w: A shielded TBM erects precast concrete rings behind itself as it advances, built by a steel erector arm — the lining half of the same real machine.

3225.w: A motor spins an X-ray tube and its detectors around the patient; a computer turns the angled measurements into cross-sectional slices — Hounsfield's 1972 invention.

3226.w: At Hoover Dam, water drops through penstocks reaching 85mph before it ever touches a turbine — the concrete arch-gravity structure exists to hold that head of water up.

3227.w: A planetary mixer's motor drives a set of gears so the beater spins on its own axis while it also orbits the bowl — the motion the machine is named for.

3228.w: A stationary plate tilted by hydraulic actuators changes a rotating plate's angle, which pitch links carry to each rotor blade differently through the turn — a helicopter's actual steering.

3229.w: It's the swashplate, not the rotor alone, that lets a pilot steer: tilting it cycles each blade's pitch as it passes through the turn, pushing the whole helicopter sideways.

3230.w: An electric car's only source of propulsion is the electricity stored in its battery — no combustion, no gearbox in most designs, and full torque from a standing start.

3231.w: Contrary to the popular idea of a ship climbing onto ice to crush it, most icebreaking happens at cruising speed: a reinforced steel bow simply breaks the low-strength ice under the hull.

3232.w: A tracked vehicle with a front blade and a rear tiller combs a ski slope into the ridged pattern called corduroy, winched by cable up gradients too steep to grip.

3233.w: A turboprop is a gas turbine that sends almost all its power through a reduction gearbox to a propeller instead of out the exhaust — unlike a turbojet, the jet thrust is a rounding error.

3234.w: The M1 Abrams runs on a 1,500-horsepower Honeywell/Lycoming AGT1500 gas turbine, not a diesel — the engine choice that set it apart from its rival design from the start.

3235.w: The Tiger I's armor plates were flat and vertical, not sloped like the Panther's — its protection came from raw thickness and an 88mm gun instead of angled steel.

3236.w: Radar sends a short radio pulse and times how long its reflection takes to return — half the round-trip delay, times the speed of light, gives the range to the object.

3237.w: A stealth aircraft's faceted panels fling radar's radio waves off at an angle instead of straight back at the receiver, which is what actually makes it hard to see on a screen.

3238.w: Heated to a 'cherry red' near 900°C, driven through two plates and hammered into a second head, a rivet only grips tight as it cools and contracts back down.

3239.w: Titanic's hull was closed by three million rivets and divided by watertight bulkheads — but the bulkheads stopped short of the top deck, so water simply spilled over them.

3240.w: An elliptical planform gives the lowest induced drag of any wing shape for a given span — the aerodynamic reason the Spitfire's wing has its famous curved outline.

3241.w: A box's rigid walls are traditionally just flat wooden panels, cut square and joined edge to edge with nails.

3242.w: Veils have traditionally been woven from fine, often sheer cloth like silk, worn to cover the head or face.

3243.w: Convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens, Socrates was sentenced to death and executed in 399 BCE by drinking poison hemlock.

3244.w: Socrates wrote nothing himself — everything known of him comes from later accounts, chiefly the dialogues of his student Plato.

3245.w: Plato held that everything we perceive is an imperfect, changing copy of a perfect, unchanging Form — the dogs we meet are just copies of one Form of Dog.

3246.w: In Plato's Allegory of the Cave, people chained since birth face a wall and mistake shadows cast by a fire behind them for the whole of reality.

3247.w: In 343 BCE Aristotle was summoned to the Macedonian court to tutor Philip II's thirteen-year-old son — the boy who became Alexander the Great.

3248.w: Descartes united algebra and geometry into analytic geometry, plotting equations on a grid — the x-y coordinate system still called Cartesian.

3249.w: Descartes doubted everything he possibly could, until he realized the very act of doubting proved a doubter existed — 'I think, therefore I am.'

3250.w: Locke argued the mind at birth is a tabula rasa, a blank slate with no innate ideas — everything we know is written on afterward by experience.

3251.w: Locke split an object's qualities in two: primary qualities like an apple's shape, built into the object, and secondary qualities like its redness, only a power to trigger a sensation in the mind.

3252.w: Kant's own example of the categorical imperative: a person who borrows money on a promise to repay it that he knows is false — a rule that collapses the moment everyone follows it.

3253.w: Kant closed his Critique of Practical Reason with the line: 'the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me' fill the mind with ever-growing wonder.

3254.w: Wittgenstein imagined everyone holding a private box with a 'beetle' inside that only they can see — proof, he argued, that a word for a private sensation can't work like the name of a thing.

3255.w: Wittgenstein helped design a starkly modernist house for his sister in Vienna, once having a finished ceiling raised 30mm to get its exact proportions right.

3256.w: Beauvoir's 1949 book The Second Sex argued that femininity is made, not born: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, woman.'

3257.w: At 21, Simone de Beauvoir passed France's difficult philosophy agrégation exam — the youngest person, and only the eighth woman, ever to do so.

3258.w: Asked for one word to live by, Confucius offered reciprocity: 'What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others' — the negative form now called the Silver Rule.

3259.w: Confucius taught that a ruler who leads by virtue and example, not by law and punishment, gives people a sense of shame and makes them good, not just afraid of being caught.

3260.w: Meditating beneath a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment and became known as the Buddha — the tree is still venerated as the Bodhi Tree.

3261.w: Buddhist tradition compares the Buddha to a lotus, which rises up through muddy water to bloom unstained above it — a symbol of enlightenment transcending the world.

3262.w: Avicenna imagined a man created fully formed but floating in the air, sensing nothing of his own body — he argued the man would still know his own mind exists.

3263.w: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin in the 12th century and used as a standard medical textbook in European universities into the 18th century.

3264.w: Plutarch became a Roman citizen, likely taking the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus, and around 95 CE was made a priest at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.

3265.w: Epicurus taught philosophy in a garden outside Athens known simply as The Garden, unusually for the time admitting women alongside men as students.

3266.w: Epicurus argued death is nothing to fear: 'where death is, we are not; where we are, death is not' — it can never actually be experienced, only imagined in advance.

3267.w: Searle imagined a person locked in a room, following a rulebook to match Chinese symbol cards without understanding a word of Chinese — his Chinese Room argument against machine understanding.

3268.w: Alan Turing proposed judging a machine's intelligence by written conversation alone: if a human judge can't tell it apart from a real person, it passes the Turing Test.

3269.w: In 1936 Turing described an imagined machine reading and writing symbols on an endless tape, following simple rules — the Turing machine, a blueprint for every computer since.

3270.w: Philippa Foot's 1967 trolley problem asks whether it's right to divert a runaway tram onto a track with one worker instead of five — showing consequences alone don't settle what's right.

3271.w: John Rawls asked people to choose the rules of a just society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' hiding their own future wealth, talent, and status — forcing a genuinely fair choice.

3272.w: Aquinas argued that everything that moves is moved by something else, and that chain cannot regress forever — it must start with an unmoved first mover, which he called God.

3273.w: After a mystical experience during Mass in 1273, Aquinas stopped writing, telling his secretary: 'all that I have written seems like straw to me' — his Summa Theologiae stayed unfinished.

3274.w: Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) argues Being's meaning is bound up with time: existence is fundamentally temporal, understood only from the finite vantage of a mortal life headed toward death.

3275.w: Sartre's classic example of 'bad faith' is a cafe waiter whose movements are a little too precise, too eager — overplaying the role of 'waiter' as if it were his fixed essence, to hide from himself that he remains radically free to be otherwise.

3276.w: In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus retells the Greek myth of a king condemned to push a rock up a mountain forever; accepting the task's futility without illusion, he concludes 'one must imagine Sisyphus happy.'

3277.w: Reporting on Adolf Eichmann's 1961 Jerusalem trial, Arendt watched him testify from inside a bulletproof glass booth — an ordinary bureaucrat, not a monster, prompting her phrase 'the banality of evil.'

3278.w: In Discipline and Punish, Foucault used the Panopticon — a prison ringed with cells around a central watchtower — as a metaphor for modern power: people behave because they might be watched at any moment.

3279.w: Derrida coined 'différance,' a deliberate misspelling of the French 'différence' pronounced identically to the correct word — a difference invisible to the ear but legible only to the eye on the page.

3280.w: Popper illustrated falsifiability with black swans, first seen by Europeans in the 17th century: no number of white swans could prove 'all swans are white,' but one black swan disproves it.

3281.w: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) names the 1543 shift from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy — Earth and Sun swapping places at the center — as a classic paradigm shift.

3282.w: With Edward Herman, Chomsky's Manufacturing Consent describes a 'propaganda model' in which mass media, filtered by ownership and advertising, manufactures public consent rather than reporting independently.

3283.w: Singer's 1975 Animal Liberation, founding text of the modern animal rights movement, argues any being capable of suffering deserves equal consideration, and popularized the term 'speciesism.'

3284.w: Ockham's razor, the principle 'entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity,' took William of Ockham's name for his frequent use of it: given two explanations, cut away the more complicated one.

3285.w: Having emigrated from Soviet Russia in 1926, Rand founded Objectivism, calling egoism 'the virtue of selfishness' and reason 'his only absolute' — condemning altruism as incompatible with human happiness.

3286.w: Said's book Orientalism (1978) argued Western scholarship about the East was tied to the imperial powers that produced it — colonial pageantry, like the British Raj's elephant processions, dressed conquest as civilization.

3287.w: Habermas traced the emergence of a 'public sphere' to 18th-century institutions like Britain's coffeehouses, where private individuals gathered to debate freely, putting the state in touch with public opinion.

3288.w: Berlin's 1958 lecture Two Concepts of Liberty distinguishes negative liberty — freedom from external restraint — from positive liberty, the ability to be one's own master and pursue self-chosen goals.

3289.w: Adorno and Horkheimer's 'culture industry' describes mass-produced film, radio, and television as a factory system manipulating audiences into passivity, homogenizing culture and dulling independent judgment.

3290.w: Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man (1964) argues advanced industrial society manufactures 'false needs' — for goods like cars — that integrate people into the system and wither critical, oppositional thought.

3291.w: Levinas argued that ethics arises from face-to-face encounters with others — even walking past someone in need without helping, their need has already made an unavoidable ethical claim on you.

3292.w: Merleau-Ponty rejected Descartes' picture of mind and body as separate substances, arguing consciousness is always embodied — not a ghost piloting a body, but a single 'body-subject' whose senses are inseparable from thought.

3293.w: Quine imagined a linguist hearing a stranger shout 'gavagai' at the sight of a rabbit — it might mean 'rabbit,' or 'undetached rabbit-part,' or 'dinner': all equally compatible with the evidence.

3294.w: Barthes's 1967 essay The Death of the Author argues a text's meaning is not fixed by its writer's intention: once written, the author is no longer reflected in it, and the reader takes over as the source of meaning.

3295.w: Fanon's 1952 Black Skin, White Masks is a psychoanalytic study of how colonialism and racism damage Black identity, examining the dependency and inferiority colonized people are made to feel.

3296.w: Naess's 'deep ecology' built on ecologist Aldo Leopold's injunction to 'think like a mountain' — after shooting a wolf, Leopold watched 'a fierce green fire' die in her eyes and rethought his place in nature.

3297.w: Bruno argued the universe is infinite, with countless stars like our own sun each possibly hosting inhabited worlds — a heresy for which the Roman Inquisition burned him alive in Rome in 1600.

3298.w: Ryle's The Concept of Mind (1949) mocked Cartesian mind-body dualism as belief in 'the ghost in the machine' — the myth of a separate, non-physical mind piloting the physical brain and body like an operator at a machine.

3299.w: Girard theorized that early communities defused their own rivalries by polarizing blame onto a single victim, the scapegoat, whose expulsion or killing united the rest and founded archaic religion.

3300.w: Dennett's Consciousness Explained rejects a single 'Cartesian theater' where experience is watched by an inner self, proposing consciousness emerges from many parallel drafts of content across the brain.

3301.w: Nussbaum's capabilities approach, developed with economist Amartya Sen, judges a society's justice not by wealth alone but by the real freedoms — including a full emotional life — each person has to flourish.

3302.w: Hypatia taught mathematics and astronomy in Alexandria; her student Synesius described her instructing him in constructing a silver astrolabe. In 415 CE a mob murdered her with sharpened pottery shards.

3303.w: The chlor-alkali process: run current through brine and chlorine bubbles off one electrode, hydrogen the other, leaving sodium hydroxide dissolved in what's left. Almost the world's entire supply is made this way.

3304.w: Drop sodium into water and it reacts vigorously enough to ignite the hydrogen it releases, leaving caustic sodium hydroxide behind in solution — the fast, dangerous way to reach what the chlor-alkali cell makes quietly.

3305.w: Potassium reacts with water hard enough to ignite the hydrogen it releases on its own, burning with a lilac flame. What's left dissolved is potassium hydroxide, caustic potash.

3306.w: Add potash — the potassium carbonate lye carries — to a strong lime solution and calcium carbonate precipitates out, leaving potassium hydroxide behind. Causticizing ran the show until electrolysis replaced it in the late 19th century.

3307.w: Calcium reacts with water on its own — more slowly than sodium or potassium, but the same pattern: hydrogen gas comes off, and a caustic hydroxide, calcium hydroxide, is left dissolved.

3308.w: Electrolysing acetic acid was Hermann Kolbe's 1848 discovery: current strips CO2 off the acetate ion at the electrode, and the methyl radicals left over pair up into ethane.

3309.w: Hydrogenation saturates ethylene's double bond: add hydrogen across it and the two carbons settle for a single bond instead. Industry mostly runs this the other way, cracking ethane back into ethylene.

3310.w: Before the anthraquinone process took over, hydrogen peroxide was made by electrolysing a strong sulfuric-acid solution: current builds peroxydisulfate at the anode, and that hydrolyses in water to hydrogen peroxide.

3311.w: Dissolve silver in nitric acid and evaporate the solution down: what crystallises out is silver nitrate, the precursor to nearly every other silver compound made in a lab.

3312.w: A straightforward acid-base swap: potassium hydroxide neutralises acetic acid, and evaporating off the water leaves potassium acetate — the de-icer airports favour because it doesn't chew up concrete the way chloride salts do.

3313.w: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. The same acid that strips oxide off a joint before soldering will dissolve the zinc metal itself, given time.

3314.w: Zinc oxide is amphoteric — it dissolves in acid as readily as it would in a base. ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O is the cleaner industrial route, since it skips handling raw zinc metal at all.

3315.w: Hydrogen chloride is a gas until it meets water. Dissolved in fully, HCl becomes hydrochloric acid — commercial solutions reach up to 38%, about the strongest concentration that still ships safely.

3316.w: Aluminium reacts straight through with sulfuric acid, 2 Al + 3 H2SO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + 3 H2 — the same coagulant water-treatment plants use by the million tonnes to pull grit out of cloudy river water.

3317.w: Ammonia neutralises phosphoric acid outright, H3PO4 + 3 NH3 → (NH4)3PO4 — the reaction behind the diammonium and monoammonium phosphates that supply most of the world's fertiliser nitrogen and phosphorus.

3318.w: Methane chlorinates all the way through: CH4 + 4 Cl2 → CCl4 + 4 HCl. It was once everywhere — fire extinguishers, dry-cleaning fluid, refrigerant feedstock — until its liver toxicity and ozone damage ended that.

3319.w: Magnesium is reactive enough to displace hydrogen straight out of phosphoric acid, 3 Mg + 2 H3PO4 → Mg3(PO4)2 + 3 H2 — one of the magnesium phosphates the FDA lists as generally recognised as safe.

3320.w: The Mannheim process runs salt straight through sulfuric acid, 2 NaCl + H2SO4 → 2 HCl + Na2SO4 — sodium sulfate is what settles out, hydrochloric acid is the process's other half.

3321.w: Ammonia and carbon dioxide combine in water, CO2 + NH3 + H2O → NH4HCO3, precipitating as a white solid if kept cold. Bakers call it hartshorn — it pushes more gas than baking soda and leaves no salty taste.

3322.w: Ammonia and hydrochloric acid meet head-on, NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl — sal ammoniac, mildly acidic in solution and the electrolyte packed inside an ordinary zinc-carbon battery.

3323.w: Nitric acid dissolves limestone outright, CaCO3 + 2 HNO3 → Ca(NO3)2 + CO2 + H2O — first made this way in Norway in 1905, which is why calcium nitrate is still sometimes called Norwegian saltpetre.

3324.w: Barium is a metal readily attacked by acids. Dropped into nitric acid it displaces hydrogen and leaves barium nitrate behind, Ba + 2 HNO3 → Ba(NO3)2 + H2 — the oxidiser that burns fireworks green.

3325.w: Vinegar reacts straight with limestone's mineral, CaCO3 + 2 CH3COOH → Ca(CH3COO)2 + H2O + CO2 — the fizz is the carbon dioxide leaving. Both ingredients are ancient, and so is this preparation.

3326.w: The wet process treats phosphate rock with sulfuric acid: the calcium in it precipitates out as gypsum, and phosphoric acid is left behind in solution. About ninety percent of world output becomes fertiliser.

3327.w: Phosphoric acid neutralised with three equivalents of lye, H3PO4 + 3 NaOH → Na3PO4 + 3 H2O, gives trisodium phosphate — a food buffer in small doses and a paint-stripping degreaser in industrial ones.

3328.w: Citric acid neutralised with sodium hydroxide, the same preparation that turns acetic acid into sodium acetate: a sharp acid becomes its calm, food-safe salt.

3329.w: Sodium's own salt of the nitrite ion, NaNO2 — the E250 curing agent that turns cured meat pink and holds back the bacteria that make botulinum toxin.

3330.w: Sulfur dioxide dissolving into rain oxidises toward sulfuric acid, and sulfate is what's left in the soil and water where that rain lands — acid rain's own signature ion, the same road nitrogen dioxide takes to nitrate.

3331.w: Calcined together under an inert atmosphere, barium and sulfur combine directly: Ba + S → BaS. It also phosphoresces after exposure to light — the 'Bologna stone' that fascinated 17th-century alchemists.

3332.w: Barium sulfide takes up carbon dioxide and water and gives up hydrogen sulfide, leaving barium carbonate behind — witherite, sold for a century as rat poison because it dissolves so readily in stomach acid.

3333.w: Sulfuric acid is a strong acid at its first proton but not its second: dissolved in water it ionises completely to hydronium and hydrogen sulfate, and only some of that goes on to bare sulfate.

3334.w: Manganese dioxide fused with potassium hydroxide and air makes potassium manganate, which is oxidised further to the deep-purple permanganate ion — the first real stage of how the world's supply is actually made.

3335.w: A soluble silver salt meeting a soluble phosphate precipitates Ag3PO4 straight out of solution — a yellow solid that darkens under light just like silver's other insoluble salts.

3336.w: Silver metal ignores oxygen even at red heat, but a soluble silver salt is a different story: silver nitrate and sodium hydroxide precipitate dark-brown silver oxide straight out of solution.

3337.w: Ammonia gas meeting hydrogen bromide gas is a direct acid-base reaction, NH3 + HBr → NH4Br, no water or evaporation needed.

3338.w: Ca3(PO4)2, tricalcium phosphate — the anticaking agent that keeps powdered spices and table salt from clumping, and the same mineral chemistry that, with a hydroxide added, becomes the calcium half of bone.

3339.w: Chromium(III) oxide oxidised in molten alkali with air converts to sodium chromate — industrially it's soda ash roasted at 1,100°C, but sodium hydroxide with an oxidiser does the same chemistry at far lower temperature.

3340.w: Acidify a chromate solution and two chromate ions condense into one dichromate: 2 CrO4²⁻ + 2 H⁺ ⇌ Cr2O7²⁻ + H2O. Chromate is what you get in alkali; dichromate is the same chromium caught on the acid side.

3341.w: Fructose is simply fruit sugar: it's already there in tree fruit, vine fruit and berries before anything is done to them. Crushing only lets it out.

3342.w: Potassium's own salt of the cyanide ion, KCN — colourless, soluble, and the reagent gold mining runs on to dissolve the metal straight out of crushed ore as a soluble complex.

3343.w: Zinc oxide meeting phosphate gives Zn3(PO4)2 directly — the same conversion coating that etches onto bare steel before primer goes on, run here as a precipitation instead of a dip.

3344.w: Benzene chlorinated with an iron catalyst gives para-dichlorobenzene alongside its ortho cousin. The game's coal tar stands in for the ring, the same shortcut its azo-dye recipes already take for a benzene the game doesn't model directly.

3345.w: Rhubarb's leaf blade — never the stalk — carries about 0.5% oxalic acid by weight. Crush it and this is the ion that makes it dangerous.

3346.w: Spinach runs 0.65 to 1.3% oxalic acid by fresh weight, among the highest of any common vegetable — crushed, it releases the same ion rhubarb leaves do.

3347.w: Potassium's answer to baking soda: KHCO3. Purple-K, the dry-chemical fire-extinguisher blend, is built on it, because potassium bicarbonate smothers a fire faster than sodium bicarbonate does.

3348.w: Chlorine gas bubbled through potassium hydroxide disproportionates: Cl2 + 2 KOH → KCl + KOCl + H2O. Berthollet made the very first bleach this exact way in 1789, in a Paris workshop called Javel.

3349.w: Potassium's own salt of the nitrite ion, KNO2 — a meat-curing preservative like its sodium cousin, distinct from potassium nitrate despite the near-identical name.

3350.w: Two fault blocks grinding past each other shatter the rock between them into sharp, angular fragments. Mineral-laden groundwater seeping through cements the wreckage back into solid stone before anything wears the edges round.

3351.w: Granite eroded and buried fast enough — floodwater off a rising fault block, say — entombs its feldspar grains before rain and time get the chance to rot them into clay. Slow weathering leaves bare quartz; speed leaves arkose.

3352.w: A submarine earthquake can shake a slope's sediment loose as a turbidity current — a dense underwater avalanche of sand, mud and rock scraps that drops everything at once, with no time left for the grains to sort themselves.

3353.w: A moraine is unsorted glacial rubble sitting on the surface. Buried under later sediment and left long enough, that same jumble of striated, poorly sorted stones compacts and cements into solid rock: tillite.

3354.w: Radiolarian skeletons raining onto the seafloor pile up as siliceous ooze. Buried and left long enough, the silica slowly recrystallises grain by grain into microcrystalline quartz — the rock is chert.

3355.w: Roll a grain through warm, wave-agitated water saturated with calcium carbonate and it grows a coat, then another, in concentric layers around itself — the same way a pearl grows, just built from calcite instead of nacre.

3356.w: Ooids settle out, pile up and cement together. Enough of these tiny layered spheres in one place make an oolite — a limestone built entirely from grains, not from shell hash.

3357.w: Early photosynthesising cyanobacteria breathed oxygen into iron-rich Precambrian oceans, and the iron dropped out as hematite, banding in rhythm with layers of chert — a record that stops appearing once the ocean ran out of iron to rust.

3358.w: Heat gypsum past about 200°C and it gives up both water molecules locked in its structure, leaving anhydrous calcium sulfate behind. Wet it again and anhydrite grabs the water straight back, swelling into gypsum once more.

3359.w: The same undecayed algae that pressure-cooks into crude oil, sealed instead into fine mudrock without ever reaching the roughly 100°C petroleum needs. The kerogen stays kerogen, and the rock is oil shale.

3360.w: Where a deep, nutrient-rich current wells up along a coast, bone and fish debris raining onto the seafloor concentrate faster than anything can carry them away, building phosphate-rich rock instead of just scattering.

3361.w: Croatian mercenaries serving France in the Thirty Years' War tied silk kerchiefs at the throat. Parisians called the look cravate, and Louis XIV made it court fashion by 1646.

3362.w: The big toe carries two phalanges; the other four toes carry three each — fourteen small bones bundled at the front of one foot, doing the final push-off of every stride.

3363.w: Seth Wheeler's 1883 patent split a roll into sheets by perforation alone, no blade needed — the feature that turned paper into something torn off one square at a time.

3364.w: Alexander Cumming's 1775 S-trap held a slug of standing water in a bent pipe below the bowl — the water itself was the seal, keeping foul sewer air from ever reaching the room.

3365.w: Saliva is roughly 99% water, with mucus for lubrication and the enzyme amylase mixed through it — starch digestion begins the moment food enters the mouth, not in the stomach.

3366.w: Like an octopus arm or elephant trunk, the tongue is a muscular hydrostat: no skeleton, its own interwoven muscle both moves it and holds its shape, kept slick by saliva.

3367.w: A boar's back and neck grow coarser, stiffer hair than the rest of the coat — cut and bundled into tufts, it holds its shape well enough to scrub with.

3368.w: Jailed in 1780, William Addis saved a bone from a meal, drilled holes in it, and tied in tufts of boar bristle bought from a guard, sealed with glue. He later got rich selling them.

3369.w: Middle Kingdom Egyptian paddle dolls, found in Middle Kingdom burials, had hair made of small beads of black Nile mud threaded onto string.

3370.w: Turkish hammam cloths from 17th-century Bursa grew loops standing up from the weave, havlu, 'with loops' — the terry pile that still defines an absorbent towel, once cotton made it cheap.

3371.w: Early tractors mounted an internal combustion engine onto the running gear of a horse-drawn plough, replacing a team of draft animals with one machine that never needed to eat or rest.

3372.w: A freight wagon is unpowered by design, built only to be coupled behind a locomotive — hook enough of them to one engine, and the coupled string is what 'train' actually means.

3373.w: A triangle is a steel or brass rod bent to shape with one corner deliberately left unclosed — closing the loop would let it ring at one clean pitch, and players want overtones instead.

3374.w: Stephan Farffler, a paraplegic watchmaker, built the first recorded three-wheeled self-propelled vehicle in 1680, worked by hand cranks instead of pedals.

3375.w: Gastric juice is acidic enough to dissolve tissue, so the stomach's lining constantly secretes a mucus-and-bicarbonate layer over itself — without it, the stomach would digest its own wall.

3376.w: Samuel Fox's 1852 steel-ribbed frame replaced the wood or baleen ribs of earlier umbrellas, which were heavy and hard to fold once wet — steel let the canopy fold small and spring back open.

3377.w: Linen, woven from flax, has been worn as underclothes for as long as flax has been spun into cloth — a light, breathable layer worn next to skin, distinct from the clothing worn over it.

3378.w: The spinning jenny and cotton gin made cotton fabric cheap in the late 1700s, letting factories mass-produce washable cotton undergarments instead of linen finery sewn at home.

3379.w: James Murray Spangler, an asthmatic janitor, built a motor-driven suction cleaner in 1907 that collected dust in a cloth pillowcase bag — he sold the patent to William Hoover a year later.
