3380.w: Antonio Pasin hand-built his first child's wagon in a rented one-room New York workshop in 1917, calling it the Liberty Coaster — pulled along by a rope handle.

3381.w: A washcloth is toweling cut down to a roughly 12-by-12-inch square — the same absorbent terry loop pile as a bath towel, scaled to wash a face or a baby instead of drying a whole body.

3382.w: Early 1500s Nuremberg clockmakers built drum-shaped brass movements driven by a coiled mainspring instead of a hanging weight — the innovation that let a clock leave the wall for a pocket.

3383.w: Joseph Hudson's 1883 pea whistle put a small pea loose inside a brass chamber; its rattle chops the airstream into a trilling shriek, and Scotland Yard adopted it for police use in 1884.

3384.w: A glazier beds the pane in a wooden sash and drives in small headless nails called glazier's points, or sprigs, to hold it firm on the rebate before putty is run around the edge to seal it.

3385.w: Pedro Flores, a Filipino immigrant, opened a yo-yo factory in California in 1928 using a traditional Filipino design: the string loops around the axle rather than tying to it, letting it 'sleep' at the bottom of its spin.

3386.w: Gideon Sundback redesigned Whitcomb Judson's jam-prone 'clasp locker' into two rows of interlocking brass teeth pulled together by a slider — patented as the Separable Fastener in 1917.

3387.w: Iron dissolves cleanly in dilute sulfuric acid, Fe + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2 — the plain +2 salt, not the +3 chloride that burning iron in chlorine gas gives instead.

3388.w: A strong acid displaces the weaker one out of its own salt: sulfuric acid added to a cyanide salt drives hydrogen cyanide gas out of solution — exactly why cyanide salts and acid must never be mixed in the same container.

3389.w: Methanol and carbon monoxide combine directly over a strong base catalyst — carbonylation — to give methyl formate. It's the cheapest large-scale door in to formic acid.

3390.w: Passed into a hot concentrated hydroxide solution, chlorine disproportionates instead of just dissolving: 3 Cl2 + 6 NaOH → NaClO3 + 5 NaCl + 3 H2O. Cold and dilute gives ordinary bleach; hot and concentrated pushes all the way to chlorate.

3391.w: In strong acid solution, sulfur dioxide reduces chlorate down to chlorine dioxide: 2 NaClO3 + SO2 → 2 ClO2 + Na2SO4 — how pulp mills bleach paper without using elemental chlorine.

3392.w: An electric current at a platinum electrode oxidises chlorate straight to perchlorate — anodic oxidation, the same electrochemical idea that splits brine into chlorine and lye.

3393.w: Chlorine disproportionates the same way in any hot concentrated metal hydroxide, not just sodium's — run it through barium hydroxide instead of lye and the chlorate that forms is barium's.

3394.w: Chlorine dioxide absorbed into a hydroxide solution alongside a reducing agent converts to the chlorite salt — the same reaction industry runs against sodium hydroxide, done here with barium hydroxide instead.

3395.w: Nitrogen dioxide disproportionates the moment it meets water: 2 NO2 + H2O → HNO3 + HNO2 — one molecule of the dioxide gets oxidised, the other reduced, and both acids come out of the same reaction.

3396.w: Chlorine gas doesn't just dissolve in water, it reacts with it: Cl2 + H2O ⇌ HOCl + HCl. The hypochlorous acid that forms is what actually does the disinfecting in a chlorinated pool.

3397.w: Sulfuric acid displaces the weaker chlorous acid out of its barium salt, and the barium sulfate that forms alongside it is so insoluble it drops straight out of solution and can be filtered away.

3398.w: The same trick that isolates chlorous acid works one oxidation state up: sulfuric acid pulls chloric acid free of its barium salt, leaving insoluble barium sulfate behind to filter out.

3399.w: Hydrochloric acid displaces perchloric acid from its sodium salt; sodium chloride is far less soluble in the concentrated mix and precipitates out, leaving perchloric acid behind to be distilled off.

3400.w: Phosphorus trichloride reacts fast and completely with water: PCl3 + 3 H2O → H3PO3 + 3 HCl. It's the standard industrial route to the acid.

3401.w: Scheele made it exactly this way in 1776: concentrated nitric acid tears sucrose apart, oxidising it all the way down to oxalic acid — he called the product ‘sugar acid’ before anyone connected it to the acid already known from wood sorrel.

3402.w: A mineral acid displaces the weaker boric acid straight out of borax: Na2B4O7·10H2O + 2 HCl → 4 B(OH)3 + 2 NaCl + 5 H2O.

3403.w: Silica dissolves only sparingly in water, but what little does goes in as silicic acid — the same slow chemistry that leaches silicon out of rock and carries it to the sea.

3404.w: Ammonia gas is extremely soluble in water — this is simply what results, sold under a dozen names from ammonia water to aqua ammonia.

3405.w: Magnesium oxide reacts with water to form the hydroxide, MgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2 — slower than the same reaction with calcium oxide, but the same idea.

3406.w: Barium oxide dissolves straight into water and reacts as it goes: BaO + H2O → Ba(OH)2.

3407.w: Within seconds of alum meeting water, the aluminium ions begin precipitating out as this hydroxide — a fine floc that drags suspended dirt down with it, the entire point of using alum to clarify water.

3408.w: Hydroxide ions from lye swap places with sulfate: FeSO4 + 2 NaOH → Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4, and iron(II) hydroxide falls out of solution as a precipitate.

3409.w: Sodium hydroxide added to a solution of iron(III) chloride precipitates the oxide-hydroxide straight out: FeCl3 + 3 NaOH → Fe(OH)3 + 3 NaCl.

3410.w: Zinc oxide dissolves into concentrated sodium hydroxide; diluted back down, zinc hydroxide comes back out of that same solution as a precipitate.

3411.w: Lithium oxide reacts slowly with water to form the hydroxide: Li2O + H2O → 2 LiOH.

3412.w: Hydrogen iodide gas is extremely soluble in water, and dissolving it gives simply this: hydroiodic acid, a colourless solution of the same molecule.

3413.w: Methyl formate hydrolyses straight into formic acid and methanol, HCO2CH3 + H2O → HCOOH + CH3OH — the industrial route in from methanol and carbon monoxide.

3414.w: Hydrogen fluoride gas dissolves completely in water to give this: a weak acid by strength, but ferociously reactive all the same, because the fluoride ion attacks silicon-oxygen bonds directly.

3415.w: Hydrogen cyanide gas dissolves in water to give hydrocyanic acid, HCN(aq) — the same molecule, just wet.

3416.w: Passed together over an aluminosilicate catalyst, methanol and ammonia trade an –OH for an –NH2 group and come out as methylamine, plus water.

3417.w: The real industrial route condenses acetaldehyde and formaldehyde first, then closes the ring with ammonia over an alumina catalyst at 400-450°C. Acetaldehyde and ammonia carry the real chemistry the direct pairing skipped — formaldehyde and ammonia condense into something else entirely, hexamine, not this ring.

3418.w: NiO + 2 HNO3 + 5 H2O -> Ni(NO3)2.6H2O. Nickel oxide dissolves straight into nitric acid and the hexahydrate crystallises out green.

3419.w: 2 Cr2O3 + 4 Na2CO3 + 3 O2 -> 4 Na2CrO4 + 4 CO2 — chromium oxide fused with soda ash under air at around 1,000C, the roasting step every chromium chemical starts from.

3420.w: Any strong acid pulls chromate over to the dichromate side of the same equilibrium — hydrochloric acid does it to sodium chromate just as sulfuric acid does, yielding the specific sodium salt rather than the generic ion.

3421.w: Tartaric acid is already dissolved in the juice, and its potassium salt — cream of tartar — crystallises out of its own accord as the juice sits and ferments, the 'wine stone' that once crusted barrel walls.

3422.w: Zn + I2 -> ZnI2, direct combination in water or refluxing ether — the elements alone, dry, will not react at room temperature; the solvent is what gets it started.

3423.w: 2 Al + 3 Br2 -> Al2Br6. Aluminium foil dropped into liquid bromine reacts immediately, the same direct-combination route used for aluminium chloride.

3424.w: Carbonating sodium hydroxide is one of the standard routes to soda ash — the strong base soaks up CO2 straight out of the gas phase.

3425.w: 2 BaO + O2 <-> 2 BaO2. The peroxide forms around 500C and gives its extra oxygen back above 820C — reversible enough that it once ran an entire industrial oxygen-separation process.

3426.w: Thenard's 1818 method, improved: barium peroxide dissolved in acid and precipitated with sulfuric acid, which pulls the barium out as insoluble barium sulfate and leaves peroxide behind in solution.

3427.w: Sodium percarbonate is produced industrially by crystallising a solution of sodium carbonate and hydrogen peroxide together, with the pH and concentrations watched closely.

3428.w: Nickel(II) acetate is made by treating a nickel compound — the oxide, hydroxide or carbonate — with acetic acid; whichever nickel source you start from, the same green salt crystallises out.

3429.w: SO2 + Na2CO3 -> Na2SO3 + CO2. This is the industrial route to sodium sulfite; the lab version swaps in sodium hydroxide instead of the carbonate.

3430.w: Sodium thiosulfate is prepared by oxidation of sodium sulfite with sulfur — boil the two together and a sulfur atom bonds onto the sulfite ion.

3431.w: Smaller quantities are made by partial oxidation of ethanol, run over a silver catalyst at about 500 to 650C — the same reaction your liver's alcohol dehydrogenase runs at body temperature.

3432.w: Mannitol concentrations in seaweed can reach 20% of dry weight, and isolation from seaweed is still the most common way it is produced, especially in China.

3433.w: Styrene is found in coal tar in small quantities alongside toluene and benzene — one more aromatic fraction separated out of the same distillation.

3434.w: Eduard Simon isolated styrene from storax resin in 1839 and noticed that left exposed to air, light or heat it slowly turned into a hard, rubber-like solid — spontaneous polymerisation, the same reaction industry now speeds up with heat and initiators.

3435.w: Made industrially by high-temperature chlorinolysis of light hydrocarbons: heating a chlorinated hydrocarbon like 1,2-dichloroethane with more chlorine to 400C strips it all the way down to tetrachloroethylene.

3436.w: 3 I2 + 6 KOH -> KIO3 + 5 KI + 3 H2O. Iodine disproportionates in hot potassium hydroxide — part oxidised up to iodate, part reduced back down to iodide.

3437.w: PbO + 2 CH3CO2H -> Pb(CH3CO2)2 + H2O. Litharge dissolved straight into acetic acid — the historic 'sugar of lead' preparation.

3438.w: Potassium thiocyanate is made by fusing sulfur with potassium cyanide, then extracting the melt with hot aqueous alcohol and crystallising it out.

3439.w: Maltose is the principal sugar in wort, the barley-water malt's own beta-amylase has already sugared — boil the water back off and this is the biggest single crystal left.

3440.w: 2 NO2 + O3 -> N2O5 + O2. The cleanest lab route to dinitrogen pentoxide skips heat: ozone oxidises nitrogen dioxide straight across, though the product then turns around and helps destroy more ozone.

3441.w: An iron(II) ion pulls six cyanide ions around itself into one tightly bound octahedral complex, [Fe(CN)6]4- — and because the complex barely lets any cyanide escape, it is far less toxic than the free ion that built it.

3442.w: Historically made by fusing nitrogenous animal waste — torrefied horn, hoof, dried blood — with iron filings and potassium carbonate; modern production instead builds the ferrocyanide first, from hydrogen cyanide and iron, then adds the potassium.

3443.w: Equal parts xenon and fluorine gas react at low pressure under ordinary sunlight — the synthesis works even on a cloudy day, sealed in a plain Pyrex bulb, no furnace needed unlike the tetrafluoride.

3444.w: Iodine vapour on molten lead between 500 and 700C gives lead iodide directly -- or, more commonly, mixing dissolved lead and iodide ions precipitates the same nearly-insoluble compound as gold-glittering hexagonal crystals: the 'golden rain' demonstration.

3445.w: A bus is an automobile's engine and wheels under a much bigger body: Daimler's 1898 double-decker sat 20 passengers, enclosed below and open-air on top, one of the first successful motor buses on the road — and today that body is welded steel.

3446.w: Medieval French guild rules split button-makers into those who worked horn, bone and ivory, those who worked metal, and those who worked precious metal and glass — horn buttons, cut and punched from a flattened sheet, are still made the same way.

3447.w: A CD is 1.2 millimetres of polycarbonate plastic, moulded with a spiral of microscopic pits, then coated with a thin layer of aluminium to make it reflective enough for a laser to read.

3448.w: John Harvey Kellogg patented his toasted-flake process in 1891 and launched the Corn Flakes brand in 1895 — grain cooked, rolled thin and toasted crisp, the same basic idea behind sweetened breakfast cereal ever since.

3449.w: Furniture-making has been a specialised part of the carpenter's trade for as long as there have been carpenters — a chair is wood cut, joined and shaped into a raised seat, the same craft behind the carved wooden chairs buried with ancient Egyptian nobles.

3450.w: A compass does one geometric trick: fix one leg and swing the other, and the point traces every location the same distance from the centre — that fixed-distance rule is the actual definition of a circle, automated instead of laid out with a rope and a stake.

3451.w: A whiteface clown covers the entire face and neck in clown-white greasepaint, a look Joseph Grimaldi originated in the early 1800s, finished with a red foam or rubber nose on most clowns working today.

3452.w: Tortoiseshell — keratin cut from a hawksbill turtle's carapace — was once, alongside horn and whalebone, a common comb material, prized for taking a shine no plain wood or bone could match.

3453.w: Ruth Wakefield mixed chopped chocolate straight into her cookie dough at the Toll House Inn in the 1930s, expecting it to melt into the batter; it held its shape instead, and the chocolate chip cookie was born.

3454.w: Jonathan Dodgson Carr's 1836 Carlisle 'water biscuit' took ship's hardtack — flour, water, baked hard for storage — and rolled it much thinner and saltier: more palatable, still dry enough to keep, and the direct ancestor of the modern cracker.

3455.w: Encaustic painters in Egypt, Greece and Rome bound powdered pigment — an iron-oxide ochre for red — into melted beeswax to hold colour; the same pairing, pigment locked into wax, underlies the wax crayon millennia later.

3456.w: Gold does not oxidise on the way to melting, so it can be melted, cast, remelted and cast again indefinitely without loss. Almost all the gold ever mined is still in circulation for that reason.

3457.w: Softened glass pressed into a mould, rather than blown into a bubble, is how most inexpensive mass-produced glassware — cups and tumblers included — has been made since the mid-19th century.

3458.w: A cupcake takes its name literally — batter baked one to a cup, whether a pottery cup, a ramekin or a mould, instead of one large cake to a single pan.

3459.w: A flat curtain is a hemmed panel of fabric hung from a pole by rings or a threaded rod — the same basic idea that replaced England's very first window coverings, leather panels threaded on iron rods, with woven wool.

3460.w: 'Diaper' first named a pattern of repeated diamond shapes, then the white cotton or linen fabric woven with it — a usage on record in England from the 1590s, centuries before the word settled on the baby garment.

3461.w: Ancient doors did not swing on hinges; a wooden peg called a pintle, at top and bottom, turned in sockets cut into the lintel and sill, and the lower socket was often cut into a hard stone such as basalt or granite to resist the wear.

3462.w: Dolphins are toothed whales, not baleen ones — conical teeth built to grab fast prey, and a fat-filled 'melon' in the forehead that focuses the clicks they use to echolocate fish in water too dark or murky to see through.

3463.w: Doughnuts are leavened dough deep-fried rather than baked, then finished with a sugar glaze or coating once they come out of the oil.

3464.w: A dress is a single garment — bodice sewn to skirt — hanging from the torso over the legs in one piece, tailored rather than cut into the separate top and bottom most other clothing is.

3465.w: A dressing table is furniture built for exactly one job, the toilette — dressing, makeup, grooming — and a mirror became standard on it by the middle of the 18th century, mounted to swivel or folding straight into the table.

3466.w: The earthen darabukkeh pairs a fired-clay pot body with a stretched skin head — goblet drums like it go back to ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and are among the oldest drum shapes anyone has found.

3467.w: The outer ear is a single piece of elastic cartilage; deeper in, hair cells in the cochlea convert the fluid's movement into an electrical signal — a nerve current — that the brain reads as sound.

3468.w: Carl Baudin of Leipzig's Stadttheater invented modern greasepaint by binding zinc white and other pigments in lard for a smooth, opaque, stage-lit finish; it caught on with other actors and he began selling it commercially.

3469.w: Clostridium acetobutylicum — the 'Weizmann organism' — ferments a sugar or starch feedstock into acetone, butanol and ethanol together; Chaim Weizmann's version of the process supplied Britain with wartime acetone for cordite once demand outstripped every other source.

3470.w: Bisphenol A is made by condensing two molecules of phenol with one of acetone under a strong acid catalyst — the reaction that gives the compound its name, acetone plus phenol, 'A' for acetone.

3471.w: Industrially, phosgene is made by passing purified carbon monoxide and chlorine gas together over a bed of activated carbon, which catalyses the reaction; it is also remembered as the chemical weapon responsible for roughly 85,000 deaths after it was first used as a weapon in 1915.

3472.w: Industrial polycarbonate is made by reacting bisphenol A with phosgene, which links the BPA units end to end into long carbonate chains — about a billion kilograms of it are produced this way every year.

3473.w: Steam-distilling thyme drives the oil out with the water vapour, and thymol is the antiseptic compound inside it — the same one now used as an active ingredient in mouthwash.

3474.w: Bromine added to thymol blue in glacial acetic acid gives bromothymol blue, and thymol blue itself starts from thymol. The game has no sulfonation step for that intermediate, so this skips straight there — the same shortcut already used for Brilliant Blue FCF.

3475.w: Ammonia neutralises hydroiodic acid in a plain acid-base reaction, NH3 + HI -> NH4I, the same shape as ammonia meeting nitric or any other strong acid.

3476.w: Ammonium nitrite forms wherever ammonia meets a nitrite salt, and it is never kept pure: it decomposes into nitrogen gas and water, NH4NO2 -> N2 + 2H2O, even sitting at room temperature.

3477.w: Bromine disproportionates in base to bromide and hypobromite, and hot hypobromite disproportionates again into bromide and bromate. The same chemistry once strengthened bread dough and now turns up as an unwanted trace in ozonated drinking water.

3478.w: Mix nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide in equal parts and cool the mixture below -21°C: N2O3 condenses out, deep blue as a liquid or solid, and falls back apart into the two gases the moment it warms.

3479.w: Sulfites reduce iodine readily in acidic solution, straight to iodide — the reaction analytical chemists still use to strip iodine's colour out of a titration.

3480.w: Lead dissolves into acetic acid, with air's oxygen or a splash of hydrogen peroxide helping it along, leaving lead acetate — the 'sugar of lead' Roman winemakers sweetened wine with, not knowing what it was doing to them.

3481.w: Sulfur dioxide taken onto a potassium base gives potassium sulfite, K2SO3 — the same reaction sodium undergoes for plain sulfite, run with potassium instead.

3482.w: Heat baking soda hard enough and it drives off water and carbon dioxide, leaving the stronger base behind: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 — washing soda, made from its own milder cousin.

3483.w: Mix silver nitrate and sodium carbonate solutions and silver carbonate falls out at once: 2AgNO3 + Na2CO3 -> Ag2CO3 + 2NaNO3. It precipitates colourless, then turns yellow within minutes of standing.

3484.w: Industrially this is hydrogen cyanide neutralised with sodium hydroxide, HCN + NaOH -> NaCN + H2O; the game's cyanide ion and sodium stand in for that acid and base. Most of the world's supply goes straight into gold mining.

3485.w: Sodium metal dissolved in ammonia reacts to give sodium amide and hydrogen gas — a strong enough base afterward to pull a proton straight off an alkyne, and violent enough with water that it is handled under inert gas.

3486.w: Heated hard enough, sodium amide breaks down into sodium nitride — one of the real routes chemists use to reach a compound that otherwise falls straight back apart into sodium metal and nitrogen gas.

3487.w: Strontium is reactive enough to dissolve straight into nitric acid, displacing hydrogen as it goes: Sr + 2HNO3 -> Sr(NO3)2 + H2 — the salt that burns pure red in fireworks and road flares.

3488.w: The Hooker process: chlorine gas run into cold, dilute sodium hydroxide disproportionates at once into sodium chloride and sodium hypochlorite, Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaClO + H2O — nearly every bottle of bleach sold is made exactly this way.

3489.w: Most of the world's aluminium fluoride is made by treating alumina with hydrogen fluoride at 700°C. Mixed with cryolite it drops the melting point of the smelting bath by over 1,000°C.

3490.w: Butter left to spoil hydrolyses its own tributyrin and liberates butyric acid — rancid butter's exact smell, and the same compound gut bacteria make by fermenting fibre.

3491.w: Lithium left in moist air tarnishes fast: some of it becomes lithium hydroxide, which reacts on with carbon dioxide to give lithium carbonate — a compound better known today as a mood stabiliser shown to cut suicide risk by 87%.

3492.w: Lithium carbonate neutralised with phosphate gives lithium phosphate — the game's phosphate ion standing in for phosphoric acid. Most of what's made today feeds straight into lithium iron phosphate battery cathodes.

3493.w: Bromine added to water disproportionates at once into hypobromous acid and hydrobromic acid. Hypobromous acid is what actually does the disinfecting in a bromine-treated hot tub.

3494.w: Iodine in water barely favours hypoiodous acid on its own — real preparations nudge the equilibrium over with a silver or mercury salt. The body does something similar: hypoiodite is what lactoperoxidase makes as an antimicrobial weapon.

3495.w: Force oxygen through ethylene over a hot silver catalyst and some of it picks up an oxygen bridge instead of just burning: 2C2H4 + O2 -> 2C2H4O. Reactive enough to sterilise a hospital's plastic syringes, and carcinogenic for the same reason.

3496.w: Ethylene oxide hydrolyses straight into ethylene glycol, C2H4O + H2O -> HOCH2CH2OH — the antifreeze that drops water's freezing point by 45°C at a 60:40 mix, and tastes sweet enough to poison a pet or child who finds it first.

3497.w: Nickel metal dissolves straight into sulfuric acid to give the turquoise salt nickel sulfate — the single most common cause of a positive result on a nickel allergy patch test.

3498.w: The same felsic melt that freezes glassy as obsidian can instead sit just long enough for microscopic crystals to nucleate through it before it fully hardens — rhyolite, chemically identical to granite, textured by the surface instead of the depths.

3499.w: One of andesite's real recipes: a basaltic magma mixing with a rhyolitic one crystallizes out at an intermediate 57–63% silica — plagioclase and hornblende instead of either parent's minerals. It's common enough that Earth has been called the andesite planet.

3500.w: Push andesite's chemistry further toward rhyolite — more quartz, more sodium-rich plagioclase — and the melt crystallizes as dacite instead: the same rock that domed up inside Mount St. Helens's crater after the 1980 eruption.

3501.w: Diorite's chemistry sits exactly between its two neighbours — more silica than gabbro, less than granite — so plagioclase, not quartz, is the dominant mineral. The Akkadian Empire carved royal stelae from it, including a Code of Hammurabi copy now in the Louvre.

3502.w: Granite's mafic opposite: calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar and olivine crystallizing together, slowly, at depth, instead of feldspar and quartz. Much of the ocean floor's lower crust is gabbro — basalt's exact chemistry, cooled for far longer.

3503.w: Fractional crystallization can leave a mafic magma's late melt so enriched in alkali feldspar, and so starved of leftover silica, that quartz barely forms at all — under 5%, the line that separates syenite from granite.

3504.w: Olivine is the first mineral to crystallize from a cooling mafic melt, and it's denser than the liquid around it, so it sinks and piles up on the floor of the magma body. Enough of it settling out before anything else forms is peridotite.

3505.w: Left long enough in a cooling magma body, olivine crystals settle out almost to the exclusion of everything else: over 90% olivine by volume — dunite, named for the New Zealand mountain where it was first described.

3506.w: Komatiite is defined by its magnesium: at least 18% MgO, erupted at up to 1,600°C. Almost every known komatiite dates to the Archean Eon, when Earth's mantle still ran hot enough to produce lava this fluid.

3507.w: Plagioclase feldspar crystallizes early and floats — it's lighter than the basaltic melt around it — so the crystals raft together at the top of the chamber into a rock that's 90–100% feldspar. The Moon's magma ocean did the same thing at a planetary scale; its bright highlands are anorthosite.

3508.w: The last, most water-rich dregs of a granite magma crystallize last of all. That volatile-rich fluid has such low viscosity that atoms migrate freely to join existing crystals instead of starting new ones — which is how pegmatites grow crystals a metre or more long.

3509.w: Given enough time in contact with groundwater, obsidian hydrates: water works into the glass and cracks it into tiny concentric shells. Flash-heated past 850°C, that trapped water turns to steam and the grains pop — the perlite bagged for potting soil.

3510.w: An eruption throws ash into the air by the cubic kilometre; wind carries the fine fraction away from the vent and drops it in blanketing layers. Buried and cemented by groundwater, those ash falls lithify into tuff.

3511.w: Tuff isn't only ash: welded and ash-fall tuffs regularly carry pea-sized pumice fragments, caught up in the same eruption and cemented in alongside it.

3512.w: Magma rising through the crust tears loose fragments of the older rock it's cutting through and carries them along, often too fast for them to melt. A rock-within-a-rock like this is a xenolith — literally, a "foreign rock."

3513.w: Basaltic lava rising fast from the mantle sometimes hauls up chunks of the mantle itself — peridotite xenoliths, the closest thing geologists get to a hand sample of rock dozens of kilometres down.

3514.w: Magma that grew coarse phenocrysts slowly at depth, then erupted before it finished crystallizing, quenches its remaining melt fast into a fine matrix around them. Rome's one purple quarry in Egypt supplied every imperial porphyry column in the city.

3515.w: Direct electrolysis of a hot potassium chloride solution works too: chlorine forms at one electrode and reacts in situ with the potassium hydroxide forming at the other, oxidizing straight through to chlorate.

3516.w: Chlorine gas passed into slaked lime gives bleaching powder, calcium hypochlorite — the historically dominant industrial hypochlorite, used to disinfect water and bleach textiles for over a century before liquid bleach took over.

3517.w: The Raschig process: hypochlorite oxidizes ammonia to chloramine, and a second ammonia molecule displaces the chlorine, welding two nitrogens together into hydrazine.

3518.w: Ammonium acetate loses water on heating and leaves acetamide behind.

3519.w: Fuse silica sand with an alkali and the two combine directly into a glassy sodium silicate that dissolves in water instead of staying solid rock.

3520.w: Roast green chromium(III) oxide with an alkali in air and the metal oxidizes clean through to hexavalent chromate — several million kilograms a year are won out of chromite ore exactly this way.

3521.w: Zinc oxide dissolves straight into sulfuric acid, the metal swapping its oxide ion for a sulfate one.

3522.w: Concentrated sulfuric acid added to potassium dichromate displaces chromium trioxide directly, one step past the chromate-to-dichromate acidification.

3523.w: Acetic acid and methanol condense into an ester and water — a Fischer esterification, faster with a strong acid catalyst prodding it along.

3524.w: Passed together over an aluminium oxide catalyst, methanol and hydrogen sulfide trade a hydroxyl for a sulfur, releasing water and leaving dimethyl sulfide.

3525.w: Oxidize dimethyl sulfide — a byproduct of pulping wood for paper — with oxygen or nitrogen dioxide and one more oxygen bonds onto the sulfur, making DMSO.

3526.w: Fractional distillation pulls hexane out of crude oil around its own 65-70°C boiling point — the light-naphtha cut also used to leach oil out of soybeans and canola seed at scale.

3527.w: Crush clove buds and the oil that comes out is almost pure eugenol by weight — the same compound dentists once packed straight into an aching cavity.

3528.w: Chilled wine sheds potassium bitartrate as fine crystals — cold stabilization, the same process behind the crust of "wine diamonds" left on a cask or a cork.

3529.w: Cream of tartar still carries one acidic hydrogen. Neutralizing it with an alkali swaps that hydrogen for sodium, pairing sodium and potassium onto the same tartrate ion — Seignette's 17th-century recipe for Rochelle salt.

3530.w: Formaldehyde and ammonia condense directly into one cage-shaped molecule, six carbons and four nitrogens knit into a single lattice — made industrially just by combining the two.

3531.w: Phosphorus trichloride simply adds a second molecule of chlorine, no substitution needed: PCl3 + Cl2 goes straight to PCl5.

3532.w: Potassium metal reduces its own nitrate outright: ten potassium atoms strip the oxygen off two nitrate ions, freeing nitrogen gas and leaving nothing behind but potassium oxide.

3533.w: Phosphoric acid neutralized with an alkali all the way to its third proton gives potassium phosphate — three hydrogens traded for three potassiums on the same phosphate ion.

3534.w: Mix solutions of silver nitrate and sodium acetate and silver acetate precipitates straight out — sodium and silver swap partners, silver pairing off with acetate instead.

3535.w: Cartilage caps every bone in the joint, and the calf's own tendon runs straight across it to the heel — why a sprain hurts exactly there.

3536.w: A humerus above the elbow, radius and ulna below — all three strung together by sinew so the muscle wrapped around them has something to pull against.

3537.w: Human reproduction begins with fertilisation between two people. What it produces gets its own name for its first year or so: baby.

3538.w: The oldest bags were exactly this: cloth or leather folded up at the edges and cinched shut with a cord of the same fibre.

3539.w: Boiled 60 to 90 seconds before it ever reaches the oven — the boiling water is what gives a bagel its shiny crust and dense, chewy bite.

3540.w: Sew two leather straps onto a bag and move the load off one hand and onto both shoulders — the whole invention in one sentence.

3541.w: Michael Faraday made the first rubber balloons in 1824 to hold hydrogen for lecture demonstrations. A puff of air does exactly what the hydrogen did.

3542.w: Mesoamerican ballplayers mixed raw latex with sap from the white morning-glory vine — the sap turned slippery, sticky polymer into a rubber that actually bounces.

3543.w: Barn is Old English for 'barley house'. Raise a granary's storage job into a full timber frame and that's what you get — hay in the loft, grain below.

3544.w: Turned on a lathe from a single billet — ash was the standard for a century, until maple bats won MLB approval in 1997.

3545.w: Vitreous enamel is glass, fused onto metal by heat. Kohler's foundry started by enamelling cast-iron horse troughs after an 1880 fire — turn the ears into a rim and it's a bathtub.

3546.w: Medieval mattresses were feathers, hair or wool stuffed into a cover and laid on a wood frame, off the cold and the draughts of the floor.

3547.w: Leather bends, folds and cinches tight without tearing, which is why it became the standard strap — closed with a steel buckle.

3548.w: Every one of the roughly 11,000 living species carries the same kit: feathers, and a toothless, horn-covered beak.

3549.w: Wool is the classic fill because it's thick, warm cloth in its own right — many blankets today swap in cotton or synthetic fibre, but the idea started here.

3550.w: Birch takes a fine, splinter-free polish once it's sanded — cut it to size, round the corners, and it's safe in a toddler's hands.

3551.w: The only real difference from a shoe is height: enough extra leather to cover the ankle, sometimes the calf or the knee.

3552.w: A calabash gourd, dried hard and hollow. Split the shell in half and it is already the exact shape you wanted.

3553.w: A clapper bridge is nothing but a flat slab of stone, cut and laid across two piers — engineering by leaving everything else out.

3554.w: A besom: birch twigs bound to a handle with cord. English kept the word 'broom' for it long after it stopped literally being the plant.

3555.w: Fibres tied to a handle — split palm leaf in ancient Egypt, plant fibre or animal hair ever since.

3556.w: Soap cuts water's surface tension enough that a puff of air can stretch it into a film about a micrometre thick without tearing.

3557.w: A cooper's trade scaled down: staves bent into a cylinder and cinched tight with a metal hoop — tin, once tin-plating got cheap.

3558.w: Many bulbs need a cold spell before they will flower — vernalisation. Without a winter, they simply sit.

3559.w: Earth up the stems with straw and the buried part makes more tubers. The potato grows in the dark, not in the soil's nutrients.

3560.w: Bone char is carbon with the calcium left in. Sugar refineries used it for centuries to whiten syrup.

3561.w: Jupiter's mass is nearly 2.5 times that of every other planet in the Solar System combined — so much gravity that nothing else was left to out-crush it.

3562.w: The second-largest planet, after Jupiter, with upper clouds sitting around 100–160 K — and the only planet in the Solar System less dense than water, by about 30%.

3563.w: Uranus is tipped 82° onto its side. The cause isn't known for certain, but the leading idea is a collision with an Earth-sized or larger protoplanet early in the Solar System's history.

3564.w: Neptune was found by mathematics before anyone saw it — Uranus's orbit wasn't behaving as predicted, and when Johann Galle checked the calculated spot on 23 September 1846, Neptune was within a degree of it.

3565.w: With over 400 active volcanoes, Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System — heated not by radioactive decay like Earth, but by tidal forces from Jupiter roughly 20,000 times stronger than the Moon's pull on Earth.

3566.w: Massive enough for its own gravity to crush it round, like a planet — but not massive enough to dominate and clear its orbit of everything else nearby. That line between the two is what the IAU drew in 2006.

3567.w: The Kuiper Belt is a disc of icy planetesimals beyond Neptune, running from 30 out to about 50 AU — and Neptune's gravity, through orbital resonances, still shapes which parts of it stay stable.

3568.w: Gravitational interactions with the young gas giants, Jupiter foremost, scattered leftover icy planetesimals into extremely wide orbits, building a shell now thought to reach anywhere from 2,000 to well over 100,000 AU out.

3569.w: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt: round under its own gravity, but far too small to have cleared its orbit of everything else out there — the reasoning behind its 2006 reclassification.

3570.w: Ceres is round under its own gravity like a planet, but it shares its orbit with thousands of other asteroids and makes up only about 40% of the asteroid belt's total mass — so it stays a dwarf planet.

3571.w: Neptune's Great Dark Spot was an Earth-sized anticyclonic storm Voyager 2 photographed in 1989 — and when Hubble looked again in 1994, it had disappeared completely, while a new dark spot had formed elsewhere.

3572.w: Over time, Earth's gravity locked the Moon's rotation to its orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces us — most of the far side stayed unseen until Luna 3's photographs in 1959.

3573.w: A stream of charged particles blows constantly off the Sun's corona. It is what strips thin atmospheres away over time — MAVEN measured Mars losing about 100 grams of atmosphere to it every second.

3574.w: Phaseolus lunatus, a species apart from the common bean — first domesticated in the Andes of Peru around 2000 BC. Spanish export crates stamped ‘Lima, Peru’ gave it the name it still carries.

3575.w: Vigna unguiculata, the cowpea — a different genus from the common bean, domesticated in Africa and bred for exactly the ground other legumes fail on: soil up to 85% sand, and low rainfall.

3576.w: A small white cultivar of the common bean. The name is American military history, not botany — the US Navy has served it to sailors as a staple ration since the mid-1800s.

3577.w: A cone doesn't crack open the way a shell does — it's bagged and set in the sun until the heat dries it open, about 20 days, then struck against a hard surface to shatter the seed loose.

3578.w: Bertholletia excelsa fruits almost only in undisturbed forest, because its flower can only be pollinated by a few large-bodied bee genera — Bombus, Centris, Epicharis, Eulaema, Xylocopa — that don't live in cleared plantation land.

3579.w: Ground into a spreadable paste the same way peanuts are for peanut butter — the nut's own oil is what holds it together.

3580.w: Almond meal worked with sugar, up to 35% of it by some recipes, until it's pliable enough to shape by hand. Toledo's version of the confection is documented back to 1512.

3581.w: Scooped out once the pumpkin is opened. Some cultivars are bred huskless on purpose, so the seed inside never needs shelling at all.

3582.w: Pressed roasted, hull-less pumpkin seed gives up a thick oil that reads green in a thin layer and dark red in a thick one — the same pigment seen two different ways.

3583.w: Soaked beans, ground with water, then boiled 15 to 20 minutes and strained — the base liquid tofu is curdled from.

3584.w: The same coagulant that curdles a whole soybean's worth of milk at once works directly on the milk itself, once it's already been ground, boiled and strained out of the bean.

3585.w: Whole beans, not curdled — the mould Rhizopus oligosporus is what binds them. Its mycelium knits the beans into a solid cake in about a day, leaving more fibre and protein in than tofu keeps.

3586.w: Picked green and immature, 35 to 40 days after the plant flowers — well before the beans would dry on the vine, and sweeter for it, before the sugar in them converts to starch.

3587.w: The same species as kidney and pinto beans, harvested and eaten pod and all before the seeds inside mature — a fresh legume, picked young instead of left to dry.

3588.w: Frying at 180 °C sets the outside of the ball before the inside can absorb oil. Below about 160 the falafel drinks the fryer; above 190 the crust colours before the middle cooks.

3589.w: Frijoles refritos — ‘well fried,’ not fried a second time. Cooked beans mashed to a paste, then fried in lard until they hold together.

3590.w: Held at boiling, lentil starch gelatinises and the cell walls give way, so the pulse breaks down into the sauce rather than sitting in it. Lentils need no soaking because the seed coat is thin enough for water to get in at once.

3591.w: Black-eyed peas simmered together with rice, eaten across the US South on New Year's Day for luck — the peas are meant to stand in for coins.

3592.w: Colonial New England grafted its own pantry onto a Native cooking method — beans baked in a covered pot for hours, maple sugar and bear fat swapped for molasses and salt pork. The molasses version is the one that stuck to Boston's name.

3593.w: Steam-cracking petroleum's long hydrocarbon chains apart at around 850°C is the dominant route to propylene, which comes off as a major co-product alongside ethylene.

3594.w: Steam-cracking petroleum throws off a C4 fraction alongside the ethylene and propylene; extractive distillation with a polar solvent pulls 1,3-butadiene out of it.

3595.w: The Sohio process ammoxidizes propylene with ammonia and oxygen over a bismuth-molybdate catalyst — 2 CH3CH=CH2 + 2 NH3 + 3 O2 → 2 CH2=CHCN + 6 H2O — though this recipe can't also carry the oxygen the real reaction needs.

3596.w: Nitrile rubber is a copolymer of butadiene and acrylonitrile built by emulsion polymerization — around 33% acrylonitrile content is the usual balance of oil resistance against low-temperature flexibility.

3597.w: CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + H2O. Hydrochlorinating methanol is the modern industrial route to chloromethane, cleaner than chlorinating methane directly, which also throws off dichloromethane, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride.

3598.w: The Müller-Rochow direct process reacts chloromethane with elemental silicon over a copper catalyst in a fluidized bed near 300°C, yielding dimethyldichlorosilane as its main product.

3599.w: n Si(CH3)2Cl2 + n H2O → [Si(CH3)2O]n + 2n HCl. Hydrolyzing dimethyldichlorosilane is how polydimethylsiloxane — silicone — gets its backbone.

3600.w: Aniline can be made by catalytic amination of phenol with ammonia — an alternative to the more common nitrobenzene-hydrogenation route, using phenol from the cumene process.

3601.w: RNH2 + COCl2 → RNCO + 2 HCl, through a carbamoyl-chloride intermediate. Phosgenating a primary amine like aniline is the general industrial route to isocyanates.

3602.w: Polyether polyols are built by ring-opening alkylene oxides onto a starter alcohol; glycerol is one of the classic low-molecular-weight starters, here reacted with ethylene oxide in place of the propylene oxide more common in industry.

3603.w: A polyurethane is produced by reacting a diisocyanate with a polyol, forming the alternating carbamate — urethane — linkages that give the polymer its name.

3604.w: Inconel 625 runs at least 58% nickel, with 8-10% molybdenum the alloying element that most sets it apart from plainer nickel-chromium alloys — 20-23% chromium and 3-4% niobium are real too, but this recipe can't carry a four-metal blend.

3605.w: Borosilicate glass is silica sand melted together with boric oxide, plus soda ash and alumina this recipe can't carry — about 80% silica and 13% boric oxide by mass, melting near 1,650°C.

3606.w: SiO2 + 3C → SiC + 2CO. Edward Acheson's 1893 process fuses silica sand with carbon in a graphite-resistance furnace between 1,600 and 2,500°C.

3607.w: Zr + 2 H2O → ZrO2 + 2 H2 — slow below 100°C but rapid above 900°C. The same reaction that worries nuclear engineers about zirconium cladding is a direct route from the metal to its oxide.

3608.w: Most commercial PAN is made by free-radical polymerization of acrylonitrile monomer, usually with a percent or two of another vinyl comonomer mixed in.

3609.w: PAN fiber is stabilized by oxidizing it in air near 230°C, then carbonized above 1,000°C in an inert atmosphere, driving off everything that isn't carbon. PAN is the precursor for about 90% of carbon fiber made today.

3610.w: Dow's glycerol-to-epichlorohydrin process reacts glycerol with hydrogen chloride, with a carboxylic-acid catalyst this recipe can't carry, giving the same chlorohydrin intermediate the older propylene route produces before base converts it to the epoxide.

3611.w: Epichlorohydrin added to bisphenol A, then condensed with sodium hydroxide this recipe can't carry, makes DGEBA — the most widely produced epoxy resin.

3612.w: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer pairs carbon fiber with a binding matrix — most often epoxy resin, sometimes polyester or nylon instead.

3613.w: Reinforcement-grade glass fiber is drawn by forcing molten glass from a furnace through a spinneret — bushings full of tiny holes the fiber is pulled through under its own tension.

3614.w: Fiberglass (GFRP) is glass fiber embedded in a plastic matrix — most often epoxy, polyester or vinyl ester resin.

3615.w: Wood flour is wood waste — sawdust and shavings from woodworking and furniture-making — ground fine enough to feel like sand, and it's the main filler in wood-plastic composite decking.

3616.w: Wood-plastic composite is wood fiber or wood flour compounded with a thermoplastic — polyethylene is by far the most common resin used.

3617.w: Anhydrous formaldehyde, freed by heating and strung together through anionic catalysis into long -CH2O- chains, is acetal homopolymer — the material sold as Delrin.

3618.w: n ClC6H4Cl + n Na2S → [C6H4S]n + 2n NaCl, run hot in NMP solvent. This is still the industrial route to polyphenylene sulfide, first commercialized by Phillips Petroleum.

3619.w: EPDM is a terpolymer built on an ethylene-propylene backbone with a few percent of a diene comonomer — commonly ethylidene norbornene — copolymerized in for sulfur-vulcanization sites this recipe can't carry.

3620.w: One of the four French fines herbes, and the fussiest: it wants a cool, moist bed, or it bolts to seed before there's anything to pick.

3621.w: A tropical grass that grows in dense clumps to 2 metres. Its lemon smell is geraniol and citronellol in the leaf oil — no citrus involved at all.

3622.w: Summer savory is sown, grown and harvested within a single season — unlike its evergreen cousin winter savory, or the perennial mints and thyme it grows beside.

3623.w: Celery's own family, Apiaceae, sown once the ground has warmed in spring. Its dry, curved fruit is what gets sold as aniseed.

3624.w: Reclassified in 2010 from its own species into a cultivar group of the onion — but it still multiplies in clustered offsets the way a garlic bulb does, not as one single bulb.

3625.w: Pulled and cut for its hollow green leaves before the bulb underneath has had any chance to swell.

3626.w: Allium tuberosum grows from small bulbs the way common chives do, but its flat leaves taste of garlic rather than onion.

3627.w: Fully ripe pepper berries are soaked in water for about a week until the flesh softens and rots away; rubbing removes what's left, and the bare seed dries pale.

3628.w: The vine's unripe drupes, packed in brine or vinegar before they can darken — dried green pepper uses sulphur dioxide or freeze-drying instead to hold the colour.

3629.w: Capsicum annuum again, the species behind paprika too — bred and picked the other way, for capsaicin rather than sweetness, then dried and ground.

3630.w: Left to bolt instead of being cut for its stalk, celery flowers and sets seed — grown for exactly this in temperate countries, then sold whole or ground as a spice.

3631.w: Nutmeg's own fruit carries two spices at once: the crimson, lacy aril peeled off and dried into mace, and the seed inside it dried separately into nutmeg.

3632.w: William Gebhardt's 1894 blend — dried chile peppers ground with other spices, cumin and garlic chief among them — was the first chili powder sold commercially in the US.

3633.w: Brazil nut trees fruit almost only in undisturbed forest, because only large-bodied orchid bees can pollinate their flowers — logging removes the bee long before it removes the tree.

3634.w: Its spiny bur splits open on its own once the fruit is ripe. The unrelated horse chestnut looks similar and is named for it, but is mildly poisonous.

3635.w: Striped, thin-hulled seeds are the confectionery type, bred to be eaten whole as a snack rather than pressed — the solid black-hulled kind goes to the oil press instead.

3636.w: Traditional balsamic starts as white grape juice boiled down to a thick must, then ages through a series of wooden barrels — oak, chestnut, cherry, mulberry — for a legal minimum of 12 years.

3637.w: Oil pressed from raw seed is pale and mild; toast the seed first and the oil that comes out is darker, stronger, and no longer suited to frying.

3638.w: Heinz 57 built its steak sauce on a ketchup-like base fortified with malt vinegar and seasoned with mustard, garlic and onion — tangier and more savoury than ketchup alone.

3639.w: Chopped rather than sliced. American pickle relish — a cooked, pickled dish of chopped vegetables — is the base of tartar sauce and the standard hot-dog topping.

3640.w: Most French recipes tie thyme, bay leaf and parsley together with string, simmer the bundle in the pot, then fish it back out before the dish is served.

3641.w: A marinade balances acid, oil and spice — vinegar, lemon juice or wine on one side, oil on the other. Too much acid toughens the food instead of tenderising it.

3642.w: The haloform reaction: sodium hypochlorite chlorinates and cleaves acetone's methyl groups off as chloroform. This is how chloroform was first made; industry has since switched to chlorinating methane directly.

3643.w: Two of chloroform's three chlorines swap for fluorine: HCCl3 + 2 HF -> HCF2Cl + 2 HCl. This refrigerant gas, R-22, is also the raw material for most of the world's Teflon.

3644.w: Pyrolyzed at 550-750°C, R-22 loses its chlorine and pairs up: 2 CHClF2 -> C2F4 + 2 HCl, through a fleeting difluorocarbene intermediate. This is the monomer behind Teflon.

3645.w: Free-radical polymerization in pressurized water, initiated by a persulfate, strings TFE end to end into a carbon backbone wrapped entirely in fluorine -- the same high-pressure trick that turns ethylene into polyethylene.

3646.w: At high pyrolysis temperature two TFE molecules combine and rearrange into one heavier, branched cousin: 3 CF2=CF2 -> 2 CF3CF=CF2. It's TFE's own byproduct, not a separate feedstock.

3647.w: Copolymerize TFE with a trace of a perfluoroether comonomer -- perfluoromethyl vinyl ether, in Wikipedia's own description of the class -- and the chain gains just enough of a kink to melt-process, unlike PTFE, which can only be sintered.

3648.w: Hydrofluoric acid adds across perchloroethylene's double bond and swaps chlorine for fluorine at the same time, giving CFC-113 -- an alternative route to the more common hexachloroethane-plus-HF process.

3649.w: Zinc dust strips two chlorines off CFC-113 and the freed electrons form a new double bond: CFCl2-CF2Cl + Zn -> CClF=CF2 + ZnCl2. This dechlorination is how CTFE, the monomer behind ECTFE, is made commercially.

3650.w: Ethylene and chlorotrifluoroethylene alternate almost perfectly along the chain, giving ECTFE roughly the toughness of a polyolefin with the chemical resistance of a fluoropolymer.

3651.w: Oxychlorination: ethylene, hydrogen chloride and oxygen combine over a copper catalyst to give 1,2-dichloroethane, recycling the very HCl that cracking it back apart will release downstream.

3652.w: Cracked in a fired heater, EDC falls apart into vinyl chloride monomer and hydrogen chloride -- the highly endothermic reaction that has supplied most of the world's PVC since the late 1950s.

3653.w: Suspension polymerization: vinyl chloride, water and an initiator are stirred in a pressurized, continuously cooled reactor until the double bonds link up into PVC's chain -- about 80% of the world's PVC is made exactly this way.

3654.w: Add HCl across vinyl chloride's double bond, Lewis-acid catalyzed at 20-50°C: H2C=CHCl + HCl -> CH3CHCl2. The first stop on the way to 1,1,1-trichloroethane.

3655.w: UV light drives one more chlorine onto 1,1-dichloroethane's remaining C-H bond: CH3CHCl2 + Cl2 -> CH3CCl3 + HCl, at 80-90% yield -- the industrial route to 1,1,1-trichloroethane.

3656.w: Antimony pentachloride catalyzes the exchange of two of 1,1,1-trichloroethane's chlorines for fluorine, at 0-80°C, giving HCFC-142b -- the feedstock for polyvinylidene fluoride.

3657.w: HCFC-142b loses a hydrogen chloride under heat and becomes vinylidene fluoride, CH2=CF2 -- the monomer both PVDF and Viton-type fluoroelastomers are built from.

3658.w: Free-radical polymerization of vinylidene fluoride, usually run as an aqueous emulsion or suspension, strings the CH2=CF2 monomer into PVDF's chain.

3659.w: Standard-type FKM -- the fluoroelastomer sold as Viton -- is a copolymer of vinylidene fluoride and hexafluoropropylene; some grades add a third monomer, tetrafluoroethylene, for extra chemical resistance.

3660.w: The same free-radical route that gave ICI its first polyethylene in 1933, run hotter and at higher pressure, keeps the chains short and branched -- LDPE, still made this way at industrial scale.

3661.w: Ziegler-Natta catalysis -- titanium chloride, the classic catalyst of the process -- strings ethylene into chains averaging millions of daltons instead of thousands, long enough that the result no longer melts cleanly.

3662.w: The lightest liquid fraction to come off a barrel of crude, boiling near 0°C -- drawn off before hexane's turn comes at a higher cut of the same still.

3663.w: The Houdry Catadiene process runs butane over a chromia-alumina catalyst and pulls off two pairs of hydrogens, leaving the conjugated double bonds of 1,3-butadiene.

3664.w: Ziegler-Natta catalysts (or, for a different chain geometry, alkyllithium initiators) polymerize butadiene into polybutadiene -- the synthetic rubber in nearly every tire tread.

3665.w: Ziegler-Natta or metallocene catalysts polymerize liquid propylene at 60-80°C and 30-40 atmospheres -- enough pressure to keep the gas liquid while the chains grow.

3666.w: Copolymerized in roughly a 75:25 ratio by weight, styrene and acrylonitrile give SAN -- clear and rigid on its own, and the resin half of ABS before the rubber gets grafted in.

3667.w: ABS is SAN grafted onto a backbone of polybutadiene rubber: a long chain of polybutadiene crisscrossed with shorter chains of poly(styrene-co-acrylonitrile), tough where SAN alone is brittle.

3668.w: Coal carbonisation, the same coking process that yields coal tar, gives up xylene too, alongside the toluene and styrene already found in the same light-oil fraction.

3669.w: The Amoco process oxidizes p-xylene's two methyl groups straight to carboxylic acids with compressed air over a cobalt-manganese-bromide catalyst in acetic acid -- the feedstock for nearly all polyester.

3670.w: Esterified at 220-260°C, then polycondensed as the water is driven off, terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol link up into PET -- the polyester of soda bottles and clothing fibre alike.

3671.w: Hydrogenating phenol saturates the aromatic ring and rearranges the hydroxyl into a ketone in one step, C6H5OH + 2 H2 -> cyclohexanone -- a smaller share of the world's supply than direct cyclohexane oxidation, but a real industrial route.

3672.w: Catalytic hydrogenation of nitric oxide over platinum adds three hydrogens and gives hydroxylamine, NH2OH -- one of two industrial routes to it, the other building it up from ammonium nitrite instead.

3673.w: Hydroxylamine condenses onto cyclohexanone's carbonyl, swapping the oxygen for =N-OH -- the oxime a Beckmann rearrangement will later crack open into nylon's own ring.

3674.w: Strong acid triggers the Beckmann rearrangement: the oxime's ring expands by one atom as a nitrogen inserts itself next to the old carbonyl carbon, giving caprolactam -- the source of 90% of the world's supply.

3675.w: Heated to about 260°C in an inert atmosphere for several hours, caprolactam's seven-membered ring breaks open and the monomers link end to end into nylon 6.

3676.w: Real nitrobenzene comes from nitrating benzene with a nitric-and-sulfuric-acid mixture. The game's coal tar stands in for a benzene it doesn't model directly, the same shortcut its azo-dye and terephthalic-acid recipes already take.

3677.w: Industrial aniline is nitrobenzene's nitro group reduced straight to an amine by catalytic hydrogenation at 200-300°C over a metal catalyst -- about 4 million tonnes a year made exactly this way.

3678.w: Nitrous acid diazotizes aniline's amine group: ArNH2 + HNO2 + HCl -> [ArN2]+Cl- + 2 H2O. The salt is dangerously explosive dry, so it is made cold, in solution, and used within the hour.

3679.w: Boric acid dissolved straight into hydrofluoric acid: B(OH)3 + 4 HF -> H3O+ + BF4- + 2 H2O, four fluorines clamping onto one boron.

3680.w: Swap the diazonium salt's chloride for tetrafluoroborate and the same unstable compound crystallises out as a stable solid, shock-insensitive where the chloride was dangerously explosive.

3681.w: Heating the solid salt triggers the Balz-Schiemann reaction: it decomposes exothermically into fluorobenzene, boron trifluoride and nitrogen gas.

3682.w: Benzophenone itself is made this way -- benzene plus carbon tetrachloride, Friedel-Crafts, then hydrolysis of the resulting diphenyldichloromethane. Run the same reaction on fluorobenzene and the product is the fluorinated version PEEK is built from.

3683.w: Catalytic hydroxylation of phenol with hydrogen peroxide gives a mixture of hydroquinone and its ortho isomer, catechol -- one of hydroquinone's real industrial routes.

3684.w: Hydroquinone's bisphenolate salt displaces fluoride from 4,4'-difluorobenzophenone in a nucleophilic aromatic substitution, run in molten diphenyl sulfone at around 300°C -- the step-growth polymerization that builds PEEK.

3685.w: Modern potassium carbonate is made the opposite way from old potash: carbon dioxide passed into potassium hydroxide solution, 2KOH + CO2 → K2CO3 + H2O, putting the carbonate back that potassium hydroxide-making took out.

3686.w: Sodium metal added to its own hydroxide steals the extra oxygen back: 2NaOH + 2Na → 2Na2O + H2, a cleaner route than plain burning, which tends to overshoot to the peroxide instead.

3687.w: Zinc metal dissolves straight into nitric acid, Zn + 2HNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + H2, a plain acid-metal reaction with hydrogen gas as the tell.

3688.w: Zinc oxide dissolves in nitric acid just as readily as the metal does, without the hydrogen: ZnO + 2HNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + H2O.

3689.w: o-Xylene run over a catalyst with oxygen at 320–400°C oxidises straight through to phthalic anhydride — the reaction that displaced the older naphthalene route once petrochemical xylene got cheap.

3690.w: Adolf von Baeyer condensed phthalic anhydride with two molecules of phenol under acid conditions in 1871 and got an indicator that stays colourless in acid and turns pink the moment a solution turns alkaline.

3691.w: Magnesium metal dissolves in nitric acid the same way zinc does: Mg + 2HNO3 → Mg(NO3)2 + H2, hydrogen fizzing off as the metal disappears.

3692.w: Straight acid-base neutralisation: glacial acetic acid saturated with ammonia gas, or the acid neutralised with ammonium carbonate, and ammonium acetate is what crystallises out either way.

3693.w: Toluene methylated with methanol over an HZSM-5 zeolite catalyst adds the second methyl group directly — one of the two industrial routes into xylene, alongside naphtha reforming.

3694.w: Carbonic acid loses a proton almost as fast as it forms: H2CO3 sits in equilibrium with H+ and HCO3-, and at ordinary pH the bicarbonate ion is what is left a moment later.

3695.w: Chromium(III) oxide roasted with an alkali under a stream of oxygen drives the metal up to its +6 state — the same oxidative roast chromite ore goes through on an industrial scale to make chromate.

3696.w: Chlorine gas reacts with acetic acid over a red phosphorus catalyst, replacing all three of the methyl group's hydrogens one at a time until only chlorine is left there: CH3CO2H + 3Cl2 → CCl3CO2H + 3HCl.

3697.w: Magnesite dissolved in sulfuric acid swaps its carbonate for sulfate and lets the carbon go as gas: MgCO3 + H2SO4 → MgSO4 + H2O + CO2.

3698.w: Sulfur dioxide run into sodium hydroxide solution is absorbed directly as the sulfite salt, SO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SO3 + H2O — the laboratory route into the same compound industry makes from sodium carbonate instead.

3699.w: Sulfur dioxide passed over vanadium pentoxide with more oxygen at 400–600°C oxidises straight through to the trioxide — the middle step of the contact process, on its way to becoming sulfuric acid.

3700.w: Aluminium oxide and phosphate combine to precipitate the phosphate salt directly — close to the same one-to-one chemistry that makes up most of turquoise's structure by weight once copper is added for colour.

3701.w: Fat and hot water alone will hydrolyse a triglyceride apart, splitting off its fatty acids — tallow's share of stearic acid is what gets distilled back out of the mixture afterward.

3702.w: Ammonium nitrate heated carefully to about 250°C decomposes cleanly into nitrous oxide and water vapour — the same industrial method that can just as easily run away into detonation if the heat isn't controlled.

3703.w: Chromate and potassium combine directly as the salt precipitates — the same +6 chromium the ore gives up in an oxidative alkaline roast, just paired with potassium instead of sodium.

3704.w: Chromate and dichromate sit in a pH-driven equilibrium in solution, 2CrO4(2-) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7(2-) + H2O — acidify a potassium chromate solution and dichromate is what crystallises out as it cools.

3705.w: Zinc metal dissolves directly in acetic acid to give the acetate salt, the same reaction path zinc carbonate takes to the identical compound.

3706.w: Magnesium dissolved in groundwater precipitates out as the carbonate wherever carbon dioxide is around to combine with it — the same mineral-forming chemistry limestone runs on calcium instead.

3707.w: MEK's industrial route runs through petroleum-derived butenes twice over: acid-catalysed hydration to 2-butanol first, then dehydrogenation strips the hydrogen back off to leave the ketone.

3708.w: Almost none of it is made on purpose. Ammoxidising petroleum-derived propylene with ammonia targets acrylonitrile, and acetonitrile falls out as the byproduct — most of it gets burned for fuel rather than sold.

3709.w: Propane comes off two ways: stripped from raw natural gas before it can condense in the pipeline, or as a by-product when refineries crack crude into petrol and heating oil. It boils at about −42°C, the lightest cut there is.

3710.w: Pentane's 36°C boiling point sits right at the bottom of the naphtha cut — the lightest hydrocarbon in crude that's still liquid at room temperature rather than boiling straight off as a gas.

3711.w: Octane is one straight-run cut among many in petrol, boiling around 126°C — but its branched cousin, iso-octane, became fuel quality's own ruler: the 100 on an octane rating is defined against it.

3712.w: Hydrodealkylation strips toluene of its methyl group with hydrogen over a chromium, molybdenum or platinum catalyst at 500 to 650°C: C6H5CH3 + H2 → C6H6 + CH4. It supplies a real share of world benzene, alongside reforming crude naphtha directly.

3713.w: Clostridium acetobutylicum ferments starch into a fixed ratio of solvents: 3 parts acetone to 6 of butanol and 1 of ethanol. Chaim Weizmann’s process supplied Britain’s acetone for cordite manufacture through the First World War.

3714.w: Hydrogen bromide gas dissolved in water is hydrobromic acid outright — no further reaction needed. At its azeotrope it boils at 124.3°C, still 47.6% HBr by mass.

3715.w: Dissolved carbon dioxide sits in equilibrium with carbonic acid — the same reaction, sped up a million-fold by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, that keeps blood pH steady with every breath. It's also the entire fizz in a soda bottle.

3716.w: Straight acid-base neutralisation: 2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4. The result is 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, and because the ammonium ion acidifies soil as it releases, it’s the fertiliser of choice on alkaline ground.

3717.w: Copper oxide dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid gives copper sulfate outright. Mixed with slaked lime it becomes Bordeaux mixture, sprayed on vines since 1885 and still farming’s default fungicide.

3718.w: A stronger acid displaces a weaker one from its salt: an acid added to a sulfite releases sulfur dioxide, which is what 'sulfurous acid' actually is in water — it has never been isolated as a free molecule, only as SO2 in equilibrium with H2O.

3719.w: Whey, drained off cut curd, still carries milk’s lactose in solution. Concentrated and cooled to 60–65% solids, lactose crystallises straight out of it — the standard industrial way to isolate it from cheesemaking’s own runoff.

3720.w: Lactase splits lactose's glycosidic bond with a molecule of water, handing back the two simple sugars it was built from: glucose, and galactose, its mirror-image twin.

3721.w: Sodium hydroxide neutralised with nitric acid gives sodium nitrate outright: HNO3 + NaOH → NaNO3 + H2O. The natural version, Chile saltpetre, was mined from Atacama desert crusts a metre thick and once called ‘white gold.’

3722.w: Iodine holds its electrons tightly enough that only a strong oxidiser moves it — hot concentrated nitric acid does the job, driving iodine up to iodic acid, HIO3.

3723.w: Steam driven through pine resin in a copper still carries the volatile oil off as vapour; what's left behind, no longer liquid, is rosin. What distils over and condenses is turpentine.

3724.w: Turpentine's pinene converts through isobornyl acetate and isoborneol to camphor by oxidation — the route supplying most world camphor since it undercut the tree around 1900. The game has no intermediate elements, so three steps collapse into one heat.

3725.w: Mix a silver salt with an iodide and silver iodide drops straight out of solution — it barely dissolves in water at all. That same insolubility is what makes it useful seeded into clouds: a nucleus for ice to form around.

3726.w: Arsenic burns readily in air into arsenic trioxide — 'white arsenic,' the same compound arsenopyrite ore gives up when roasted, which is how almost all of the world's supply turns up: an unwanted by-product of smelting gold and copper ores.

3727.w: Sodium hydroxide precipitates gold hydroxide from a gold chloride solution — HAuCl4 + 4NaOH → Au(OH)3 + 4NaCl + H2O — and above 140°C it dehydrates to the oxide. Not a stable resting point: past 298°C it falls back apart into metallic gold.

3728.w: Hydrogen sulfide gas passed through a gold chloride solution precipitates gold(I) sulfide directly — gold, true to its nobility, would rather bond loosely to sulfur than stay dissolved.

3729.w: Steel drawn cold through a die, the same way copper is: the metal doesn't lose volume, only cross-section, so it gets longer as it gets thinner.

3730.w: A dry cell's casing is zinc sheet metal, doubling as the negative terminal; the paste packed inside is manganese dioxide, which soaks up the electrons at the positive terminal.

3731.w: Skin is two tissue layers doing different jobs: an epidermis of keratin-forming epithelial tissue on top, and a collagen-rich dermis of connective tissue underneath.

3732.w: A ligament is dense connective tissue built from bundled collagen fibres — the same construction as a tendon, just anchored bone to bone instead of muscle to bone.

3733.w: Gold is soft enough to hammer thin and bend into a hoop small enough for a pierced ear — the earliest known earrings, gold pieces from Ur and Lothal, are about 4,500 years old.

3734.w: The elbow is a hinge joint where the humerus meets the radius and ulna; ulnar and radial collateral ligaments run either side of the joint capsule to stop it swinging sideways.

3735.w: Traditional envelopes are paper sheets cut into a rhombus, a kite or a short-armed cross and folded, with the overlapping flaps pasted or gummed together.

3736.w: The retina and optic nerve begin as outgrowths of the embryonic brain's diencephalon, which is why the retina counts as central nervous system tissue and carries its signal onward as electric current.

3737.w: Smooth or barbed wire strung between wooden posts fences a field with a fraction of the timber a solid rail fence needs — farmers who had wood but little else used it wherever it reached.

3738.w: A fingernail is alpha-keratin, the same protein as claws, hooves and horns, growing from a matrix under the skin at the fingertip — flattened and blunt where a claw stays curved and pointed.

3739.w: Each finger is built on phalanx bones — three of them, except the thumb's two — wrapped in skin all the way to the fingertip.

3740.w: A fire engine is a combustion-engine vehicle built to carry hose and pump to a blaze; motorised engines date back to a Paris funding request in January 1897 and were commonplace within a decade.

3741.w: David Misell's 1899 patent laid dry-cell batteries front to back in a paper tube, with a small light bulb and a rough brass reflector at the end — the first practical flashlight.

3742.w: Roman forks were bronze or silver; it was Catherine de' Medici's entourage that carried the table fork to the French court in the 16th century, and the rest of Europe took two more centuries to accept it.

3743.w: Galvanising coats steel in zinc, which is more reactive than iron and oxidises first, protecting the steel underneath from rusting through — exactly what an outdoor steel bin needs.

3744.w: Peripheral vision is far more sensitive to faint movement than fine detail, and pareidolia primes the brain to see faces and figures in ambiguous shapes — psychologists point to both as sources of ghost sightings.

3745.w: Ground glass lenses set in a metal frame — the first glasses were made in Pisa or Florence around 1290, though the wire temples that hook over your ears weren't developed until before 1727.

3746.w: Sheepskin turned to leather with the fleece left on — shearling — gives a glove its own wool lining in one piece, warm in a way a plain leather glove is not.

3747.w: Hide glue comes from soaking and liming animal hide, then heating it in water around 70°C to draw off a 'glue liquor' — the same collagen hydrolysis as gelatin, just dried coarse rather than refined.

3748.w: John Alexander Brodie invented the football goal net in 1889 — rope netting slung from a frame so a goal no longer had to be argued over — and called it the invention he was proudest of.

3749.w: Hair is a keratin protein filament that grows from a follicle rooted in the dermis; only the follicle's base is living tissue, which is why a cut hair doesn't hurt.

3750.w: A wire coat hanger is one length of wire cut to size and bent into a flattened triangle with a hook at the top — most are still, as the earliest ones reputedly were, just steel wire.

3751.w: Felt hats are stitched and can be stretched afterward to fit — a fedora is simply a soft felt hat with a lengthwise crease pressed into the crown.

3752.w: The skull is a bony enclosure built around the brain of a vertebrate — one continuous case, hinged only at the jaw.

3753.w: James Naismith nailed up a peach basket in 1891; by 1906 it had been replaced by an open metal rim with a net, so the ball could simply pass through instead of being fished out.

3754.w: A hose is extruded rubber reinforced with an internal web of fibres — fabric plies wrapped between rubber layers so it can survive being dragged over rocks and stepped on without splitting.

3755.w: Spring steel gets its snap-back from being hardened and tempered, not from any special metal — heat it, then quench it cold to lock the hardness in, and ordinary steel wire starts returning to shape instead of staying bent.

3756.w: Naval engineer Richard James spent about a year testing coils of wire after watching a torsion spring 'walk' off a shelf in 1943, before finding the one gauge that would do it on purpose — 400 sold in 90 minutes at the first Gimbels demonstration in 1945.

3757.w: Knitted fabric stretches in every direction, which is exactly what a garment shaped to a foot needs — the oldest surviving knitted garments are cotton socks from medieval Egypt.

3758.w: Gas solubility rises as water gets colder, so chilled carbonic-acid solution holds far more dissolved CO2 before it fizzes back out — the same reason bottling and soda fountains run cold. Joseph Priestley worked the basic process out in 1767, over a brewery vat in Leeds.

3759.w: A soft drink is carbonated water diluted with flavoured, sweetened syrup — commercial syrup is typically cut about 1:5 with carbonated water, with sugar carrying most of the rest of the taste.

3760.w: A couch frame is usually wood, and its covering is traditionally soft leather, corduroy or linen over padding — the Chesterfield's deep-buttoned leather look was commissioned by Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield.

3761.w: Spiders spin silk protein from spinneret glands at the tip of the abdomen, using different silks for a web's frame, spiral and sticky capture threads. A finished web is commonly about 20 times the size of the spider that built it.

3762.w: Ordinary spoons stayed wood or horn for most of history, carved by hand with a blade, while bronze and silver were the rare, wealthy exception. Carved antler spoons from the last ice age work the same way.

3763.w: Squirrels live and shelter in trees, and among the seeds and nuts they eat, an oak's acorns matter enough that squirrels bite out the embryo before burying one — keeping it from germinating in storage, out of several thousand caches a season.

3764.w: Brick stairs are laid the same way a brick wall is, course by course, each step its own short run of bricks — a cheap, durable alternative to carving steps directly into stone.

3765.w: A twig is a tree's thinnest, outermost branch — thin and dry enough that wind breaks it off before anything thicker moves. A stick on the ground is a twig that already fell.

3766.w: A label needs a coat of adhesive on the back, and gelatin is glue's kitchen name: prepared hide glue and gelatin are, in the words of one glue chemist, 'a similar composition,' both made by boiling collagen out of connective tissue.

3767.w: Iron cast around a fire, rather than a fire built in the open: the first cast-iron stove went up in 1642 at Lynn, Massachusetts, and was little more than an iron box with no grates yet — meant to keep the heat rather than lose it up a chimney.

3768.w: Rowland Hill's 1837 proposal for adhesive postage called for paper 'just large enough to bear the stamp, and covered at the back with a glutinous wash' — starch paste gummed onto a printed square of paper, first sold as the Penny Black on 1 May 1840.

3769.w: Stools are one of the oldest forms of wooden furniture; 17th-century joined stools built bigger seats out of thin spindles and rails joined at right angles — a carpenter's basic joinery, applied to a hardwood like oak.

3770.w: String, more precisely 'twine', is built the same way as thread or rope, just one step further: strands are twisted, then plied together in the opposite direction from their own twist — exactly what stops it unravelling.

3771.w: Early suitcases were leather stretched over a rigid frame, with leather or brass caps reinforcing the corners — the leather-over-frame design that lighter cardboard and plastic replaced once a 1938 US weight limit made every pound count.

3772.w: The first sunglasses were flat panes of smoky quartz, called Ai Tai ('dark clouds') in 12th-century China — worn for the glare, not vision correction, and reportedly used by judges to hide their expressions while questioning witnesses.

3773.w: Two needles loop one continuous strand of wool into a garment; the word 'sweater' itself dates only to 1882, first meaning a woolen vest worn rowing. Unscoured wool, as in an Aran jumper, keeps its natural lanolin and sheds water even wet.

3774.w: Before the 1930s a swimsuit was wool cut and sewn to a body shape — a fit that never quite worked, since wool does not hug the body and turns heavy soaked with water, which is exactly why rayon, then latex and nylon, replaced it.

3775.w: A swing needs almost nothing: something to hang from — chains, ropes or bars — and a seat at the end. The oldest version is exactly a rope thrown over a tree branch, no frame required.

3776.w: A table is a flat top on one or more legs, nailed together by the carpenter who built it — Egyptian tables from around 2500 BC were wood, and medieval trestle tables were built to fold and clear away after a meal.

3777.w: 3M's Richard Drew invented masking tape in 1925 after watching autobody painters fight tape that stripped fresh paint off the car — his fix was a gentler rubber-based adhesive coated onto paper backing, the recipe pressure-sensitive tape still uses.

3778.w: Steeping loose tea leaves — a brewing method that only caught on late in China's Yuan dynasty, replacing whipped powdered tea — needed its own vessel. The earliest surviving teapot, made by Gong Chun, is dated to 1513.

3779.w: The external nose's tip and sides are shaped entirely by cartilage — only the upper bridge is true bone — and the whole framework is covered in skin that varies from paper-thin at the tip to thicker over the bridge.

3780.w: Olfactory receptor neurons sit in the nasal lining; their fibers thread up through tiny holes in the ethmoid bone's cribriform plate to synapse in the olfactory bulb, making this the one cranial nerve wired straight into the nose.

3781.w: The optic nerve carries the retina's visual signal to the brain, but it isn't a typical peripheral nerve: it forms as an outgrowth of the embryonic diencephalon, myelinated by oligodendrocytes rather than Schwann cells, and wrapped in true meninges.

3782.w: The trigeminal nerve is the face's main sensory line, its three branches covering the forehead, cheeks, and jaw, while its own motor branch alone drives the muscles of chewing — the largest and most complex of the twelve cranial nerves.

3783.w: The vestibulocochlear nerve is really two nerves fused in one sheath: a cochlear branch carrying sound from the cochlea's hair cells, and a vestibular branch carrying balance information from the inner ear's semicircular canals and otolith organs.

3784.w: Named for wandering (Latin vagus), it is the longest cranial nerve, its right branch reaching all the way to the heart's own pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, to slow the heartbeat as the parasympathetic brake on the chest and abdomen.

3785.w: The accessory nerve is purely motor, its only job driving two neck and shoulder muscles: the sternocleidomastoid that turns the head, and the trapezius that shrugs the shoulder.

3786.w: The hypoglossal nerve carries no sensory fibers at all — it is a pure motor line driving the tongue's extrinsic and intrinsic muscles, the movements behind speech, chewing, and swallowing.

3787.w: Lavandula, grown across the Mediterranean for its flower spikes — and famous enough as bee forage that lavender honey is its own named variety.

3788.w: Carum carvi is a biennial that overwinters as a low rosette before flowering its second year — cold-hardy enough that its root is also harvested as a winter vegetable, eaten like a parsnip.
