3789.w: Sambucus nigra colonises disturbed, moisture-holding ground — hedgerows and waste places — and is picked in flower, before it sets fruit, for cordial or pressé.

3790.w: Mertensia maritima grows on gravelly, humus-rich shingle within reach of the highest winter tides, from Britain north to Svalbard.

3791.w: Trigonella foenum-graecum, a Fabaceae annual — the same family as peas and beans — grown for both its leaf and its seed.

3792.w: Acmella oleracea, native to Brazil's warm, wet ground — the flower bud alone carries spilanthol, the numbing compound behind its toothache-plant name.

3793.w: An F1 hybrid of mandarin and the wild ichang papeda, and it inherited that parent's frost tolerance — yuzu is grown through Japanese winters as cold as -7°C that ordinary citrus can't survive.

3794.w: Undaria pinnatifida, same order as kelp — Laminariales — cultivated in the cool coastal waters of Japan and Korea for centuries.

3795.w: Capsaicin barely dissolves in water — 0.0013 g per 100 mL — but readily in alcohol, which is why a chilli tincture is made with spirit, not water.

3796.w: Crushing the kernel inside an apricot pit exposes its amygdalin to water and its own enzyme, and one product of that breakdown is benzaldehyde — the same molecule that gives almonds and cherries their scent.

3797.w: Crushing ruptures the seed's cells and lets myrosinase reach sinigrin for the first time, releasing allyl isothiocyanate — the compound behind mustard's sting.

3798.w: The same reaction mustard runs: grinding the rhizome breaks its cells open, myrosinase meets its own glucosinolate, and allyl isothiocyanate is what stings.

3799.w: Present at only a few parts per million, but it is grapefruit's single most valuable aroma compound.

3800.w: A whole cucumber holds almost none of its own smell. Cutting exposes the flesh to oxygen, and (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal — cucumber aldehyde — is what forms.

3801.w: The character-impact compound of hazelnuts — no other nut carries it, which is why nothing else quite smells like one.

3802.w: One of dozens of aroma molecules a banana makes as it ripens, and the one that reads most like the fruit itself — it's also what banana-flavoured candy is built from.

3803.w: Sotolon is the major aroma and flavour component of fenugreek seed — the same molecule that reads as curry at high concentration and burnt sugar or maple at low.

3804.w: Cultured buttermilk owes its buttery aroma to diacetyl, a byproduct lactic-acid bacteria make while souring the cream — the same molecule that gives butter its taste.

3805.w: Retting the berries to strip their skin can go wrong: left too long in stagnant rather than running water, the process throws off 3-methylindole — pig manure's own smell — as an off-flavour.

3806.w: Lavender's scent is overwhelmingly one molecule, (R)-linalool — the reference plant chemists use for linalool itself.

3807.w: Cutting or zesting the peel releases citrus oil, and limonene is the major component of that oil in every citrus fruit's rind.

3808.w: Cooking breaks down the amino acid methionine through the same Strecker reaction that gives fried potato its cooked-potato smell — raw green beans lack it, cooked ones develop it.

3809.w: Kiwi's green, grassy edge comes from the aldehyde hexanal, released the moment its cell walls break.

3810.w: Slicing an apple lets enzymes turn its fatty acids into hexanal within seconds — the same green aldehyde behind kiwi's grassy note, and the smell of cut grass generally.

3811.w: Vanillin sits locked to sugar as glucovanillin in a fresh pod; curing lets an enzyme cut it free during ripening, releasing the pod's full scent.

3812.w: The first commercial vanillin, sold from 1874 into the 1920s, was synthesized from clove oil's eugenol rather than extracted from any vanilla pod.

3813.w: Furaneol builds as a strawberry ripens, reaching its highest concentration at full ripeness — the molecule also called strawberry furanone.

3814.w: The same furanone that ripens in strawberries is partly responsible for fresh pineapple's smell, which is why it doubles as 'pineapple ketone'.

3815.w: Cinnamon bark's essential oil is mostly this one compound — chemically, it is what cinnamon flavour and smell are.

3816.w: Cassia bark contains the same cinnamaldehyde as true cinnamon, in different proportions, which is why the two spices are so often sold interchangeably.

3817.w: Sweet basil's citrusy edge comes from linalool, the same terpene alcohol also present in lavender and bay laurel.

3818.w: Linalool is a major constituent of coriander seed oil — the same molecule that gives basil its citrus note, in an unrelated plant.

3819.w: Lemongrass oil runs 65 to 85 percent citral by weight, the richest common source of the compound.

3820.w: Citral is used commercially to fortify lemon oil, precisely because it is already the dominant note in the fruit's own peel oil.

3821.w: Limonene is the major component of citrus peel oil and the compound behind orange peel's characteristic smell.

3822.w: Beyond citrus, limonene is also a major component of the aromatic resins of numerous conifers, several pine species included.

3823.w: Capsaicin concentrates in the pith holding a chilli's seeds rather than the seeds themselves — cutting one open exposes where nearly all the heat sits.

3824.w: Whole garlic barely smells; crushing breaks the cell walls keeping the enzyme alliinase apart from alliin, and the enzyme converts it to allicin within seconds.

3825.w: Shiitake's earthy scent, like that of mushrooms generally, comes from octenol — first isolated from crushed matsutake in the 1930s.

3826.w: The mushroom alcohol behind matsutake's aroma is common across mushroom species generally, shiitake included.

3827.w: Eucalyptol makes up 70 to 90 percent of eucalyptus oil, by far the tree's dominant scent compound.

3828.w: The same camphor-like compound that dominates eucalyptus oil is also present in rosemary's, part of why the two smell distantly related.

3829.w: Theobromine is the primary alkaloid in cocoa and chocolate, a milder relative of caffeine.

3830.w: Theobromine is present in tea leaves as well as chocolate, extracted into the cup alongside caffeine when the leaves steep.

3831.w: Celeriac is the same species as celery, Apium graveolens, bred toward a swollen root instead of the stalk.

3832.w: Agave sap, or aguamiel, ferments into pulque driven by the bacterium Zymomonas mobilis rather than yeast — the drink Aztecs called this tequila's forerunner.

3833.w: Ethanol boils out of fermented agave wort at 78°C, before the water does; Mexican law requires two distillations to produce tequila.

3834.w: Cognac is twice-distilled wine aged at least two years in French oak barrels, which is where nearly all of its final flavour comes from.

3835.w: Cassia comes from a different tree than true cinnamon, Cinnamomum cassia — its bark is stripped and dried much the same way, then sold as 'cinnamon' in most supermarkets.

3836.w: Trigonella foenum-graecum is an annual of the legume family — beans, peas, peanuts — grown to pod and dried in the field before the seed is threshed out.

3837.w: Carum carvi is a biennial of the carrot family, Apiaceae. Its root is eaten like a parsnip in year one; only in year two does it flower and set the seed sold as caraway.

3838.w: Lavandula flourishes best in dry, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils in full sun — thin, poor ground it does not fight to grow in.

3839.w: A rhizome of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, native to and grown across the wet tropics of South and Southeast Asia.

3840.w: Dried at about 60 °C, low enough to leave the alliinase enzyme working. Take it hotter and the enzyme denatures, so the powder has no allicin and no smell when it meets water.

3841.w: Onion powder is dehydrated, ground onion, used wherever a cook wants the flavour without the water or the sting.

3842.w: Garam masala regularly incorporates cardamom, cinnamon, cumin, cloves, bay leaves, star anise and peppercorns — cardamom and cinnamon are its two most-cited spices.

3843.w: In the United States, curry powder is expected to contain at least turmeric, coriander, fenugreek, cinnamon, cumin, black pepper, ginger and cardamom — turmeric gives it colour, coriander its citrus-sweet base.

3844.w: Five-spice powder commonly mixes star anise, cloves, Chinese cinnamon, Sichuan pepper and fennel seeds — star anise and clove anchor the blend.

3845.w: Berbere's ingredients include chili peppers, coriander, garlic, ginger and fenugreek — fenugreek's bitter edge is one of the blend's hard-to-place background notes, carried here by a cultivated hot pepper standing in for the fresh chile.

3846.w: Common ras el hanout ingredients include cardamom, cumin, clove, cinnamon, nutmeg, mace, allspice and dry ginger — cinnamon and ginger are two of its most consistently named spices.

3847.w: North American commercial herbes de Provence typically add dried lavender to a base of thyme and other herbs, even though lavender does not appear in Jean-Baptiste Reboul's 1910 compendium of authentic Provençal cooking — a modern addition, not a heritage one.

3848.w: Quatre épices contains ground pepper, cloves, nutmeg and dried ginger — cloves and nutmeg are two of its fixed four, unlike the pepper base some versions swap for allspice or cinnamon.

3849.w: Za'atar is a prepared mixture of dried herb, toasted sesame, sumac and salt — traditionally wild Origanum syriacum, with thyme, oregano or marjoram named as the substitutes cooks reach for where that herb isn't sold.

3850.w: Harissa's main ingredients are roasted red peppers, Baklouti peppers, garlic paste and caraway seeds — caraway is one of its two or three defining spices, alongside a hot red pepper standing in for the fresh chile.

3851.w: Tabil is a Tunisian spice mixture generally consisting of ground coriander seed, caraway seed, garlic and chili powder.

3852.w: Chermoula's common ingredients are garlic, cumin, coriander, oil, lemon juice and salt — garlic and cumin are two of its fixed anchors across regional versions.

3853.w: Dukkah's composition varies by family and vendor, but coriander and cumin are named among its common ingredients, alongside sesame, salt and black pepper.

3854.w: Gomashio is made by toasting sesame seeds and then mixing them with salt.

3855.w: A typical shichimi togarashi blend's main ingredient is coarsely ground red chile pepper, cut with black or white sesame seed — represented here by a cultivated hot pepper.

3856.w: Lemongrass and galangal are named among the common ingredients across Thai curry pastes, alongside chiles, shallots, garlic and coriander root.

3857.w: Jerk seasoning principally consists of allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers — allspice, Jamaica's own pimento, is the blend's namesake spice, paired here with a hot pepper standing in for the Scotch bonnet.

3858.w: The Lebanese spice blend, also called Lebanese seven-spice, is a mixture of equal parts allspice, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves, fenugreek, nutmeg and ginger.

3859.w: Baharat's main ingredients are often cloves, black pepper, allspice and cinnamon — black pepper and cinnamon anchor the blend across its Turkish, Gulf and Levantine versions.

3860.w: The basic soup hawaij is made from cumin, black pepper, turmeric and cardamom.

3861.w: Common advieh ingredients include turmeric, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, rose petals, cumin and ginger — cumin and cardamom are two of its everyday anchors.

3862.w: Mustard seed is one of the antimicrobial spices pickling spice leans on, alongside dill — the herb most identified with pickled cucumbers, and a standard component of homemade pickling brine.

3863.w: The canonical fines herbes of French haute cuisine comprise finely chopped parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil — parsley and tarragon are two of its four.

3864.w: Gingerbread is typically flavoured with ginger, cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon — ginger and clove are two of its four defining spices.

3865.w: Speculaas cookies contain speculaas spices, a mix of cinnamon with other spices such as nutmeg, clove, ginger, cardamom and black pepper — cinnamon and nutmeg anchor the blend.

3866.w: Apple pie spice blends nutmeg with mace, its own lacy aril, alongside cinnamon and allspice — two spices from the same nutmeg fruit, dried apart, ending up in the same jar.

3867.w: Pumpkin pie spice is generally a blend of ground cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and sometimes allspice — ginger and nutmeg are two of its fixed base.

3868.w: Sage is traditionally served in sage and onion stuffing alongside roast turkey or chicken, and remains the dominant herb in American poultry seasoning, typically rounded out with thyme.

3869.w: Homemade crab and crawfish boil recipes call for abundant cayenne pepper, salt, bay leaf, lemon and garlic — bay leaf and cayenne are two of its constants.

3870.w: Cajun seasonings consist of salt blended with a variety of spices, most commonly cayenne pepper and garlic, with paprika named among the other flavour components.

3871.w: This style of blend mixes about 18 herbs and spices including celery salt, red and black pepper and paprika, with others such as bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger.

3872.w: Adobo seco consists of garlic powder, onion powder, turmeric, salt, black pepper and dried oregano — a dry rub distinct from the Filipino braise that shares its name.

3873.w: A basic dry rub generally contains brown sugar, paprika, black pepper, chili powder, garlic powder and onion powder along with salt — paprika and garlic powder anchor its savoury-smoky base.

3874.w: Recado rojo, or achiote paste, typically includes annatto, oregano, cumin, clove, cinnamon, black pepper, allspice, garlic and salt, ground with sour orange juice or vinegar.

3875.w: Zhoug is made from fresh hot chile peppers seasoned with coriander, garlic, salt, black cumin and parsley, then mixed with olive oil — coriander and garlic anchor its herbal base.

3876.w: Animism holds that soul or spirit exists not only in humans but in animals, plants, rocks, and rivers alike — summed up by the Ainu saying that even a rock has a spirit.

3877.w: Sami and Siberian shamans beat a sacred drum and, in some traditions, ate the psychoactive fly agaric mushroom to fall into the trance that let them travel to the spirit world.

3878.w: Andean peoples believed the spirits of the dead resided in the mountains and land as living ancestors, to be fed and honored so they would guide and provide for their descendants.

3879.w: The Dreaming is a 'timeless time' of ongoing creation in which ancestral beings — including figures like the Rainbow Serpent — shaped the land and left it charged with spiritual power.

3880.w: Aztec priests cut the heart from a sacrificial victim with a blade, believing the sun needed a steady offering of human hearts and blood to keep crossing the sky.

3881.w: Ahura Mazda, the 'Wise Lord' and sovereign creator of Zoroastrianism, is honored through the sacred fire that Zoroastrian temples keep burning as a mark of his eternal authority.

3882.w: Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit who opposes Ahura Mazda with darkness and lies, is said to have created the serpent-demon Aži Dahāka as one of his agents of chaos.

3883.w: Zoroaster reported that around age 30 he received a riverbank revelation of Ahura Mazda's 'Good Purpose,' becoming the prophet who composed the Gathas and founded Zoroastrianism.

3884.w: Zoroastrianism holds that the good creator Ahura Mazda is locked in an eternal struggle with Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit, and that humans must choose good to help tip the balance.

3885.w: Legend holds that the aging Laozi rode out of China on an ox, and at the western border a guard refused to let him pass until he set down his wisdom — the resulting text became the Daode Jing.

3886.w: Laozi's Daode Jing describes the dao, or Way, as an enigmatic, unseen process of transformation underlying and sustaining all reality — as intangible and ever-moving as the wind.

3887.w: Wu wei, Daoism's 'non-action,' is action carried out in such silent harmony with the dao that it 'may even seem motionless and effortless' — like water, which shapes the land by yielding rather than striving.

3888.w: Daoism, founded on Laozi's Daode Jing, holds that the dao sustains and orders the universe, and that one aligns with it not through force but through wu wei, effortless action.

3889.w: Prince Vardhamana renounced his throne and family at age 30 to live as a wandering ascetic; after 12 years of extreme austerity he attained enlightenment and became known as Mahavira.

3890.w: Ahimsa, Jainism's vow of nonviolence, is held to extend even to the microorganisms in water and the smallest flying insects — why strict Jains strain their drinking water and take care where they walk.

3891.w: Tirthankaras, the 'ford-builders' who show the way across the ocean of rebirth, are traditionally 24 enlightened teachers per era; Mahavira, often shown seated on a lotus, is honored as the most recent.

3892.w: Jainism as practiced today was shaped by Mahavira in the 6th century BCE around ahimsa, nonviolence toward all living things, which the faith holds as its highest ethical duty.

3893.w: Confucianism grew from the individual records Confucius's disciples kept of their conversations with him, which they collected and jointly edited into the Analects after his death.

3894.w: Confucius held that the junzi, or 'superior man,' governs by acting virtuously himself rather than by force, on the belief that pure virtue leads others to follow by simple example.

3895.w: Marduk defeated the primordial sea-dragon Tiamat in battle and was crowned king of the Babylonian gods, going on to fashion the ordered world from her body.

3896.w: The Enûma Eliš, Babylon's epic of creation, was recorded on seven clay tablets telling how Marduk defeated Tiamat and organized the cosmos — legitimizing Babylonian kingship.

3897.w: Egyptian embalmers dried the body for 70 days in natron, a natural salt, before wrapping it in linen — a rite myth credits to the jackal-headed god Anubis, who first embalmed his father Osiris.

3898.w: Wealthy Egyptians were buried with the Book of the Dead, a collection of spells written to guide the deceased safely through the underworld and into the afterlife.

3899.w: Shinto venerates kami, the sacred spirits of Japan, tracing its roots to the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami, who according to the Kojiki were instructed by the gods to bring the land into being.

3900.w: Kami are the sacred spirits Shinto venerates in nature, ancestors, and history; the sun goddess Amaterasu, most revered of all, is enshrined at Ise and represented there by the Sacred Mirror.

3901.w: A torii is the gateless gate marking a Shinto shrine's entrance, traditionally built of wood, symbolically marking the transition from the ordinary world into sacred ground.

3902.w: Ragnarok is the Norse apocalypse in which Odin and Loki, once allies, end up on opposing sides of a final battle between gods and giants that destroys the world before it rises again.

3903.w: In Valhalla, slain warriors feast nightly on meat from the boar Sæhrímnir, cooked and whole again by morning, and on mead milked from the udder of the goat Heiðrún.

3904.w: The Pythia, Apollo's oracle at Delphi, entered a trance state — possibly from gases seeping through the rock — to deliver the god's cryptic prophecies to those who sought her counsel.

3905.w: The lares were Roman guardian spirits, often linked to the ancestral dead, honored at a shrine by the household hearth-fire and, in their wider civic role, at crossroads across the community.

3906.w: The Bhagavad-Gita is a dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna set within the epic Mahabharata, and is probably the single most popular scripture in all of Hinduism.

3907.w: In the Bhagavad-Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna he must perform his dharma, or duty, even against his own feelings — dharma being the moral responsibility that varies by role, as a soldier's differs from a farmer's.

3908.w: Karma is the seed sown by every intentional deed, whose fruit — good or bad — ripens across lifetimes to turn the great wheel of rebirth.

3909.w: Samsara, the wheel of birth, death, and rebirth, is kept turning by karma, the residue of past actions — a cycle broken only by moksha, liberation.

3910.w: The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that the atman, one's innermost self, dwells within the heart, 'smaller than a corn of rice' — illustrated by cracking open a fig seed to reveal an essence too fine to see, yet real.

3911.w: The Upanishads teach 'tat tvam asi' — 'that thou art' — meaning Brahman, ultimate reality, is identical to the atman within: just as a fig's invisible essence pervades and defines it, Brahman pervades and equals the self.

3912.w: Moksha, liberation from the endless round of samsara, comes through realizing that the atman, one's innermost self, is identical to Brahman, ultimate reality itself.

3913.w: The four Vedas — Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda — are Hinduism's oldest and most authoritative scriptures; the four-headed creator Brahma is traditionally shown with each head reciting one.

3914.w: The Upanishads are the Vedas' philosophical final layer, moving from ritual toward the exploration of atman and Brahman — 'Upanishad' itself meaning 'sitting down near' a teacher to receive this deeper knowledge.

3915.w: A guru is a teacher who passes on the Upanishads' most advanced teachings — the very word 'Upanishad' means 'sitting down near' the guru who imparts them.

3916.w: The four ashramas take a Hindu man from student — learning at a guru's side — to householder, tending the sacred domestic fire, and finally to forest-dweller and wandering ascetic.

3917.w: Yoga combines physical postures with breath control — the literal stilling of one's wind — to calm the mind until it can perceive the atman, the true self, and so attain liberation.

3918.w: Puja is Hindu ritual worship — the loving offering of light, flowers, water, or food before the image of a deity such as Lakshmi — open to any devotee, not only priests.

3919.w: Bhakti, loving devotion to a personal god, finds its most celebrated expression in the romantic devotion between Krishna and Radha, likened by worshippers to the soul's own passionate bond with the divine.

3920.w: Adi Shankara wrote an influential commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, one of the texts that made him the most consequential systematizer of Advaita Vedanta.

3921.w: Adi Shankara's Advaita ('non-dual') Vedanta holds that Brahman alone is ultimately real, while the everyday world of separate, multiple things is not fully real.

3922.w: Shakti is feminine divine power personified as the Great Goddess, taking many forms across Hindu tradition — from the gentle Parvati to the fierce Durga and Kali, all facets of one creative, preserving, destroying energy.

3923.w: As an infant, Moses was hidden among the reeds of the Nile River in a basket, according to the Torah's account of his birth.

3924.w: In Genesis, God promises the childless, desert-dwelling Abraham that his descendants will be as numerous as the stars in the sky.

3925.w: At the Last Supper, Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples and told them, 'Do this in remembrance of me' — the origin of the Christian Eucharist.

3926.w: Before his first revelation, Muhammad worked as a merchant leading camel caravans on the trade route to Syria for the wealthy widow Khadija, whom he later married.

3927.w: Prince Siddhartha Gautama renounced his crown and sat beneath a fig tree, meditating until he reached enlightenment and became known as the Buddha.

3928.w: A Hindu poet who debated with Hindu and Muslim holy men alike, Guru Nanak vanished into a river for three days and returned declaring, 'There is no Hindu, no Muslim.'

3929.w: Legend holds that the aging Laozi, disillusioned with society, rode an ox out through a mountain pass, dictating the Tao Te Ching to the pass's gatekeeper before vanishing.

3930.w: At about age 30, Zoroaster experienced a revelation of Ahura Mazda, the 'Wise Lord,' and described existence as an ongoing battle between truth and the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu — a struggle Zoroastrian fire temples still keep alight.

3931.w: Born a prince, Vardhamana renounced his wealth and royal life at 30 to seek release from reincarnation; after roughly twelve years of fasting and meditation he achieved enlightenment as Mahavira, Jainism's last Tirthankara.

3932.w: Known as 'Darwin's Bulldog' for his fierce public defense of evolution, biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the word 'agnostic' in 1869.

3933.w: The words for 'spirit' in Latin (spiritus) and Greek (pneuma) both mean 'breath' or 'wind' — many traditions picture the soul as the breath that animates a body and departs at death.

3934.w: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism all teach that after death, the soul begins a new life in a new body, shaped by the karma accumulated in the last one.

3935.w: In Hindu thought, dharma is an individual's righteous duty, the moral order running through the Vedas and through karma alike; Buddhists later used the same word for the Buddha's own body of teaching.

3936.w: Moksha, liberation from the endless cycle of reincarnation, is described in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist texts as something reached only after countless lifetimes of accumulated spiritual effort.

3937.w: Nirvana literally means 'blowing out' or 'quenching' — early Buddhist texts pictured it as a flame going out once the fires of craving, hatred, and ignorance have burned themselves to nothing.

3938.w: Tradition holds that the sage Vyasa — regarded by many Hindus as a partial incarnation of Vishnu — arranged ancient hymns passed down by word of mouth into the four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur, and Atharva.

3939.w: The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally believed to have been revealed by God to Moses atop Mount Sinai.

3940.w: Compiled by rabbis over centuries of debate on how to interpret and apply the Torah, the Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.

3941.w: An acronym for its three sections — Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings) — the Tanakh is the canon of the Hebrew Bible.

3942.w: Muslims believe the Quran's first verses were revealed to Muhammad by the angel Gabriel in the Cave of Hira, near Mecca, in 610 CE; revelations continued for 23 years.

3943.w: The Christian Bible unites the Hebrew scriptures as its Old Testament with a New Testament of gospels and letters recounting the life and teachings of Jesus.

3944.w: Composed predominantly by six Sikh Gurus and compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, the Guru Granth Sahib was declared the Sikhs' eternal, living Guru by Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.

3945.w: The doctrine that God exists as three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one being; the New Testament describes the Holy Spirit descending 'like the blowing of a violent wind' at Pentecost.

3946.w: The five obligatory acts of Islam: declaring the faith (Shahada), praying five times daily (Salat), giving to charity (Zakat), fasting during Ramadan (Sawm), and, if able, a pilgrimage to Mecca (Hajj).

3947.w: Hinduism has no single founder; many of its traditions hold that a single Supreme Reality, Brahman, is expressed through gods such as the Trimurti and taught in the ancient Vedas.

3948.w: Founded on the dharma the Buddha taught after his enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, Buddhism holds that suffering ends by following the Noble Eightfold Path.

3949.w: The oldest of the Abrahamic religions, built on God's covenant with Abraham and on the Torah, the law revealed to Moses.

3950.w: Centered on Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe to be the Son of God; God is understood as a Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

3951.w: Founded in 7th-century Arabia when Muhammad began receiving revelations later collected as the Quran, Islam teaches submission to the one God, Allah.

3952.w: Traditionally traced to the sage Laozi, Taoism teaches that harmony comes from living according to the Tao ('the Way') and keeping yin and yang in balance.

3953.w: Founded by Guru Nanak in 15th-century Punjab, Sikhism's line of living Gurus ended in 1708, when Guru Gobind Singh named the Guru Granth Sahib itself as his eternal successor.

3954.w: Founded by the prophet Zoroaster in ancient Persia, one of the world's oldest continuously practiced religions; its fire temples keep a sacred flame burning as a symbol of Ahura Mazda.

3955.w: An ancient Indian religion built on ahimsa, strict non-violence toward all living things, as the path to moksha; its most revered teacher is Mahavira, the tradition's last Tirthankara.

3956.w: The absence of belief in gods; Charles Darwin's 1859 On the Origin of Species offered a natural explanation for life's diversity that many atheists point to as evidence a creator isn't needed.

3957.w: The view that God's existence can never be proven or disproven; biologist Thomas Henry Huxley coined the term in 1869, from the Greek for 'not knowable.'

3958.w: Yin and yang: two complements, neither of which exists or means anything at all without the other.

3959.w: Considered the primordial sound of the universe, the sacred syllable Om (or Aum) is chanted across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism alike.

3960.w: Islam's holiest city, in Saudi Arabia: birthplace of Muhammad and home to the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine built around the sacred Black Stone at the center of the Grand Mosque.

3961.w: A Jewish house of worship built around an ark that holds its Torah scrolls; full communal prayer traditionally requires a minyan, a quorum of at least ten adults.

3962.w: An Islamic place of worship with a mihrab, a niche set into the wall to indicate the direction of Mecca, so that everyone can pray facing the same way.

3963.w: Names both a building used for Christian worship and, more broadly, the entire community of Christian believers gathered around it.

3964.w: Most everyday Hindu worship happens at home shrines, but grand stone temples such as the Brihadisvara Temple, built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE, host puja, ritual devotional worship, on a monumental scale.

3965.w: A teacher and spiritual leader qualified to interpret Jewish law; the title comes from the Hebrew for 'my master,' and rabbis are the primary voices behind the Talmud's centuries of legal debate.

3966.w: Carum carvi is Apiaceae, family to carrot, and unlike its warm-climate lookalike cumin it grows wild as far north as Scandinavia. What is sold as caraway ‘seed’ is the dried fruit of the plant's second year.

3967.w: Piper cubeba is a climbing pepper vine of humid Sumatran and Javan rainforest; its berries are picked unripe and dried whole, stalk and all — the ‘tail’ that gives tailed pepper its name.

3968.w: Trigonella foenum-graecum is an annual Fabaceae legume of the Near East, grown for its cuboid amber seed. It has long been used to try to raise milk supply and manage diabetes, but no good evidence confirms either use works.

3969.w: Glycyrrhiza glabra is a Fabaceae legume harvested in autumn, two to three years after planting, for its sweet root — the source of glycyrrhizin, which can be 7 to 10 percent of the dried root by weight.

3970.w: Myrtus communis is an evergreen Myrtaceae shrub of the Mediterranean, growing to 5 metres, with white-pink flowers giving way to blue-black berries — the same berries steeped in alcohol to make the Sardinian liqueur Mirto.

3971.w: Quassia amara is a Simaroubaceae tree of tropical South America; its intensely bitter bark, dried into chips, is named after Graman Quassi, a formerly enslaved man in Suriname credited with discovering its medicinal use in the eighteenth century.

3972.w: Carthamus tinctorius is an Asteraceae thistle bred for two different oils — one high in monounsaturated oleic acid, one high in polyunsaturated linoleic — and for petals that yield both a yellow and a red dye.

3973.w: Zanthoxylum peppers are Rutaceae, the citrus and rue family, not related to true pepper or chili despite the name. What is sold as the peppercorn is the dried pericarp — the husk — with the shiny black seed discarded.

3974.w: Capers are the unopened flower buds of Capparis spinosa, hand-picked in the morning before they can bloom and preserved by pickling in a salt or salt-and-vinegar solution.

3975.w: Alpinia officinarum is a Chinese ginger-family plant grown for its rhizome, thin and orange-fleshed under a brown skin, dug up and dried for use in curries and Chinese herbal medicine.

3976.w: Alpinia galanga is the same ginger-family genus as lesser galangal but a far bigger plant, growing to ten feet in Java's tropical warmth; red cultivars are used mainly as medicine, white mainly as a spice.

3977.w: Ferula assa-foetida is a foul-smelling Apiaceae; harvesters expose the taproot's crown and score it repeatedly over several weeks, and the oleo-gum-resin that oozes out is collected and dried into the lump ground into asafoetida.

3978.w: Aframomum melegueta is Zingiberaceae, the ginger family that also holds cardamom, native to West African wetlands. Its purple flowers give way to pods holding small, pyramid-shaped reddish-brown seeds.

3979.w: Capsaicin binds TRPV1, the same heat-sensing nerve channel piperine and gingerol open, which is why an unrelated fruit reads as ‘hot’. A transdermal capsaicin patch, Qutenza, was FDA-approved in 2009 for nerve pain after shingles.

3980.w: S-(+)-carvone makes up 60 to 70 percent of caraway's essential oil and gives it that rye-bread spiciness. Its mirror-image molecule, R-(−)-carvone, is the main scent of spearmint — same formula, opposite shape, a completely different smell.

3981.w: Glycyrrhizin, 7 to 10 percent of dried licorice root by weight, is 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar. It also blocks the enzyme that breaks down cortisol, which is why overuse raises blood pressure and drops potassium — a real, dose-dependent risk.

3982.w: Hydroxy-alpha-sanshool is the compound behind Sichuan pepper's signature sensation — food writer Harold McGee describes it as tingling and buzzing, closer to a carbonated drink than to the burn of chili or black pepper.

3983.w: Safflower petals hold both a water-soluble yellow dye and an alcohol-soluble red one, carthamin, that needs no mordant to fix to cotton or silk — the same red used for centuries as a natural rouge and lip colour.

3984.w: About 15 percent of a dried cubeb berry is essential oil. In Victorian England it was distilled out and sold as an antiseptic marketed specifically against gonorrhoea, and 1908 medical literature described it as acting directly on the genitourinary tract.

3985.w: Nigella seed is about a third oil, and the thymoquinone in it is under active laboratory study rather than settled medicine: it is flagged as a pan-assay interference compound, meaning it binds many proteins nonspecifically and can produce misleading lab results.

3986.w: Quassin and neo-quassin, the quassinoids that give quassia bark its bitterness, are the compounds behind its historic use flavouring bitters and beer. Modern research has tested quassin alongside artesunate against malaria and classes quassia as a plant-toxin insecticide.

3987.w: Elecampane root's bitter, camphor-scented resin, historically called helenin, is made largely of the sesquiterpene lactones alantolactone and isoalantolactone. Herbal medicine still uses the root as an expectorant for bronchitis.

3988.w: The Ganges is worshipped in Hinduism as the goddess Ganga and considered sacred along its entire length, and cattle are honored as sacred, protected from slaughter across most of India.

3989.w: Buddhism's eight-spoked dharmachakra represents the Noble Eightfold Path taught by the Buddha, while the lotus, rising unstained from muddy water to bloom, symbolizes the purity of enlightenment.

3990.w: The Star of David is a widely recognized symbol of Jewish identity, and the eight-day festival of Hanukkah is marked by lighting candles on a nine-branched menorah each night.

3991.w: The ichthys fish was reportedly used by early Christians as a secret sign to identify fellow believers during Roman persecution, alongside the cross, Christianity's principal symbol.

3992.w: Traced to Laozi, and water is its central image: it yields to everything and wears away what will not yield to it.

3993.w: Sikhism's central scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, was declared the eternal, living Guru in 1708; initiated Sikhs also carry a kirpan, a small sword of iron or steel, as one of the Five Ks.

3994.w: Zoroastrians hold fire sacred as a symbol of Ahura Mazda and worship at fire temples, while the winged Faravahar figure is Zoroastrianism's best-known emblem.

3995.w: Shinto kami are typically tied to a natural feature such as a mountain, waterfall, or tree, and a sacred mirror, the Yata no Kagami, is one of Japan's three Imperial Regalia, associated with the sun goddess Amaterasu.

3996.w: Confucianism is built on sayings attributed to Confucius, compiled by his followers into the Analects; Confucian temples still hold ceremonies honoring Confucius and ancestors with ritual offerings and incense.

3997.w: The belief that souls or spirits are in animals, plants, rocks and rivers, and not only in people.

3998.w: Monotheism, belief in one God, characterizes the Abrahamic religious traditions of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

3999.w: Hinduism, which reveres deities such as Vishnu, and ancient Greek religion, led by Zeus and the Twelve Olympians, are two of many traditions built around the worship of numerous gods.

4000.w: Shinbutsu-shūgō, the syncretic blending of Shinto kami worship with Buddhism, was Japan's dominant organized religion from Buddhism's arrival until the Meiji era.

4001.w: In Buddhism, dharma refers to the Buddha's teachings and to the true nature of reality those teachings point to — one of the "Three Jewels," with the Buddha and the monastic Sangha, in which Buddhists take refuge.

4002.w: Karma is the Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Sikh principle that good or bad intent and deeds shape a person's fortune and the quality of their rebirth, turning the "wheel" of samsara that dharma's teaching aims to still.

4003.w: Nirvana literally means "blowing out" or "quenching" — Buddhism describes it as the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, as a flame is snuffed out and left as ash.

4004.w: Eggs have served as a symbol of fertility and rebirth since prehistory, while South Asian traditions describe the endless cycle of rebirth itself as a turning "wheel," samsara.

4005.w: Andrei Rublev's 15th-century icon "The Trinity" depicts the three winged angels who visited Abraham in Genesis 18, an image that came to represent the three persons of the Christian Trinity.

4006.w: The Five Pillars of Islam are the testimony of faith, prayer, almsgiving, fasting during Ramadan, and pilgrimage (Hajj) to Mecca — the obligatory acts of worship at the center of Muslim life.

4007.w: The idea of a god taking bodily form links Hinduism's avatars of Vishnu with Christianity's doctrine of the Incarnation, though theologians debate whether "avatar" and "incarnation" truly describe the same thing.

4008.w: "Messiah" comes from the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed," from a verb meaning "to rub with oil" — originally describing kings and priests ritually anointed before it came to mean an expected deliverer of Israel.

4009.w: The covenant between God and Israel, given to Moses at Sinai, contains the foundations of the written Torah and lies at the heart of Jewish religious law.

4010.w: Ancestor veneration — honoring and making offerings to the dead — is central to Chinese folk religion and many African traditions; incense sticks are burned before a household's ancestral spirit tablet, sometimes made of wood.

4011.w: Filial piety (xiao) — a person's duty to respect, obey, and care for their parents and ancestors — is the cardinal virtue of Confucianism, said by Confucius to be "the root of virtue."

4012.w: Rooted in animist belief in a spirit world, shamans enter trance states — sometimes through drumming, chanting, or the smoke of burned herbs — to travel between worlds on their community's behalf.

4013.w: Christianity's Desert Fathers withdrew into the Egyptian desert to live lives of prayer, fasting, and self-denial — a pattern of ascetic renunciation echoed by Hindu sadhus and by Jain and Buddhist monks elsewhere.

4014.w: A journey to a sacred place, undertaken for devotion, in nearly every major religion.

4015.w: Sikhism recognizes ten human Gurus beginning with founder Guru Nanak in 1469; in 1708 the tenth Guru passed the title to the Guru Granth Sahib scripture, which Sikhs have treated as their living Guru ever since.

4016.w: The Guru Granth Sahib is Sikhism's central scripture, compiled from hymns of the Sikh Gurus and other saints; since 1708 Sikhs have honored it as their eternal, living Guru.

4017.w: Tibetan Buddhist prayer wheels are inscribed with a written mantra, often "Om mani padme hum"; spinning the wheel is believed to carry much the same spiritual benefit as reciting the mantra aloud.

4018.w: Incense, made by burning aromatic plant materials such as resins and fragrant woods, is used in ceremonies across Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, Jewish, Islamic, and Chinese religious practice.

4019.w: Trigonella foenum-graecum is a legume grown three ways at once — as a seed spice, a dried herb and a fresh vegetable leaf. Charred seeds have turned up in Tutankhamun's tomb.

4020.w: Alpinia galanga (greater) and Alpinia officinarum (lesser) are both Zingiberaceae rhizomes, ginger's own family, dug up and used fresh or dried. Each has its own heat and its own flowery, peppery edge.

4021.w: Carum carvi is an Apiaceae herb; what's sold as a caraway seed is really the dried fruit, an achene about 3mm long. It looks so like cumin that many languages never separated the two.

4022.w: Physalis philadelphica and P. ixocarpa were domesticated in Mexico before European contact and outranked the tomato in Aztec and Maya cooking. The fruit is picked once it fills out the papery husk formed by its calyx.

4023.w: Physalis peruviana is a perennial shrub in the tropics but behaves as an annual anywhere frost cuts it back. Its papery calyx keeps expanding after the petals drop, sealing the ripening berry inside its own husk.

4024.w: Citrus microcarpa is a hybrid of kumquat and mandarin orange, native to the Philippines and nearby islands — standing in here for those two unmodelled parents. It's crushed whole for juice and used as a lemon or lime substitute across Filipino, Malaysian and Indonesian cooking.

4025.w: Ilex paraguariensis is a species of holly, native to Paraguay, northern Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, first cultivated by the Guaraní. Harvested branches are dried over a wood fire, which is where the drink's smoky flavour comes from.

4026.w: Citrus bergamia is a probable hybrid of lemon and bitter orange, standing in here for that unmodelled bitter-orange parent. Its rind is cold-pressed for the oil that flavours Earl Grey tea, and Reggio Calabria in southern Italy supplies nearly the entire world's crop.

4027.w: Jasminum sambac flowers are harvested as unopened white buds in the early morning, then open at night before closing for good the next day. About 70 percent of the scent is indole — foul in high concentration, floral in trace amounts.

4028.w: Most plantains are sterile AAB-group triploids, hybrids of Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana. They carry far more starch and far less sugar than dessert bananas, so they're cooked rather than eaten raw, and Musa's poor wind tolerance leaves plantations vulnerable to hurricanes.

4029.w: Amomum subulatum is Zingiberaceae like green cardamom but a separate species; its pods are dried over open flames, which is where its smoky flavour comes from. Nepal is the largest producer, ahead of India and Bhutan.

4030.w: Cucurbita moschata; the butternut cultivar was bred in 1944 by Charles Leggett of Stow, Massachusetts, crossing two older squashes. Its orange flesh carries over 4,500 micrograms of beta-carotene per 100g.

4031.w: Tropaeolum majus, native to the Andes, has flowers, leaves and seed pods that are all edible, with a peppery bite close to watercress. Its leaf is a textbook case of the lotus effect: water gathers into beads and rolls off instead of wetting the surface.

4032.w: Perilla frutescens is a Lamiaceae annual native to Southeast Asia and the Indian highlands, grown for its aromatic leaves — shiso, in Japanese cooking. In the United States it has escaped into pastures, where cattle grazing on it can develop acute respiratory distress, called panting disease.

4033.w: Nigella sativa is a Ranunculaceae flowering annual, unrelated to true cumin despite the 'black cumin' name. Its seeds carry thymoquinone alongside p-cymene, carvacrol and thymol, and are dry-roasted before use in blends like Bengali panch phoron.

4034.w: Artemisia absinthium, the herb that gives absinthe its name and much of its bitterness, is a hardy plant of temperate and cold climates — the Ukrainian city of Chernobyl takes its name from the local word for it. Its thujone can cause convulsions at high doses, but studies have found no evidence it caused the 19th-century 'absinthism' panic.

4035.w: Boiled, pounded soybeans are shaped into meju bricks and air-dried until a wild mould coats them, then aged in brine inside earthenware jars, sometimes for months. Jars used for doenjang production appear in 4th-century Goguryeo tomb murals.

4036.w: Traditional gochujang blends red chilli powder with fermented soybean and glutinous rice, aged for years in sun-exposed earthenware jars — simplified here to chilli fermented against an existing fermented-soybean base. Sunchang has been renowned for its gochujang since the Joseon dynasty's founding in the 14th century.

4037.w: Steam distillation, not crushing, is how geraniol is actually drawn out of lemongrass — a monoterpenoid alcohol and, together with citronellol, one of the two compounds that give lemongrass its lemon scent despite no citrus being involved. It is also a major component of rose and palmarosa oil.

4038.w: Oxidative cleavage breaks beta-carotene down into beta-ionone, the compound behind the scent of violets and a reason cooked carrots and squash smell more floral than raw ones. It's synthesized industrially from citral and acetone for the fragrance trade.

4039.w: Ethyl hexanoate is a fruity, pineapple-and-apple-peel ester formed from hexanoic acid and ethanol. Penicillium roqueforti produces it as blue cheese ripens, and food-chemistry surveys list it among the compounds most responsible for the cheese's aroma.

4040.w: A sulphur compound whose smell is foul at high concentration and pungently savoury in the trace amounts found in food. It has been identified among the volatile sulphur compounds of Tuber melanosporum black truffle, and separately in the aroma profile built by Penicillium roqueforti in blue cheese.

4041.w: Sufi practitioners cultivate dhikr, the remembrance of God, sometimes visualizing his name as written upon the heart -- an inward path toward union with the divine that complements Islam's outward law.

4042.w: In 1889, Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founded the Ahmadiyya movement, claiming through revelation that he was the Mahdi ('rightly guided one') and Messiah that Islamic tradition expected to appear at the end times.

4043.w: Shia Muslims trace legitimate leadership of the Muslim community through Muhammad's bloodline, beginning with his son-in-law Ali, rather than through election -- a hereditary claim to succession that Sunnis reject.

4044.w: Sunni Islam holds that Muhammad did not appoint a successor; instead the first caliph, Abu Bakr, was chosen by the consensus of the community -- the elected, communally bound model of leadership followed by roughly 85-90 percent of Muslims today.

4045.w: The word sharia literally means 'path to the watering hole,' a metaphor rooted in the importance of a reliable route to water across the Arabian desert -- sharia is likewise conceived as the path God has laid out to a good life.

4046.w: Jihad, Arabic for "striving," is traditionally divided into the "greater jihad" — the internal struggle against one's own base desires — and the "lesser jihad" of external effort, guided directly by the Quran's own teaching.

4047.w: In 1744, the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed a pact with the Najdi ruler Muhammad bin Saud, uniting his puritanical desert movement with a ruling dynasty in an alliance that founded the first Saudi state.

4048.w: Salafi, Arabic for 'predecessors,' names a movement that looks to the salaf -- the first three generations of Muslims, from Muhammad onward -- as the root and purest model of Islamic practice.

4049.w: The Nation of Islam grew out of and reinterprets Islam in an African-American context; its own flag places a star beside the crescent moon, on a design modeled on the flag of Turkey.

4050.w: The Druze faith, which took shape in Cairo around 1017 CE, teaches that the soul is eternal and passes through successive reincarnations until it reunites with the Cosmic Mind; the five-pointed star is its principal religious emblem.

4051.w: The nine-pointed star, the Baha'i Faith's most widely used symbol, reflects the numerical value of 9 that the word 'Baha' -- meaning glory -- carries in the Abjad numeral system used in Baha'i scripture.

4052.w: Haile Selassie's full imperial title, 'Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah, Elect of God and King of the Kings of Ethiopia,' taken at his 1930 coronation, was seen by Jamaican Rastafarians as fulfilling prophecy and confirming him as their returned savior.

4053.w: In Santeria, the Yoruba orisha Chango -- god of thunder, lightning, and fire -- was concealed by enslaved worshippers in Cuba behind the image of the Catholic martyr Santa Barbara, since both are depicted wearing red.

4054.w: In Haitian Vodou, the lwa spirit Papa Legba, who guards the crossroads between the human and spirit worlds, was syncretized with the Catholic Saint Peter, keeper of heaven's gate, since Legba is likewise the 'door' to the spirit realm.

4055.w: After World War II ended and military cargo deliveries stopped, some Melanesian islanders built life-size replicas of airplanes out of straw and cut new landing strips from the jungle, hoping the ritual would attract more cargo-bearing aircraft.

4056.w: Scientology grew from L. Ron Hubbard's 1950 book Dianetics; its central practice, auditing, uses a wired device called the E-meter, which the Church describes as a spiritual tool for detecting areas of mental or spiritual trauma.

4057.w: Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954; it became known worldwide for mass 'Blessing' wedding ceremonies, including one in 1982 that joined 2,000 couples at Madison Square Garden.

4058.w: Wicca, popularized by Gerald Gardner in 1950s England, is typically duotheistic, venerating a goddess and a god traditionally conceived as the Triple Goddess and the Horned God.

4059.w: Unitarian Universalism, formed in 1961 by the merger of the Unitarian and Universalist churches, uses the flaming chalice as its most widely recognized symbol.

4060.w: Tenrikyo, founded in 1838 by Nakayama Miki, teaches that eight kinds of mental 'dust' -- including greed, anger, and self-love -- must be swept away through acts of kindness to live the Joyous Life.

4061.w: Cao Dai, founded in Vietnam in 1926, represents God with the Left Eye of God, or Divine Eye, enshrined at its Tay Ninh Holy See, reminding believers that God witnesses everything, everywhere, constantly.

4062.w: Jehovah's Witnesses are widely recognized for their door-to-door ministry, distributing literature such as The Watchtower magazine as they visit homes to spread their beliefs.

4063.w: Joseph Smith said the angel Moroni directed him to a set of golden plates buried near Palmyra, New York, which he translated into the Book of Mormon, published in 1830 alongside the founding of his church.

4064.w: Quakers, founded by George Fox in mid-17th-century England, traditionally practice waiting worship, gathering mostly in silence and speaking only when moved by the Inner Light.

4065.w: In 1693, Jakob Ammann led a stricter schism from the Swiss and Alsatian Mennonites, founding the Amish, whose communities remain distinctive today for traveling by horse-drawn buggy rather than motor vehicle.

4066.w: Mennonites trace their name to the Frisian reformer Menno Simons; the movement's Anabaptist founders baptized one another as adults near Zurich in January 1525, rejecting infant baptism.

4067.w: The Shakers, founded by Ann Lee around 1747, were originally nicknamed 'Shaking Quakers' for the ecstatic trembling, marching, and dancing that characterized their worship services.

4068.w: Formally established in 1863 in Battle Creek, Michigan, the Seventh-day Adventist Church has advocated a vegetarian diet since its founding, alongside observing Saturday, the Bible's seventh day, as the Sabbath.

4069.w: Pentecostalism takes its name from the Christian Pentecost, when the Bible describes the Holy Spirit descending as 'tongues of fire'; the modern movement began at the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles.

4070.w: Mary Baker Eddy founded the Church of Christ, Scientist in Boston in 1879; her textbook Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, alongside the Bible, is regarded by the church as its 'dual impersonal pastor.'

4071.w: The Salvation Army, founded by William Booth in 1865, is famous for its Christmas-season red kettles, where volunteers ring bells to invite passers-by to drop coins and cash into donation pots.

4072.w: In 1534, King Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy severed the Church of England from Rome and declared the English crown its supreme head, founding Anglicanism.

4073.w: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses, written in 1517, protested the Church's sale of indulgences -- payments believed to reduce punishment for sin -- and are traditionally seen as having sparked the Protestant Reformation and Lutheranism.

4074.w: John Knox, who studied under John Calvin in Geneva, carried Calvin's Reformed theology back to Scotland, establishing the Presbyterian tradition of church government by elected elders bound together in representative assemblies.

4075.w: John Wesley, founder of Methodism, described his 1738 conversion experience at a Moravian meeting in Aldersgate, London, saying he felt his 'heart strangely warmed' -- the spark that ignited the Methodist revival within the Church of England.

4076.w: In 1609, John Smyth baptized adult believers by full immersion in Amsterdam, founding the Baptist tradition on the principle -- laid out in his own tract -- that only professing believers, not infants, should be baptized.

4077.w: Reform Judaism's 1885 Pittsburgh Platform declared that ceremonial rituals were binding only insofar as they enhanced the religious life of the modern Jew, elevating ethics over ritual observance.

4078.w: Orthodox Judaism emerged as a self-conscious movement during the 1818-1821 Hamburg Temple dispute, when Rabbi Moses Sofer led rabbis across Europe in defending traditional, unaltered observance of halakha against Reform-influenced changes.

4079.w: Hasidic Judaism was founded around 1730-1740 by Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov ('Master of the Good Name'), who taught a joyful, mystical path to God centered on ecstatic devotion rather than solely scholarly study.

4080.w: Conservative Judaism developed as a deliberate middle path between Reform and Orthodox Judaism, institutionalized around the Jewish Theological Seminary of America, founded in New York in 1887.

4081.w: Kabbalah's foundational text, the Zohar, describes ten sefirot -- emanations through which God sustains the universe -- traditionally diagrammed as a Tree of Life.

4082.w: The Heliodorus pillar, a stone column erected around 110 BCE by an Indo-Greek envoy who inscribed himself as a devotee of the 'God of gods' Vasudeva, is among the earliest archaeological evidence of organized Vaishnava worship of Vishnu.

4083.w: Shaktism's oldest scriptural evidence is the Rigveda's Devi Sukta hymn, in which the Goddess proclaims herself 'the Queen, the gatherer-up of treasures' -- the supreme reality later known as Devi or Shakti.

4084.w: Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875 as a Hindu reform movement; it became the first Hindu organization to actively seek converts, and today runs more than 1,000 colleges and 10,000 schools across India.

4085.w: Maharishi Mahesh Yogi introduced Transcendental Meditation to the West in 1955; practitioners silently repeat a personal mantra for 15-20 minutes twice a day, a technique popularized in the 1960s by the Beatles and the Beach Boys.

4086.w: The Pali Canon, scriptural foundation of Theravada Buddhism -- the oldest surviving Buddhist school -- was committed to writing in the 1st century BCE, the most complete Buddhist canon in a classical Indian language.

4087.w: Mahayana Buddhism, which spread from India to become the dominant tradition in China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan, emphasizes the bodhisattva vow -- a pledge binding practitioners to postpone their own final liberation to help save all beings.

4088.w: Zen Buddhism, which developed as Chan in Tang-dynasty China and is traditionally said to have been brought from India by the monk Bodhidharma, centers its practice on zazen -- seated meditation in profound stillness.

4089.w: In 1578, the Mongol ruler Altan Khan bestowed the title Dalai Lama on the Tibetan Buddhist monk Sonam Gyatso, a title of spiritual authority that has passed by recognized reincarnation ever since.

4090.w: Pure Land Buddhism teaches that Amitabha Buddha vowed to create a paradise, Sukhavati, described in Buddhist scripture as covered in beryl and gold and free of filth or evil, reached by the faithful through devoted recitation of his name.

4091.w: Nichiren, a 13th-century Japanese monk, taught that chanting devotion to the Lotus Sutra -- Namu Myoho Renge Kyo -- was Buddhism's sole valid practice for this age, founding the school that bears his name.

4092.w: In 1930, Japanese educators Tsunesaburo Makiguchi and Josei Toda founded Soka Gakkai as a lay society grounded in Nichiren Buddhism's veneration of the Lotus Sutra; Makiguchi died in prison in 1944 after refusing to recant his beliefs during WWII.

4093.w: Sumerian scribes pressed a sharpened reed stylus into wet clay tablets, first as pictographs and, by the mid-3rd millennium BCE, as wedge-shaped signs -- faster to make in soft clay.

4094.w: Hammurabi's roughly 4,130 lines of cuneiform law were cut into a 2.25 m basalt stele, using a layout already old-fashioned by his own reign.

4095.w: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro rose along the Indus in standardized fired brick, sharing a single measuring system -- the Mohenjo-daro ruler, marked off in 34 mm units -- across a civilization larger than Egypt or Mesopotamia.

4096.w: Shang diviners scorched turtle plastrons and ox scapulae with a hot rod until thermal stress cracked them, then read the crack pattern as an answer from the ancestors.

4097.w: The Shang court that commissioned oracle-bone divinations also cast some of the ancient world's most elaborate bronze vessels, reserved for ritual rather than daily use.

4098.w: By around 2650 BCE, masted Cretan ships -- and bronze that had by then moved from arsenical alloys to tin bronze -- carried Minoan trade beyond the Aegean to Egypt and Syria.

4099.w: By 1450 BCE the palace of Knossos had passed to a Mycenaean elite, who adapted the Minoans' undeciphered Linear A into Linear B -- the earliest written record of the Greek language.

4100.w: Within decades around 1200 BCE, Mycenaean palace centers were destroyed, the Hittite Empire collapsed entirely, and Ugarit was sacked, even as ironworking -- which needed no long, vulnerable bronze trade routes -- was spreading in from Bulgaria and Romania.

4101.w: The Phoenicians' maritime trading culture carried their compact, phonetic script across the Mediterranean to North Africa and southern Europe, where it became the direct ancestor of the Greek alphabet.

4102.w: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, which began in 911 BCE with the accession of Adad-nirari II, administered its territory in Akkadian cuneiform and conquered Egypt in 671 BCE -- where iron only replaced bronze in the wake of that conquest.

4103.w: Cyrus the Great's Achaemenid empire, built on cavalry-heavy conquests of Media and Lydia, overran Nebuchadnezzar's Neo-Babylonian empire in 539 BCE, entering Babylon with almost no resistance and freeing its Jewish exiles per the Cyrus Cylinder.

4104.w: Two generations after Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Empire, his successor Darius I sent it against Greece; Athenian hoplite spearmen, outnumbered roughly two to one, broke the Persian line at Marathon in 490 BCE.

4105.w: Two centuries after Cyrus founded it, Alexander's ten-year campaign broke Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, conquering the entire Achaemenid Persian Empire in his father's stead.

4106.w: China's First Emperor was buried near Xi'an behind an army of thousands of individually crafted, life-sized terracotta soldiers, chariots, and horses -- fired clay meant to guard him in the afterlife.

4107.w: After the Kalinga War left him remorseful, Ashoka had edicts of Buddhist dharma carved into rock and stone pillars across his empire -- the Dhauli inscription's rock face shaped into a standing elephant.

4108.w: Carthage grew from a Phoenician colony of Tyrian traders on the North African coast into the capital of its own Punic empire, its people still writing and speaking a Canaanite tongue.

4109.w: The Carthaginian general Hannibal led 38,000 troops and 38 war elephants across the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE; almost none of the elephants survived the crossing.

4110.w: In January 49 BCE Caesar led his legion across the Rubicon, the river marking Italy's northern boundary -- an act forbidden to any general under arms -- igniting the civil war that ended the Republic.

4111.w: When Alexander's empire fractured on his death in 323 BCE, his general Ptolemy I took Egypt and founded the Ptolemaic dynasty; Cleopatra VII, who became queen in 51 BCE, was its last ruler.

4112.w: Caesar's adopted heir Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, taking Egypt, and in 27 BCE was granted the title Augustus by the Senate -- Rome's first emperor.

4113.w: Following Han envoy Zhang Qian's reports on Central Asia around 130 BCE, camel caravans carried Chinese silk as far as Rome, where the Senate tried in vain to ban it as a decadent drain of gold.

4114.w: The Nubian kingdom of Kush, on the Nile south of Egypt, conquered Egypt under King Piye around 727 BCE to found its 25th Dynasty, and its later capital Meroe grew into a major ironworking center rich in ore and hardwood fuel.

4115.w: Hinduism evolved over more than 3,000 years from the Vedic religion of the Indus-Ganges region and rests on scriptures such as the Vedas and Upanishads, with no single founder.

4116.w: After his conversion, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka issued edicts protecting dozens of animal species from slaughter and cutting the animals killed daily for his own kitchen, putting ahimsa into imperial policy.

4117.w: Mohandas Gandhi built his campaigns of nonviolent civil disobedience, which he called satyagraha, on ahimsa, the principle of nonviolence.

4118.w: Buddhism traces its origin to the 6th-century-BCE teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, later gathered by his followers into scriptures such as the Pali Canon.

4119.w: After the Buddha's death, his teaching was carried on by a growing community of monks and teachers, who over the centuries split into the Theravada and Mahayana traditions.

4120.w: In Buddhist thought, karma is the principle that intentional actions shape future rebirths, keeping beings tied to samsara until the Buddhist path leads them out.

4121.w: In Hindu philosophy, karma in the present shapes the nature and quality of a person's future lives, or samsara.

4122.w: In Hinduism, dharma refers to a person's moral and religious duty appropriate to their place in life — the dharma of a farmer differs from that of a soldier.

4123.w: Nirvana comes from a Sanskrit word meaning 'blown out': Buddhists describe it as the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion that cause suffering.

4124.w: Buddhists hold that following the Noble Eightfold Path ends craving and leads to nirvana, a state of liberation the Buddha described as attainable in this life.

4125.w: In Hindu belief, samsara is the beginningless cycle of death and rebirth, driven onward by karma, the residue of past actions.

4126.w: Buddhism inherited the idea of samsara, an endless cycle of rebirth driven by karma, from earlier Indian religion, while denying that any fixed self passes between lives.

4127.w: The Buddha's first sermon set out Four Noble Truths: dukkha (suffering), samudaya (its origin), nirodha (its ending), and magga (the path to its ending).

4128.w: Buddhist tradition holds that the Buddha first taught the Four Noble Truths in a sermon called 'Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion,' delivered after his enlightenment.

4129.w: The Noble Eightfold Path is the content of Buddhism's Fourth Noble Truth: eight practices of right view, speech, and action grouped into wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline.

4130.w: The earliest description of the Buddhist path may have been simply 'the Middle Way'; over time this short description was elaborated into the fuller Eightfold Path.

4131.w: Having tried both a life of luxury and years of extreme asceticism, Siddhartha Gautama taught that a balanced Middle Way between these extremes leads to enlightenment.

4132.w: In Mahayana Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a being on the path to enlightenment who, out of compassion, vows to delay or forgo their own nirvana to help all others reach it too.

4133.w: Bodhisattva images are often shown holding a lotus, an ancient symbol of purity said to rise from muddy water unstained, representing the enlightened mind above worldly suffering.

4134.w: Zen, called Chan in China, is a Buddhist meditation tradition traditionally traced to the monk Bodhidharma, said to have brought it from India to China around the 5th-6th century CE.

4135.w: Japanese Zen gardens of carefully raked gravel or sand serve as aids to meditation, and Zen monks practice the raking itself to help their concentration.

4136.w: The Dalai Lama, leading figure of Tibetan Buddhism's Gelug school, is traditionally regarded as the living incarnation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

4137.w: When a Dalai Lama dies, monks search for his successor among young children and test candidates by having them identify personal belongings of their predecessor, taken as a sign of true reincarnation.

4138.w: Ashoka, emperor of the Mauryan Empire, converted to Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE after a bloody war of conquest, and thereafter promoted Buddhist principles including protection of animal life.

4139.w: Many of Ashoka's edicts survive carved onto rock faces and stone pillars across the Indian subcontinent, among the oldest deciphered inscriptions in Indian history.

4140.w: Judaism's practice and identity are organized around a series of covenants between God and the Israelites, first with Abraham and renewed through Moses, recorded in the Torah.

4141.w: A Torah scroll is handwritten entirely by a trained scribe on parchment, using a quill dipped in special ink, a task that can take about a year and a half.

4142.w: According to the Torah, God inscribed the Ten Commandments onto two stone tablets and gave them to Moses on Mount Sinai.

4143.w: The Ten Commandments form the core of the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai, prohibiting the worship of other gods and mandating a weekly Sabbath day of rest.

4144.w: The Torah describes a covenant God made with the Israelites at Mount Sinai, promising to make them 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' if they kept his commandments.

4145.w: The Torah also describes an earlier covenant with Noah after the flood, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood — a promise it says the rainbow was given to signify.

4146.w: Kabbalah is a body of Jewish mystical teaching, originally transmitted orally and collected in a text called the Zohar, or 'Divine Splendor,' traditionally dated to 13th-century Spain.

4147.w: The influential 16th-century kabbalist Isaac Luria taught that creation involved vessels shattering under the strain of holding divine light, scattering sparks that people gather and restore through good deeds.

4148.w: In Jewish tradition, 'messiah' (Hebrew for 'anointed one') originally meant any anointed king, but came to mean a specific future ruler descended from King David who would restore Israel.

4149.w: Among the traditional reasons for sounding the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, the medieval scholar Saadia Gaon listed arousing belief in the future ingathering of the exiles and the coming of the Messiah.

4150.w: After Rome crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE and barred Jews from Jerusalem, the Jewish diaspora — communities dispersed beyond their homeland — became the center of Jewish life for centuries.

4151.w: Displaced first by Babylon in the 6th century BCE and again by Rome in 70 CE, Jewish communities scattered across the Mediterranean world, forming the diaspora that would shape Jewish life for two millennia.

4152.w: The 12th-century philosopher Moses Maimonides argued that God's absolute oneness means God has no parts or describable attributes, a position known as negative theology.

4153.w: Early Christians adopted the ichthys, a simple two-arc fish outline, as a visual shorthand for their faith, evoking the Gospel image of the apostles as 'fishers of men.'

4154.w: The doctrine of the Trinity was settled in its classic form at the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE and expanded at the Council of Constantinople in 381 CE, in the Nicene Creed.

4155.w: In 325 CE the Roman emperor Constantine convened bishops from across his empire at Nicaea to agree a common statement of Christian belief, aiming to end disputes dividing the newly tolerated faith.

4156.w: The Nicene Creed condemned the teaching of Arius, known as Arianism, that the Son was not co-eternal with God the Father but a distinct being of merely similar substance.

4157.w: In the Eucharist, Christians reenact Jesus's Last Supper, at which he shared bread and wine with his disciples, calling the bread 'my body' and the cup 'the blood of my covenant.'

4158.w: The 13th-century theologian Thomas Aquinas gave classic form to the doctrine of transubstantiation, teaching that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ while their outward appearance does not.

4159.w: Baptism, one of Christianity's most widespread rites, marks a person's entry into the Church through ritual washing with water, following the example of Jesus's own baptism by John the Baptist in the Jordan.

4160.w: Christian monasticism traces its roots to 3rd-century hermits such as Anthony of Egypt, who withdrew into the desert to live simple lives of prayer and ascetic discipline.

4161.w: Medieval European monasteries became centers of learning where monks copied and illuminated manuscripts, preserving much of the West's literary heritage through the Middle Ages.

4162.w: Martin Luther was angered by the Church's sale of indulgences, payments believed to reduce punishment for sin, and in 1517 wrote 95 Theses opposing the practice, helping ignite the Protestant Reformation.

4163.w: The recently invented printing press let Martin Luther's 1522 German translation of the New Testament spread rapidly and cheaply, letting ordinary people read scripture for themselves and fueling the Reformation.

4164.w: Metal rods are heated soft, bent into rings, and forge-welded shut before they cool, then linked together — a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

4165.w: Once doors could be barred, a metal sliver shaped to match one lock's internal wards let its owner — and no one else — open it.

4166.w: Prometheus fashioned the first humans from clay, then stole fire from the gods' own forge, hidden inside a hollow fennel stalk, and gave it to his creations.

4167.w: For stealing fire, Zeus chained Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus and sent an eagle to eat his liver; it regrew every night so the torment never ended, until Heracles freed him.

4168.w: Prometheus's brother Epimetheus — "Afterthought" to Prometheus's "Forethought" — ignored his warning never to accept a gift from Zeus, and married Pandora anyway.

4169.w: Hephaestus molded Pandora, the first woman, from clay on Zeus's orders; every god then added a gift, from beauty to a dangerously curious mind.

4170.w: Hesiod's original jar (later mistranslated "box") that Pandora opened despite the warning, loosing every evil into the world — only Hope stayed trapped inside.

4171.w: Punished by Zeus for leading the Titans against the Olympians, Atlas was condemned to hold up the heavens forever — a burden Heracles briefly shouldered so Atlas could fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides.

4172.w: Son of Prometheus, Deucalion built a wooden chest that let him and his wife Pyrrha survive nine days of the flood Zeus sent to destroy a corrupt humanity.

4173.w: Told by an oracle to throw "the bones of their mother" behind them, Deucalion and Pyrrha cast stones over their shoulders — his became men, hers became women, repopulating the earth.

4174.w: Crete's exiled master craftsman built the Labyrinth to hold the Minotaur, then fashioned wings of feathers bound with beeswax so he and his son Icarus could fly free of the island.

4175.w: Wearing wings his father built, Icarus ignored every warning and flew too close to the sun; the wax melted and he fell into the sea that now bears his name.

4176.w: Son of the sun god Helios, Phaethon begged to drive his father's chariot for a day, lost control near the earth, and was struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt before he could burn the world.

4177.w: Daedalus built this maze on Crete at King Minos's order to contain the Minotaur — its passages so winding that no one inside could find the way out unaided.

4178.w: Born when Queen Pasiphaë mated with a bull sent by Poseidon, the half-man half-bull Minotaur was imprisoned by King Minos inside the Labyrinth built to contain it.

4179.w: Sent as one of Athens's tribute youths to Crete, Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth and used Ariadne's ball of thread to find his way back out.

4180.w: After her ball of thread saved Theseus from the Labyrinth, Ariadne was abandoned on Naxos — where the god Dionysus found and married her.

4181.w: Conceived when Zeus visited the imprisoned princess Danaë as a shower of gold, Perseus grew up to behead the Gorgon Medusa using a mirrored shield to avoid her petrifying gaze.

4182.w: One of three Gorgon sisters but the only mortal one, Medusa's living snake hair and stone-turning gaze made her deadly until Perseus beheaded her with Athena's mirrored shield.

4183.w: When Perseus beheaded the pregnant Medusa, the winged horse Pegasus sprang fully formed from her blood, along with his brother, the giant Chrysaor.

4184.w: Chained to a sea cliff as a sacrifice to the monster Poseidon sent to punish her mother Cassiopeia's boast, Andromeda was rescued — and later married — by Perseus.

4185.w: The fleece of the winged golden ram Chrysomallus, hung on an oak in a sacred grove of Colchis and guarded by a dragon that never slept.

4186.w: Rightful heir to Iolcos, Jason sailed the Argo to Colchis to win the Golden Fleece for his crown — a quest only the sorceress Medea's love and magic made possible.

4187.w: The Colchian sorceress helped Jason win the Golden Fleece by lulling its sleepless dragon guardian with narcotic herbs — a mortal reaching into a god of sleep's own domain.

4188.w: Unlike Egypt's benevolent guardian statues, the Greek Sphinx — a woman's head on a winged lion's body — strangled every traveler at Thebes who failed her riddle.

4189.w: Fated by a Delphic prophecy to kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus fulfilled it unknowingly, then won the Theban throne by solving the Sphinx's riddle about man's three ages.

4190.w: Greek mythology's greatest musician, Orpheus charmed the lord of the underworld with his lyre after his wife Eurydice died of a snakebite, winning permission to lead her back to the living.

4191.w: Orpheus's bride was allowed to follow him out of the underworld on one condition — that he not look back until both reached the surface. He looked back too soon, and she was lost forever.

4192.w: Mortal princess loved by Cupid (Eros), Psyche was set impossible tasks by jealous Venus, including fetching a jar of beauty from Persephone in the Underworld — which she opened despite every warning.

4193.w: As thanks for kindly hosting the satyr Silenus, King Midas won a wish from Dionysus: everything he touched would turn to gold — a blessing that became a curse the moment his food and wine did too.

4194.w: The nymph Echo used to distract Hera with long stories so other nymphs could escape notice while Zeus pursued them; when Hera realized the trick, she cursed Echo to only ever repeat the last words spoken to her.

4195.w: The beautiful youth who spurned Echo's love fell instead for his own reflection in a woodland pool, wasted away staring at it, and was transformed into the flower that bears his name.

4196.w: A Lydian weaver so skilled she claimed to surpass Athena, Arachne wove a tapestry mocking the gods' misdeeds; after the contest that followed ended in her disgrace, she was reborn as the first spider.

4197.w: Described by Plato as an advanced island empire beyond the Pillars of Heracles that grew corrupt and warred on Athens, Atlantis was swallowed by the sea "in a single day and night" as divine punishment.

4198.w: Roman god of doorways, gates, and transitions, Janus was shown with two faces looking in opposite directions at once; no Greek god matches him, and the month of January bears his name.

4199.w: First of Kronos's children swallowed, and the last disgorged, Hestia is the Greek goddess of the hearth fire that burned at the heart of every home and city.

4200.w: Vesta is Hestia's Roman counterpart, virgin goddess of the hearth; the Vestal Virgins tended her eternal flame in the Roman Forum for over a thousand years.

4201.w: Twin son of the war god Mars and the priestess Rhea Silvia, Romulus was suckled by a she-wolf after being abandoned as an infant, then founded Rome in 753 BCE.

4202.w: Romulus's twin, also suckled by the she-wolf as an infant; when Remus mocked the walls of his brother's new city, Romulus (or one of his supporters) killed him.

4203.w: Son of the goddess Aphrodite (Venus) and the Trojan Anchises, Aeneas carried his father from burning Troy on his back and, per Virgil's Aeneid, became the legendary ancestor of Rome's founders.

4204.w: Succeeding Romulus as Rome's second king, the Sabine Numa Pompilius held nightly consultations with the nymph Egeria and founded the Vestal cult, the priesthoods, and the Roman calendar.
