4205.w: The Anatolian "Great Mother" goddess, worshipped in Phrygia since the Bronze Age, is shown enthroned with a lion; Rome formally adopted her in 204 BCE as a black meteoric stone carried from Pessinus.

4206.w: Cybele's devoted companion Attis castrated himself in a fit of madness beneath a pine tree and bled to death; the goddess mourned him into a yearly spring resurrection, and the pine became sacred to her cult.

4207.w: Center of a secretive Roman mystery religion practiced in underground temples, Mithras dragged the cosmic bull into a cave and killed it with a dagger — the scene, called the tauroctony, decorated every one of his shrines.

4208.w: A Cypriot sculptor carved an ivory woman so beautiful he fell in love with his own creation; when he prayed at her festival, Venus (Aphrodite) brought the statue to life.

4209.w: Apollo granted the Sibyl of Cumae as many years of life as grains of dust in her hand, but not eternal youth, so she withered for centuries; she later guided Aeneas into the Underworld.

4210.w: Mecca sat at the crossroads of major desert caravan routes, its trade — much of it by camel — making it the wealthiest Arabian trading town by the 6th century.

4211.w: Muhammad grew up in Mecca and, before any revelation, led camel caravans on trade routes to Syria for the merchant Khadija, whom he later married.

4212.w: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad received his first revelation from the angel Gabriel in a cave near Mecca in 610, the event Muslims mark as Islam's origin.

4213.w: Threatened in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers accepted an invitation from Yathrib's feuding tribes to migrate there in 622 and mediate between them — the hijra that renamed the city Medina.

4214.w: After the civil war following Caliph Ali's assassination, Mu'awiyah founded the Umayyad dynasty in 661, moving the caliphate's capital from Medina to Damascus.

4215.w: The Abbasid Revolution of 750 overthrew the Umayyads, the new dynasty claiming legitimacy through descent from Muhammad's uncle Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

4216.w: Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris River in 762 as the Abbasid capital, and within a generation it had grown into a center of learning, home to the House of Wisdom.

4217.w: The Seljuk chieftain Tugrul Beg took Baghdad in 1055; from then on the Abbasid caliphs kept only religious authority while the Seljuk sultans held the real power.

4218.w: Around 552, Nestorian monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of Central Asia for Emperor Justinian, breaking China's monopoly and founding a silk industry that, with its stable gold solidus coin, helped fund the empire for centuries.

4219.w: In 1095, Byzantine Emperor Alexius I appealed to Pope Urban II for help against Seljuk Turk advances; the Pope's call at Clermont that November launched the First Crusade toward Jerusalem.

4220.w: Chinese gunsmiths cast the earliest known cannons in bronze by the 13th century — the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the oldest confirmed survivor — before the technology reached Europe in the 1320s.

4221.w: In 1453, Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II's cannons — including a Hungarian engineer's 27-foot bombard — battered gaps in Constantinople's walls after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire.

4222.w: Raised among horse-mounted nomads who lived in felt-covered gers on the steppe, Temüjin united the rival Mongol clans and, in 1206, was proclaimed Genghis Khan at an assembly on the Onon River.

4223.w: Genghis Khan's conquests unified Central Asia under Mongol rule, and the resulting Pax Mongolica secured the Silk Road for merchants and travelers — Marco Polo among them.

4224.w: Mongol forces besieging the Genoese trading post of Caffa in Crimea let the plague reach the Black Sea in 1346; fleeing Genoese ships carried it to Sicily by October 1347, launching it in Europe.

4225.w: The bubonic plague bacterium Yersinia pestis is carried by fleas living on rats — the transmission mechanism behind the pandemic that killed between a third and half of Europe's population.

4226.w: Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai pushed Mongol armies past the Great Wall frontier to conquer Song China, founding the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completing the conquest by 1279.

4227.w: Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty issued jiaochao, paper banknotes that circulated nationwide — a currency so novel that Marco Polo described it to disbelieving Europeans.

4228.w: Born into a poor rice-farming family, Zhu Yuanzhang joined the agrarian Red Turban Rebellion against Yuan rule in 1352 and, by 1368, had overthrown the Mongols to found the Ming as the Hongwu Emperor.

4229.w: The Ming Yongle Emperor built his new Beijing palace complex from 1406 to 1420 using whole logs of precious phoebe zhennan timber hauled from southwestern China's jungles, alongside specially baked brick.

4230.w: The Yongle Emperor commissioned the eunuch admiral Zheng He to lead seven treasure-fleet voyages between 1405 and 1433, reaching as far as the Swahili coast of East Africa.

4231.w: With the Ming capital falling to a rebel army in 1644, Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to Manchu forces, who defeated the rebels and founded the Qing dynasty in Beijing.

4232.w: As Japan's national conscript army dissolved by the late 8th century, wealthy landholding families who could afford horses, iron weapons, and years of archery training formed the mounted warrior class that became the samurai.

4233.w: A katana's blade is folded and welded from steel, then differentially quenched under a layer of clay slurry to harden its edge; the Tokugawa shogunate required samurai to wear one as a mark of rank.

4234.w: Minamoto no Yoritomo's samurai crushed the rival Taira clan at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, and in 1192 he was appointed shogun, founding Japan's first military government at Kamakura.

4235.w: Turkic cavalry armies carried Islam into northern India, routing Rajput defenders in 1192 under Muhammad of Ghor; after his death in 1206, his former slave-general Qutb-ud-din Aibak became the first Sultan of Delhi.

4236.w: Timur styled himself the restorer of Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire, and in 1398 his armies captured and sacked Delhi, devastating the Sultanate so badly the city took nearly a century to recover.

4237.w: Babur, descended from Tamerlane and Genghis Khan, used matchlock guns and field cannon behind a barricade of carts to rout the Delhi Sultanate's far larger army at Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire.

4238.w: Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire in 802, and its wealth rested on a vast hydraulic network of canals and reservoirs that irrigated rice paddies fed by the Tonlé Sap and its rivers.

4239.w: King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1122 and 1150 as a temple-mountain, its central towers symbolizing the five peaks of Mount Meru, the Hindu gods' sacred mountain.

4240.w: After defeating the Sosso at the Battle of Kirina around 1235, Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire, which taxed the desert caravan trade and became one of the richest sources of gold in the medieval world.

4241.w: Mansa Musa's 1324-25 pilgrimage to Mecca passed through Cairo, where the chronicler al-Umari reported he gave away so much gold that its price stayed depressed there for over a decade.

4242.w: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and grew maize on artificial chinampa islands in Lake Texcoco, while obsidian-edged weapons like the macuahuitl armed the empire they built by the 15th century.

4243.w: Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and linked to the mainland by causeway-bridges whose sections could be pulled away to defend the city, while chinampas expanded the island itself.

4244.w: Centered on Cuzco high in the Andes, the Inca Empire expanded explosively from 1438 under Pachacuti, growing wealthy on gold worked by skilled metalsmiths — though the Spanish would melt almost all of it down.

4245.w: Inca ruler Pachacuti ordered Machu Picchu built as a royal estate on a mountain ridge around 1450, after his conquest of the Urubamba valley; it was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest.

4246.w: Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with only about 500 men and 13 horses — animals unknown to the Aztecs — and, allied with the Aztecs' Tlaxcalan enemies, besieged and captured Tenochtitlan by August 1521.

4247.w: With roughly 168 men and a few dozen horses, Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 during a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother, then had him executed in 1533 after his gold ransom was paid.

4248.w: A smallpox epidemic, introduced by an infected member of a Spanish expedition in 1520, swept Tenochtitlan and killed the newly chosen emperor Cuitláhuac within 80 days of taking power, crippling Aztec resistance.

4249.w: Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and theology professor at Wittenberg, protested the Church's sale of indulgences by nailing his 95 Theses to the church door on 31 October 1517.

4250.w: Gutenberg's printing press let Luther's 95 Theses and his German Bible translation spread rapidly across Europe in the vernacular, turning a local theological protest into the continent-wide Protestant Reformation.

4251.w: Sparked by Edward III's claim to the French throne, the war saw England's earliest cannons fire at Crécy in 1346, and ended in 1453 when French field artillery under Jean Bureau won at Castillon — Europe's first major battle decided by field artillery.

4252.w: Claiming divine visions, Joan of Arc helped break the English siege of Orléans in 1429, reviving French fortunes in the Hundred Years' War, but was captured and burned at the stake as a heretic in 1431.

4253.w: Sumerian city-states arose in southern Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates from the 4th millennium BCE, their irrigation canals and mudbrick building turning river silt into the world's first cities -- Uruk alone held over 50,000 people by 2900 BCE.

4254.w: Sargon of Akkad defeated Lugal-zage-si of Umma and conquered Sumer's independent city-states around 2334 BCE, founding the first empire in world history and making Akkadian, not Sumerian, the language of government.

4255.w: The Hittite kingdom, centred on Hattusa in Anatolia, fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh in 1274 BCE; the peace that followed in 1259 BCE is history's earliest surviving treaty -- its lost original on silver tablets, the Hittite copy in cuneiform on clay.

4256.w: Neo-Assyrian kings pioneered large-scale cavalry and siege-warfare, and ruled through deliberate terror -- mass deportations, mutilations -- building an empire of some 1.4 million square kilometres, reaching its height with the conquest of Egypt in 671 BCE.

4257.w: By around 1050 BCE Phoenician traders had reduced Near Eastern scripts like cuneiform to a 22-sign consonantal alphabet and carried it across the Mediterranean aboard their merchant ships -- the direct ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets.

4258.w: Minoan Crete built its wealth on Mediterranean sea trade to Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant, and the palace of Knossos is covered in frescoes of bull-leaping acrobats -- a bull cult later Greek myth wove into the legend of the Minotaur in its labyrinth.

4259.w: Mycenaean Greeks took control of Knossos around 1450 BCE, adapting the Minoans' Linear A into Linear B -- the earliest written form of Greek -- while fortifying mainland citadels at Mycenae and Tiryns with Cyclopean walls the open Minoan palaces never had.

4260.w: Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, a brick-built tank 12 by 7 metres and 2.4 metres deep, was sealed watertight with a lining of bitumen -- one of the oldest public water tanks in the ancient world, at the heart of a city built around 2500 BCE.

4261.w: China's Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE) cast ritual bronze vessels for ancestor worship and cracked heated turtle shells and ox bones to divine the future, inscribing the answers in China's earliest confirmed writing -- oracle bones found since the 1920s.

4262.w: The Olmecs, Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization (c. 1200-400 BCE), carved colossal basalt heads up to 55 tonnes and worked obsidian traded from Guatemala, building their religious art around 'werejaguar' beings blending human and jaguar features.

4263.w: The Chavín culture (900-250 BCE) spread a shared religion of fanged jaguar deities across Peru's highlands and coast from its temple at Chavín de Huántar -- through religious authority alone, not war -- centred on a 4.53-metre carved granite shaft, the Lanzón.

4264.w: Cyrus the Great defeated Croesus of Lydia in 546 BCE, and his cavalry went on to build the largest empire the world had yet seen -- some 5.5 million square kilometres stretching from the Aegean to the Indus.

4265.w: Cyrus the Great's forces won at Opis on the Tigris in October 539 BCE, then took Babylon itself without a fight -- ending the Neo-Babylonian dynasty Nebuchadnezzar had built and absorbing Mesopotamia into the new Achaemenid Empire.

4266.w: Darius I founded Persepolis around 515 BCE as the Achaemenid Empire's ceremonial capital, its Apadana reception hall built to hold thousands of tribute-bearers from across the empire -- until Alexander's troops burned the palace to the ground in 330 BCE.

4267.w: Aristotle tutored the teenage Alexander at the Macedonian court; riding his warhorse Bucephalus, Alexander went on to shatter the last Achaemenid king Darius III at Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BCE, conquering the entire Persian Empire.

4268.w: After capturing Persepolis in 330 BCE, Alexander's troops burned the Achaemenid ceremonial capital to the ground -- ancient sources blame either revenge for Athens or a drunken celebration -- a fire that symbolically ended the empire he had just conquered.

4269.w: After Alexander died in 323 BCE his generals -- the Diadochi -- split his empire into rival Hellenistic kingdoms, chiefly Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Syria, and Antigonid Macedon, spreading Greek temples, cities and language across the Near East for centuries.

4270.w: Rome expelled its last king, Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BCE, then after decades of plebeian pressure against patrician rule wrote its first law code, the Twelve Tables, and had it posted on bronze in the Forum in 449 BCE.

4271.w: Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome around 390 BCE and, by legend, weighed out its gold ransom on rigged scales, meeting Roman protests with the taunt 'Vae victis' -- woe to the vanquished -- a humiliation Rome remembered for centuries.

4272.w: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul's Celtic tribes between 58 and 51 BCE, and the wealth and battle-hardened legions it gave him let him cross the Rubicon in 49 BCE and seize control of the Republic he served; he was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.

4273.w: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BCE, opening the Second Punic War, and destroyed a Roman army of some 86,000 men at Cannae in 216 BCE before Scipio finally broke Carthage at Zama in 202 BCE.

4274.w: Carthage, founded generations earlier by settlers from the eastern Mediterranean, grew into Rome's greatest rival; three Punic Wars between 264 and 146 BCE ended with Carthage stormed, sacked, and its territory annexed as the Roman province of Africa.

4275.w: Caesar's assassination by knife-wielding senators on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, left his 18-year-old adopted heir Octavian to avenge him and outmanoeuvre every rival, taking the title Augustus from the Senate in 27 BCE.

4276.w: Octavian's fleet crushed Antony and Cleopatra's navy at Actium in 31 BCE; when Egypt fell the next year the last independent Hellenistic kingdom was gone, and Octavian stood unchallenged as Rome's first emperor.

4277.w: Huns pressing in from Central Asia forced Goths into Roman land from 376 CE; they sacked Rome in 410 -- the first time in 800 years an outside enemy had taken the city -- and in 476 CE Odoacer deposed the last emperor, ending the empire Augustus founded.

4278.w: Iron Age Celtic Europe's La Tène culture, from around 450 BCE, saw iron production explode while druids held their rites in sacred oak groves and tribes sheltered in hilltop forts.

4279.w: Scythian nomads of the Pontic-Caspian steppe were expert mounted archers -- their name likely derives from a root meaning 'archer' -- who buried their rulers in kurgans, earthen mounds furnished with gold objects from as early as the 8th century BCE.

4280.w: Huns sweeping out of Central Asia crushed the Alans and the Sarmatians -- who had displaced the Scythians on the Pontic steppe centuries earlier -- east of the Don around 375 CE, then turned their mounted archers on the Goths and, eventually, Rome.

4281.w: Chandragupta Maurya founded India's first empire around 320 BCE, and around 302 BCE struck a treaty with Seleucus I -- one of Alexander's former generals -- ceding him 500 war elephants in exchange for territory stretching toward the Hindu Kush.

4282.w: Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta, conquered Kalinga around 261-260 BCE in a war his own edicts say killed or displaced hundreds of thousands, then turned to Gautama Buddha's teachings, carving edicts of dhamma onto stone pillars across his empire.

4283.w: Chandragupta I built the Gupta dynasty into an empire from around 319 CE, ruling from Pataliputra -- the old Mauryan capital -- and marrying into the Licchavi line to claim 'king of great kings'; his successors presided over India's later golden age.

4284.w: Qin Shi Huang conquered the last Warring State, Qi, in 221 BCE to unify China, then standardized coinage, weights and script under Legalist rule -- and in 213-212 BCE had rival texts burned and, by one tradition, some 460 scholars buried alive.

4285.w: Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum was guarded underground by more than 8,000 life-sized terracotta soldiers, 130 chariots and 520 horses, each face individually finished from ten base moulds -- discovered by farmers digging a well in March 1974.

4286.w: Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty in 202 BCE after Qin's collapse, and under Emperor Wudi Han campaigns against the Xiongnu opened the Silk Road through the Tarim Basin by 60 BCE -- a trade network that eventually carried Chinese silk as far as Rome.

4287.w: Teotihuacan grew into the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas, its population reaching 100,000-200,000 by around 400-500 CE on the back of a monopoly over obsidian trade from the Pachuca mines, centred on the Pyramid of the Sun, completed by 100 CE.

4288.w: The Zapotecs founded Monte Albán on a defensible mountaintop above Oaxaca's three valleys around 700-500 BCE, neutral ground between competing rival polities, and carved the Danzante stones there with some of Mesoamerica's earliest writing.

4289.w: Classic Maya civilization (c. 250-900 CE) built city-states like Tikal and Palenque on an economy of maize, while jaguar imagery marked royal authority -- Maya kings sat enthroned on jaguar-skin cushions beneath temples like Tikal's Temple of the Great Jaguar.

4290.w: Cleisthenes's reforms of 508-507 BCE organized Athenian citizens into ten tribes supplying a Council of 500 chosen by lot, and gave the Assembly the power of ostracism -- exile by a vote scratched onto broken pottery shards, ostraka.

4291.w: Spartan citizens were freed for lifelong military training, the agoge starting at age seven, because a subjugated population of helots -- conquered Messenian and Laconian Greeks -- farmed their land and surrendered half the harvest to their Spartan masters.

4292.w: In 480 BCE, Spartan king Leonidas and a rearguard of roughly 300 Spartans plus Thespian and Theban allies held the pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes's Achaemenid army for three days before being outflanked and wiped out -- buying Greece time to win the war.

4293.w: The 27-year Peloponnesian War pitted democratic, sea-based Athens against oligarchic, land-based Sparta; it ended in 405 BCE when Sparta's fleet destroyed the Athenian navy beached at Aegospotami, and Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, tearing down its own walls.

4294.w: Thales held that everything is ultimately water, the first attempt in the West to explain the cosmos through a single natural substance rather than the will of the gods.

4295.w: Thales is said to have predicted a bumper olive harvest, buying up the region's olive presses cheaply and renting them out at a high price once demand peaked — proof, Aristotle said, that philosophers could be rich if they cared to.

4296.w: Pythagoras has been credited since antiquity with proving that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

4297.w: According to legend, Pythagoras discovered that musical harmony follows mathematical ratios after hearing blacksmiths' hammers of different sizes ring out different, pleasing tones against their anvils.

4298.w: Heraclitus taught that the cosmos is in permanent flux: step into a river, and by the time your foot touches it, different waters are already flowing past — even as we still call it one and the same river.

4299.w: Heraclitus held that the world is united only through the tension of its opposites: night and day, he said, are one, each endlessly turning into the other.

4300.w: Parmenides argued through logic alone that what truly exists must be a single, eternal, indivisible whole, unchanging and complete — an idea later thinkers pictured as a perfect, well-rounded unity.

4301.w: Protagoras taught that 'man is the measure of all things': a person from a cold country may call the weather warm while a person from a hot country calls the very same day cold, and Protagoras held both perceptions equally true.

4302.w: Democritus, developing the theory with Leucippus, held that the only true realities are atoms and the void: everything we perceive, from water to human beings, is just atoms combined in empty space.

4303.w: Quoting an old verse, Mozi taught that 'when one throws to me a peach, I return to him a plum' — kindness given is kindness returned, the basis of his doctrine of impartial, universal love.

4304.w: Diogenes lived by choice in a large ceramic storage jar — later Latin writers rendered it as a 'tub' or barrel — and embraced the nickname Cynic, Greek for 'dog-like', for living as shamelessly as a stray.

4305.w: Zeno of Citium was a merchant shipwrecked near Athens with the loss of his entire cargo; wandering into the city, a chance find in a bookseller's shop turned him toward philosophy, and he went on to found Stoicism.

4306.w: Central to the Stoicism Zeno of Citium founded is the idea that living well means living in agreement with nature, aligning one's will with the rational order of the world.

4307.w: After the Oracle at Delphi called him the wisest man in Greece, Socrates treated the claim as a paradox to test, pressing people with question after question until their confident beliefs collapsed under their own contradictions.

4308.w: Augustine argued that evil is not a thing God created but a privation, an absence of good, and that moral evil enters the world only because rational creatures have the free will to choose it — as Adam did in Eden.

4309.w: In his Confessions, Augustine describes his conversion in a garden: hearing what sounded like a child's voice chanting 'take up and read', he picked up a book of Paul's letters and, opening it at random, read the passage that changed his life.

4310.w: Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while imprisoned and awaiting execution on a charge of treason; in it, Philosophy herself is asked whether an all-knowing God's foreknowledge leaves any room for human free will.

4311.w: Anselm's Ontological Argument defines God as 'that than which no greater can be conceived', then reasons that a being existing both in the mind and in reality is greater than one existing in the mind alone — so God must exist.

4312.w: Averroes argued that philosophy and Islamic revelation cannot truly contradict, since both are methods of reaching the same truth; where reasoned conclusions and a literal reading of scripture appear to clash, he held that the text must be read allegorically.

4313.w: Erasmus's 1509 satire In Praise of Folly is delivered as a mock speech by Folly herself, who praises naivety and simple faith over intellectual pride — a paradox that ultimately turns worldly foolishness into a figure for Christian wisdom.

4314.w: In The Prince, Machiavelli advises a ruler to be 'a fox to recognize snares, and a lion to frighten off wolves' — combining an animal's cunning with another's ferocity, unconstrained by conventional morality.

4315.w: In 1513 Machiavelli was arrested, tortured with the strappado, and imprisoned after being falsely implicated in a conspiracy against the Medici; released weeks later, he retired to his farm and wrote The Prince.

4316.w: In 1571 Montaigne retired to the tower of his family château, inscribing its beams with maxims, to write his Essays — arguing that chasing enduring fame, the good opinion of others, only corrodes one's own tranquility.

4317.w: Francis Bacon is credited with the phrase 'knowledge is power' and is called the father of empiricism, arguing that scientific knowledge must be built from careful observation and inductive reasoning rather than assumption.

4318.w: According to a story recorded by his friend John Aubrey, Bacon caught his final, fatal chill on a snowy road while personally testing whether stuffing a chicken with snow would preserve the meat — dying, if the tale is true, in the course of an experiment.

4319.w: Pascal's 1654 correspondence with Pierre de Fermat about gambling problems founded mathematical probability theory; his triangle of binomial coefficients still bears his name.

4320.w: During a mystical experience on the night of November 23, 1654, Pascal wrote 'Fire...' and sewed the note into his coat lining, moving it to each new garment; a servant found it only after his death.

4321.w: Spinoza's central claim was 'Deus sive Natura' -- God or Nature -- naming a single infinite substance, not a separate creator standing outside the world it made.

4322.w: Leibniz argued the universe is built of monads: simple substances that never interact with each other directly, yet each one represents the whole universe from its own unique point of view.

4323.w: Berkeley denied that matter exists independent of the mind, holding 'esse est percipi' -- to be is to be perceived; an apple no one is perceiving, he argued, simply is not there.

4324.w: In 1728 Berkeley sailed for Rhode Island to found a college for the New World on a promised parliamentary grant that never arrived; he abandoned the project and returned to London in 1732.

4325.w: The 1755 Lisbon earthquake convinced Voltaire that Leibniz's claim we live in 'the best of all possible worlds' was untenable; he satirized the idea in Candide (1759).

4326.w: Voltaire was staggeringly prolific, writing more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets, and publishing much of it under pen names -- he used at least 178 over his lifetime.

4327.w: Hume argued causation is never something we perceive directly, only inferred from a 'constant conjunction' of events grown so familiar that habit, not reason, makes us expect one to follow the other.

4328.w: Rousseau wrote that 'the first person who, having enclosed a plot of land, took it into his head to say this is mine... was the true founder of civil society' -- the moment private property, and inequality, began.

4329.w: Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) opens with a pin factory split into about eighteen steps -- 'one man draws out the wire; another straights it; a third cuts it' -- letting ten workers turn out 48,000 pins a day.

4330.w: Smith argued that a person pursuing only their own gain is 'led by an invisible hand' to promote the interest of society more effectually than if they had set out to do so directly.

4331.w: Burke described society as 'a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born' -- obligations running root-deep across generations.

4332.w: Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) condemned the Revolution for having 'completely pulled down to the ground' France's monarchy, church, and law; it sold 17,500 copies within a year.

4333.w: Bentham arranged for his skeleton to be dressed, seated, and preserved as an 'auto-icon'; it has been kept at University College London since 1850, today in a glass display case.

4334.w: Bentham designed the Panopticon, a circular prison he described as 'an iron cage, glazed,' with a central watchtower letting one guard observe every inmate without them knowing if they were being watched.

4335.w: Wollstonecraft died on September 10, 1797, eleven days after giving birth to her daughter Mary, from a childbirth infection; that daughter grew up to write Frankenstein as Mary Shelley.

4336.w: Hegel wrote that 'the owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering' -- philosophy, he meant, only understands a historical moment after it has already passed.

4337.w: Hegel's dialectic holds that a concept's internal contradictions are resolved not by discarding it but by transforming it into a higher, more comprehensive unity -- much as carbon under pressure becomes diamond.

4338.w: Schopenhauer lived largely alone in Frankfurt from 1833, keeping a succession of pet poodles he named Atman, after the Hindu concept of the self, or Butz.

4339.w: Feuerbach argued 'God is nothing else than man: he is, so to speak, the outward projection of man's inward nature' -- we make gods by idealizing our own best qualities and calling the result divine.

4340.w: Mill's On Liberty (1859) holds that "the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others" -- a threshold the individual's own liberty stops at.

4341.w: Kierkegaard proposed to Regine Olsen in September 1840, then broke off the engagement in August 1841, writing in his journals only that his melancholy made him unsuited to marriage.

4342.w: The Communist Manifesto (1848) opens 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism' and declares 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'

4343.w: Thoreau built a small cabin near Walden Pond for $28.12 and lived there from July 1845 to September 1847, testing whether he could live simply by 'stripping away all superfluous luxuries.'

4344.w: Peirce's pragmatic maxim holds that the whole of our conception of an object lies in conceiving its practical, conceivable effects -- an idea's meaning is what it would do, not some hidden essence.

4345.w: James argued that an idea's truth lies in its practical 'cash-value': 'you must bring out of each word its practical cash-value, set it at work within the stream of your experience.'

4346.w: In The Gay Science (1882), Nietzsche's madman declares 'God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him' -- not a claim about a literal death, but about the collapse of the values Christianity once anchored.

4347.w: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-85), Nietzsche argues mankind's goal must be to create something superior to itself -- a new type of human he called the Übermensch.

4348.w: Saussure argued the linguistic sign is arbitrary -- 'any sensible image could in principle be paired with any concept' -- nothing in a word's sound inherently connects it to its meaning.

4349.w: Martin Heidegger became Husserl's assistant at Freiburg in 1919 and succeeded him to the philosophy chair there when Husserl retired in 1928.

4350.w: Bergson's Creative Evolution (1907) described an élan vital, a 'vital impetus,' driving evolution in a more dynamic and creative way than any purely mechanical process could.

4351.w: Dewey argued in his essay Kant and the Philosophic Method that we only think when we are confronted with problems -- philosophy exists to work through the contradictions life presents, not to describe the world from afar.

4352.w: Santayana's The Life of Reason (1905) contains his famous aphorism: 'those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.'

4353.w: Unamuno's The Tragic Sense of Life (1913) grounded human existence in an awareness of death and the desire to exist rather than in pure reason; the Spanish Church placed it on its Index of banned books in 1957.

4354.w: Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk (1903) named 'the problem of the Twentieth Century' as 'the problem of the colour-line,' a phrase he first delivered at the 1900 Pan-African Conference in London.

4355.w: Russell's essay In Praise of Idleness (1932) argued 'the belief in the virtue of labour causes great evils in the modern world,' and that a four-hour workday would free everyone for a fuller life.

4356.w: A 12th-century monk described Slavs invoking two gods over a shared bowl at their feasts, one good and one bad -- the bad one, called Chernobog, 'the black god,' was said to arrange all misfortune.

4357.w: Belobog, the 'White God,' has no genuine ancient source. Unlike Chernobog, who is named in a 12th-century chronicle, Belobog first appears in 16th-century writing, invented as his opposite.

4358.w: She travels in a wooden mortar, wielding a pestle, and lives deep in the forest in a hut that stands and turns on chicken legs.

4359.w: The Baltic god of the daylit sky, who walked the earth disguised as a beggar to find out who would be kind to one.

4360.w: Known across Aboriginal Australia by dozens of names, the Rainbow Serpent pushed up from beneath the ground to carve mountains and gorges, and lives in the permanent waterholes it created.

4361.w: The sky father who came down, shaped the rivers and mountains, and went back up.

4362.w: Before creation there was only Ta'aroa, alone inside a huge cosmic shell. He broke it open and used its two halves to build the dome of the sky and the rocky foundation of the earth.

4363.w: Tane, first of the gods Ta'aroa summoned forth, took charge of decorating creation -- placing the stars, sun and moon in the sky -- and became god of forests and birds.

4364.w: Where his brothers failed, Tane separated his sky father and earth mother by lying on his back and pushing them apart with his legs, letting light into the cramped darkness between them.

4365.w: The sky father, held in an embrace with the earth mother Papa so tight that their children grew up in the dark between them.

4366.w: Papatuanuku, the Maori earth mother, is the ground itself -- held so close in sky father Rangi's embrace that their children lived for generations in total darkness between them.

4367.w: The only child of Rangi and Papa who protested their separation, and answered it with an army of storms.

4368.w: Tumatauenga, god of war, was the only brother who stood and fought Tawhirimatea's storm rather than flee -- afterward he turned on his siblings in turn, felling Tane's forests for the first weapons.

4369.w: Maui hauled up islands of the Pacific from a canoe, tricking his brothers into paddling hard while his magic hook dragged land up from the sea floor behind them.

4370.w: Days were too short to dry cloth, so Maui climbed to where the sun rises and lassoed its rays with a rope, forcing it to slow down and lengthen the day.

4371.w: Makemake, creator god and chief deity of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, is carved into the island's rocks as a face with huge eyes, worshipped through the seabirds that nest on its cliffs.

4372.w: Haua shared Makemake's role at the heart of Rapa Nui's birdman cult, the two gods honored together through the island's nesting seabirds.

4373.w: In the Navajo Dine Bahane' creation narrative, Spider Woman and Spider Man introduced the spindle and the loom to the people.

4374.w: In Hopi tradition, Spider Grandmother guided the people through the underground worlds, teaching them to weave and to make clay pots along the way.

4375.w: The Haida credit this shapeshifting trickster with finding the first humans hiding inside a clam shell, and bringing them berries and salmon to eat.

4376.w: Iktomi, the Lakota trickster, is the first-born son of Inyan, the Rock -- and became a spider, the meaning of his name, through his own cunning.

4377.w: Nanabozho, the Ojibwe trickster and culture hero, is called Michabo -- 'the Great Hare who created the Earth' -- and is credited as the inventor of fishing.

4378.w: Kiviuq is an Inuit hero said to travel eternally by kayak and sled across the Arctic regions of Canada, Alaska and Greenland, known by different names in each place.

4379.w: An inua is the spirit the Inuit believe exists in every person, animal, lake, mountain and plant -- not one individual soul, but the shared life-force of an entire kind, including the whale's own.

4380.w: He rose out of Lake Titicaca in darkness and made humankind by breathing into stone.

4381.w: Viracocha's first people -- brainless giants -- displeased him, so he sent a flood down from the Andes to destroy them, then remade humanity, better this time, from smaller stones.

4382.w: Addressed as the possessor of brightness, and said to rest on Mount Kenya — the mountain is where he is, not what he is made from.

4383.w: Amma, the Dogon sky god, is said to have united with the earth goddess through a termite mound standing in her place -- only after it was cleared away could he father true offspring.

4384.w: Nommo, the first living creature made by the Dogon sky god Amma, are hermaphroditic water spirits pictured with a human body and a fish's tail.

4385.w: Papa Legba, intermediary between gods and humanity in Haitian Vodou, traces his origins to Yoruba and Fon traditions carried across the Atlantic by enslaved West Africans, among them the trickster Eshu.

4386.w: Fearing he sought to be king, a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar to death on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, shortly after he was proclaimed dictator in perpetuity.

4387.w: In 27 BCE the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus, 'the revered,' making him Rome's first emperor; he later boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.

4388.w: In 343 BCE, King Philip II hired Aristotle to tutor his 13-year-old son at the Temple of the Nymphs at Mieza — the boy who would become Alexander the Great.

4389.w: As consul in 63 BCE, Cicero exposed Catiline's conspiracy to overthrow the Republic, denouncing the plot in four famous speeches and earning the title 'father of the fatherland.'

4390.w: Forced into exile in 58 BCE after his enemy Clodius passed legislation targeting him, Cicero returned to Italy in triumph on 5 August 57 BCE.

4391.w: In 610 CE, at age 40, Muhammad received his first Quranic revelation from the angel Gabriel in a cave on Mount Hira, in the hills outside Mecca.

4392.w: In 622 CE Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina — the Hijra, an event that marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

4393.w: In August 386 Augustine underwent a sudden conversion in a garden in Milan, hearing a child's voice say 'take up and read' before opening St. Paul's letters to a passage that ended his inner turmoil.

4394.w: Augustine composed his autobiographical Confessions in 397-398, a work of unsparing self-examination often called the first Western autobiography.

4395.w: On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne 'emperor of the Romans' during Mass at St. Peter's Basilica, reviving the western imperial title for the first time since 476.

4396.w: In 774 Charlemagne besieged and captured Pavia, defeating the Lombard King Desiderius and adding King of the Lombards to his own titles.

4397.w: In 1206, at a kurultai assembly by the Onon River, Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan, uniting the Mongol tribes into a disciplined army of mounted archers.

4398.w: In 1215 the Mongols captured Zhongdu, the Jin dynasty capital near modern Beijing, a major milestone in Genghis Khan's campaign against northern China.

4399.w: At the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066, William's forces defeated and killed King Harold II — later legend, shown on the Bayeux Tapestry, holds he was struck in the eye by an arrow.

4400.w: In 1086 William ordered a nationwide survey of England's land and wealth for taxation, compiled as the Domesday Book.

4401.w: In 1429 Joan of Arc, a 17-year-old peasant claiming divine visions, led French troops that lifted the English siege of Orléans, a turning point in the Hundred Years' War.

4402.w: Convicted of heresy by a pro-English church court, Joan of Arc was tied to a stake and burned in Rouen on 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen.

4403.w: Leonardo began the Mona Lisa in October 1503 using layers of translucent oil glazes, and kept reworking the portrait until his death in 1519.

4404.w: Michelangelo carved his statue of David from a single block of marble, completing the Renaissance masterpiece in 1504.

4405.w: From 1508 to 1512 Michelangelo worked from scaffolding to fresco the Sistine Chapel ceiling with over 300 figures, including the Creation of Adam.

4406.w: On 31 October 1517 Luther is said to have nailed his Ninety-Five Theses, protesting the sale of indulgences, to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church.

4407.w: Henry VIII married six times between 1509 and 1547 — Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr — beheading two of them.

4408.w: In 1534 the Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII 'Supreme Head of the Church of England,' severing ties with the papacy after Rome refused to annul his first marriage.

4409.w: On 28-29 July 1588, English fire ships scattered the anchored Spanish Armada off Gravelines, leading to a decisive battle that shattered Spain's invasion fleet.

4410.w: Elizabeth I was crowned queen at Westminster Abbey on 15 January 1559, beginning a 44-year reign later remembered as the Elizabethan Age.

4411.w: In 1543, the year of his death, Copernicus published De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, proposing that the Sun, not Earth, sits at the center of the universe.

4412.w: In March 1610 Galileo published Sidereus Nuncius after turning his telescope on the sky, describing the Moon's cratered surface and four moons orbiting Jupiter.

4413.w: Galileo's 1632 book Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, defending the Sun-centered model, led the Roman Inquisition to try him for heresy in 1633; he recanted and lived under house arrest.

4414.w: Newton described how watching an apple fall started his thinking about gravity; his 1687 Principia Mathematica united that force with the mathematics of planetary motion.

4415.w: During 1665-66, while Cambridge closed for the Great Plague, Newton worked out the basics of calculus, the mathematics he later used to describe planetary motion.

4416.w: After Cardinal Mazarin's death in 1661, Louis XIV began his personal rule of France and later moved his court to the newly built Palace of Versailles.

4417.w: In 1685 Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking a century of religious tolerance for Protestants and forcing many Huguenots to flee France or convert.

4418.w: At the Battle of Naseby in 1645, Cromwell's cavalry broke the Royalist lines, a decisive victory that effectively ended the First English Civil War in Parliament's favor.

4419.w: Cromwell was the third man to sign Charles I's death warrant; the king was beheaded on a scaffold outside the Banqueting House on 30 January 1649, and England briefly became a republic.

4420.w: Voltaire was imprisoned in the Bastille fortress in Paris from May 1717 to April 1718 after writing a satirical verse accusing the French regent of incest.

4421.w: Published anonymously in early 1759, Voltaire's Candide became his most enduring work, satirizing the Leibnizian idea that we live in 'the best of all possible worlds.'

4422.w: Unanimously elected the first U.S. president, Washington voluntarily stepped down after two terms in 1797, a precedent nearly every successor followed for over a century.

4423.w: Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, which the Second Continental Congress voted to adopt on 4 July 1776.

4424.w: In 1803 Jefferson's administration purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, doubling the young nation's size and securing control of the Mississippi River.

4425.w: In June 1752 Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm to demonstrate that lightning is an electrical phenomenon, work that led him to invent the lightning rod — a grounded wire that lets a strike pass harmlessly to earth.

4426.w: In December 1804 Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame, and had his own portrait struck onto the new imperial coinage.

4427.w: Defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in June 1815, Napoleon was exiled to the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

4428.w: Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto on 21 February 1848, opening with the line 'A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of Communism.'

4429.w: From 1831 to 1836 Darwin sailed around the world aboard HMS Beagle, collecting specimens including finches from the Galápagos Islands that later shaped his theory of evolution.

4430.w: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, opening his case for evolution by natural selection with evidence from the artificial selection long practiced by dog and pigeon breeders.

4431.w: On 30 September 1862 Bismarck told the Prussian parliament that the great questions of the age would be decided not by speeches but 'by iron and blood,' a phrase that became shorthand for his politics.

4432.w: On 18 January 1871 Bismarck had Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, staging German unification inside a defeated France.

4433.w: In 1930 Gandhi led a 24-day, 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi to make salt from seawater in defiance of the British crown's salt tax, launching a mass civil disobedience campaign.

4434.w: Gandhi was shot three times at close range by Nathuram Godse during an evening prayer meeting in Delhi on 30 January 1948.

4435.w: On 29 June 1613 a theatrical cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII misfired and ignited the Globe Theatre's thatched roof, burning it to the ground within an hour.

4436.w: Seven years after Shakespeare's death, his colleagues John Heminges and Henry Condell published the First Folio in 1623, a collected edition preserving 36 of his plays.

4437.w: In May 1747 Bach visited the court of King Frederick the Great in Potsdam, where the king gave him a theme and challenged him to improvise a fugue on the spot, later worked into The Musical Offering.

4438.w: Sun-dried mud brick and organized temple precincts let Uruk grow into the world's first true city by around 3200 BC, ringed by its own city walls.

4439.w: Uruk's temple administrators needed to track livestock and grain, so around 3300 BC they began pressing a reed stylus into wet clay tablets -- the world's first writing system.

4440.w: Sumerian poems about Uruk's king Gilgamesh, first written down in cuneiform around 2100 BC, grew into the world's oldest surviving narrative epic.

4441.w: Sargon tore down Uruk's walls and captured its king, and went on to conquer Ur, Lagash, and Umma -- uniting Sumer into the world's first known empire around 2334 BC.

4442.w: Some 5,000-6,000 bronze-fitted chariots collided at Kadesh in 1274 BC between Ramesses II's Egyptians and Muwatalli II's Hittites -- the largest chariot battle in recorded history, and a stalemate.

4443.w: Fifteen years after neither side won at Kadesh, Egypt and the Hittites exchanged treaty tablets of silver in 1259 BC -- the oldest peace treaty for which both parties' own copies have survived.

4444.w: Five centuries after Caesar's legions crossed the Rubicon, the Germanic king Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in AD 476, ending the Western Roman Empire.

4445.w: Having conquered most of Western Europe on horseback and sponsored a revival of book-copying and learning known as the Carolingian Renaissance, Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800 AD.

4446.w: William of Normandy ferried his cavalry across the Channel by ship and defeated King Harold's English army at Hastings on 14 October 1066, the last successful invasion of England.

4447.w: Twenty years after conquering England at Hastings, William ordered a survey of every manor, ox, and peasant in his new kingdom, compiled by 1086 into the Domesday Book.

4448.w: Facing an armed baronial revolt over taxation and abuses of royal power, King John sealed the Great Charter at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, the first document to put the English crown under the law.

4449.w: The Mongol peace that Genghis Khan's empire imposed across Central Asia made the Silk Road safe enough for the young Venetian merchant Marco Polo to travel it to Kublai Khan's court, starting in 1271.

4450.w: A dispute over the French crown between the English and French royal houses erupted into intermittent warfare in 1337 -- fought partly with iron-tipped English longbow volleys at battles like Crecy and Agincourt -- that dragged on until 1453.

4451.w: Sultan Mehmed II's gunpowder cannons, some hurling 600-pound stone balls over a mile, breached Constantinople's ancient walls after a 53-day siege in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire nearly 1,500 years after it began.

4452.w: Cinnamon bark carries caryophyllene alongside cinnamaldehyde — a sesquiterpene also found in cloves and black pepper, and one of the few plant compounds shown to directly activate a cannabinoid receptor, CB2.

4453.w: What gets sold as 'cinnamon' is usually cassia bark, and cassia carries far more coumarin than true Ceylon cinnamon does — over 1mg per gram against barely a trace — which is why food regulators set separate safe limits for the two.

4454.w: Anethole is what makes star anise taste of liquorice, and it measures about 13 times sweeter than table sugar on the tongue's own sweetness receptors — a compound three unrelated plant families arrived at independently.

4455.w: Anise and star anise are not related plants — one is a carrot-family herb, the other a magnolia relative from China — but both concentrate the same anethole in their seeds, a case of convergent chemistry rather than shared ancestry.

4456.w: Star anise pods are the commercial source of shikimic acid, the starting molecule for synthesizing the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — a dependency real enough that a 2005 shortage of the acid tightened world Tamiflu supply during a flu scare.

4457.w: Vanillin is the single dominant compound in cured vanilla pods among several hundred flavour compounds altogether, and it's cheap enough to synthesize that most vanilla-flavoured food today is flavoured with lab vanillin rather than the orchid.

4458.w: Myristicin is nutmeg's own defensive chemical, a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that clears certain neurotransmitters, and a high-quality nutmeg seed can carry up to 13mg of it per gram — enough that a couple of whole seeds is a real overdose.

4459.w: Mace and nutmeg come from the same fruit — mace is the seed's lacy red covering — and both carry sabinene, a woody, peppery terpene also documented in black pepper and carrot seed oil.

4460.w: Mace and nutmeg both carry safrole in their oil, the same compound sassafras is named for. The US banned safrole as a food additive in 1960 after it proved to cause liver tumours in rats at high, sustained dose.

4461.w: Dill seed's essential oil is dominated by carvone but also carries a real share of limonene, the same citrus terpene found in orange peel and pine resin — part of why dill reads as both spicy and bright.

4462.w: Liquorice root's sweetness is almost entirely glycyrrhizin, 30 to 50 times sweeter than table sugar by weight, and shaped like a soap molecule — it drags oil and water into the same mixture rather than just adding sweetness.

4463.w: Cardamom oil runs 20 to 50 percent 1,8-cineole — in Java cardamom sometimes up to 70 — the same eucalyptus-smelling compound that makes up most of eucalyptus oil itself, which is why cardamom carries a cooling, medicinal edge.

4464.w: Cuminaldehyde is the molecule responsible for cumin's characteristic aroma — spicy, green, distinctly cumin — and it's why cumin doesn't smell like its close carrot-family relatives caraway, dill, and fennel.

4465.w: Beneath fennel's anethole sweetness sits fenchone, a bitter, camphor-toned compound in the same chemical family as camphor itself — part of what keeps fennel from tasting like pure liquorice.

4466.w: Caraway is cumin's own close cousin in the carrot family, sometimes called 'meridian fennel' or Persian cumin — the two seeds look alike enough to mix up by sight despite tasting nothing alike.

4467.w: Liquorice is a legume, not an aromatic herb, and harvest means digging up the whole plant and cutting the sweet root free from three to five years of growth.

4468.w: Score the bark of a Chios mastic tree and the resin oozes out, hardening into brittle tears over roughly 15 to 20 days as it dries in the open air.

4469.w: Damask rose petals are hand-picked at bloom and either dried whole as a spice or steam-distilled with oil-bearing steam to make attar of roses.

4470.w: Aframomum melegueta's trumpet-shaped flowers develop into 5 to 7cm pods holding numerous small reddish-brown seeds, dried and sold as grains of paradise.

4471.w: Ajwain is a small annual in the parsley family, the same family as caraway, cumin and fennel, grown for its thymol-rich seed.

4472.w: Asafoetida is literally dried latex — a gum oleoresin exuded from a Ferula taproot after repeated shallow cuts, collected and dried between bleeds.

4473.w: Berberis vulgaris's thorny branches are difficult to harvest by hand, so the tart red berries are often knocked down and then dried for use as zereshk.

4474.w: Amchoor is made from unripe green mangoes, harvested early, peeled, thinly sliced, and sun-dried before being ground into a sour powder.

4475.w: Lemon myrtle's leaves are harvested year-round from the tree and dried for their intensely citral-rich oil.

4476.w: Black cardamom's pods are dried over open flames for days, and that traditional smoke-drying is where the spice's campfire flavour actually comes from.

4477.w: Xylopia aethiopica's dried fruits are sold as grains of Selim; in Senegal the immature pods are smoked before drying, elsewhere they are simply sun-dried.

4478.w: A dried lime has simply lost its water content, spending most of its drying time out in the sun until it turns hard, dark, and musky.

4479.w: Wattleseed is the roasted, milled seed of Australian Acacia species — specialised seed-grinding stones for processing it date back at least 1,000 years.

4480.w: For anardana, pomegranate seeds and their fleshy pulp are separated from the bitter white membrane and dried in the sun until reddish-brown.

4481.w: Germacrene D is the single most abundant compound in annatto seed's essential oil, measured at nearly 18 percent — more than caryophyllene or pinene.

4482.w: Alpha-pinene is mastic gum's dominant compound; analyses of Pistacia lentiscus essential oil have measured it at up to 79 percent.

4483.w: Steam-distilling damask rose petals yields rose oil, in which geraniol is one of the three major components alongside citronellol and nonadecane.

4484.w: Nigella sativa seeds are dry-roasted before use in spice blends, a step that draws out thymoquinone, the phytochemical dominating the seed's own aroma profile, alongside dihydrothymoquinone and other minor compounds.

4485.w: Nigellone — better known chemically as dithymoquinone — forms when sunlight photodimerises two thymoquinone molecules together during the separation and extraction of nigella oil.

4486.w: (6)-Paradol gives grains of paradise its pungent, black-pepper-like heat with hints of citrus — structurally a close relative of ginger's gingerol.

4487.w: Picrocrocin, saffron's bitter glucoside, makes up as much as 4 percent of the dried spice's weight after the stigmas are harvested and cured.

4488.w: When saffron is dried after harvest, heat combined with enzymatic action splits picrocrocin into D-glucose and free safranal, the volatile molecule behind most of saffron's aroma.

4489.w: Wikipedia credits sedanolide, alongside butylphthalide, as the main chemicals responsible for celery's aroma and taste.

4490.w: 1-Phenylethanethiol is named as one of the major odour compounds in curry leaves, giving them their sulphury, meaty note alongside citrusy linalool and resinous pinene.

4491.w: 2-Pentylfuran is identified as poppy seed's primary flavour compound.

4492.w: Turmerones are a group of sesquiterpene compounds found in turmeric's steam-distilled essential oil, chemically distinct from the curcumin that gives turmeric its colour.

4493.w: Terpenes including ocimene, myrcene, and limonene have been identified in the dried unripe mango used to make amchoor, alongside the citric acid behind its sourness.

4494.w: Panch phoron, the Bengali five-spice blend used whole rather than ground, consists of fenugreek, cumin, nigella, black mustard, and fennel seed in equal parts.

4495.w: Chaat masala typically consists of amchoor, cumin, coriander, dried ginger, black salt, black pepper, asafoetida, and chilli powder — the tangy, savoury seasoning behind Indian street-food chaat.

4496.w: Bart Bok first described these small, dense, isolated clouds in 1947 — among the coldest objects in the universe, and one of the few places a collapsing pocket of a molecular cloud can be picked out from outside.

4497.w: Near-infrared observations confirmed in 1990 that stars really do form inside Bok globules — usually as a double or multiple system rather than a single star.

4498.w: Ultraviolet light from a nearby hot star strips material off one side of a Bok globule, leaving a bright ionized rim and a trailing dark tail — a cometary globule.

4499.w: Material ejected from an accreting protostar rams into the surrounding gas at hundreds of kilometres a second, lighting up glowing shock fronts — more than a thousand of these are now catalogued.

4500.w: As infall dies down and the shrouding envelope clears, a low-mass protostar becomes visible as a T Tauri star — still contracting toward the main sequence, not yet fusing hydrogen in its core.

4501.w: An intermediate-mass protostar of 2 to 8 solar masses, still wrapped in its accretion disc, is a Herbig Ae/Be star — the heavier counterpart to a T Tauri star, first identified by George Herbig in 1960.

4502.w: Sometimes a T Tauri star's own accretion disc dumps a burst of mass onto it all at once, brightening the star by several magnitudes for decades — the average young star erupts like this 10 to 20 times over its life.

4503.w: Thousands of ATP-bound globular actin subunits polymerize head-to-tail into a helical filament with a fast-growing plus end and a slow minus end; muscle cells pack them densest, as the thin filaments of the sarcomere.

4504.w: Myosin-II's two heads bind actin and hydrolyze ATP in a cycle — phosphate release powers the stroke, ADP release locks it into rigor, and fresh ATP finally lets go — walking the motor toward the filament's plus end.

4505.w: Keratin is only one branch of a whole family — vimentin, desmin, lamins, neurofilaments — that all assemble into 10 nm ropes tougher and more stretchable than actin or microtubules, built for mechanical strength rather than movement.

4506.w: Integrins are transmembrane heterodimers that grip the extracellular matrix outside the cell and couple, inside it, to the actin cytoskeleton through focal adhesions — signaling runs both directions across that same membrane.

4507.w: Myosin heads on the thick filament repeatedly bind actin, pull, and let go, sliding the thin filaments deeper into the sarcomere without either filament changing length — the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.

4508.w: Actin polymerizing at the front pushes out lamellipodia and filopodia, while integrins grip the substrate like feet and recycle from back to front, so the cell body is pulled forward.

4509.w: GPCRs snake across the membrane in seven transmembrane helices; a ligand binding outside twists the whole bundle, and the new shape lets the receptor act as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor on an associated G protein inside.

4510.w: A growth factor binding outside pairs up two receptors, and each one then spends ATP autophosphorylating tyrosines on its partner's cytosolic tail — the docking sites that launch the signal inward.

4511.w: A GPCR's activated G protein alpha subunit diffuses along the membrane and switches on adenylyl cyclase — Earl Sutherland's Nobel-winning 1971 discovery tying a hormone outside the cell to a new enzyme inside it.

4512.w: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP directly into cyclic AMP plus pyrophosphate — one of biology's oldest and most widespread second messengers, relaying signals like adrenaline and glucagon that never cross the membrane themselves.

4513.w: PKA sits locked as two regulatory and two catalytic subunits until four cAMP molecules bind the regulatory pair; the complex falls apart and the freed catalytic subunits phosphorylate target serines and threonines.

4514.w: A different flavor of G protein, Gq, activates phospholipase C instead of adenylyl cyclase; PLC then cleaves the membrane lipid PIP2 into two separate second messengers in a single reaction.

4515.w: Cleaving PIP2 releases IP3, the water-soluble half of the split, carrying three phosphate groups and enough charge to diffuse straight into the cytosol, where it opens calcium channels on the ER.

4516.w: The other half of the same PIP2 cut, diacylglycerol is too lipophilic to leave the membrane, so it stays anchored there and waits for calcium to arrive before it can finish activating protein kinase C.

4517.w: Diacylglycerol and a rise in cytosolic calcium — the second half of the same phospholipase C signal — together pull PKC to the membrane and switch it on to phosphorylate serine and threonine residues.

4518.w: Docking proteins recruited to a phosphorylated RTK tail switch Ras from its GDP-bound off state to its GTP-bound on state — a binary molecular switch whose stuck-on mutants are found in 20–25% of all human tumors.

4519.w: Active Ras kicks off a three-kinase relay — each one phosphorylating and activating the next using ATP — until the last kinase reaches the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors, changing which genes get read.

4520.w: Cortisol is built from cholesterol through a chain of enzyme reactions in the adrenal cortex's zona fasciculata — as with every steroid hormone, the raw material is the same molecule that also stiffens cell membranes.

4521.w: Because cortisol is small and lipophilic, it needs no surface receptor at all — it diffuses across the membrane and binds a receptor sitting inside the cell, which then acts directly on DNA as a transcription factor.

4522.w: Continental crust is thicker but far less dense than oceanic crust, so it floats higher on the mantle — built from granitic rock old enough, in places, to exceed 3 billion years, since subduction rarely destroys it.

4523.w: Magma constantly rises through mid-ocean ridges to add new basaltic seafloor, driving the plates apart and widening the ocean basin — the ridge system runs 65,000 km, longer than any mountain range on land.

4524.w: A peninsula extends from a mainland, connected to it on only one side while mostly surrounded by water — the Peloponnese, for instance, is tied to the rest of Greece by the narrow Isthmus of Corinth.

4525.w: An archipelago is a chain, cluster, or collection of islands — the Hawaiian Islands and the Azores are two well-known examples, both built up by repeated volcanic activity rather than any single eruption.

4526.w: A strait is a water body connecting two seas or larger basins, with surface water flowing through in either direction — the Strait of Gibraltar does exactly that between two continents, Europe and Africa.

4527.w: The Isthmus of Panama closed a seaway between the Pacific and Atlantic around 3 million years ago, as colliding plates threw up volcanoes whose gaps filled with sediment until North and South America were welded into one strip of land.

4528.w: The equator is the circle of latitude at 0°, running around Earth's midpoint exactly between the poles — the line that divides the planet into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

4529.w: Cut along the equator and Earth divides into a Northern Hemisphere, holding about 68% of the planet's land and 90% of its population, and a Southern Hemisphere with the rest.

4530.w: Latitude measures north-south position as an angle from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles; lines of constant latitude, called parallels, are circles running east-west, parallel to the Equator and shrinking as they near the poles.

4531.w: Meridians are imaginary lines running from pole to pole, perpendicular to the circles of latitude, that measure a point's position east or west — cut across the parallels and you get the other half of the coordinate grid.

4532.w: In October 1884, delegates at the International Meridian Conference chose the meridian through Greenwich, England as the common zero of longitude, from which every other line is measured east or west.

4533.w: Because Earth spins once every 24 hours, the world is split into time zones, each defined by a standard offset from Coordinated Universal Time — the successor to Greenwich Mean Time, measured from the Prime Meridian.

4534.w: The Tropic of Cancer, at about 23°26'N, is Earth's northernmost circle of latitude where the Sun appears directly overhead — a moment that occurs once a year, on the June solstice.

4535.w: The Tropic of Capricorn, at about 23°26'S, is the southernmost latitude that contains the subsolar point — the Sun sits directly overhead there once a year, on the December solstice.

4536.w: A steppe is grassland plains without closed forest, getting 250-500 mm of rain a year — too dry to support trees, not dry enough to be desert. The Eurasian Steppe, the largest, helped spread the horse, the wheel, and Indo-European languages.

4537.w: Savanna is grassy woodland where the trees, like acacia, stand far enough apart that the canopy never closes; it covers about a fifth of Earth's land, with most of its 500-1,270 mm of yearly rain falling in a single season.

4538.w: Political borders are imposed by human agency — war, colonization, or treaty — and often follow rivers or mountain ranges, though ones formalized recently, especially in Africa, more often run the straight lines colonial powers drew instead.

4539.w: A country is a political entity or its territory, ranging from a fully sovereign state to an unrecognized state or dependent territory — a bordered piece of a continent claimed as its own.

4540.w: A nation-state is where the state and the nation — a population sharing a common identity — are congruent; the model became dominant in the 19th century, after the Peace of Westphalia had already set the norm of sovereign, recognized territories.

4541.w: A capital city holds primary status as a country's seat of government — not always its largest city. Brazil built Brasília, Australia built Canberra as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, and Canada chose Ottawa on the old Upper/Lower Canada boundary.

4542.w: Population density is population size per unit of land area. Monaco packs in over 18,000 people per km², Singapore over 8,000 — while Mongolia, with vast arid land unable to support crops, has one of the lowest densities of any country.

4543.w: A supply chain is the network of facilities that convert raw materials into finished products and distribute them onward — ports and freight wagons are two of its physical links.

4544.w: Logistics is the flow of goods, services and information from origin to consumption; the English word arrived around 1846 from the French logistique, which Antoine-Henri Jomini tied to logis, 'lodgings.'

4545.w: Supply chain management coordinates procurement, operations, logistics and marketing from raw material to end customer; computers made that coordination practical through EDI and ERP systems from the 1960s on.

4546.w: Sales forecasting uses past sales figures to predict short- or long-term future performance and enable sound financial planning, drawing on historical sales and economic data.

4547.w: Demand planning predicts future customer demand using predictive analytics; it's described as an important tool for optimizing business profitability through efficient supply chain management.

4548.w: S&OP is a business management process that integrates demand forecasting with supply planning to balance demand against available resources; its modern form is credited to consultant Richard Ling of Oliver Wight in the 1980s.

4549.w: A warehouse is simply a building for storing goods — used by manufacturers, importers, exporters, wholesalers and transport businesses, usually fitted with loading docks, cranes and forklifts.

4550.w: Inventory is the quantity of goods and materials a business holds for the ultimate goal of resale, production or utilisation — stock on the shelf, not money in the till.

4551.w: Inventory management software records and tracks stock levels, orders and deliveries; the first retail barcode scan was in 1974, and personal computers made computerized inventory records practical for smaller firms by the early 1980s.

4552.w: Safety stock is a level of extra stock maintained to mitigate the risk of stockouts caused by uncertainty in demand, supply, or the accuracy of the forecast itself.

4553.w: Economic order quantity is the order quantity that minimizes total holding costs and ordering costs in inventory management; Ford W. Harris derived the original formula in 1913.

4554.w: The bullwhip effect is a supply-chain phenomenon where orders to suppliers show larger swings than sales to buyers, amplifying demand variability upstream; Jay Forrester first modeled it in 1961, so it's also called the Forrester effect.

4555.w: Just-in-time manufacturing receives goods only as needed to reduce cost and waste; Toyota engineer Taiichi Ohno developed it after noticing American supermarkets restock shelves based on what customers actually take.

4556.w: Kanban — Japanese for 'signboard' — is a scheduling system for just-in-time manufacturing in which a card authorizes production only once it's requested downstream; Taiichi Ohno modeled it on how supermarkets restock only what shoppers take.

4557.w: Lean manufacturing is built on producing only what's needed when it's needed, correcting abnormalities immediately, and empowering workers to improve the process; it grew out of Toyota's postwar system and was formally named 'Lean' by John Krafcik in 1988.

4558.w: Material requirements planning is a production planning, scheduling and inventory control system; Joseph Orlicky developed it in 1964, it first ran at Black and Decker that year, and roughly 700 companies had adopted it by 1975.

4559.w: Enterprise resource planning is the integrated, software-mediated management of an organization's main business processes; the acronym was coined by research firm Gartner in the 1990s as a functional extension of material requirements planning.

4560.w: In vendor-managed inventory, the supplier — usually the manufacturer — takes responsibility for optimizing the inventory held by a distributor, deciding order sizes itself; Walmart and Procter & Gamble are among the retailers built around the model.

4561.w: Distribution requirements planning applies material-requirements-style logic to a distribution network, letting planners set inventory-control parameters such as safety stock and calculate time-phased inventory requirements across warehouses.

4562.w: Chinese soldiers packed gunpowder and a slow match into a bamboo tube strapped to a spear; the earliest fire lances appeared by 950 and saw combat at the 1132 siege of De'an, ancestor of the gun.

4563.w: Bronze Age bowyers glued a horn belly and sinew backing onto a wood core with animal glue; composite bows buried with Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BC, show the design was already standard in Egypt.

4564.w: The spoked wheel, far lighter than a solid wooden disk, was the invention that let horses pull a cart fast enough for war; chariots fielded by both sides decided the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BC.

4565.w: The Ghaznavids fielded 1,300 iron-armored war elephants by 1023; centuries earlier Hannibal marched armored elephants over the Alps in 218 BC, and Chandragupta Maurya commanded some 9,000 of them.

4566.w: Eurasian steppe cavalry paired the compact composite bow with the horse, shooting on the gallop and wheeling away before contact; Parthian horse archers annihilated a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC.

4567.w: India's earliest stirrup was a rope loop for the big toe, used by the 2nd century BC; China then developed the sturdier paired stirrup, cast in bronze and iron by 415 AD, freeing riders to fight from horseback.

4568.w: Devised around 672 AD by Kallinikos, a refugee engineer from Syria, Greek fire was pumped from bow-mounted siphons and helped Byzantine ships repel Arab sieges of Constantinople between 674 and 678 AD.

4569.w: French gunsmith Marin le Bourgeoys built the first true flintlock for Louis XIII around 1610 to 1615, its flint-on-steel spark replacing the smoldering match cord and making loaded muskets safer to carry.

4570.w: Patented by Hiram Maxim in 1883, his water-cooled gun used the energy of its own recoil to eject and reload each cartridge, sustaining 600 rounds per minute and becoming the weapon most associated with imperial conquest.

4571.w: Robert Whitehead's self-propelled torpedo, presented to the Austrian navy on 21 December 1866, was driven by a compressed-air engine inside a body of polished steel or phosphor bronze — the largest models used either metal.

4572.w: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin's rigid, aluminum-framed hydrogen airship first flew in 1900; between 1915 and 1918 German Zeppelins flew 51 raids on England, dropping 5,806 bombs that killed 557 people.

4573.w: Mikhail Kalashnikov's rifle, accepted by the Soviet Armed Forces in early 1949, diverts propellant gas from the barrel to drive a piston that cycles the bolt — a rugged, cheap design later carried on every continent.

4574.w: Manhattan Project scientists used reactors like Hanford's B Reactor to breed plutonium-239 from uranium-238; that plutonium armed the Fat Man bomb dropped on Nagasaki in August 1945.

4575.w: On 22 April 1915 German troops released 168 tons of chlorine from 5,730 cylinders along a 4-mile front at Ypres; a north-easterly breeze carried the cloud onto French lines, tearing open a 3.7-mile gap.

4576.w: Voltage-gated sodium channels are transmembrane proteins embedded in the axon's membrane, permeable specifically to sodium ions; when the membrane depolarizes they open, and the resulting sodium influx constitutes the action potential's rising phase.

4577.w: Voltage-gated potassium channels open during and after an action potential, and the resulting outward flow of potassium ions is what returns the depolarized membrane to its resting state.

4578.w: For a short interval after firing, an axon's voltage-gated sodium channels sit inactivated rather than merely closed, so no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second action potential until they reset.

4579.w: A myelin sheath doesn't cover an axon continuously; it leaves short gaps exposed to extracellular fluid, and it's exactly at those gaps that voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at high density, concentrating where the signal actually regenerates.

4580.w: Because ion exchange can only happen at an axon's exposed nodes of Ranvier, the action potential appears to jump node to node rather than propagate continuously, reaching speeds up to 150 m/s versus 0.5-10 m/s in an unmyelinated axon.

4581.w: Schwann cells are the principal glia of the peripheral nervous system; myelinating Schwann cells wrap around the axons of motor and sensory neurons the way oligodendrocytes do in the brain and spinal cord, but each one insulates only a single axon.

4582.w: A mechanoreceptor is a sensory receptor that responds to mechanical pressure or distortion; the skin is packed with dendritic nerve endings tuned to exactly that stimulus, converting touch into an electrical signal for the nervous system.

4583.w: Nociceptors are sensory neurons that respond to damaging or potentially damaging stimuli; besides the skin, they're distributed through internal tissue such as muscle, where sustained contraction cutting off blood supply is itself enough to trigger them.

4584.w: The Pacinian corpuscle is a low-threshold mechanoreceptor built from 20 to 70 concentric connective-tissue lamellae wrapped around a nerve ending, situated deep in the dermis, where it rapidly adapts to detect vibration and gross pressure changes.

4585.w: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors embedded within the body of a skeletal muscle, a specialized mechanoreceptor that primarily detects changes in the muscle's own length and feeds that information back to the central nervous system.

4586.w: The retina and the optic nerve both originate as outgrowths of the embryonic diencephalon, so the retina is classified as part of the central nervous system, and is, developmentally, actual brain tissue rather than a peripheral sense organ.

4587.w: A photoreceptor cell's membranous opsin protein pairs with the pigment retinal; in rod cells the two together are called rhodopsin, and absorbing a single photon changes the pigment's shape, the first step in converting light into a nerve signal.

4588.w: The cornea is the eye's transparent front layer, and its stroma is built from roughly 200 layers of type I collagen fibrils; the fibrils are spaced so precisely that light scattered by one is cancelled by destructive interference from its neighbors.

4589.w: The vertebrate eye's lens is built almost entirely from crystallin proteins, which make up over 90% of its protein content; densely packed crystallins raise the lens's refractive index while keeping it transparent.

4590.w: The iris is a thin, muscular diaphragm controlling pupil size: a circular sphincter muscle contracts to narrow the pupil, while a separate set of dilator muscles pulls the iris outward to widen it.

4591.w: The oculomotor nerve innervates most of the eye's own movement muscles, but it also carries parasympathetic fibers that reach the iris directly, driving the sphincter muscle that constricts the pupil and controlling the lens's focus for near objects.

4592.w: Hair cells are the sensory receptors of both the auditory and vestibular systems in the inner ear, a mechanoreceptor whose named tuft of stereocilia bends in response to fluid motion, converting that mechanical deflection into an electrical signal.

4593.w: The cochlea is a spiral-shaped, fluid-filled cavity of the inner ear making about 2.75 turns; running along it is the organ of Corti, whose hair cells sense the fluid's motion through their stereocilia and convert it into the electrical signal of hearing.

4594.w: The eardrum is a thin, cone-shaped membrane separating the outer ear from the middle ear; it flexes with incoming sound pressure and transmits that vibration to the ossicles, the middle ear's chain of tiny bones.
