6074.w: Barbara McClintock discovered transposons in the 1940s while studying maize: a mobile DNA segment jumped into a pigment gene and switched it off, producing the mottled, variegated kernel colors that first revealed 'jumping genes.'

6075.w: Transposable elements, first described in maize, were later discovered in bacteria too, where a mobile DNA segment can excise itself from one site and insert into another, often inactivating whichever gene it lands in.

6076.w: An F+ cell's pilus, built from genes on the F plasmid, attaches to an F- cell and draws the two together so a single strand of plasmid DNA can cross through a channel between them.

6077.w: First described by Esther Lederberg, the F-plasmid (sex factor) is a specific plasmid of E. coli whose tra genes build a pilus and transfer the plasmid, converting an F- recipient into F+.

6078.w: While assembling inside a host, a phage occasionally packages a stray piece of bacterial DNA into its protein coat instead of its own genome; that transducing particle then injects the bacterial DNA into the next cell it infects.

6079.w: A prophage sitting in the chromosome can excise itself imprecisely, dragging along a nearby bacterial gene into the new phage particle — specialized transduction, limited to genes near the old integration site.

6080.w: R factors can carry up to ten resistance genes on one plasmid, turning resistance to drugs like streptomycin into a package that spreads by conjugation between bacteria, even across species.

6081.w: Resistance plasmids are frequently loaded with genes for toxic heavy metals like mercury alongside their antibiotic-resistance genes, riding together on the same mobile piece of DNA.

6082.w: A block of chromosomal DNA larger than 10 kilobases with nucleotide composition unlike its surroundings marks a genomic island acquired by horizontal transfer; disease-gene-carrying ones are called pathogenicity islands.

6083.w: Devised by Joshua and Esther Lederberg, the technique presses a velvet-covered stamp onto a master agar plate, then onto fresh plates in the same orientation, revealing which colonies fail on a selective medium without exposing the mutant itself.

6084.w: A genomic DNA library is built by cutting an organism's chromosome into fragments with restriction enzymes, then cloning that pool into host cells so each cell carries, on average, just one fragment — together they preserve the whole genome.

6085.w: Reverse transcriptase copies mature messenger RNA back into DNA. Because that mRNA has already been spliced, the resulting cDNA contains only exons and no introns, so bacteria — which cannot splice — can still read it and make a working eukaryotic protein.

6086.w: Placing an antibiotic-resistance gene on a cloning vector makes it a selectable marker: on medium containing that antibiotic, only cells that actually took up and expressed the vector survive and form colonies.

6087.w: Green fluorescent protein was first purified from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria and glows green when exposed to blue-to-ultraviolet light; fused to a gene of interest, it lets researchers see exactly when and where that gene switches on.

6088.w: Colonies growing on an agar plate are pressed onto a membrane filter, the cells are lysed open in place, and their DNA is probed with a labeled sequence — autoradiography then reveals exactly which colonies in a library carry the gene of interest.

6089.w: A short single strand of DNA, labeled radioactively or fluorescently, hybridizes only to its exact complementary sequence, so wherever the probe lights up marks the target sequence's location.

6090.w: FISH detects a target sequence inside an intact cell on a slide; for identifying bacteria, probes are commonly aimed at the 16S rRNA region because each cell holds thousands of rRNA copies, giving a far stronger signal than a single-copy gene.

6091.w: A DNA microarray is a solid surface spotted with as many as millions of microscopic DNA probes; fluorescently labeled cDNA from a sample hybridizes to matching spots, and the resulting signal pattern reveals which genes an organism was expressing all at once.

6092.w: Plant genomes can be engineered by using Agrobacterium to deliver a gene of interest carried in T-DNA binary vectors derived from the Ti plasmid, integrating the foreign gene into the plant's own chromosome to produce a transgenic plant.

6093.w: Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, makes crystal Cry proteins while forming spores that bind gut-cell receptors unique to certain insects and rupture them; the gene was engineered into cotton so the plant makes its own insect toxin, harmless to humans.

6094.w: Golden Rice is rice genetically engineered to biosynthesize beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A, in the edible grain — developed from 1982 by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer to address vitamin A deficiency in regions where rice is the dietary staple.

6095.w: Golden Rice grain was engineered to carry beta-carotene, vitamin A's biological precursor, directly in the part of the plant people actually eat, so a staple food itself can supply a nutrient its ordinary grain lacks.

6096.w: The Ti plasmid occurs naturally in the soil bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens; its T-DNA region is transferred by conjugation into a wounded plant cell and integrates into the plant's chromosome, causing crown gall disease.

6097.w: A brief high-voltage electric pulse destabilizes a cell's lipid bilayer, opening nanoscale pores that let plasmid DNA enter — a standard way to transform E. coli and other cells that are not naturally competent to take up DNA on their own.

6098.w: S. pyogenes colonies on blood agar clear a wide zone of beta-hemolysis — complete destruction of the red blood cells around them — which is exactly how the species is told apart from the many other, gentler streptococci that share its usual haunts.

6099.w: S. pyogenes typically colonizes the throat, and when the infection is there it's strep throat by name. It spreads on the respiratory droplets a cough or sneeze sends into someone else's nose and mouth.

6100.w: The most common routes of entry for C. diphtheriae are the nose, tonsils, and throat — a club-shaped, palisade-forming rod that sets up in exactly the passage air takes on the way in.

6101.w: Diphtheria's damage isn't the bacterium invading tissue directly — it barely does. Its toxin spreads through the blood instead, and that's what causes the life-threatening complications in the heart and kidneys, and the nerve damage that can lead to paralysis.

6102.w: Streptococcus pneumoniae, cells paired up as a diplococcus, is the main cause of community-acquired pneumonia in children and the elderly — a species defined by the organ it targets.

6103.w: It's the most common bacterial pneumonia found in adults. Pneumonia's own mechanism is mechanical: it fills the lung's alveoli, the tiny air sacs, with fluid, and that fluid is what hinders oxygen from crossing into the blood.

6104.w: Bordetella pertussis is a tiny, encapsulated coccobacillus that attaches to the ciliated epithelial cells lining the respiratory tract using surface proteins built specifically for that job — cilia are the whole reason this species exists as a distinct thing.

6105.w: Whooping cough is what Bordetella pertussis causes once it's down in the airway: paroxysms of coughing, and following a fit of coughing, a high-pitched whoop or gasp as the next breath forces its way back in.

6106.w: An alveolar macrophage phagocytoses M. tuberculosis but can't kill or digest it, and the body's attempt to wall the infection off produces the caseating granulomas — tubercles — the bacterium is named for and characterized by in tissue.

6107.w: Tuberculosis initially infects the lungs, though it can spread elsewhere from there. Most infections stay latent, showing no symptoms at all, for years before some ever progress to active disease.

6108.w: Human rhinoviruses grow best at 33°C, noticeably colder than the body's 37°C core, which is exactly why they primarily infect nasal epithelial cells rather than settling deeper in the airway.

6109.w: Rhinoviruses alone cause up to 40% of common colds, and there are more than 100 known types of just that one genus — which is why no single vaccine has ever covered the disease.

6110.w: S. aureus is a usual member of the skin's own microbiota, frequently found there and in the nostrils — and it turns opportunist, becoming a common cause of skin infections, only once a barrier it normally respects gets breached.

6111.w: Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles, and most carbuncles, boils, and other cases of it are infected with exactly this species.

6112.w: S. aureus's exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1, the protein holding the epidermis's granulosum and spinosum layers together — the layers sitting just beneath the fully keratinized stratum corneum — so the skin separates from itself like a scald.

6113.w: Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection of the superficial skin, and it's typically due to either Staphylococcus aureus or, as here, Streptococcus pyogenes — the same species behind strep throat, just at a different portal.

6114.w: After a bite from an infected tick, R. rickettsii rides tick salivary secretions straight into the bloodstream, where it goes on to invade the endothelial cells lining the host's own blood vessels.

6115.w: R. rickettsii's invasion of blood vessel walls is what produces the disease's signature rash — small spots of bleeding starting on the wrists and ankles, then working toward the trunk.

6116.w: After spreading through the lymphatic system, measles virions circulate in the blood and go on to target epithelial cells in the skin and respiratory tract — the skin being exactly where the disease's signature rash comes from.

6117.w: Humans are the only natural host of measles virus, and it is one of the most contagious diseases known — nine in ten non-immune people sharing a home with a case will catch it.

6118.w: Rubella virus is found in the blood five to seven days after infection and spreads throughout the body from there — viremia is how this virus gets everywhere it goes, skin and placenta included.

6119.w: Rubella's rash is typically pink or light red, not as bright as measles' — a lighter disease on the skin, but the virus that causes it can also cross the placenta and interrupt fetal cell development.

6120.w: Dermatophytes are defined by their diet: they obtain nutrients from keratinized material, which is exactly why this whole group of fungi is restricted to skin, hair, and nails and nowhere else on the body.

6121.w: Dermatophytosis, better known as ringworm or tinea, is a fungal infection of the skin producing a red, itchy, scaly, circular rash — tinea is Latin for worm, but no worm is ever actually involved.

6122.w: Warts are caused by human papillomavirus, and the virus is believed to infect the host through the entrance of a skin wound — a break too small to notice is all the opening it needs.

6123.w: C. tetani cannot grow in the presence of oxygen at all, and once its toxin is loose it is taken up specifically into the nervous system, blocking the inhibitory neurotransmitters that motor nerve endings need to let a contracted muscle relax.

6124.w: Tetanus often begins with mild spasms in the jaw muscles — lockjaw — the direct result of the toxin blocking the nerve signal that would otherwise let those muscles relax between contractions.

6125.w: C. perfringens has the shortest reported generation time of any known organism, 6.3 minutes — an anaerobic spore-former whose alpha toxin embeds in and disrupts cell membranes, muscle cells included, faster than almost anything else can react.

6126.w: Gas gangrene is myonecrosis — outright muscle tissue death — with gas production alongside it, and progression to toxemia and shock is often very rapid once it starts.

6127.w: Pseudomonas aeruginosa forms tenacious biofilms on catheters, contact lenses and cystic-fibrosis lungs alike, and thrives in soil, water and skin flora, essentially anywhere there is moisture.

6128.w: P. aeruginosa is the most common cause of infections in burn injuries — a breach in the skin is the opening this ordinarily-environmental organism needs to become a serious opportunist.

6129.w: Actinomyces israelii is a normal colonizer of the mouth — present in ordinary saliva-bathed tissue — harmless there as long as it stays confined to the small, anoxic pockets it usually occupies.

6130.w: About 70% of actinomycosis cases trace to this one species, and it takes real tissue damage to get there — dental work, a broken jaw, or another trauma that lets a normal mouth commensal spread slowly through tissue it never usually reaches.

6131.w: Bartonella henselae is transmitted to humans through scratches, bites, or flea vectors associated with domestic and feral cats — the cat itself is this species' whole reservoir.

6132.w: Most cases of cat scratch disease trace to a scratch or bite from a kitten rather than an adult cat — the bacterium riding straight through the broken skin the scratch itself made.

6133.w: Nearly all domestic and wild rats are colonized by Streptobacillus moniliformis, and most of them carry it without any symptoms of their own — a completely silent passenger until it changes hosts.

6134.w: A bite or scratch from a colonized rat, gerbil, or mouse is enough to transmit it, and the resulting fever is a genuinely systemic one — high prostrating fevers, shivering, headache, and joint pain.

6135.w: H. pylori's helical shape is built for progressing through the stomach's own viscous mucosa lining, and its urease neutralizes the acid immediately around it as it corkscrews through — a bacterium engineered for one specific, hostile organ.

6136.w: H. pylori is one of the major causative factors of peptic ulcer disease — most people infected never experience symptoms, but a real fraction develop an actual ulcer in the stomach lining it's been living in.

6137.w: Mumps virus is transmitted via contact with respiratory secretions and saliva specifically, and humans are its only natural host — a virus whose entire spread depends on exactly this fluid.

6138.w: Humans are the only natural host of mumps virus, and once inside one, painful swelling of the parotid salivary glands in front of the ears is the single most common symptom the infection produces.

6139.w: Hepatitis A virus is a non-enveloped RNA picornavirus that spreads primarily by the fecal-oral route, most often through water or food that's been contaminated with infected feces.

6140.w: Once contracted, hepatitis A usually resolves completely and without any ongoing liver disease left behind — the acute illness runs its course and the liver recovers.

6141.w: C. difficile is normally held in check by a healthy gut microbiome — if an antibiotic disrupts that microbiome, it can grow freely as its competitors die off around it.

6142.w: Signs and symptoms of C. difficile infection range from mild diarrhea to severe, life-threatening inflammation of the colon, with a pseudomembrane of inflammatory cells and fibrin sometimes forming right there in the large intestine.

6143.w: As few as ten norovirus virions are needed to infect a person, making it one of the most contagious viruses known — and humans are its host throughout.

6144.w: Norovirus is usually spread by the fecal-oral route, through contaminated food or water, or through direct person-to-person contact — any one of which is enough given how few virions it takes to infect someone.

6145.w: Cyclospora spreads fecal-orally through oocysts shed in feces, but those oocysts aren't infectious the moment they're passed — sporulation takes one to several weeks outdoors first.

6146.w: Cyclospora cayetanensis causes cyclosporiasis, a diarrheal disease, once its slow-sporulating oocysts finally reach a human gut — the same weeks-long delay that makes direct person-to-person spread unlikely.

6147.w: Cryptosporidium affects the distal small intestine, resulting in watery diarrhea, sometimes alongside an unexplained cough if it reaches the respiratory tract too.

6148.w: Unlike the nontyphoidal Salmonella that causes ordinary food poisoning in a wide range of animal hosts, Salmonella Typhi is believed to infect and replicate only within humans — the same genus, a completely different epidemiology.

6149.w: A short mucosa-lined muscular tube from bladder to skin surface — about 4 cm in women versus roughly 20 cm in men, leaving women far less distance for bacteria to travel before reaching the bladder.

6150.w: The vaginal wall is a mucosa-lined muscular tube kept acidic, pH 3.8 to 4.5, by resident Lactobacillus that ferment glycogen stored in its epithelial cells into lactic acid, a barrier most pathogens can't tolerate.

6151.w: Leptospira interrogans is a hook-ended spirochete that colonizes the kidneys of chronically infected rodents without making them sick, then is shed continuously in their urine to contaminate soil and water.

6152.w: Gardnerella vaginalis is a small, gram-variable rod that can live in a healthy vagina without causing any problem — it becomes a marker of trouble only once Lactobacillus numbers fall and an anaerobic community grows in its place.

6153.w: Neisseria gonorrhoeae attaches to non-ciliated mucosal cells using retractable pili, then reshuffles its pilin and Opa surface genes into over a hundred antigenic variants — one reason no vaccine against it exists.

6154.w: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that infects cells lining the urethra and cervix, alternating between a rigid infectious form and a dividing form that never leaves the host cell it invaded.

6155.w: Treponema pallidum is a corkscrew-shaped spirochete driven by internal endoflagella, too thin to see by ordinary staining — it shows up only under dark-field microscopy, and still cannot be grown outside living tissue.

6156.w: True to its genus name, Haemophilus ducreyi is 'blood-loving' — it grows only on blood-enriched chocolate agar under humid, CO2-rich conditions, and its cytolethal distending toxin helps disable nearby immune cells.

6157.w: A compressed core of cotton, rayon, or a blend of the two. The most absorbent rayon blends of the late 1970s could soak up nearly 20 times their own weight in fluid, a property later tied to a rise in toxic shock syndrome.

6158.w: Uropathogenic E. coli causes roughly 75% of uncomplicated bladder infections by climbing the urethra and attaching to bladder cells with fimbriae — a much shorter trip in women, whose urethra averages just 4 cm.

6159.w: Left untreated, a bladder infection can climb the ureters into the kidneys, becoming pyelonephritis — a more serious infection that strikes 1 to 2 women per 1,000 each year and can leave lasting kidney scarring.

6160.w: Leptospira interrogans enters through mucous membranes or broken skin after contact with water or soil fouled by infected animal urine, then spreads through the bloodstream to the kidneys, liver, and other organs.

6161.w: Bacterial vaginosis develops when the vagina's normal Lactobacillus-dominated community collapses and anaerobic species, commonly signaled by Gardnerella vaginalis, overgrow in its place, raising the pH above 4.5 and producing a thin, fishy-smelling discharge.

6162.w: Candida albicans already lives in the vagina of many women without causing symptoms. When something disrupts the normal microbiota — oral antibiotics trigger it in about 30% of courses — the yeast overgrows, causing itching and a thick, white discharge.

6163.w: Certain Staphylococcus aureus strains growing in a blood-soaked, high-absorbency tampon release TSST-1, a superantigen that floods the bloodstream and triggers a massive cytokine release, crashing blood pressure within days.

6164.w: Gonorrhea infects roughly 88 million people worldwide each year. About half of infected women have no symptoms at all, letting the infection climb silently into the fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease or infertility.

6165.w: Chlamydial infection is the most frequently reported bacterial STI in the US. About 70% of infected women and half of infected men have no symptoms, so it often goes untreated long enough to scar the fallopian tubes and cause infertility.

6166.w: Syphilis begins with a painless ulcer at the site of entry, then can progress through a systemic rash, a silent latent phase lasting years, and — in a minority of untreated cases — late damage to the heart, brain, and blood vessels.

6167.w: Chancroid produces one or more painful, soft genital ulcers, unlike the painless hard chancre of syphilis, and often swells the lymph nodes in the groin into tender, pus-filled buboes that can rupture.

6168.w: Formaldehyde crosslinks an exotoxin's structure, destroying its toxicity while leaving enough shape intact for the immune system to recognize — this is exactly how tetanus and diphtheria vaccines are made.

6169.w: Clostridium tetani's toxin, tetanospasmin, blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine at synapses, so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles can't relax, producing the rigid spasms of lockjaw.

6170.w: Botulinum toxin from Clostridium botulinum blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, the opposite target from tetanus toxin — instead of rigid spasms, this produces flaccid, descending paralysis.

6171.w: Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae cause most bacterial meningitis; even treated, overall mortality is roughly one in six, and higher still in newborns.

6172.w: Enteroviruses and other viruses inflame the same meninges, but viral meningitis follows a far more benign course than the bacterial kind and is rarely fatal.

6173.w: When Neisseria meningitidis enters the bloodstream it can release endotoxin at up to 1,000 times normal levels, hemorrhaging small vessels into the telltale petechial rash; untreated, case-fatality reaches roughly 80%.

6174.w: About three-quarters of poliovirus infections cause no symptoms at all; only rarely does the virus reach and destroy motor neurons in the spinal cord, producing the disease's characteristic asymmetric, flaccid paralysis.

6175.w: Arbovirus is short for arthropod-borne virus — mosquitoes, ticks, and other blood-feeding arthropods pick it up from a reservoir host whose blood carries enough virus to infect the next bite, then pass it to the next host.

6176.w: West Nile virus cycles mainly between mosquitoes and birds, which is why it spread across North America within a few years of its 1999 arrival; humans rarely carry enough virus in their blood to pass it on, making them a dead-end host.

6177.w: Epidemic viral encephalitis in the US is caused mainly by arboviruses like La Crosse, eastern equine, and West Nile virus — mosquito-borne infections that occasionally spread from the blood into the brain itself.

6178.w: Herpes simplex virus, latent for years in a facial nerve ganglion, can reactivate and travel by the nerve into the brain instead of just the skin — herpes encephalitis is still fatal in about a third of cases even when treated.

6179.w: Rabies virus rides retrograde transport backward up motor-neuron axons to reach the brain, where it triggers acute encephalitis; once that stage begins and symptoms appear, treatment is almost never effective and mortality exceeds 99%.

6180.w: Y. pestis multiplies in a flea's gut until a clot of bacteria blocks its foregut; the starving flea bites repeatedly, regurgitating the blockage — and the bacteria — into the wound.

6181.w: A flea bite delivers Y. pestis into the lymphatic system; it multiplies in the nearest lymph node until acute inflammation swells it into the hard, tender bubo that gives bubonic plague its name.

6182.w: Rabbits and other small mammals are reservoir hosts for F. tularensis, and handling an infected one is a classic route of infection — the source of the name 'rabbit fever.'

6183.w: In the most common form, a skin ulcer marks where the bacteria got in, and the regional lymph node draining that site swells and becomes tender within days.

6184.w: Brucella melitensis, the species most often behind human illness, keeps mainly to goats and sheep as its natural host.

6185.w: Brucella abortus is the cattle-adapted species of the genus, the counterpart to B. melitensis in goats and B. suis in pigs.

6186.w: Undulant fever, its old name, for how the fever recurs in waves over weeks; most human cases trace to unpasteurized milk or cheese, or direct contact with an infected animal.

6187.w: Sepsis is the body's own dysregulated response to a bloodstream infection, not the microbe's damage directly — Gram-negative bacteria releasing endotoxin is a well-studied trigger of the resulting cytokine storm.

6188.w: Left uncontrolled, sepsis can progress to blood pressure so low it doesn't recover with fluids alone — septic shock, which carries a mortality rate near 40%.

6189.w: Bacteria seed a thin clot that forms on a damaged heart valve and build a biofilm there — since a heart valve has no blood supply of its own, the immune system has no direct way to reach them.

6190.w: Lymph nodes are strung along the vessels that drain lymph fluid from tissue and skin, and act as filters — B cells fill the outer cortex, T cells and dendritic cells the paracortex, macrophages the sinuses.

6191.w: Tucked behind the stomach in the upper left abdomen, the spleen filters blood the way lymph nodes filter lymph — its red pulp clears out worn and damaged red blood cells.

6192.w: Every lymphocyte — B cell, T cell, or NK cell — descends from a common progenitor born of hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow.

6193.w: EBV is an enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus whose defining trick is B lymphocytes: it infects them, then persists there for life once the initial infection clears.

6194.w: Nicknamed 'kissing disease' because EBV spreads mainly through saliva — weeks of fever, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes follow, with fatigue that can linger for months.

6195.w: Outside cities, yellow fever virus keeps a sylvatic cycle running between forest mosquitoes and monkeys — mostly without making the monkeys sick — long before any human is bitten.

6196.w: Named for the jaundice liver damage causes in severe cases — among patients who develop jaundice, the fatality rate is 20% to 50%.

6197.w: Untreated, HIV floods the bloodstream in the first weeks after infection, producing a flu-like illness in most people 2 to 4 weeks after exposure — the acute retroviral syndrome.

6198.w: After acute symptoms subside, HIV keeps replicating at a stable 'viral set point' for years — an asymptomatic period that, without treatment, lasts three to over twenty years, averaging about eight.

6199.w: Years of continuous HIV replication gradually exhausts the CD4+ T cell supply; AIDS is diagnosed once the count falls below 200 cells per microliter or a defining opportunistic disease appears.

6200.w: A single needlestick exposure to HIV-infected blood infects a health care worker about 0.3% of the time, well below the roughly 10% seroconversion risk from a hepatitis B needlestick.

6201.w: Without antiretroviral treatment, HIV passes from mother to child around birth in about 20% of cases, rising to 35% with breastfeeding; treatment cuts that risk below 5%.

6202.w: Human herpesvirus 8 packages a large double-stranded DNA genome and was first identified in 1994 by analyzing DNA extracted directly from Kaposi's sarcoma tumor tissue.

6203.w: HHV-8 infects the endothelial cells lining blood and lymphatic vessels; up to 50% of AIDS patients developed Kaposi's sarcoma during the early epidemic, before antiretroviral therapy could suppress it.

6204.w: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus so adapted to mammalian lung tissue that every life stage occurs there, and it has never been successfully grown outside a host.

6205.w: Pneumocystis colonizes most people harmlessly, but once CD4+ counts fall below 200 cells per microliter it can cause a severe pneumonia that was once the most common AIDS-defining illness in the US.

6206.w: Severe immunodeficiency lets latent Toxoplasma cysts reactivate in brain tissue, causing encephalitis; treatment is recommended once CD4+ counts drop below 200 cells per microliter.

6207.w: Cytomegalovirus carries roughly 235,000 base pairs of double-stranded DNA in an icosahedral capsid inside a lipid envelope — longer than the genome of any other human herpesvirus.

6208.w: Reactivated cytomegalovirus infects the retina in 15% to 40% of people with AIDS, historically one of the leading causes of AIDS-related blindness before antiviral treatment.

6209.w: Chronic, uncontrolled HIV infection causes cachexia — muscle and fat loss without another explanation — which presented as the first sign of AIDS in about a fifth of early cases.

6210.w: Zidovudine mimics thymidine closely enough that reverse transcriptase incorporates it into the growing DNA chain, but it lacks the 3' hydroxyl group needed to add the next nucleotide, so the chain stops.

6211.w: Combining antiretrovirals from different drug classes creates multiple simultaneous obstacles to replication, suppressing HIV to a low viral set point for years — though it never clears the latent provirus, so it is not a cure.

6212.w: Big Bang nucleosynthesis produced the universe's first elements within minutes of its beginning — overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, the same two that still make up nearly all its ordinary matter today.

6213.w: The Big Bang describes how the universe expanded from that early hot, dense state into everything it now is: all space, time, matter and energy, roughly 93 billion light-years across at its observable edge.

6214.w: Bacteria and fungi are two of the domains microorganism actually spans — any organism of microscopic size, found in nearly every one of the three domains of life. (Viruses are generally excluded: not considered alive.)

6215.w: Most microbes never harm a host at all. A pathogen is specifically one equipped with virulence factors — the traits that let it actually cause disease, which is exactly why the word exists separately from microbe.

6216.w: Infection is the pathogen actually establishing itself and multiplying in a host -- the event itself, which can happen with or without producing any visible symptom.

6217.w: The same infection can stay silent (asymptomatic carriage) or progress into disease -- the actual harm and symptoms an infection produces once it overwhelms the host's defenses.

6218.w: The English word 'geyser' comes from Geysir in Iceland's Haukadalur, meaning 'gusher' in Icelandic; the island is volcanically active because it straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

6219.w: Norway's coast is cut by roughly 1,200 fjords — U-shaped valleys gouged by glaciers and then drowned by the sea — which stretch its coastline from about 2,500 km to about 29,000 km.

6220.w: Malta is a limestone archipelago in the central Mediterranean about 80 km south of Italy, and that soft stone was quarried for its megalithic temples around 3500 BC.

6221.w: Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean and was antiquity's great copper source — the Latin 'aes Cyprium', metal of Cyprus, was shortened to cuprum.

6222.w: Georgia borders Türkiye to the south and holds the earliest known winemaking sites in the world, dating to around 6000 BCE.

6223.w: The Kingdom of Kush ruled the Nile valley of what is now Sudan, leaving the pyramids of Meroë, and the Blue and White Niles converge at Sudan's capital Khartoum.

6224.w: Rwanda's highest ground is the Virunga volcanic chain on its north-western border with the DR Congo, crowned by Mount Karisimbi at 4,507 m.

6225.w: Zambia borders the DR Congo to the north, and its population and mining industry are concentrated in the Copperbelt Province along that border.

6226.w: The Kalahari covers up to 70% of Botswana, and the Okavango, one of the largest inland deltas in the world, spreads into those desert sands instead of reaching the sea.

6227.w: The Namib, the oldest desert in the world, runs the length of Namibia's Atlantic shore as the Skeleton Coast, making it the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa.

6228.w: Angola's oil-producing province of Cabinda is an exclave cut off from the rest of the country by DR Congo territory.

6229.w: Mauritius is a volcanic island in the Indian Ocean that became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony before independence in 1968.

6230.w: Seychelles is unusual in combining 42 granitic islands, including Mahé and Praslin, with far-flung coral atolls such as Aldabra.

6231.w: Cabo Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands in the eastern Atlantic, uninhabited until Portuguese and Genoese navigators settled it from the 1460s.

6232.w: The equator crosses the country's islet of Ilhéu das Rolas, and by 1905 São Tomé was the world's largest producer of cocoa, still its most important crop.

6233.w: Gabon straddles the equator in Central Africa and is 89.3% forested, with about 10% of its territory set aside in thirteen national parks.

6234.w: The Republic of the Congo borders Gabon to the west and lies on the western side of the Congo River, its capital Brazzaville facing Kinshasa across the water.

6235.w: Mali takes its name from the medieval Mali Empire that grew rich on trans-Saharan trade, and its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara.

6236.w: The Guinea Highlands hold the sources of the Niger, Gambia and Senegal rivers, and Guinea is the world's second-largest producer of bauxite.

6237.w: The ruins of Carthage, the Mediterranean power Rome destroyed in 146 BC, stand beside modern Tunis on Tunisia's northeastern Mediterranean coast.

6238.w: Barbuda is a flat island built almost entirely of coral limestone, while Antigua's English Harbour held the Royal Navy's Nelson's Dockyard until Britain granted independence in 1981.

6239.w: The Bahamian archipelago of some 700 islands and 2,500 cays supports a queen conch fishery that employs over 9,000 Bahamian fishers.

6240.w: Belize holds Maya cities of the Mesoamerican lowlands on land and the Belize Barrier Reef, the second-longest barrier reef in the world, offshore.

6241.w: The maple leaf on Canada's flag names the tree that gives the country more than 75 percent of the world's maple syrup, most of it from Quebec.

6242.w: Costa Rica occupies a narrow stretch of the Central American isthmus, with the Caribbean Sea on its northeast coast and the Pacific Ocean on its southwest.

6243.w: Sugarcane was central to Cuba's development and sugar remains one of its principal exports alongside tobacco and coffee.

6244.w: Columbus sighted the island on Sunday 3 November 1493 and named it for dies Dominica; it is the youngest island of the Lesser Antilles volcanic arc and still volcanically active.

6245.w: El Salvador is called the Land of Volcanoes for its more than twenty volcanic cones, among them Santa Ana at 2,365 m and the still-active San Miguel and Izalco.

6246.w: Nutmeg introduced to Grenada in 1843 became a mainstay of its economy and earned the island the name Island of Spice.

6247.w: Guatemala hosted the core of the Maya civilization, with cities such as Tikal, across highlands defined by its chain of volcanoes.

6248.w: Rainforest covers over 80 percent of Guyana and contains Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's most powerful waterfalls.

6249.w: Honduras holds the Maya city of Copán, and its banana trade was so dominated by fruit companies that O. Henry coined 'banana republic' about it in 1904.

6250.w: Bauxite discovered in the 1940s reshaped Jamaica's economy; by 1998 it produced 10.4 percent of world bauxite, and bauxite and alumina made 55.2 percent of exports in 1999.

6251.w: Mexico takes its name from Mēxihko, the Nahuatl term for the Aztec heartland, and Mexico City stands on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan.

6252.w: Nicaragua is called the land of lakes and volcanoes, and Lake Nicaragua holds Ometepe, an island formed where the volcanoes Concepción and Maderas join at a low isthmus.

6253.w: Panama occupies the isthmus that joined North and South America about three million years ago, cut through by the 83 km Panama Canal completed in 1914.

6254.w: Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans covered the volcanic slopes of Saint Kitts until the state-owned sugar company was closed in 2005.

6255.w: England and France fought fourteen times for control of Saint Lucia, whose position was so contested it was nicknamed the Helen of the West.

6256.w: William Bligh's 1791 Providence expedition carried seedless breadfruit from Tahiti to Saint Vincent, where it took hold on the volcanic slopes below La Soufriere, still an active volcano — it erupted explosively in April 2021.

6257.w: Suriname was Dutch until independence on 25 November 1975, and at 90.2 percent forest cover it is the most forested nation in the world.

6258.w: The epidermis is dead stratified squamous keratinized epithelium — the skin's outer layer is epithelial tissue, and like all epithelium it has no blood vessels of its own.

6259.w: The airways are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium: about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times a second to sweep mucus up toward the pharynx.

6260.w: Tendon is dense connective tissue — collagen fibres laid down one way by fibroblasts in the ground substance they secrete.

6261.w: Cartilage is 'special' connective tissue: sparse cells in a collagen-rich matrix, the same pattern that also covers bone and the fluid types, blood and lymph.

6262.w: Muscle tissue is myocytes doing all the work — a skeletal muscle fibre is a single multinucleate cell that can run from a few millimetres to several inches long.

6263.w: Actin and myosin are the contractile proteins that define muscle tissue; troponin and tropomyosin decide when the two are allowed to interact.

6264.w: Nervous tissue is exactly two cell classes — neurons that carry impulses and neuroglia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells) that feed and support them.

6265.w: Two tissue types in one wall is what makes an organ: the intestine lines itself with epithelium and wraps that lining in smooth muscle.

6266.w: The nervous system is one of the eleven organ systems in the human body — the tier above the organ, where several organs share a single function.

6267.w: Glycolysis is catabolism's opening move, splitting glucose to pyruvate and banking the energy as ATP — the currency every anabolic reaction then spends.

6268.w: Metabolism is enzyme-catalysed chains of reactions, and the mitochondrion runs the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation that pay for the rest of them.

6269.w: Salivary amylase breaks down about 30% of dietary starch before you swallow, and gastric juice — roughly 0.5% hydrochloric acid, pH 1 to 3 — then takes over on protein.

6270.w: Digestion runs on two tracks at once: mechanical churning and peristaltic waves moving food along, while enzymes cut it into water-soluble pieces the blood can absorb.

6271.w: Heart, blood vessels and blood are the three parts of the circulatory system; William Harvey published the proof in 1628 that blood goes round and round rather than being used up.

6272.w: Inhalation at rest is simply the diaphragm contracting and dropping, pulling air down to 300 million alveoli and about 145 m² of gas-exchange surface.

6273.w: Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus — about nine metres of tract, the last stretch taking 30 to 40 hours over what was not absorbed.

6274.w: The pancreas is an accessory digestive organ: no food passes through it, it just pipes enzymes into the small intestine downstream of the stomach.

6275.w: Around 270 bones at birth fuse to about 206 in an adult, split 80 axial to 126 appendicular — support, movement, protection and blood production in one system.

6276.w: The skeleton doubles as a mineral bank, storing the body's calcium and iron and releasing them on demand.

6277.w: Skeletal muscles pull on bone through tendons; more than 600 of them make up roughly 40% of body mass and hold posture as well as move it.

6278.w: The anterior pituitary's tropic hormones — TSH, ACTH, growth hormone — ride the bloodstream to command other glands, TSH being the order that brings thyroxine out of the thyroid.

6279.w: The pancreas doubles as an endocrine organ, releasing insulin directly into the circulation rather than down a duct.

6280.w: Kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra: 180 litres of filtrate a day with 99% reabsorbed, which is how blood volume, electrolytes and pH are held steady.

6281.w: Roughly 800 lymph nodes plus spleen, thymus and tonsils on a network with no pump — muscle contraction alone returns about 3 litres of leaked fluid to the blood each day.

6282.w: Leukocytes are the immune system's workforce: phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils engulf whatever gets in, while lymphocytes mount the response tailored to that pathogen.

6283.w: Adaptive immunity's two halves — B cells raise antibodies that tag a pathogen for complement or phagocytes, T cells handle infected cells, and both leave long-lived memory cells behind.

6284.w: The only organ system an individual can survive without: testicles make sperm, ovaries make ova, and every other part of the tract exists to bring the two together.

6285.w: The female tract runs ovary to fallopian tube to uterus to cervix to vagina — the ovum comes down it and the sperm go up, meeting in the tube.

6286.w: Skin, hair, nails, scales and claws are one system — in humans 1.5 to 2 m² of covering weighing 12 to 15% of the body.

6287.w: The kidney is where a mammal does its osmoregulation — about 180 litres of filtrate a day, with fluid volume, osmolality, acid-base balance and electrolyte levels all set by how much is reabsorbed.

6288.w: The liver converts ammonia into urea through the urea cycle, and the urea is carried away in the blood to be excreted in the urine.

6289.w: About 80% of the body's daily cholesterol production happens in the liver and intestines, and the liver oxidises cholesterol into bile acids — the same organ that banks roughly 100 g of glycogen.

6290.w: The liver makes 400 to 800 ml of bile a day; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, then releases it when fatty food arrives, where bile salts wrap triglyceride droplets into micelles.

6291.w: Peristaltic contractions of the oesophageal muscle push a swallow down to the stomach, past a lower sphincter that then closes to prevent reflux of acidic stomach contents.

6292.w: The airway down to the lungs is held permanently open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, each 4 mm high.

6293.w: The trachea divides at the carina into a main bronchus for each lung — three secondary bronchi for the right lung's three lobes, two for the left's two.

6294.w: An artery's middle layer, the tunica media, packs smooth muscle with elastic tissue and collagen — far thicker than a vein's, which is how it carries blood away from the heart against the circulatory system's highest pressure.

6295.w: Blood comes back at low pressure, so contracting skeletal muscle presses on the intramuscular veins to drive it toward the heart while one-way valves prevent backflow.

6296.w: Capillaries convey blood from the smallest arteries, the arterioles, to the smallest veins, the venules — and that 5 to 10 micrometre gap is where water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose and urea are exchanged.

6297.w: The branching airway ends in about 480 million alveoli, each wrapped in capillaries across a membrane between 0.2 and 0.6 micrometres thick, giving 70 to 80 square metres of gas exchange.

6298.w: The blastocyst implants in the endometrium lining the uterus, whose middle layer — the myometrium — is smooth muscle that grows to several times its size and contracts in labour.

6299.w: The ovary both releases the ovum, one per menstrual cycle, and secretes oestrogen, androgen, inhibin and progestogen directly into the bloodstream.

6300.w: Leydig cells sit next to the sperm-making seminiferous tubules and shuttle cholesterol into their mitochondria, where it becomes pregnenolone and eventually testosterone.

6301.w: Fetal tissue builds the placenta against the uterine wall, exchanging nutrients and oxygen with no intermingling of fetal and maternal blood, and it is expelled in the third stage of labour.

6302.w: Twenty-two bones make up the skull, and the mandible is the only freely-jointed one, articulating with the temporal bones at the paired temporomandibular joints.

6303.w: Joints are classed by what connects the bones — dense collagen in a fibrous joint, cartilage in a cartilaginous one, and in a synovial joint no direct connection at all, just a capsule and a fluid-filled cavity.

6304.w: The head of the femur sits in the acetabulum of the pelvis as the hip joint and its lower end meets tibia and patella at the knee; neck and shaft meet at roughly 130 degrees.

6305.w: Twelve pairs of ribs cage the heart, lungs and great vessels, and evert on inhalation so the chest circumference expands by 3 to 5 cm.

6306.w: Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary drives the follicle cells that concentrate iodide out of the bloodstream and build it into the colloid's thyroglobulin.

6307.w: One gland, two tissues: the outer cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, while the medulla inside it releases roughly 80% adrenaline and 20% noradrenaline.

6308.w: Glucagon from the pancreatic alpha cells drives glycogenolysis in the liver, breaking stored glycogen back down into circulating glucose.

6309.w: Pituitary luteinizing hormone tells the testes' Leydig cells — the source of over 95% of a man's testosterone — to build it out of cholesterol.

6310.w: One enzyme makes every estrogen: aromatase strips the C19 methyl group off testosterone and aromatizes the A ring, turning it into estradiol.

6311.w: The follicle left behind once the ovum is released becomes the corpus luteum, which converts cholesterol through pregnenolone into about 30 mg of progesterone a day.

6312.w: Somatotropic cells in the anterior pituitary release a 191-amino-acid chain that divides growth-plate cartilage directly, and grows bone again indirectly by making the liver secrete IGF-1.

6313.w: Vitamin K — the K is for Koagulation — carboxylates prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X into Gla residues that can chelate calcium, and without it blood will not clot.

6314.w: Calcium is factor IV: it bridges factors IXa and Xa onto phospholipid surfaces through their gamma-carboxy residues, and the cascade stalls without it.

6315.w: The clot is only the first of four phases — fibroblasts arrive two to five days in and lay down type III collagen, later swapped for type I during remodeling.

6316.w: The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus is the body's thermostat, correcting in both directions: sweating and vasodilation above the setpoint, shivering and brown fat below it.

6317.w: Rising estrogen thickens the endometrium in the proliferative half; progesterone from the corpus luteum holds it for about 14 days, and when that gland fails the lining sheds.

6318.w: The hypothalamus resumes pulses of GnRH, the pituitary answers with LH and FSH, and the gonads answer with testosterone or estradiol.

6319.w: Growth hormone drives the growth-plate spurt and estrogen ends it — rising estrogen in both sexes kills off the plate's chondrocytes until cartilage is replaced by bone.

6320.w: Bile is cholesterol turned into detergent plus bilirubin, the pigment macrophages make from the heme of destroyed red blood cells.

6321.w: Deep in the epithalamus between the two halves of the thalamus sits the gland that N-acetylates serotonin and then methylates it into melatonin.

6322.w: Melanopsin ganglion cells run straight from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, resetting a clock that otherwise free-runs at about 24 hours 11 minutes.

6323.w: Two enzymes do it in the dark — AANAT acetylates serotonin, ASMT methylates the result — and the pineal gland releases about 30 micrograms a day, 80% of it at night.

6324.w: The ventral part of the striatum is where the ventral tegmental area's mesolimbic dopamine axons terminate, on the medium spiny neurons that are 95% of the cells there.

6325.w: Struck, the fork's two tines swing apart and together and drive pressure pulses into the air — nearly a pure sine wave at the fundamental, most often A440.

6326.w: Pitch lives in the listener, not the air — the ear ordering sounds high to low on a frequency-related scale, which is why it counts as a psychoacoustic attribute rather than a physical one.

6327.w: Halve a vibrating string and it sounds at twice the frequency, a pitch exactly one octave higher — the 2:1 ratio demonstrated on the monochord since antiquity.

6328.w: A scale is the series of notes running from one pitch up to its octave; the keyboard divides each octave into twelve equal semitones, of which a major scale selects seven.

6329.w: A chord is two or more notes sounding together, most often a triad of root, third and fifth built on a scale degree — a guitar lets one hand stop all three at once.

6330.w: Rhythm is sound placed in time, accented beats against unaccented ones — and an unpitched drum stroke carries almost no information except when it lands.

6331.w: Tempo sets how fast the beats go by, counted in beats per minute — the same unit as a pulse, and a resting adult heart's 60–100 bpm sits inside the Andante band of 56–108.

6332.w: In its most literal sense a melody is a combination of pitch and rhythm — a linear succession of tones the listener perceives as one entity.

6333.w: Harmony is the vertical dimension to melody's horizontal one — pitches combined at once and chords moving in progression, the basis of Western tonal practice since about 1600.

6334.w: Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody and rhythm — melody running in sequence, harmony stacked beneath it.

6335.w: Put music on a page and you get notation: neumes written above chant text in 9th-century monasteries, which Guido of Arezzo ruled onto a staff around 1000.

6336.w: A full orchestra runs seventy to over a hundred players across four sections; the violins head the strings and the timpani head the percussion, which in Baroque scoring were called for whenever trumpets were.

6337.w: A symphony is an extended orchestral work notated in a score holding every instrument's part, from which each player reads only their own line.

6338.w: Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, premiered at Mantua on 24 February 1607, sets exactly this myth — the descent to Hades and the failed attempt to lead Eurydice back — and is the earliest opera still regularly performed.

6339.w: Jazz came out of New Orleans at the turn of the 20th century on swung rhythm and improvisation; the saxophone entered its instrumentation around 1912.

6340.w: The lungs are the pump: their airflow sets the vocal folds in the larynx vibrating into audible pulses, which the tongue, palate and lips then filter into speech.

6341.w: The cello's top three strings, G2–D3–A3, sit exactly one octave below the violin's lowest three, G3–D4–A4, with a low C2 added underneath.

6342.w: Both are strung frames, but a lyre's strings stretch from a yoke across a bridge in the plane of the sound table, while a harp's rise almost perpendicular out of the soundboard.

6343.w: Human language is a structured system of grammar and vocabulary, the primary means by which humans convey meaning -- spoken, signed, or written down. The spoken form is shaped by the vocal tract, tongue included.

6344.w: A phoneme is defined by perception: a set of similar speech sounds that a language's own speakers hear as a single basic sound. Those are the contrasts that let one word be told from another.

6345.w: Phonemes are the smallest units that distinguish one word from another; strung together they build the words that carry meaning.

6346.w: Grammar is the system of rules governing how a natural language's words combine into phrases and clauses, as its speakers and writers actually use them.

6347.w: Cuneiform is one of the earliest conventional writing systems: a fixed set of symbols, plus the rules they encode, for representing a particular spoken language. Such systems first appear in the late 4th millennium BC.

6348.w: Alphabetic writing starts in Egypt: the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt repurposed Egyptian hieroglyphs as signs for single sounds, and later alphabets descend from them.

6349.w: A writing system is the abstract set of symbols and rules; a script is the concrete character set put on the page. They are coded separately because one script can serve many different languages.

6350.w: In a dialect continuum neighbouring varieties stay mutually intelligible while distant ones do not, so the line is usually drawn politically: one variety gets codified as a state's standard language and serves as the authority for that part of the chain.

6351.w: Sogdian, the Eastern Iranian language of Samarkand and Bukhara, became the most important lingua franca of Mongolia, China and Inner Asia, carried along the trade routes by Sogdian merchants.

6352.w: Every family descends from a single proto-language, and the split typically happens through geographical separation: speakers move apart, their regional dialects change differently, and daughter languages result.

6353.w: When two groups with no language in common have to deal with each other -- typically to trade -- they improvise a pidgin, grammatically simplified, its words pulled from both sides.

6354.w: A pidgin becomes a creole once children acquire it as their first language. That is the dividing line: creoles have native speakers, systematized grammar and stable vocabularies; pidgins have none of the three.

6355.w: Sign languages convey meaning through manual articulation combined with non-manual markers rather than spoken words -- a different modality for language, not a gestured version of speech.

6356.w: Where languages meet, words cross. Indonesian's vocabulary has taken words from Javanese, Sundanese, Minangkabau and Balinese, and also from Arabic, Dutch, Hokkien, Portuguese, Sanskrit and English.

6357.w: Literacy -- the ability to read and write -- has spread in step with the invention of writing systems and the expansion of education, and rates have risen substantially worldwide since the mid-twentieth century.

6358.w: Esperanto is a constructed auxiliary language: Zamenhof designed its vocabulary and grammar deliberately and published them in 1887 as 'the International Language', intended as a neutral second language for international communication.

6359.w: The Steppe theory -- the most widely accepted answer to the Proto-Indo-European homeland question -- places the proto-language on the steppe, from which the Indo-European migrations carried its daughters across Europe, Iran and northern India.

6360.w: Beyond the Sinitic giants, most Sino-Tibetan languages are spoken by small communities in the Himalayas, the Southeast Asian Massif and the eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, and are poorly documented as a result.

6361.w: Afroasiatic's roughly 400 languages are spoken across West Asia, North Africa, the Horn of Africa and parts of the Sahara and the Sahel, by more than 500 million native speakers.

6362.w: Niger-Congo is spoken over the majority of sub-Saharan Africa and unites the Mande and Atlantic-Congo groups; Yoruba, spoken across south-west Nigeria, is one of its Atlantic-Congo languages.

6363.w: Austronesian spread by sea: its languages are spoken across Taiwan, Maritime Southeast Asia, Madagascar and the islands of the Pacific, making it the fifth-largest family by number of speakers.

6364.w: The Dravidian family's 250 million speakers are concentrated in South India, spilling into north India, Bangladesh, Nepal, north-east Sri Lanka and south-west Pakistan.

6365.w: Proto-Turkic is thought to have been spoken in a region of East Asia spanning Mongolia and northwest China, from which the Turkic languages expanded into Central Asia and further west during the first millennium.

6366.w: The Greeks took the Phoenician alphabet in the late 9th or early 8th century BC and added something no earlier script had: systematic letters for vowels alongside the consonants.

6367.w: The Latin script began as the Greek alphabet in use at Cumae in Magna Graecia; the Etruscans altered it, and the Romans altered the Etruscan version in turn.

6368.w: Cyrillic is a writing system used for languages across Eurasia, and the national script of Russia and of many countries in Southeastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

6369.w: Devanagari is an Indic abugida based on the ancient Brahmi script, developed and in regular use by the 8th century CE; it is one of the official scripts of India and Nepal.

6370.w: Of the four independently invented writing systems scholars accept, Chinese characters are the only one to have remained in continuous use -- a documented history spanning more than three millennia.

6371.w: Korean had been written with Chinese characters, which suited the language poorly and left illiteracy high, so Joseon king Sejong the Great had a new alphabet announced in 1443-44 and published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum.

6372.w: Both Japanese syllabaries descend from magana: Chinese characters used purely for their sound to transcribe Japanese, rather than for their meaning.

6373.w: Ge'ez was first used to write the Ge'ez language, now the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and has since been adapted for Amharic, Tigrinya and at least 20 other languages of Ethiopia.

6374.w: Latin was originally spoken by the Latins in Latium, the lower Tiber valley around Rome, and spread through the Italian peninsula with the expansion of the Roman Republic.

6375.w: English is a West Germanic language that emerged in early medieval England, named after the Angles who migrated to Britain after Roman rule ended; the British Empire and then the United States made it a global lingua franca.

6376.w: Mandarin is the largest branch of the Sinitic languages, stretching from Yunnan to Xinjiang to Heilongjiang; its spread is generally credited to how much easier the North China Plain is to travel than the mountainous south.

6377.w: Modern Standard Hindi is an Indo-Aryan language written in the Devanagari script, an official language of the government of India and the lingua franca of most of the northern half of the country.

6378.w: Spanish originated in the Kingdom of Castile in north-central Spain, evolving out of the Vulgar Latin spoken on the Iberian Peninsula, and is now one of the six official languages of the United Nations.

6379.w: Castilian is what became of the Vulgar Latin spoken on the Iberian Peninsula -- the most widely spoken Romance language today.

6380.w: Arabic is a Central Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family spoken primarily across the Arab world, whose varieties share a literary standard derived from Classical Arabic.

6381.w: French descends from the Vulgar Latin of Roman Gaul, marked by native Celtic languages and by the Germanic Frankish of the post-Roman invaders, and over time supplanted most of France's other regional Romance varieties.

6382.w: French and its closest relatives, the langues d'oil of northern France and southern Belgium, all descend from the Vulgar Latin of the Roman Empire.

6383.w: Bengali, known by its endonym Bangla, is the Indo-Aryan language of the Bengal region, spoken natively across Bangladesh and eastern India.

6384.w: Portuguese is a Western Romance language of the Indo-European family, written in the Latin script and official in Portugal, with approximately 267 million native speakers worldwide.

6385.w: Portuguese is the official language of eight countries -- Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Sao Tome and Principe and Timor-Leste -- and the most widely spoken language of the Southern Hemisphere.

6386.w: Russian is an East Slavic language of the Balto-Slavic branch, and remains a lingua franca in Ukraine, Moldova, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

6387.w: Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language spoken primarily in South Asia, and is the national language and lingua franca of Pakistan.

6388.w: Indonesian is a standardised variety of Malay, the Austronesian language that had served as the lingua franca of the multilingual Indonesian archipelago for centuries before it was made the national language.

6389.w: German is a West Germanic language of the Indo-European family, spoken mainly in Western and Central Europe, with sizeable communities across the Americas.

6390.w: Japanese is the principal language of the Japonic family, spoken by the Japanese people and by the Japanese diaspora worldwide.

6391.w: Swahili, or Kiswahili, is a Bantu language of the Atlantic-Congo family, originally spoken by the Swahili people of Tanzania, Kenya and Mozambique.

6392.w: Swahili's speaker estimates run from 150 to 200 million once second-language speakers are counted -- far beyond the coastal Swahili people who speak it natively.

6393.w: Korean is a Koreanic language native to Korea and the official language of both North and South Korea; it is written in the Hangul alphabet.

6394.w: Turkish is the most widely spoken of the Turkic languages: the national language of Turkey, one of two official languages of Cyprus, and spoken by sizeable communities in Germany, Bulgaria and the Caucasus.

6395.w: Vietnamese is an Austroasiatic language of the Vietic subgroup and the official language of Vietnam, where it also serves as a second language for other ethnic groups.

6396.w: Tamil is the Dravidian language of the Tamil people, concentrated in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry in India and in the Northern and Eastern Provinces of Sri Lanka.

6397.w: Tamil is the Dravidian language of Tamil Nadu in South India, and one of the longest-surviving classical languages anywhere.

6398.w: Persian, or Farsi, is a Western Iranian language of the Indo-European family, spoken and used officially within Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan.

6399.w: Italian is a standardised form of literary Florentine Tuscan and, together with Sardinian, the Romance language least differentiated from Latin.

6400.w: Thai is a Tai language of the Kra-Dai family, spoken in Central Thailand and the sole official language of the country.

6401.w: Polish is a West Slavic language of the Lechitic subgroup, written in the Latin script, and the official language of Poland.

6402.w: Dutch is the native language of most of the population of the Netherlands and of Flanders; it was an official language of South Africa until 1925, when Afrikaans, its daughter language, replaced it.

6403.w: Greek constitutes an independent Hellenic branch of Indo-European, native to Greece, Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean; before the alphabet it was recorded in Linear B and the Cypriot syllabary.

6404.w: Hebrew was spoken natively by the Israelites, remained in regular first-language use until after 200 CE, survived as the liturgical language of Judaism, and was revived as a spoken language in the 19th century.

6405.w: Amharic is an Ethio-Semitic language within the Semitic branch of Afroasiatic, spoken as a first language by the Amhara and as a common language by other city populations of Ethiopia.

6406.w: Hausa is a Chadic language spoken primarily by the Hausa people of Niger and Nigeria, and used as a common language far beyond them across West Africa.

6407.w: Tagalog is an Austronesian language spoken as a first language by the ethnic Tagalog people and as a second language by the majority of the Philippine population.

6408.w: Yoruba is a pluricentric Atlantic-Congo language spoken across a dialect area spanning south-west Nigeria, Benin and Togo, with migrated communities in Cote d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone and the Gambia.

6409.w: Punjabi is an Indo-Aryan language native to the Punjab region, which straddles Pakistan and India.

6410.w: Javanese is the Austronesian language of the Javanese people of Java; Indonesian, the national language, has borrowed heavily from it.

6411.w: Telugu is the Dravidian language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where it is the official language -- one of the few Indian languages with primary official status in more than one state.

6412.w: Sanskrit is a classical Indo-Aryan language and the sacred language of Hinduism; its most archaic form, Vedic Sanskrit, is the language of the Rigveda's 1,028 hymns, composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE.

6413.w: The Arabic script is the writing system used for Arabic and for several other languages of Asia and Africa -- Persian, for one, is written in a derivative of it.

6414.w: An adult male lion needs about 7 kg of meat a day and takes all of it from animal tissue. Obligate carnivores like the big cats cannot get nutrients such as taurine and retinol any other way, so meat is not a preference for them but a requirement.

6415.w: A cow's rumen holds no cellulase of the cow's own — the mutualistic bacteria and protozoans fermenting inside it break the grass's cross-linked cellulose down instead. That outsourcing is what lets a herbivore live on a diet no vertebrate enzyme can handle.

6416.w: An omnivore takes energy and nutrients from both plant and animal matter, feeding across more than one trophic level at once — which is exactly why bears, pigs, crows and humans cannot be pinned to a single rung of any food chain.

6417.w: Lions hunt medium-to-large hooved mammals — plains zebra, blue wildebeest, buffalo — killing and eating them. That is the whole definition of predation: one organism kills another and eats it.

6418.w: The prey is the organism the predator kills and eats, and plains zebra are among the lion's principal prey. Prey numbers drive predator numbers in turn — the lynx and the snowshoe hare cycle together on a 10-year period across the boreal forest.

6419.w: A bee working a flower picks up pollen on its body and rubs it onto the stigma of the next one. This is the biotic route, and over 87.5% of flowering plants depend on pollination of some kind to fertilise their ovules and set seed.

6420.w: The pollinator is the animal doing the moving — all bee families qualify, and honey bee pollination alone adds more than $15 billion of value to United States crops each year.

6421.w: The orchid Angraecum sesquipedale is pollinated by Morgan's sphinx moth and effectively nothing else. Pollination can narrow to a single species on each side, which is why losing one moth can strand a whole plant.

6422.w: The tapetum lucidum is a mirror behind the retina that sends light back through it a second time — the eyeshine you get in a torch beam. It is one of the night-adapted features mammals kept from their long nocturnal past, alongside acute hearing and whiskers.

6423.w: Most animals were originally diurnal and some adapted into the night; lineages have since re-evolved daytime activity, geckos about 20 separate times. The suprachiasmatic nucleus reads incoming light to set which way round an animal runs.

6424.w: An Ophrys orchid's lip mimics a female bee closely enough in shape and pheromone that males attempt to mate with it — pseudocopulation — and leave carrying pollen on their head or abdomen. The flower offers no nectar at all; the whole transaction is a deception.

6425.w: Venom is defined by being actively delivered into another animal through a wound — a bite, a sting, a penetrating strike — rather than passively ingested or absorbed the way a poison is. About 450 snake species carry it.

6426.w: Both are skeletons; what differs is which side the soft tissue sits on. An endoskeleton of bone and cartilage grows with its owner, while an arthropod has to moult its exoskeleton repeatedly through its juvenile stages just to get bigger.

6427.w: Gestation is the stretch during which an embryo, and later a fetus, develops inside a viviparous mother. The African bush elephant runs it for 22 months and ends with a calf of 100 to 120 kg.

6428.w: A butterfly's egg hatches into a caterpillar, not a small butterfly. The larva has structures and organs the adult never has, a different diet, and often a different habitat — it eats to fuel the metamorphosis that will replace it.

6429.w: Habitat is a species-specific term: the array of resources and biotic factors present in an area that lets that particular species survive and reproduce. Savanna grass, water and open space is what makes savanna zebra habitat rather than merely scenery.

6430.w: Add the abiotic half — soil, water, climate — to the living food web occupying a habitat and you have an ecosystem: biotic and abiotic components tied together by nutrient cycles and energy flows, which is precisely the definition Tansley published in 1935.

6431.w: Habitat is where a species lives; the niche is what it does there — Elton defined it in 1927 as an animal's place in the biotic environment, its relations to food and enemies. A species' habitat is the physical manifestation of the niche its adaptations fit it for.

6432.w: A biome is a distinct geographical region with its own climate, vegetation and animal life. Whittaker's classification needs nothing but average annual temperature and average annual precipitation to tell one from another.

6433.w: Scavengers feed on dead and decaying organic matter. The spotted hyena is a facultative one — its bone-crushing bite lets it take the parts of a carcass other carnivores abandon — while obligate scavenging is nearly a vulture monopoly, and diclofenac cutting Asia's Gyps vultures by at least 95% was followed by rises in rabies, plague and anthrax.

6434.w: A bat's wing is a hand. It is built from the same ancestral tetrapod forelimb bones as a whale's flipper, a horse's foreleg and a human arm, reshaped for a different job — similarity of structure from shared ancestry, regardless of what the structure now does.

6435.w: Mendel crossed round-seeded peas with wrinkled ones and got an F1 generation that was entirely round: the round allele masked the wrinkled one in every heterozygote. Self-cross that F1 and the hidden version reappears, in the characteristic 3:1 ratio.

6436.w: Punnett drew the square in 1905 to make Mendel's arithmetic visible. Cross two heterozygotes and the four cells read 25% BB, 50% Bb and 25% bb — three offspring showing the dominant phenotype for every one showing the recessive.

6437.w: A spontaneous mutation that happens to blunt a drug becomes an advantage the instant that drug is present. Tuberculosis regimens built on streptomycin alone selected for exactly that and failed — which is why TB is now treated with several drugs at once.

6438.w: Selection pressure from overuse in medicine and agriculture does the sorting, and horizontal gene transfer spreads the result: bacteria hand resistance genes sideways between species by conjugation, transformation and transduction, so a trait selected in one lineage need not stay there.

6439.w: Selection can only see reproductive success: an allele spreads when its carriers average more offspring than the alternatives, and adaptation is what accumulates from that. Spencer's 1864 phrase 'survival of the fittest' describes this arithmetic, not strength or health — a frail organism that leaves more offspring is the fitter one.

6440.w: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour; Wundt made it a laboratory discipline at Leipzig, and psychologists in Germany, Denmark, Austria, England and the United States soon set up laboratories of their own.

6441.w: The discipline's two founding lines: Wundt breaking mental processes into basic components in the laboratory, by analogy to chemistry, and Freud's clinical account of unconscious phenomena — psychology covers conscious and unconscious alike.

6442.w: Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies inside the substantia nigra's dopamine neurons; by the time motor symptoms appear, 50-80% of those neurons have degenerated.

6443.w: Autism is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder: the differences in social communication, sensory processing and repetitive interests emerge in early childhood and usually persist for life, and twin studies show genetic factors explain most of the variation.

6444.w: ADHD involves the dopamine and norepinephrine systems that modulate executive function, with the greatest volume reduction found in the left prefrontal cortex; stimulant medication works by increasing activity in exactly those two systems.

6618.w: A potato tuber is storage parenchyma: thin-walled living cells with big central vacuoles, packed with starch.

6619.w: The strings you pull off a celery stalk are collenchyma strands — living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls of cellulose and pectin, bracing a shoot that is still growing.

6620.w: Cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin in a thick secondary wall; the cell then dies and is pure structure — long fibres like flax, or stubby sclereids like the grit in a pear.

6621.w: Mesophyll is the leaf's parenchyma: palisade cells stacked upright for light under the upper epidermis, spongy cells below with air spaces wide enough that CO2 from the stomata reaches every one of them.

6622.w: The wall they share is riddled with plasmodesmata, so the nucleated companion cell keeps its enucleate sieve tube element alive and loads sugar into it.

6623.w: Water crosses from one dead tracheid to the next through bordered pits in the side walls — an arrangement that passes water while limiting how far an air embolism can spread.

6624.w: Water evaporating from mesophyll walls and out through the stomata puts the whole xylem column under tension, and cohesion between water molecules drags the next one up behind it.

6625.w: Autogamy: pollen from a flower's own anther landing on its own stigma. Tomatoes go further with cleistogamy, setting seed inside a flower that never opens.

6626.w: Cross-pollination moves pollen to a genetically distinct plant of the same species, so the offspring combine two parents' alleles rather than one's — the reason most flowering plants have mechanisms to avoid pollinating themselves.

6627.w: A maple's winged samara flutters off on the wind. Other seeds pay a bird with fruit, hook onto fur, float across an ocean, or get carried underground by ants.

6628.w: Stomata sunk into pits, leaves reduced to spines, and CAM photosynthesis that takes CO2 in at night so the pores can stay shut through the heat of the day.

6629.w: Water is banked in swollen parenchyma, most of it inside enormous vacuoles — an aloe does it in the leaf, a cactus in the stem, and about 60 unrelated families arrived at it separately.

6630.w: An epiphyte uses the host purely for support, taking its water and minerals from rain, air and the debris that collects around it — unlike a parasite, it draws nothing out of the tree.

6631.w: Three tactics are available: exclude the salt at the root, push it out through leaf glands, or dump it into leaves the plant then sheds. A mangrove filters most of it out at the root and offloads the rest into old leaves.

6632.w: Physiological dormancy is chemical: abscisic acid blocks germination until cold, damp or fire tips the balance toward gibberellin. Physical dormancy is simpler — a coat too hard to let water in.

6633.w: Cold and moisture together are what break physiological dormancy, so the seed cannot germinate in autumn into a winter it would not survive.

6634.w: Cold recruits VIN3 and the VRN2 complex to shut the FLC repressor down by chromatin remodelling. Lysenko coined the term in 1928, then wrongly claimed the change was inherited.

6635.w: Ethylene drives leaf senescence and shedding far harder than abscisic acid does; cytokinin pulls the other way, and keeping cytokinin synthesis switched on late will hold a leaf green.

6636.w: The vascular cambium makes xylem inward and phloem outward while the cork cambium makes bark outward. Most monocots have neither — a palm thickens by enlarging parenchyma instead.

6637.w: A dicot stem sets its bundles in a neat ring with cambium between the xylem and phloem; a monocot scatters them through the stem in an atactostele, with no ring left to thicken.

6638.w: Pith is parenchyma at the dead centre of a eudicot stem, ringed by xylem and then phloem. Monocot stems have none — and sago palm pith is a starch staple across Melanesia.

6639.w: Krupp began casting steel cannon in the 1840s, and Prussia's 1870-71 victory over France demonstrated the superiority of breech-loaded steel guns over muzzle-loaded brass.

6640.w: A revolution in firepower unmatched by any advance in mobility: rapid-firing guns like the French 75 and machine guns handed the defender the advantage, and by the end of October 1914 the whole front had dug in.

6641.w: Caterpillar-track tractors hauling guns in France showed what tracks could do; the commission that followed asked for a machine able to cross a four-foot trench and carry its own gun over ground swept by fire.

6642.w: The design brief was written by the deadlock itself — an armoured machine that could cross a 4 ft trench, first tried at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916.

6643.w: The deadlock machine guns helped create is what 167 tons of chlorine, released from 5,730 cylinders near Ypres on 22 April 1915, was meant to break; gas killed roughly 90,000 and broke nothing.

6644.w: The Western Front solidified into a near-continuous line of fortified trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, and Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele all failed to break it.

6645.w: HMS Dreadnought put ten 12-inch guns on the first capital ship driven by steam turbines, reaching 21.6 knots on trials in October 1906.

6646.w: The 1922 Washington Naval Treaty capped capital-ship building, so surplus battlecruiser hulls became the first large carriers — Lexington, Akagi, Kaga — and by Taranto in 1940 their aircraft had outclassed the guns.

6647.w: A submersible hull whose weapon is the torpedo: U-20 sank the Lusitania on 7 May 1915, and unrestricted campaigns ran in 1915, again from February 1917, and through the whole of the next war.

6648.w: Guderian ordered in 1933 that every German tank carry a radio; at the outbreak of war only the German army's tanks were all radio-equipped, which is what let armoured columns be handled as one mass.

6649.w: Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, the Soviet Union from the east on 17 September, and organised resistance ended on 6 October — the campaign Liddell Hart called a full demonstration of the theory.

6650.w: The wartime programme spent over 80 percent of its near-$2 billion budget on the plants that enriched uranium at Oak Ridge and bred plutonium at Hanford.

6651.w: In the Teller-Ulam design the fission primary's X-rays compress a secondary of deuterium fuel by radiation implosion; Ivy Mike, using liquid deuterium, gave 10.4 megatons.

6652.w: The R-7, burning liquid oxygen and kerosene, threw a multi-megaton warhead 6,000 km to Kamchatka on 21 August 1957.

6653.w: Castles were not communal defences but the private fortified residences of feudal lords — the men who granted land in return for the military service a mounted vassal owed.
