6654.w: Bonaparte was commissioned a second lieutenant in the La Fère artillery regiment in September 1785, and made his name massing guns above the harbour at Toulon in 1793.

6655.w: Bamboo slips unearthed at Yinqueshan in Shandong in 1972, sealed in the tomb between 134 and 118 BC, carry an early version of the Art of War closely matching the text still read.

6656.w: Compressed inert gas, usually nitrogen, drives heated oil through a hose to a pilot flame at the barrel, throwing fire 50 to 100 metres.

6657.w: Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia, where Sumer arose, and Baghdad, founded in 762 as the Abbasid capital, is its capital today.

6658.w: Bahrain is an archipelago of 33 natural islands famed since antiquity for pearl fisheries considered the best in the world into the 19th century.

6659.w: Oman's Dhofar is the UNESCO Land of Frankincense of the medieval incense trade, and its Musandam exclave is bounded by the Strait of Hormuz.

6660.w: Archery is the national sport of Bhutan, contested regularly in most villages of this Vajrayana Buddhist kingdom.

6661.w: The Tian Shan mountains cover over 80% of Kyrgyzstan, and its Lake Issyk-Kul was a stopover on the Silk Road between the Far East and Europe.

6662.w: Nan Madol, on Pohnpei in Micronesia, is 92 artificial islets built of columnar basalt in a lagoon from around AD 1180.

6663.w: On 25 September 2009 Palau announced the world's first shark sanctuary, protecting reef sharks across waters that include the Southern Lagoon of its Rock Islands.

6664.w: Marshallese navigators invented stick charts that map ocean swell and wave patterns, letting sailors locate atolls still below the horizon.

6665.w: Kiribati's 32 atolls straddle the equator and the 180th meridian, stretching from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east.

6666.w: Phosphate was discovered on the island of Nauru in 1900, and income from the mines made Nauruans among the richest people in the world.

6667.w: The atolls of Tuvalu hold the .tv internet domain, whose royalties supplied 8.4% of government revenue by 2019.

6668.w: The Tonga Trench's Horizon Deep drops 10,800 m into the hadal zone, second on Earth only to the Mariana, and the Hunga Tonga volcano erupted there in January 2022.

6669.w: Mount Yasur, a near-continuously erupting volcano on Vanuatu's Tanna Island, is the sacred site of the John Frum cargo cult.

6670.w: Mendana's 1568 expedition sailed west chasing Inca stories of gold, and the archipelago was named Islas Salomon when reports of it were conflated with the wealth of the biblical King Solomon.

6671.w: Animals are the multicellular eukaryotes that have muscle cells, breathe oxygen, consume organic material, and develop through a blastula.

6672.w: A sea squirt larva carries a notochord and a hollow dorsal nerve cord just as any vertebrate does — those, plus an endostyle, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail, define the phylum Chordata.

6673.w: Vertebrates are the chordates whose vertebral column surrounds and protects the nerve cord, with a cranium around the brain.

6674.w: Mammals are the vertebrates that feed their young on milk from mammary glands; around 6,640 living species have been described.

6675.w: Synapsida is the amniote clade that contains all mammals and their extinct relatives; hair and mammary glands mark the surviving branch, which split from the reptile line over 300 million years ago.

6676.w: Sauropsida is the amniote clade broadly equivalent to class Reptilia; reptiles are its ectothermic members, developing inside an amniotic egg.

6677.w: Amphibians are the anamniotic tetrapods: four-limbed vertebrates that never gained the amniotic egg, so most begin as gilled aquatic larvae and metamorphose into air-breathing adults.

6678.w: Arthropods are the invertebrates with a chitin exoskeleton, segmented bodies and paired jointed appendages — and they must moult that shell to keep growing.

6679.w: In every mollusk the dorsal body wall forms a mantle, and it is the mantle that secretes the calcareous plates or shell.

6680.w: Cnidaria is named for the cnidocyte, the stinging cell that fires the nematocyst, and most of its species alternate between a sessile polyp and a free-swimming medusa.

6681.w: Insects are the largest group within the arthropods, marked by a three-part body, three pairs of jointed legs, one pair of antennae and compound eyes.

6682.w: Primates are the mammals that adapted to life in the treetops: large brains, binocular colour vision, mobile shoulders and opposable thumbs for grasping.

6683.w: Rodentia is defined by a single pair of continuously growing incisors in each of the upper and lower jaws — and it accounts for about 40% of all mammal species.

6684.w: A beaver and a house mouse are both Rodentia, gnawing with the same pair of ever-growing incisors — the order is native to every major landmass except Antarctica.

6685.w: Metamorphosis grows the legs, swaps gills for lungs, and draws the tadpole's tail inward as an internal urostyle — leaving an adult of Anura, 'without tail'.

6686.w: Frogs make up about 87% of all amphibian species — over 7,700 of them in 59 families — and almost all start as jelly-wrapped spawn laid in water.

6687.w: Speciation is the point where diverging populations can no longer interbreed; taxonomy then treats the result as the basic unit of classification, a species.

6688.w: The first half of a two-part Latin name is the genus, the rank just above species and below family: Panthera leo and Panthera onca share theirs.

6689.w: Arthropoda and Chordata are two of the roughly 32 phyla in the animal kingdom — the rank sitting below kingdom and above class.

6690.w: Fungi and Plantae are separate kingdoms, alongside Animalia — the rank Linnaeus put at the top of his 1735 hierarchy.

6691.w: Kingdoms are the rank divided into phyla: Animalia contains about 32 of them, Plantae about 14.

6692.w: Woese, Kandler and Wheelis introduced domain in 1990 as a rank above kingdom, splitting all cellular life into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

6693.w: Comparing 16S ribosomal RNA in 1977, Woese found Archaea were no kind of bacterium at all — which forced a new highest rank to hold the three branches.

6694.w: Aristotle's History of Animals investigates animal structure, development and the function of the parts — formal zoology is said to originate with him.

6695.w: Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance; he, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen founded ethology, the branch of zoology studying animal behaviour, and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for it.

6696.w: Homo sapiens emerged around 300,000 years ago from a big-brained heidelbergensis-grade population, then spread out of Africa and replaced the archaic humans it met.

6697.w: Carl Linnaeus coined the binomial Homo sapiens in 1758 — and is himself the designated type specimen of the species he named.

6698.w: A. ramidus, described in 1994 from 4.4-million-year-old deposits at Aramis, is the type species of the genus Ardipithecus; the older A. kadabba at 5.6 million years is the other.

6699.w: Every known Ardipithecus fossil comes from the Afar region of Ethiopia, unearthed at Aramis and in the Middle Awash between 1992 and 1993.

6700.w: Ardipithecus walked upright but kept a divergent grasping big toe for the trees; by 3.7 million years ago Australopithecus afarensis had lost it, and the Laetoli footprints record a committed two-legged stride.

6701.w: Two legs have been invented over and over: all the early dinosaurs and the theropod clade that became birds, and among mammals kangaroos, hopping mice and hominins, each independently.

6702.w: Gene flow carries alleles between populations and mixes their gene pools — the set of all genetic information a population holds.

6703.w: A species' gene pool is the sum of its genetic diversity; a large one survives bouts of intense selection, while a small one drifts toward extinction.

6704.w: With no oxygen, Saccharomyces cerevisiae takes about 2 ATP from each sugar and dumps the leftover carbon as ethanol and carbon dioxide.

6705.w: Fermentation is what the ferment verb does: yeast, starved of oxygen, breaks each glucose molecule into two ethanol and two carbon dioxide molecules — the reaction behind beer, wine and a risen loaf.

6706.w: Gluten is 75–85% of the total protein in bread wheat, as two storage proteins: glutenin supplying elasticity and gliadin supplying extensibility.

6707.w: Kneading wet flour cross-links glutenin molecules through disulfide bonds into a submicroscopic network that gliadin attaches to.

6708.w: It needs both halves — amino acids from the protein and a reducing sugar — which is exactly what separates it from caramelization, where sugar alone pyrolyses.

6709.w: The TAS1R1+TAS1R3 receptor pair, identified at the University of Miami in 2000, is what reports free glutamate as a taste in its own right.

6710.w: Kikunae Ikeda traced the palatability of kombu broth to glutamate in 1908 and coined the word; the symposium that accepted it as a basic taste met in Hawaii in 1985.

6711.w: Two liquids that will not mix, forced into a dispersed phase inside a continuous one — it takes energy input to make, and it separates again on its own.

6712.w: Lecithin is amphiphilic: one end dissolves in water, the other in oil, so it sits on the interface and lowers the tension holding the droplets apart.

6713.w: Each sugar has its own threshold, and glucose starts at 150 °C — twenty degrees below sucrose. No amino acids are involved at all, which is what separates caramelization from the Maillard reaction.

6714.w: Every sugar has its own threshold: fructose at 105 °C, glucose at 150 °C, sucrose at 170 °C, maltose at 180 °C.

6715.w: The same class of molecule in two states: saturated chains pack tight and set solid, unsaturated ones kink and stay liquid.

6716.w: Rendered pig fat and rendered beef suet are both esters of fatty acids on glycerol; how saturated those chains are decides how hard the fat sits at room temperature.

6717.w: Equal proportions by weight: the fat is heated first, the flour stirred in and cooked until it loses its raw taste.

6718.w: Cajun cooks use oil or lard rather than butter and take it to dark brown for gumbo; Hungarian cooks stir paprika into theirs.

6719.w: Velouté is exactly this — a pale stock thickened with roux — and it is one of Escoffier's five mother sauces.

6720.w: Béchamel, a butter-and-flour roux loosened with milk, was named in Vincent La Chapelle's The Modern Cook of 1733.

6721.w: A leaf and a root land in the same category because cooks group by how a plant part is eaten, not by which organ it is.

6722.w: One is a swollen underground stem and the other a berry, yet Nix v. Hedden (1893) taxed the tomato as a vegetable because it arrives with the main course.

6723.w: Cinnamon is bark and ginger a rhizome — spices come from seed, fruit, root, bark or flower bud, never from the leaf.

6724.w: Same shelf, different anatomy: herbs are the leaves, flowers and stems of a plant, spices everything else it offers.

6725.w: Escoffier drew the line here: salt, acids and spices are seasonings, while onions, mustard and fats he counted as condiments.

6726.w: Salt draws water out and magnifies the flavours already present; used properly the seasoning itself cannot be tasted.

6727.w: Served alongside rather than stirred in during cooking — that timing is what separates a condiment from a seasoning.

6728.w: The archetypes of the narrow definition: prepared compounds made in advance, added after cooking, dosed by the eater.

6729.w: Carbohydrates, amino acids and fatty acids are the macronutrients an animal needs in bulk; vitamins and minerals are the trace list beside them.

6730.w: An essential nutrient is one the body cannot make in sufficient quantity — 9 amino acids, 2 fatty acids, 13 vitamins, 14 minerals — so it has to arrive on the plate.

6731.w: Biological leavening: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments the dough's sugars and the carbon dioxide is caught in the starch-and-gluten matrix.

6732.w: Chemical leavening: a bicarbonate salt and a dry acid that only meet once moisture arrives, so quick breads need no fermentation time.

6733.w: The juices meat and vegetables run naturally during cooking, thickened with flour or cornstarch — that is the whole definition.

6734.w: Drippings let down with stock: cream gravy in the American South, onion gravy in Britain, giblet gravy at Thanksgiving.

6735.w: Butter holds almost no lactose because it is milk fat, while milk itself carries the most — the category spans that entire range.

6736.w: Cattle were domesticated about 12,000 years ago, but the earliest evidence of milking them is seventh-millennium-BC northwestern Anatolia.

6737.w: Ethanol boils at 78.1 °C, but at 95.6% by mass it forms an azeotrope with water where vapour and liquid match and ordinary distilling can go no further.

6738.w: Selective boiling and condensing the vapour in a still — a physical separation, not a chemical reaction. Alexandria's alchemists were doing it by the 1st century CE.

6739.w: Air, sun, wind and smoke all do one job: remove the moisture that bacteria, yeasts and mould need to grow. Jerky and prosciutto are the meat version.

6740.w: Lofoten stockfish hangs unsalted on wooden racks from February to May at just above 0 °C and loses about 80% of its water.

6741.w: Salt does the osmosis; nitrite breaks down to nitric oxide, binds myoglobin's heme group for the pink colour, and inhibits the bacteria that cause botulism.

6742.w: Osmotic pressure pulls water out of the microbes rather than killing them, and this was the main way to keep meat and fish until the late 19th century.

6743.w: Hot smoking runs 52–80 °C and cooks as it flavours; cold smoking at 20–30 °C leaves the food raw and leans entirely on the smoke's antimicrobials.

6744.w: Smoke's phenols are antioxidant and antimicrobial, but it is nearly always paired with salt because smoke mainly seals the outer layer.

6745.w: Lactic acid bacteria ferment at room temperature in 20–40 grams of salt per litre and generate the required acidity themselves — no sterilisation needed.

6746.w: The other route: sterilised jars, vinegar and spices, holding the solution at pH 4.6 or below so enzyme activity and microbial growth both stop.

6747.w: The coating fats and oils leave is a texture sensation, distinct from taste and smell, and research shows viscosity alone can shift how full you feel.

6748.w: Wine tasters rate mouthfeel from first perception on the palate through chewing to aftertaste; tannin drops protein out of solution, so its grip is felt, not tasted.

6749.w: The first of the WHO's five keys is keeping pathogens off food from people, pets and pests; the rest are separating raw from cooked, cooking through, storing right, and safe water.

6750.w: Spoilage organisms announce themselves by smell; pathogens do not, which is why safety is governed by the 5–60 °C danger zone rather than by taste.

6751.w: Malting, mashing, lautering, boiling, fermenting: the yeast only gets to work after amylase has turned the grain's starch into sugar it can eat.

6752.w: Mashing steeps barley malt at 60–70 °C, where alpha- and beta-amylase cut starch into dextrins and fermentable sugars such as maltose.

6753.w: The surface must pass about 150 °C to brown, and since water boils off at 100 °C it has to be dry first. The browning is Maillard, not caramelization.

6754.w: Experiments from the 1930s found seared roasts lost as much moisture or more; the high heat ruptures more cells and releases extra liquid. The payoff is flavour and contrast.

6755.w: A combination method — dry heat first for the browning, then moist heat in a covered pot, with less liquid and bigger cuts than a stew.

6756.w: Wine, stock or beer, often with something acidic: coq au vin and osso buco work because connective tissue and collagen break down and lubricate the fibres.

6757.w: Adolphe Sax put the clarinet's single-reed mouthpiece onto a conical brass body — Wikipedia calls the saxophone 'a type of single-reed woodwind instrument with a conical body, usually made of brass' whose mouthpiece is 'similar to that of the clarinet'. The saxophone's own fact says this; no recipe did.

6758.w: The bassoon is the oboe's double reed on a long maple bore: a 'Double-reed woodwind instrument', 'generally made of maple', standing 1.34 m tall with a sounding length of 2.54 m because the tube doubles back on itself.

6759.w: The bag is animal skin — 'the skins of local animals such as goats, dogs, sheep, and cows' — and every pipe it feeds is sounded by a reed, 'single... or double reed'. The current recipe is air plus hide and never touches the reed.

6760.w: The two things that make a modern piano: 'a massive, strong, cast iron frame' to hold the string tension, and 'firm felt hammer coverings instead of layered leather or cotton' to strike the strings.

6761.w: Tuning forks are 'traditional sources of standard pitch for tuning musical instruments', and 'the most common tuning fork sounds the note of A = 440 Hz, the standard concert pitch'. That is exactly how a piano gets its reference.

6762.w: Pitch is made in the cochlea: hair cells 'are tuned to certain sound frequencies by way of their location in the cochlea, due to the degree of stiffness in the basilar membrane' — 'this spatial arrangement of sound reception is referred to as tonotopy'.

6763.w: The hunting bow is the bowed instrument's ancestor — the military bow 'could easily have served the inventor as a temporary way to hold horsehair at high tension' — and the hair only grips once tree resin is on it: 'Rosin... a hard, sticky substance made from resin... is regularly applied to the bow hair to increase friction.'

6764.w: 'The first electric guitars used in jazz were hollow archtop acoustic guitar bodies with electromagnetic transducers' — an ordinary guitar plus magnets: pickups are 'magnets wound with coils of very fine wire'.

6765.w: Moog built a theremin at 14 from magazine plans, founded R.A. Moog Co. in 1954 selling theremin kits, and was still selling them from Ithaca when he built 'his first synthesizer components' at Cornell. The theremin business is where the synthesizer came from.

6766.w: Stephenson's Rocket was a steam engine set on rail wheels: an 0-2-2 locomotive whose 'large front pair of wooden wheels was driven by two external cylinders', with 'the pistons... connected directly to the driving wheels'. The recipe went straight from wheel and piston, skipping the engine.

6767.w: Bardeen and Brattain worked from 17 November to 23 December 1947 at Bell Labs until 'two gold point contacts were applied to a crystal of germanium' and gave power gain — the solid-state replacement for the vacuum tube's triode.

6768.w: Marconi's 1896 British Patent 12039 was for wireless telegraphy: 'a Righi spark gap powered by an induction coil with a telegraph key to switch it on and off to spell out text messages in Morse code'. Radio began as a telegraph without the wire.

6769.w: The competition 'gained Western public attention with the Sputnik crisis' of 4 October 1957, and the Moon landing is 'considered as the final act of the Space Race by many observers'. Sputnik's beep is what pointed the United States at the Moon.

6770.w: Whitney's gin cleaned short-staple cotton fast enough to flood the mills: 'the greatly expanded supply of cotton created strong demand for textile machinery and improved machine designs that replaced wooden parts with metal'. The gin fed the loom; the loom made the cloth.

6771.w: Edison conceived recorded sound 'as a byproduct of his efforts to play back recorded telegraph messages and to automate speech sounds for transmission by telephone', and his first machine 'recorded onto a thin sheet of metal, normally tinfoil'.

6772.w: The computer inherited its keyboard whole from the typewriter: 'the first computer terminals such as the Teletype were typewriters that could produce and be controlled by computer codes. These used the QWERTY layouts' — the layout fixed by the 1873 Sholes and Glidden machine.

6773.w: The press is a machine 'that transfers ink onto materials such as paper... by applying pressure to an inked surface', and by 1500 Europe's presses had produced 'more than twenty million copies' where 'hand-copying was slow and expensive'. Books were only craftable by hand before this.

6774.w: Pesto alla genovese is basil crushed with garlic, pine nuts, cheese and extra virgin olive oil, and is 'a sauce used to dress pasta'. Its first written recipe is Giovanni Battista Ratto's La Cuciniera Genovese, 1863.

6775.w: Ratto's 1863 pesto instructs the cook to take garlic and basil, 'grated Dutch and Parmigiano cheese and mix them with pine nuts and crush it all together in a mortar'. The pine nut is not a garnish here — it is what makes the sauce a paste.

6776.w: Mole poblano is built on 'two or more of the following types of chili pepper: ancho, pasilla, mulato and chipotle', and 'chocolate, if used, is added at the end of cooking' to balance it — roughly twenty ingredients reduced to one sauce.

6777.w: British mint sauce is exactly these two things: 'finely chopped spearmint leaves soaked in vinegar, and a small amount of sugar'. Mint currently connects to nothing downstream at all.

6778.w: Mint sauce 'is a traditional accompaniment to roast lamb', established in English cooking before the mid-18th century and with roots reaching back to Roman practice.

6779.w: 'Honey mustard is a blend of mustard and honey', used on sandwiches and as a dip; the pairing is old — Apicius's De re coquinaria mustard calls for ground mustard with 'honey, vinegar, fish sauce, and oil'.

6780.w: The default seasoning of the Western table: salt's 'pairing with pepper as table accessories dates to seventeenth-century French cuisine, which considered black pepper... the only spice that did not overpower the true taste of food'.

6781.w: Marinara: 'a tomato sauce usually made with tomatoes, garlic, herbs, and onions', and in Italy 'typically made with tomatoes, basil, olive oil, garlic, and oregano'. Tomato and garlic are the two that cannot be left out.

6782.w: Guacamole is mashed avocado and salt, and 'recipes often call for lime juice, cilantro..., onions, and jalapeños'. The game currently makes it from avocado alone.

6783.w: Alongside lime, 'cilantro (known as coriander outside the US)' is one of the ingredients guacamole recipes most often call for.

6784.w: The aromatic base of the kimchi seasoning: 'commonly used seasonings include gochugaru (chili powder), scallions, garlic, ginger, and jeotgal' — and kimchi's smell is 'especially tied to the sulfur compounds from garlic and ginger'.

6785.w: 'Aztecs from the central highlands of Mexico invaded the Totonacs in 1427, developed a taste for the vanilla pods, and began using vanilla to flavor their foods and drinks, often mixing it with cocoa in a drink called xocolatl' — with no sugarcane, vanilla was what tamed the bitterness.

6786.w: Pizza Margherita is a base 'seasoned with hand-crushed peeled tomatoes, mozzarella (buffalo mozzarella or fior di latte), fresh basil leaves, and extra virgin olive oil'. Mozzarella was used in no recipe at all.

6787.w: Sufism is 'a mystic body of religious practices within Islam', 'the inward dimension of Islam', turning on the qalb — the heart — as 'a faculty of spiritual intuition' to be purified. Its recipe was human plus heart, with Islam nowhere in it.

6788.w: 'Wahhabism is a Salafi revivalist movement within Sunni Islam named after the 18th-century Hanbali scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab', and 'was initially established in the central Arabian region of Najd' before spreading across the peninsula.

6789.w: Salafism is 'a cluster of contemporary Sunni renewal and reform movements' whose name 'claims a return to the traditions of the predecessors (salaf), the first three generations of Muslims' — a movement defined by going back to the root.

6790.w: 'Hasidic thought draws heavily on Lurianic Kabbalah, and, to an extent, is a popularization of it', pursuing devekut — communion — through 'the common man's more humble yet no less significant emotion during prayer'.

6791.w: 'When Pope Clement VII, under pressure from Emperor Charles V, refused the annulment, Henry acted to resolve the issue domestically'; Parliament's Act of Supremacy 1534 made him 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England. Henry VIII was used in no recipe at all.

6792.w: 'The Greek translation of Messiah is Khristós, anglicized as Christ' — Christians 'refer to Jesus of Nazareth as either the Christ or the Messiah, believing that the Old Testament messianic prophecies were fulfilled' in him. The claim is the whole of what makes Christianity a separate religion.

6793.w: 'The Kaaba is the holiest site in Islam', and the Quran has it raised by Abraham: 'And remember Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House' (2:127). Abraham currently links only to Judaism.

6794.w: The Dalai Lamas are a tulku line: the office is filled by finding a rebirth, and 'the lineage of Dalai Lama tulkus became firmly established with the third incarnation, Sonam Gyatso (1543-1588)'. The two elements' facts cross-reference each other and no recipe did.

6795.w: Egypt is the Nile's last stretch and its mouth: the main Nile runs 'from Khartoum to Cairo', then the delta 'extends from Cairo to the Mediterranean Sea'.

6796.w: Greece is 'a peninsular mainland jutting out into the Mediterranean Sea at the southernmost tip of the Balkan Peninsula, and a large number of islands' — 'an archipelago of about 3,000 islands', a fifth of its territory.

6797.w: Italy 'consists of a peninsula that extends into the Mediterranean Sea, with the Alps on its northern land border'. The Mediterranean had zero recipes using it as an ingredient.

6798.w: The other half of the same sentence: the country is the peninsula plus the Alpine arc that closes it off — 'a peninsula that extends into the Mediterranean Sea, with the Alps on its northern land border'. The Alps previously produced only Switzerland.

6799.w: What turns a storm into a hurricane is spin: 'the stronger the force from the Coriolis effect, the faster the wind spins and picks up additional energy, increasing the strength of the hurricane', and 'cyclones rarely form along the equator due to the weak Coriolis effect present in this region'.

6800.w: The Great Dying: 'the scientific consensus is that the main cause of the extinction was the flood basalt eruptions that created the Siberian Traps', which took 81% of marine species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species.

6801.w: Krakatoa 1883 blew two-thirds of the island away into a caldera and shoved the sea aside doing it: 'the town of Merak was destroyed by a tsunami that was 46 metres high', and of at least 36,417 dead, most were killed by the waves rather than the eruption.

6802.w: Reef limestone is a named rock: 'most limestone is formed by the activities of living organisms near reefs', where 'the core of a reef is typically massive and unbedded'. The corals deposit calcium carbonate skeletons and the reef becomes the rock.

6803.w: Rising magma cracks the rock above it, and that is how a volcano announces itself: the USGS finds active volcanoes by 'earthquake swarms, ground inflation, or unusually high levels of carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide', and Pinatubo was 'not seismically monitored before its unanticipated and catastrophic eruption of 1991'.

6804.w: The fire lance's bamboo tube was replaced by a cast metal one around the mid-13th century; by 1276 the Chinese character for the weapon had switched from the wood radical to the metal radical. Those independent metal barrels are the direct ancestors of the cannon.

6805.w: Gunpowder is what ended the trebuchet: counterweight and traction machines were phased out from about the mid-15th century in favour of guns, and in China 1480 was the last time trebuchets were seriously considered for war.

6806.w: The janissaries were the Ottoman sultan's household infantry, founded in the 14th century and levied from Christian boys of the Balkans. Under Murad II they took up firearms, becoming perhaps the first infantry force anywhere equipped primarily with guns.

6807.w: Orban's 8.2 m bombard threw 270 kg stones at the Theodosian walls for weeks; when the assault came before dawn on 29 May 1453 the last wave was the janissaries, who pressed through the breach and into the city.

6808.w: At Crecy on 26 August 1346 English and Welsh longbowmen outshot the French and broke charge after charge of mounted men-at-arms, largely by killing the horses. The battle established the longbow as the dominant weapon of the war's early phase.

6809.w: The true flintlock, built by Marin le Bourgeoys for Louis XIII between 1610 and 1615, replaced the arquebus's smouldering match with flint struck against a frizzen. Matchlock and flintlock overlapped for most of a century before the flint won.

6810.w: Sea biscuit — bizcocho, twice-baked — was the staple of Columbus's crews, soaked in water or stew to be edible, and kept at least a year if dry. It is the ration that made an Atlantic crossing in a caravel provisionable at all.

6811.w: Hannibal commanded the forces of Carthage and left New Carthage in the spring of 218 BC with 38,000 infantry, 8,000 cavalry and 38 war elephants; almost none of the elephants survived the Alps.

6812.w: Hannibal's march into Italy in 218 BC opened the Second Punic War against the Roman Republic, fought 218-201 BC — the war the game's own punic_wars fact describes.

6813.w: Rome met Celtiberian swords in Carthaginian service during the Second Punic War and copied the design; Polybius records the adoption before the war ended, probably promoted by Scipio after 209 BC. The blade was forged from bloomery iron.

6814.w: Kadesh, dated to about May 1274 BC, is the largest chariot battle ever fought: roughly 2,000 Egyptian and 2,500 Hittite chariots, five to six thousand vehicles in all, each drawn by a horse team.

6815.w: The wars set the Greek city-states against the Achaemenid Empire of Darius I and Xerxes. The Greek answer to Persian numbers was the hoplite phalanx, with spears longer than the Persians' — decisive at Marathon, Thermopylae and Plataea.

6816.w: On 12 September 490 BC democratic Athens summoned every available hoplite — 9,000 Athenians with 1,000 Plataeans — and the phalanx broke Darius I's lighter-armed infantry despite being outnumbered roughly two to one.

6817.w: The Delian League, formed to continue the Persian war after 480 BC, was turned by Athens into an empire over the next fifty years. Thucydides names the cause directly: the growth of Athenian power and the alarm it inspired in Sparta made war inevitable in 431 BC.

6818.w: Urban II preached at Clermont on 27 November 1095 for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem; the armies that answered were led by the knights and nobility of western Europe, and took the city on 15 July 1099.

6819.w: The crusaders spent about three weeks building two wheel-mounted siege towers from ship timber landed at Jaffa, and it was from the towers' assault on the walls that Jerusalem fell on 15 July 1099.

6820.w: The flamethrower's origin is the Byzantine cheirosiphon, a hand-held pump that shot Greek fire down a siphon-hose. The modern weapon is the same idea with a gas propellant: fuel forced along a flexible pipe and lit at the nozzle.

6821.w: Active underwater sound detection was built to find submarines. Britain's Anti-Submarine Division gave ASDIC its name; Boyle and Wood's quartz prototype was tested in mid-1917 and Langevin's work on submarine detection began in 1915.

6822.w: TNT is what turned a gun barrel into modern artillery. The German army adopted it as a shell filling in 1902 and Britain switched from Lyddite in 1907; it also filled naval mines, bombs, depth charges and torpedo warheads.

6823.w: A detonator is a small charge used to set off a much larger one it cannot ignite directly. Nobel's 1867 copper capsules of mercury fulminate are what made dynamite usable in drilled blast-holes for mining and quarrying.

6824.w: A Zeppelin is a rigid airship: a steerable gas envelope built around a load-bearing frame of duralumin, an aluminium-copper alloy whose exact composition was kept secret for years.

6825.w: The M249 is the US adaptation of the FN Minimi: a belt-fed light machine gun chambered in the same 5.56x45mm NATO round as the M16, and able to feed from M16 STANAG magazines as a backup.

6826.w: The M2 is essentially John Browning's M1917 machine gun scaled up to .50 BMG, firing from a closed bolt on the short-recoil principle. Its M903 SLAP round drives a 7.6 mm tungsten penetrator through 34 mm of armour plate at 500 m.

6827.w: The M1 Abrams is the main battle tank that took its powerplant from aviation practice: a Honeywell AGT1500 multi-fuel gas turbine of 1,500 shaft horsepower rather than a diesel.

6828.w: The Manhattan Project bred plutonium in the world's first industrial-scale reactors at Hanford. Because Hanford plutonium carried too much Pu-240 for a gun-type weapon, it forced the implosion design tested at Trinity on 16 July 1945 and dropped as Fat Man that August.

6829.w: Tactical weapons are the low-yield fission devices built from the 1950s for use on a battlefield rather than against cities — artillery shells among them, down to the 10-20 ton W54 fired from the Davy Crockett recoilless gun.

6830.w: ICBMs with thermonuclear warheads are the primary strategic nuclear weapons: yields from about 100 kilotons into the megatons, aimed at an enemy's home territory from thousands of miles away rather than at forces in the field.

6831.w: The Soviet RDS-1 test at Semipalatinsk on 29 August 1949 ended the American atomic monopoly. US detection of the fallout triggered a crash thermonuclear programme, opening the nuclear arms race of the Cold War.

6832.w: Phosgene was first used as a weapon by the French in 1915, released from cylinders and mixed with chlorine so the lighter gas would carry the heavier one downwind into the trenches. It is credited with about 85,000 deaths.

6833.w: The Mongol army was a horse-archer army: its primary weapon was the composite bow of horn, wood and sinew, small enough to shoot from the saddle and good past 150 m. At Liegnitz 20,000 horse archers beat a force of 30,000.

6834.w: Logistics is the part of supply chain management handling the forward and reverse flow of goods from origin to consumption — order processing, inventory and freight — with warehouses as the storage nodes it moves between.

6835.w: The bands are cyanobacterial oxygen written into rock: "Banded iron formations are theorized to have formed in sea water as the result of oxygen production by photosynthetic cyanobacteria", which "combined with dissolved iron in Earth's oceans to form insoluble iron oxides, which precipitated out". The game's own BIF fact calls it a record of when oxygen first filled the sea, yet it was only reachable from hematite+chert.

6836.w: Banded iron formations "account for more than 60% of global iron reserves and provide most of the iron ore presently mined" — so the ore fed to a charcoal furnace is, in practice, Precambrian BIF. Mirrors the existing ore+charcoal route.

6837.w: "In late September 1838, he started reading Thomas Malthus's An Essay on the Principle of Population... Darwin related this to the struggle for existence among wildlife" — the moment the mechanism arrived. Malthus's own game fact says his essay sparked the idea, yet he was an ingredient in nothing.

6838.w: Darwin wrote the book, published 24 November 1859. The game could previously craft the Origin from natural_selection+book without Darwin himself being an ingredient in it.

6839.w: The branching diagram of divergence "is the only illustration in the Origin of Species" — nodes standing for common ancestors. The game's phylogenetic_tree fact already says exactly this, but nothing linked the two.

6840.w: Cladistics groups on synapomorphies to produce "a cladogram - a tree-shaped diagram", and since PCR "genetic sequencing data and computational phylogenetics are now commonly used" as its input. Cladistics is the method that makes the tree; neither was an ingredient in anything.

6841.w: The finches are "a classic example of adaptive radiation", about 18 species "thought to have evolved from a single finch species that came to the islands more than a million years ago".

6842.w: Abzhanov, Tabin and the Grants showed deep broad finch beaks come from earlier, stronger Bmp4 expression around the prenasal cartilage and long pointed ones from the calmodulin pathway — the textbook evo-devo result, and the link between the finches and the beak that shapes them.

6843.w: "Between 1856 and 1863 Mendel cultivated and tested some 28,000 plants, the majority of which were pea plants"; crossing true-breeding yellow with green gave all yellow, then 3:1, and "Mendel coined the terms 'recessive' and 'dominant'".

6844.w: The square is "a tabular summary of possible combinations of maternal alleles with paternal alleles" used "to determine the probability of an offspring having a particular genotype" — alleles in, genotypes out.

6845.w: ABO is the standard classroom case of genotype versus phenotype: "AO and AA both test as type A; BO and BB test as type B" — two genotypes, one visible blood type.

6846.w: Selection cannot see a genotype: it "affects the genetic structure of a population indirectly via the contribution of phenotypes", and what it measures is offspring left — fitness. Phenotype went nowhere despite this being the definition.

6847.w: Hardy-Weinberg is the null: frequencies hold "in the absence of other evolutionary influences". Drift is first on the list of influences that break it, and a broken equilibrium is allele frequencies shifting — microevolution.

6848.w: "Genetic bottlenecks exist in cheetahs", and "the genetic drift caused by a population bottleneck can change the proportional random distribution of alleles and even lead to loss of alleles" — the cheetah is the standard worked example.

6849.w: The founder effect is a bottleneck at colonisation: "A slightly different form of bottleneck can occur if a small group becomes reproductively (e.g., geographically) separated from the main population, such as through a founder event."

6850.w: "Polyploidization can be a mechanism of sympatric speciation because polyploids are usually unable to interbreed with their diploid ancestors" — and wheat is the worked case, with diploid, tetraploid (durum) and hexaploid (bread) strains.

6851.w: In the explosion "almost all present-day animal phyla appeared", and the Burgess Shale is where they are preserved: "Many Burgess Shale organisms represent stem group members of the modern animal phyla, though crown group representatives of certain phyla are also present."

6852.w: LUCA is "the hypothesized latest common ancestral population... from which all subsequent life forms descend under the three-domain system of Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya", drawn "as 'LUCA' at the root". It is the root of that tree and was attached to neither.

6853.w: "After the K-Pg extinction, mammals evolved to fill the niches left vacant by the dinosaurs", and "morphological diversification rates among eutherians after the extinction event were thrice those of before it" — emptying the niches is what let placentals radiate.

6854.w: Chloroplasts are engulfed cyanobacteria: "a second merger some 1.6 Gya added chloroplasts", and "both chloroplasts and cyanobacteria have a double membrane, DNA, ribosomes, and chlorophyll-containing thylakoids".

6855.w: Sarich and Wilson turned human-chimpanzee albumin cross-reactions into a date, putting the split at roughly 4-6 million years — the molecular clock's first real use. The game's molecular_evidence fact is literally about the human-chimp difference.

6856.w: Morganucodon is caught mid-transition, carrying "an anterior 'mammalian' joint between the dentary and squamosal and a posterior 'reptilian' joint between the quadrate and articular" — the very bones that became incus and malleus, in a cynodont descendant.

6857.w: "The quadrate and articular bones have evolved into the incus and malleus bones in the middle ear" — jaw bones turned into hearing bones, and three middle-ear ossicles is one of the traits that defines a mammal, as the game's own mammal fact says.

6858.w: Coelacanths "were thought to have become extinct in the Late Cretaceous, around 66 million years ago" until a live one was landed in 1938; Latimeria "is often considered an example of a 'living fossil'... known only from fossils". The game's living_fossil entry is dated 1938 for this reason.

6859.w: "Penguin wings have the same general bone structure as flighted birds, but the bones are shorter and stouter to allow them to serve as fins" — humerus, radius, ulna, phalanges, Owen's same organ under a different form. The penguin's own game fact says this and linked to nothing.

6860.w: Whales keep reduced pelvic and hind-limb bones, and "hind limbs in cetaceans and sirenians" is a listed atavism — the vestige occasionally switching back on as a full ancestral trait.

6861.w: "Boas and pythons have vestigial pelvis remnants, which are externally visible as two small pelvic spurs on each side of the cloaca" — and vestigiality is established exactly this way, by "comparison with homologous features in related species".

6862.w: Pale moths "were able to blend in with the light-coloured lichens and tree bark" while "dark-coloured moths... were camouflaged very well by the blackened trees"; predation on the mismatched form drove the population average all the way to melanic. Research settled on "camouflage and bird predation as the overriding explanation".

6863.w: Cuttlefish camouflage is chromatophores doing the work: coleoid cephalopods "have complex multicellular organs that they use to change colour rapidly, producing a wide variety of bright colours and patterns".

6864.w: Resembling a twig is masquerade, the branch of mimicry "used when the models are inanimate, and the mimicry's purpose is crypsis" — animals that "resemble twigs, bark, leaves, bird droppings or flowers".

6865.w: Sesiidae, the clearwing moths, are "known for their Batesian mimicry in both appearance and behaviour of various Hymenoptera", hovering flight included. The game's wasp fact ends on Batesian mimicry and the wasp was an ingredient in nothing.

6866.w: A mammal arriving independently at the insect solution: "the social structure of naked mole-rats is similar to that of ants, termites, and some bees and wasps", and eusociality "has evolved among the insects, crustaceans, trematodes and mammals" separately, on different genetic systems.

6867.w: Brassica oleracea "has been bred into a wide range of cultivars, including cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, brussels sprouts, collards, and kale, some of which are hardly recognizable as being members of the same genus, let alone species". Cabbage spawns four cultivar recipes and the mechanism touched none of them.

6868.w: "The dog was the first species and the only large carnivore to have been domesticated", and "the grey wolf is the closest living relative of the dog". Dog spawns 36 breed recipes; domestication itself fed into none of them.

6869.w: The canonical case, and the one that unnerved Darwin: "The sight of a feather in a peacock's tail, whenever I gaze at it, makes me sick!" Female choice produces "the ornate plumage of birds-of-paradise and peafowl".

6870.w: Selection observed in real time: "the types of microorganisms that are able to survive over time with continued attack by certain antimicrobial agents will naturally become more prevalent", a process "heavily driven by the natural selection processes that happen during antibiotic use or misuse".

6871.w: Wikipedia's opening line for pathogen is 'any organism, agent or micro-organism that can produce disease' - the game's own pathogen fact says the same thing, and this is the recipe that finally encodes it.

6872.w: Koch's postulates are 'four criteria designed to establish a causal relationship between a microbe and a disease' - hand them a disease and what you get out is the microbe behind it.

6873.w: A zoonosis is 'an infectious disease of humans caused by a pathogen ... transmitted from a non-human animal to a human' - an animal plus a disease is exactly the definition.

6874.w: Prevalence is 'the proportion of a particular population found to be affected by a medical condition at a specific time' - it takes a disease and a head count of the population and nothing else.

6875.w: Prions 'cause neurodegenerative disease by aggregating extracellularly within the central nervous system', and prion's own fact ends 'the disease still spreads' - until now prion was used in no recipe at all.

6876.w: Sepsis 'arises when the body's dysregulated response to infection causes injury to its own tissues and organs' - the immune system, not the microbe, is the second ingredient, exactly as sepsis's own fact says.

6877.w: A fomite is 'any inanimate object that, when contaminated with or exposed to infectious agents ... can transfer disease to a new host' - contaminated object plus pathogen is a transmitted infection.

6878.w: A disease vector is 'any living agent that carries and transmits an infectious pathogen ... to another living organism', and mosquitoes head Wikipedia's list of arthropod vectors.

6879.w: TLRs 'recognize molecules that are broadly shared by pathogens ... collectively referred to as pathogen-associated molecular patterns', and activation 'leads to production of inflammatory cytokines'.

6880.w: 'C3b binds to the surface of pathogens, leading to greater internalization by phagocytic cells by opsonization' - complement tagging a pathogen is what makes phagocytosis happen.

6881.w: An inactivated vaccine is made when 'an entire pathogen is killed using heat, chemicals, or radiation', and of those chemicals 'only formaldehyde and beta-propiolactone exposure are widely used in human vaccines'.

6882.w: Attenuation is serial passage over time: the pathogen adapts to a foreign host until 'it is no longer harmful to the subject that is to receive the vaccine' - attenuated_vaccine's own fact names the pathogen it starts from.

6883.w: 'Up to 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic in origin' and Wikipedia tracks how spillovers grow into outbreaks - counting cases of a zoonosis in a population is how one is recognised as an epidemic.

6884.w: A vaccine 'stimulates the immune system to recognize the agent as a threat, destroy it, and recognize further and destroy any of the microorganisms associated with that agent that it may encounter in the future' - the game's vaccine fact says the same and linked to neither.

6885.w: Adjuvants work by provoking the innate immune system - they 'increase the capacity to cause local reactions at the injection site' and drive dendritic cells to secrete interleukin-1 beta - which is what adjuvant's own fact means by making the immune system take a weak antigen seriously.

6886.w: Conjugating the polysaccharide to a carrier protein lets it be 'presented on the MHC molecule and the T cell can be activated', which promotes 'a more rapid and long-lasting immunologic memory' in infants who ignore the sugar alone.

6887.w: 'The dendritic cells use their internal machinery (ribosomes) to read the mRNA and produce the viral antigens that the mRNA encodes' - the host's own ribosome is the missing ingredient in mrna_vaccine's fact.

6888.w: A purified antigen 'may lack pathogen-associated molecular patterns', so for subunit vaccines 'addition of adjuvants is necessary during manufacturing to increase the efficacy' - antigen plus adjuvant is what makes a usable vaccine.

6889.w: IgG 'is the only antibody isotype that has receptors to facilitate passage through the human placenta, thereby providing protection to the fetus in utero' - passive immunity, and both elements were dead ends.

6890.w: In Burnet's theory 'a specific antigen activates (i.e. selects) only its counter-specific cell, which then induces that particular cell to multiply, producing identical clones for antibody production' - the selected lymphocyte's output is the plasma cell.

6891.w: 'NK cells recognize and kill stressed cells that are lacking the MHC class I molecules', and their perforin/granzyme delivery induces apoptosis - the missing-self rule natural_killer_cell's own fact states.

6892.w: Type I hypersensitivity is the IgE-mediated one: B cells 'produce IgE antibodies specific to an antigen', those arm mast cells, and re-exposure gives the allergic reaction. Allergy is simply hypersensitivity of the IgE type.

6893.w: 'Every B cell is specific to a single antigen, but each cell can produce several thousand matching antibodies per second' - plasma_cell's own fact says this and it was used in no recipe.

6894.w: 'AIDS is defined as an HIV infection with either a CD4+ T cell count below 200 cells per microlitre of blood or the occurrence of specific diseases' - and the CD4+ cell is the helper T cell. Immunodeficiency's own fact is that number.

6895.w: 'Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease that occurs when the body's immune system destroys beta cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone insulin' - autoimmune_disease's own fact says exactly this and linked to nothing.

6896.w: The trypanosome's genome 'has over 1,000 genes that code for different variants of the VSG protein', swapped one after another as the host immune system catches up - the textbook case of antigenic variation, and trypanosoma's own fact.

6897.w: 'At high levels of LPS, the syndrome of septic shock supervenes' - free lipopolysaccharide in the circulation binds LPS-binding protein and CD14 on monocytes, and the cytokine surge collapses blood pressure.

6898.w: Pneumocystis is 'a source of opportunistic infection and can cause lung infections in people with a weak immune system', and the rise in cases 'was the first clue to the existence of AIDS in the early 1980s'.

6899.w: Conjugation is 'the transfer of DNA via a plasmid from a donor cell to a recombinant recipient cell during cell-to-cell contact', and 'horizontal gene transfer is the primary mechanism for the spread of antibiotic resistance in bacteria'.

6900.w: Transduction is 'the process in which bacterial DNA is moved from one bacterium to another by a virus (a bacteriophage, or phage)' - one of the three named routes of horizontal gene transfer.

6901.w: Transformation is 'the genetic alteration of a cell resulting from the introduction, uptake and expression of foreign genetic material' - naked DNA taken from the surroundings, the third route of horizontal gene transfer.

6902.w: R-factors ride the conjugative mating bridge between cells, 'even across different species', and carry as many as ten resistance genes at once - so 'antibiotic resistance can be easily spread among a population of bacteria'.

6903.w: 'Common to all engineered vectors are the origin of replication, a multicloning site, and a selectable marker' - a plasmid only becomes a cloning vector once a marker lets you find the cells that took it up.

6904.w: 'The absence of peptidoglycan makes them naturally resistant to antibiotics such as the beta-lactam antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis' - mycoplasma's own fact calls it naturally immune to penicillin.

6905.w: MRSA is 'a group of Staphylococcus aureus strains that are resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics' - the species plus acquired resistance, and antibiotic_resistance was an ingredient in nothing.

6906.w: 'One in ten hospital-acquired infections is from Pseudomonas' - P. aeruginosa reaching a patient through catheters and ventilators in a healthcare setting is the classic nosocomial route.

6907.w: 'C. difficile colitis is associated most strongly with the use of these antibiotics: fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, and clindamycin' - the drug clears the competing gut flora, which is precisely C. diff's own fact.

6908.w: Lysozyme hydrolyses the peptidoglycan bond, and 'this hydrolysis in turn compromises the integrity of bacterial cell walls causing lysis of the bacteria' - lysozyme's own fact, unencoded until now.

6909.w: 'Batch culture is the most common laboratory growth method in which bacterial growth is studied', giving the lag, log, stationary and death phases - the curve is a property of bacteria in a medium, not of bacteria alone.

6910.w: Metchnikoff's founding proposal was that fermented milk would 'seed the intestine with harmless lactic-acid bacteria' and suppress the proteolytic ones - probiotics are defined by what they do to the resident gut community.

6911.w: Metagenomics profiles 'environmental and clinical samples without the need for time-consuming culture of individual species', reaching the 'large groups of microorganisms in many environments that cannot be cultured'.

6912.w: Clostridium tetani 'causes tetanus' - the toxin blocks inhibition of motor neurons and the muscles lock. The genus's own fact names tetanus, botulism and gas gangrene, and it was an ingredient in no recipe.

6913.w: Clostridium botulinum 'can produce botulinum toxin in food or wounds and can cause botulism' - the toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, the opposite end of the same synapse tetanus attacks.

6914.w: Clostridium perfringens causes 'necrotic enteritis and gas gangrene', and C. septicum 'can also cause rapidly progressive myonecrosis (gas gangrene type)' - the genus growing in devitalised tissue.

6915.w: Once rabies virus reaches the CNS 'the virus rapidly causes encephalitis' - encephalitis was made two ways and used in none.

6916.w: In immunocompromised people latent Toxoplasma reactivates and 'the tachyzoites can run rampant and cause significant neurological damage', listed as damage to the brain (encephalitis).

6917.w: 'Carried by twelve Genoese galleys, plague arrived by ship in Sicily in October 1347' - plague's own fact says 'Called the Black Death' and black_death's fact names the ships, yet nothing connected them.

6918.w: 'Pasteur patented the process, to fight the diseases of wine, in 1865' - the method is named after him and nothing in the game was made from him.

6919.w: Pasteur's rabies vaccine was made by 'growing the virus in rabbits, and then weakening it by drying the affected nerve tissue' - the first deliberately attenuated vaccine.

6920.w: In the swan-neck flask experiments 'nothing grew in the broths unless the flasks were tilted, making the liquid touch the contaminated walls of the neck' - the result that displaced spontaneous generation.

6921.w: On 24 March 1882 Koch reported 'the causative agent of the disease to be the slow-growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis' - the game's robert_koch fact says so and no recipe used him.

6922.w: 'In 1881, Koch started using agar to grow and isolate pure cultures', on a suggestion that reached him through his assistant Walther Hesse - the agar plate is Koch's lab's contribution, and culture_medium was a dead end too.

6923.w: 'Using single-lensed microscopes of his own design and make, Van Leeuwenhoek was the first to observe and to experiment with microbes', finding them 'in rotten water, in ditches'.

6924.w: 'Soon after Koch's discovery, Paul Ehrlich developed a stain for mycobacterium tuberculosis' - Ziehl and Neelsen only modified it, and Ehrlich was used in zero recipes.

6925.w: Snow counted deaths house by house and showed the Southwark and Vauxhall supply carried 'a cholera rate fourteen times that of those supplied by Lambeth Waterworks' - comparing new cases per population is incidence, and it made him the founder of the field.

6926.w: The herd immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0, and 'the primary way to boost levels of immunity in a population is through vaccination' - R0 sets the number, the vaccine reaches it.

6927.w: Palisade cells sit directly beneath the upper epidermis and cuticle, above the spongy mesophyll — first in line for the light that gets through, which is why their large central vacuole shoves the chloroplasts out to the cell edge.

6928.w: Enceladus's south-polar geysers are the direct source of Saturn's E ring — the icy grains they throw off don't fall back, they spread into a ring the moon orbits inside.

6929.w: Cassini imaged geyser-like jets of icy particles rising from Enceladus's south pole in November 2005, turning a bright little moon into the most promising place in the outer solar system.

6930.w: Halley-type comets — 20 to 200 year periods, orbits tilted every which way — are long-period comets the giant planets have pulled inward. Halley itself most likely started in the Oort cloud, 20,000 to 50,000 AU out.

6931.w: Short-period comets come from the Kuiper belt and its scattered disc, and Jupiter is what puts them on those orbits: more than twice the mass of every other planet combined, its perturbations deflect icy bodies into the Jupiter-family comets, 816 of them catalogued by 2024.

6932.w: Triton orbits Neptune backwards, the signature of a captured world. It is only slightly larger than Pluto and nearly identical in composition — nitrogen ice with traces of methane and carbon monoxide — so the two are read as siblings from the same Kuiper belt.

6933.w: Voyager 2 reached Neptune in 1989 and caught nitrogen-gas geysers erupting through Triton's icy crust in plumes up to 8 km high — one of the very few worlds ever seen actively erupting.

6934.w: Voyager 1's flyby on 25 February 1979 returned the first detailed image of the Great Red Spot, resolving cloud features 160 km across, and its time-lapse movies confirmed the storm's counterclockwise circulation.

6935.w: New Horizons is the only spacecraft ever to visit Charon. Its closest approach on 14 July 2015 produced the only detailed images that exist of Pluto's giant moon.

6936.w: Pluto and Charon are gravitationally locked to each other, so each permanently shows the other the same face — mutual tidal locking, of which this is the best-known example in the solar system.

6937.w: From September 1610 Galileo watched Venus run through crescent, gibbous and full phases. Ptolemy's model kept Venus on one side of the Sun and could never produce a full phase; the telescope made the old cosmos untenable.

6938.w: On 7 January 1610 Galileo saw what he took for three fixed stars beside Jupiter; by 15 January he had four of them and knew they were circling the planet. Callisto is the outermost of that catch.

6939.w: Io, Europa and Ganymede are locked in the 4:2:1 Laplace resonance — two Io orbits per Europa orbit, two Europa orbits per Ganymede orbit — held so tightly that a triple conjunction is impossible.

6940.w: Ring particles at the inner edge of the Cassini Division orbit twice for every one orbit of Mimas. The 2:1 resonance means Mimas tugs them in the same direction every time, and it has swept the 4,800 km gap clear.

6941.w: The closest planet to the Sun keeps water ice in craters at its poles that sunlight never reaches. Goldstone and VLA radar found the bright patches in the early 1990s; MESSENGER's images of the north polar craters confirmed them.

6942.w: Eris, found in January 2005 and reported as a tenth planet, forced the question. The IAU's answer on 24 August 2006 was a new class, and Ceres — demoted from planet once already — and Eris were its founding members alongside Pluto.

6943.w: Eight observatories on four continents linked into one Earth-sized dish produced the first direct image of a black hole in 2019: M87*, 6.5 billion solar masses, its event horizon 40 billion km across.

6944.w: Adaptive optics on the 10-metre Keck telescopes cancelled the atmosphere's blur well enough to follow individual stars orbiting the galactic centre for decades. S2 was clocked at 2.55% of light speed, and four million solar masses in that volume left only one answer — the 2020 Nobel Prize.

6945.w: Harlow Shapley assumed the globular clusters were spread symmetrically about the galaxy's centre, plotted where they actually are, and found the centre lay off in Sagittarius — not near the Sun at all. That is how we learned we live in the suburbs.

6946.w: 3C 273's spectrum matched no known star until Maarten Schmidt read it in 1963 as ordinary lines shifted 15.8% to the red. That redshift put it billions of light-years away, which is what made it the first object identified as a quasar.

6947.w: Penzias and Wilson's horn antenna at Holmdel measured an excess 4.2 K of noise on 20 May 1964 that they could not get rid of. The leftover heat of a hot dense beginning is the key experimental evidence for the Big Bang.

6948.w: The CMB's temperature ripples, a few parts in 100,000, are the seeds of every structure there is. They only grew in time because dark matter feels no radiation pressure: it collapsed into halos first, and ordinary matter fell in afterwards. Without it, galaxies would still be forming.

6949.w: The books balance at 68% dark energy, 27% dark matter and about 5% ordinary matter — everything ever observed is the rounding error.

6950.w: The Virgo Supercluster is defined by the Virgo Cluster it is centred on, with our own Local Group sitting out near one edge of it, on a filament running toward Fornax.

6951.w: Parallax is how nearness is measured, and the largest parallax any star has is Proxima Centauri's 0.7685 arcseconds. That number is the whole reason we can call it the closest star.

6952.w: Delta Cephei is the prototype the entire class is named for. John Goodricke watched it swing in brightness through the autumn of 1784 and found the period that later became astronomy's distance ladder.

6953.w: Sirius in Canis Major and Procyon in Canis Minor are two of the triangle's three corners; Betelgeuse in Orion is the third.

6954.w: Deneb in Cygnus and Altair in Aquila make two corners of the Summer Triangle, with Vega in Lyra closing it — each the brightest star of its own constellation.

6955.w: A coronagraph blocks the direct light of the star so that whatever sits beside it stops being drowned out. That is how Fomalhaut b was seen directly in Hubble images from 2004 and 2006.

6956.w: The ELODIE spectrograph caught 51 Pegasi wobbling toward and away from us as an unseen companion tugged it. Mayor and Queloz announced it on 6 October 1995 — the first planet found around a Sun-like star.

6957.w: Webb's near-infrared spectrograph found the first clear evidence of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of a planet outside the solar system, in the hot Saturn WASP-39b, in 2022.

6958.w: Polaris stands almost exactly over the north celestial pole, so its measured altitude above the horizon is your latitude. A sextant sight of it at night is the oldest one-step fix there is.

6959.w: The Almagest's catalogue of 1,022 stars in 48 constellations — 12 zodiacal, 21 northern, 15 southern — absorbed and revised Hipparchus's lost catalogue, and those 48 are the backbone of the modern 88.

6960.w: In the surviving manuscript of De revolutionibus Copernicus wrote that 'some even say that Aristarchus was of that opinion' — that the Earth moves — and then struck the passage out before publication.

6961.w: Bruno took the Copernican model and refused to stop at the edge of it: the stars are other suns, each with its own planets, in a universe that is infinite and has no centre. It cost him his life in 1600.

6962.w: Having measured the Earth, Eratosthenes drew it: in the Geography he laid grids of parallels and meridians over the whole surface to fix the positions of more than 400 cities — the first coordinate system for a planet.

6963.w: The mechanism's back dial is a spiral of 223 lunar months — the Saros. Glyphs in 51 of its cells name 38 lunar and 27 solar eclipses, with the day and the hour.

6964.w: Zhang Heng is the first person known to have driven an armillary sphere by water power, coupling a waterwheel and a clepsydra to turn a model of the sky on its own around 125 CE.

6965.w: The Great Pyramid's sides sit within about 3 minutes 38 seconds of true north. The pole-star method proposed for that alignment is exactly the merkhet's trade: track a circumpolar star with a movable sight against a fixed plumb line and bisect its extremes.

6966.w: The 21.5 kg Apollo 11 brought home from Mare Tranquillitatis were basalts — lava-plain rock, unusually rich in titanium. Sample 10047 also gave up tranquillityite, a mineral then unknown on Earth.

6967.w: Two physicists at Johns Hopkins tracked Sputnik's beep and realised the Doppler shift told them where along its orbit the satellite was. Inverting the problem — satellite known, find yourself — produced TRANSIT, and TRANSIT produced GPS.

6968.w: Curiosity's laser spectrometer found background methane in Gale crater rising and falling with the Martian seasons, and a tenfold spike averaging 7.2 ppb across late 2013 and early 2014 — a gas that should not last long in that air.

6969.w: On 18 August 1868 a bright yellow line at 587.49 nm turned up in the spectrum of the Sun's chromosphere. Lockyer decided it belonged to an unknown element and named it for Helios — an element found on the Sun 27 years before anyone found it on Earth.

6970.w: With no atmosphere and no magnetic field to stop it, the solar wind has been implanting helium straight into the lunar soil for billions of years — 1.4 to 15 parts per billion of helium-3 in sunlit regolith, and up to 50 in the permanent shadows.

6971.w: Element 93 was named for the planet beyond Uranus, because element 92 had been named for Uranus. Fittingly, you make it by firing a neutron into uranium: U-238 becomes U-239, which beta-decays in 23 minutes to neptunium-239.

6972.w: Neptunium-239 beta-decays with a 2.36-day half-life into element 94 — and since 93 had been named for Neptune, McMillan proposed naming 94 for what was then the next planet out.

6973.w: Klaproth dissolved pitchblende in nitric acid in 1789, precipitated a yellow compound, and named what he had after the planet William Herschel had found eight years earlier.

6974.w: The melon is the fat-filled forehead organ that 'focuses and modulates the animal's vocalizations and acts as a sound lens' — it is how a dolphin aims its biosonar clicks. The game's own dolphin fact already says this and no recipe encoded it.

6975.w: Orcas sit at the very top of the marine food chain: they are apex predators, meaning they themselves have no natural predators.

6976.w: The white shark is an apex predator that opportunistically feeds on fish, cephalopods, marine mammals, sea birds and sea turtles — it eats across the whole web rather than one chain.

6977.w: Methylmercury is absorbed efficiently and excreted only very slowly, so it concentrates at every step up the chain: herring carries about 0.01 ppm, shark over 1 ppm. Apex predators end up with the load.

6978.w: Countershading is a method of camouflage in which an animal is darker above and lighter below. The orca is the pattern at its starkest — mostly black with sharply bordered white underside.

6979.w: The cuticle forms a largely inelastic exoskeleton, so growth is otherwise constrained by its rigidity: shedding it is the only way a crab gets bigger.

6980.w: Frogs have permeable skin that easily absorbs toxic chemicals and a poor ability to detoxify what it takes in, which is exactly why anurans are the standard early-warning bioindicator for pollution.

6981.w: Echolocation evolved separately in bats and in toothed whales, but from the same genetic mutations — studies find convergence in the amino acid sequences of echolocating bats and the dolphin.

6982.w: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere primarily through photosynthesis and returned by respiration — the two halves of the fast carbon cycle. The game's carbon_cycle fact says this outright and nothing linked them.

6983.w: Solutes entering a guard cell pull water in osmotically and raise turgor pressure; cellulose microfibril rings stop the cell widening, so the extra pressure elongates it and the pore opens. Turgor change IS the stomatal mechanism.

6984.w: Ethylene stimulates the formation of amylase, the enzyme that breaks the banana's stored starch down into sugar — the whole reason a green banana turns sweet.

6985.w: Synthetic auxins, especially NAA and IBA, are commonly applied to stimulate root initiation when rooting cuttings — auxin is literally the active ingredient in rooting powder.

6986.w: Gibberellins break dormancy: they diffuse from the embryo to the aleurone cells and induce alpha-amylase, which hydrolyses the seed's stored starch to glucose and powers germination.

6987.w: Most water absorption happens through the root hairs; where root cells hold a more negative water potential than the soil, water moves in by osmosis, and the resulting positive root pressure forces sap up the xylem.

6988.w: The chloroplast is the organelle that conducts photosynthesis, and the green chlorophyll is contained in its stacks of disk-like thylakoids. The most basic pairing in plant cell biology, and it had no edge.

6989.w: A cotyledon is a seed leaf — a part of the embryo within the seed, formed during embryogenesis and present before germination. It anchors embryo to plant development rather than only animal development.

6990.w: Mycorrhizal fungi form a mutualistic relationship with the roots of most plant species, trading water and minerals for photosynthate — a legume root runs this alongside its rhizobial nodules, two mutualisms at once.

6991.w: The function of cork cambium is to produce the cork, and it is one of the many layers of bark, sitting between the cork and the phelloderm.

6992.w: Flowers pay in both currencies to the same visitor: nectar provides the energy, pollen provides the protein, and pollen rubbed off the anthers rides to the next stigma.

6993.w: Carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis passes through stomata by gaseous diffusion — the pores are the only way the raw material gets in, which is why most plants must open them by day.

6994.w: Almost all gymnosperms are anemophilous, and many pines, spruces and firs are wind-pollinated — no animal involved.

6995.w: Water reaches the atmosphere by evapotranspiration — water transpired from plants and evaporated from the soil taken together as one limb of the cycle.

6996.w: Wheat endosperm is ground into flour; for white flour the endosperm is selectively retained and the embryo and seed coat removed.

6997.w: As auxin drains from an ageing leaf the abscission zone becomes sensitive to ethylene, which switches on cellulase and polygalacturonase — the wall-degrading enzymes that cut the leaf loose.

6998.w: Vitamin D exists to increase intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate — without it the mineral never reaches the skeleton, which is why deficiency gives rickets and osteomalacia.

6999.w: Glycogenesis is activated by insulin in response to high glucose levels — the storage half of the story whose opposite, glucagon, the game already encodes.

7000.w: Cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis in the liver — synthesising new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources — which is the defining action of the stress hormone.

7001.w: Adrenaline increases cardiac output by binding beta-1 receptors, acting on the SA node to raise rate, contractility and AV conduction — the heart's half of the fight-or-flight response the game only ever slowed, via the vagus.

7002.w: The stretch reflex is a monosynaptic arc: afferent signal into the spinal cord, efferent straight back out to the muscle, the shortest path a reflex can take and no brain involved.

7003.w: The ligand for rhodopsin is the vitamin A-based chromophore 11-cis-retinal, covalently bound to a lysine of the opsin protein in the eye's rod cells — dim-light vision starts there.

7004.w: Two calcium ions bind troponin C, the troponin-Ca complex slides tropomyosin aside and unblocks the actin binding site — calcium is the trigger for every contraction, and it releases again as calcium falls.

7005.w: Glucagon's effect is opposite to insulin's, and the two are part of a feedback system that keeps blood glucose levels stable — the game's own homeostasis fact opens with exactly this example.

7006.w: The adrenal glands are endocrine glands found above the kidneys — 'suprarenal' means just that — and the game's adrenal_gland fact already calls them a cap on each kidney.

7007.w: In humans and placental mammals the urinary system consists of the kidneys, ureters, bladder and the urethra — filter at one end, exit at the other.

7008.w: The human digestive system is the gastrointestinal tract plus the accessory organs of digestion — tongue, salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gallbladder. The game's digestive_system fact names the liver and no recipe used it.

7009.w: Bile is produced by the liver, flows down the biliary tree into the gallbladder and is stored there, concentrated three to tenfold — which is what the gallbladder is for.

7010.w: The vagus is a key part of the parasympathetic nervous system, carrying motor parasympathetic fibres to every organ from the neck down to the transverse colon — the rest-and-digest supply to the gut.

7011.w: Birds are a specialised subgroup of theropod dinosaurs and are reptiles in the modern cladistic sense — feathers, toothless beaked jaws and hard-shelled eggs are what mark the branch off.

7012.w: Almost all cacti are succulents, with thickened fleshy organs that store water, and most specialise in surviving hot dry environments — they are xerophytes. The cactus is both habits at once.

7013.w: In holometabolous insects the immature stages are very different from the adult: larvae never have wings or compound eyes, and their whole form is tuned for feeding and growth while the adult's is tuned for dispersal and mating.

7014.w: Pegasus sprang fully grown from Medusa's severed neck the instant Perseus beheaded her with the mirrored shield -- the game's own pegasus fact already says this, with no recipe behind it.

7015.w: Poseidon coupled with Medusa -- in Athena's own temple, the transgression Athena punished by making her a Gorgon. Pegasus was sired by Poseidon in his horse-god role and foaled by Medusa.

7016.w: Perseus took Andromeda in marriage after cutting her free of the sea-cliff. Their son Electryon fathered Alcmene, who bore Heracles -- Wikipedia calls Perseus the half-brother and great-grandfather of Heracles.

7017.w: Theseus volunteered as tribute, went into the Labyrinth paying out Ariadne's thread behind him, and killed the Minotaur at its centre.

7018.w: Ariadne's ball of thread got Theseus out of the Labyrinth; he then abandoned her on Naxos, where Dionysus found her sleeping and married her.

7019.w: In Book 8 of the Odyssey the singer Demodocus makes Aphrodite Hephaestus's wife -- and has Hephaestus forge a near-invisible net to catch her in bed with Ares.

7020.w: Cronus was the youngest child of the primordial pair Gaia and Uranus, and castrated his father with Gaia's sickle to take the throne.

7021.w: Cronus swallowed each child Rhea bore him. At the sixth she hid the infant Zeus in Crete and handed Cronus a swaddled stone instead -- the trick rhea's own fact describes.

7022.w: Hesiod's Theogony makes sun, moon and dawn siblings: Helios, Selene and Eos, all children of the Titans Hyperion and Theia.

7023.w: Infant Hermes stole Apollo's cattle and built the first lyre from a tortoise shell; Apollo traded the herd for the instrument, which became one of his identifying attributes.

7024.w: The twelfth labour sent Heracles down to fetch Cerberus from Hades -- Cerberus's only myth, and the one time the dog left the gate.

7025.w: Epimetheus, 'afterthought', accepted Pandora as a gift against his brother's warning; in Hesiod's telling it is that marriage that puts the jar in reach of the lid.

7026.w: Aeneas hired the Cumaean Sibyl before descending to the dead; she showed him the way to Avernus and guided him through the underworld, leaving it with him at the end of Aeneid VI.

7027.w: Virgil has the road fork for Aeneas: right to Elysium, left to Tartarus. The two are the opposite ends of the same Greek afterlife.

7028.w: After his birth Pegasus flew up to Olympus, where Greco-Roman poets have him enter Zeus's service carrying the god's thunder and lightning.

7029.w: Prometheus is catalogued among the Greek tricksters: he cheated Zeus over the sacrificial portions, then stole fire back for humanity and was chained to a rock for it.

7030.w: At Memphis the creator Ptah absorbed the falcon necropolis god Sokar and then Osiris, producing the composite funerary deity Ptah-Sokar-Osiris -- which the game's sokar fact already names.

7031.w: The Theban Triad: Khonsu is the moon-god son of Amun and Mut, worshipped with them at Karnak.

7032.w: Shu and his twin sister Tefnut, air and moisture, were the parents of Geb the earth and Nut the sky -- the generation Shu then had to force apart.

7033.w: Ra crossed the night with defenders aboard his barque, Set among them: the chaos god speared the world-encircling serpent Apep so the sun could rise.

7034.w: Wadjet of Lower Egypt and Nekhbet of Upper Egypt appear together as the Two Ladies -- the cobra and the vulture set side by side on the pharaoh's crown, and the Nebty name in his titulary.

7035.w: Freyr and Freyja are twin Vanir, fathered by the sea god Njord on his unnamed twin sister.

7036.w: The peace that ended the Aesir-Vanir war was sealed with hostages: the Vanir sent Njord and his son Freyr to live among the Aesir, in the walled enclosure that is Asgard.

7037.w: Frigg made every object swear not to harm Baldr and overlooked the mistletoe. Loki -- the one god who did not love him -- guided the shaft that killed him, and Baldr went down to Hel.

7038.w: Hel agreed to release Baldr if everything alive and dead wept for him. Everything did except one giantess, Thokk, generally taken to be Loki in disguise -- so Baldr stayed.

7039.w: Heimdall watches from Himinbjorg for the onset of Ragnarok and sounds Gjallarhorn; he and Loki, long antagonists, are foretold to kill one another in it.

7040.w: Yggdrasil means 'Odin's horse', a kenning for gallows: the Havamal's Runatal has Odin hang himself on the tree as a sacrifice to himself and take up the runes.

7041.w: Fenrir swallows Odin at Ragnarok, and Odin's silent son Vidar avenges him by stabbing the wolf through the heart -- what the huge shoe in vidar's own fact is for.

7042.w: Comparative mythology sets Thor beside the Slavic Perun and the Baltic Perkunas as reflexes of one Proto-Indo-European thunder god, and particularly beside Indra, whose vajra parallels Mjolnir.

7044.w: The Three Precious Children born of Izanagi's purification: Amaterasu the sun, Tsukuyomi the moon, and Susanoo the storm.

7045.w: Ryujin, 'dragon god', is the Japanese dragon of the sea -- tutelary deity of the ocean, ruling from a coral palace beneath the waves.

7046.w: Fujin with his bag of winds and his twin brother Raijin with his ring of drums are paired in Japanese art -- Sotatsu's screens the most famous -- as the kami of storms.

7047.w: The torii marks the boundary of a Shinto shrine: the passage from the mundane into the sacred, and the spot where the kami are welcomed through.

7048.w: Parvati made Ganesha to guard her door; Shiva, not knowing him, beheaded him, then set an elephant's head in place of the one he had struck off.

7049.w: Lakshmi descends with Vishnu at each avatar -- as Sita to his Rama, as Rukmini to his Krishna. Sita is regarded as Lakshmi incarnate.
