With no intermediate forms known, all of them appear to have radiated from a single close ancestor that already had the pitcher.

7492.w: Lophophora williamsii grows in desert scrub and limestone ground in the Chihuahuan Desert — Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas down to San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas, crossing into southern Texas — mostly between 100 and 1,500 m. In the wild it is extremely slow growing, where a cultivated plant can go from seedling to flowering in under three years.

7493.w: Conium maculatum is an umbellifer, in the carrot and parsley family, native to Europe, Central Asia and the Mediterranean. It reached the United States from Europe in the 1800s as a garden ornamental sold as 'winter fern', and has since naturalised across Asia, North America, Australia and New Zealand — it is the poison that killed Socrates after his trial.

7494.w: The psilocybin pathway is a cluster of five genes — a tryptophan decarboxylase, a P450 monooxygenase, a methyltransferase, a phosphotransferase and a transporter — and it has not simply descended down one family tree. The analyses support horizontal transfer of the whole cluster between divergent dung decomposers in the genera Psilocybe and Panaeolus, the first such case found in mushroom-forming fungi.

7495.w: In 1989 morphological and genetic studies showed that the trout of the Pacific basin are closer to the Pacific salmon than to the Atlantic genus Salmo, and the rainbow trout was moved into Oncorhynchus. Its native range runs from Kamchatka east along the Aleutians and south to northern Mexico, and the sea-going form, the steelhead, is iteroparous — able to spawn several times instead of dying after one run.

7496.w: One saguaro fruit holds around 2,000 seeds, and predation and lack of moisture leave only about 1% of them to germinate. A survivor may be 6.4 mm tall after two years and take 20 to 50 years to reach a metre; the first arm comes at 75 to 100 years, and the plant can live 150 to 200.

7497.w: Zygentoma are primitive wingless insects — apterygotes, which never had wings to lose — and the order goes back to the Pennsylvanian. A silverfish is also one of the few insects that keeps moulting after it is adult: 17 to 66 times over a life of two to eight years, sometimes 30 times in one year.

7498.w: Springtails are hexapods but no longer counted as insects: their mouthparts are held inside the head capsule, which is what puts Collembola with the Protura and Diplura in the Entognatha. Rhyniella praecursor, from the Rhynie chert of Scotland about 400 million years ago, is the oldest known, and soil today is estimated to hold 100,000 springtails per square metre.

7499.w: Charles H. Sternberg found the holotype skull in the summer of 1913 along the Red Deer River in Alberta, about 19 km below the mouth of Berry Creek, and Lawrence Lambe named the animal that same year. The rock is the Dinosaur Park Formation, 75.5 to 74.5 million years old; the rest of the skeleton was dug out in 1935 and reunited with the skull in 1955.

7500.w: Ticks are arachnids — parasitic mites of the order Ixodida within the superorder Parasitiformes, about 980 species in 37 genera. They are obligate hematophages, unable to pass from one life stage to the next without a meal of vertebrate blood, and the oldest tick fossils, around 100 million years old, come from Cretaceous amber.

7501.w: Fruiting underground costs a fungus the wind and water that would otherwise carry its spores away, and fungi have arrived at it more than once, by convergent evolution in water-limited places. Instead a truffle exudes volatile compounds that draw animal vectors — deer, voles, squirrels, flying squirrels — and the spores come through digestion intact behind thick chitin walls.

7502.w: Carl Limone's find of a large claw in October 1991 led to excavation at the Gaston Quarry in Grand County, Utah, and Kirkland, Gaston and Burge named the animal in June 1993. It comes from the Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, 139 to 134.6 million years old; the sickle claw measured about 24 cm, and a nine-ton sandstone block found in 2001 held at least seven individuals.

7503.w: The genus Equus arose in North America — paleogenomic work puts the most recent common ancestor of all living equines at about 4.07 million years ago — and dispersed into the Old World during the Early and Middle Pleistocene. Zebras and asses split from each other around 2 million years ago, and the three zebra species live in eastern and southern Africa.

7504.w: Equus is the only recognised living genus of the horse family, seven species of horse, ass and zebra, and every one of them takes its weight on a single digit — the middle one, the side toes shrinking away through the Pleistocene until the single-toed form emerged. The dentition tracks the same shift: large incisors that clip grass blades, and tall ridged molars for grinding it.

7505.w: Sauropods carried a system of air sacs, as other saurischians including birds do, and it hollowed the skeleton out from the inside — some vertebrae ran to 60% air. That is what made the necks possible: the spaces cut the weight they had to hold up, and one-way airflow through stiff lungs got enough oxygen into an animal that size.

7506.w: Myriapods breathe through spiracles opening into a tracheal system, and all of the roughly 13,000 species across their four classes are terrestrial — trace fossils have them on land by the Ordovician, and the oldest body fossils are about 427 million years old. They carry a single pair of antennae, simple eyes, and a long tubular heart.

7507.w: Herpestidae runs to 34 living species in 14 genera, across southern Europe, Africa and Asia. Mongooses are one of at least four mammal groups carrying a mutation in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that stops snake venom's α-neurotoxin binding to it — and the only one in which the change is made by glycosylation.

7508.w: A dromedary jawbone dated to 8,200 BC was found in Saudi Arabia on the southern coast of the Red Sea, thousands of years before any herder took the animal in. Nothing like it is left standing: the dromedary has not occurred naturally in the wild for nearly 2,000 years.

7509.w: Lycaon is not a wolf and not a dog: a 2019 study puts the split of its lineage from Canis and Cuon at 1.7 million years ago, after which it specialised in Africa for a hypercarnivorous life. It has no dewclaws at all, the heel of its lower carnassial is a shearing blade — the trenchant heel — and its premolars are the largest relative to body size of any carnivore but the hyenas.

7510.w: Linnaeus filed these plants under Datura in 1753, and it took until 1973, when T. E. Lockwood settled the question, for Brugmansia to stand unchallenged as a separate genus — woody trees and shrubs 3 to 11 m tall against Datura's herbs. All seven species are listed Extinct in the Wild; no wild plant has ever been confirmed, and the suspicion is that whatever animal once dispersed their seed is gone as well.

7511.w: Colchicum autumnale is a monocot of the family Colchicaceae, in the order Liliales, growing from a bulb-like corm across mainland Europe from Portugal to Ukraine — the only member of its family native to Great Britain and Ireland. Its flowers come up long before the leaves, which is why it is called naked ladies, and the corms carry colchicine, a drug with a famously narrow therapeutic index.

7512.w: Bees are descended from stinging wasps: molecular work published in 2018 recovers Ammoplanidae, predators of other insects, as their closest relatives. The switch is thought to have started with prey that were themselves flower visitors, partly covered in pollen and carried back to wasp larvae, and bees appear during the Early Cretaceous about 124 million years ago on West Gondwana.

7513.w: On 4 July 1900 the field assistant Harold Menke found a humerus in the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation, in the valley of the Colorado River near Fruita, Colorado, and Elmer Riggs named Brachiosaurus altithorax from that material in 1903. The African Tendaguru skeletons long carried under the same genus were taken out in 2009, when Michael Taylor found significant divergences in every element known from both and made them Giraffatitan, leaving Brachiosaurus a North American animal.

7514.w: William Harlow Reed found the first remains on 4 September 1879 in Albany County, Wyoming; Marsh named them Camptonotus that year and changed it to Camptosaurus in 1885, the first name already belonging to a cricket. It is a basal member of Ankylopollexia within Iguanodontia, standing between the small early ornithopods and the iguanodonts and hadrosaurs that came after.

7515.w: Sequoia sempervirens carries six chromosome sets, 2n=66, which is unusual among conifers; Yang and colleagues argued in 2010 that it is an allopolyploid, AAAABB, formed from ancestors of the giant sequoia and the dawn redwood. Those extra copies come with the largest genome measured in any plant up to 2020, 26.5 gigabases.

7516.w: The coyote's line is American throughout: Eucyon davisi in the Miocene 6 million years ago in the southwestern US and Mexico, the larger Canis lepophagus by the Pliocene, and fossils inside the range of the modern species by 0.74 to 0.85 million years ago at Hamilton Cave, West Virginia. A 2016 genome study placed the split between North American wolves and coyotes at about 51,000 years ago, and the two have never fully separated — every coyote carries some wolf ancestry and every North American wolf some coyote.

7517.w: Cervidae is the mammal family that grows antlers: single structures of bone, cartilage, fibrous tissue, skin, nerve and blood vessel, shed and regrown every year and growing faster than any other mammal bone, extending at the tip as cartilage under the highly vascular skin called velvet that feeds them until the bone dies and the velvet comes off. That is the line between deer and the horned mammals — a bovid's horn is a two-part structure, bone under a keratin sheath, and it is not shed. The first antlered cervids, Dicrocerus, Euprox and Heteroprox, appear in the Eurasian Miocene, and as antlers came in the tusks of their antlerless ancestors went out.

7518.w: Every donkey descends from the African wild ass, Equus africanus, by way of its Nubian and Somali subspecies, domesticated in Africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago — pastoralists in Nubia and Cushitic-speaking peoples of the Horn of Africa appear to have done it separately. Domestic donkey remains from the fourth millennium BC turn up at Ma'adi in Lower Egypt, while the wild ancestor is down to a few hundred animals in the deserts of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia.

7519.w: The stem group earwigs came from is the Protelytroptera, Permian insects with shell-like forewings and a large, unequal anal fan, known from North America, Europe and Australia. The earwig record itself starts on the far side of that boundary, in the Late Triassic about 208 million years ago in England and Australia, with around 70 specimens of the extinct suborder Archidermaptera — animals with veined tegmina and cerci not yet curled into the pincers of a modern earwig.

7520.w: A flatfish starts as an ordinary symmetrical larva, and thyroid hormone then remakes it: one eye migrates across the top of the head to join the other, and the fish spends the rest of its life lying on its blind side. Amphistium and Heteronectes, about 50 million years old, catch the change partway — still an eye on each side, but one carried up towards the midline — and over 800 living species in 16 families descend from that reorganisation.

7521.w: Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska found the largest skeleton at Tsaagan Khushuu in 1964, during the Polish and Mongolian academies' expeditions of 1963 to 1965 into the Nemegt Formation of the Gobi. Halszka Osmólska, Ewa Roniewicz and Rinchen Barsbold named Gallimimus bullatus from it in 1972 and placed it in the family Ornithomimidae, within Ornithomimosauria.

7522.w: Helodermatid lizards have a long North American history: the genus Heloderma has been present since the Miocene, in H. texana, while the family's roots run back to the Cretaceous. The splits inside the genus fall in the Late Miocene around 10 million years ago and the Pliocene at about 4.4 and 3.0 million years, and Gila monster osteoderms turn up in Late Pleistocene deposits near Las Vegas dated 10,000 to 8,000 years old.

7523.w: Hammerheads evolved out of the requiem sharks, Carcharhinidae, the family the bull shark belongs to, with DNA estimates putting the family's origin in the Miocene about 20 million years ago. The hammer is a sensory spread rather than a shape: distributing the ampullae of Lorenzini over a wider area lets the shark sweep for prey like a larger antenna, and the winghead, sister to all other hammerheads and owner of the widest head, suggests the first hammerheads were already broad.

7524.w: Aesculus belongs to Sapindaceae, the maple, soapberry and lychee family. The conker tree now planted around the world is a Balkan relict: natively it grows only in Albania, Bulgaria, mainland Greece and North Macedonia, and Bulgaria's share is 9 hectares in the Preslav Mountain, in the valleys of the Dervishka and Lazarska rivers — enough for the IUCN to list a globally familiar tree as Vulnerable.

7525.w: Koalas and wombats are the two surviving branches of Vombatiformes; the koala's lineage possibly split off around 40 million years ago in the Eocene, and Phascolarctos separated from the smaller Litokoala in the late Miocene. What the eucalypt diet has cost it since shows in the anatomy — a caecum 200 cm long and 10 cm across, and a brain 60% smaller than a typical diprotodont's, averaging 19.2 g.

7526.w: Lemurs are strepsirrhine primates whose ancestors crossed from Africa on tangled mats of vegetation flushed out of rivers, over a Mozambique Channel at least 560 km wide; 60 million years ago Madagascar and Africa both sat 1,650 km further south, where the currents could have cut the trip to 30 days or less. From that founding population, dated to 62 to 65 million years ago by genetics or 50 to 55 on more conservative estimates, came about 100 living species in 15 genera and eight families.

7527.w: Liverworts descend from the charophyte green algae that made the move onto land, and they sit at the base of the plants that resulted. Five different types of fossilised liverwort spore, found in Argentina in 2010, date to the Middle Ordovician around 470 million years ago; some 9,000 species live now, at least 85% of them in the leafy group.

7528.w: A mantis is a cockroach's close kin: mantises, cockroaches and termites together make up Dictyoptera. The mantis line's own fossils begin with the Jurassic Lovec, reported in 2024 from the Karabastau Formation, and the earliest confidently identified mantises of the Early Cretaceous, among them the 10 mm Santanmantis axelrodi described in 2003 — from which over 2,400 species in about 460 genera and 33 families are recognised today.

7529.w: The megamouth is a mackerel shark, Lamniformes, the same order as the basking shark, but its filter-feeding adaptations are thought to have evolved independently of every other living filter feeder, the basking shark included — the resemblance is convergence, not inheritance. It is the smallest of the three filter-feeding sharks and one of the least seen: as of 25 March 2025 only 296 had been caught or sighted, the first on 15 November 1976, snagged on a US Navy vessel's sea anchor at about 165 m off Kahuku, Hawaii.

7530.w: A mosquito is a true fly like the housefly — one pair of wings, the hind pair reduced to halteres for balance — but from the older long-antennaed side of Diptera, in the infraorder Culicomorpha. The group diversified in the Cretaceous: Burmaculex in Burmese amber dates to about 99 million years ago, Paleoculicis minutus in Canadian amber to about 79, and a 2023 claim for Libanoculex in Lebanese amber reaches about 125 million years, though other authors read that fossil as a chaoborid instead.

7531.w: Crocodylus is an Indo-Pacific genus that reached Africa secondarily, and the Nile crocodile's own lineage shows up in the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene of Kenya, in fossils dated about 7 to 5 million years old. It now ranges across 26 African countries, from the Nile tributaries of Sudan and Lake Nasser to the Cunene in Angola and the Olifants in South Africa, and the West African animals long counted with it stand separated as Crocodylus suchus on morphology, genetics and habitat alike.

7532.w: Oysters are bivalves like the mussel, but where a mussel spins byssal threads that harden in seawater and tether it to rock, an oyster cements a valve down permanently. Ostreidae evolved in the Early Triassic — the genus Liostrea grew on the shells of living ammonoids — and a mature oyster filters 11 to 45 litres of water a day, up to 190 in ideal laboratory conditions.

7533.w: Every pig breed but the Timor and Papua New Guinea stock descends from the wild boar, Sus scrofa, and it happened twice over: in the Tigris Basin of the Near East as early as 13,000 to 12,700 BCE, and separately in China about 8,000 years ago. Remains on Cyprus dated earlier than 11,400 BCE show domestic pigs were already being carried off the mainland by then.

7534.w: Pokeweed is native to eastern North America, the Midwest, the Gulf Coast and the West Coast, and it belongs to Caryophyllales, the order of amaranth, beets and cacti, whose members colour themselves with betalains where other plants use anthocyanins — the two have never been found together in one plant. The magenta of a pokeweed stem and berry is betanin, and the same fruit that birds strip safely has killed infants who ate only a few raw berries.

7535.w: Psittacosaurus is known from hundreds of individuals, most of them Chinese — the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, the Qingshan Formation of Shandong, the Jiufotang — in strata of the Aptian and Albian, roughly 125 to 100 million years ago. Osborn named the type species in 1924 from material of the 1922 Third Asiatic Expedition, and with up to 13 species it is the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus, an early ceratopsian standing below the horned dinosaurs that followed.

7536.w: A ram is a male lamb that kept its testes. Castration, now usually done at around three or four weeks of age, takes away the gonads and the testosterone with them and produces a wether instead; left intact, a ram reaches sexual maturity at four to six months, ahead of ewes at six to eight.

7537.w: Salvia divinorum is a sage of the mint family, hollow square stems and all, endemic to the Sierra Mazateca of Oaxaca and known only as a plant people keep: it reproduces vegetatively, no seed has ever been observed on a wild plant, and even in flower it sets few viable ones. Botanists have not settled whether it is a cultigen or a hybrid, and what carries it forward is cuttings 5 to 20 cm long, taken below a node, which root in plain tap water in two or three weeks.

7538.w: Anatomy, molecules and genetics all place seahorses inside the pipefish family Syngnathidae — a seahorse is a highly modified pipefish, the two lineages having diverged in the Late Oligocene. The upright posture is thought to answer new shallow water raised by tectonic movement, which let seagrass beds spread and gave an upright fish cover; the oldest seahorse fossils, from the Tunjice Hills of Slovenia, are about 13 million years old and still pipefish-like.

7539.w: Sloths and anteaters are the two branches of the order Pilosa, within the xenarthrans, placental mammals thought to have evolved in South America around 60 million years ago. The common ancestor of the two living sloth genera dates to about 28 million years ago, and Bradypus and Choloepus come from different, distantly related families — their shared life hanging in trees is one of the most striking cases of convergent evolution known among mammals.

7540.w: Lawrence Lambe collected three partial skull domes from the Belly River Group along the Red Deer River in Alberta, two in 1898 and one in 1901, and named Stegoceras validus from them in 1902 — roof-horn, for the thickened cap. It is a basal member of Pachycephalosauridae, the family whose best-known animal is Pachycephalosaurus, and its type material comes from the Dinosaur Park and Oldman Formations, about 77.5 to 74 million years old.

7541.w: Helarctos malayanus is the smallest bear, standing near 70 cm at the shoulder at 25 to 65 kg, and its line diverged from the two black bears between about 6.26 and 5.09 million years ago — the sloth bear and the sun bear were the first ursine bears to radiate away from the Ursus group. Its range is the forest belt from Northeast India through Bangladesh, mainland Southeast Asia, Brunei and Indonesia, reaching into Yunnan.

7542.w: The tiger's closest living relative is the snow leopard, the two lineages splitting from each other between 2.70 and 3.70 million years ago within Panthera. Glaciation then squeezed the tiger hard: the population contracted around 115,000 years ago, every living tiger traces to a common ancestor from between 108,000 and 72,000 years ago, and modern populations spread back across Asia from a refuge in Indochina after the Last Glacial Maximum.

7543.w: Tunas are the tribe Thunnini inside Scombridae, the mackerel family — 15 species in five genera, built on the same finletted, deeply forked plan. What separates them is heat: a rete mirabile, veins and arteries interwoven at the body's periphery, reclaims nearly all the metabolic warmth from venous blood, letting a bluefin hold a core of 25 to 33 °C in water as cold as 6 °C.

7544.w: Peter Kaisen found the holotype skull on 11 August 1923 at the Flaming Cliffs, in the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia, and Osborn named Velociraptor mongoliensis the following year. It is a dromaeosaurid, kin to Microraptor and Deinonychus, and in 2007 Alan Turner and colleagues reported six quill knobs on an ulna spaced so that 14 were likely present — the marks a feathered forearm leaves in bone.

7545.w: The zebra shark is the only living member of Stegostomatidae, and there is robust morphological support for placing it in a single clade with the whale shark and the nurse sharks among the carpet sharks — one analysis makes it the sister group to Rhincodon and Ginglymostoma together. Its name comes from the young: juveniles wear light vertical stripes on brown, which break up at 50 to 90 cm into the adult's dark spots on pale, a change so complete that the two stages were once described as separate species.

7546.w: Equus arose in North America and spread quickly into the Old World, and molecular dating puts the split between the caballine horses and the non-caballine line at about 4 million years ago, within a genus whose most recent common ancestor lived some 5.6 million years back. The African wild ass, Equus africanus, sits on the non-caballine side in the subgenus Asinus — nearer kin to the zebras it shares a continent with than to any horse.

7547.w: Mitochondrial studies place the origin of Sus scrofa on the islands of Southeast Asia, from which it spread onto mainland Eurasia and North Africa; the earliest fossils of the species, from Europe and Asia alike, are Early Pleistocene. Moving west it displaced Sus strozzii, a large, possibly swamp-adapted suid, by the late Villafranchian restricting that animal to insular Asia — and the sixteen or so subspecies recognised in 2005 still sort into Western, Indian, Eastern and Indonesian groups by skull height and lacrimal bone length.

7548.w: Syngnathids — pipefishes, seahorses and seadragons — are fish rebuilt around one set of traits: an elongated snout with the jaws fused shut, no pelvic fins, and thick plates of bony armour in place of scales. Carrying the eggs falls to the male throughout the family, and the family is old, the earliest syngnathids coming from Paleocene strata of the Dakhla Formation in Egypt and the Eocene of Monte Bolca in Italy.

7549.w: Scombridae holds 51 living species in 15 genera, divided into the mackerels proper, the Spanish mackerels, the bonitos and the tunas, and the family reaches back to the Danian, the first age of the Paleocene. What the branches share is the swimming gear: two dorsal fins with a row of finlets behind them, a stiff, deeply divided tail on a slender ridged base, and a spiny dorsal and pelvic fins that retract into grooves in the body.

7550.w: Albertosaurus is a tyrannosaurid — the same family as Tyrannosaurus, in its own subfamily Albertosaurinae — and at 8–9 m it stayed much smaller than its famous relative. Its type skull was collected on 9 June 1884 from an outcrop of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation alongside the Red Deer River in Alberta, and a bonebed Barnum Brown found nearby on 11 August 1910 has since given up 1,128 bones from at least 12 individuals.

7551.w: Ants evolved from vespoid wasp ancestors in the Cretaceous; the oldest ant fossils date to about 113–100 million years ago, and the modern subfamilies appear around 80–70 million years ago. What separates them from those wasps is the caste system — one or more reproducing queens and castes of sterile, wingless females — which is why a colony is described as a superorganism.

7552.w: The axolotl is a salamander that reaches sexual maturity without ever metamorphosing, a condition called neoteny: it lacks the thyroid-stimulating hormone that would set off the thyroxine surge other amphibians use to leave the water. Dose it with thyroid hormone and it metamorphoses after all. Within Ambystomatidae its closest relative is the eastern tiger salamander, and it is native to the lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco in the Valley of Mexico.

7553.w: The betel nut is the seed of Areca catechu, a palm native to the Philippines that grows straight to 20 m on a trunk only 10–15 cm across. It is not a true nut at all but the seed of a fruit classed as a berry, and the palm is grown commercially for that one seed crop.

7554.w: Bracken is a fern, so like other ferns it reproduces by spores rather than seeds — but the fronds themselves come up from an underground rootstock that may travel a metre or more between them and makes up about 90% of the plant. That creeping rhizome lets a stand extend its area by 1–3% a year, which is how one pioneer plant becomes a hillside.

7555.w: Toads are frogs, and this one is American: the cane toad's native range runs from the Rio Grande Valley in south Texas down to the central Amazon and southeastern Peru. Its Australian population is an import — 102 toads were collected in Hawaiʻi and released into Queensland cane fields in August 1935, and by March 1937 62,000 toadlets had been let loose.

7556.w: The chanterelle you pick is the fruiting body of a mycelium living in mycorrhizal partnership with tree roots — with oaks in California, Texas and Mexico, with silver birch and Scots pine in Scotland, under beech in Fife. That dependence is also the catch: their mycorrhizal nature makes the species very difficult to cultivate, so there is no chanterelle farming to speak of.

7557.w: All four cultivated cocas were domesticated from the wild shrub Erythroxylum gracilipes, and genomic analysis indicates it happened two or three separate times, by different South American groups during the Holocene. Chewing the leaf goes back at least 8,000 years — leaves and calcite turn up in house floors in Peru's Nanchoc Valley — and the plant, which is not frost-resistant, will not grow above 2,600 m.

7558.w: The crab shape — broad flattened body with the tail folded underneath — has evolved independently in at least five groups of living decapod crustaceans, among the anomurans (king crabs, porcelain crabs, hairy stone crabs, some hermit crabs) as well as in the true crabs. Lancelot Borradaile named the pattern carcinisation in 1916, describing it as nature's repeated attempts to make a crab.

7559.w: Deinonychus is a dromaeosaurid, a close relative of Velociraptor inside the subfamily Velociraptorinae, but its bones come from the other side of the world: the Cloverly Formation of Montana and Wyoming and the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma. John Ostrom published the name in February 1969, and the fast, bird-like animal he described led him to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs — the start of the dinosaur renaissance.

7560.w: Dragonflies are hemimetabolous: there is no pupa, only a run of nymphal stages, and they moult between six and 15 times depending on the species before the adult emerges. That underwater stage lasts up to five years in large species and between two months and three years in smaller ones, ending when the nymph climbs an emergent plant, splits its skin and pumps its wings out with hydraulic pressure.

7561.w: Edelweiss belongs to Leontopodium, a genus of 30–41 species whose centre of diversity is the Sino-Himalayan region of south-western China, where about 15 species grow. AFLP data put the rarest genetic variation in Yunnan, pointing to a long in-situ history there; only two species are native to Europe, so the flower that stands for the Alps is an outlier from an Asian lineage.

7562.w: A ewe is a female sheep old enough to breed, and that line is crossed early: ewes generally reach sexual maturity at six to eight months old. Breeds pull hard in both directions — Finnsheep ewe lambs may reach puberty at three to four months, Merinos sometimes not until 18 to 20 months.

7563.w: Giant hogweed is native to the western Caucasus, at the Asian end of Eurasia, and was carried to Europe for its size: the first British record is 1817, on the seed list at Kew. It grows 2 to 5 m tall and a single flowering plant averages 20,000 seeds — between 10,000 and 50,000 — which is how one ornamental becomes a river-bank thicket.

7564.w: The giraffe and the okapi are the only living members of the family Giraffidae, and a 2016 genetic study placed their common ancestor at about 11.5 million years ago. The okapi — 1.5 m at the shoulder, 200 to 350 kg, confined to forest north and east of the Congo River — shows how much of the giraffe is the derived half of that split.

7565.w: The white shark's ancestor is Carcharodon hastalis, a broad-toothed shark long carried in the mako genus as Isurus hastalis. Around 8–6 million years ago a Pacific population of C. hastalis became C. hubbelli, whose teeth gained serrations over the next few million years, and the white shark itself first appears in the fossil record of the Pacific basin about 6–5 million years ago. Megalodon was not its parent — white sharks replaced it.

7566.w: A housefly is holometabolous — egg, maggot, pupa, adult, with no stage resembling the next. Larvae hatch within a day and feed where they were laid, taking two weeks under optimal conditions or 30 days and more when it is cool, and the pupa finishes in two to six days at 35 °C but 20 days or more at 14 °C. Warm enough, the whole cycle runs in seven to ten days.

7567.w: Monitor lizards originated in Asia and spread to Africa and Australasia, and the Komodo dragon's own fossil record starts in Australia: specimens from across Queensland run from the Early Pliocene, about 3.8 million years ago, to at latest 330,000 years ago. It only shows up on Flores around 1.4 million years ago, and its closest living relative is the Australian lace monitor.

7568.w: Within Panthera the leopard's sister group is the clade holding the lion and the jaguar, and the lineages split 3.1–1.95 million years ago. The oldest unambiguous leopard fossils are eastern African, about 2 million years old; leopards only reached Eurasia between 1.2 and 0.6 million years ago, though the genus itself most likely arose in northern Central Asia.

7569.w: Lizards belong to Squamata, which with over 11,991 species is the second-largest order of living vertebrates, and it parted from the other reptiles early: crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic, with the oldest unambiguous squamate fossils from the Middle Jurassic. A 2018 study argued that Megachirella, from about 240 million years ago in the Middle Triassic, was a stem-squamate and so the oldest known, though a 2021 study left its position unresolved.

7570.w: The mescal bean is the seed of Dermatophyllum secundiflorum, a flowering shrub of the pea family native to Texas, New Mexico and Mexico from Chihuahua and Coahuila south to Hidalgo, Puebla and Querétaro. Its 10 cm pods hold hard orange-red seeds carrying cytisine, a bicyclic alkaloid chemically related to nicotine; a single seed is enough to kill an adult.

7571.w: Mosses are among the first land plants, and land plants emerged from multicellular charophytes — freshwater green algae similar to today's Klebsormidiophyceae — that invaded the land during the Ordovician. Spore microfossils from Argentina carry that step back to the Early Middle Ordovician, around 470 million years ago.

7572.w: Cephalopods descended from a mollusc resembling the Monoplacophora some 530 million years ago, and most molluscs kept the external shell — the nautiloids and the extinct ammonoids among them. Octopuses did not: they arose from the Muensterelloidea within Vampyropoda in the Jurassic, and with no skeletal support left, their arms work as muscular hydrostats of longitudinal, transverse and circular muscle around a central axial nerve.

7573.w: The pink frogmouth is an anglerfish — order Lophiiformes, family Chaunacidae, the sea toads — and it fishes the way the rest of the order does, with an illicium tipped by an esca that is a mop-like tuft of filaments. Where its deep-sea cousins hang in open water, this one is bathydemersal, resting on the bottom between 200 and 1,000 m.

7574.w: Polar bears are brown bears that went out onto the ice: glaciation events over hundreds of thousands of years drove both the split and the later hybridisation between the two, and mass hybridisation appears to have stopped about 200,000 years ago. Estimates of the divergence still range widely — 150,000 years in a 2010 study, 600,000 in a 2012 study, over a million in a 2022 one — and the oldest known polar bear fossil is a jawbone 130,000 to 110,000 years old, found on Prince Charles Foreland, Norway, in 2004.

7575.w: Pteranodon is a pterosaur, not a dinosaur, though both sit inside the clade Avemetatarsalia. Of the roughly 1,200 known specimens, most come from the Late Cretaceous Smoky Hill Chalk of western Kansas, with others from Wyoming, South Dakota and Alabama; Othniel Charles Marsh found the first in 1870 or 1871 and coined the name — 'wing without tooth' — in 1876.

7576.w: The 36 rattlesnake species are native only to the Americas, from southern Canada to central Argentina, and the most probable ancestral area for the group is the Sierra Madre Occidental of Mexico — pine-oak forest, not desert. The diversity still sits there and just north of it: Arizona alone holds 13 species.

7577.w: Echinopsis pachanoi is native to Ecuador and Peru, growing in the Andes at 2,000–3,000 m, and it is quick for a columnar cactus at up to 30 cm a year. Most plants in cultivation began as cuttings rather than seed, which makes them genetic clones of the parent — and the species has been used for healing and divination in the Andes for over 3,000 years.

7578.w: The shaggy mane is the fruiting body a club-fungus mycelium raises out of lawns, gravel roads and waste ground, and it does not keep: the gills turn white, then pink, then black, and the cap dissolves itself within hours of shedding its spores. The same fungus is nematophagous, killing and digesting nematodes such as Panagrellus redivivus and Meloidogyne arenaria.

7579.w: The snow leopard's closest relative in Panthera is the tiger; the two probably diverged between 3.7 and 2.7 million years ago, out of a genus that most likely originated in northern Central Asia. The earliest definitive record of the modern species is Late Pleistocene, from Niuyan Cave in China.

7580.w: Sundews are flowering plants — at least 194 species — that took up insects to supplement the poor mineral nutrition of the soil they grow in; the pygmy species have gone so far as to lose enzymes for processing soil nitrogen. Their flowers are held far above the leaves on a long stem, commonly read as an adaptation to avoid trapping the pollinators the plant still needs.

7581.w: Cultivated tobacco is not a wild species but an allotetraploid, 2n = 4x = 48: within the last 200,000 years, in the Andes, the diploid ancestors of Nicotiana sylvestris and N. tomentosiformis — 24 chromosomes each — crossed, and the hybrid kept both full genomes instead of halving them. N. sylvestris, woodland tobacco of Argentina and Bolivia, is still there to compare it against.

7582.w: The domestic turkey comes from the south Mexican wild subspecies, Meleagris gallopavo gallopavo — the one subspecies that is not found in the United States or Canada — domesticated in Mexico or by Preclassic peoples in Mesoamerica. The wild bird it was taken from is no small animal: an adult tom weighs 5 to 11 kg and measures 100–125 cm, and at twilight it heads for the trees to roost well off the ground.

7583.w: The snap trap evolved only once, in the common ancestor of Dionaea and the waterwheel plant Aldrovanda, and a 2009 study found it developed out of the flypaper traps of an ancestor shared with the sundews. What that ancient lineage has left in the wild is tiny: the Venus flytrap is native only to the coastal bogs of North and South Carolina, within about 100 km of Wilmington.

7584.w: The dog whelk is a predatory sea snail that bores through barnacles and mussels with a modified radula, helped by an organ on the foot secreting a shell-softening chemical; a small prey animal is eaten in about a day, a mussel can take a week to digest. Its own shell records where it grew — the overall shape varies widely with how exposed to wave action the shore is.

7585.w: The okapi is endemic to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, occurring north and east of the Congo River and nowhere else on Earth: about 1.5 m at the shoulder, 2.5 m long, 200 to 350 kg. The striping is a resemblance to a zebra and nothing more — it is most closely related to the giraffe, and a 2016 genetic study put their common ancestor at about 11.5 million years ago.

7586.w: Pterosaurs are the earliest vertebrates known to have evolved powered flight, and they held it for most of the Mesozoic — from the Late Triassic to the end of the Cretaceous, 228 to 66 million years ago. They are archosaurs, avemetatarsalians closer to birds and other dinosaurs than to crocodiles or any other living reptile, and the oldest ones known were already fully adapted to flying.

7587.w: Palms are monocots, and Areca catechu is one: a medium-sized palm native to the Philippines, growing straight to 20 m on a trunk only 10–15 cm in diameter, since a monocot has no vascular cambium to thicken a trunk the way a ring-forming tree does. It is grown across the tropics for one commercially important seed crop, the areca nut.

7588.w: Erythroxylum is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Erythroxylaceae — Kew's Plants of the World Online listed 259 species as of 2021, and many of the roughly 200 examined carry the tropane alkaloid cocaine. Erythroxylum gracilipes is the wild South American member of that genus from which every cultivated coca was domesticated.

7589.w: Nicotiana sylvestris is a wild flowering plant of the Andes, a diploid carrying the S-genome at 2n = 2x = 24. Within the last 200,000 years, in those same mountains, its ancestors crossed with the ancestors of N. tomentosiformis — another diploid at 2n = 2x = 24 — and the hybrid kept both genomes, which is where cultivated tobacco comes from.

7590.w: The wild turkey is a North American bird in six subspecies, only one of which — the nominate south Mexican form — is absent from the United States and Canada. It came close to going: game managers estimate the entire US population fell as low as 30,000 by the late 1930s, against 1.3 million by 1973 and roughly 7 million today.

7591.w: The bulk of Allosaurus comes out of the Morrison Formation of Utah, Wyoming and Colorado, where the Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry alone preserves a minimum of 73 dinosaurs, at least 46 of them A. fragilis. Then a specimen turned up in 1988 near Andrés in Portugal's Leiria District, with further material from the Lourinhã, Bombarral and Alcobaça formations, making A. fragilis the first dinosaur species known from both Europe and North America. The two occurrences together are evidence of a land connection between the continents in the Late Jurassic.

7592.w: Apatosaurus and Diplodocus are the two branches of one family, Diplodocidae, and the difference between them is build rather than plan: Apatosaurus's neck vertebrae are shorter and far more heavily constructed, its leg bones stockier though longer. The 2015 study that scored 477 morphological characters across 81 dinosaur individuals sorted the family out again, and in the process gave Brontosaurus back a genus of its own, 112 years after Elmer Riggs folded it into Apatosaurus in 1903.

7593.w: Banisteriopsis caapi is a Malpighiaceae liana of the western Amazon, native to Ecuador and Peru, climbing up to 30 metres and flowering only infrequently. Its bark carries harmine at 0.31 to 8.43 percent, harmaline at 0.03 to 0.83 and tetrahydroharmine at 0.05 to 2.94 — the monoamine oxidase inhibitors that make the brew work at all.

7594.w: Panellus stipticus is a gilled fungus of the Agaricales, the same order as the button mushroom, and sits in the mycenoid lineage that holds most known luminous fungi. Its glow is a strain trait rather than a species trait: collections from eastern North America light up, while those from the Pacific coast, Europe, Russia, Japan and New Zealand do not.

7595.w: Jumping bristletails branch off below every other insect alive: Archaeognatha is the sister taxon to the Dicondylia, the line that leads on to the winged insects. The order appears in the Middle Devonian, at about the same time as the arachnids, and specimens closely resembling living species turn up as both body and trace fossils right through the Paleozoic. After all that time it still holds only about 600 species in two families, small animals that spring up to 30 cm into the air off their tails when disturbed.

7596.w: Genetic and archaeological evidence puts the first domestication of cannabis about 12,000 years ago in East Asia, in the early Neolithic. The oldest hard traces are Chinese: hemp fibre imprints pressed into Yangshao culture pottery from the 5th millennium BC.

7597.w: The cheetah's closest living relatives are not the big cats but the cougar and the jaguarundi; the three make up the Puma lineage, which diverged from the rest of the cat family 6.7 million years ago. Two later bottlenecks — one about 100,000 years ago tied to the crossing from North America into Asia, one 10,000 to 12,000 years ago in Africa — left it with roughly 0.1 to 4 percent of the genetic variation an average species carries.

7598.w: Dactylopius coccus is a scale insect native to tropical and subtropical America, from South America north through Mexico and the southwestern United States, and one of the very few insects people ever took into cultivation. Indigenous growers moved it into gardens and kept the strains carrying more dye; the colour was in use by the second century BC, and codices were being painted with it by the thirteenth.

7599.w: Freshwater crayfish fall into two superfamilies that divide by hemisphere: Astacoidea across Eurasia and North America, and Parastacoidea, whose single family Parastacidae has a Gondwanan spread over South America, Madagascar and Australasia. That line follows the break-up of Pangaea into Laurasia and Gondwana, and the crayfish sit with the lobsters in one infraorder, Astacidea.

7600.w: Almost every domestic duck breed descends from the mallard, Anas platyrhynchos, the exceptions being a few Muscovy breeds, and whole-genome sequencing points to a single domestication event. It happened around 2000 BC in southern China among rice-paddy farmers, after which selection split the lineages sharply between meat birds and egg birds.

7601.w: Hadrosaurids like Edmontosaurus sit inside Iguanodontia, the clade Iguanodon anchors — phylogenetic work makes the traditional iguanodontids a paraphyletic grade leading up to the duck-bills. That line ends in the most sophisticated chewing apparatus any non-avian dinosaur developed, worked by bulk feeders taking tough, low-value plants: E. annectens reached about 12 metres and 5.6 tonnes, with exceptional individuals near 15 metres and 15.9 tonnes. Lawrence Lambe named the genus in 1917 from two partial skeletons found along the Red Deer River in Alberta, in the rock then called the Edmonton Formation.

7602.w: Fiddler crabs are ocypodid crabs, sharing that family with the ghost crabs, and more than 100 species of them fill 11 of the family's 13 genera. Until 2016 nearly all sat inside the single genus Uca; that year most of its subgenera were raised to genera in their own right, split between the subfamilies Gelasiminae and Ucinae.

7603.w: Bathynomus belongs to the order Isopoda, the same order as the woodlouse under a garden log, and shows deep-sea gigantism at its most extreme: the giant species run 8 to 15 cm, the supergiants 17 to 50. They live from about 170 metres down to 2,140, with B. kensleyi recorded at 2,500.

7604.w: The domestic goat descends from the bezoar ibex, Capra aegagrus, a wild goat now confined to the Zagros Mountains but formerly spread right across Anatolia. The oldest remains of domesticated goats, 10,000 years old, come from Ganj Dareh in Iran, with further early finds at Jericho, Choga Mami, Djeitun and Çayönü.

7605.w: The grey reef shark is Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, a requiem shark in the same genus as the bull shark; within that genus, vertebral counts, tooth shape and a 1992 allozyme phylogeny put it closest to the silvertip shark. It stays small for a Carcharhinus — most are under 1.88 metres, the maximum recorded 2.6 metres and 33.7 kg — and lives at least 25 years.

7606.w: Every anatomically modern human fossil older than about 200,000 years is African: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco at roughly 315,000 years, Florisbad in South Africa at 259,000, Omo-Kibish in Ethiopia at 233,000. The Middle Pleistocene African populations usually filed under Homo heidelbergensis are the pool those first moderns emerged from, though which lineage is the direct ancestor is still argued.

7607.w: Kerria lacca is a scale insect of the family Kerriidae, in the superfamily Coccoidea alongside the cochineal, and it is native to Asia. India alone produces around 20,000 tonnes of raw lac a year, at least half the world's supply, from insects farmed on host trees.

7608.w: Molecular work makes Triakis semifasciata the most basal member of the houndshark family Triakidae, with the banded houndshark as its nearest relative. Genetics also shows how little it travels: seven discrete gene pools lie along the Californian coast between Humboldt Bay and San Diego, inside a range that runs only from Coos Bay in Oregon to Mazatlán in Mexico.

7609.w: Decapods go back about 455 million years, and after the swimming prawns branched off first, the remainder split again into the swimming shrimp and the Reptantia — the crawling line that produced lobsters and crabs. The oldest known decapod body fossil, Palaeopalaemon, is Late Devonian; nearly 15,000 decapod species are alive today.

7610.w: Marlins are the family Istiophoridae, between 9 and 11 species depending on the authority, and their closest relative is the swordfish, the only member of Xiphiidae; the two families together make up the billfish superfamily Xiphioidea. The Atlantic blue marlin reaches 5 metres and 820 kg, the black marlin over 5 metres and 670 kg.

7611.w: The pupa inside a cocoon does not chew its way out. It releases proteolytic enzymes that dissolve a hole through the wall of raw silk — 300 to about 900 metres of one unbroken thread — and the adult moth walks out through it. In Bombyx mori that adult cannot fly: its body is too heavy for a wingspan of 3 to 5 cm, unlike the wild B. mandarina it was bred from.

7612.w: Nerium oleander is the only species currently placed in its genus, a dogbane-family shrub native from Morocco and Portugal east through the Mediterranean to India and Myanmar, and cultivated around the Mediterranean basin for millennia. Every part of it carries cardenolide glycosides — oleandrin, odorosiside, adigoside — with a narrow therapeutic index: about 100 grams of leaf is enough to kill an adult horse.

7613.w: Hadrosauridae divides into two subfamilies and these two sit one on each side: the lambeosaurines carry hollow crests with air chambers inside, the saurolophines a solid crest or none at all. The type specimen of P. walkeri, found in 1920 near Sand Creek on the Red Deer River in Alberta and named by William Parks in 1922, has a skull about 1.6 metres long including that crest.

7614.w: Pinnipeds are caniform carnivorans — the branch of the order that also holds the bears, the weasels and the red panda — that went back to the water, diverging from their land relatives around 50 million years ago in the Eocene. Puijila, an otter-shaped Early Miocene animal from Arctic Canada, was still swimming on four legs in fresh water; Enaliarctos, 24 to 22 million years ago off California, already had flippers and a flexible spine.

7615.w: A cnidarian egg hatches into a planula: a flattened, ciliated larva with no mouth and no gut, living on stored yolk while its cilia carry it through the water. When it reaches hard substrate it anchors there and grows into a polyp — and from that fixed sac a coral colony builds itself, or a jellyfish buds off.

7616.w: A puffball is a gilled mushroom that gave up its gills and shut its spores inside instead. That rebuild, gasteromycetation, happened convergently in a number of independent events out of ordinary hymenomycetes, which is why puffballs are a shape rather than a single lineage. A mature giant puffball, Calvatia gigantea, holds about 7 × 10¹² spores, more than any other known organism.

7617.w: The Pacific razor clam, Siliqua patula, is a bivalve mollusc of the family Pharidae whose two hinged valves are drawn out into a blade — the shape the muscular foot drives down through wet sand, valves closing to force it deeper. It runs 8 to 15 cm at the southern end of a range that reaches from Alaska to California, and up to 28 cm in Alaska itself.

7618.w: Sand dollars are the order Clypeasteroida, sea urchins flattened for burrowing; they diverged from the other irregular echinoids, the cassiduloids, in the early Jurassic, and the first true sand dollar genus, Togocyamus, appears in the Paleocene. The rebuild moved the anus from the top of the test round to the back and cut the long defensive spines down to a velvet of ciliated ones.

7619.w: Ovis aries descends from the Asiatic mouflon, Ovis gmelini; the European mouflon is a direct descendant of that same domestic population rather than a second wild source. Domestication ran between 11,000 and 9000 BC in Mesopotamia and reached Mehrgarh in the Indus Valley by about 7000 BC, and the FAO listed 1,229 breeds as of 2006.

7620.w: The snowy owl was long given a genus of its own, Nyctea, until mtDNA cytochrome b sequences placed it inside Bubo, the horned owls, with the great horned owl as its closest living relative. What it did evolve on that branch is insulation: toe feathers averaging 33.3 mm against 13 mm in the great horned owl, the next longest of any owl.

7621.w: The bulkiest of the stick insects are Malay Archipelago animals: Heteropteryx dilatata lives on the Malay Peninsula, in Thailand and Singapore, on Sumatra and in Sarawak on Borneo, and the female reaches 14 to 17 cm and 30 to 65 grams against a male's slender 9 to 13 cm. Its genus holds that one species and no other.

7622.w: Acorus is the first branch off the monocot line — sister to all other monocots — and stands alone in its family, four species in the genus. The sweet flag that spread through Europe and North America is a sterile triploid, 3n = 36, probably a hybrid of the diploid and tetraploid cytotypes and probably from the Himalayan region; it sets no seed and travels only as cut rhizome, and unlike the diploid strains it carries β-asarone.

7623.w: The tope is a houndshark, family Triakidae — the same family as the leopard shark, which a 2006 analysis makes the most basal member of the group — and it is the only living species in the genus Galeorhinus. Where the leopard shark barely moves, this one crosses oceans: fish tagged in the United Kingdom have been recovered in the Azores, the Canary Islands and Iceland, and Australian-tagged fish have turned up in New Zealand.

7624.w: Trametes versicolor is a white-rot fungus of the Polyporales, the basidiomycete order that holds most white rotters, and it takes lignin apart with class II peroxidases — lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, versatile peroxidase — backed by laccase. A 2012 study of 31 fungal genomes traced that enzymatic machinery to about the end of the Permian, which is where the great burial of undecayed wood as coal falls away.

7625.w: The walrus is the only surviving odobenid, and its family separated from the eared seals — the sea lions and fur seals — roughly 15 to 20 million years ago, after both had split from the true seals 20 to 26 million years ago. The tusks are elongated canines carried by both sexes, reaching 1 metre and 5.4 kg.

7626.w: Tremella mesenterica is not rotting the wood it sits on; it grows parasitically on the mycelium of Peniophora, the corticioid crust fungi that are. Its gelatinous lobes reach 7.5 cm across and 2.5 to 5 cm high, shrivel within a few days into a thin film, and revive with the next rain.

7627.w: Geese and the mallard sit in one family, Anatidae — around 174 species in 43 genera — the geese and swans in the subfamily Anserinae, the mallard among the dabbling ducks of the Anatinae, genus Anas. Its own species boundary leaks badly: Anas platyrhynchos has hybridised with more than 40 species in the wild and 20 more in captivity, and the fertile hybrids have swamped the American black duck, the Hawaiian duck and the New Zealand grey duck.

7628.w: Goats and sheep are the two large genera of one bovid subfamily, Caprinae — Capra with about ten species, Ovis with seven — separate wild lines that people took in separately. Ovis gmelini, the Asiatic mouflon, is the wild half of the sheep story, ranging across Turkey, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Iran, and a mature ram's horns curve almost a full revolution, up to 85 cm.

7629.w: The aurochs and the wild goat are both bovids, but from opposite halves of the family — Bovinae for the cattle, Caprinae for the goats and sheep — and the Bovinae are thought to have diverged from the rest in the early Miocene, when bovids first appear about 20 million years ago. Of that family 143 species are alive now against 300 known extinct ones, and Capra aegagrus is the one holding the Zagros Mountains of Iran, formerly spread across Anatolia.

7630.w: Guillermo Rougier found the only known skeleton in February 1984, on an expedition led by Jose Bonaparte, in the La Amarga Formation of Neuquen Province in northern Patagonia — sandstone and mudstone dropped by braided river channels, lakes and alluvial plains, and the oldest Cretaceous terrestrial rock in the Neuquen Basin at 130 to 120 million years old. Salgado and Bonaparte named it in 1991, and that one near-complete skeleton is still the whole of what is known.

7631.w: Through spring and summer an aphid colony is entirely female, each mother giving live birth to clones of herself, and the daughters arrive already carrying their own developing embryos, so generations telescope one inside another. Cabbage aphids can run through as many as 41 such generations in a season, each lasting 20 to 40 days, before shortening days and falling temperatures finally bring out males and the mated females lay eggs that overwinter outside the body.

7632.w: The olive baboon belongs to Papio, a genus of the Old World monkey family Cercopithecidae, and baboons are an African radiation: no species of the genus lives wild beyond Africa and a corner of the Arabian Peninsula. This one is the most wide-ranging of them all, spread across 25 equatorial African countries from Mali east to Ethiopia and Tanzania, with isolated populations holding on in mountains of the Sahara.

7633.w: Bird's nest fungi belong to the Agaricales, inside the euagarics clade of mostly gilled mushrooms, but they gave up handing their spores to the wind the way most fungi do. The spores travel packed into disc-shaped peridioles sitting in the tiny cup, and a raindrop striking that cup at the right angle throws one about a metre; in some species a sticky funicular cord catches a passing twig and whips the packet around it.

7634.w: The domestic water buffalo descends from Bubalus arnee, the wild water buffalo, now down to fewer than 4,000 mature animals in fragments of Assam, Nepal and mainland Southeast Asia. It was taken in twice over and independently: the river type in western India about 6,300 years ago, the swamp type in mainland Southeast Asia between 3,000 and 7,000 years ago. Their descendants now number some 208 million head across 77 countries.

7635.w: Abelisaurids were the dominant predators of Late Cretaceous Gondwana, occupying the niche tyrannosaurids held on the northern continents, and Carnotaurus sits in Brachyrostra, a short-snouted branch of them restricted to South America. Its single known skeleton came out of the La Colonia Formation of Chubut Province, Argentina, in 1984, from rock 69 to 66 million years old.

7636.w: Every breed of chicken traces back to the red junglefowl of South and Southeast Asian forest; a 2020 study put all domestic chickens down to a single domestication of Gallus gallus spadiceus in Southeast Asia around 9,500 years ago. One trait came in from a neighbour — the gene behind the yellow skin of domestic birds most likely originated in the closely related grey junglefowl.

7637.w: A cockroach does not lay loose eggs: it wraps them in an ootheca, a case of structural proteins hardened by tanning agents, and a German cockroach packs about 30 to 40 long thin eggs into one. The female glues the case to a surface, wedges it into a protective crevice, or carries it about until just before hatching, when the young break out on the combined pressure of all of them gulping air — though some species keep the eggs inside the body instead, and the genus Diploptera is fully viviparous. One female may produce up to eight cases in her life, and in good conditions 300 to 400 offspring.

7638.w: Datura is a genus of the nightshade family whose centre of origin is Mexico, where most of its nine to fourteen species are native. Populations long taken for native elsewhere — D. ferox in China, D. metel in India and Southeast Asia, D. leichhardtii in Australia — are almost certainly post-Columbian introductions carried out of Central America.

7639.w: Jesse Williams, a Navajo man, found the bones in 1940 in the Kayenta Formation of northern Arizona, about 32 km north of Cameron on the Navajo Reservation, and Charles Camp's field party excavated three skeletons from the site in 1942. The Kayenta's red and brown sandstones outcrop across the Colorado Plateau and date the animal to roughly 198 to 179 million years ago; Welles called it Megalosaurus in 1954 and only gave it its own genus in 1970.

7640.w: Duckweeds are flowering plants that selection has stripped almost bare — no obvious stem and no leaves, just a floating thallus a few cells thick, often pocketed with air, and in some species no roots at all. They sit inside the arum family, Araceae, so all that structure was lost from ancestors that had it. Wolffia's flower, 0.3 mm long, is the smallest known, and the plants mostly skip flowering altogether, budding daughters from a meristem at the base of the frond fast enough to double their biomass in four and a half days.

7641.w: The specimen came out of a ravine in the Pierre Shale near Fort Wallace, Kansas, in 1867 — marine rock laid down in the Western Interior Seaway between about 80.6 and 77 million years ago. Cope named it in 1868 and reconstructed it with the skull on the wrong end of the vertebral column, at the tail; Marsh made sure the mistake was public. Of its 10.3 m length about 7.1 m was neck, carried on 72 vertebrae.

7642.w: Salamandra salamandra is the salamander of southern and central Europe, usually found between 250 and 1,000 m of altitude and higher in Spain and the Balkans, and split into thirteen recognised subspecies. Most are ovoviviparous — the eggs develop inside the female and she deposits the hatched larvae straight into water — while fastuosa and bernardezi go further and bear live young.

7643.w: The panda's line split from the common ancestor of the bears about 19 million years ago, which makes it the most basal member of Ursidae and equally distant from every other living bear. It has stayed where it began: six montane regions of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, up to 3,000 m, hold the entire wild population of roughly 1,900 animals.

7644.w: The first known specimen was a 107 cm immature male caught in Sagami Bay near Yokohama; shipmaster Alan Owston passed it to Kakichi Mitsukuri at the University of Tokyo, who sent it on to David Starr Jordan, and Jordan named it Mitsukurina owstoni in 1898 for both men. It is the only surviving member of the family Mitsukurinidae, whose fossil record reaches back about 125 million years to the Aptian.

7645.w: The European hedgehog belongs to the family Erinaceidae in the order Eulipotyphla, a branch of placental mammals quite separate from the rodents its habits might suggest. Its range runs from Iberia and Italy north into Scandinavia and reaches its western limit in Ireland, and a single animal carries up to 6,000 brown and white spines.

7646.w: The Malheur National Forest fungus is not a population but one individual, spreading underground on black rhizomorphs — 'shoestrings' that carry nutrients between distant roots — and growing rather than breeding, so every cell of it is a copy. That single Armillaria ostoyae genet has been at it for an estimated 8,000 years, and now covers 3.5 square miles, about 2,200 acres, at a weight that may reach 35,000 tons.

7647.w: A ladybird is a beetle, one of more than 6,000 species in the family Coccinellidae, and the adult is assembled out of a larva that looks nothing like it. In Adalia bipunctata the eggs hatch after four to eight days, the larva spends about three weeks growing through four stages and three moults, then hunches into a pupa for seven to ten days before the hardened forewings, the elytra, colour up over the following hours.

7648.w: Leptocyon is the oldest known canine, the earliest member of the subfamily Caninae, and it lived in North America from about 34 million years ago until 10.3 million years ago. While the heavy-jawed borophagines alongside it specialised in a powerful killing bite, Leptocyon stayed small — as little as 2 kg — and built for snatching fast little prey.

7649.w: No taxonomic line separates locusts from grasshoppers; what makes a locust is that the animal changes phase. Increased tactile stimulation of the hind legs raises serotonin, and several contacts a minute sustained over about four hours tips a solitary grasshopper into the gregarious form, which changes colour, eats much more and breeds much more readily — in swarms reaching 80 million insects per square kilometre.

7650.w: The government surveyor Joseph Millard Orpen and his brothers dug the first bones out of a farm in the Drakensberg near Harrismith in 1853 and 1854, and Richard Owen described the animal in 1854. Most later material comes from the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho, rock spanning roughly 201 to 184 million years ago — the fossils are common enough that they are used to date the beds themselves.

7651.w: A mussel starts as a drifting larva that spends anywhere from three weeks to six months in the plankton before finding a hard surface and settling as a young mussel about 1 mm across. Only then is it the bivalve mollusc anyone would recognise, holding its place with byssal threads that it can attach and detach to shuffle slowly into a better position.

7652.w: Papaver somniferum is known only as a cultivated plant, and its wild ancestor has never been identified. Papaver setigerum, native to southwestern Europe and North Africa and long the favoured candidate, is tetraploid with n=22 while the opium poppy is diploid with n=11, so it cannot be the wild ancestral species. What is left is archaeology: small botanical remains around the Mediterranean and west of the Rhine push cultivation back beyond about 5000 BC.

7653.w: Charles Hazelius Sternberg, collecting on commission for Uppsala University, recovered a skull and a rump at Meyers Creek near the Kimbetoh Wash in the San Juan Basin of New Mexico in 1921. The Kirtland Formation he dug them from is sandstone with shale, mudstone and conglomerate, alluvial deposits of old river channels and floodplains dated between 75.02 and 73.49 million years ago; Osborn named the animal Pentaceratops sternbergii after him in 1923.

7654.w: Piranhas are characiform fish of the family Serrasalmidae, and they are confined to South America — the Amazon basin, the Orinoco, the rivers of the Guianas, the Paraguay-Parana and the Sao Francisco. Estimates of how many species there are run from fewer than 30 to more than 60, and the same continent produced the extinct Megapiranha of 8 to 10 million years ago, far larger than anything alive.

7655.w: Boletus edulis cannot raise a fruit body alone: it is ectomycorrhizal, trading nutrients with tree roots across at least 30 host species in more than 15 genera, from pines, spruces and firs to oaks, chestnuts and beech. That partnership is also how it travels — it reached Christchurch in the mid-19th century on the roots of imported beech, birch and oak, and has been in South African pine plantations for over 50 years. The largest one recorded, from the Isle of Skye in 1995, weighed 3.2 kg with a 42 cm cap.

7656.w: Douglas Lawson, then a graduate student, found a 0.91 m bone in an arroyo on the western edge of Big Bend National Park, Texas, in 1971, in the Javelina Formation, and published the name in 1975. It is a pterosaur rather than a dinosaur — an azhdarchid — and while early wingspan estimates ranged from 5.2 all the way to 25.8 m, recent work settles around 10 to 11 m.

7657.w: The fox-like genus Leptocyon appears about 34 million years ago and splits 11.9 million years ago into two lines: Vulpes, the foxes, and the Canini. The red fox sits on the first of those branches, which is why it is unmistakably a member of the dog family and yet not a close relative of the wolf and the dog on the other side of that division.

7658.w: Constantine Rafinesque described Carcharias taurus in 1810 from a specimen caught off Sicily, and that Mediterranean fish still fixes the species name. Very few individuals ever descend from a given female: she may begin with as many as 50 embryos, but once one reaches about 10 cm it eats every smaller embryo in its uterine horn, so two pups are born, each already about a metre long and fully independent.

7659.w: Dendrobranchiate prawns hatch as a nauplius — three head segments under a single carapace, with one unpaired naupliar eye — and only take on a shrimp's shape after a long planktonic passage through the zoea stage, which carries thoracic swimming appendages and a large dorsal spine. Most other decapods brood their eggs on the female's pleopods and take the short route, with at most nine larval stages; a shrimp's post-larva has a name of its own, the parva.

7660.w: Sphynx hairlessness is a recessive 'hr' allele of KRT71 that knocks the gene out completely, so a hair never forms a solid root or bulb; DNA work in 2010 showed that a different allele of the very same gene gives the Devon Rex its short curly coat. The breed was assembled from a handful of spontaneous carriers — Prune, born in Toronto in 1966 to a domestic shorthair called Elizabeth, the Minnesota kittens Epidermis and Dermis in 1975, and Toronto street kittens found in 1978 and crossed to a Devon Rex in the Netherlands.

7661.w: Phallus impudicus does not hand its spores to the wind. Its sticky spore mass gives off methanethiol, hydrogen sulfide, dimethyl sulfide and dimethyl trisulfide — the chemistry of decomposing flesh — and an Austrian study found blow-flies such as Calliphora vicina and Lucilia caesar, which normally feed on dead animals, coming to the fungus instead and carrying spores away. The fruit body rises out of its egg at 10 to 15 cm an hour to meet them.

7662.w: Termites are not a separate order at all: 21st-century phylogenetics places the infraorder Isoptera deep inside Blattodea, making them highly derived cockroaches whose closest living relatives are the wood-eating cockroaches of the genus Cryptocercus. The symbiosis gave it away long before the genetics did — the similarity of their symbiotic gut flagellates prompted the suggestion as early as 1925, and the two groups also share trophallaxis and social habits.

7663.w: Othniel Charles Marsh named Torosaurus in 1891 from a skull John Bell Hatcher took out of the Lance Formation in Niobrara County, southeastern Wyoming, where badlands of buff-coloured sandstone and drab green shale are cut along Cow Creek beside the formation's type locality — stream deposits on a coastal plain at the edge of the Western Interior Seaway, 69 to 66 million years ago. Its largest known skull, 'Adam', is 3 m long, the longest of any land animal.

7664.w: New World vultures are not close kin to the Old World ones; the bare head and the scavenging life evolved twice over, and the two groups do not form a single clade. The turkey vulture is one of seven surviving Cathartidae in five genera, spread from southern Canada to South America, and taxonomists still disagree about whether to keep them in their own order Cathartiformes or fold them into Accipitriformes.

7665.w: Cicuta is a genus of four species in the carrot family, Apiaceae, native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere and mainly to North America — three of them, C. maculata, C. bulbifera and C. douglasii, are North American. All carry cicutoxin, an unsaturated aliphatic alcohol that blocks GABA receptors and lets neurons fire unchecked, and seizures can begin as soon as 15 minutes after a mouthful.

7666.w: From Leptocyon the Canini branch runs on through Eucyon davisi about 6 to 5 million years ago, Canis lepophagus around 5 million, Canis etruscus about 2 million, and Canis mosbachensis in the Middle Pleistocene before Canis lupus itself. The oldest wolf tooth known comes from Old Crow in the Yukon, in sediment a million years old, and Alaskan specimens dated to 810,000 years point to an origin in eastern Beringia.

7667.w: Gallus gallus is a bird of South and Southeast Asia and nowhere else: the range opens in Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh, runs east across southern China into Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, then south through Malaysia and Singapore to the Philippines, Indonesia and Timor-Leste. Every chicken on every other continent arrived there with people, out of a single domestication in Southeast Asia around 9,500 years ago.

7668.w: Bubalus arnee is a South and Southeast Asian bovid down to fewer than 4,000 mature animals, and Nepal holds one of its last strongholds in the Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, the source for recent translocations founding new herds. It has been listed as Endangered since 1986 and sits in CITES Appendix III, protected by law in Bhutan, India, Nepal and Thailand — and it is already gone from Bangladesh, Laos, Vietnam and Sri Lanka.

7669.w: The suborder Caelifera has split into roughly 2,400 valid genera and about 11,000 described species, with many more undescribed in tropical wet forest. They are among the most ancient living groups of chewing herbivorous insects, reaching back to the early Triassic around 250 million years ago — and a few species in the family Acrididae keep a second identity in reserve, turning into locusts when they are crowded.

7670.w: The genus Alligator has only two species left, one in the southeastern United States and one on China's Yangtze. The American one lives farther from the equator than any other crocodilian, and when its water freezes over it holds its snout up through the surface to breathe above the ice.

7671.w: A farmer near Plaza Huincul in Neuquen Province found the first bone in 1987 and took it for a petrified log; Jose Bonaparte's 1989 excavation of the Huincul Formation yielded the vertebrae and sacrum that became the holotype, named in 1993. Everything known of this 30-35 m titanosaur comes from those few fragments, scaled against more complete relatives.

7672.w: The bald eagle forms a species pair with the white-tailed eagle of Eurasia: one white-headed, one tan-headed, much the same size, each filling the same role on its own side of the world. The pair had split from the other sea eagles by the Early Miocene, around 10 million years ago.

7673.w: Carcharhinus radiated so recently that its branches resist untangling: a 1998 allozyme analysis left the blacktip reef shark in an unresolved polytomy with ten other species of the genus, of which it is the type species. It also keeps extremely small home ranges, staying in one patch of reef for years at a time.

7674.w: Every true bug carries the same piece of equipment: a beak of piercing-sucking mouthparts, the one arrangement shared across more than 80,000 species that otherwise drink sap, other insects, or blood. Hemiptera is also the largest order that never pupates, more than 95,000 named species whose nymphs hatch already resembling small wingless adults; every insect order with more species than that passes through a pupa instead.

7675.w: Ricinus communis is the only species in its genus and in its subtribe, a spurge indigenous to East Africa, the southeastern Mediterranean basin and India, and spread from there through the tropics. India now grows over three-quarters of the world's roughly two million tonnes of castor seed a year.

7676.w: Chimpanzees are one of the four surviving great-ape genera, and the African ones have left almost no fossils: three teeth found in Kenya in 2005 and dated to about 500,000 years ago are the only Pan fossils known. The split from the human line is placed 7 to 10 million years ago.

7677.w: One of the earliest known dinosaurs, and among the best represented, because of a single place. David Baldwin collected the first bones in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico in 1881, and in June 1947 Edwin Colbert's crew struck a Chinle Formation bonebed at Ghost Ranch packed with skeletons of an animal that lived 215 to 201 million years ago.

7678.w: The dingo descends from domesticated dogs whose lineage branched off early from today's breeds and can be traced back through Maritime Southeast Asia. The oldest dingo remains in Australia are 3,450 years old, and the skull has barely changed since: nobody bred it, it simply lived wild.

7679.w: Dung beetles are not one branch of the family tree. Dung feeding turns up in several beetle families within the Scarabaeoidea, so the habit cannot have arisen only once; the true dung beetles alone, the subfamily Scarabaeinae, number more than 5,000 species.

7680.w: The elephant order opens with Eritherium, a 3-8 kg animal from the Ouled Abdoun phosphate beds of Morocco about 60 million years ago, the oldest and most primitive proboscidean known. Elephants proper appeared in Africa around 10 million years ago, and the lineage only reached Eurasia after Afro-Arabia collided with it 18-19 million years ago.

7681.w: Lampyridae are elateroid beetles, more than 2,400 described species. The light is thought to have begun as a warning that the larvae taste bad and was later taken over as a mating signal, and females of the genus Photuris now mimic the flash pattern of Photinus males in order to eat them.

7682.w: The giant sequoia and the coast redwood are surviving genera of the same redwood subfamily, split between the Sierra Nevada and the coast. The Sierra tree holds its cones green and shut for as long as 20 years and it takes the heat of a fire to dry them open; bark up to 90 cm thick and full of tannic acid carries the parent through that same fire.

7683.w: It lives in one stretch of the Choco rainforest on Colombia's Pacific coast, a range under 5,000 square kilometres, and nowhere else on earth; it was described in 1978 from specimens collected at Quebrada Guangui and La Brea. At about 6 cm it is the largest of the poison dart frogs.

7684.w: Every known fossil comes from the Ischigualasto Formation of northwestern Argentina, where a goatherd named Victorino Herrera first noticed the bones in 1959 and Osvaldo Reig described them in 1963; the rock is about 231 million years old. Where exactly it sits has been argued ever since — basal saurischian or primitive theropod — with the near-complete skull found by Paul Sereno's team in 1988 pushing the theropod reading.

7685.w: Hyenas are feliforms, the cat branch of the carnivores, closer to felines and civets than to any dog. The dog-like build, the running feet with blunt claws and the catching of prey with the teeth are convergence; the family began about 22 million years ago in Miocene Eurasia with civet-like animals such as Plioviverrops.

7686.w: A sunfish native to the eastern and central United States, southeastern Canada and northern Mexico, carried far beyond that by anglers. A 2022 phylogenomic study found that Lacepede's 1802 type specimen from near Charleston was really a Florida bass, so the largemouth took Cuvier's name instead, typed on Lake Huron.

7687.w: Convallaria sits in the asparagus family, Asparagaceae, having been shunted through Ruscaceae, a family of its own and the lilies before that. The species is native to Europe and northern Asia; the plants in eastern North America and East Asia, long treated as its varieties, are now split off as separate species, and a colony that is all one clone sets no seed, because the plant will not fertilise itself.

7688.w: The first dinosaur eggs ever found in the Western Hemisphere came out of a Montana hillside in 1979, the year after Jack Horner and Bob Makela found the bonebed south of Choteau and named the animal 'good mother lizard'. The site held nests and juveniles as well, which is why the hill is called Egg Mountain and why this hadrosaur is Montana's state fossil.

7689.w: The mayapple belongs to the barberry family, but as a herb of eastern North American and southeastern Canadian woodland rather than a shrub. It spreads by a creeping rhizome, so a whole colony can descend from one root, and it depends obligately on mycorrhizal fungi to feed itself.

7690.w: The narwhal and the beluga are the only two living monodontids; a 2020 analysis puts their split about 5 million years ago, and they still meet, because a strange skull found in West Greenland around 1990 was confirmed by DNA in 2019 as a narwhal-beluga hybrid. The narwhal itself never leaves the Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland and Russia.
