7691.w: Orangutans are the only great apes outside Africa, the last of the subfamily Ponginae, which parted from the African hominids between 19.3 and 15.7 million years ago. In the Pleistocene they ranged across Southeast Asia and southern China; they are now down to Borneo and Sumatra, in three species, the third recognised only in 2017.

7692.w: The falcon family, around 65 species of falcons and caracaras, likely originated in South America during the Paleocene. From that start the peregrine ended up with the widest natural breeding distribution of any bird, ranging from Greenland to Fiji.

7693.w: Johann Friedrich Engelhardt found it in 1834 and Hermann von Meyer described it three years later, making it the fifth named dinosaur genus still considered valid — named before Owen coined the word dinosaur in 1842. Over 100 skeletons have since come out of the Late Triassic rock of Swabia, enough that Germans call it the Swabian lindworm.

7694.w: The giant river prawn lives its adult life entirely in fresh water, but its larvae still depend on brackish water to develop — the mark of a lineage that came into the rivers from the sea and never fully cut the tie. It is native across the Indo-Pacific from India to Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and grows past 30 cm.

7695.w: The European rabbit is the only rabbit ever domesticated, and every breed alive descends from it. It has been raised for food since at least the first century BC, out of a wild range covering only the Iberian Peninsula and southwestern France, and has since been put ashore on at least 800 islands and every continent except Antarctica.

7696.w: The Indian rhinoceros is an odd-toed ungulate: it carries its weight on the third toe and digests plant cellulose in its intestines rather than in a chambered stomach, and horses and tapirs are its only living relatives. It holds on in 12 protected areas of the Indo-Gangetic plain in northern India and southern Nepal, under 20,000 square kilometres, where about 4,075 animals were counted by March 2025.

7697.w: It has a cryptic sister species, Sphyrna gilberti, which differs from it in the number of vertebrae and little else. Females return to the coast where they were born to drop their own pups, which keeps the nursery populations apart generation after generation.

7698.w: The breed has been selectively bred since the end of the 19th century from the Wichianmat, a colourpointed landrace of Thailand, which was called Siam until 1939. Those cats appear far earlier in the Tamra Maew manuscripts of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, 1351 to 1767; the pale body with dark points is a temperature-sensitive form of albinism.

7699.w: Silk came before spiders. Attercopus, from rock about 390 million years old at Gilboa in New York, made silk from plates on an abdomen that was still segmented and carried a whip-scorpion-like tail, and it had no spinnerets at all. It belongs to the extinct order Uraraneida, thought to sit close to the origin of the spiders proper.

7700.w: Synanceia is a scorpionfish, from the venom-spined family; Linnaeus described its type species in 1766 from Ambon Island in Indonesia, and a 2018 revision moved the stonefishes out into a family of their own. The venom sits in glands at the base of needle-like dorsal spines that stand up when the fish is disturbed, and it is injected in proportion to the pressure put on them.

7701.w: A Mongolian field expedition turned up the first bones in the Gobi in 1948, in the Nemegt Formation, and Evgeny Maleev described them in 1954 as a giant turtle-like reptile, which is why the species is still called cheloniformis. It is now placed firmly among the theropods, as a maniraptoran, with hand claws over 50 cm long.

7702.w: Ceratopsians began small and bipedal in Asia: Psittacosaurus and the other basal forms all come from northern China or Mongolia. The huge horned quadrupeds came later, on Laramidia, the island continent that is now western North America, and Triceratops prorsus was the last ceratopsian of all, gone at the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction 66 million years ago.

7703.w: The shell was built belly-first. Odontochelys semitestacea, from 220-million-year-old marine rock in Guizhou, China, still had teeth in both jaws and a complete plastron underneath, but no carapace over its back at all, only broadened ribs like those of a turtle embryo before the plates ossify.

7704.w: Water lilies sit near the base of the flowering plants, and genetic work confirmed the Nymphaeaceae as basal angiosperms, which is why their large, many-parted flowers were once read as the original floral plan. Comparison with their sister family Cabombaceae says otherwise: the beetle-pollinated flowers of Nymphaea and Victoria, with the most parts, are the derived kind rather than the ancestral one.

7705.w: Woodlice are the isopods that finished the move onto land, one of very few crustacean lineages to manage it; molecular clocks put the crossing in the late Paleozoic, though the oldest known fossils are only about 100 million years old. They breathe through pleopods, the old swimming legs, and the female carries her eggs in a marsupium that supplies them with water, oxygen and nutrients.

7706.w: Apes are the Old World primates that lost the tail, and the loss traces to a mutation in the TBXT gene. The superfamily is native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia and has two branches: the gibbons, and the great apes proper, four genera holding three orangutan species, two gorillas, two chimpanzees and ourselves.

7707.w: The front pair of wings is hardened into cases, the elytra, folded over the flight wings and the body beneath — the character that separates a beetle from most other insects, and one that water beetles even use to trap a bubble of air for diving. About 400,000 species have been described, the largest order of anything: 40% of described arthropods and a quarter of all known animals.

7708.w: A crocodilian's closest living relatives are birds: the two are the only surviving archosaurs, and everything else on that branch is gone. The crocodilian total group appeared about 250 million years ago in the Early Triassic, and the order itself 83.5 million years ago.

7709.w: Theropods first appear 231.4 million years ago and supplied most of the large land carnivores from the Early Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous — and they are the one dinosaur branch that came through the extinction, because birds evolved from small feathered coelurosaurs among them. That leaves about 11,000 theropod species alive today.

7710.w: Rabbits, hares and pikas were classed as a suborder of rodents until 1912, and they are the rodents' nearest kin rather than their descendants. The teeth separate them: four upper incisors instead of two, the second pair a small peg tucked behind the front ones, plus more cheek teeth and no pads on the feet.

7711.w: About 17 species survive in three families — horses, rhinos and tapirs — and two things mark them off from the cloven-hoofed mammals. Weight passes through the third toe rather than being split evenly between two, and they break down plant cellulose in the intestine instead of in one or more stomach chambers.

7712.w: Isopods carry seven pairs of jointed legs on the thorax and five pairs of branching abdominal appendages used for breathing. The female does not release her eggs into the water at all: she broods them in a marsupium, a pouch under her own thorax, which is what let the group reach dry land as well as the seabed.

7713.w: Milky latex runs through the Euphorbioideae and Crotonoideae, poisonous in the first and harmless in the second; the rubber tree's latex is the world's main source of natural rubber, and spurge latex was once taken as a laxative. The flowers are unisexual and radially symmetrical, usually with both sexes on one plant.

7714.w: Antoine Risso described the family in 1826, and it holds many of the most venomous fish alive: the sting is delivered by sharp spines coated in venomous mucus. They are spread through tropical and temperate seas and are richest in the Indo-Pacific; a 2018 revision moved several groups, the stonefishes among them, into families of their own.

7715.w: Requiem sharks do not lay eggs. A blacktip reef shark's embryo lives on its yolk sac for the first months, and at about four months that sac converts into a placental connection anchored to the uterine wall; by five months the placenta is complete and the pup is 24 cm long.

7716.w: The American bullfrog is an anuran native to eastern North America, found in every US state east of the Mississippi and ranging from the Canadian Maritimes west to Idaho and Texas. It has since been carried to more than 40 countries, where it usually turns invasive. Its tadpole takes anywhere from a few months in the south of that range to three years in the cold north before metamorphosis finishes.

7717.w: Armadillos are xenarthrans, a mammal group that arose in South America in the Late Paleocene about 60 million years ago and diversified through the continent's long isolation, only spreading north from around 10 million years ago in the Great American Interchange. The name refers to extra vertebral joints found in no other mammal. The three-banded armadillo Tolypeutes tricinctus is confined to Brazil, and its genus is the only one whose armour closes into a sealed ball.

7718.w: The basking shark is the only living member of Cetorhinidae, a lamniform in the same order as the great white, the mako and the thresher. Filter feeding arrived separately in three unrelated shark lineages, and by different means: the whale shark and the megamouth can suck or pump water across their gills, while the basking shark strains only what its own swimming pushes through — calculated at up to 450 tonnes of water an hour for a five-metre animal.

7719.w: In 2007 a nine-year-old female blacktip at the Virginia Aquarium became pregnant having never been housed with a male, and genetic analysis confirmed automictic parthenogenesis: an ovum merged with a polar body to make a zygote, with no fertilisation at all. Blacktips normally breed every other year and carry four to seven pups for ten to twelve months, so the case suggested asexual reproduction runs wider among sharks than had been supposed.

7720.w: Butterflies came out of the moths: they are a single clade nested inside Lepidoptera, which is why the moths left over do not form a natural group at all. From a Late Cretaceous origin, probably North American, the line fanned into roughly 18,500 species, most of that diversification falling in the Cenozoic. The oldest known fossil butterfly, Protocoeliades kristenseni, comes from Paleocene Denmark about 55 million years ago.

7721.w: The small-spotted catshark is one of the oviparous sharks: the female anchors a horny capsule roughly 4 cm by 2 cm, trailing long tendrils, to the seabed, and the embryo develops inside it for five to eleven months depending on how warm the sea is. The pup that leaves the case is 9 to 10 cm long.

7722.w: Chitons are Polyplacophora, about 940 living species carrying eight separate shell valves rather than one shell, with a fossil record reaching back to the Cambrian. Some of them have turned the light-sensing aesthetes under the shell surface into true eyes, each with a lens of aragonite - the shell mineral itself - grown as large, crystallographically aligned grains that scatter little light and form a clear image. The eyes are paid for out of the armour: as they grow larger and more complex the shell's mechanical performance drops, and they show up only in fossils of the last 10 million years or so, the most recent eyes known to have evolved in a mollusc.

7723.w: Hadrosaurids are descendants of the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous iguanodontians and keep much the same body plan, the differences lying in their stacked dental batteries and, among lambeosaurines, the hollow crest. Barnum Brown found the first Corythosaurus in 1911 on the Red Deer River in Alberta, in Belly River Group rock laid down 77 to 75.7 million years ago. The crest's looping internal passages are modelled as producing loud, low calls, closer to a trombone than a shout.

7724.w: Atropa belladonna and Datura sit in different tribes of the nightshade family and arrived at the same chemistry: atropine, hyoscyamine and scopolamine. Datura's centre of origin is Mexico, while belladonna is a plant of Europe and western Asia, growing from England east to Ukraine and the Iranian province of Gilan. Every part of it is loaded — 1.3% tropane alkaloid in the root, 1.2% in the leaf, 0.7% in the ripe berry, which is the part that tastes sweet.

7725.w: Dinosaurs diverged from their archosaur relatives in the Middle to Late Triassic, roughly 20 million years after the end-Permian extinction, and the first of them were small bipedal predators on the pattern of Eoraptor. The oldest substantial dinosaur fossils come from Carnian rock in South America: the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina at 231 to 230 million years, and the Santa Maria Formation of Brazil dated radiometrically to 233.23 million.

7726.w: Spotted eagle rays belong to the Myliobatidae along with the manta ray, both of them open-water swimmers rather than bottom-dwellers. What was once treated as one ocean-spanning species has been split three ways: Aetobatus narinari is now restricted to the Atlantic, with A. ocellatus in the Indo-Pacific and A. laticeps in the eastern Pacific. Females carry their young about a year and bear at most four pups, 17 to 35 cm across.

7727.w: Euoplocephalus is an earlier member of Ankylosaurini, the same tribe of armoured dinosaurs as Ankylosaurus, and differs from it in skull ornament and nostril structure. Lawrence Lambe found the first piece — part of a cranium and five scutes — on 18 August 1897 beside the Red Deer River in Alberta, in beds 76.4 to 75.6 million years old. Only the far half of its tail was stiffened by bundles of ossified tendons, so the club swung on a flexible shaft with force enough to break bone.

7728.w: Fish are chordates that turned the notochord, dorsal nerve cord and pharyngeal slits into a body built around a backbone. The first vertebrates appear in the Cambrian about 518 million years ago — Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, jawless, with rudimentary vertebrae and a defined head and tail — and jawed vertebrates followed in the Late Ordovician around 445 million years ago. Ray-finned fish alone account for over 32,000 living species, roughly half of all described vertebrates.

7729.w: Squid and cuttlefish are both Decapodiformes, the ten-limbed branch of cephalopods that made tentacles of arm pair IV while the octopus line lost arm pair II instead; the giant squid is an oegopsid within that branch. Its eyes reach at least 27 cm across with a 9 cm pupil, the largest of any living animal except perhaps the colossal squid — an investment that only repays in deep water, where a big eye gathers what little light, bioluminescence included, is there to be had.

7730.w: Most domestic goose breeds come down from the greylag, Anser anser, domesticated at least as early as 1360 BCE, while the Chinese goose descends separately from the swan goose of eastern Asia. The oldest evidence of goose domestication is about 7,000 years old, from the Hemudu culture on the lower Yangtze, and geese were being kept in Egypt more than 4,000 years ago.

7731.w: Where heterodontosaurids sit among the ornithischians is still unsettled, but one standing proposal ties them to the marginocephalians - Heterodontosauriformes is the name for the clade of heterodontosaurids plus pachycephalosaurs and ceratopsians - and a 2020 analysis went further, recovering the traditional heterodontosaurs as paraphyletic within Pachycephalosauria itself. They were fox-sized animals under 2 m long including the tail, about eight named genera across four continents, and southern Africa holds much the most diverse fauna of them; the Heterodontosaurus holotype came out of the Cape Province on the British-South African expedition of 1961-62. Its jaw carries three kinds of tooth at once - small incisor-like teeth, long canine-like tusks, and eleven tall chisel-shaped cheek teeth - which is what the name records.

7732.w: Marsupials reached Australia from South America across the Antarctic land bridge in the Early Eocene, around 50 million years ago, in what looks like one dispersal of a single species. With terrestrial placentals gone from the continent early in the Cenozoic they radiated into roles filled elsewhere by placentals, large grazers included, and close to 70% of the 334 living marsupial species are Australian. The kangaroos are macropods that expanded from the Late Miocene on, as forest gave way to grassland.

7733.w: 'Limpet' names a shape rather than a lineage: the same low cone has been arrived at independently by patellogastropods, by vetigastropods such as the keyhole limpets, by neritimorphs and by several heterobranch groups. True limpets wander the rock at high tide and follow their own mucus trail back to a home scar worn into the stone. Their iron-mineralised teeth test at 3.0 to 6.5 GPa in tension, above spider silk.

7734.w: Majungasaurus is an abelisaurid, the Gondwanan theropod family that also produced Carnotaurus; the family splits into western and eastern Gondwanan branches, and the most recent analyses put Majungasaurus with the Indian forms rather than the South American ones. It comes from the Maevarano Formation of Mahajanga Province in northwestern Madagascar, in the Maastrichtian, 70 to 66 million years ago. Bones bearing tooth marks of the same size and spacing as its own teeth make it the one non-avian dinosaur with direct evidence of cannibalism.

7735.w: Moulting is most of what a mayfly does: the nymph works through anywhere between ten and fifty post-embryonic moults underwater, more numerous than in most other insect orders, over months or in some species years. Then it does the thing no other insect does - it moults once more after its wings already work, the winged subimago flying for a day or two, or in some species only a few minutes, before shedding again into the imago. Little is left of the animal afterwards: the adult females of Dolania americana live less than five minutes.

7736.w: Morning glories are Ipomoea, a genus of over 600 species in the Convolvulaceae, and the sweet potato, Ipomoea batatas, is one of them — a morning glory grown for its root rather than its flower. The Mexican morning glory, Ipomoea tricolor, and its relatives carry lysergamides in their seeds, which Aztec and Zapotec specialists used in divination.

7737.w: The nautilus is the only living cephalopod that still carries its shell on the outside; squid, cuttlefish and octopus all internalised or lost theirs after the lineages parted, and the nautilus has changed remarkably little since. Its fossil record runs from about 230 million years ago in the Triassic, and unlike the ammonites it came through the end-Cretaceous extinction. A hatchling starts with roughly four gas-filled chambers and an adult has thirty or more, the siphuncle drawing salt out of them to set buoyancy.

7738.w: The orca is the largest member of Delphinidae, the oceanic dolphins. Its ecotypes have diverged far enough that a 2024 study argued the eastern North Pacific resident and transient forms should be raised to separate species, Orcinus ater and Orcinus rectipinnus; the Society for Marine Mammalogy has so far recognised them provisionally as subspecies instead, and the species as a whole remains listed as data deficient.

7739.w: The common periwinkle is a littorinid sea snail of the higher and middle intertidal on rocky shores, native to the northeastern Atlantic — Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia. It reached North America around the middle of the 19th century, probably carried in rock ballast, and was first recorded in the Gulf of St Lawrence in 1840. A female packs 10,000 to 100,000 eggs into one horny capsule, and the animals live five to ten years, occasionally twenty.

7740.w: The platypus is a monotreme, one of the egg-laying mammals, endemic to eastern Australia including Tasmania, and it split from the echidnas somewhere between 19 and 48 million years ago. The female lays two leathery eggs about 17 mm long, after roughly 28 days of internal development and ten more days of incubation outside. Its bill carries about 40,000 electroreceptors in rows, reading the currents thrown off by a prey animal's muscles while eyes, ears and nose are all shut underwater.

7741.w: Henri Filhol named Proailurus in 1879 from fossils at the Saint-Gerand site in France, and it is generally taken as the first true cat and the ancestor of the whole family, giving rise to Pseudaelurus, which lived 20 to 10 million years ago and produced the major felid lineages. Proailurus itself ranged across Europe and Asia between about 30.8 and 25 million years ago; the type species weighed around 9 kg, was proportioned like a modern viverrid, and was at least partly a tree-climber.

7742.w: Rafflesia is a flowering plant that has thrown away nearly everything a plant has — no stems, leaves or roots, only an absorptive organ spread through a Tetrastigma vine — and genetic work places it inside the Euphorbiaceae. Joseph Arnold found Rafflesia arnoldii at Bengkulu on Sumatra in 1818, and its blooms pass 100 cm across and 10 kg. The genus has taken up a large number of genes horizontally from its hosts, and one Philippine species appears to have lost its chloroplast genome outright.

7743.w: Rhododendron and blueberry are both Ericaceae, plants of acid ground with a pH of roughly 4.5 to 5.5, feeding through fungal partners in soil high in organic matter. The genus runs to about 1,024 woody species, at their densest in the Sino-Himalayan region, southwest China and northern Burma. Some load grayanotoxin into pollen and nectar, and Xenophon recorded Greek soldiers behaving oddly after eating the honey in 401 BCE.

7744.w: Scorpions are among the oldest known arachnids: the earliest found so far is Dolichophonus loudonensis, from the Silurian of what is now Scotland, about 430 million years ago. Over 2,500 species survive in 22 families, and unlike the great majority of arachnids, which lay eggs, scorpions appear to be universally viviparous, the young riding on the mother's back until their exoskeletons harden. All of them glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.

7745.w: Every domestic silk moth descends from Bombyx mandarina, a wild moth ranging from inland China through Korea to Japan, whose males still fly perfectly well; the domestic stock traces to the inland Chinese population, and the earliest archaeological evidence for its keeping belongs to the Yangshao culture of northern China more than 5,000 years ago. Breeding since has cost Bombyx mori its colouring and its flight, and it does not exist in the wild; one cocoon unwinds into 300 to 900 m of raw silk, and a kilogram takes 4,000 to 7,000 of them.

7746.w: Spiny lobsters are Achelata, a decapod group whose nearest relatives are the slipper lobsters rather than the clawed true lobsters: they never grew pincers on the first four pairs of walking legs, carrying long spiny antennae instead. In place of a claw they have a sound, made by dragging a soft plectrum at the antenna base across a file — a sticking and slipping like rubber on a hard surface, which keeps working even when a fresh moult has left the shell soft. They sometimes cross the sea floor in single files more than 50 animals long.

7747.w: Strychnos nux-vomica is a deciduous flowering tree of the family Loganiaceae, native to India and southeast Asia. Its seeds run to about 1.5% strychnine and its dried blossoms about 1.0%, and the alkaloid is still used in baits to kill feral mammals. Most accidental human poisonings come not from eating it but from breathing the powder or taking it up through the skin.

7748.w: Threshers are Alopiidae, lamniforms sitting alongside the Lamnidae of the great white and the mako, and two of the three species share that family's rare trick of regional endothermy — a counter-current heat exchanger warming a strip of red muscle along each flank. The lineage's own specialisation is the upper tail lobe, grown as long as the whole rest of the body; a 2013 study confirmed threshers swat schooling fish with it, stunning them before turning to feed. The common thresher reaches 6.1 m and over 500 kg.

7749.w: Troodontids and dromaeosaurs such as Velociraptor are the two branches of Paraves closest to birds, similar enough that derived troodontids convergently evolved the dromaeosaur's enlarged second toe claw. The genus rests on a single tooth found in October 1855 in the Judith River Formation of Montana and described by Joseph Leidy in 1856; it was taken for a lizard's until 1877. Eggshell work published in 2023 found that several females laid into one nest, with reptile-like slow calcification and two working ovaries limiting how many eggs each could produce.

7750.w: Tyrannosaurs started out as small theropods, and only some of them grew large in the Early Cretaceous: Yutyrannus, a basal tyrannosauroid from the 125-million-year-old Yixian Formation of Liaoning, weighed about 1,414 kg and carried filamentous feathers up to 20 cm long. Barnum Brown found the first partial Tyrannosaurus in eastern Wyoming in 1900 and a better skeleton in Montana's Hell Creek Formation in 1902, which Osborn named in 1905. The specimen 'Sue' is 12.3 to 12.8 m long at an estimated 8.4 to 9.2 tonnes.

7751.w: Welwitschia is a gnetophyte and the only living genus of both its family and its order, a relict with nothing else beside it. It grows in the Namib of Namibia and Angola, where the coast gets almost no rain and the interior under 100 mm a year, so the plants gather along ephemeral water courses and draw on fog as well as groundwater. It never makes a third leaf: the two it starts with keep growing from the crown, up to 4 m long, on plants that may be 2,000 years old.

7752.w: Several conifer lineages independently traded the woody cone for something fleshy a bird will swallow, and each built it from different parts: a juniper's galbulus is cone scales fused together, while the yew's cone is reduced to a single seed half-wrapped in a soft red aril 8 to 15 mm across. Thrushes and waxwings pass the hard seed undamaged in their droppings. The aril is the only part of a yew free of the alkaloid taxine, and the seed inside it is the dangerous piece.

7753.w: Grey geese and swans sit together in Anserinae, the true goose and swan subfamily of the duck family Anatidae. Anser, the grey geese, has split into 11 living species spread right across the Holarctic, with at least one of them breeding in open wet country somewhere in the subarctic and cool temperate north. The greylag is the type species of the genus, the one Linnaeus described in 1758 as Anas anser, and at up to about 4 kg it is among the largest.

7754.w: Bombyx mandarina is the wild moth from which every domesticated silkworm descends, ranging from inland China through Korea to Japan. Those populations have already drifted apart in the karyotype - Chinese specimens carry 56 chromosomes and Japanese ones 54 - and the domestic stock's affinities lie with the inland Chinese birds of the species, taken from wild stock as far back as 5,000 years ago. Unlike its descendant it is a fairly ordinary moth, the males with well-developed wings that still work.

7755.w: Pangaea assembled around 335 million years ago and began breaking up by about 180. Africa is the piece that stayed: it lay near the middle of the supercontinent and has moved least since, which is why every other southern continent is described as having rifted away from it.

7756.w: A rift opened between them around 190 million years ago at Falkland latitudes, and once a spreading ridge took over about 130 to 135 million years ago the two halves were being actively pushed apart. The South Atlantic was fully open by roughly 83 million years ago; the matching coastlines are what first suggested the whole idea.

7757.w: Laurasia was Pangaea's northern half from about 335 to 175 million years ago, and separated from Gondwana between roughly 215 and 175 million years ago. Asia is the eastern bulk of it, assembled by collision as block after block was welded on.

7758.w: The Uralian orogeny ran through the late Carboniferous into the early Triassic, roughly 300 to 250 million years ago, as Laurasia's eastern edge collided with Kazakhstania and the island arcs between them. That suture is the line Europe is conventionally divided from Asia along — the two are one landmass, and the Urals are the seam.

7759.w: Laurasia came apart when the North Atlantic opened about 56 million years ago. The same event made Greenland a plate in its own right, separated from North America by the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay rift.

7760.w: An annelid is an invertebrate built as a repeating series: a chain of segments called metameres, ringed externally by annuli and partitioned internally by septa, most carrying their own pair of coelomic cavities and their own set of organs. Chaetae of beta-chitin push through the skin for grip. Over 22,000 species live now, and the oldest confident fossil, Phragmochaeta from Sirius Passet, is about 518 million years old.

7761.w: Development slowed or stopped short while sexual maturity arrives on time, so an animal breeds still wearing its larval body. It is not progenesis, where maturity is instead brought forward. Cold water and altitude select for it because metamorphosis is expensive, and a salamander short of iodine cannot complete it at all.

7762.w: A skeleton worn on the outside: chitin laid down in layers as a cuticle, stiffened where support is needed and left flexible at the joints. It cannot grow with its owner, so anything wearing one has to shed it and expand before the new one hardens.

7763.w: Not a group so much as everything left over: every animal that never evolved a vertebral column, which is about 95% of described animal species. The name records what they lack rather than anything they share, which is why it holds sponges and squid and beetles at once.

7764.w: The branch of the amniotes that leads to reptiles and birds rather than to mammals — Huxley's 1864 division, with Synapsida on the other side. They excrete nitrogen as uric acid, which needs almost no water and goes out with the faeces, and their skin carries no glands of the kind mammals inherited from amphibians. That combination is what let the group hold arid ground.

7765.w: Lepidoptera means scale-wing, from lepis and pteron, and the scales are the order: blade-like lamellae each on a stalk, their surface structured finely enough to make colour from interference as well as pigment. About 180,000 species have been described, 8.6% of all known living things, and all but roughly 18,000 of them are moths.

7766.w: Feathers came before birds and before flight. The genes for them sit at the base of the archosaurs, around 250 million years ago, and branched feathers with barbs and barbules are preserved on theropods like Sinosauropteryx and on Anchiornis, which is older than Archaeopteryx. They are built from beta-keratin, hydrogen-bonded into pleated sheets and tougher than the alpha-keratin of hair and horn. The first ones could not have generated lift, so warmth, waterproofing and display came first.

7767.w: Theropoda means beast-foot, from therion and pous. The group is diagnosed on the skeleton rather than the diet: hollow bones, three weight-bearing toes with claws, digit V lost early and digit I lifted clear of the ground, a ball-and-socket joint at the head of the neck, five or more sacral vertebrae, and a furcula. They appear about 231.4 million years ago and have not stopped — the 11,000-odd living birds are theropods, the smallest of them a bee hummingbird at 1.9 grams.

7768.w: The arthropods that kept the two-branched limb: a crustacean's appendages are biramous, forking into two parts, and the second pair of antennae usually shows it plainly. What really unites a group this varied is the larva — the nauplius, with three pairs of appendages all on the head and a single eye. About 67,000 species are described, from Stygotantulus at 0.1 mm to a Japanese spider crab spanning 3.8 metres.

7769.w: A gymnosperm that carries its seeds naked on the scales of a cone rather than inside a fruit. Most bear needle leaves, from 2 mm on the scale-leaved species to 600 mm on some pines, though cypresses flatten theirs to triangular scales instead. Pine cones open their scales to let winged seeds blow out; fir and cedar cones fall apart to release them. Just over 600 species survive, from a lineage in the fossil record for more than 300 million years.

7770.w: Delphinium — about 300 species in the buttercup family, named for a flower whose five petal-like sepals fuse into a hollow pocket ending in a spur, which the Greeks thought looked like a dolphin. Every part of the plant carries diterpenoid alkaloids, methyllycaconitine chief among them, which block neuromuscular transmission and poison the heart; a fatal dose can act within hours. Aconitum turns out to sit inside this genus rather than beside it.

7771.w: An antler is bone, and unlike a horn it is not sheathed in keratin — it is bone, cartilage, fibrous tissue, skin, nerve and blood vessel, grown fresh each year from a pedicle on the skull. It extends at the tip as cartilage that then turns to bone, fed the whole time by velvet, a highly vascular skin. It grows faster than any other mammal bone. When it is finished the velvet is shed, the bone dies, and osteoclasts eat through the base until the whole thing drops.

7772.w: Eight legs on a cephalothorax, no antennae and no wings, the body in two parts — prosoma and opisthosoma — with chelicerae for feeding and pedipalps repurposed for feeding, walking or mating. Most are carnivores that cannot chew: they flood prey with enzymes and drink the pre-digested remains. Over 110,000 species are named, 51,000 of them spiders, and the true total may pass a million.

7773.w: Not taming, which is one animal learning to tolerate you, but a multi-generational mutualism: the domesticator builds an environment where it manages another species' survival and breeding, and that species becomes dependent on the arrangement. It needed people to stay put. After the Last Glacial Maximum a warmer Holocene and growing populations made it possible from about 11,700 years ago — cereals in the Near East 13,000 to 11,000 years ago, livestock in the Fertile Crescent 11,000 to 10,000. Early farmers were not trying to make new species; they became entangled with them.

7774.w: Fenton's reaction: iron(II) hands one electron to hydrogen peroxide and the peroxide comes apart into hydroxide and a hydroxyl radical — Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → Fe³⁺ + OH⁻ + •OH. Henry Fenton published it in 1894, from work on oxidising tartaric acid. The same chemistry runs inside cells wherever loose iron and peroxide meet.

7775.w: Radiolysis. A gamma photon ionises water and the wreckage includes hydroxyl radicals, hydrated electrons, hydrogen atoms and peroxide. Because a cell is mostly water, this indirect route — radicals diffusing far enough to reach DNA — is the main damage mechanism for photons in radiation therapy, rather than a photon striking the DNA itself.

7776.w: Homolysis: light of the right energy splits a shared pair down the middle instead of handing both electrons to one side, and each fragment leaves with one unpaired electron. It costs real energy — 435 kJ/mol to break H–H that way, 243 kJ/mol for Cl–Cl — which is why photodissociation, not gentle warmth, is a standard route to a radical.

7777.w: The hydroxyl radical attacks guanine and leaves 8-oxoguanine, one of the commonest oxidative DNA lesions there is. The altered base pairs with adenine instead of cytosine, so the next round of copying writes G-to-T and C-to-A substitutions — a mutation rate above background, which is exactly what defines a mutagen. The glycosylase OGG1 cuts most of them back out first.

7778.w: A mutagen turns carcinogenic when the damage lands in the genes that govern division — a proto-oncogene pushed into an oncogene, or a tumour suppressor switched off. The sets overlap without coinciding: around 90% of known carcinogens registered as mutagenic in the early Ames screens, yet sodium azide is mutagenic and has never been shown to cause cancer, and non-genotoxic carcinogens such as some hormones promote growth without binding DNA at all.

7779.w: Muller showed in 1927 that X-rays raise the mutation rate in fruit flies and leave visible changes to the chromosomes themselves; the 1946 Nobel followed. Agents that break chromosomes outright are called clastogens, and a break put back wrong returns as a deletion, an inversion or a translocation rather than a single swapped base.

7780.w: Gastrulation ends with three germ layers and no organs. Hox genes then fix which position along the head-to-tail axis is which, and the layers build to match: ectoderm into epidermis and neurons, mesoderm into heart, kidney and red cells, endoderm into lung, thyroid, pancreas and gut. In humans that work runs from about week three to week eight after fertilisation.

7781.w: Two conditions make an agent a teratogen, and they are Wilson's fourth and second principles: it has to get across the placenta, and it has to arrive while the part it will damage is being built. Thalidomide is the whole argument in one drug — day 20 of gestation took the brain, day 21 the eyes, day 22 the ears and face, day 24 the arms, and after day 42 the same dose did nothing to the fetus.

7782.w: A mutagen that reaches an embryo while the organs are forming can act as a teratogen too, damaging the cells doing the building. The categories overlap and are not the same: thalidomide alters no base at all — it works by making the cereblon ubiquitin ligase destroy developmental transcription factors — and what it caused was never inherited, which is what non-heritable means in the definition.

7783.w: Wilson's fifth principle lists the four ways development can deviate: death, malformation, growth retardation, functional defect. Which one, and where, is set by the week — rubella between weeks five and ten damages eyes and ears, a cleft palate is decided between weeks four and seven. About 3% of US newborns have a birth defect, and around 65% of those have no cause anyone can name.

7784.w: CYP2E1 in the liver oxidises vinyl chloride into chloroethylene oxide, an alkylating epoxide that binds DNA and disturbs proto-oncogene and tumour-suppressor expression — which is why the tumour turns up in the liver and not the lung that breathed the gas in. Dr John Creech found three cases of hepatic angiosarcoma among workers at B.F. Goodrich's Louisville PVC plant and reported them to NIOSH on 22 January 1974.

7785.w: A flame short of oxygen builds rings instead of burning them. In the hydrogen-abstraction/acetylene-addition cycle an aromatic loses a hydrogen, the radical left behind adds a molecule of acetylene, and the sequence repeats until a new ring closes onto the old one. HACA is the route that assembles naphthalene both in flames and in the envelopes of carbon-rich stars.

7786.w: Naphthalene is the most abundant single component of coal tar — typical tar is about 10% naphthalene by weight — and it melts at 80 °C, so it drops out of the distilled middle oil as pale crystals as that oil cools. Alexander Garden reported crystallising a silvery, camphor-like solid from coal-tar distillate in 1819; John Kidd named it in 1821 after the naphtha it came out of.

7787.w: Coal tar is only about 1.5% anthracene, and it comes over late, in the heavy cut still called anthracene oil. Jean-Baptiste Dumas and Auguste Laurent crystallised it from that fraction in 1832; Laurent first took it for an isomer of naphthalene and called it paranaphthalene before renaming it from anthrax, the Greek for coal. Industry kept distilling for it because oxidising anthracene gives anthraquinone, and anthraquinone gives the red dye alizarin.

7788.w: The same acetylene-addition cycle that closed naphthalene's second ring can close a third onto it, and the third ring goes on at an angle far more often than in line. The proof is in the tar: phenanthrene, the bent isomer, makes up around 4–6% of coke-oven coal tar, where anthracene, the straight one with the identical formula, manages about 1.5%. Fittig with Ostermayer, and Graebe independently, both pulled it out of coal tar in 1872.

7789.w: A fourth ring fused onto the side of anthracene's three, which is exactly what the name records. Flames grow PAHs by adding whole rings as well as by adding acetylene: a phenyl radical adds to an aromatic and then cyclises onto it, the phenyl-addition/dehydrocyclization route, which runs efficiently at high temperatures and reaches structures that acetylene addition alone finds hard to build. The fusion leaves a bay region — the crowded inner pocket that makes four-ring PAHs easy prey for the enzymes that turn them into mutagens.

7790.w: One more benzo ring fused on and the count reaches five: dibenz[a,h]anthracene, C22H14, first synthesised in 1918. It is barely volatile and barely soluble, so it travels stuck to particles in polluted air, soil and sediment, and it is genotoxic in both bacterial and mammalian cells — it slides between the base pairs of DNA and causes mutations there.

7791.w: Fat dripping onto hot coals does not burn cleanly; benzo[a]pyrene is what incomplete combustion of organic matter yields between 300 and 600 °C, and the smoke carries it back up onto the meat. A 2001 National Cancer Institute study found levels far higher in food cooked well-done on a barbecue; cooked meat products have been measured at up to 4 ng/g, fried chicken at 5.5 ng/g and overcooked charcoal-barbecued beef at 62.6 ng/g.

7792.w: A soot particle begins when two PAH molecules collide and stay together. Dimers held by nothing but attraction come apart again; when the pair goes on to form a covalent bond it survives, and putting that step into a flame simulation raises the predicted soot concentration by four orders of magnitude, matching what laser-induced incandescence measures. Trimers account for under 3% of the nuclei formed, so a bonded pair is essentially the whole of nucleation.

7793.w: The definition the IPCC adopted turns on cooling: soot is what forms during the "quenching of gases at the outer edge of flames" of organic vapours — mostly carbon, with a little oxygen and hydrogen, in an imperfect graphitic structure. What settles on a flue wall is that: clumps of 6 to 30 nm particles, mixed with mineral matter and sometimes coated in sulfuric acid. Enough of it collecting in a chimney is what makes a chimney fire possible.

7794.w: The burning cone reaches 700–950 °C during a puff, but hardly any of the smoke is made there. Just behind the fire sits an oxygen-starved distillation zone where the temperature falls from about 600 °C to 200 °C, and it is below roughly 350 °C, in that zone, that the majority of the toxicants are generated — which is the point heated tobacco products were designed around.

7795.w: In 1775 Percivall Pott traced the scrotal cancer common among London's chimney sweeps to soot lodging in the skin — the first occupational cancer anyone described, and the first time a chemical mixture was tied to cancer at all. The sweeps had been in contact with soot since early childhood; one review puts the median age at first symptoms at 37.7 years, with cases in boys as young as 8. In 1922 R. D. Passey raised malignant skin tumours in mice using an extract of soot, which showed the cause was carried in the soot itself.

7796.w: Benzo[a]pyrene is a procarcinogen: it does nothing until the body's own cytochrome P450 1A1 and epoxide hydrolase convert it, in three steps, into the diol epoxide BPDE. That electrophile is attacked by guanine, leaving a bulky adduct that distorts the double helix. Nucleotide excision repair clears most of them; the ones it misses produce G-to-T transversions, clustered in hotspots of the tumour-suppressor gene p53.

7797.w: Chlorine substitutes into an alkane under ultraviolet light, or adds straight across the double bond of an alkene to give a di- or tetrachloro compound. Nothing in the chemistry stops at one chlorine, so controlling how far the reaction goes is the hard part. The largest single product is vinyl chloride — 13 million tonnes a year by 1985, nearly all of it polymerised into PVC.

7798.w: Acetic acid dehydrated thermally gives ketene, and ketene attacks an aldehyde to close a four-membered beta-lactone — with formaldehyde, over an aluminium or zinc chloride catalyst, that lactone is beta-propiolactone. Ketene only does this under Lewis acid catalysis or against an electron-poor carbonyl, which formaldehyde is.

7799.w: Ammonia opens the strained oxygen ring of ethylene oxide to give aminoethanol, and the aminoethanol is then closed back up around nitrogen — dehydrated over an oxide catalyst in the Nippon Shokubai process, or converted to a sulfate ester and eliminated in the older Wenker synthesis. Older routes aminated 1,2-dichloroethane or cyclised 2-chloroethylamine instead.

7800.w: Proline's nitrogen sits inside its ring, which makes it a secondary amine, and nitrous acid from acidified nitrite nitrosates secondary amines directly. Ohshima and Bartsch turned that into a measurement in 1981: 300 mg of nitrate and 500 mg of proline by mouth, then N-nitrosoproline counted in 24 hours of urine, to see how much nitrosation is going on inside a living stomach.

7801.w: Nitrosating nicotine and its relative nornicotine during tobacco curing produces the tobacco-specific nitrosamines NNN and NNK. IARC evaluated the pair in 2009 and placed both in Group 1, carcinogenic to humans. American dip snuff carries markedly more of them than Swedish snus.

7802.w: Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus are ordinary weedy moulds, and on maize held warm and damp they make aflatoxin B1 as they grow. A contaminated maize harvest in Kenya in 2004 caused an acute outbreak with 125 confirmed deaths. FDA action levels for aflatoxin in food and feed run from 20 to 300 ppb depending on what it is for.

7803.w: Phthalic anhydride condenses with L-glutamine, with triethylamine and acetic anhydride, at around 110 °C; the modern version of the route gives 85–93% yield at 99% purity. The molecule is a single ring system joined to a glutarimide, and that glutarimide end is the part that binds cereblon.

7804.w: Mercury becomes methylmercury only when a microbe methylates it, and three groups do: sulfate-reducing bacteria, iron-reducing bacteria and methanogens, all working where oxygen has run out. From there it climbs — in top aquatic predators the concentration can reach a million times the level in the surrounding water.

7805.w: Sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic sediment are the main methylators of mercury in most waters, which is what turned an industrial discharge into a poisoning. Chisso's factory at Minamata used a mercury catalyst to make acetaldehyde — 210 tonnes in 1932, 45,245 at the 1960 peak — and released waste into the bay from 1951 to 1968. Sediment at the mouth of the wastewater canal measured 2 kg of mercury per tonne.

7806.w: Partial oxidation of toluene with oxygen, over cobalt or manganese naphthenate catalysts, turns the methyl group into a carboxylic acid. Abundant feedstock, high yield, and it is how nearly all of it is made now. The older route was dry distillation of gum benzoin, first described in 1556.

7807.w: The precursor is 4-methoxyphenol, which is hydroquinone with one of its two hydroxyls methylated. Alkylating it with isobutylene — the branched four-carbon alkene from the same refinery cut that yields butane — hangs a tert-butyl group on the ring. It lands in two positions, and BHA is sold as the mixture of 2-tert-butyl and 3-tert-butyl-4-hydroxyanisole.

7808.w: BHT is a cresol wearing two tert-butyl groups. p-Cresol — toluene with a hydroxyl on the far corner of the ring — is alkylated with isobutylene over sulfuric acid, and the two bulky groups settle either side of that hydroxyl. Isobutylene is the branched four-carbon alkene from the same refinery cut that yields butane.

7809.w: A fresh cheese made from cream holds more water than its curd can keep, and whey weeps out on the shelf. Carob galactomannan binds that loose water at a fraction of a percent, which is why industrial cream cheese lists carob bean gum.

7810.w: The emulsifier crowds milk protein off the fat globules, so fat part-coalesces into a network as the mix freezes. That network is what lets soft serve stand up dry at −4 °C holding 33 to 45% air, where ice cream needs −15 °C to keep shape.

7811.w: Gluten's cross-linked network is what traps the carbon dioxide yeast makes; without it a batter cannot hold a bubble. Xanthan gum, used at 0.5% or less, supplies the stickiness gluten would have given, so the loaf rises and sets.

7812.w: Kappa carrageenan forms strong rigid gels with potassium ions and binds hard to dairy protein, so it sets milk rather than merely thickening it. Boiling the whole red weed in milk is the old version; E407 is that extract, purified.

7813.w: About 0.5 g of alginate per 100 g of juice, dripped into a bath of 0.5 g calcium chloride per 100 g of water. Calcium cross-links the alginate on contact, so a skin sets in seconds while the middle is still juice.

7814.w: Milled oat solids settle out of water. Gellan sets a network too weak to taste but strong enough to hold plant particles suspended for the life of the carton, at about half the concentration agar would need to gel.

7815.w: The fluid runs about 90% water, 9.5% sand and 0.5% chemicals, and thin water drops its sand at the wellbore. Guar gel, cross-linked by borate above pH 9, carries grains into the fracture; a breaker or pH 3–4 thins it for flowback.

7816.w: Calcium is what holds the casein network together, and heating that network gives strings and free oil. Sodium citrate takes the calcium, so the freed protein emulsifies the fat into a sauce — Gerber and Stettler's 1911 Swiss trick.

7817.w: Casein precipitates at pH 4.6 and coffee is acid enough to take it there — the white flecks called feathering. Dipotassium phosphate buffers the creamer, holding the mix off that point so the protein stays dissolved in the cup.

7818.w: Curcumin is turmeric's yellow, sold on its own as E100, and it is what makes American mustard that colour rather than the dull tan of ground seed and vinegar. It is poorly soluble in water, so it is carried as a suspension rather than dissolved.

7819.w: Betanin is beetroot red, E162. Light, heat and oxygen all break it down, which confines it to chilled or short-lived foods like yoghurt, and at yoghurt's pH of 4 to 5 it reads bright bluish-red. As a food additive it raises no safety concern.

7820.w: The brown of a cola is caramel colour. Soft drinks take Class IV, E150d, sugar cooked with both ammonia and sulfite, which gives a dark colour and almost no flavour of its own; JECFA sets its acceptable intake at 200 mg per kg of body weight a day.

7821.w: Gelatin sets clear, so a red jelly is a coloured one. Ponceau 4R, E124, is a synthetic azo red permitted across Europe, Asia and Australia at a European acceptable intake of 0.7 mg per kg of body weight; the US FDA has never approved it.

7822.w: Sorbate is fungistatic, not lethal: surviving yeast cannot multiply, so the sugar stays in the bottle. Up to 200 mg a litre is allowed in wine above 5 g/L of residual sugar, always alongside sulfur dioxide — lactobacilli left to eat sorbate turn it geranium.

7823.w: Benzoate only preserves acid drinks. Benzoic acid's pKa is 4.2 and only the undissociated molecule crosses into a microbe; once inside, an internal pH of 5 or lower cuts its fermentation of glucose by 95%. Food use runs 0.05 to 0.1%.

7824.w: Six percent benzoic acid with three percent salicylic acid makes one fungistatic and keratolytic ointment: the second sheds the infected outer skin, the first holds back the dermatophyte in it. It is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.

7825.w: Sulfite blocks the browning reactions that darken fruit as it dries. The EU allows dried apricots up to 2,000 mg of sulfur dioxide per kg and sulphured fruit typically carries 200 to 2,000, so the 10 mg/kg declaration threshold is always crossed.

7826.w: Nitrite in the brine is what leaves cured beef pink rather than grey, and it holds back Clostridium botulinum. Since 9 October 2025 the EU has capped what may be added to a meat product at 80 mg per kg, down from 150, to limit the nitrosamines that follow.

7827.w: A saturated solution of calcium acetate poured into ethanol leaves a semisolid flammable gel that burns for around twenty minutes — the Sterno trick. The same salt is E263 in confectionery and a phosphate binder for failing kidneys.

7828.w: Airfields spray potassium acetate solution instead of chloride salts because it is far less corrosive and easier on soils. It freezes near -60 °C, and it is fully biodegraded within about twenty days at an oxygen demand of 0.3 g per gram.

7829.w: Washed fish mince will not set into a gel again once it has been frozen: the actomyosin denatures in storage and the gel strength goes with it. Sorbitol is blended in before freezing to hold that structure. A 2018 trial on freshwater fish ran four cryoprotectant blends and the strongest gel came from the highest of them — 4% sucrose, 4% sorbitol and 0.3% sodium tripolyphosphate.

7830.w: Streptococcus mutans ferments sugar into the acid that dissolves enamel, and xylitol inhibits that species specifically — about three times as effectively as sorbitol does. Gum is mostly sweetener to begin with, 40 to 50% sugar alcohol by weight, so the swap is nearly the whole product. Dose matters: below 3.44 grams of xylitol a day there is no effect, and above 10.32 grams no further one.

7831.w: Aspartame is about 200 times as sweet as sucrose, so the sugar in a soft drink is replaced by very little of it: a 12-fl-oz (350 ml) can of diet soda contains 0.18 grams. The FDA approved aspartame for carbonated beverages in 1983, which is what made the category possible; the acceptable daily intake is 50 mg per kg of body weight in the US and 40 mg/kg in the EU.

7832.w: Sucralose is about 600 times as sweet as sucrose, so a spoonful of the pure compound is not a thing anyone could measure. The tabletop product is almost entirely carrier: Splenda granular is roughly 1.1% sucralose spread over dextrose and maltodextrin, which is what lets it be spooned against sugar one for one. A one-gram packet carries 3.36 kcal, under the 5 kcal per serving below which US labelling permits a zero-calorie claim.

7833.w: Dried potato has to keep for a year in a cardboard box, and the fat left in the flake is what turns first — BHA is an antioxidant used in fat-containing foods to stop that rancidification. US regulation names the use and the amount: 21 CFR 172.110 permits 50 parts per million of BHA in potato flakes and in dehydrated potato shreds, and 10 ppm in potato granules.

7834.w: Hydrogenation sets liquid oil solid, and shortening was sold from the start as a fat that needed no refrigeration — which leaves it a year of slow oxidation to survive. BHT is generally recognised as safe for that job as long as total antioxidants stay under 0.02% of the food's fat or oil content, and 21 CFR 172.115 separately allows 200 ppm in emulsion stabilisers for shortenings.

7835.w: Nobody mines indium. It rides in sphalerite at trace level, and in the roast-leach-electrowin route to zinc it accumulates in the iron-rich residues left behind; from those it is leached out and finished pure by electrolysis.

7836.w: Thallium is a trace passenger in iron pyrite. Roast the pyrite to make sulfuric acid and the thallium goes up the flue; it is leached back out of the flue dust with alkali or acid. Crookes first caught it there in 1861, by its green line.

7837.w: 209Bi + 70Zn → 278Nh + n — Riken began firing zinc-70 at a bismuth target in September 2003, took one atom in July 2004, a second in 2005, and a third after 450 more days of beam in 2012.

7838.w: 244Pu + 48Ca → 289Fl + 3n. Calcium-48 is both neutron-rich and doubly magic, so a fused nucleus made with it survives long enough to be seen — the hot-fusion trick that got Dubna elements 114 to 118.

7839.w: 243Am + 48Ca → 288Mc + 3n — Dubna and Livermore bombarded an americium-243 target with calcium-48 in August 2003 and got four atoms, each alpha-decaying on to element 113 in about 100 milliseconds.

7840.w: 248Cm + 48Ca → 293Lv + 3n — Dubna fired calcium-48 at a curium-248 target on 19 July 2000 and caught a single atom, identified by the flerovium it alpha-decayed into.

7841.w: Didymium was never an element. Von Welsbach split it in 1885 into neodymium and a green-salted twin, and fractional crystallisation of the ammonium nitrate double salts is still how high-purity praseodymium is parted from its neighbours.

7842.w: The richest terbium going is not an ore body but weathered granite. In South China's regolith the heavy rare earths cling as loose cations to kaolinite, and 0.3M ammonium sulfate pumped through the clay swaps NH4+ in and washes them straight out.

7843.w: Boisbaudran worked on holmium oxide in Paris in 1886, dissolving it in acid and dropping the hydroxide back out with ammonia. He had to run the cycle more than thirty times before a new oxide separated, and named it 'hard to get at'.

7844.w: Erbia was not one earth either. Cleve ran Mosander's nitrate method on erbium oxide, stripping out everything already known, and two new materials were left — one brown, one green. Soret had already seen the brown one's lines and called it element X.

7845.w: Most erbium now comes from the ion-adsorption clays of southern China. Yttrium is about two thirds of the rare earth in that concentrate and erbia 4–5% of it; dissolved in acid, the erbium ion gives the pink colour Mosander saw at Ytterby.

7846.w: Thulia was the green half of what Cleve took out of erbia in 1879, and nobody had enough to see the colour. Charles James got there in 1911 by fractional crystallisation of the bromate — 15,000 operations before the material came out homogeneous.

7847.w: Ytterbium has europium's back door. Treat a buffered solution of the trivalent rare earths with molten sodium amalgam and only Yb3+ is reduced and pulled into the alloy, leaving the rest behind. Marignac found the earth inside erbia in 1878.

7848.w: Marignac's ytterbia was two elements. Urbain split it in 1907, publishing 44 days ahead of von Welsbach, and lutetium — 0.0001% of monazite — still comes out last, crystallised as an ammonium nitrate double salt and finished by ion exchange.

7849.w: Actinium-227 mostly beta-decays, but about one atom in a hundred goes by alpha instead, and what is left behind is francium-223 — long called actinium K. Perey caught it that way in 1939, and it is why uranium ore carries a trace of francium.

7850.w: Ivy Mike, 1 November 1952: uranium-238 in the device swallowed fifteen neutrons inside a microsecond, then beta-decayed seven times over. Aircraft flew filter papers through the cloud, and Ghiorso's team found element 99 on them that December.

7851.w: Element 100 was an order of magnitude scarcer in the debris than element 99, so filter papers were not enough: contaminated coral from Enewetak Atoll was shipped to Berkeley, and 255Fm — uranium-238 plus seventeen neutrons — came out of it.

7852.w: 253Es + 4He → 256Md + n. The target was a billion einsteinium atoms, and the arithmetic promised about one atom of element 101 per run; Berkeley's 60-inch cyclotron made seventeen in all, one at a time.

7853.w: 248Cm + 12C → 255No + 5n. Element 102 was claimed by four countries before Dubna's 1966 report settled it, and carbon-12 fired at a curium or californium target is still how the working isotope is made.

7854.w: On 14 February 1961 Ghiorso's team fired boron-10 and boron-11 from Berkeley's heavy-ion linear accelerator at a three-milligram target of mixed californium isotopes. They reported 257Lr; later work showed they had actually made 258Lr.

7855.w: Metal in the ground is an oxide or a sulfide — its atoms have already handed their outer electrons to oxygen or sulfur. Carbon monoxide off burning coke takes those away again, and the freed atoms pool their electrons into the sea that makes a metal.

7856.w: Every gastropod does this as a larva: the visceral mass, mantle and shell rotate 180° anti-clockwise against the head and foot, carrying the mantle cavity and the anus forward over the head. The first 90° can take minutes.

7857.w: Torsion is the gastropod synapomorphy: it happens in all of them during larval development and in no other mollusk. Snail, slug, limpet, whelk and nudibranch are one class of 65,000-plus species, second only to the insects.

7858.w: Cephalopods are the only molluscs with a closed circulatory system: blood stays inside vessels the whole way round, driven by two branchial hearts at the gills plus one systemic heart for the rest of the body.

7859.w: One shell split into left and right valves, joined by an organic ligament that works against the adductor muscles: the muscles pull the shell shut, the ligament springs it open. The head and the radula are gone entirely.

7860.w: Clam is not a taxon but a way of living: the bivalves that spend life half-buried in the sand of a sea floor or riverbed, digging with a powerful foot and attached to nothing — unlike an oyster or a mussel.

7861.w: The squid did not so much lose the ancestral mollusc shell as swallow it. What is left is the gladius, or pen: a feather-shaped chitinous blade in the functionally dorsal mantle, stiffening the body and anchoring muscle.

7862.w: A jellyfish is a life stage, not a species. In strobilation the sessile polyp reabsorbs its tentacles and narrows into a stack of discs; each ephyra detaches, swims off, and grows into the bell-shaped medusa.

7863.w: Worm names a shape, not a clade — the old taxon Vermes is paraphyletic and abandoned. Flatworms, roundworms and annelids are separate phyla; what they share is a long limbless tube of muscle, usually with no eyes.

7864.w: Acoelomate, with no circulatory or respiratory organs, so oxygen has to diffuse in through the body surface and out again the same way. That only works if no cell is far from the skin — hence flat, ribbon-like, or microscopic.

7865.w: Once Animalia, Plantae and Fungi had been carved out of the eukaryotes, everything left over was filed as Protista. It is a definition by exclusion: a paraphyletic group with no unique trait that unites all of them.

7866.w: Carl Sagan's formulation, adopted as NASA's working definition: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of undergoing Darwinian evolution. Metabolism is the self-sustaining half, and heredity supplies the rest.

7867.w: Life is a property; an organism is one packet of it — any living thing that functions as an individual, built of a single cell or of many. Where one individual stops is still genuinely argued over.

7868.w: The gastropods that kept a coiled calcium-carbonate shell big enough to withdraw into. Slugs are the ones that lost it, or reduced it to an internal remnant, in several separate lineages.

7869.w: An oyster reef builds itself out of oysters. Larvae need hard substrate, so spat settle and cement onto the shells of older and dead oysters, and each generation adds its shells to the structure under it.

7870.w: A hen deposits gram amounts of calcium carbonate in about 20 hours: 95 to 97% of the finished shell, stabilised by a protein matrix without which the calcite would be too brittle to keep its form.

7871.w: A turtle's spine and expanded ribs fuse by ossification to dermal plates under the skin, making one bony box, and scutes of keratin much like horn or nail overlay it. The ribs are in the shell, so it cannot be left behind.

7872.w: Take enough heat out of anything and its particles stop sliding and lock into fixed positions. A solid keeps both its shape and its volume, and the atoms can do nothing but vibrate where they stand.

7873.w: Put enough heat in and the pull between particles stops mattering. A gas keeps neither shape nor volume: it spreads until the container runs out, and it is the only common state you can squeeze.

7874.w: A solid taken past its melting point is a liquid: the lattice is gone but the particles still touch. It keeps its volume and gives up its shape, and it is nearly impossible to compress.

7875.w: The other way in. Cool a gas to its saturation point and it condenses to the middle state. Liquids need a narrow band of temperature and pressure, which makes them the rarest of the four in the universe.

7876.w: Solid to liquid. At the melting point the ordered arrangement breaks down, and the temperature stops climbing while the latent heat of fusion goes entirely into taking the lattice apart.

7877.w: Liquid to solid, and exothermic: the latent heat has to come back out. Without something to nucleate on, pure water will supercool to −40°C and still refuse to start.

7878.w: Liquid to gas, by two different routes. Below the boiling point it happens only at the surface and is called evaporation; once the vapour pressure beats the air, bubbles form inside and it is boiling.

7879.w: Gas back to liquid, the reverse of vaporisation. It starts when a vapour is cooled to its saturation limit — the dew point — which is every cloud, every fogged window and half of the water cycle.

7880.w: Some solids never bother with the liquid step. Leave dry ice out and it goes straight to gas at −78.5°C; leave naphthalene mothballs out and they simply shrink away, never wetting the shelf.

7881.w: Sublimation run backwards: vapour to solid with no liquid in between, giving out heat where sublimation takes it in. Frost on a cold window is deposition, and so is soot laid down on a chimney wall.

7882.w: Heat a gas far enough and collisions start knocking electrons clean off the atoms. What is left is charged and mobile: it conducts electricity and bends to magnetic fields as a neutral gas never does.

7883.w: Ionise a gas and you have the fourth state. The classical four run solid, liquid, gas, plasma, and the transition between the last two is exactly this one.

7884.w: Cut the universe into what it actually contains. Under 5% of it is matter — anything with mass that takes up space. The other 95% is dark matter and dark energy, and nobody can pick either up.

7885.w: Every particle has a twin of the same mass and opposite charge. Dirac's equation demanded them in 1928, and they only ever appear in pairs: a gamma ray above 1.022 MeV can become one particle and one anti.

7886.w: Send silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field and the beam splits in two rather than smearing out. That is Stern and Gerlach in 1922: angular momentum that is intrinsic, and quantised in halves of ħ.

7887.w: Half-integer spin makes a fermion, and fermions are what matter is built from. The Standard Model has twenty-four: six quarks, six leptons, and an antiparticle for each one.

7888.w: Push two identical fermions into the same quantum state and they refuse. Pauli wrote the rule in 1925; it fills electron shells in order, gives the periodic table its shape, and holds up a white dwarf.

7889.w: Spin sorts every particle into two camps. Half-integer and you are a fermion, one to a state. Whole-integer and you are a boson, and any number can pile into the same state — which is what a laser is.

7890.w: Every force is a boson passed between matter particles: the photon for electromagnetism, gluons for the strong force, W and Z for the weak. Gravity is the fourth, and the one this scheme still cannot fit.

7891.w: The force gluons carry. At a femtometre it is about 100 times electromagnetism and 10^38 times gravity, and unlike either it does not weaken with distance — which is why no quark ever gets out.

7892.w: The force the W and Z carry, and the only one that can change a quark's flavour — so it is the force behind beta decay and behind hydrogen fusing at all. It also violates parity, which no other force does.

7893.w: The force the photon carries: second strongest of the four and unlimited in range, though its two signs of charge cancel out at large scales. Every chemical bond and every push on a solid object is this.

7894.w: Cut into a proton and it is not three quarks sitting quietly. Most of what is in there is the field between them: eight kinds of massless gluon, which carry colour charge themselves and so pull on each other.

7895.w: The half of matter that feels the strong force, so gluons never let one go: colour confinement means no quark has ever been seen alone. They are also the only particles whose charge is not a whole multiple of e.

7896.w: The other half of matter: the fermions that do not feel the strong force, so they travel alone instead of being locked inside a hadron. Six of them — electron, muon, tau, and a neutrino for each.

7897.w: Quarks bound by the strong force, and always colourless: three quarks, or a quark with an antiquark. The free proton is the only stable hadron; a free neutron half-lives in about 611 seconds.

7898.w: Three quarks means an odd number of half-spins, so every baryon is a fermion. Protons and neutrons are baryons, and they are very nearly all of the mass of everything you can pick up.

7899.w: A quark with an antiquark means an even number of half-spins, so a meson is a boson. Yukawa predicted them in 1935 as the glue between nucleons; every one is unstable, the best lasting a fraction of a nanosecond.

7900.w: The second-generation copy of the down quark: same −1/3 charge, about twenty times the mass. It got its name from the oddly long-lived 'strange particles' spotted in cosmic rays in 1947.

7901.w: The second-generation copy of the up quark: same +2/3 charge, 1.27 GeV instead of a few MeV. Brookhaven and SLAC announced the J/psi on the same day in November 1974, and it is a charm-anticharm pair.

7902.w: One generation further up the same −1/3 column: 4.18 GeV. Lederman's group found it at Fermilab in 1977 inside the upsilon. It decays reluctantly, which is what lets detectors tag b-jets today.

7903.w: One generation further up the +2/3 column, and a staggering jump: about 173 GeV, heavier than an atom of gold. CDF and DØ found it at Fermilab in 1995. It decays too fast to form a hadron at all.

7904.w: A cosmic-ray proton hits a nucleus high in the air, makes pions, and the pions decay to muons. Around 10,000 land on every square metre of ground a minute — only time dilation gets them down.

7905.w: Perl's group found it at SLAC's SPEAR ring between 1974 and 1977, as events that made no sense any other way. At 1777 MeV it outweighs a proton, and it is the only lepton heavy enough to decay into hadrons.

7906.w: Pauli invented it in 1930 to save the books: when a neutron becomes a proton and an electron, the energy does not add up unless something neutral leaves too. It took until 1956 to catch one.

7907.w: The first-generation neutrino, paired with the electron. Cowan and Reines caught it beside a reactor in 1956. About 65 billion of them from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you each second.

7908.w: Lederman, Schwartz and Steinberger aimed a neutrino beam at a detector at Brookhaven in 1962 and got only muons, never electrons. That proved neutrinos come in more than one kind. Nobel Prize, 1988.

7909.w: The third-generation neutrino, and the last Standard Model fermion to be seen directly: DONUT at Fermilab announced it in July 2000, a quarter of a century after the tau itself turned up.

7910.w: A neutron decays because one of its down quarks emits a W− and turns into an up quark. That is beta decay, and the W is the thing that does it. At 80.4 GeV it is heavier than a whole silver atom.

7911.w: The neutral weak carrier, 91.19 GeV. The proof came in 1973, when a neutrino was seen bouncing off matter and staying a neutrino — a neutral current. CERN made real W and Z in 1983 with UA1 and UA2.

7912.w: ATLAS and CMS announced it on 4 July 2012 at about 125 GeV, after a forty-year search. It has zero spin — the first elementary scalar ever found — and its field is what gives the W, the Z and the fermions mass.

7913.w: Twelve matter fermions, five bosons, and three of the four forces. Settled in the mid-1970s, it has survived every test since — and still says nothing about gravity, dark matter, or the matter-antimatter imbalance.

7914.w: A muon lasts 2.2 microseconds and then always ends the same way: an electron, a muon neutrino and an electron antineutrino. There is nothing lighter and charged for it to become.

7915.w: Beta decay, drawn properly. A down quark of charge −1/3 emits a virtual W− and is left an up quark of +2/3; the W then becomes an electron and an antineutrino. Only the weak force can change a flavour like this.

7916.w: Any compound with oxygen bonded to another element, oxygen sitting at oxidation state −2. Most of the Earth's crust is oxides, and even a sheet of aluminium foil is wearing a skin of Al2O3.

7917.w: Heat a metal in air and its surface turns. Zinc powder burns outright: 2 Zn + O2 makes 2 ZnO. Gold and platinum are prized precisely because they refuse to do it.

7918.w: Mendeleev laid the elements out by weight in 1869 and left gaps for what he could not find. Moseley showed in 1913 that the real order is the proton count. 118 now, of which 94 occur on Earth.

7919.w: Not shared between two atoms and not handed over, but pooled: positive ions sitting in a sea of electrons that belongs to all of them at once. That sea is the conduction, the lustre, and the bend.

7920.w: IUPAC's test is an atom with a partly filled d sub-shell — groups 3 to 12. That half-empty shell gives several oxidation states a step apart, which is why their salts are coloured and why so many catalysts are these.

7921.w: Group 2, with two electrons filling the outer s orbital. They are named for their oxides: quicklime, magnesia and baryta were 'earths' — fireproof and water-insoluble — and they turn water alkaline.

7922.w: The fifteen from lanthanum to lutetium, filling the 4f shell. Because 4f hides beneath the outer electrons they behave almost identically, so the table floats them out below and separating them needs solvent extraction.

7923.w: The second floated row: actinium to lawrencium, filling 5f as the lanthanides fill 4f. Seaborg proposed the family in 1944. Every single one is radioactive, and only thorium and uranium are left on Earth in quantity.

7924.w: Every raindrop is an acid before it lands. Carbon dioxide dissolves into it and becomes carbonic acid, which is why clean rain sits above pH 5 and below 7 instead of neutral. No acid went in; one came out.

7925.w: Quicklime is an oxide, not a base: no hydroxide in it. Slake it and CaO plus water becomes calcium hydroxide, and a saturated solution of that sits at pH 12.4, caustic enough to burn skin.

7926.w: Berzelius called them salt-formers, and a salt is where you get one back. Drive a current through sodium chloride and chloride ions surrender an electron at the anode: 2Cl- becomes Cl2, chlorine gas, 97 million tonnes of it a year.

7927.w: A spiral is a galaxy whose gas settled into one flat disc where everything orbits the same way. The disc turns at different speeds by radius, so the arms cannot be fixed strings of stars: they are density waves that material drifts into and out of.

7928.w: The nearest large barred spiral to us, 2.54 million light-years off, named for the patch of sky it sits in: the constellation Andromeda, itself named for the princess chained to the sea cliff.

7929.w: Two suns circling a common centre every 79.8 years, swinging from 11.2 AU apart to 35.6, with a red dwarf bound to the pair 13,000 AU further out. That third star, Proxima, is the closest star to the Sun and still too faint to see.

7930.w: A requiem shark that rewires its own salt balance. Entering fresh water it throttles the rectal gland back to hold on to sodium and chloride, the gills take ions up from the river, and the kidneys pour out dilute urine while reabsorbing solutes.

7931.w: An antennariid frogfish, so an anglerfish. Its pink and white fingerprint stripes echo the hermatypic corals it lives among, and when it leaves the bottom it balls up until it reads as a piece of debris bouncing along rather than a fish.

7932.w: The echinoderm that grew a jaw. Five calcium-carbonate teeth hang in a muscular frame Aristotle compared to a lantern, and they grasp, scrape, pull and tear well enough to cut a kelp holdfast or bore into rock.

7933.w: The echinoderm that eats outside itself. It pulls a shell apart until the gap is a fraction of a millimetre, pushes its cardiac stomach through, digests the animal inside its own shell, then hauls the stomach back on ligaments in the arms.

7934.w: An invertebrate built out of calcite. Its skeleton sits in the dermis as plates called ossicles, each a porous mesh named stereom, laced together by collagen fibres. Nothing outside this phylum makes a skeleton that way.

7935.w: The annelid that eats the ground. Soil goes into a muscular gizzard where grit grinds it, and comes out as casts. Darwin put 53,000 of them in an acre of arable land and doubted many animals had done more to the surface of the world.

7936.w: A sea star under a coat of thorn-like spines that drive saponin-bearing tissue into whatever presses on them, causing a sharp stinging pain. It eats what almost nothing else will: living hard coral, up to 6 square metres of reef a year.

7937.w: Chiroptera means hand-wing. Five elongated digits radiate from the wrist and frame the patagium, a skin membrane running from arm and fingers to the flank and hind limbs — the only mammal capable of true sustained flight.

7938.w: The pinniped that went without the eared seal's kit: ear holes rather than flaps, hind flippers that will not rotate forward, so on land it galumphs on its belly. It regulates heat by diverting blood into a smooth layer of blubber under the skin.

7939.w: Build a chamber round the fire instead of standing the ware in it. A kiln is a thermally insulated chamber — a type of oven — and charcoal inside one reaches temperatures an open wood fire never will.

7940.w: The masonry oven is a kiln you bake in: a chamber of fireproof brick, fired with wood, then swept of ash so the bread meets the heat the brick has stored. Same chamber, lower temperature.

7941.w: Cast iron replaced masonry and the range shrank to fit a kitchen. A modern stove has an oven in it — an enclosed box beside the fire, for baking rather than direct heat.

7942.w: A stovetop kettle is a metal pot built for one job, taking its heat from the hob below. Lid, spout and handle; stainless steel now, copper and cast iron in the 1800s.

7943.w: The electric kettle moved the element off the hob and put it inside the water. Nothing heats but the water itself, which is why it beats a pan on a stove.

7944.w: A toaster is heating elements with slots between them. It waited on nichrome, patented by Albert Marsh in 1906 — the oldest resistance heating alloy, and the first wire that would sit at red heat in open air day after day.
