7945.w: A freezer is a specialised refrigerator: the same vapour-compression loop pushed below the freezing point of water, about -18 °C. Home freezer compartments arrived in 1940.

7946.w: A stationary blender is a container with a rotating blade at the bottom, powered by an electric motor in the base. The jar is only there to keep the food against the blade.

7947.w: The tinsmith John Landis Mason patented the pattern in 1858: a glass jar with a thread moulded into its neck, and a metal band that screws down to press a flat lid against the rim.

7948.w: A tin can is not tin. It is a steel can with a thin tin coating, and the coating is the whole point — it stops the contents rusting the steel they sit against.

7949.w: Withies crossed over and under each other until they hold their own shape. Willow was the material of choice for its flexibility and for how easily it can be grown and cut.

7950.w: A sink is a bowl-shaped plumbing fixture. The basin is the old part; what makes it a sink is the pipework — water arriving under pressure and a drain taking it away.

7951.w: A tap is a screw with a washer on the end of it, wound down onto a seat to shut off the flow. The first screw-down mechanism was patented by the Rotherham brass founders Guest and Chrimes in 1845.

7952.w: A broad, mainly flat vessel with a lip, thrown on the potter's wheel and fired hard enough for daily use. Give it a rounder, deeper profile and you have made a bowl instead.

7953.w: A mug is a type of cup: one with a handle, straight-sided, holding 250 to 350 ml. Thick stoneware walls are what let you hold it while the drink inside stays hot.

7954.w: Brickwork is masonry made of bricks and mortar. The mortar is not glue so much as bedding: a uniform 10 mm joint that lets units that are never quite identical stack true.

7955.w: Thatching lays bundles of straw so each course sheds water onto the one below, fixed down with horizontal sways and hairpin spars of twisted hazel. The packed straw traps air and insulates as well.

7956.w: Solid floors are planks milled from single pieces of timber and laid at right angles across the joists. They were structural first — the floor was the thing holding you up, not a surface.

7957.w: A room is any enclosed space in a structure, bounded by walls, which you can enter only through a door or similar dividing structure. Without the door it is not a room, only a cavity.

7958.w: Walls and a roofing system to keep the rain out of the dwelling space — everything else a house has is added to that. The social unit living inside it is called a household.

7959.w: Masonry built to carry the smoke of a fire out past the living space, kept as near vertical as possible so the gases draw themselves up. Domestic chimneys appear in northern Europe in the 12th century; England's oldest survivor is at Conisbrough, 1185.

7960.w: Locks have been in use over 6,000 years. The Egyptian wooden pin lock was a bolt, a door fixture and a key that lifted the pins clear — and the modern Yale is a developed version of exactly that.

7961.w: A shelf is a flat horizontal plane fixed to a wall or other vertical surface. The board is nothing on its own; the wall is what turns it into storage.

7962.w: It was a cup board: open shelved tiers for displaying plates, cups and saucers. Put doors on the front and the display becomes storage, which is what the word now means.

7963.w: A woven carpet comes off a loom much like woven cloth; a knotted pile carpet adds a supplementary weft that rises at right angles from the weave. Rug meant a coarse coverlet until about 1808.

7964.w: Teeth cut into the edge of a steel strip, then bent alternately left and right. That set is the whole trick: the cut ends up wider than the blade, so the blade never binds in its own kerf.

7965.w: A hand drill's crank was replaced by an electric motor geared down for torque — patented in Melbourne in 1889 by Arnot and Brain, and made portable by the Fein brothers of Stuttgart in 1895.

7966.w: A helical thread cut round a shank, so a twist becomes a pull. Every wood screw was filed by hand until Job and William Wyatt patented a screw machine in 1760; by the 1780s the works made 16,000 a day with 30 people.

7967.w: The tool exists only because the fastener does. A screwdriver is classified entirely by its tip, because the tip has to match the driving surfaces cut into the screw head.

7968.w: The other way to turn a threaded fastener: grip its flats from outside instead of a slot in its head. A wrench gives grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to nuts and bolts.

7969.w: A stone head lashed to a wooden haft — birch tar and rawhide held the blade on. Hafted axes date back at least 46,000 years in northern Australia; the unhafted hand axe is a million years older still.

7970.w: A broad blade of sheet steel, its back folded into a socket, on a hardwood handle chosen for a wood that will not snap. The blade digs; the handle is the lever.

7971.w: Two long stiles with rungs let into them. Rigid ladders were wood until aluminium took over in the 20th century — and one is painted on a wall of the Spider Caves in Valencia at least 10,000 years ago.

7972.w: A table becomes a workbench when it gains a way to fix the workpiece to the surface, so the work can be attacked with both hands. Roubo drew the standard pattern in 1769.

7973.w: Tailors used unmarked cloth tapes, notched by hand. James Chesterman's 1821 retractable design was a spring-loaded cloth strip with markings, in a compact case; he later repurposed surplus pannier-dress wire for the first steel tape.

7974.w: A gear is a toothed wheel, and nothing more: cut teeth into the rim and its rotation can be handed to another wheel instead of slipping against it. Two meshed gears are a gear train.

7975.w: Woven cloth cut to the shape of a body and sewn. The world's oldest preserved garment is a linen shirt from a First Dynasty tomb at Tarkhan in Egypt, and it is already sophisticatedly cut.

7976.w: Trousers came from riding. The oldest known pair, from the Yanghai cemetery at Turpan and dated between the 13th and 10th centuries BC, is wool with straight legs and a wide crotch, and was likely made for horseback.

7977.w: Wallets were developed after paper currency reached the West in the 1600s. Before that people carried drawstring leather coin purses — a pouch, not a flat folded case sized to a note.

7978.w: Sheet metal cut and worked to one thin edge, kept only for hair. Excavations in Egypt have turned up solid gold and copper razors in tombs from the 4th millennium BC.

7979.w: A printed promise standing in for metal. Banknotes were first issued by commercial banks, legally required to redeem them for coin on demand at the chief cashier's counter.

7980.w: The quill pen is a flight feather cut to a nib, holding a bead of ink in its hollow shaft. It replaced the reed pen from about the 7th century, because it wrote finer on skin.

7981.w: A graphite core in a wooden case that stops it snapping and keeps it off your hand. Red cedar was the favoured timber because it is aromatic and does not splinter when sharpened.

7982.w: The eraser exists because the pencil does — and the material is named after the job. Edward Nairne sold natural rubber cubes for lifting pencil marks off paper from 1770, at three shillings a half inch.

7983.w: Two blades joined at a pivot so their sharpened edges slide past each other. Roman pivoted shears survive from the 2nd century AD, but they were not made in numbers until Hinchliffe of Sheffield, 1761.

7984.w: Printing gives you copies; the wire gives you news worth printing today. Few papers could afford foreign bureaus, so they bought telegraphed copy from agencies — Havas from 1835, the Associated Press from 1846.

7985.w: A portolan chart is drawn from compass observations: a web of windrose lines showing constant bearings, coastlines, and place names written perpendicular to the shore. No latitude, no longitude at all.

7986.w: A road is a prepared surface. Asphalt concrete is mineral aggregate bound with bitumen, laid in layers and compacted — the stone carries the load and the bitumen keeps it from scattering.

7987.w: A street is a public thoroughfare lined with buildings on one or both sides. A road's job is transport; a street's job is the people beside it — which is why the buildings are what make one.

7988.w: A market is a place people gather regularly to buy and sell — a souk, a bazaar, a mercado, a tianguis, a palengke. It needs somewhere public to stand and a coin everyone will take.

7989.w: A shop is a market stall that stopped packing up. Retail shops grew over centuries from little more than rude booths into permanent premises, selling to the person who will use the goods.

7990.w: What makes a town rather than a village is the market: it supplies goods and services to the countryside around it. Domesday listed 50 markets in England in 1086, and some 2,000 more were founded between 1200 and 1349.

7991.w: A school is the institution and, for in-person learning, the building: a place designed to hold learners under a teacher's direction. Many early public schools were literally one room and one teacher taking seven grades.

7992.w: The word means a place of hospitality, and that is what these were first: somewhere to lie down. Historically hospitals were founded and funded by Christian religious orders, and staffed by their members rather than physicians.

7993.w: The chain is what made the bicycle safe. Running it from frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel let both wheels shrink to the same size and the seat drop — the safety bicycle, about 1885, barely changed since.

7994.w: A goods wagon that stopped needing to be pulled. Gottlieb Daimler built the Motor-Lastwagen in 1896; trucks still use body-on-frame construction, with the cab independent of the load behind it.

7995.w: Four fixed propellers cannot be flown by hand — control comes only from varying each rotor's speed, thousands of times a second. Cheap lightweight flight controllers and accelerometers arrived around 2005-2010, and the quadcopter arrived with them.

7996.w: Every adult fluke carries two cup-shaped muscular suckers, an oral and a ventral one, and a tapeworm's scolex carries four. A parasite with no legs still has to hold on.
7996.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

7997.w: The anterior end of a tapeworm is a knob under 2 mm across carrying four radially arranged acetabula, and in armed species a hooked rostellum between them. It is not a head: it has no mouth.
7997.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

7998.w: The rostellum is a fleshy protuberance in the middle of the four suckers, retractable in some species and armed in others. Taenia solium's carries two rows of 22 to 32 spiny hooks.
7998.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

7999.w: Segments bud from germinal tissue behind the scolex and are pushed backwards as newer ones form. Each is hermaphroditic; the gravid ones at the far end break off and leave in the feces.
7999.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

8000.w: An adult tapeworm has no mouth, no digestive tract and no blood vessels. Its outer surface is metabolically active, releasing enzymes from microtriches and taking everything in through the skin.
8000.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

8001.w: A gravid proglottid is a uterus packed with eggs, and inside each egg sits a hexacanth embryo — an oncosphere carrying six hooklets it uses to bore through the intermediate host's intestinal wall.
8001.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

8002.w: Once through the gut wall the oncosphere settles in tissue and becomes a cysticercus: a small fluid-filled bladder with the scolex inverted inside it. The bladder worm is the stage that infects the next host.
8002.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

8003.w: An Echinococcus oncosphere that reaches the liver grows slowly into a hydatid cyst, its brood capsules budding scolices into the fluid. Rupture spills that fluid, and can cause anaphylactic shock.
8003.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 38

8004.w: Flukes are hermaphrodites with one exception: the blood flukes have separate sexes. The male's body curls up at its edges into a long channel, and the larger female lies inside it for their whole adult lives.
8004.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8005.w: A fluke egg hatches in fresh water into a ciliated, free-swimming miracidium. It must penetrate the right species of snail to go any further, and it is specific to that one species.
8005.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8006.w: Inside the snail the miracidium multiplies asexually through sporocysts and rediae, so hundreds of cercariae leave for every one larva that entered. Each has a swimming tail; the blood flukes' is forked.
8006.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8007.w: The cercariae of the gut, liver and lung flukes never pierce skin. They shed the tail, secrete a thick wall and encyst on water plants or inside a fish or a crab, and wait there to be swallowed.
8007.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8008.w: The exterior surface of a roundworm is a collagen-rich cuticle tough enough to resist a host's digestive enzymes. Because it cannot stretch far, the growing larva has to moult out of it four times over.
8008.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

8009.w: The anterior end of a roundworm may carry hooks, teeth or cutting plates inside a hardened mouth cavity, used to grip. Ancylostoma's holds two pairs of teeth; Necator's holds a pair of cutting plates instead.
8009.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

8010.w: Trichuris eggs are barrel-shaped and brown with a transparent protuberance at each pole. The two plugs are the whole identification, and the egg needs two to three weeks in soil before it can infect anyone.
8010.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8011.w: A Trichinella larva enters a striated muscle cell and reprograms it: the cell stops being muscle and becomes a collagen-walled capsule around the worm. Stomach acid is what releases the larva in the next host.
8011.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8012.w: Adult filariae in the tissues do not lay eggs; they release live embryos, microfilariae, into blood or skin. Wuchereria's peak in peripheral blood at night, matched to when the mosquito that carries them feeds.
8012.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 27

8013.w: The Mastigophora are the protists that move by lashing flagella rather than by pseudopodia or by cilia — the group that holds Giardia, Trichomonas, the trypanosomes and Leishmania.
8013.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

8014.w: The ventral surface of Giardia is dished into a rigid concavity built on a spiral of microtubules. It grips the intestinal epithelium, which is why the parasite is shed into the stool only intermittently.
8014.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

8015.w: In Trichomonas and in the trypanosomes a flagellum runs backwards attached to the body wall instead of trailing free, and its beat sends a visible ripple down the membrane it is fastened to.
8015.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

8016.w: Trichomonas has four flagella at the front and a fifth behind, all joined to an undulating membrane, and a barb-like rod of microtubules projecting opposite them. The axostyle is thought to anchor the cell and to do some of the tissue damage.
8016.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

8017.w: A network of interlocked circular DNA packed inside a single mitochondrion, holding many copies of the mitochondrial genome. Only one class of flagellates carries one, and it is named after it: the Kinetoplastida.
8017.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

8018.w: Nearly every apicomplexan is a parasite, and this is the machine that makes it one: a polar ring of microtubules with secretory rhoptries and micronemes behind it, used to force entry into a host cell.
8018.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 70

8019.w: A blood-feeding parasite that digests haemoglobin releases free heme, which would kill it. Plasmodium crystallises the heme instead into hemozoin — inert, iron-rich, and dark enough to see down a microscope.

8020.w: A roundworm named for its shape: a slender anterior three-fifths threaded into the mucosa of the large intestine, with a thicker handle behind. It feeds on tissue secretions rather than on blood.
8020.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8021.w: The parasitic females reproduce parthenogenetically, with no male anywhere in the cycle. Their eggs hatch inside the gut wall, so it is larvae that appear in the stool, and those larvae can reinfect the same host.
8021.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8022.w: The gravid female is close to a metre long and almost entirely uterus — a bag of larvae. About a year after infection she raises a burning blister in a limb, and cold water on it makes her expel them in a milky cloud.
8022.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 26

8023.w: Adult pairs live for years coiled in fibrous nodules the host builds around them, called onchocercomas. Those adults do little harm; it is the microfilariae they release, wandering the skin and the eye, that blind people.
8023.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 27

8024.w: The adult is tiny — 3 to 6 mm, three or four proglottids — and lives in a dog's intestine. Nearly all the animal's mass is on the other side of its cycle, in a hydatid cyst growing for years in a sheep or a person.
8024.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 46

8025.w: A pseudophyllid tapeworm whose scolex grips with two slit-like grooves rather than four suckers. It competes for dietary vitamin B12 directly, and in about 1% of infections that causes a macrocytic anaemia.
8025.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 45

8026.w: Its cercariae never touch skin. They encyst as metacercariae on raw water vegetation such as watercress, and whatever grazes or eats that plant swallows them; the young flukes then bore to the bile ducts.
8026.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8027.w: A thick, spined-tegument fluke that settles in pairs inside cysts in the lung and lays eggs that leave in sputum. The chronic bloody cough it produces is routinely mistaken for tuberculosis.
8027.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8028.w: A ciliate alveolate rowed along by a full coat of cilia — the only member of the phylum Ciliophora known to be pathogenic to humans. Its main reservoir is domestic and wild pigs, not people.
8028.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 96

8029.w: Unlike most protozoan parasites it never enters a cell; it swims free in blood and lymph, driven by a flagellum bound along its side into an undulating membrane, and swaps its surface coat to stay ahead of the immune system.
8029.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 110

8030.w: A kinetoplastid: its single mitochondrion holds a disc of interlocked DNA circles so large it is visible under a light microscope. In a blood smear the parasite takes a characteristic C shape.
8030.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

8031.w: Glossina is a true fly like the housefly, but an obligate parasite: both sexes feed only on vertebrate blood, and the crop stretches enough to take a meal equal to the fly's own weight.

8032.w: Phlebotomine sandflies are small — a body around 3 mm — and densely hairy, which helps them escape notice. Only the female takes blood, and she is the vector of every form of leishmaniasis.

8033.w: Simulium lays its eggs in running water and the larvae hold onto submerged rocks with hooks. That is the whole reason river blindness is called river blindness: the vector cannot breed away from a fast stream.

8034.w: A blood-feeding bug that bites at night, usually on the face. The parasite passes in the insect's feces, not its saliva — unusual among bloodsucking vectors — and enters when the bite is scratched.

8035.w: It makes the worm's membranes permeable to calcium ions; the influx locks the muscles in contraction. It also disrupts the tegument, exposing the parasite's own antigens to the host's immune system.
8035.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 172

8036.w: It binds the worm's beta-tubulin so microtubules cannot assemble, and glucose uptake fails with them. The parasite is forced onto its glycogen stores and dies when the ATP runs out.
8036.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 172

8037.w: It binds the colchicine site of beta-tubulin, blocking tubulin from polymerising in the parasite's intestinal cells. The worm is immobilised gradually rather than killed outright, and passes out.
8037.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

8038.w: Omura's soil Streptomyces yielded the avermectins, and Campbell's screen showed they paralysed nematodes. The drug binds glutamate-gated chloride channels found in invertebrate nerve and muscle, and not in ours.
8038.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 178

8039.w: A nitroimidazole that only becomes toxic once its nitro group is reduced, which happens in anaerobic metabolism. One drug therefore covers Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba and the anaerobic bacteria, and spares aerobes.
8039.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 173

8040.w: It uncouples the worm's oxidative phosphorylation and blocks its glucose uptake, so the scolex loses its grip and is digested. It is not taken up from the gut, which is why it reaches worms in the lumen and nothing else.
8040.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

8041.w: It inhibits arachidonic acid metabolism in microfilariae, which leaves them open to innate immune attack rather than killing them directly. The adult worms in the tissues survive it.
8041.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 173

8042.w: A depolarising neuromuscular blocker: the roundworm contracts suddenly and is then paralysed, so it loses its grip on the intestinal wall and is passed out rather than killed in place.
8042.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

8043.w: It interferes with pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase, an electron-transfer enzyme essential to anaerobic energy metabolism and absent from us. It is first-line for Cryptosporidium and for Giardia.
8043.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 176

8044.w: Powdered cinchona bark was the only thing that worked against malaria for three centuries. Pelletier and Caventou pulled the alkaloid out of the bark in 1820, and quinine is still the fallback where chloroquine has failed.
8044.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 178

8045.w: A person becomes the definitive host by eating undercooked pork carrying cysticerci. The bladder everts in the small intestine, the scolex hooks into the wall, and the worm buds segments behind it for years.
8045.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

8046.w: The same disease from the other animal: Cysticercus bovis in raw or undercooked beef. Humans are the only known definitive host of either species, and usually carry just the one worm.
8046.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

8047.w: Swallowing Taenia solium eggs, rather than larvae in pork, puts a person in the pig's place: the oncospheres hatch, cross the gut wall and form cysticerci in muscle, skin, eye or brain. Contaminated vegetables are a main source.
8047.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

8048.w: Around 60% of people with cysticercosis have larvae in the brain. Seizures are the commonest symptom, and in developing countries this is one of the leading causes of them; the disease is called the great imitator.
8048.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

8049.w: Eggs pass out in feces and need two to three weeks in warm, moist soil before they can infect anyone; then they persist there for ten years or more. Swallowed, they hatch, and the larvae set off through liver and lungs.
8049.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8050.w: Eggs in feces hatch in warm damp soil and the filariform larvae penetrate skin directly — walking barefoot is the risk factor. Chronic blood loss from the attached adults makes it a leading cause of anaemia.
8050.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8051.w: Whipworm eggs pass in feces, embryonate in soil for two to three weeks, and are swallowed on unwashed vegetables or from hands. Heavy loads cause bloody diarrhoea, growth faltering and rectal prolapse.
8051.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8052.w: The gravid female crawls out at night and lays on the perianal skin; the eggs are infective within hours. Scratching moves them to the mouth, and they are light enough to go airborne in bedding and house dust.
8052.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8053.w: Larvae penetrate skin from soil, but the disease is unusual because larvae in the gut can become infective before they leave. That autoinfective cycle has kept infections alive in people for decades.
8053.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8054.w: Simulium black flies pass the larvae on, usually over many bites. The damage comes from the microfilariae the adults release, wandering the skin and every structure of the eye, and from the allergy to them.
8054.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 29

8055.w: The larvae travel inside copepods in drinking water; stomach acid digests the copepod and frees the worm. Filtering water through cloth breaks the cycle, which is why the disease has almost been eradicated.
8055.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 26

8056.w: The adult worm lives in dogs and other canines; sheep are the usual intermediate host. A person who swallows eggs from close contact with an infected dog takes the sheep's place, and grows a hydatid cyst instead.
8056.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 40

8057.w: A plant-borne trematode zoonosis: metacercariae encysted on raw watercress and other water vegetation are swallowed whole. The young flukes bore out of the gut to the liver and settle in the bile ducts.
8057.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8058.w: The metacercariae sit in the flesh of freshwater fish, so raw or undercooked fish is the route in. The adults live in the bile ducts for up to thirty years, and long infection is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
8058.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8059.w: The metacercariae are in raw or undercooked freshwater crabs and crayfish. The young flukes cross the diaphragm into the lungs, and the chronic fibrotic cough that follows is easily mistaken for tuberculosis.
8059.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8060.w: The plerocercoid larva waits in the flesh of freshwater fish, salmon and pike among them, so sashimi and ceviche have carried it well outside its old range. Vitamin B12 deficiency follows in about 1% of cases.
8060.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 45

8061.w: Female phlebotomine sandflies inject metacyclic promastigotes while feeding. Where the parasite settles decides the disease: skin for the cutaneous form, mucous membranes for the mucocutaneous, spleen and liver for the visceral.
8061.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 94

8062.w: An infected tsetse fly injects the parasite while feeding. It multiplies in blood and lymph first, then crosses into the central nervous system, and untreated it is generally fatal.
8062.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 110

8063.w: The kissing bug defecates as it feeds and the parasite enters through the scratched bite, not the bite itself. Decades later, chronic infection damages the heart in up to a third of cases, and can enlarge the gut.
8063.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

8064.w: Pigs are the main reservoir, and human infection is commonest where people and pigs live close together. Cysts pass in feces and are swallowed in contaminated food or water; fewer than 1% of people carry it.
8064.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 111

8065.w: Spread by direct sexual contact — the parasite forms no cyst and cannot survive a trip through the environment. Women get the symptoms; men are usually asymptomatic carriers, which is how it keeps circulating.
8065.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 86

8066.w: Undercooked pork and wild game are how the encysted larvae get in; stomach acid frees them from their nurse cells. Migration into muscle a week later brings the muscle pain and the swollen face.
8066.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8067.w: The vehicle is fresh water, but the engine is the snail: one miracidium multiplies inside it into hundreds of cercariae, and those are what pierce the skin of anyone wading. No snail, no transmission.
8067.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8068.w: Cysts shed in feces contaminate water and survive nearly three months in cold water. Swallowing a handful is enough, which is why the disease turns up in hikers, in nurseries and in whole water supplies at once.
8068.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

8069.w: A hermaphroditic fluke holding on with an oral sucker and a ventral one, living in the common bile duct and the gall bladder and feeding on bile. It can survive thirty years in one host.
8069.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 54

8070.w: Four anterior flagella, a fifth at the back, all joined to an undulating membrane, and a barb-like axostyle projecting opposite them. It never makes a cyst, which is why only direct contact passes it on.
8070.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 82

8071.w: The blood flukes are the ones whose cercariae pierce skin instead of encysting: a fork-tailed larva leaves the snail, burrows into a foot or a leg on contact with fresh water, and sheds its tail to become a schistosomule.
8071.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8072.w: The apicomplexan genus that does its growing inside red blood cells: it digests their haemoglobin and dumps the leftover heme as hemozoin, the dark malaria pigment pathologists find in the tissues afterwards.
8072.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 100

8073.w: A tapeworm is a flatworm of the class Cestoda, and the scolex is what makes it one: a holdfast under 2 mm long with four suckers, gripping the gut wall while the segmented body streams behind it.
8073.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 39

8074.w: The armed tapeworm. Its scolex carries a rostellum between the four suckers, ringed with two rows of 22 to 32 spiny hooks, and that crown is exactly what separates it from the beef tapeworm.
8074.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

8075.w: The unarmed tapeworm: four suckers on the scolex and no hooks and no rostellum at all. That absence is the identifying feature against the other Taenia, and it can still exceed twenty metres.
8075.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 43

8076.w: A roundworm whose head bends back into a hook, holding the gut wall with a hardened mouth cavity — two pairs of teeth in the Old World species, a pair of cutting plates in the New World one. Feeding that way is what makes it a cause of anaemia.
8076.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 10

8077.w: Alone among the flukes the blood flukes have separate sexes, and the male's body curls into a long channel that holds the larger female for the whole of their adult lives, in the veins of the gut or bladder.
8077.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 52

8078.w: The large intestinal roundworm: a female runs 22 to 35 cm and lays as many as 200,000 eggs a day. A thick, digestion-resistant cuticle is what lets an animal that size sit in a small intestine undigested.
8078.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8079.w: It does not simply hide in muscle: the larva enters a striated muscle cell and reprograms it into a collagen-walled nurse cell, then lives inside the thing it made. Nothing else among the roundworms does this.
8079.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 13

8080.w: A flagellate with four pairs of flagella and a rigid dished underside built on microtubules. That ventral disc clamps it to the lining of the small intestine, and it never invades any further than that.
8080.b: Leventhal R & Cheadle RF, Medical Parasitology: A Self-Instructional Text, 6th ed. (F. A. Davis, 2012), p. 83

8081.w: Break the wire and the current stops; close it again and it flows. A switch is a deliberate, repeatable gap, and it has exactly two states. Every digital machine in this chain rests on that fact.

8082.w: Put the switch's contacts next to an electromagnet instead of a finger. A small current through the coil pulls them closed, switching a much larger circuit. One circuit can now command another.

8083.w: Aristotle pulled the form of an argument away from its content. All A are B, all B are C, so all A are C — that holds whatever A, B and C stand for. Validity became a property of structure, like grammar.

8084.w: Al-Khwarizmi, at Baghdad's House of Wisdom around 820, wrote out rules for restoring and balancing equations. Let letters stand for the unknown quantities and a single line states a method, not one sum.

8085.w: Boole's Laws of Thought, 1854, gave logic the form of an algebra: the variables hold true and false instead of numbers, and the operations are and, or and not. Reasoning turned into calculation.

8086.w: A Boolean operation has finitely many cases, so you can simply list them: write every combination the inputs can take, one per row, and fill in the output. The table is the complete definition.

8087.w: Shannon's 1937 master's thesis proved Boolean algebra describes relay arrangements exactly: contacts in series behave as and, in parallel as or. An equation and a circuit became the same object.

8088.w: Diodes pass a signal but cannot reverse one, so diode logic alone is incomplete. A transistor can: wire it to pull the output low whenever the input is high and you have negation in a circuit.

8089.w: Point two diodes into a shared resistor. Current arriving at either input reaches the output, and neither input can push back through the other diode into its neighbour. That is disjunction, in parts.

8090.w: De Morgan's law: A and B is exactly not(not A or not B). Invert both inputs, OR them, invert the result — conjunction assembled from the two gates already on the bench, with no new part.

8091.w: Put an inverter after an AND: the output is false only when both inputs are true. This is Sheffer's stroke, and it is functionally complete — every Boolean function whatsoever can be written with it.

8092.w: OR is true when either input is true, including both. Subtract the both case — OR and not AND — and what is left is true only when the inputs disagree: exclusive or.

8093.w: Invert the select line so exactly one branch is enabled, gate each input against its own branch, and merge the two. A handful of NANDs and an inverter let a control signal choose which input gets through.

8094.w: Cross-couple two NAND gates so each feeds the other's input. The pair has two stable states and sits in whichever one you last pushed it to. Gates could only react; this one remembers.

8095.w: Add two bits and there are two answers to produce. XOR gives the sum digit (1+1 is 0), AND gives the carry into the next column. Two gates, and arithmetic has come out of pure logic.

8096.w: A half adder ignores the carry coming in from the column below. Chain two of them and OR the two carries out, and you have a stage that can be stacked as wide as the numbers you want to add.

8097.w: Run the adder and the bitwise AND, OR and NOT circuits all at once on the same operands, then let a multiplexer choose which result leaves. The code that steers the multiplexer is the opcode.

8098.w: A switch has exactly two states, so knowing which one it is in answers exactly one yes-or-no question. That answer is the unit of information — Tukey contracted 'binary digit' to bit, Shannon made it a measure.

8099.w: One bit cannot hold a letter. Group as many as it takes to encode a single character and you have a byte: eight, once IBM settled the matter, and the smallest piece of memory with its own address.

8100.w: Split a byte down the middle. Four bits have sixteen possible values, so give each one symbol: 0 to 9, then A to F. Now any byte is two characters instead of eight, and the grouping is exact.

8101.w: Telegraph and teleprinter codes had numbered the alphabet for decades. ASCII fixed 128 of those code points in seven bits, so any machine receiving the number 65 produces the same letter A.

8102.w: 128 slots hold English and almost nothing else. Unicode set out to give every script on Earth one number per character; version 17 defines 159,801 characters across 172 scripts, ASCII first among them.

8103.w: Stand eight flip-flops side by side and wire them to one control line: they load or hold a whole byte together. Nothing is closer to the arithmetic, so nothing is quicker to read.

8104.w: Charge on a microscopic capacitor is the 1; a transistor beside it gates access. Two parts per bit packs densely — but the charge drains in milliseconds, so every cell is read and written back over and over. That is what 'dynamic' means.

8105.w: Lay out a grid and put a diode at every crossing that should read 1, leaving the rest empty. The diode matrix is decided at manufacture, so the contents cannot be altered — and cannot be forgotten.

8106.w: Registers are instant but tiny; main memory is vast but tens to hundreds of times slower. Put a small fast memory between them holding copies of recently used locations and most requests never travel.

8107.w: A quartz crystal is piezoelectric and flexes at one precise frequency. Build an oscillator around it and the chip gets a steady beat, so every flip-flop in the machine changes state at the same instant.

8108.w: A private wire between every pair of registers grows as the square of their number. Run one shared bundle of traces instead and arbitrate who may drive it, and any component can send to any other.

8109.w: The ALU already takes an opcode saying which operation to perform. Store that code as a number in memory and it stops being a setting on a wire and becomes a command the machine can be handed.

8110.w: Write the whole program as those numbers, one after another: load a word into a register, run an ALU operation, jump elsewhere. No translation happens; the processor's own wiring decodes it.

8111.w: Add a control unit that fetches the next instruction, points the ALU at the right operands, files the result and moves on. Fetch and execute, over and over — that loop is the whole processor.

8112.w: Nobody can write raw opcodes all day. Give each instruction a short mnemonic and each address a label, then let a program do the substitution. Kathleen Booth co-wrote the first one in the late 1940s.

8113.w: Assembly still names the machine's own instructions, one for one. Write the method in a language of its own and have a program translate it down instead — so the algorithm outlives the machine it ran on.

8114.w: A compiler can only translate what it can parse, so the language needs a formal grammar — every legal program spelled out by rules. Fix the grammar and people write readably while the machine still gets its numbers.

8115.w: When every job needs loading, compiling and running by hand, the operator is the slowest part. GM-NAA I/O, built for the IBM 704 in 1956, read the next job in and ran it itself — software minding the machine.

8116.w: A reel of tape is just bytes in a row, found by counting. Give a run of them a name and a length and it becomes a thing you can ask for, without knowing where on the reel it actually sits.

8117.w: One name is easy to keep track of; ten thousand are not. The operating system keeps a table of names against the blocks holding them, and hands out files while nobody else thinks about the disk.

8118.w: Files hold bytes; they answer no questions. Codd's relational model holds data as relations and defines an algebra of operations over them, so you state what you want and the system works out how to fetch it.

8119.w: Bouchon in 1725 and Falcon in 1728 drove a loom from punched paper: a hole or no hole at each fixed position, read by a row of pins. Information became a physical pattern you could hand to a machine.

8120.w: Jacquard's 1804 machine laced the cards into a continuous chain, one complete card per row of the pattern. The design now lived on the cards, so new cloth meant new cards, not a new loom.

8121.w: Hollerith punched facts about people onto cards instead of patterns for cloth. A pin dropping through a hole closes a circuit and steps a counter, so a whole census could be summed electrically.

8122.w: Turing stripped an algorithm down to the least a machine could possibly need: a strip of tape, one symbol under the head, and a finite table of rules. Anything computable at all is computable on it.

8123.w: Simply wait. Gordon Moore noticed in 1965 that components per integrated circuit kept doubling, and later revised the interval to about two years. It describes an industry's learning curve, not physics.

8124.w: A photosite's charge becomes a number, and that number is one sample of light at one point. Arrange the samples in a grid and the picture is addressable: any point can be named and changed.

8125.w: Set aside a block of memory with one number per pixel and wire it to be read out continuously to a screen. Whatever is written there appears: the picture and the memory become the same object.

8126.w: Movable type held each letter as a shape cast on a slug of metal. A digital font holds the same glyphs as data — a grid of pixels, or outlines to fill — so one file replaces a whole case of sorts.

8127.w: Cut the image into 8x8 blocks and express each as cosine frequencies (Ahmed's 1972 transform). Keep the coarse ones, throw away the fine, and the file shrinks about tenfold. Standardised in 1992.

8128.w: Divide a register's bits into three fields: sign, exponent and significand. The point floats with the exponent, so the same 32 bits reach the enormous and the minute. IEEE 754 fixed the layout in 1985.

8129.w: Add the bytes of a block together and send the total alongside them. Recompute it at the far end: if the two disagree, something was corrupted in transit or in storage, and the block is not to be trusted.

8130.w: A checksum only says that something broke. Hamming, in 1950, spread check bits over overlapping subsets of the message, so the pattern of failing checks spells out the number of the wrong bit — flip it back.

8131.w: Lease telephone lines between computers, give each machine an address, and data can move without a person carrying it. ARPANET, built this way, was the first wide-area packet-switched network.

8132.w: Do not hold a line open for a whole file. Cut it into short pieces, each with a header giving source and destination, and let them find their own way independently — Baran at RAND and Davies at the NPL, in the 1960s.

8133.w: Packets are useless unless both ends agree where the address sits, what each field means, when to speak and what to do when one goes missing. That whole agreement, written down, is the protocol.

8134.w: A packet needs somewhere to go. Give every network interface a number: IPv4 uses 32 bits, which is four bytes — which is why they are written as four numbers separated by dots.

8135.w: IP delivers a packet to an address and promises nothing else. TCP numbers the bytes, checksums them, and asks again for whatever never arrived — so the application sees one reliable ordered stream.

8136.w: Nobody remembers a four-number address. DNS lets machines be named in words instead, and a hierarchy of servers — one level per dot — translates the name into the address before the packet leaves.

8137.w: Combine three things in one string: which protocol to speak, which machine to ask for by name, and the path to the file on it. Now any document anywhere can be pointed at from anywhere else.

8138.w: A URL says what you want; HTTP is the protocol for asking. The client opens a connection, sends a request naming the resource, and the server returns one response. Simple enough that anything can serve.

8139.w: Keep the document as plain characters and put the structure in the same stream: mark this a heading, that a paragraph, this other a link to another document. Text and its wiring travel as one file.

8140.w: One program that speaks HTTP to fetch whatever a URL names, parses the HTML for its structure, and draws the result. Every document on every server, through a single window.

8141.w: Put a computer on the network whose only work is answering requests from others for data, resources or computation. The machines that ask become clients, and one server can serve many of them.

8142.w: Give every station one shared cable rather than a link to each neighbour. A station listens first, transmits, and if it hears a collision it stops and retries after a random wait. Standardised as IEEE 802.3.

8143.w: A telephone line carries sound, not bits. Modulate the bits onto audio tones to send and demodulate them at the far end — AT&T's Bell 103, 1963, managed 300 bits per second over an ordinary line.

8144.w: Fix a rule for replacing each letter, and a key that decides which replacement. The rule can be published; only the key needs guarding — which is what makes a cipher different from a secret alphabet.

8145.w: Once the message is bits, enciphering becomes arithmetic: combine each bit with a bit of key. Vernam did exactly this in 1917, and with a truly random key as long as the message it cannot be broken.

8146.w: Write out the counting numbers, then strike out every multiple of two, of three, of five, and so on. What survives has no smaller factors. Eratosthenes' sieve is among the oldest algorithms there is.

8147.w: Multiplying two large primes is easy; recovering them from the product is not. That one-way gap lets you hand out a key for locking while keeping the key that unlocks. Diffie and Hellman 1976, RSA 1977.

8148.w: A checksum catches accidents but not liars. Harden the same idea so that reversing it, or finding two inputs that agree, is infeasible, and a short fingerprint becomes evidence about the data behind it.

8149.w: Hash the document, then encrypt the hash with your private key. Anyone can decrypt it with your public key and hash the document themselves: matching hashes prove both the author and that nothing changed.

8150.w: Keep the typewriter's key arrangement but put an electrical switch under each key instead of a lever and a typebar. Which switch closed becomes a number, and the number is the character.

8151.w: How much can a noisy line carry? Nyquist and Hartley asked it of telegraphy in the 1920s; Shannon answered in the 1940s, in bits per second, and proved every channel has a hard capacity you cannot exceed.

8152.w: A halophyte is defined by tolerance, not by address: a plant that can grow in soil or water of high salinity. Only about 2% of plant species manage it — everything else is a glycophyte and dies there.

8153.w: Resin is a stem secretion, mostly terpenes, that a conifer pushes into a wound. Cut the bark and it bleeds. Sap and latex are different fluids doing different jobs; only resin sets hard.

8154.w: A thorn is a whole shoot that gave up on being a branch: it arises from a bud, keeps vascular tissue inside, and lignifies to a point. A spine is a modified leaf; a prickle is only epidermis.

8155.w: In a berry the whole fruit wall ripens into fleshy parenchyma with the seeds embedded in it. The endocarp is what separates it from a drupe: a drupe hardens that inner layer into a stone.

8156.w: A berry comes from a single flower with one ovary, whose wall becomes flesh rather than stone. Grapes, tomatoes, bananas, kiwifruit and persimmons all qualify; strawberries and raspberries do not.

8157.w: Aerenchyma is parenchyma turned to sponge: gas-filled channels that give oxygen a low-resistance path from shoot to submerged root. Some of it leaks out of the root pores into the mud around them.

8158.w: Take the oxygen away and the plant builds its own airway. Low oxygen makes it produce ethylene, and cortical parenchyma cells then die and lyse on purpose, leaving lysigenous cavities behind.

8159.w: Isoprene comes off a sunlit leaf, and emission climbs steeply with leaf temperature to a peak near 40 °C. Oaks and poplars are the great emitters: in a deciduous forest isoprene is about 80% of the hydrocarbons in the air.

8160.w: Industrially it is a byproduct of thermally cracking petroleum naphtha — about 800,000 tonnes recovered a year, and 95% of that goes straight back into making cis-1,4-polyisoprene.

8161.w: Polyisoprene is what isoprene becomes when it is polymerised — anionically with n-butyllithium, or by coordination over a Ziegler–Natta catalyst.

8162.w: The monomer chains to itself, thousands of units long. Natural rubber is that same chain in the cis-1,4 arrangement, and it is about 99.99% of what comes out of the tree.

8163.w: Rubber is the polymer cis-1,4-polyisoprene, whether a tree made it or a reactor did, and sulfur cross-links the chains the same way either way — around 10% by weight at the optimum.

8164.w: The category, not any one member: an artificial elastomer polymerised from petroleum monomers rather than tapped from a tree. Fritz Hofmann made the first in 1909; two thirds of US rubber is now synthetic.

8165.w: Carbon black is made on purpose: petroleum feedstock — fuel oil, cracking tar — burned in a deliberately limited supply of air. Unlike soot it has a huge surface area and negligible polycyclic aromatics.

8166.w: Coal tar is the other classic feedstock. Burn it in too little air and what you collect is near-pure carbon: world consumption was 13.2 million tonnes in 2015.

8167.w: Carbon black is the reinforcing filler in tire rubber, and 70% of all carbon black made goes into tires. It is also the reason every tire is black.

8168.w: The tire is forced onto the wheel, bead into the channel between the rims. Most of the rubber is synthetic — styrene-butadiene copolymer alone is about half of it — alongside natural rubber, fabric and wire.

8169.w: Hevea brasiliensis, a eudicot of the spurge family. Its latex vessels spiral up the bark in a right-handed helix; harvesters cut across them just deep enough to bleed the tree without harming it.

8170.w: Mangrove is not a taxon but a habit: salt-tolerant trees that convergent evolution produced separately in several unrelated families — 35 true species in 5 families. The salt tolerance is the definition, not the shore.

8171.w: Adansonia is a stem succulent the size of a tree: the swollen trunk is water-storing tissue holding up to 120,000 litres, which is how it crosses a drought that would kill an ordinary tree.

8172.w: Pinus is the conifer the world taps: turpentine and rosin are both got from its resin. Its needles grow bundled in fascicles, one to seven per sheath and usually two to five.

8173.w: Salix, twice over: it flowers as catkins, male and female on separate trees, and it roots so readily that almost any cutting — or a broken branch left lying on wet ground — becomes a new tree.

8174.w: Illicium verum is the anethole tree. Aniseed and fennel are herbs that converged on the same molecule from unrelated families; only this one is an evergreen tree, and the spice is its whorl of six to eight boat-shaped follicles.

8175.w: Durio is named for its armour — Malay duri, thorn, plus -an — and the rind carries thorns sharp enough to draw blood on a fruit 30 cm long and up to 3 kg. The smell is separate chemistry: diethyl disulfide and relatives.

8176.w: Diospyros kaki is botanically a berry — one fleshy fruit from the ovary of a single flower — and its defining property is soluble tannin: astringent enough to pucker the mouth until ripening turns that tannin insoluble.

8177.w: Actinidia is dioecious: a vine is male or female and never both, so no female sets fruit unless pollen is carried in from a male. Orchards plant one male for every three to eight females.

8178.w: Olea europaea's drupe stores oil in its flesh where other fruit store sugar, which is why it is pressed rather than eaten — and why it is inedibly bitter with oleuropein until it is cured.

8179.w: Vitis: botanically a berry, borne in clusters on a deciduous woody vine. Wine grapes are picked at about 24% sugar by weight, against roughly 15% for the table grapes juice is pressed from.

8180.w: Oryza sativa survives flooding on plumbing, not luck: lysigenous aerenchyma forms in its roots even in air and increases when oxygen runs short, piping oxygen from shoot down to a drowned root tip.

8181.w: Saccharum is a tall perennial grass that banks its sugar in the stalk instead of the seed: 12–16% of a mature cane stalk is soluble sugars, stored in the internodes, on C4 photosynthesis.

8182.w: Agave is a monocot built for drought rather than merely found in it: large succulent, xerophytic rosettes of fibre-packed leaves, each rosette flowering once and then dying.

8183.w: An empire is a state that keeps ruling what it conquers. Rome, the Mongols and the Ottomans all worked the same way: permanent troops annexed the neighbours, who were then governed from the centre as subjects rather than as fellow citizens.

8184.w: War ends in writing. The oldest surviving international treaty, between Ramesses II and Hattusili III around 1259 BCE, survives in Egyptian hieroglyphs at Karnak and in Akkadian cuneiform on clay tablets found at Hattusa.

8185.w: The treaties of Osnabrück and Münster, signed 24 October 1648, ended the Thirty Years' War. By convention they begin the system of states answerable to no higher authority — though historians argue over how much the texts actually say so.

8186.w: Self-determination is the principle; independence is a people exercising it and taking sovereignty. Four waves carried it: the Americas from the 1770s, Europe after 1918, decolonisation after 1945, and the Soviet collapse of the early 1990s.

8187.w: Not a coup and not a riot. A revolution is a rapid, fundamental remaking of a state's institutions, and it needs two things a palace plot does not: mass mobilisation, and action outside the institutions — demonstrations, strikes or force.

8188.w: The document the winners put in place of the government they removed. The United States wrote its constitution in 1787 and it is still the oldest codified one in force; France wrote its first in 1791.

8189.w: A state whose head of state is not born to the job, its powers written down instead of inherited. Europe held 55 monarchies and 9 republics in 1815; by 2015 it held 12 monarchies and 35 republics.

8190.w: The same voting machinery, asked a question instead of asked to pick a representative. Switzerland has run almost 600 national votes since 1848; Italy, the next most frequent user, has run 78.

8191.w: What separates a colonial empire from a land empire is the sea between the ruler and the ruled. European powers held roughly 35% of the world's land in 1800 and about 84% of it by 1914.

8192.w: UN General Assembly Resolution 1514, passed in 1960, declared that colonial rule violated human rights and that independence should be immediate. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies became sovereign states.

8193.w: Ireland in 1920, British India in 1947, Korea, Vietnam, Cyprus: one territory cut in two, so that the new border and the new states arrive on the same day. Brendan O'Leary distinguishes it from secession, which works within existing units.

8194.w: Fichte's argument was that those who speak one language are already bound together; the Grimms collected folk tales to prove it. Twenty-five German states were proclaimed one empire on 18 January 1871 on that reasoning.

8195.w: Uruk, Athens, Venice and the eighty-odd free imperial cities: a walled city that was the whole of its own country and answered to nobody above it. Three sovereign city-states survive — Vatican City, Monaco and Singapore.

8196.w: In 1278 Peter III of Aragon mediated a paréage — a feudal treaty splitting a disputed lordship — between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix. Andorra has had two heads of state ever since.

8197.w: By 1920 it covered 35.5 million km², about 24% of the Earth's land, and in 1913 it ruled some 412 million people, 23% of humanity — the largest empire in history, held together by control of the oceans.

8198.w: Beaten by Prussia in 1866 and close to bankruptcy, Franz Joseph bought Hungarian consent. The Compromise ratified on 29 May 1867 gave one monarch two separate states, each with its own parliament, sharing only foreign affairs, defence and their funding.

8199.w: Masaryk, Beneš and Štefánik argued the Czechoslovak case to the Allies as one of self-determination and won recognition for their National Council; the state was proclaimed on 28 October 1918 as Austria-Hungary collapsed.

8200.w: On 1 December 1918 the South Slav lands of the collapsed Austria-Hungary joined the Kingdom of Serbia as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. King Alexander renamed it Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929.

8201.w: Andorra had two co-princes for 715 years and no constitution. The one approved by referendum on 14 March 1993, with 74.2% in favour, made it a sovereign parliamentary co-principality; it joined the UN the same year.

8202.w: Latvia did not write a new constitution. On 4 May 1990 its Supreme Council readopted articles of the 1922 Satversme, holding that the 1940 annexation was unlawful and the pre-war republic had never ended; restoration completed 21 August 1991.

8203.w: The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 cut the Grand Duchy in two: the French-speaking part became Belgium's Province of Luxembourg, and the remainder became an independent grand duchy. Its personal union with the Dutch crown lapsed in 1890.

8204.w: Hans-Adam I bought Schellenberg in 1699 and Vaduz in 1712 because they owed no lord but the emperor; on 23 January 1719 Charles VI merged them into an imperial principality. The prince owed no suzerain once the Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806.

8205.w: The 1830 rising in Brussels broke the United Kingdom of the Netherlands apart. The Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 recognised Belgium and had five great powers guarantee its neutrality — the guarantee invoked in 1914.

8206.w: Constitutional Act 542, passed on 25 November 1992, agreed the federation's end. Czechoslovakia ceased to exist at midnight on 31 December 1992 and two sovereign states existed from 1 January 1993. No referendum was ever held.

8207.w: The push came from the Slovak side: on 17 July 1992 the Slovak National Council adopted a declaration of the sovereignty of the Slovak nation, and six days earlier Klaus and Mečiar had agreed to split the state.

8208.w: The Treaty of Trianon, signed 4 June 1920, fixed the borders of an independent Hungary after Austria-Hungary dissolved. It left about 28% of the old kingdom's territory and 36% of its people.

8209.w: Yugoslavia's last remnant was renamed the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro on 4 February 2003. When Montenegro left, Serbia's parliament declared the Republic of Serbia its legal successor on 5 June 2006.

8210.w: A referendum on 19 May 1991 authorised the declaration made on 25 June 1991, the same day as Slovenia's. The European Community recognised Croatia on 15 January 1992; the war that followed ran to 1995.

8211.w: In the plebiscite of 23 December 1990, 88.5% of the electorate voted to leave. Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991 and secured it in the Ten-Day War.

8212.w: Recognised on 6 April 1992 after a referendum, then fought over for three and a half years. The agreement negotiated at Dayton, Ohio in November 1995 carries the country's constitution as its Annex 4, still in force.

8213.w: On 21 May 2006, 55.5% voted to leave the state union on an 86.5% turnout — just over the 55% threshold the EU had set. Parliament declared independence on 3 June 2006.

8214.w: It voted to leave Yugoslavia on 8 September 1991 and left without fighting. The Prespa Agreement with Greece, signed 17 June 2018, settled the naming dispute; the name North Macedonia took effect on 12 February 2019.

8215.w: Forty delegates under Ismail Kemal declared independence at Vlorë on 28 November 1912, as Ottoman rule collapsed in the First Balkan War. The London Conference of Ambassadors recognised Albania de facto on 17 December 1912.

8216.w: The Treaty of Berlin of 1878 made Bulgaria an autonomous principality still under Ottoman suzerainty. Prince Ferdinand declared full independence at Tarnovo on 5 October 1908; the powers recognised it by spring 1909.

8217.w: Moldavia and Wallachia exploited a drafting gap and elected the same prince, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, in 1859; on 3 February 1862 they merged as Romania. The Congress of Berlin recognised independence from the Ottomans in 1878.

8218.w: On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Council voted 124 to 0, with six abstentions, that the sovereign powers abolished in 1940 were re-established. Lithuania was the first of the fifteen Soviet republics to declare independence.

8219.w: On 16 November 1988 Estonia declared its own laws supreme over Soviet law and claimed its resources — the first union republic to declare state sovereignty. Full independence was restored on 20 August 1991.

8220.w: On 1 December 1991, 92.3% of voters backed the independence act on an 84.2% turnout. A week later Ukraine, Russia and Belarus signed the accords declaring the USSR had ceased to exist.

8221.w: The Belovezha Accords were signed on 8 December 1991 at Viskuli, a hunting lodge in the Belovezhskaya Pushcha in Belarus. Shushkevich, Yeltsin and Kravchuk declared the USSR was ceasing to exist.

8222.w: The independence movement began with a language law: on 31 August 1989 the republic made Moldovan in the Latin script its state language and declared it identical with Romanian. Independence was declared on 27 August 1991.

8223.w: The last of the fifteen union republics to declare independence, on 16 December 1991. Five days later Alma-Ata hosted the protocol at which eleven republics jointly declared the USSR at an end.

8224.w: Menton and Roquebrune were about 95% of Monaco's territory and wanted out. Charles III ceded them to France for compensation, and the Franco-Monégasque Treaty of 1861 recognised his sovereignty over the 2 km² that remained.

8225.w: A commune on Monte Titano that never joined Italy. Its Statutes of 1600 are the earliest written governing documents still in force, and a treaty of friendship with the new Kingdom of Italy in 1862 confirmed its independence.

8226.w: The only state founded by a successful revolt of the enslaved. The insurrection that began in 1791 destroyed French Saint-Domingue, and Dessalines declared independence on 1 January 1804.

8227.w: Duarte's Trinitaria seized the Puerta del Conde in Santo Domingo on 27 February 1844, ending 22 years of Haitian rule over the whole island. Spain re-annexed the country in 1861 and the Restoration War won it back by 1865.

8228.w: The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and India became a sovereign dominion on 15 August. It replaced the Act with its own constitution on 26 January 1950.

8229.w: The same 1947 Act partitioned British India into two dominions and cut Bengal and Punjab in half to do it. Pakistan's independence day is 14 August 1947; its eastern wing became Bangladesh in 1971.

8230.w: East Pakistan declared independence on 26 March 1971; Pakistani forces surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December after nine months of war. Pakistan itself recognised Bangladesh in 1974.

8231.w: The Soulbury constitution gave Ceylon dominion status and independence was proclaimed on 4 February 1948, six months after India's. It became a republic and took the name Sri Lanka in 1972.

8232.w: The Federation of Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957. On 16 September 1963 it merged with three British colonies — Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo — to form Malaysia.

8233.w: Two years after joining, Singapore left. The Malaysian parliament passed the separation bill 126 votes to nil on 9 August 1965, and Singapore became a sovereign state that day.

8234.w: A Portuguese colony until 1975 and then under Indonesian rule. In a UN-run popular consultation on 30 August 1999, 78.5% chose independence on a 98.9% turnout; sovereignty was restored on 20 May 2002.

8235.w: A monocot germinates with a single seed leaf. Parallel veins, vascular bundles scattered through the stem rather than set in a ring, flower parts in threes — over 70,000 species, some 25,000 of them orchids.

8236.w: The eudicots were called tricolpates first, for pollen grains with three furrows where every other seed plant has one. Two seed leaves, netted veins, and over 70% of all flowering-plant species.

8237.w: The first plants to wrap an embryo in a seed instead of casting a spore. The ovule sits naked on a scale or a leaf with no ovary around it — over 1,000 living species, nearly all of them conifers and cycads.

8238.w: Club fungi are named for the basidium, which buds its spores on the outside rather than shutting them in a sac — 31,515 described species: mushrooms, boletes, puffballs, brackets, and the rusts and smuts.

8239.w: Ophiuroidea, not a sea star: the disc is sharply cut off from the arms and no organ reaches into them. It hides under rocks, rows along on snake-like arms, and sheds one to a predator rather than be held.

8240.w: Holothuroidea: an echinoderm gone long and leathery, grubbing through seabed mud on tube feet. Some reef species fire sticky Cuvierian tubules out of the anus to snare a predator, and regrow them within weeks.

8241.w: Crinoidea is the oldest echinoderm class, back about 480 million years, and only some 700 species survive. A feather star grips the reef with claw-like cirri and strains plankton from the current with feathered arms.

8242.w: Pycnogonida is not a spider and not even an arachnid — its own chelicerate class, over 1,300 species. The trunk is too small to hold the animal, so gut and gonads branch into the legs, which absorb oxygen straight through the cuticle.

8243.w: One of about 116 species of Sepiida, cousin to octopus and squid. It trims the gas-to-liquid ratio inside the chambered cuttlebone to hold almost any depth, and its W-shaped pupil reads polarised light rather than colour.

8244.w: Every fern frond comes up tightly coiled — circinate vernation — and is cut at that stage or not at all. Ostrich fern is the one usually eaten; bracken fiddleheads carry ptaquiloside, a carcinogen.

8245.w: Ceratosaurus is 'horn lizard': a blade of fused nasal bone about 13 cm long, sheathed in keratin and grooved for blood vessels. Marsh named it in 1884 from a Morrison Formation skeleton dug at Garden Park, Colorado.

8246.w: Peel a mushroom gill and its whole surface is basidia — club-shaped cells, each budding four spores on slender horns called sterigmata and flicking them away with a bead of fluid.

8247.w: The sharks are the elasmobranchs that stayed torpedo-shaped with gill slits on the flank, and they carry the group's teeth to its extreme — rows of replacements lying flat behind the working row, rotating forward as teeth are lost, for thousands over a lifetime.

8248.w: The shortfin mako is a lamnid, one of the few sharks that keeps its swimming muscle warmer than the sea using a rete mirabile — a countercurrent mesh of blood vessels that traps muscle heat instead of losing it at the gills. Warm muscle contracts faster, and the mako is the fastest shark measured.

8249.w: A lamnid shark of the subarctic North Pacific that holds its core 8 to 11 degrees Celsius above the water around it — the widest gap of any shark — which is what lets it hunt in seas near freezing.

8250.w: Named for the dark vertical bars along its flanks, strongest in young animals and fading with age, which break up its outline against dappled water.

8251.w: A shark of the open ocean rather than the coast, ranging the warm surface layer far from land on very long, rounded, white-tipped pectoral fins that let it glide slowly over huge distances between meals.

8252.w: Named for its skin. Shark scales are dermal denticles, tooth-like and normally rough enough to abrade; the silky shark's are unusually small, flat and tightly packed, so the hide feels smooth to the hand.

8253.w: A slender reef shark that spends the day resting in caves and under coral ledges — unusual among sharks, most of which must keep moving to pass water over the gills — and hunts through the reef at night.

8254.w: A bottom-dwelling shark with a pair of fleshy barbels hanging beside the nostrils, used to taste and feel for prey buried in sand, which it then draws out by expanding its throat into a suction pump.

8255.w: The largest fish alive, and a filter feeder. It swims with its mouth open or pumps water through it, straining plankton and small fish on twenty pads of fine mesh across the throat.

8256.w: A ray that left the sea floor for open water, flying on its disc rather than resting on it, and feeds by funnelling plankton into its mouth with two unrolled head fins and straining it through mesh plates in the gills.

8257.w: The largest bony fish on coral reefs, reaching about 2.7 metres. It hunts by opening its very large mouth fast enough that the drop in pressure pulls prey in whole.

8258.w: A lionfish is a scorpionfish, and carries the family's grooved venomous spines — thirteen dorsal, three anal, two pelvic. What sets it apart from its relatives is that it does not lie camouflaged on the bottom: it hovers in the open over the reef, fins spread, and herds small fish with them.

8259.w: A South American river fish with a single row of triangular blade-like teeth that interlock when the jaw closes, so the bite shears rather than grips.

8260.w: A bottom-feeding freshwater fish with two pairs of barbels at the mouth, the longer pair at the corners, which it uses to find food by touch and taste in water too silty to see through.

8261.w: Europe's largest freshwater fish, and scaleless — the skin is bare and heavily coated in mucus, which is where the slipperiness of a catfish comes from.

8262.w: A large predatory fish of the Nile and the rivers and lakes of tropical Africa, reaching about two metres. Introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, where it drove much of the lake's cichlid fauna to extinction.

8263.w: It lives among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone, which kill other small fish. A mucus coat lets it move through them unstung; it gets shelter, and the anemone gets a defender and its waste as fertiliser.

8264.w: The only known cephalopod that does not hunt living prey. It lives in the oxygen minimum zone and streams out a long sticky filament to gather marine snow — sinking flakes of dead plankton and faecal matter — which it wipes off and eats.

8265.w: A wolf-sized four-legged mammal from Eocene Pakistan that lived beside fresh water and is counted the earliest known whale — not from its shape but from its ear, whose thickened involucrum bone is found in whales and in nothing else.

8266.w: A large plant-eating dinosaur that cropped with a horny beak at the front of the jaw and ground with packed rows of cheek teeth behind it. It also carried a conical spike in place of a thumb, which Mantell's first reconstruction put on the nose as a horn.

8267.w: A wingless insect flattened side to side so it can run between the hairs of a mammal, with hind legs that store energy in a pad of resilin and release it to jump many times its own length, and mouthparts that pierce skin to drink blood.

8268.w: Sharks, rays and skates are the vertebrates whose skeleton never turns to bone. It stays cartilage for life, stiffened at the jaws and spine with a crust of mineral prisms rather than replaced, which is lighter than bone and helps hold a body heavier than water off the bottom.

8269.w: The rays are the elasmobranchs that went flat to live on the bottom: the body is pressed dorsoventrally, the pectoral fins have grown forward and fused to the head into a disc, and the gill slits have moved to the underside.

8270.w: A thyreophoran dinosaur carrying two staggered rows of tall bony plates down its back. They were not armour — thin, and threaded with blood vessels — so they are read as display or heat exchange, with the defence left to four tail spikes.

8271.w: A dinosaur whose skull roof thickened into a dome of solid bone up to 25 centimetres deep, ringed with knobs and short spikes, over a body otherwise built like any other two-legged plant-eater.

8272.w: The myriapods that gave up hunting for leaf litter. Their trunk segments are fused in pairs, so each apparent segment carries two pairs of legs rather than one — many short legs pushing a body built to burrow rather than to chase.

8273.w: A vascular plant that never evolved seeds. It scatters spores from the underside of its fronds, and those grow into a separate tiny plant that makes the egg and sperm, so the fern alternates between two independent generations.

8274.w: The oldest surviving lineage of vascular plants. Despite the name it is not a moss: it has xylem to carry water up a stem, true roots, and small single-veined leaves, all of which the mosses lack.

8275.w: The largest nematode of poultry, reaching about 12 centimetres in the small intestine of a chicken. Birds pick it up by swallowing eggs that have matured in the litter.

8276.w: The pinworm, and the commonest human worm in temperate countries. Humans are its only host. The female leaves the gut at night to lay her eggs on the skin around the anus, which is what makes the infection itch and how it spreads.

8277.w: A thread-thin nematode whose adults live in the lymphatic vessels. Its larvae circulate in the blood mostly at night, timed to when the mosquito that carries them between people is biting.

8278.w: A wingless insect found on no animal but us, with claws curved to exactly the diameter of a human hair so it can grip the shaft, and mouthparts that pierce the scalp to drink blood.
