8279.w: The same species as the head louse, living in the seams of clothing and moving onto the skin only to feed. Because it cannot exist without clothes, dating the split between the two gives an estimate of when people began wearing them.

8280.w: A mite under half a millimetre long. The female tunnels into the outer layer of the skin and lays her eggs along the burrow; the itch is an allergic reaction to the mite and its waste, and takes weeks to begin.

8281.w: A true bug, flattened side to side and about the size of an apple pip, which spends the day in seams and crevices near where people sleep and feeds on blood at night.

8282.w: A barnacle that settles on nothing but whale skin, growing its plates down into it so it cannot be shed. It never has to search for food: the whale swims, and the water brings it.

8283.w: The parasitic flukes. Almost every one of them passes through a snail first, where a single larva multiplies into many before moving on to its next host.

8284.w: A marine mammal with no blubber at all. It stays warm on fur alone, the densest of any animal at up to a million hairs per square inch, which traps a layer of air against the skin.

8285.w: A theropod with a long narrow crocodile-like snout and conical unserrated teeth, unlike the blades of other big predators. The first skeleton found had scales of the fish Scheenstia in its gut.

8286.w: Known for fifty years from nothing but a pair of arms 2.4 metres long, which is how it got its name, the horrible hand. Skeletons described in 2014 showed a large humped ornithomimosaur with a duck-like bill.

8287.w: Named the egg seizer from a skeleton found lying on a nest, assumed to have been raiding it. An embryo found inside the same kind of egg in the 1990s showed the eggs were its own and it had been sitting on them.

8288.w: A small feathered dinosaur with long asymmetric flight feathers on its hind limbs as well as its arms, giving it four wing surfaces rather than two.

8289.w: A bird that fishes with a throat pouch of bare skin slung under a long bill, using it as a net; it drains the water out at the surface before swallowing.

8290.w: An ash-grey bird found wild only in the forests of New Caledonia. It has wings large enough to display but not to fly, and nasal flaps covering its nostrils that no other bird has.

8291.w: An amphibian that gave up its legs for burrowing. It drives a bone-reinforced skull through soil, its eyes are covered by skin or bone, and it finds its way with a chemical-sensing tentacle between eye and nostril.

8292.w: One of the few mammals that lays eggs, and covered in spines that are not a separate structure at all but single hairs thickened with keratin.

8293.w: The only mammal with true scales: overlapping plates of keratin, the same material as a fingernail, covering everything but the belly. It rolls into a ball that a lion cannot open.

8294.w: An American marsupial whose blood carries a protein that neutralises snake venom, letting it survive bites that would kill an animal its size. It is also the animal that plays dead, an involuntary collapse rather than a decision.

8295.w: A marsupial that eats nothing but termites, up to twenty thousand a day, gathered on a tongue longer than its own head. Unusually for an Australian marsupial it is active only by day, because that is when termites are near the surface.

8296.w: An insect with a waist so narrow the abdomen hangs from a stalk, and a sting that is a modified egg-laying tube — which is why only females have one.

8297.w: A small African mammal with a long flexible snout it swings to sniff out insects. Despite looking like a shrew it belongs with elephants and aardvarks, and it keeps a network of cleared trails it can sprint along.

8298.w: A tall yellow-flowered daisy grown for its thick root, which stores its carbohydrate as inulin rather than starch — the substance was first isolated from this plant, and is named after it.

8299.w: A Swedish province for six centuries, then an autonomous Grand Duchy under the Russian tsar from 1809. It declared independence in December 1917, weeks after the Russian empire it belonged to collapsed.

8300.w: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, drawn together on the Jutland peninsula and the islands east of it during the Viking age. The Jelling stone raised by Harald Bluetooth about 965 is the first thing to call the place Denmark.

8301.w: The first state in the world to adopt Christianity, in 301. Absorbed by the Russian empire and then the Soviet Union, and independent again in 1991. Ararat, the mountain on its coat of arms, has stood over the border in Turkey since 1921.

8302.w: Baku was pumping about half the world's oil by 1900, which is why the Soviet Union held the region so tightly and why the German army drove for it in 1942. Independent in 1991.

8303.w: The newest country in the world. After two long civil wars, a 2011 referendum in the south of Sudan returned 98.8 per cent for separation, and it became independent that July.

8304.w: An Italian colony, then federated to Ethiopia and annexed by it. Thirty years of war ended in a 1993 referendum in which almost everyone voted to leave, taking Ethiopia's entire coastline with them.

8305.w: French Somaliland until 1977, held for its position on the Bab-el-Mandeb, the strait every ship between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean must pass through.

8306.w: Made in 1960 by joining two colonies that became independent five days apart: British Somaliland in the north and Italian Somaliland, which Italy had continued to administer under a UN trusteeship.

8307.w: A British protectorate from 1894 to 1962, assembled around the kingdom of Buganda and around Lake Victoria, where the White Nile begins.

8308.w: Half of Ruanda-Urundi, a German colony taken by Belgium after the First World War and split in two at independence in 1962. It sits on the western branch of the Great Rift Valley.

8309.w: The British protectorate of Nyasaland until 1964, named for the lake that fills the southern end of the rift and takes up a fifth of the country.

8310.w: Southern Rhodesia, run from London and then by a white settler government that declared its own independence in 1965; majority rule came in 1980. It takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, a dry-stone city built without mortar.

8311.w: Portuguese East Africa for nearly five centuries, a base on the sea route to India, until a ten-year war and the 1974 revolution in Lisbon ended the empire.

8312.w: A kingdom that survived colonisation as a British protectorate and came out of it in 1968 still a monarchy. It changed its name from Swaziland in 2018.

8313.w: Basutoland, which asked for British protection in 1868 to avoid being swallowed by its neighbour, and is now the only country lying entirely above 1,000 metres.

8314.w: A French colony until 1975, and a chain of volcanic islands; Karthala on the largest is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.

8315.w: Spanish Guinea until 1968, and the only sovereign African state where Spanish is official. Its capital stands not on the mainland but on a volcanic island 200 kilometres offshore.

8316.w: German Kamerun, divided between France and Britain after the First World War and reunited at independence in 1960. Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, is the highest point in West Africa.

8317.w: Ubangi-Shari, a French territory of savanna between the Sahel and the rainforest, independent in 1960.

8318.w: A French territory until 1960, stretching from the deep Sahara in the north to the lake in the south that gives it its name — a lake that has lost most of its area since the 1960s.

8319.w: French until 1960, named for the river that clips its south-western corner. Uranium found at Arlit in the 1960s became most of what it sells abroad.

8320.w: Upper Volta under France, named for the three rivers that rise in it, until it renamed itself in 1984 Burkina Faso — the land of upright people.

8321.w: German Togoland, split between Britain and France after the First World War; the French part became Togo in 1960. Phosphate rock is its main export.

8322.w: Dahomey under France, and before that a kingdom powerful enough to field a regiment of women soldiers. It took the name Benin in 1975 from the bight it faces.

8323.w: French until 1960, and named for the Mauri, the Berber people of the Roman province of Mauretania. Its iron ore leaves on a train more than two kilometres long.

8324.w: A British colony until 1965, and barely a country at all in shape: a strip of land following the Gambia river inland, nowhere much wider than the valley itself.

8325.w: Portuguese Guinea, which won its independence in 1974 after a war that helped bring down the government in Lisbon. Its coast is a maze of mangrove and tidal creeks.

8326.w: A British colony from 1808, founded as a settlement for freed slaves. The name is Portuguese, Serra Leoa, the lion mountains — for the hills behind Freetown, or the thunder over them.

8327.w: Settled from 1822 by free-born and formerly enslaved Black Americans, and a republic from 1847 — the only country in Africa never brought under European colonial rule.

8328.w: An Italian colony from 1911, then under British and French administration, and in 1951 the first country to become independent through the United Nations. Nine-tenths of it is desert.

8329.w: English from 1627 and British until 1966, and the island where the plantation and its slave code were worked out before being carried across the Caribbean.

8330.w: Spanish, then British from 1797, and independent in 1962. Its Pitch Lake is the largest natural asphalt deposit on earth, and oil and gas still pay for the country.

8331.w: Thirteen British colonies that declared independence in 1776 and won it by 1783.

8332.w: Under Ottoman rule for four centuries, then a French mandate from 1920, and independent in 1946. Damascus had been the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, which ruled from Spain to the Indus.

8333.w: Transjordan, carved out of the British mandate east of the river in 1921 and independent in 1946. Four-fifths of it is desert.

8334.w: A British protectorate from 1899 to 1961, and one of the first Gulf states where oil was found in commercial quantity, at Burgan in 1938.

8335.w: A peninsula under British protection until 1971, and the holder of a third of the world's proven natural gas after the North Field was found offshore in 1971.

8336.w: Seven emirates known as the Trucial States, for the truces they signed with Britain in the nineteenth century to end raiding at sea. They federated as one country in 1971 when Britain withdrew.

8337.w: Contested by the Ottomans for centuries, and the country that first cultivated coffee for export — the drink is named for Mocha, the Yemeni port it shipped from.

8338.w: Burma, annexed to British India in three wars and independent in 1948, renamed Myanmar in 1989. The Mogok valley has produced most of the world's finest rubies.

8339.w: A Soviet republic until 1991, and the most mountainous country in central Asia; the Fedchenko glacier in the Pamirs is the longest outside the polar regions.

8340.w: A Soviet republic until 1991. The Karakum desert covers about four-fifths of it, and a gas crater at Darvaza has been alight since Soviet geologists set it burning.

8341.w: A French colony from 1897 to 1960. It broke from Africa about 88 million years ago and its wildlife evolved alone: most of what lives there lives nowhere else.

8342.w: Sawing a log lengthways rather than splitting it along the grain is what gives a flat board of even thickness, and it is the step that turns a tree into a building material.

8343.w: A blade is not cast to shape. Steel is worked flat and then ground away on one or both sides until the edge is a few thousandths of a millimetre thick, which is what lets it wedge material apart.

8344.w: Cut and shaped from a plank so the grain runs the length of it — across the grain and it snaps at the first hard pull, which is why an axe handle is split along the wood rather than sawn across it.

8345.w: A modern pole is steel tube rather than solid bar: a hollow section resists bending almost as well as a solid one of the same outside width while using a fraction of the metal, and it is galvanised so the inside does not rust out of sight.

8346.w: Ground from coloured rock and earth — ochre, malachite, cinnabar. A pigment is insoluble, so unlike a dye it sits in the film rather than staining the fibre, and the grinding is what makes the particles small enough to hold an even colour.

8347.w: Pigment alone is a powder that brushes off. Suspended in a drying oil it can be spread thin, and the oil then hardens by taking up oxygen from the air rather than by evaporating, leaving the colour bound in a tough film.

8348.w: Bare wire can only be strung through air on insulators. Sheathing it in rubber lets conductors run side by side, be buried, and be handled — which is the difference between a telegraph line and wiring a building.

8349.w: Metal squeezed between rollers or beaten flat comes out far thinner than it can be cast, and the working hardens it as it goes. A folded edge then makes it far stiffer than the flat sheet — which is why almost everything made from it has a lip.

8350.w: Wire mesh is genuinely woven, on a loom built for metal rather than thread — warp wires held under tension while weft wires are driven across them.

8351.w: A road sheds water sideways because it is built with a camber, and the drain is where that water leaves. Below it sits a trap holding a plug of water, so the sewer's air cannot come back up.

8352.w: A pavement is the road's surface repeated at a different level: the same made ground, laid in slabs or poured, but held above the carriageway so that water, and traffic, run past rather than across it.

8353.w: A kerb is a retaining wall a hand's width tall. It stops the made-up pavement spreading sideways under load, and its face forms one side of the channel that carries surface water to the nearest drain.

8354.w: The first was set outside the Palace of Westminster in 1868, gas-lit and worked by a policeman with a lever; it exploded within a month. The colours were taken from railway signalling, which had already settled on red for stop.

8355.w: Lighting the street rather than the doorway is what a pole buys: raising the lamp spreads its light over a long stretch of road instead of a pool at the foot of a wall, so far fewer are needed to light a whole street.

8356.w: It works by being immovable rather than by being seen: most of a bollard is below ground, set in a concrete foundation deep enough that a vehicle striking it stops rather than pushes it over.

8357.w: The stripes are the whole mechanism: nothing is built, only painted, and the pattern reads at a distance and at a glance from a moving vehicle. Britain's striped version was trialled in 1949 and named the zebra.

8358.w: Shape carries meaning before the words do — a triangle warns, a circle orders, a rectangle informs — so a sign can be understood at speed, in a language the driver may not read. The 1968 Vienna Convention settled much of it internationally.

8359.w: The cover is cast iron and heavy on purpose: weight alone holds it down under traffic without a fastening, so it can still be lifted by one person with a bar. Round is the shape that cannot fall through its own hole.

8360.w: Public bins are often open mesh rather than solid, so that what is inside can be seen at a glance — a precaution against concealment adopted widely after bombings in British and Irish cities.

8361.w: It only works once postage is paid by the sender. Before the stamp, letters were paid for on delivery and had to be handed to someone; a box that anyone can post into unattended is what the prepaid stamp made possible, in Britain from 1852.

8362.w: The body is pressed from a single disc of sheet metal so there is no seam to fail, and the handle is set out on a thin stalk — the narrower the bridge, the less heat crosses it, which is why a pan handle can be held while the pan is boiling.

8363.w: The holes are punched rather than drilled, so each one leaves a slightly raised rim on the outside; that is also why a colander stands on a foot, keeping the holes clear of whatever has just drained through them.

8364.w: A sieve sorts purely by size, which is why the same tool sifts flour, strains stock and grades sand. Mesh is counted in wires per inch, so a higher number means a finer sieve.

8365.w: The wires do not mix so much as tear the liquid apart and drag air in behind them. More loops means more edges doing that at once, which is why a balloon whisk beats egg white faster than a fork.

8366.w: Each hole is punched and its lip left standing proud, so the sheet carries hundreds of tiny raised cutting edges. The sharpest modern kind came from a woodworking rasp: a photo-etched blade a cook borrowed from a hardware shop.

8367.w: The slot is what makes it a peeler rather than a knife: the blade floats and follows the surface, so the cut stays the same thin depth over a curve instead of digging in.

8368.w: Wood closes back around a cut, which both spares the edge and gives bacteria less to sit in than a scored plastic surface. It is oiled rather than varnished so it takes up oil instead of water.

8369.w: The helix does not bite into the cork so much as thread through it, spreading the pull along its whole length so the cork comes out in one piece. Samuel Henshall patented the first improvement in 1795, a disc that stops the worm going too deep.

8370.w: The bowl is set at an angle to the handle so it stays level as the arm swings, and the handle is long enough to reach the bottom of a stockpot without putting a hand over the steam.

8371.w: Flexibility is the whole point: the blade bends to the shape of the pan or bowl so it can get under something without breaking it, or clear the sides of a bowl in one pass.

8372.w: Weight does the work rather than force, which is why it is solid wood. The French kind has no handles at all: rolling with the palms on the pin itself gives more feel for where the dough is still thick.

8373.w: A mainspring stores the energy and a train of gears steps it down, but neither keeps time. The escapement does: it lets the train advance by exactly one tooth per swing of the oscillator, which is also what makes the ticking.

8374.w: The flutes are the whole trick. Standing on edge between two liners they act as a row of tiny arches, so the board resists a load far out of proportion to its weight — and collapses at once if the flutes are crushed.

8375.w: It does two unrelated jobs at once: the straight edge guides a pen, and the graduations measure. Only the first needs it to be straight, which is why a bent ruler still measures correctly and still draws badly.

8376.w: The fold is what fastens it, not the puncture. A small anvil under the paper turns the legs inward as they come through, so the staple closes on itself; turn the anvil round and it clinches outward instead, for a staple meant to be pulled out again.

8377.w: Nothing is fastened and nothing is pierced: the wire is sprung slightly open by the paper and the grip is it trying to close again. The familiar double-oval shape is the Gem pattern, made in Britain from the 1890s.

8378.w: Sheets are folded into sections and sewn through the fold, section to section. A sewn book opens flat because nothing crosses the spine but thread — which is exactly what a glued one cannot do.

8379.w: It is relief printing at hand scale: only the raised parts take ink, so the design must be cut in reverse. Rubber rather than metal because it gives slightly, and so prints evenly onto a surface that is not quite flat.

8380.w: Ordinary ink covers. Highlighter ink is a fluorescent dye in a see-through carrier, so the words read straight through it, and the dye throws back more visible light than falls on it — which is why the colour looks brighter than the paper.

8381.w: The simplest possible container: one fold, no fastening. It works because paper slides out of a stack but not out of a crease, and because the folded edge tells you which way up the contents go.

8382.w: Punched holes and openable rings make the order of the pages a thing you can change afterwards, which a sewn or glued book cannot do. Friedrich Soennecken patented both the ring binder and the hole punch for it, in 1886.

8383.w: The rivet is the whole machine. Because the handles are several times longer than the jaws, the hand's grip arrives at the jaws multiplied by that ratio — which is why a small pair can hold what fingers cannot.

8384.w: Every grain is a tiny cutting edge presented at a random angle, and the grit number is the mesh that graded them — a count of wires per inch of the sieve the grains just fit through, which is why a higher number means finer.

8385.w: The spirit it is named for is ethanol: thin enough to let the bubble move quickly and not liable to freeze. The vial is very slightly curved, so the bubble — being the lightest thing in there — always sits at the highest point of the curve, and reads centre only when the tool is level.

8386.w: It exists because glue needs pressure and time at once. The screw converts a turn into a squeeze and, being a screw, does not undo itself when let go — so the joint can be left overnight.

8387.w: Fixing it to the bench is the difference: a clamp holds two things to each other, a vice holds one thing to the world. That is what lets you file, saw or hammer against it without the work moving.

8388.w: The bend is the point of it. It puts a fulcrum right beside the wedge, so the long bar swings on the short end and the force arriving at the joint is many times what the arm applied.

8389.w: A shelf is only usable at its front edge. Pulling the box out instead turns the whole depth into the front, which is the entire reason for a drawer and why the handle is the only part of it you ever touch.

8390.w: A table becomes a desk when the storage arrives at the sitter rather than the room: drawers under the top put paper, pens and ink within reach of a seated arm.

8391.w: Hanging rather than folding is what the height buys. A folded coat creases along the fold and takes the shape of the pile; hung from the shoulders it keeps the shape it was cut to.

8392.w: Springs under a soft layer do what neither does alone: the springs push back in proportion to how far each is pressed, so a heavy part of the body sinks further and a light part less, and the whole line of the spine stays supported.

8393.w: Lying on one side leaves the head unsupported by the width of a shoulder. The pillow fills exactly that gap, which is why a side sleeper wants a thicker one than someone lying on their back.

8394.w: The pole is the whole invention: it puts the cloth on the floor and the hands at waist height. Strands rather than a sheet because loose ends reach into corners and hold far more water for their weight.

8395.w: A tower is not a tall house. It is built to see from, be seen from, or drop something down, and the stairs are what make the height usable — which is why the stair is often the whole interior.

8396.w: The battery is what makes it a laptop rather than a small desktop: it cuts the last cable, so the machine can be used anywhere rather than merely moved between places with sockets.

8397.w: It turns a grid of numbers back into a physical mark. An inkjet does it by firing droplets a few picolitres at a time, steered to a spot far smaller than the eye resolves, which is why the page looks continuous rather than dotted.

8398.w: The whole image is a grid of pixels, each one three subpixels of red, green and blue lit to different amounts. There is no yellow in the screen: yellow is red and green next to each other, too close for the eye to separate.

8399.w: A coil of wire sits in the field of a permanent magnet and is glued to a paper cone. Current through the coil pushes it along the magnet, the cone moves with it, and the air in front is pressed and released — which is what sound is.

8400.w: Being at the ear rather than across a room changes what is needed: microwatts instead of watts, and each ear hears only its own channel, with none of the crossover that makes a room's stereo image collapse when you move.

8401.w: It is not simply a supply. It must force current backwards through the cell against its own voltage, then taper off as the cell fills — charge too fast at the end and lithium plates out as metal on the anode, which is what ruins a battery.

8402.w: Rails in the road are what separate it from a bus: steel on steel has a fraction of the rolling resistance of rubber on asphalt, so far less power moves the same load, and the vehicle cannot wander from its line.

8403.w: Everything follows from putting a box where the back seats were: a flat floor, a high roof, doors at the side and rear, and windows only where the driver needs them.

8404.w: It began as exactly that — Daimler's 1885 Reitwagen was a wooden bicycle with a petrol engine — but power meant heavier frames, real brakes and wider tyres, because a machine that can reach speed must also be able to stop and to hold the road.

8405.w: Standing rather than sitting is the whole design: one foot stays on the board and the other pushes, so the rider can step off at any moment, which is why it needs no gears, no chain and no seat.

8406.w: It exists because some work has no material to be near. Once the product is paper or numbers rather than cloth or steel, the workplace can be anywhere, and what it is built around is the desk.

8407.w: The building is the easy part. What makes a library is the ordering: without an agreed scheme, a million books and no book are the same thing, which is why every library is really a catalogue with shelves attached.

8408.w: Gaps between the boards are deliberate. They save weight and wood, let the contents be seen and let air through, and the strength comes from the corners rather than the faces.

8409.w: It has to shut. A pocket holds what is put in it only while you are upright; a purse has a fastening, which is what makes it safe to carry loose coins at all.

8410.w: The buttons are what make it outerwear. A coat has to be put on and taken off over other clothes and closed against wind, so it opens all the way down the front — unlike anything worn next to the skin.

8411.w: Stopping at the hip is what it is for: the leg swings freely, so it can be worn to work in rather than only to travel in, and the zip closes it in one movement with one hand.

8412.w: A day is one rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun — which is about four minutes longer than one rotation relative to the stars, because the Earth has also moved along its orbit and must turn a little further to face the Sun again.

8413.w: The Moon takes 27.3 days to go round the Earth, but 29.5 days to return to the same phase — because the Earth has moved along its own orbit meanwhile, so the Moon must travel further to line up with the Sun again.

8414.w: The mismatch is the whole problem. Twelve months fall eleven days short, so lunar calendars drift through the seasons and lunisolar ones insert a whole extra month every few years to catch up.

8415.w: It is a reconciliation, not a measurement. The Julian year overshot by 11 minutes, which by the 1500s had moved the equinox ten days; the Gregorian reform of 1582 dropped those ten days and changed the leap rule for century years.

8416.w: The oldest known accounting is Mesopotamian clay tokens — one small shape per sheep or per measure of grain, sealed inside a clay envelope. Counting begins as a record of goods owed, not as mathematics.

8417.w: It was invented for accounts before literature. The pressed marks on Sumerian clay begin as pictures of the goods being counted and become, over centuries, signs for the sounds of words instead of the things.

8418.w: The step is abstraction: once the mark for five sheep can be split into a mark for five and a mark for sheep, five can be added to anything. That separation is what makes arithmetic possible at all.

8419.w: Used as a placeholder in several places, but treated as a number in its own right — one you can add, subtract and calculate with — by Brahmagupta in India in 628, who also set down the rules for negative numbers.

8420.w: The name means earth-measuring, and Herodotus says that is literally what it was: the Nile flood erased field boundaries every year, and Egyptian surveyors had to re-establish who owned what, which meant measuring land.

8421.w: It is not simply farming but the surplus farming makes: one family growing more than one family eats is what allows anyone at all to do something other than get food, which is where every other trade comes from.

8422.w: That is the definition and the consequence together: once people are fed by others, they can specialise, and the density that follows makes trade, writing, law and disease all far more likely than they were in a village.

8423.w: Writing is what changes a custom into a law. Hammurabi's code was cut into a stone pillar and set in public around 1750 BC — the point of which is not the rules but that everyone can see them and they cannot quietly change.

8424.w: It is stored as change rather than as a copy: synapses that fire together strengthen, so a memory is a pattern of connections made easier to re-run. The hippocampus builds new ones; damage it and old memories survive while new ones stop forming.

8425.w: The line between history and prehistory is writing, and it is drawn there because it is the point where the past can say something about itself rather than being inferred from what it left. Everything before is archaeology.

8426.w: It is both at once, and neither description alone works. It arrives as countable photons and it interferes with itself like a wave, and which one you see depends only on what you set up to catch it.

8427.w: Mass is what resists being accelerated, and mass is also what produces and responds to gravity. There is no obvious reason those should be the same number — they are, to about one part in a thousand trillion, and general relativity says that is because they are the same thing.

8428.w: Mass and energy are the same quantity in different units, and c squared is the exchange rate between them. Because c is so large, a very small amount of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy — which is the whole of nuclear power and the whole of why the Sun shines.

8429.w: Since 1967 the second has not been a fraction of a day. It is defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the radiation from a caesium-133 atom — because atoms are identical everywhere and the Earth's rotation is not even constant.

8430.w: Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That means the speed of light is no longer measured at all: it is fixed by definition, and measuring it now measures the metre.

8431.w: It is always relative to something. There is no experiment that reveals absolute speed — which is why nothing feels different in a smoothly flying aircraft, and why the speed of light being the same for every observer forced everything else to bend instead.

8432.w: It is what you actually feel. Constant speed feels like standing still; only a change in it presses you into the seat, which is why acceleration and gravity are indistinguishable from inside a closed box.

8433.w: Newton's second law: force equals mass times acceleration. It is a definition as much as a discovery — it says what we mean by force, and the content is that the same force always gives twice the mass half the acceleration.

8434.w: Its importance is that it is conserved. Add up the momentum of everything before a collision and after, and the totals match exactly, whatever happened in between — which is what lets you work out the result of a crash without knowing anything about the crash.

8435.w: Nothing moves, no work is done, however hard you push — a person holding a heavy box still does no work on it in this sense. It is the bridge between force and energy: work done is energy transferred.

8436.w: A person and an engine can do the same work; the engine does it in a second. That is the entire difference power measures, and it is why the horsepower was defined by comparing an engine to the animal it replaced.

8437.w: It is an average, not a total, which is why a spark at 1500 degrees will not burn you and a bath at 50 will: the spark has a high temperature and almost no energy in it. Temperature says how hot, never how much.

8438.w: There are vastly more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, so a system left alone drifts into disorder for the same reason a shuffled deck comes out unsorted — not a law of force but of counting. It is also the only physical quantity that picks a direction for time.

8439.w: It needs a surplus in one place and a want in another, with distance between them — which is why it begins as soon as farming produces more than a household eats, and why obsidian from a single volcano turns up hundreds of miles away in the Stone Age.

8440.w: Barter requires a coincidence of wants. Money removes it by being wanted by definition. The first coins were struck in Lydia around 600 BC from electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, stamped to certify weight and purity so it need not be weighed again.

8441.w: It is older than coinage, not younger: Mesopotamian tablets record interest-bearing loans of grain and silver centuries before anyone struck a coin. What money added was a way to settle a debt with a stranger.

8442.w: It is what separates a government from anyone else who wants your money, and the reason the earliest writing is accounts: someone had to record who had paid.

8443.w: A city cannot run on custom the way a village can — too many people, too many strangers, too much stored grain to defend and divide. Government is what appears when the rules must be administered rather than simply known.

8444.w: Athens from about 508 BC decided by assembly, and filled most offices by lot rather than election, on the reasoning that election favours the well known and the rich. Its citizenship excluded women, slaves and foreigners — most of the people there.

8445.w: Inheritance is the point of it, not the crown: it settles the succession in advance, which is the problem that has destroyed more states than any other. What it buys in continuity it pays for in whoever happens to be born next.

8446.w: Writing is what makes it one. A spoken promise depends on memory and on both parties agreeing what was said; a written one can be produced years later in front of someone who was not there.

8447.w: It is the one unit every society has, and almost the only thing they organise differently: who counts as family, who lives with whom, and what is owed to whom vary enormously, while the raising of children in a small group does not.

8448.w: That is the difference from a family or a band: beyond about a hundred and fifty people you cannot know everyone, so cooperation has to run on rules, reputation and exchange instead of on personal knowledge.

8449.w: It is a claim rather than a fact of geography. Shared language, story and printed books did most of the work of making people who had never met feel like one thing — which is why nations and printing arrive so close together.

8450.w: It is a relation between people, not between a person and an object: what you own is everyone else's obligation not to use it, which is why property only means anything where there is law to enforce it.

8451.w: The line between boat and ship is seaworthiness, not size alone: a ship is decked and framed to take a wave over the bow and stay watertight, which is what lets it leave the coast at all.

8452.w: Almost everything about it is arranged for waiting at the water's edge: eyes, ears and nostrils on one plane along the top of the skull, so it can see, hear and breathe with the rest of itself submerged.

8453.w: It hunts underwater and has to stay warm doing it, which is why the fur is the densest of any animal and why an otter spends so much of its day grooming: the insulation is trapped air, and dirty fur does not trap it.

8454.w: It got that big by eating some of the smallest things in the sea. Lunge-feeding on krill takes in a volume of water greater than the whale's own body, which is only worth the effort at enormous scale — the size and the diet each require the other.

8455.w: Flightlessness is not a failure to fly but a return: its ancestors flew, and on a continent with few ground predators the keel that anchors flight muscle was lost, leaving the wing a stub and the legs everything.

8456.w: The spray is thiols — sulfur compounds the nose detects at a few parts per billion, which is why it carries so far and lasts so long. The bold black and white is the warning that makes using it rarely necessary.

8457.w: It has no roots, no vessels and no need of them: surrounded by water, it takes what it needs across its whole surface, and the holdfast at its base is a clamp rather than a root.

8458.w: The line is the whole invention. Free, it would simply blow away; held, it is forced to move through the air rather than with it, and a surface moving through air at an angle generates lift.

8459.w: Distilling concentrates what fermentation made, but new spirit is harsh and clear. Years in oak give it the colour and most of the flavour, drawn out of the charred wood — which is why the barrel matters as much as the grain.

8460.w: Waterlogged soil has no oxygen in it, so the trees that manage it breathe another way — cypress knees and mangrove stilts are roots reaching up into the air rather than down.

8461.w: The water is not local rain but rain that fell somewhere else, often long ago, travelling underground until the rock or the land surface brings it up — which is why an oasis can sit in a place that gets no rain at all.

8462.w: The six arms grow in the same conditions at the same time, which is why they match each other — and no two flakes match because each one took its own path through the cloud, and every twist of temperature and humidity along it is recorded in the shape.

8463.w: The word is younger than the idea and came from a play — Capek's R.U.R., 1920, from a Czech word for forced labour. What separates a robot from a machine is the decision: a lathe repeats, a robot responds.

8464.w: Carving is subtractive and unforgiving — every cut is final, so the figure has to be seen inside the block before it is begun, and the stone that remains is chosen rather than shaped.

8465.w: It stands because nothing has to hold anything else up: every course is smaller than the one below and the load runs straight down through solid mass. The Great Pyramid held the record for tallest structure for about 3,800 years.

8466.w: The name is the rice, not the fish. It began as a preservation method — fish packed in fermenting rice for months, the rice discarded — and the modern version keeps the sourness while throwing away the wait.

8467.w: Most infections cause nothing worse than a stomach upset. In roughly one in two hundred the virus reaches the motor neurons of the spinal cord, and the paralysis that follows is permanent because those neurons do not regrow.

8468.w: Its surface proteins drift a little each year, which is why immunity fades and the vaccine is remade annually. Rarely two strains infect one animal and swap whole gene segments — a shift rather than a drift, and the reason pandemics happen.

8469.w: It moves through nerve tissue rather than blood, which is slow and is the whole reason treatment works: vaccination after a bite can still outrun the virus to the brain. Untreated, once symptoms begin, survival is close to unknown.

8470.w: It killed more sailors than storms and battle together. James Lind's 1747 trial aboard HMS Salisbury gave six pairs of sick men six different remedies and is one of the first controlled clinical trials; the pair given oranges and lemons recovered.

8471.w: It became a disease of industrial cities rather than of poverty alone: skin makes vitamin D from ultraviolet light, and coal smoke over a northern city takes enough of it out of the sky to matter.

8472.w: John Snow mapped the 1854 Broad Street cases and found them clustered on one pump — evidence that it travelled in water years before anyone had seen the bacterium, and the founding piece of work in epidemiology.

8473.w: Sugar is not there for energy. Glucose and sodium are carried across the gut wall together by the same transporter, so adding glucose lets water follow salt back into a body that is losing both — a mechanism found in the 1960s, and The Lancet called it potentially the most important medical advance of the century.

8474.w: It is the cofactor that lets the body cross-link collagen. Without it, the connective tissue holding skin, gums, blood vessels and old scars together is built wrong and slowly comes apart — which is scurvy.

8475.w: It is a creature of estuaries first and a pathogen second — which is why cholera is seasonal in the Bay of Bengal, rising and falling with the plankton the bacteria ride on.

8476.w: Green wood is half water by weight and shrinks across the grain as it dries, so it is seasoned — air-dried under cover, or kilned — to about the moisture content of the room it will live in. Build with it wet and the joints open after the house is finished.

8477.w: It works by bending: the top of a loaded beam is squeezed and the bottom is stretched, with a neutral line between them doing almost nothing. That is why an I-beam puts most of its metal at the top and bottom and almost none in the middle.

8478.w: Depth beats width: a joist twice as deep is eight times as stiff, while one twice as wide is only twice as stiff, which is why floor joists stand on edge rather than lying flat.

8479.w: The rounding is the record of how it travelled. Angular fragments are crushed rock; rounded ones have been rolled along a riverbed or a beach long enough to lose their corners.

8480.w: The building is not held up by strength but by area. A footing works by making the load per square metre small enough that the ground does not move — which is why the size of a foundation is set by the soil, not by the wall.

8481.w: It is the oldest way to cross an opening and the weakest: stone is strong in compression and poor in tension, so a stone lintel cracks from underneath. The arch was invented to avoid needing one.

8482.w: Gypsum plaster sets by taking back the water that was driven off when it was burnt, rather than by drying — so it goes off on a timetable of its own and a plasterer works to it rather than to the weather.

8483.w: The paper is structural, not packaging: gypsum has almost no tensile strength, and the liners carry the tension so the board can be handled and fixed at all. It also gives a house most of its fire resistance — the water bound in the gypsum has to be boiled off before the board can burn.

8484.w: It is weaker than cement mortar on purpose. Soft mortar lets a wall move and cracks itself rather than the brick, and it can be raked out and replaced — which is why old buildings repointed in cement start losing their faces.

8485.w: Almost nothing insulates as well as air; the trick is stopping it moving, because moving air carries heat away. Wool, foam and fibre all work the same way — a great many small pockets too small for a convection current to form in.

8486.w: It is rarely the underside of anything. Fixing a separate surface to the joists leaves a void for pipes, cables and insulation, and breaks the path sound would otherwise take straight through the structure.

8487.w: Laid across the joists rather than along them, so each board is supported at several points, and tongued and grooved along its edges so the boards carry each other and a foot between joists does not simply push one down.

8488.w: A roof sheds a surprising amount: 25 millimetres of rain on a modest house is a couple of thousand litres, and all of it arrives at the eaves. Without somewhere to go it lands at the foot of the wall, which is where damp begins.

8489.w: One degree of freedom out of six is the whole design. Everything else — lifting, sliding, twisting — is resisted by the knuckle and the pin, which is why a sagging door is almost always a screw pulling out rather than a hinge wearing.

8490.w: It heats the air at its surface, which rises and pulls cold air in underneath, so the room turns over. That is convection, not radiation — which is why a radiator is put under a window, to meet the cold draught coming down the glass.

8491.w: It is a structure whose whole purpose is to be taken down, so it is bolted and clamped rather than fixed, and every part is a standard length — which is what lets the same tubes go up around any shape of building.

8492.w: Everything depends on how round it is. A piston seals against the wall by its rings, so the bore is honed to a few thousandths of a millimetre and given a fine cross-hatch of scratches on purpose, to hold a film of oil.

8493.w: The cylinder and piston only give a push. Turning that into rotation needs a crank, and turning an intermittent push into steady rotation needs stored inertia — which is why every engine has a heavy wheel somewhere on the shaft.

8494.w: It is the piece that makes engines possible, and it is far older than engines: the same geometry turns a grindstone, a hand drill and a bicycle. Force applied at the throw becomes torque about the axis, and the length of the throw is the leverage.

8495.w: One of the six classical simple machines, and the one the others are explained with. Force times distance from the fulcrum is the same on both sides, so a bar ten times longer on your side lifts ten times the weight through a tenth of the distance.

8496.w: Where it sits decides everything the lever does. Close to the load it multiplies force; close to the hand it multiplies speed and distance instead — the same bar, two different machines.

8497.w: Cast to a rough bar in a mould and then drawn: metal pulled through a die comes out at a diameter set by the hole, work-hardened by the pull, and straighter than anything poured can be.

8498.w: It stores energy in motion rather than in a spring or a fuel, and how much depends on where the mass sits: doubling the radius stores four times as much, which is why a flywheel is heavy at the rim and light at the centre.

8499.w: Water expands about 1,700 times when it boils, and holding that expansion in is where the power comes from and where the danger is. The whole history of the boiler is the history of containing it: staying, riveting, testing, and the safety valve that admits defeat on purpose.

8500.w: A one-way valve needs no operator at all: pressure from the wrong side pushes it shut. That is the heart, the pump and the engine using the same idea, and it is why a valve is the first thing added to any pipe that matters.

8501.w: A piston pump does not suck. It lowers the pressure above the water and the atmosphere pushes it up — which is why no such pump can lift water more than about ten metres, however hard it is worked.

8502.w: Rolling friction is a small fraction of sliding friction, so putting hardened balls between two races turns a rubbing joint into a rolling one. It is the reason a wheel spins for minutes rather than seconds.

8503.w: It does not destroy the energy, it moves it: everything the vehicle had as speed comes out as heat in the pads and discs. That is why brakes fade — hot enough, they stop being able to accept any more.

8504.w: It does not depend on how large the contact area is, which is deeply counter-intuitive: pressing twice as hard doubles it, spreading the same load over twice the area does not change it at all. Amontons worked that out in 1699.

8505.w: Almost everything interesting happens there rather than inside: friction, corrosion, catalysis, wetting, adhesion. It is also never as flat as it looks — polished steel under a microscope is a landscape of peaks touching at a few points.

8506.w: It grows as the square of size while volume grows as the cube, which is the single most useful fact in biology and engineering: double a thing and its skin quadruples while its bulk goes up eightfold, so large animals overheat and small ones starve.

8507.w: Crude oil is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons and useless as it comes. A refinery separates them by boiling point in a fractionating column — petrol comes off high up where it is cool, diesel lower down, bitumen never leaves the bottom.

8508.w: An engine makes useful power over a narrow band of speed and a car has to move from nothing to motorway pace. The gearbox trades turns for torque: a low gear turns the wheels slowly and pushes hard, a high gear the reverse.

8509.w: It works by slipping on purpose. Two plates pressed together transmit only as much torque as friction between them allows, so a clutch can take up drive gradually instead of stalling the engine or snatching the car forward.

8510.w: It has to twist and not break: a shaft transmits torque by being wound up slightly along its length, and because only the outside is highly stressed, it is usually a tube rather than a bar.

8511.w: Going round a corner the outer wheel travels further than the inner one. Locked together they must scrub; disconnected, only one drives. The differential splits torque evenly while allowing any difference in speed, which is a genuinely clever piece of geometry.

8512.w: It has to carry tens of thousands of volts to a gap inside a combustion chamber, so its body is an insulator — a ceramic strong enough to survive the pressure and hot enough not to foul, which is why the ribbed white porcelain is the whole design.

8513.w: Spinning a magnet inside coils of wire makes current whichever way the field moves, so the output alternates and has to be rectified back to direct current for the battery — which is why an alternator has diodes and a dynamo did not.

8514.w: Getting gas out matters almost as much as getting mixture in: a cylinder still full of its last burn cannot take a full fresh charge, so exhaust design is about the pressure wave leaving, not just the hole it leaves through.

8515.w: It converts carbon monoxide and unburnt fuel to carbon dioxide and water and splits nitrogen oxides back apart, using platinum, palladium and rhodium as catalysts. Leaded petrol poisons it permanently, which is why lead had to go before it could be fitted.

8516.w: The reduction is the point: several turns lock to lock means a small force at the rim becomes a large one at the tyre, and a bump at the tyre arrives back at the hands much reduced.

8517.w: The name is older than cars: a dashboard was the board on a carriage that stopped mud dashed up by the horse's hooves from reaching the driver. The instruments arrived on it later and kept the name.

8518.w: A pointer is read faster than a number because the eye takes in an angle at a glance and has to decode a digit. That is why the instruments that matter in a hurry are dials and the ones you study are numbers.

8519.w: The classic mechanical kind measures nothing directly: a magnet spun by the wheels drags a metal cup around against a hairspring, and how far it drags is proportional to speed. There is no gearing to the needle at all, only eddy currents.

8520.w: The reflector does most of the work. A bulb alone lights the whole sphere; a parabolic mirror with the filament at its focus turns almost all of that into a beam, and the dipped pattern is made by deliberately putting part of the filament off-focus.

8521.w: A seat is a compromise between support and pressure: too soft and the pelvis rolls back and the lower spine takes the load, too hard and the weight arrives on two small bones. Foam over a sprung base is an attempt at both.

8522.w: Almost all of it is air, so its properties come from the walls between bubbles rather than the material itself. Open cells let air through and squash easily; closed cells trap it and push back — the same plastic, two different materials.

8523.w: The hollow needle is the hard part and the late one: Alexander Wood and Charles Pravaz arrived at it independently around 1853, and it is what turned a drug into a dose that could bypass the gut entirely.

8524.w: Holding the edges together is the whole treatment: skin knits edge to edge in days and across a gap in weeks, with a scar in proportion. Catgut, which is sheep intestine and never cat, dissolves so internal stitches need not be removed.

8525.w: A wound heals faster kept slightly moist than dried to a scab, which reverses what everyone was taught: the scab is not a repair but an obstacle the new skin has to grow underneath.

8526.w: Repair runs in a fixed order whatever caused it: bleeding stops, the site inflames and is cleaned by white cells, new tissue and vessels are built, and then the patch is remodelled and shrunk for months afterwards.

8527.w: It is a lever pair, so the grip at the tip is set by where the hinge sits — and surgical patterns are shaped for one job each, which is why there are hundreds of named kinds and a surgeon asks for one by name.

8528.w: Before it, surgery was measured in seconds and limited to what a held-down patient could survive. Its public demonstration in Boston in 1846 changed what could be attempted more than any instrument ever has, and how the general kind works is still not fully settled.

8529.w: It waited on three things and none of them is a technique: anaesthesia so the patient could be still, antisepsis so the wound would not kill them afterwards, and haemostasis so they did not bleed to death first. All three arrived within fifty years.

8530.w: Nightingale's contribution was statistical as much as practical: her records at Scutari showed most deaths were from infection rather than wounds, and her polar-area diagrams made the case to people who would not read a table.

8531.w: The diagnosis is the harder half. Treatment follows from it, and for most of history the treatments were useless or worse while the diagnosis was still worth having — knowing what is coming is a different service from changing it.

8532.w: It is reasoning under uncertainty, not lookup: the same symptom belongs to many diseases and any disease shows only some of its symptoms in any one person. Tests move the probability rather than settling it.

8533.w: Some are the illness doing damage and some are the body's answer to it: fever, inflammation and coughing are all defences, which is why suppressing them is sometimes exactly wrong.

8534.w: Larrey's flying ambulances in the 1790s were the first, and the idea behind them is still the whole point: survival after major injury falls sharply with time, so the hour after it happens is worth more than anything done later.

8535.w: It is what makes a clock a clock rather than a weight falling. It does two jobs at once — counting the oscillation and keeping it going — and every tick is the sound of one tooth being released.

8536.w: Galileo noticed that the period barely changes with how far it swings, which is what makes it a timekeeper. It depends on length and gravity, so the same clock runs slow at the equator and on a mountain.

8537.w: It is a counterweight as much as a handle. The pommel behind the hand moves the balance point back toward it, and a sword balanced near the hand feels light and turns quickly whatever it actually weighs.

8538.w: It protects the person from the edge and the edge from the weather, and it has to do the second without holding damp against steel — which is why a scabbard is lined with something that breathes and oiled fleece was used for centuries.

8539.w: It does two things at once and they fight: a small hole is dimmer but brings a deeper slice of the world into focus, a wide one is bright with only a thin plane sharp. Every photograph is a decision about that trade.

8540.w: Together with the aperture it fixes the exposure, and separately it fixes the motion: a thousandth of a second freezes a bird, a second turns moving water into a smear. The same brightness, two entirely different pictures.

8541.w: It is what a candle actually burns, though not as a solid: the flame melts wax, the wick draws the liquid up, and the heat vaporises it at the top. A candle is a small oil lamp that carries its own fuel in solid form.

8542.w: It is a pump with no moving parts. A modern candle wick is braided so it curls into the hot edge of the flame and burns itself away at the same rate the wax goes down, which is why it needs no trimming and older ones did.

8543.w: It has to be stiff enough not to fold under the arch and flexible enough to let the foot roll from heel to toe, which is why almost every sole is layered rather than a single slab.

8544.w: It started as a riding aid — a heel stops the foot sliding through a stirrup — and became fashion afterwards. Raising it tips the body forward and shifts load onto the front of the foot, which is the whole ergonomic argument about it.

8545.w: Threading is what distributes the pull: each crossing shares the tension, so a single cord closes the whole opening evenly rather than pinching wherever it happens to be tied.

8546.w: The metal ring spreads the load around the whole circumference. Without it the cord bears on a few threads and the hole becomes a tear, which is the reason a grommet exists at all.

8547.w: The twist is what makes it work: it presses the fibres against each other so friction stops them sliding apart, and the load is shared instead of falling on whichever strand is shortest.

8548.w: It is the whole basis of spinning and of rope. Twisted one way the strands grip; twisted the same way again at the next level up they would unwind, which is why rope is laid in alternating directions at each stage.

8549.w: It turns a continuous instrument into a stepped one. Spacing follows a fixed ratio — each fret is about 5.95 per cent of the remaining length from the last — so the twelfth lands at the halfway point and sounds the octave.

8550.w: A set of steel strings pulls with something like 80 kilograms of force, all of it trying to fold the neck forward, which is why a modern one has a steel rod buried along its length to pull back.

8551.w: Resin gives the film its hardness and oil its flexibility, and the ratio decides everything: too hard and it cracks as the wood moves, too soft and it never stops being sticky. On an instrument it also changes how the wood vibrates.

8552.w: The enclosure is the technology, not the fire: brick keeps the heat in and a draught forces it hotter, and the difference between a hearth that warms a room and a furnace that melts iron is entirely how well it does both.

8553.w: Pure silica melts near 1,700 degrees, which was out of reach for most of history. Adding soda drops it by hundreds of degrees — and because that also makes the glass water-soluble, lime has to go in as well to make it durable.

8554.w: It has to stay slightly flexible for years. Glass and timber move at different rates with heat and damp, so anything rigid between them cracks the pane — putty works by never quite finishing setting.

8555.w: It is the idea that a structure can be lines rather than surfaces. A triangulated frame cannot change shape without a member changing length, which is why bridges, bicycles and roofs are all made of triangles and why a rectangle needs a brace.

8556.w: A wire wheel does not stand on its spokes, it hangs from them: the hub is suspended from the upper spokes while the lower ones slacken. That is why they are tensioned in a set, and why one loose spoke puts a wheel out of true.

8557.w: It is squeezed, not stretched: every spoke pulls inward, so the rim is a ring in compression trying to buckle, and its depth is what stops it. Take the tension off and a wheel can be reshaped by hand.

8558.w: Everything about a wheel is decided here: the bearings set how freely it spins, and the flange spacing sets how wide the spokes splay, which is what makes a wheel stiff sideways rather than just round.

8559.w: It carries the load on air rather than on rubber: the casing is a pressure vessel and the contact patch is only as large as the load divided by the pressure. Grip comes from the rubber deforming into the road's texture, which is why a hot tyre grips better and a worn one does not.

8560.w: Separating the two jobs is what made the pneumatic tyre practical: a thin tube can be made airtight cheaply, and a thick casing can be made tough, and neither has to be both.

8561.w: The teeth do not mesh, they seat: each one sits inside a link, so the chain and the sprocket must share exactly the same pitch. Wear stretches a chain and it then rides high on the teeth, which is how a worn chain destroys a good sprocket.

8562.w: Force is only useful over part of the circle — near the top and bottom the foot is pushing along the crank and achieving nothing — which is why pedalling well is about spreading effort round the stroke rather than stamping.

8563.w: It is a lever on the steering axis, so its width sets how much leverage there is over the front wheel: wide bars turn easily and slowly, narrow ones are quick and twitchy, and neither is better in general.

8564.w: The cut is the point, which is why the blade is flat and sharpened rather than curved: a spade slices a clean edge and a shovel scoops what is already loose, and using either for the other's job is hard work.

8565.w: The gaps do the work. Teeth spaced wider than soil crumbs and narrower than leaves sort one from the other as they pass, which is the whole design.

8566.w: Several thin points enter ground far more easily than one broad edge, because each concentrates the same push onto a much smaller area — the reason a garden fork beats a spade in heavy clay.

8567.w: The bricklayer's and the gardener's are different tools with one name: one is a flat plate for spreading a bed, the other a scoop for making a hole. Both are shaped for one hand and one motion.

8568.w: Its invention around the first century BC is what made glass an everyday material rather than a luxury: before it, vessels were ground or cast one at a time, and after it a gather could be blown into a bottle in a minute.

8569.w: Silver halide crystals in gelatin darken where light strikes them, and the image is latent until developed — a few atoms of silver per grain, invisible, waiting for a chemical that will amplify them a billionfold.

8570.w: It decides how the book behaves more than the paper does: sewn sections open flat and survive a century, glued spines are cheap and crack, and the difference shows the first time anyone tries to photocopy one.

8571.w: Concrete is strong squeezed and weak pulled — about a tenth as strong — so it is put where the squeezing happens and steel where the stretching does. The pairing only works because the two expand at almost exactly the same rate with heat.

8572.w: A pair of rafters leaning together push outward at the feet as well as down, which is what spreads walls apart. The tie across the bottom is not optional: it turns two struts into a triangle and cancels the thrust.

8573.w: It is where the rafters lean on each other, and where the roof is most exposed and least able to shed water sideways — which is why the ridge tile is the one bedded in mortar and the one that fails first.

8574.w: It is what makes a tiled roof possible without nailing every tile: each one hangs by a nib over a batten, held down by its own weight and the tile above, so any single tile can be lifted out and replaced.

8575.w: It does not seal, it sheds. Each course overlaps the two below so there is no straight path through, and the whole roof relies on gravity and slope rather than on any joint being watertight.

8576.w: Every leak is at a junction, never in the middle of a slope, so flashing exists only for those places — and it is traditionally lead because lead can be dressed by hand into any shape and moves with the building instead of cracking.

8577.w: One of them handles a surprising flow, so it is sized by roof area rather than by looks, and it must discharge somewhere that leads away — a downpipe emptying at the foot of a wall is worse than no gutter at all.

8578.w: It has to be softer than what it covers or it cracks and traps water behind itself, which is why cement render over soft old brick does more damage than the weather it was meant to stop.

8579.w: It does two jobs paint cannot: it grips a surface paint would slide off, and it seals a porous one that would otherwise drink the topcoat unevenly. That is why a primed wall takes fewer coats, not more.

8580.w: It works by never setting hard. Glass, timber and masonry all expand differently with heat and damp, and anything rigid in the gap between them either cracks or pushes them apart.

8581.w: The slab below is strong and rarely flat; the screed is flat and not strong. Separating those two jobs is why it exists, and why it is laid to a level rather than to a thickness.

8582.w: It does three jobs at once: evens out the small irregularities left in the screed, deadens the sound of footsteps into the room below, and takes the wear that would otherwise reach the covering itself.

8583.w: One block replaces about six bricks, so a wall goes up faster with fewer joints — and because it is cast rather than fired, it can be made light and full of air, which is how a wall becomes insulation as well as structure.

8584.w: The groove on its underside is the whole point: water running back along the soffit stops at the drip and falls, instead of tracking back to the wall and soaking it. A sill without one is decoration.

8585.w: For centuries it was small because glass could only be made small — blown into a cylinder, split and flattened — and the Georgian window of many small panes is that limit made visible rather than a style.

8586.w: The sprung bevel is what makes it work one-handed: the sloping face is pushed aside by the striker as the door closes and springs back behind it, so a door latches by being pushed and needs a handle only to open.

8587.w: It is the second most abundant compound in the Earth's crust and the reason glass is cheap. Molten it does not crystallise readily on cooling, so it sets as a disordered solid, which is what glass is.

8588.w: Unlike a screw it does not hold in the work at all — the nut does the holding, and the bolt is stretched between them like a very stiff spring. That tension is what stops the joint moving, not friction on the threads.

8589.w: A blade breaks at the handle or nowhere. A full tang running the whole length and width of the grip is why a good knife outlives its handle, and a short stub tang is why a cheap one snaps at the bolster.

8590.w: It is not mainly for catching another blade. Its first job is stopping the hand sliding forward onto the edge when a thrust hits something solid, which is why even knives that never fenced have one.

8591.w: Wrapping is functional twice over: it gives the hand something to key into when wet, and it lets the shape be adjusted with the sword in hand rather than fixed when it was made.

8592.w: It is a counterweight, and it is why a heavy sword can feel light: mass behind the hand moves the balance point back toward it, and a blade balanced near the hand turns quickly whatever it actually weighs.

8593.w: It does not sharpen so much as remove: an edge is blunted by rolling over, and the stone cuts steel away on both sides until the two surfaces meet again at a line. Which is why a knife gets smaller over its life.

8594.w: Slow-cooled steel is soft; cooled in seconds the carbon has no time to move and the crystal locks into martensite, which is hard and would shatter. Tempering afterwards gives some of the hardness back for toughness — a blade is always a compromise between the two.

8595.w: Fired clay is full of pores and drinks whatever is put in it. The glaze is a glass melted onto the surface, and it has to shrink at the same rate as the body on cooling or it crazes into a net of fine cracks.

8596.w: Two pieces of leather-hard clay will not stick, because there is nothing wet to knit them. Slip painted into a scored joint is the glue, and it works because it is the same material and shrinks identically in the kiln.

8597.w: It is not drying. Above about 600 degrees the chemically bound water leaves the clay lattice and it can never be softened with water again — the pot stops being clay, which is why a shard survives ten thousand years.

8598.w: The plough turns the soil over in slabs and the harrow makes a seedbed of it. Seed needs contact with fine soil to take up water, so the harrow is the difference between a furrow and a crop.

8599.w: It is the oldest large-scale engineering there is, and it makes its own problem: water carries dissolved salt, and evaporating year after year it leaves the salt behind. Fields salted this way are why some of the earliest farmed land is now desert.

8600.w: A harvest is an export of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium off the field. Everything before the Haber process — manure, guano, marl, clover — was a way of moving those back, and the whole history of yields is the history of that accounting.

8601.w: Sealing is the mechanism: cut fodder respires, uses up the oxygen, and then ferments instead of rotting, preserving itself in its own acid. Grain keeps for the opposite reason — kept dry and cool it simply never starts.
