9314.w: The facades are cut into the cliff rather than built against it, which means working downward from the top and getting it right first time. The approach is a natural fissure three metres wide, so the city could be closed by a handful of people.

9315.w: A relic mound with no door. The form spread from India across Asia and kept its logic everywhere: the building is not a shelter, it is an object to circle.

9316.w: Fifty-five thousand cubic metres of andesite from the Progo riverbed, stacked into nine terraces. Three kilometres of relief run along the galleries, so a pilgrim reads the story by walking it and arrives at the plain dome with nothing left to look at.

9317.w: Desert pavement is a surface of dark weathered stones over pale ground. Lift the stones aside and the pale ground is your line — no pigment, no tool marks, and nothing to fade.

9318.w: Rust-coated pebbles moved off yellow-grey subsoil, ten to fifteen centimetres deep. The subsoil is limey and hardens into a crust, and the plateau is windless and rainless, which is the entire reason two thousand years of drawing is still legible.

9319.w: A mud wall needs replastering every year, and a ladder every year is a nuisance. Building the sticks in permanently means the scaffolding is already there when the rains have finished with the wall.

9320.w: Henri Christophe put it 900 m up and several kilometres inland, so a landing force would have to come to him. The guns were taken off the Europeans who had just been beaten with them.

9321.w: A fired glaze is glass, and glass does not fade. Cut the fired tile into shaped pieces and set them into mortar and the pattern outlives the mortar, the roof and usually the dynasty.

9322.w: Rooms round a courtyard, all facing in: a mosque on one side, lecture halls on the others, cells above. The plan puts everyone within earshot of the same teacher and out of earshot of the street.

9323.w: Three colleges facing one square across two centuries, and the last of them has tigers carrying the sun on their backs across its portal. Figurative animals on a madrasah are close to forbidden, which is why they are famous.

9324.w: Laying stone so it stays up is not obvious and cannot be worked out twice. The knowledge travels as a trade — apprentice to journeyman to master — which is why medieval cathedrals across a continent share details nobody wrote down.

9325.w: A trade in one town can set who may practise it, what it charges and who it teaches. That is a monopoly, and it is also the mechanism by which a craft outlives every individual who holds it.

9326.w: Sun-dried earth brick on a platform three metres above the market, so the Bani flood cannot reach it. The hereditary masons' guild directs a replastering by the whole town each year, which is the only reason a mud building survives a monsoon climate.

9327.w: Grass roots bind the top few centimetres of soil into a mat you can cut and stack. A turf wall a metre thick holds heat better than stone, which is why Iceland and Newfoundland built in it and Rome did not.

9328.w: Taro wants wet ground but drowns in standing water, so it has to be drained rather than irrigated. Three grades of ditch — field, feeder and disposal — turned a highland swamp into fields about nine thousand years ago, by people who had worked farming out for themselves with no contact with anyone else who had.

9329.w: Standard fired brick, laid on a grid, with drains along the streets and a well for every three houses. It is a plumbing city before it is anything else, and the plumbing is the same in every quarter — which suggests somebody was enforcing a standard.

9330.w: A brick tank waterproofed with bitumen, twelve metres by seven, with steps down at both ends. It holds water, which brick alone does not, and that is the entire technical claim; what it was for is guesswork.

9331.w: No quarry, no kiln, no metal. Fifty-five million cubic feet of earth moved at Cahokia in baskets on people's backs, which makes the scale a measure of how many people agreed to do it.

9332.w: Maize arrived on the Mississippi floodplain and the population went from under 3,000 to over 10,000 in fifty years. Monks Mound went up in that window: 622,000 cubic metres of earth, and the city was empty again by 1400.

9333.w: Two kilometres of avenue, a pyramid of over a million cubic metres, and apartment compounds for a hundred thousand people. Around 550 CE the palaces along the avenue were burned and the ordinary houses were not, which points inward rather than at an invader.

9334.w: A sloping batter carries the load and a framed panel above it carries the decoration, so the wall is structurally sound and flat where it needs to be painted. Finding it outside Teotihuacan is how influence gets traced.

9335.w: A field has to be come back to, so somebody has to stay. Everything else about a settled society follows from that one constraint — stores, ownership, inheritance and the year measured in seasons rather than in journeys.

9336.w: A rib vault pushes outward as well as down. Put a half-arch outside the wall to catch that push and walk it out to a pier, and the wall itself no longer has to be thick — which is the whole reason a Gothic wall can be window.

9337.w: Pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress are each ordinary on their own. Together they take the load off the wall entirely, and a builder who no longer needs the wall spends it on glass.

9338.w: A cathedral is defined by holding a bishop's chair, not by its size — but a bishop's church is the one with the money and the reason to be the tallest thing for fifty miles, so the definition and the ambition arrive together.

9339.w: The 1194 fire left only the crypt, the towers and the west front. The rest went up in about twenty-five years — fast enough that the whole building is one design, which is why its 167 windows agree with each other.

9340.w: A leucogranite plug that resisted what eroded around it, standing 92 m out of a bay whose tide runs 14 m. That makes it defensible for free twice a day, which is why an abbey and then a fortress ended up on top of it.

9341.w: A capital sited on a mountain where trade routes met, so it could tax what passed and see anyone coming. Its stone palace and churches went up under Afonso, and the kingdom outlasted four centuries of Portuguese contact before it was abolished in 1915.

9342.w: The first Christian monks went into the Egyptian desert alone. Withdrawal was the point, but withdrawing together turned out to be more durable than withdrawing alone — a rule, a timetable and a shared roof are what let the practice outlive the practitioner.

9343.w: Benedictines built up the rock in stages from the eighth century, each new church raised on the crypts of the last because there is no flat ground. The abbey is stacked rather than laid out.

9344.w: Rome spent five centuries refusing to have a king and then acquired one under another name. Augustus kept every republican office and title and simply held them all at once, which is why the empire has no founding date anyone can agree on.

9345.w: A Greek theatre is a half-bowl facing a stage. Close the half into a full ring and the performance has to move to the middle, which changes what can be performed there — no scenery, no backdrop, and everyone equidistant.

9346.w: Diocletian abdicated, which no Roman emperor had done, and had somewhere to go because he had built it first: white limestone and marble from the Brač quarries, laid out like a fortified camp rather than a villa.

9347.w: A small maritime republic with no army bought its independence twice over — in tribute, and in masonry. Six metres of wall on the landward side and one and a half on the sea, because the sea was where its own ships were.

9348.w: Built into a slope so the seating needs less substructure, and faced in the local limestone. It is the only Roman amphitheatre whose outer ring survives all the way round, because Pula never grew big enough to quarry it for its own buildings.

9349.w: Dry heat snaps starch's long chains into shorter ones. The flour browns, stops absorbing as much water and thickens far less — which is exactly why a dark roux is a weaker thickener than a pale one.

9350.w: Grass cut at flowering and dried below about 15% moisture will keep. Cut it too wet and the bale respires, heats, and can reach ignition on its own.

9351.w: Salt draws water out of the cucumber and holds off everything except the lactic acid bacteria already on its skin. They drop the pH below 4.6, which is where nothing dangerous grows.

9352.w: Honey holds more glucose than water can dissolve, so crystals form around any speck of pollen or dust. Higher-glucose honeys set in weeks and acacia honey can stay liquid for years.

9353.w: Bread is a set foam, so cutting it opens thousands of gas cells at once. That is why a cut loaf goes stale faster than a whole one: the starch retrogrades wherever moisture can leave.

9354.w: Water leaves and the capsaicin stays, so heat concentrates. Sugars and amino acids also get months at low temperature to react, which builds flavours a fresh chilli has never had.

9355.w: Seal cut grass away from air and its own lactic acid bacteria drop the pH to about 4. It is pickling on a field scale, and it works in weather too wet to make hay in.

9356.w: Cutting removes the tall grasses before they shade everything else out, so cutting a sward once a year is what makes a meadow rather than a monoculture. Stop cutting and it goes to scrub.

9357.w: Ale yeast stops below about 10 °C. The lager strain is a hybrid, carrying a cold-tolerant genome from a wild Patagonian species, so it keeps working slowly in the cold and settles out at the bottom rather than rising.

9358.w: The stupa's stacked discs become stacked roofs when the material is wood. The floors sit loose around a central pillar rather than being fixed to it, so the storeys slide out of phase in a quake and damp each other instead of resonating.

9359.w: A wet year makes a wide ring and a dry one a narrow ring, and every tree in a region records the same weather. Overlap enough sequences and you get an unbroken calendar thousands of years long, against which a single beam can be dated to the year.

9360.w: Ring-counting dates the felling of the five-storey pagoda's central pillar to 594. That is a date taken off the wood rather than out of a chronicle, which is why these are securely the oldest wooden buildings anywhere.

9361.w: A Paleocene lava flow cooled and contracted, and the cracks worked downward from the surface into about 40,000 columns. The sea then cut the coast back through them, which is the only reason the inside of a lava flow is standing in the open.

9362.w: The lintels are held on with mortise and tenon, and joined end to end with tongue and groove — carpenters' joints, cut into sarsen by people with no metal. The uprights taper upward so they do not look top-heavy from below.

9363.w: Three legions, about 15,000 men, built it in roughly six years from AD 122 — the eastern two thirds in stone and the western third in stacked turf, later rebuilt. The wall is the least of it: a ditch in front, the Vallum behind, a milecastle every Roman mile and a turret every third. A monitored frontier rather than a barrier.

9364.w: His Sydney shells had no defined geometry and could not be costed or built. The answer, found years later, was to cut every one from the surface of a single sphere — so a thousand unique curves became repeats of one precast rib.

9365.w: Water sinks through porous sandstone until it meets a shale band it cannot pass, then runs sideways and out of the cliff face. Freezing and salt crystallisation at that seep line quarry the rock away from the inside.

9366.w: Maize will grow on the mesa tops and the alcoves in the canyon walls are dry, shaded in summer and sunlit in winter. Farming above and living below is the whole settlement pattern, and it depends entirely on the rain.

9367.w: Six hundred dwellings of shaped sandstone in adobe mortar, built inside overhangs that keep the rain off them. That is why they are still standing after seven hundred years while the mesa-top villages are not.

9368.w: A hospital order from the Third Crusade that was invited north to fight pagans and stayed to rule. By the fourteenth century it was a sovereign state with its own coinage, run from a castle rather than a court.

9369.w: There is no building stone on the north German plain, so the order fired its own. 21 hectares of brick inside the outer walls, built in phases over 132 years — the largest brick complex in Europe because brick was the only option.

9370.w: A ruler's house has to hold a court, a treasury, an audience and a garrison, so it grows into a building type of its own. Its plan is about who may get how close, which is why the last room is always the smallest.

9371.w: Limestone dissolves in slightly acid rainwater until a cave roof gives way. On the Yucatán this is the entire hydrology: no surface river anywhere, and every settlement sited on a hole in the ground.

9372.w: Four cenotes in one place means water all year, and that is why a city is there rather than somewhere else. El Castillo's 91 steps on each of four faces plus the top step come to 365, and around the equinoxes the corner casts a serpent of shadow down the balustrade.

9373.w: A magma plug cools underground harder than the rock it pushed into. Strip the softer rock off over tens of millions of years and the plug is left standing alone on a plain, with no foothills, because there was never a mountain around it.

9374.w: Kashyapa put his palace on top of a 180 m granite plug reached by one stair through a gateway built as a lion's mouth. The water gardens at the foot run on gravity alone and some of the fountains still work in the rains.

9375.w: Spin an arch about its vertical axis and every section through it is still an arch, so the whole surface works in compression. Nothing is in tension, which means it can be built of stone or brick and span far more than any beam of the same material.

9376.w: A dome wants a circular wall beneath it and a room is square. The pendentive is the curved triangle that fills each corner and gathers the dome's ring down onto four piers, so the weight lands where the walls are and the corners can be opened up.

9377.w: Anthemius and Isidore raised it in five years and ten months. Their first dome was too shallow and came down in 558 after two earthquakes; the ribbed replacement sits 6.25 m higher, which steepens the thrust and is why it is still up.

9378.w: Blocks up to about 200 tonnes, hauled some 35 km, dressed by pounding rather than cutting and set without mortar so closely that paper will not pass between them. Irregular joints interlock, which is also why the walls survive the earthquakes that flatten mortared ones.

9379.w: Bloomery iron comes out full of slag, and working it hot squeezes most of that out and draws the rest into threads along the grain. The stringers are why it tears along its length and bends across it, and why a wrought iron chain gives warning before it fails.

9380.w: Eiffel designed for wind before anything else, and solved the shape graphically rather than by formula: at every height the leg leans exactly enough that wind load and weight balance. The top sways 9 cm in a gale and moves 18 cm away from the sun as one side warms.

9381.w: A defensive maze does not stop anyone; it costs them time under fire from above. Himeji's keep is 130 m from the gate in a straight line and 325 m along the only path there, all of it overlooked.

9382.w: Every exposed timber surface is coated in lime plaster, which is what makes it white and what makes it hard to burn. Eighty-three buildings survived the 1945 firebombing of the city around them.

9383.w: Water finds its own level, so a trough of it is a straight horizontal you can sight along. The Roman chorobates was exactly that: a bench with a water channel cut in the top. You cannot see a slope of one in three thousand, so it has to be measured.

9384.w: The whole 50 km aqueduct falls one metre in three thousand, and across this bridge it drops 2.5 cm in 456 m. Getting that wrong by a hand's breadth over that distance means the water stops. The blocks are laid dry and held by friction, and the stones left sticking out are the scaffold supports nobody bothered to trim.

9385.w: At 3,700 m on a fault, walls three metres thick and five at the base are battered inward so their own weight resists the shake, and copper was poured into the foundations to tie them. The outside took three years; the inside took forty-five.

9386.w: The spoil from the ditch becomes the bank, so one act of digging gives you the obstacle twice over. Around Benin City that makes 17 m from ditch floor to rampart top in places, and it is still largely there.

9387.w: An oasis on the road across the Karakum, where the caravans had to stop. Each dynasty built its own walled city on empty ground beside the last rather than over it, which is why the site is four cities in a row and each one is legible.

9388.w: Fired clay has already lost its water and done all the shrinking it will ever do. Ground up and mixed back into wet clay it acts as a skeleton, so the pot shrinks less on drying and is far less likely to crack. Almost every ancient pottery has it.

9389.w: Obsidian is a glass with no crystal grain, so a blow does not follow any plane — the fracture spreads as a cone and leaves a curved shell-shaped scar. The edge that results is a few molecules thick, sharper than a modern scalpel.

9390.w: Quartz has no cleavage plane to split along, so it does not break down into flakes the way feldspar and mica do; it just wears rounder. Everything else in the granite becomes clay and washes away, and the quartz is what is left on the beach.

9391.w: Breaking the same mass into smaller pieces multiplies the surface touching the drink, so heat moves out faster — and so does meltwater in. A cocktail on crushed ice is colder sooner and weaker sooner, and the two are the same fact.

9392.w: Barley starch is not fermentable until malting wakes the grain's own amylase and cuts it into sugar. Yeast can then take it, which is why beer needs a malting floor and wine needs only a bucket.

9393.w: Acetobacter is airborne and everywhere, and it oxidises ethanol to acetic acid as long as it can reach oxygen. An open bottle turns; a sealed one does not. Vinegar is not spoiled wine so much as the next step wine takes if you let it.

9394.w: Rain that is warm and relentless dissolves limestone downward far faster than it wears it sideways, so the valleys deepen and the ridges between them are left standing as separate towers. Cooler climates get caves and sinkholes; the tropics get towers.

9395.w: The towers formed on land over about twenty million years and the sea rose into them. It then cut a notch into every tower at exactly its own working level, so the whole bay is undercut at one height — which is how you read a drowned landscape.

9396.w: A cistern holds a household through a dry week. Scale it up and line it, and it holds a city through a dry season — at which point whoever holds the key is no longer just a builder.

9397.w: There is no river, lake or cenote at Tikal. The whole city ran on rain caught off plastered plazas and stored in reservoirs, so the rulers who maintained them held the year in their hands. A drought that fouled the water is the leading explanation for why it emptied between 830 and 950.

9398.w: Building a temple earned merit, so a rich century meant thousands of them going up on one plain — more than 10,000 in about two hundred years. The brickwork is good enough that most of what the 1975 earthquake left standing is still standing.

9399.w: Fill a loose-woven bag with rubble and stack the bags. The platform settles and flexes in a quake instead of cracking, and every bag is woven from a plant that grew in a known year — so the building dates itself.

9400.w: Six pyramid complexes built of stacked shicra bags, the largest 150 m by 110 and 28 high, and not a weapon or a battlement anywhere on the site. It is a city 1,500 years before the Olmec, and it had no pottery.

9401.w: One wall means the fight is decided at one line. Put a second ring inside the first and build it taller, and both walls shoot together — so an attacker who takes the outer one has walked into a corridor overlooked from above on every side.

9402.w: The Hospitallers built it out to a full concentric plan with a steeply sloping glacis that defeats a battering ram and stiffens the wall against earthquakes. It was never taken by force: Baibars sent in a forged letter from the Grand Master telling the garrison to give up, and they did.

9403.w: A beam on a pivot with a known mass on one side does not measure weight at all — it compares two of them. Gravity cancels out of both arms, so the reading is the same wherever you take it, which is why trade ran on balances for four thousand years.

9404.w: Steel cooled slowly gives its carbon time to move and comes out soft. Dropped into water it cannot, and the structure locks mid-transformation as martensite: hard, and brittle enough to shatter until heat is put back in to temper it.

9405.w: A wet sheet pressed against felt gives up most of its water to the felt and the rest to the air. Do it too fast and the sheet cockles as the edges shrink before the middle, which is why drying is the step that takes the time.

9406.w: Cut a recess in marble to a drawn outline and set a piece of coloured stone into it flush. Everything is mineral, so nothing fades and nothing lifts — a pietra dura flower is the same colour now as the day it was cut.

9407.w: White marble from Makrana and red sandstone from Fatehpur Sikri, inlaid with twenty-eight kinds of stone brought from as far as China and Afghanistan. The minarets are set leaning very slightly outward, so a collapse would drop them away from the tomb rather than onto it.

9408.w: Hang the deck from a cable and the span works in tension, where steel is strongest, instead of in bending, where it is not. The towers only have to hold the cable up, so the water underneath can be as deep as it likes.

9409.w: Sink an upturned box and pump air in until the pressure holds the water out, and men can dig the riverbed dry inside it. The cost is the pressure itself: nitrogen dissolves into the blood down there and comes out as bubbles if you rise too fast.

9410.w: Two hundred thousand conifer beams carried in on foot from as far as 110 km, along roads nine metres wide and straight through whatever was in the way. Chetro Ketl alone is estimated at 29,135 man-hours, and most of its rooms show no sign of anyone living in them.

9411.w: Pueblo Bonito covers nearly two acres and has at least 650 rooms, and it stands on a line with Chetro Ketl that runs precisely east to west — the axis the equinox sun crosses. All of it built with no wheel and no draught animal.

9412.w: A 486 m span with diagonal stays as well as vertical hangers, so it is stiffer than a pure suspension bridge. Its contractor substituted bad wire in the cables; Washington Roebling could not have it removed, so he added 150 wires per cable to cover the shortfall.

9413.w: Notch each log near its ends and lay it across the last, and the weight of the wall above locks every joint. No saw, no nail and no mortar are needed, which is why the method appears independently across the whole northern forest.

9414.w: Split a block along the grain rather than sawing across it and the fibres stay whole from end to end, so water runs off along them instead of wicking into cut ends. A split shingle outlasts a sawn one by decades.

9415.w: The Transfiguration Church is notched pine, 37 m to the top of twenty-two domes, with no nails anywhere in the log structure. The domes and roof are another matter: about 180,000 nails hold 60,000 aspen shingles. 'Built without a single nail' is a good story and the roof is where it stops being true.

9416.w: A hemisphere holds snow and a point does not, so the northern dome is drawn out taller than it is wide and bulges past its drum. It is a timber frame with a metal or tiled skin, carrying nothing but itself — decoration on top of the roof rather than part of the structure.

9417.w: Nine chapels on one foundation, eight arranged around a central Intercession. The story that Ivan had the architect blinded so he could never build its equal is a myth — he is recorded working on other Moscow projects afterwards.

9418.w: The design is British military engineering and the work was done by enslaved Africans, over generations. It was called the Gibraltar of the Caribbean, and it fell anyway: cut off and outnumbered, the garrison surrendered to the French after a month in 1782.

9419.w: Bones fall into a dolomite cave, get cemented into breccia, and stay. Cosmogenic dating in 2022 pushed most of the Australopithecus here back to about 3.4 million years — contemporary with afarensis in East Africa rather than descended from it, which is a different family tree.

9420.w: Copper corrodes at once and then stops. The oxide gives way to carbonates and sulfates that lock into a dense adherent layer, and that layer is airtight — the opposite of rust, which flakes and lets the next layer corrode.

9421.w: Pressed from flax seed. It is a drying oil: the double bonds in it take oxygen from the air and cross-link into a solid, so it hardens rather than evaporating — and the reaction is exothermic enough that heaped oily rags can reach ignition on their own.

9422.w: Breaking the cells lets an enzyme reach a sulfur compound the onion keeps separately, and the product is volatile. It drifts to your eye, dissolves in the film of tears there and becomes sulfuric acid, which is what the nerve endings are reacting to.

9423.w: Copper hung over vinegar fumes grows a bright green crust of copper acetate. Painters used it for a thousand years because nothing else was that green, and it is mildly acidic, so it slowly eats the paper and the pigment beside it.

9424.w: A bay with a narrow mouth and deep water inside, on the side of the Caribbean where the current sets for Spain. Every treasure fleet gathered there before the crossing, which made the town rich, and then made it a target: a French corsair burned it in 1555 and the first fortress was begun in 1558.

9425.w: A hull deep enough for a season's cargo and strong enough to carry guns above it. That is why the Atlantic silver route existed at all, and why it sailed in convoy: a lone galleon is a prize and a fleet of them is a campaign.

9426.w: Quartzite weathers to sand with almost no nutrients in it. What grows there has to be frugal and fire-adapted, and the result is one of the densest floras on Earth — poverty of soil producing richness of species, which is the general rule and not the exception.

9427.w: The flat top is a syncline — the floor of a valley, folded down and hardened. Softer rock above it eroded away and the quartzite platform did not, so what is left standing 1,084 m over Cape Town is the bottom of something rather than the top.

9428.w: A wall only becomes a prison when a law says who must stay behind it and for how long. Imprisonment as the punishment itself — rather than as a wait for one — is barely two centuries old as a normal sentence.

9429.w: Colonial rule left a state that already sorted people by race for administrative convenience. From 1948 that sorting was made statute: registration by race, pass laws, separate areas, enforced until the early 1990s.

9430.w: An island is a prison that needs fewer guards, which is why this one held prisoners from the late seventeenth century to 1996. Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years there; it was declared a World Heritage Site in 1999.

9431.w: Carved stucco niches stacked in tiers, each row set a little proud of the one below, until the corner of a room becomes a curved surface. It is a facing rather than a structure: the vault behind it does the work, and the honeycomb only has to hold itself up.

9432.w: A fortress became a palace-city when the Sultan's Canal brought water from the mountains up onto the plateau. Everything that makes it famous — the courts, the pools, the running channels — depends on that one piece of hydraulic engineering.

9433.w: A hall whose roof rests on rows of very tall slender columns, which only works if the beams are long and light — cedar, brought a very long way. The reliefs on the stairs show delegations from across the empire arriving with gifts, which is what the building was for.

9434.w: You are not assembling a building, you are removing everything that is not one. There is no foundation to settle and no joint to fail, and equally no way to put back a column you cut too thin. Everything has to be right the first time, from the top down.

9435.w: Thirty monasteries and halls cut into a basalt cliff over two widely separated periods, the second of them possibly as short as 460 to 480. The paintings inside are dry fresco rather than true fresco, which is why so much of them survived at all.

9436.w: Septimius Severus was born here and spent imperial money on his home town: a new forum, a basilica, rebuilt docks. Then it was abandoned and the sand covered it, and burial is the best conservation there is — nothing was quarried away because nothing was visible.

9437.w: Air burns off the flame's fuel — the volatile gases coming out of the wood — faster than the wood can make more. What is left is charcoal glowing at a higher temperature than the flame ever reached, which is why you cook on embers and not on flames.

9438.w: A fire draws its own air only as fast as convection allows, which caps it well below the temperature that melts iron. Push air in and the cap comes off — every smelting technology in history is a way of solving that one problem.

9439.w: A spark lands in tinder and makes a coal the size of a pinhead. Blowing on it feeds oxygen faster than the coal consumes it, so the ember spreads instead of dying — gently, because a hard breath cools it faster than it feeds it.

9440.w: Cut the air and the flame stops, but the wick stays hot and the wax in it stays liquid, which is why a snuffed candle relights far more easily than a fresh one. Blowing it out sends a trail of vaporised wax up; smothering it does not.

9441.w: Silica melts near 1,700 °C and a kiln left to draw its own air does not get there. Forced draught does, which is why glass and iron both had to wait for bellows rather than for anyone to have the idea.

9442.w: Cut into a cliff at the oasis where the road divided to go round the Taklamakan, so everyone travelling either way stopped here and left something. Cave 17 was sealed early in the 11th century and opened on 25 June 1900, with about 50,000 documents still inside it.

9443.w: Its evenness is the giveaway: a stratovolcano builds itself out of its own ash and lava in alternating layers, and one that has not been disturbed grows into a cone. There are four of them stacked here, and the visible one is the youngest by about 90,000 years.

9444.w: A nucleosome is 146 base pairs wound on eight histones. Thread the linker DNA between them and you have chromatin — beads on a string, which is the form the genome actually spends most of its life in.

9445.w: Chromatin becomes a chromosome when it has ends and a middle: telomeres to stop the ends being read as breakage, and a centromere for the spindle to pull on. Without those it is just a very long thread.

9446.w: Meiosis in a female germ line divides the cytoplasm unequally on purpose: one cell keeps almost all of it and becomes the egg, and the others are discarded as polar bodies. The egg is the largest human cell and that is why.

9447.w: Meiosis is mitosis run twice with one round of copying, and with the homologous pairs swapping stretches first. That swap is the point: it is where the shuffling happens, and it is why no two gametes from one person are the same.

9448.w: Cooling magma sweats out water carrying whatever metals would not fit into the crystals forming around it. That fluid travels along cracks and drops its load where pressure or temperature changes, which is why ore is in veins rather than spread evenly through the rock.

9449.w: Bone is mostly calcium phosphate, and acid pulls the phosphate straight back out of it. That is how the first phosphate fertiliser was made — ground bones and sulfuric acid — and it is why bone meal works at all.

9450.w: A glial cell wraps its own membrane round an axon dozens of times, and membrane is mostly fat, which does not conduct. The insulated stretches force the signal to jump between the gaps instead of creeping along, which is about fifty times faster.

9451.w: Copper is drawn rather than rolled: pulled through a hole slightly smaller than itself, again and again. It stays ductile the whole way because it work-hardens slowly, which is precisely why it and not iron became the metal electricity travels through.

9452.w: The two cells never touch. A gap of about twenty nanometres is crossed chemically — the arriving signal empties vesicles of transmitter into it, and the next cell reads the concentration. That gap is what makes a nervous system programmable rather than merely wired.

9453.w: The cortex is grey because it is where the cell bodies and their dendrites are, and dendrites are where a neuron does its adding up. Folding it is how a large sheet of that fits inside a skull.

9454.w: The cord runs inside the vertebral column, which is armour that also has to bend. Each vertebra lets a pair of nerves out through a gap at its own level, so the segmenting of the backbone and the segmenting of the body are the same fact.

9455.w: An axon is one process of the cell drawn out very long, and everything about it is membrane: the signal is a wave of ions crossing that membrane, regenerated at every point, which is why it arrives at the far end as strong as it left.

9456.w: Tubulin dimers stack into a hollow tube that grows at one end and shrinks at the other. That instability is the function, not a flaw — it is how a cell searches space, and how a chromosome gets found and pulled.

9457.w: Both are brown algae holding themselves up with gas floats rather than with wood, because water carries the weight. Kelp does it at a scale that makes a forest, and grows toward the light at up to half a metre a day.

9458.w: An archaeal host took in a bacterium and did not digest it. That bacterium is the mitochondrion, which still has its own genome and its own double membrane — the eukaryotic cell is a merger, not a step up a ladder.

9459.w: A sheet of photoreceptors tells you how much light; put a lens in front of it and it tells you where the light came from. Everything else about an eye is the business of keeping that image steady and clean.

9460.w: A coral reef grows on a volcano that is sinking. If the coral keeps pace with the subsidence the volcano disappears and the ring of reef is left as an atoll — an island made entirely by animals, standing where a mountain used to be.

9461.w: Multicellular, and living by eating rather than by making its own food. That single constraint explains the rest of the body plan: a gut, a way to move to the food, and a nervous system to decide which way.

9462.w: A sponge has no organs and no nerves, and if you push it through a sieve the separated cells crawl back together and rebuild it. That is multicellularity at its most minimal: cells that stay stuck together and divide the work.

9463.w: Collagen is the animal kingdom's signature: a triple helix that makes a sheet cells can sit on, and no plant or fungus makes it. Everything with a body plan is built on that scaffold.

9464.w: The swim bladder and the lung are the same organ, and in the lobe-finned lineage it went the other way — an outpouching of the gut used for buoyancy became one used for air. Fish that gulp air do it with the organ that became ours.

9465.w: Twist short fibres one way and twist the resulting strands the other, and the two twists fight each other so the thing cannot unwind. That is the whole invention, and it is at least thirty thousand years old.

9466.w: Steamed to soften and stop the enzymes, then pressed flat. The flattening splits the cell walls so water gets in at once, which is the whole difference between a five-minute breakfast and an hour of simmering.

9467.w: Bacillus subtilis lives on rice straw, which is why the traditional method is to wrap boiled beans in it. The bacterium builds long chains of glutamic acid outside itself — the threads you can pull a foot into the air are a bacterial polymer, not the bean.

9468.w: A piece of root or stem put in soil will regrow the parts it is missing, because plant cells keep the ability to become other kinds of cell. Every apple of a given variety is a cutting of one original tree, which is why they are all clones.

9469.w: Bark is loaded with tannins because they bind protein, and binding protein is how a tree makes itself unpleasant to eat. The same reaction turns hide into leather, and it is why tea is astringent.

9470.w: The yellow is curcumin, and it is a pH indicator: alkaline conditions turn it red, which is why turmeric-stained cloth changes colour with soap. It is also barely absorbed when eaten, which most claims made for it quietly skip.

9471.w: A field has to be come back to, so the house stops being a shelter and becomes an address. Everything else follows from staying: stores worth stealing, boundaries worth arguing over, and a reason to know your neighbours' names.

9472.w: The wheel is the easy half. The hard half is the axle — a round hole and a round shaft that fit closely enough not to wobble and loosely enough to turn, in wood, without a lathe. That is why the wheel arrives late and only where there were already carpenters.

9473.w: Three pairs of glands, about a litre a day, and almost all of it water. What it carries matters more than what it is: amylase to start on starch, mucin to make food slide, and bicarbonate to hold the mouth near neutral so teeth do not dissolve.

9474.w: A sound that stands for a thing is not language yet. Language is that plus a rule for combining them, so a finite vocabulary makes an unlimited number of sentences — including ones nobody has ever said before, which is the part animals do not do.

9475.w: Two thirds of bone by weight is this one mineral, grown as plates a few nanometres thick between the collagen fibres. Mineral alone shatters and collagen alone bends; together they do neither, which is the whole trick of bone.

9476.w: A scaly skin that loses almost no water, and a metabolism that costs about a tenth of a mammal's. Both are what let a lizard live where there is very little to eat and nothing to drink.

9477.w: Snake venom is modified saliva, made in a gland that is a modified salivary gland, and delivered through a tooth with a groove or a tube in it. Every part of the apparatus is an ordinary mouth part doing something else.

9478.w: Quartz is silicon already bonded to oxygen, and carbon wants the oxygen more at high enough temperature. Heat them together in an arc furnace and the carbon leaves as carbon monoxide, taking the oxygen and leaving the silicon behind.

9479.w: A weight falling turns a gear train, and left alone it accelerates until the weight hits the floor. The escapement lets the train advance one tooth at a time against a swinging control, which is what turns falling into counting.

9480.w: Collagen fibres holding a mesh of water in place. It is that trapped water that carries the load, which is why cartilage is slippery under pressure and why it does not repair — there are almost no blood vessels in it.

9481.w: Wind drags on the surface and the drag grows with the roughness it has already made, so a small chop builds a bigger one. How big it gets depends on wind speed, how long it blows, and how much open water it blows across.

9482.w: Each year's snow is buried by the next and the crystals weld at their contact points, squeezing the air out slowly. Firn is the halfway stage: denser than snow, still breathable, and one more year from becoming glacier ice.

9483.w: Hot water holds far more sugar than cold. Cool a saturated syrup and it holds more than it can, so any seed — a string, a speck — starts the sugar coming out of solution in an orderly repeating stack, which is what a crystal is.

9484.w: Held near 80 °C for hours, the fat globules rise and the proteins at the surface denature into a crust. Take it much hotter and it curdles; much cooler and it never sets. Nothing is added at any point.

9485.w: Shell is calcium carbonate, the same as limestone, and the coast has it where the ground does not. Crushed and burned it gives the same quicklime, which is why shell middens turn up beside old lime kilns.

9486.w: Glass is not cut so much as scored and snapped: the scratch concentrates stress along one line and the break follows it. The offcuts go back into the furnace, where they melt at a lower temperature than raw batch and save fuel.

9487.w: Same magma, two endings. Cooled slowly at depth it grows crystals and becomes nepheline syenite; erupted at the surface it chills too fast for that and becomes phonolite — the same silica-poor, alkali-rich chemistry with the grain size of a lava.

9488.w: Building began about 270 BC and went on for over 700 years. They stand 6 to 30 m tall and are inclined at roughly 70°, where Egyptian pyramids of similar height had footprints at least five times larger and slopes of 40–50°. Narrow and steep is the Nubian signature, not a smaller copy of Giza.

9489.w: Mudbrick houses crammed into one aggregate structure with no footpaths or streets between them. Most were entered through holes in the ceiling, reached by ladders — so the rooftops were effectively the streets, and the plan of the town follows from how you get into a house.

9490.w: 167 arches of unmortared, brick-like granite blocks, 28.5 m high at the deepest point of the valley. With no mortar the arch does all of the work: every block is held in place by the compression of the ones beside it.

9491.w: About 1,500 m above sea level, built largely by hand with retaining walls of stone and rammed earth, and fed by an irrigation system running down from the rainforest above. The forest is part of the machine: it is what holds the water the terraces are watered with.

9492.w: Ur-Nammu began it around 2040 BC on a plain with no stone and no hill: a three-layered solid mass of mud brick faced with burnt bricks set in bitumen. The bulk is cheap mud, and the waterproof skin is the only reason four thousand years of rain has not returned it to the plain.

9493.w: Reptile scales are outgrowths of the epidermis with a hard beta-keratin layer over a softer alpha-keratin one, joined by flexible hinges. Because the covering is one continuous sheet rather than separate plates, a snake sheds it entire and inside out.

9494.w: Each scale is a modified seta — a bristle flattened into a blade and left on its stalk — and they overlap over the wing membrane like roof tiles. Their surface is ridged finely enough to make colour by interference as well as by pigment, which is why a blue morpho has no blue pigment in it.

9495.w: Naive set theory let any describable collection be a set, and Russell broke it in a line: the set of all sets that are not members of themselves both is and is not a member of itself. Modern set theory replaces the description with a list of axioms saying which sets exist — and one of them, the axiom of infinity, has to assert an infinite set outright, because nothing else on the list produces one.

9496.w: A mass on a spring oscillates because the spring pulls back harder the further it is pushed. Line the oscillators up so each one pulls on the next, and the disturbance travels while the oscillators themselves stay put. That is the whole definition, and it is the same statement for a string, the sea and the air.

9497.w: Dermal bone: it ossifies within the skin itself rather than growing out of the skeleton, which is how scutes on a crocodile, a shell on an armadillo and plates on a Stegosaurus can all be the same structure in animals that are not close relatives.

9498.w: Spin a right triangle about one of its legs and it sweeps a cone: a circle for a base, an apex over its centre, and a straight line from every point of the rim to that apex. Being ruled by straight lines is the useful part — a cone can be cut and rolled from flat sheet, and a sphere cannot.

9499.w: Ditch and bank, and the bank is the ditch's own spoil: in places the drop from rampart top to ditch floor reaches 17 m. The Inner City Iya alone runs about 12 km, built around 1460, and the combined earthworks across Edo State have been estimated at some 16,000 km enclosing about 6,500 km². One estimate puts the inner work at 5,000 men working ten-hour days for 97 days.

9500.w: Ashlar masonry in sandstone pillars and smaller blocks, cut well enough that the geometry is the argument for the skill. Founded around AD 110, at its height from about AD 375 to 700, and holding somewhere over 10,000 people before it collapsed around AD 1000. The largest block at Pumapunku is estimated at 131 tonnes.

9501.w: Cut as reliefs on the outside and as excavated caves within, into limestone cliffs, from 493 to 1127 — about 30% Northern Wei and 60% Tang. 2,345 caves and roughly 100,000 statues, from 25 mm to 17 m; the Vairocana Buddha is 17.14 m with ears two metres long.

9502.w: Over 100 caves cut from the basalt of the Deccan Traps, AD 600–1000, with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain excavations side by side. The Kailasa temple was cut downward out of a single rock: about 85,000 m³ of stone removed, a courtyard 82 m by 46 m and 30 m high, and not one block added.

9503.w: Andesite is soft enough to carve with an iron chisel and each block was cut to interlock with its neighbours, so the temples stand without mortar. That is also why they could be rebuilt: after the 16th-century earthquake brought them down, anastylosis put them back using the original stones, and the 47 m Shiva temple was finished in 1953.

9504.w: Harald Bluetooth's stone says it outright: "that Haraldr who won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian." Runes are cut in straight strokes because a horizontal line would follow the grain, and enough specks of the original paint survived to recover the colours it was first shown in.

9505.w: The critique came out of the factory rather than the study: Engels wrote up the condition of the working class in Manchester and sent it to him, and Capital is an argument about what happens to labour once the machine sets the pace.

9506.w: The prairie and its grazer made each other. Grass grows from the base, so it survives being cropped; a herd that grazes hard and moves on leaves the roots alive, and it is those roots dying and regrowing for ten thousand years that built two metres of the best soil on Earth.

9507.w: A paved court 44 by 60 m with an ahu of basalt and coral, and the centre of learning where priests and navigators from across the Pacific met. A new marae elsewhere was founded by carrying a stone away from this one, so the alliance was made of rock rather than of memory.

9508.w: Two pieces: an upright shaft, the haligi, and a hemispherical cap, the tasa, set in spaced parallel rows to carry a building clear of the ground. The ones at the House of Taga stood 4.6 m and were quarried about 1,200 m away; of the twelve George Anson sketched in 1742, one is still standing.

9509.w: It exists to close one harbour mouth, and everything about it follows from that: begun in 1539 and not finished until 1787, six levels of sandstone and brick over rubble fill, walls from 5.5 to 12.2 m thick, rising 43 m from the water. Drake failed against it in 1595 and Abercromby in 1797.

9510.w: The cliff is the least of it. Hunters dressed as coyotes and wolves moved a herd three kilometres from the Porcupine Hills into drive lanes marked by hundreds of cairns, and at a gallop the animals in front went over from the weight of those behind. Used for some 5,500 years, and the bone below is 12 m deep.

9511.w: The dome is 15 m across and 12.5 m high, and its heavy ribbed fluting exists to carry glazed tile: fluting turns one curved surface into strips a tiler can actually cover, and it catches the light so the blue reads as blue from the ground.

9512.w: The site is the boundary itself. Grassland in the north survives from the last ice age 15,000 years ago and the rainforest has been advancing into it ever since, so the same ground carries both — and the open Ogooué valley through it may have served as the corridor from the coast into the interior. Over 1,600 petroglyphs were cut here about the time iron-working arrived, some 2,000 years ago.

9513.w: José Garanger located the grave on Eretoka in 1967 by reading the local folklore as evidence and digging where it pointed. He found a chief buried with more than 25 of his retinue — the story and the ground agreeing, which is rare enough that it is the reason the site is listed.

9514.w: Shaft 12 opened in 1932 to a design by Fritz Schupp and Martin Kremmer: cubical buildings of reinforced concrete and steel trusses, with a Doppelbock winding tower. It handled up to 12,000 tons a day, and the point of the architecture was that a pithead could be composed rather than accumulated.

9515.w: Not a temple with chariot decoration — a temple built as the chariot, because Surya crosses the sky in one drawn by seven horses. Twenty-four carved stone wheels about 3 m across stand along the plinth as the vehicle's own, and the sanctum tower, estimated at 70 m, fell in 1837.

9516.w: What makes it primeval is what was never taken out. Almost half the wood in it is dead, ten times the share in a managed forest, and half of its 12,000 species depend on decaying logs. The European bison went extinct in the wild — 54 left alive in zoos by 1923 — and four were brought back here in 1929; there are now more than 800.

9517.w: Three canals dug as one plan in the 17th century, west to east across the whole layout — Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht in order outward from the old town, the north-west sector begun in 1613 and finished around 1625. Over 100 km of canals, about 90 islands and 1,500 bridges, and the street plan is still the plan.

9518.w: A chamber with a gate at each end, and nothing else. Close both, let water in and the boat floats up with it; let water out and it settles down. The lift costs no power at all — every metre a boat rises is paid for by water running downhill somewhere above.

9519.w: The continental divide is too high to cut through, so the canal goes over it: three locks up to Gatun Lake at 26 m, 82 km across, and three down the other side. The lake is both the summit and the reservoir, and each transit spends about 200 million litres of fresh water on the lift.

9520.w: Ashoka commissioned it in the 3rd century BCE as a hemispherical brick structure over relics of the Buddha. The Shungas then roughly doubled its diameter and cased the brick in stone, and the four carved toranas came later still, in the 1st century BCE — so the building is three claims from three dynasties standing on top of each other.

9521.w: High-fired bricks 27 by 27 by 5 cm laid in gypsum mortar, tapering from 9 m at the base to 6 m at the top over 45.6 m. Gypsum sets fast and does not need to dry out, which is what lets a tower that slender be built course upon course without waiting a season between lifts.

9522.w: Two concentric walls with 52 towers and barbicans, set far enough apart that a siege engine cannot reach the inner one — one stretch still Roman, in red brick courses under shallow terracotta. Viollet-le-Duc restored it from 1853 and roofed the towers in slate, which is northern practice and not local: there is no slate to quarry anywhere near.

9523.w: It burned in 1833 and was rebuilt between 1834 and 1862 by subscription from across the country, which is why it looks like one building rather than eight centuries of them: striped arcades running the full height of the courtyard, 300 chambers, and frescoes finished in 1846. Only Hrelja's tower of 1334–35 came through the fire.

9524.w: Laterite — tropical soil left as iron and aluminium oxides once the silica has leached out — hardens on exposure, so a bank cut from it stands where loose earth would slump. More than 160 km of it rings the old Ijebu kingdom, with up to 20 m from ditch floor to the rim of the inner bank.

9525.w: Dissolved gas comes out of solution as the magma rises and shatters it from the inside: an explosive eruption is melt torn into fragments finer than 2 mm before it has time to cool as anything else. It is rock, not smoke, which is why it settles as a blanket and stays.

9526.w: The ash fell cool and fast — 4 to 8 m in a few hours, 10 m in the end — so the village was sealed rather than burned. That is why a manioc field survived to be excavated, the first identified anywhere in the New World, and why there are no bodies: the position of the artefacts says they left in the early evening.

9527.w: The mountain top was levelled by hand around 500 BC and built on for fourteen centuries, 400 m above the valley floor. Building J is set askew to everything else because it is not aligned to the plaza: its steps face the point where Capella rose at the time, so a person in the doorway looked straight at it.

9528.w: Brown basalt for the walls and local wine-coloured tuff for the ornament — a hard stone carrying a soft one, which is how you get carved detail on a building made of lava. Founded by Fasilides in 1645, with Portuguese, Indian and Arab influence in the same compound; a Yemeni ambassador in 1648 credited the design of Fasilides' palace to an Indian named Abdal Kerim.

9529.w: Twenty-three devices between 1946 and 1958, about 77 megatons in total. Castle Bravo yielded 15 megatons instead of the predicted figure because of an unforeseen lithium-7 reaction, and its crater is still visible on the north-west cape. The lagoon holds the target fleet, Saratoga and Nagato among them.

9530.w: Capital of Fiji from 1871 until the government left in 1877, and the reason it survives is the reason it was abandoned: 600 m hills, many of them cliffs, ring the town and left it nowhere to expand. Cakobau signed the Deed of Cession at Nasova on 10 October 1874.

9531.w: 7,463 km² across the Republic of the Congo, Cameroon and the Central African Republic, held as one because the animals do not stop at the borders. The natural clearings in it, the bais, are the only places a forest elephant can be seen in the open — which is why a forest this dense can be counted at all.

9532.w: The dome gets lighter as it rises. Heavy travertine in the aggregate at the base, then terracotta, then tufa and pumice at the crown; the shell thins from 6.4 m to 1.2 m; and the oculus removes the material at the weakest point instead of adding to it. Interior diameter and height to the oculus are the same 43.3 m, so a sphere would fit exactly.

9533.w: Almost no line in it is straight. The stylobate bulges upward by 10.3 cm over 70 m, the columns swell and taper, and both columns and walls lean inward — refinements measured in the 19th century and made in Pentelic marble in the 15 years from 447 BC, cut to size in the quarry before it ever reached the hill.

9534.w: It is lit from above. Light wells bring daylight and air down to rooms too deep in the building to reach a wall, which is what lets it be dense and multi-storey at once, with drains, water channels and timber-reinforced masonry running through. That plan is probably where the Greeks got the Labyrinth from — the palace came first and the story second.

9535.w: Sandstone and conglomerate laid down in a delta, lifted into a plateau about 60 million years ago and cut along vertical faults until only pillars were left. Twenty-four monasteries went up on top of them from the second half of the 14th century, and until the 1600s everything and everyone arrived by rope, basket or a ladder that could be pulled up.

9536.w: Four to six metres of ash and pumice set around the dead, and the bodies rotted away inside it, leaving voids. Giuseppe Fiorelli worked out that the void was the cast: fill it with plaster and the person comes back. The method is still used, with resin now, because it does not destroy the bones inside.

9537.w: A stratovolcano is built out of its own eruptions, so its height is a running total rather than a fact: 3,403 m in September 2024, and different after the next summit eruption. Diodorus Siculus reports one around 1400 BCE, sixteen happened in 2001 alone, and the 1669 flows destroyed at least ten villages before reaching Catania.

9538.w: An octagon 60 m across and 36 m high, with a wooden dome about 20 m in diameter carried on a drum standing on sixteen supports — four piers and twelve columns — and an inner arcade of twenty-four more around the rock itself. Completed in 72 AH, 691–2 CE, for Abd al-Malik; the original dome fell in 1015 and was rebuilt in 1022–3.

9539.w: A plateau 550 by 270 m standing over 400 m above the desert has no water on it, so Herod put the water in: cisterns of about 40,000 m³ filled from runoff. That is the fortress. The Romans answered it with a ramp 114 m high and breached the wall on 16 April; Yadin's excavation found at most 28 bodies, against Josephus's 960.

9540.w: Thick ash deposits from Erciyes, Hasan and Göllüdağ, with harder layers on top of softer ones. The hard cap shelters the column beneath it while everything unprotected around it washes away, which leaves standing towers of rock soft enough to be dug out with hand tools — so the houses, the churches and the underground cities are all subtraction.

9541.w: Uplift did half of it. Raising the Colorado Plateau steepened the river without moving it, and when the Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago the base level dropped again — so the river cut down instead of wandering. It has reached the Vishnu Schist, two billion years old, with 270-million-year-old Kaibab Limestone still on the rim.

9542.w: A closed basin at 3,656 m with nowhere for water to leave except upward. Lake Minchin, then Tauca 140 m deep, then Coipasa 11,500 to 13,400 years ago, each evaporating and leaving its salt: eight metres of crust whose elevation varies by less than a metre across 10,582 km², over brine about 0.3% lithium.

9543.w: A stave church stands on upright posts rather than on horizontal sills, which keeps the timber out of the wet ground and is why any of them survive at all. Dendrochronology puts this one at about 1132, and the north portal is carved in the Urnes style — the last of the Viking animal ornament, on a Christian building.

9544.w: Flat-roofed brick houses on a semi-orthogonal plan with drainage running through it, holding as many as 23,500 people over about 150 hectares in the Mature Harappan phase, 2600–1900 BC. The bricks were good enough that in about 1857 the Lahore–Multan railway dug the site up and used them for track ballast.

9545.w: An arch-gravity dam only works in a canyon: the curve throws the water's push sideways into the rock walls, so the wall can be thick at the bottom and thin at the top. Curing was the harder problem — 2,480,000 m³ poured as one mass would have taken 125 years to cool and cracked, so it went in as columns threaded with 937 km of pipe carrying first river water and then refrigerated water.

9546.w: A canal that crosses a watershed has to climb, and the summit in the Shandong foothills is 42 m up. Qiao Weiyue invented the pound lock for it in 984 — a gated chamber a boat waits in while the level changes — and the Ming dug four reservoirs and dammed the Wen to send 60% of its water north to keep the top of it wet.

9547.w: Star-fort geometry exists so that every stretch of wall is covered by fire from another stretch, and that geometry assumes flat ground you can lay it out on. Ehrensvärd began in 1748 bending it instead onto eight islands, six of them fortified, each carrying its own works. It surrendered on 3 May 1808 after two months.

9548.w: A 500-tonne bronze Buddha nearly 15 m tall needs a roof, and the roof became the argument: until 1998 the Daibutsuden was the largest wooden building in the world. The statue took much of Japan's bronze and all of its gold imported; the present hall, finished in 1709, is 30% smaller than its predecessor — 7 bays instead of 11, for want of funds.

9549.w: About 40,000 km of road across what are now six countries, with no wheeled vehicle on any of it and no draught animal bigger than a llama — so it can climb stairs, and it does. Where it meets a gorge it crosses on cable spun from ichu grass, which rots: the bridges had to be rebuilt about every two years, and that maintenance was a tax.

9550.w: Begun 15 August 1248, halted around 1560, resumed 1842 and finished 15 October 1880 — 632 years, with a gap of about 282 in the middle. It could be finished at all because the medieval plans and drawings survived it; the 19th century built to them and used iron roof girders to do it. Fourteen aerial bomb hits, and it was still standing in a flattened city.

9551.w: The buttresses take the roof's weight entirely outside the building — the 14th-century ones reach fifteen metres from wall to counter-support — so the wall stops being structure and can become window. Inside that shell sat the oak roof frame called the forest, and when it and the flèche burned on 15 April 2019 the flèche brought down 750 tonnes of stone and lead, while the walls, towers, buttresses and glass survived.

9552.w: A geyser needs a heat source shallow enough to boil groundwater, and here that is a caldera 72 by 45 km left by an eruption 640,000 years ago that threw out over 1,000 km³. At least 1,283 geysers have erupted in the park and about 465 are active in a year, out of at least 10,000 hydrothermal features. Protected as the first national park on 1 March 1872.

9553.w: Three layers of basalt of the Serra Geral formation, and the falls step down them twice: hard rock over softer, so the lip holds while what is beneath it is cut away. About 275 drops across 2.7 km, the longest 82 m, and roughly half the river goes into the Devil's Throat, 80–90 m wide.

9554.w: A tepui is a table mountain with a vertical edge, so a river on top does not descend — it leaves. 979 m in total with an uninterrupted plunge of 807 m, then about 400 m of cascade and a final 30 m drop. Jimmie Angel first flew over it on 16 November 1933 looking for ore, and in 1937 landed on the top and could not take off again.

9555.w: A dome cut from granite blocks and held together by stone rivets, with no mortar anywhere. The gaps that leaves are the ventilation: the grotto breathed, and stayed dry, until an early 20th-century restoration cased it in concrete and sealed it — after which humidity, leaks and erosion of the sculptures followed. Begun 751 and completed by the Silla court in 774.

9556.w: The geography does the guarding. A peninsula joined to the rest of Tasmania by a neck 30 m wide needs only that neck fenced, guarded, trapped and lined with dogs, and everything else is water. Running from 1830 to 1877; the Separate Prison of 1853 then moved the punishment inside the head instead, hooding prisoners and enforcing silence.

9557.w: Iron-rich earth on sandstone under an overhang: pigment that does not fade and rock that does not get rained on. More than 5,000 recorded sites, some paintings up to 20,000 years old, on ground where the archaeology shows occupation for at least 40,000 years and possibly 65,000.

9558.w: Thirty-one square rooms, each carried up to a dome on squinches and lit only through a hole at its top — rubble stone on clay mortar with gypsum sealing the joints, at 3,200 m where there is no timber to roof anything with. A caravanserai has to shelter strangers and their animals at the pass, and stone vaulting is what is available to do it.

9559.w: Adobe cannot span or carry much, so the walls are thickened into twelve conical buttresses and threaded with horizontal timbers that both reinforce them and give the replasterers something to stand on. A 1970s repair rendered it in sand and cement, which trapped moisture in the mud behind and started it rotting; the 2023 work went back to adobe.

9560.w: Fifty-eight oil-pressing complexes have been excavated in one town of about 42 hectares — mills, decantation basins and presses — which is what a Roman city on the far edge of the empire was for: it exported oil. About 20,000 people at its late-2nd-century peak; wrecked by the 1755 earthquake and then quarried for stone to build Meknes.

9561.w: The site is an island because a river meander was closed off by a canal on the eastern side, which turns a bend in the water into a moat around the whole city — a defence that costs one cut instead of a circuit. It held until a fourteen-month Burmese siege took it on 7 April 1767.

9562.w: The limit of the technique is on show, because it was reached. The largest block known from the ancient world was uncovered in 2014 in the quarry above the site — about 19.6 by 6 by 5.5 m and an estimated 1,650 tonnes — cut free and then left there. Everything at Baalbek that did get moved is the answer to the question that stone asks.

9563.w: Nothing was done to the lake. In the early 1960s the Amu Darya and Syr Darya were diverted to irrigate desert for cotton, and a lake with no outlet loses whatever its rivers stop bringing: 60% of the surface and 80% of the volume gone by 1998, a tenth of the original size by 2007, salinity from 10 g/L to about 30, and a fishery employing 40,000 down to nothing by 1987.

9564.w: Gaudí worked out his structure by hanging weighted strings from a ceiling and photographing the result upside down: a chain hanging free takes pure tension, so inverted it stands in pure compression and needs no buttress at all. Begun 19 March 1882, less than a quarter done when he died in 1926, and the 172.5 m central tower now makes it the tallest church in the world.

9565.w: Brick instead of stone alone, and pulleys and cranes instead of numbers — both from the Silhak argument that a state should build with what works rather than with what is customary. 5.74 km of wall in two years, 1794 to 1796, on 700,000 person-hours of paid labour, and the whole thing written up in the ten volumes of the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe down to the wages.

9566.w: Delta mud is anoxic, so a tree standing in it cannot get oxygen through its roots — pneumatophores grow upward out of the mud to breathe instead. That single adaptation is what allows 10,277 km² of forest on the Ganges delta, and the forest is what stands between the cyclones and millions of people behind it.

9567.w: A bone tube, pigment blown through it, and a hand held against the rock: the image is the gap. Over 2,000 hands, 829 left against 31 right, because the pipe goes in the hand you are better with and the other one gets stencilled. Iron oxides for red, natrojarosite yellow, pyrolusite black, and gypsum to make them stick; from about 7,300 BC.
